concept_tested: Base unit recall
stem: The SI unit of luminous intensity is
solution: Luminous intensity is one of the seven SI base quantities and its base unit is the candela (cd).
formula_principle: SI base quantities and units
common_misconception: Confusing luminous intensity (candela) with luminous flux (lumen) or illuminance (lux).

concept_tested: Identify base quantity
stem: Which of the following is a fundamental (base) quantity in the SI system?
solution: Electric current (ampere) is one of the seven SI base quantities; force, momentum and charge are all derived.
formula_principle: SI base quantities
common_misconception: Assuming charge is fundamental; current is the base quantity, charge is derived.

concept_tested: Number of base quantities
stem: The number of base (fundamental) quantities in the SI system is
solution: The SI system defines seven base quantities: length, mass, time, electric current, temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity.
formula_principle: SI base quantities
common_misconception: Forgetting amount of substance or luminous intensity in the count.

concept_tested: Base unit recall
stem: The SI unit of the amount of substance is the
solution: Amount of substance is a base quantity with SI unit the mole (mol).
formula_principle: SI base quantities
common_misconception: Confusing amount of substance (mole) with mass (kilogram).

concept_tested: Same unit pair
stem: Which pair of physical quantities has the same SI unit?
solution: Work and energy are both measured in joule (J), since energy is the capacity to do work.
formula_principle: Units of derived quantities
common_misconception: Assuming force and momentum share a unit because both involve mass and motion.

concept_tested: Parsec meaning
stem: The unit 'parsec' is used to measure
solution: A parsec is a large astronomical unit of distance, equal to about 3.26 light years.
formula_principle: Astronomical units of length
common_misconception: Linking 'parsec' to 'sec' and wrongly treating it as a time unit.

concept_tested: Parsec value
stem: One parsec is approximately equal to
solution: By definition 1 parsec is the distance at which 1 AU subtends 1 arc second, which works out to about 3.26 light years.
formula_principle: 1 parsec ~ 3.26 ly
common_misconception: Assuming a parsec and a light year are the same size.

concept_tested: Light year value
stem: One light year is approximately equal to
formula_principle: distance = speed x time
common_misconception: Reporting the distance light travels in one second instead of one year.

concept_tested: Astronomical unit
stem: One astronomical unit (AU) is defined as the average distance between the
solution: 1 AU is the mean Sun to Earth distance, about 1.5 x 10^11 m.
formula_principle: Astronomical units
common_misconception: Confusing the AU (Sun to Earth) with the Earth to Moon distance.

concept_tested: Odd one out (time)
stem: Which of the following is NOT a unit of time?
solution: A light year is a unit of distance, not time, despite containing the word 'year'.
formula_principle: Units of time vs length
common_misconception: Being misled by the word 'year' in 'light year'.

concept_tested: Solid angle unit
stem: The SI unit of solid angle is the
solution: Solid angle is measured in steradian (sr); plane angle is measured in radian (rad).
formula_principle: Radian and steradian
common_misconception: Interchanging radian (plane angle) and steradian (solid angle).

concept_tested: Radian meaning
stem: In the SI system the radian is the unit used to measure
solution: The radian is the SI unit of plane angle, defined as arc length divided by radius. Modern SI treats plane angle as a dimensionless derived quantity with the special unit name radian; older texts call it a supplementary unit.
formula_principle: Radian and steradian
common_misconception: Confusing plane angle (radian) with solid angle (steradian).

concept_tested: Fermi
stem: One fermi is equal to
solution: The fermi is used for nuclear sizes: 1 fermi = 1 femtometre = 10^-15 m.
formula_principle: 1 fermi = 10^-15 m
common_misconception: Confusing the fermi (10^-15 m) with the angstrom (10^-10 m).

concept_tested: Angstrom
stem: One angstrom is equal to
solution: The angstrom is used for atomic sizes and wavelengths: 1 A = 10^-10 m.
formula_principle: 1 angstrom = 10^-10 m
common_misconception: Mixing up angstrom (10^-10 m) with nanometre (10^-9 m).

concept_tested: Barn
stem: The unit 'barn' used in nuclear physics is a unit of
solution: The barn measures nuclear cross-sectional area, with 1 barn = 10^-28 m^2.
common_misconception: Assuming barn is a length or volume rather than an area.

concept_tested: CGS system
stem: The system of units that uses centimetre, gram and second as base units is the
solution: CGS stands for centimetre, gram, second.
formula_principle: Systems of units
common_misconception: Confusing CGS with MKS, which uses metre and kilogram.

concept_tested: Pascal
stem: In the SI system the unit of pressure, the pascal, is equivalent to
solution: Pressure is force per unit area, so 1 pascal = 1 N m^-2.
formula_principle: Pressure = Force / Area
common_misconception: Writing N m (joule) instead of N m^-2 for pressure.

concept_tested: Atmospheric pressure
stem: One atmosphere of pressure is approximately
solution: Standard atmospheric pressure is about 1.013 x 10^5 Pa (about 760 mm of Hg).
formula_principle: Standard atmospheric pressure
common_misconception: Losing track of the power of ten for standard atmospheric pressure.

concept_tested: Force
stem: The dimensional formula of force is
solution: Force = mass x acceleration = [M][L T^-2] = [M L T^-2].
formula_principle: F = m a
common_misconception: Confusing force [M L T^-2] with momentum [M L T^-1].

concept_tested: Work and energy
stem: The dimensional formula of work (or energy) is
solution: Work = force x displacement = [M L T^-2][L] = [M L^2 T^-2].
formula_principle: W = F d
common_misconception: Dropping a length factor and writing force dimensions instead.

concept_tested: Power
stem: The dimensional formula of power is
solution: Power = work / time = [M L^2 T^-2] / [T] = [M L^2 T^-3].
formula_principle: P = W / t
common_misconception: Forgetting the extra time factor that distinguishes power from energy.

concept_tested: Pressure
stem: The dimensional formula of pressure is
solution: Pressure = force / area = [M L T^-2] / [L^2] = [M L^-1 T^-2].
formula_principle: P = F / A
common_misconception: Forgetting to divide the force dimensions by area.

concept_tested: Torque
stem: Which physical quantity has the dimensional formula [M L^2 T^-2]?
solution: Torque = r x F = [L][M L T^-2] = [M L^2 T^-2], the same as energy.
formula_principle: Torque = force x perpendicular distance
common_misconception: Not realising torque shares its dimensions with work and energy.

concept_tested: Impulse and momentum
stem: Which pair of quantities has the same dimensional formula?
solution: Impulse = F t = [M L T^-2][T] = [M L T^-1], identical to momentum [M L T^-1].
formula_principle: Impulse = change in momentum
common_misconception: Assuming work and power are dimensionally the same.

concept_tested: Gravitational constant
stem: The dimensional formula of the universal gravitational constant G is
formula_principle: F = G m1 m2 / r^2
common_misconception: Forgetting to invert the mass dimension when solving for G.

concept_tested: Planck's constant
stem: The dimensional formula of Planck's constant is
solution: h = E / nu = [M L^2 T^-2] / [T^-1] = [M L^2 T^-1], the same as angular momentum.
formula_principle: E = h nu
common_misconception: Treating Planck's constant as if it had the dimensions of energy.

concept_tested: Coefficient of viscosity
stem: The dimensional formula of the coefficient of viscosity is
solution: From F = 6 pi eta r v, eta = F / (r v) = [M L T^-2] / ([L][L T^-1]) = [M L^-1 T^-1].
formula_principle: F = 6 pi eta r v (Stokes' law)
common_misconception: Confusing the coefficient of viscosity with pressure, which is [M L^-1 T^-2].

concept_tested: Surface tension
stem: The dimensional formula of surface tension is
solution: Surface tension = force per unit length = [M L T^-2] / [L] = [M T^-2].
formula_principle: Surface tension = Force / length
common_misconception: Forgetting to divide force by length, giving force dimensions instead.

concept_tested: Frequency
stem: The dimensional formula of frequency is
solution: Frequency = 1 / period = [T^-1], a purely temporal dimension.
formula_principle: f = 1 / T
common_misconception: Writing time dimension [T] instead of its reciprocal [T^-1].

concept_tested: Angular velocity
stem: The dimensional formula of angular velocity is
solution: Angular velocity = angle / time; angle is dimensionless, so omega = [T^-1].
formula_principle: omega = angle / time
common_misconception: Treating the radian as if it carried a length dimension.

concept_tested: Strain
stem: Which of the following quantities is dimensionless?
solution: Strain is a ratio of two like quantities (for example change in length over original length), so it is dimensionless.
formula_principle: Strain = change in dimension / original dimension
common_misconception: Assuming every physical quantity must have non-zero dimensions.

concept_tested: Momentum
stem: The dimensional formula of linear momentum is
solution: Momentum = mass x velocity = [M][L T^-1] = [M L T^-1].
formula_principle: p = m v
common_misconception: Confusing momentum [M L T^-1] with force [M L T^-2].

concept_tested: Young's modulus
stem: Which of the following has the dimensional formula [M L^-1 T^-2]?
solution: Young's modulus has the dimensions of stress (pressure) since strain is dimensionless, giving [M L^-1 T^-2].
formula_principle: Young's modulus = stress / strain
common_misconception: Not recognising that stress, pressure and Young's modulus share dimensions.

concept_tested: Electric charge
stem: Taking current as a base quantity, the dimensional formula of electric charge is
solution: Charge = current x time = [A][T] = [A T].
formula_principle: q = I t
common_misconception: Dividing by time instead of multiplying, giving [A T^-1].

concept_tested: Permittivity
stem: The dimensional formula of the permittivity of free space is
formula_principle: F = q1 q2 / (4 pi eps0 r^2)
common_misconception: Errors in tracking the time power when squaring the charge dimension.

concept_tested: Simple pendulum by dimensions
stem: Using dimensional analysis, the period T of a simple pendulum depends on its length l and acceleration due to gravity g as
option_d: T is proportional to l g
solution: Assume T proportional to l^a g^b. Matching [T] to [L]^a [L T^-2]^b gives a = 1/2, b = -1/2, so T is proportional to sqrt(l/g).
formula_principle: Homogeneity of dimensions
common_misconception: Inverting the ratio and writing sqrt(g/l), which has the dimension of frequency.

concept_tested: Speed of sound by dimensions
stem: The speed v of sound in a medium is assumed to depend on pressure P and density rho. Dimensional analysis gives
option_d: v is proportional to P rho
solution: Assume v proportional to P^a rho^b. Matching [L T^-1] to [M L^-1 T^-2]^a [M L^-3]^b gives a = 1/2, b = -1/2, so v is proportional to sqrt(P/rho).
formula_principle: Homogeneity of dimensions
common_misconception: Choosing the inverted ratio sqrt(rho/P), which gives the reciprocal of speed.

concept_tested: What dimensional analysis cannot do
stem: Dimensional analysis alone cannot determine
option_a: whether a given equation is dimensionally consistent
option_b: the value of a dimensionless constant in a formula
option_c: the dimensions of a derived physical quantity
option_d: a conversion factor between two systems of units
correct_answer_text: the value of a dimensionless constant in a formula
solution: Dimensional analysis cannot fix numerical constants such as 2, pi or 1/2, since they are dimensionless.
formula_principle: Limitations of dimensional analysis
common_misconception: Believing dimensional analysis yields the complete formula including constants.

concept_tested: Statement
stem: The principle of homogeneity of dimensions states that
option_a: all physical quantities in an equation must be dimensionless
option_b: the two sides of an equation may differ only by a constant of different dimensions
option_c: only the largest term in an equation need be dimensionally consistent
option_d: every term on both sides of a valid physical equation has the same dimensions
correct_answer_text: every term on both sides of a valid physical equation has the same dimensions
solution: For an equation to be physically valid, each additive term must carry identical dimensions.
formula_principle: Principle of homogeneity
common_misconception: Thinking only the two whole sides, not each individual term, must match.

concept_tested: van der Waals constant a
stem: In the van der Waals equation (P + a/V^2)(V - b) = RT, the dimensional formula of the constant a is
solution: Since a/V^2 must have the dimensions of pressure, a = P V^2 = [M L^-1 T^-2][L^3]^2 = [M L^5 T^-2].
formula_principle: Homogeneity: a/V^2 has dimensions of pressure
common_misconception: Forgetting that V^2 carries [L^6], and stopping at pressure dimensions.

concept_tested: Odd one out
stem: Which of the following quantities is NOT dimensionless?
solution: Relative velocity has dimensions [L T^-1]; the other three are pure ratios and are dimensionless.
formula_principle: Dimensionless ratios
common_misconception: Assuming anything called a 'velocity' ratio must be dimensionless.

concept_tested: Mass in F, v, T
stem: If force F, velocity v and time T are taken as fundamental quantities, the dimensional formula of mass is
solution: From F = m v / T, mass m = F T / v = [F v^-1 T].
formula_principle: F = m a = m v / T
common_misconception: Rearranging F = m v / T incorrectly and misplacing the time factor.

concept_tested: Surface tension in E, v, T
stem: If energy E, velocity v and time T are the fundamental quantities, the dimensional formula of surface tension is
solution: Length L = v T and mass M = E v^-2 (from E = M L^2 T^-2). Surface tension = M T^-2 = E v^-2 T^-2.
formula_principle: Express M and L via E, v, T
common_misconception: Failing to substitute both L = vT and M = E v^-2 before simplifying.

concept_tested: Boltzmann constant
stem: The dimensional formula of the Boltzmann constant is
solution: From E = k T, k = E / T(temperature) = [M L^2 T^-2] / [K] = [M L^2 T^-2 K^-1].
formula_principle: E = k T
common_misconception: Omitting the temperature dimension when dividing energy by temperature.

concept_tested: Thermal conductivity
stem: The dimensional formula of coefficient of thermal conductivity is
formula_principle: Q = k A (dT/dx) t
common_misconception: Mishandling the length factors from area and thickness.

concept_tested: Different dimensions pair
stem: Which pair of quantities does NOT have the same dimensions?
solution: Force is [M L T^-2] while surface tension is [M T^-2]; they differ by a length factor. The other pairs match.
formula_principle: Compare dimensional formulae
common_misconception: Assuming force and surface tension match because both involve force.

concept_tested: Electric field
stem: The dimensional formula of electric field intensity is
solution: E = force / charge = [M L T^-2] / [A T] = [M L T^-3 A^-1].
formula_principle: E = F / q
common_misconception: Forgetting the extra time factor introduced by dividing by charge [A T].

concept_tested: Capacitance
stem: The dimensional formula of electrical capacitance is
formula_principle: C = Q / V
common_misconception: Errors in dividing charge dimensions by potential difference dimensions.

concept_tested: Leading zeros
stem: The number of significant figures in 0.00340 is
solution: Leading zeros are not significant; the significant figures are 3, 4 and the trailing 0, giving 3.
formula_principle: Rules for significant figures
common_misconception: Counting leading zeros as significant figures.

concept_tested: Sandwiched and trailing zeros
stem: The number of significant figures in 0.06900 is
solution: Leading zeros do not count; 6, 9 and the two trailing zeros are significant, giving 4.
formula_principle: Rules for significant figures
common_misconception: Dropping the significant trailing zeros after the decimal point.

concept_tested: Embedded zeros
stem: The number of significant figures in 2.0035 is
solution: All digits including the zeros trapped between non-zero digits are significant, so there are 5.
formula_principle: Rules for significant figures
common_misconception: Ignoring zeros that lie between non-zero digits.

concept_tested: Trailing zeros with decimal
stem: The number of significant figures in 100.00 is
solution: When a decimal point is present, trailing zeros are significant, so 100.00 has 5 significant figures.
formula_principle: Rules for significant figures
common_misconception: Treating the trailing zeros as placeholders even though a decimal point is shown.

concept_tested: Single significant digit
stem: The number of significant figures in 0.0001 is
solution: Only the digit 1 is significant; the leading zeros merely fix the decimal place.
formula_principle: Rules for significant figures
common_misconception: Counting the placeholder leading zeros as significant.

concept_tested: Multiplication rule
stem: The product 2.5 x 1.25, expressed to the correct number of significant figures, is
solution: 2.5 x 1.25 = 3.125. The factor 2.5 has two significant figures, so the answer is rounded to 3.1.
formula_principle: Product keeps least significant figures
common_misconception: Reporting all calculator digits instead of limiting to the least significant figures.

concept_tested: Addition rule
stem: The sum 12.11 + 8.5 + 1.013, to the correct number of decimal places, is
solution: 12.11 + 8.5 + 1.013 = 21.623. The least precise term 8.5 has one decimal place, so the answer is 21.6.
formula_principle: Sum keeps least decimal places
common_misconception: Applying the significant-figure (product) rule instead of the decimal-place (sum) rule.

concept_tested: Division rule
stem: The quotient 5.74 / 2.0, to the correct number of significant figures, is
solution: 5.74 / 2.0 = 2.87. The divisor 2.0 has two significant figures, so the answer is 2.9.
formula_principle: Quotient keeps least significant figures
common_misconception: Keeping three significant figures because the dividend has three.

concept_tested: Round to three figures
stem: The number 4.567 rounded to three significant figures is
solution: Dropping the 7 (greater than 5) rounds the 6 up to 7, giving 4.57.
formula_principle: Rounding rules
common_misconception: Rounding down when the dropped digit exceeds 5.

concept_tested: Round-half-to-even (even preceding)
stem: Using the rounding rule for a trailing 5, the number 2.745 rounded to three significant figures is
solution: When the digit to be dropped is exactly 5, the preceding digit is left unchanged if it is even. Here 4 is even, so 2.745 becomes 2.74.
formula_principle: Round half to even
common_misconception: Always rounding a trailing 5 upward, ignoring the even-preceding-digit rule.

concept_tested: Round-half-to-even (odd preceding)
stem: Using the rounding rule for a trailing 5, the number 3.135 rounded to three significant figures is
solution: When the dropped digit is 5, an odd preceding digit is raised by one. Here 3 is odd, so 3.135 becomes 3.14.
formula_principle: Round half to even
common_misconception: Leaving the odd preceding digit unchanged when the dropped digit is 5.

concept_tested: Scientific notation
stem: The number of significant figures in 1.6 x 10^-19 is
solution: In scientific notation only the mantissa digits count; 1.6 has 2 significant figures.
formula_principle: Significant figures in scientific notation
common_misconception: Counting the exponent as part of the significant figures.

concept_tested: Measured value zeros
stem: A mass is recorded as 5.00 kg. The number of significant figures in this value is
solution: The trailing zeros after the decimal point indicate measured precision, so 5.00 has 3 significant figures.
formula_principle: Significant figures in measurements
common_misconception: Discarding trailing zeros that actually convey measurement precision.

concept_tested: Identify four figures
stem: Which of the following numbers has exactly four significant figures?
solution: In 2.500 the trailing zeros after the decimal are significant, giving four significant figures.
formula_principle: Rules for significant figures
common_misconception: Assuming 0.0025 has four figures by counting the leading zeros.

concept_tested: Area to correct figures
stem: The length and breadth of a plate are 2.53 cm and 1.27 cm. Its area to the correct number of significant figures is
solution: Area = 2.53 x 1.27 = 3.2131 cm^2. Both factors have three significant figures, so the answer is 3.21 cm^2.
formula_principle: Product keeps least significant figures
common_misconception: Reporting the full product without rounding to three significant figures.

concept_tested: Zeros within a number
stem: The number of significant figures in 0.00204 is
solution: Leading zeros do not count, but the zero between 2 and 4 does, giving 3 significant figures.
formula_principle: Rules for significant figures
common_misconception: Either counting leading zeros or dropping the significant embedded zero.

concept_tested: Trailing zeros with decimal point
stem: Trailing zeros in a number that contains a decimal point are
option_c: significant only if followed by a non-zero digit
solution: A decimal point signals that trailing zeros are meaningful measured digits, so they are significant.
formula_principle: Rules for significant figures
common_misconception: Treating trailing zeros as mere placeholders even with a decimal point present.

concept_tested: Energy value
stem: The number of significant figures in the measured value 6.320 J is
solution: The digits 6, 3, 2 and the trailing 0 are all significant, giving 4.
formula_principle: Rules for significant figures
common_misconception: Dropping the significant trailing zero after the decimal point.

concept_tested: Surface area of sphere
stem: The radius of a sphere is measured as 2.1 cm. Its surface area, to the correct number of significant figures, is (take pi = 3.14)
solution: A = 4 x 3.14 x (2.1)^2 = 4 x 3.14 x 4.41 = 55.4 cm^2. With two significant figures in r, the answer is 55 cm^2.
formula_principle: A = 4 pi r^2
common_misconception: Keeping extra figures although the radius limits the result to two significant figures.

concept_tested: Addition decimal places
stem: The sum 3.8 + 4.29, to the correct number of decimal places, is
solution: 3.8 + 4.29 = 8.09. The term 3.8 has one decimal place, so the answer is 8.1.
formula_principle: Sum keeps least decimal places
common_misconception: Retaining two decimal places from 4.29 instead of rounding to one.

concept_tested: Multiplication rule statement
stem: In multiplication or division, the number of significant figures in the result equals
option_a: the largest number of significant figures among the quantities
option_b: the least number of significant figures among the quantities
option_c: the sum of the significant figures of the quantities
option_d: the number of decimal places in the least precise quantity
correct_answer_text: the least number of significant figures among the quantities
solution: A product or quotient is limited to the least number of significant figures among the factors.
formula_principle: Significant-figure rules
common_misconception: Applying the decimal-place (addition) rule to a multiplication.

concept_tested: Subtraction decimal places
stem: The result of 24.36 - 0.0623, to the correct number of decimal places, is
solution: 24.36 - 0.0623 = 24.2977. The least precise term 24.36 has two decimal places, so the answer is 24.30.
formula_principle: Difference keeps least decimal places
common_misconception: Retaining the extra decimal places of the more precise term.

concept_tested: Absolute error definition
stem: The magnitude of the difference between the true value and a measured value of a quantity is called the
solution: The absolute error in a measurement is the magnitude of the difference between the measured value and the true (mean) value.
formula_principle: Absolute error
common_misconception: Confusing the absolute error (a difference) with the relative error (a ratio).

concept_tested: Relative error definition
stem: The relative error in a measurement is defined as
option_a: mean absolute error multiplied by the mean value
option_b: mean value divided by the mean absolute error
option_d: mean absolute error divided by the mean value
correct_answer_text: mean absolute error divided by the mean value
solution: Relative error = mean absolute error / mean value, a dimensionless ratio.
formula_principle: Relative error
common_misconception: Inverting the ratio or mixing relative error with percentage error.

concept_tested: Percentage error
stem: The percentage error in a measurement is equal to the relative error
solution: Percentage error is the relative error expressed per hundred, so it equals the relative error times 100.
formula_principle: Percentage error = relative error x 100
common_misconception: Dividing by 100 instead of multiplying.

concept_tested: Gross error
stem: Errors that arise from carelessness of the observer, such as misreading a scale, are classified as
solution: Gross errors are due to human mistakes such as wrong readings or recording, and can be avoided with care.
formula_principle: Classification of errors
common_misconception: Confusing avoidable gross errors with instrument-based systematic errors.

concept_tested: Systematic error
stem: A zero error in a screw gauge that shifts every reading by the same amount is an example of a
solution: A constant, repeatable offset such as a zero error is a systematic error and can be corrected by calibration.
formula_principle: Classification of errors
common_misconception: Mistaking a constant instrument offset for a random error.

concept_tested: Averaging
stem: Random errors in a measurement can be minimised by
option_a: taking a large number of readings and averaging them
option_d: choosing an instrument with a larger least count
correct_answer_text: taking a large number of readings and averaging them
solution: Because random errors are equally likely to be positive or negative, averaging many readings reduces their net effect.
formula_principle: Reducing random errors
common_misconception: Believing zero-error correction removes random rather than systematic error.

concept_tested: Least count meaning
stem: The least count of a measuring instrument is
option_a: the smallest measurement that can be made with it
option_b: the largest measurement it can display
option_c: the average of its scale readings
option_d: the zero error of the instrument
correct_answer_text: the smallest measurement that can be made with it
solution: The least count is the smallest value that an instrument can measure, setting its resolution.
formula_principle: Least count
common_misconception: Confusing the least count with the zero error of the instrument.

concept_tested: Mean of readings
stem: Five readings of a length are 2.63, 2.65, 2.64, 2.62 and 2.66 cm. The mean value is
formula_principle: Mean = sum of readings / number of readings
common_misconception: Adding incorrectly or dividing by the wrong count of readings.

concept_tested: Mean absolute error
stem: For the five readings 2.63, 2.65, 2.64, 2.62 and 2.66 cm with mean 2.64 cm, the mean absolute error is
solution: Deviations are 0.01, 0.01, 0.00, 0.02, 0.02; their sum is 0.06 and the mean absolute error is 0.06/5 = 0.012 cm.
formula_principle: Mean absolute error = mean of |deviations|
common_misconception: Taking the maximum deviation instead of the average of the deviations.

concept_tested: From relative error
stem: If the relative error in a measurement is 0.02, the percentage error is
solution: Percentage error = 0.02 x 100 = 2 percent.
formula_principle: Percentage error = relative error x 100
common_misconception: Misplacing the decimal point when multiplying by 100.

concept_tested: Sum rule
stem: If Z = A + B, the maximum absolute error in Z is
solution: For a sum, the maximum absolute error is the sum of the absolute errors: delta Z = delta A + delta B.
formula_principle: Error in a sum
common_misconception: Subtracting errors for A + B instead of adding them.

concept_tested: Difference rule
stem: If Z = A - B, the maximum absolute error in Z is
solution: For a difference, the maximum absolute error is still the sum of the absolute errors: delta Z = delta A + delta B.
formula_principle: Error in a difference
common_misconception: Assuming errors cancel when quantities are subtracted.

concept_tested: Product rule
stem: If Z = A B, the maximum relative error in Z is
solution: For a product, the relative errors add: delta Z / Z = delta A / A + delta B / B.
formula_principle: Error in a product
common_misconception: Adding absolute errors instead of relative errors for a product.

concept_tested: Quotient rule
stem: If Z = A / B, the maximum relative error in Z is
solution: For a quotient, the relative errors add: delta Z / Z = delta A / A + delta B / B.
formula_principle: Error in a quotient
common_misconception: Subtracting the relative errors because the quantities are divided.

concept_tested: Power rule (square)
stem: If Z = A^2, the maximum relative error in Z is
solution: For Z = A^n, delta Z / Z = n (delta A / A). With n = 2 this is 2 (delta A / A).
formula_principle: Error in a power
common_misconception: Forgetting that squaring doubles the relative error.

concept_tested: General power rule
stem: For Z = A^a B^b / C^c, the maximum relative error in Z is
option_a: a(delta A)/A + b(delta B)/B - c(delta C)/C
option_c: a(delta A)/A + b(delta B)/B + c(delta C)/C
option_d: a(delta A)/A + b(delta B)/B + c(delta C)/C, all multiplied
correct_answer_text: a(delta A)/A + b(delta B)/B + c(delta C)/C
solution: Each relative error is multiplied by the magnitude of its power and all terms are added for the maximum error.
formula_principle: General rule for combination of errors
common_misconception: Subtracting the term for C because it is in the denominator.

concept_tested: Numerical sum
stem: Two lengths are A = (10.0 +/- 0.1) cm and B = (5.0 +/- 0.1) cm. The percentage error in Z = A + B is about
solution: delta Z = 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.2 cm and Z = 15.0 cm, so percentage error = (0.2/15.0) x 100 ~ 1.3 percent.
formula_principle: Error in a sum then percentage
common_misconception: Adding the individual percentage errors of A and B instead of using the combined absolute error.

concept_tested: Resistance from V and I
stem: A resistance is found using R = V / I with V = (100 +/- 5) V and I = (10 +/- 0.2) A. The percentage error in R is
solution: Percentage error in V = 5 percent and in I = 2 percent; for R = V/I they add to 7 percent.
formula_principle: Relative errors add for a quotient
common_misconception: Taking only the larger of the two percentage errors instead of their sum.

concept_tested: Density from mass and volume
stem: The density of a body is found from rho = m / V with m = (10.0 +/- 0.1) g and V = (5.0 +/- 0.1) cm^3. The percentage error in rho is
solution: Percentage error in m = 1 percent and in V = 2 percent; for rho = m/V they add to 3 percent.
formula_principle: Relative errors add for a quotient
common_misconception: Using only the mass error and ignoring the larger volume error.

concept_tested: Kinetic energy
stem: The percentage errors in mass and speed of a body are 2 percent and 3 percent. The maximum percentage error in its kinetic energy (1/2 m v^2) is
solution: Percentage error in KE = (error in m) + 2 x (error in v) = 2 + 2(3) = 8 percent.
formula_principle: Error in a product with a power
common_misconception: Forgetting to double the speed error since kinetic energy depends on v squared.

concept_tested: g from pendulum
stem: In g = 4 pi^2 L / T^2, the percentage errors in L and T are 1 percent and 2 percent. The maximum percentage error in g is
solution: Percentage error in g = (error in L) + 2 x (error in T) = 1 + 2(2) = 5 percent.
formula_principle: Error with a squared term
common_misconception: Not doubling the period error although T appears squared in the formula.

concept_tested: Product statement
stem: When two measured quantities are multiplied, the percentage error in the product is
option_a: the difference of their percentage errors
option_b: the sum of their percentage errors
option_c: the product of their percentage errors
option_d: the larger of their percentage errors
correct_answer_text: the sum of their percentage errors
solution: For a product the relative (and hence percentage) errors add.
formula_principle: Error in a product
common_misconception: Taking only the larger percentage error instead of the sum.

concept_tested: Absolute error in sum
stem: For Z = A + B with A = (4.0 +/- 0.2) and B = (6.0 +/- 0.3), the value of Z with its absolute error is
formula_principle: Error in a sum
common_misconception: Averaging the absolute errors instead of adding them.

concept_tested: Complex power expression
stem: A quantity is P = a^3 b^2 / (c d^(1/2)). If the percentage errors in a, b, c and d are 1, 2, 3 and 4 percent, the maximum percentage error in P is
formula_principle: General combination of errors
common_misconception: Using the full 4 percent for d instead of halving it for the square-root power.

concept_tested: Volume of cube
stem: The side of a cube is measured as (2.00 +/- 0.01) cm. The percentage error in its volume is
solution: Relative error in side = 0.01/2.00 = 0.5 percent; volume goes as side^3, so percentage error = 3 x 0.5 = 1.5 percent.
formula_principle: Error in a cube
common_misconception: Forgetting to multiply the side error by three for a volume.

concept_tested: Area of circle
stem: The radius of a circle is (2.0 +/- 0.1) cm. The percentage error in its area is
solution: Relative error in radius = 0.1/2.0 = 5 percent; area goes as radius^2, so percentage error = 2 x 5 = 10 percent.
formula_principle: Error in a square
common_misconception: Not doubling the radius error although area depends on radius squared.

concept_tested: Momentum
stem: The percentage errors in mass and speed of a body are 2 percent and 3 percent. The maximum percentage error in its momentum (m v) is
solution: Momentum p = m v is a simple product, so percentage error = 2 + 3 = 5 percent.
formula_principle: Error in a product
common_misconception: Doubling the speed error as if computing kinetic energy rather than momentum.

concept_tested: Power rule statement
stem: The relative error in a quantity raised to the power n is
option_a: equal to the relative error in the quantity
option_b: 1/n times the relative error in the quantity
option_c: n squared times the relative error in the quantity
option_d: n times the relative error in the quantity
correct_answer_text: n times the relative error in the quantity
solution: For Z = A^n, the relative error is delta Z / Z = n (delta A / A).
formula_principle: Error in a power
common_misconception: Assuming a power leaves the relative error unchanged.

concept_tested: Fractional and negative powers
stem: For Y = A^2 B^(1/2) / C^(1/3), the percentage errors in A, B and C are 1, 2 and 3 percent. The maximum percentage error in Y is
solution: Percentage error = 2(1) + (1/2)(2) + (1/3)(3) = 2 + 1 + 1 = 4 percent.
formula_principle: General combination of errors
common_misconception: Using the full percentage errors of B and C instead of scaling by their fractional powers.

concept_tested: Most precise measurement
stem: In g = 4 pi^2 L / T^2, to minimise the error in g the quantity that must be measured most precisely is
option_a: the length L, since it appears to the first power
option_d: the period T, since it appears squared
correct_answer_text: the period T, since it appears squared
solution: Since T appears squared, its relative error is doubled in g, so T must be measured most carefully.
formula_principle: Weighting of errors by power
common_misconception: Assuming the length, appearing to the first power, dominates the error.

concept_tested: Cubed quantity
stem: The percentage error in a measured quantity is 4 percent. If this quantity is cubed, the percentage error in the result is
solution: For a cube the percentage error is 3 x 4 = 12 percent.
formula_principle: Error in a power
common_misconception: Cubing the percentage error itself instead of multiplying it by three.

concept_tested: Series resistance
stem: Two resistances R1 = (100 +/- 3) ohm and R2 = (200 +/- 4) ohm are joined in series. The equivalent resistance with its absolute error is
solution: Series R = R1 + R2 = 300 ohm and delta R = 3 + 4 = 7 ohm, so R = (300 +/- 7) ohm.
formula_principle: Series resistance and error in a sum
common_misconception: Averaging the absolute errors rather than adding them for a sum.

concept_tested: Implied uncertainty
stem: A time interval is recorded as 4.6 s. The implied absolute uncertainty in this reading is about
solution: The uncertainty is taken to lie in the last significant digit, here the tenths place, giving about 0.1 s.
formula_principle: Uncertainty from significant figures
common_misconception: Reading the uncertainty from the wrong digit position.

concept_tested: Product with power
stem: For Z = A B^2 with A = (1.0 +/- 0.1) and B = (2.0 +/- 0.1), the maximum percentage error in Z is
solution: Percentage error in A = 10 percent and in B = 5 percent; for Z = A B^2 it is 10 + 2(5) = 20 percent.
formula_principle: Combination of errors with a power
common_misconception: Not doubling the B error although B is squared.

concept_tested: Difference and precision
stem: When two nearly equal quantities are subtracted, the percentage error in the result usually
solution: The absolute errors add while the difference itself is small, so the relative (percentage) error grows sharply.
formula_principle: Error in a difference of close values
common_misconception: Believing subtraction reduces error because the numbers are close.

concept_tested: Below root ten
stem: The order of magnitude of 2.5 x 10^6 is
solution: Writing the number as a x 10^b, the order is 10^b if a is less than 3.16. Here a = 2.5, so the order is 10^6.
formula_principle: Order of magnitude rule
common_misconception: Rounding the exponent up even though the mantissa is below 3.16.

concept_tested: Above root ten (negative)
stem: The order of magnitude of 8.2 x 10^-4 is
solution: The mantissa 8.2 exceeds 3.16 (root ten), so the exponent -4 is rounded up to -3.
formula_principle: Order of magnitude rule
common_misconception: Ignoring the rule that a mantissa above 3.16 raises the exponent.

concept_tested: Atomic size
stem: The order of magnitude of the diameter of a hydrogen atom (about 1.06 x 10^-10 m) is
solution: With mantissa 1.06 below 3.16, the order of magnitude of an atomic diameter is 10^-10 m.
formula_principle: Order of magnitude rule
common_misconception: Confusing atomic (10^-10 m) and nuclear (10^-15 m) length scales.

concept_tested: Small decimal
stem: The order of magnitude of 0.0000734 is
solution: 0.0000734 = 7.34 x 10^-5; since 7.34 exceeds 3.16 the exponent rounds up to -4.
formula_principle: Order of magnitude rule
common_misconception: Reading the order directly as 10^-5 without applying the root-ten rule.

concept_tested: Electron mass
stem: The order of magnitude of the mass of an electron (9.1 x 10^-31 kg) is
solution: With mantissa 9.1 above 3.16, the exponent -31 rounds up, giving order 10^-30 kg.
formula_principle: Order of magnitude rule
common_misconception: Taking the order as 10^-31 without applying the root-ten rounding rule.

concept_tested: Three-digit number
stem: The order of magnitude of the number 149 is
solution: 149 = 1.49 x 10^2; the mantissa 1.49 is below 3.16, so the order of magnitude is 10^2.
formula_principle: Order of magnitude rule
common_misconception: Rounding up to 10^3 although the mantissa is well below 3.16.

concept_tested: Seconds in a day
stem: The order of magnitude of the number of seconds in one day is
solution: One day = 24 x 3600 = 86400 s = 8.64 x 10^4 s; since 8.64 exceeds 3.16 the order is 10^5.
formula_principle: Order of magnitude of an estimate
common_misconception: Stopping at 10^4 without applying the root-ten rounding rule.

concept_tested: Above root ten (positive)
stem: The order of magnitude of 4.5 x 10^7 is
solution: With mantissa 4.5 above 3.16, the exponent 7 rounds up, giving order 10^8.
formula_principle: Order of magnitude rule
common_misconception: Reading the order as 10^7 without applying the root-ten rule.

concept_tested: Least count (10 divisions)
stem: In a vernier calliper, 10 vernier scale divisions coincide with 9 main scale divisions, and one main scale division is 1 mm. The least count is
solution: 1 VSD = 9/10 mm = 0.9 mm, so LC = 1 mm - 0.9 mm = 0.1 mm = 0.01 cm.
formula_principle: LC = 1 MSD - 1 VSD
common_misconception: Reporting the main scale division as the least count.

concept_tested: Least count formula
stem: The least count of a vernier calliper with main scale division 1 mm and 20 vernier divisions (equal to 19 main divisions) is
solution: LC = 1 MSD / N = 1 mm / 20 = 0.05 mm.
formula_principle: LC = value of 1 MSD / number of vernier divisions
common_misconception: Dividing by the wrong number of vernier divisions.

concept_tested: Least count from pitch
stem: A screw gauge has a pitch of 1 mm and 100 divisions on its circular scale. Its least count is
solution: LC = pitch / divisions = 1 mm / 100 = 0.01 mm = 0.001 cm.
formula_principle: LC = pitch / number of circular divisions
common_misconception: Making a power-of-ten slip when converting 0.01 mm to centimetre.

concept_tested: Pitch definition
stem: The circular scale of a screw gauge advances the screw by 1 mm in two complete rotations. The pitch of the screw gauge is
solution: Pitch = distance advanced per rotation = 1 mm / 2 = 0.5 mm.
formula_principle: Pitch = distance moved per rotation
common_misconception: Confusing total travel with travel per rotation.

concept_tested: Least count with pitch 0.5 mm
stem: A screw gauge has a pitch of 0.5 mm and 50 divisions on its circular scale. Its least count is
solution: LC = pitch / divisions = 0.5 mm / 50 = 0.01 mm.
formula_principle: LC = pitch / number of circular divisions
common_misconception: Dividing by the wrong number of circular divisions.

concept_tested: Least count of metre scale
stem: The least count of an ordinary metre scale graduated in millimetres is
solution: The smallest division of a millimetre scale is 1 mm = 0.1 cm, which is its least count.
formula_principle: Least count of a scale
common_misconception: Confusing the least count with a larger centimetre division.

concept_tested: Reading a screw gauge
stem: A screw gauge with least count 0.01 mm and no zero error shows a main scale reading of 3 mm, with the 45th circular scale division coinciding with the reference line. The measured diameter is
solution: Diameter = 3 mm + (45 x 0.01 mm) = 3 mm + 0.45 mm = 3.45 mm.
formula_principle: Reading = MSR + (CSD x LC)
common_misconception: Misplacing the decimal when adding the circular scale contribution.

concept_tested: A vector needs both magnitude and direction and must obey the laws of vector addition
stem: Which one of the following physical quantities is a vector?
solution: Impulse is force multiplied by the time interval for which it acts. Time is a scalar and force is a vector, so impulse is a vector directed along the force. Work, electric potential and pressure are all scalars.
formula_principle: Impulse J = F x time interval; multiplying a vector by a scalar gives a vector
common_misconception: Students assume that any quantity built out of a force must be a vector, and so mark work as a vector.

concept_tested: Scalars are completely specified by a magnitude with a suitable unit
stem: Which one of the following physical quantities is a scalar?
solution: Kinetic energy is one half m v squared. It depends only on the magnitude of the velocity, so reversing the direction of motion does not change it. Torque, angular velocity and magnetic moment all require a direction to be stated.
formula_principle: A scalar is fully specified by a magnitude and a unit alone
common_misconception: Students think kinetic energy inherits the direction of velocity, since velocity appears in its expression.

concept_tested: A unit vector carries direction information only and has magnitude exactly one
stem: The unit vector drawn along a given non zero vector has
option_a: magnitude one and the unit of the given vector
option_b: the magnitude of the given vector and no unit
option_c: magnitude one and no unit of any kind
option_d: magnitude zero and no fixed direction at all
correct_answer_text: magnitude one and no unit of any kind
solution: A unit vector is defined as the vector divided by its own magnitude. Both the numerical size and the physical unit cancel in that division, leaving a pure number of value one that only specifies direction.
formula_principle: Unit vector n = P / |P|
common_misconception: Students believe a unit vector along a velocity of 5 m s^-1 still carries the unit m s^-1.

concept_tested: The null vector has zero magnitude and an arbitrary direction
stem: Which statement about the null vector is correct?
option_a: Its magnitude is zero and its direction is indeterminate
option_b: Its magnitude is zero and its direction is always along the x axis
option_c: Its magnitude is one and its direction is indeterminate
option_d: Its magnitude is zero and it can never be written as the sum of two non zero vectors
correct_answer_text: Its magnitude is zero and its direction is indeterminate
solution: A null vector is an arrow of zero length, so no direction can be assigned to it. It arises whenever a vector is added to its own negative, or when a closed polygon of vectors is traversed once completely.
formula_principle: P + (-P) = null vector; magnitude zero, direction arbitrary
common_misconception: Students insist every vector must point somewhere and so reject the idea of an indeterminate direction.

concept_tested: Dividing a vector by its magnitude gives the unit vector along it
stem: The unit vector along the vector 3 i + 4 j is
solution: The magnitude is sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5. Dividing the vector by 5 gives 0.6 i + 0.8 j, whose magnitude is sqrt(0.36 + 0.64) = 1.
formula_principle: n = P / |P| with |P| = sqrt(Px^2 + Py^2)
common_misconception: Students add the components directly to get the magnitude rather than using the Pythagorean form.

concept_tested: Equality of vectors requires equality of both magnitude and direction
stem: Two vectors are said to be equal if
option_a: they have the same magnitude and the same direction
option_b: they have the same magnitude, whatever their directions may be
option_c: they have the same direction, whatever their magnitudes may be
option_d: they act at the same point of the body
correct_answer_text: they have the same magnitude and the same direction
solution: Two vectors are equal only when their magnitudes are equal and their directions are identical. Their positions in space are irrelevant, so two equal arrows drawn at different places still represent the same vector.
formula_principle: P = Q if and only if |P| = |Q| and the directions coincide
common_misconception: Students treat vectors with equal magnitudes, such as 5 N east and 5 N west, as equal vectors.

subtopic: Direction alone does not make a vector
concept_tested: A quantity is a vector only if it also obeys the laws of vector addition
stem: Electric current has a magnitude and an associated direction along the conductor, yet it is classified as a scalar. This is because electric current
option_a: always has a positive numerical value
option_b: is measured by a single instrument, the ammeter
option_c: is defined as a ratio of the two scalars charge and time
option_d: does not obey the triangle law of vector addition
correct_answer_text: does not obey the triangle law of vector addition
solution: At a junction where two wires carrying 3 A and 4 A at right angles meet, the outgoing current is 7 A and not 5 A. Currents add algebraically, not by the triangle law, so current fails the third requirement and is classified as a scalar.
formula_principle: Vector test: magnitude, direction and addition by the triangle or parallelogram law
common_misconception: Students assume that any quantity with an arrow drawn for it in a circuit diagram must be a vector.

concept_tested: Three vectors of unequal magnitudes can sum to zero only if they are coplanar
stem: The minimum number of coplanar vectors of unequal magnitudes whose vector sum can be a null vector is
solution: Two unequal vectors can never cancel, since their resultant lies between the difference and the sum of their magnitudes and both bounds are non zero. Three unequal vectors can be arranged as the sides of a triangle taken in order, and a closed triangle gives a null resultant.
formula_principle: Closed polygon law: vectors forming a closed figure taken in order sum to zero
common_misconception: Students answer two, forgetting that the magnitudes are specified to be unequal.

concept_tested: Magnitude of a position vector gives the distance from the origin
stem: The position vector of a point P is r = 3 i + 4 j + 12 k metre. The distance of P from the origin is
common_misconception: Students extend the two dimensional habit of using only two components and drop the third one.

concept_tested: Collinear vectors act along the same line or along parallel lines
stem: Two non zero vectors are collinear. Which statement about them is necessarily true?
option_a: The angle between them is either 0 degree or 180 degree
option_b: The angle between them is 0 degree and nothing else
option_c: The angle between them is 90 degree and nothing else
option_d: The angle is 0 degree and their magnitudes are equal
correct_answer_text: The angle between them is either 0 degree or 180 degree
solution: Collinear vectors lie along one line. They may point the same way, giving an angle of 0 degree, or opposite ways, giving 180 degree. In either case the sine of the angle is zero, which is why their vector product vanishes.
formula_principle: Collinear vectors are parallel or antiparallel, so sin theta = 0
common_misconception: Students equate collinear with parallel only and forget the antiparallel case.

concept_tested: The negative of a vector has the same magnitude and the reversed direction
stem: Vector Q is the negative of vector P. Which statement is correct?
option_a: Q has the same magnitude as P, points opposite to P, and P + Q has magnitude 2|P|
option_b: Q has magnitude equal to |P| and points along the same line and sense as P
option_c: Q has the same magnitude as P, points opposite to P, and P + Q is a null vector
option_d: Q has magnitude smaller than |P| and points opposite to P
correct_answer_text: Q has the same magnitude as P, points opposite to P, and P + Q is a null vector
solution: Multiplying a vector by the scalar minus one keeps its length unchanged and turns it through 180 degree. Placing the two arrows head to tail returns to the starting point, so their sum is the null vector.
formula_principle: -P has magnitude |P| with direction reversed; P + (-P) = null vector
common_misconception: Students think a negative sign in front of a vector makes its magnitude negative.

concept_tested: Displacement is the difference of position vectors, and dividing it by its magnitude gives direction
stem: A particle moves from the point (1, 2, 3) m to the point (4, 6, 3) m. The unit vector along its displacement is
solution: The displacement is (4 - 1) i + (6 - 2) j + (3 - 3) k = 3 i + 4 j. Its magnitude is sqrt(9 + 16) = 5 m, so the unit vector is (3 i + 4 j) / 5 = 0.6 i + 0.8 j.
formula_principle: Displacement d = r2 - r1; unit vector = d / |d|
common_misconception: Students subtract the coordinates in the wrong order or forget to normalise the displacement.

concept_tested: A vector may be shifted parallel to itself without changing it
stem: A vector drawn from a point P to a point Q is shifted parallel to itself so that its tail now lies at a different point of the plane. The shifted vector
option_a: has the same magnitude as the original vector but a different direction
option_b: is equal to the original vector
option_c: is the negative of the original vector
option_d: has the same direction as the original vector but a different magnitude
correct_answer_text: is equal to the original vector
solution: Vectors in elementary mechanics are free vectors. Shifting the arrow parallel to itself alters neither its length nor its orientation, so the shifted arrow represents the same vector and the two are equal.
formula_principle: Equality of vectors depends on magnitude and direction only, not on position
common_misconception: Students believe the point of application is part of the identity of a vector, so a shifted vector must be different.

concept_tested: In three dimensions the directions perpendicular to a given vector form a whole plane
stem: How many distinct unit vectors in three dimensional space are perpendicular to one given non zero vector?
solution: Every direction perpendicular to a given vector lies in the plane drawn normal to that vector through its tail. That plane contains a continuous circle of unit vectors, so the number of such unit vectors is unlimited. Restricting the problem to a plane would leave only two.
formula_principle: All vectors perpendicular to a given vector lie in the plane normal to it
common_misconception: Students carry over the two dimensional answer of two perpendicular unit vectors into three dimensions.

concept_tested: Division by a vector is not defined in vector algebra
stem: Which one of the following operations is not defined in vector algebra?
option_a: Division of one vector by another vector
option_b: Multiplication of a vector by a scalar
option_c: Addition of a vector to another vector of the same physical kind
option_d: Multiplication of two vectors to give a scalar
correct_answer_text: Division of one vector by another vector
solution: Vector algebra defines multiplication by a scalar, addition and subtraction of like vectors, the scalar product and the vector product. No operation inverse to vector multiplication exists, because knowing a scalar or vector product does not determine one factor uniquely from the other.
formula_principle: Defined operations: scalar multiplication, vector addition, scalar product, vector product
common_misconception: Students expect that because vectors can be multiplied they can also be divided.

concept_tested: A vector is a unit vector only when the sum of the squares of its components is one
stem: The vectors a (i + j + k) and b (i - j) are each unit vectors, where a and b are positive numbers. The value of a / b is
solution: For a (i + j + k): a^2 (1 + 1 + 1) = 1, so 3 a^2 = 1 and a = 1 / sqrt(3). For b (i - j): b^2 (1 + 1) = 1, so 2 b^2 = 1 and b = 1 / sqrt(2). Hence a / b = sqrt(2) / sqrt(3) = sqrt(2 / 3), which is about 0.816.
formula_principle: |P| = 1 requires Px^2 + Py^2 + Pz^2 = 1
common_misconception: Students set the sum of the components rather than the sum of their squares equal to one.

concept_tested: For perpendicular vectors the resultant follows the Pythagorean rule
stem: Two forces of 3 N and 4 N act at a point at right angles to each other. The magnitude of their resultant is
solution: With theta = 90 degree, cos theta = 0, so R = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5 N.
formula_principle: R = sqrt(P^2 + Q^2 + 2 P Q cos theta), with theta = 90 degree giving R = sqrt(P^2 + Q^2)
common_misconception: Students add the magnitudes of forces without regard to the angle between them.

concept_tested: The resultant is largest when the two vectors point the same way
stem: The resultant of two vectors of magnitudes P and Q has its maximum possible magnitude when the angle between them is
solution: The angle enters only through cos theta, and R increases with cos theta. The cosine has its largest value of one at theta = 0 degree, giving R = sqrt(P^2 + Q^2 + 2 P Q) = P + Q.
formula_principle: R = sqrt(P^2 + Q^2 + 2 P Q cos theta); R is maximum when cos theta = 1
common_misconception: Students memorise that the resultant is greatest at 90 degree by confusing the maximum with the perpendicular case.

concept_tested: The resultant is smallest when the two vectors are antiparallel
stem: Two vectors have magnitudes 7 units and 4 units. The smallest magnitude their resultant can have is
solution: At theta = 180 degree, cos theta = -1, so R = sqrt(49 + 16 - 56) = sqrt(9) = 3 units. This equals the difference of the magnitudes, 7 - 4 = 3 units.
formula_principle: R minimum = |P - Q| at theta = 180 degree
common_misconception: Students think the resultant of two unequal vectors can always be made zero.

concept_tested: The triangle law states how two vectors placed head to tail combine
stem: According to the triangle law of vector addition, if two vectors are represented in magnitude and direction by two sides of a triangle taken in order, their resultant is represented by
option_a: the third side taken in the same order
option_b: the third side taken in the reverse order
option_c: the median drawn to the third side
option_d: half of the third side taken in the reverse order
correct_answer_text: the third side taken in the reverse order
solution: Placing the tail of the second vector at the head of the first traces two sides of a triangle in order. The closing side drawn from the tail of the first to the head of the second, that is in the reverse order, represents the resultant in magnitude and direction.
formula_principle: Triangle law of vector addition
common_misconception: Students state the closing side in the same order and end up describing a null resultant.

concept_tested: Vectors along one line add algebraically with signs
stem: Two forces of magnitudes 8 N and 6 N act at a point in exactly opposite directions. The magnitude of their resultant is
solution: With theta = 180 degree, cos theta = -1, so R = sqrt(64 + 36 - 96) = sqrt(4) = 2 N, directed along the 8 N force.
formula_principle: R = sqrt(P^2 + Q^2 + 2 P Q cos 180) = |P - Q|
common_misconception: Students apply the Pythagorean rule regardless of the actual angle between the forces.

concept_tested: Vector addition is commutative and associative
stem: Which property is obeyed by the addition of two vectors?
option_c: |P + Q| is larger than both |P| and |Q|
solution: The parallelogram built on the two vectors is the same whichever vector is drawn first, so the diagonal representing the sum is unchanged. Hence vector addition is commutative.
formula_principle: Commutative law of vector addition
common_misconception: Students assume magnitudes always add, so that the length of the resultant is the sum of the two lengths.

concept_tested: Two equal vectors inclined at 120 degree give a resultant of the same magnitude
stem: Two vectors, each of magnitude 10 units, are inclined at 120 degree to each other. The magnitude of their resultant is
solution: With P = Q = 10 and cos 120 degree = -0.5, R = sqrt(100 + 100 + 2 x 100 x (-0.5)) = sqrt(200 - 100) = sqrt(100) = 10 units.
formula_principle: R = sqrt(P^2 + Q^2 + 2 P Q cos theta)
common_misconception: Students take cos 120 degree as +0.5 and obtain a resultant of 10 sqrt(3) units.

concept_tested: For equal vectors R = 2 P cos(theta / 2)
stem: Two vectors, each of magnitude 6 units, act at an angle of 60 degree to each other. The magnitude of their resultant is
solution: R = 2 x 6 x cos 30 degree = 12 x (sqrt(3) / 2) = 6 sqrt(3), which is about 10.4 units. The same follows from R = sqrt(36 + 36 + 2 x 36 x 0.5) = sqrt(108).
formula_principle: R = 2 P cos(theta / 2) for two equal vectors of magnitude P
common_misconception: Students use cos theta instead of cos(theta / 2) in the shortcut formula for equal vectors.

concept_tested: Vectors add component by component
stem: Two vectors are P = 2 i + 3 j and Q = 4 i - 3 j. The magnitude of P + Q is
solution: P + Q = (2 + 4) i + (3 - 3) j = 6 i. Its magnitude is sqrt(6^2 + 0^2) = 6 units, directed along the positive x axis.
formula_principle: P + Q = (Px + Qx) i + (Py + Qy) j
common_misconception: Students ignore the signs of the components and add magnitudes of like components blindly.

subtopic: Direction of the resultant of equal vectors
concept_tested: The resultant of two equal vectors bisects the angle between them
stem: Two vectors of equal magnitude are inclined at an angle theta. Their resultant makes an angle with the first vector equal to
solution: Putting P = Q gives tan alpha = P sin theta / (P + P cos theta) = sin theta / (1 + cos theta) = tan(theta / 2). Hence alpha = theta / 2, so the resultant bisects the angle. The parallelogram is a rhombus and its diagonal bisects the vertex angle.
formula_principle: tan alpha = Q sin theta / (P + Q cos theta); with P = Q this gives alpha = theta / 2
common_misconception: Students assume the resultant always lies closer to the larger vector without noticing that here the vectors are equal.

concept_tested: Vectors forming a closed polygon taken in order have a null resultant
stem: Several forces acting at a point are represented in magnitude and direction by the sides of a closed polygon taken in order. Their resultant is
option_a: a vector equal to the longest side
option_b: a null vector of zero magnitude
option_c: a vector of magnitude equal to the perimeter
option_d: a vector equal to twice the shortest side
correct_answer_text: a null vector of zero magnitude
solution: Drawing the vectors head to tail traces the polygon. Since the polygon closes, the head of the last vector coincides with the tail of the first, so the displacement from start to finish is zero and the resultant is the null vector. The point is therefore in equilibrium.
formula_principle: Polygon law of vector addition
common_misconception: Students confuse the scalar perimeter of the polygon with the vector sum of its sides.

subtopic: Finding the angle from the resultant
concept_tested: When two equal vectors have a resultant equal to either one, the angle is 120 degree
stem: Two vectors have equal magnitudes P, and the magnitude of their resultant is also P. The angle between the two vectors is
solution: Setting R = P = Q gives P^2 = P^2 + P^2 + 2 P^2 cos theta, so 0 = P^2 + 2 P^2 cos theta and cos theta = -1 / 2. Hence theta = 120 degree.
formula_principle: R^2 = P^2 + Q^2 + 2 P Q cos theta
common_misconception: Students expect the answer 60 degree by pattern matching with the equilateral triangle.

concept_tested: The resultant is the diagonal of the parallelogram drawn from the common tail
stem: Two vectors acting at a point are represented by the two adjacent sides of a parallelogram. Their resultant is represented by
option_a: the diagonal of the parallelogram drawn from the opposite corner
option_b: either diagonal of the parallelogram, since both have the same length
option_c: the diagonal of the parallelogram drawn from the point where the two vectors meet
option_d: the longer side of the parallelogram
correct_answer_text: the diagonal of the parallelogram drawn from the point where the two vectors meet
solution: With both vectors drawn from a common point as adjacent sides, the diagonal starting from that same common point gives the resultant in magnitude and direction. The other diagonal, joining the two heads, represents the difference of the vectors.
formula_principle: Parallelogram law of vector addition
common_misconception: Students pick whichever diagonal is drawn in the figure without checking where it starts.

concept_tested: The angle can be recovered from the magnitudes of the two vectors and the resultant
stem: Two forces of 6 N and 8 N acting at a point have a resultant of magnitude 10 N. The angle between the two forces is
solution: 100 = 36 + 64 + 2 x 6 x 8 x cos theta, so 100 = 100 + 96 cos theta, giving cos theta = 0 and theta = 90 degree. The numbers form the 6, 8, 10 right triangle.
formula_principle: R^2 = P^2 + Q^2 + 2 P Q cos theta
common_misconception: Students recognise the triple 6, 8, 10 but read the 90 degree as the angle of the resultant with one force instead of the angle between the forces.

concept_tested: The resultant lies between the difference and the sum of the magnitudes
stem: Two vectors of magnitudes 5 units and 3 units act at a point. Which of the following can NOT be the magnitude of their resultant?
solution: The resultant can range only from |5 - 3| = 2 units to 5 + 3 = 8 units. A value of 1 unit lies below this range and is therefore impossible for any angle between the two vectors.
formula_principle: |P - Q| is less than or equal to R which is less than or equal to P + Q
common_misconception: Students believe the resultant of two vectors can be made as small as zero whatever their magnitudes.

concept_tested: Three equal coplanar vectors at 120 degree to one another add to zero
stem: Three forces, each of magnitude 10 N, act at a point in one plane, and the angle between any two adjacent forces is 120 degree. The magnitude of their resultant is
solution: Any two of the forces at 120 degree have a resultant of 10 N directed exactly opposite to the third force. That resultant and the third force cancel, so the total is zero. The three vectors placed head to tail form a closed equilateral triangle.
formula_principle: R = sqrt(P^2 + Q^2 + 2 P Q cos theta) applied twice, or symmetry of a closed equilateral triangle
common_misconception: Students add the magnitudes and report 30 N, forgetting the symmetric directions.

subtopic: Angle from magnitudes of vectors and resultant
concept_tested: The cosine of the angle follows from the resultant equation
stem: Two vectors of magnitudes 3 units and 5 units have a resultant of magnitude 7 units. The angle between the two vectors is
solution: 49 = 9 + 25 + 2 x 3 x 5 x cos theta, so 49 = 34 + 30 cos theta and 30 cos theta = 15. Hence cos theta = 0.5 and theta = 60 degree.
formula_principle: R^2 = P^2 + Q^2 + 2 P Q cos theta
common_misconception: Students forget the factor of two in the cross term and obtain cos theta = 1, which has no solution consistent with the data.

subtopic: Finding two vectors from sum and resultant
concept_tested: Simultaneous use of the sum of magnitudes and the perpendicular resultant
stem: The sum of the magnitudes of two forces acting at a point is 14 N. When they act at right angles to each other their resultant has magnitude 10 N. The magnitudes of the two forces are
solution: From (P + Q)^2 = P^2 + Q^2 + 2 P Q, 196 = 100 + 2 P Q, so P Q = 48. With P + Q = 14 and P Q = 48 the two magnitudes are the roots of x^2 - 14 x + 48 = 0, which are 6 and 8.
common_misconception: Students try to guess the pair without using the identity linking the sum, the product and the sum of squares.

concept_tested: When the resultant is perpendicular to one vector a right triangle relation applies
stem: Two vectors of magnitudes 5 units and 13 units act at a point, and their resultant is perpendicular to the vector of magnitude 5 units. The magnitude of the resultant is
solution: Since the resultant is perpendicular to the 5 unit vector, that vector and the resultant are the two legs of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is the 13 unit vector. Hence R = sqrt(13^2 - 5^2) = sqrt(169 - 25) = sqrt(144) = 12 units.
formula_principle: If R is perpendicular to P then P, R and Q form a right triangle with Q as hypotenuse, so R^2 = Q^2 - P^2
common_misconception: Students apply the Pythagorean rule to the two given vectors instead of recognising which vector is the hypotenuse.

concept_tested: The direction of the resultant is fixed by tan alpha = Q sin theta / (P + Q cos theta)
stem: Two vectors, each of magnitude 3 units, are inclined at 60 degree to each other. The resultant makes an angle with the first vector equal to
solution: tan alpha = 3 sin 60 / (3 + 3 cos 60) = (3 x 0.866) / (3 + 1.5) = 2.598 / 4.5 = 0.577, so alpha = 30 degree. This agrees with the rule that the resultant of two equal vectors bisects the angle between them.
formula_principle: tan alpha = Q sin theta / (P + Q cos theta)
common_misconception: Students put the sine and cosine terms in the wrong places in the direction formula.

concept_tested: The velocity of a boat relative to the ground is the vector sum of two velocities
stem: A boat can move at 4 m s^-1 in still water. It is steered exactly perpendicular to the banks of a river whose water flows at 3 m s^-1. The magnitude of the velocity of the boat relative to the ground is
solution: The two velocities are at right angles, so the resultant speed is sqrt(4^2 + 3^2) = sqrt(16 + 9) = 5 m s^-1. The boat crosses along a slanting path even though it is pointed straight across.
formula_principle: v resultant = sqrt(v boat^2 + v river^2) for perpendicular velocities
common_misconception: Students think that steering perpendicular to the bank makes the actual path perpendicular to the bank as well.

subtopic: Resultant perpendicular to the smaller force
concept_tested: Combining the sum condition with the right triangle condition
stem: The sum of the magnitudes of two forces acting at a point is 18 N. Their resultant has magnitude 12 N and is perpendicular to the smaller force. The magnitude of the smaller force is
solution: Since the resultant is perpendicular to the smaller force Q, the relation R^2 = P^2 - Q^2 holds, so P^2 - Q^2 = 144. Writing this as (P - Q)(P + Q) = 144 and using P + Q = 18 gives P - Q = 8. Solving, P = 13 N and Q = 5 N, so the smaller force is 5 N.
formula_principle: P + Q = 18 with R perpendicular to Q, giving R^2 = P^2 - Q^2
common_misconception: Students apply the Pythagorean rule as R^2 = P^2 + Q^2 without noticing that the resultant, not the larger force, is one of the legs.

subtopic: Effect of scaling and reversing one vector
concept_tested: Three conditions on the resultant fix the ratio of the squares of the magnitudes
stem: The resultant of two vectors P and Q has magnitude R. If Q is doubled the new resultant becomes 2 R, and if instead Q is reversed the resultant is again 2 R. Then P^2 : Q^2 : R^2 is
solution: The three conditions give P^2 + Q^2 + 2 P Q cos theta = R^2, P^2 + 4 Q^2 + 4 P Q cos theta = 4 R^2 and P^2 + Q^2 - 2 P Q cos theta = 4 R^2. Adding the first and third gives 2 P^2 + 2 Q^2 = 5 R^2. Subtracting them gives 4 P Q cos theta = -3 R^2. Substituting in the second gives P^2 + 4 Q^2 = 7 R^2. Solving, Q^2 = 1.5 R^2 and P^2 = R^2, so P^2 : Q^2 : R^2 = 1 : 1.5 : 1 = 2 : 3 : 2.
formula_principle: R^2 = P^2 + Q^2 + 2 P Q cos theta applied to each of the three cases
common_misconception: Students set up only two of the three equations and cannot eliminate the unknown angle.

concept_tested: If three vectors sum to zero, any two of them must have a resultant equal and opposite to the third
stem: Three coplanar vectors of magnitudes 5 units, 12 units and 13 units are arranged so that their vector sum is zero. The angle between the vectors of magnitudes 5 units and 12 units is
solution: For the sum to vanish, the resultant of the 5 unit and 12 unit vectors must have magnitude 13 units. Hence 169 = 25 + 144 + 2 x 5 x 12 x cos theta, giving 120 cos theta = 0 and cos theta = 0. Therefore theta = 90 degree, which is consistent with the 5, 12, 13 right triangle.
formula_principle: Zero resultant requires the resultant of two vectors to be equal in magnitude and opposite to the third
common_misconception: Students take the three vectors to be inclined at 120 degree to one another by analogy with three equal vectors.

concept_tested: Subtracting a vector means adding its negative
stem: The subtraction of a vector Q from a vector P is carried out as
solution: There is no separate rule for subtraction. The vector Q is reversed to give -Q, and this reversed vector is then added to P by the triangle or parallelogram law.
formula_principle: P - Q = P + (-Q)
common_misconception: Students subtract magnitudes directly without reversing one vector and applying the addition law.

concept_tested: Parallel vectors subtract algebraically
stem: Two vectors of magnitudes 8 units and 5 units point in the same direction. The magnitude of their difference is
solution: With theta = 0 degree, |P - Q| = sqrt(64 + 25 - 2 x 8 x 5 x 1) = sqrt(89 - 80) = sqrt(9) = 3 units.
formula_principle: |P - Q| = sqrt(P^2 + Q^2 - 2 P Q cos theta), with theta = 0
common_misconception: Students apply the formula for the sum when the question asks for the difference.

concept_tested: A vector subtracted from itself gives the null vector
stem: For any non zero vector P, the quantity P - P is
option_c: a vector of magnitude 2|P| along P
solution: Reversing P gives -P, and adding this to P places the head of the second arrow exactly at the tail of the first. The displacement from start to finish is zero, so the result is the null vector, a vector of zero magnitude.
formula_principle: P - P = P + (-P) = null vector
common_misconception: Students report the answer as the number zero rather than as the null vector.

concept_tested: The difference formula carries a minus sign in the cross term
stem: For two vectors of magnitudes P and Q with an angle theta between them, the magnitude of P - Q is
option_a: sqrt(P^2 + Q^2 + 2 P Q cos theta)
option_b: sqrt(P^2 - Q^2 - 2 P Q cos theta)
option_c: sqrt(P^2 + Q^2 - 2 P Q sin theta)
option_d: sqrt(P^2 + Q^2 - 2 P Q cos theta)
correct_answer_text: sqrt(P^2 + Q^2 - 2 P Q cos theta)
solution: Replacing Q by -Q in the addition formula changes the angle from theta to 180 degree minus theta, and cos(180 - theta) = -cos theta. Hence the cross term changes sign while the squares of the magnitudes remain positive.
formula_principle: |P - Q| = sqrt(P^2 + Q^2 - 2 P Q cos theta)
common_misconception: Students also flip the sign of Q squared when reversing the second vector.

concept_tested: For perpendicular vectors the sum and difference have equal magnitudes
stem: Two vectors of magnitudes 3 units and 4 units are perpendicular to each other. The magnitude of their difference is
solution: With theta = 90 degree the cross term vanishes, so |P - Q| = sqrt(9 + 16) = 5 units. This equals the magnitude of the sum, which is the signature of perpendicular vectors.
formula_principle: |P - Q| = sqrt(P^2 + Q^2 - 2 P Q cos 90) = sqrt(P^2 + Q^2)
common_misconception: Students assume the difference of two vectors must always be smaller in magnitude than the sum.

concept_tested: Components subtract one by one
stem: Two vectors are P = 5 i + 3 j and Q = 2 i - j. The magnitude of P - Q is
solution: P - Q = (5 - 2) i + (3 - (-1)) j = 3 i + 4 j. Its magnitude is sqrt(9 + 16) = 5 units.
formula_principle: P - Q = (Px - Qx) i + (Py - Qy) j
common_misconception: Students mishandle the double negative and take the j component of the difference as 2 instead of 4.

concept_tested: Reversing the order of subtraction reverses the resulting vector
stem: For two vectors P and Q, the relation between P - Q and Q - P is that
option_a: they are equal in both magnitude and direction
option_b: they have equal magnitudes and opposite directions
option_c: they have equal directions but different magnitudes
option_d: they have different magnitudes and opposite directions
correct_answer_text: they have equal magnitudes and opposite directions
solution: Q - P = -(P - Q), so the two differences are negatives of each other. They therefore have the same magnitude but point in exactly opposite directions, which shows that subtraction of vectors is not commutative.
formula_principle: Q - P = -(P - Q)
common_misconception: Students carry over the commutative property of vector addition to vector subtraction.

concept_tested: For equal vectors |P - Q| = 2 P sin(theta / 2)
stem: Two vectors, each of magnitude 8 units, are inclined at 60 degree to each other. The magnitude of their difference is
solution: |P - Q| = 2 x 8 x sin 30 degree = 16 x 0.5 = 8 units. Directly, sqrt(64 + 64 - 2 x 64 x 0.5) = sqrt(128 - 64) = sqrt(64) = 8 units.
formula_principle: |P - Q| = 2 P sin(theta / 2) for equal magnitudes P
common_misconception: Students use the cosine half angle form, which belongs to the sum, when computing the difference.

concept_tested: Equality of the magnitudes of the sum and the difference means the vectors are perpendicular
stem: For two non zero vectors P and Q it is found that |P + Q| = |P - Q|. The angle between P and Q is
solution: Squaring both sides gives P^2 + Q^2 + 2 P Q cos theta = P^2 + Q^2 - 2 P Q cos theta, so 4 P Q cos theta = 0. Since neither magnitude is zero, cos theta = 0 and theta = 90 degree. Geometrically, the diagonals of a parallelogram are equal only when it is a rectangle.
formula_principle: |P + Q|^2 - |P - Q|^2 = 4 P Q cos theta
common_misconception: Students conclude that the two vectors must be equal in magnitude rather than perpendicular in direction.

subtopic: Angle from the magnitude of the difference
concept_tested: The half angle form gives the angle directly for equal vectors
stem: Two vectors have equal magnitudes P, and the magnitude of their difference is sqrt(3) P. The angle between them is
solution: 2 P sin(theta / 2) = sqrt(3) P gives sin(theta / 2) = sqrt(3) / 2, so theta / 2 = 60 degree and theta = 120 degree. Checking, sqrt(P^2 + P^2 - 2 P^2 cos 120) = sqrt(2 P^2 + P^2) = sqrt(3) P.
formula_principle: |P - Q| = 2 P sin(theta / 2)
common_misconception: Students solve sin theta = sqrt(3) / 2 and report 60 degree, forgetting the half angle.

concept_tested: Change in velocity is the vector difference of the final and initial velocities
stem: A particle is moving due east with a speed of 5 m s^-1. A little later it is moving due north with a speed of 5 m s^-1. The magnitude of the change in its velocity is
solution: Taking east as i and north as j, the initial velocity is 5 i and the final velocity is 5 j. The change is 5 j - 5 i, whose magnitude is sqrt(25 + 25) = 5 sqrt(2), about 7.07 m s^-1, directed to the north west.
formula_principle: Change in velocity = v final - v initial, evaluated by components
common_misconception: Students equate change of velocity with change of speed and answer zero.

concept_tested: Two simultaneous conditions fix both the angle and the ratio of magnitudes
stem: For two vectors P and Q it is given that |P + Q| = |P - Q| = 2 |P|. The ratio |Q| / |P| is
solution: Equality of the sum and difference magnitudes forces the two vectors to be perpendicular. Then |P + Q| = sqrt(P^2 + Q^2) = 2 P, so P^2 + Q^2 = 4 P^2 and Q^2 = 3 P^2. Hence |Q| / |P| = sqrt(3).
formula_principle: |P + Q| = |P - Q| implies perpendicularity, after which |P + Q| = sqrt(P^2 + Q^2)
common_misconception: Students use only one of the two conditions and cannot pin down the ratio of the magnitudes.

concept_tested: A vector in a plane splits into components along two perpendicular axes
stem: A vector of magnitude P makes an angle theta with the x axis. Its rectangular components along the x and y axes are
option_a: P cos theta and P sin theta
option_b: P sin theta and P cos theta
option_c: P tan theta and P cot theta
option_d: P cos theta and P cos theta
correct_answer_text: P cos theta and P sin theta
