solution: Dropping perpendiculars from the head of the vector onto the two axes gives a right triangle in which the side adjacent to theta is P cos theta along x and the side opposite is P sin theta along y.
formula_principle: Px = P cos theta, Py = P sin theta, with theta measured from the x axis
common_misconception: Students interchange sine and cosine when the angle is measured from the x axis.

concept_tested: Standard angles give exact component values
stem: A force of 10 N acts at 60 degree to the x axis. Its x and y components are
solution: Px = 10 cos 60 = 10 x 0.5 = 5 N and Py = 10 sin 60 = 10 x (sqrt(3) / 2) = 5 sqrt(3) N, about 8.66 N. A check gives sqrt(25 + 75) = 10 N.
formula_principle: Px = P cos theta, Py = P sin theta
common_misconception: Students use sin 60 for the x component because 60 degree feels like a steep angle.

concept_tested: The magnitude is the square root of the sum of the squares of the components
stem: The magnitude of the vector 6 i + 8 j is
formula_principle: |P| = sqrt(Px^2 + Py^2)
common_misconception: Students add components directly, forgetting that the components are perpendicular to each other.

concept_tested: The unit vectors i, j and k form a right handed mutually perpendicular set
stem: The unit vectors i, j and k used in Cartesian resolution are
option_a: mutually perpendicular vectors, each of magnitude one
option_b: mutually perpendicular vectors, each of magnitude equal to the length of the axis
option_c: mutually parallel vectors, each of magnitude one
option_d: mutually perpendicular vectors with magnitudes one, two and three respectively
correct_answer_text: mutually perpendicular vectors, each of magnitude one
solution: The Cartesian unit vectors point along the positive x, y and z axes. Each has magnitude one and each is perpendicular to the other two, which is what makes the components of a vector along them independent.
formula_principle: i . i = j . j = k . k = 1 and i . j = j . k = k . i = 0
common_misconception: Students think the magnitudes of i, j and k depend on the scale chosen for the axes.

concept_tested: A vector at 45 degree has equal rectangular components
stem: A vector in the xy plane has equal x and y components. The angle it makes with the x axis is
solution: Equal components give tan theta = Py / Px = 1, so theta = 45 degree. Each component then has magnitude P / sqrt(2).
formula_principle: tan theta = Py / Px
common_misconception: Students think equal components mean each component equals the magnitude of the vector.

concept_tested: The direction follows from the ratio of the components
stem: The vector 3 i + 3 j makes an angle with the positive x axis of
solution: tan theta = 3 / 3 = 1, so theta = 45 degree. The magnitude of the vector is 3 sqrt(2), about 4.24 units.
formula_principle: tan theta = Py / Px
common_misconception: Students take the angle from the numerical size of the components rather than from their ratio.

concept_tested: Knowing the magnitude and one component fixes the angle
stem: A force of magnitude 20 N has a component of 10 N along the x axis. The angle between the force and the x axis is
solution: 10 = 20 cos theta gives cos theta = 0.5, so theta = 60 degree. The y component is then 20 sin 60 = 10 sqrt(3), about 17.3 N.
formula_principle: Px = P cos theta
common_misconception: Students use the sine instead of the cosine when relating a component along the x axis to the angle from that axis.

concept_tested: The three dimensional magnitude uses all three components
stem: The magnitude of the vector 2 i + 3 j + 6 k is
formula_principle: |P| = sqrt(Px^2 + Py^2 + Pz^2)
common_misconception: Students apply the two dimensional formula and ignore the third component.

concept_tested: Direction cosines are the ratios of the components to the magnitude
stem: For the vector 2 i + 3 j + 6 k, the cosine of the angle it makes with the x axis is
solution: The magnitude is sqrt(4 + 9 + 36) = 7, so cos alpha = 2 / 7, which is about 0.286. A check gives (2/7)^2 + (3/7)^2 + (6/7)^2 = (4 + 9 + 36) / 49 = 1.
formula_principle: cos alpha = Px / |P|, cos beta = Py / |P|, cos gamma = Pz / |P|
common_misconception: Students divide a component by another component instead of by the magnitude of the vector.

concept_tested: The inverse tangent of the component ratio gives the direction
stem: A vector in the xy plane has an x component of 3 units and a y component of 4 units. The angle it makes with the x axis is closest to
solution: tan theta = 4 / 3 = 1.333, so theta is about 53 degree. The magnitude of the vector is sqrt(9 + 16) = 5 units, giving the standard 3, 4, 5 triangle.
formula_principle: tan theta = Py / Px
common_misconception: Students compute the angle from the x axis but form the ratio as Px over Py.

concept_tested: Rectangular components must satisfy the Pythagorean relation with the magnitude
stem: A vector of magnitude 13 units is resolved into two perpendicular components. If one component is 5 units, the other component is
solution: Py = sqrt(13^2 - 5^2) = sqrt(169 - 25) = sqrt(144) = 12 units. The three numbers form the 5, 12, 13 right triangle.
formula_principle: Px^2 + Py^2 = P^2 for two perpendicular components
common_misconception: Students subtract the given component from the magnitude, treating the components as if they acted along one line.

concept_tested: Weight resolves into components along and perpendicular to an incline
stem: A block of mass m rests on a smooth plane inclined at angle theta to the horizontal. The component of its weight along the inclined surface is
solution: The angle between the vertical weight and the normal to the inclined surface equals the angle of the incline. Resolving the weight along the two directions gives m g cos theta perpendicular to the surface and m g sin theta down the slope, which is the accelerating component.
formula_principle: Components of weight: m g sin theta along the incline and m g cos theta normal to it
common_misconception: Students interchange the sine and cosine and predict that a block accelerates fastest on a nearly horizontal surface.

concept_tested: Standard 3, 4, 5 angles give tidy components
stem: A velocity of 5 m s^-1 is directed at 37 degree above the x axis. Taking sin 37 degree as 0.6 and cos 37 degree as 0.8, its components along x and y are
solution: vx = 5 x 0.8 = 4 m s^-1 and vy = 5 x 0.6 = 3 m s^-1. A check gives sqrt(16 + 9) = 5 m s^-1.
formula_principle: vx = v cos theta, vy = v sin theta
common_misconception: Students recall the numbers 3 and 4 but attach them to the wrong axes.

subtopic: Vector equally inclined to the axes
concept_tested: The direction cosines of a vector satisfy cos^2 alpha + cos^2 beta + cos^2 gamma = 1
stem: A vector makes equal angles with all three coordinate axes. The cosine of each of these angles is
solution: With all three angles equal, 3 cos^2 alpha = 1, so cos^2 alpha = 1 / 3 and cos alpha = 1 / sqrt(3), about 0.577. The angle is then about 54.7 degree, and the vector lies along i + j + k.
formula_principle: cos^2 alpha + cos^2 beta + cos^2 gamma = 1
common_misconception: Students set the sum of the direction cosines rather than the sum of their squares equal to one.

concept_tested: Two direction angles fix the third through the direction cosine identity
stem: A vector makes an angle of 45 degree with the x axis and 60 degree with the y axis. The angle it makes with the z axis is
solution: cos^2 45 + cos^2 60 + cos^2 gamma = 1 gives 0.5 + 0.25 + cos^2 gamma = 1, so cos^2 gamma = 0.25 and cos gamma = 0.5. Hence gamma = 60 degree.
formula_principle: cos^2 alpha + cos^2 beta + cos^2 gamma = 1
common_misconception: Students assume the three direction angles must add up to 180 degree.

concept_tested: Interchanging components and flipping one sign gives a perpendicular vector
stem: A unit vector in the xy plane perpendicular to the vector 4 i - 3 j is
solution: Testing the scalar product, (4 i - 3 j) . (3 i + 4 j) = 12 - 12 = 0, so the two vectors are perpendicular. The magnitude of 3 i + 4 j is 5, so dividing by 5 gives the required unit vector 0.6 i + 0.8 j.
formula_principle: Two vectors are perpendicular when their scalar product is zero
common_misconception: Students interchange the components but forget that exactly one sign must be reversed.

concept_tested: The launch velocity resolves into a horizontal and a vertical component
stem: A ball is thrown with a speed of 20 m s^-1 at 60 degree to the horizontal. The ratio of the horizontal component to the vertical component of its initial velocity is
solution: vx = 20 cos 60 = 10 m s^-1 and vy = 20 sin 60 = 10 sqrt(3), about 17.3 m s^-1. The ratio is 10 to 10 sqrt(3), that is 1 to sqrt(3), which equals cot 60 degree.
formula_principle: vx = v cos theta, vy = v sin theta, so vx / vy = cot theta
common_misconception: Students take the ratio as tan theta rather than cot theta when the angle is measured from the horizontal.

subtopic: Component of one vector along another
concept_tested: The component of one vector along another can be negative
stem: Two forces, each of magnitude 10 N, act at a point with an angle of 120 degree between them. The component of one force along the direction of the other is
solution: The component is 10 cos 120 = 10 x (-0.5) = -5 N. The negative sign shows that this force has a projection pointing opposite to the second force, which is why an obtuse angle reduces the resultant.
formula_principle: Component of P along Q = P cos theta
common_misconception: Students take the magnitude of the projection and lose the sign that shows the two forces partly oppose each other.

concept_tested: A stated ratio of components together with the magnitude fixes both components
stem: A vector of magnitude 5 sqrt(5) units lies in the xy plane, and its y component is twice its x component. Both components are positive. The components are
solution: Let Px = a, so Py = 2 a. Then a^2 + 4 a^2 = (5 sqrt(5))^2 = 125, giving 5 a^2 = 125 and a^2 = 25, so a = 5. Hence Px = 5 units and Py = 10 units. The vector makes an angle whose tangent is 2, about 63.4 degree, with the x axis.
formula_principle: Px^2 + Py^2 = P^2 with Py = 2 Px
common_misconception: Students split the magnitude in the ratio 1 to 2 directly, obtaining components that do not satisfy the Pythagorean relation.

subtopic: Rotation of a vector in a plane
concept_tested: Rotating a vector through 90 degree exchanges its components with one sign change
stem: The vector 3 i + 4 j is rotated through 90 degree in the anticlockwise sense within the xy plane, without changing its length. The rotated vector is
solution: The original vector has magnitude 5 and makes an angle of about 53 degree with the x axis. After an anticlockwise turn of 90 degree it makes about 143 degree, so it lies in the second quadrant with a negative x component and a positive y component. The rule (x, y) to (-y, x) gives -4 i + 3 j, whose magnitude is again sqrt(16 + 9) = 5 and whose scalar product with the original vector is -12 + 12 = 0.
formula_principle: Anticlockwise rotation by 90 degree sends (x, y) to (-y, x); the magnitude is unchanged
common_misconception: Students interchange the components but attach the minus sign to the wrong one, producing a clockwise rotation.

concept_tested: The scalar product of two vectors is the product of their magnitudes and the cosine of the angle between them
stem: The scalar product of two vectors of magnitudes P and Q with an angle theta between them is
option_c: P Q cos theta directed along P
solution: The scalar product multiplies the magnitude of one vector by the projection of the other on it, that is Q cos theta. The outcome is a scalar with no direction associated with it.
formula_principle: P . Q = P Q cos theta
common_misconception: Students attach a direction to the scalar product because both factors are vectors.

concept_tested: The Cartesian unit vectors are orthonormal
stem: For the Cartesian unit vectors, the values of i . i and i . j are respectively
solution: i . i = 1 x 1 x cos 0 = 1, while i . j = 1 x 1 x cos 90 = 0. These relations are what let the scalar product of two vectors be written as the sum of the products of like components.
formula_principle: i . i = j . j = k . k = 1 and i . j = j . k = k . i = 0
common_misconception: Students confuse these results with the corresponding vector product relations, where i x i = 0.

concept_tested: Work done is the scalar product of force and displacement
stem: The work done by a constant force F in producing a displacement d is given by
solution: Only the component of the force along the displacement does work, and that component is F cos theta. Multiplying it by the displacement d gives W = F d cos theta, which is exactly the scalar product.
formula_principle: W = F . d = F d cos theta
common_misconception: Students use the vector product for work because torque, which also involves a force, uses the vector product.

concept_tested: The scalar product vanishes for perpendicular vectors
stem: The scalar product of two non zero perpendicular vectors is
option_a: equal to the product of their magnitudes
option_b: equal to the magnitude of their vector product
option_c: zero, whatever their magnitudes may be
option_d: the negative of the product of their magnitudes
correct_answer_text: zero, whatever their magnitudes may be
solution: Since cos 90 degree is zero, the scalar product of perpendicular vectors vanishes. This is the standard test for perpendicularity, and it is why a force at right angles to the displacement does no work.
formula_principle: P . Q = P Q cos 90 = 0
common_misconception: Students think a zero scalar product means one of the vectors must itself be zero.

concept_tested: Like components multiply and the products are summed
stem: The scalar product of the vectors 3 i + 4 j and 4 i + 3 j is
solution: P . Q = (3)(4) + (4)(3) = 12 + 12 = 24. Since both magnitudes are 5, cos theta = 24 / 25 = 0.96, so the angle between them is about 16 degree.
formula_principle: P . Q = Px Qx + Py Qy + Pz Qz
common_misconception: Students multiply unlike components, pairing the i term of one vector with the j term of the other.

concept_tested: Work follows from the component form of the scalar product
stem: A force F = 5 i + 3 j newton acts on a body that undergoes a displacement d = 2 i - j metre. The work done by the force is
formula_principle: W = F . d = Fx dx + Fy dy
common_misconception: Students drop the negative sign of a component and so overestimate the work done.

concept_tested: The scalar product is commutative and distributive over addition
stem: Which relation is correct for the scalar product of vectors?
option_d: P . Q is a vector along the direction of P
solution: The definition P Q cos theta is symmetric in the two magnitudes and the angle between the vectors is the same whichever is named first, so the scalar product is commutative. It is also distributive over vector addition.
formula_principle: P . Q = Q . P and P . (Q + S) = P . Q + P . S
common_misconception: Students transfer the anticommutative property of the vector product to the scalar product.

subtopic: Scalar product of a vector with itself
concept_tested: A vector dotted with itself gives the square of its magnitude
stem: For a vector P of magnitude 6 units, the value of P . P is
solution: The angle between a vector and itself is zero and cos 0 = 1, so P . P = 6 x 6 x 1 = 36. This relation is used constantly, for example in expanding |P + Q|^2.
formula_principle: P . P = P^2 cos 0 = P^2
common_misconception: Students confuse P . P with P x P, which is the null vector.

concept_tested: A vanishing scalar product identifies perpendicular vectors
stem: The angle between the vectors 2 i + 3 j and 3 i - 2 j is
solution: P . Q = (2)(3) + (3)(-2) = 6 - 6 = 0. Since both magnitudes are sqrt(13) and non zero, cos theta = 0 and theta = 90 degree.
formula_principle: cos theta = (P . Q) / (P Q)
common_misconception: Students conclude from a zero scalar product that one of the vectors must be a null vector.

subtopic: Projection of one vector on another
concept_tested: The projection is the scalar product divided by the magnitude of the second vector
stem: The projection of the vector 3 i + 4 j on the vector 4 i + 3 j is
solution: P . Q = 12 + 12 = 24 and |Q| = sqrt(16 + 9) = 5, so the projection is 24 / 5 = 4.8 units. It is slightly less than 5, as it must be, since the two vectors are not quite parallel.
formula_principle: Projection of P on Q = (P . Q) / |Q|
common_misconception: Students divide by the product of both magnitudes and report the cosine of the angle as the projection.

subtopic: Scalar product from magnitudes and angle
concept_tested: Direct use of the defining formula
stem: Two vectors of magnitudes 4 units and 5 units are inclined at 60 degree to each other. Their scalar product is
formula_principle: P . Q = P Q cos theta
common_misconception: Students substitute sin theta for cos theta, mixing up the two kinds of vector multiplication.

subtopic: Expansion of the square of a sum
concept_tested: Expanding |P + Q|^2 introduces the scalar product as the cross term
stem: For two non zero vectors it is found that |P + Q|^2 = |P|^2 + |Q|^2. It follows that
option_a: P and Q are parallel to each other
option_b: P and Q have equal magnitudes
option_c: P and Q are antiparallel to each other
option_d: P and Q are perpendicular to each other
correct_answer_text: P and Q are perpendicular to each other
solution: Expanding the left side gives P^2 + Q^2 + 2 P . Q. Comparing with the given relation forces P . Q = 0. Since neither vector is null, the angle between them must be 90 degree.
common_misconception: Students read the Pythagorean form as a statement about magnitudes being equal rather than about the angle.

concept_tested: The angle follows from cos theta = (P . Q) / (P Q)
stem: The angle between the vectors i + j and j + k is
solution: The scalar product is (1)(0) + (1)(1) + (0)(1) = 1. Each magnitude is sqrt(2), so cos theta = 1 / (sqrt(2) x sqrt(2)) = 1 / 2 and theta = 60 degree.
formula_principle: cos theta = (P . Q) / (|P| |Q|)
common_misconception: Students forget the j component is shared by both vectors and take the scalar product as zero.

concept_tested: Equality of the two products gives tan theta = 1
stem: For two non zero vectors the magnitude of their vector product equals their scalar product. The angle between them is
solution: Setting P Q sin theta = P Q cos theta and cancelling the non zero magnitudes gives tan theta = 1, so theta = 45 degree. At this angle both products equal P Q / sqrt(2).
formula_principle: P Q sin theta = P Q cos theta gives tan theta = 1
common_misconception: Students equate the vector product with the scalar product but then solve sin theta = cos theta as sin theta = 1.

concept_tested: Perpendicularity supplies one equation for the unknown component
stem: The vectors i + x j + 2 k and 2 i - j + k are perpendicular to each other. The value of x is
solution: The scalar product is (1)(2) + (x)(-1) + (2)(1) = 2 - x + 2 = 4 - x. Setting this equal to zero gives x = 4.
formula_principle: P . Q = 0 for perpendicular vectors
common_misconception: Students omit the contribution of the k components when writing the perpendicularity condition.

concept_tested: Only the component of the force along the displacement does work
stem: A constant force of 10 N acts at 60 degree to the direction of motion of a body while the body moves 5 m. The work done by this force is
solution: W = 10 x 5 x cos 60 = 50 x 0.5 = 25 J. The effective force along the motion is 10 cos 60 = 5 N, and 5 N over 5 m gives 25 J.
formula_principle: W = F d cos theta
common_misconception: Students multiply force and displacement magnitudes without projecting the force on the displacement.

subtopic: Deducing the angle from three magnitudes
concept_tested: Knowing the magnitudes of two vectors and of their sum determines their scalar product
stem: Two vectors have magnitudes 3 units and 4 units, and the magnitude of their sum is 5 units. Their scalar product is
solution: 25 = 9 + 16 + 2 (P . Q), so 25 = 25 + 2 (P . Q) and P . Q = 0. The two vectors are therefore perpendicular, which is consistent with the 3, 4, 5 right triangle.
common_misconception: Students assume the vectors are parallel because 3, 4 and 5 look like a simple arithmetic pattern.

concept_tested: Squaring a vector equation converts it into a scalar relation
stem: Three vectors P, Q and S of magnitudes 3, 4 and 5 units satisfy P + Q + S = 0. The value of P . Q + Q . S + S . P is
solution: Taking the scalar product of the equation with itself gives 0 = 9 + 16 + 25 + 2 (P . Q + Q . S + S . P), so 0 = 50 + 2 X where X is the required sum. Hence X = -25.
common_misconception: Students try to find each scalar product separately instead of squaring the whole vector equation at once.

concept_tested: The magnitude of the vector product is the product of the magnitudes and the sine of the angle
stem: The magnitude of the vector product of two vectors of magnitudes P and Q with an angle theta between them is
option_d: P Q sin theta measured along the larger vector
solution: The vector product has magnitude P Q sin theta and points along the normal to the plane containing the two vectors, with the sense fixed by the right hand rule. Its magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram formed by the two vectors.
formula_principle: |P x Q| = P Q sin theta, directed normal to the plane of P and Q
common_misconception: Students use the cosine of the angle, confusing the vector product with the scalar product.

concept_tested: The unit vectors follow a right handed cyclic rule
stem: For the Cartesian unit vectors, the value of j x k is
solution: The three relations i x j = k, j x k = i and k x i = j follow the cyclic order i, j, k, i. So j x k = i, a unit vector along the positive x axis.
formula_principle: i x j = k, j x k = i, k x i = j; reversing the order changes the sign
common_misconception: Students break the cyclic order and write j x k as k or as -i.

subtopic: Vector product of a vector with itself
concept_tested: The vector product of parallel vectors vanishes
stem: For any vector P, the vector product P x P is
option_a: a vector of magnitude P^2 perpendicular to P
solution: The angle between a vector and itself is zero, and sin 0 = 0, so the magnitude of the product is zero. The result is therefore the null vector. The same holds for any two parallel vectors.
formula_principle: P x P = P P sin 0 = 0
common_misconception: Students carry over the result P . P = P^2 to the vector product and answer P^2.

concept_tested: Torque is the vector product of position vector and force
stem: The torque of a force F acting at a point whose position vector relative to the axis is r is given by
solution: Torque is defined as r x F. Its magnitude r F sin theta is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance of its line of action from the axis, and its direction along the axis fixes the sense of rotation by the right hand rule.
formula_principle: torque = r x F, with magnitude r F sin theta
common_misconception: Students write the factors in the reverse order and obtain a torque of the wrong sense.

concept_tested: The right hand rule fixes the direction of the vector product
stem: The direction of the vector product of two non parallel vectors is
option_a: along the bisector of the angle between the two vectors
option_b: along the vector of larger magnitude
option_c: in the plane of the two vectors and perpendicular to the first one
option_d: perpendicular to the plane containing both vectors
correct_answer_text: perpendicular to the plane containing both vectors
solution: The vector product is normal to the plane of the two vectors. Curling the fingers of the right hand from the first vector towards the second makes the extended thumb point along the product. Reversing the order reverses this direction.
formula_principle: Right hand rule for P x Q
common_misconception: Students place the product inside the plane of the two vectors, along the bisector of the angle.

concept_tested: Interchanging the order of the vector product reverses the result
stem: For two vectors P and Q, the vector product satisfies
option_a: P x Q = Q x P
solution: The magnitude P Q sin theta is unchanged when the order is reversed, but the right hand rule then points the thumb the other way. The two products are therefore equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
formula_principle: P x Q = -(Q x P); the vector product is anticommutative
common_misconception: Students assume both kinds of vector multiplication are commutative.

concept_tested: Products of vectors along the axes follow from the unit vector rules
stem: The vector product of 3 i and 4 j is
solution: (3 i) x (4 j) = 12 (i x j) = 12 k. The magnitude is 3 x 4 x sin 90 = 12, and the direction is along the positive z axis.
formula_principle: (a i) x (b j) = a b (i x j) = a b k
common_misconception: Students apply the cyclic rule in the wrong sense and attach a minus sign to the answer.

concept_tested: Direct use of the defining formula for the vector product
stem: Two vectors of magnitudes 4 units and 5 units are inclined at 30 degree. The magnitude of their vector product is
solution: |P x Q| = 4 x 5 x sin 30 = 20 x 0.5 = 10 units.
formula_principle: |P x Q| = P Q sin theta
common_misconception: Students use cos 30 in place of sin 30 while evaluating a vector product.

concept_tested: The magnitude of the vector product is the area of the parallelogram on the two vectors
stem: Two adjacent sides of a parallelogram are represented by the vectors 3 i and 4 j. The area of the parallelogram is
solution: |3 i x 4 j| = 12, so the area is 12 square units. Since the sides are perpendicular the figure is a rectangle of sides 3 and 4, which confirms the result.
formula_principle: Area of parallelogram = |P x Q|; area of triangle = |P x Q| / 2
common_misconception: Students use the triangle formula with the one half factor when the question asks for a parallelogram.

subtopic: Angular momentum as a vector product
concept_tested: Angular momentum is the vector product of position vector and linear momentum
stem: The angular momentum of a particle of linear momentum p at a position r relative to the origin is given by
solution: Angular momentum is defined as L = r x p. Its magnitude r p sin theta equals the momentum multiplied by the perpendicular distance of its line from the origin, and it vanishes for a particle moving directly towards or away from the origin.
formula_principle: L = r x p, with magnitude r p sin theta
common_misconception: Students write the factors in the order p x r, reversing the direction of the angular momentum.

concept_tested: The vector product vanishes when the vectors are collinear
stem: The vector product of two non zero collinear vectors is
option_a: the null vector, of zero magnitude
option_b: a vector whose magnitude is the product of theirs
option_c: a vector directed along either of the two
option_d: a scalar equal to the product of their magnitudes
correct_answer_text: the null vector, of zero magnitude
solution: Collinear vectors are at 0 degree or 180 degree, and the sine of both angles is zero. The product therefore has zero magnitude and is the null vector. This is the standard test for two vectors being parallel.
formula_principle: |P x Q| = P Q sin theta, with sin 0 = sin 180 = 0
common_misconception: Students expect a non zero answer whenever both vectors are non zero.

concept_tested: The two dimensional vector product reduces to a single k component
stem: The vector product (2 i + 3 j) x (i + 2 j) is
solution: P x Q = (2 x 2 - 3 x 1) k = (4 - 3) k = k. The magnitude is 1, which is also the area of the parallelogram formed by the two vectors.
formula_principle: For plane vectors, P x Q = (Px Qy - Py Qx) k
common_misconception: Students forget that j x i equals -k and so add the two contributions instead of subtracting.

concept_tested: Torque follows from the determinant form of r x F
stem: A force F = 3 i + 2 j newton acts at the point whose position vector is r = 2 i + 3 j metre. The magnitude of the torque about the origin is
solution: torque = (2 x 2 - 3 x 3) k = (4 - 9) k = -5 k N m. Its magnitude is 5 N m and it is directed along the negative z axis, so the rotation is clockwise as seen from the positive z axis.
formula_principle: torque = r x F = (x Fy - y Fx) k for vectors in the xy plane
common_misconception: Students compute x Fx - y Fy, mixing the scalar and vector product patterns.

concept_tested: The ratio of the vector and scalar products gives the tangent of the angle
stem: For two non zero vectors, the magnitude of their vector product is sqrt(3) times their scalar product. The angle between the vectors is
solution: P Q sin theta = sqrt(3) P Q cos theta gives tan theta = sqrt(3), so theta = 60 degree.
formula_principle: |P x Q| / (P . Q) = tan theta
common_misconception: Students set sin theta equal to sqrt(3) and find no valid angle, since the sine cannot exceed one.

concept_tested: Proportional components signal parallel vectors and a vanishing product
stem: The vector product of i + 2 j + 3 k and 2 i + 4 j + 6 k is
solution: The second vector is exactly twice the first, so the two are parallel and the angle between them is zero. Since sin 0 = 0, the vector product is the null vector. Expanding the determinant gives the same result, as each of the three minors is 2 x 6 - 3 x 4 = 0 in turn.
formula_principle: P x Q = 0 when P and Q are parallel
common_misconception: Students expand the determinant mechanically without noticing that the two vectors are proportional.

concept_tested: Half the magnitude of the vector product gives the area of the triangle
stem: Two sides of a triangle are represented by the vectors 3 i + 4 j and 4 i + 3 j. The area of the triangle is
solution: P x Q = (3 x 3 - 4 x 4) k = (9 - 16) k = -7 k, whose magnitude is 7. Half of this is 3.5 square units.
formula_principle: Area of triangle = |P x Q| / 2
common_misconception: Students omit the factor of one half and quote the parallelogram area for a triangle.

concept_tested: The two products cannot both vanish for two non zero vectors
stem: For two vectors P and Q it is found that both P . Q = 0 and P x Q = 0. It follows that
option_a: the two vectors are perpendicular to each other
option_b: the two vectors are parallel to each other
option_c: at least one of the two vectors must be a null vector
option_d: the two vectors are equal in magnitude
correct_answer_text: at least one of the two vectors must be a null vector
solution: If both magnitudes were non zero, the first condition would need cos theta = 0 and the second would need sin theta = 0. No angle satisfies both, since the squares of the sine and the cosine add to one. Hence at least one of the magnitudes must be zero.
formula_principle: P . Q = P Q cos theta and |P x Q| = P Q sin theta
common_misconception: Students pick perpendicular or parallel from habit without noticing that the two conditions clash.

subtopic: Unit vector normal to two vectors
concept_tested: Normalising the vector product gives a unit normal to both vectors
stem: A unit vector perpendicular to both i + j and j + k is
solution: With P = (1, 1, 0) and Q = (0, 1, 1), the components of P x Q are (1 x 1 - 0 x 1), (0 x 0 - 1 x 1) and (1 x 1 - 1 x 0), that is 1, -1 and 1. Its magnitude is sqrt(3), so the unit normal is (i - j + k) / sqrt(3). A check gives a scalar product of 1 - 1 + 0 = 0 with the first vector and 0 - 1 + 1 = 0 with the second.
formula_principle: Unit normal = (P x Q) / |P x Q|
common_misconception: Students expand the determinant without changing the sign of the middle term.

subtopic: Derivative as a rate of change
concept_tested: The derivative of position with respect to time is the instantaneous velocity
stem: For a particle moving along a straight line with position x at time t, the quantity dx / dt represents
option_a: the average velocity of the particle over the whole motion
option_b: the instantaneous acceleration of the particle
option_c: the total distance travelled by the particle
option_d: the instantaneous velocity of the particle
correct_answer_text: the instantaneous velocity of the particle
solution: The derivative dx / dt is the limit of the ratio of a small change in position to the small time interval in which it occurs, which is the velocity at that instant.
formula_principle: v = dx / dt and a = dv / dt
common_misconception: Students treat the derivative as an average rather than as an instantaneous rate.

subtopic: Differentiation of a power of t
concept_tested: The power rule for differentiation
stem: The derivative of 5 t^2 with respect to t is
solution: Applying the power rule, d(5 t^2) / dt = 5 x 2 x t^(2-1) = 10 t.
formula_principle: d(t^n) / dt = n t^(n-1)
common_misconception: Students integrate when the question asks them to differentiate.

concept_tested: Differentiating the position function and substituting the time gives the instantaneous velocity
stem: The position of a particle is given by x = 5 t^2 + 3 t, where x is in metre and t in second. Its velocity at t = 2 s is
formula_principle: v = dx / dt
common_misconception: Students divide the position by the time and report an average velocity as the instantaneous velocity.

concept_tested: Acceleration is the derivative of velocity with respect to time
stem: The velocity of a particle is v = 3 t^2 + 2 t metre per second. Its acceleration at t = 1 s is
formula_principle: a = dv / dt
common_misconception: Students substitute the time into the velocity expression rather than into its derivative.

subtopic: Integration as area under a graph
concept_tested: The area under a velocity time graph gives the displacement
stem: For a particle moving in a straight line, the area under its velocity time graph between two instants represents
option_c: the average velocity during that interval
option_d: the change in acceleration during that interval
solution: Since v = dx / dt, the displacement is the integral of v with respect to t, and that integral is exactly the area enclosed between the velocity curve and the time axis. Areas below the axis count as negative displacements.
formula_principle: Displacement = integral of v dt
common_misconception: Students associate the area under the graph with acceleration, confusing area with slope.

concept_tested: Integrating a constant acceleration gives velocity linear in time
stem: A particle starts with velocity u and moves with constant acceleration a. Integrating a with respect to time gives its velocity at time t as
solution: Integrating the constant a with respect to t gives a t plus a constant. Setting t = 0 makes the velocity equal to u, so the constant is u and v = u + a t.
formula_principle: v = integral of a dt = a t + constant, with the constant fixed by v = u at t = 0
common_misconception: Students omit the constant of integration and lose the initial velocity term.

concept_tested: Setting the derivative to zero locates the instants of momentary rest
stem: The position of a particle is x = t^3 - 6 t^2 + 9 t metre, with t in second. The particle is momentarily at rest at
solution: v = dx / dt = 3 t^2 - 12 t + 9 = 3 (t^2 - 4 t + 3) = 3 (t - 1)(t - 3). This vanishes at t = 1 s and t = 3 s, so the particle is momentarily at rest at those two instants.
formula_principle: The particle is at rest where v = dx / dt = 0
common_misconception: Students set the position equal to zero and report the instants when the particle passes the origin.

concept_tested: Definite integration of velocity over an interval gives the displacement
stem: A particle moves with velocity v = 6 t^2 metre per second, starting from the origin at t = 0. Its displacement during the first 2 s is
solution: The integral of 6 t^2 with respect to t is 2 t^3. Evaluating between t = 0 and t = 2 s gives 2 x 8 - 0 = 16 m.
formula_principle: Displacement = integral of v dt from t1 to t2
common_misconception: Students multiply the final velocity by the total time, which assumes the velocity was constant.

subtopic: Distance up to the instant of rest
concept_tested: Integrating the velocity up to the instant it vanishes gives the distance covered
stem: A particle moves with velocity v = 10 - 2 t metre per second along a straight line. The distance it covers before coming momentarily to rest is
solution: The particle stops when 10 - 2 t = 0, that is at t = 5 s. The integral of 10 - 2 t is 10 t - t^2, and between t = 0 and t = 5 s this gives 50 - 25 = 25 m.
formula_principle: v = 0 fixes the time; distance = integral of v dt over that interval
common_misconception: Students multiply the initial velocity by the stopping time and forget that the velocity falls steadily to zero.

subtopic: Velocity from a time dependent acceleration
concept_tested: A non constant acceleration must be integrated, not simply multiplied by time
stem: A particle starts from rest and its acceleration varies as a = 6 t metre per second squared. Its velocity at t = 2 s is
solution: Integrating a = 6 t gives v = 3 t^2 plus a constant, and starting from rest makes the constant zero. At t = 2 s, v = 3 x 4 = 12 m s^-1.
formula_principle: v = integral of a dt, with v = 0 at t = 0
common_misconception: Students use v = u + a t even though the acceleration is not constant.

concept_tested: The time is found from the position function before the derivative is evaluated
stem: A particle moves so that its position is x = 4 t^2 metre, with t in second. Its speed at the instant when it has travelled 16 m from the start is
solution: Setting 4 t^2 = 16 gives t^2 = 4, so t = 2 s. The velocity is v = dx / dt = 8 t, and at t = 2 s this equals 16 m s^-1. The average speed over the same interval is only 16 / 2 = 8 m s^-1, since the motion is accelerated.
formula_principle: v = dx / dt, with t obtained from the given displacement
common_misconception: Students substitute the displacement in place of the time in the velocity expression.

subtopic: Maximum velocity from a varying acceleration
concept_tested: The velocity is largest at the instant when the acceleration falls to zero
stem: A particle starts from rest and its acceleration varies with time as a = 4 - 2 t metre per second squared. The maximum velocity it attains is
solution: Integrating from rest gives v = 4 t - t^2. The velocity is largest where its derivative, the acceleration, vanishes, that is where 4 - 2 t = 0, so t = 2 s. Substituting gives v = 8 - 4 = 4 m s^-1.
formula_principle: v = integral of a dt; v is maximum where dv / dt = a = 0
common_misconception: Students believe the velocity keeps rising as long as the particle is moving, and evaluate it at the end of the given interval.

concept_tested: Magnitude of a position vector in two dimensions
stem: The position vector of a particle in the x y plane is r = 3 i + 4 j metre. The distance of the particle from the origin is
solution: The magnitude of r = 3 i + 4 j is sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5 m.
formula_principle: |r| = sqrt(x^2 + y^2)
common_misconception: Students add or subtract vector components directly instead of combining them through the square root of the sum of squares.

concept_tested: Distance and displacement for one complete circular lap
stem: A cyclist completes exactly one full lap of a circular track of radius R and stops at the starting point. The path length covered and the magnitude of the displacement are respectively
solution: One lap means the final position coincides with the initial position, so the change in position vector is zero and the displacement magnitude is zero. The length of path actually traversed is the circumference, 2 pi R.
formula_principle: Path length is the actual length travelled; displacement is the change in position vector
common_misconception: Students assume displacement can never be zero if the body has actually moved.

concept_tested: Direction of instantaneous velocity on a curved path
stem: A particle moves along a curved path in a plane. At any instant the direction of its instantaneous velocity is
option_a: along the normal to the path at that point
option_b: along the chord joining the initial and final positions
option_c: along the position vector drawn from the origin
option_d: along the tangent to the path at that point
correct_answer_text: along the tangent to the path at that point
solution: Instantaneous velocity is the limit of the ratio of a small displacement to a small time interval. As the interval shrinks the chord joining the two positions turns into the tangent, so the instantaneous velocity always points along the tangent to the path.
formula_principle: v = dr/dt, the limit of a chord as the interval tends to zero
common_misconception: Students confuse the direction of the average velocity over a finite interval with the direction of the instantaneous velocity.

concept_tested: Speed from a position vector linear in time
stem: The position of a particle varies with time as r = (5 t) i + (12 t) j metre, where t is in second. The speed of the particle is
solution: Differentiating gives v = 5 i + 12 j m s^-1, which is constant. Its magnitude is sqrt(5^2 + 12^2) = sqrt(25 + 144) = sqrt(169) = 13 m s^-1.
formula_principle: v = dr/dt and |v| = sqrt(vx^2 + vy^2)
common_misconception: Students add perpendicular components arithmetically instead of using the Pythagorean sum.

concept_tested: General relation between path length and displacement magnitude
stem: For any motion of a particle between two given instants, the correct relation between the path length s and the magnitude of the displacement d is
option_a: d is always exactly equal to s for every kind of motion
option_b: d is always greater than s whenever the path is curved
option_c: d is less than or equal to s, with equality only for motion along a straight line in one direction
option_d: d is greater than s when the particle reverses its direction of motion
correct_answer_text: d is less than or equal to s, with equality only for motion along a straight line in one direction
solution: The displacement is the straight line vector joining the initial and final positions, and the straight line is the shortest route between them. Hence the magnitude of the displacement can never exceed the length of the actual path, and the two are equal only when the particle moves along a straight line without reversing.
formula_principle: The straight line is the shortest route between two points
common_misconception: Students believe distance and displacement magnitude are always numerically the same.

concept_tested: Average velocity between two position vectors
stem: A particle moves from the point (2 m, 3 m) to the point (6 m, 6 m) in 5 s. The magnitude of its average velocity is
solution: The displacement is (6 - 2) i + (6 - 3) j = 4 i + 3 j m, whose magnitude is sqrt(16 + 9) = 5 m. Dividing by 5 s gives an average velocity of magnitude 1 m s^-1.
formula_principle: v_average = (r2 - r1) / t
common_misconception: Students add displacement components arithmetically rather than using the resultant.

concept_tested: Differentiating a quadratic position vector
stem: The position of a particle is r = (3 t^2) i + (4 t^2) j metre with t in second. Its speed at t = 1 s is
solution: Differentiating gives v = (6 t) i + (8 t) j m s^-1. At t = 1 s this is 6 i + 8 j m s^-1, whose magnitude is sqrt(36 + 64) = 10 m s^-1.
formula_principle: v = dr/dt, |v| = sqrt(vx^2 + vy^2)
common_misconception: Students substitute the time into the position expression and report a distance where a speed is asked for.

concept_tested: Average acceleration when only the direction of velocity changes
stem: A car moving due east at 20 m s^-1 turns and, 5 s later, is moving due north at 20 m s^-1. The magnitude of its average acceleration during this interval is
solution: Taking east as i and north as j, v1 = 20 i and v2 = 20 j m s^-1. The change in velocity is v2 - v1 = -20 i + 20 j m s^-1, of magnitude 20 sqrt 2 m s^-1. Dividing by 5 s gives 4 sqrt 2 m s^-2, about 5.7 m s^-2, directed towards the north west.
formula_principle: a_average = (v2 - v1) / t
common_misconception: Students treat velocity as a scalar and conclude that equal speeds imply zero acceleration.

concept_tested: Acceleration of a particle moving at constant speed along a curve
stem: A particle moves along a curved path in a plane with constant speed. Which statement about its acceleration is correct
option_a: The acceleration is non zero and points towards the concave side of the path
option_b: The acceleration is zero because the speed does not change
option_c: The acceleration is non zero and points along the direction of motion
option_d: The acceleration is non zero and points opposite to the direction of motion
correct_answer_text: The acceleration is non zero and points towards the concave side of the path
solution: Acceleration is the rate of change of the velocity vector. With constant speed the tangential part vanishes, but the direction of the velocity keeps turning, so a normal component survives. That normal component always points towards the centre of curvature, that is towards the concave side of the path.
formula_principle: Acceleration has a tangential part that changes speed and a normal part that changes direction
common_misconception: Students equate constant speed with zero acceleration, forgetting that velocity is a vector.

concept_tested: Ratio of average speed to average velocity for a semicircular path
stem: A particle travels along a semicircular arc of radius R from one end of a diameter to the other. The ratio of its average speed to the magnitude of its average velocity for this trip is
solution: For the same time interval t the path length is pi R and the displacement magnitude is the diameter 2 R. The ratio of average speed to the magnitude of average velocity is therefore (pi R / t) divided by (2 R / t), which is pi / 2, about 1.57.
formula_principle: Average speed = path length / time; average velocity = displacement / time
common_misconception: Students invert the ratio, or use the full circumference for a semicircular arc.

concept_tested: Distance and displacement for a three leg journey
stem: A boy walks 3 m due east, then 4 m due north, and finally 3 m due west. For the whole journey the magnitude of his displacement and the distance he walked are
solution: Taking east as i and north as j, the legs are 3 i, 4 j and -3 i metre. Their vector sum is 4 j metre, so the displacement is 4 m due north. The distance walked is 3 + 4 + 3 = 10 m.
formula_principle: Displacement is the vector sum of the legs; distance is the sum of their lengths
common_misconception: Students add the leg lengths to obtain displacement, ignoring that opposite legs cancel.

concept_tested: Instant at which a velocity vector becomes parallel to an axis
stem: The velocity of a particle in a plane is v = (4 - 2 t) i + 3 j m s^-1 with t in second. The velocity is directed along the y axis at
solution: The velocity points along the y axis when its x component vanishes, that is when 4 - 2 t = 0, giving t = 2 s. At that instant v = 3 j m s^-1.
formula_principle: A vector points along the y axis when its x component is zero
common_misconception: Students set the two components equal instead of setting the unwanted component to zero.

concept_tested: Speed at an intermediate instant under constant acceleration
stem: A particle moving in a plane with constant acceleration has velocity 3 i + 4 j m s^-1 at t = 0 and 3 i - 4 j m s^-1 at t = 4 s. Its speed at t = 2 s is
solution: The change in velocity over 4 s is (3 i - 4 j) - (3 i + 4 j) = -8 j m s^-1, so a = -2 j m s^-2. At t = 2 s the velocity is 3 i + (4 - 2 x 2) j = 3 i + 0 j m s^-1, so the speed is 3 m s^-1.
formula_principle: a = (v2 - v1) / t and v = u + a t applied component by component
common_misconception: Students assume that equal initial and final speeds mean the speed was constant throughout.

concept_tested: Ratio of path length to displacement for a quarter circle
stem: A particle moves along a circle of radius 5 m from the point (5 m, 0) to the point (0, 5 m), the centre being at the origin. The ratio of the path length travelled to the magnitude of its displacement is
solution: The quarter arc has length (1/4)(2 pi x 5) = 2.5 pi = 7.85 m. The displacement is the chord joining (5, 0) to (0, 5), of magnitude sqrt(25 + 25) = 5 sqrt 2 = 7.07 m. The ratio is 7.85 / 7.07 = pi / (2 sqrt 2), about 1.11.
formula_principle: Quarter arc length = (1/4)(2 pi R); chord of a quarter circle = R sqrt 2
common_misconception: Students use the diameter as the displacement for a quarter circle instead of the chord R sqrt 2.

concept_tested: Position of a particle starting from rest with constant vector acceleration
stem: A particle starts from rest at the origin with a constant acceleration a = 2 i + 4 j m s^-2. Its distance from the origin at t = 2 s is
solution: With u = 0 the displacement is s = (1/2) a t^2 = (1/2)(2 i + 4 j)(4) = 4 i + 8 j metre. Its magnitude is sqrt(16 + 64) = sqrt 80 = 4 sqrt 5 m, about 8.9 m.
formula_principle: s = u t + (1/2) a t^2 applied to each component with u = 0
common_misconception: Students drop the factor one half or add perpendicular components arithmetically.

concept_tested: Acceleration obtained by differentiating a velocity vector
stem: A particle moves in the x y plane with velocity v = (3 t^2) i + (2 t) j m s^-1, t being in second. Its acceleration at t = 2 s is
solution: Differentiating each component gives a = (6 t) i + 2 j m s^-2. Substituting t = 2 s gives a = 12 i + 2 j m s^-2.
formula_principle: a = dv/dt taken component by component
common_misconception: Students substitute the time before differentiating, or forget to substitute after differentiating.

subtopic: Motion with a rotating velocity vector
concept_tested: Speed and acceleration for a particle whose position is sinusoidal in two dimensions
stem: The position of a particle is r = R cos(omega t) i + R sin(omega t) j, where R and omega are positive constants. Which statement is correct
option_a: The speed is constant and equal to omega R, and the acceleration has magnitude omega^2 R directed towards the origin
option_b: The speed is constant and equal to omega R, and the acceleration is zero because the speed does not change
option_c: The speed varies between zero and omega R, and the acceleration has magnitude omega^2 R
option_d: The speed is omega^2 R and the acceleration has magnitude omega R directed away from the origin
correct_answer_text: The speed is constant and equal to omega R, and the acceleration has magnitude omega^2 R directed towards the origin
solution: Differentiating gives v = -R omega sin(omega t) i + R omega cos(omega t) j, whose magnitude is R omega sqrt(sin^2 + cos^2) = omega R, a constant. Differentiating again gives a = -R omega^2 cos(omega t) i - R omega^2 sin(omega t) j = -omega^2 r, so the acceleration has magnitude omega^2 R and points from the particle towards the origin.
formula_principle: Differentiate twice: v = dr/dt, a = dv/dt
common_misconception: Students infer zero acceleration from a constant speed, or mix up which power of omega goes with speed and which with acceleration.

concept_tested: Comparing average velocity with instantaneous velocity under constant acceleration
stem: A particle starts at the origin with velocity 4 i m s^-1 and moves with a constant acceleration 2 j m s^-2. The magnitude of its average velocity over the first 4 s and its instantaneous speed at t = 4 s are respectively
option_a: 4 sqrt 5 m s^-1 and 4 sqrt 2 m s^-1
option_b: 4 sqrt 2 m s^-1 and 4 sqrt 5 m s^-1
option_c: 4 sqrt 2 m s^-1 and 4 sqrt 2 m s^-1
correct_answer_text: 4 sqrt 2 m s^-1 and 4 sqrt 5 m s^-1
solution: In 4 s the displacement is r = (4 i)(4) + (1/2)(2 j)(16) = 16 i + 16 j metre, so the average velocity is 4 i + 4 j m s^-1 of magnitude 4 sqrt 2, about 5.66 m s^-1. The instantaneous velocity at t = 4 s is 4 i + 8 j m s^-1, of magnitude sqrt(16 + 64) = 4 sqrt 5, about 8.94 m s^-1.
formula_principle: r = u t + (1/2) a t^2; v_average = r / t; v = u + a t
common_misconception: Students assume the average velocity over an interval equals the velocity at the end of the interval.

major_topic: Equations of Motion in a Plane
concept_tested: First kinematic equation written for vectors
stem: For motion in a plane with constant acceleration a, the velocity v after time t in terms of the initial velocity u is
solution: For constant acceleration the velocity changes at a steady vector rate, so the change in velocity in time t is a t, giving v = u + a t. Each Cartesian component of this vector equation holds separately.
formula_principle: v = u + a t, valid as a vector equation for constant a
common_misconception: Students memorise the scalar relations without recognising that they apply component wise as a single vector equation.

major_topic: Equations of Motion in a Plane
concept_tested: The quantity shared by the two perpendicular component motions
stem: When motion in a plane is split into two perpendicular component motions, the quantity that is common to both of them is
solution: Splitting a plane motion into perpendicular directions gives two separate one dimensional problems. Each has its own initial velocity, acceleration and displacement, but the same instant of time applies to both, so time is the link used to connect them.
formula_principle: Perpendicular components of motion are independent but share a single clock
common_misconception: Students look for a shared displacement or a shared acceleration instead of recognising that only the clock is shared.

major_topic: Equations of Motion in a Plane
concept_tested: Displacement from the second kinematic equation in vector form
stem: A particle has initial velocity u = 3 i m s^-1 and constant acceleration a = 2 j m s^-2. Its displacement in the first 2 s is
solution: The x component gives 3 x 2 = 6 m and the y component gives (1/2)(2)(2^2) = 4 m, so the displacement is 6 i + 4 j metre.
common_misconception: Students drop the factor one half or use the wrong power of time in the second kinematic equation.

major_topic: Equations of Motion in a Plane
concept_tested: Meaning of independence of perpendicular components
stem: Which statement correctly expresses the independence of perpendicular components in plane motion
option_a: The two components must always be solved together because each has its own value of the time
option_b: The motion along x fixes the motion along y through the direction of the resultant acceleration
option_c: Each perpendicular component obeys its own one dimensional equation of motion, with the same value of t appearing in both
option_d: Only the resultant equation of motion is valid, so the components have no separate equations of motion
correct_answer_text: Each perpendicular component obeys its own one dimensional equation of motion, with the same value of t appearing in both
solution: Because the vector equations of motion hold component wise, the x motion is governed only by the x components of u and a, and the y motion only by their y components. Neither influences the other. The single link is the time t, which is the same for both.
formula_principle: A vector equation of motion is equivalent to two independent scalar equations
common_misconception: Students believe the two component motions interact, and try to transfer a velocity from one direction to the other.

major_topic: Equations of Motion in a Plane
concept_tested: Velocity after a given time with acceleration along one axis only
stem: A particle has initial velocity u = 4 i + 3 j m s^-1 and constant acceleration a = -2 i m s^-2. Its speed at t = 2 s is
solution: The x component becomes 4 + (-2)(2) = 0 m s^-1 while the y component is unaffected and stays at 3 m s^-1. The velocity is therefore 3 j m s^-1 and the speed is 3 m s^-1.
formula_principle: v = u + a t applied component wise
common_misconception: Students apply the acceleration to the wrong component or assume the speed is unchanged.

major_topic: Equations of Motion in a Plane
concept_tested: Speed from rest under a constant vector acceleration
stem: A body starts from rest and moves with constant acceleration a = 3 i + 4 j m s^-2. Its speed after 5 s is
solution: The magnitude of the acceleration is sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = 5 m s^-2. Starting from rest, the speed after 5 s is 5 x 5 = 25 m s^-1.
formula_principle: v = u + a t with u = 0, so |v| = |a| t
common_misconception: Students add perpendicular components of acceleration arithmetically.

major_topic: Equations of Motion in a Plane
concept_tested: Magnitude of displacement with perpendicular initial velocity and acceleration
stem: A particle is projected in a plane with initial velocity 10 i m s^-1 and moves with constant acceleration 5 j m s^-2. The magnitude of its displacement after 4 s is
solution: Along x, sx = 10 x 4 = 40 m. Along y, sy = (1/2)(5)(4^2) = 40 m. The magnitude is sqrt(40^2 + 40^2) = 40 sqrt 2 m, about 56.6 m.
formula_principle: s = u t + (1/2) a t^2, then |s| = sqrt(sx^2 + sy^2)
common_misconception: Students add perpendicular displacement components arithmetically instead of using the resultant.

major_topic: Equations of Motion in a Plane
concept_tested: Why equal horizontal distances are covered in equal times
stem: A projectile covers exactly the same horizontal distance during the first second of its flight as during the last second. The reason is that
option_a: gravity acts for equal lengths of time in the two intervals
option_b: the vertical component of velocity has the same value in the two intervals
option_c: the magnitude of the total acceleration stays constant throughout the flight
option_d: the horizontal component of velocity is unchanged, since there is no horizontal acceleration
correct_answer_text: the horizontal component of velocity is unchanged, since there is no horizontal acceleration
solution: With air resistance neglected the only acceleration is vertical, so the horizontal velocity component keeps its launch value u cos theta throughout. Equal time intervals therefore give equal horizontal distances, whatever is happening vertically.
formula_principle: a_x = 0 implies v_x is constant, so x = v_x t
common_misconception: Students look for a vertical reason for a horizontal result, instead of using the independence of the two component motions.

major_topic: Equations of Motion in a Plane
concept_tested: Correct vector version of the third kinematic equation
stem: For motion in a plane with constant acceleration a, which relation between the initial velocity u, the final velocity v and the displacement s is correct
option_b: v . v = u . u + 2 |a| |s| for any directions of a and s
option_c: v . v = u . u + (a . s) t
solution: Eliminating t between v = u + a t and s = u t + (1/2) a t^2 gives the scalar relation v . v = u . u + 2 (a . s). The scalar product automatically includes the cosine of the angle between a and s, so it applies whatever their relative directions.
formula_principle: v . v = u . u + 2 (a . s), the scalar product form of the third equation
common_misconception: Students replace the scalar product a . s by the product of magnitudes, which is valid only when a and s are parallel.

major_topic: Equations of Motion in a Plane
concept_tested: Velocity vector after a given time with acceleration in two directions
stem: A particle has u = 2 i + 3 j m s^-1 and a = i - j m s^-2. Its velocity at t = 2 s is
solution: The x component is 2 + (1)(2) = 4 m s^-1 and the y component is 3 + (-1)(2) = 1 m s^-1, so v = 4 i + j m s^-1.
formula_principle: v = u + a t applied component wise
common_misconception: Students mishandle the sign of a negative acceleration component.

major_topic: Equations of Motion in a Plane
concept_tested: Shape of the path for constant acceleration not parallel to the initial velocity
stem: A particle moves with a constant acceleration whose direction is not along its initial velocity. The path of the particle is
solution: Choose axes so that the acceleration is along y. Then x = u_x t is linear in t and y = u_y t + (1/2) a_y t^2 is quadratic in t. Eliminating t makes y a quadratic function of x, which is the equation of a parabola.
formula_principle: x = u_x t and y = u_y t + (1/2) a_y t^2 give y as a quadratic in x
common_misconception: Students assume any accelerated motion in a plane must be circular, or that the path always follows the acceleration.

major_topic: Equations of Motion in a Plane
concept_tested: Speed after a given vertical drop with a horizontal initial velocity
stem: A particle is projected with velocity 20 i m s^-1 and moves with acceleration -10 j m s^-2. Its speed when its displacement along the y direction is -20 m is
option_b: 20 sqrt 2 m s^-1, about 28.3 m s^-1
option_d: 20 sqrt 3 m s^-1, about 34.6 m s^-1
correct_answer_text: 20 sqrt 2 m s^-1, about 28.3 m s^-1
solution: The horizontal velocity stays at 20 m s^-1. Vertically, v_y^2 = 0 + 2 x 10 x 20 = 400, so the magnitude of v_y is 20 m s^-1. The speed is sqrt(400 + 400) = 20 sqrt 2 m s^-1, about 28.3 m s^-1.
formula_principle: v_y^2 = u_y^2 + 2 a_y s_y with u_y = 0; speed = sqrt(v_x^2 + v_y^2)
common_misconception: Students forget that the horizontal component still contributes to the speed after the fall.

major_topic: Equations of Motion in a Plane
concept_tested: Time at which the velocity becomes perpendicular to the initial velocity
stem: A particle has initial velocity u = 4 i m s^-1 and constant acceleration a = -2 i + 3 j m s^-2. The velocity becomes perpendicular to the initial velocity at
solution: Here v = (4 - 2 t) i + (3 t) j m s^-1. Requiring v . u = 0 with u = 4 i gives 4 (4 - 2 t) = 0, so 4 - 2 t = 0 and t = 2 s. At that instant the velocity is 6 j m s^-1, which is indeed perpendicular to the initial velocity.
formula_principle: Two vectors are perpendicular when their scalar product is zero
common_misconception: Students set the components equal rather than setting the scalar product with the initial velocity to zero.

major_topic: Equations of Motion in a Plane
concept_tested: Distance covered after the acceleration is switched off
stem: A body starts from rest and moves with constant acceleration 4 i + 3 j m s^-2 for 2 s, after which the acceleration ceases. The distance it covers during the next 3 s is
solution: The acceleration has magnitude sqrt(16 + 9) = 5 m s^-2, so after 2 s the speed is 10 m s^-1 and the body has covered (1/2)(5)(4) = 10 m in a straight line. With the acceleration removed it continues at 10 m s^-1, covering 10 x 3 = 30 m in the next 3 s.
formula_principle: |a| = sqrt(ax^2 + ay^2); v = a t; then uniform velocity gives distance = v t
common_misconception: Students report the total distance from the start when only the distance in the second stage is asked for.

major_topic: Equations of Motion in a Plane
concept_tested: Instant of minimum speed for a velocity with one varying component
stem: A particle has u = 6 i + 8 j m s^-1 and constant acceleration a = -2 j m s^-2. The minimum speed of the particle and the time at which it occurs are
solution: Here v = 6 i + (8 - 2 t) j m s^-1. The x component is fixed at 6 m s^-1, so the speed is least when the y component vanishes, that is when 8 - 2 t = 0, giving t = 4 s. The minimum speed is then 6 m s^-1.
formula_principle: Speed = sqrt(vx^2 + vy^2) is least when the varying component is zero
common_misconception: Students conclude that the speed becomes zero whenever one velocity component becomes zero.

major_topic: Equations of Motion in a Plane
concept_tested: Locating the point where a plane trajectory recrosses an axis
stem: A particle starts from the origin with u = 2 i + 4 j m s^-1 and moves with constant acceleration a = 2 i - 2 j m s^-2. It crosses the x axis again at a distance from the origin of
solution: Along y, y = 4 t + (1/2)(-2) t^2 = 4 t - t^2. Setting this to zero gives t (4 - t) = 0, so the non zero solution is t = 4 s. Along x, x = 2 x 4 + (1/2)(2)(4^2) = 8 + 16 = 24 m.
formula_principle: Set y = u_y t + (1/2) a_y t^2 = 0 to find t, then evaluate x
common_misconception: Students forget that a non zero horizontal acceleration also contributes a (1/2) a t^2 term to the horizontal displacement.

concept_tested: Relative velocity of one body with respect to another
stem: Two bodies P and Q move with velocities v_P and v_Q as measured in the ground frame. The velocity of P relative to Q is
solution: The velocity of P as measured by an observer moving with Q is the rate of change of the position of P relative to Q, which is v_P - v_Q.
formula_principle: v_PQ = v_P - v_Q
common_misconception: Students always add the two velocities, having learnt only the head on case.

concept_tested: Relative speed of two bodies moving in the same direction
stem: Two cars travel along the same straight road in the same direction with speeds 20 m s^-1 and 30 m s^-1. The speed of the faster car relative to the slower one is
solution: Taking the common direction of travel as positive, the relative velocity is 30 - 20 = 10 m s^-1, directed forward.
formula_principle: For collinear motion in the same sense, relative speed = difference of speeds
common_misconception: Students add the speeds without checking whether the motions are in the same or opposite directions.

concept_tested: Relative speed of two bodies approaching head on
stem: Two trains on parallel tracks approach each other with speeds 15 m s^-1 and 25 m s^-1. Their speed of approach is
solution: Taking one direction as positive, the velocities are +15 m s^-1 and -25 m s^-1. The relative velocity is 15 - (-25) = 40 m s^-1, so they approach at 40 m s^-1.
formula_principle: For collinear motion in opposite senses, relative speed = sum of speeds
common_misconception: Students subtract speeds without regard to the sense of each motion.

concept_tested: Direction in which a moving person must tilt an umbrella
stem: Rain is falling vertically downwards. A man runs horizontally along a level road. To keep himself dry he must hold his umbrella tilted
option_a: backwards, opposite to his direction of motion
option_b: forwards, in the direction of his motion
option_c: vertically, since the rain itself falls vertically
option_d: sideways, perpendicular to his direction of motion
correct_answer_text: forwards, in the direction of his motion
solution: In the man's frame the rain has velocity v_rain - v_man. Subtracting his forward velocity adds a backward horizontal component to the rain, so the rain appears to come slanting from the front. The umbrella must therefore be tilted forwards.
formula_principle: v_rain,man = v_rain - v_man
common_misconception: Students reason in the ground frame and conclude the umbrella should be held vertically.

concept_tested: Heading for the shortest time of crossing
stem: A boat whose speed in still water exceeds the speed of the river current is to cross the river in the shortest possible time. The boat should be headed
option_a: upstream at an angle to the bank
option_b: downstream at an angle to the bank
option_c: along the bank, in the direction of the current
option_d: perpendicular to the bank, straight across the river
correct_answer_text: perpendicular to the bank, straight across the river
solution: The crossing time is the width divided by the component of the boat velocity perpendicular to the bank. That component is largest when the entire boat velocity is directed across the river, so the shortest time is obtained by heading straight across. The current then simply carries the boat downstream while it crosses.
formula_principle: Crossing time = width / (component of boat velocity perpendicular to the bank)
common_misconception: Students confuse the heading for shortest time with the heading for shortest path.

concept_tested: Drift for the shortest time crossing
stem: A river 100 m wide flows at 3 m s^-1. A boat whose speed in still water is 5 m s^-1 is headed straight across. The distance downstream at which it lands from the point directly opposite its start is
solution: Since the boat is headed straight across, the crossing time is 100 / 5 = 20 s. During this time the current carries it downstream through 3 x 20 = 60 m.
formula_principle: t = width / v_boat; drift = v_current x t
common_misconception: Students use the resultant speed for the crossing time instead of the component perpendicular to the bank.

concept_tested: Crossing time along the shortest path
stem: A river 100 m wide flows at 3 m s^-1. A boat whose speed in still water is 5 m s^-1 must land at the point directly opposite its starting point. The time taken to cross is
solution: To land directly opposite, the upstream component of the boat velocity must cancel the current, so 5 sin theta = 3 with theta measured from the line straight across. The component across the river is then 5 cos theta = sqrt(25 - 9) = 4 m s^-1, and the crossing time is 100 / 4 = 25 s.
formula_principle: Effective crossing speed = sqrt(v_boat^2 - v_current^2)
common_misconception: Students use the full boat speed as the crossing speed even when part of it is spent cancelling the current.

concept_tested: Umbrella angle when the walking speed equals the rain speed
stem: Rain falls vertically downwards at 10 m s^-1. A man walks horizontally at 10 m s^-1. The angle with the vertical at which he must hold his umbrella is
solution: In the man's frame the rain has a horizontal component equal in magnitude to his own speed, 10 m s^-1, and a vertical component of 10 m s^-1. Hence tan theta = 10 / 10 = 1, so theta = 45 degrees from the vertical, tilted forwards.
formula_principle: tan(angle with the vertical) = v_man / v_rain
common_misconception: Students put the two speeds in the wrong order in the tangent, or forget the tilt entirely.

concept_tested: Umbrella angle for unequal rain and walking speeds
stem: Rain falls vertically downwards at 10 sqrt 3 m s^-1 and a man walks horizontally at 10 m s^-1. His umbrella should be tilted from the vertical through
solution: In the man's frame the horizontal component of the rain velocity has magnitude 10 m s^-1 and the vertical component is 10 sqrt 3 m s^-1. Hence tan theta = 10 / (10 sqrt 3) = 1 / sqrt 3, giving theta = 30 degrees from the vertical.
formula_principle: tan(angle with the vertical) = v_man / v_rain
common_misconception: Students invert the ratio and obtain the complement of the required angle.

concept_tested: Comparing the shortest path route with the shortest time route
stem: For a boat crossing a river whose current is slower than the boat, which comparison of the shortest path crossing with the shortest time crossing is correct
option_a: The two crossings take the same time, since the width of the river is the same
option_b: The shortest path crossing takes less time, since the boat travels a shorter distance
option_c: The shortest time crossing is impossible whenever the current is slower than the boat
option_d: The shortest path crossing takes more time than the shortest time crossing
correct_answer_text: The shortest path crossing takes more time than the shortest time crossing
solution: Heading straight across gives a crossing speed v and time d / v. Landing directly opposite requires part of the boat velocity to cancel the current, leaving only sqrt(v^2 - u^2) across the river, and a time d / sqrt(v^2 - u^2). Since sqrt(v^2 - u^2) is smaller than v, the shortest path route always takes longer.
formula_principle: t_shortest_time = d / v; t_shortest_path = d / sqrt(v^2 - u^2)
common_misconception: Students assume that the shortest path must also be the quickest.

concept_tested: Feasibility of landing directly opposite when the current is fast
stem: The speed of a river current is greater than the speed of a boat in still water. Can the boat reach the point on the far bank directly opposite its starting point
option_a: Yes, provided the boat is headed fully upstream along the bank
option_b: Yes, provided the boat is headed perpendicular to the bank
option_c: Yes, provided the river is narrow enough for the crossing to be quick
option_d: No, because the boat velocity cannot supply an upstream component large enough to cancel the current
correct_answer_text: No, because the boat velocity cannot supply an upstream component large enough to cancel the current
solution: To land directly opposite, the upstream component of the boat velocity must exactly cancel the current, that is v sin theta = u. Since sin theta cannot exceed 1, this is possible only when v is at least as large as u. If u is greater than v the boat is always carried downstream, whatever heading is chosen.
formula_principle: Landing directly opposite requires v_boat sin theta = v_current, which needs v_boat greater than or equal to v_current
common_misconception: Students believe any destination can be reached by choosing a suitable heading, whatever the current speed.

concept_tested: Relative velocity of two particles moving along perpendicular directions
stem: Two particles move with velocities 4 i m s^-1 and 3 j m s^-1. The magnitude of the velocity of the first relative to the second is
solution: The relative velocity is 4 i - 3 j m s^-1, whose magnitude is sqrt(16 + 9) = 5 m s^-1.
formula_principle: v_12 = v_1 - v_2, then take the magnitude
common_misconception: Students add or subtract the speeds arithmetically even though the velocities are perpendicular.

concept_tested: Comparing v of P relative to Q with v of Q relative to P
stem: The velocity of a body P relative to a body Q and the velocity of Q relative to P are
option_a: equal in magnitude and in the same direction
option_b: different in magnitude and opposite in direction
option_c: always zero, since each body is at rest in its own frame
option_d: equal in magnitude and opposite in direction
correct_answer_text: equal in magnitude and opposite in direction
solution: By definition v_PQ = v_P - v_Q and v_QP = v_Q - v_P. These two expressions differ only by an overall minus sign, so the two relative velocities always have the same magnitude and opposite directions.
formula_principle: v_PQ = v_P - v_Q = -(v_Q - v_P) = -v_QP
common_misconception: Students think the observer's own motion changes the magnitude of the relative velocity.

concept_tested: Minimum crossing time and the corresponding displacement
stem: A river 40 m wide flows at 3 m s^-1. A boat whose speed in still water is 4 m s^-1 is headed straight across the river. The time taken and the magnitude of the boat displacement are
solution: Headed straight across, the component of the boat velocity perpendicular to the bank is the full 4 m s^-1, so the crossing time is 40 / 4 = 10 s. In that time the current carries the boat 3 x 10 = 30 m downstream. The displacement is sqrt(40^2 + 30^2) = 50 m.
formula_principle: t = d / v_boat; drift = u t; displacement = sqrt(d^2 + drift^2)
common_misconception: Students combine the width and the drift arithmetically instead of as perpendicular components.

concept_tested: Heading angle and crossing time for the shortest path
stem: A river 200 m wide flows at 5 m s^-1. A boat whose speed in still water is 10 m s^-1 has to land directly opposite its starting point. The angle at which it must be headed, measured from the line straight across the river, and the time taken are
option_c: 30 degrees upstream and 40 / sqrt 3 s, about 23.1 s
correct_answer_text: 30 degrees upstream and 40 / sqrt 3 s, about 23.1 s
solution: The upstream component must cancel the current, so 10 sin theta = 5 giving sin theta = 0.5 and theta = 30 degrees from the line straight across. The component across the river is 10 cos 30 = 5 sqrt 3 m s^-1, about 8.66 m s^-1, so the crossing time is 200 / (5 sqrt 3) = 40 / sqrt 3 s, about 23.1 s.
formula_principle: sin theta = v_current / v_boat; t = d / (v_boat cos theta)
common_misconception: Students quote the angle from the wrong reference line, or use the full boat speed for the crossing time.

concept_tested: Finding the actual rain velocity from two observations
stem: A man walking due east at 4 m s^-1 finds that rain appears to fall vertically. When he doubles his speed to 8 m s^-1 the rain appears to come at 45 degrees to the vertical. The actual speed of the rain is
option_c: 4 sqrt 3 m s^-1, about 6.9 m s^-1
option_d: 4 sqrt 2 m s^-1, about 5.7 m s^-1
correct_answer_text: 4 sqrt 2 m s^-1, about 5.7 m s^-1
solution: Let the rain velocity be p i - q j with east as i. At 4 m s^-1 the apparent horizontal component is p - 4, and the rain seems vertical, so p = 4 m s^-1. At 8 m s^-1 the apparent horizontal component is 4 - 8 = -4 m s^-1 while the vertical component is still -q. A 45 degree slant needs q = 4 m s^-1. The actual rain speed is sqrt(4^2 + 4^2) = 4 sqrt 2 m s^-1, about 5.7 m s^-1.
formula_principle: v_rain,man = v_rain - v_man applied to both observations
common_misconception: Students assume rain that appears vertical to a moving observer really is falling vertically.

concept_tested: Separation of two bodies moving along perpendicular roads
stem: Two cars start together from the same crossing. One travels due north at 30 m s^-1 and the other due east at 40 m s^-1. After 10 s their separation and the rate at which the separation is increasing are
solution: The relative velocity of one car with respect to the other is 40 i - 30 j m s^-1, of magnitude sqrt(1600 + 900) = 50 m s^-1. Since this relative velocity is constant, the separation after 10 s is 50 x 10 = 500 m and it grows at 50 m s^-1.
formula_principle: Relative velocity magnitude = sqrt(v1^2 + v2^2) for perpendicular motions; separation = relative speed x t
common_misconception: Students add perpendicular speeds arithmetically to get the rate of separation.

concept_tested: Total time for a downstream and upstream round trip
stem: A boat whose speed in still water is 10 m s^-1 travels 96 m downstream and then returns to its starting point. The river current is 2 m s^-1. The total time for the round trip is
solution: Downstream the boat moves at 10 + 2 = 12 m s^-1, taking 96 / 12 = 8 s. Upstream it moves at 10 - 2 = 8 m s^-1, taking 96 / 8 = 12 s. The total time is 8 + 12 = 20 s, which is more than the 19.2 s the trip would take in still water.
formula_principle: Downstream speed = v + u; upstream speed = v - u; t = distance / speed for each leg
common_misconception: Students average the downstream and upstream speeds, or cancel the effect of the current.

concept_tested: Ratio of the two characteristic crossing times
stem: A swimmer whose speed in still water is 5 m s^-1 crosses a river flowing at 3 m s^-1. The ratio of the time for the shortest time crossing to the time for the shortest path crossing is
solution: For the shortest time crossing the whole swimmer velocity acts across the river, so t1 = d / 5. For the shortest path crossing only sqrt(25 - 9) = 4 m s^-1 acts across the river, so t2 = d / 4. The ratio t1 : t2 is (d / 5) : (d / 4) = 4 : 5, so the shortest path route takes a quarter longer.
formula_principle: t1 = d / v and t2 = d / sqrt(v^2 - u^2)
common_misconception: Students invert the ratio or use the resultant speed as the effective crossing speed.

concept_tested: Recovering the true rain velocity from an apparent vertical fall
stem: To a man running due east at 3 m s^-1, rain appears to fall vertically downwards at 4 m s^-1. The actual velocity of the rain is
option_b: 5 m s^-1, at 37 degrees to the vertical, slanting towards the east
option_c: 5 m s^-1, at 53 degrees to the vertical, slanting towards the east
option_d: 7 m s^-1, at 37 degrees to the vertical, slanting towards the east
correct_answer_text: 5 m s^-1, at 37 degrees to the vertical, slanting towards the east
