solution: The apparent velocity is v_rain - v_man = -4 j m s^-1 with east as i. Hence v_rain = -4 j + 3 i m s^-1, of magnitude sqrt(9 + 16) = 5 m s^-1. The angle with the vertical satisfies tan theta = 3 / 4, so theta is about 37 degrees, the rain slanting towards the east.
formula_principle: v_rain = v_rain,man + v_man
common_misconception: Students forget to add the observer velocity back when converting an apparent velocity to a ground frame velocity.

concept_tested: Shape of a projectile trajectory
stem: A body is projected obliquely near the surface of the earth. If air resistance is neglected, the path followed by the body is
option_b: a straight line inclined to the horizontal
solution: Horizontally x = u cos theta multiplied by t, so t is proportional to x. Vertically y = u sin theta t - (1/2) g t^2. Eliminating t makes y a quadratic function of x, which is the equation of a parabola.
formula_principle: y = x tan theta - g x^2 / (2 u^2 cos^2 theta)
common_misconception: Students associate any curved path in a plane with circular motion.

concept_tested: Velocity of a projectile at the top of its path
stem: A projectile is launched with speed u at an angle theta to the horizontal. At the highest point of its path its velocity is
option_d: u, directed along the tangent to the path
solution: Gravity acts vertically, so it changes only the vertical component of velocity. At the highest point the vertical component has been reduced to zero, but the horizontal component still has its launch value u cos theta, directed horizontally.
formula_principle: v_x = u cos theta throughout; v_y = 0 at the highest point
common_misconception: Students say the projectile is momentarily at rest at the top of its path.

concept_tested: Acceleration of a projectile at the highest point
stem: At the highest point of the path of a projectile, its acceleration is
option_a: zero, because the vertical velocity is zero there
solution: Once the projectile is in flight the only force on it is its weight, so its acceleration is g directed vertically downwards at every point of the trajectory, including the highest point. It is the vertical velocity, not the acceleration, that is zero there.
formula_principle: For projectile motion a = g downwards at every instant
common_misconception: Students confuse zero vertical velocity at the top with zero acceleration.

concept_tested: Why the horizontal velocity stays constant
stem: The horizontal component of the velocity of a projectile stays constant throughout its flight because
option_a: the horizontal displacement is much smaller than the vertical displacement
option_b: gravity acts on the vertical component first and only later on the horizontal one
option_c: the horizontal and vertical components of velocity are always equal in magnitude
option_d: there is no horizontal component of acceleration when air resistance is neglected
correct_answer_text: there is no horizontal component of acceleration when air resistance is neglected
solution: The only acceleration during flight is g, directed vertically. Since the horizontal component of the acceleration is zero, the horizontal component of the velocity does not change and keeps its launch value u cos theta.
formula_principle: a_x = 0 implies v_x is constant
common_misconception: Students believe gravity gradually reduces the horizontal velocity as well.

concept_tested: Horizontal component of the initial velocity
stem: A ball is projected with a speed of 20 m s^-1 at 60 degrees to the horizontal. The horizontal component of its initial velocity is
option_b: 10 sqrt 3 m s^-1, about 17.3 m s^-1
option_d: 20 sqrt 3 m s^-1, about 34.6 m s^-1
solution: The horizontal component is u cos theta = 20 x cos 60 = 20 x 0.5 = 10 m s^-1.
formula_principle: u_x = u cos theta
common_misconception: Students interchange sine and cosine when resolving the launch velocity.

concept_tested: Standard assumptions used in elementary projectile theory
stem: The standard treatment of projectile motion in a plane rests on the assumptions that
option_a: air resistance is included and the acceleration due to gravity is neglected
option_b: air resistance is neglected and the acceleration due to gravity is constant in magnitude and direction
option_c: the acceleration due to gravity falls off with height while air resistance is neglected
option_d: both the horizontal and the vertical accelerations are constant and non zero
correct_answer_text: air resistance is neglected and the acceleration due to gravity is constant in magnitude and direction
solution: Elementary projectile theory assumes that the projectile moves close to the earth so that g is constant in magnitude and direction, that air resistance is negligible, and that the range is small enough for the earth to be treated as flat and non rotating. These assumptions make the horizontal acceleration zero and the vertical acceleration a constant g.
formula_principle: Constant g, no air resistance, ranges small compared with the size of the earth
common_misconception: Students forget that constancy of g in both magnitude and direction is itself an assumption.

concept_tested: Speed of a projectile one second after launch
stem: A ball is projected at 20 m s^-1 making 30 degrees with the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, its speed 1 s after launch is
option_d: 10 sqrt 3 m s^-1, about 17.3 m s^-1
correct_answer_text: 10 sqrt 3 m s^-1, about 17.3 m s^-1
solution: Here u_x = 20 cos 30 = 10 sqrt 3 m s^-1 and u_y = 20 sin 30 = 10 m s^-1. After 1 s, v_y = 10 - 10 x 1 = 0, so the ball is at its highest point. The speed is then just the horizontal component, 10 sqrt 3 m s^-1, about 17.3 m s^-1.
formula_principle: v_x = u cos theta; v_y = u sin theta - g t; speed = sqrt(v_x^2 + v_y^2)
common_misconception: Students take the speed to be zero when the vertical component of velocity becomes zero.

concept_tested: Speed at the top for a launch at 45 degrees
stem: A stone is thrown with a speed of 20 m s^-1 at 45 degrees to the horizontal. Its speed at the highest point of the path is
option_c: 10 sqrt 2 m s^-1, about 14.1 m s^-1
correct_answer_text: 10 sqrt 2 m s^-1, about 14.1 m s^-1
solution: At the top the vertical component is zero and only the horizontal component survives. That component is u cos theta = 20 cos 45 = 20 / sqrt 2 = 10 sqrt 2 m s^-1, about 14.1 m s^-1.
formula_principle: Speed at the highest point = u cos theta
common_misconception: Students assume the speed at the top equals the launch speed, or that it is zero.

concept_tested: Correct description of the state of a projectile at the top
stem: Which statement correctly describes a projectile launched at speed u and angle theta when it is at the highest point of its path
option_a: Both components of its velocity are zero, so it is momentarily at rest
option_b: Its vertical velocity is zero while its horizontal velocity is u cos theta
option_c: Its horizontal velocity is zero while its vertical velocity is u sin theta
option_d: Its velocity is zero and its acceleration is also zero at that instant
correct_answer_text: Its vertical velocity is zero while its horizontal velocity is u cos theta
solution: At the highest point the projectile stops rising, so its vertical velocity is momentarily zero. Since there is no horizontal acceleration, the horizontal velocity is still u cos theta. The projectile is therefore moving horizontally at u cos theta, and its acceleration is still g downwards.
formula_principle: v_x = u cos theta throughout; v_y = 0 at the highest point
common_misconception: Students describe the top of the trajectory as an instant of rest.

concept_tested: Comparing two launches at the same speed and different angles
stem: Two balls are thrown with the same speed, one at 30 degrees and the other at 60 degrees to the horizontal. Comparing the two flights,
option_a: the ball at 30 degrees stays in the air longer, because its horizontal component of velocity is larger
option_b: both stay in the air for the same time, because the launch speeds are equal
option_c: both stay in the air for the same time, because the two angles are complementary
option_d: the ball at 60 degrees stays in the air longer, because its initial vertical component of velocity is larger
correct_answer_text: the ball at 60 degrees stays in the air longer, because its initial vertical component of velocity is larger
solution: The time of flight is 2 u sin theta / g and depends only on the vertical component of the launch velocity. Since sin 60 is larger than sin 30, the ball projected at 60 degrees has the greater vertical component and stays in the air longer, in the ratio sqrt 3 to 1.
formula_principle: T = 2 u sin theta / g
common_misconception: Students believe complementary angles give equal times of flight because they give equal ranges.

subtopic: Variation of velocity components with time
concept_tested: Time dependence of the two velocity components
stem: For a projectile in flight, the way in which the components of velocity depend on time is best described by saying that
option_a: both components change linearly with time
option_b: the horizontal component decreases linearly with time while the vertical component stays constant
option_c: the horizontal component stays constant while the vertical component changes linearly with time
option_d: the horizontal component stays constant while the vertical component changes as the square of the time
correct_answer_text: the horizontal component stays constant while the vertical component changes linearly with time
solution: A graph of horizontal velocity against time is a straight line parallel to the time axis, since there is no horizontal acceleration. A graph of vertical velocity against time is a straight line of slope minus g, crossing the time axis at the instant the projectile reaches its highest point.
formula_principle: v_x = u cos theta; v_y = u sin theta - g t
common_misconception: Students confuse the linear time dependence of the vertical velocity with the quadratic time dependence of the vertical displacement.

concept_tested: Velocity vector at a later instant from a vector launch velocity
stem: A body is projected with velocity 10 i + 20 j m s^-1, the acceleration due to gravity being 10 m s^-2 along the negative j direction. Its velocity 3 s after launch is
solution: The horizontal component is unchanged at 10 m s^-1. The vertical component is 20 - 10 x 3 = -10 m s^-1. Hence the velocity is 10 i - 10 j m s^-1, of magnitude 10 sqrt 2 m s^-1 directed 45 degrees below the horizontal.
formula_principle: v = u + g t applied component wise
common_misconception: Students apply gravity to the horizontal component or mishandle the sign of the vertical component.

concept_tested: Comparing the landing velocity with the launch velocity
stem: A projectile is launched from level ground and lands back on the same level. Comparing the velocity at landing with the velocity at launch,
option_a: the speeds are equal, but the angle at landing is 90 degrees minus the launch angle
option_b: the speeds are equal, and the angle below the horizontal at landing equals the launch angle above it
option_c: the landing speed is smaller, because gravity has opposed the motion during the flight
option_d: the landing speed is larger, because gravity has acted throughout the whole flight
correct_answer_text: the speeds are equal, and the angle below the horizontal at landing equals the launch angle above it
solution: The horizontal component is unchanged. Vertically, the speed lost while rising through the maximum height is exactly regained while falling through the same height, so the magnitude of the vertical component at landing equals u sin theta. Hence the landing speed is u and the velocity makes an angle theta below the horizontal.
formula_principle: Symmetry of the parabola about the vertical line through the highest point
common_misconception: Students expect the projectile to land faster or slower than it was launched.

concept_tested: Horizontal distance covered in a given time
stem: A ball is projected at 40 m s^-1 at 60 degrees to the horizontal from level ground. The horizontal distance it covers during the first 2 s of its flight is
solution: The horizontal component of the launch velocity is 40 cos 60 = 20 m s^-1 and it stays constant. In 2 s the horizontal distance covered is 20 x 2 = 40 m.
formula_principle: x = (u cos theta) t, since the horizontal motion is uniform
common_misconception: Students apply a (1/2) a t^2 term to the horizontal motion, or use the wrong component.

concept_tested: Angle between velocity and acceleration at the highest point
stem: At the highest point of the path of a projectile, the angle between its velocity and its acceleration is
solution: At the highest point the velocity is purely horizontal, of magnitude u cos theta, while the acceleration is g directed vertically downwards. Two such directions are mutually perpendicular, so the angle between them is 90 degrees.
formula_principle: At the top, velocity is horizontal while acceleration is vertically downwards
common_misconception: Students assume the acceleration must be along the velocity, or take the velocity to be zero at the top.

concept_tested: Extracting the launch angle and speed from the trajectory equation
stem: The path of a projectile is given by y = x - x^2 / 20, with x and y in metre and g = 10 m s^-2. The angle of projection and the speed of projection are
solution: Comparing coefficients, tan theta = 1 so theta = 45 degrees. Also g / (2 u^2 cos^2 theta) = 1 / 20. With cos^2 45 = 1/2 this gives 10 / u^2 = 1 / 20, so u^2 = 200 and u = 10 sqrt 2 m s^-1, about 14.1 m s^-1.
formula_principle: y = x tan theta - g x^2 / (2 u^2 cos^2 theta)
common_misconception: Students read the coefficient of x as sin theta rather than tan theta, or drop the cos^2 theta factor.

concept_tested: Instant at which the velocity makes a given angle with the horizontal
stem: A projectile is fired at 20 m s^-1 at 60 degrees to the horizontal, with g = 10 m s^-2. The velocity makes 45 degrees with the horizontal at
solution: Here v_x = 20 cos 60 = 10 m s^-1 and v_y = 20 sin 60 - 10 t = 10 sqrt 3 - 10 t. For the velocity to make 45 degrees with the horizontal on the way up, v_y must equal v_x, so 10 sqrt 3 - 10 t = 10, giving t = sqrt 3 - 1, about 0.73 s.
formula_principle: tan(angle with horizontal) = v_y / v_x with v_y = u sin theta - g t
common_misconception: Students set the vertical component to zero instead of equating it with the horizontal component.

concept_tested: Magnitude of the change in velocity from launch to the highest point
stem: A ball is projected at 40 m s^-1 at 30 degrees to the horizontal, with g = 10 m s^-2. The magnitude of the change in its velocity between the instant of launch and the instant it reaches the highest point is
option_b: 20 sqrt 3 m s^-1, about 34.6 m s^-1
solution: The launch velocity is 40 cos 30 i + 40 sin 30 j, that is 20 sqrt 3 i + 20 j m s^-1. At the top the velocity is 20 sqrt 3 i m s^-1. The change is -20 j m s^-1, so the magnitude is 20 m s^-1, directed vertically downwards.
formula_principle: Change in velocity = v_top - u; only the vertical component changes
common_misconception: Students include the unchanged horizontal component in the change of velocity, or double the correct answer.

concept_tested: Instant at which the velocity points below the horizontal at the launch angle
stem: A stone is thrown at 20 m s^-1 at 30 degrees above the horizontal, with g = 10 m s^-2. The velocity of the stone is directed 30 degrees below the horizontal at
solution: Here v_x = 20 cos 30 = 10 sqrt 3 m s^-1 and v_y = 10 - 10 t. For the velocity to point 30 degrees below the horizontal, v_y must equal -10 sqrt 3 tan 30 = -10 m s^-1. Solving 10 - 10 t = -10 gives t = 2 s, which is exactly the time of flight, as the symmetry of the parabola requires.
formula_principle: v_y = u sin theta - g t; symmetry gives v_y = -u sin theta at the landing level
common_misconception: Students forget the sign of the vertical velocity when the direction is below the horizontal.

subtopic: Position at a given velocity direction
concept_tested: Locating the projectile when its velocity has a specified direction
stem: A projectile is launched from the origin with velocity 10 i + 10 j m s^-1, g being 10 m s^-2 along the negative j direction. Its position vector at the instant its velocity makes 45 degrees below the horizontal is
solution: The velocity is 45 degrees below the horizontal when v_y = -v_x = -10 m s^-1, that is when 10 - 10 t = -10, giving t = 2 s. Then x = 10 x 2 = 20 m and y = 10 x 2 - (1/2)(10)(4) = 20 - 20 = 0. The position vector is therefore 20 i metre, which is the landing point on the launch level.
formula_principle: v_y = u_y - g t; x = u_x t; y = u_y t - (1/2) g t^2
common_misconception: Students stop at the highest point instead of continuing to the instant when the velocity turns downwards through 45 degrees.

concept_tested: Radius of curvature of the trajectory at the highest point
stem: A shell is fired at 40 m s^-1 at 30 degrees to the horizontal, with g = 10 m s^-2. The radius of curvature of its path at the highest point is
solution: At the top the velocity is horizontal, of magnitude 40 cos 30 = 20 sqrt 3 m s^-1, and the acceleration g is perpendicular to it. Hence g = v^2 / r gives r = v^2 / g = (20 sqrt 3)^2 / 10 = 1200 / 10 = 120 m.
formula_principle: At the highest point the whole of g is normal to the path, so g = v^2 / r
common_misconception: Students use the launch speed rather than the speed at the highest point when applying v^2 / r.

concept_tested: Independence of the speed at a given height from the launch angle
stem: Several balls are projected from the ground with the same speed 20 m s^-1 but at different angles, with g = 10 m s^-2. For every ball that reaches a height of 15 m, its speed at that height is
option_a: 10 m s^-1 only for the ball projected vertically upwards, and larger for the others
option_b: 10 sqrt 3 m s^-1, the same for all of them
option_c: 10 m s^-1, the same for all of them
option_d: 5 m s^-1, the same for all of them
correct_answer_text: 10 m s^-1, the same for all of them
solution: Write v^2 = v_x^2 + v_y^2 with v_x = u cos theta and v_y^2 = u^2 sin^2 theta - 2 g h. Adding gives v^2 = u^2 - 2 g h, which contains no trace of theta. Here v^2 = 400 - 2 x 10 x 15 = 100, so v = 10 m s^-1 for every ball that reaches that height.
formula_principle: v^2 = u^2 - 2 g h, obtained by combining the two component motions
common_misconception: Students believe the speed at a given height must depend on the launch angle.

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
concept_tested: Formula for the time of flight on level ground
stem: A projectile is launched from level ground with speed u at an angle theta to the horizontal. Its time of flight is
solution: Vertically the projectile returns to its launch level, so the vertical displacement is zero. Putting 0 = u sin theta T - (1/2) g T^2 gives T = 2 u sin theta / g.
formula_principle: T = 2 u sin theta / g
common_misconception: Students quote the time to the highest point in place of the full time of flight.

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
concept_tested: Formula for the maximum height of a projectile
stem: The maximum height reached by a projectile launched with speed u at an angle theta to the horizontal is
solution: At the highest point the vertical velocity is zero. Using v_y^2 = u_y^2 - 2 g H with u_y = u sin theta gives H = u^2 sin^2 theta / (2 g).
formula_principle: H = u^2 sin^2 theta / (2 g)
common_misconception: Students confuse sin^2 theta with sin 2 theta and so mix up the height and range formulae.

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
concept_tested: Formula for the horizontal range on level ground
stem: The horizontal range of a projectile launched from level ground with speed u at an angle theta to the horizontal is
solution: The range is the horizontal velocity multiplied by the time of flight, that is R = (u cos theta)(2 u sin theta / g) = u^2 (2 sin theta cos theta) / g = u^2 sin 2 theta / g.
formula_principle: R = u^2 sin 2 theta / g
common_misconception: Students interchange sin 2 theta and sin^2 theta between the range and height formulae.

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
concept_tested: Angle for maximum range and its value
stem: For a given launch speed u on level ground, the horizontal range is greatest when the launch angle is
option_a: 45 degrees, the greatest range then being u^2 / g
option_b: 90 degrees, the greatest range then being u^2 / g
option_c: 60 degrees, the greatest range then being u^2 / (2 g)
option_d: 30 degrees, the greatest range then being 2 u^2 / g
correct_answer_text: 45 degrees, the greatest range then being u^2 / g
solution: Since R = u^2 sin 2 theta / g, the range is largest when sin 2 theta takes its greatest value of 1, that is when 2 theta = 90 degrees and theta = 45 degrees. The maximum range is then u^2 / g.
formula_principle: R = u^2 sin 2 theta / g is greatest when sin 2 theta = 1
common_misconception: Students take the largest launch angle to give the largest range.

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
concept_tested: Numerical time of flight for a given launch
stem: A ball is projected at 20 m s^-1 at 30 degrees to the horizontal from level ground, with g = 10 m s^-2. Its time of flight is
solution: The vertical component is 20 sin 30 = 10 m s^-1, so T = 2 x 10 / 10 = 2 s.
formula_principle: T = 2 u sin theta / g
common_misconception: Students report the time to the highest point as the time of flight.

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
concept_tested: Pair of launch angles giving equal range
stem: Two projectiles launched with the same speed from level ground have equal horizontal ranges. A possible pair of launch angles is
solution: Since R = u^2 sin 2 theta / g, two angles give the same range whenever their doubles have the same sine, that is when the angles add up to 90 degrees. The pair 30 degrees and 60 degrees satisfies this, both giving sin 60 in the range formula.
formula_principle: R depends on sin 2 theta, and sin 2 theta = sin (180 - 2 theta)
common_misconception: Students look for angles that differ by a fixed amount instead of angles that add up to 90 degrees.

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
concept_tested: Numerical maximum height for an oblique launch
stem: A stone is projected at 20 m s^-1 at 30 degrees to the horizontal, with g = 10 m s^-2. The maximum height it reaches is
solution: The vertical component is 20 sin 30 = 10 m s^-1. Hence H = 10^2 / (2 x 10) = 100 / 20 = 5 m.
formula_principle: H = u^2 sin^2 theta / (2 g)
common_misconception: Students drop the factor 2 in the denominator or resolve the launch velocity with the wrong trigonometric function.

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
concept_tested: Numerical range for a launch at 30 degrees
stem: A ball is projected at 20 m s^-1 at 30 degrees to the horizontal from level ground, with g = 10 m s^-2. Its horizontal range is
solution: Here R = 20^2 x sin 60 / 10 = 400 x (sqrt 3 / 2) / 10 = 20 sqrt 3 m, about 34.6 m. The same result follows from multiplying the horizontal velocity 10 sqrt 3 m s^-1 by the time of flight of 2 s.
formula_principle: R = u^2 sin 2 theta / g
common_misconception: Students use sin theta instead of sin 2 theta in the range formula.

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
concept_tested: Range and maximum height for a 45 degree launch
stem: A projectile is fired at 20 m s^-1 at 45 degrees from level ground, with g = 10 m s^-2. Its horizontal range and maximum height are respectively
solution: At 45 degrees, sin 2 theta = sin 90 = 1, so R = 400 / 10 = 40 m. Also sin^2 45 = 1/2, so H = 400 x 0.5 / 20 = 10 m. Note that R = 4 H here, as expected for a 45 degree launch.
formula_principle: R = u^2 sin 2 theta / g and H = u^2 sin^2 theta / (2 g)
common_misconception: Students mix the two formulae and use sin 2 theta where sin^2 theta is needed.

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
concept_tested: Maximum range for a given launch speed
stem: A boy can throw a ball with a maximum speed of 40 m s^-1. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the greatest horizontal distance he can throw it on level ground is
solution: The greatest range is obtained at 45 degrees and equals u^2 / g = 1600 / 10 = 160 m.
formula_principle: R_max = u^2 / g at theta = 45 degrees
common_misconception: Students confuse the maximum range u^2 / g with the maximum height for vertical projection u^2 / (2 g).

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
concept_tested: Ratio of maximum heights for 30 and 60 degrees at the same speed
stem: Two balls are thrown with the same speed, one at 30 degrees and the other at 60 degrees to the horizontal. The ratio of their maximum heights is
solution: Since H = u^2 sin^2 theta / (2 g), the ratio of the heights is sin^2 30 : sin^2 60 = (1/4) : (3/4) = 1 : 3.
formula_principle: H is proportional to sin^2 theta for a fixed launch speed
common_misconception: Students use the first power of the sine instead of its square when comparing heights.

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
concept_tested: Ratio of times of flight for 30 and 60 degrees at the same speed
stem: Two projectiles are fired with the same speed, one at 30 degrees and the other at 60 degrees to the horizontal. The ratio of their times of flight is
solution: Since T = 2 u sin theta / g, the ratio of the times of flight is sin 30 : sin 60 = 0.5 : (sqrt 3 / 2) = 1 : sqrt 3.
formula_principle: T is proportional to sin theta for a fixed launch speed
common_misconception: Students assume equal ranges imply equal times of flight for complementary angles.

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
concept_tested: Which quantities agree for complementary launch angles
stem: Two projectiles are fired from level ground with the same speed at complementary angles. Which statement about them is correct
option_a: They have equal horizontal ranges but different maximum heights and different times of flight
option_b: They have equal ranges, equal maximum heights and equal times of flight
option_c: They have different ranges but equal maximum heights
option_d: They have equal maximum heights but different times of flight
correct_answer_text: They have equal horizontal ranges but different maximum heights and different times of flight
solution: Replacing theta by 90 minus theta leaves sin 2 theta unchanged, so the ranges are equal. However sin theta and sin^2 theta both change, so the steeper launch has the larger time of flight and the larger maximum height.
formula_principle: R depends on sin 2 theta; H depends on sin^2 theta; T depends on sin theta
common_misconception: Students extend the equality of ranges for complementary angles to every other quantity.

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
concept_tested: Ratio of range to maximum height for a 45 degree launch
stem: For a projectile launched at 45 degrees from level ground, the ratio of the horizontal range to the maximum height is
solution: Dividing R = u^2 sin 2 theta / g by H = u^2 sin^2 theta / (2 g) gives R / H = 2 sin 2 theta / sin^2 theta = 4 cot theta, that is R = 4 H / tan theta. At theta = 45 degrees, tan theta = 1, so R / H = 4.
formula_principle: R = 4 H / tan theta
common_misconception: Students misremember the numerical factor in the relation between range and maximum height.

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
concept_tested: Effect of doubling the launch speed at a fixed angle
stem: A projectile is fired at a fixed angle. If its launch speed is doubled, its horizontal range becomes
solution: The horizontal velocity u cos theta and the time of flight 2 u sin theta / g are each proportional to u, and the range is their product. Doubling u therefore multiplies the range by 2 x 2 = 4.
formula_principle: R = u^2 sin 2 theta / g, so R is proportional to u^2 at fixed theta
common_misconception: Students treat the range as proportional to the launch speed rather than to its square.

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
concept_tested: Effect of a smaller acceleration due to gravity
stem: A projectile fired on the earth with a certain speed and angle has range R. The same launch is repeated on a planet where the acceleration due to gravity is half that on the earth. The range there is
solution: For fixed launch speed and angle the range is inversely proportional to g. Halving g therefore doubles the range, so the new range is 2 R.
formula_principle: R = u^2 sin 2 theta / g, so R varies as 1 / g
common_misconception: Students assume the range is independent of g, or make it directly proportional to g.

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
concept_tested: Launch angle when range equals maximum height
stem: A projectile is fired from level ground so that its horizontal range equals its maximum height. The angle of projection satisfies
option_a: tan theta = 1, so theta is 45 degrees
option_b: tan theta = 1/4, so theta is about 14 degrees
option_c: tan theta = 4, so theta is about 76 degrees
option_d: tan theta = 2, so theta is about 63 degrees
correct_answer_text: tan theta = 4, so theta is about 76 degrees
solution: Setting R = H in R = 4 H / tan theta gives tan theta = 4, so theta = tan inverse 4, about 76 degrees. Equivalently, u^2 sin 2 theta / g = u^2 sin^2 theta / (2 g) reduces to 4 cos theta = sin theta.
formula_principle: R = 4 H / tan theta
common_misconception: Students invert the relation between range and height and obtain the complementary angle.

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
subtopic: Working back from T and R
concept_tested: Finding launch speed and angle from the time of flight and the range
stem: A projectile launched from level ground has a time of flight of 4 s and a horizontal range of 80 m, with g = 10 m s^-2. Its angle of projection and launch speed are
option_b: 45 degrees and 20 sqrt 2 m s^-1, about 28.3 m s^-1
correct_answer_text: 45 degrees and 20 sqrt 2 m s^-1, about 28.3 m s^-1
solution: From T = 4 s, u sin theta = g T / 2 = 10 x 4 / 2 = 20 m s^-1. From R = (u cos theta) T, u cos theta = 80 / 4 = 20 m s^-1. Since the two components are equal, theta = 45 degrees and u = sqrt(20^2 + 20^2) = 20 sqrt 2 m s^-1, about 28.3 m s^-1.
formula_principle: T = 2 u sin theta / g and R = (u cos theta) T
common_misconception: Students quote a single velocity component as the launch speed.

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
concept_tested: Finding the range from the launch speed and the maximum height
stem: A projectile fired at 40 m s^-1 from level ground rises to a maximum height of 20 m, with g = 10 m s^-2. Its horizontal range is
solution: From H = 20 m, sin^2 theta = 2 g H / u^2 = 2 x 10 x 20 / 1600 = 0.25, so sin theta = 0.5 and theta = 30 degrees. Then R = 1600 x sin 60 / 10 = 160 x (sqrt 3 / 2) = 80 sqrt 3 m, about 138.6 m.
formula_principle: H = u^2 sin^2 theta / (2 g), then R = u^2 sin 2 theta / g
common_misconception: Students forget to double the angle when moving from the height formula to the range formula.

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
concept_tested: General ratio of maximum heights for complementary angles
stem: Two projectiles fired with the same speed at complementary angles theta and (90 - theta) have maximum heights H1 and H2 respectively. The ratio H1 / H2 is
solution: H1 is proportional to sin^2 theta and H2 to sin^2(90 - theta) = cos^2 theta. Their ratio is therefore sin^2 theta / cos^2 theta = tan^2 theta. For theta = 30 degrees this gives 1/3, in agreement with the ratio 1 : 3 for 30 and 60 degrees.
formula_principle: H is proportional to sin^2 theta
common_misconception: Students invert the ratio, or use the first power of the trigonometric function.

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
concept_tested: Launch angle from given values of range and maximum height
stem: A projectile fired from level ground has a horizontal range of 60 m and a maximum height of 15 m. Its angle of projection is
solution: Using R = 4 H / tan theta gives tan theta = 4 H / R = 4 x 15 / 60 = 1, so theta = 45 degrees. As a check, the ratio R / H is 4, which is the value expected for a 45 degree launch.
formula_principle: tan theta = 4 H / R
common_misconception: Students invert the relation and obtain the complement of the correct angle.

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
concept_tested: Greatest vertical height for a thrower of known maximum range
stem: A cricketer can throw a ball to a maximum horizontal distance of 80 m on level ground. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the greatest height to which he can throw the same ball is
solution: The maximum range gives u^2 / g = 80, so u^2 = 800 m^2 s^-2. Throwing the ball vertically upwards with the same speed gives a rise of u^2 / (2 g) = 800 / 20 = 40 m, which is exactly half the maximum range.
formula_principle: R_max = u^2 / g; greatest height for vertical projection = u^2 / (2 g)
common_misconception: Students equate the greatest vertical height with the greatest horizontal range.

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
concept_tested: Difference of maximum heights for two launch angles
stem: Two balls are thrown from level ground with the same speed 20 m s^-1, one at 30 degrees and the other at 60 degrees, with g = 10 m s^-2. The difference between their maximum heights is
solution: With u^2 / (2 g) = 400 / 20 = 20 m, the heights are 20 sin^2 30 = 5 m and 20 sin^2 60 = 15 m. Their difference is 15 - 5 = 10 m.
formula_principle: H = u^2 sin^2 theta / (2 g)
common_misconception: Students add the two heights, or compute only one of them.

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
concept_tested: Separation of two projectiles launched simultaneously
stem: From the top of a tall tower two balls are thrown simultaneously with the same speed 20 m s^-1, one vertically upwards and the other horizontally. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the distance between them 2 s later, both still being in flight, is
solution: Taking horizontal as i and vertical as j, the launch velocities are 20 j and 20 i m s^-1. Since both balls have the same acceleration g, the relative acceleration is zero and the relative velocity stays at 20 j - 20 i m s^-1, of magnitude 20 sqrt 2 m s^-1. After 2 s the separation is 20 sqrt 2 x 2 = 40 sqrt 2 m, about 56.6 m.
formula_principle: Both projectiles have the same acceleration, so their relative acceleration is zero and their relative velocity is constant
common_misconception: Students try to compute two separate trajectories and forget that gravity cancels out in the relative motion.

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
concept_tested: Interval between the landings of two projectiles
stem: Two stones are thrown simultaneously from the same point on level ground with the same speed 20 m s^-1, one at 30 degrees and the other at 60 degrees to the horizontal, with g = 10 m s^-2. The time interval between their landings is
solution: The times of flight are 2 x 20 sin 30 / 10 = 2 s and 2 x 20 sin 60 / 10 = 2 sqrt 3 s, about 3.46 s. Their difference is 2 sqrt 3 - 2 = 2 (sqrt 3 - 1) s, about 1.46 s, even though both stones land at the same distance from the throwing point.
formula_principle: T = 2 u sin theta / g
common_misconception: Students assume that complementary launch angles give the same time of flight because they give the same range.

major_topic: Time of Flight Maximum Height Range
concept_tested: Ratio of the range at 30 degrees to the maximum range
stem: A projectile fired at 45 degrees from level ground has range R. Fired with the same speed at 30 degrees, its range is
solution: The range at 45 degrees is u^2 sin 90 / g = u^2 / g = R. At 30 degrees it is u^2 sin 60 / g = (sqrt 3 / 2) u^2 / g. The ratio of the second to the first is sqrt 3 / 2, about 0.87, so the range at 30 degrees is smaller, as it must be since 45 degrees gives the largest possible range.
formula_principle: R = u^2 sin 2 theta / g
common_misconception: Students forget to double the launch angle inside the sine, and so obtain a ratio of one half.

concept_tested: What the time of fall for a horizontal projection depends on
stem: A body is projected horizontally from the top of a tower. The time it takes to reach the ground depends on
option_a: the horizontal speed of projection alone
option_b: the height of the tower alone, for a given value of g
option_c: both the height of the tower and the horizontal speed of projection
option_d: the mass of the body as well as the height of the tower
correct_answer_text: the height of the tower alone, for a given value of g
solution: For a horizontal projection the initial vertical velocity is zero, so h = (1/2) g t^2 and t = sqrt(2 h / g). This contains only h and g, so the time of fall is the same as for a body simply dropped from the same height, whatever the horizontal speed.
formula_principle: t = sqrt(2 h / g), obtained from h = (1/2) g t^2 with zero initial vertical velocity
common_misconception: Students expect a faster horizontal launch to keep the body in the air longer.

concept_tested: Numerical time of fall from a given height
stem: A stone is projected horizontally from a height of 20 m above level ground, with g = 10 m s^-2. It reaches the ground after
solution: Here t = sqrt(2 x 20 / 10) = sqrt 4 = 2 s.
formula_principle: t = sqrt(2 h / g)
common_misconception: Students omit the factor 2 or forget to take the square root.

concept_tested: Horizontal distance for a projection from a tower
stem: A ball is thrown horizontally at 15 m s^-1 from the top of a 20 m tower, with g = 10 m s^-2. It strikes the ground at a horizontal distance from the foot of the tower of
solution: The time of fall is sqrt(2 x 20 / 10) = 2 s. The horizontal velocity stays at 15 m s^-1, so the horizontal distance is 15 x 2 = 30 m.
formula_principle: t = sqrt(2 h / g); x = u t
common_misconception: Students compute the time of fall incorrectly, or mix the vertical and horizontal distances.

concept_tested: Landing speed for a horizontal projection
stem: A ball is projected horizontally at 15 m s^-1 from a height of 20 m, with g = 10 m s^-2. Its speed just before it strikes the ground is
solution: The fall takes sqrt(2 x 20 / 10) = 2 s, so the vertical component on landing is 10 x 2 = 20 m s^-1 while the horizontal component stays at 15 m s^-1. The landing speed is sqrt(15^2 + 20^2) = sqrt(225 + 400) = 25 m s^-1.
formula_principle: v_y = g t with t = sqrt(2 h / g); speed = sqrt(v_x^2 + v_y^2)
common_misconception: Students add perpendicular components arithmetically, or ignore one of them.

concept_tested: Comparing a dropped body with one projected horizontally
stem: From the top of the same tower one ball is simply dropped and another is thrown horizontally at the same instant. Neglecting air resistance,
option_a: the dropped ball reaches the ground first, since it travels a shorter path
option_b: the ball thrown horizontally reaches the ground first, since it has the greater initial speed
option_c: the dropped ball reaches the ground first, since gravity acts wholly on it while it is shared for the other
option_d: both reach the ground at the same instant, since their vertical motions are identical
correct_answer_text: both reach the ground at the same instant, since their vertical motions are identical
solution: Both balls start with zero vertical velocity and fall through the same height under the same acceleration g. Their vertical equations are identical, so both take t = sqrt(2 h / g) to reach the ground. The horizontal velocity of the second ball only determines where it lands, not when.
formula_principle: Vertical motion is governed only by g and the initial vertical velocity, which is zero for both
common_misconception: Students believe a horizontally launched body stays in the air longer than a dropped one.

concept_tested: Package released from a moving aeroplane
stem: An aeroplane flying horizontally at 100 m s^-1 at a height of 500 m releases a package, with g = 10 m s^-2. The horizontal distance travelled by the package before it strikes the ground is
solution: The fall takes sqrt(2 x 500 / 10) = sqrt 100 = 10 s. The package keeps the horizontal velocity of the aeroplane, 100 m s^-1, so it travels 100 x 10 = 1000 m horizontally.
formula_principle: t = sqrt(2 h / g); x = u t
common_misconception: Students forget that the released package retains the horizontal velocity of the aeroplane.

subtopic: Motion seen from the moving frame
concept_tested: Path of a released package as seen by the pilot
stem: A package is released from an aeroplane flying horizontally with constant velocity. As seen by the pilot, the package appears to move
option_a: vertically downwards, staying directly below the aeroplane
option_b: backwards along a curved path, falling behind the aeroplane
option_c: forwards along a curved path, moving ahead of the aeroplane
option_d: vertically downwards but drifting steadily behind the aeroplane
correct_answer_text: vertically downwards, staying directly below the aeroplane
solution: The package leaves with the same horizontal velocity as the aeroplane, and no horizontal force acts on either afterwards. Their horizontal velocities therefore stay equal, so relative to the pilot the package has only a vertical velocity and appears to drop straight down, remaining directly below the aeroplane. To a ground observer the same package traces a parabola.
formula_principle: Relative horizontal velocity of the package with respect to the aeroplane is zero
common_misconception: Students assume the package must fall behind because the aeroplane is moving fast.

concept_tested: Finding the launch speed from the landing direction
stem: A ball thrown horizontally from a cliff strikes the ground 3 s later, its velocity then making 60 degrees with the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the speed with which it was thrown is
option_a: 30 sqrt 3 m s^-1, about 52.0 m s^-1
option_c: 10 sqrt 3 m s^-1, about 17.3 m s^-1
correct_answer_text: 10 sqrt 3 m s^-1, about 17.3 m s^-1
solution: After 3 s the vertical component is v_y = 10 x 3 = 30 m s^-1. Since the velocity makes 60 degrees with the horizontal, tan 60 = 30 / v_x, so v_x = 30 / sqrt 3 = 10 sqrt 3 m s^-1, about 17.3 m s^-1. This horizontal component is the launch speed.
formula_principle: v_y = g t; tan(angle with horizontal) = v_y / v_x
common_misconception: Students multiply by the tangent instead of dividing by it when working back to the horizontal component.

concept_tested: Direction and magnitude of the landing velocity
stem: A stone is thrown horizontally at 20 m s^-1 from a tower 20 m high, with g = 10 m s^-2. The angle its velocity makes with the horizontal on striking the ground, and its speed there, are
option_c: 45 degrees and 20 sqrt 2 m s^-1, about 28.3 m s^-1
correct_answer_text: 45 degrees and 20 sqrt 2 m s^-1, about 28.3 m s^-1
solution: The fall takes sqrt(2 x 20 / 10) = 2 s, so v_y = 10 x 2 = 20 m s^-1 while v_x stays at 20 m s^-1. Since the components are equal, the velocity makes 45 degrees with the horizontal, and its magnitude is sqrt(400 + 400) = 20 sqrt 2 m s^-1, about 28.3 m s^-1.
formula_principle: t = sqrt(2 h / g); v_y = g t; tan(angle) = v_y / v_x
common_misconception: Students report the launch speed as the landing speed even after finding the correct direction.

concept_tested: Launch speed for which the horizontal distance equals the height
stem: A body is projected horizontally from a height of 20 m and lands at a horizontal distance from the launch point equal to that height, with g = 10 m s^-2. Its speed of projection was
option_d: 10 sqrt 2 m s^-1, about 14.1 m s^-1
solution: The time of fall is sqrt(2 x 20 / 10) = 2 s. Requiring the horizontal distance to equal the 20 m height gives u x 2 = 20, so u = 10 m s^-1. In general the condition x = h gives u = sqrt(g h / 2).
formula_principle: x = u sqrt(2 h / g); setting x = h gives u = sqrt(g h / 2)
common_misconception: Students confuse the launch speed with the landing speed, or mis-evaluate the fall time.

concept_tested: Relation between linear speed, radius and angular speed
stem: A particle moves in a circle of radius r with angular speed omega. Its linear speed v is given by
solution: In time t the particle sweeps an angle omega t, so the arc length covered is r omega t. Dividing by t gives the linear speed v = r omega.
formula_principle: v = r omega
common_misconception: Students confuse the expression for speed with the expression for centripetal acceleration.

concept_tested: Direction of the acceleration in uniform circular motion
stem: In uniform circular motion the acceleration of the particle is directed
option_a: away from the centre, along the outward radius
option_b: along the tangent, in the direction of motion
option_c: along the tangent, opposite to the direction of motion
option_d: towards the centre of the circle, along the radius
correct_answer_text: towards the centre of the circle, along the radius
solution: In uniform circular motion the speed does not change, so there is no tangential acceleration. What does change is the direction of the velocity, and the change in the velocity vector always points towards the centre of the circle. The acceleration is therefore radially inward, with magnitude v^2 / r.
formula_principle: a = v^2 / r directed towards the centre
common_misconception: Students take the acceleration to be directed outwards, confusing it with the outward pull they feel in a turning vehicle.

concept_tested: Centripetal acceleration from radius and angular speed
stem: A particle moves in a circle of radius 2 m with a constant angular speed of 5 rad s^-1. Its centripetal acceleration is
solution: Here a = r omega^2 = 2 x 5^2 = 2 x 25 = 50 m s^-2, directed towards the centre. The same result follows from v = r omega = 10 m s^-1 and a = v^2 / r = 100 / 2 = 50 m s^-2.
formula_principle: a = r omega^2
common_misconception: Students omit the radius or forget to square the angular speed.

concept_tested: Centripetal acceleration from linear speed and radius
stem: A car goes round a circular bend of radius 5 m at a steady speed of 10 m s^-1. Its centripetal acceleration is
solution: Here a = v^2 / r = 10^2 / 5 = 100 / 5 = 20 m s^-2, directed towards the centre of the bend.
formula_principle: a = v^2 / r
common_misconception: Students forget to square the speed, or forget to divide by the radius.

concept_tested: Centripetal acceleration from a stated rate of revolution
stem: A particle makes 60 revolutions per minute on a circle of radius 0.5 m. Its centripetal acceleration is
option_a: 2 pi^2 m s^-2, about 19.7 m s^-2
option_b: 4 pi^2 m s^-2, about 39.5 m s^-2
option_c: pi^2 m s^-2, about 9.87 m s^-2
option_d: pi m s^-2, about 3.14 m s^-2
correct_answer_text: 2 pi^2 m s^-2, about 19.7 m s^-2
solution: Sixty revolutions per minute is one revolution per second, so omega = 2 pi rad s^-1. Then a = r omega^2 = 0.5 x (2 pi)^2 = 0.5 x 4 pi^2 = 2 pi^2 m s^-2, about 19.7 m s^-2. The linear speed is v = r omega = pi m s^-1.
formula_principle: omega = 2 pi n; a = r omega^2
common_misconception: Students forget to convert revolutions per minute into radian per second, or quote the speed where the acceleration is asked for.

concept_tested: Comparing two points on the same rotating disc
stem: Two particles are fixed on a rotating disc, one at distance r and the other at distance 2 r from the axis. Comparing them,
option_a: their linear speeds are equal and their centripetal accelerations are in the ratio 1 : 2
option_b: their angular speeds are in the ratio 2 : 1 and their centripetal accelerations are equal
option_c: their angular speeds are equal and their centripetal accelerations are in the ratio 1 : 4
option_d: their angular speeds are equal and their centripetal accelerations are in the ratio 1 : 2
correct_answer_text: their angular speeds are equal and their centripetal accelerations are in the ratio 1 : 2
solution: All points of a rigid rotating disc turn through the same angle in the same time, so omega is the same for both. Their linear speeds v = r omega are therefore in the ratio 1 : 2, and their centripetal accelerations a = r omega^2 are also in the ratio 1 : 2.
formula_principle: For a rigid body omega is common; v = r omega and a = r omega^2
common_misconception: Students use a = v^2 / r with a common v, or make the acceleration proportional to the square of the radius.

concept_tested: Constancy of the magnitude and direction of the acceleration
stem: For a particle in uniform circular motion, the acceleration is such that
option_a: both its magnitude and its direction are constant
option_b: it is zero, since the speed of the particle does not change
option_c: it is directed along the tangent and its magnitude changes continuously
option_d: its magnitude is constant while its direction changes continuously
correct_answer_text: its magnitude is constant while its direction changes continuously
solution: The magnitude of the centripetal acceleration is v^2 / r, which stays fixed because both v and r are fixed. Its direction, however, always points from the particle to the centre, and as the particle moves round the circle this direction turns continuously. Uniform circular motion is therefore an accelerated motion with an acceleration of constant magnitude but varying direction.
formula_principle: a = v^2 / r in magnitude, always directed towards the centre
common_misconception: Students describe uniform circular motion as unaccelerated, or as having a constant acceleration vector.

concept_tested: Average acceleration over half a revolution
stem: A particle moves at constant speed round a circle of radius 10 m, completing half a revolution in 5 s. The magnitude of its average acceleration over that half revolution is
option_a: 2 pi^2 / 5 m s^-2, about 3.9 m s^-2
option_c: 4 pi / 5 m s^-2, about 2.5 m s^-2
option_d: 2 pi / 5 m s^-2, about 1.26 m s^-2
correct_answer_text: 4 pi / 5 m s^-2, about 2.5 m s^-2
solution: The half circumference is pi x 10 = 10 pi m, covered in 5 s, so the speed is 2 pi m s^-1. After half a revolution the velocity has the same magnitude but the opposite direction, so the change in velocity has magnitude 2 x 2 pi = 4 pi m s^-1. Dividing by 5 s gives an average acceleration of 4 pi / 5 m s^-2, about 2.5 m s^-2.
formula_principle: Average acceleration = change in velocity / time; over half a revolution the velocity reverses
common_misconception: Students quote the instantaneous centripetal acceleration when the average acceleration over an interval is asked for, or set the change in velocity to zero because the speed is unchanged.

concept_tested: The first law identifies inertia as a property of matter
stem: Newton's first law of motion is essentially a statement about which property of matter?
option_a: The tendency of a body to resist any change in its total mass
option_b: The tendency of a body to return to its original position after being displaced
option_c: The tendency of a body to move towards a region of lower potential energy
option_d: The tendency of a body to resist any change in its state of rest or of uniform motion
correct_answer_text: The tendency of a body to resist any change in its state of rest or of uniform motion
solution: The first law says a body cannot change its own state of rest or of uniform straight line motion. This built in resistance to a change of state is called inertia, which is why the first law is also called the law of inertia. Mass is the quantitative measure of inertia.
formula_principle: First law: a body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless a net external force acts on it.
common_misconception: Students think the first law says a force is needed to keep a body moving, because in daily life friction always acts.

concept_tested: Second law in momentum form
stem: According to Newton's second law, the net external force acting on a body is equal to
option_a: the rate of change of its kinetic energy
option_b: the rate of change of its linear momentum
option_c: the product of its mass and its velocity
option_d: the rate of change of its displacement
correct_answer_text: the rate of change of its linear momentum
solution: The general statement of the second law is that the net external force equals the time rate of change of linear momentum. For a body of constant mass, dp/dt = m dv/dt = m a, giving the familiar form F = m a.
formula_principle: F = dp/dt, which reduces to F = m a when the mass is constant.
common_misconception: Students memorise only F = m a and cannot state the law for situations where mass changes, such as a rocket.

concept_tested: Action and reaction act on different bodies
stem: A book lies at rest on a horizontal table. The reaction to the gravitational force exerted by the earth on the book is
option_a: the gravitational force exerted by the book on the earth
option_b: the normal force exerted by the table on the book
option_c: the normal force exerted by the book on the table
option_d: the weight of the table pressing on the floor
correct_answer_text: the gravitational force exerted by the book on the earth
solution: The pull of the earth on the book is gravitational. Its third law partner must be gravitational, of the same magnitude, opposite in direction, and must act on the earth. That force is the gravitational pull of the book on the earth.
formula_principle: Third law: forces occur in pairs that are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, of the same nature, and act on two different bodies.
common_misconception: Students pick the normal reaction as the reaction to weight because the two happen to balance in this static situation.

concept_tested: Dimensions of force
stem: A student checks an equation by dimensions and needs the dimensions of force. These are
solution: Force is mass times acceleration. Acceleration has dimensions [L T^-2], so force has dimensions [M^1 L^1 T^-2]. The corresponding SI unit is the newton, equal to kg m s^-2.
formula_principle: F = m a, so [F] = [M][L T^-2].
common_misconception: Students confuse the dimensions of force with those of energy by carrying an extra factor of length.

concept_tested: Direct use of F = m a
stem: A net force of 20 N acts on a body of mass 5 kg lying on a smooth horizontal surface. The acceleration produced is
solution: Using a = F/m with F = 20 N and m = 5 kg gives a = 20/5 = 4 m s^-2, directed along the applied force.
formula_principle: a = F/m.
common_misconception: Students invert the ratio and divide mass by force when the numbers make either order look reasonable.

concept_tested: Recognising a non inertial frame
stem: Which of the following is a non inertial frame of reference?
option_a: A car moving along a circular track at constant speed
option_b: A train moving on a straight track with constant velocity
option_c: A lift moving upward with constant velocity
option_d: A ship sailing along a straight line at steady speed
correct_answer_text: A car moving along a circular track at constant speed
solution: A car on a circular track has a centripetal acceleration even though its speed is constant, because the direction of its velocity keeps changing. An accelerated frame is non inertial, so Newton's laws need a pseudo force there. The other three frames move with constant velocity and are inertial.
formula_principle: A frame is inertial if it has zero acceleration. Any accelerated frame, including one turning at constant speed, is non inertial.
common_misconception: Students equate constant speed with zero acceleration and forget that a change of direction is also an acceleration.

concept_tested: Force from a uniform change of velocity
stem: A body of mass 2 kg moving with a velocity of 10 m s^-1 is brought to rest uniformly in 4 s. The magnitude of the retarding force is
solution: The retardation is (10 - 0)/4 = 2.5 m s^-2. Hence the force is F = 2 x 2.5 = 5 N, directed opposite to the motion. The same result follows from impulse, since the momentum change is 2 x 10 = 20 kg m s^-1 over 4 s, giving 20/4 = 5 N.
formula_principle: F = m (v - u)/t.
common_misconception: Students report the acceleration or the momentum change as the answer instead of completing the calculation of force.

concept_tested: Third law pair acts on different bodies
stem: A horse pulls a cart forward and the cart pulls the horse backward with an equal and opposite force. The cart nevertheless accelerates forward because
option_a: the force exerted by the horse on the cart is slightly greater than the force exerted by the cart on the horse
option_b: the two forces of the pair act on different bodies, and the net force on the cart alone is forward
option_c: the force exerted by the cart on the horse acts only after a short time delay
option_d: the weight of the cart cancels the backward pull exerted by the cart
correct_answer_text: the two forces of the pair act on different bodies, and the net force on the cart alone is forward
solution: To find the motion of the cart, only the forces on the cart are collected. These are the forward pull of the horse and the backward friction on the wheels. The backward pull of the cart on the horse appears in the equation of motion of the horse, not of the cart. When the forward pull exceeds the friction on the cart, the cart accelerates.
formula_principle: Third law forces are equal and opposite but act on two different bodies, so they never cancel in the equation of motion of either body.
common_misconception: Students add the action and reaction of a third law pair into one free body diagram and conclude that nothing can ever accelerate.

concept_tested: Apparent weight when the lift accelerates upward
stem: A man of mass 50 kg stands on a weighing machine inside a lift that is accelerating upward at 2 m s^-2. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the reading of the machine is
solution: The machine reads the normal reaction N. For the man, N - m g = m a with the acceleration upward, so N = m(g + a) = 50 x (10 + 2) = 50 x 12 = 600 N.
formula_principle: For a lift accelerating upward with acceleration a, the normal reaction is N = m(g + a).
common_misconception: Students use m(g - a) whenever the lift is in motion, without checking the direction of the acceleration.

concept_tested: Apparent weight in free fall
stem: The cable of a lift snaps and the lift falls freely. A person of mass 60 kg inside stands on a weighing machine. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the machine reads
solution: In free fall the lift and the person both accelerate downward at g. The equation for the person is m g - N = m g, which gives N = 0. The person and the machine fall together and press on each other with no force, a state described as weightlessness.
formula_principle: N = m(g - a). In free fall a = g, so N = 0.
common_misconception: Students think weightlessness means gravity has disappeared, whereas gravity is precisely what is producing the free fall.

concept_tested: Acceleration is inversely proportional to mass for a given force
stem: The same constant force acts separately on two bodies X and Y of masses 2 kg and 8 kg, both initially at rest on a smooth horizontal surface. The ratio of the acceleration of X to that of Y is
solution: With F fixed, a = F/m, so a_X/a_Y = m_Y/m_X = 8/2 = 4. The lighter body accelerates four times as fast.
formula_principle: For a fixed force, a is proportional to 1/m.
common_misconception: Students take acceleration to be proportional to mass because heavier bodies feel harder to move.

concept_tested: Pseudo force in an accelerated frame
stem: Consider two statements. Statement P: Newton's laws in their usual form are valid only in inertial frames. Statement Q: They may still be used in an accelerated frame provided a pseudo force equal in magnitude to the mass times the acceleration of the frame, and opposite to it, is added to every body.
option_a: P is correct and Q is incorrect
option_b: P is incorrect and Q is correct
option_c: Both P and Q are incorrect
option_d: Both P and Q are correct
correct_answer_text: Both P and Q are correct
solution: Newton's laws hold in their simple form only in unaccelerated frames. In a frame accelerating with a0, the observed acceleration of a body differs from the true one by a0, and the discrepancy is absorbed by including a pseudo force of magnitude m a0 opposite to a0. Both statements are therefore correct.
formula_principle: In a frame with acceleration a0, add a pseudo force of magnitude m a0 directed opposite to a0 on every body of mass m.
common_misconception: Students believe a pseudo force is a real interaction and try to find its third law partner, which does not exist.

concept_tested: Resultant of perpendicular forces then acceleration
stem: Two perpendicular forces of magnitudes 3 N and 4 N act simultaneously on a body of mass 5 kg lying on a smooth horizontal surface. The magnitude of the acceleration produced is
solution: The resultant of the two forces is the square root of (3^2 + 4^2), which is 5 N. Dividing by the mass gives a = 5/5 = 1 m s^-2.
formula_principle: For perpendicular forces the resultant is the square root of the sum of the squares; then a = F/m.
common_misconception: Students add force magnitudes arithmetically instead of combining them as vectors.

concept_tested: Kinematics combined with the second law
stem: A constant force of 10 N acts for 5 s on a body of mass 2 kg initially at rest on a smooth horizontal surface. The distance covered in this time is
solution: The acceleration is a = 10/2 = 5 m s^-2. Starting from rest, s = (1/2) x 5 x 5^2 = (1/2) x 5 x 25 = 62.5 m.
formula_principle: a = F/m and s = u t + (1/2) a t^2 with u = 0.
common_misconception: Students drop the factor of one half or square the time incorrectly when combining the second law with kinematics.

concept_tested: Slope of a momentum against time graph
stem: The linear momentum of a body is plotted against time and the graph is a straight line through the origin whose slope is 6 kg m s^-2. The magnitude of the net force acting on the body is
solution: The second law in its general form states that force equals the rate of change of momentum, which is the slope of the graph. A slope of 6 kg m s^-2 therefore corresponds to a constant force of 6 N.
formula_principle: F = dp/dt, so the force is the slope of the momentum against time graph.
common_misconception: Students confuse a straight line graph with an unchanging quantity and answer that the force is zero.

concept_tested: Deducing the motion of a lift from the balance reading
stem: A man of mass 50 kg stands on a spring balance inside a lift and the balance reads 400 N. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the lift must be
solution: The true weight is 50 x 10 = 500 N, and the balance reads less than this, so the acceleration must be directed downward. Writing N = m(g - a) gives 400 = 50(10 - a), so 10 - a = 8 and a = 2 m s^-2 downward. Note that the lift could be moving upward while slowing down, since only the acceleration matters.
formula_principle: N = m(g - a) for a lift accelerating downward with acceleration a.
common_misconception: Students assume a reduced reading means the lift is moving downward, whereas it only means the acceleration is downward.

concept_tested: Plumb line in a uniformly accelerating vehicle
stem: A small bob hangs from the roof of a car by a light string. The car moves along a horizontal road with a constant acceleration of 10 m s^-2. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the string settles at an angle with the vertical of
solution: Resolving the tension, the vertical component balances the weight, so T cos of the angle equals m g, and the horizontal component supplies the acceleration, so T sin of the angle equals m a. Dividing gives tan of the angle equal to a/g = 10/10 = 1, so the angle is 45 degrees. The bob tilts backward, that is, opposite to the acceleration.
formula_principle: For a bob hanging in a vehicle with horizontal acceleration a, tan of the angle with the vertical equals a/g.
common_misconception: Students think the string stays vertical because gravity is vertical, forgetting that the bob must also accelerate horizontally.

concept_tested: Identifying a genuine action and reaction pair
stem: A block rests on a horizontal floor. Which of the following is a correct action and reaction pair under the third law?
option_a: The weight of the block and the normal force of the floor on the block
option_b: The weight of the block and the push of the block on the floor
option_c: The push of the floor on the block and the push of the block on the floor
option_d: The weight of the block and the weight of the floor
correct_answer_text: The push of the floor on the block and the push of the block on the floor
solution: The contact interaction between block and floor gives one force on the block from the floor and one force on the floor from the block. These form the pair. The weight of the block is gravitational and its partner is the pull of the block on the earth. Weight and normal reaction act on the same body and so can never be a third law pair, even though they are numerically equal when the block is in equilibrium on a horizontal floor.
formula_principle: A third law pair is equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, of the same nature, and consists of one force on each of the two interacting bodies.
common_misconception: Students treat any two equal and opposite forces as an action and reaction pair without checking that they act on different bodies.

concept_tested: Direction of acceleration when a lift moving down slows
stem: A lift of total mass 500 kg is moving downward and is slowing down at the rate of 2 m s^-2. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the tension in the supporting cable is
solution: The lift moves downward but its speed decreases, so its acceleration points upward with magnitude 2 m s^-2. Then T - m g = m a gives T = m(g + a) = 500 x 12 = 6000 N, which is larger than the weight of 5000 N.
formula_principle: T - m g = m a with a taken positive upward. A body moving down while slowing has an upward acceleration.
common_misconception: Students set the sign of the acceleration from the direction of motion instead of from the direction of the change of velocity.

concept_tested: Force from a given position time relation
stem: The position of a particle of mass 2 kg moving along a straight line is given by x = 3 t^2 + 4 t, where x is in metre and t in second. The magnitude of the net force acting on the particle is
solution: Differentiating once gives the velocity 6 t + 4, and differentiating again gives a constant acceleration of 6 m s^-2. Hence F = m a = 2 x 6 = 12 N, and the force is constant in time.
formula_principle: Differentiate the position twice to get the acceleration, then apply F = m a.
common_misconception: Students stop after one differentiation and use the velocity expression in place of the acceleration.

concept_tested: Maximum acceleration set by a breaking tension
stem: A monkey of mass 20 kg climbs a rope that can withstand a maximum tension of 300 N. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the greatest upward acceleration with which the monkey can climb without breaking the rope is
solution: The rope tension must satisfy T = m(g + a) and cannot exceed 300 N. Hence 20(10 + a) is at most 300, so 10 + a is at most 15 and a is at most 5 m s^-2. If the monkey merely hangs on, the tension is 200 N, and if it climbs with acceleration 5 m s^-2 the tension reaches exactly 300 N.
formula_principle: For a body climbing with upward acceleration a, T - m g = m a, so T = m(g + a).
common_misconception: Students forget that the rope must support the weight as well as supply the accelerating force, and so allow far too large an acceleration.

concept_tested: Accelerating a smooth wedge so the block does not slide
stem: A block is placed on the smooth face of a wedge whose inclined face makes 45 degrees with the horizontal. The wedge is given a horizontal acceleration such that the block stays at rest relative to the wedge. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, this acceleration is
solution: Only the weight and the normal reaction act on the block. The normal reaction is perpendicular to the inclined face, so its vertical component must balance the weight while its horizontal component supplies the acceleration. Writing N cos theta equal to m g and N sin theta equal to m a and dividing gives a = g tan theta. With theta equal to 45 degrees, tan theta is 1, so a = 10 m s^-2.
formula_principle: For a block riding on a smooth wedge of inclination theta without sliding, a = g tan theta.
common_misconception: Students think a body on a smooth incline must always slide, and do not see that a suitable acceleration of the support can hold it in place.

concept_tested: Unit of impulse
stem: The SI unit of impulse, the newton second, is identical to the SI unit of
solution: One newton second equals one kg m s^-2 multiplied by one second, that is one kg m s^-1, which is the unit of linear momentum. This equality of units reflects the impulse momentum theorem, which states that impulse equals the change in momentum.
formula_principle: Impulse = F t and momentum = m v, both measured in N s, equivalently kg m s^-1.
common_misconception: Students assume impulse must share its unit with force because the newton appears in its name.

concept_tested: Direct use of p = m v
stem: A body of mass 2 kg moves with a speed of 5 m s^-1. Its linear momentum is
solution: Linear momentum is the product of mass and velocity, so p = 2 x 5 = 10 kg m s^-1, directed along the velocity.
formula_principle: p = m v.
common_misconception: Students confuse momentum with kinetic energy and insert the factor of one half and the square of the speed.

concept_tested: Statement of the impulse momentum theorem
stem: The impulse of a force acting on a body during a time interval is equal to
option_a: the change in the kinetic energy of the body
option_b: the linear momentum of the body at the end of the interval
option_c: the rate of change of momentum of the body
option_d: the change in the linear momentum of the body
correct_answer_text: the change in the linear momentum of the body
solution: Integrating the second law F = dp/dt over the interval of action gives the impulse on the left and the change of momentum on the right. Hence impulse equals final momentum minus initial momentum, a vector relation.
formula_principle: Impulse J = F t for a constant force, and J equals the change in momentum p2 - p1.
common_misconception: Students confuse the impulse momentum theorem with the work energy theorem and equate impulse to a change of energy.

concept_tested: Dimensions of impulse
stem: The dimensional formula of impulse is
solution: Multiplying the dimensions of force, [M^1 L^1 T^-2], by the dimension of time, [T^1], gives [M^1 L^1 T^-1]. This matches the dimensions of momentum, [M][L T^-1], as it must.
formula_principle: Impulse = force x time, so [J] = [M L T^-2][T] = [M L T^-1].
common_misconception: Students carry the dimensions of force straight over to impulse and forget the extra factor of time.

concept_tested: Impulse of a constant force
stem: A constant force of 5 N acts on a body for 4 s. The magnitude of the impulse imparted is
solution: Impulse is the product of the constant force and the time for which it acts, so J = 5 x 4 = 20 N s. The body therefore gains 20 kg m s^-1 of momentum along the direction of the force.
formula_principle: For a constant force, impulse = F t.
common_misconception: Students treat impulse as an average rate and divide instead of multiplying.

concept_tested: Impulse when a ball rebounds with the same speed
stem: A ball of mass 0.2 kg strikes a rigid wall normally with a speed of 10 m s^-1 and rebounds with the same speed. The magnitude of the impulse received by the ball is
solution: Take the direction towards the wall as positive. The initial momentum is 0.2 x 10 = 2 kg m s^-1 and the final momentum is -2 kg m s^-1. The change is -2 - 2 = -4 kg m s^-1, so the impulse has magnitude 4 N s directed away from the wall.
formula_principle: Impulse equals the change in momentum. For a reversal at the same speed the magnitude is 2 m v.
common_misconception: Students treat momentum as a scalar, see the same speed before and after, and conclude that the impulse is zero.

subtopic: Force from rate of change of momentum
concept_tested: Average force during a catch
stem: A cricket ball of mass 0.15 kg moving at 20 m s^-1 is brought to rest by a fielder in 0.1 s. The average force exerted on the ball is
solution: The momentum change has magnitude 0.15 x 20 = 3 kg m s^-1. Dividing by the contact time gives F = 3/0.1 = 30 N.
formula_principle: F = change in momentum divided by the time of contact.
common_misconception: Students apply the factor of two that belongs to a rebound to a case where the body is merely stopped.

subtopic: Force from rate of change of momentum
concept_tested: Why a fielder pulls his hands back
stem: A fielder draws his hands backward while catching a fast moving ball. This action
option_a: reduces the impulse received by the hands so that the force becomes smaller
option_b: reduces the momentum of the ball before it reaches the hands
option_c: increases the impulse but spreads it over a larger area of the palm
option_d: increases the time of impact so that the average force on the hands is reduced, the impulse being the same
correct_answer_text: increases the time of impact so that the average force on the hands is reduced, the impulse being the same
solution: The ball must lose all its momentum, so the impulse delivered is fixed at m v whatever the fielder does. Since the impulse equals the average force times the contact time, lengthening the contact time by moving the hands back reduces the average force proportionately, and the catch hurts less.
formula_principle: Impulse is fixed at m v; since F t equals the impulse, a larger t means a smaller average F.
common_misconception: Students say the impulse is reduced, confusing the fixed total impulse with the peak force felt.

concept_tested: Momentum of two bodies with equal kinetic energy
stem: Two bodies X and Y of masses 1 kg and 4 kg have the same kinetic energy. The ratio of the magnitude of the momentum of X to that of Y is
solution: Writing p as the square root of 2 m K shows that for the same K the momentum varies as the square root of the mass. Hence p_X/p_Y is the square root of 1/4, which is 1/2, so the ratio is 1 to 2.
formula_principle: Since K = p^2/(2m), for equal K the momentum is proportional to the square root of the mass.
common_misconception: Students use the mass ratio directly instead of the square root, forgetting that momentum enters the energy as a square.

concept_tested: Impulse from a change of velocity
stem: A body of mass 5 kg has its velocity changed from 2 m s^-1 to 8 m s^-1 along the same straight line by a constant force acting for 3 s. The impulse received by the body is
solution: The change of velocity is 8 - 2 = 6 m s^-1, so the impulse is 5 x 6 = 30 N s. Dividing by 3 s would give the constant force, 10 N, but the question asks for the impulse itself.
formula_principle: Impulse = m(v - u); the force follows as impulse divided by time.
common_misconception: Students answer with the force because the time of action is quoted in the question.

concept_tested: Impulse from the floor on a bouncing ball
stem: A ball of mass 0.1 kg is dropped from a height of 5 m onto a floor and rebounds to the same height. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the magnitude of the impulse the floor gives the ball is
solution: The speed just before impact is the square root of (2 x 10 x 5), which is 10 m s^-1. Since it rebounds to the same height, it leaves at 10 m s^-1 upward. The momentum changes from 1 kg m s^-1 downward to 1 kg m s^-1 upward, a change of magnitude 2 N s.
formula_principle: v = square root of (2 g h); impulse = 2 m v for a rebound to the same height.
common_misconception: Students count only one leg of the journey and halve the correct impulse.

concept_tested: Speed acquired from a given impulse
stem: A body of mass 6 kg initially at rest on a smooth horizontal surface receives an impulse of 30 N s. Its final speed is
solution: Starting from rest, the whole impulse appears as final momentum, so m v = 30 and v = 30/6 = 5 m s^-1.
formula_principle: Impulse = m v - m u; with u = 0 this gives v = J/m.
common_misconception: Students confuse impulse with momentum per unit mass and skip the division by the mass.

concept_tested: Impulse as the area under a force time graph
stem: A force acting on a body rises uniformly from zero to 20 N in 0.2 s and then falls uniformly back to zero in the next 0.2 s. The impulse imparted is
solution: The graph is a triangle of base 0.4 s and height 20 N. Its area is (1/2) x 0.4 x 20 = 4 N s, which is the impulse imparted.
formula_principle: Impulse equals the area under the force against time graph.
common_misconception: Students take the product of the peak force and the total time and forget the factor of one half for a triangular pulse.

subtopic: Force from rate of change of momentum
concept_tested: Average force needed to hold a machine gun
stem: A machine gun fires 10 bullets per second, each of mass 20 g, with a muzzle speed of 500 m s^-1. The average force needed to hold the gun steady is
solution: Each bullet leaves with momentum 0.02 x 500 = 10 kg m s^-1. Ten such bullets leave every second, so the gun must supply momentum at the rate of 10 x 10 = 100 kg m s^-1 per second, which is an average force of 100 N. By the third law the gun pushes back on the holder with the same average force.
formula_principle: Average force = (momentum carried by one bullet) x (number of bullets fired per second).
common_misconception: Students compute the impulse of one bullet and forget to multiply by the number fired per second.

subtopic: Force from rate of change of momentum
concept_tested: Force of a water jet that does not rebound
stem: Water strikes a wall normally at the rate of 2 kg per second with a speed of 10 m s^-1 and then runs down the wall without rebounding. The force on the wall is
solution: Every second, 2 kg of water arrives with momentum 2 x 10 = 20 kg m s^-1 and leaves with no momentum along the original direction. The wall therefore destroys 20 kg m s^-1 of momentum per second, which is a force of 20 N. Had the water rebounded with the same speed, the force would have been 40 N.
formula_principle: F = (dm/dt) v when the striking matter is brought to rest, and F = 2 (dm/dt) v when it rebounds elastically.
common_misconception: Students automatically insert a factor of two, which belongs only to the case of an elastic rebound.

concept_tested: Impulse of a force that grows linearly with time
stem: A force F = 6 t newton, with t in second, acts on a body of mass 3 kg initially at rest. The speed of the body at t = 2 s is
solution: The force grows from zero at t = 0 to 12 N at t = 2 s, so the graph is a triangle of base 2 s and height 12 N. Its area is (1/2) x 2 x 12 = 12 N s, which is the impulse. Then m v = 12 gives v = 12/3 = 4 m s^-1.
formula_principle: For a time dependent force the impulse is the area under the force time graph, here (1/2) x t x (6 t) = 3 t^2.
common_misconception: Students substitute the instantaneous final force into F t and so double the impulse of a linearly rising force.

concept_tested: Kinetic energy of two bodies with equal momentum
stem: Two bodies X and Y of masses 2 kg and 8 kg have equal linear momentum. The ratio of the kinetic energy of X to that of Y is
