solution: With p the same for both, K is inversely proportional to the mass. Hence K_X/K_Y = m_Y/m_X = 8/2 = 4, giving 4 to 1. The lighter body carries the larger kinetic energy, which is why a light fragment of an explosion is the dangerous one.
formula_principle: K = p^2/(2m), so for equal p the kinetic energy varies as 1/m.
common_misconception: Students mix up the equal momentum case with the equal energy case and use a square root where none belongs.

concept_tested: Impulse when the rebound height is smaller
stem: A ball of mass 0.5 kg is dropped from a height of 20 m and rebounds from the floor to a height of 5 m. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the magnitude of the impulse the floor gives the ball is
solution: The speed just before impact is the square root of (2 x 10 x 20), which is 20 m s^-1 downward. The speed just after is the square root of (2 x 10 x 5), which is 10 m s^-1 upward. Taking upward as positive, the momentum changes from -10 kg m s^-1 to +5 kg m s^-1, a change of 15 N s.
formula_principle: v = square root of (2 g h) for each leg; impulse = m(v_up + v_down) because the directions are opposite.
common_misconception: Students subtract the two speeds because the numbers look like a change, forgetting that the directions are opposite so the magnitudes add.

concept_tested: Impulse in an oblique bounce off a smooth wall
stem: A ball of mass 0.2 kg strikes a smooth vertical wall with a speed of 20 m s^-1 along a direction making 60 degrees with the normal to the wall, and rebounds with the same speed at the same angle. The magnitude of the impulse received by the ball is
solution: Resolve the velocity into a component along the normal, 20 cos 60 = 10 m s^-1, and a component along the wall, 20 sin 60 m s^-1. The smooth wall leaves the parallel component untouched and reverses the normal component. The change of momentum is therefore 2 x 0.2 x 10 = 4 N s, directed along the outward normal.
formula_principle: A smooth wall reverses only the normal component of velocity; impulse = 2 m v cos theta with theta measured from the normal.
common_misconception: Students use the whole speed rather than resolving it, and so double the impulse for an oblique impact.

concept_tested: Impulse when the direction of motion turns through a right angle
stem: A ball of mass 1 kg moving due east with a speed of 10 m s^-1 is struck so that it afterwards moves due north with the same speed. The magnitude of the impulse given to the ball is
solution: The initial momentum is 10 kg m s^-1 due east and the final momentum is 10 kg m s^-1 due north. The change is the final minus the initial, that is 10 north together with 10 west. These are perpendicular and equal, so the magnitude is the square root of (10^2 + 10^2), which is 10 sqrt(2), about 14.1 N s, directed north west.
formula_principle: Impulse is the vector difference of the final and initial momenta; for perpendicular vectors of equal magnitude p, the difference has magnitude p sqrt(2).
common_misconception: Students treat momentum as a scalar and conclude that no impulse is needed when only the direction changes.

concept_tested: Condition for conservation of linear momentum
stem: The total linear momentum of a system of particles stays constant in time provided
option_a: the net external force on the system is zero
option_b: the net internal force on the system is zero
option_c: the total kinetic energy of the system is constant
option_d: all the particles of the system have equal masses
correct_answer_text: the net external force on the system is zero
solution: Summing the second law over all the particles, the internal forces cancel in pairs by the third law, leaving dP/dt equal to the net external force. If that force is zero the total momentum P does not change, whatever violent interactions take place inside the system.
formula_principle: dP/dt equals the net external force, so P is constant when that force is zero.
common_misconception: Students look for the internal forces to vanish, not realising that they always cancel in pairs anyway.

concept_tested: Recoil as a consequence of momentum conservation
stem: When a bullet is fired from a gun, the gun recoils backward. This happens because
option_a: the total kinetic energy of the gun and bullet must stay zero
option_b: the gun is pushed back by the air displaced by the bullet
option_c: the total momentum of the gun and bullet must stay zero, so the two momenta are equal and opposite
option_d: the gun has a larger mass than the bullet
correct_answer_text: the total momentum of the gun and bullet must stay zero, so the two momenta are equal and opposite
solution: Before firing, the system is at rest and has zero total momentum. The explosion involves only internal forces, so the total momentum stays zero. The forward momentum of the bullet must therefore be matched by an equal backward momentum of the gun.
formula_principle: For an isolated gun and bullet system, m_bullet v_bullet + M_gun V_gun = 0.
common_misconception: Students explain the recoil by the mass of the gun rather than by conservation of momentum.

concept_tested: Recoil speed of a gun
stem: A gun of mass 4 kg fires a bullet of mass 20 g with a muzzle speed of 400 m s^-1. The recoil speed of the gun is
solution: The bullet carries momentum 0.02 x 400 = 8 kg m s^-1. The gun must carry 8 kg m s^-1 backward, so its recoil speed is 8/4 = 2 m s^-1.
formula_principle: M V = m v for a system starting from rest.
common_misconception: Students equate the speeds instead of the momenta of the gun and the bullet.

concept_tested: Basis of rocket propulsion
stem: A rocket accelerates forward in outer space because
option_a: the gases ejected backward carry momentum, so the rocket gains an equal momentum forward
option_b: the ejected gases push against the surrounding air
option_c: the burning of fuel reduces the weight of the rocket
option_d: the pressure of the burning gases is the same in all directions inside the rocket
correct_answer_text: the gases ejected backward carry momentum, so the rocket gains an equal momentum forward
solution: The rocket and its fuel form a system with no external force in free space, so the total momentum stays constant. The exhaust gases stream backward with large momentum, and the remaining rocket must acquire an equal forward momentum. Equivalently, by the third law the rocket pushes the gases back and the gases push the rocket forward.
formula_principle: Thrust = u (dm/dt), where u is the exhaust speed relative to the rocket and dm/dt the rate of ejection of mass.
common_misconception: Students think the exhaust must push against something outside, and so imagine that rockets cannot work in vacuum.

concept_tested: What is conserved in a collision
stem: In any collision between two bodies of an isolated system,
option_a: both the total linear momentum and the total kinetic energy are always conserved
option_b: the total kinetic energy is conserved but the total linear momentum need not be
option_c: the total linear momentum is conserved whether or not the kinetic energy is conserved
option_d: neither quantity is conserved unless the two bodies have equal masses
correct_answer_text: the total linear momentum is conserved whether or not the kinetic energy is conserved
solution: The impulsive forces during a collision are internal to the two body system and cancel in pairs, so the total momentum before equals the total momentum after. Kinetic energy, in contrast, can be converted into heat, sound and permanent deformation, and is conserved only in an elastic collision.
formula_principle: External forces are absent during the brief collision, so the total momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is conserved only if the collision is elastic.
common_misconception: Students assume that whenever momentum is conserved kinetic energy must be conserved too.

concept_tested: Two fragment explosion from rest
stem: A body at rest explodes into two pieces of masses 2 kg and 3 kg. If the 2 kg piece moves off with a speed of 6 m s^-1, the speed of the 3 kg piece is
solution: The 2 kg piece carries momentum 2 x 6 = 12 kg m s^-1. The 3 kg piece must carry 12 kg m s^-1 in the opposite direction, so its speed is 12/3 = 4 m s^-1.
formula_principle: Total momentum stays zero, so m1 v1 = m2 v2 in magnitude, in opposite directions.
common_misconception: Students equate the speeds of the fragments rather than their momenta.

concept_tested: Common velocity in a perfectly inelastic collision
stem: A body of mass 2 kg moving at 6 m s^-1 collides with a stationary body of mass 4 kg and the two move off together. Their common speed is
solution: The momentum before is 2 x 6 = 12 kg m s^-1 and the combined mass afterwards is 6 kg. Hence v = 12/6 = 2 m s^-1. Some kinetic energy is lost, but momentum is unchanged.
formula_principle: m1 u1 = (m1 + m2) v for a perfectly inelastic collision with the second body at rest.
common_misconception: Students take the arithmetic mean of the two speeds, which is right only when the masses are equal.

concept_tested: Recoil of a man on frictionless ice
stem: A man of mass 50 kg standing at rest on a frictionless horizontal ice surface throws a stone of mass 5 kg horizontally at 4 m s^-1. His recoil speed is
solution: The stone carries momentum 5 x 4 = 20 kg m s^-1. The man must carry the same momentum in the opposite direction, so his speed is 20/50 = 0.4 m s^-1.
formula_principle: M V = m v when the system starts from rest and there is no external horizontal force.
common_misconception: Students forget that on frictionless ice the man really does move, and answer zero or the speed of the stone.

concept_tested: Boat and passenger on still water
stem: A boy of mass 40 kg stands at rest on a boat of mass 160 kg floating on still water. He then walks along the boat with a speed of 1 m s^-1 relative to the water. Neglecting the resistance of the water, the speed of the boat relative to the water is
solution: Before the boy walks, the system is at rest, and the water offers no horizontal force, so the total momentum stays zero. The boy carries 40 x 1 = 40 kg m s^-1 forward, so the boat carries 40 kg m s^-1 backward and its speed is 40/160 = 0.25 m s^-1.
formula_principle: Total momentum stays zero: m_boy v_boy = m_boat v_boat, in opposite directions.
common_misconception: Students think the boat stays still because the boy pushes only on its floor, missing that this push is an internal force.

concept_tested: Two trolleys pushed apart by a spring
stem: Two trolleys X and Y of masses 2 kg and 6 kg are held together on a smooth horizontal track with a compressed spring between them. When they are released, the ratio of the speed of X to that of Y is
solution: The spring exerts internal forces only, so the total momentum stays zero. Hence 2 v_X = 6 v_Y, giving v_X/v_Y = 6/2 = 3. The light trolley moves off three times as fast.
formula_principle: For a system released from rest, m_X v_X = m_Y v_Y, so speed is inversely proportional to mass.
common_misconception: Students assume the spring gives both trolleys the same speed because it pushes both ends equally hard.

concept_tested: Bullet embedding in a block
stem: A bullet of mass 10 g moving at 500 m s^-1 embeds itself in a block of mass 990 g resting on a smooth horizontal surface. The common speed just after impact is
solution: The bullet brings momentum 0.01 x 500 = 5 kg m s^-1. The combined mass is 0.01 + 0.99 = 1 kg, so the common speed is 5/1 = 5 m s^-1.
formula_principle: m u = (m + M) v for a perfectly inelastic capture.
common_misconception: Students mix grams and kilograms and end up with a combined mass that is out by a factor of ten.

concept_tested: Momentum and energy in an explosion
stem: A stationary bomb explodes into several fragments. Which statement about the fragments is correct?
option_a: Both their total momentum and their total kinetic energy are zero
option_b: Their total momentum is greater than zero because the explosion supplies momentum
option_c: Their total kinetic energy is unchanged because momentum is conserved
option_d: Their total momentum is zero while their total kinetic energy is greater than before the explosion
correct_answer_text: Their total momentum is zero while their total kinetic energy is greater than before the explosion
solution: The explosive forces are internal, so the total momentum stays at its initial value of zero, with the fragment momenta cancelling as vectors. The chemical energy stored in the charge is released and appears largely as kinetic energy of the fragments, so the total kinetic energy rises from zero to a positive value.
formula_principle: Internal forces conserve total momentum but stored chemical energy can be converted into kinetic energy.
common_misconception: Students believe an explosion must supply momentum as well as energy, and so expect the total momentum to grow.

concept_tested: Three fragment explosion with two at right angles
stem: A shell at rest explodes into three fragments. Two of them, each of mass 1 kg, fly off at right angles to each other, each with a speed of 10 m s^-1. The third fragment has mass 2 kg. Its speed is
solution: Each 1 kg fragment carries momentum 1 x 10 = 10 kg m s^-1, and the two are perpendicular, so their resultant has magnitude 10 sqrt(2) kg m s^-1. The third fragment must carry an equal momentum in the opposite direction, so 2 v = 10 sqrt(2) and v = 5 sqrt(2), about 7.1 m s^-1.
formula_principle: The vector sum of all fragment momenta must be zero; perpendicular momenta of equal magnitude p combine to p sqrt(2).
common_misconception: Students add the two fragment momenta as numbers rather than combining perpendicular vectors.

concept_tested: Ballistic pendulum
stem: A bullet of mass 10 g moving horizontally at 400 m s^-1 embeds itself in a wooden block of mass 1.99 kg hanging from a long light string. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the height through which the block rises is
solution: The impact is perfectly inelastic, so 0.01 x 400 = 4 kg m s^-1 is shared by a total mass of 2 kg, giving a common speed of 2 m s^-1. The block and bullet then rise until this kinetic energy becomes potential energy, so h = v^2/(2 g) = 4/20 = 0.2 m.
formula_principle: Momentum conservation for the impact, m u = (m + M) v; then energy conservation for the swing, h = v^2/(2g).
common_misconception: Students apply energy conservation right through the impact, forgetting that a large part of the kinetic energy is lost when the bullet embeds itself.

concept_tested: Thrust developed by a rocket
stem: The exhaust gases of a rocket leave with a speed of 2000 m s^-1 relative to the rocket, and fuel is burnt at the steady rate of 5 kg s^-1. The thrust developed is
solution: Each second, 5 kg of gas is thrown backward at 2000 m s^-1 relative to the rocket, carrying away 5 x 2000 = 10000 kg m s^-1 of momentum. The rocket therefore experiences a forward force of 10000 N. The net acceleration is found by subtracting the weight where gravity acts.
formula_principle: Thrust = u (dm/dt), with u the exhaust speed relative to the rocket.
common_misconception: Students divide instead of multiplying, or confuse the thrust with the net force by forgetting the weight of the rocket.

concept_tested: Sharing of energy between gun and bullet
stem: A gun of mass 10 kg fires a bullet of mass 20 g with a muzzle speed of 500 m s^-1. The ratio of the kinetic energy of the bullet to that of the recoiling gun is
solution: Momentum conservation gives the gun a recoil speed of 0.02 x 500/10 = 1 m s^-1. The bullet has kinetic energy (1/2) x 0.02 x 500^2 = 2500 J while the gun has (1/2) x 10 x 1^2 = 5 J, a ratio of 500 to 1. This is just the inverse mass ratio, 10/0.02.
formula_principle: The two bodies have equal momenta, and K = p^2/(2m), so the kinetic energies are in the inverse ratio of the masses.
common_misconception: Students assume that equal and opposite momenta imply equal kinetic energies, and so expect a ratio of one to one.

concept_tested: Fraction of kinetic energy lost in a perfectly inelastic collision
stem: A body of mass 2 kg moving at 10 m s^-1 collides head on with a stationary body of mass 3 kg, and the two move off together. The percentage of the initial kinetic energy that is lost is
solution: Momentum conservation gives 2 x 10 = 5 v, so v = 4 m s^-1. The initial kinetic energy is (1/2) x 2 x 100 = 100 J and the final is (1/2) x 5 x 16 = 40 J. The loss is 60 J out of 100 J, that is 60 percent. In general the fraction lost is m2/(m1 + m2), here 3/5.
formula_principle: m1 u = (m1 + m2) v; then compare (1/2)(m1 + m2)v^2 with (1/2) m1 u^2.
common_misconception: Students quote the fraction that survives instead of the fraction lost, or expect no loss because momentum is conserved.

concept_tested: Man jumping off a trolley
stem: A man of mass 60 kg stands on a trolley of mass 40 kg, both at rest on a smooth horizontal track. The man jumps off horizontally with a speed of 4 m s^-1 with respect to the ground. The speed of the trolley just afterwards is
solution: The track is smooth, so there is no external horizontal force and the total momentum stays zero. The man carries 60 x 4 = 240 kg m s^-1 forward, so the trolley must carry 240 kg m s^-1 backward. Its speed is 240/40 = 6 m s^-1, and it is directed opposite to the jump.
formula_principle: Total momentum stays zero: m_man v_man = m_trolley v_trolley, in opposite directions.
common_misconception: Students divide by the combined mass of man and trolley, although the man is no longer on the trolley after the jump.

concept_tested: Condition for equilibrium under concurrent forces
stem: A set of concurrent forces keeps a body in equilibrium. This requires that
option_a: the sum of the magnitudes of all the forces is zero
option_b: the vector sum of all the forces is zero
option_c: all the forces have equal magnitudes
option_d: the largest force is equal to the sum of the remaining forces
correct_answer_text: the vector sum of all the forces is zero
solution: Equilibrium under concurrent forces means no net force, and force is a vector, so the requirement is that the vector sum vanishes. In practice this is applied by resolving all the forces along two perpendicular directions and setting each set of components to sum to zero.
formula_principle: For concurrent forces, equilibrium requires the vector sum to vanish, equivalently the sum of the components along any two perpendicular directions to vanish.
common_misconception: Students add force magnitudes as ordinary numbers and do not resolve them into components.

concept_tested: Components of a force
stem: A force of 20 N acts in a direction making 60 degrees with the horizontal. Its horizontal and vertical components are
solution: With the angle measured from the horizontal, the horizontal component is 20 cos 60 = 20 x 0.5 = 10 N and the vertical component is 20 sin 60 = 20 x (sqrt(3)/2) = 10 sqrt(3) N, about 17.3 N.
formula_principle: Component along the reference direction = F cos theta; component perpendicular to it = F sin theta.
common_misconception: Students interchange sine and cosine because they do not check which axis the given angle is measured from.

concept_tested: Scope of Lami's theorem
stem: Lami's theorem can be applied to
option_a: any number of forces acting at a point
option_b: three coplanar concurrent forces that keep a body in equilibrium
option_c: two forces acting on a body in equilibrium
option_d: three parallel forces acting on a rigid body
correct_answer_text: three coplanar concurrent forces that keep a body in equilibrium
solution: Lami's theorem follows from representing three equilibrium forces by the sides of a triangle taken in order and applying the sine rule. It therefore needs exactly three forces, all in one plane and all passing through one point.
formula_principle: Lami's theorem: each of three concurrent coplanar forces in equilibrium is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two.
common_misconception: Students apply Lami's theorem to four or more forces, or to parallel forces that are not concurrent.

concept_tested: Direction of the normal reaction
stem: The normal reaction exerted by a surface on a body resting on it
option_a: always has magnitude equal to the weight of the body
option_b: acts along the perpendicular to the surface of contact
option_c: acts along the direction in which the body tends to slide
option_d: acts vertically upward whatever the orientation of the surface
correct_answer_text: acts along the perpendicular to the surface of contact
solution: The contact force between two surfaces is resolved into a component perpendicular to the plane of contact, called the normal reaction, and a component along that plane, called friction. On an incline of angle theta the normal reaction is m g cos theta, which is less than the weight.
formula_principle: The contact force splits into a normal component perpendicular to the surface and a frictional component along it.
common_misconception: Students take the normal reaction to be equal to the weight and vertical in every situation.

concept_tested: Third force needed for equilibrium
stem: Three concurrent coplanar forces keep a body in equilibrium. Two of them have magnitudes 3 N and 4 N and act at right angles to each other. The magnitude of the third force is
solution: The resultant of the perpendicular forces 3 N and 4 N has magnitude equal to the square root of (9 + 16), which is 5 N. For equilibrium, the third force must be 5 N directed exactly opposite to this resultant.
formula_principle: The third force must be equal and opposite to the resultant of the other two.
common_misconception: Students add or subtract force magnitudes without regard to the angle between them.

concept_tested: Three equilibrium forces equally inclined
stem: Three coplanar concurrent forces keep a particle in equilibrium, and the angle between every pair of them is 120 degrees. If one of them has magnitude 20 N, the other two are
solution: By Lami's theorem, each force is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two. Here every such angle is 120 degrees, so all three sines are equal and hence all three forces are equal in magnitude. Since one is 20 N, the other two are 20 N each.
formula_principle: Lami's theorem: each force divided by the sine of the angle between the other two is the same for all three.
common_misconception: Students think the two unknown forces must be smaller because their resultant has to balance only one given force.

concept_tested: Hanging body pulled aside by a horizontal force
stem: A body of mass 5 kg hangs from a light string fixed to the ceiling. A horizontal force holds the string steadily at 45 degrees to the vertical. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the magnitude of the horizontal force is
solution: The vertical component of the tension balances the weight, so T cos 45 = 50 N, and the horizontal component balances the applied force, so T sin 45 = F. Dividing gives F = m g tan 45 = 50 x 1 = 50 N. The tension itself is 50/cos 45 = 50 sqrt(2), about 70.7 N.
formula_principle: For a string at angle theta to the vertical, F = m g tan theta and T = m g/cos theta.
common_misconception: Students quote the tension when the horizontal force is asked for, since both come out of the same pair of equations.

concept_tested: Normal reaction when the pull is inclined
stem: A block is dragged along a rough horizontal floor by a rope inclined at an angle above the horizontal. In the free body diagram of the block, the normal reaction of the floor is
option_a: equal to the weight, because the floor is horizontal
option_b: greater than the weight, because the rope adds an extra downward pull
option_c: equal to the horizontal component of the tension, because the block slides horizontally
option_d: less than the weight, because the upward component of the rope tension carries part of the weight
correct_answer_text: less than the weight, because the upward component of the rope tension carries part of the weight
solution: Four forces act on the block: the weight downward, the normal reaction upward, the friction backward, and the tension along the rope. Resolving the tension, its vertical component T sin theta acts upward, so the vertical equation gives N = m g - T sin theta, which is less than the weight. This is why an inclined pull also reduces the friction, since friction is mu N.
formula_principle: Vertical equilibrium: N + T sin theta = m g, so N = m g - T sin theta.
common_misconception: Students take the normal reaction to be m g in every situation and so overestimate the friction when the pull is inclined.

concept_tested: Block held on a smooth incline by a string along the plane
stem: A body of weight 100 N rests on a smooth plane inclined at 30 degrees to the horizontal and is held in place by a light string parallel to the plane. The tension in the string and the normal reaction are
solution: Resolving the weight along and perpendicular to the plane gives components W sin 30 = 100 x 0.5 = 50 N down the plane and W cos 30 = 100 x (sqrt(3)/2) = 50 sqrt(3) N into the plane. The string balances the first and the normal reaction balances the second, giving T = 50 N and N = 50 sqrt(3), about 86.6 N.
formula_principle: On a smooth incline of angle theta, T = W sin theta and N = W cos theta.
common_misconception: Students interchange the sine and cosine of the inclination when resolving the weight on an incline.

concept_tested: Dynamic equilibrium
stem: A body moves along a straight line with constant speed while several forces act on it. It follows that
option_a: each of the forces acting on the body must separately be zero
option_b: exactly two forces must be acting on the body
option_c: the vector sum of the forces is zero, although the individual forces need not be zero
option_d: the body must appear to be at rest in every frame of reference
correct_answer_text: the vector sum of the forces is zero, although the individual forces need not be zero
solution: Constant speed along a straight line means zero acceleration, so by the second law the net force must vanish. This is called dynamic equilibrium. A block sliding at steady speed on a rough floor under an applied force is a standard example: the applied force and friction are individually large but they cancel.
formula_principle: Zero acceleration means zero net force, which is the condition of equilibrium whether the body is at rest or moving uniformly.
common_misconception: Students believe equilibrium means being at rest and therefore expect a moving body to have a net force on it.

concept_tested: Tension when a hanging lamp is pulled aside
stem: A lamp of weight 40 N hangs from the ceiling by a light string. A horizontal string pulls it aside until the first string makes 60 degrees with the vertical. The tension in the string attached to the ceiling is
solution: The vertical component of the tension must carry the whole weight, so T cos 60 = 40. Since cos 60 = 0.5, T = 40/0.5 = 80 N. The horizontal string then carries T sin 60 = 80 x (sqrt(3)/2) = 40 sqrt(3), about 69.3 N.
formula_principle: For a string at angle theta to the vertical supporting a weight W with a horizontal pull, T = W/cos theta and the horizontal pull is W tan theta.
common_misconception: Students multiply the weight by the cosine instead of dividing, and so obtain a tension smaller than the weight.

concept_tested: Numerical use of Lami's theorem
stem: Three coplanar concurrent forces P, Q and R keep a particle in equilibrium. The angle between Q and R is 90 degrees, and the angle between R and P and the angle between P and Q are each 135 degrees. If R has magnitude 10 N, then P is
solution: Applying the theorem, P divided by sin 90 equals R divided by sin 135. Since sin 90 = 1 and sin 135 = 1/sqrt(2), we get P = 10 x 1 x sqrt(2) = 10 sqrt(2), about 14.1 N. The three angles sum to 360 degrees as they must.
formula_principle: Lami's theorem: P/sin(angle between Q and R) = Q/sin(angle between R and P) = R/sin(angle between P and Q).
common_misconception: Students pair each force with the angle adjacent to it instead of with the angle between the other two forces.

concept_tested: Tension in a supporting wire
stem: A weight of 60 N hangs from the outer end of a light horizontal rod that is hinged to a wall. A wire runs from that same outer end to a point on the wall above the hinge, making 30 degrees with the rod. The tension in the wire is
solution: Consider the outer end of the rod. The forces there are the load of 60 N downward, the tension T along the wire towards the wall, and the push of the light rod along its own length, which is horizontal. Only the wire has a vertical component, so T sin 30 = 60. With sin 30 = 0.5, T = 120 N.
formula_principle: At the loaded end, the vertical component of the wire tension supports the load: T sin theta = W.
common_misconception: Students multiply by the sine instead of dividing and obtain a tension smaller than the load it must support.

concept_tested: Geometrical condition on three balancing forces
stem: If three non parallel forces keep a rigid body in equilibrium, then they must
option_b: be coplanar and pass through a single point
option_c: all lie along the same straight line
option_d: be such that each is perpendicular to the other two
correct_answer_text: be coplanar and pass through a single point
solution: Zero net force makes the three forces form a closed triangle, which requires them to be coplanar. Taking torques about the point where two of the lines of action meet, those two contribute nothing, so the third must also pass through that point or its torque would be unbalanced. Hence all three lines of action meet at a single point.
formula_principle: For a rigid body, equilibrium needs zero net force and zero net torque; for three non parallel forces this forces them to be concurrent and coplanar.
common_misconception: Students check only that the forces add to zero and forget the torque condition, which is what makes them concurrent.

concept_tested: Body hung from two strings at different angles
stem: A body of weight 100 N hangs from the point where two light strings meet. One string makes 30 degrees with the horizontal and the other makes 60 degrees with the horizontal, on opposite sides. The tensions are
option_a: 50 N in the string at 30 degrees and 50 sqrt(3) N in the string at 60 degrees
option_b: 50 sqrt(3) N in the string at 30 degrees and 50 N in the string at 60 degrees
option_c: 50 N in the string at 30 degrees and 50 N in the string at 60 degrees
option_d: 100 N in the string at 30 degrees and 100 N in the string at 60 degrees
correct_answer_text: 50 N in the string at 30 degrees and 50 sqrt(3) N in the string at 60 degrees
solution: Let T1 be the tension in the string at 30 degrees and T2 that in the string at 60 degrees. Horizontal balance gives T1 cos 30 = T2 cos 60, so T2 = T1 sqrt(3). Vertical balance gives T1 sin 30 + T2 sin 60 = 100, that is 0.5 T1 + (sqrt(3) T1)(sqrt(3)/2) = 100, which simplifies to 2 T1 = 100. Hence T1 = 50 N and T2 = 50 sqrt(3), about 86.6 N. The strings are perpendicular to each other, so a check is that 50^2 + (50 sqrt(3))^2 = 100^2.
formula_principle: Resolve horizontally and vertically at the junction: T1 cos 30 = T2 cos 60 and T1 sin 30 + T2 sin 60 = W.
common_misconception: Students assume the two tensions are equal because both strings support the same body.

concept_tested: Block on a smooth incline held by a horizontal force
stem: A block of mass 10 kg rests on a smooth plane inclined at 45 degrees to the horizontal and is held in place by a horizontal force. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the horizontal force and the normal reaction are
solution: Resolving along the plane, the component of the weight down the plane is m g sin 45 and the component of the horizontal force up the plane is F cos 45. Equating gives F = m g tan 45 = 100 x 1 = 100 N. Resolving perpendicular to the plane, N = m g cos 45 + F sin 45 = 100 x 0.707 + 100 x 0.707, which is 100 sqrt(2), about 141.4 N. The normal reaction is thus larger than the weight because the horizontal force presses the block into the plane.
formula_principle: For a horizontal holding force on a smooth incline of angle theta, F = m g tan theta and N = m g/cos theta.
common_misconception: Students take the normal reaction to be m g cos theta as on a free incline and forget the extra pressing caused by the horizontal force.

concept_tested: Acceleration of two blocks pushed together
stem: Two blocks of masses 2 kg and 3 kg are placed in contact on a smooth horizontal surface and a horizontal force of 10 N is applied to the outer face of the 2 kg block. The acceleration of the blocks is
solution: The two blocks stay in contact and so share a common acceleration. Treating them as a single body of mass 5 kg, a = 10/5 = 2 m s^-2.
formula_principle: For bodies that move together, a = F/(m1 + m2).
common_misconception: Students apply the force to only the block it touches and forget that the whole system must be accelerated.

concept_tested: Tension in a light string over a smooth pulley
stem: For a light inextensible string passing over a frictionless pulley, the tension
option_a: has the same magnitude at every point along the string
option_b: is greater on the side carrying the heavier mass
option_c: increases steadily with the length of string paid out
option_d: is zero at the point where the string touches the pulley
correct_answer_text: has the same magnitude at every point along the string
solution: Any short element of a massless string has zero mass, so the net force on it must vanish however it accelerates. The tensions pulling on its two ends must therefore be equal, and this holds all along the string. A frictionless pulley merely changes the direction of the string without changing its tension.
formula_principle: A massless string over a frictionless pulley transmits a single value of tension throughout.
common_misconception: Students give the two sides of a pulley different tensions when the masses are unequal.

concept_tested: Acceleration of an Atwood machine
stem: Two masses of 3 kg and 2 kg hang from the two ends of a light string passing over a frictionless pulley. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the acceleration of the system is
solution: The net driving force is the difference of the weights, (3 - 2) x 10 = 10 N, while the mass being accelerated is the total, 3 + 2 = 5 kg. Hence a = 10/5 = 2 m s^-2, with the heavier mass descending.
common_misconception: Students divide by the difference of the masses instead of by their sum, since both masses must be set in motion.

concept_tested: Constraint imposed by an inextensible string
stem: Two blocks joined by a taut light inextensible string are set in motion. At every instant
option_a: their velocities are equal in both magnitude and direction whatever the arrangement
option_b: the heavier block has the larger acceleration
option_c: their accelerations are in the inverse ratio of their masses
option_d: the magnitudes of their accelerations along the string are equal
correct_answer_text: the magnitudes of their accelerations along the string are equal
solution: Since the string cannot stretch, the speed at which one end moves along the string must equal the speed at which the other end moves along it. Differentiating, the magnitudes of the accelerations along the string are equal, even though the directions may differ, as they do on either side of a pulley.
formula_principle: An inextensible string keeps the distance along the string constant, so the components of acceleration along the string are equal in magnitude.
common_misconception: Students assign different accelerations to the two connected blocks because their masses differ.

concept_tested: Tension between two blocks pulled on a smooth surface
stem: Two blocks of masses 2 kg and 3 kg lie on a smooth horizontal surface joined by a light string. A horizontal force of 10 N is applied to the 2 kg block so that the pair is dragged along. The tension in the string is
solution: The common acceleration is a = 10/5 = 2 m s^-2. The string is the only thing pulling the 3 kg block, so T = 3 x 2 = 6 N. Equivalently T = m2 F/(m1 + m2) = 3 x 10/5 = 6 N.
formula_principle: a = F/(m1 + m2) and the tension is the mass being towed times a, that is T = m2 F/(m1 + m2).
common_misconception: Students use the mass of the block that the force is applied to when computing the tension.

concept_tested: Contact force in a row of three blocks
stem: Three blocks of masses 1 kg, 2 kg and 3 kg are placed in contact in that order on a smooth horizontal surface, and a horizontal force of 12 N is applied to the outer face of the 1 kg block. The force that the 2 kg block exerts on the 3 kg block is
solution: The common acceleration is a = 12/6 = 2 m s^-2. The only horizontal force on the 3 kg block is the push from the 2 kg block, so that push is 3 x 2 = 6 N. The force between the first and second blocks would be (2 + 3) x 2 = 10 N.
formula_principle: a = F/(total mass); the contact force at any junction equals the mass beyond that junction times a.
common_misconception: Students take the contact force to be the same at every junction, instead of counting only the mass beyond the junction.

concept_tested: Tension in an Atwood machine
stem: Two masses of 3 kg and 2 kg hang from the two ends of a light string over a frictionless pulley. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the tension in the string is
solution: Using the standard result, T = 2 x 3 x 2 x 10/(3 + 2) = 120/5 = 24 N. A check from the lighter mass: it accelerates upward at 2 m s^-2, so T - 20 = 2 x 2, giving T = 24 N.
common_misconception: Students take the tension to be the weight of the heavier mass, forgetting that this mass is accelerating downward.

concept_tested: Block on a smooth table pulled by a hanging mass
stem: A block of mass 3 kg on a smooth horizontal table is joined by a light string over a frictionless pulley at the edge of the table to a mass of 2 kg hanging freely. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the tension in the string is
solution: The driving force is the weight of the hanging mass, 20 N, and the total mass in motion is 5 kg, so a = 20/5 = 4 m s^-2. The only horizontal force on the block on the table is the tension, so T = 3 x 4 = 12 N. A check on the hanging mass: 20 - 12 = 8 = 2 x 4.
formula_principle: a = m2 g/(m1 + m2) for a smooth table, and T = m1 a.
common_misconception: Students set the tension equal to the weight of the hanging mass, which is true only when the system is held at rest.

concept_tested: Size of the tension compared with the weights
stem: In an Atwood machine with two unequal masses released from rest, the tension in the string is
option_a: equal to the total weight of the two masses
option_b: less than the weight of the heavier mass and greater than the weight of the lighter mass
option_c: equal to the weight of the heavier mass
option_d: equal to the difference of the two weights
correct_answer_text: less than the weight of the heavier mass and greater than the weight of the lighter mass
solution: The heavier mass accelerates downward, so the upward tension on it must be less than its weight. The lighter mass accelerates upward, so the tension on it must exceed its weight. The tension therefore lies strictly between the two weights, and it equals both of them only when the masses are equal.
formula_principle: T = 2 m1 m2 g/(m1 + m2), which is the harmonic type mean lying between m2 g and m1 g.
common_misconception: Students set the tension equal to one of the weights, forgetting that both masses are accelerating.

concept_tested: Atwood machine with equal masses
stem: Two masses of 5 kg each hang from the two ends of a light string over a frictionless pulley. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the tension in the string is
solution: Equal masses give no net driving force, so the acceleration is zero and each mass is in equilibrium. For either mass, T = m g = 5 x 10 = 50 N. The standard formula agrees, since 2 x 5 x 5 x 10/10 = 50 N.
formula_principle: With m1 = m2 = m, a = 0 and T = m g.
common_misconception: Students confuse zero acceleration with zero tension and answer that the string carries no force.

concept_tested: Distance moved by an Atwood machine
stem: In an Atwood machine the two masses are 6 kg and 4 kg. Starting from rest and taking g = 10 m s^-2, the distance moved by each mass in 2 s is
solution: The acceleration is (6 - 4) x 10/(6 + 4) = 20/10 = 2 m s^-2. Starting from rest, s = (1/2) x 2 x 2^2 = 4 m. One mass descends 4 m while the other rises 4 m.
common_misconception: Students drop the factor of one half or use g in place of the much smaller acceleration of the machine.

concept_tested: Force on the pulley of an Atwood machine
stem: In an Atwood machine the masses are 6 kg and 4 kg and the pulley is light and frictionless. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the downward force exerted on the pulley by the string is
solution: The tension is T = 2 x 6 x 4 x 10/10 = 48 N. Both vertical portions of the string hang from the pulley and each pulls down with T, so the force on the pulley is 2 T = 96 N. This is less than the combined weight of 100 N because the masses are accelerating.
formula_principle: T = 2 m1 m2 g/(m1 + m2); the two vertical portions of the string pull down on the pulley, giving 2 T.
common_misconception: Students expect the pulley to carry the full weight of both masses and overlook the effect of the acceleration.

concept_tested: Connected blocks with friction on the table
stem: A block of mass 2 kg lies on a rough horizontal table for which the coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.5. It is joined by a light string over a frictionless pulley at the edge to a block of mass 3 kg hanging freely. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the acceleration of the system is
solution: The driving force is the weight of the hanging block, 3 x 10 = 30 N. The resisting friction is mu m1 g = 0.5 x 2 x 10 = 10 N. The net force is 20 N and the total mass in motion is 5 kg, so a = 20/5 = 4 m s^-2.
formula_principle: a = (m2 g - mu m1 g)/(m1 + m2) with m1 on the table and m2 hanging.
common_misconception: Students forget the friction on the horizontal block and so obtain too large an acceleration.

concept_tested: Tensions in a chain of three blocks
stem: Three blocks of masses 1 kg, 2 kg and 3 kg lie in that order on a smooth horizontal surface, joined by light strings. A horizontal force of 12 N is applied to the 1 kg block so that all three are dragged along. The tension in the string joining the 1 kg and 2 kg blocks is
solution: The acceleration is a = 12/6 = 2 m s^-2. The first string has to tow the 2 kg and 3 kg blocks, a total of 5 kg, so its tension is 5 x 2 = 10 N. The second string tows only the 3 kg block and so carries 6 N.
formula_principle: a = F/(total mass); the tension in any string equals the total mass behind it times a.
common_misconception: Students use the mass of the block in front of the string instead of the total mass being towed behind it.

concept_tested: Effect of which block is pulled
stem: Two blocks of unequal mass are joined by a light string and dragged along a smooth horizontal surface by a force of fixed magnitude, applied first to one block and then to the other. The tension in the string is
option_a: larger when the force is applied to the heavier block
option_c: zero in one of the two cases
option_d: larger when the force is applied to the lighter block
correct_answer_text: larger when the force is applied to the lighter block
solution: The common acceleration a = F/(m1 + m2) is the same in both cases. The tension equals the towed mass times a. When the force is applied to the lighter block, the string must tow the heavier one, so the tension is larger. As a numerical illustration, with masses 2 kg and 3 kg and F = 10 N, the tension is 6 N when the 2 kg block is pulled and 4 N when the 3 kg block is pulled.
formula_principle: T = (mass being towed) x F/(m1 + m2).
common_misconception: Students think the tension depends only on the applied force and not on which block it is applied to.

concept_tested: Hanging mass connected to a block on a smooth incline
stem: A block of mass 2 kg lies on a smooth plane inclined at 30 degrees, and is joined by a light string over a frictionless pulley at the top of the incline to a block of mass 4 kg hanging vertically. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the acceleration of the system is
solution: The hanging block pulls with 4 x 10 = 40 N, while the block on the incline is held back by the component of its weight along the plane, 2 x 10 x sin 30 = 10 N. The net driving force is 30 N and the total mass is 6 kg, so a = 30/6 = 5 m s^-2.
formula_principle: a = (m2 g - m1 g sin theta)/(m1 + m2) for a smooth incline of angle theta.
common_misconception: Students use the full weight of the block on the incline instead of its component along the plane.

concept_tested: A hanging weight compared with an equal steady pull
stem: A block of mass 10 kg on a smooth horizontal table is joined by a light string over a frictionless pulley at the edge to a hanging block of mass 10 kg. In a second experiment the hanging block is removed and the free end of the string is pulled straight down with a steady force of 100 N. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the acceleration of the block on the table is
option_a: 10 m s^-2 in the first case and 5 m s^-2 in the second
option_b: 5 m s^-2 in the first case and 10 m s^-2 in the second
correct_answer_text: 5 m s^-2 in the first case and 10 m s^-2 in the second
solution: In the first case the driving force is 100 N but the moving mass is 20 kg, so a = 100/20 = 5 m s^-2 and the tension is 50 N, not 100 N. In the second case the 100 N acts directly on the string and only the 10 kg block has to be accelerated, so a = 100/10 = 10 m s^-2. A hanging weight is therefore not the same as an equal steady pull, because the hanging body must itself be accelerated.
formula_principle: With a hanging mass, a = m2 g/(m1 + m2); with a fixed applied force, a = F/m1.
common_misconception: Students replace a hanging mass by a force equal to its weight, which is valid only when the system is in equilibrium.

concept_tested: Reading of a balance supporting the pulley
stem: In an Atwood machine, masses of 5 kg and 3 kg hang from the ends of a light string over a light frictionless pulley, and the pulley itself hangs from a spring balance. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the reading of the spring balance is
solution: The acceleration is (5 - 3) x 10/8 = 2.5 m s^-2 and the tension is 2 x 5 x 3 x 10/8 = 37.5 N. The pulley is light, so the balance must simply support the two string portions, giving a reading of 2 x 37.5 = 75 N. This is less than the combined weight of 80 N, the shortfall of 5 N being exactly the net downward rate of change of momentum of the two masses, since (5 - 3) x 2.5 = 5 N.
formula_principle: a = (m1 - m2)g/(m1 + m2), T = 2 m1 m2 g/(m1 + m2), and the balance reads 2 T for a light pulley.
common_misconception: Students expect the balance to read the total weight and do not allow for the acceleration of the two masses.

concept_tested: Laws of limiting friction
stem: The limiting force of static friction between two surfaces in contact is
option_a: directly proportional to the normal reaction between the surfaces
option_b: directly proportional to the apparent area of contact
option_c: directly proportional to the relative speed of the two surfaces
option_d: independent of the nature of the two surfaces in contact
correct_answer_text: directly proportional to the normal reaction between the surfaces
solution: The first law of friction states that the limiting friction is proportional to the normal reaction, with the coefficient of static friction as the constant of proportionality. The coefficient depends on the nature and finish of the surfaces but not on their apparent area.
formula_principle: Limiting friction f = mu_s N, where mu_s is the coefficient of static friction.
common_misconception: Students believe a wider block experiences more friction because more surface appears to be touching.

concept_tested: Independence of friction from the apparent area
stem: A rectangular brick can be made to rest on a table on its broad face or on its narrow face. The limiting friction between the brick and the table
option_a: is greater when the brick rests on its broad face, in proportion to the larger area
option_b: is greater when the brick rests on its narrow face, in inverse proportion to the area
option_c: is the same in both positions, since it does not depend on the apparent area of contact
option_d: is zero when the brick rests on its narrow face, since the contact is too small
correct_answer_text: is the same in both positions, since it does not depend on the apparent area of contact
solution: The normal reaction equals the weight of the brick in both positions, and the coefficient of friction depends only on the pair of materials. Hence the limiting friction is unchanged. The real area of microscopic contact adjusts itself so that the friction depends only on the load.
formula_principle: f = mu N; the apparent area of contact does not appear in the relation.
common_misconception: Students expect the broad face to give more grip because more of the surface seems to be in contact.

concept_tested: Limiting friction on a horizontal floor
stem: A block of mass 5 kg rests on a horizontal floor for which the coefficient of static friction is 0.4. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the limiting force of friction is
solution: The normal reaction is N = 5 x 10 = 50 N. Hence the limiting friction is 0.4 x 50 = 20 N. Any applied horizontal force smaller than 20 N will be exactly balanced by friction and the block will stay at rest.
formula_principle: f_limiting = mu_s N, with N = m g on a horizontal surface.
common_misconception: Students forget to multiply the mass by g and so lose a factor of ten in the normal reaction.

concept_tested: Comparing kinetic friction with limiting static friction
stem: For a given pair of surfaces, the force of kinetic friction is
option_a: somewhat less than the limiting force of static friction
option_b: somewhat greater than the limiting force of static friction
option_c: exactly equal to the limiting force of static friction
option_d: zero once the body has started sliding
correct_answer_text: somewhat less than the limiting force of static friction
solution: It takes a larger force to start a body sliding than to keep it sliding, because the microscopic junctions between the surfaces have less time to form once relative motion has begun. Hence mu_k is smaller than mu_s, and the friction drops slightly at the instant sliding starts.
formula_principle: mu_k is less than mu_s for a given pair of surfaces.
common_misconception: Students think friction must increase once the body starts moving because motion is being opposed.

concept_tested: Relation between the angle of repose and the angle of friction
stem: The angle of repose for a body resting on an inclined surface is
option_a: equal to twice the angle of friction
option_b: independent of the coefficient of friction between the surfaces
option_c: the angle whose sine is the coefficient of static friction
option_d: equal to the angle of friction, and its tangent is the coefficient of static friction
correct_answer_text: equal to the angle of friction, and its tangent is the coefficient of static friction
solution: A body on an incline is on the point of sliding when the component of the weight along the plane equals the limiting friction, that is m g sin theta = mu_s m g cos theta. Cancelling m g gives tan theta = mu_s. Since the angle of friction is defined by tan of that angle equal to mu_s as well, the two angles are equal.
formula_principle: At the angle of repose, m g sin theta = mu_s m g cos theta, so tan theta = mu_s.
common_misconception: Students write sin of the angle of repose equal to mu because the driving component involves a sine, forgetting the cosine in the normal reaction.

concept_tested: Angle of repose from a given coefficient
stem: The coefficient of static friction between a body and an inclined surface is 1/sqrt(3). The angle of repose is
solution: Setting tan theta = 1/sqrt(3) gives theta = 30 degrees, since tan 30 = 1/sqrt(3), about 0.577. A body placed on this surface will stay at rest for inclinations up to 30 degrees and will begin to slide beyond that.
formula_principle: tan(angle of repose) = mu_s.
common_misconception: Students invert the coefficient and read off 60 degrees, since tan 60 is sqrt(3).

concept_tested: Friction when the applied force is below the limit
stem: A block of mass 10 kg rests on a horizontal floor for which the coefficient of static friction is 0.4. A horizontal force of 30 N is applied to it. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the force of friction acting on the block is
solution: The limiting friction here is 0.4 x 10 x 10 = 40 N. The applied force of 30 N is smaller than this, so the block does not move. Since it is in equilibrium, the friction must exactly balance the applied force and is therefore 30 N, not 40 N.
formula_principle: Static friction is self adjusting: it equals the applied force up to a maximum of mu_s N.
common_misconception: Students always compute mu N and quote it as the friction, even when the body is not on the point of sliding.

concept_tested: Stopping distance on a rough floor
stem: A block sliding on a rough horizontal floor with an initial speed of 10 m s^-1 comes to rest. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.2 and g = 10 m s^-2. The distance travelled before it stops is
solution: The only horizontal force is friction, so the retardation is a = mu_k g = 0.2 x 10 = 2 m s^-2. Using v^2 = u^2 - 2 a s with v = 0 gives s = 100/(2 x 2) = 25 m. Note that the mass cancels, so the distance does not depend on how heavy the block is.
formula_principle: Retardation a = mu_k g; then distance = u^2/(2a).
common_misconception: Students expect a heavier block to travel a shorter distance, not seeing that the mass cancels out of the calculation.

concept_tested: Coefficient of friction from sliding at constant velocity
stem: A block placed on a plane inclined at 30 degrees to the horizontal slides down it with constant velocity. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the plane is
solution: Sliding with constant velocity means the net force along the plane is zero, so the friction exactly balances the component of the weight down the plane. Hence mu_k m g cos 30 = m g sin 30, and mu_k = tan 30 = 1/sqrt(3), about 0.58.
formula_principle: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so m g sin theta = mu_k m g cos theta and mu_k = tan theta.
common_misconception: Students equate the coefficient to the sine of the angle and forget that the normal reaction carries a cosine.

concept_tested: Angle of friction for a given coefficient
stem: If the coefficient of friction between two surfaces is 1, the angle of friction is
solution: The angle of friction is the angle between the total contact force and the normal to the surface when friction is limiting, and it satisfies tan of that angle equal to mu. With mu = 1, the angle is 45 degrees, and it equals the angle of repose for the same pair of surfaces.
formula_principle: tan(angle of friction) = mu.
common_misconception: Students use the sine or take the coefficient itself as the angle in degrees.

concept_tested: Rolling friction compared with sliding friction
stem: For the same pair of surfaces and the same normal reaction, rolling friction is
option_a: much larger than sliding friction, which is why brakes work by rolling
option_b: exactly equal to sliding friction, since the same two surfaces are involved
option_c: much smaller than sliding friction, which is why wheels and ball bearings are used
option_d: independent of the normal reaction, unlike sliding friction
correct_answer_text: much smaller than sliding friction, which is why wheels and ball bearings are used
solution: In rolling, the surfaces are in contact only momentarily at each point and there is no sliding at the contact, so far less resistance arises. This is why loads are moved on wheels and why ball bearings are placed between a shaft and its housing to convert sliding into rolling.
formula_principle: Rolling friction is typically one to two orders of magnitude smaller than sliding friction for the same load.
common_misconception: Students think that any contact between the same two materials must give the same friction whatever the type of motion.

concept_tested: Friction as the force that drives a car
stem: A car of mass 1000 kg accelerates from rest along a level road. The forward force that accelerates the car is
option_a: the force exerted by the engine directly on the body of the car
option_b: the static friction exerted by the road on the driving wheels
option_c: the kinetic friction between the tyres and the road, acting forward
option_d: the normal reaction of the road on the tyres
correct_answer_text: the static friction exerted by the road on the driving wheels
solution: The engine turns the wheels so that the contact patch tends to slip backward on the road. Friction opposes this tendency and therefore acts forward on the car. Since the tyre does not actually slide when the car grips well, this is static friction. On an icy road the available friction is small and the car cannot accelerate briskly, which shows that friction really is the driving force.
formula_principle: The wheels push backward on the road and, by the third law, the road pushes forward on the wheels; this forward push is static friction.
common_misconception: Students treat friction as always opposing motion and cannot accept that it is the very force that propels a car.

concept_tested: Braking distance of a car
stem: A car moving at 20 m s^-1 on a level road brakes so hard that its wheels lock and it skids to rest. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.5 and g = 10 m s^-2. The distance the car skids is
solution: The retardation is 0.5 x 10 = 5 m s^-2. Then s = u^2/(2 a) = 400/10 = 40 m. Doubling the speed would quadruple this distance, which is why speed limits matter so much.
formula_principle: Retardation a = mu_k g; skidding distance = u^2/(2 a).
common_misconception: Students think a heavier car needs a longer distance to stop, whereas the mass cancels from the calculation.

concept_tested: Force needed to push a block up a rough incline
stem: A block of mass 2 kg rests on a plane inclined at 45 degrees, with coefficient of friction 0.5 between the block and the plane. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the force applied parallel to the plane and directed up the plane that will just move the block upward is
solution: The component of the weight along the plane is 2 x 10 x sin 45 = 20/sqrt(2) = 10 sqrt(2) N, about 14.1 N. The normal reaction is 2 x 10 x cos 45 = 10 sqrt(2) N, so the friction, which now acts down the plane, is 0.5 x 10 sqrt(2) = 5 sqrt(2) N. The required force is the sum, 15 sqrt(2) N, about 21.2 N.
formula_principle: F = m g sin theta + mu m g cos theta for motion up a rough incline.
common_misconception: Students make friction act up the plane, forgetting that it opposes the intended upward motion.

concept_tested: Coefficient of friction from a comparison of sliding times
stem: A body takes twice as long to slide from rest down a rough plane inclined at 45 degrees as it takes to slide down a smooth plane of the same inclination and the same length. The coefficient of friction is
solution: For the same length travelled from rest, doubling the time means the acceleration is one quarter as large. On the smooth plane a = g sin theta, and on the rough plane a = g(sin theta - mu cos theta). Setting the second equal to one quarter of the first gives sin theta - mu cos theta = (1/4) sin theta, so mu cos theta = (3/4) sin theta and mu = (3/4) tan theta. With theta = 45 degrees, tan theta = 1 and mu = 0.75.
formula_principle: For the same distance from rest, s = (1/2) a t^2, so a is proportional to 1/t^2; and a_rough/a_smooth = 1 - mu cot theta.
common_misconception: Students take the time ratio to equal the ratio of accelerations rather than the ratio of their square roots.

concept_tested: Largest acceleration a stacked block can be given
stem: A block of mass 2 kg rests on top of a larger block, and the coefficient of static friction between the two blocks is 0.4. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the greatest horizontal acceleration that can be given to the lower block without the upper block slipping is
solution: The upper block is accelerated solely by the friction from the block beneath it. That friction cannot exceed mu_s m g = 0.4 x 2 x 10 = 8 N, so the largest acceleration it can give the 2 kg block is 8/2 = 4 m s^-2. The mass of the upper block cancels, giving the general result a_max = mu_s g.
formula_principle: The only horizontal force on the upper block is friction, so a_max = mu_s g.
common_misconception: Students look for the mass of the lower block, not realising that the limit is set entirely by the upper block.

concept_tested: Block held against a vertical wall
stem: A block of mass 2 kg is pressed against a vertical wall by a horizontal force. The coefficient of static friction between the block and the wall is 0.5 and g = 10 m s^-2. The least horizontal force that will prevent the block from sliding down is
solution: Here the applied force is horizontal and presses the block into the wall, so the normal reaction is N = F. The friction acts vertically upward and must support the weight, so mu F = m g. Hence F = m g/mu = 20/0.5 = 40 N. Note that the friction here is vertical, unlike the usual case of a block on the floor.
formula_principle: The horizontal push supplies the normal reaction, so friction is mu F, and equilibrium requires mu F = m g.
common_misconception: Students multiply the weight by mu instead of dividing, and so obtain a force far too small to hold the block.

concept_tested: Friction on a body with no applied horizontal force
stem: A block lies at rest on a rough horizontal floor and no horizontal force is applied to it. The force of friction acting on the block is
option_a: equal to mu times the weight, since that is the value of the frictional force
option_b: equal to the weight of the block, since the block does not move
option_c: zero, since friction appears only in response to an applied force or a tendency to slide
option_d: equal to the normal reaction, since the two surfaces are in contact
correct_answer_text: zero, since friction appears only in response to an applied force or a tendency to slide
solution: With no horizontal force applied there is no tendency to slide, so the horizontal equilibrium equation reads simply that friction equals zero. The quantity mu_s N is the greatest friction the surfaces can supply, not the value they always supply. The vertical equilibrium is looked after by the normal reaction balancing the weight.
formula_principle: Static friction is self adjusting and lies between zero and mu_s N; it takes whatever value the equilibrium demands.
common_misconception: Students treat mu N as a fixed force that always acts whenever rough surfaces touch.

concept_tested: Least force to move a block, applied at the best angle
stem: A block of mass 10 kg rests on a horizontal floor with coefficient of static friction 0.75. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the least force that can just set the block moving, when applied at the most favourable angle above the horizontal, is
solution: A pull inclined upward reduces the normal reaction and hence the friction, so it can be more economical than a horizontal pull. Balancing forces at the point of sliding gives F cos theta = mu(m g - F sin theta), so F = mu m g/(cos theta + mu sin theta). The denominator is largest when tan theta = mu, and then F = mu m g/sqrt(1 + mu^2). With mu = 0.75 and m g = 100 N this is 75/sqrt(1 + 0.5625) = 75/1.25 = 60 N, against 75 N for a horizontal pull.
formula_principle: For a pull at angle theta above the horizontal, F = mu m g/(cos theta + mu sin theta), which is least when tan theta = mu, giving F_min = mu m g/sqrt(1 + mu^2).
common_misconception: Students assume the easiest way to move a block is to pull it horizontally and never consider inclining the pull.

concept_tested: Largest force on the lower of two stacked blocks
stem: A block of mass 2 kg rests on a block of mass 3 kg which lies on a smooth horizontal floor. The coefficient of static friction between the two blocks is 0.5 and g = 10 m s^-2. The largest horizontal force that can be applied to the lower block so that the two still move together is
solution: The upper block can only be accelerated by friction from below, and that friction is at most 0.5 x 2 x 10 = 10 N. This gives the upper block a largest possible acceleration of 10/2 = 5 m s^-2, which is just mu_s g. While the two move together the whole 5 kg accelerates at this rate, so the largest applied force is 5 x 5 = 25 N. A larger force would make the lower block slide out from under the upper one.
formula_principle: Friction on the upper block gives it at most a_max = mu_s g; the two move together while F is at most (m1 + m2) a_max.
common_misconception: Students quote the limiting friction of 10 N as the answer, forgetting that the applied force must accelerate both blocks.

concept_tested: Statement of the work energy theorem
stem: The work energy theorem states that the net work done on a body by all the forces acting on it equals
option_a: the change in its linear momentum
option_b: its total mechanical energy at the end of the motion
option_c: the impulse delivered to it by those forces
option_d: the change in its kinetic energy
correct_answer_text: the change in its kinetic energy
solution: Starting from F = m a and using v^2 = u^2 + 2 a s, multiplying by m/2 gives F s equal to the difference of the two kinetic energy terms. Hence the net work done equals the change in kinetic energy, whatever forces are involved.
formula_principle: W_net = K_final - K_initial.
common_misconception: Students confuse the work energy theorem with the impulse momentum theorem and equate work to a change of momentum.

concept_tested: Head on elastic collision of equal masses
stem: A body moving with speed u collides head on and elastically with an identical body at rest. After the collision
option_a: both move forward together with speed u/2
option_b: the first body stops and the second moves off with speed u
option_c: both move off with speed u in opposite directions
option_d: the first rebounds with speed u and the second stays at rest
correct_answer_text: the first body stops and the second moves off with speed u
solution: Momentum conservation gives v1 + v2 = u and kinetic energy conservation gives v1^2 + v2^2 = u^2. Solving these together gives either the initial state or the exchanged state v1 = 0 and v2 = u. Since the bodies must separate, the exchange is the physical solution. This is what is seen when one carrom coin strikes another squarely.
formula_principle: For a head on elastic collision of equal masses, the two velocities are simply exchanged.
common_misconception: Students apply the perfectly inelastic result of a common speed u/2 to an elastic collision.

concept_tested: Definition of the coefficient of restitution
stem: The coefficient of restitution for a collision between two bodies is defined as
option_a: the ratio of the relative speed of approach to the relative speed of separation
option_b: the ratio of the total kinetic energy after the collision to that before it
option_c: the ratio of the relative speed of separation to the relative speed of approach
option_d: the ratio of the total momentum after the collision to that before it
correct_answer_text: the ratio of the relative speed of separation to the relative speed of approach
solution: The coefficient of restitution measures how much of the relative motion survives the collision. It is 1 for a perfectly elastic collision, in which the bodies separate as fast as they approached, and 0 for a perfectly inelastic collision, in which they move off together with no relative velocity at all. Real collisions lie between these two limits.
formula_principle: e = (relative velocity of separation)/(relative velocity of approach); e = 1 for a perfectly elastic collision and e = 0 for a perfectly inelastic one.
common_misconception: Students invert the ratio and obtain values greater than one, which no ordinary collision can give.

concept_tested: Coefficient of restitution from rebound height
stem: A ball dropped from a height of 10 m onto a floor rebounds to a height of 2.5 m. The coefficient of restitution between the ball and the floor is
solution: The speed at any height is proportional to the square root of that height, since v is the square root of 2 g h. Hence e equals the square root of (2.5/10), which is the square root of 0.25, that is 0.5. Equivalently, the height ratio is the square of the coefficient.
formula_principle: e = v_up/v_down and v is proportional to the square root of h, so e = square root of (h_rebound/h_drop).
common_misconception: Students quote the ratio of the heights directly and forget that speed goes as the square root of the height.

concept_tested: Kinetic energy lost when two bodies stick together
stem: A body of mass 1 kg moving at 10 m s^-1 collides with a stationary body of mass 4 kg and the two move off together. The loss in kinetic energy is
solution: Momentum conservation gives 1 x 10 = 5 v, so v = 2 m s^-1. The initial kinetic energy is (1/2) x 1 x 100 = 50 J and the final kinetic energy is (1/2) x 5 x 4 = 10 J. The loss is 50 - 10 = 40 J, which appears as heat, sound and deformation.
formula_principle: m1 u = (m1 + m2) v; then the loss is (1/2) m1 u^2 - (1/2)(m1 + m2)v^2.
common_misconception: Students quote the surviving kinetic energy instead of the loss, or expect no loss because momentum is conserved.

concept_tested: Head on elastic collision with a heavier body at rest
stem: A body of mass 2 kg moving at 8 m s^-1 makes a head on elastic collision with a stationary body of mass 6 kg. The velocity of the 2 kg body just after the collision is
option_a: 4 m s^-1 in the original direction
option_b: 4 m s^-1 in the reverse direction
option_c: 2 m s^-1 in the reverse direction
option_d: 8 m s^-1 in the reverse direction
correct_answer_text: 4 m s^-1 in the reverse direction
solution: Substituting m1 = 2 kg, m2 = 6 kg and u = 8 m s^-1 gives v1 = (2 - 6) x 8/8 = -4 m s^-1, so the 2 kg body rebounds at 4 m s^-1. The 6 kg body moves forward at v2 = 2 x 2 x 8/8 = 4 m s^-1. A check: momentum before is 16 kg m s^-1 and after is -8 + 24 = 16 kg m s^-1, while the kinetic energy is 64 J before and 16 + 48 = 64 J after.
formula_principle: For a head on elastic collision with the target at rest, v1 = (m1 - m2)u/(m1 + m2) and v2 = 2 m1 u/(m1 + m2).
common_misconception: Students assume the incident body always continues forward and miss the reversal that occurs when the target is heavier.

concept_tested: Force between two point masses varies as the product of the masses and inversely as the square of the separation
stem: Two point masses m1 and m2 are separated by a distance r. According to Newton's law of gravitation the magnitude of the force of attraction between them is proportional to
solution: Newton's law of gravitation states that every particle attracts every other particle with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. Hence F is proportional to m1 m2 / r^2.
formula_principle: F = G m1 m2 / r^2
common_misconception: Students sometimes remember an inverse first power or an inverse cube dependence by confusing force with potential or with dipole fields.

concept_tested: SI unit of the universal gravitational constant G
stem: The SI unit of the universal gravitational constant G is
solution: Rearranging F = G m1 m2 / r^2 gives G = F r^2 / (m1 m2). The unit is therefore newton times metre squared divided by kilogram squared, that is N m^2 kg^-2.
common_misconception: Students often quote N m^2 kg^-1 by forgetting that the product of two masses divides the numerator.

concept_tested: Effect of doubling the separation on the gravitational force
stem: The gravitational force between two point masses is F when their separation is r. If the separation is made 2r while the masses are unchanged, the new force is
solution: Since F is proportional to 1 / r^2, doubling r multiplies the force by 1 / 2^2 = 1 / 4. Hence the new force is F / 4.
formula_principle: F is proportional to 1 / r^2
common_misconception: Students forget that the inverse square law makes the force fall four fold, not two fold, when the distance doubles.

concept_tested: Gravitational force is always attractive and is unaffected by the intervening medium
stem: Which one of the following statements about the gravitational force between two bodies is correct?
option_a: It is always attractive and its value does not depend on the nature of the medium between the bodies
option_b: It is always attractive and its value becomes smaller when a dense medium fills the space between the bodies
option_c: It may be attractive or repulsive depending on the nature of the two bodies
option_d: It acts only when the two bodies are joined by a material medium that can transmit it
correct_answer_text: It is always attractive and its value does not depend on the nature of the medium between the bodies
solution: Gravitation is always an attraction because mass is of one sign only. It is a central force that acts along the line joining the bodies, it obeys Newton's third law, and unlike the electrostatic force it is not screened or modified by any intervening medium.
formula_principle: Properties of the gravitational interaction
common_misconception: Students transfer the electrostatic idea that a medium of high permittivity weakens the force, which has no gravitational analogue.

concept_tested: G is a universal constant with the same value everywhere
stem: The universal gravitational constant G
option_a: has a larger value on the surface of the Earth than on the surface of the Moon
option_b: has the same value at every place in the universe
option_c: has a value that decreases as the separation between the interacting bodies increases
option_d: has a value that depends on the two particular masses that are interacting
correct_answer_text: has the same value at every place in the universe
solution: G is a universal constant. Its measured value 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2 is the same for every pair of bodies, at every location and at every separation. Only the acceleration due to gravity g changes from place to place.
formula_principle: G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2 everywhere
common_misconception: Students confuse the universal constant G with the local acceleration due to gravity g.

concept_tested: Computing the gravitational force between two given masses
stem: Two small spheres, each of mass 100 kg, are placed with their centres 1 m apart. Taking G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2, the gravitational force between them is
formula_principle: F = G m1 m2 / r^2
common_misconception: Students slip on the power of ten when multiplying the two mass factors into the small value of G.

concept_tested: Combined effect of changing both masses and the separation
stem: The gravitational force between two point masses is F. One mass is doubled, the other is made three times as large, and the separation between them is doubled. The new force is
solution: The new force is G (2 m1)(3 m2) / (2 r)^2 = 6 G m1 m2 / (4 r^2) = 1.5 G m1 m2 / r^2 = 1.5 F.
formula_principle: F = G m1 m2 / r^2
common_misconception: Students square the mass factors or forget to square the factor by which the separation changes.

concept_tested: The mutual gravitational forces on two bodies are equal in magnitude
stem: The Earth attracts a stone of mass 1 kg with a gravitational force of magnitude F. The magnitude of the force with which the stone attracts the Earth is
option_a: much smaller than F, in the ratio of the mass of the stone to the mass of the Earth
option_b: much larger than F, in the ratio of the mass of the Earth to the mass of the stone
option_c: equal to F, since the two forces form an action reaction pair
option_d: effectively zero, because the Earth is far too massive to be pulled by the stone
correct_answer_text: equal to F, since the two forces form an action reaction pair
solution: The single expression G M m / r^2 gives the force on each body. The Earth pulls the stone and the stone pulls the Earth with forces equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. The accelerations differ enormously because the masses differ, but the forces do not.
formula_principle: F = G M m / r^2 acting on both bodies
common_misconception: Students confuse the equal forces with the very unequal accelerations they produce.

concept_tested: Dimensional formula of the universal gravitational constant
stem: Newton's law of gravitation is F = G m1 m2 / r^2. From this relation the dimensional formula of G is
solution: G = F r^2 / (m1 m2). The dimensions are [M L T^-2][L^2] / [M^2] = [M^-1 L^3 T^-2].
common_misconception: Students forget that the force itself already contains one power of mass, and so miscount the net power of M.

concept_tested: Resultant force on one of three equal masses at the corners of an equilateral triangle
stem: Three particles, each of mass m, are fixed at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side a. The magnitude of the resultant gravitational force on any one particle is
solution: Each of the other two particles pulls with force F = G m^2 / a^2 and the angle between these two forces is 60 degrees. The resultant is sqrt(F^2 + F^2 + 2 F F cos 60) = F sqrt(2 + 1) = sqrt(3) G m^2 / a^2, directed towards the centroid.
formula_principle: Superposition principle with resultant of two equal forces at 60 degrees
common_misconception: Students add the two equal forces arithmetically instead of using the parallelogram law at 60 degrees.

concept_tested: Gravitational force cannot be screened by an intervening body
stem: Two heavy spheres attract each other with a force F. A thick lead slab is now introduced so that it completely fills the space between the two spheres. The force of attraction between the spheres becomes
option_a: equal to F, apart from the small extra pull of the slab itself on each sphere
option_b: smaller than F, because the slab partly screens the gravitational pull
option_c: larger than F, because the dense slab strengthens the gravitational field between the spheres
option_d: exactly zero, because lead is opaque to the gravitational interaction
correct_answer_text: equal to F, apart from the small extra pull of the slab itself on each sphere
solution: The gravitational interaction between two masses depends only on the two masses and their separation. There is no known gravitational screening, so the mutual force between the two spheres is unchanged. The slab merely adds its own separate attraction on each sphere.
formula_principle: Gravitational force is independent of the intervening medium
common_misconception: Students carry over electrostatic shielding by a conductor and expect a similar screening for gravity.

concept_tested: Splitting a fixed total mass so that the mutual force is greatest
stem: A total mass M is divided into two parts, which are then placed a fixed distance r apart. The mutual gravitational force between the parts is greatest when the two parts have masses
solution: With one part m the other is M - m, so F = G m (M - m) / r^2. The product m (M - m) = M m - m^2 is maximum when its derivative M - 2m is zero, that is m = M / 2. Both parts are therefore M / 2.
