option_a: 1 degree Celsius, and of 0.56 degree Fahrenheit
option_b: 274.15 degree Celsius, and of 33.8 degree Fahrenheit
option_c: 1 degree Celsius, and of 1.8 degree Fahrenheit
option_d: 1.8 degree Celsius, and of 1 degree Fahrenheit
correct_answer_text: 1 degree Celsius, and of 1.8 degree Fahrenheit
solution: The Kelvin and Celsius scales use divisions of exactly the same size, so a rise of 1 K is a rise of 1 degree Celsius. The Fahrenheit scale puts 180 divisions between the ice point and the steam point where Celsius puts 100, so one Celsius degree equals 180/100 = 1.8 Fahrenheit degrees.
formula_principle: delta K = delta C = (5/9) delta F, so delta F = 1.8 delta C.
common_misconception: Converting a temperature interval as though it were a temperature reading.

concept_tested: Temperature at which the Fahrenheit reading is twice the Celsius reading
stem: At a certain temperature the Fahrenheit reading is exactly twice the Celsius reading. That temperature on the Celsius scale is
solution: 2C = 1.8 C + 32 gives 0.2 C = 32, so C = 160. Checking, (9/5) x 160 + 32 = 288 + 32 = 320, which is indeed twice 160.
formula_principle: Put F = 2C in F = (9/5) C + 32.
common_misconception: Reporting the Fahrenheit value when the Celsius value was asked for.

concept_tested: Relative size of the Celsius and Fahrenheit degree
stem: Comparing the size of one degree on the Celsius scale with the size of one degree on the Fahrenheit scale,
option_a: one Celsius degree is the larger, being equal to 1.8 Fahrenheit degrees
option_b: one Fahrenheit degree is the larger, being equal to 1.8 Celsius degrees
option_c: the two are of the same size, since both scales are used for the same range of temperatures
option_d: one Celsius degree equals 32 Fahrenheit degrees
correct_answer_text: one Celsius degree is the larger, being equal to 1.8 Fahrenheit degrees
solution: Between the ice point and the steam point there are 100 Celsius degrees and 180 Fahrenheit degrees. Hence 1 Celsius degree = 180/100 = 1.8 Fahrenheit degrees, so the Celsius degree is the larger of the two.
formula_principle: 100 Celsius divisions span the same interval as 180 Fahrenheit divisions.
common_misconception: Assuming that a scale with larger numbers must have larger divisions.

concept_tested: Absolute temperature from pressure readings referred to the triple point
stem: A constant volume gas thermometer records a pressure of 40 kPa when its bulb is at the triple point of water, 273.16 K, and a pressure of 60 kPa when the bulb is placed in a hot bath. The temperature of the bath is
solution: T = 273.16 x (60/40) = 273.16 x 1.5 = 409.74. The bath is at 409.74 K, since at constant volume the pressure of an ideal gas is proportional to the absolute temperature.
formula_principle: For a constant volume gas thermometer, T = 273.16 x (P / P_triple).
common_misconception: Adding pressure differences to temperatures instead of using the ratio of pressures.

concept_tested: Correcting a reading from a thermometer with displaced fixed points
stem: A mercury thermometer is wrongly graduated. It reads 2 degree Celsius in melting ice and 102 degree Celsius in steam at normal pressure, its scale being uniform. When this thermometer reads 52 degree Celsius, the true temperature is
solution: The wrong scale spans 102 - 2 = 100 of its own divisions between the two fixed points. So t = (52 - 2) x 100 / 100 = 50. The true temperature is 50 degree Celsius. Here the span happens to be 100 divisions, so only the shift of the ice point matters.
formula_principle: True temperature t satisfies (reading - lower fixed point) / (upper fixed point - lower fixed point) = t / 100.
common_misconception: Applying the ice point correction in the wrong direction, or ignoring the calibration entirely.

concept_tested: Converting a reading on a new linear scale into Celsius
stem: On a new temperature scale X the ice point of water is marked 20 X and the steam point 220 X, the scale being uniform. A body whose temperature reads 80 X has a Celsius temperature of
solution: (80 - 20) / (220 - 20) = C / 100, so 60/200 = C/100 and C = 30. The temperature is 30 degree Celsius. Two X divisions correspond to one Celsius degree, and the X scale starts 20 divisions above its own ice point mark.
formula_principle: (X - X_ice) / (X_steam - X_ice) = (C - 0) / 100
common_misconception: Forgetting that both the offset and the scale factor must be handled when passing between two linear scales.

concept_tested: Doubling a Celsius reading does not double the absolute temperature
stem: A body is heated from 27 degree Celsius to 54 degree Celsius. A student claims that its absolute temperature has doubled. Taking K = C + 273.15, the correct statement is that
option_a: the absolute temperature rises from 300.15 K to 600.30 K, so the claim is right
option_b: the absolute temperature rises only from 300.15 K to 327.15 K, a factor of about 1.09
option_c: the absolute temperature is unchanged, since only the Celsius reading was altered
option_d: the absolute temperature rises from 27 K to 54 K, so the claim is right
correct_answer_text: the absolute temperature rises only from 300.15 K to 327.15 K, a factor of about 1.09
solution: 27 degree Celsius is 300.15 K and 54 degree Celsius is 327.15 K. The ratio is 327.15/300.15 = 1.09 approximately, nowhere near 2. Ratios of Celsius readings carry no physical meaning because the Celsius zero is arbitrary.
formula_principle: K = C + 273.15; ratios of temperature are meaningful only on the absolute scale.
common_misconception: Taking ratios of Celsius readings as though the Celsius zero were an absolute zero.

concept_tested: Finding the Celsius temperature corresponding to a given reading on a new scale
stem: On a scale Y the ice point of water is marked -30 Y and the steam point 120 Y, the scale being uniform. The Celsius temperature that corresponds to the reading 0 Y is
solution: The Y scale has 120 - (-30) = 150 divisions for 100 Celsius degrees, so 1 Celsius degree equals 1.5 Y divisions. For Y = 0, (0 - (-30))/150 = C/100, that is 30/150 = C/100, so C = 20. The answer is 20 degree Celsius.
formula_principle: (Y - Y_ice) / (Y_steam - Y_ice) = C / 100
common_misconception: Assuming the zero of an arbitrary scale must be its ice point.

concept_tested: Reading at which a wrongly graduated thermometer happens to be right
stem: A faulty thermometer reads 5 degree Celsius in melting ice and 95 degree Celsius in steam at normal pressure, its scale being uniform. The true temperature at which this thermometer gives a reading numerically equal to the true temperature is
solution: The faulty scale has 95 - 5 = 90 divisions for 100 true degrees, so r = 5 + 0.9 t. Setting r = t gives t = 5 + 0.9 t, that is 0.1 t = 5 and t = 50. The thermometer reads 50 when the true temperature is 50 degree Celsius; above that it reads low and below it reads high.
formula_principle: Reading r and true temperature t are related by (r - 5)/(95 - 5) = t/100.
common_misconception: Assuming that a thermometer with displaced fixed points is wrong at every temperature, or that the agreement occurs at the ice point.

concept_tested: Definition and SI unit of alpha
stem: The coefficient of linear expansion of a solid is the fractional increase in length per unit rise in temperature. Its SI unit is
solution: Since delta L / L is a ratio of two lengths it is a pure number. Dividing it by a temperature interval leaves the unit as per kelvin, that is K^-1. Numerically the same value holds if degree Celsius is used, because the two scales have equal division sizes.
formula_principle: alpha = (1/L)(delta L / delta T)
common_misconception: Leaving a stray metre in the unit by forgetting that alpha uses the fractional and not the absolute change in length.

concept_tested: Areal expansion coefficient in terms of the linear one
stem: For an isotropic solid, the coefficient of areal expansion beta is related to the coefficient of linear expansion alpha by
solution: An area is the product of two lengths, each growing by the factor (1 + alpha delta T). The product is (1 + alpha delta T)^2, which is 1 + 2 alpha delta T when the very small term in (alpha delta T)^2 is dropped. Hence beta = 2 alpha.
formula_principle: beta = 2 alpha for an isotropic solid.
common_misconception: Interchanging the areal and cubical relations.

concept_tested: Cubical expansion coefficient in terms of the linear one
stem: For an isotropic solid, the coefficient of cubical expansion gamma and the coefficient of linear expansion alpha are related by
solution: A volume is the product of three lengths, each growing by the factor (1 + alpha delta T). The product is (1 + alpha delta T)^3, which is 1 + 3 alpha delta T when higher powers of the very small quantity alpha delta T are dropped. Hence gamma = 3 alpha.
formula_principle: gamma = 3 alpha for an isotropic solid.
common_misconception: Cubing alpha rather than tripling it.

concept_tested: Behaviour of a hole cut in a plate when the plate is heated
stem: A circular hole is cut in a uniform metal plate. When the whole plate is heated uniformly, the diameter of the hole
option_a: decreases, because the surrounding metal expands inward into the hole
option_b: stays unchanged, because empty space cannot expand
option_c: decreases at first and then increases once the whole plate is hot
option_d: increases, in exactly the same proportion as any length marked on the plate
correct_answer_text: increases, in exactly the same proportion as any length marked on the plate
solution: Imagine the disc of metal that was removed to make the hole. On heating, that disc would expand and still fit the hole exactly, so the hole must expand by the same amount. All distances in the plate, filled or empty, are multiplied by the same factor (1 + alpha delta T).
formula_principle: Every linear dimension of a heated body, including the diameter of a cavity, scales by (1 + alpha delta T).
common_misconception: Picturing the metal as growing inward and squeezing the hole shut.

concept_tested: Temperature of maximum density of water
stem: Water has its maximum density at
option_a: 4 degree Celsius, and it expands both on cooling below this temperature and on heating above it
option_b: 0 degree Celsius, and it contracts steadily as it is cooled further
option_c: 100 degree Celsius, just before it turns into steam
option_d: -4 degree Celsius, at which the last of it freezes
correct_answer_text: 4 degree Celsius, and it expands both on cooling below this temperature and on heating above it
solution: Unlike most liquids, water contracts as it is warmed from 0 degree Celsius to 4 degree Celsius and expands on further warming. Its volume for a given mass is therefore least, and its density greatest, at 4 degree Celsius. Water also expands on freezing, so ice floats.
formula_principle: Water contracts from 0 degree Celsius to 4 degree Celsius and expands above 4 degree Celsius.
common_misconception: Assuming water behaves like an ordinary liquid and is densest just at its freezing point.

concept_tested: Direction of bending of a bimetallic strip on heating
stem: A bimetallic strip is made by riveting together a strip of brass and a strip of iron, brass having the larger coefficient of linear expansion. When the strip is heated it bends so that
option_a: the iron lies along the outer side of the curve and the brass along the inner side
option_b: both strips curve equally, so the strip stays straight and merely becomes longer
option_c: the strip twists about its own long axis instead of bending
option_d: the brass lies along the outer side of the curve and the iron along the inner side
correct_answer_text: the brass lies along the outer side of the curve and the iron along the inner side
solution: For the same temperature rise the brass tries to become longer than the iron. Being riveted together, the pair can only accommodate this by curving, with the longer brass on the outside of the arc and the shorter iron on the inside. This bending is used to open and close contacts in thermostats.
formula_principle: The metal of larger alpha becomes the longer of the two and forms the convex side.
common_misconception: Assuming that the metal expanding more ends up on the inside of the curve.

concept_tested: Straightforward use of delta L = L alpha delta T
stem: A metal rod 1 m long has a coefficient of linear expansion 2 x 10^-5 K^-1. Its increase in length when it is heated through 50 K is
solution: delta L = 1 x 2 x 10^-5 x 50 = 1 x 10^-3 m, that is 1 mm.
formula_principle: delta L = L alpha delta T
common_misconception: Using 2 alpha or 3 alpha where the simple linear coefficient is required.

concept_tested: Linear expansion with a stated temperature range
stem: A steel rod of length 2 m and coefficient of linear expansion 1.2 x 10^-5 K^-1 is heated from 20 degree Celsius to 120 degree Celsius. The increase in its length is
solution: delta T = 120 - 20 = 100 K. delta L = 2 x 1.2 x 10^-5 x 100 = 2.4 x 10^-3 m, that is 2.4 mm.
formula_principle: delta L = L alpha delta T
common_misconception: Substituting the final temperature in place of the temperature rise.

concept_tested: Increase in the area of a plate using beta = 2 alpha
stem: A square metal plate of side 10 cm is made of a metal for which alpha = 2 x 10^-5 K^-1. When its temperature is raised by 100 K, the increase in its area is
formula_principle: delta A = A beta delta T with beta = 2 alpha
common_misconception: Forgetting the factor of two that converts alpha into the areal coefficient.

concept_tested: Increase in volume of a solid using gamma = 3 alpha
stem: A solid sphere of volume 1000 cm^3 is made of a metal for which alpha = 1 x 10^-5 K^-1. The increase in its volume when it is heated through 100 K is
formula_principle: delta V = V gamma delta T with gamma = 3 alpha
common_misconception: Applying alpha or 2 alpha to a volume change.

concept_tested: Numerical treatment of a hole in a heated plate
stem: A copper plate has a circular hole of diameter 2.0000 cm. Copper has alpha = 1.7 x 10^-5 K^-1. When the plate is heated through 100 K, the diameter of the hole becomes
formula_principle: delta d = d alpha delta T, a cavity expanding exactly like the material around it.
common_misconception: Believing that the surrounding metal expands into the hole and reduces its size.

concept_tested: Relating percentage change in volume to percentage change in length
stem: The length of an edge of a solid metal cube increases by 0.1 percent when the cube is heated. For the same heating, the percentage increase in its volume is about
solution: V is proportional to L^3, so for small changes delta V / V = 3 delta L / L = 3 x 0.1 percent = 0.3 percent. Cubing the small quantity 0.001 would give 10^-9, which is negligible and is not what is asked.
formula_principle: delta V / V = 3 (delta L / L) for small changes.
common_misconception: Cubing the fractional change instead of multiplying it by three.

concept_tested: Relation between apparent and real expansion of a liquid
stem: A liquid is heated in a glass vessel. The coefficient of apparent expansion of the liquid, as judged from the change in its level in the vessel, is
option_a: the real coefficient of cubical expansion of the liquid minus the coefficient of cubical expansion of the glass
option_b: the real coefficient of cubical expansion of the liquid plus the coefficient of cubical expansion of the glass
option_c: the real coefficient of cubical expansion of the liquid minus the coefficient of linear expansion of the glass
option_d: the coefficient of cubical expansion of the glass minus the real coefficient of cubical expansion of the liquid
correct_answer_text: the real coefficient of cubical expansion of the liquid minus the coefficient of cubical expansion of the glass
solution: The container expands at the same time as the liquid, so part of the extra liquid volume is taken up by the extra vessel volume. Only the difference shows as a rise in level, giving gamma_apparent = gamma_real - gamma_vessel.
formula_principle: gamma_apparent = gamma_real - gamma_vessel, with gamma_vessel = 3 alpha_vessel.
common_misconception: Adding the vessel expansion, or using the linear rather than the cubical coefficient of the vessel.

concept_tested: Numerical value of the apparent expansion coefficient
stem: Mercury has a real coefficient of cubical expansion 1.8 x 10^-4 K^-1 and is held in a glass vessel whose glass has alpha = 9 x 10^-6 K^-1. The apparent coefficient of expansion of the mercury in this vessel is
formula_principle: gamma_apparent = gamma_real - 3 alpha_glass
common_misconception: Subtracting the linear coefficient of the container instead of three times it.

concept_tested: Why a pond freezes from the top downward
stem: In a cold country the water in a pond freezes at the surface first, while fish survive in the water below. The chief reason is that
option_a: ice is denser than water and so forms at the surface, where the cooling is fastest
option_b: water is densest at 4 degree Celsius, so water colder than this is lighter and stays on top to freeze, while water at 4 degree Celsius collects at the bottom
option_c: water conducts heat so well that the whole pond cools uniformly and then freezes downward
option_d: the pressure at the bottom of the pond raises the freezing point of the water there
correct_answer_text: water is densest at 4 degree Celsius, so water colder than this is lighter and stays on top to freeze, while water at 4 degree Celsius collects at the bottom
solution: As the pond cools, water sinks until it reaches 4 degree Celsius, the temperature of maximum density. Cooled below that, the water becomes lighter and remains at the surface, where it freezes. Ice, being less dense still, floats and forms an insulating lid, leaving water at about 4 degree Celsius below in which fish can live.
formula_principle: Water is densest at 4 degree Celsius, so colder water rises and ice floats.
common_misconception: Assuming ice is denser than water, or forgetting the anomalous behaviour between 0 and 4 degree Celsius.

concept_tested: Use of a bimetallic strip as a thermostat
stem: A bimetallic strip is fitted in an electric iron. Its role there is to
option_a: bend as the temperature rises and break the circuit at a set temperature, so acting as a thermostat
option_b: expand uniformly so that the heating element is stretched and its resistance is increased
option_c: conduct heat quickly from the heating element to the sole plate of the iron
option_d: store heat while the iron is on and give it back when the iron is switched off
correct_answer_text: bend as the temperature rises and break the circuit at a set temperature, so acting as a thermostat
solution: As the iron heats, the strip curves because the two metals expand by different amounts. At the set temperature the curvature is enough to separate the contacts and cut off the current. As the iron cools the strip straightens and the circuit closes again, so the temperature is held between narrow limits.
formula_principle: Unequal linear expansion of two riveted metals converts a temperature change into a mechanical movement.
common_misconception: Treating the strip as a conductor of heat rather than as a temperature operated switch.

subtopic: Effect of heating on physical quantities
concept_tested: Which property of a solid is unaffected by heating
stem: A solid metal block is heated so that its temperature rises, with no melting and no loss of material. Of the following, the quantity that stays the same is
solution: Heating does not add or remove any material, so the mass is unchanged. Every length grows by (1 + alpha delta T), so areas grow by (1 + 2 alpha delta T) and the volume by (1 + 3 alpha delta T). Since density is mass divided by volume, the density must fall.
formula_principle: Heating changes dimensions and density but conserves mass.
common_misconception: Assuming density is a fixed property of a material at all temperatures.

concept_tested: Time lost by a pendulum clock when the temperature rises
stem: The pendulum of a clock is made of a metal of coefficient of linear expansion 2 x 10^-5 K^-1, and the clock keeps correct time at 20 degree Celsius. The fractional change in the time period is (1/2) alpha delta T. If the temperature rises to 30 degree Celsius, the time lost by the clock in one day of 86400 s is
solution: delta T = 30 - 20 = 10 K, so the fractional change is (1/2) x 2 x 10^-5 x 10 = 1 x 10^-4. Time lost in one day = 1 x 10^-4 x 86400 = 8.64 s. The pendulum lengthens, the period rises and the clock runs slow.
formula_principle: delta T_period / T_period = (1/2) alpha delta T; time lost per day = (1/2) alpha delta T x 86400.
common_misconception: Dropping the factor of one half that comes from the square root in the period formula.

concept_tested: Stress in a rod prevented from expanding
stem: A steel rod is clamped rigidly between two fixed walls at 20 degree Celsius and is then heated to 70 degree Celsius. For steel, Young's modulus is 2 x 10^11 Pa and alpha = 1.2 x 10^-5 K^-1. The thermal stress developed in the rod is
solution: delta T = 70 - 20 = 50 K. The strain the rod would have taken up freely is alpha delta T = 1.2 x 10^-5 x 50 = 6 x 10^-4. Stress = Y x strain = 2 x 10^11 x 6 x 10^-4 = 1.2 x 10^8 Pa. The stress does not depend on the length of the rod.
formula_principle: Thermal stress = Y alpha delta T, since the prevented strain is alpha delta T.
common_misconception: Thinking the thermal stress depends on the length or the cross section of the rod.

concept_tested: Change in the density of a liquid on heating
stem: A liquid has a coefficient of cubical expansion 3 x 10^-5 K^-1. When it is heated through 100 K, its density
solution: gamma delta T = 3 x 10^-5 x 100 = 3 x 10^-3, that is 0.3 percent. The volume of the fixed mass rises by 0.3 percent, so the density falls by very nearly the same 0.3 percent.
formula_principle: rho' = rho / (1 + gamma delta T), so delta rho / rho is about -gamma delta T for small changes.
common_misconception: Getting the direction of the density change wrong, or using alpha in place of gamma.

concept_tested: Condition for two rods to keep a constant difference of length
stem: A copper rod with alpha = 1.8 x 10^-5 K^-1 and a steel rod with alpha = 1.2 x 10^-5 K^-1 are cut so that the steel rod is 10 cm longer than the copper rod, and this difference stays the same at every temperature. The length of the copper rod is
solution: The two rods must expand by equal amounts, so L_steel x 1.2 x 10^-5 = L_copper x 1.8 x 10^-5, giving L_steel = 1.5 L_copper. With L_steel - L_copper = 10 cm, 0.5 L_copper = 10 cm, so L_copper = 20 cm and L_steel = 30 cm.
formula_principle: For the difference of lengths to be independent of temperature, L1 alpha1 = L2 alpha2.
common_misconception: Setting the lengths in the ratio of the coefficients rather than in the inverse ratio.

concept_tested: Overflow from a vessel filled to the brim
stem: A glass vessel of volume 1000 cm^3 is filled to the brim with a liquid of coefficient of cubical expansion 1.8 x 10^-4 K^-1. The glass has alpha = 1 x 10^-5 K^-1. The volume of liquid that overflows when the whole is heated through 100 K is
formula_principle: Overflow = V (gamma_liquid - gamma_vessel) delta T, with gamma_vessel = 3 alpha.
common_misconception: Forgetting that the vessel also grows, so that only the difference of the two expansions spills over.

concept_tested: Comparing the volume increases of two spheres of different size
stem: Two solid spheres of the same metal have radii in the ratio 1:2 and are heated through the same temperature rise. The ratio of the increases in their volumes is
solution: Both spheres are of the same metal and get the same delta T, so delta V is proportional to V, which is proportional to r^3. With radii in the ratio 1:2, the volumes and hence the volume increases are in the ratio 1:8.
formula_principle: delta V = gamma V delta T, and V is proportional to the cube of the radius.
common_misconception: Using the ratio of radii or of areas where the ratio of volumes is required.

concept_tested: Shape of the volume against temperature graph for water
stem: The graph of the volume of a fixed mass of water plotted against temperature, over the range 0 degree Celsius to 10 degree Celsius, is
option_a: a straight line of positive slope throughout the range
option_b: a curve that rises to a maximum at 4 degree Celsius and falls on either side of it
option_c: a curve that falls to a minimum at 4 degree Celsius and rises on either side of it
option_d: a horizontal straight line, since water does not expand over this range
correct_answer_text: a curve that falls to a minimum at 4 degree Celsius and rises on either side of it
solution: From 0 degree Celsius up to 4 degree Celsius the volume of a fixed mass of water decreases with rising temperature, an unusual contraction on heating. Above 4 degree Celsius it increases in the normal way. The curve therefore has a minimum at 4 degree Celsius, mirroring the maximum in the density curve there.
formula_principle: For water, volume is minimum and density maximum at 4 degree Celsius.
common_misconception: Drawing the volume curve with a maximum at 4 degree Celsius by confusing it with the density curve.

concept_tested: Correcting a reading taken with an expanded metal scale
stem: A steel measuring scale is correct at 20 degree Celsius. On a hot day at 40 degree Celsius the scale is used to measure a rod and reads 100.000 cm. Steel has alpha = 1.2 x 10^-5 K^-1. The true length of the rod is
solution: At 40 degree Celsius each division of the scale is longer than its marked value by the factor (1 + 1.2 x 10^-5 x 20) = 1 + 2.4 x 10^-4. Since each division now covers more length than it claims, the reading is an underestimate. True length = 100.000 x (1 + 2.4 x 10^-4) = 100.024 cm.
formula_principle: True length = reading x (1 + alpha delta T) when the scale is used above its calibration temperature.
common_misconception: Assuming an expanded scale reads too high; in fact its enlarged divisions make it read too low.

concept_tested: Condition for the empty volume above a liquid to stay constant
stem: A glass vessel of volume 1000 cm^3 is partly filled with mercury. The volume of the empty space above the mercury is to stay the same at every temperature. Mercury has gamma = 1.8 x 10^-4 K^-1 and the glass has alpha = 9 x 10^-6 K^-1. The volume of mercury required is
solution: gamma_glass = 3 x 9 x 10^-6 = 2.7 x 10^-5 K^-1. The empty space is V_vessel - V_mercury, and for it to be unchanged the two expansions must be equal, so V_mercury x 1.8 x 10^-4 = 1000 x 2.7 x 10^-5. Hence V_mercury = 1000 x 2.7 x 10^-5 / 1.8 x 10^-4 = 150 cm^3.
formula_principle: Empty volume stays constant when V_mercury gamma_mercury = V_vessel gamma_vessel.
common_misconception: Balancing volumes instead of balancing the increases in volume, or using alpha in place of 3 alpha for the vessel.

concept_tested: SI unit of specific heat capacity
stem: The specific heat capacity of a substance is the heat needed to raise the temperature of unit mass of it by one kelvin. Its SI unit is
solution: Heat is measured in joules, mass in kilograms and temperature interval in kelvin, so c has the unit J kg^-1 K^-1. For water this quantity is 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1.
formula_principle: c = Q / (m delta T)
common_misconception: Confusing specific heat capacity with the heat capacity of the body or with latent heat.

concept_tested: Direct use of the heat equation for water
stem: How much heat must be supplied to raise the temperature of 2 kg of water by 10 K? Take the specific heat capacity of water to be 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1.
solution: Q = 2 x 4200 x 10 = 84000 J, that is 84 kJ.
formula_principle: Q = m c delta T
common_misconception: Omitting the mass, or dividing by it, in Q = m c delta T.

concept_tested: Why water is used as a coolant
stem: Water is used as the coolant in a car radiator chiefly because
option_a: it has a small specific heat capacity, so it heats up quickly and so carries the heat away quickly
option_b: it has a large specific heat capacity, so it can carry away much heat for a small rise in its own temperature
option_c: it has a large latent heat of fusion, so it stays cold for a long time
option_d: it is a better conductor of heat than the metal of the radiator itself
correct_answer_text: it has a large specific heat capacity, so it can carry away much heat for a small rise in its own temperature
solution: With c = 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1, water has one of the largest specific heat capacities of any common substance. Each kilogram absorbs 4200 J for every kelvin it warms, so a modest flow of water can carry a large amount of heat away from the engine without itself becoming very hot.
formula_principle: Q = m c delta T; a large c means a large Q for a modest delta T.
common_misconception: Supposing that a coolant should heat up easily, that is have a small specific heat capacity.

concept_tested: SI unit of the heat capacity of a body
stem: The heat capacity, or thermal capacity, of a body is the product of its mass and its specific heat capacity. Its SI unit is
solution: Multiplying the mass in kilograms by the specific heat capacity in J kg^-1 K^-1 cancels the kilogram and leaves J K^-1. The heat capacity tells how much heat the whole body needs for a rise of one kelvin.
formula_principle: Heat capacity = m c, so its unit is kg x J kg^-1 K^-1 = J K^-1.
common_misconception: Confusing the heat capacity of a body with the specific heat capacity of its material.

concept_tested: Statement of the principle of calorimetry
stem: The principle of calorimetry, used when hot and cold bodies are mixed in a well insulated container, states that
option_a: the temperature lost by the hotter bodies equals the temperature gained by the colder bodies
option_b: the heat lost by the hotter bodies equals the heat lost by the colder bodies
option_c: the final temperature is always the arithmetic mean of the initial temperatures
option_d: the heat lost by the hotter bodies equals the heat gained by the colder bodies
correct_answer_text: the heat lost by the hotter bodies equals the heat gained by the colder bodies
solution: In an insulated container no heat escapes to the surroundings, so all the heat given out by the hotter bodies is taken up by the colder ones. Writing this balance as m1 c1 (T1 - T) = m2 c2 (T - T2) gives the equation from which the final temperature is found.
formula_principle: Heat lost = heat gained, in an insulated system with no change of state.
common_misconception: Balancing temperatures rather than quantities of heat.

concept_tested: Using molar specific heat capacity in Q = n C delta T
stem: A gas has a molar specific heat capacity of 25 J mol^-1 K^-1. The heat needed to raise the temperature of 0.5 mol of it by 40 K is
formula_principle: Q = n C delta T, where C is the molar specific heat capacity.
common_misconception: Mixing up the molar form Q = n C delta T with the mass form Q = m c delta T.

concept_tested: Finding the specific heat capacity from measured data
stem: Supplying 2000 J of heat to a 500 g block of metal raises its temperature by 20 K. The specific heat capacity of the metal is
formula_principle: c = Q / (m delta T)
common_misconception: Leaving the mass in grams when the answer is wanted in J kg^-1 K^-1.

concept_tested: Mixing equal masses of the same liquid
stem: 100 g of water at 80 degree Celsius is mixed with 100 g of water at 20 degree Celsius in an insulated container of negligible heat capacity. The final temperature of the mixture is
solution: The masses and the specific heat capacities are equal, so 80 - T = T - 20, giving 2T = 100 and T = 50 degree Celsius.
formula_principle: m c (80 - T) = m c (T - 20) for equal masses of the same liquid.
common_misconception: Assuming the mixture always ends nearer the hotter sample.

concept_tested: Mixing unequal masses of the same liquid
stem: 200 g of water at 90 degree Celsius is mixed with 300 g of water at 40 degree Celsius in an insulated vessel of negligible heat capacity. The final temperature is
formula_principle: m1 c (T1 - T) = m2 c (T - T2), so T = (m1 T1 + m2 T2) / (m1 + m2) for one liquid.
common_misconception: Taking the simple mean of the two temperatures when the masses are unequal.

concept_tested: Temperature rises for equal heat given to different materials
stem: Two bodies of equal mass are made of materials whose specific heat capacities are in the ratio 1:2. When the same quantity of heat is given to each, and neither changes state, the ratio of their rises in temperature is
solution: With the same Q and the same m, delta T is inversely proportional to c. Since the specific heats are in the ratio 1:2, the temperature rises are in the ratio 2:1, the body with the smaller specific heat capacity getting hotter.
formula_principle: delta T = Q / (m c), so for fixed Q and m, delta T varies as 1/c.
common_misconception: Assuming the temperature rise follows the specific heat capacity directly rather than inversely.

concept_tested: Water equivalent of a calorimeter
stem: A calorimeter of mass 0.21 kg is made of a metal of specific heat capacity 400 J kg^-1 K^-1. Taking the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1, the water equivalent of the calorimeter is
solution: The heat capacity of the calorimeter is 0.21 x 400 = 84 J K^-1. The mass of water with the same heat capacity is 84 / 4200 = 0.02 kg, that is 20 g.
formula_principle: Water equivalent w satisfies w c_water = m c, so w = m c / c_water.
common_misconception: Quoting the heat capacity in J K^-1 as if it were the water equivalent in grams.

concept_tested: Distinguishing an intensive from an extensive property
stem: Two blocks of the same metal have masses 1 kg and 3 kg. Comparing the two blocks,
option_a: their heat capacities are equal, while the specific heat capacity of the heavier block is three times that of the lighter one
option_b: both the specific heat capacity and the heat capacity of the heavier block are three times those of the lighter one
option_c: their specific heat capacities are equal, while the heat capacity of the heavier block is three times that of the lighter one
option_d: both the specific heat capacity and the heat capacity are the same for the two blocks
correct_answer_text: their specific heat capacities are equal, while the heat capacity of the heavier block is three times that of the lighter one
solution: Both blocks are of the same metal, so both have the same c. The heat capacity is m c, so for the 3 kg block it is three times that for the 1 kg block. The heavier block therefore needs three times as much heat for the same temperature rise.
formula_principle: Specific heat capacity depends only on the material; heat capacity = m c depends on the mass as well.
common_misconception: Treating specific heat capacity as though it grew with the size of the sample.

concept_tested: Heat needed for a stated temperature range
stem: The heat required to raise the temperature of 5 kg of water from 20 degree Celsius to 100 degree Celsius, with none of it boiling away, is (specific heat capacity of water 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1)
solution: delta T = 100 - 20 = 80 K. Q = 5 x 4200 x 80 = 1680000 J, that is 1.68 x 10^6 J. No latent heat is involved because the water is only brought to the boiling point and not boiled.
formula_principle: Q = m c delta T
common_misconception: Substituting the final temperature rather than the temperature difference.

concept_tested: Equal heat given to equal masses of water and of oil
stem: Equal masses of water, of specific heat capacity 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1, and of an oil, of specific heat capacity 2100 J kg^-1 K^-1, are given the same quantity of heat, with no change of state in either. Then
option_a: the oil ends up hotter, its temperature rise being twice that of the water
option_b: the water ends up hotter, its temperature rise being twice that of the oil
option_c: both reach the same temperature rise, since they were given the same quantity of heat
option_d: the oil ends up hotter, its temperature rise being four times that of the water
correct_answer_text: the oil ends up hotter, its temperature rise being twice that of the water
solution: The oil has half the specific heat capacity of the water, so for the same mass and the same heat its temperature rise is twice as large. Starting from the same temperature, the oil therefore ends up hotter.
formula_principle: delta T = Q / (m c); for equal Q and m, delta T varies inversely as c.
common_misconception: Associating a large specific heat capacity with getting hot quickly.

concept_tested: Specific heat of a metal from a calorimetry experiment
stem: A 200 g block of metal at 100 degree Celsius is dropped into 400 g of water at 20 degree Celsius held in a calorimeter of negligible heat capacity, and the final temperature is 25 degree Celsius. Taking the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1, the specific heat capacity of the metal is
solution: Heat gained by the water = 0.4 x 4200 x (25 - 20) = 8400 J. The metal falls from 100 degree Celsius to 25 degree Celsius, a drop of 75 K, so 0.2 x c x 75 = 8400, that is 15 c = 8400 and c = 560 J kg^-1 K^-1.
formula_principle: Heat lost by metal = heat gained by water: m_m c_m (100 - T) = m_w c_w (T - 20).
common_misconception: Using the initial temperature of the hot body as its temperature drop.

concept_tested: Mixing two different liquids with equal heat capacities
stem: 2 kg of a liquid of specific heat capacity 2100 J kg^-1 K^-1 at 90 degree Celsius is mixed with 1 kg of water of specific heat capacity 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1 at 30 degree Celsius, in an insulated vessel of negligible heat capacity. The final temperature of the mixture is
solution: Heat capacity of the liquid = 2 x 2100 = 4200 J K^-1. Heat capacity of the water = 1 x 4200 = 4200 J K^-1. The two are equal, so 90 - T = T - 30, giving 2T = 120 and T = 60 degree Celsius.
common_misconception: Weighting the average by mass alone when the specific heat capacities differ.

concept_tested: Time for a heater of known power to warm water
stem: An electric heater of power 500 W is immersed in 1 kg of water and the whole of its output goes into the water. Taking the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1, the time needed to raise the temperature of the water by 20 K is
formula_principle: P t = m c delta T
common_misconception: Mixing up power in watts with energy in joules when dividing.

concept_tested: Reading specific heat capacities from temperature against time graphs
stem: Equal masses of two liquids X and Y are heated by identical heaters, and the temperature of each is plotted against time. The line for X has the steeper slope. It follows that
option_a: X has the larger specific heat capacity, since its temperature climbs faster
option_b: Y has the larger specific heat capacity, since it needs more heat for the same rise in temperature
option_c: the two have equal specific heat capacities, since the heaters supply heat at the same rate
option_d: Y has the larger latent heat of fusion, which is what sets the slope of the line
correct_answer_text: Y has the larger specific heat capacity, since it needs more heat for the same rise in temperature
solution: The heaters give the same power P and the masses are equal, so the slope of each line is P / (m c). A steeper slope therefore corresponds to a smaller c. Since X has the steeper line, X has the smaller specific heat capacity and Y the larger.
formula_principle: P t = m c delta T, so the slope delta T / t = P / (m c).
common_misconception: Reading a steep temperature rise as a sign of a large specific heat capacity.

concept_tested: Power of a heater from the flow rate and temperature rise
stem: Water flows steadily through an electric heater at the rate of 0.1 kg s^-1 and leaves 10 K hotter than it enters. Taking the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1 and assuming no heat is lost, the power of the heater is
solution: In one second, 0.1 kg of water is warmed by 10 K, needing 0.1 x 4200 x 10 = 4200 J. Energy of 4200 J supplied each second is a power of 4200 W.
formula_principle: P = (mass per second) x c x delta T
common_misconception: Forgetting that a rate of flow already carries the per second factor, so no extra division by time is needed.

concept_tested: Heat given out by water and by copper cooling over the same range
stem: A 1 kg mass of water and a 1 kg mass of copper of specific heat capacity 400 J kg^-1 K^-1 are each cooled from 90 degree Celsius to 40 degree Celsius. Taking the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1, the heat given out
option_a: is 2.1 x 10^5 J for the water and 2 x 10^4 J for the copper
option_b: is 2 x 10^4 J for the water and 2.1 x 10^5 J for the copper
option_c: is 2.1 x 10^5 J for each, since the masses and the temperature falls are the same
option_d: is 4.2 x 10^5 J for the water and 4 x 10^4 J for the copper
correct_answer_text: is 2.1 x 10^5 J for the water and 2 x 10^4 J for the copper
solution: delta T = 90 - 40 = 50 K. For the water, Q = 1 x 4200 x 50 = 210000 J = 2.1 x 10^5 J. For the copper, Q = 1 x 400 x 50 = 20000 J = 2 x 10^4 J. The water gives out about ten and a half times as much heat.
formula_principle: Q = m c delta T applied separately to each body.
common_misconception: Assuming equal masses cooling over the same range must give out equal amounts of heat.

concept_tested: Final temperature when a hot metal is dropped into water in a calorimeter
stem: A calorimeter of water equivalent 100 g contains 900 g of water at 20 degree Celsius. A 2.5 kg block of metal of specific heat capacity 420 J kg^-1 K^-1 at 100 degree Celsius is dropped into it. Taking the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1, the final temperature is
solution: The calorimeter and its water together behave like 900 + 100 = 1000 g = 1 kg of water, of heat capacity 1 x 4200 = 4200 J K^-1. The metal has heat capacity 2.5 x 420 = 1050 J K^-1. Balancing, 1050 (100 - T) = 4200 (T - 20), so 100 - T = 4 (T - 20) = 4T - 80. Hence 5T = 180 and T = 36 degree Celsius.
formula_principle: m_metal c_metal (100 - T) = (m_water + water equivalent) c_water (T - 20).
common_misconception: Forgetting that the calorimeter itself absorbs heat, expressed through its water equivalent.

concept_tested: Deducing an unknown mixture temperature from two given mixtures
stem: Equal masses of three liquids X, Y and Z are at 10 degree Celsius, 20 degree Celsius and 30 degree Celsius respectively. When equal masses of X and Y are mixed the final temperature is 15 degree Celsius, and when equal masses of Y and Z are mixed the final temperature is 25 degree Celsius. When equal masses of X and Z are mixed the final temperature is
solution: Mixing X and Y gives 15 degree Celsius, exactly midway between 10 and 20, so c_X (15 - 10) = c_Y (20 - 15), that is c_X = c_Y. Mixing Y and Z gives 25 degree Celsius, midway between 20 and 30, so c_Y = c_Z. Hence all three specific heat capacities are equal, and mixing X at 10 degree Celsius with Z at 30 degree Celsius gives the midpoint, 20 degree Celsius.
formula_principle: For equal masses, m c1 (T1 - T) = m c2 (T - T2), so the mixture temperature is midway only when c1 = c2.
common_misconception: Failing to see that a mixture landing exactly midway proves the two heat capacities are equal.

major_topic: Latent Heat and Change of State
concept_tested: Definition of latent heat of fusion
stem: The latent heat of fusion of a substance is the heat needed to
option_a: change unit mass of it from solid to liquid at its melting point, with no change of temperature
option_b: raise the temperature of unit mass of the solid by one kelvin
option_c: change unit mass of it from liquid to vapour at its boiling point, with no change of temperature
option_d: raise the temperature of unit mass of the liquid from its melting point to its boiling point
correct_answer_text: change unit mass of it from solid to liquid at its melting point, with no change of temperature
solution: Latent heat of fusion is the energy per unit mass needed to break down the ordered solid structure into a liquid at the melting point. Its defining feature is that the temperature does not change while the heat is being absorbed. For ice it is 3.36 x 10^5 J kg^-1.
formula_principle: Q = m L, with the temperature constant during the change of state.
common_misconception: Confusing latent heat of fusion with specific heat capacity or with the latent heat of vaporisation.

major_topic: Latent Heat and Change of State
concept_tested: Temperature behaviour while a solid melts
stem: A block of ice at 0 degree Celsius is being supplied with heat steadily and is melting. While the melting goes on,
option_a: its temperature rises steadily from 0 degree Celsius towards room temperature
option_b: its temperature stays at 0 degree Celsius, the heat supplied going into breaking up the solid structure
option_c: its temperature falls, since melting is a cooling process
option_d: its temperature stays at 0 degree Celsius because no heat is actually being absorbed by the ice
correct_answer_text: its temperature stays at 0 degree Celsius, the heat supplied going into breaking up the solid structure
solution: The heat supplied during melting is used to overcome the forces holding the molecules in their fixed lattice positions rather than to increase their average kinetic energy. Since temperature is a measure of that average kinetic energy, the temperature stays at the melting point until the last of the ice has melted.
formula_principle: During a change of state the heat supplied is latent heat and the temperature is constant.
common_misconception: Believing that supplying heat must always raise the temperature.

major_topic: Latent Heat and Change of State
concept_tested: Direct use of Q = m L for melting ice
stem: The latent heat of fusion of ice is 3.36 x 10^5 J kg^-1. The heat needed to melt 2 kg of ice already at 0 degree Celsius is
solution: Q = 2 x 3.36 x 10^5 = 6.72 x 10^5 J. No m c delta T term appears because the ice is already at its melting point and the temperature does not change.
formula_principle: Q = m L
common_misconception: Adding a sensible heat term when the substance is already at the melting point.

major_topic: Latent Heat and Change of State
concept_tested: Meaning of sublimation
stem: Sublimation is the process in which
option_a: a solid changes directly into vapour without passing through the liquid state, as camphor does
option_b: a liquid changes into vapour at a temperature below its boiling point
option_c: a vapour changes directly into a liquid on being cooled
option_d: a solid melts and then at once boils away at the same temperature
correct_answer_text: a solid changes directly into vapour without passing through the liquid state, as camphor does
solution: Camphor, iodine and solid carbon dioxide pass straight from the solid state to the vapour state at ordinary pressures. The heat absorbed per unit mass in doing so is the latent heat of sublimation, and the temperature stays constant while it happens.
formula_principle: Sublimation: solid to vapour directly, with its own latent heat.
common_misconception: Confusing sublimation with evaporation or with rapid boiling.

major_topic: Latent Heat and Change of State
concept_tested: Why steam burns are more severe than boiling water burns
stem: A burn from steam at 100 degree Celsius is more severe than a burn from water at 100 degree Celsius because
option_a: the steam is at a higher temperature than the boiling water
option_b: the steam has a much larger specific heat capacity than the water
option_c: the steam gives out its latent heat of vaporisation, 22.6 x 10^5 J kg^-1, as it condenses on the skin, in addition to any heat given out on cooling
option_d: the steam is a much better conductor of heat than the water
correct_answer_text: the steam gives out its latent heat of vaporisation, 22.6 x 10^5 J kg^-1, as it condenses on the skin, in addition to any heat given out on cooling
solution: Each kilogram of steam that condenses on the skin gives up 22.6 x 10^5 J of latent heat while still at 100 degree Celsius, and the water so formed then cools and gives up more heat. Boiling water at the same temperature only supplies the cooling part, so it delivers far less energy per kilogram.
formula_principle: Q = m L for condensation, released at constant temperature.
common_misconception: Assuming steam must be hotter than boiling water for its burn to be worse.

major_topic: Latent Heat and Change of State
concept_tested: SI unit of latent heat
stem: The SI unit of latent heat is
solution: Latent heat is the heat per unit mass needed for a change of state, so its unit is joule per kilogram. No kelvin appears, because the temperature does not change during the process.
formula_principle: L = Q / m
common_misconception: Adding a per kelvin to the unit of latent heat by analogy with specific heat capacity.

major_topic: Latent Heat and Change of State
concept_tested: Heat needed to boil away water already at 100 degree Celsius
stem: The latent heat of vaporisation of water is 22.6 x 10^5 J kg^-1. The heat needed to convert 0.5 kg of water already at 100 degree Celsius into steam at 100 degree Celsius is
formula_principle: Q = m L_vaporisation
common_misconception: Omitting the mass factor when the mass is a fraction of a kilogram.

major_topic: Latent Heat and Change of State
concept_tested: Heat needed to take ice at 0 degree Celsius to water at 100 degree Celsius
stem: Taking the latent heat of fusion of ice as 3.36 x 10^5 J kg^-1 and the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1, the heat needed to change 1 kg of ice at 0 degree Celsius into water at 100 degree Celsius is
solution: Melting: 1 x 3.36 x 10^5 = 3.36 x 10^5 J. Warming the water from 0 to 100 degree Celsius: 1 x 4200 x 100 = 4.2 x 10^5 J. Total = 3.36 x 10^5 + 4.2 x 10^5 = 7.56 x 10^5 J.
formula_principle: Q = m L_fusion + m c delta T
common_misconception: Counting only one of the two stages, or adding a vaporisation term that does not occur.

major_topic: Latent Heat and Change of State
subtopic: Effect of pressure on melting point
concept_tested: Melting point of a substance that expands on freezing
stem: Ice expands on freezing. In consequence, an increase in the pressure applied to ice
option_a: raises its melting point, so that ice melts only above 0 degree Celsius
option_b: lowers its melting point, so that ice can melt at a temperature below 0 degree Celsius
option_c: leaves the melting point unchanged, since ice always melts at 0 degree Celsius
option_d: raises its melting point and at the same time raises the boiling point of the water formed
correct_answer_text: lowers its melting point, so that ice can melt at a temperature below 0 degree Celsius
solution: Pressure favours the state of smaller volume. Since water contracts on melting, increased pressure encourages melting and the solid can turn liquid at a temperature below 0 degree Celsius. Most other substances contract on freezing, so their melting points rise with pressure.
formula_principle: For a substance that expands on freezing, increased pressure lowers the melting point.
common_misconception: Applying the ordinary rule for melting points to ice, whose expansion on freezing reverses it.

major_topic: Latent Heat and Change of State
subtopic: Effect of pressure on boiling point
concept_tested: Why a pressure cooker works
stem: Food cooks faster in a pressure cooker because
option_a: the raised pressure lowers the boiling point of water, so steam is produced sooner
option_b: the sealed vessel prevents any heat at all from escaping, so the flame is used to the full
option_c: the latent heat of vaporisation of water becomes zero at the raised pressure
option_d: the raised pressure inside raises the boiling point of water, so the food is cooked at a temperature above 100 degree Celsius
correct_answer_text: the raised pressure inside raises the boiling point of water, so the food is cooked at a temperature above 100 degree Celsius
solution: A liquid boils when its saturated vapour pressure equals the pressure above it. Sealing the cooker lets the pressure build up, so a higher temperature is needed before boiling starts. Water inside can reach about 120 degree Celsius, and chemical processes in cooking run much faster at that temperature.
formula_principle: Boiling point rises with external pressure.
common_misconception: Thinking the cooker works by trapping heat rather than by raising the boiling point.

major_topic: Latent Heat and Change of State
concept_tested: Explanation of regelation
stem: A wire loaded at both ends is laid across a block of ice. It slowly cuts its way through the block, which is nevertheless left in one piece. This happens because
option_a: the wire conducts heat from the room and simply melts a channel that then stays open
option_b: the pressure under the wire raises the melting point there, so the ice melts and then refreezes
option_c: the pressure under the wire lowers the melting point there so the ice melts, and the water refreezes above the wire where the pressure is normal again
option_d: friction between the wire and the ice melts the ice, and the block reunites as it cools
correct_answer_text: the pressure under the wire lowers the melting point there so the ice melts, and the water refreezes above the wire where the pressure is normal again
solution: Under the loaded wire the pressure is large, and since ice expands on freezing this lowers its melting point below the ambient temperature, so the ice melts. The water flows to the region just above the wire, where the pressure is back to normal, and there it freezes again, giving out its latent heat. The wire therefore passes through while the block stays solid.
formula_principle: Regelation: pressure melting followed by refreezing when the pressure is removed.
common_misconception: Attributing the effect to conduction or friction rather than to pressure melting.

major_topic: Latent Heat and Change of State
concept_tested: Meaning of the flat portions of a heating curve
stem: A solid is heated at a steady rate from below its melting point until it is well above its boiling point, and its temperature is plotted against time. The horizontal portions of the graph correspond to
option_a: the intervals during which the substance is simply being warmed within a single state
option_b: the intervals during which the substance is changing state, the heat supplied being used as latent heat
option_c: the intervals during which no heat at all is being supplied to the substance
option_d: the intervals during which the specific heat capacity of the substance falls to zero
correct_answer_text: the intervals during which the substance is changing state, the heat supplied being used as latent heat
solution: Along the sloping portions the heat goes into m c delta T and the temperature climbs. At the melting point and at the boiling point the heat goes into m L instead, so the temperature holds still and the graph runs flat. The lengths of the flat parts are proportional to the latent heats.
formula_principle: Q = m L during a change of state, so temperature stays constant while heat is absorbed.
common_misconception: Reading a flat portion as a period during which no heat is being supplied.

major_topic: Latent Heat and Change of State
concept_tested: Comparing the heat to melt ice with the heat to warm water
stem: Taking the latent heat of fusion of ice as 3.36 x 10^5 J kg^-1 and the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1, compare the heat needed to melt 1 kg of ice at 0 degree Celsius with the heat needed to warm 1 kg of water from 0 degree Celsius to 80 degree Celsius. The correct comparison is that
option_a: melting needs about twice as much heat as the warming
option_b: the warming needs about twice as much heat as the melting
option_c: melting needs about eighty times as much heat as the warming
option_d: the two are equal, each being 3.36 x 10^5 J
correct_answer_text: the two are equal, each being 3.36 x 10^5 J
solution: Melting: 1 x 3.36 x 10^5 = 3.36 x 10^5 J. Warming: 1 x 4200 x 80 = 3.36 x 10^5 J. The two are exactly equal, which is a convenient way to remember that the latent heat of fusion of ice matches an 80 K rise in the temperature of water.
formula_principle: Compare m L with m c delta T.
common_misconception: Underestimating latent heat by comparing it against small temperature rises only.

major_topic: Latent Heat and Change of State
concept_tested: Mass melted by a given quantity of heat
stem: A quantity of heat equal to 8.4 x 10^5 J is supplied to ice at 0 degree Celsius. Taking the latent heat of fusion of ice as 3.36 x 10^5 J kg^-1, the mass of ice that melts is
solution: m = 8.4 x 10^5 / 3.36 x 10^5 = 2.5 kg. All the heat goes into melting because the ice starts at its melting point and the water formed stays at 0 degree Celsius.
formula_principle: m = Q / L
common_misconception: Inverting the ratio when the unknown is the mass rather than the heat.

major_topic: Latent Heat and Change of State
concept_tested: How evaporation differs from boiling
stem: Evaporation differs from boiling in that evaporation
option_a: takes place throughout the body of the liquid, and only at one fixed temperature
option_b: needs no latent heat, whereas boiling needs latent heat
option_c: takes place only at the free surface of the liquid, and at all temperatures
option_d: raises the temperature of the liquid left behind, whereas boiling lowers it
correct_answer_text: takes place only at the free surface of the liquid, and at all temperatures
solution: Molecules leave the free surface of a liquid at any temperature, so evaporation goes on continually and takes latent heat from the liquid, cooling it. Boiling begins only when the saturated vapour pressure equals the external pressure, and then bubbles of vapour form throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature.
formula_principle: Evaporation: surface process at all temperatures. Boiling: bulk process at the boiling point.
common_misconception: Believing that evaporation involves no latent heat because no thermometer reading is fixed.

major_topic: Latent Heat and Change of State
concept_tested: Mixing ice and hot water when the heat exactly melts the ice
stem: 1 kg of ice at 0 degree Celsius is added to 1 kg of water at 80 degree Celsius in an insulated vessel of negligible heat capacity. Take the latent heat of fusion of ice as 3.36 x 10^5 J kg^-1 and the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1. The final contents of the vessel are
option_a: 2 kg of water at 0 degree Celsius
option_b: 2 kg of water at 40 degree Celsius
option_c: 1 kg of ice and 1 kg of water, both at 0 degree Celsius
option_d: 2 kg of water at 20 degree Celsius
correct_answer_text: 2 kg of water at 0 degree Celsius
solution: Cooling the hot water to 0 degree Celsius releases 1 x 4200 x 80 = 336000 J. Melting the ice needs 1 x 3.36 x 10^5 = 336000 J. The two are exactly equal, so all the ice just melts and the mixture is left at 0 degree Celsius, giving 2 kg of water at 0 degree Celsius.
formula_principle: Heat given out by water cooling to 0 degree Celsius = m c delta T; heat needed to melt ice = m L.
common_misconception: Taking a weighted average of temperatures without paying for the latent heat of melting.

major_topic: Latent Heat and Change of State
concept_tested: Final temperature after ice is dropped into warm water
stem: 100 g of ice at 0 degree Celsius is dropped into 500 g of water at 40 degree Celsius in an insulated vessel of negligible heat capacity. Take the latent heat of fusion of ice as 3.36 x 10^5 J kg^-1 and the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1. The final temperature is
solution: Cooling the 500 g of water all the way to 0 degree Celsius would give 0.5 x 4200 x 40 = 84000 J. Melting all the ice needs 0.1 x 3.36 x 10^5 = 33600 J, which is less, so all the ice melts. The remaining 84000 - 33600 = 50400 J warms the whole 0.6 kg of water, giving delta T = 50400 / (0.6 x 4200) = 20 K above 0 degree Celsius. The final temperature is 20 degree Celsius.
formula_principle: m_w c (40 - T) = m_ice L + m_ice c (T - 0)
common_misconception: Warming only the original water at the last stage, or forgetting to check whether all the ice can melt.

major_topic: Latent Heat and Change of State
concept_tested: Heat needed to take ice below its melting point up to water at 0 degree Celsius
stem: Take the specific heat capacity of ice as 2100 J kg^-1 K^-1 and the latent heat of fusion of ice as 3.36 x 10^5 J kg^-1. The heat needed to convert 2 kg of ice at -20 degree Celsius into water at 0 degree Celsius is
solution: Warming the ice: 2 x 2100 x 20 = 84000 J. Melting the ice: 2 x 3.36 x 10^5 = 672000 J. Total = 84000 + 672000 = 756000 J, that is 7.56 x 10^5 J.
formula_principle: Q = m c_ice delta T + m L_fusion
common_misconception: Using the specific heat capacity of water for solid ice, or skipping one of the two stages.

major_topic: Latent Heat and Change of State
concept_tested: Case in which the hot water cannot melt all the ice
stem: 500 g of ice at 0 degree Celsius is placed in 250 g of water at 32 degree Celsius in an insulated vessel of negligible heat capacity. Take the latent heat of fusion of ice as 3.36 x 10^5 J kg^-1 and the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1. Then
option_a: the final temperature is 0 degree Celsius and 100 g of the ice melts
option_b: the final temperature is 0 degree Celsius and all the ice melts
option_c: the final temperature is 10.7 degree Celsius and all the ice melts
option_d: the final temperature is 16 degree Celsius, the mean of the two starting temperatures
correct_answer_text: the final temperature is 0 degree Celsius and 100 g of the ice melts
solution: Cooling the 250 g of water to 0 degree Celsius gives 0.25 x 4200 x 32 = 33600 J. Melting all 500 g of ice would need 0.5 x 3.36 x 10^5 = 168000 J, which is far more. So only part of the ice melts: mass melted = 33600 / 3.36 x 10^5 = 0.1 kg, that is 100 g. Ice remains, so the mixture settles at 0 degree Celsius.
formula_principle: Compare the heat available, m c delta T, with the heat needed to melt all the ice, m L.
common_misconception: Assuming all the ice must melt, and so predicting a final temperature above 0 degree Celsius.

major_topic: Latent Heat and Change of State
concept_tested: Opposite effects of pressure on the boiling point and the melting point of water
stem: Which of the following statements about the effect of an increase in pressure on the changes of state of water is correct?
option_a: It raises both the boiling point of water and the melting point of ice
option_b: It lowers both the boiling point of water and the melting point of ice
option_c: It lowers the boiling point of water but raises the melting point of ice
option_d: It raises the boiling point of water but lowers the melting point of ice
correct_answer_text: It raises the boiling point of water but lowers the melting point of ice
solution: A liquid boils when its saturated vapour pressure matches the external pressure, so raising the pressure demands a higher temperature and the boiling point rises. For melting, pressure favours the denser state, and water is denser than ice, so extra pressure encourages melting and the melting point falls. The two effects therefore run in opposite directions for water.
formula_principle: Boiling point rises with pressure; melting point of ice falls with pressure because ice expands on freezing.
common_misconception: Assuming pressure must shift all transition temperatures in the same direction.

major_topic: Latent Heat and Change of State
concept_tested: Time for a heater to melt ice and then heat the water
stem: 0.5 kg of ice at 0 degree Celsius is heated by a 1000 W heater, all of whose output goes into the ice and the water formed. Take the latent heat of fusion of ice as 3.36 x 10^5 J kg^-1 and the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1. The time taken to bring it all to water at 100 degree Celsius is
solution: Melting: 0.5 x 3.36 x 10^5 = 168000 J. Warming the water from 0 to 100 degree Celsius: 0.5 x 4200 x 100 = 210000 J. Total = 378000 J. Time = 378000 / 1000 = 378 s.
formula_principle: P t = m L_fusion + m c delta T
common_misconception: Counting only one of the two stages when a heater acts over a change of state and a temperature rise.

major_topic: Latent Heat and Change of State
concept_tested: Case in which not all the steam can condense
stem: 200 g of steam at 100 degree Celsius is passed into 1 kg of water at 20 degree Celsius in an insulated vessel of negligible heat capacity. Take the latent heat of vaporisation of water as 22.6 x 10^5 J kg^-1 and the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1. The final temperature of the contents is
option_a: 60 degree Celsius, the mean of the two starting temperatures
option_b: 33.3 degree Celsius, the mass weighted average of the two temperatures
option_c: 20 degree Celsius, since steam at the same pressure cannot warm water
option_d: 100 degree Celsius, with some of the steam remaining uncondensed
correct_answer_text: 100 degree Celsius, with some of the steam remaining uncondensed
solution: Warming the 1 kg of water from 20 degree Celsius to 100 degree Celsius needs 1 x 4200 x 80 = 336000 J. If all 200 g of steam condensed it would release 0.2 x 22.6 x 10^5 = 452000 J, which is more than the water can take before reaching 100 degree Celsius. So only about 336000 / 22.6 x 10^5 = 0.149 kg of the steam condenses, the rest stays as steam, and the whole system settles at 100 degree Celsius.
formula_principle: Compare the heat the cold water can absorb up to 100 degree Celsius with the heat all the steam would release on condensing.
common_misconception: Assuming that all the steam must condense, and so calculating a final temperature below 100 degree Celsius.

concept_tested: SI unit of thermal conductivity
stem: The SI unit of the coefficient of thermal conductivity is
solution: Rearranging gives k in units of W x m divided by m^2 x K, which is W m^-1 K^-1.
formula_principle: Q/t = k A (T1 - T2) / L, so k = (Q/t) L / (A delta T).
common_misconception: Dropping the factor of length and quoting W m^-2 K^-1 instead.

concept_tested: Meaning of the steady state in conduction
stem: A laterally insulated rod is conducting heat between a hot and a cold reservoir. It is said to have reached the steady state when
option_a: the temperature has become the same at every point of the rod
option_b: the temperature at each point of the rod has stopped changing with time, although it still varies from point to point along the rod
option_c: no heat flows through the rod any longer
option_d: both ends of the rod have come to the temperature of the surroundings
correct_answer_text: the temperature at each point of the rod has stopped changing with time, although it still varies from point to point along the rod
solution: At first part of the heat entering the rod is used to warm the rod itself. Once the steady state is reached, each cross section passes on exactly as much heat as it receives, so no point changes its temperature further. The temperature still falls steadily from the hot end to the cold end, and it is this gradient that drives the flow.
formula_principle: In the steady state every cross section passes the same rate of heat flow and no section is storing energy.
common_misconception: Equating the steady state with a uniform temperature along the rod.

concept_tested: SI unit of temperature gradient
stem: The temperature gradient along a conducting rod is the rate of change of temperature with distance along the rod. Its SI unit is
solution: A temperature difference in kelvin divided by a distance in metres gives K m^-1. For a uniform rod with ends at 100 degree Celsius and 0 degree Celsius and length 0.5 m the gradient is 200 K m^-1.
formula_principle: Temperature gradient = delta T / L.
common_misconception: Inverting the ratio or confusing the gradient with the conductivity.

concept_tested: Direct use of the conduction equation
stem: A metal slab of thermal conductivity 50 W m^-1 K^-1 has a face area of 0.02 m^2 and a thickness of 0.5 m. Its two faces are held at 100 degree Celsius and 0 degree Celsius. The rate of flow of heat through it is
formula_principle: Q/t = k A (T1 - T2) / L
common_misconception: Multiplying by the thickness instead of dividing by it.

concept_tested: Effect of doubling the thickness of a slab
stem: The thickness of a conducting slab is doubled while its face area, its material and the temperature difference across it are all unchanged. The rate of heat conduction through it becomes
option_b: one quarter of its earlier value
option_c: one half of its earlier value
correct_answer_text: one half of its earlier value
solution: Doubling L doubles the thermal resistance L/(kA) and so halves the rate of heat flow for the same temperature difference.
formula_principle: Q/t = k A delta T / L, so the rate varies as 1/L.
common_misconception: Assuming the rate falls as the square of the thickness, or confusing it with the area dependence.

concept_tested: SI unit of thermal resistance
stem: For a slab of thickness L, face area A and thermal conductivity k, the thermal resistance is L / (k A). Its SI unit is
solution: Substituting units, R has the units m divided by (W m^-1 K^-1 x m^2), which reduces to K W^-1. The relation Q/t = delta T / R is the exact analogue of Ohm's law with temperature difference for potential difference and rate of heat flow for current.
formula_principle: R = L / (k A), and Q/t = delta T / R.
common_misconception: Quoting the unit of thermal conductance in place of that of thermal resistance.

concept_tested: Rules that govern slabs placed one behind the other
stem: Two slabs of different materials are placed one behind the other, so that all the heat that passes through the first also passes through the second. For this arrangement,
option_a: the thermal resistances add, and the same rate of heat flow passes through both
option_b: the thermal conductances add, and the same temperature difference exists across both
option_c: the thermal resistances add, and the same temperature difference exists across both
option_d: the thermal conductances add, and the same rate of heat flow passes through both
correct_answer_text: the thermal resistances add, and the same rate of heat flow passes through both
solution: Since no heat is lost sideways, the same rate of flow passes through both slabs in the steady state. The total temperature drop is the sum of the two individual drops, and dividing by the common rate of flow shows that the resistances add. The slab of larger resistance carries the larger share of the temperature drop.
formula_principle: Series combination: R_total = R1 + R2, with the same Q/t through each element.
common_misconception: Applying the parallel rule of adding conductances to a series arrangement.

concept_tested: Rules that govern rods placed side by side
stem: Two rods of the same length are placed side by side, both connecting the same hot reservoir to the same cold reservoir. For this arrangement,
option_a: the same rate of heat flow passes through both, and the thermal resistances add
option_b: the same temperature difference acts across both, and the thermal conductances add
option_c: the same temperature difference acts across both, and the thermal resistances add
option_d: the same rate of heat flow passes through both, and the thermal conductances add
correct_answer_text: the same temperature difference acts across both, and the thermal conductances add
solution: Both rods span the same pair of reservoirs, so each has the same temperature difference across it. The total rate of heat flow is the sum of the two individual rates, and dividing by the common temperature difference shows that the conductances k A / L add.
formula_principle: Parallel combination: 1/R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2, with the same delta T across each element.
common_misconception: Carrying the series rule over to a side by side arrangement.

concept_tested: Why metals are good conductors of heat
stem: Metals conduct heat far better than non metals chiefly because
option_a: a metal contains free electrons that move through the lattice and carry energy rapidly from the hot end to the cold end
option_b: the atoms of a metal are much lighter and so vibrate faster than those of a non metal
option_c: metals have a much larger specific heat capacity than non metals
option_d: metals expand more on heating, and the expansion itself carries the heat along the metal
correct_answer_text: a metal contains free electrons that move through the lattice and carry energy rapidly from the hot end to the cold end
solution: In a non metal, energy passes only from one vibrating atom to the next, which is slow. In a metal the free electrons travel large distances between collisions and carry kinetic energy with them, so they transport energy much faster. This is also why good electrical conductors are good thermal conductors.
formula_principle: Conduction in metals is dominated by free electrons; in insulators only lattice vibrations carry energy.
common_misconception: Attributing thermal conduction in metals to expansion or to specific heat capacity.

concept_tested: Junction temperature of two rods of different conductivity
stem: Two rods of the same length and the same cross section are joined end to end. The thermal conductivity of the first is three times that of the second. The free end of the first is held at 100 degree Celsius and the free end of the second at 0 degree Celsius. In the steady state the temperature of the junction is
solution: With k1 = 3k and k2 = k and equal L and A, 3(100 - T) = T, so 300 = 4T and T = 75 degree Celsius. The better conductor takes the smaller share of the temperature drop, here 25 K against 75 K.
formula_principle: In series, the same Q/t gives k1 A (100 - T)/L = k2 A (T - 0)/L.
common_misconception: Placing the junction midway, or giving the better conductor the larger temperature drop.

concept_tested: Effective conductivity of two equal rods joined end to end
stem: Two rods of equal length and equal cross section, of thermal conductivities 600 W m^-1 K^-1 and 300 W m^-1 K^-1, are joined end to end. The effective thermal conductivity of the combination is
solution: k_eff = 2 x 600 x 300 / (600 + 300) = 360000 / 900 = 400 W m^-1 K^-1. The effective value is the harmonic mean and always lies nearer the smaller of the two conductivities.
formula_principle: For two equal rods in series, k_eff = 2 k1 k2 / (k1 + k2).
common_misconception: Taking the arithmetic mean of the two conductivities for a series combination.

concept_tested: Total heat conducted in a given time
stem: A rod of length 1 m and cross sectional area 4 cm^2 has a thermal conductivity of 400 W m^-1 K^-1. Its ends are held at 100 degree Celsius and 0 degree Celsius, and its sides are insulated. The heat that flows through it in 10 minutes is
formula_principle: Q = k A (T1 - T2) t / L
common_misconception: Forgetting to convert square centimetres to square metres, or to convert minutes to seconds.

concept_tested: Comparing series and parallel arrangements of two identical rods
stem: Two identical rods are first joined end to end and then instead placed side by side, and in each case the same pair of temperatures is applied across the whole combination. The ratio of the rate of heat flow in the side by side arrangement to that in the end to end arrangement is
solution: Let each rod have thermal resistance R. End to end gives 2R, so the rate is delta T / (2R). Side by side gives R/2, so the rate is 2 delta T / R. The ratio of the second to the first is (2 delta T / R) divided by (delta T / 2R) = 4. The ratio is 4:1.
formula_principle: Q/t = delta T / R, with R_series = 2R and R_parallel = R/2 for two identical rods of resistance R.
common_misconception: Counting only the change in one of the two arrangements and answering 2:1.

concept_tested: Junction temperature from thermal resistances of unequal rods
stem: Rod P has length 0.1 m, thermal conductivity 200 W m^-1 K^-1 and cross sectional area 1 x 10^-3 m^2. Rod Q has length 0.2 m, thermal conductivity 100 W m^-1 K^-1 and the same cross sectional area. They are joined end to end, the free end of P being held at 100 degree Celsius and the free end of Q at 0 degree Celsius. In the steady state the temperature of the junction is
solution: R_P = 0.1 / (200 x 1 x 10^-3) = 0.5 K W^-1. R_Q = 0.2 / (100 x 1 x 10^-3) = 2 K W^-1. Total = 2.5 K W^-1, so Q/t = 100 / 2.5 = 40 W. The drop across P is 40 x 0.5 = 20 K, so the junction is at 100 - 20 = 80 degree Celsius.
formula_principle: R = L / (k A); in series R adds, Q/t = delta T / R_total, and the drop across each rod is (Q/t) R.
common_misconception: Comparing conductivities alone and ignoring that the rods have different lengths.

subtopic: Growth of ice on a lake
concept_tested: Time dependence of the thickness of ice formed on a pond
stem: The time taken for the layer of ice on a lake to grow from zero thickness to a thickness x is proportional to x^2. If it takes 1 hour for the ice to reach a thickness of 2 cm, the further time needed for it to grow from 2 cm to 4 cm is
solution: Time to reach 2 cm corresponds to 2^2 = 4 units, and this is given as 1 hour, so one unit is 0.25 hour. Time to reach 4 cm corresponds to 4^2 = 16 units, that is 4 hours in all. The further time from 2 cm to 4 cm is 4 - 1 = 3 hours.
formula_principle: t is proportional to x^2, because the growing ice layer is itself the conducting slab.
common_misconception: Assuming ice thickens at a constant rate, and so scaling the time linearly with the thickness.

concept_tested: Junction temperature in a network of three rods
stem: Three rods of the same material and the same cross section have lengths L, L and 2L. The two rods of length L are joined side by side, and this pair is joined end to end with the rod of length 2L. The free end of the long rod is held at 100 degree Celsius and the free end of the side by side pair at 0 degree Celsius. In the steady state the junction between the pair and the long rod is at
solution: Let R0 = L / (k A) be the resistance of one short rod. The pair side by side has resistance R0/2. The rod of length 2L has resistance 2R0. In series the total is 2.5 R0, so the whole 100 K drop is shared in the ratio 2R0 to 0.5R0, that is 4 to 1. The long rod takes 80 K of the drop, leaving the junction at 100 - 80 = 20 degree Celsius.
formula_principle: R = L / (k A); resistances add in series and conductances add in parallel.
common_misconception: Treating two rods placed side by side as though they were a single rod of the same resistance.

concept_tested: Mode by which solar energy reaches the Earth
stem: Heat from the Sun reaches the Earth mainly by
option_a: conduction through the air lying between the Sun and the Earth
option_b: convection currents set up in the space between the Sun and the Earth
option_c: conduction through the vacuum, since a vacuum is a good conductor of heat
option_d: radiation, which needs no material medium
correct_answer_text: radiation, which needs no material medium
solution: Between the Sun and the Earth there is almost perfect vacuum, so neither conduction nor convection can operate over that path. Radiation is electromagnetic and requires no medium, which is why it alone can carry the Sun's energy across space.
