formula_principle: Thermal radiation is an electromagnetic wave and travels through vacuum.
common_misconception: Assuming every mode of heat transfer requires some material medium.

concept_tested: Mechanism of heat transfer by convection
stem: In convection, heat is carried through a fluid by
option_a: the bulk movement of the heated fluid itself from one place to another
option_b: the vibration of the molecules about fixed mean positions, with no bulk movement
option_c: electromagnetic waves that travel through the fluid at the speed of light
option_d: the drift of free electrons through the fluid
correct_answer_text: the bulk movement of the heated fluid itself from one place to another
solution: When part of a fluid is heated it expands, becomes less dense and rises, while cooler denser fluid sinks to take its place. Energy is carried along bodily with the moving fluid. Because it needs matter that can flow, convection is impossible in solids and in vacuum.
formula_principle: Convection: heat carried by the actual movement of a heated fluid.
common_misconception: Confusing convection with conduction, in which the particles stay in place.

concept_tested: Speed of thermal radiation in vacuum
stem: Thermal radiation travels through vacuum with a speed of
option_a: 3 x 10^5 m s^-1, considerably less than that of light
option_b: 340 m s^-1, the same as that of sound in air
option_c: a speed that depends on the temperature of the source that emits it
option_d: 3 x 10^8 m s^-1, the same as that of light
correct_answer_text: 3 x 10^8 m s^-1, the same as that of light
solution: Thermal radiation is an electromagnetic wave, differing from visible light only in wavelength. In vacuum all electromagnetic waves travel at 3 x 10^8 m s^-1 regardless of their wavelength or of the temperature of the source.
formula_principle: Thermal radiation is part of the electromagnetic spectrum and travels at 3 x 10^8 m s^-1 in vacuum.
common_misconception: Assuming hotter sources emit radiation that travels faster.

concept_tested: Identifying an example of forced convection
stem: Which of the following is an example of forced convection?
option_a: the cooling of a computer processor by a fan that blows air over its heat sink
option_b: the rising of warm air above a hot road on a summer afternoon
option_c: the warming of your face when you stand facing a fire from a distance
option_d: the warming of a metal spoon whose lower end is dipped in hot soup
correct_answer_text: the cooling of a computer processor by a fan that blows air over its heat sink
solution: In natural convection the fluid circulates by itself because heated fluid is less dense and rises. In forced convection an outside agency, here a fan, drives the fluid past the hot surface. Forced convection removes heat much faster, which is why fans and pumps are used in cooling systems.
formula_principle: Forced convection: the fluid is driven by an external agency such as a fan or a pump.
common_misconception: Labelling every case of moving air as forced convection, or confusing radiation with convection.

concept_tested: Origin of the daytime sea breeze
stem: During the day a sea breeze blows from the sea towards the land because
option_a: the sea warms faster than the land, so the air over the sea rises and cooler air moves in from over the land
option_b: water conducts heat better than soil, so heat is carried through the ground from the sea to the land
option_c: the land warms faster than the sea, so the air over the land rises and cooler air moves in from over the sea
option_d: the radiation from the Sun pushes the air bodily from over the sea towards the land
correct_answer_text: the land warms faster than the sea, so the air over the land rises and cooler air moves in from over the sea
solution: Water has a much larger specific heat capacity than soil and rock, so for the same sunshine the land becomes hotter than the sea during the day. Air over the hot land expands, becomes less dense and rises, and cooler air from over the sea flows in to replace it, giving the sea breeze. At night the land cools faster and the flow reverses as a land breeze.
formula_principle: Natural convection driven by unequal heating of land and sea, whose specific heat capacities differ greatly.
common_misconception: Getting the direction of the flow wrong by forgetting the large specific heat capacity of water.

concept_tested: Dominant mode of heat transfer in a heated beaker of water
stem: When a beaker of water is heated with a flame placed below it, the heat is carried through the bulk of the water chiefly by
option_a: conduction, since water is an excellent conductor of heat
option_b: radiation from the flame passing straight through the body of the water
option_c: convection currents, the warm water rising and the cooler water sinking to take its place
option_d: conduction through the glass walls of the beaker only
correct_answer_text: convection currents, the warm water rising and the cooler water sinking to take its place
solution: The water just above the flame expands, becomes less dense and rises. Cooler water from the upper part sinks to take its place and in turn gets heated. A steady circulation is set up which distributes heat through the whole beaker far faster than the poor conduction of water ever could.
formula_principle: In fluids heated from below, natural convection is the dominant mode of heat transfer.
common_misconception: Assuming water conducts heat well because it heats up readily on a stove.

concept_tested: Part of the spectrum in which everyday thermal radiation lies
stem: The thermal radiation given out by a body at everyday temperatures lies mainly in
option_a: the ultraviolet part of the electromagnetic spectrum
option_b: the visible part of the electromagnetic spectrum
option_c: the infrared part of the electromagnetic spectrum
option_d: the radio wave part of the electromagnetic spectrum
correct_answer_text: the infrared part of the electromagnetic spectrum
solution: A body at room temperature or a little above emits most strongly at wavelengths of a few tens of micrometres, which lie in the infrared. As the temperature is raised the peak shifts towards shorter wavelengths, so a body first glows dull red and then white hot. This is why infrared cameras can see warm objects in the dark.
formula_principle: The wavelength at which emission peaks falls as the temperature rises.
common_misconception: Supposing that a warm body must give out visible light in order to be radiating.

concept_tested: Media in which convection cannot occur
stem: Convection cannot take place
option_a: in a vacuum only, since a solid can also set up convection currents
option_b: in a solid or in a vacuum, since it needs a fluid that is free to move in bulk
option_c: in a solid only, since a vacuum can carry convection currents
option_d: in any medium unless that medium is also transparent to infrared radiation
correct_answer_text: in a solid or in a vacuum, since it needs a fluid that is free to move in bulk
solution: Convection is the transport of energy by the bodily movement of heated matter. A solid holds its particles at fixed mean positions so they cannot circulate, and a vacuum has no particles at all. Hence convection is confined to liquids and gases, while radiation alone can cross a vacuum.
formula_principle: Convection requires a fluid that can move in bulk; conduction needs matter; radiation needs neither.
common_misconception: Believing that any heating of a solid must involve some convection within it.

concept_tested: How the features of a vacuum flask suppress the three modes
stem: In a vacuum flask the space between the two walls is evacuated and the two facing surfaces are silvered. These two features respectively
option_a: cut down radiation, and cut down conduction and convection
option_b: cut down conduction only, and cut down convection only
option_c: cut down conduction and convection, and cut down radiation
option_d: cut down convection only, and cut down conduction only
correct_answer_text: cut down conduction and convection, and cut down radiation
solution: Conduction and convection both need a material medium, so evacuating the gap between the walls removes both. Radiation crosses a vacuum freely, so it is dealt with separately by silvering the facing surfaces, which makes them poor emitters and good reflectors. The stopper and the thin glass neck limit the small amount of conduction that remains.
formula_principle: Conduction and convection need matter; radiation is reduced by polished reflecting surfaces.
common_misconception: Attributing the silvering to conduction, or forgetting that a vacuum stops convection as well.

subtopic: Convection and poor conduction of water
concept_tested: Heating water at the top of a tube
stem: A tube of water is heated near its upper end while ice is held at the bottom. The water at the top can be made to boil while the ice at the bottom is still unmelted. The reason is that
option_a: water conducts heat so well that the heat is carried out sideways through the glass instead of downward
option_b: the ice at the bottom radiates heat upward and so keeps itself cold
option_c: convection currents carry the heat upward and out of the open top of the tube, away from the ice
option_d: the warm water at the top is less dense and stays where it is, so no convection current reaches the bottom, and water is itself a very poor conductor
correct_answer_text: the warm water at the top is less dense and stays where it is, so no convection current reaches the bottom, and water is itself a very poor conductor
solution: Heated water expands and becomes less dense, so it can only rise. Heating the top therefore sets up no circulation at all, since the warm water is already above the cold. The only route left downward is conduction, and water conducts heat so poorly that the ice at the bottom stays frozen even while the top boils.
formula_principle: Convection carries heat only upward, and water conducts heat very poorly.
common_misconception: Assuming heat must eventually reach the bottom because it does so when a beaker is heated from below.

concept_tested: Quantity to which the rate of cooling is proportional
stem: Newton's law of cooling states that the rate of loss of heat by a body is proportional to
option_a: the absolute temperature of the body alone, irrespective of the surroundings
option_b: the square of the excess of its temperature over that of its surroundings
option_c: the fourth power of the absolute temperature of the surroundings
option_d: the excess of its temperature over that of its surroundings, provided that excess is small
correct_answer_text: the excess of its temperature over that of its surroundings, provided that excess is small
solution: The law holds when the excess of the body's temperature over that of the surroundings is small. The rate of fall of temperature is then proportional to that excess, so a hot body cools quickly at first and ever more slowly as it approaches the temperature of its surroundings.
formula_principle: dQ/dt is proportional to (theta - theta_0), so d theta / dt = -k (theta - theta_0).
common_misconception: Applying a fourth power law, which belongs to black body radiation, to ordinary Newtonian cooling.

subtopic: Rate of cooling and excess temperature
concept_tested: Comparing the cooling rates of two bodies at different temperatures
stem: Two identical cups of tea, one at 90 degree Celsius and the other at 50 degree Celsius, are left in a room at 20 degree Celsius. According to Newton's law of cooling,
option_a: the cup at 90 degree Celsius cools at the greater rate, since its excess temperature is larger
option_b: the cup at 50 degree Celsius cools at the greater rate, since it is nearer the room temperature
option_c: both cool at the same rate, since the cups and the surroundings are the same
option_d: neither cools until the two cups have reached the same temperature as each other
correct_answer_text: the cup at 90 degree Celsius cools at the greater rate, since its excess temperature is larger
solution: The excess temperatures are 90 - 20 = 70 K and 50 - 20 = 30 K. Since the rate of cooling is proportional to the excess, the hotter cup cools 70/30, that is about 2.3 times as fast at that instant.
formula_principle: d theta / dt is proportional to (theta - theta_0).
common_misconception: Thinking a body close to room temperature loses heat faster because there is less left to lose.

concept_tested: Time for a second equal fall in temperature
stem: A body cools from 80 degree Celsius to 70 degree Celsius in 5 minutes while the surroundings stay at 25 degree Celsius. Using Newton's law of cooling with the average excess temperature over each interval, the time taken to cool from 70 degree Celsius to 60 degree Celsius is
solution: First interval: average temperature 75 degree Celsius, excess 75 - 25 = 50 K, and 10/5 = k x 50. Second interval: average temperature 65 degree Celsius, excess 65 - 25 = 40 K, and 10/t = k x 40. Dividing, t/5 = 50/40, so t = 6.25 minutes.
formula_principle: (fall in temperature)/(time) = k x (average temperature during the interval minus surroundings temperature).
common_misconception: Assuming equal falls in temperature take equal times.

concept_tested: Conditions under which Newton's law of cooling is a good approximation
stem: Newton's law of cooling is a good approximation
option_a: when the excess of the body's temperature over that of the surroundings is very large
option_b: only when the body is a perfect black body placed in a vacuum
option_c: only when the body is losing heat by conduction through a solid contact
option_d: when the excess of the body's temperature over that of the surroundings is small, and the surroundings stay at a steady temperature
correct_answer_text: when the excess of the body's temperature over that of the surroundings is small, and the surroundings stay at a steady temperature
solution: For small excess temperatures the loss of heat, whether by convection in the surrounding air or by radiation, is very nearly proportional to the excess. For large excesses this breaks down, since radiation depends on the fourth power of the absolute temperature. The surroundings must also be large and steady, so that they do not warm up appreciably.
formula_principle: Newton's law is the small excess temperature limit of the more general radiation and convection loss.
common_misconception: Applying the law to very hot bodies, where the loss is dominated by radiation and grows much faster.

concept_tested: Time for the next equal fall in temperature of a cooling liquid
stem: A liquid cools from 60 degree Celsius to 50 degree Celsius in 10 minutes while the surroundings are held at 25 degree Celsius. Working with the average excess temperature over each interval, the time it takes to cool further from 50 degree Celsius to 40 degree Celsius is
solution: First interval: average 55 degree Celsius, excess 55 - 25 = 30 K, so 10/10 = k x 30. Second interval: average 45 degree Celsius, excess 45 - 25 = 20 K, so 10/t = k x 20. Dividing gives t/10 = 30/20, so t = 15 minutes.
formula_principle: (fall in temperature)/(time) = k x (average temperature minus surroundings temperature).
common_misconception: Treating cooling as a steady process in which equal falls take equal times.

subtopic: Factors affecting the rate of cooling
concept_tested: What the rate of fall of temperature of a hot body depends on
stem: For a hot body losing heat to its surroundings, the rate of fall of its temperature depends on
option_a: the excess temperature alone, all the other factors cancelling out of the problem
option_b: the mass of the body alone, since the heat capacity is settled by the mass
option_c: the excess temperature, the exposed surface area, the nature of the surface, and the heat capacity of the body
option_d: the surface area alone, the excess temperature having no further effect once cooling has begun
correct_answer_text: the excess temperature, the exposed surface area, the nature of the surface, and the heat capacity of the body
solution: The rate of loss of heat grows with the exposed surface area, with the excess temperature and with the emitting quality of the surface, a dull black surface losing heat faster than a polished one. That heat loss is converted into a fall of temperature by dividing by the heat capacity m c, so a body of large heat capacity cools more slowly for the same heat loss.
formula_principle: d theta / dt = -(k A / m c)(theta - theta_0), where the constant depends on the nature of the surface.
common_misconception: Forgetting that the same rate of heat loss produces a smaller temperature fall in a body of large heat capacity.

concept_tested: Temperature reached after a second equal interval of time
stem: A body cools from 70 degree Celsius to 60 degree Celsius in 5 minutes while the surroundings are held at 30 degree Celsius. Using Newton's law of cooling with the average excess temperature over each interval, its temperature at the end of the next 5 minutes is
solution: First interval: (70 - 60)/5 = 2 = k x (65 - 30) = 35k, so k = 2/35. Second interval with final temperature T: (60 - T)/5 = k x ((60 + T)/2 - 30) = (2/35) x (T/2) = T/35. So 35(60 - T) = 5T, giving 2100 = 40T and T = 52.5 degree Celsius.
formula_principle: (theta_1 - theta_2)/t = k x ((theta_1 + theta_2)/2 - theta_0)
common_misconception: Assuming the temperature falls by the same 10 degree in each successive equal interval of time.

concept_tested: Shape of the graph of the logarithm of excess temperature against time
stem: A hot body cools in surroundings held at a constant temperature theta_0. If theta is the temperature of the body at time t, the graph of log_e (theta - theta_0) against t is
option_a: a straight line with a negative slope
option_b: a straight line with a positive slope
option_c: a curve that bends upward, because the cooling itself is exponential
option_d: a horizontal straight line, since the excess temperature falls at a steady rate
correct_answer_text: a straight line with a negative slope
solution: Separating the variables in d theta / (theta - theta_0) = -k dt and integrating gives log_e (theta - theta_0) = -k t + constant, so theta - theta_0 falls exponentially with time. Plotting log_e (theta - theta_0) against t therefore gives a straight line whose slope is -k, and the value of k can be read off from that slope.
formula_principle: d theta / dt = -k (theta - theta_0), which integrates to log_e (theta - theta_0) = -k t + constant.
common_misconception: Expecting the logarithmic plot to remain curved, or getting the sign of the slope wrong.

concept_tested: Sound in a fluid is a longitudinal mechanical wave
stem: Sound travelling through air is correctly described as
option_a: a transverse mechanical wave in which the particles of air oscillate at right angles to the direction of propagation
option_b: a longitudinal mechanical wave in which the particles of air oscillate along the direction of propagation
option_c: an electromagnetic wave produced by the vibrating charges in the source
option_d: a longitudinal electromagnetic wave whose speed is fixed by the electrical properties of air
correct_answer_text: a longitudinal mechanical wave in which the particles of air oscillate along the direction of propagation
solution: In a sound wave the layers of air are alternately pushed together and pulled apart along the line of travel. Each particle oscillates about its mean position parallel to the direction in which the disturbance advances, which is the defining feature of a longitudinal wave. Because the restoring force comes from the elasticity of the air, the wave is mechanical, not electromagnetic.
formula_principle: Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave requiring an elastic material medium.
common_misconception: Students picture the familiar sine curve drawn for a sound wave and conclude that the air particles move up and down across the direction of travel.

concept_tested: Sound cannot propagate through vacuum
stem: An electric bell is suspended inside a glass jar and kept ringing while the air is slowly pumped out of the jar. As the pumping continues, the sound heard outside
option_a: stays equally loud because the sound travels out through the glass wall of the jar
option_b: becomes louder because the removal of air reduces the resistance offered to the wave
option_c: becomes fainter and fainter and finally cannot be heard at all, although the hammer is still seen striking the gong
option_d: first becomes louder and then dies away once the pressure falls below atmospheric pressure
correct_answer_text: becomes fainter and fainter and finally cannot be heard at all, although the hammer is still seen striking the gong
solution: Sound is carried by the successive pushing of one layer of the medium on the next. As the air is removed there are fewer and fewer particles to pass the disturbance on, so the sound grows steadily fainter. In a good vacuum there is no medium at all and no sound reaches the jar wall, even though light still travels and the hammer is seen to move.
formula_principle: A mechanical wave needs a material medium; sound cannot travel through vacuum.
common_misconception: Treating air as an obstruction to sound rather than as the carrier of the disturbance.

concept_tested: Physical meaning of a compression in a sound wave
stem: In a sound wave travelling through air, a compression is a region in which
option_a: the particles are crowded together, so that the density is above normal while the pressure falls below normal
option_b: the particles are spread apart, so that the density and the pressure are both above their normal values
option_c: the particles are momentarily at rest, so that the density stays normal while the pressure rises
option_d: the particles are crowded together, so that the density and the pressure are above their normal values
correct_answer_text: the particles are crowded together, so that the density and the pressure are above their normal values
solution: As the source vibrates it pushes the neighbouring layer of air forward, squeezing the particles into a smaller volume. In this region the number of particles per unit volume rises, so the density rises, and since the gas is compressed its pressure also rises above the undisturbed value. The opposite region, where the particles are pulled apart, is a rarefaction of reduced density and reduced pressure.
formula_principle: Compression: density and pressure above normal. Rarefaction: density and pressure below normal.
common_misconception: Believing that the pressure and the density can vary in opposite senses within the same region of a gas.

concept_tested: Elasticity and inertia are both required for wave propagation
stem: The two properties that a material medium must possess if it is to carry a sound wave are
option_a: elasticity, which supplies the restoring force, and inertia, which allows the disturbance to overshoot the mean position
option_b: elasticity, which supplies the restoring force, and high thermal conductivity, which allows heat to move with the wave
option_c: low density and low viscosity, so that the layers of the medium can slide over one another freely
option_d: inertia, which stores the energy, and electrical conductivity, which carries the disturbance forward
correct_answer_text: elasticity, which supplies the restoring force, and inertia, which allows the disturbance to overshoot the mean position
solution: When a layer of the medium is displaced, its elasticity pulls it back towards the mean position. Its inertia then carries it past that position, displacing the next layer in turn. The alternation of these two effects is what passes the disturbance along, so both elasticity and inertia are essential.
formula_principle: A mechanical wave needs elasticity for a restoring force and inertia for continued motion.
common_misconception: Assuming that a light or thin medium carries sound better, because it is easier to set moving.

concept_tested: Distance between successive compressions equals one wavelength
stem: In a sound wave travelling through air, the distance between the centres of two successive compressions is equal to
option_a: one half of the wavelength of the wave
option_b: one quarter of the wavelength of the wave
option_c: twice the wavelength of the wave
solution: Two successive compressions are the nearest pair of points that are in exactly the same state of motion and the same state of pressure. The distance between two such consecutive points in phase is by definition one wavelength. A compression and the rarefaction next to it are in opposite phase and are separated by half a wavelength.
formula_principle: Wavelength is the distance between two consecutive points in the same phase.
common_misconception: Mixing up the compression to compression distance with the compression to rarefaction distance.

concept_tested: A wave transports energy without bulk transport of matter
stem: A loudspeaker sounds a steady note in a still room. Regarding the air between the speaker and the listener,
option_a: both energy and air travel steadily from the speaker to the listener, producing a slow breeze in the room
option_b: air travels from the speaker to the listener but the energy stays localised near the speaker
option_c: energy travels from the speaker to the listener while each air particle merely oscillates about a fixed mean position
option_d: neither energy nor air moves through the room, since each particle simply vibrates in place
correct_answer_text: energy travels from the speaker to the listener while each air particle merely oscillates about a fixed mean position
solution: Each particle of air executes a small oscillation about its own mean position and hands its energy on to the next particle. Over one full cycle the net displacement of any particle is zero, so no air is carried across the room, yet the energy given out by the cone of the speaker travels outward continuously and reaches the ear.
formula_principle: Progressive waves transport energy and momentum, not the medium itself.
common_misconception: Imagining that the air itself is blown from the source to the listener along with the sound.

concept_tested: Longitudinal waves cannot be polarised
stem: Sound waves in air cannot be polarised. The reason is that
option_a: the frequency of a sound wave is far too low for a polariser to act on it
option_b: the vibrations of the particles are along the direction of propagation, so there is no preferred direction across the wave to select
option_c: the wave carries too little energy to be affected by a polarising sheet
option_d: air is an isotropic medium and isotropic media never allow polarisation of any wave
correct_answer_text: the vibrations of the particles are along the direction of propagation, so there is no preferred direction across the wave to select
solution: Polarisation means restricting the vibration to one particular direction in the plane perpendicular to the direction of travel. A longitudinal wave has all its vibration along the direction of travel, so that perpendicular plane contains no vibration to restrict. Hence sound in air, being longitudinal, cannot be polarised, and the failure of a polarisation test is itself evidence that a wave is longitudinal.
formula_principle: Only transverse waves can be polarised, since only they have vibration directions across the line of travel.
common_misconception: Thinking polarisation depends on frequency or intensity rather than on the direction of particle vibration.

concept_tested: Separation between a compression and the nearest rarefaction
stem: A sound wave of frequency 200 Hz travels in air with speed 340 m s^-1. The distance between the centre of a compression and the centre of the nearest rarefaction is
solution: The wavelength is lambda = v / f = 340 / 200 = 1.7 m. A compression and the rarefaction next to it are in opposite phase, so they are separated by half a wavelength, that is 1.7 / 2 = 0.85 m.
formula_principle: v = f lambda; a compression and the nearest rarefaction are lambda/2 apart.
common_misconception: Quoting the full wavelength as the compression to rarefaction distance.

concept_tested: Distinction between the speed of a particle and the speed of the wave
stem: For a progressive sound wave in air, the particle velocity and the wave velocity are related as follows.
option_a: the wave velocity is constant for the medium, while the particle velocity changes continuously with time and is generally much smaller
option_b: the wave velocity is constant for the medium and the particle velocity is constant and equal to it at every instant
option_c: both the wave velocity and the particle velocity change continuously and are equal at every instant
option_d: the particle velocity is constant for the medium while the wave velocity changes continuously with time
correct_answer_text: the wave velocity is constant for the medium, while the particle velocity changes continuously with time and is generally much smaller
solution: The wave speed depends only on the elasticity and density of the medium and is the same everywhere in a uniform medium. The particle velocity is the derivative of the oscillatory displacement, so it varies sinusoidally between a maximum and zero and reverses direction twice in every cycle. For ordinary sounds the maximum particle speed is only a few metres per second, far below the wave speed of about 340 m s^-1.
formula_principle: Wave speed v = f lambda is a property of the medium; particle velocity is the time rate of change of the particle displacement.
common_misconception: Confusing the steady advance of the disturbance with the oscillation of the individual particles.

concept_tested: No sound in vacuum and the practical consequence
stem: Two astronauts working outside their spacecraft cannot hear each other even when their helmets are only a metre apart. They communicate by radio because
option_a: the very low temperature of space reduces the speed of sound almost to zero
option_b: space contains no material medium, so the mechanical vibrations of sound have nothing to travel through, while radio waves need no medium
option_c: their helmets are made of a material that completely absorbs all sound falling on it
option_d: radio waves travel much faster than sound and therefore drown the sound out
correct_answer_text: space contains no material medium, so the mechanical vibrations of sound have nothing to travel through, while radio waves need no medium
solution: Sound propagates by the successive compression of layers of a material medium. Outer space is very nearly empty, so there are no layers of matter to be compressed and no sound can cross the gap. Radio waves are electromagnetic and propagate through vacuum without any medium, which is why they are used for communication in space.
formula_principle: Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a material medium; electromagnetic waves do not.
common_misconception: Blaming the temperature or the helmet material instead of the absence of a medium.

subtopic: Waves in different states of matter
concept_tested: Which media can carry transverse and longitudinal mechanical waves
stem: Consider mechanical waves in bulk matter. Which of the following statements describes the situation correctly?
option_a: transverse waves can travel through solids, liquids and gases, while longitudinal waves can travel through the bulk of solids only
option_b: both longitudinal and transverse mechanical waves can travel through the bulk of any of the three states of matter
option_c: longitudinal waves travel only through gases and transverse waves only through liquids
option_d: longitudinal waves can travel through solids, liquids and gases, while transverse mechanical waves can travel through the bulk of solids only
correct_answer_text: longitudinal waves can travel through solids, liquids and gases, while transverse mechanical waves can travel through the bulk of solids only
solution: A longitudinal wave alternately compresses and expands the medium, and every state of matter resists a change of volume, so all three can carry it. A transverse wave requires the medium to resist a shearing displacement of one layer past another. Only solids possess a modulus of rigidity, so only solids can carry transverse mechanical waves through their bulk. Ripples on the surface of water are a surface effect governed by gravity and surface tension, not a bulk transverse wave.
formula_principle: Transverse bulk waves need shear elasticity, which only solids possess; longitudinal waves need only volume elasticity.
common_misconception: Citing water ripples as proof that liquids carry bulk transverse waves.

concept_tested: Phase relation between displacement and excess pressure
stem: In a progressive longitudinal sound wave in air, the excess pressure and the particle displacement are
option_a: exactly in step, so that the excess pressure is largest where the particle displacement is largest
option_b: out of step by half a cycle, so that a maximum of pressure coincides with a maximum negative displacement
option_c: unrelated in phase, since the pressure change is set by the source and the displacement by the medium
option_d: out of step by a quarter of a cycle, so that the excess pressure is largest where the particle displacement is zero
correct_answer_text: out of step by a quarter of a cycle, so that the excess pressure is largest where the particle displacement is zero
solution: The excess pressure at a point depends on how much the medium there has been squeezed, which is governed by the way the displacement changes from point to point rather than by the displacement itself. At the centre of a compression the particles on either side have moved towards that point, so the point itself has zero displacement while the crowding, and hence the excess pressure, is maximum. This gives a phase difference of a quarter of a cycle between displacement and excess pressure.
formula_principle: Excess pressure is proportional to the rate of change of displacement with position, giving a quarter cycle phase difference.
common_misconception: Assuming that the biggest push corresponds to the biggest displacement of the particles.

concept_tested: Number of compressions crossing a point per second
stem: A tuning fork of frequency 480 Hz is sounded in air. The number of compressions that pass a fixed point in the air in one second is
solution: In every complete vibration the prong of the fork moves forward once, producing one compression, and backward once, producing one rarefaction. The fork completes 480 vibrations each second, so 480 compressions and 480 rarefactions leave it each second and 480 compressions cross any fixed point in the path in one second.
formula_principle: Each complete vibration of the source sends out one compression and one rarefaction, so compressions pass at the rate of the frequency.
common_misconception: Doubling the count by including the rarefactions when only compressions were asked for.

concept_tested: Difference between the speeds of light and sound
stem: During a thunderstorm the flash of lightning is seen well before the thunder is heard, even though both are produced at the same instant. This is because
option_a: light travels through air about a million times faster than sound, so the sound takes far longer to cover the same distance
option_b: the thunder is produced a few seconds after the flash by the cooling of the air along the channel
option_c: sound is absorbed by the clouds and is released only after some delay
option_d: the ear responds much more slowly than the eye, and this response time accounts for the gap
correct_answer_text: light travels through air about a million times faster than sound, so the sound takes far longer to cover the same distance
solution: The lightning and the thunder begin at the same moment. Light covers a few kilometres in a small fraction of a millisecond, so the flash is effectively seen at once. Sound covers the same few kilometres at about 340 m s^-1 and so takes several seconds. The gap therefore grows in proportion to the distance of the storm, which is why the delay is used to estimate that distance.
formula_principle: Speed of light is about 3 x 10^8 m s^-1; speed of sound in air is about 340 m s^-1.
common_misconception: Supposing that the thunder is generated later than the flash rather than merely arriving later.

concept_tested: Speed of sound does not depend on the properties of the source
stem: A drum and a whistle are sounded together at one end of a long corridor. A listener at the far end
option_a: hears the whistle first, because a higher frequency sound travels faster through air
option_b: hears both sounds at the same instant, because the speed of sound in air does not depend on the frequency or the loudness of the source
option_c: hears the drum first, because a louder sound of larger amplitude travels faster through air
option_d: hears the whistle first only if the corridor is longer than about a hundred metres
correct_answer_text: hears both sounds at the same instant, because the speed of sound in air does not depend on the frequency or the loudness of the source
solution: The speed of a sound wave follows from the elastic and inertial properties of the medium through v = sqrt(gamma P / rho). Nothing in that expression refers to the source. Hence a loud low note and a soft high note travel through the same air at the same speed and arrive together. This is exactly why an orchestra heard from the back of a hall still sounds in time.
formula_principle: The speed of sound is fixed by the elasticity and density of the medium, not by the frequency or amplitude of the source.
common_misconception: Believing that higher pitched or louder sounds travel faster.

concept_tested: Particle displacement at the centre of a compression is zero
stem: At the exact centre of a compression in a progressive sound wave in air, the particle displacement and the excess pressure are respectively
solution: Consider the particles just on either side of the centre of a compression. The particle behind has moved forward and the particle ahead has moved backward, so both have crowded towards the centre. The particle at the centre itself has nothing to push it one way rather than the other, so its displacement is zero. The crowding around it, however, is greatest there, so the density and the excess pressure are maximum. The two quantities therefore differ in phase by a quarter of a cycle.
formula_principle: Excess pressure is proportional to the negative of the space gradient of displacement, so it leads or lags the displacement by a quarter cycle.
common_misconception: Assuming that the region of greatest squeezing is also the region of greatest particle displacement.

concept_tested: Using the speed of sound to find the distance of a source
stem: A flash of lightning is seen and the thunder is heard 5 s later. Taking the speed of sound in air as 340 m s^-1 and neglecting the time taken by the light, the storm is at a distance of
solution: The light reaches the observer almost instantaneously, so the full 5 s is the time taken by the sound to travel one way from the storm to the observer. Hence d = v t = 340 x 5 = 1700 m. There is no factor of two here because the sound makes a single one way journey, unlike an echo where the pulse travels out and back.
formula_principle: distance = speed x time, with the travel time of light neglected.
common_misconception: Applying the echo formula d = v t / 2 to a one way journey.

concept_tested: Comparing maximum particle speed with wave speed
stem: A sound wave of frequency 500 Hz travels in air with speed 340 m s^-1. The amplitude of oscillation of an air particle is 1 mm. Taking pi = 3.14, the maximum speed of an air particle is about
solution: The angular frequency is omega = 2 pi f = 2 x 3.14 x 500 = 3140 rad s^-1. The amplitude is A = 1 mm = 1 x 10^-3 m. Hence the maximum particle speed is A omega = 1 x 10^-3 x 3140 = 3.14 m s^-1. This is roughly a hundred times smaller than the wave speed of 340 m s^-1, which confirms that the particles only jiggle while the disturbance races ahead.
formula_principle: Maximum particle speed = A omega = 2 pi f A, quite distinct from the wave speed v = f lambda.
common_misconception: Quoting the wave speed as the particle speed, or omitting the factor 2 pi.

concept_tested: Intensity of a sound wave varies as the square of the amplitude
stem: The amplitude of a sound wave of fixed frequency travelling in air is increased to three times its original value. The energy carried by the wave across unit area per second becomes
option_b: one third of the original value
option_d: one ninth of the original value
solution: The energy of an oscillating particle is proportional to the square of its amplitude, and the intensity of the wave is the energy crossing unit area per unit time. With the frequency and the medium unchanged, I is proportional to A^2. Tripling A therefore multiplies the intensity by 3^2 = 9.
formula_principle: Intensity of a wave is proportional to the square of the amplitude for a fixed frequency and medium.
common_misconception: Scaling the intensity linearly with the amplitude instead of using the square law.

concept_tested: Identifying the correct set of statements about the nature of sound
stem: Four statements about sound waves in air are listed. P: they are longitudinal. Q: they transport the air itself from the source to the listener. R: they require a material medium. S: they can be polarised. The statements that are correct are
solution: P is correct, since the air particles oscillate along the direction of travel. Q is wrong, because although energy travels forward each particle only oscillates about a fixed mean position and no net mass is carried across. R is correct, since a mechanical wave has nothing to propagate through in vacuum. S is wrong, because polarisation requires vibration across the line of travel and a longitudinal wave has none. Hence only P and R are correct.
formula_principle: Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave: it needs a medium, transports energy without matter, and cannot be polarised.
common_misconception: Confusing the forward transport of energy with a forward transport of the medium, and forgetting that longitudinal waves cannot be polarised.

concept_tested: Wavelength as the distance covered in one period
stem: The wavelength of a progressive wave is best defined as
option_a: the distance travelled by a particle of the medium during one full oscillation
option_b: the distance travelled by the wave in the time taken by one particle of the medium to complete one full oscillation
option_c: the maximum distance of a particle of the medium from its mean position
option_d: the distance travelled by the wave in one second
correct_answer_text: the distance travelled by the wave in the time taken by one particle of the medium to complete one full oscillation
solution: In the time T taken by a particle to complete one oscillation, the disturbance advances by a distance v T. After that time the pattern has moved forward by exactly one repeat unit, so v T is the wavelength. Writing T = 1/f gives the standard relation v = f lambda.
formula_principle: lambda = v T, so the wavelength is the distance advanced by the wave in one period.
common_misconception: Confusing the distance travelled by the wave with the path length covered by an oscillating particle.

concept_tested: Finding wavelength from frequency and speed
stem: A source produces a note of frequency 500 Hz in air, in which the speed of sound is 340 m s^-1. The wavelength of the note is
solution: lambda = v / f = 340 / 500 = 0.68 m. The note therefore repeats itself in space every 68 cm as it travels through the air.
formula_principle: v = f lambda, so lambda = v / f.
common_misconception: Inverting the formula and dividing the frequency by the speed.

concept_tested: Relation between period and frequency
stem: The period of a sound wave of frequency 2000 Hz is
solution: T = 1 / f = 1 / 2000 s = 5 x 10^-4 s = 0.5 ms. Each complete vibration of the source therefore takes half a millisecond.
common_misconception: Slipping by a factor of a thousand when converting between hertz and kilohertz.

concept_tested: Physical meaning of the amplitude of a sound wave
stem: The amplitude of a sound wave in air is
option_a: the total distance covered by an air particle in one complete oscillation
option_b: the greatest displacement of an air particle from its mean position during the passage of the wave
option_c: the distance between a compression and the nearest rarefaction
option_d: the distance advanced by the wave during one complete oscillation of a particle
correct_answer_text: the greatest displacement of an air particle from its mean position during the passage of the wave
solution: As the wave passes, each particle swings to one side and then to the other about its mean position. The largest displacement reached on either side is the amplitude. Over a full cycle the particle covers a path of four amplitudes, but the amplitude itself is only the extreme displacement in one direction.
formula_principle: Amplitude is the maximum displacement of a particle of the medium from its mean position.
common_misconception: Reporting the total path in one cycle, or the peak to peak swing, as the amplitude.

concept_tested: Frequency of a wave is decided by the source
stem: A sound wave passes from air into water. The quantity that certainly remains unchanged is
solution: The particles at the boundary are driven by the wave arriving from the air, so they vibrate at exactly the rate at which the source vibrates. That rate is carried unchanged into the water. The speed, however, is fixed by the elasticity and density of the new medium and is much larger in water. Since lambda = v / f with f fixed and v larger, the wavelength in water is correspondingly larger.
formula_principle: Frequency is set by the source; speed is set by the medium; lambda = v / f then follows.
common_misconception: Assuming the wavelength stays the same and letting the frequency change instead.

concept_tested: Using v = f lambda with the unknown reversed
stem: A sound wave in air has a wavelength of 2 m. Taking the speed of sound in air as 340 m s^-1, the frequency of the wave is
solution: f = v / lambda = 340 / 2 = 170 Hz. The note lies comfortably within the audible range, since the human ear responds from about 20 Hz to about 20 kHz.
formula_principle: f = v / lambda.
common_misconception: Multiplying rather than dividing when the unknown is the frequency.

subtopic: Wavelength on entering a new medium
concept_tested: Wavelength change when sound passes from air into water
stem: A sound of frequency 500 Hz travels from air, where its speed is 340 m s^-1, into water, where its speed is 1500 m s^-1. The wavelength of the sound in water is
solution: The frequency stays at 500 Hz because it is imposed by the source. In water lambda = v / f = 1500 / 500 = 3.0 m. Comparing with the air value of 340 / 500 = 0.68 m shows that the wavelength has grown in the same ratio as the speed, which is about 4.4 to 1.
formula_principle: The frequency is unchanged on crossing a boundary, so lambda = v / f with the new speed.
common_misconception: Keeping the wavelength fixed across the boundary and adjusting the frequency instead.

concept_tested: Converting a path difference into a phase difference
stem: Two points on the path of a sound wave are separated by a distance equal to one quarter of the wavelength. The phase difference between the oscillations at these two points is
solution: Using phi = (2 pi / lambda) x delta x with delta x = lambda / 4 gives phi = (2 pi / lambda) x (lambda / 4) = pi / 2 rad, which is 90 degrees or a quarter of a cycle.
formula_principle: phase difference = (2 pi / lambda) x path difference.
common_misconception: Forgetting the factor 2 pi and reading the fraction of a wavelength directly as radians.

concept_tested: Reversing the path and phase relation
stem: Two particles in the path of a sound wave of wavelength lambda oscillate with a phase difference of 60 degrees. The distance between them is
solution: One complete cycle of 360 degrees corresponds to a path difference of one wavelength. A phase difference of 60 degrees is therefore 60 / 360 = 1 / 6 of a cycle, so the separation is lambda / 6.
formula_principle: path difference = (lambda / 2 pi) x phase difference; equivalently a full cycle of 360 degrees corresponds to lambda.
common_misconception: Dividing by 180 degrees instead of 360 degrees when converting a phase angle into a fraction of a wavelength.

concept_tested: Extracting speed from the equation of a progressive wave
stem: A progressive sound wave is described by y = A sin 2 pi (t / 0.01 - x / 3.4), where t is in seconds and x is in metres. The speed of the wave is
solution: Comparison with the standard form shows T = 0.01 s and lambda = 3.4 m. Hence the frequency is f = 1 / T = 100 Hz and the speed is v = f lambda = 100 x 3.4 = 340 m s^-1, the usual speed of sound in air.
formula_principle: Comparing with y = A sin 2 pi (t / T - x / lambda) gives T and lambda, then v = lambda / T.
common_misconception: Inverting the ratio and dividing the period by the wavelength.

concept_tested: Computing phase difference from a given separation
stem: A sound wave of frequency 200 Hz travels in air with speed 340 m s^-1. Two points on the direction of propagation are 0.85 m apart. The phase difference between the oscillations at these points is
solution: First lambda = v / f = 340 / 200 = 1.7 m. The separation 0.85 m is therefore exactly lambda / 2. The phase difference is (2 pi / 1.7) x 0.85 = pi rad, so the two points always move in exactly opposite directions.
formula_principle: lambda = v / f, then phase difference = (2 pi / lambda) x path difference.
common_misconception: Skipping the calculation of the wavelength and comparing the separation with the speed or the frequency instead.

concept_tested: Units and meaning of the propagation constant
stem: For a progressive wave written as y = A sin (omega t - k x), the SI unit of the propagation constant k is
solution: The argument of a sine must be a pure angle, so k x must be an angle. Since x is measured in metres, k must carry the unit rad m^-1. This is consistent with k = 2 pi / lambda, in which 2 pi is an angle in radians and lambda is a length. The ratio omega / k then has the unit m s^-1, correctly giving the wave speed.
formula_principle: k = 2 pi / lambda, so k has the unit of inverse length; omega = 2 pi f has the unit of inverse time.
common_misconception: Interchanging the units of the propagation constant and the angular frequency.

concept_tested: Amplitude changes do not alter speed or frequency
stem: The amplitude of a sound wave travelling in air is doubled while the source frequency is kept the same. As a result,
option_a: the speed is doubled while the wavelength and the energy carried per second are unchanged
option_b: the wavelength is doubled while the speed and the energy carried per second are unchanged
option_c: the speed and the wavelength are both unchanged, while the energy carried per second becomes four times as large
option_d: the speed, the wavelength and the energy carried per second are all doubled
correct_answer_text: the speed and the wavelength are both unchanged, while the energy carried per second becomes four times as large
solution: The wave speed follows from the elasticity and the density of the air and does not involve the amplitude, so it stays at about 340 m s^-1. The frequency is set by the source and is unchanged, so lambda = v / f is unchanged too. The intensity, however, is proportional to the square of the amplitude, so doubling the amplitude makes the wave four times as intense.
formula_principle: v depends only on the medium; lambda = v / f; intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude.
common_misconception: Assuming that a louder sound is also a faster sound.

concept_tested: Obtaining amplitude and wavelength from a snapshot graph
stem: A snapshot graph of a progressive sound wave shows the particle displacement plotted against distance at one instant. The graph is a sine curve whose peaks reach 4 mm above the axis and whose successive peaks are 1.7 m apart. If the speed of sound is 340 m s^-1, the amplitude and frequency of the wave are
solution: The maximum displacement above the axis is the amplitude, so A = 4 mm. The distance between successive peaks is one wavelength, so lambda = 1.7 m. Hence f = v / lambda = 340 / 1.7 = 200 Hz.
formula_principle: From a snapshot graph the peak height gives A and the peak to peak spacing gives lambda; then f = v / lambda.
common_misconception: Taking the full peak to trough height of the curve as the amplitude.

concept_tested: Extracting frequency, wavelength and speed together
stem: A sound wave is represented by y = 0.005 sin (660 pi t - 2 pi x) in SI units. The frequency and the speed of this wave are
solution: Here omega = 660 pi rad s^-1, so f = omega / 2 pi = 660 pi / 2 pi = 330 Hz. Also k = 2 pi rad m^-1, so lambda = 2 pi / k = 1 m. The speed is v = f lambda = 330 x 1 = 330 m s^-1, which may also be obtained directly as omega / k = 660 pi / 2 pi = 330 m s^-1.
formula_principle: Compare with y = A sin (omega t - k x): omega = 2 pi f and k = 2 pi / lambda, then v = omega / k.
common_misconception: Reading the coefficients of t and x as the frequency and the wave number in cycles rather than in radians.

concept_tested: Converting a phase difference into a time delay
stem: Two points in the path of a sound wave of frequency 250 Hz oscillate with a phase difference of pi / 2 rad. The time interval between the instants at which the two points pass through their mean positions moving in the same direction is
solution: The period is T = 1 / f = 1 / 250 = 4 x 10^-3 s = 4 ms. A phase difference of pi / 2 rad is a quarter of a full cycle of 2 pi rad, so the time lag is T / 4 = 4 / 4 = 1 ms.
formula_principle: A phase difference phi corresponds to a time lag (phi / 2 pi) T, where T = 1 / f.
common_misconception: Equating the phase difference with a fraction of the period without first converting from radians to cycles.

concept_tested: Frequency from the number of waves produced in a given time
stem: A vibrating source sends out 600 complete waves into air in 3 s. Taking the speed of sound in air as 340 m s^-1, the wavelength of these waves is
solution: The frequency is f = 600 / 3 = 200 Hz. The wavelength then follows as lambda = v / f = 340 / 200 = 1.7 m.
formula_principle: f = number of waves / time taken, then lambda = v / f.
common_misconception: Reading the total number of waves as the frequency without dividing by the time interval.

concept_tested: Ratio of wavelengths for the same note in air and water
stem: A note of a single fixed frequency is sounded so that it travels both through air, where the speed of sound is 340 m s^-1, and through water, where it is 1500 m s^-1. The ratio of the wavelength in air to that in water is
solution: The frequency is the same in both media because it is fixed by the source. Hence lambda is proportional to v and lambda_air / lambda_water = 340 / 1500. Dividing both numbers by 20 gives 17 / 75. The wavelength in water is therefore several times longer than in air.
formula_principle: At fixed frequency lambda is proportional to v, so lambda_air / lambda_water = v_air / v_water.
common_misconception: Inverting the ratio because sound seems to be squeezed into the denser medium.

subtopic: Phase relation over a long separation
concept_tested: Reducing a large phase difference to within one cycle
stem: A sound wave of frequency 250 Hz travels through air at 340 m s^-1. Two points on the line of propagation are 2.04 m apart. The oscillations at these two points are
option_a: exactly in phase, the separation being an integral number of wavelengths
option_b: a quarter of a cycle apart, the separation being one and a quarter wavelengths
option_c: exactly opposite in phase, the separation being one and a half wavelengths
option_d: one third of a cycle apart, the separation being one and one third wavelengths
correct_answer_text: exactly opposite in phase, the separation being one and a half wavelengths
solution: The wavelength is lambda = v / f = 340 / 250 = 1.36 m. The separation in wavelengths is 2.04 / 1.36 = 1.5. A whole wavelength contributes a phase difference of 2 pi, which brings the oscillation back to the same state, so only the extra half wavelength matters. That half wavelength gives a phase difference of pi rad, so the two points are always moving in opposite directions.
formula_principle: lambda = v / f; a separation of (n + 1/2) lambda gives a phase difference of pi rad.
common_misconception: Failing to strip off the whole number of wavelengths before deciding the phase relation.

subtopic: Quantities that change across a boundary
concept_tested: Behaviour of f, v, lambda and T when sound enters a new medium
stem: A sound wave travels from air into water. Four statements are made. P: the frequency is unchanged. Q: the period is unchanged. R: the wavelength is unchanged. S: the speed is unchanged. The statements that are correct are
solution: The particles at the boundary are driven at the rate of the incoming wave, so the frequency crosses unchanged and the period T = 1 / f is unchanged with it. The speed depends on the bulk modulus and density of the new medium and rises from about 340 m s^-1 to about 1500 m s^-1. Since lambda = v / f with f fixed, the wavelength grows in the same proportion. Hence only P and Q hold.
formula_principle: Frequency, and hence period, is imposed by the source; speed is set by the medium; lambda = v / f adjusts accordingly.
common_misconception: Treating the wavelength rather than the frequency as the quantity carried unchanged across a boundary.

concept_tested: Assumption behind Newton's expression for the speed of sound
stem: In deriving his formula v = sqrt(P / rho) for the speed of sound in a gas, Newton assumed that the compressions and rarefactions take place
option_a: isothermally, so that the temperature of the gas stays constant throughout the passage of the wave
option_b: adiabatically, so that no heat enters or leaves any element of the gas
option_c: at constant volume, so that the density of the gas never changes
option_d: at constant pressure, so that the elastic modulus involved is simply the atmospheric pressure
correct_answer_text: isothermally, so that the temperature of the gas stays constant throughout the passage of the wave
solution: Newton argued that the heat produced in a compression would have time to flow into the neighbouring rarefaction, keeping the temperature uniform. For an isothermal change of an ideal gas the bulk modulus equals the pressure P, so his formula became v = sqrt(P / rho). Numerically this gives about 280 m s^-1 for air, some fifteen per cent below the measured value.
formula_principle: Newton assumed isothermal changes, giving the isothermal bulk modulus P and hence v = sqrt(P / rho).
common_misconception: Attributing the adiabatic assumption to Newton and the isothermal one to Laplace.

concept_tested: Correct expression for the speed of sound in a gas
stem: According to the Laplace correction, the speed of sound in a gas of pressure P, density rho and ratio of specific heats gamma is
solution: Laplace pointed out that the compressions and rarefactions succeed each other far too rapidly for heat to be conducted between them, so each element behaves adiabatically. The adiabatic bulk modulus of an ideal gas is gamma P instead of P, and inserting this into v = sqrt(E / rho) gives v = sqrt(gamma P / rho). For air with gamma = 1.4 this raises Newton's value by a factor sqrt(1.4), bringing it into agreement with experiment.
formula_principle: Adiabatic bulk modulus of a gas is gamma P, so v = sqrt(gamma P / rho).
common_misconception: Writing gamma outside the square root or in the denominator.

concept_tested: Using v_t = v_0 + 0.61 t
stem: The speed of sound in air at 0 degree Celsius is 332 m s^-1 and it increases by 0.61 m s^-1 for each degree Celsius rise in temperature. The speed of sound in air at 20 degree Celsius is
solution: v_20 = 332 + 0.61 x 20 = 332 + 12.2 = 344.2 m s^-1. The rule holds well for ordinary room temperatures, being a straight line approximation to the exact square root dependence on absolute temperature.
formula_principle: v_t = v_0 + 0.61 t, with v_0 = 332 m s^-1 and t in degree Celsius.
common_misconception: Getting the sign wrong and reducing the speed as the air gets warmer.

subtopic: Speed in solids, liquids and gases
concept_tested: Ordering the speed of sound in the three states of matter
stem: For most ordinary materials, the speed of sound is
option_a: greatest in gases, smaller in liquids and least in solids
option_b: greatest in liquids, smaller in gases and least in solids
option_c: the same in all three states, being fixed only by the temperature
option_d: greatest in solids, smaller in liquids and least in gases
correct_answer_text: greatest in solids, smaller in liquids and least in gases
solution: Going from a gas to a liquid to a solid, the density rises by a factor of roughly a thousand, but the relevant elastic modulus rises by a factor of about a million. Since v = sqrt(E / rho), the modulus wins and the speed increases. Typical values are about 340 m s^-1 in air, about 1500 m s^-1 in water and about 5000 m s^-1 in steel.
formula_principle: v = sqrt(E / rho); the elastic modulus rises far more steeply from gas to solid than the density does.
common_misconception: Reasoning only from density and concluding that the heaviest medium must be the slowest.

concept_tested: Sound travels faster in moist air
stem: Other things being equal, the speed of sound in moist air compared with that in dry air at the same temperature and pressure is
option_a: greater, because water vapour is less dense than the air it displaces
option_b: smaller, because the water vapour adds extra mass that the wave must set into motion
option_c: the same, because humidity does not enter the expression v = sqrt(gamma P / rho)
option_d: smaller, because the water droplets scatter the sound and slow it down
correct_answer_text: greater, because water vapour is less dense than the air it displaces
solution: Water vapour has a molar mass of 18 g, while nitrogen has 28 g and oxygen has 32 g. When water vapour is added at fixed total pressure and temperature it displaces some of these heavier molecules, so the density of the mixture falls. Since v = sqrt(gamma P / rho), a smaller rho gives a larger speed, and sound therefore travels faster on a humid day.
formula_principle: v = sqrt(gamma P / rho); moist air has a lower rho because water has a smaller molar mass than nitrogen and oxygen.
common_misconception: Assuming that adding water to air must make it heavier and therefore slower.

concept_tested: Speed of sound does not depend on frequency
stem: The speed of sound in a given sample of air at a fixed temperature is
option_a: the same for all audible frequencies, which is why a distant band is heard in tune and in time
option_b: greater for higher frequencies, which is why the shriller instruments of a distant band are heard first
option_c: greater for lower frequencies, because long wavelengths meet less resistance from the air
option_d: greater for louder sounds of any frequency, because they carry more energy
correct_answer_text: the same for all audible frequencies, which is why a distant band is heard in tune and in time
solution: The speed of sound follows entirely from the elastic and inertial properties of the medium. Neither the frequency nor the amplitude of the disturbance appears in the expression. Hence all audible frequencies travel through the same air at the same speed, which is why a chord played at a distance still sounds as a chord.
formula_principle: v = sqrt(gamma P / rho) contains no reference to frequency or amplitude.
common_misconception: Believing that shrill notes outrun deep notes over long distances.

concept_tested: Ratio of the Laplace and Newton values
stem: Newton's formula gives the speed of sound in air as 280 m s^-1. Taking gamma = 1.4 for air and sqrt(1.4) = 1.18, the value given by the Laplace corrected formula is about
solution: The two formulas differ only by the factor gamma inside the square root, so v_Laplace = sqrt(gamma) x v_Newton = 1.18 x 280 = 330.4, about 331 m s^-1. This is close to the measured speed of sound in air near 0 degree Celsius and shows why the adiabatic assumption is the correct one.
formula_principle: v_Laplace / v_Newton = sqrt(gamma).
common_misconception: Applying gamma as a direct multiplier rather than taking its square root.

concept_tested: Speed of sound is independent of pressure at constant temperature
stem: The pressure of a fixed mass of air is doubled while its temperature is held constant. The speed of sound in the air then
option_a: remains unchanged, because the density doubles along with the pressure so that P / rho is unaltered
option_b: becomes sqrt(2) times as large, because the speed varies as the square root of the pressure
option_c: becomes twice as large, because the speed is directly proportional to the pressure
option_d: is halved, because the denser gas offers twice the inertia to the passing wave
correct_answer_text: remains unchanged, because the density doubles along with the pressure so that P / rho is unaltered
solution: Doubling the pressure of a gas at constant temperature packs the same molecules into half the volume, so the density also doubles. In v = sqrt(gamma P / rho) the numerator and the denominator change by the same factor, leaving the ratio and hence the speed unchanged. This is confirmed by the ideal gas relation P / rho = R T / M, which shows that P / rho depends only on temperature for a given gas.
formula_principle: For an ideal gas P / rho = R T / M, so at constant temperature P / rho is constant and v = sqrt(gamma P / rho) is unchanged.
common_misconception: Reading v = sqrt(gamma P / rho) as if rho were a constant of the gas, so that raising P must raise v.

concept_tested: Speed of sound varies as the square root of the absolute temperature
stem: The speed of sound in air at 27 degree Celsius is 330 m s^-1. The speed of sound in the same air at 927 degree Celsius is
solution: In kelvin the two temperatures are T_1 = 27 + 273 = 300 K and T_2 = 927 + 273 = 1200 K, a ratio of 4. Since v is proportional to sqrt(T), the speed changes by a factor sqrt(4) = 2, giving v_2 = 2 x 330 = 660 m s^-1.
formula_principle: v is proportional to sqrt(T) with T in kelvin.
common_misconception: Using Celsius readings directly in a proportionality that requires absolute temperature.

concept_tested: Using v = sqrt(Y / rho) for a long thin rod
stem: The Young modulus of steel is 2 x 10^11 N m^-2 and its density is 8000 kg m^-3. The speed of a longitudinal wave along a long thin steel rod is
solution: Y / rho = 2 x 10^11 / 8 x 10^3 = 2.5 x 10^7 m^2 s^-2. Taking the square root gives v = 5 x 10^3 = 5000 m s^-1. Sound therefore travels through steel about fifteen times faster than through air.
formula_principle: For a long thin rod, v = sqrt(Y / rho).
common_misconception: Forgetting to take the square root, or inverting the ratio of modulus to density.

concept_tested: Using v = sqrt(B / rho) for a liquid
stem: The bulk modulus of water is 2.25 x 10^9 N m^-2 and its density is 1000 kg m^-3. The speed of sound in water is
solution: B / rho = 2.25 x 10^9 / 1.0 x 10^3 = 2.25 x 10^6 m^2 s^-2. The square root of 2.25 is 1.5 and the square root of 10^6 is 10^3, so v = 1.5 x 10^3 = 1500 m s^-1. This is the value used in SONAR calculations for sea water.
formula_principle: For a liquid or a gas, v = sqrt(B / rho) with B the bulk modulus.
common_misconception: Losing the square root or mishandling the powers of ten.

concept_tested: Comparing speeds in two gases at the same temperature
stem: Hydrogen and oxygen are both diatomic gases with the same value of gamma. At the same temperature, the molar masses being 2 g and 32 g respectively, the ratio of the speed of sound in hydrogen to that in oxygen is
solution: Writing P / rho = R T / M turns the Laplace formula into v = sqrt(gamma R T / M). With gamma and T the same for both gases, v is proportional to 1 / sqrt(M). Hence v_H / v_O = sqrt(M_O / M_H) = sqrt(32 / 2) = sqrt(16) = 4. Sound travels four times faster in hydrogen than in oxygen at the same temperature.
formula_principle: v = sqrt(gamma R T / M), so at fixed T and gamma the speed varies as 1 / sqrt(M).
common_misconception: Using the ratio of molar masses without taking its square root, or getting the direction of the comparison the wrong way round.

concept_tested: Finding the temperature from a measured speed
stem: The speed of sound in air is measured to be 350.3 m s^-1. Given that the speed is 332 m s^-1 at 0 degree Celsius and rises by 0.61 m s^-1 for each degree Celsius, the temperature of the air is
solution: The excess over the value at the ice point is v_t - v_0 = 350.3 - 332 = 18.3 m s^-1. Dividing by the coefficient gives t = 18.3 / 0.61 = 30. The air is therefore at 30 degree Celsius.
common_misconception: Forgetting to subtract the value at 0 degree Celsius before dividing by the coefficient.

concept_tested: Physical reason for the failure of the isothermal assumption
stem: Newton's isothermal assumption fails for sound in air because
option_a: air is such a good conductor of heat that the temperature can never be held constant during a compression
option_b: the pressure of the atmosphere is far too small for the isothermal bulk modulus to be meaningful
option_c: the compressions and rarefactions follow one another too rapidly for heat to be conducted between them, and air is in any case a poor conductor
option_d: sound waves in air are transverse rather than longitudinal, so no compression takes place
correct_answer_text: the compressions and rarefactions follow one another too rapidly for heat to be conducted between them, and air is in any case a poor conductor
solution: For an audible note there are hundreds or thousands of compressions per second, so each region is squeezed and released in a fraction of a millisecond. Air is a poor conductor of heat, so in that short time almost no heat can flow from a warm compression to a cool rarefaction. Each element therefore behaves adiabatically, its bulk modulus is gamma P rather than P, and the speed comes out about eighteen per cent higher than Newton predicted.
formula_principle: Rapid alternation plus the low thermal conductivity of air make the changes adiabatic rather than isothermal.
common_misconception: Believing that the failure is caused by air conducting heat too well rather than too poorly.

concept_tested: Verifying that sqrt(P / rho) has the dimensions of speed
stem: The dimensions of the quantity sqrt(P / rho), where P is a pressure and rho is a density, are
solution: Pressure is force per area, so [P] = M L T^-2 / L^2 = M L^-1 T^-2. Density is mass per volume, so [rho] = M L^-3. Dividing, [P / rho] = M L^-1 T^-2 / M L^-3 = L^2 T^-2, which is the square of a speed. Taking the square root gives L T^-1, confirming that both Newton's formula and Laplace's corrected form are dimensionally sound. Note that gamma is a pure number and does not affect the dimensions.
formula_principle: [P] = M L^-1 T^-2 and [rho] = M L^-3, so [P / rho] = L^2 T^-2 and its square root is L T^-1.
common_misconception: Stopping at L^2 T^-2 and forgetting that the square root has still to be taken.

subtopic: Effect of density at constant pressure
concept_tested: Speed varies inversely as the square root of density
stem: Two gases are kept at the same pressure and have the same value of gamma, but the density of the first is four times that of the second. The ratio of the speed of sound in the first gas to that in the second is
solution: With gamma and P the same for the two gases, v varies as 1 / sqrt(rho). If rho_1 = 4 rho_2 then v_1 / v_2 = sqrt(rho_2 / rho_1) = sqrt(1/4) = 1/2. The denser gas therefore carries sound at half the speed.
formula_principle: At constant P and gamma, v = sqrt(gamma P / rho) is proportional to 1 / sqrt(rho).
common_misconception: Comparing the speeds in direct proportion to the densities, or forgetting to take the square root.

concept_tested: Consequence of the temperature dependence in an everyday setting
stem: A boy measures the time between a clap and its echo from a distant wall on a cold winter morning, and repeats the measurement from the same spot on a hot afternoon. Compared with the morning value, the afternoon time interval is
option_a: longer, because the warmer air is less dense and so offers less elastic restoring force
option_b: the same, because the distance to the wall has not changed
option_c: shorter, because the warmer air carries the sound faster over the same total path
option_d: longer, because the extra heat is absorbed by the sound wave and delays it
correct_answer_text: shorter, because the warmer air carries the sound faster over the same total path
solution: The total path is twice the distance to the wall and is the same on both occasions. The speed of sound rises with temperature, so on the hot afternoon v is larger. Since t = 2 d / v with d fixed, a larger v means a shorter measured interval. A rise of 20 degree Celsius raises v by about 12 m s^-1, roughly three and a half per cent, and shortens the interval by the same fraction.
formula_principle: v_t = v_0 + 0.61 t, and time of travel = total path / v.
common_misconception: Assuming that the lower density of hot air must slow the sound down.

concept_tested: Direct application of the Laplace formula
stem: A gas has pressure 1.2 x 10^5 N m^-2, density 2.0 kg m^-3 and ratio of specific heats 1.5. The speed of sound in this gas is
solution: gamma P = 1.5 x 1.2 x 10^5 = 1.8 x 10^5 N m^-2. Dividing by rho gives 1.8 x 10^5 / 2.0 = 9.0 x 10^4 m^2 s^-2. The square root of 9.0 x 10^4 is 3.0 x 10^2, so v = 300 m s^-1.
formula_principle: v = sqrt(gamma P / rho).
common_misconception: Leaving out gamma or failing to take the square root at the end.

concept_tested: Temperature needed to double the speed of sound
stem: The speed of sound in air at 0 degree Celsius is 332 m s^-1. Taking the speed to vary as the square root of the absolute temperature and 0 degree Celsius as 273 K, the temperature at which the speed becomes 664 m s^-1 is
solution: Since v is proportional to sqrt(T), the ratio of speeds gives sqrt(T_2 / T_1) = 664 / 332 = 2, so T_2 / T_1 = 4. With T_1 = 273 K this gives T_2 = 4 x 273 = 1092 K. Converting back, t_2 = 1092 - 273 = 819 degree Celsius.
formula_principle: v is proportional to sqrt(T), so doubling v requires T to be multiplied by four.
common_misconception: Doubling the absolute temperature to double the speed, or forgetting the final conversion from kelvin to Celsius.

concept_tested: Linking the square root law to the linear temperature rule
stem: Sound travels in air at 332 m s^-1 at 0 degree Celsius, that is at 273 K, and its speed varies as the square root of the absolute temperature. The increase in speed produced by a rise of 1 K near this temperature is closest to
solution: Since v varies as the square root of T, a small change gives delta v / v = (1/2) x (delta T / T). Putting delta T = 1 K, T = 273 K and v = 332 m s^-1 gives delta v = 332 / (2 x 273) = 332 / 546 = 0.608 m s^-1. This is precisely the familiar rule that the speed of sound in air rises by about 0.61 m s^-1 for each degree Celsius, and it shows that the linear rule is just the square root law used over a small range.
formula_principle: For v proportional to sqrt(T), the fractional change is delta v / v = (1/2)(delta T / T).
common_misconception: Ignoring the factor of one half that arises because the dependence is on the square root of temperature.

subtopic: Percentage difference of the two formulas
concept_tested: How far Newton's value falls below the true value
stem: Taking gamma for air as 1.4 and sqrt(1.4) as 1.18, the speed of sound predicted by Newton's formula falls below the Laplace value by about
solution: The ratio of the two predictions is v_Newton / v_Laplace = 1 / sqrt(gamma) = 1 / 1.18 = 0.847. The shortfall is therefore 1 - 0.847 = 0.153, that is about 15 per cent of the true value. Looked at the other way round, the Laplace value exceeds the Newton value by 18 per cent of the Newton value, and both statements describe the same pair of numbers.
formula_principle: v_Newton / v_Laplace = 1 / sqrt(gamma).
common_misconception: Failing to notice which of the two values is being used as the base of the percentage.

concept_tested: Shape of the graph of v against absolute temperature
stem: For a fixed sample of air, the graph of the speed of sound v plotted against the absolute temperature T is
option_a: a straight line through the origin, while the graph of v against sqrt(T) is a curve
option_b: a curve that rises with increasing steepness, while the graph of v against sqrt(T) is also a curve
option_c: a curve that rises with decreasing steepness, while the graph of v against sqrt(T) is a straight line through the origin
option_d: a horizontal straight line, since the speed of sound in a given gas is a constant of that gas
correct_answer_text: a curve that rises with decreasing steepness, while the graph of v against sqrt(T) is a straight line through the origin
solution: Writing the Laplace formula with the gas relation gives v = sqrt(gamma R T / M), so v is proportional to the square root of T. A square root curve rises steeply at first and then flattens, so v against T bends over. If instead sqrt(T) is plotted along the horizontal axis the relation becomes linear and the graph is a straight line through the origin whose slope is sqrt(gamma R / M).
formula_principle: v = sqrt(gamma R T / M), so v is proportional to sqrt(T).
common_misconception: Assuming that the well known linear rule v_t = v_0 + 0.61 t means v is exactly proportional to absolute temperature.

concept_tested: Identifying which quantities affect the speed of sound in a gas
stem: Four quantities are listed for a sample of air. P: the temperature. Q: the pressure at constant temperature. R: the humidity. S: the loudness of the sound. The quantities that affect the speed of sound in the air are
solution: Temperature raises the speed as the square root of the absolute temperature, so P is correct. A change of pressure at constant temperature changes rho in exactly the same proportion, leaving P / rho and hence v unaltered, so Q is wrong. Humidity replaces heavier nitrogen and oxygen molecules by lighter water molecules, lowering rho and raising the speed, so R is correct. Loudness is a matter of amplitude and does not enter the formula at all, so S is wrong.
formula_principle: v = sqrt(gamma P / rho) = sqrt(gamma R T / M): only temperature and composition matter.
common_misconception: Reading the symbol P in the formula as evidence that raising the pressure must raise the speed.

concept_tested: Temperature at which two different gases carry sound equally fast
stem: Two diatomic gases X and Y have the same value of gamma, and the molar mass of Y is four times that of X. Gas X is at 300 K. The temperature at which the speed of sound in Y equals that in X is
