solution: Since gamma is the same for both, equal speeds require T_X / M_X = T_Y / M_Y. With M_Y = 4 M_X this gives T_Y = 4 T_X = 4 x 300 = 1200 K. Physically, the heavier gas is four times as sluggish in molar mass, so its absolute temperature must be four times as high to give its molecules the same characteristic speed and hence the same speed of sound.
formula_principle: v = sqrt(gamma R T / M); equal speeds require T / M to be equal for the two gases.
common_misconception: Matching the temperatures in the same ratio as the molar masses raised to the power one half instead of one.

concept_tested: Sound obeys the same reflection laws as light
stem: When a sound wave is reflected from a large smooth wall,
option_a: the angle of reflection is always zero, so that the sound returns straight back along the incident path
option_b: the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, and the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal lie in one plane
option_c: the angle of reflection equals twice the angle of incidence, because sound is a longitudinal wave
option_d: the frequency of the sound is halved on reflection while the direction obeys the law of reflection
correct_answer_text: the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, and the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal lie in one plane
solution: Reflection is a general property of waves and does not depend on whether the wave is longitudinal or transverse. A sound wave striking a large rigid surface obeys exactly the same two laws as a light ray, and this is what makes sound reflectors, whispering galleries and megaphones work.
formula_principle: Laws of reflection: angle of incidence equals angle of reflection, and both rays and the normal are coplanar.
common_misconception: Assuming that because sound is longitudinal it must obey different reflection rules from light.

concept_tested: Persistence of hearing and the 17 m rule
stem: The sensation of a sound persists in the human ear for about 0.1 s. Taking the speed of sound in air as 340 m s^-1, the minimum distance of a reflecting wall from a listener if a distinct echo is to be heard is
solution: For the echo to be heard as a separate sound the reflected pulse must arrive at least 0.1 s after the original. In that time the sound travels 340 x 0.1 = 34 m, but this is the total path out to the wall and back. The wall must therefore be at least 34 / 2 = 17 m away.
formula_principle: d = v t / 2, with t equal to the persistence of hearing.
common_misconception: Omitting the factor of two that accounts for the return journey.

concept_tested: Definition of reverberation
stem: Reverberation in a hall is best described as
option_a: a single clearly separated repetition of a sound heard after a distinct time interval
option_b: the gradual change in the pitch of a sound as it travels across a large hall
option_c: the persistence of sound caused by repeated reflections from the walls, floor and ceiling after the source has stopped
option_d: the complete absorption of sound by soft furnishings so that no reflection reaches the listener
correct_answer_text: the persistence of sound caused by repeated reflections from the walls, floor and ceiling after the source has stopped
solution: In a hall the sound reaches a listener directly and also after one, two or many reflections from the surrounding surfaces. These reflected contributions arrive at slightly different times and overlap, so the sound seems to linger after the source has fallen silent. Excessive reverberation blurs speech and is reduced by hanging curtains and using porous absorbing materials.
formula_principle: Reverberation is the prolongation of sound in an enclosure due to multiple reflections.
common_misconception: Using the words echo and reverberation as though they meant exactly the same thing.

concept_tested: Principle and waves used in SONAR
stem: SONAR is used to find the depth of the sea. It works by
option_a: sending a beam of light downward and timing the return of the beam reflected from the sea bed
option_b: sending a pulse of ultrasonic waves downward and timing the return of the pulse reflected from the sea bed
option_c: sending a pulse of infrasonic waves downward, since only very low frequencies penetrate water
option_d: measuring the pressure at the bottom of a long cable lowered to the sea bed
correct_answer_text: sending a pulse of ultrasonic waves downward and timing the return of the pulse reflected from the sea bed
solution: A transmitter on the ship sends a short pulse of ultrasound into the water. The pulse travels down, reflects from the sea bed and returns to a receiver. If the total time is t and the speed of sound in sea water is v, the depth is d = v t / 2. Ultrasound is chosen because its short wavelength gives a narrow, well directed beam.
formula_principle: SONAR times the echo of an ultrasonic pulse and uses d = v t / 2.
common_misconception: Supposing that light or radio waves could be used for sounding at depth in sea water.

concept_tested: What is needed for a distinct echo
stem: For a distinct echo to be heard, the reflecting surface must be
option_a: small compared with the wavelength of the sound, so that the sound is reflected from a sharp point
option_b: polished to a mirror finish, since only optically smooth surfaces can reflect waves
option_c: made of a soft absorbing material such as cloth, which returns the sound most efficiently
option_d: large compared with the wavelength of the sound and far enough away for the reflected sound to arrive after the direct sound has ceased to be sensed
correct_answer_text: large compared with the wavelength of the sound and far enough away for the reflected sound to arrive after the direct sound has ceased to be sensed
solution: Two conditions must be met. Geometrically, the reflector must be large compared with the wavelength, otherwise the sound bends around it. In time, the echo must arrive at least about 0.1 s after the direct sound, which for air at 340 m s^-1 places the reflector at least 17 m away. A hard dense surface reflects far better than a soft porous one.
formula_principle: Echo requires a large hard reflector at least about 17 m away in air at 340 m s^-1.
common_misconception: Applying the optical requirement of a polished surface to sound, whose wavelength is enormous by comparison.

concept_tested: Using d = v t / 2 for a wall
stem: A man fires a gun and hears its echo from a cliff after 3 s. Taking the speed of sound in air as 340 m s^-1, the cliff is at a distance of
solution: In 3 s the sound covers v t = 340 x 3 = 1020 m. This is the journey to the cliff and back, so the distance to the cliff is 1020 / 2 = 510 m.
formula_principle: 2 d = v t, so d = v t / 2.
common_misconception: Quoting the total path length as the distance to the reflector.

concept_tested: Depth of the sea from an echo time
stem: A SONAR pulse sent vertically downward from a ship returns after 4 s. Taking the speed of sound in sea water as 1500 m s^-1, the depth of the sea at that point is
solution: The total path length is v t = 1500 x 4 = 6000 m. The pulse travels down and back over equal distances, so the depth is 6000 / 2 = 3000 m.
formula_principle: d = v t / 2 for an echo sounding.
common_misconception: Forgetting that the echo time covers a down and up journey.

subtopic: Echo time from a known distance
concept_tested: Reversing the echo relation
stem: A boy claps his hands while standing 170 m from a large wall. Taking the speed of sound in air as 340 m s^-1, he hears the echo after
solution: The sound travels 170 m to the wall and 170 m back, a total of 340 m. The time taken is t = 340 / 340 = 1 s. Since this exceeds 0.1 s, the echo is heard as a distinct repetition of the clap.
formula_principle: t = 2 d / v.
common_misconception: Computing the one way time and quoting it as the echo interval.

subtopic: Minimum distance at a different speed
concept_tested: How the 17 m rule changes with the assumed speed
stem: If the speed of sound in air is taken as 330 m s^-1 and the persistence of hearing as 0.1 s, the minimum distance of a reflector needed for a distinct echo is
solution: In 0.1 s the sound travels 330 x 0.1 = 33 m. Since this is the out and back path, the minimum distance to the reflector is 33 / 2 = 16.5 m. The familiar figure of 17 m corresponds to taking the speed as 340 m s^-1, so the answer depends on which value of the speed is used.
formula_principle: d_min = v t / 2 with t = 0.1 s.
common_misconception: Quoting the memorised figure of 17 m without checking which speed of sound the question specifies.

subtopic: Why small rooms give no echo
concept_tested: Applying the minimum distance condition indoors
stem: A person shouts in an ordinary room about 5 m across and hears no separate echo. The reason is that
option_a: the walls of an ordinary room are too smooth to reflect sound back to the speaker
option_b: the reflected sound returns in far less than the persistence of hearing, so it merges with the original sound
option_c: sound cannot be reflected at all unless the reflector is at least a hundred metres away
option_d: the sound is completely absorbed by the air over the few metres of its journey
correct_answer_text: the reflected sound returns in far less than the persistence of hearing, so it merges with the original sound
solution: In a room 5 m across the reflected sound travels about 10 m, taking roughly 10 / 340 = 0.03 s. This is well within the 0.1 s for which the ear retains the sensation of the original sound, so the reflection is not perceived as a separate event. It still reaches the listener and contributes to the reverberation, which is why an empty room sounds hollow.
formula_principle: An echo is distinguished only if the reflected sound arrives at least 0.1 s later, needing about 17 m in air.
common_misconception: Concluding that no reflection takes place at all, rather than that the reflection is not separately audible.

concept_tested: Behaviour of a compression reflected from a denser medium
stem: A compression pulse travelling through air is incident normally on a rigid wall. The reflected pulse is
option_a: a rarefaction, and the displacement of the particles suffers no phase change on reflection
option_b: a compression, and neither the pressure nor the displacement suffers any phase change
option_c: a rarefaction, and the pressure suffers a phase change of pi while the displacement does not
option_d: a compression, and the displacement of the particles suffers a phase change of pi on reflection
correct_answer_text: a compression, and the displacement of the particles suffers a phase change of pi on reflection
solution: The wall cannot move, so the particles right at the wall must stay at rest. This forces the reflected displacement wave to be opposite in sign to the incident one, a phase change of pi. Because excess pressure and displacement are related through the space gradient, this reversal leaves the pressure variation unchanged in sign, so a compression comes back as a compression and the wall experiences a doubled pressure change.
formula_principle: At a rigid boundary the displacement reverses (phase change pi) while the pressure change does not; a compression returns as a compression.
common_misconception: Assuming that a phase reversal of displacement must also turn a compression into a rarefaction.

concept_tested: Behaviour of a compression reflected from a rarer medium
stem: A compression pulse travelling along the air in a tube reaches the open end of the tube. The pulse reflected back into the tube is
option_a: a rarefaction, since a compression arriving at a free boundary is returned with the sign of the pressure change reversed
option_b: a compression, since the sign of the pressure change is preserved at every kind of boundary
option_c: a compression of half the original amplitude, since only half the energy is returned
option_d: neither a compression nor a rarefaction, since no reflection occurs at an open end
correct_answer_text: a rarefaction, since a compression arriving at a free boundary is returned with the sign of the pressure change reversed
solution: At the open end the air is free to move outward into the large body of atmosphere, so the excess pressure there must fall to the ambient value. The reflected pulse must therefore cancel the incident excess pressure at that point, which requires it to be a rarefaction. The displacement, in contrast, suffers no reversal at a free boundary. This is the exact opposite of what happens at a rigid wall.
formula_principle: At a free or open boundary the pressure change reverses while the displacement does not; a compression returns as a rarefaction.
common_misconception: Applying the rigid wall rule at an open end and expecting a compression to return as a compression.

concept_tested: Use of reflected ultrasound in imaging
stem: Ultrasonic waves are preferred to audible sound for medical imaging mainly because
option_a: they travel much faster through body tissue than audible sound does
option_b: they are the only waves that can be reflected from a boundary between two tissues
option_c: their short wavelength allows them to be sent as a narrow beam and to resolve small structures inside the body
option_d: they pass through bone without any reflection, giving a clear view of the tissue behind
correct_answer_text: their short wavelength allows them to be sent as a narrow beam and to resolve small structures inside the body
solution: The ability of a wave to be sent as a beam and to reveal fine detail improves as the wavelength becomes small compared with the objects of interest. A 2 MHz ultrasound pulse in tissue, where the speed is about 1500 m s^-1, has a wavelength of less than a millimetre, so it can outline structures of that size. An audible 2 kHz wave would have a wavelength of the order of a metre and would simply diffract around the organs.
formula_principle: Ultrasound has frequency above 20 kHz and hence wavelength below about 1.7 cm in air and less in tissue, giving good directionality and resolution.
common_misconception: Thinking that ultrasound is useful because it is faster rather than because it is shorter in wavelength.

concept_tested: Separation of two cliffs from two echo times
stem: A man standing between two parallel cliffs fires a gun and hears the first echo after 1.5 s and the second after 2.5 s. Taking the speed of sound in air as 340 m s^-1, the distance between the two cliffs is
solution: The nearer cliff is at d_1 = 340 x 1.5 / 2 = 255 m and the farther cliff at d_2 = 340 x 2.5 / 2 = 425 m. The man stands between them, so the separation is d_1 + d_2 = 255 + 425 = 680 m. As a check, the sum of the two times is 4 s, and 340 x 4 / 2 = 680 m gives the same answer directly.
formula_principle: For each cliff d = v t / 2; the separation is the sum of the two distances.
common_misconception: Forgetting the factor of two for one of the two journeys, or subtracting the distances instead of adding them.

subtopic: Change of echo time with position
concept_tested: Effect of moving towards the reflector
stem: A man standing 85 m from a wall claps and notes the echo interval. He then walks 17 m towards the wall and claps again. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m s^-1, the second echo interval is shorter than the first by
solution: At 85 m the interval is t_1 = 2 x 85 / 340 = 0.5 s. At 68 m it is t_2 = 2 x 68 / 340 = 0.4 s. The reduction is 0.5 - 0.4 = 0.1 s, which also follows directly from 2 x 17 / 340 = 0.1 s. Note that at the closer position the interval is exactly at the limit of 0.1 s, so the echo is only just distinguishable.
formula_principle: t = 2 d / v, so a change delta d in distance changes the interval by 2 delta d / v.
common_misconception: Applying the change in distance once instead of twice, since both the outward and the return path are shortened.

concept_tested: Distinguishing the two phenomena
stem: The essential difference between an echo and reverberation is that
option_a: an echo is a single reflection arriving late enough to be heard separately, while reverberation is a succession of reflections arriving too soon to be separated
option_b: an echo occurs only in closed halls while reverberation occurs only in the open air
option_c: an echo involves a change in the frequency of the sound while reverberation does not
option_d: an echo is produced by absorption at a soft surface while reverberation is produced by reflection at a hard surface
correct_answer_text: an echo is a single reflection arriving late enough to be heard separately, while reverberation is a succession of reflections arriving too soon to be separated
solution: Both effects are caused by the reflection of sound from surrounding surfaces. If a single reflection arrives more than about 0.1 s after the direct sound, which needs a reflector more than about 17 m away in air, the ear registers it as a separate repetition and it is called an echo. In a hall the many surfaces are close together, so a large number of reflections arrive within that 0.1 s window and merge with the direct sound into a prolonged trailing sound, which is reverberation.
formula_principle: Both arise from reflection; the difference lies in the time separation compared with the 0.1 s persistence of hearing.
common_misconception: Treating the two as physically different processes rather than as the same process with different time separations.

concept_tested: Combining echo timing with the wave relation
stem: A SONAR set works at a frequency of 50 kHz. The speed of sound in sea water is 1500 m s^-1 and the echo from the sea bed returns 2 s after the pulse is sent. The wavelength of the pulse in water and the depth of the sea are respectively
solution: The wavelength is lambda = v / f = 1500 / 50000 = 0.03 m = 3 cm, short enough to give a well directed beam. The total path is v t = 1500 x 2 = 3000 m, so the depth is 3000 / 2 = 1500 m.
formula_principle: lambda = v / f for the wavelength and d = v t / 2 for the depth.
common_misconception: Halving the wavelength instead of the path length, or failing to convert kilohertz to hertz.

concept_tested: Determining the speed of sound from echo data
stem: A student stands 165 m from a wall, claps, and finds that the echo returns after 1 s. From this measurement the speed of sound in the air is
solution: The sound covers 165 m to the wall and 165 m back, a total of 330 m, in 1 s. Hence v = 330 / 1 = 330 m s^-1. This kind of open air measurement is the simplest classroom determination of the speed of sound.
formula_principle: v = 2 d / t.
common_misconception: Using the one way distance in v = d / t and obtaining half the true speed.

concept_tested: Multiple reflections in a valley
stem: A man standing between two parallel cliffs 1020 m apart fires a gun. He hears the first echo after 1 s and the second after 5 s. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m s^-1, a further echo formed by sound reflected from both cliffs in turn reaches him after
solution: The near cliff is at 340 x 1 / 2 = 170 m and the far cliff at 340 x 5 / 2 = 850 m, and indeed 170 + 850 = 1020 m as stated. A pulse that goes to the near cliff, reflects across to the far cliff and returns to the man travels 170 + 1020 + 850 = 2040 m, taking 2040 / 340 = 6 s. Equivalently this is the time for a round trip across the full separation, 2 x 1020 / 340 = 6 s.
formula_principle: For each path, time = path length / v; the doubly reflected pulse travels the full separation and back.
common_misconception: Adding or subtracting the two echo times instead of tracing the actual path of the doubly reflected pulse.

concept_tested: Statements about echo, reverberation and absorption
stem: Four statements are made about sound in a large hall. P: reverberation is caused by repeated reflections. Q: hanging heavy curtains reduces reverberation. R: a distinct echo needs the reflector to be at least about 17 m away when the speed of sound is 340 m s^-1. S: reflection of sound from a stationary wall raises its frequency. The correct statements are
solution: P is correct, since reverberation is the overlapping of many reflected contributions. Q is correct, because porous heavy fabric absorbs sound energy and shortens the reverberation time. R is correct, since d = v t / 2 = 340 x 0.1 / 2 = 17 m. S is wrong, because a frequency shift on reflection requires the reflector to be moving, which is the Doppler effect and not ordinary reflection.
formula_principle: Reverberation arises from multiple reflections and is reduced by absorbers; echo needs v t / 2 with t about 0.1 s; a stationary reflector preserves frequency.
common_misconception: Believing that reflection by itself alters the pitch of a sound.

concept_tested: Pitch is determined by frequency
stem: The characteristic of a musical note that decides whether it is heard as shrill or as flat is
option_a: its loudness, which is determined by the frequency of the vibration
option_b: its pitch, which is determined by the frequency of the vibration
option_c: its pitch, which is determined by the amplitude of the vibration
option_d: its quality, which is determined by the amplitude of the vibration
correct_answer_text: its pitch, which is determined by the frequency of the vibration
solution: A note of high frequency is heard as shrill and a note of low frequency as flat or deep. The sensation of pitch therefore corresponds to frequency. Turning up the volume increases the amplitude and hence the loudness, but the note keeps exactly the same pitch, which shows that pitch and loudness are independent characteristics.
formula_principle: Pitch is the subjective sensation corresponding to the frequency of the sound.
common_misconception: Interchanging the physical quantity behind pitch with the one behind loudness.

concept_tested: Loudness depends on intensity and hence on amplitude
stem: The loudness of a sound of a given frequency reaching the ear depends mainly on
option_a: the frequency of the wave, higher frequencies always being louder
option_b: the wavelength of the wave, longer wavelengths always being louder
option_c: the speed of the wave in the medium, faster waves always being louder
option_d: the intensity of the wave, which is proportional to the square of the amplitude
correct_answer_text: the intensity of the wave, which is proportional to the square of the amplitude
solution: The energy carried by a wave, and therefore its intensity, depends on the square of the amplitude of vibration. The ear perceives a more intense sound as louder. Frequency and wavelength decide pitch, while the speed is a property of the medium, so none of these settles the loudness.
formula_principle: Intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude, and loudness increases with intensity.
common_misconception: Assuming that a shrill high frequency sound is automatically a loud one.

concept_tested: Quality is decided by the overtones present
stem: A violin and a flute both sound the note of the same frequency and the same loudness, yet the two can easily be told apart. The characteristic that differs is
option_a: the pitch, which depends on the shape of the instrument producing the note
option_b: the loudness, which depends on the material of the instrument
option_c: the speed of the sound, which depends on the size of the sounding body
option_d: the quality, which depends on the number and relative strength of the overtones present along with the fundamental
correct_answer_text: the quality, which depends on the number and relative strength of the overtones present along with the fundamental
solution: Every real instrument produces a fundamental together with a set of overtones whose relative strengths depend on the way the instrument vibrates and on its shape and material. This mixture gives the resultant wave its characteristic shape. Two notes with the same fundamental frequency and the same energy therefore have the same pitch and loudness, but different waveforms, and the ear recognises this difference as quality or timbre.
formula_principle: Quality or timbre is set by the overtone content, which shapes the waveform of the note.
common_misconception: Believing that a difference in the sound of two instruments must mean a difference in pitch or loudness.

concept_tested: Limits of the audible range of frequency
stem: The range of frequencies to which the normal human ear responds is about
solution: Frequencies below about 20 Hz are called infrasonic and are felt rather than heard, while frequencies above about 20000 Hz are ultrasonic and lie beyond the response of the human ear. The upper limit falls steadily with age, so the figure of 20 kHz applies to young ears.
formula_principle: Audible range is approximately 20 Hz to 20000 Hz.
common_misconception: Slipping by a factor of ten in one or both limits of the range.

concept_tested: Classifying waves by frequency
stem: A mechanical wave in air of frequency 40 kHz is described as
option_a: infrasonic, since its frequency lies below the lower limit of human hearing
option_b: audible, since it lies within the range 20 Hz to 20 kHz
option_c: ultrasonic, since its frequency lies above the upper limit of human hearing
option_d: supersonic, since its frequency exceeds that of an audible note
correct_answer_text: ultrasonic, since its frequency lies above the upper limit of human hearing
solution: A frequency of 40 kHz is 40000 Hz, which is twice the upper limit of human hearing, so the wave is ultrasonic. Such waves are used in SONAR, in industrial flaw detection and in medical imaging. The word supersonic is quite different and describes a body moving faster than sound, not a high frequency wave.
formula_principle: Infrasonic: below 20 Hz. Audible: 20 Hz to 20 kHz. Ultrasonic: above 20 kHz.
common_misconception: Confusing the word ultrasonic, which describes a frequency, with supersonic, which describes a speed.

concept_tested: Wavelengths corresponding to the ends of the audible range
stem: Taking the speed of sound in air as 340 m s^-1, the wavelengths corresponding to the two ends of the audible range of 20 Hz to 20 kHz are respectively
solution: At the low end, lambda = 340 / 20 = 17 m. At the high end, lambda = 340 / 20000 = 0.017 m = 1.7 cm. The audible range therefore spans wavelengths from about the height of a house down to less than the width of a finger, a factor of a thousand.
formula_principle: lambda = v / f applied at each end of the audible range.
common_misconception: Pairing the shortest wavelength with the lowest frequency.

concept_tested: Waveform as the signature of quality
stem: Two notes sounded on different instruments have identical waveforms when displayed on an oscilloscope. It follows that the two notes
option_a: have the same pitch but necessarily different quality, since they come from different instruments
option_b: have the same quality but necessarily different pitch, since the instruments are of different sizes
option_c: have the same pitch, the same loudness and the same quality, so the ear cannot distinguish them
option_d: must differ in loudness, since two instruments cannot deliver the same energy
correct_answer_text: have the same pitch, the same loudness and the same quality, so the ear cannot distinguish them
solution: The repeat period of the trace gives the frequency and hence the pitch. The height of the trace gives the amplitude and hence the loudness. The detailed shape within one period reflects the overtones present and hence the quality. If two traces coincide in every respect, all three characteristics agree and the ear has nothing left to distinguish. In practice the traces of different instruments do differ in shape, which is exactly why they sound different.
formula_principle: The waveform of a note encodes its frequency, its amplitude and its overtone content, hence its pitch, loudness and quality.
common_misconception: Assuming that different sources must sound different even when they produce identical waveforms.

concept_tested: Comparing intensities of two sources
stem: Two sources of the same frequency send sound into the same air, the amplitude of the second wave being twice that of the first. The intensity of the second wave compared with the first is
solution: The energy of an oscillating particle varies as the square of its amplitude, so the intensity of a wave of fixed frequency in a given medium is proportional to A^2. Doubling the amplitude therefore multiplies the intensity by 2^2 = 4.
formula_principle: For a fixed frequency and medium, intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude.
common_misconception: Scaling the intensity in direct proportion to the amplitude.

concept_tested: Everyday sources of infrasonic waves
stem: Which of the following is a source of infrasonic waves?
option_a: the ground vibrations that travel ahead of an earthquake
option_b: the navigation pulses emitted by a bat in flight
option_c: the transmitter of a SONAR set on a ship
option_d: an ultrasonic cleaning bath used for spectacles
correct_answer_text: the ground vibrations that travel ahead of an earthquake
solution: Large slow moving masses produce very low frequencies. The ground motion associated with an earthquake contains components well below 20 Hz, which is why some animals appear to sense an earthquake before humans hear anything. Bats, SONAR transmitters and cleaning baths all operate above 20 kHz and are therefore ultrasonic sources.
formula_principle: Infrasonic waves have frequency below about 20 Hz; ultrasonic waves have frequency above about 20 kHz.
common_misconception: Grouping all inaudible sounds together instead of separating those below the range from those above it.

concept_tested: Echolocation by bats and dolphins
stem: A bat finds its way in complete darkness by
option_a: emitting short pulses of ultrasound and listening for the reflections from obstacles and prey
option_b: emitting short pulses of infrasound whose long wavelength bends easily around obstacles
option_c: detecting the heat radiated by objects in its path with sensitive receptors in its ears
option_d: sensing changes in the pressure of the air produced by nearby stationary walls
correct_answer_text: emitting short pulses of ultrasound and listening for the reflections from obstacles and prey
solution: The bat sends out bursts of ultrasound, often above 40 kHz, whose wavelength in air is less than a centimetre. Such a short wavelength reflects strongly from small objects such as insects rather than diffracting around them. From the time delay of the returning echo the bat judges distance, exactly as a SONAR set does under water. Dolphins use the same principle in water.
formula_principle: Echolocation uses the reflection of short wavelength ultrasound, with distance found from d = v t / 2.
common_misconception: Assuming that low frequency sound would serve equally well, without considering how wavelength governs reflection.

concept_tested: Separating the two sensations
stem: The volume control of a music system is turned up while the same note continues to play. As a result,
option_a: both the amplitude and the frequency increase, so the note sounds both louder and shriller
option_b: the frequency increases while the amplitude stays the same, so the note sounds shriller but not louder
option_c: the wavelength decreases so the note sounds louder, the speed of sound being unchanged
option_d: the amplitude of the wave increases so the note sounds louder, while its frequency and therefore its pitch remain unchanged
correct_answer_text: the amplitude of the wave increases so the note sounds louder, while its frequency and therefore its pitch remain unchanged
solution: The volume control adjusts the electrical power fed to the loudspeaker, which changes how far the cone moves and hence the amplitude of the sound wave. The rate of vibration is set by the recorded signal and is untouched, so the frequency and pitch are unchanged. Since v is fixed by the air and f is fixed by the source, the wavelength is unchanged as well.
formula_principle: Loudness follows amplitude; pitch follows frequency; the two are independent characteristics.
common_misconception: Supposing that a louder sound must also be a higher pitched one.

concept_tested: Change of intensity level for a given intensity ratio
stem: The intensity of a sound is increased to 100 times its original value. Given that the intensity level in decibel is 10 log10 (I / I_0), the increase in the intensity level is
solution: The change in level is L_2 - L_1 = 10 log10 (I_2 / I_0) - 10 log10 (I_1 / I_0) = 10 log10 (I_2 / I_1) = 10 log10 (100) = 10 x 2 = 20 dB. Each factor of ten in intensity adds 10 dB, so two factors of ten add 20 dB.
formula_principle: Intensity level L = 10 log10 (I / I_0), so a change of intensity by a factor r changes L by 10 log10 r.
common_misconception: Reading the decibel scale as a linear rather than a logarithmic measure of intensity.

concept_tested: Audibility and wavelength of a very low frequency
stem: A large machine vibrates 17 times per second and sets up a wave in air, in which the speed of sound is 340 m s^-1. This wave
option_a: is audible and has a wavelength of 20 m
option_b: is infrasonic and has a wavelength of 0.05 m
option_c: is ultrasonic and has a wavelength of 20 m
option_d: is infrasonic and has a wavelength of 20 m
correct_answer_text: is infrasonic and has a wavelength of 20 m
solution: The frequency 17 Hz lies below the lower limit of about 20 Hz, so the wave is infrasonic and is felt as a vibration rather than heard as a note. Its wavelength is lambda = v / f = 340 / 17 = 20 m, which is very long compared with ordinary objects, so such a wave diffracts freely around buildings.
formula_principle: Audible range is 20 Hz to 20 kHz; lambda = v / f.
common_misconception: Classifying every inaudible frequency as ultrasonic without checking which side of the audible range it lies on.

concept_tested: Does pitch change when sound enters water?
stem: A swimmer with his head under water listens to a bell rung in the air above. Compared with what a listener in the air hears, the swimmer hears the note with
option_a: the same pitch, because the frequency is unchanged on entering the water even though the wavelength increases
option_b: a higher pitch, because sound travels faster in water than in air
option_c: a lower pitch, because the wavelength of the sound is longer in water than in air
option_d: no definite pitch, because the sound is completely reflected at the surface of the water
correct_answer_text: the same pitch, because the frequency is unchanged on entering the water even though the wavelength increases
solution: The water at the surface is driven by the air above it at exactly the rate at which the bell vibrates, so the frequency carried into the water is the same. Pitch corresponds to frequency, so the note sounds the same in pitch. What does change is the speed, which rises to about 1500 m s^-1, and the wavelength, which rises in the same proportion since lambda = v / f. The loudness is reduced because much of the energy is reflected at the surface.
formula_principle: Frequency is preserved across a boundary, so pitch is preserved; v and lambda both change in the same ratio.
common_misconception: Reasoning from the change of wavelength to a change of pitch, forgetting that the speed changes in the same ratio.

concept_tested: Comparing intensities at different frequencies
stem: Two sound waves travel in the same air with the same amplitude, but the frequency of the second is twice that of the first. Taking the intensity to be proportional to the square of the amplitude and to the square of the frequency, the intensity of the second wave compared with the first is
option_b: equal to that of the first
solution: The energy of an oscillating particle is proportional to A^2 omega^2, since the maximum particle speed is A omega and the energy goes as the square of that speed. With A the same for the two waves, the intensity varies as f^2. Doubling the frequency therefore multiplies the intensity by 2^2 = 4. Physically, the particles of the higher frequency wave cover the same amplitude in half the time and so move twice as fast.
formula_principle: Intensity is proportional to (amplitude)^2 x (frequency)^2 for a wave in a given medium.
common_misconception: Assuming that equal amplitude automatically means equal energy, regardless of frequency.

concept_tested: Matching each characteristic with the quantity that decides it
stem: Four claims are made about the characteristics of a musical note. P: pitch is decided by frequency. Q: loudness is decided by intensity. R: quality is decided by the overtones present. S: pitch is decided by the speed of sound in the medium. The correct claims are
solution: P is correct, since a note of higher frequency is heard as shriller. Q is correct, since the ear judges loudness by the energy arriving per unit area per second, which is proportional to the square of the amplitude. R is correct, since two notes of the same fundamental frequency are told apart by the relative strengths of their overtones. S is wrong, because a note keeps its pitch when it passes into water even though the speed there is more than four times larger; it is the frequency, imposed by the source, that decides pitch.
formula_principle: Pitch follows frequency, loudness follows intensity, quality follows overtone content.
common_misconception: Letting the change of speed or wavelength in a new medium suggest a change of pitch.

concept_tested: Meaning of the Doppler effect for sound
stem: The Doppler effect for sound is the
option_a: real change in the frequency emitted by a source caused by its own motion through the air
option_b: apparent change in the frequency heard by an observer caused by relative motion between the source and the observer along the line joining them
option_c: change in the speed of sound in air caused by the motion of the source through the air
option_d: change in the loudness of a sound caused by the increasing distance between source and observer
correct_answer_text: apparent change in the frequency heard by an observer caused by relative motion between the source and the observer along the line joining them
solution: The source continues to emit at its own frequency, and the sound continues to travel through the air at the fixed speed of sound. What changes is the rate at which wavefronts arrive at the ear, because the relative motion crowds them together or spreads them out. This alters the received frequency and hence the pitch heard, which is the Doppler effect.
formula_principle: Doppler effect: apparent frequency changes when source and observer have relative motion along the line joining them.
common_misconception: Believing that the source itself begins to vibrate faster or that the speed of sound changes.

concept_tested: Approach raises pitch and recession lowers it
stem: A police siren of fixed frequency passes a stationary listener at speed. The listener hears
option_a: a lower pitch while the siren approaches and a higher pitch after it has passed
option_b: a steadily rising pitch throughout, from long before the siren arrives until long after
option_c: the same pitch throughout, only the loudness changing as the siren comes near and goes away
option_d: a higher pitch while the siren approaches and a lower pitch after it has passed
correct_answer_text: a higher pitch while the siren approaches and a lower pitch after it has passed
solution: While the siren approaches, each successive wavefront is emitted from a point nearer the listener, so the fronts are packed closer together and arrive more often. The received frequency is therefore higher than the emitted one. Once the siren has passed, each front is emitted from a point further away, the fronts are stretched apart and the received frequency falls below the emitted value. The drop occurs at the moment of passing.
formula_principle: n' = n v / (v -/+ v_s): the minus sign for approach gives a larger n', the plus sign for recession a smaller n'.
common_misconception: Getting the sense of the shift the wrong way round, or attributing the effect to loudness alone.

concept_tested: Apparent frequency for an approaching source
stem: A source emitting a note of 500 Hz moves towards a stationary observer at 30 m s^-1. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m s^-1, the frequency heard by the observer is
solution: n' = 500 x 330 / (330 - 30) = 500 x 330 / 300 = 500 x 1.1 = 550 Hz. The approach raises the frequency, as expected.
formula_principle: n' = n v / (v - v_s) for a source approaching a stationary observer.
common_misconception: Placing the source speed in the numerator, or using the plus sign for an approaching source.

concept_tested: Apparent frequency for a receding source
stem: A source emitting a note of 480 Hz moves away from a stationary observer at 30 m s^-1. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m s^-1, the frequency heard by the observer is
solution: n' = 480 x 330 / (330 + 30) = 480 x 330 / 360 = 480 x 11 / 12 = 440 Hz. The recession lowers the frequency, as expected.
formula_principle: n' = n v / (v + v_s) for a source receding from a stationary observer.
common_misconception: Choosing the sign in the denominator by habit instead of by checking whether the pitch must rise or fall.

concept_tested: Apparent frequency for a moving observer
stem: A stationary source emits a note of 440 Hz. An observer moves towards the source at 30 m s^-1. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m s^-1, the frequency heard by the observer is
solution: n' = 440 x (330 + 30) / 330 = 440 x 360 / 330 = 440 x 12 / 11 = 480 Hz. The observer runs into the wavefronts and therefore meets more of them each second.
formula_principle: n' = n (v + v_o) / v for an observer approaching a stationary source.
common_misconception: Applying the moving source formula when it is in fact the observer who is moving.

concept_tested: Apparent frequency for an observer moving away
stem: A stationary source emits a note of 550 Hz. An observer moves away from the source at 30 m s^-1. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m s^-1, the frequency heard by the observer is
solution: n' = 550 x (330 - 30) / 330 = 550 x 300 / 330 = 550 x 10 / 11 = 500 Hz. The observer is running away from the advancing wavefronts and so meets fewer of them each second.
formula_principle: n' = n (v - v_o) / v for an observer receding from a stationary source.
common_misconception: Interchanging the moving source and moving observer formulas.

concept_tested: No shift for motion perpendicular to the line of sight
stem: A source of sound moves along a straight track at constant speed. At the instant when it is at the point of closest approach to a stationary observer beside the track, the frequency heard by the observer is
option_a: greater than the true frequency, since the source is at its closest and the sound is loudest there
option_b: equal to the true frequency of the source, since at that instant the source has no component of velocity along the line joining it to the observer
option_c: less than the true frequency, since the source has already begun to move away in the sense of its own motion
option_d: greater than the true frequency by the same amount as it is less a moment later, so that the two are equal
correct_answer_text: equal to the true frequency of the source, since at that instant the source has no component of velocity along the line joining it to the observer
solution: The Doppler shift is governed by the rate at which the distance between source and observer changes. At the point of closest approach the velocity of the source is entirely at right angles to the line joining it to the observer, so that distance is momentarily neither increasing nor decreasing. The wavefronts therefore arrive at exactly the rate at which they are emitted, and the observer hears the true frequency. Just before this instant the pitch is higher and just after it is lower.
formula_principle: Only the component of relative velocity along the line joining source and observer produces a Doppler shift.
common_misconception: Assuming that any motion of the source, in any direction, must produce a shift in pitch.

concept_tested: Source and observer moving together
stem: A motorcyclist sounding a horn of constant frequency is followed by a car at exactly the same speed, both travelling along a straight road in still air. The driver of the car hears
option_a: a frequency higher than the true value, since both vehicles are moving through the air
option_b: a frequency lower than the true value, since the horn is running away from the car
option_c: a frequency higher than the true value when the speed is large and the true value when it is small
option_d: the true frequency of the horn, since the separation between the horn and the car is not changing
correct_answer_text: the true frequency of the horn, since the separation between the horn and the car is not changing
solution: Take the direction from the horn to the car as positive. Both move at the same speed u in the same direction, so the general expression n' = n (v + u) / (v + u) reduces to n' = n. Physically, each wavefront that leaves the horn has to cover a separation that stays constant, so the fronts arrive at exactly the rate at which they are sent out. There is no Doppler shift when the separation does not change.
formula_principle: n' = n (v + v_o) / (v + v_s); with v_o = v_s the two factors cancel and n' = n.
common_misconception: Supposing that motion relative to the air, rather than relative to each other, is what produces the shift.

concept_tested: Practical uses of the Doppler effect
stem: The Doppler effect is used in a traffic speed gun. The instrument works by
option_a: sending a wave at the vehicle and measuring the shift in frequency of the wave reflected back from it
option_b: measuring the loudness of the engine noise reaching it from the vehicle
option_c: timing how long the vehicle takes to travel between two marked points on the road
option_d: measuring the change in the speed of the reflected wave caused by the motion of the vehicle
correct_answer_text: sending a wave at the vehicle and measuring the shift in frequency of the wave reflected back from it
solution: The gun emits a wave of known frequency towards the vehicle. The vehicle, moving towards the gun, receives a raised frequency, and on reflecting the wave it acts as a moving source and raises the frequency again. The instrument compares the returning frequency with the emitted one and computes the speed from the double shift. The same double shift principle is used in medical Doppler ultrasound to measure the speed of blood.
formula_principle: A moving reflector acts first as a moving observer and then as a moving source, giving a shift that depends on its speed.
common_misconception: Thinking that the reflected wave travels faster, rather than that its frequency is shifted.

concept_tested: Using the general formula
stem: A source emitting a note of 500 Hz moves towards an observer at 30 m s^-1 while the observer moves towards the source at 30 m s^-1. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m s^-1, the frequency heard is
solution: n' = 500 x (330 + 30) / (330 - 30) = 500 x 360 / 300 = 500 x 1.2 = 600 Hz. Both motions are approaches, so both push the frequency up: the observer meets the wavefronts more often and the source packs them closer together.
formula_principle: n' = n (v + v_o) / (v - v_s) when both approach each other.
common_misconception: Cancelling the two equal speeds and concluding wrongly that there is no shift.

concept_tested: Doppler effect seen as a change of wavelength
stem: A source emitting a note of 300 Hz moves through still air at 30 m s^-1. Taking the speed of sound as 330 m s^-1, the wavelengths of the sound in front of the source and behind it are respectively
solution: In one period the wave advances v / n while the source itself advances v_s / n, so ahead of the source the fronts are separated by (v - v_s) / n = (330 - 30) / 300 = 300 / 300 = 1.0 m. Behind the source they are separated by (v + v_s) / n = (330 + 30) / 300 = 360 / 300 = 1.2 m. For a stationary source both would be 330 / 300 = 1.1 m.
formula_principle: lambda_front = (v - v_s) / n and lambda_behind = (v + v_s) / n.
common_misconception: Applying the speed correction to the final wavelength rather than to the distance advanced in one period.

concept_tested: The two cases are not equivalent for sound
stem: A source of frequency 330 Hz and an observer are in still air where the speed of sound is 330 m s^-1. In case X the source moves towards the stationary observer at 30 m s^-1; in case Y the observer moves towards the stationary source at 30 m s^-1. The frequencies heard are
option_a: 360 Hz in case X and 363 Hz in case Y, so the two cases are not equivalent
option_b: 363 Hz in both cases, since only the relative velocity of source and observer matters
option_c: 360 Hz in both cases, since only the relative velocity of source and observer matters
option_d: 363 Hz in case X and 360 Hz in case Y, so the two cases are not equivalent
correct_answer_text: 363 Hz in case X and 360 Hz in case Y, so the two cases are not equivalent
solution: In case X, n' = 330 x 330 / (330 - 30) = 330 x 330 / 300 = 363 Hz. In case Y, n' = 330 x (330 + 30) / 330 = 360 Hz. The results differ because the air itself provides a frame of reference for sound: a moving source alters the wavelength in the air, while a moving observer alters only the rate at which unchanged wavefronts are met. The two answers approach each other when the speeds are small compared with the speed of sound.
formula_principle: Moving source: n' = n v / (v - v_s). Moving observer: n' = n (v + v_o) / v. The two differ except in the limit of small speeds.
common_misconception: Assuming that only the relative velocity matters, as it does for light, and expecting the two cases to give identical answers.

concept_tested: Double Doppler shift at a moving reflector
stem: A stationary source emits a note of 500 Hz towards a large wall that is moving towards the source at 30 m s^-1. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m s^-1, the frequency of the sound reflected back to the source is
solution: The wall approaches the wavefronts, so it receives n_1 = 500 x (330 + 30) / 330 = 500 x 360 / 330 Hz. It then re-radiates this frequency while itself approaching the source, so the source receives n_2 = n_1 x 330 / (330 - 30) = 500 x (360 / 330) x (330 / 300) = 500 x 360 / 300 = 600 Hz. The two shifts multiply, giving n'' = n (v + u) / (v - u).
formula_principle: The moving wall first acts as a moving observer, then re-emits as a moving source: n'' = n (v + u) / (v - u).
common_misconception: Applying the Doppler formula only once and forgetting that the moving wall plays both roles in turn.

subtopic: Change in pitch as a train passes
concept_tested: Difference between the approach and recession frequencies
stem: A train whistle of frequency 1200 Hz passes a stationary observer standing beside the track, the train moving at 30 m s^-1. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m s^-1, the drop in the frequency heard as the train goes past is
solution: While approaching, n_1 = 1200 x 330 / 300 = 1320 Hz. While receding, n_2 = 1200 x 330 / 360 = 1100 Hz. The observed frequency falls from 1320 Hz to 1100 Hz, a drop of 220 Hz. Note that the rise of 120 Hz on approach and the fall of 100 Hz on recession are not equal, because the two expressions are not symmetric.
formula_principle: n_approach = n v / (v - v_s), n_recede = n v / (v + v_s), and the drop is the difference.
common_misconception: Assuming the rise and the fall are equal and simply doubling one of them.

concept_tested: Reversing the Doppler formula
stem: A stationary observer hears a note of true frequency 500 Hz as 550 Hz while the source approaches him along the line joining them. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m s^-1, the speed of the source is
formula_principle: n' = n v / (v - v_s), so v_s = v (1 - n / n').
common_misconception: Using the moving observer formula, or reading the frequency difference as though it were a speed.

concept_tested: Validity of the Doppler expressions for sound
stem: The standard Doppler expressions for sound cease to apply when
option_a: the frequency of the source is greater than 20 kHz, since ultrasonic waves do not show a Doppler shift
option_b: the source and the observer are more than a few hundred metres apart, since the shift dies away with distance
option_c: the speed of the source becomes equal to or greater than the speed of sound in the medium, since the wavefronts then pile up into a shock front
option_d: the medium is a liquid or a solid rather than a gas, since the formulas were derived for air
correct_answer_text: the speed of the source becomes equal to or greater than the speed of sound in the medium, since the wavefronts then pile up into a shock front
solution: In deriving n' = n (v +/- v_o) / (v -/+ v_s) it is assumed that the source moves more slowly than the sound it emits, so that it always stays behind its own wavefronts. If the source speed reaches the speed of sound the denominator vanishes and the expression fails, because the wavefronts pile up into a single shock front. The formulas also assume that the medium is at rest and that the motion is along the line joining source and observer.
formula_principle: The formulas assume v_s < v and v_o < v, and that the motion is along the line joining source and observer in a still medium.
common_misconception: Looking for limitations in frequency or distance instead of in the assumed speeds and geometry.

concept_tested: A steady wind produces no Doppler shift
stem: A source and an observer are both at rest, and a steady wind blows from the source towards the observer at 30 m s^-1. Taking the speed of sound in still air as 330 m s^-1, the frequency heard by the observer is
option_a: higher than the true frequency, because the wind carries the sound to the observer faster
option_b: lower than the true frequency, because the moving air drags energy away from the observer
option_c: equal to the true frequency, because the wind raises the speed of the sound and stretches its wavelength in the same proportion
option_d: higher than the true frequency in the ratio 360 to 330, exactly as for an approaching source
correct_answer_text: equal to the true frequency, because the wind raises the speed of the sound and stretches its wavelength in the same proportion
solution: In the frame of the moving air nothing has changed: the source and the observer are simply drifting together with the air, so the separation between them is constant. Relative to the ground the sound now travels at v + w = 360 m s^-1, but the wavelength is also stretched to (v + w) / n. The number of wavefronts arriving per second is (v + w) divided by that wavelength, which is exactly n. A steady wind therefore changes the travel time and the range of audibility but not the pitch.
formula_principle: With a wind of speed w along the line of sight, both the effective speed and the wavelength become (v + w) / v times their still air values, so n' = n.
common_misconception: Substituting the wind speed into the Doppler formula as though the wind were an approaching source.

concept_tested: Driver hearing the echo of his own horn
stem: A car moving at 30 m s^-1 towards a large vertical wall sounds a horn of frequency 600 Hz. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m s^-1, the frequency of the reflected sound heard by the driver of the car is
solution: The wall is a stationary observer of an approaching source, so it receives n_1 = 600 x 330 / (330 - 30) = 600 x 330 / 300 = 660 Hz. The wall reflects this without change, acting as a stationary source of 660 Hz. The driver is now an observer approaching that source, so he hears n_2 = 660 x (330 + 30) / 330 = 660 x 360 / 330 = 720 Hz. Combining, n_2 = n (v + u) / (v - u) = 600 x 360 / 300 = 720 Hz.
formula_principle: The wall receives n_1 = n v / (v - u) and re-emits it; the driver then receives n_2 = n_1 (v + u) / v, so n_2 = n (v + u) / (v - u).
common_misconception: Applying the Doppler formula only once, forgetting that the car is a moving source on the outward trip and a moving observer on the return trip.

concept_tested: Finding source speed from the apparent wavelength
stem: A source moves through still air and the wavelength of the sound ahead of it is found to be 0.9 times the wavelength that the same source produces when at rest. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m s^-1, the speed of the source is
solution: Dividing the two expressions gives lambda_front / lambda_rest = (v - v_s) / v = 0.9. Hence v - v_s = 0.9 x 330 = 297 m s^-1 and v_s = 330 - 297 = 33 m s^-1. Note that the shift in wavelength gives the source speed directly, while a frequency ratio would have involved the reciprocal of the same factor.
formula_principle: lambda_front = (v - v_s) / n while lambda_rest = v / n, so lambda_front / lambda_rest = (v - v_s) / v.
common_misconception: Quoting 0.9 v as the answer instead of the difference between v and 0.9 v.

concept_tested: Identifying correct statements about the Doppler effect for sound
stem: Four statements are made about the Doppler effect for sound in still air. P: a source approaching an observer raises the frequency heard. Q: there is no shift when the source moves at right angles to the line joining it to the observer. R: a moving source and a moving observer of the same speed produce exactly the same apparent frequency. S: the speed of the sound in the air is changed by the motion of the source. The correct statements are
solution: P is correct, since an approaching source packs the wavefronts closer together. Q is correct, since at right angles the separation is momentarily unchanging and the shift vanishes. R is wrong: with v = 330 m s^-1, a source of 330 Hz approaching at 30 m s^-1 gives 363 Hz while an observer approaching at 30 m s^-1 gives 360 Hz, because the moving source changes the wavelength in the air while the moving observer does not. S is wrong, since the sound travels through the air at the speed set by the air itself, whatever the source does.
formula_principle: n' = n (v +/- v_o) / (v -/+ v_s); the speed v belongs to the medium, and only the component of motion along the line of sight matters.
common_misconception: Carrying over from light the idea that only relative velocity matters, and believing that a fast source drags the sound along with it.

concept_tested: Angles in reflection are always measured from the normal, not from the mirror surface
stem: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror so that it makes an angle of 30 degrees with the reflecting surface. The angle of reflection is
solution: The normal is perpendicular to the mirror surface. A ray making 30 degrees with the surface makes 90 - 30 = 60 degrees with the normal, so the angle of incidence is 60 degrees. By the law of reflection the angle of reflection is also 60 degrees.
formula_principle: Law of reflection: angle of incidence equals angle of reflection, both measured from the normal
common_misconception: Students quote the angle measured from the mirror surface as the angle of incidence.

concept_tested: A plane mirror forms a virtual image as far behind the mirror as the object is in front
stem: A small bulb is kept 40 cm in front of a plane mirror. The distance between the bulb and its image is
solution: The image lies 40 cm behind the mirror. The object is 40 cm in front. The two are on opposite sides of the mirror, so the separation is 40 + 40 = 80 cm.
formula_principle: For a plane mirror, image distance behind the mirror equals object distance in front
common_misconception: Students report the mirror to image distance instead of the object to image distance.

concept_tested: When an object approaches a fixed plane mirror with speed v, the image approaches the object with speed 2v
stem: A boy walks straight towards a fixed vertical plane mirror at 2 m s^-1. The speed with which his image approaches him is
solution: The mirror is at rest, so v_image = -v_object with respect to the mirror. The boy moves towards the mirror at 2 m s^-1 and the image moves towards the mirror at 2 m s^-1 from the other side. Their approach speed is 2 + 2 = 4 m s^-1.
formula_principle: Image position x_i = 2x_mirror - x_object, so v_image = 2v_mirror - v_object
common_misconception: Students forget that both the object and its image move, so the closing speed is double.

subtopic: Minimum size of a plane mirror
concept_tested: A plane mirror of half the height of a person is enough to show the full image, whatever the distance
stem: A person 1.8 m tall wishes to see his complete image in a fixed vertical plane mirror on a wall. The smallest vertical length of mirror that will do this is
solution: Rays from the top of the head and from the feet reach the eye after reflection at points midway in height between the eye and those extremes. The mirror therefore needs to span only half the height of the person, that is 1.8 / 2 = 0.9 m. The result does not depend on how far the person stands.
formula_principle: Minimum mirror length for full view equals half the height of the object
common_misconception: Students think a taller person needs a taller mirror in direct proportion, or that the distance from the mirror matters.

concept_tested: Number of images for two inclined plane mirrors from 360 divided by the angle between them
stem: Two plane mirrors are inclined to each other at 45 degrees. The number of images of a small object placed between them is
solution: Here 360 / 45 = 8, which is an even integer. For an even value of n the number of images is n - 1 = 7, whatever the position of the object between the mirrors.
formula_principle: If n = 360 / theta is an even integer, the number of images is n - 1
common_misconception: Students quote 360 divided by the angle itself as the number of images.

concept_tested: Working backwards from the number of images to the angle between two plane mirrors
stem: A small object placed between two inclined plane mirrors produces exactly 5 images. The angle between the mirrors is
solution: Five images require n - 1 = 5, so n = 6. Then theta = 360 / 6 = 60 degrees. A check confirms 360 / 60 = 6 is even, so the rule n - 1 applies and gives 5 images.
formula_principle: Number of images = n - 1 with n = 360 / theta when n is an even integer
common_misconception: Students set 360 divided by the angle equal to the number of images and get 72 degrees.

concept_tested: Rotating a plane mirror through an angle turns the reflected ray through twice that angle
stem: A ray of light falls on a plane mirror and is reflected. Keeping the incident ray fixed, the mirror is rotated through 10 degrees about an axis lying in the mirror and perpendicular to the plane of incidence. The reflected ray turns through
solution: When the mirror turns by 10 degrees the normal also turns by 10 degrees, so the angle of incidence changes by 10 degrees. The reflected ray is measured on the other side of the normal, so its direction changes by 10 degrees from the change in angle plus 10 degrees from the turning of the normal, a total of 20 degrees.
formula_principle: For a fixed incident ray, a mirror rotation of theta rotates the reflected ray by 2 theta
common_misconception: Students assume the reflected ray simply follows the mirror through the same angle.

concept_tested: Lateral inversion is a left to right reversal along the direction perpendicular to the mirror, not a vertical flip
stem: Consider the two statements about the image formed by a plane mirror. Statement P: the image is always virtual and of the same size as the object. Statement Q: lateral inversion means the image appears upside down. Which of the following is true
option_a: Both P and Q are correct
option_b: P is wrong and Q is correct
option_c: P is correct and Q is wrong
option_d: Both P and Q are wrong
correct_answer_text: P is correct and Q is wrong
solution: A plane mirror always gives a virtual erect image of the same size as the object, so P is correct. Lateral inversion is a reversal of the front to back direction which appears as a left to right exchange; the image stays erect and is not turned upside down, so Q is wrong.
formula_principle: Plane mirror image: virtual, erect, same size, laterally inverted
common_misconception: Students describe lateral inversion as an inversion of the image top to bottom.

concept_tested: Two mirrors at right angles send a ray back parallel to itself after two reflections
stem: Two plane mirrors are fixed at right angles to each other. A ray of light in the plane perpendicular to both mirrors strikes one mirror, reflects, then strikes the second mirror and reflects again. The final emergent ray is
option_a: parallel to the original incident ray and travelling in the same direction
option_b: perpendicular to the original incident ray
option_c: along the bisector of the angle between the mirrors
option_d: antiparallel to the original incident ray
correct_answer_text: antiparallel to the original incident ray
solution: With theta = 90 degrees the total deviation is 360 - 180 = 180 degrees. A deviation of 180 degrees means the emergent ray travels back exactly opposite to the incident ray, that is antiparallel to it. This is the principle of a corner reflector.
formula_principle: Total deviation after two reflections from mirrors inclined at theta is 360 - 2 theta
common_misconception: Students assume the two reflections cancel and return a ray travelling in the original direction.

concept_tested: Deviation produced by a single plane mirror is 180 degrees minus twice the angle of incidence
stem: A ray of light is incident on a plane mirror at an angle of incidence of 25 degrees. The angle through which the ray is deviated by the mirror is
solution: The deviation is the angle between the original direction of travel and the final direction. With i = 25 degrees, delta = 180 - 2 x 25 = 180 - 50 = 130 degrees.
formula_principle: Deviation delta = 180 degrees - 2i for reflection at a plane surface
common_misconception: Students report the angle between the incident and reflected rays rather than the deviation from the original path.

subtopic: Minimum size and position of a mirror
concept_tested: The position of the mirror strip is fixed by the midpoints between the eye and the extreme points of the object
stem: A man of height 180 cm has his eyes 10 cm below the top of his head. He wants to see his full image in a vertical plane mirror fixed on a wall. The lower edge of the shortest such mirror must be at a height above the floor of
solution: The eyes are at 180 - 10 = 170 cm above the floor. A ray from the feet reaches the eye after reflecting at a point midway in height between the feet and the eye, that is at 170 / 2 = 85 cm above the floor. So the lower edge of the mirror must be at 85 cm. The upper edge lies midway between the eye and the top of the head, at 175 cm, giving a mirror length of 175 - 85 = 90 cm as expected.
formula_principle: Lower edge height = (height of eye above floor) / 2; mirror length = half the height of the person
common_misconception: Students place the lower edge at half the total height, forgetting that the eye is not at the top of the head.

concept_tested: The angle between the incident ray and the ray emerging after reflection at both of two inclined mirrors is twice the mirror angle
stem: Two plane mirrors are inclined at 70 degrees. A ray of light in the plane perpendicular to both suffers one reflection at each mirror. The angle between the original incident ray and the finally emergent ray is
solution: The net deviation is 360 - 2 x 70 = 220 degrees. Turning through 220 degrees in one sense is the same as turning through 360 - 220 = 140 degrees in the other, so the angle between the incident and emergent rays is 140 degrees, which equals 2 x 70. A useful check is the right angle case, where 2 x 90 = 180 degrees gives the antiparallel ray.
formula_principle: Total deviation after two reflections from mirrors inclined at theta is 360 - 2 theta, equivalent to an angle 2 theta between incident and emergent rays
common_misconception: Students think the answer depends on the angle of incidence at the first mirror; it does not.

subtopic: Images when 360 over the angle is not an integer
concept_tested: When 360 divided by the mirror angle is not a whole number, the number of images is the integer part
stem: Two plane mirrors are inclined at 50 degrees to each other. The number of images of a point object placed between them is
solution: Here 360 / 50 = 7.2, which is not a whole number. In that case the standard result is that the number of images equals the integer part of the ratio, that is 7. The rule of subtracting one applies only when 360 / theta comes out an even integer.
formula_principle: If 360 / theta is not an integer, the number of images equals the integer part of 360 / theta
common_misconception: Students apply the n - 1 rule blindly even when 360 divided by the angle is not a whole number.

subtopic: Image velocity with a moving mirror
concept_tested: Image position is twice the mirror position minus the object position, so image velocity is 2v_mirror - v_object
stem: A plane mirror faces a man and both move along the same straight line normal to the mirror. With respect to the ground the man moves towards the mirror at 2 m s^-1 while the mirror moves away from him at 1 m s^-1 along the same direction. The speed of the man's image with respect to the ground is
solution: Take the direction of the man's motion as positive. Then v_object = +2 m s^-1 and v_mirror = +1 m s^-1. Differentiating x_image = 2x_mirror - x_object gives v_image = 2(1) - 2 = 0. The image is momentarily at rest with respect to the ground, even though both the man and the mirror are moving. Relative to the man the image still approaches at 2 m s^-1.
formula_principle: x_image = 2 x_mirror - x_object, hence v_image = 2 v_mirror - v_object
common_misconception: Students automatically double the object speed and forget that a moving mirror contributes twice its own velocity.

subtopic: Focal length and radius of curvature
concept_tested: For a spherical mirror of small aperture the focal length is half the radius of curvature
stem: A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 30 cm. Its focal length is
solution: For a spherical mirror of small aperture f = R / 2. With R = 30 cm the focal length is 30 / 2 = 15 cm. The negative sign in the Cartesian convention for a concave mirror concerns direction only; the magnitude is 15 cm.
formula_principle: f = R / 2 for a spherical mirror
common_misconception: Students take the focal length equal to the radius of curvature, as for refraction at a single surface.

subtopic: Nature of the image in a convex mirror
concept_tested: A convex mirror gives a virtual, erect and diminished image for every real object position
stem: For every position of a real object in front of a convex mirror, the image formed is
option_d: real, inverted and of the same size
solution: The reflected rays from a convex mirror always diverge, so they can only appear to come from a point behind the mirror. That image is virtual and erect, and it always lies between the pole and the focus, so it is smaller than the object.
formula_principle: A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image between the pole and the focus
common_misconception: Students expect a convex mirror to behave like a concave mirror for distant objects and give a real image.

concept_tested: Applying the mirror formula with the Cartesian sign convention for an object beyond the centre of curvature
stem: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Using the Cartesian sign convention, the image is formed at a distance from the mirror of
option_b: 15 cm in front of the mirror
option_c: 7.5 cm in front of the mirror
option_d: 60 cm in front of the mirror
correct_answer_text: 15 cm in front of the mirror
solution: With the Cartesian convention u = -30 cm and f = -10 cm. Then 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = -1/10 + 1/30 = (-3 + 1)/30 = -2/30, so v = -15 cm. The negative value means the image is real and lies 15 cm in front of the mirror.
formula_principle: Mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f with u and f negative for a concave mirror and a real object
common_misconception: Students drop the sign convention and obtain a positive image distance for a real image.

subtopic: Object at the centre of curvature
concept_tested: For a concave mirror an object at the centre of curvature gives an image at the centre of curvature
stem: An object is placed at the centre of curvature of a concave mirror. The image formed is
option_a: real, inverted, magnified and beyond the centre of curvature
option_b: virtual, erect, magnified and behind the mirror
option_c: real, inverted, diminished and at the focus
option_d: real, inverted, of the same size and at the centre of curvature
correct_answer_text: real, inverted, of the same size and at the centre of curvature
solution: Putting u = -R and f = -R/2 in 1/v + 1/u = 1/f gives 1/v = -2/R + 1/R = -1/R, so v = -R. The image is real and also at the centre of curvature, and m = -v/u = -1, so it is inverted and of the same size.
formula_principle: For u = R the mirror formula gives v = R and magnification m = -1
common_misconception: Students confuse the centre of curvature with the focus and expect the image at the focus.

concept_tested: Rays from a point object at the focus of a concave mirror emerge parallel to the axis
stem: A point source of light is placed at the principal focus of a concave mirror. After reflection the rays
option_a: converge to the centre of curvature
option_b: diverge as if coming from the pole
option_c: travel parallel to the principal axis
option_d: converge to a point midway between the focus and the pole
correct_answer_text: travel parallel to the principal axis
solution: By the reversibility of light rays, since a parallel beam converges to the focus, a source at the focus sends out a beam that is parallel to the principal axis after reflection. Formally u = f gives 1/v = 1/f - 1/f = 0, so v is infinite.
formula_principle: Object at focus gives image at infinity, the reverse of the definition of the focus
common_misconception: Students think a source at the focus produces a sharply focused image somewhere near the mirror.

concept_tested: Applying the mirror formula to a convex mirror with a positive focal length
stem: An object is placed 30 cm from a convex mirror whose radius of curvature is 30 cm. The image is formed
option_a: 10 cm in front of the mirror
solution: For the convex mirror f = +R/2 = +15 cm and u = -30 cm. Then 1/v = 1/15 + 1/30 = (2 + 1)/30 = 3/30 = 1/10, so v = +10 cm. A positive v means the image is virtual and lies 10 cm behind the mirror.
formula_principle: f = R / 2 = +15 cm for a convex mirror; 1/v + 1/u = 1/f
common_misconception: Students give the focal length of a convex mirror a negative sign and end up with a real image.

subtopic: Virtual image from a concave mirror
concept_tested: A concave mirror forms an erect magnified virtual image only when the object lies inside the focus
stem: A concave mirror of focal length 20 cm forms an erect image twice the size of the object. The object distance from the mirror is
solution: An erect image from a concave mirror must be virtual, so m = +2 gives -v/u = 2, that is v = -2u. With u = -x, v = +2x. Substituting in 1/v + 1/u = 1/f gives 1/(2x) - 1/x = -1/20, that is -1/(2x) = -1/20, so 2x = 20 and x = 10 cm. The object lies 10 cm from the mirror, inside the focus, as required for a virtual image.
formula_principle: m = -v/u = +2 for an erect image, combined with 1/v + 1/u = 1/f
common_misconception: Students use m = +2 with the real image relation v = 2u and place the object outside the focus.

concept_tested: Sign of the magnification tells whether the image is erect or inverted
stem: An object is placed 20 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. The magnification produced is
solution: With u = -20 cm and f = -15 cm, 1/v = -1/15 + 1/20 = (-4 + 3)/60 = -1/60, so v = -60 cm. Then m = -v/u = -(-60)/(-20) = -3. The image is real, inverted and three times the size of the object.
formula_principle: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f followed by m = -v/u
common_misconception: Students forget the minus sign in m = -v/u for a mirror and report a positive magnification for a real image.

concept_tested: All distances are measured from the pole, positive along the direction of the incident light
stem: In the Cartesian sign convention used for spherical mirrors, which of the following is always true for a real object placed in front of the mirror
option_a: the object distance u is positive
option_b: the focal length of a concave mirror is positive
option_c: the object distance u is negative
option_d: the image distance v of a real image is positive
correct_answer_text: the object distance u is negative
solution: Distances are measured from the pole and taken positive in the direction in which the incident light travels. A real object always lies on the side from which light comes, so u is always negative. A concave mirror has its focus in front of it, so f is negative, and a real image also forms in front, so v is negative.
formula_principle: Distances measured against the direction of incident light are negative; heights above the axis are positive
common_misconception: Students apply the convention only to some quantities and leave others with their arithmetical magnitudes.

subtopic: Convex mirror as a rear view mirror
concept_tested: A convex mirror gives an erect diminished image and therefore a wide field of view
stem: A convex mirror rather than a plane mirror is preferred as a rear view mirror in vehicles mainly because
option_a: it always gives an erect image and covers a much wider field of view
option_b: it gives a magnified image so that distant vehicles look nearer
option_c: it forms a real image on the retina directly without any inversion
option_d: it has a longer focal length so the image is formed farther away
correct_answer_text: it always gives an erect image and covers a much wider field of view
solution: Because the image is diminished, a large region behind the vehicle is compressed into the small mirror, giving a wide field of view. The image is also always erect, which makes it easy to interpret. The cost is that objects appear smaller and therefore farther away than they really are.
formula_principle: Convex mirror: virtual, erect, diminished image lying between the pole and the focus
common_misconception: Students believe a convex mirror is used because it magnifies approaching vehicles.

concept_tested: The mirror formula can be used in reverse to find the focal length and hence the radius of curvature
stem: A concave mirror forms a real image 20 cm from the mirror when the object is 60 cm from it. The radius of curvature of the mirror is
solution: Both object and image are in front of the mirror, so u = -60 cm and v = -20 cm. Then 1/f = -1/20 - 1/60 = (-3 - 1)/60 = -4/60 = -1/15, giving f = -15 cm. The radius of curvature is R = 2f, of magnitude 30 cm.
formula_principle: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f and R = 2f
common_misconception: Students stop at the focal length and forget that the question asks for the radius of curvature.

subtopic: Object between the pole and the focus
concept_tested: Object inside the focus of a concave mirror gives an enlarged erect virtual image behind the mirror
