stem: A small object is placed between the pole and the principal focus of a concave mirror. Compared with the object, the image is
option_a: inverted, magnified and formed in front of the mirror
option_b: erect, magnified and formed behind the mirror
option_c: erect, diminished and formed behind the mirror
option_d: inverted, of the same size and formed at the centre of curvature
correct_answer_text: erect, magnified and formed behind the mirror
solution: Take f = -20 cm and u = -10 cm as an example. Then 1/v = -1/20 + 1/10 = 1/20, so v = +20 cm, behind the mirror, and m = -v/u = -20/(-10) = +2. The image is virtual, erect and magnified. This is the shaving mirror or make up mirror arrangement.
formula_principle: For a concave mirror with |u| < |f| the image is virtual, erect and magnified
common_misconception: Students assume a concave mirror can only give real inverted images.

concept_tested: The mirror formula written as 1/v = -1/u + 1/f is the equation of a straight line
stem: For a concave mirror a graph is plotted with 1/v on the vertical axis and 1/u on the horizontal axis. The graph is a straight line whose
option_a: slope is -1 and whose intercept on either axis has magnitude 1/f
option_b: slope is +1 and whose intercept on either axis has magnitude 1/f
option_c: slope is -1 and whose intercept on either axis has magnitude f
option_d: slope is -1/f and which passes through the origin
correct_answer_text: slope is -1 and whose intercept on either axis has magnitude 1/f
solution: Writing the mirror formula as 1/v = -(1/u) + 1/f shows a straight line of slope -1 with vertical intercept 1/f. By symmetry the intercept on the horizontal axis also has magnitude 1/f. Reading either intercept gives the focal length at once.
formula_principle: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f rearranges to 1/v = -(1/u) + 1/f
common_misconception: Students expect the slope to depend on the focal length and read the intercept directly as f.

subtopic: Image size in a convex mirror
concept_tested: Linear magnification relates image height to object height through m = -v/u
stem: An object 6 cm tall is placed 15 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 10 cm. The height of the image is
solution: For the convex mirror f = +10 cm and u = -15 cm, so 1/v = 1/10 + 1/15 = (3 + 2)/30 = 5/30 = 1/6, giving v = +6 cm. Then m = -v/u = -6/(-15) = +0.4. The image height is 0.4 x 6 = 2.4 cm, erect and diminished.
formula_principle: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, then m = -v/u and h_image = m x h_object
common_misconception: Students invert the magnification ratio and obtain an image larger than the object.

subtopic: Mirror focal length and the surrounding medium
concept_tested: Reflection does not involve the refractive index, so the focal length of a mirror is independent of the medium
stem: A concave mirror of focal length 20 cm in air is completely immersed in water of refractive index 4/3. Its focal length in water becomes
solution: The focal length of a spherical mirror is fixed by f = R / 2, which contains only the radius of curvature. Reflection obeys the same law whatever the medium, so immersing the mirror in water leaves the focal length at 20 cm. Only the brightness of the reflected beam changes.
formula_principle: f = R / 2 depends only on the geometry of the mirror, not on the refractive index
common_misconception: Students transfer the lens result, where the focal length grows in water, to a mirror.

subtopic: Diminished real image from a concave mirror
concept_tested: A diminished image from a concave mirror must be real and inverted, so the magnification is negative
stem: A concave mirror of focal length 20 cm produces an image half the size of the object. The distance of the object from the mirror is
solution: A concave mirror can only diminish an image when that image is real and inverted, so m = -1/2. Then -v/u = -1/2 gives v = u/2. With u = -x this means v = -x/2. Substituting, 1/v + 1/u = -2/x - 1/x = -3/x = -1/20, so x = 60 cm. Check: u = -60 gives v = -30 and m = -(-30)/(-60) = -0.5.
formula_principle: m = -v/u with m = -1/2 for a diminished real image, together with 1/v + 1/u = 1/f
common_misconception: Students take m = +1/2 and obtain an object position that a concave mirror cannot in fact use.

concept_tested: When the object lies inside the focus of a concave mirror the image distance comes out positive
stem: An object is placed 20 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 30 cm. The image is
option_a: virtual, erect and 60 cm behind the mirror
option_b: real, inverted and 60 cm in front of the mirror
option_c: virtual, erect and 12 cm behind the mirror
option_d: real, inverted and 12 cm in front of the mirror
correct_answer_text: virtual, erect and 60 cm behind the mirror
solution: Here u = -20 cm and f = -30 cm, so 1/v = -1/30 + 1/20 = (-2 + 3)/60 = 1/60 and v = +60 cm. The positive sign shows the image is virtual and lies 60 cm behind the mirror. The magnification is m = -v/u = -60/(-20) = +3, so the image is erect and three times as large.
formula_principle: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f with |u| < |f| gives v positive, meaning a virtual image
common_misconception: Students assume a concave mirror can never give a positive image distance and force a negative answer.

concept_tested: Object and image distances measured from the focus satisfy the product relation x_object x_image = f squared
stem: An object is placed on the axis of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm at a point 10 cm beyond the focus, on the side away from the mirror. The image is formed at a distance from the pole of
solution: The object is 20 + 10 = 30 cm from the pole. Using the mirror formula with u = -30 cm and f = -20 cm, 1/v = -1/20 + 1/30 = (-3 + 2)/60 = -1/60 and v = -60 cm, so the image is 60 cm in front of the pole. The same result follows from x_object x_image = f^2, since 10 x x_image = 400 gives x_image = 40 cm from the focus, that is 40 + 20 = 60 cm from the pole.
formula_principle: Newton relation x_object x_image = f^2, with distances measured from the focus
common_misconception: Students mix distances measured from the focus with distances measured from the pole.

subtopic: Speed of the image along the axis
concept_tested: For motion along the principal axis the image speed is m squared times the object speed
stem: An object moves along the principal axis towards a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm with a speed of 1 cm s^-1. At the instant the object is 15 cm from the mirror, the speed of its image is
solution: With u = -15 cm and f = -10 cm, 1/v = -1/10 + 1/15 = (-3 + 2)/30 = -1/30, so v = -30 cm. Differentiating the mirror formula gives dv/du = -v^2/u^2 = -(30/15)^2 = -4. Hence the image speed is 4 times the object speed, that is 4 cm s^-1, and the minus sign shows the image moves away from the mirror as the object approaches.
formula_principle: Differentiating 1/v + 1/u = 1/f gives dv/du = -v^2/u^2 = -m^2
common_misconception: Students use the linear magnification for axial motion instead of the square of the magnification.

subtopic: Convex mirror with a given magnification
concept_tested: Working back from magnification to object distance for a convex mirror
stem: A convex mirror of radius of curvature 40 cm forms an image one fifth the size of the object. The object distance from the mirror is
solution: The image in a convex mirror is erect, so m = +1/5. With u = -x, m = -v/u gives v = x/5. Then 1/v + 1/u = 5/x - 1/x = 4/x = 1/f = 1/20, so x = 80 cm. Check: u = -80 gives 1/v = 1/20 + 1/80 = 5/80, v = 16 cm and m = -16/(-80) = 0.2.
formula_principle: f = R/2 = +20 cm for a convex mirror; m = -v/u = +1/5 with 1/v + 1/u = 1/f
common_misconception: Students use the focal length as negative for a convex mirror and get an impossible object position.

concept_tested: Every part of a mirror forms a complete image; blocking part of it only reduces the light collected
stem: The lower half of a concave mirror is covered with an opaque black paint. An object is kept in front of it so that a real image is formed on a screen. The image now
option_a: is complete but less bright than before
option_b: shows only the upper half of the object
option_c: shows only the lower half of the object
correct_answer_text: is complete but less bright than before
solution: Light from each point of the object spreads over the whole aperture of the mirror. The uncovered upper half still receives rays from every point of the object and brings each set to its own image point, so the full image is formed. Only half as much light is now collected, so the image is dimmer.
formula_principle: Rays from every point of the object reach the whole mirror, so any part of the mirror can form the full image
common_misconception: Students think each half of the mirror is responsible for the corresponding half of the image.

concept_tested: For a convex mirror the image is confined to the region between the pole and the focus
stem: As a real object is moved from a very large distance right up to the pole of a convex mirror, the image always lies
option_a: between the focus and the centre of curvature, behind the mirror
option_b: between the pole and the centre of curvature, in front of the mirror
option_c: beyond the centre of curvature, behind the mirror
option_d: between the pole and the focus, behind the mirror
correct_answer_text: between the pole and the focus, behind the mirror
solution: Put u = -x with x positive in 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = 1/f + 1/x. As x tends to infinity, v tends to f, so a very distant object gives an image at the focus. As x tends to zero, v tends to zero, so an object touching the mirror gives an image at the pole. In between the image always lies between the pole and the focus, virtual, erect and diminished.
formula_principle: For a convex mirror, u from minus infinity to 0 gives v from f to 0
common_misconception: Students expect a convex mirror image to move out to the centre of curvature as the object approaches.

concept_tested: Output of the first mirror serves as the object for the second mirror
stem: A concave mirror of focal length 20 cm and a convex mirror of focal length 20 cm face each other with their poles 100 cm apart on a common axis. A point object is placed on the axis 40 cm from the concave mirror. Light reflects first at the concave mirror and then at the convex mirror. The final image lies
option_a: 15 cm in front of the convex mirror
option_c: 40 cm in front of the convex mirror
solution: At the concave mirror u = -40 cm and f = -20 cm, so 1/v = -1/20 + 1/40 = -1/40 and v = -40 cm. The intermediate image is 40 cm in front of the concave mirror, and therefore 100 - 40 = 60 cm in front of the convex mirror. For the convex mirror u = -60 cm and f = +20 cm, so 1/v = 1/20 + 1/60 = (3 + 1)/60 = 1/15 and v = +15 cm. The final image is virtual and lies 15 cm behind the convex mirror.
formula_principle: Apply 1/v + 1/u = 1/f twice, treating the first image as the object for the second mirror
common_misconception: Students measure the intermediate image distance from the wrong mirror when setting up the second step.

subtopic: Image of an object lying along the axis
concept_tested: An object lying along the axis is imaged by treating its two ends separately
stem: A thin rod 10 cm long lies along the principal axis of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm, with its nearer end 20 cm and its farther end 30 cm from the pole. The length of the image of the rod is
solution: For the nearer end u = -20 cm gives 1/v = -1/15 + 1/20 = (-4 + 3)/60 = -1/60, so v = -60 cm. For the farther end u = -30 cm gives 1/v = -1/15 + 1/30 = (-2 + 1)/30 = -1/30, so v = -30 cm. The image therefore stretches from 30 cm to 60 cm in front of the mirror, a length of 60 - 30 = 30 cm.
formula_principle: Apply 1/v + 1/u = 1/f to each end separately; the axial image length is the difference of the image distances
common_misconception: Students multiply the rod length by the transverse magnification, which is valid only for objects perpendicular to the axis.

subtopic: Refractive index and speed of light
concept_tested: Absolute refractive index is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to that in the medium
stem: The refractive index of a glass is 1.5. Taking the speed of light in vacuum as 3 x 10^8 m s^-1, the speed of light in this glass is
solution: From mu = c / v we get v = c / mu = (3 x 10^8) / 1.5 = 2 x 10^8 m s^-1. Light always travels more slowly in a medium of refractive index greater than one.
formula_principle: mu = c / v, so v = c / mu
common_misconception: Students multiply the vacuum speed by the refractive index and get a speed larger than c.

concept_tested: Light entering a denser medium bends towards the normal
stem: A ray of light travelling in air is incident obliquely on the flat surface of water of refractive index 4/3. Compared with the angle of incidence, the angle of refraction is
option_a: larger, the ray bending away from the normal
option_b: equal, the ray continuing without any bending
option_c: smaller, the ray bending towards the normal
option_d: smaller, the ray bending away from the normal
correct_answer_text: smaller, the ray bending towards the normal
solution: Snell law gives sin i / sin r = mu_water / mu_air = 4/3, which is greater than one. Hence sin r is less than sin i and r is less than i. A smaller angle with the normal means the ray has bent towards the normal on entering the denser medium.
formula_principle: Snell law: mu_1 sin i = mu_2 sin r, so a larger refractive index gives a smaller angle
common_misconception: Students remember that the ray bends but not the direction, and reverse it for a denser medium.

concept_tested: Real depth divided by apparent depth equals the refractive index of the liquid
stem: A swimming pool is filled with water of refractive index 4/3 to a depth of 4 m. Seen from directly above, the bottom appears to be at a depth of
solution: Apparent depth = real depth / mu = 4 / (4/3) = 4 x 3/4 = 3 m. The bottom appears raised by 4 - 3 = 1 m, which is why pools always look shallower than they are.
formula_principle: mu = real depth / apparent depth
common_misconception: Students multiply by the refractive index and conclude that the pool looks deeper.

concept_tested: Frequency is set by the source and does not change on refraction; speed and wavelength do change
stem: When a beam of monochromatic light passes from air into glass, the quantity that remains unchanged is its
solution: The number of wave crests arriving per second at the boundary equals the number leaving it, so the frequency is the same in both media. Since v = f lambda and v falls to c/mu inside the glass, the wavelength must also fall to lambda/mu.
formula_principle: v = f lambda with f fixed by the source, so lambda changes in the same ratio as v
common_misconception: Students think the wavelength is a property of the source and that the frequency changes instead.

concept_tested: Refractive index from a measured pair of incidence and refraction angles
stem: A ray of light passes from air into a transparent medium. The angle of incidence is 45 degrees and the angle of refraction is 30 degrees. The refractive index of the medium is
solution: mu = sin 45 / sin 30 = 0.7071 / 0.5 = 1.414, that is the square root of 2. To one decimal place this is 1.4.
formula_principle: mu = sin i / sin r for light entering a medium from air
common_misconception: Students take the ratio sin r / sin i and obtain a refractive index less than one.

concept_tested: A parallel slab raises the apparent position of an object by t times one minus one over mu
stem: A mark on a sheet of paper is viewed from directly above through a glass slab 6 cm thick of refractive index 1.5. The mark appears to be raised by
solution: The shift is t(1 - 1/mu) = 6(1 - 1/1.5) = 6(1 - 2/3) = 6 x 1/3 = 2 cm. Equivalently the slab of real thickness 6 cm looks only 6/1.5 = 4 cm thick, so the mark rises by 6 - 4 = 2 cm.
formula_principle: Normal shift = t (1 - 1/mu)
common_misconception: Students report the apparent thickness of the slab as the shift.

concept_tested: Lateral shift depends on thickness, angle of incidence and refractive index
stem: A ray of light strikes a glass slab of thickness 6 cm at an angle of incidence of 60 degrees. The refractive index of the glass is the square root of 3. The lateral shift of the emergent ray is
solution: Snell law gives sin r = sin 60 / sqrt(3) = (0.866)/(1.732) = 0.5, so r = 30 degrees. The lateral shift is t sin(i - r)/cos r = 6 x sin 30 / cos 30 = 6 x 0.5 / 0.866 = 3.46 cm, which is 2 times the square root of 3 centimetres.
formula_principle: sin i = mu sin r, then lateral shift = t sin(i - r) / cos r
common_misconception: Students forget the factor 1/cos r and simply multiply the thickness by sin(i - r).

subtopic: Emergent ray from a parallel slab
concept_tested: The two refractions at parallel faces of a slab are equal and opposite in their bending
stem: A ray of light passes obliquely through a glass slab with plane parallel faces and emerges into air. The emergent ray is
option_a: parallel to the incident ray with no sideways shift
option_b: inclined to the incident ray by twice the angle of refraction
option_c: parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways
option_d: inclined to the incident ray by the angle of deviation at the first face
correct_answer_text: parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways
solution: At the first face sin i = mu sin r and at the second face mu sin r = sin e, so sin e = sin i and e = i. The emergent ray is therefore parallel to the incident ray. It is however displaced sideways by the lateral shift t sin(i - r)/cos r.
formula_principle: For plane parallel faces the angle of emergence equals the angle of incidence
common_misconception: Students expect a net deviation, forgetting that the two parallel faces bend the ray in opposite senses.

concept_tested: Relative refractive index of one medium with respect to another is the ratio of their absolute values
stem: The absolute refractive indices of glass and water are 3/2 and 4/3 respectively. The refractive index of glass with respect to water is
solution: The refractive index of glass with respect to water is mu_glass / mu_water = (3/2) / (4/3) = (3/2) x (3/4) = 9/8 = 1.125. It exceeds one, confirming that glass is optically denser than water.
formula_principle: Refractive index of medium 2 with respect to medium 1 is mu_2 / mu_1
common_misconception: Students invert the ratio and quote a value less than one for the denser medium.

concept_tested: Each layer contributes its own thickness divided by its own refractive index
stem: A tank contains a layer of water 8 cm deep of refractive index 4/3, over which floats a layer of oil 6 cm deep of refractive index 1.5. Seen from directly above, the bottom of the tank appears at a depth below the oil surface of
solution: Apparent depth = 8/(4/3) + 6/1.5 = 6 + 4 = 10 cm. Each layer is separately reduced by its own refractive index and the two apparent depths are then added.
formula_principle: Apparent depth = sum over layers of t_i / mu_i for near normal viewing
common_misconception: Students use a single average refractive index for the whole column of liquid.

concept_tested: Wavelength in a medium is the vacuum wavelength divided by the refractive index
stem: Light of wavelength 600 nm in vacuum enters a medium of refractive index 1.5. Its wavelength in the medium is
solution: The frequency stays the same, so lambda_medium / lambda_vacuum = v / c = 1/mu. Hence lambda_medium = 600 / 1.5 = 400 nm. The light still appears the same colour to the eye because colour is set by frequency.
formula_principle: lambda_medium = lambda_vacuum / mu, since frequency is unchanged and v = c / mu
common_misconception: Students apply the change to the frequency instead of the wavelength.

concept_tested: The apparent rise of an object under a liquid fixes the real depth once mu is known
stem: A coin lying at the bottom of a beaker appears to be raised by 3 cm when the beaker is filled with water of refractive index 4/3. The depth of the water is
solution: The rise is h(1 - 1/mu) = h(1 - 3/4) = h/4. Setting h/4 = 3 cm gives h = 12 cm. As a check the apparent depth is 12/(4/3) = 9 cm, which is 3 cm less than the real depth.
formula_principle: Apparent rise = h (1 - 1/mu)
common_misconception: Students set the apparent depth itself equal to the given shift.

concept_tested: The general form of Snell law applies when neither medium is air
stem: A ray of light travels from water of refractive index 4/3 into glass of refractive index 3/2. If the angle of incidence in water is 30 degrees, the sine of the angle of refraction in the glass is
solution: Snell law gives (4/3) sin 30 = (3/2) sin r, so (4/3)(1/2) = (3/2) sin r, that is 2/3 = (3/2) sin r and sin r = (2/3)(2/3) = 4/9. Since 4/9 is less than 1/2, the ray bends towards the normal, as expected on entering the denser medium.
formula_principle: mu_1 sin i = mu_2 sin r
common_misconception: Students write sin i / sin r = mu_1 / mu_2 instead of mu_2 / mu_1.

concept_tested: The distance a microscope must be raised equals the normal shift produced by the liquid
stem: A microscope is focused on a mark at the bottom of an empty beaker. Water of refractive index 4/3 is poured in to a depth of 8 cm and the microscope has to be raised to refocus. The water is then poured out and replaced by the same depth of a liquid of refractive index 1.6. Compared with the water setting, the microscope must now be raised further by
solution: With water the shift is 8(1 - 3/4) = 8 x 0.25 = 2 cm. With the new liquid the shift is 8(1 - 1/1.6) = 8(1 - 0.625) = 8 x 0.375 = 3 cm. The microscope was already raised by 2 cm, so it must be raised a further 3 - 2 = 1 cm.
formula_principle: Normal shift = t (1 - 1/mu); the extra raising is the difference of the two shifts
common_misconception: Students quote the total shift for the second liquid instead of the additional movement required.

concept_tested: The number of waves in a given path equals the path length divided by the wavelength in that medium
stem: Light of wavelength 600 nm in air travels through a 6 cm thickness of a medium of refractive index 1.5. The number of complete waves contained in this path is
solution: Inside the medium the wavelength is 600/1.5 = 400 nm = 4 x 10^-7 m. The path is 6 cm = 6 x 10^-2 m. The number of waves is (6 x 10^-2)/(4 x 10^-7) = 1.5 x 10^5. Equivalently the optical path is mu x 6 cm = 9 cm and dividing that by the air wavelength gives the same count.
formula_principle: lambda_medium = lambda_air / mu; number of waves = path length / lambda_medium
common_misconception: Students use the air wavelength inside the medium and undercount the waves.

concept_tested: As the angle of incidence approaches ninety degrees the lateral shift tends to the slab thickness
stem: A ray of light passes through a glass slab of thickness t. As the angle of incidence is increased towards grazing incidence, the lateral shift of the emergent ray tends to a maximum value equal to
solution: As i tends to 90 degrees the refraction angle r tends to the critical angle C, where sin C = 1/mu. The shift becomes t sin(90 - C)/cos C = t cos C / cos C = t. So however large the refractive index, the sideways displacement can never exceed the thickness of the slab.
formula_principle: Lateral shift = t sin(i - r)/cos r, evaluated as i tends to 90 degrees
common_misconception: Students assume a very dense slab can shift the ray by more than its own thickness.

concept_tested: Light takes longer to cross a slab than to cross the same length of vacuum
stem: A slab of transparent material of thickness 3 m has refractive index 1.5. Taking the speed of light in vacuum as 3 x 10^8 m s^-1, the extra time taken by light to cross the slab compared with crossing the same 3 m in vacuum is
solution: In vacuum the time is t/c = 3/(3 x 10^8) = 1 x 10^-8 s. Inside the slab the speed is c/mu, so the time is mu t/c = 1.5 x 10^-8 s. The extra time is (mu - 1)t/c = 0.5 x 3/(3 x 10^8) = 5 x 10^-9 s.
formula_principle: Time in medium = mu t / c; extra time = (mu - 1) t / c
common_misconception: Students report the total transit time in the slab instead of the increase over the vacuum time.

concept_tested: Intermediate refractive indices cancel out when the final medium is the same as the first
stem: A ray of light in air passes normally through the sides of a stack of three slabs of different transparent materials whose faces are all parallel, and finally emerges into air again. If the ray enters the stack at 40 degrees to the normal, it leaves the stack at
option_a: an angle that depends on the largest of the three refractive indices
option_c: an angle that depends on the order in which the slabs are stacked
option_d: an angle equal to the refraction angle inside the last slab
solution: For parallel boundaries the product mu sin theta is the same in every layer. Since the first and last media are both air with mu = 1, sin(emergent angle) = sin(incident angle), so the emergent angle is 40 degrees. Only the total sideways displacement depends on the individual thicknesses and indices.
formula_principle: mu_1 sin theta_1 = mu_2 sin theta_2 = mu_3 sin theta_3 = ... is constant across parallel boundaries
common_misconception: Students try to apply Snell law slab by slab and think the emergent angle depends on the intermediate materials.

subtopic: Slab in front of a plane mirror
concept_tested: A slab shifts the effective object position towards the mirror by the normal shift
stem: A point object is 30 cm in front of a plane mirror. A glass slab of thickness 6 cm and refractive index 1.5 is placed between the object and the mirror with its faces parallel to the mirror. The image formed by the mirror now lies behind the mirror at a distance of
solution: The slab shifts the apparent position of the object towards the mirror by t(1 - 1/mu) = 6(1 - 2/3) = 2 cm. As seen by the mirror the object is therefore effectively at 30 - 2 = 28 cm. A plane mirror places the image as far behind as the object is in front, so the image is 28 cm behind the mirror.
formula_principle: Normal shift = t (1 - 1/mu); the mirror images the shifted object with equal distances
common_misconception: Students forget the slab entirely, or shift the object away from the mirror instead of towards it.

subtopic: Apparent depth of two equal layers
concept_tested: Apparent depths of separate layers simply add for near normal viewing
stem: A vessel of depth 2d is filled to half its depth with a liquid of refractive index mu_1 and the upper half with an immiscible liquid of refractive index mu_2. Viewed from directly above, the apparent depth of the bottom of the vessel is
solution: Each layer of real thickness d contributes an apparent thickness d/mu. The total apparent depth is d/mu_1 + d/mu_2 = d(mu_2 + mu_1)/(mu_1 mu_2). As a check, putting mu_1 = mu_2 = mu gives 2d/mu, the standard single liquid result.
formula_principle: Apparent depth = sum of t_i / mu_i over the layers
common_misconception: Students define an effective refractive index as the average of the two and divide the total depth by it.

concept_tested: Critical angle for a medium and air satisfies sin C = 1 / mu
stem: A transparent medium has refractive index 2 with respect to air. Its critical angle for the medium to air boundary is
solution: sin C = 1/mu = 1/2, so C = 30 degrees. Any ray inside the medium striking the boundary at more than 30 degrees to the normal is totally internally reflected.
formula_principle: sin C = 1 / mu for a denser medium in contact with air
common_misconception: Students use cos C = 1/mu or take the critical angle as the refraction angle in the rarer medium.

concept_tested: Total internal reflection needs a denser to rarer passage and an angle greater than the critical angle
stem: Total internal reflection can take place only when light travels
option_a: from a rarer medium to a denser medium at an angle greater than the critical angle
option_b: from a denser medium to a rarer medium at an angle smaller than the critical angle
option_c: from a denser medium to a rarer medium at an angle greater than the critical angle
option_d: from a rarer medium to a denser medium at exactly the critical angle
correct_answer_text: from a denser medium to a rarer medium at an angle greater than the critical angle
solution: Going from denser to rarer the refracted ray bends away from the normal. At the critical angle the refracted ray grazes the surface, and beyond it Snell law would require a sine greater than one, so no refracted ray exists and all the light is reflected back into the denser medium.
formula_principle: Denser to rarer passage plus angle of incidence greater than the critical angle
common_misconception: Students remember only the angle condition and forget that the light must start in the denser medium.

concept_tested: Compare the angle of incidence inside the denser medium with the critical angle
stem: A ray of light travelling inside a glass block strikes the glass to air surface at 60 degrees to the normal. The critical angle for this glass and air is 42 degrees. At the surface the light is
option_a: completely refracted out into the air along the surface
option_b: partly reflected and partly refracted out into the air
option_c: completely reflected back into the glass
option_d: refracted out into the air at 42 degrees to the normal
correct_answer_text: completely reflected back into the glass
solution: The angle of incidence, 60 degrees, is greater than the critical angle of 42 degrees, and the light is going from the denser glass to the rarer air. Both conditions for total internal reflection are met, so none of the light emerges and all of it is reflected back into the glass.
formula_principle: Total internal reflection when the angle of incidence in the denser medium exceeds the critical angle
common_misconception: Students think some light always leaks out even beyond the critical angle.

concept_tested: Light is guided along an optical fibre by repeated total internal reflection at the core cladding boundary
stem: Light is transmitted over long distances along a thin optical fibre mainly because of
option_a: repeated ordinary reflection from a silvered coating on the outside of the fibre
option_b: repeated total internal reflection at the boundary between the core and the cladding
option_c: continuous refraction that keeps bending the ray back towards the axis of the fibre
option_d: dispersion of the light into its component colours inside the core
correct_answer_text: repeated total internal reflection at the boundary between the core and the cladding
solution: The core has a slightly larger refractive index than the cladding, so rays that meet the boundary at more than the critical angle are totally internally reflected. Because total internal reflection returns all the energy, the light can bounce thousands of times with very little loss.
formula_principle: Core of higher refractive index surrounded by cladding of lower refractive index gives total internal reflection
common_misconception: Students attribute fibre transmission to a reflecting metal coating rather than to total internal reflection.

concept_tested: Air layers of different temperature have different refractive indices, allowing total internal reflection
stem: On a hot day a distant patch of road appears wet and reflects the sky. This mirage arises because
option_a: air near the hot road is optically denser, so light from the sky is totally internally reflected upwards
option_b: air near the hot road is optically rarer, so light from the sky is totally internally reflected upwards
option_c: water vapour on the road surface reflects the sky like a mirror
option_d: the hot road emits its own light which is mistaken for the reflected sky
correct_answer_text: air near the hot road is optically rarer, so light from the sky is totally internally reflected upwards
solution: Air close to the hot road expands, becomes less dense and so has a smaller refractive index. A ray from the sky travelling downwards passes from denser upper layers into rarer lower layers, bending steadily away from the vertical until it meets a layer at more than the critical angle. It is then totally internally reflected and curves back up to the eye, which traces it back to a point on the road.
formula_principle: sin C = mu_rarer / mu_denser applied to layers of air with a temperature gradient
common_misconception: Students say the hot air near the ground is denser, which would bend the light the other way.

concept_tested: The denser the medium, the smaller its critical angle with air
stem: The refractive indices of water, crown glass, dense flint glass and diamond are 1.33, 1.50, 1.65 and 2.42 respectively. The medium among them with the smallest critical angle for a boundary with air is
solution: Since sin C = 1/mu, a larger refractive index gives a smaller sine and hence a smaller critical angle. Diamond has the largest index, 2.42, so sin C = 0.413 and C is about 24 degrees, the smallest of the four. Water gives about 49 degrees, crown glass about 42 degrees and dense flint glass about 37 degrees.
formula_principle: sin C = 1 / mu, so C decreases as mu increases
common_misconception: Students assume a denser medium must have a larger critical angle because the index is larger.

concept_tested: A very small critical angle traps light inside a cut diamond through many total internal reflections
stem: A cut diamond sparkles brilliantly chiefly because
option_a: its critical angle is very large, so almost all the light that enters escapes at the first face it meets
option_b: its critical angle is very small, so light entering it undergoes many total internal reflections before emerging
option_c: it absorbs light strongly and re-emits it in all directions
option_d: its surfaces are coated with a thin reflecting metallic film
correct_answer_text: its critical angle is very small, so light entering it undergoes many total internal reflections before emerging
solution: For diamond sin C = 1/2.42 = 0.413, so C is about 24 degrees. Almost any ray inside the stone therefore meets a face at more than the critical angle and is totally internally reflected. The faces are cut so that the light finally leaves through the top, concentrating the brilliance where it is seen.
formula_principle: sin C = 1/mu with mu about 2.42 gives C about 24 degrees
common_misconception: Students believe the sparkle comes from strong ordinary reflection at the polished surfaces.

subtopic: Ray inside water striking the surface
concept_tested: Comparing an angle of incidence in water with the water to air critical angle
stem: A ray of light inside water of refractive index 4/3 strikes the water to air surface at 50 degrees to the normal. Given that the critical angle for water is about 48.6 degrees, the ray
option_a: emerges into the air bending towards the normal
option_b: undergoes total internal reflection and stays inside the water
option_c: emerges into the air at 48.6 degrees to the normal
option_d: grazes exactly along the water surface as it emerges
correct_answer_text: undergoes total internal reflection and stays inside the water
solution: The critical angle satisfies sin C = 3/4, giving C about 48.6 degrees. Since 50 degrees is greater than 48.6 degrees and the light is going from the denser water to the rarer air, total internal reflection occurs and no light emerges at that point.
formula_principle: Compare i with C where sin C = 1/mu = 3/4
common_misconception: Students assume that a difference of only a degree or two beyond the critical angle still lets some light through.

subtopic: Critical angle for two dense media
concept_tested: For a boundary between two media the critical angle satisfies sin C = mu_rarer / mu_denser
stem: The refractive indices of glass and water are 3/2 and 4/3 respectively. For a ray travelling inside the glass and meeting a glass to water boundary, the sine of the critical angle is
solution: Here the denser medium is glass and the rarer is water, so sin C = mu_water / mu_glass = (4/3)/(3/2) = (4/3)(2/3) = 8/9 = 0.889. The critical angle is about 62.7 degrees, larger than the 41.8 degrees for glass and air, because water is closer in density to glass than air is.
formula_principle: sin C = mu_rarer / mu_denser
common_misconception: Students always use 1/mu for the critical angle even when the second medium is not air.

subtopic: Speed of light from the critical angle
concept_tested: The critical angle gives the refractive index, which then gives the speed of light in the medium
stem: The critical angle of a certain transparent medium with respect to air is 30 degrees. Taking the speed of light in vacuum as 3 x 10^8 m s^-1, the speed of light inside this medium is
solution: From sin 30 = 1/mu we get 1/2 = 1/mu, so mu = 2. Then v = c/mu = (3 x 10^8)/2 = 1.5 x 10^8 m s^-1.
formula_principle: sin C = 1/mu, then v = c / mu
common_misconception: Students take the refractive index as the sine of the critical angle rather than its reciprocal.

subtopic: Why total internal reflection is total
concept_tested: Total internal reflection returns the whole of the incident energy, unlike reflection at a metal mirror
stem: Compared with reflection at a good metal mirror, total internal reflection at a glass to air boundary
option_a: returns a smaller fraction of the light because some is always refracted out
option_b: returns light only for angles of incidence smaller than the critical angle
option_c: returns essentially the whole of the incident light energy
option_d: changes the frequency of the reflected light slightly
correct_answer_text: returns essentially the whole of the incident light energy
solution: Above the critical angle Snell law admits no real refracted ray, so no energy is carried away into the rarer medium and the reflection is complete. A metal mirror always absorbs a few per cent at each reflection. This is why totally reflecting prisms are preferred to mirrors in periscopes and binoculars.
formula_principle: Beyond the critical angle no refracted ray exists, so reflection carries all the energy
common_misconception: Students think some light must always leak through any boundary.

concept_tested: An observer under water sees the whole outside world within a cone whose half angle is the critical angle
stem: A fish under still water of refractive index 4/3 looks upwards. The entire world above the water surface appears to it compressed into a cone whose half angle is about
solution: Light arriving at the surface from just above the horizon enters the water at the critical angle, since sin C = 1/mu = 3/4 gives C about 48.6 degrees. Light from directly overhead enters along the vertical. Everything above the water therefore reaches the fish within a cone of half angle about 49 degrees, and outside that cone the fish sees only the totally internally reflected image of the bottom.
formula_principle: Rays from the whole hemisphere above refract into a cone of half angle C, where sin C = 1/mu
common_misconception: Students expect the outside world to fill the whole upper hemisphere as it would in air.

subtopic: Light patch on a liquid surface
concept_tested: Light from a submerged point source escapes only through a circle of radius h tan C
stem: A small lamp lies at the bottom of a tank of liquid of refractive index 5/3, at a depth of 4 m below the surface. Light escapes from the surface only through a circular patch of radius
solution: sin C = 1/mu = 3/5, so cos C = 4/5 and tan C = 3/4. The radius is R = h tan C = 4 x 3/4 = 3 m. Rays meeting the surface further out than this strike it beyond the critical angle and are totally internally reflected back into the liquid.
formula_principle: Radius R = h tan C with sin C = 1 / mu
common_misconception: Students use R = h sin C, forgetting that the horizontal distance involves the tangent.

concept_tested: A right angled isosceles glass prism turns a beam through ninety degrees by total internal reflection
stem: A glass prism of refractive index 1.5 has angles of 45, 45 and 90 degrees. A beam of light enters normally through one of the shorter faces and meets the hypotenuse. The beam is
option_a: totally internally reflected at the hypotenuse and turned through 90 degrees
option_b: refracted out through the hypotenuse with a small deviation
option_c: totally internally reflected at the hypotenuse and turned through 180 degrees
option_d: split into a reflected part and a refracted part of comparable brightness
correct_answer_text: totally internally reflected at the hypotenuse and turned through 90 degrees
solution: Entering normally, the beam is undeviated and meets the hypotenuse at 45 degrees to its normal. The critical angle is given by sin C = 1/1.5 = 0.667, so C is about 41.8 degrees. Since 45 degrees is greater than 41.8 degrees, total internal reflection occurs. A single reflection at a surface inclined at 45 degrees to the beam turns it through 90 degrees.
formula_principle: sin C = 1/1.5 gives C about 41.8 degrees, which is less than the 45 degree angle of incidence
common_misconception: Students compare 45 degrees with the prism angle rather than with the critical angle of the glass.

subtopic: Effect of covering a surface with water
concept_tested: Replacing air by water above a glass surface raises the critical angle
stem: A ray inside a glass block of refractive index 3/2 meets the top surface. When the surface is in contact with air the critical angle is about 42 degrees. If a layer of water of refractive index 4/3 is poured on top, the critical angle at the glass surface
option_b: stays at about 42 degrees since the glass is unchanged
option_d: increases to about 90 degrees so that no ray can be totally reflected
solution: With air above, sin C = 1/(3/2) = 0.667 and C is about 42 degrees. With water above, sin C = (4/3)/(3/2) = 8/9 = 0.889 and C is about 62.7 degrees. Bringing the two refractive indices closer together makes it harder to trap the light, so a larger angle of incidence is now needed for total internal reflection.
formula_principle: sin C = mu_rarer / mu_denser
common_misconception: Students hold the critical angle fixed as a property of the glass alone.

subtopic: Refractive index from the escaping patch
concept_tested: The radius of the illuminated circle and the depth together determine the critical angle
stem: A point source of light lies 3 m below the surface of a still liquid. Light emerges from the surface only within a circle of radius 4 m centred vertically above the source. The refractive index of the liquid is
solution: From the geometry tan C = R/h = 4/3, so the right angled triangle with sides 3 and 4 has hypotenuse 5 and sin C = 4/5 = 0.8. Then mu = 1/sin C = 1/0.8 = 1.25.
formula_principle: R = h tan C and sin C = 1 / mu
common_misconception: Students set sin C equal to R/h instead of tan C, and so obtain the wrong refractive index.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
concept_tested: The thin lens formula 1/v - 1/u = 1/f with the Cartesian sign convention
stem: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a thin convex lens of focal length 20 cm. Using the Cartesian sign convention, the image is formed at
option_a: 60 cm on the far side of the lens
option_b: 12 cm on the far side of the lens
option_c: 60 cm on the same side as the object
option_d: 10 cm on the far side of the lens
correct_answer_text: 60 cm on the far side of the lens
solution: With u = -30 cm and f = +20 cm, 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/20 - 1/30 = (3 - 2)/60 = 1/60, so v = +60 cm. The positive value means a real image 60 cm beyond the lens.
formula_principle: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f with u negative for a real object
common_misconception: Students use the mirror formula, with a plus sign between the reciprocals, for a lens.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
concept_tested: Power is the reciprocal of the focal length expressed in metres, measured in dioptre
stem: A thin convex lens has a focal length of 20 cm. Its power is
solution: Convert the focal length to metres first: f = 20 cm = 0.20 m. Then P = 1/f = 1/0.20 = 5 D. The power is positive because the lens is converging.
formula_principle: P = 1 / f with f in metres; the unit of power is the dioptre
common_misconception: Students forget to convert centimetres to metres and quote a power that is a hundred times too small.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
subtopic: Nature of the image in a concave lens
concept_tested: A concave lens gives a virtual, erect, diminished image for every real object position
stem: For every position of a real object, a thin concave lens forms an image which is
option_c: real, erect and of the same size
solution: A concave lens always diverges the rays, so they can only appear to come from a point on the object side. The image is therefore virtual and erect, and it always lies between the lens and the focus, making it smaller than the object.
formula_principle: For a concave lens with u negative and f negative, v is always negative with |v| < |u|
common_misconception: Students expect a concave lens to give a real image when the object is far away.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
concept_tested: A negative power identifies a diverging lens and fixes the magnitude of its focal length
stem: The power of a certain thin lens is -4 D. The lens is
option_a: converging with a focal length of 25 cm
option_b: diverging with a focal length of 4 cm
option_c: diverging with a focal length of 25 cm
option_d: diverging with a focal length of 40 cm
correct_answer_text: diverging with a focal length of 25 cm
solution: f = 1/P = 1/(-4) = -0.25 m = -25 cm. The negative sign shows that the lens is concave and diverging, and the magnitude of the focal length is 25 cm.
formula_principle: P = 1/f in metres; a negative power means a concave, diverging lens
common_misconception: Students treat the numerical value of the power as a focal length in centimetres.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
concept_tested: Powers of thin lenses in contact simply add
stem: A converging lens of power +5 D is placed in contact with a diverging lens of power -2 D. The power of the combination is
solution: The powers add algebraically: P = 5 + (-2) = +3 D. The combination therefore behaves as a converging lens of focal length 1/3 m, about 33.3 cm.
formula_principle: For thin lenses in contact P = P_1 + P_2, equivalently 1/F = 1/f_1 + 1/f_2
common_misconception: Students add the magnitudes of the two powers without regard to sign.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
concept_tested: Lens maker formula relates focal length to the refractive index and the two radii
stem: An equiconvex lens is made of glass of refractive index 1.5, each surface having a radius of curvature of 20 cm. The focal length of the lens in air is
solution: For an equiconvex lens R_1 = +20 cm and R_2 = -20 cm. Then 1/f = (1.5 - 1)(1/20 - 1/(-20)) = 0.5 x (2/20) = 1/20, so f = 20 cm.
common_misconception: Students take both radii as positive and lose the doubling that comes from the two curved surfaces.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
subtopic: Object at twice the focal length
concept_tested: A convex lens with the object at twice the focal length gives an image of the same size
stem: An object is placed at a distance of twice the focal length from a thin convex lens. The image formed is
option_a: real, inverted, of the same size and at twice the focal length on the other side
option_b: real, inverted, magnified and beyond twice the focal length on the other side
option_c: virtual, erect, magnified and on the same side as the object
option_d: real, inverted, diminished and at the focus on the other side
correct_answer_text: real, inverted, of the same size and at twice the focal length on the other side
solution: Putting u = -2f in 1/v = 1/f + 1/u gives 1/v = 1/f - 1/(2f) = 1/(2f), so v = 2f. The magnification is m = v/u = 2f/(-2f) = -1, so the image is real, inverted and of the same size. This is the arrangement used in a one to one copying camera.
formula_principle: u = -2f gives v = +2f and m = v/u = -1
common_misconception: Students confuse the focus with twice the focal length and place the image at f.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
subtopic: Object inside the focus of a convex lens
concept_tested: A convex lens with the object inside the focus acts as a magnifying glass
stem: An object is placed 10 cm from a thin convex lens of focal length 15 cm. The image is
option_a: real, inverted and 30 cm from the lens on the far side
option_b: virtual, erect and 6 cm from the lens on the same side as the object
option_c: real, inverted and 6 cm from the lens on the far side
option_d: virtual, erect and 30 cm from the lens on the same side as the object
correct_answer_text: virtual, erect and 30 cm from the lens on the same side as the object
solution: With u = -10 cm and f = +15 cm, 1/v = 1/15 - 1/10 = (2 - 3)/30 = -1/30, so v = -30 cm. The image is virtual and lies 30 cm from the lens on the same side as the object. Its magnification is m = v/u = -30/(-10) = +3, so it is erect and three times as large.
formula_principle: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f with |u| < f gives a negative v, that is a virtual image
common_misconception: Students assume a convex lens always produces a real image on the opposite side.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
concept_tested: Applying the lens formula to a diverging lens with a negative focal length
stem: An object is placed 30 cm from a thin concave lens of focal length 20 cm. The magnification produced is
solution: With u = -30 cm and f = -20 cm, 1/v = -1/20 - 1/30 = (-3 - 2)/60 = -1/12, so v = -12 cm. Then m = v/u = -12/(-30) = +0.4. The image is virtual, erect and 0.4 times the size of the object.
formula_principle: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f with f negative for a concave lens; m = v/u
common_misconception: Students give the focal length of a concave lens a positive sign and get a real image.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
concept_tested: One flat face contributes nothing to the power of a lens
stem: A plano-convex lens is made of glass of refractive index 1.5, the curved surface having a radius of curvature of 10 cm. The focal length of the lens in air is
solution: Taking the curved face first, R_1 = +10 cm and R_2 is infinite so 1/R_2 = 0. Then 1/f = (1.5 - 1)(1/10 - 0) = 0.5/10 = 1/20, giving f = 20 cm. The flat face has no curvature and so contributes no power.
formula_principle: 1/f = (mu - 1)(1/R_1 - 1/R_2) with one radius infinite
common_misconception: Students set the flat surface radius to zero rather than to infinity.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
concept_tested: Focal length of a combination from the reciprocal addition rule
stem: Two thin convex lenses of focal lengths 10 cm and 15 cm are placed in contact along a common axis. The focal length of the combination is
solution: 1/F = 1/10 + 1/15 = (3 + 2)/30 = 5/30 = 1/6, so F = 6 cm. The combination is more strongly converging than either lens alone, as expected when two positive powers add.
formula_principle: 1/F = 1/f_1 + 1/f_2 for thin lenses in contact
common_misconception: Students add the focal lengths directly, as though the lenses were in series like resistors.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
subtopic: Converging and diverging lenses in contact
concept_tested: Adding a diverging lens reduces the power of the combination
stem: A thin convex lens of focal length 20 cm is placed in contact with a thin concave lens of focal length 25 cm. The combination behaves as a single lens of focal length
solution: The convex lens has P_1 = 1/0.20 = +5 D and the concave lens has P_2 = 1/(-0.25) = -4 D. The combination has P = 5 - 4 = +1 D, so F = 1/1 = 1 m = 100 cm. A positive power means the combination converges.
formula_principle: P = P_1 + P_2 with P = 1/f in metres
common_misconception: Students treat the focal length of the concave lens as positive and get a much shorter combined focal length.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
subtopic: Refraction at a single spherical surface
concept_tested: The relation mu_2 / v - mu_1 / u = (mu_2 - mu_1) / R applies at one curved boundary
stem: A point object in air lies on the axis 30 cm from the convex end of a long glass rod of refractive index 1.5 whose end face has a radius of curvature of 10 cm. Measured from that face, the image inside the glass is formed at
solution: Take mu_1 = 1, mu_2 = 1.5, u = -30 cm and R = +10 cm. Then 1.5/v - 1/(-30) = (1.5 - 1)/10, that is 1.5/v + 0.0333 = 0.05, so 1.5/v = 0.01667 and v = 90 cm. The image lies 90 cm inside the glass, on the far side of the surface.
formula_principle: mu_2 / v - mu_1 / u = (mu_2 - mu_1) / R
common_misconception: Students use the thin lens formula for a single refracting surface and omit the refractive indices.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
concept_tested: For a real image the object to screen distance is the sum of the two magnitudes
stem: A thin convex lens of focal length 20 cm throws a real inverted image twice the size of the object onto a screen. The distance between the object and the screen is
solution: For a real inverted image twice the size, m = v/u = -2. With u = -x this gives v = 2x. Substituting in the lens formula, 1/(2x) - 1/(-x) = 1/20, that is 1/(2x) + 1/x = 3/(2x) = 1/20, so x = 30 cm and v = 60 cm. The object to screen distance is 30 + 60 = 90 cm.
formula_principle: m = v/u = -2 for a real inverted image of twice the size, with 1/v - 1/u = 1/f
common_misconception: Students give only the image distance and forget that the screen distance is measured from the object.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
concept_tested: Refractive index is larger for violet light, so the focal length is shorter for violet
stem: A thin convex lens is used with white light. Compared with the focal length for red light, the focal length of the same lens for violet light is
option_a: shorter, because the refractive index is larger for violet
option_b: longer, because the refractive index is larger for violet
option_c: the same, because the focal length depends only on the radii of curvature
option_d: shorter, because the wavelength of violet light is longer than that of red light
correct_answer_text: shorter, because the refractive index is larger for violet
solution: In the lens maker formula the power is proportional to mu minus one. Since mu is larger for violet than for red, the power is greater for violet and the focal length correspondingly shorter. The two focal points therefore separate, which is chromatic aberration along the axis.
formula_principle: 1/f = (mu - 1)(1/R_1 - 1/R_2), with mu larger for shorter wavelengths
common_misconception: Students think the focal length is fixed by the shape of the lens alone and does not depend on colour.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
subtopic: Parallel beam at an angle to the axis
concept_tested: A parallel beam converges to a point in the focal plane, off the axis if the beam is tilted
stem: A parallel beam of light falls on a thin convex lens of focal length 20 cm, making a small angle of 0.02 radian with the principal axis. The beam is brought to a focus at a point in the focal plane at a distance from the axis of
solution: All rays of a parallel beam meet at one point in the focal plane. The chief ray through the optical centre is undeviated, so it fixes the image point at a distance f tan theta from the axis, which for small theta is f theta = 20 x 0.02 = 0.4 cm.
formula_principle: A parallel beam at angle theta focuses in the focal plane at a distance f theta from the axis for small theta
common_misconception: Students think a tilted parallel beam still focuses at the principal focus on the axis.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
subtopic: Finding an unknown lens in a combination
concept_tested: The power of an unknown lens follows by subtraction when the combination power is known
stem: A converging lens of power 4 D is placed in contact with a diverging lens. The combination has a power of -1 D. The focal length of the diverging lens is
solution: P_2 = P - P_1 = (-1) - (4) = -5 D. Hence f_2 = 1/(-5) = -0.20 m, so the diverging lens has a focal length of magnitude 20 cm.
formula_principle: P = P_1 + P_2 for thin lenses in contact
common_misconception: Students subtract the powers the wrong way round and obtain a lens that is far too weak.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
concept_tested: The power of a glass lens falls sharply when it is immersed in water
stem: A thin glass lens of refractive index 1.5 has a focal length of 10 cm in air. When it is completely immersed in water of refractive index 4/3, its focal length becomes
solution: Write the bracket of radii as K. In air 1/f_air = (1.5 - 1)K = 0.5K. In water 1/f_water = (1.5/(4/3) - 1)K = (1.125 - 1)K = 0.125K. Dividing, f_water/f_air = 0.5/0.125 = 4, so f_water = 4 x 10 = 40 cm. The lens becomes four times weaker because glass and water differ far less than glass and air.
formula_principle: 1/f = (mu_lens/mu_medium - 1)(1/R_1 - 1/R_2)
common_misconception: Students divide or multiply the air focal length by the water index instead of using the ratio of the two brackets.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
concept_tested: Two lens positions between a fixed object and screen give sharp images
stem: An object and a screen are fixed 100 cm apart. A thin convex lens placed between them forms a sharp image on the screen for two positions of the lens which are 20 cm apart. The focal length of the lens is
solution: Here D = 100 cm and d = 20 cm, so f = (100^2 - 20^2)/(4 x 100) = (10000 - 400)/400 = 9600/400 = 24 cm. Note that the two positions exist only when D is at least four times the focal length, which is satisfied since 4f = 96 cm is less than 100 cm.
formula_principle: f = (D^2 - d^2) / (4D) where D is the object to screen distance and d the separation of the two positions
common_misconception: Students use f = D/4, which holds only in the special case when the two positions coincide.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
concept_tested: When the separation equals the sum of the focal lengths a parallel beam emerges parallel
stem: Two thin convex lenses of focal lengths 20 cm and 30 cm are mounted coaxially with their centres 50 cm apart. A parallel beam of light is incident along the axis on the 20 cm lens. The beam finally emerges
option_a: converging to a point 30 cm beyond the second lens
option_b: converging to a point 20 cm beyond the second lens
option_c: diverging as if from a point 50 cm before the second lens
option_d: as a parallel beam travelling along the principal axis
correct_answer_text: as a parallel beam travelling along the principal axis
solution: The parallel beam converges to the focus of the first lens, 20 cm beyond it. That point is 50 - 20 = 30 cm before the second lens, that is exactly at its focus, so u = -30 cm and f = +30 cm give 1/v = 1/30 - 1/30 = 0 and v is infinite. The emergent beam is therefore parallel. This is the telescopic or afocal arrangement used in a refracting telescope.
formula_principle: Apply 1/v - 1/u = 1/f twice, using the first image as the object for the second lens
common_misconception: Students apply the contact formula 1/F = 1/f_1 + 1/f_2 even though the lenses are 50 cm apart.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
subtopic: Lens in a medium of the same index
concept_tested: A lens loses all its power when the surrounding medium matches the lens material
stem: A thin convex lens made of glass of refractive index 1.5 is immersed in a liquid whose refractive index is also 1.5. The lens then behaves as
option_a: a converging lens of unchanged focal length
option_b: a diverging lens of the same focal length magnitude
option_c: a converging lens of half the original power
option_d: a plane sheet of glass with zero power
correct_answer_text: a plane sheet of glass with zero power
solution: The bracket mu_lens/mu_medium - 1 becomes 1.5/1.5 - 1 = 0, so 1/f = 0 and the focal length is infinite. There is no refraction at either surface because there is no change of refractive index, so the lens simply becomes invisible and passes light straight through.
formula_principle: 1/f = (mu_lens/mu_medium - 1)(1/R_1 - 1/R_2)
common_misconception: Students believe a lens shape guarantees a focusing action whatever the surrounding medium.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
concept_tested: Object distance and image distance follow from the magnification and their sum
stem: An object and a screen are 100 cm apart. A convex lens between them forms a real image four times the size of the object on the screen. The focal length of the lens is
solution: A real image four times the size needs |v| = 4|u|. With |u| + |v| = 100 cm we get 5|u| = 100, so |u| = 20 cm and |v| = 80 cm. Then 1/f = 1/80 - 1/(-20) = 1/80 + 4/80 = 5/80 = 1/16, giving f = 16 cm.
formula_principle: |v| = 4|u| with |u| + |v| = 100 cm, then 1/v - 1/u = 1/f
common_misconception: Students split the 100 cm in the ratio one to four but then forget to apply the lens formula.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
concept_tested: Cutting a lens perpendicular to the axis leaves each half with a longer focal length
stem: An equiconvex lens of focal length 20 cm is cut into two identical plano-convex lenses by a plane perpendicular to the principal axis. The focal length of each half is
solution: The whole lens has 1/f = (mu - 1)(2/R), giving f = 20 cm. Each plano-convex half retains only one curved surface, so 1/f_half = (mu - 1)(1/R), which is half the original power. The focal length of each half is therefore 2 x 20 = 40 cm. Cutting along the axis instead would leave both curved surfaces intact and the focal length unchanged.
formula_principle: 1/f = (mu - 1)(1/R_1 - 1/R_2); removing one curved surface halves the power
common_misconception: Students assume that halving the lens must halve the focal length as well.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
subtopic: Size of the image of a distant object
concept_tested: The size of the image of a distant object equals the focal length times its angular size
stem: The Sun subtends an angle of 0.01 radian at the Earth. A thin convex lens of focal length 50 cm is used to form an image of the Sun on a screen. The diameter of the image is
solution: The Sun is effectively at infinity, so its image lies in the focal plane. Rays from the two edges pass undeviated through the optical centre and arrive at the focal plane separated by f x theta = 50 x 0.01 = 0.5 cm. Note that the image size depends only on the focal length and the angular size, not on the aperture of the lens.
formula_principle: Image size = f x angular size for a very distant object
common_misconception: Students think a larger lens gives a larger image of the Sun; a larger lens gives only a brighter one.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
subtopic: Glass sphere as a thick lens
concept_tested: Two successive refractions at the spherical surfaces of a solid sphere
stem: A parallel beam of light travelling along a diameter falls on a solid glass sphere of radius 10 cm and refractive index 1.5. Measured from the far surface of the sphere, the beam is brought to a focus at a distance of
solution: At the first surface mu_1 = 1, mu_2 = 1.5, u is infinite and R = +10 cm, so 1.5/v = 0.5/10 = 0.05 and v = 30 cm. This point lies 30 - 20 = 10 cm beyond the second surface, so it acts as a virtual object with u = +10 cm there. At the second surface mu_1 = 1.5, mu_2 = 1 and R = -10 cm, so 1/v - 1.5/10 = (1 - 1.5)/(-10) = 0.05, giving 1/v = 0.05 + 0.15 = 0.2 and v = 5 cm. The focus is 5 cm beyond the sphere.
formula_principle: mu_2 / v - mu_1 / u = (mu_2 - mu_1) / R applied at each surface in turn
common_misconception: Students measure the intermediate image from the wrong surface, or treat it as a real object for the second refraction.

major_topic: Refraction at a Spherical Surface and Lenses
concept_tested: A lens with one face silvered behaves as an equivalent mirror whose power is 2P_lens + P_mirror
stem: An equiconvex lens of glass of refractive index 1.5 has a focal length of 20 cm in air. One of its faces is silvered. The silvered lens now behaves as a mirror of focal length
option_a: 10 cm, converging like a concave mirror
option_b: 5 cm, converging like a concave mirror
option_c: 20 cm, converging like a concave mirror
option_d: 5 cm, diverging like a convex mirror
correct_answer_text: 5 cm, converging like a concave mirror
solution: For an equiconvex lens 1/f = (mu - 1)(2/R) gives 1/20 = 0.5 x 2/R = 1/R, so R = 20 cm. The silvered face acts as a mirror of focal length R/2 = 10 cm. Light crosses the lens, reflects and crosses the lens again, so the equivalent power is 1/F = 2/f_lens + 1/f_mirror = 2/20 + 1/10 = 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.2, giving F = 5 cm. The positive total power means it converges like a concave mirror.
formula_principle: Equivalent mirror power P = 2 P_lens + P_mirror, with P_mirror = 2/R for the silvered surface
common_misconception: Students count the passage through the lens only once, or use the radius rather than R/2 for the silvered surface.

concept_tested: For refraction through a prism, A + D = i + e
stem: A ray of light passes through a prism of refracting angle 60 degrees. The angle of incidence is 45 degrees and the angle of emergence is 55 degrees. The angle of deviation is
solution: Rearranging A + D = i + e gives D = i + e - A = 45 + 55 - 60 = 40 degrees.
formula_principle: A + D = i + e for a prism
common_misconception: Students add all three angles or forget to subtract the refracting angle of the prism.

concept_tested: Violet light has the largest refractive index in glass and so suffers the largest deviation
stem: A narrow beam of white light passes through a glass prism and forms a spectrum on a screen. The colour that is deviated most from the original direction is
solution: The refractive index of glass increases as the wavelength decreases, so violet, having the shortest visible wavelength, has the largest refractive index. Since deviation increases with refractive index, violet is deviated most and red least.
formula_principle: Deviation increases with refractive index, and mu is largest for the shortest wavelength
common_misconception: Students associate the largest deviation with the longest wavelength.

concept_tested: For a thin prism the deviation is (mu - 1) times the refracting angle
stem: A thin prism of refracting angle 5 degrees is made of glass of refractive index 1.5. The deviation produced by it is
solution: D = (mu - 1)A = (1.5 - 1) x 5 = 0.5 x 5 = 2.5 degrees. The relation holds only for small refracting angles and small angles of incidence, where the sines may be replaced by the angles themselves.
formula_principle: D = (mu - 1) A for a thin prism
common_misconception: Students use mu A instead of (mu - 1)A for a thin prism.

concept_tested: The prism formula relates mu to the refracting angle and the angle of minimum deviation
stem: A prism of refracting angle 60 degrees gives an angle of minimum deviation of 30 degrees. The refractive index of its material is
solution: mu = sin((60 + 30)/2) / sin(60/2) = sin 45 / sin 30 = 0.7071/0.5 = 1.414, that is the square root of 2.
formula_principle: mu = sin((A + D_min)/2) / sin(A/2)
common_misconception: Students divide the angles directly instead of dividing their sines.

concept_tested: At minimum deviation the passage of light through the prism is symmetric
stem: When a ray passes through a prism in the position of minimum deviation
option_a: the angle of incidence is zero and the ray enters along the normal to the first face
option_b: the angle of emergence is ninety degrees and the ray grazes the second face
option_c: the angle of incidence equals the angle of emergence and the ray inside runs parallel to the base
option_d: the angle of incidence equals the refracting angle of the prism
correct_answer_text: the angle of incidence equals the angle of emergence and the ray inside runs parallel to the base
solution: The deviation curve is symmetric in i and e, and its single minimum occurs where the two are equal. Then r_1 = r_2 = A/2 and the ray inside the prism is parallel to the base. This symmetric path is the one used in the standard prism formula.
formula_principle: At minimum deviation i = e and r_1 = r_2 = A/2
common_misconception: Students associate minimum deviation with normal incidence on the first face.

concept_tested: Angular dispersion for a thin prism is the difference in deviation between violet and red
stem: A thin prism of refracting angle 5 degrees has refractive indices 1.66 for violet and 1.62 for red light. The angular dispersion produced is
solution: Angular dispersion = (1.66 - 1.62) x 5 = 0.04 x 5 = 0.2 degrees. Individually the violet is deviated by 0.66 x 5 = 3.3 degrees and the red by 0.62 x 5 = 3.1 degrees, whose difference is 0.2 degrees.
formula_principle: Angular dispersion = (mu_violet - mu_red) A for a thin prism
common_misconception: Students report the difference in refractive index itself as an angle.

concept_tested: Dispersive power is the ratio of the angular dispersion to the mean deviation
stem: For a certain glass the refractive indices are 1.66 for violet, 1.64 for yellow and 1.62 for red. The dispersive power of this glass is
solution: omega = (1.66 - 1.62)/(1.64 - 1) = 0.04/0.64 = 0.0625. Dispersive power is a pure number depending only on the material, not on the refracting angle of the prism.
formula_principle: Dispersive power omega = (mu_violet - mu_red) / (mu_yellow - 1)
common_misconception: Students divide by mu_yellow rather than by mu_yellow minus one.

subtopic: Minimum deviation of a standard prism
concept_tested: Solving the prism formula for the angle of minimum deviation
stem: A prism of refracting angle 60 degrees is made of glass of refractive index 1.5. Its angle of minimum deviation is about
solution: From the prism formula sin((60 + D)/2) = mu sin 30 = 1.5 x 0.5 = 0.75. Hence (60 + D)/2 = 48.6 degrees, so 60 + D = 97.2 and D = 37.2 degrees, about 37 degrees.
formula_principle: mu = sin((A + D_min)/2) / sin(A/2)
common_misconception: Students stop at the half angle 48.6 degrees and quote it as the minimum deviation.

subtopic: Limit on the prism angle for emergence
concept_tested: Light can emerge from the second face only if the refracting angle is at most twice the critical angle
stem: For a prism made of a material of refractive index equal to the square root of 2, the largest refracting angle for which light entering the first face can still emerge from the second face is
solution: Inside the prism r_1 + r_2 = A. For the ray to emerge, r_2 must not exceed the critical angle C, and r_1 can never exceed C either. So A cannot exceed 2C. Here sin C = 1/sqrt(2) gives C = 45 degrees, so the limiting refracting angle is 2 x 45 = 90 degrees.
formula_principle: r_1 + r_2 = A with both angles at most C; hence emergence requires A less than or equal to 2C
common_misconception: Students compare the refracting angle with the critical angle instead of with twice the critical angle.

concept_tested: Two thin prisms placed oppositely can cancel the deviation while leaving some dispersion
stem: A thin prism of refracting angle 6 degrees made of glass of refractive index 1.5 is combined with a second thin prism of refractive index 1.6, placed with its refracting edge opposite to the first, so that the mean ray suffers no net deviation. The refracting angle of the second prism is
solution: The first prism deviates the mean ray by (1.5 - 1) x 6 = 3 degrees. For the second prism, placed oppositely, to cancel this we need (1.6 - 1) A_2 = 3, that is 0.6 A_2 = 3, so A_2 = 5 degrees. The two dispersive powers differ, so a spectrum is still produced even though the mean ray goes straight through.
formula_principle: For zero net deviation (mu_1 - 1) A_1 = (mu_2 - 1) A_2
common_misconception: Students equate the refracting angles or use the refractive indices instead of the mu minus one factors.

subtopic: Deviation as a function of angle of incidence
concept_tested: The deviation curve for a prism has a single minimum, so a given deviation above the minimum corresponds to two angles of incidence
stem: For a given prism the angle of deviation is plotted against the angle of incidence. For any value of the deviation that is greater than the minimum deviation, the number of angles of incidence that produce it is
solution: By the reversibility of light, a path with incidence i and emergence e can be traversed the other way with incidence e and emergence i, and both give the same deviation. Since i and e are different everywhere except at the minimum, each deviation above the minimum is produced by two distinct angles of incidence. Only at the minimum do the two merge into the single symmetric path with i = e.
formula_principle: A + D = i + e with the roles of i and e interchangeable, so the deviation curve is symmetric about its minimum
common_misconception: Students assume each angle of incidence and each deviation are in one to one correspondence.

concept_tested: An achromatic combination cancels the dispersion but leaves a net deviation
stem: A thin crown glass prism of refracting angle 6 degrees, refractive index 1.5 for the mean ray and dispersive power 0.02, is combined with a flint glass prism of dispersive power 0.04 placed with its refracting edge opposite. The combination is achromatic for the extreme colours. The net mean deviation produced is
solution: The crown prism deviates the mean ray by D_1 = (1.5 - 1) x 6 = 3 degrees. The achromatic condition omega_1 D_1 = omega_2 D_2 gives 0.02 x 3 = 0.04 x D_2, so D_2 = 1.5 degrees. Because the prisms are oppositely directed the deviations subtract, leaving a net mean deviation of 3 - 1.5 = 1.5 degrees with no net spread of colour.
formula_principle: Achromatic condition omega_1 D_1 = omega_2 D_2; net deviation = D_1 - D_2
common_misconception: Students confuse the achromatic condition with the direct vision condition and answer zero.

concept_tested: Magnifying power of a simple microscope with the image at the near point is 1 + D/f
stem: A simple microscope has a converging lens of focal length 5 cm. Taking the least distance of distinct vision as 25 cm, its magnifying power when the final image is formed at the near point is
formula_principle: M = 1 + D/f for a simple microscope with the image at the near point
common_misconception: Students omit the added one and quote the value appropriate to an image at infinity.

concept_tested: Magnifying power of a telescope in normal adjustment is the ratio of the focal lengths
stem: An astronomical telescope has an objective of focal length 100 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm. In normal adjustment its magnifying power is
solution: M = f_o / f_e = 100/5 = 20. A telescope needs a long focus objective and a short focus eyepiece for high magnification.
formula_principle: M = f_objective / f_eyepiece for a telescope in normal adjustment
common_misconception: Students invert the ratio, using the eyepiece focal length in the numerator.

concept_tested: In normal adjustment the tube length is the sum of the two focal lengths
stem: An astronomical telescope in normal adjustment has an objective of focal length 150 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm. The distance between the objective and the eyepiece is
solution: In normal adjustment the image formed by the objective lies at its focus, which must also be at the focus of the eyepiece so that the final image is at infinity. The separation is therefore f_o + f_e = 150 + 5 = 155 cm.
formula_principle: Tube length L = f_objective + f_eyepiece in normal adjustment
common_misconception: Students subtract the focal lengths, as would be right for a Galilean telescope with a concave eyepiece.

concept_tested: Total magnifying power is the product of the objective and eyepiece magnifications
stem: In a compound microscope the objective produces a linear magnification of 10 and the eyepiece has a focal length of 5 cm. If the final image is formed at the near point, 25 cm from the eye, the total magnifying power is
solution: The eyepiece acts as a simple microscope with M_e = 1 + D/f_e = 1 + 25/5 = 6. The total magnifying power is the product m_o x M_e = 10 x 6 = 60.
formula_principle: M = m_objective x (1 + D/f_eyepiece) for the final image at the near point
common_misconception: Students add the two magnifications instead of multiplying them.

concept_tested: Relaxed viewing with the image at infinity gives slightly less magnification than near point viewing
stem: A magnifying glass of focal length 5 cm is used with the least distance of distinct vision taken as 25 cm. Compared with the setting in which the final image is at the near point, the setting in which the final image is at infinity gives a magnifying power that is
option_b: smaller by a factor of D over f
solution: At the near point M = 1 + 25/5 = 6, while for the image at infinity M = 25/5 = 5. The difference is exactly one, and it is the same for any focal length because the two expressions differ only by the added one. The infinity setting is preferred for long observation because the eye is relaxed.
formula_principle: M = 1 + D/f at the near point and M = D/f for the image at infinity
common_misconception: Students think the relaxed setting must be the one that gives the larger magnification.

concept_tested: Magnifying power depends on the focal lengths while resolving power depends on the aperture
stem: For an astronomical telescope, which single change increases the resolving power without changing the magnifying power
option_a: increasing the focal length of the objective while keeping its diameter fixed
option_b: decreasing the focal length of the eyepiece while keeping the objective unchanged
option_c: increasing the separation between the objective and the eyepiece beyond normal adjustment
option_d: increasing the diameter of the objective while keeping both focal lengths fixed
correct_answer_text: increasing the diameter of the objective while keeping both focal lengths fixed
solution: The magnifying power depends only on the ratio of the two focal lengths, so keeping both fixed keeps it unchanged. The smallest angular separation that can be resolved is proportional to lambda divided by the aperture, so widening the objective lowers this limit and raises the resolving power. It also gathers more light, making faint objects visible.
formula_principle: Magnifying power = f_o / f_e; limit of resolution is proportional to lambda / D where D is the aperture
common_misconception: Students believe that magnifying an image more must automatically reveal finer detail.

subtopic: Limit of resolution of a telescope
concept_tested: Smallest resolvable angular separation is about 1.22 lambda divided by the aperture
stem: A telescope objective has a diameter of 12 cm and is used with light of wavelength 600 nm. Taking the limit of resolution as 1.22 times the wavelength divided by the aperture, the smallest angular separation it can resolve is about
solution: Convert to metres: lambda = 600 nm = 6 x 10^-7 m and D = 12 cm = 0.12 m. Then theta = 1.22 x (6 x 10^-7)/0.12 = (7.32 x 10^-7)/0.12 = 6.1 x 10^-6 radian. The resolving power is the reciprocal of this, about 1.6 x 10^5 per radian.
