formula_principle: Limit of resolution theta = 1.22 lambda / D, with lambda and D in the same units
common_misconception: Students mix centimetres and metres, or quote the reciprocal as the limit of resolution.

concept_tested: The objective magnification must be computed from the lens formula before combining with the eyepiece
stem: In a compound microscope the objective has a focal length of 2 cm and the object is placed 2.5 cm from it. The eyepiece has a focal length of 5 cm and the final image is formed at the near point, 25 cm from the eye. The magnifying power of the microscope is
solution: For the objective u = -2.5 cm and f = 2 cm, so 1/v = 1/2 - 1/2.5 = 0.5 - 0.4 = 0.1 and v = 10 cm. The objective magnification is m_o = v/u = 10/(-2.5) = -4, of magnitude 4. The eyepiece, with the final image at the near point, gives M_e = 1 + 25/5 = 6. The total magnifying power is 4 x 6 = 24.
formula_principle: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f for the objective, m_o = v/u, then M = |m_o| x (1 + D/f_e)
common_misconception: Students take the objective magnification as v/f or forget to add one in the eyepiece term.

concept_tested: Number of electronic charges in one coulomb
stem: The magnitude of the charge on one electron is 1.6 x 10^-19 C. A body carrying a charge of 1 C therefore carries a number of electronic charges equal to about
solution: n = q / e = 1 / (1.6 x 10^-19) = 0.625 x 10^19 = 6.25 x 10^18. So one coulomb corresponds to about 6.25 x 10^18 electronic charges.
formula_principle: q = n e, so n = q / e
common_misconception: Confusing the count n with the value of the elementary charge e itself.

concept_tested: Statement of the principle of quantisation
stem: The observation that the charge on any body is always an integral multiple of the elementary charge e is known as
solution: Charge exists only in packets of size e. Writing q = n e with n a positive or negative integer expresses exactly this, and the property is named quantisation of charge.
formula_principle: q = n e with n an integer and e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C
common_misconception: Mixing up the names of the three basic properties of charge.

concept_tested: Direction of electron transfer during rubbing
stem: A glass rod rubbed with a silk cloth is found to be positively charged. During the rubbing
option_a: electrons move from the silk cloth to the glass rod
option_b: protons move from the silk cloth to the glass rod
option_c: protons move from the glass rod to the silk cloth
option_d: electrons move from the glass rod to the silk cloth
correct_answer_text: electrons move from the glass rod to the silk cloth
solution: Only the loosely bound electrons can be transferred by rubbing. The glass rod ends up positive, so it must have lost electrons, that is electrons went from the glass to the silk. The silk becomes equally negative.
formula_principle: Charging by friction transfers electrons only; the body losing electrons becomes positive
common_misconception: Believing that positive charging happens by gaining protons rather than by losing electrons.

concept_tested: Interpretation of leaf divergence
stem: A charged body is touched to the disc of an uncharged gold leaf electroscope. The two gold leaves are seen to diverge because
option_a: the leaves receive charges of opposite sign and attract each other
option_b: both leaves receive charge of the same sign and repel each other
option_c: the air between the leaves is heated and pushes them apart
option_d: the leaves become heavier and sag away from the vertical
correct_answer_text: both leaves receive charge of the same sign and repel each other
solution: Charge given to the disc spreads over the whole conductor, so each leaf gets charge of the same sign. Like charges repel, so the leaves swing apart. The angle of divergence is a rough measure of the charge given.
formula_principle: Like charges repel; the electroscope shares charge between disc, stem and leaves
common_misconception: Thinking that induction inside the electroscope gives the two leaves opposite charges.

concept_tested: Charge conservation in an isolated system
stem: Two neutral bodies are rubbed together inside a closed insulated box. After rubbing, the algebraic sum of the charges on the two bodies is
option_a: positive and equal to the charge on the body that gained electrons
option_b: negative and equal in magnitude to the total charge transferred
option_c: twice the charge transferred from one body to the other
solution: Rubbing only transfers electrons from one body to the other. If a charge -q appears on one body then +q appears on the other, so the algebraic total remains zero, the value it had before rubbing.
formula_principle: Conservation of charge in an isolated system
common_misconception: Believing that friction creates new charge rather than separating existing charge.

concept_tested: Algebraic addition of charges on a body
stem: Three small charged beads carrying +3 microC, -5 microC and +7 microC are stuck on to one insulating rod. The total charge on the rod is
solution: Total charge = (+3) + (-5) + (+7) microC = +5 microC. Charge is a scalar and adds algebraically, so signs must be carried through the sum.
formula_principle: Charge is additive, so total q = q1 + q2 + q3 with signs included
common_misconception: Adding magnitudes of charges instead of adding them algebraically with signs.

concept_tested: Counting excess electrons from a measured charge
stem: A small sphere carries a charge of -3.2 x 10^-18 C. Taking the magnitude of the electronic charge to be 1.6 x 10^-19 C, the number of excess electrons on the sphere is
solution: n = (3.2 x 10^-18) / (1.6 x 10^-19) = 2 x 10^1 = 20. The sphere carries 20 electrons more than the number needed for neutrality.
formula_principle: q = n e, so n = |q| / e
common_misconception: Careless handling of powers of ten when dividing charges in scientific notation.

concept_tested: Sharing of charge between identical conducting spheres
stem: Two identical metal spheres carry charges of +7 microC and -3 microC. They are brought into contact and then separated. The charge on each sphere after separation is
solution: Total charge = (+7) + (-3) = +4 microC. Because the spheres are identical, contact shares this equally, giving (+4)/2 = +2 microC on each. Note that 6.25 x 10^12 electrons had to move for this redistribution.
formula_principle: Identical conductors in contact share the total charge equally: q each = (q1 + q2) / 2
common_misconception: Sharing the magnitudes rather than the algebraic sum when charges have opposite signs.

concept_tested: Testing whether a stated charge is permissible
stem: Taking e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, which of the following can be the charge on a body?
solution: Divide each value by e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C. For 4.8 x 10^-19 C the quotient is exactly 3, a whole number, so this charge is allowed. The other quotients are 0.5, 1.5 and 0.35, none of which is a whole number.
formula_principle: Permissible charge must satisfy q = n e with n a whole number
common_misconception: Forgetting that only whole number multiples of e are physically permissible charges.

concept_tested: Charge distribution on a neutral conductor near a charged rod
stem: A positively charged rod is held close to, but not touching, an isolated neutral metal sphere. The sphere then has
option_a: negative charge on the near face, positive charge on the far face and a net negative charge
option_b: positive charge on the near face, negative charge on the far face and zero net charge
option_c: uniform positive charge over its whole surface and a net positive charge
option_d: negative charge on the near face, positive charge on the far face and zero net charge
correct_answer_text: negative charge on the near face, positive charge on the far face and zero net charge
solution: Free electrons in the metal are drawn towards the positive rod, so the near face acquires negative charge and the far face is left positive. Since the sphere is isolated, no charge enters or leaves it and its net charge stays zero.
formula_principle: Electrostatic induction separates charge inside a conductor while the net charge is conserved
common_misconception: Assuming induction gives the isolated conductor a net charge rather than just separating charge within it.

concept_tested: Sign of the final charge produced by induction with earthing
stem: A negatively charged rod is brought near an isolated metal sphere. The sphere is momentarily earthed while the rod is still held in place, and then the earth connection and the rod are removed in that order. The sphere is left
option_d: charged only on the face that was near the rod
solution: The negative rod repels free electrons to the far side of the sphere. Earthing lets those electrons flow away to the ground. Breaking the earth connection first traps a deficiency of electrons, so when the rod is removed the sphere is left positively charged, opposite in sign to the rod.
formula_principle: Charging by induction leaves a charge opposite in sign to the inducing charge
common_misconception: Assuming the induced body ends up with the same sign of charge as the inducing body.

concept_tested: Charge produced by a known loss of electrons
stem: A metal ball loses 10^12 electrons. Taking e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, the charge acquired by the ball is
solution: q = n e = 10^12 x 1.6 x 10^-19 = 1.6 x 10^-7 C. Because electrons have been removed, the ball is left with a deficiency of negative charge and so carries +1.6 x 10^-7 C.
formula_principle: q = n e, with the body becoming positive when it loses electrons
common_misconception: Getting the sign wrong by associating loss of electrons with negative charging.

concept_tested: Why quantisation is not noticed at laboratory scale
stem: Quantisation of charge is not evident in everyday laboratory measurements because
option_a: charge stops being quantised once the number of electrons is very large
option_b: laboratory instruments measure current rather than charge
option_c: charge behaves as a continuous fluid inside conductors
option_d: the elementary charge is so small that ordinary charges correspond to enormous values of n
correct_answer_text: the elementary charge is so small that ordinary charges correspond to enormous values of n
solution: A charge of only 1 microC already corresponds to n = 10^-6 / (1.6 x 10^-19), which is about 6.25 x 10^12. Adding or removing one electron changes such a charge by a fraction of order 10^-13, far below any measurable resolution, so the charge appears to vary continuously.
formula_principle: q = n e with e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, so n is astronomically large for macroscopic charges
common_misconception: Believing that quantisation of charge fails for large charges rather than merely becoming unnoticeable.

concept_tested: Judging statements about the basic properties of charge
stem: Consider the two statements. Statement P: the total charge of an isolated system remains constant. Statement Q: the charge on a particle depends on how fast the particle is moving. Which is correct?
option_a: Both P and Q are true
option_b: P is true and Q is false
option_c: P is false and Q is true
option_d: Both P and Q are false
correct_answer_text: P is true and Q is false
solution: Charge conservation says the algebraic total charge of an isolated system never changes, so P is true. Charge is also invariant, meaning a given particle carries the same charge whether it is at rest or moving fast, so Q is false. Mass, unlike charge, does depend on speed at relativistic speeds.
formula_principle: Charge is conserved in an isolated system and is invariant with the speed of the carrier
common_misconception: Carrying over the speed dependence of mass and assuming charge behaves in the same way.

concept_tested: Repeated sharing between a charged sphere and identical neutral spheres
stem: A metal sphere carries a charge q. An identical uncharged sphere is touched to it and removed, and then a second identical uncharged sphere is touched to the first sphere and removed. The charge finally left on the original sphere is
solution: The first contact shares q equally between two identical spheres, leaving q/2 on the original. The second contact shares that q/2 equally with the next neutral sphere, leaving q/4 on the original sphere.
formula_principle: Identical conductors in contact share their total charge equally
common_misconception: Assuming the total charge is divided at once among all the spheres involved.

concept_tested: Charges on two bodies after a measured electron transfer
stem: Two neutral bodies X and Y are rubbed together and 6.25 x 10^12 electrons are transferred from X to Y. Taking e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, the charges on X and Y are
option_a: X carries -1 microC and Y carries +1 microC
option_b: X carries +1 microC and Y carries +1 microC
option_c: X carries +1 microC and Y carries -1 microC
option_d: X carries +2 microC and Y carries -1 microC
correct_answer_text: X carries +1 microC and Y carries -1 microC
solution: Charge transferred = n e = 6.25 x 10^12 x 1.6 x 10^-19 = 1.0 x 10^-6 C = 1 microC. X has lost these electrons, so X is left with +1 microC, and Y which received them carries -1 microC. The algebraic total is still zero.
formula_principle: q = n e together with conservation of charge for an isolated pair of bodies
common_misconception: Reversing the signs by forgetting which body actually lost the electrons.

concept_tested: Physical consequences of transferring electrons during rubbing
stem: An ebonite rod acquires a charge of -1.6 x 10^-7 C when rubbed with fur. Taking the electron mass as 9.1 x 10^-31 kg and e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, the mass of the rod
option_d: remains exactly the same because charge has no mass
solution: Number of electrons gained n = (1.6 x 10^-7) / (1.6 x 10^-19) = 10^12. Mass gained = 10^12 x 9.1 x 10^-31 = 9.1 x 10^-19 kg. Since the rod becomes negative it has gained electrons, so its mass increases by this utterly negligible amount.
formula_principle: n = q / e, and the mass change equals n times the electron mass
common_misconception: Assuming charging by friction leaves the mass of a body completely unaltered.

concept_tested: Attraction is not a reliable test for charge
stem: A charged rod is brought near a small light ball hanging on a silk thread, and the ball moves towards the rod. It follows that
option_a: the ball must carry a charge opposite to that on the rod
option_b: the ball must carry a charge of the same sign as the rod
option_d: the ball is either oppositely charged or uncharged
correct_answer_text: the ball is either oppositely charged or uncharged
solution: A charged rod attracts an oppositely charged ball directly. It also attracts a neutral ball, because it induces opposite charge on the near face and like charge on the far face, and the nearer induced charge feels the stronger force. So attraction is consistent with two different states of the ball, and only repulsion would prove the ball is charged.
formula_principle: Repulsion is the only sure test of charge; attraction can arise from induction on a neutral body
common_misconception: Treating attraction as proof that a body carries charge of the opposite sign.

concept_tested: Smallest possible change in the charge of a body
stem: The charge on an isolated body is changed by transferring electrons only. The smallest possible change in its charge is
option_c: zero, because charge can be varied continuously
solution: Because charge exists only in packets of size e, the change in charge on transferring n electrons is n e. The smallest non zero value corresponds to n = 1, that is a change of 1.6 x 10^-19 C.
formula_principle: Quantisation means every change in charge is a whole number multiple of e
common_misconception: Assuming charge can be varied by arbitrarily small amounts because macroscopic charges look continuous.

concept_tested: Repeated contact with a sphere that is discharged each time
stem: An isolated metal sphere P carries charge Q. An identical sphere R, initially uncharged, is touched to P, removed and fully discharged to earth. This process of touching, removing and discharging R is carried out three times in all. The charge finally on P is
solution: R is uncharged at the start of every contact because it is discharged each time. So each contact shares the charge on P equally and halves it. After the first contact P holds Q/2, after the second Q/4, and after the third Q/8.
formula_principle: Each contact between identical conductors halves the charge on the charged sphere
common_misconception: Losing track of the fact that R returns uncharged each time, so every contact halves the charge afresh.

concept_tested: Dependence of the electrostatic force on charge and separation
stem: According to Coulomb's law, the magnitude of the force between two point charges at rest is
option_a: directly proportional to the sum of the charges and inversely proportional to the separation
option_b: directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the separation
option_c: directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the separation
option_d: directly proportional to the product of the charges and directly proportional to the square of the separation
correct_answer_text: directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the separation
solution: Coulomb's law states F = k q1 q2 / r^2. The numerator carries the product of the two charges and the denominator the square of the distance between them, so the force falls to one quarter when the separation is doubled.
formula_principle: F = k q1 q2 / r^2 with k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2
common_misconception: Replacing the product of the charges by their sum, or using an inverse first power of distance.

concept_tested: Numerical value of the Coulomb constant in free space
stem: In free space the constant k appearing in F = k q1 q2 / r^2 has the value
solution: With epsilon_0 = 8.85 x 10^-12 C^2 N^-1 m^-2, the combination 1 / (4 pi epsilon_0) works out to about 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2. This is the standard value of k used in numerical problems.
formula_principle: k = 1 / (4 pi epsilon_0) = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2
common_misconception: Quoting epsilon_0 or the gravitational constant in place of the Coulomb constant.

concept_tested: SI unit of the permittivity of free space
stem: The SI unit of the permittivity of free space epsilon_0 is
solution: Rearranging gives epsilon_0 = q1 q2 / (4 pi F r^2). The units are therefore C x C divided by N x m^2, that is C^2 N^-1 m^-2. An equivalent form often quoted is farad per metre.
formula_principle: From F = q1 q2 / (4 pi epsilon_0 r^2), epsilon_0 = q1 q2 / (4 pi F r^2)
common_misconception: Quoting the unit of k instead of the unit of epsilon_0.

concept_tested: Direct application of Coulomb's law in vacuum
stem: Two point charges of 1 microC and 2 microC are held 3 m apart in vacuum. Taking k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, the force between them is
solution: F = 9 x 10^9 x (1 x 10^-6) x (2 x 10^-6) / 3^2 = 9 x 10^9 x 2 x 10^-12 / 9 = 2 x 10^-3 N. The force is repulsive if both charges have the same sign.
formula_principle: F = k q1 q2 / r^2
common_misconception: Dividing by r instead of r squared when substituting into Coulomb's law.

concept_tested: Force between charges immersed in a dielectric medium
stem: Two point charges separated by a fixed distance experience a force F in vacuum. When the whole space around them is filled with a medium of dielectric constant K, the force becomes
solution: In a medium the permittivity becomes epsilon = K epsilon_0, so the force is F' = q1 q2 / (4 pi K epsilon_0 r^2) = F / K. For water with K about 80 the force falls to one eightieth of its vacuum value.
formula_principle: F_medium = q1 q2 / (4 pi K epsilon_0 r^2) = F_vacuum / K
common_misconception: Multiplying rather than dividing by the dielectric constant.

concept_tested: Value of the dielectric constant for vacuum
stem: The dielectric constant of vacuum is
solution: The dielectric constant is defined as the ratio of the permittivity of the medium to the permittivity of free space, K = epsilon / epsilon_0. For vacuum epsilon equals epsilon_0, so K = 1. For air the value is very close to 1.
formula_principle: K = epsilon / epsilon_0, so K = 1 for vacuum
common_misconception: Confusing the dimensionless dielectric constant with the value of epsilon_0.

concept_tested: Effect of doubling the separation between two charges
stem: Two fixed point charges repel each other with a force of 16 N. Keeping the charges unchanged, the separation between them is doubled. The new force of repulsion is
solution: F2 = F1 x (r1 / r2)^2 = 16 x (1/2)^2 = 16 / 4 = 4 N. Doubling the separation reduces the force to one quarter of its original value.
formula_principle: F is proportional to 1 / r^2, so F2 / F1 = (r1 / r2)^2
common_misconception: Treating the electrostatic force as inversely proportional to distance rather than to its square.

concept_tested: Simultaneous change of charges and separation
stem: The force between two point charges is F. Each charge is doubled and at the same time the separation between them is doubled. The new force is
solution: Doubling each charge multiplies the numerator by 2 x 2 = 4. Doubling the separation multiplies the denominator by 2^2 = 4. The two effects cancel exactly, so the force is unchanged at F.
formula_principle: F = k q1 q2 / r^2, so F scales as (product of charges) / (separation squared)
common_misconception: Applying the change to only one of the two quantities in the formula.

concept_tested: Ratio of electrostatic to gravitational force between two protons
stem: For two protons separated by any given distance, the ratio of the electrostatic force of repulsion to the gravitational force of attraction is of the order of
solution: Both forces vary as the inverse square of the separation, so the distance cancels in the ratio. Substituting k = 9 x 10^9, e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, G = 6.67 x 10^-11 and m_p = 1.67 x 10^-27 kg gives a ratio of about 10^36. Electrostatic forces are therefore overwhelmingly dominant at the level of individual particles.
formula_principle: F_electric / F_gravitational = k e^2 / (G m_p^2), and both forces vary as 1 / r^2
common_misconception: Assuming gravity dominates because it is the force we notice in everyday life.

concept_tested: Force between charges placed in water
stem: Two small charged spheres a fixed distance apart experience a force of 8 N in air. Without changing the charges or the separation, they are completely immersed in water of dielectric constant 80. The force between them becomes
solution: F' = F / K = 8 / 80 = 0.1 N. Water polarises strongly, so it reduces the electrostatic force to one eightieth of its value in air.
formula_principle: F_medium = F_air / K
common_misconception: Multiplying by K rather than dividing, so that the force appears to grow in a dielectric.

concept_tested: Finding the charge from a measured force
stem: Two identical point charges placed 1 m apart in vacuum repel each other with a force of 0.9 N. Taking k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, the magnitude of each charge is
solution: q^2 = F r^2 / k = 0.9 x 1 / (9 x 10^9) = 1 x 10^-10 C^2. Taking the square root gives q = 1 x 10^-5 C, that is 10 microC on each sphere.
formula_principle: F = k q^2 / r^2 for two equal charges, so q = sqrt(F r^2 / k)
common_misconception: Reporting q squared as the answer instead of taking the square root.

concept_tested: Neutral point between two like charges
stem: Charges of +4 microC and +1 microC are fixed 3 m apart in vacuum. A small test charge placed on the line joining them feels no net force at a point that is
option_d: 3 m from the +1 microC charge on the side away from the +4 microC charge
solution: Let the null point be at distance x from the +1 microC charge, so it is (3 - x) from the +4 microC charge. Then 4 / (3 - x)^2 = 1 / x^2, giving 2 x = 3 - x, so x = 1 m. The point is 1 m from the smaller charge and 2 m from the larger one.
formula_principle: At the null point k q1 / x1^2 = k q2 / x2^2, so x1 / x2 = sqrt(q1 / q2)
common_misconception: Placing the null point nearer the larger charge instead of nearer the smaller one.

subtopic: Newton's third law and Coulomb forces
concept_tested: Forces on two unequal charges
stem: A charge of +1 microC and a charge of +9 microC are held a certain distance apart. Comparing the electrostatic force on the smaller charge with that on the larger charge,
option_a: the force on the smaller charge is nine times the force on the larger charge
option_b: the force on the larger charge is nine times the force on the smaller charge
option_c: the two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction
option_d: the two forces are equal in magnitude and in the same direction
correct_answer_text: the two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction
solution: Coulomb's law gives the same expression k q1 q2 / r^2 for the force on each charge, because the same product of charges and the same separation appear. The forces act along the line joining the charges and point in opposite senses, forming a Newton third law pair, even though the charges and the masses may be very different.
formula_principle: Coulomb forces form an action and reaction pair: F = k q1 q2 / r^2 for both charges
common_misconception: Assuming a bigger charge pushes harder than it is pushed back.

concept_tested: Dimensional formula of the permittivity of free space
stem: The dimensional formula of the permittivity of free space epsilon_0 is
solution: Charge has dimensions A T, so the product of two charges gives A^2 T^2. Force has dimensions M L T^-2 and r^2 has L^2. Hence epsilon_0 has dimensions A^2 T^2 / (M L T^-2 x L^2) = M^-1 L^-3 T^4 A^2.
formula_principle: epsilon_0 = q1 q2 / (4 pi F r^2), with charge having dimensions A T
common_misconception: Forgetting that each charge contributes a factor of time as well as of current.

concept_tested: Net force on a charge placed between two identical charges
stem: Two identical charges of +2 microC are fixed at the two ends of a straight line of length 2 m. A charge of -3 microC is placed exactly at the midpoint of that line. The net electrostatic force on the -3 microC charge is
option_b: directed towards the nearer of the two fixed charges
option_c: equal to twice the force due to one fixed charge, directed along the line
option_d: perpendicular to the line joining the two fixed charges
solution: Each fixed charge is 1 m from the midpoint and both have the same magnitude, so each exerts a force of the same size on the -3 microC charge. These two attractions act along the same line but in opposite senses, so their vector sum is zero.
formula_principle: Superposition: the net force is the vector sum of the individual Coulomb forces
common_misconception: Adding the magnitudes of the two Coulomb forces without regard to their opposite directions.

concept_tested: Effect of tripling one charge and halving the separation
stem: The force between two point charges is F. One of the charges is made three times larger and the separation is reduced to half its original value. The new force is
solution: Tripling one charge multiplies the numerator by 3. Halving the separation divides the denominator by 4, which multiplies the force by 4. The overall factor is 3 x 4 = 12, so the new force is 12 F.
formula_principle: F is proportional to q1 q2 / r^2
common_misconception: Using the first power of the distance factor rather than its square.

concept_tested: Resultant of two perpendicular Coulomb forces
stem: A small charged bead experiences a force of 3 N due to one fixed charge and, at right angles to it, a force of 4 N due to a second fixed charge. The magnitude of the net force on the bead is
solution: Since the two forces are perpendicular, the resultant is sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5 N. It makes an angle whose tangent is 4/3 with the 3 N force.
formula_principle: For perpendicular forces the resultant is sqrt(F1^2 + F2^2)
common_misconception: Adding force magnitudes arithmetically instead of combining them as vectors.

concept_tested: Net force on one charge at a corner of an equilateral triangle
stem: Three equal point charges q are fixed at the three corners of an equilateral triangle of side r. If F = k q^2 / r^2 is the force between any two of them, the magnitude of the net force on any one charge is
solution: Each of the other two charges exerts a force of magnitude F on the chosen charge, and the angle between these two forces is 60 degrees. The resultant is 2 F cos 30 degrees = 2 F x (sqrt(3) / 2) = sqrt(3) F, directed away from the centre of the triangle for like charges.
formula_principle: Resultant of two equal forces F at angle theta is 2 F cos(theta / 2)
common_misconception: Adding the two forces as if they were collinear and reporting 2 F.

concept_tested: Change in force after two spheres are touched together
stem: Two identical small spheres carrying +5 microC and -3 microC are held 10 cm apart and attract each other. They are brought into contact, separated and replaced at the same 10 cm separation. The ratio of the magnitude of the original force to that of the new force is
solution: Before contact the product of the magnitudes is 5 x 3 = 15 in units of (microC)^2. On contact the total charge (+5) + (-3) = +2 microC is shared equally, giving +1 microC on each sphere, so the product becomes 1 x 1 = 1. Since the separation is unchanged, the ratio of the forces is 15 : 1. The force also changes from attractive to repulsive.
formula_principle: F is proportional to q1 q2, and identical spheres in contact share the total charge equally
common_misconception: Adding the magnitudes rather than the algebraic values when sharing charge on contact.

concept_tested: Separation needed to restore the force inside a dielectric
stem: Two point charges a distance r apart in vacuum experience a force F. The space around them is filled with a medium of dielectric constant K. To restore the force to its original value F, the separation must be changed to
solution: In the medium the force at separation r is F / K. Writing the required separation as r', the condition is q1 q2 / (4 pi K epsilon_0 r'^2) = q1 q2 / (4 pi epsilon_0 r^2), which gives K r'^2 = r^2 and hence r' = r / sqrt(K).
formula_principle: F = q1 q2 / (4 pi K epsilon_0 r^2)
common_misconception: Scaling the separation by K instead of by the square root of K, forgetting the inverse square dependence.

concept_tested: Common and differing features of the two inverse square laws
stem: Comparing Coulomb's law with Newton's law of gravitation, the correct statement is
option_a: both vary as the inverse square of distance, but only the Coulomb force can be repulsive and depends on the medium
option_b: both vary as the inverse square of distance and both can be attractive or repulsive
option_c: only the gravitational force varies as the inverse square of distance, while the Coulomb force varies as the inverse first power
option_d: both are independent of the medium between the interacting bodies
correct_answer_text: both vary as the inverse square of distance, but only the Coulomb force can be repulsive and depends on the medium
solution: Both forces act along the line joining the two bodies and both fall off as 1 / r^2. The differences are that charge comes in two signs so the Coulomb force can attract or repel while gravitation only attracts, that the Coulomb force is reduced by a factor K in a dielectric while gravitation is unaffected by the intervening medium, and that the Coulomb force is about 10^36 times stronger for two protons.
formula_principle: F_electric = k q1 q2 / r^2 and F_gravitational = G m1 m2 / r^2
common_misconception: Assuming the two inverse square forces behave identically in every respect.

concept_tested: Deducing the ratio of two charges from the position of the null point
stem: Two positive point charges are placed 60 cm apart on a line. A test charge placed on the line between them experiences no net force at a point 40 cm from the charge X and 20 cm from the charge Y. The ratio of the magnitude of X to that of Y is
solution: Balancing the two forces gives qX / 40^2 = qY / 20^2, so qX / qY = (40 / 20)^2 = 4. Charge X is therefore four times charge Y, and the null point sits nearer the weaker charge as expected.
formula_principle: At the null point k qX / x1^2 = k qY / x2^2, so qX / qY = (x1 / x2)^2
common_misconception: Taking the charge ratio as the distance ratio rather than as the square of the distance ratio.

subtopic: Equilibrium of a system of charges
concept_tested: Third charge that keeps a two charge system in equilibrium
stem: Point charges q and 4 q are fixed a distance d apart. A third charge is placed on the line joining them so that all three charges are in equilibrium. The third charge is
option_a: +4 q / 9, placed at a distance d / 3 from the charge q
option_b: -4 q / 9, placed at a distance d / 3 from the charge q
option_c: -4 q / 9, placed at a distance 2 d / 3 from the charge q
option_d: -q / 9, placed at a distance d / 3 from the charge q
correct_answer_text: -4 q / 9, placed at a distance d / 3 from the charge q
solution: The third charge must sit where the forces from q and 4 q cancel, so x / (d - x) = sqrt(q / 4 q) = 1 / 2, giving x = d / 3 from q. For the charge q itself to be in equilibrium, the attraction of the third charge Q3 at d / 3 must balance the repulsion of 4 q at d: |Q3| / (d/3)^2 = 4 q / d^2, so |Q3| = 4 q / 9. It must be negative so that the outer charges are pulled inward against their mutual repulsion.
formula_principle: Each charge must have zero net force: null point condition plus balance on the outer charges
common_misconception: Getting the position right but forgetting that the sign of the third charge must be opposite for the outer charges to be held in place.

concept_tested: Separation of two suspended charged pith balls
stem: Two identical pith balls hang from the same point by threads of equal length. Each carries a charge q and at equilibrium they are a small distance x apart, with the threads making a small angle with the vertical. If the charge on each ball is doubled, the equilibrium separation becomes
option_a: x multiplied by 2 to the power two thirds
option_d: x multiplied by the square root of 2
correct_answer_text: x multiplied by 2 to the power two thirds
solution: For small deflections the balance of forces gives x / (2 L) = k q^2 / (x^2 m g), so x^3 is proportional to q^2 and hence x is proportional to q raised to the power two thirds. Doubling q multiplies the separation by 2 raised to the power two thirds, which is about 1.59.
formula_principle: For small angles, tan theta is about x / (2 L) and equals F / (m g) with F = k q^2 / x^2
common_misconception: Assuming the separation is simply proportional to the charge because the Coulomb force is.

concept_tested: Definition and SI unit of electric field intensity
stem: The electric field intensity at a point is defined as the force per unit positive charge placed at that point. Its SI unit is
solution: Since E = F / q, the unit is newton divided by coulomb, written N C^-1. An equivalent unit is volt per metre, because potential difference divided by distance also gives field intensity.
formula_principle: E = F / q
common_misconception: Inverting the definition and quoting charge per unit force.

subtopic: Field due to a point charge
concept_tested: Direct calculation of the field of a point charge
stem: A point charge of 1 microC is placed in vacuum. Taking k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, the magnitude of the electric field at a point 3 m from the charge is
solution: E = 9 x 10^9 x 1 x 10^-6 / 3^2 = 9 x 10^3 / 9 = 1000 N C^-1. The field points radially outward because the charge is positive.
formula_principle: E = k q / r^2
common_misconception: Using the first power of the distance in the denominator instead of the square.

concept_tested: Where electric field lines begin and end
stem: In an electrostatic field, the lines of force
option_a: start on negative charges and end on positive charges
option_b: start on positive charges and end on negative charges
option_c: form closed loops around the charges
option_d: always lie along the surface of the nearest conductor
correct_answer_text: start on positive charges and end on negative charges
solution: A positive test charge is pushed away from a positive charge and pulled towards a negative charge. So lines of force originate on positive charges and terminate on negative charges. For an isolated positive charge the lines run outward to infinity.
formula_principle: Field lines trace the direction of the force on a positive test charge
common_misconception: Reversing the convention and drawing lines into positive charges.

concept_tested: Reason why two field lines can never cross
stem: Two electric lines of force can never intersect because at the point of intersection
option_a: the electric field would have to be zero
option_b: the charge density would become infinite
option_c: the potential would have two different values
option_d: the electric field would have two different directions at the same point
correct_answer_text: the electric field would have two different directions at the same point
solution: The tangent to a line of force at any point gives the direction of the electric field there. If two lines crossed, two different tangents would exist at the crossing point, so the field would have two directions at once. Since the force on a test charge at a point is unique, this is impossible.
formula_principle: The tangent to a line of force gives the unique direction of E at that point
common_misconception: Believing lines cannot cross because the field would become infinite there.

subtopic: Field due to a point charge
concept_tested: Direction of the field of an isolated negative charge
stem: The electric field at any point in the neighbourhood of an isolated negative point charge is directed
option_b: along circles centred on the charge
option_c: parallel to a fixed direction everywhere
solution: A positive test charge placed near a negative charge is attracted, so the force on it points towards the charge. Since E has the direction of this force, the field is radially inward everywhere around a negative point charge.
formula_principle: E points along the force on a positive test charge
common_misconception: Drawing outward radial lines for every point charge irrespective of its sign.

subtopic: Force on a charge in a field
concept_tested: Force on a positive charge placed in a known field
stem: A charge of 2 microC is placed at a point where the electric field intensity is 5 x 10^5 N C^-1. The force on the charge is
solution: F = q E = 2 x 10^-6 x 5 x 10^5 = 1 N. The force acts along the field direction because the charge is positive.
formula_principle: F = q E
common_misconception: Dividing instead of multiplying when applying F = q E.

subtopic: Field due to a point charge
concept_tested: Change in field when the distance is doubled
stem: The electric field at a distance r from a point charge is 400 N C^-1. At a distance 2 r from the same charge the field is
solution: E2 = E1 x (r1 / r2)^2 = 400 x (1/2)^2 = 400 / 4 = 100 N C^-1. Doubling the distance reduces the field to one quarter.
formula_principle: E is proportional to 1 / r^2
common_misconception: Applying an inverse first power dependence to the field of a point charge.

subtopic: Field due to a system of charges
concept_tested: Field at the midpoint between two opposite charges
stem: Charges of +5 microC and -5 microC are fixed 20 cm apart in vacuum. Taking k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, the magnitude of the electric field at the midpoint of the line joining them is
solution: Each charge is 0.10 m from the midpoint. Field due to each is 9 x 10^9 x 5 x 10^-6 / (0.10)^2 = 4.5 x 10^6 N C^-1. At the midpoint the field of the positive charge points away from it and the field of the negative charge points towards it, so both point the same way and add to give 9 x 10^6 N C^-1, directed from the positive charge towards the negative one.
formula_principle: E = k q / r^2 for each charge, combined by vector addition
common_misconception: Assuming that equal and opposite charges always give zero field at the midpoint.

subtopic: Field due to a system of charges
concept_tested: Field at the midpoint between two like charges
stem: Two equal positive point charges are held a fixed distance apart. At the midpoint of the line joining them, the electric field is
option_a: zero, while the potential there is not zero
option_b: zero, and the potential there is also zero
option_c: maximum along the line joining the charges
correct_answer_text: zero, while the potential there is not zero
solution: At the midpoint each charge produces a field of the same magnitude but the two point in opposite directions along the line, so they cancel and E = 0. Potential is a scalar, and both charges contribute positive potentials that add, so V is not zero there.
formula_principle: E adds as a vector while V adds as a scalar
common_misconception: Assuming that wherever the field vanishes the potential must vanish too.

concept_tested: Line pattern that represents a uniform field
stem: A uniform electric field in a region of space is represented by lines of force that are
option_a: parallel to one another but progressively closer together
option_b: radial and equally spaced around a central point
option_c: parallel to one another and equally spaced
correct_answer_text: parallel to one another and equally spaced
solution: A field is uniform when it has the same magnitude and the same direction at every point. Constant direction means the lines are straight and parallel, and constant magnitude means the spacing between them is the same everywhere. The field in the middle region between two large oppositely charged parallel plates is of this kind.
formula_principle: Direction of E is along the lines and its magnitude is indicated by the density of lines
common_misconception: Thinking any set of parallel lines represents a uniform field even when their spacing changes.

concept_tested: Orientation of field lines at a conductor surface
stem: At every point on the surface of a charged conductor in electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field is
option_b: inclined at 45 degrees to the surface
solution: If the field had a component along the surface, it would exert a force on the free charges and set them moving, contradicting the assumption of equilibrium. Hence the surface field can only be normal to the surface. Inside the conductor the field is zero, so no lines exist there.
formula_principle: In electrostatic equilibrium the tangential component of E at a conductor surface must be zero
common_misconception: Drawing field lines meeting a conductor surface at an oblique angle.

subtopic: Motion of a charge in a uniform field
concept_tested: Comparing accelerations of an electron and a proton
stem: An electron and a proton are placed in the same uniform electric field. Taking the proton to be about 1836 times as massive as the electron, the ratio of the magnitude of the acceleration of the electron to that of the proton is about
solution: Both particles carry the same magnitude of charge, so both experience the same magnitude of force q E in the same field. Since a = F / m, the accelerations are inversely proportional to the masses, giving a_electron / a_proton = m_proton / m_electron, about 1836. Their directions are opposite because the charges have opposite sign.
formula_principle: a = q E / m, with equal charge magnitudes for electron and proton
common_misconception: Assuming both particles pick up the same acceleration because they carry the same magnitude of charge.

subtopic: Motion of a charge in a uniform field
concept_tested: Path of a charge released from rest in a uniform field
stem: A charged particle is released from rest in a uniform electric field, and gravity is negligible. The particle moves
option_a: along a straight line with constant acceleration
option_b: along a straight line with constant speed
option_d: along a circular path of constant radius
correct_answer_text: along a straight line with constant acceleration
solution: The field is uniform, so the force q E is constant in both magnitude and direction. Starting from rest, the particle moves along the direction of that force, that is along the field for a positive charge and opposite to it for a negative one, with uniform acceleration q E / m.
formula_principle: F = q E is constant in magnitude and direction, so a = q E / m is constant
common_misconception: Assuming any motion in a field must be curved.

subtopic: Motion of a charge in a uniform field
concept_tested: Path of a charge projected across a uniform field
stem: A charged particle enters a uniform electric field with an initial velocity perpendicular to the field. Neglecting gravity, its subsequent path inside the field region is
option_a: a straight line along the initial velocity
option_b: a straight line along the field direction
solution: Along the initial direction of motion there is no force, so that velocity component stays constant. Along the field there is a constant acceleration q E / m starting from zero velocity. Uniform velocity in one direction combined with uniform acceleration perpendicular to it produces a parabolic path, exactly as in projectile motion under gravity.
formula_principle: Constant velocity across the field with uniform acceleration along it gives a parabola
common_misconception: Assuming the particle simply turns and travels along the field lines.

concept_tested: How fields of several charges combine
stem: The resultant electric field at a point due to a system of point charges is obtained by
option_a: adding the magnitudes of the individual fields
option_b: adding the individual fields as scalars with their signs
option_c: taking the field due to the nearest charge only
option_d: adding the individual fields as vectors
correct_answer_text: adding the individual fields as vectors
solution: Each charge sets up its own field at the point as though the others were absent, and the resultant field is the vector sum of these contributions. Because the field is a vector, both magnitude and direction of every contribution must be taken into account.
formula_principle: Principle of superposition for the electric field
common_misconception: Adding field magnitudes arithmetically, which works only for collinear fields in the same sense.

subtopic: Force on a charge in a field
concept_tested: Direction of the force on a negative charge
stem: An electron is placed at a point in an electric field that points vertically downward. The force on the electron is
option_a: vertically downward and of magnitude e E
option_b: vertically upward and of magnitude e E
option_c: vertically upward and of magnitude E / e
option_d: zero, because the electron is not a source of the field
correct_answer_text: vertically upward and of magnitude e E
solution: The magnitude of the force is |q| E = e E. Because the electron has negative charge, the force is opposite in direction to the field, so a downward field pushes an electron upward.
formula_principle: F = q E, with the direction reversed for a negative charge
common_misconception: Applying the field direction as the force direction regardless of the sign of the charge.

concept_tested: Resultant of two perpendicular fields
stem: At a point, one charge produces a field of 300 N C^-1 directed east and a second charge produces a field of 400 N C^-1 directed north. The magnitude of the resultant field at that point is
solution: The two fields are at right angles, so the resultant has magnitude sqrt(300^2 + 400^2) = sqrt(90000 + 160000) = sqrt(250000) = 500 N C^-1. Its direction makes an angle whose tangent is 4/3 with the easterly field.
formula_principle: For perpendicular vectors the resultant magnitude is sqrt(E1^2 + E2^2)
common_misconception: Adding perpendicular field magnitudes as if they were collinear.

subtopic: Field due to a point charge
concept_tested: Distance at which the field falls to a stated fraction
stem: The electric field of an isolated point charge has magnitude E at a distance r from it. The field has magnitude E / 9 at a distance
solution: Since E is proportional to 1 / r^2, reducing the field by a factor 9 requires r^2 to grow by a factor 9, so r must grow by a factor sqrt(9) = 3. The required distance is therefore 3 r.
formula_principle: E is proportional to 1 / r^2, so r2 / r1 = sqrt(E1 / E2)
common_misconception: Scaling the distance by the same factor as the field rather than by its square root.

subtopic: Field due to a system of charges
concept_tested: Field at the centre of a square with equal charges at the corners
stem: Four equal point charges, each of magnitude q and all of the same sign, are fixed at the four corners of a square. The electric field at the centre of the square is
option_a: four times the field due to one charge, directed along a diagonal
option_b: twice the field due to one charge, directed along a side
option_c: equal to the field due to one charge, directed towards the nearest corner
solution: The centre is equidistant from all four corners, so each charge produces a field of the same magnitude there. The charges at the two ends of a diagonal produce fields along that diagonal in opposite senses, so they cancel in pairs. Both diagonals cancel in this way, so the resultant field at the centre is zero. The potential at the centre, however, is four times that due to one charge.
formula_principle: Superposition together with the symmetry of the arrangement
common_misconception: Adding the four field magnitudes and reporting four times the single charge field.

subtopic: Motion of a charge in a uniform field
concept_tested: Kinetic energy gained by an electron in a uniform field
stem: An electron starting from rest moves through a distance of 1 cm under the action of a uniform electric field of magnitude 1 x 10^4 N C^-1. Taking e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, the kinetic energy gained by the electron is
solution: Force on the electron F = e E = 1.6 x 10^-19 x 1 x 10^4 = 1.6 x 10^-15 N. Work done over d = 1 cm = 1 x 10^-2 m is W = 1.6 x 10^-15 x 1 x 10^-2 = 1.6 x 10^-17 J. Starting from rest, this whole amount appears as kinetic energy, which is 100 eV.
formula_principle: Work done by a constant force: W = F d = q E d, and this equals the kinetic energy gained from rest
common_misconception: Failing to convert the distance from centimetres to metres before computing the work.

concept_tested: Field of a point charge inside a dielectric medium
stem: The electric field at a point a distance r from a point charge q in vacuum is E. If the whole space is filled with a medium of dielectric constant 2, the field at the same distance from the same charge becomes
solution: In a medium the permittivity is epsilon = K epsilon_0, so the field becomes E' = q / (4 pi K epsilon_0 r^2) = E / K. With K = 2 the field is halved. Physically, the medium polarises and the induced bound charges partly oppose the field of the free charge.
formula_principle: E = q / (4 pi K epsilon_0 r^2)
common_misconception: Treating the field of a point charge as independent of the surrounding medium.

subtopic: Field due to a system of charges
concept_tested: Null point for two unlike charges of different magnitude
stem: Charges of +4 microC and -1 microC are fixed 3 m apart in vacuum. The resultant electric field is zero at a point on the line through them that lies
option_a: 1 m from the -1 microC charge, on the side away from the +4 microC charge
option_b: 2 m from the +4 microC charge, between the two charges
option_c: 1.5 m from each charge, at the midpoint
option_d: 3 m from the -1 microC charge, on the side away from the +4 microC charge
correct_answer_text: 3 m from the -1 microC charge, on the side away from the +4 microC charge
solution: Between two unlike charges the two fields point the same way, so the null point must lie outside, and beyond the smaller charge because only there can the two magnitudes match. Let the point be a distance x beyond the -1 microC charge. Then 4 / (3 + x)^2 = 1 / x^2, so 2 x = 3 + x, giving x = 3 m. The null point is 3 m from the -1 microC charge and 6 m from the +4 microC charge.
formula_principle: Null point requires k q1 / d1^2 = k q2 / d2^2 with the two fields opposite in direction
common_misconception: Looking for the null point between the charges, as one would for two like charges.

subtopic: Motion of a charge in a uniform field
concept_tested: Dependence of transverse deflection on entry speed
stem: A charged particle is projected with speed v perpendicular to a uniform electric field and is deflected sideways by a distance y while crossing a field region of fixed length. If the same particle is projected into the same region with speed 2 v, the sideways deflection becomes
solution: The time in the field is t = L / v. The transverse deflection is y = (1/2) (q E / m) t^2 = q E L^2 / (2 m v^2). Doubling v divides y by 2^2 = 4, so the new deflection is y / 4.
formula_principle: y = (1/2) (q E / m) t^2 with t = L / v, so y is proportional to 1 / v^2
common_misconception: Taking the deflection to be inversely proportional to the speed rather than to its square.

concept_tested: Angle of a charged pendulum bob in a horizontal field
stem: A small ball of mass 2 g carrying a charge of 2 microC hangs from an insulating thread. A uniform horizontal electric field of 1 x 10^4 N C^-1 is switched on. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the thread settles at an angle with the vertical of
solution: Electric force q E = 2 x 10^-6 x 1 x 10^4 = 2 x 10^-2 N. Weight m g = 2 x 10^-3 x 10 = 2 x 10^-2 N. Since the horizontal and vertical forces are equal, tan(theta) = 1 and the thread makes 45 degrees with the vertical.
formula_principle: At equilibrium tan(theta) = q E / (m g)
common_misconception: Forgetting to convert the mass from grams to kilograms before comparing the two forces.

concept_tested: Expression and SI unit of electric flux through a plane area
stem: A plane surface of area S is placed in a uniform electric field E, with theta the angle between the field and the normal to the surface. The electric flux through the surface is
option_a: E S sin(theta), measured in N m^2 C^-1
option_b: E S cos(theta), measured in N m^2 C^-1
option_c: E S tan(theta), measured in N m^2 C^-1
option_d: E S cos(theta), measured in N C^-1 m^-2
correct_answer_text: E S cos(theta), measured in N m^2 C^-1
solution: Flux counts the field lines crossing the surface. Only the component of E along the normal, that is E cos(theta), contributes, so phi = E S cos(theta). The unit is newton metre squared per coulomb, equivalently volt metre.
formula_principle: phi = E S cos(theta), where theta is the angle between E and the outward normal
common_misconception: Using the sine of the angle because the angle is wrongly measured from the plane rather than from the normal.

concept_tested: Scalar character of electric flux
stem: Electric flux is
option_a: a vector quantity directed along the normal to the surface
option_b: a scalar quantity that can never be negative
option_c: a vector quantity directed along the electric field
option_d: a scalar quantity that can be positive, negative or zero
correct_answer_text: a scalar quantity that can be positive, negative or zero
solution: Flux is defined as the scalar product of the field and the area vector, so it is a scalar. Its sign depends on the angle theta: it is positive when lines leave the surface, negative when they enter, and zero when the field lies in the plane of the surface.
formula_principle: phi is the scalar product of E and the area vector
common_misconception: Assuming flux is a vector because both the field and the area vector are vectors.

concept_tested: Orientation giving maximum flux
stem: A flat sheet of fixed area is placed in a uniform electric field. The flux through the sheet is maximum when the plane of the sheet is
option_b: inclined at 45 degrees to the field
option_c: inclined at 60 degrees to the field
solution: The flux is E A cos(theta), where theta is measured from the normal. It is greatest when theta is zero, that is when the normal to the sheet lies along the field. The plane of the sheet is then perpendicular to the field, and the maximum flux is E A.
formula_principle: phi = E A cos(theta) is maximum when theta = 0, that is when the normal is along E
common_misconception: Measuring the angle from the plane of the surface instead of from its normal.

concept_tested: Numerical flux for an inclined surface
stem: A plane surface of area 2 m^2 is held in a uniform electric field of 100 N C^-1 so that the normal to the surface makes an angle of 60 degrees with the field. The flux through the surface is
solution: phi = E A cos(theta) = 100 x 2 x cos 60 degrees = 100 x 2 x 0.5 = 100 N m^2 C^-1.
formula_principle: phi = E A cos(theta)
common_misconception: Substituting the angle between the field and the plane rather than the angle with the normal.

concept_tested: Orientation giving zero flux
stem: The electric flux through a flat surface placed in a uniform electric field is zero when the field
option_a: is perpendicular to the plane of the surface
option_b: makes an angle of 60 degrees with the normal to the surface
option_c: lies entirely in the plane of the surface
option_d: makes an angle of 45 degrees with the plane of the surface
correct_answer_text: lies entirely in the plane of the surface
solution: The flux vanishes when the angle between the field and the normal is 90 degrees, that is when the field lies in the plane of the surface. Geometrically the lines run alongside the surface without piercing it, so no lines are counted.
formula_principle: phi = E A cos(theta), so phi = 0 when theta = 90 degrees
common_misconception: Confusing the orientation for zero flux with the one for maximum flux.

concept_tested: Flux depending only on the enclosed charge
stem: A closed surface encloses a net charge of 8.85 microC. Taking epsilon_0 = 8.85 x 10^-12 C^2 N^-1 m^-2, the total electric flux through the closed surface is
solution: phi = q / epsilon_0 = (8.85 x 10^-6) / (8.85 x 10^-12) = 1 x 10^6 N m^2 C^-1. The result depends only on the enclosed charge, not on where inside the surface that charge sits.
formula_principle: Total flux through a closed surface = q_enclosed / epsilon_0
common_misconception: Multiplying by epsilon_0 instead of dividing by it.

concept_tested: Flux when the enclosed charge is zero
stem: A closed surface is drawn in a region where a strong electric field exists, but the surface encloses no net charge. The total flux through the surface is
option_a: zero, although the field on the surface is not zero
option_b: zero, and the field must also be zero everywhere on the surface
option_c: non zero and proportional to the strength of the external field
option_d: non zero and proportional to the area of the surface
correct_answer_text: zero, although the field on the surface is not zero
solution: The total flux depends only on the net charge inside. With no enclosed charge the net flux is zero. This does not make the field zero on the surface: field lines from outside charges enter on one side and leave on the other, so the incoming negative flux exactly cancels the outgoing positive flux.
formula_principle: Total flux through a closed surface = q_enclosed / epsilon_0
common_misconception: Concluding that zero net flux through a surface means zero field on that surface.

concept_tested: Independence of flux from the shape of the surface
stem: A point charge q is enclosed inside a closed surface. The total flux through the surface
option_a: depends on the shape of the surface but not on its size
option_b: depends only on q and not on the shape, size or the position of the charge inside
option_c: depends on the distance of the charge from the surface
option_d: is largest when the surface is a sphere centred on the charge
correct_answer_text: depends only on q and not on the shape, size or the position of the charge inside
solution: Every line of force starting on the enclosed charge must eventually cross the surface, whatever its shape or size and wherever the charge sits inside. So the total flux is fixed at q / epsilon_0. Only the way that flux is distributed over the surface changes when the charge is moved.
formula_principle: Total flux through a closed surface = q_enclosed / epsilon_0
common_misconception: Assuming a bigger enclosing surface intercepts more total flux.

concept_tested: Flux through one face of a cube with a charge at its centre
stem: A point charge q is placed at the centre of a cube. The electric flux through any one face of the cube is
solution: The total flux emerging from the closed cubical surface is q / epsilon_0. The charge sits at the centre, so the six faces are equivalent by symmetry and each carries the same share. Flux through one face is therefore q / (6 epsilon_0).
formula_principle: Total flux q / epsilon_0 is shared equally among faces related by symmetry
common_misconception: Quoting the total flux for the whole cube when only one face is asked for.

concept_tested: Effect of a charge lying outside the surface
stem: A point charge is placed just outside a closed surface. The total electric flux through that surface is
option_c: dependent on how close the charge is to the surface
solution: Field lines from a charge outside the surface enter it on one side and leave on the other. Every incoming line contributes negative flux and the same line contributes an equal positive flux where it emerges, so the contributions cancel exactly. Since no charge is enclosed, the net flux is zero however near the charge is placed.
formula_principle: Total flux through a closed surface is determined by the enclosed charge alone
common_misconception: Assuming that a nearby external charge must contribute some net flux because it produces a strong field on the surface.

concept_tested: Simultaneous change of enclosed charge and surface radius
stem: A point charge q is at the centre of a spherical surface of radius R and the flux through the sphere is phi. The charge is now doubled and the radius of the sphere is also doubled. The new flux is
solution: Flux through a closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by epsilon_0 and is completely independent of the radius. Doubling the charge therefore doubles the flux, and doubling the radius changes nothing. The new flux is 2 phi. Note that the field at the surface does fall to one half, since the charge doubles while r^2 quadruples.
formula_principle: Total flux = q_enclosed / epsilon_0, independent of the size of the surface
common_misconception: Applying an inverse square reduction to the flux as though it were the field.

concept_tested: Flux through a hemisphere placed in a uniform field
stem: A hemispherical shell of radius R is placed in a uniform electric field E with its axis parallel to the field, so that the field enters through the flat circular face. The flux through the curved surface of the hemisphere is
solution: Treat the hemisphere plus its flat circular face as a closed surface enclosing no charge, so the total flux is zero. The flux entering through the flat face is E times its area pi R^2. Hence the same amount, E pi R^2, must leave through the curved surface. Equivalently, the curved surface presents a projected area pi R^2 to the field.
formula_principle: Net flux through a closed surface with no enclosed charge is zero, so flux out of the curved part balances flux into the flat part
common_misconception: Using the actual curved area 2 pi R^2 rather than the area projected perpendicular to the field.

concept_tested: Definition and SI unit of electric potential
stem: The electric potential at a point is the work done in bringing unit positive charge from infinity to that point. Its SI unit is
option_a: volt, equal to one coulomb per joule
option_c: joule, since potential is a form of energy
option_d: volt, equal to one joule per coulomb
correct_answer_text: volt, equal to one joule per coulomb
solution: Potential is work per unit charge, V = W / q, so its unit is joule per coulomb. This combination is named the volt. One volt means one joule of work per coulomb of charge moved.
formula_principle: V = W / q
common_misconception: Confusing the unit of potential with that of electric field or of energy.

subtopic: Potential due to a point charge
concept_tested: Direct calculation of potential near a point charge
stem: A point charge of 2 microC is placed in vacuum. Taking k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, the electric potential at a point 3 m from the charge is
solution: V = 9 x 10^9 x 2 x 10^-6 / 3 = 18 x 10^3 / 3 = 6000 V. Note that potential falls off as 1 / r while the field falls off as 1 / r^2.
formula_principle: V = k q / r
common_misconception: Using r squared in the denominator, which belongs to the field and not to the potential.

concept_tested: Scalar addition of potentials
stem: When several point charges are present, the resultant electric potential at a point is found by
option_a: adding the individual potentials algebraically with their signs
option_b: adding the individual potentials as vectors
option_c: adding the magnitudes of the individual potentials
option_d: taking the potential of the largest charge only
correct_answer_text: adding the individual potentials algebraically with their signs
solution: Potential is energy per unit charge and therefore a scalar. Contributions from different charges add algebraically, positive for positive charges and negative for negative charges. This is why potentials are far easier to combine than fields, which require vector addition.
formula_principle: V is a scalar, so V_total = V1 + V2 + V3 with signs included
common_misconception: Applying vector addition to potentials because fields are added that way.

concept_tested: Value of the electron volt in joule
stem: One electron volt is equal to
solution: One electron volt is the kinetic energy gained by an electron accelerated through a potential difference of one volt. Since W = q V, this is 1.6 x 10^-19 C multiplied by 1 V, which gives 1.6 x 10^-19 J.
common_misconception: Treating the electron volt as a unit of charge or of potential rather than of energy.

concept_tested: Work done in moving a charge on an equipotential surface
stem: A charge of 5 microC is carried from one point to another point on the same equipotential surface. The work done by the electric force is
option_b: equal to the charge multiplied by the value of the potential on that surface
option_d: dependent on the length of the path followed on the surface
solution: By definition, every point on an equipotential surface has the same potential, so V2 - V1 = 0. Hence W = q (V2 - V1) = 0, whatever the value of the charge and whatever path is taken on that surface.
formula_principle: W = q (V2 - V1), and V2 = V1 on an equipotential surface
common_misconception: Multiplying the charge by the value of the potential instead of by the potential difference.

subtopic: Potential due to a system of charges
concept_tested: Potential at a point equidistant from equal and opposite charges
stem: Charges of +2 microC and -2 microC are placed so that a point P is 1 m from each of them. The electric potential at P is
solution: The potential due to the positive charge is +k (2 x 10^-6) / 1 and that due to the negative charge is -k (2 x 10^-6) / 1. These are equal in size and opposite in sign, so the total potential at P is zero. The field at P, being a vector sum, is generally not zero.
formula_principle: V = k q / r summed algebraically over all charges
common_misconception: Adding potential magnitudes without taking the sign of each charge into account.

concept_tested: Distinguishing zero potential from zero field
stem: Charges of +5 microC and -5 microC are held 20 cm apart. At the midpoint of the line joining them,
option_a: the potential is zero but the electric field is not zero
option_b: both the potential and the electric field are zero
option_c: the electric field is zero but the potential is not zero
option_d: both the potential and the electric field are maximum
correct_answer_text: the potential is zero but the electric field is not zero
solution: Potentials from the two charges are +k q / r and -k q / r, which cancel to give V = 0. The field of the positive charge points away from it and that of the negative charge points towards it, so at the midpoint both point in the same direction and add to 2 k q / r^2. Zero potential therefore does not imply zero field.
formula_principle: V adds as a signed scalar while E adds as a vector
common_misconception: Assuming that a point of zero potential must also be a point of zero field.

concept_tested: Work done in moving a charge through a potential difference
stem: A charge of 2 C is moved from a point at potential 3 V to a point at potential 8 V. The work that must be done against the electric force is
solution: Potential difference V2 - V1 = 8 - 3 = 5 V. Work done W = q (V2 - V1) = 2 x 5 = 10 J. The work is positive because a positive charge has to be pushed towards the region of higher potential.
formula_principle: W = q (V2 - V1)
common_misconception: Using the value of the potential at one point instead of the difference between the two points.

concept_tested: Energy gained by an electron accelerated through a potential difference
stem: An electron initially at rest is accelerated through a potential difference of 100 V. Taking e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, the kinetic energy it acquires is
solution: Kinetic energy = e V = 1.6 x 10^-19 x 100 = 1.6 x 10^-17 J. This is exactly 100 eV, which is why the electron volt is such a convenient unit for such problems.
formula_principle: Kinetic energy gained = q V = e V
common_misconception: Treating the number of volts as an energy in joule without multiplying by the charge.

concept_tested: Shape of the equipotential surfaces of a point charge
stem: The equipotential surfaces around an isolated point charge are
option_a: concentric cylinders with the charge on the axis
option_b: parallel planes perpendicular to the radius
option_c: concentric spheres centred on the charge
option_d: radial straight lines drawn from the charge
correct_answer_text: concentric spheres centred on the charge
solution: Since V = k q / r depends only on the distance from the charge, all points at the same distance are at the same potential. The locus of such points is a sphere centred on the charge, so the equipotentials are a family of concentric spheres, spaced more widely as one moves further out.
formula_principle: V = k q / r depends only on r, so surfaces of constant V are surfaces of constant r
common_misconception: Confusing the equipotential surfaces with the radial lines of force.

concept_tested: Relation between equipotential surfaces and lines of force
stem: An equipotential surface and the electric lines of force passing through it always meet
option_d: at an angle that depends on the charge distribution
solution: Moving a charge along an equipotential surface requires no work. Since work equals force multiplied by displacement along the direction of the force, the electric force and hence the field can have no component along the surface. So the field, and with it every line of force, must be normal to the equipotential surface.
formula_principle: No work is done in moving a charge on an equipotential surface, so E has no component along it
common_misconception: Assuming lines of force can run along an equipotential surface.

subtopic: Potential due to a point charge
concept_tested: Comparing the fall of potential and field with distance
stem: At a distance r from an isolated point charge the potential is V and the field is E. At a distance 2 r from the same charge, the potential and the field are respectively
solution: Potential varies as 1 / r, so doubling the distance halves it to V / 2. Field varies as 1 / r^2, so doubling the distance reduces it to one quarter, E / 4. This difference of one power of r is why V = E r for a point charge.
formula_principle: V = k q / r and E = k q / r^2
common_misconception: Applying the inverse square law to the potential as well as to the field.

concept_tested: Relation between uniform field and potential difference
stem: Two large parallel plates are held 2 cm apart with a potential difference of 100 V between them. The magnitude of the uniform electric field between the plates is
solution: E = V / d = 100 / 0.02 = 5000 V m^-1. The field points from the plate at higher potential towards the plate at lower potential.
formula_principle: For a uniform field, E = V / d
common_misconception: Failing to convert centimetres to metres before dividing.

concept_tested: Potential and field inside a charged spherical conductor
stem: A hollow metal sphere is given a charge and left in electrostatic equilibrium. At a point inside the sphere,
option_a: both the field and the potential are zero
option_b: the field is zero and the potential falls steadily towards the centre
option_c: both the field and the potential have their maximum values at the centre
option_d: the field is zero and the potential equals the potential at the surface
correct_answer_text: the field is zero and the potential equals the potential at the surface
solution: In electrostatic equilibrium the field inside the conducting material and in the hollow is zero. Since the field measures how fast the potential changes with distance, a zero field means the potential does not change. So the potential everywhere inside equals its value on the surface, which is k q / R for a sphere of radius R.
formula_principle: E = 0 inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium, so V is constant throughout it
common_misconception: Assuming that a zero field must go with a zero potential.

subtopic: Potential due to a system of charges
concept_tested: Locating the point of zero potential between two unlike charges
stem: Charges of +2 microC and -4 microC are fixed 3 m apart in vacuum. On the line joining them, the potential is zero at a point that lies between the charges at a distance from the +2 microC charge of
solution: Let the point be at a distance x from the +2 microC charge. The condition V = 0 gives 2 / x = 4 / (3 - x), so 2 (3 - x) = 4 x, that is 6 = 6 x and x = 1 m. The point is 1 m from the +2 microC charge and 2 m from the -4 microC charge. Note the electric field there is not zero.
formula_principle: Setting k q1 / x + k q2 / (d - x) = 0 with signs included
common_misconception: Locating the zero potential point by balancing squares of distances, which is the rule for zero field instead.

subtopic: Work done in moving a charge
concept_tested: Work done in moving a charge between two radii of a point charge
stem: A charge of 3 microC is moved from a point 20 cm from a fixed charge of 5 microC to a point 50 cm from it. Taking k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, the work done by the external agent is
solution: V at 0.20 m is 9 x 10^9 x 5 x 10^-6 / 0.20 = 2.25 x 10^5 V. V at 0.50 m is 9 x 10^9 x 5 x 10^-6 / 0.50 = 0.90 x 10^5 V. So V_final - V_initial = -1.35 x 10^5 V, and W = 3 x 10^-6 x (-1.35 x 10^5) = -0.405 J. The negative sign means the electric force does 0.405 J of work while the charge moves outward.
formula_principle: W_external = q (V_final - V_initial) with V = k Q / r
common_misconception: Getting the sign wrong by subtracting the final potential from the initial one.

concept_tested: Point where the field vanishes but the potential does not
stem: At the midpoint of the line joining two equal positive point charges,
option_a: both the electric field and the potential are zero
option_b: the potential is zero while the electric field has twice the value due to one charge
option_c: the electric field is zero while the potential has twice the value due to one charge
option_d: both the electric field and the potential are twice their values due to one charge
correct_answer_text: the electric field is zero while the potential has twice the value due to one charge
solution: Each charge produces a field of the same magnitude at the midpoint but the two point in opposite senses along the line, so they cancel and E = 0. The potentials are each +k q / r with r half the separation, and being scalars of the same sign they add to 2 k q / r. So a zero field can coexist with a large potential.
formula_principle: E is a vector sum while V is a signed scalar sum
common_misconception: Believing that a vanishing field forces the potential to vanish as well.

concept_tested: Energy gained by a doubly charged ion
stem: An alpha particle, which carries a charge of +2 e, is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 1 x 10^6 V. Taking e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, the kinetic energy gained is
solution: Charge q = 2 x 1.6 x 10^-19 = 3.2 x 10^-19 C. Kinetic energy = q V = 3.2 x 10^-19 x 1 x 10^6 = 3.2 x 10^-13 J. In electron volt this is 2 MeV, because a charge 2 e accelerated through 1 MV gains 2 MeV.
formula_principle: Kinetic energy gained = q V with q = 2 e for an alpha particle
common_misconception: Forgetting that the alpha particle carries twice the elementary charge.

subtopic: Work done in moving a charge
concept_tested: Work done in bringing a charge from infinity
stem: A charge of 2 microC is brought from infinity to a point where the electric potential is 500 V. The work done in the process is
solution: Potential at infinity is zero by convention, so the potential difference through which the charge moves is 500 V. Work done W = q V = 2 x 10^-6 x 500 = 1 x 10^-3 J. This is exactly the definition of potential applied to a charge of 2 microC rather than to unit charge.
formula_principle: W = q V, since the potential at infinity is taken as zero
common_misconception: Reporting the numerical value of the potential as the work done, ignoring the size of the charge moved.

concept_tested: Work done around a closed path
stem: A charge is carried once around a closed loop of any shape in an electrostatic field and returns to its starting point. The work done by the electric force over the whole loop is
option_a: zero only if the loop lies entirely on one equipotential surface
option_b: equal to the charge multiplied by the largest potential encountered
option_d: proportional to the length of the loop
solution: The electrostatic force is conservative, so the work done depends only on the initial and final positions. For a closed path these are the same point, so V_final equals V_initial and the work is q times zero, that is zero, whatever the shape or length of the loop.
formula_principle: W = q (V_final - V_initial), and the endpoints coincide for a closed path
common_misconception: Assuming a longer path around the loop means more work is done.

concept_tested: Comparing final speeds of an electron and a proton
stem: An electron and a proton, both starting from rest, are accelerated through the same potential difference. Taking the proton to be about 1836 times as massive as the electron, the ratio of the final speed of the electron to that of the proton is about
solution: Both particles carry the same magnitude of charge and cross the same potential difference, so both gain the same kinetic energy q V. From (1/2) m v^2 = q V, the speed is v = sqrt(2 q V / m), so v is inversely proportional to the square root of the mass. The ratio is sqrt(m_proton / m_electron) = sqrt(1836), which is about 42.8, close to 43.
formula_principle: q V = (1/2) m v^2, so v = sqrt(2 q V / m)
