common_misconception: Using the mass ratio directly instead of its square root when equal energies are involved.

subtopic: Potential due to a system of charges
concept_tested: Second zero potential point outside the pair of charges
stem: Charges of +2 microC and -4 microC are fixed 3 m apart. Besides the point between them, the potential on the line through the charges is also zero at a point that lies
option_a: 3 m from the +2 microC charge, on the side away from the -4 microC charge
option_b: 3 m from the -4 microC charge, on the side away from the +2 microC charge
option_c: 6 m from the +2 microC charge, on the side away from the -4 microC charge
option_d: 1.5 m from the +2 microC charge, on the side away from the -4 microC charge
correct_answer_text: 3 m from the +2 microC charge, on the side away from the -4 microC charge
solution: Let the point lie a distance x beyond the +2 microC charge, on the side away from the negative charge. Its distance from the -4 microC charge is then (3 + x). Setting the total potential to zero gives 2 / x = 4 / (3 + x), so 2 (3 + x) = 4 x, that is 6 = 2 x and x = 3 m. The point lies 3 m from the +2 microC charge and 6 m from the -4 microC charge. A pair of unlike charges of unequal magnitude has two such points on the line.
formula_principle: V = k q1 / r1 + k q2 / r2 = 0 with signs included
common_misconception: Assuming there is only one point of zero potential on the line through two unlike charges.

concept_tested: Field inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium
stem: A solid metal block is placed in an external electric field and allowed to reach electrostatic equilibrium. The electric field at every point inside the metal is then
option_b: equal to the external field divided by the dielectric constant of the metal
option_d: larger than the external field because of the induced charges
solution: Free electrons in the metal move under the applied field and pile up on the surfaces. Their own field opposes the applied field, and the movement continues until the two cancel exactly. Once that happens no force acts on the remaining free charges, so equilibrium is reached with zero field everywhere inside the conductor.
formula_principle: Free charges redistribute until the net field inside a conductor is zero
common_misconception: Assuming the external field simply passes through a conductor unchanged.

concept_tested: Meaning of electrostatic shielding
stem: Sensitive electronic equipment is enclosed in a metal box so that external electric fields do not affect it. This use of a conducting enclosure is called
solution: Charges induced on the outside of the metal enclosure arrange themselves so that the field inside the cavity is zero, whatever the external field. The interior is therefore protected, and this protection is called electrostatic shielding. The same principle keeps a person safe inside a car during a lightning strike.
formula_principle: Field inside a hollow conductor is zero, so the interior is shielded
common_misconception: Naming the mechanism, induction, instead of the effect, shielding.

concept_tested: Location of excess charge on a charged conductor
stem: A solid metal sphere is given an excess charge. In electrostatic equilibrium this charge resides
option_a: uniformly throughout the volume of the sphere
option_b: mostly at the centre of the sphere
option_c: entirely on the outer surface of the sphere
option_d: in a thin shell just inside the surface with none on the surface itself
correct_answer_text: entirely on the outer surface of the sphere
solution: If any excess charge remained inside the metal, it would produce a field there and drive further motion, contradicting equilibrium. The mutual repulsion of like charges also pushes them as far apart as possible. Both arguments lead to the same conclusion: the excess charge sits entirely on the outer surface.
formula_principle: E = 0 inside a conductor in equilibrium, which forces the excess charge to the outer surface
common_misconception: Picturing the charge as spread evenly through the material of the conductor.

concept_tested: Charge induced on the faces of a conductor
stem: A neutral metal slab is placed in a uniform external electric field pointing to the right. In equilibrium the slab carries
option_a: negative charge on its left face and equal positive charge on its right face
option_b: positive charge on its left face and equal negative charge on its right face
option_c: negative charge on both faces of the slab
option_d: no charge on either face, since the slab is neutral
correct_answer_text: negative charge on its left face and equal positive charge on its right face
solution: The field pushes positive charge to the right, but only electrons are free to move, and they move to the left, against the field. The left face therefore acquires negative charge and the right face is left with an equal positive charge. These induced charges produce an internal field to the left that exactly cancels the applied field inside the metal.
formula_principle: Induced surface charges arrange themselves so that the field inside the conductor is zero
common_misconception: Placing the induced negative charge on the far face by following the direction of the field rather than the motion of the electrons.

concept_tested: What happens inside a dielectric placed in a field
stem: When a slab of dielectric is placed in an external electric field, the molecules of the dielectric
option_a: release free electrons that drift to one face of the slab
option_b: move bodily towards the face of the slab nearer the positive plate
option_c: acquire or align dipole moments, producing bound charges on the faces of the slab
option_d: lose their charge completely and become neutral atoms
correct_answer_text: acquire or align dipole moments, producing bound charges on the faces of the slab
solution: The applied field displaces the positive and negative charges within each molecule slightly, or aligns dipoles that are already present. Inside the slab the effects of neighbouring molecules cancel, but bound charges are left uncancelled on the two faces. These bound charges set up a field opposing the applied field, so the net field inside the dielectric is reduced.
formula_principle: Polarisation produces bound surface charges that set up a field opposing the applied field
common_misconception: Treating a dielectric like a conductor, with free electrons drifting to one face.

concept_tested: Definition and dimensions of the dielectric constant
stem: The dielectric constant K of a medium is defined as the ratio of the field applied to a dielectric to the reduced field inside it. The dielectric constant is therefore
option_a: a dimensionless number that is greater than or equal to 1
option_b: a dimensionless number that is always less than 1
option_c: a quantity with the unit C^2 N^-1 m^-2
option_d: a quantity with the unit farad per metre
correct_answer_text: a dimensionless number that is greater than or equal to 1
solution: K is the ratio of two quantities of the same kind, so it carries no unit and no dimensions. Because polarisation always weakens the field inside the dielectric, the reduced field is smaller than the applied one and K is at least 1, equalling 1 only for vacuum.
formula_principle: K = E_applied / E_inside = epsilon / epsilon_0
common_misconception: Assigning to the dielectric constant the unit of permittivity.

concept_tested: Everyday application of shielding
stem: During a thunderstorm, a person sitting inside a car with a metal body is comparatively safe because
option_a: the metal body keeps the field inside the car essentially zero and carries the charge on its outer surface
option_b: the rubber tyres prevent any charge from reaching the car at all
option_c: the glass windows completely block the electric field from entering
option_d: the metal body attracts the lightning away from the car and neutralises it
correct_answer_text: the metal body keeps the field inside the car essentially zero and carries the charge on its outer surface
solution: The car acts as a hollow conductor. Any charge it acquires resides on its outer surface and the field inside the cavity remains essentially zero, so the occupant experiences no large field and the current passes around the outside of the shell to the ground. This is electrostatic shielding at work, and it does not depend on the tyres.
formula_principle: Field inside a hollow conductor is zero and excess charge resides on the outer surface
common_misconception: Crediting the insulating tyres rather than the conducting shell for the protection.

concept_tested: Distinguishing polar from non polar dielectrics
stem: The essential difference between a polar and a non polar dielectric is that
option_a: molecules of a polar dielectric have a permanent dipole moment even with no field applied
option_b: a polar dielectric contains free electrons whereas a non polar dielectric does not
option_c: a non polar dielectric cannot be polarised by an external field at all
option_d: a polar dielectric has a dielectric constant less than 1
correct_answer_text: molecules of a polar dielectric have a permanent dipole moment even with no field applied
solution: In a non polar molecule such as hydrogen the centres of positive and negative charge coincide, so the molecule has no dipole moment until a field pulls the centres apart. In a polar molecule such as water the two centres are permanently separated, so a dipole moment exists even with no field. In the absence of a field these permanent dipoles point randomly, so the material shows no net polarisation until a field aligns them.
formula_principle: Polar molecules have permanent dipole moments; non polar molecules acquire induced ones
common_misconception: Assuming a non polar dielectric cannot be polarised at all.

concept_tested: Reduced field inside a dielectric slab
stem: A dielectric slab of dielectric constant 3 is placed in a uniform external electric field of 3 x 10^4 N C^-1. The net electric field inside the dielectric is
solution: E_inside = E_applied / K = 3 x 10^4 / 3 = 1 x 10^4 N C^-1. The field set up by the bound surface charges is the difference, 2 x 10^4 N C^-1, directed against the applied field.
formula_principle: E_inside = E_applied / K
common_misconception: Multiplying by K, which would make the dielectric strengthen the field instead of weakening it.

concept_tested: Comparing how a conductor and a dielectric respond to an applied field
stem: A large metal slab and a large dielectric slab of dielectric constant 4 are placed separately in the same uniform electric field E, each with its plane faces perpendicular to the field. In electrostatic equilibrium, the field deep inside the metal slab and deep inside the dielectric slab are respectively
solution: In the metal the free electrons keep moving until the induced surface charges create a field that exactly cancels the applied field, so the internal field is zero. In the dielectric the charges are bound and can only be displaced slightly, so the bound surface charges produce a partial opposing field and the net field is reduced to E / K, here E / 4. A conductor can be regarded as the limiting case of a dielectric with an infinitely large dielectric constant.
formula_principle: Free charges give complete cancellation in a conductor; bound charges give partial cancellation E / K in a dielectric
common_misconception: Assuming a dielectric with a large K reduces the field to zero just as a conductor does.

concept_tested: Defining relation and SI unit of capacitance
stem: Capacitance is defined as the charge stored on a conductor per unit rise in its potential. The SI unit of capacitance, the farad, is therefore equal to
solution: Capacitance is the charge stored per unit rise of potential, C = Q / V, so the unit is coulomb per volt. This unit is named the farad. One farad is a very large capacitance, so practical capacitors are rated in microfarad or picofarad.
formula_principle: C = Q / V
common_misconception: Inverting the defining relation and quoting volt per coulomb.

concept_tested: Direct calculation of capacitance
stem: A capacitor stores a charge of 20 microC when the potential difference across it is 5 V. Its capacitance is
formula_principle: C = Q / V
common_misconception: Multiplying charge by potential difference rather than dividing.

concept_tested: Effect of changing the plate separation
stem: The capacitance of a parallel plate air capacitor is 12 microF. Keeping the plate area unchanged, the separation between the plates is doubled. The new capacitance is
solution: Capacitance is inversely proportional to the plate separation, so doubling the separation halves it. The new value is 12 / 2 = 6 microF.
formula_principle: C = epsilon_0 A / d
common_misconception: Assuming capacitance rises when the plates are moved further apart.

concept_tested: Change in capacitance on introducing a dielectric
stem: The space between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor is completely filled with a dielectric of dielectric constant 5. The capacitance becomes
option_a: one fifth of its original value
option_c: unchanged, because the dielectric carries no free charge
solution: Filling the gap with a dielectric of constant K multiplies the capacitance by K, so with K = 5 the capacitance becomes 5 times larger. The reason is that the bound charges reduce the field between the plates, so the same charge is held at a smaller potential difference.
formula_principle: C_with dielectric = K epsilon_0 A / d = K C_air
common_misconception: Dividing by K instead of multiplying, by analogy with the reduction of force in a dielectric.

concept_tested: Numerical capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor
stem: A parallel plate air capacitor has plates of area 100 cm^2 separated by 1 mm. Taking epsilon_0 = 8.85 x 10^-12 C^2 N^-1 m^-2, its capacitance is
formula_principle: C = epsilon_0 A / d
common_misconception: Converting square centimetres to square metres using a factor of 10^-2 instead of 10^-4.

concept_tested: Dielectric introduced while the battery stays connected
stem: A parallel plate capacitor stays connected to a battery of fixed voltage while a dielectric slab of constant K is slid in to fill the gap completely. Compared with the values before the slab was inserted,
option_a: the capacitance rises K times while the stored charge and the field are both unchanged
option_b: the capacitance rises K times while the stored charge falls K times
option_c: the capacitance and the stored charge both rise K times while the field between the plates is unchanged
option_d: the capacitance is unchanged while the stored charge rises K times
correct_answer_text: the capacitance and the stored charge both rise K times while the field between the plates is unchanged
solution: The battery holds the potential difference V constant. The capacitance becomes K C_0, so the charge Q = C V becomes K times larger, drawn from the battery. The field between the plates is E = V / d, and since neither V nor d changes, the field is unchanged.
formula_principle: Battery connected means V is fixed; C = K C_0, Q = C V and E = V / d
common_misconception: Assuming the charge on the plates stays fixed even though the capacitor remains connected to the battery.

concept_tested: Dielectric introduced after the battery is disconnected
stem: A parallel plate capacitor is charged and then disconnected from the battery. A dielectric slab of constant K is now slid in to fill the gap completely. Compared with the values before insertion,
option_a: the charge rises K times, the capacitance rises K times and the potential difference is unchanged
option_b: the charge is unchanged, the capacitance rises K times and the potential difference falls K times
option_c: the charge is unchanged, the capacitance falls K times and the potential difference rises K times
option_d: the charge, the capacitance and the potential difference are all unchanged
correct_answer_text: the charge is unchanged, the capacitance rises K times and the potential difference falls K times
solution: Once the battery is disconnected the plates are isolated, so the charge Q cannot change. Filling the gap raises the capacitance to K C_0. Since V = Q / C, the potential difference falls to V_0 / K, and the field between the plates falls in the same ratio to E_0 / K.
formula_principle: Isolated capacitor means Q is fixed; C = K C_0 and V = Q / C
common_misconception: Carrying over the battery connected result and assuming the potential difference stays fixed.

concept_tested: Combined change of separation and dielectric
stem: A parallel plate capacitor with air between its plates has a capacitance of 6 microF. The plate separation is now doubled and the whole gap is filled with a dielectric of dielectric constant 4. The new capacitance is
solution: Starting from C_0 = epsilon_0 A / d = 6 microF, doubling the separation gives a factor 1/2 and filling with the dielectric gives a factor 4. The new capacitance is 6 x 4 / 2 = 12 microF.
formula_principle: C = K epsilon_0 A / d
common_misconception: Applying only one of the two changes, or multiplying by the separation factor instead of dividing.

concept_tested: Identity of the current carriers in a metal
stem: In a metallic conductor the electric current is carried mainly by
option_a: positive ions of the lattice that drift steadily towards the negative terminal
option_b: holes produced by the removal of electrons from the valence band
option_c: free electrons that are loosely bound and wander through the whole lattice
option_d: protons that are released from the nuclei of the metal atoms
correct_answer_text: free electrons that are loosely bound and wander through the whole lattice
solution: In a metal the outermost electrons of each atom are so weakly held that they detach and form a common pool. These free electrons move at random with large speeds, and when a field is applied they acquire a small drift velocity opposite to the field. The heavy positive ions stay at their lattice sites and only vibrate.
formula_principle: Free electron model of a metal: valence electrons of the atoms form a common electron gas.
common_misconception: Students often think the positive ions also move and share the current, forgetting that the lattice is rigid.

concept_tested: Order of magnitude of the resistivity of a metal
stem: At room temperature the resistivity of a good conductor such as copper lies in the range
solution: Copper has resistivity about 1.7 x 10^-8 ohm m and other metals lie within one or two powers of ten of this. The whole metallic range is therefore about 10^-8 to 10^-6 ohm m, which is separated from the semiconductor range by many powers of ten.
formula_principle: Classification by resistivity: metals about 10^-8 to 10^-6 ohm m, semiconductors about 10^-5 to 10^6 ohm m, insulators about 10^11 to 10^19 ohm m.
common_misconception: Learners confuse the numerical ranges of resistivity with those of conductivity, which are reciprocal to each other.

concept_tested: Opposite temperature behaviour of metals and semiconductors
stem: The temperature of a metal wire and of a pure semiconductor sample are both raised by the same amount. Their resistances then change so that
option_a: the resistance of the metal decreases while that of the semiconductor increases
option_d: the resistance of the metal increases while that of the semiconductor decreases
correct_answer_text: the resistance of the metal increases while that of the semiconductor decreases
solution: In a metal the number of free electrons is fixed, so heating only increases the lattice vibrations, the electrons are scattered more and the resistance rises. In a semiconductor heating breaks many more covalent bonds, so the carrier number rises steeply and the resistance falls despite the extra scattering.
formula_principle: Metals have a positive temperature coefficient of resistance; semiconductors have a negative one.
common_misconception: Students apply the metallic rule that resistance always rises with temperature to every solid.

concept_tested: Behaviour of a pure semiconductor at absolute zero
stem: A pure semiconductor crystal at absolute zero temperature behaves as
option_a: a good conductor, with a resistance comparable with that of a copper wire
option_b: a superconductor, offering exactly zero resistance to any applied voltage
option_c: a moderate conductor, with a resistance one half of its room temperature value
option_d: a perfect insulator, offering an extremely large resistance to any applied voltage
correct_answer_text: a perfect insulator, offering an extremely large resistance to any applied voltage
solution: At 0 K there is no thermal energy available to break a covalent bond. The valence band is completely full and the conduction band completely empty, so there are neither free electrons nor holes and the crystal cannot conduct at all.
formula_principle: At 0 K every valence electron of a pure semiconductor is locked in a covalent bond, so no mobile carrier exists.
common_misconception: Learners assume cooling always improves conduction because that is what happens in a metal.

concept_tested: Ordering three solids by conductivity
stem: Three materials, glass, germanium and silver, are compared at room temperature. Arranged in order of increasing electrical conductivity they are
solution: Glass is an insulator with conductivity of order 10^-12 S m^-1 or less, germanium is a semiconductor with conductivity of the order of a few S m^-1, and silver is the best metallic conductor with conductivity of the order of 10^7 S m^-1. So the increasing order is glass, germanium, silver.
formula_principle: Conductivity increases in the order insulator, semiconductor, conductor.
common_misconception: Students confuse increasing conductivity with increasing resistivity and give the reversed sequence.

concept_tested: Reciprocal relation between conductivity and resistivity
stem: A solid sample has resistivity 2 x 10^-8 ohm m at room temperature. Its conductivity and its likely classification are
solution: sigma = 1 / rho = 1 / (2 x 10^-8) = 0.5 x 10^8 = 5 x 10^7 S m^-1. A resistivity of 2 x 10^-8 ohm m lies squarely in the metallic band of 10^-8 to 10^-6 ohm m, so the sample is a conductor.
formula_principle: sigma = 1 / rho.
common_misconception: Students invert only the power of ten and leave the mantissa unchanged when taking a reciprocal.

concept_tested: Physical origin of the fall in resistance of a semiconductor on heating
stem: The resistance of a pure germanium sample falls sharply when it is heated. The main reason is that
option_a: the mobility of the carriers rises much faster than the number of carriers falls
option_b: the number of free charge carriers rises steeply and outweighs the accompanying fall in mobility
option_c: the crystal expands on heating so that the sample becomes shorter and thicker
option_d: collisions between the carriers and the lattice ions become less frequent at higher temperature
correct_answer_text: the number of free charge carriers rises steeply and outweighs the accompanying fall in mobility
solution: Heating supplies energy that breaks more covalent bonds, so the electron and hole concentrations rise very rapidly, roughly exponentially. The mobility falls slowly because of stronger lattice scattering. Since conductivity is the product of carrier number and mobility, the steep rise in number wins and the resistance falls.
formula_principle: sigma = e (n_e mu_e + n_h mu_h); in a semiconductor n rises exponentially with temperature while mu falls slowly.
common_misconception: Students credit the fall in resistance to a rise in mobility, whereas mobility actually decreases with temperature.

concept_tested: Computing resistivity from resistance and geometry and classifying the material
stem: A uniform bar of a solid has length 4 m, cross sectional area 2 x 10^-6 m^2 and resistance 20 ohm. Its resistivity and the class to which it belongs are
solution: rho = R A / l = 20 x (2 x 10^-6) / 4 = (4 x 10^-5) / 4 = 1 x 10^-5 ohm m. This lies in the semiconductor range of about 10^-5 to 10^6 ohm m, so the bar is a semiconductor.
formula_principle: R = rho l / A, so rho = R A / l.
common_misconception: Learners rearrange R = rho l / A carelessly and multiply by the length instead of dividing by it.

concept_tested: Temperature behaviour of an insulator
stem: The resistivity of an insulator such as glass, when its temperature is raised by a few hundred kelvin,
option_a: increases steadily, because the stronger lattice vibrations scatter the bound electrons
option_b: remains exactly constant, because an insulator has no charge carriers whatever at any temperature
option_c: falls to zero, because the forbidden gap of the solid disappears when it is heated
option_d: decreases slightly, because a few electrons gain just enough energy to cross the very wide gap
correct_answer_text: decreases slightly, because a few electrons gain just enough energy to cross the very wide gap
solution: An insulator has a forbidden gap wider than about 3 eV. At any temperature above 0 K a minute number of electrons are excited across it, and this number grows with temperature. The resistivity therefore falls, although it remains enormous because the gap is so wide.
formula_principle: Insulators, like semiconductors, have a negative temperature coefficient of resistance because their carriers are thermally generated.
common_misconception: Students treat insulators as having no carriers at all and conclude that their resistivity cannot change with temperature.

concept_tested: Reason for the positive temperature coefficient of a metal
stem: In a metal the number density of free electrons is almost independent of temperature. Its resistance nevertheless rises with temperature because
option_a: the free electrons combine with the lattice ions and are steadily removed from conduction
option_b: the free electron number density falls rapidly once room temperature is passed
option_c: the charge carried by each free electron becomes smaller as the temperature rises
option_d: the lattice vibrations grow stronger and scatter the electrons more often, lowering their mobility
correct_answer_text: the lattice vibrations grow stronger and scatter the electrons more often, lowering their mobility
solution: Since n and e are fixed for a metal, conductivity is controlled entirely by mobility. Heating increases the amplitude of the lattice vibrations, so an electron travels a shorter average distance between collisions, its mobility falls and the resistance rises almost linearly with temperature.
formula_principle: sigma = n e mu; in a metal n is fixed and mu falls as lattice scattering increases with temperature.
common_misconception: Learners cannot separate the two factors in sigma = n e mu and assume any change in resistance must come from a change in n.

concept_tested: Description of valence electrons in the free electron picture
stem: In the free electron model of a metal, the valence electrons are best described as
option_a: bound to their parent atoms and merely oscillating in place when a field is applied
option_b: travelling in fixed circular orbits around the lattice ions even when a field is applied
option_c: completely at rest until a field is applied and then moving together with a very large uniform speed
option_d: detached from individual atoms, moving at random through the whole crystal and drifting slowly when a field is applied
correct_answer_text: detached from individual atoms, moving at random through the whole crystal and drifting slowly when a field is applied
solution: The valence electrons of a metal leave their atoms and behave like a gas filling the crystal. Their random speeds are very large, but the random velocities cancel so no current flows. An applied field superposes a very small common drift velocity on this random motion, and that drift constitutes the current.
formula_principle: Free electron gas model: random thermal motion of order 10^5 m s^-1 with a superposed drift of order 10^-4 m s^-1.
common_misconception: Students think conduction electrons are stationary until a battery is connected and then move at the speed of the electrical signal.

concept_tested: Order of magnitude of the free electron density in a metal
stem: The number density of free electrons in a typical metal is of the order of
solution: A solid contains of the order of 10^29 atoms per cubic metre, and in a metal each atom releases about one valence electron. Hence the free electron density is of the order of 10^28 to 10^29 m^-3, which is some ten powers of ten larger than the carrier density of an intrinsic semiconductor.
formula_principle: A metal contributes roughly one free electron per atom, and a solid holds about 10^28 to 10^29 atoms per cubic metre.
common_misconception: Learners confuse the Avogadro number with a number density and quote 10^23 m^-3 for every solid.

concept_tested: Combined effect of carrier number and mobility on resistivity
stem: The resistivity of a pure semiconductor sample is 4 ohm m. On heating, its carrier number density becomes 8 times larger while the carrier mobility falls to one half of its earlier value. The new resistivity is
solution: Conductivity is proportional to n mu. The product changes by a factor 8 x (1/2) = 4, so the conductivity becomes 4 times larger. Since rho = 1 / sigma, the resistivity becomes 4 / 4 = 1 ohm m.
formula_principle: sigma = n e mu and rho = 1 / sigma, so rho is inversely proportional to the product n mu.
common_misconception: Students multiply resistivity by the same factor as conductivity instead of dividing by it.

concept_tested: Reconciling falling mobility with rising conductivity
stem: On heating a semiconductor the mobility of its carriers actually decreases, and yet its conductivity increases. The correct resolution is that
option_a: the carrier number density grows exponentially with temperature and easily dominates the modest fall in mobility
option_b: the electronic charge grows with temperature and compensates for the loss of mobility
option_c: the fall in mobility applies only to holes, while the electron mobility rises steeply with temperature
option_d: the sample shortens on heating so its resistance falls even though the conductivity is unchanged
correct_answer_text: the carrier number density grows exponentially with temperature and easily dominates the modest fall in mobility
solution: Write sigma = e n (mu_e + mu_h) for a pure sample. Raising the temperature from 300 K to 400 K may multiply n by a factor of many hundreds, while mu falls only by a factor of about two or three. The product therefore rises strongly and so does the conductivity.
formula_principle: sigma = e (n_e mu_e + n_h mu_h); in a semiconductor n rises exponentially with T while mu falls as a modest power of T.
common_misconception: Students assume that whatever raises conductivity must raise mobility as well, and cannot accept the two moving in opposite directions.

concept_tested: Current through a slab from conductivity, field and area
stem: A semiconductor slab of conductivity 2 S m^-1 and cross sectional area 5 x 10^-6 m^2 is placed in a uniform electric field of 100 V m^-1 directed along its length. The current through the slab is
solution: J = sigma E = 2 x 100 = 200 A m^-2. Then I = J A = 200 x (5 x 10^-6) = 1.0 x 10^-3 A, that is 1 mA.
formula_principle: J = sigma E and I = J A.
common_misconception: Learners forget the second step and report the current density as though it were the current.

concept_tested: Single criterion separating semiconductors from metals and insulators
stem: Which single statement correctly separates a semiconductor from both a metal and an insulator?
option_a: Its conductivity is intermediate and falls with temperature, and only electrons carry the current
option_b: Its conductivity is the highest of the three and rises with temperature
option_c: Its conductivity is intermediate and independent of temperature, and only holes carry the current
option_d: Its conductivity is intermediate and rises rapidly with temperature, and both electrons and holes carry the current
correct_answer_text: Its conductivity is intermediate and rises rapidly with temperature, and both electrons and holes carry the current
solution: A metal has very high conductivity, a positive temperature coefficient and electrons alone as carriers. An insulator has negligible conductivity. A semiconductor sits between them, its conductivity grows rapidly with temperature because bonds break, and both the freed electrons and the vacancies they leave behind carry current.
formula_principle: A semiconductor is defined by an intermediate conductivity, a negative temperature coefficient and two kinds of mobile carrier.
common_misconception: Students identify a semiconductor by its conductivity value alone and ignore the temperature behaviour and the two carrier types.

concept_tested: Identifying three unknown solids from resistivity and temperature data
stem: Three samples are tested. Sample X has resistivity 10^-8 ohm m and its resistance rises on heating. Sample Y has resistivity 10^2 ohm m and its resistance falls on heating. Sample Z has resistivity 10^14 ohm m and its resistance falls very slightly on heating. The correct identification is
option_a: X is a metal, Y is an insulator and Z is a semiconductor
option_b: X is a semiconductor, Y is a metal and Z is an insulator
option_c: X is a metal, Y is a semiconductor and Z is an insulator
option_d: X is an insulator, Y is a semiconductor and Z is a metal
correct_answer_text: X is a metal, Y is a semiconductor and Z is an insulator
solution: Sample X: resistivity 10^-8 ohm m is in the metallic band and a rising resistance means a positive temperature coefficient, so X is a metal. Sample Y: resistivity 10^2 ohm m lies inside the semiconductor band of 10^-5 to 10^6 ohm m and the resistance falls on heating, so Y is a semiconductor. Sample Z: resistivity 10^14 ohm m is in the insulating band, and insulators too show a small fall of resistance on heating, so Z is an insulator.
formula_principle: Combine the resistivity range with the sign of the temperature coefficient to classify a solid.
common_misconception: Students assume that only semiconductors show a falling resistance with temperature and misclassify the insulator.

concept_tested: Series combination made independent of temperature
stem: A metal resistor of resistance 100 ohm has temperature coefficient of resistance +0.005 per K. It is joined in series with a semiconductor resistor whose temperature coefficient is -0.05 per K. For the resistance of the combination to be independent of small changes of temperature, the resistance of the semiconductor must be
solution: The change in the total resistance for a small temperature rise is R1 alpha1 + R2 alpha2 per kelvin. Setting this to zero gives 100 x 0.005 + R2 x (-0.05) = 0, so 0.5 = 0.05 R2 and R2 = 10 ohm. The rise in the metal resistance is then exactly cancelled by the fall in the semiconductor resistance.
formula_principle: For a series pair, dR/dT = R1 alpha1 + R2 alpha2; this vanishes when R1 alpha1 + R2 alpha2 = 0.
common_misconception: Learners equate the two temperature coefficients rather than the two products of resistance and coefficient.

concept_tested: Origin of energy bands in a crystal
stem: Energy bands appear in a crystalline solid because
option_a: the sharp energy levels of the isolated atoms split into very large numbers of closely spaced levels when the atoms are brought close together
option_b: each atom of the crystal loses all its electrons into a common pool that has one fixed energy
option_c: the electrons of the crystal are free to take absolutely any energy whatever without restriction
option_d: the nuclei of neighbouring atoms merge together and produce a single very deep energy level
correct_answer_text: the sharp energy levels of the isolated atoms split into very large numbers of closely spaced levels when the atoms are brought close together
solution: In an isolated atom the electron energies are sharp levels. When about 10^29 atoms per cubic metre are packed into a crystal, the outer electron clouds overlap and no two electrons may share the same state. Each atomic level therefore splits into an enormous number of levels so close together that they form a practically continuous band.
formula_principle: Overlap of atomic wave functions in a crystal splits each atomic level into N closely spaced levels forming a band.
common_misconception: Students think bands are new energies created by the crystal rather than the splitting of the existing atomic levels.

concept_tested: Definition of the valence band
stem: The valence band of a solid is
option_a: the band of energies that stays completely empty at every temperature
option_b: the range of energies that no electron in the solid may possess
option_c: the band of energies occupied by the valence electrons of the atoms of the solid
option_d: the band in which the electrons have escaped from the crystal altogether
correct_answer_text: the band of energies occupied by the valence electrons of the atoms of the solid
solution: The valence electrons of the atoms occupy the valence band. In a pure semiconductor or insulator this band is completely full at 0 K. The next allowed band above it, separated by the forbidden gap, is the conduction band, which is empty at 0 K.
formula_principle: The valence band is the highest band containing electrons at 0 K; the conduction band is the next allowed band above it.
common_misconception: Learners mix up the valence band with the forbidden gap or with the conduction band.

concept_tested: Definition of the forbidden energy gap
stem: The forbidden energy gap of a solid is the energy interval
option_a: between the bottom of the valence band and the top of the conduction band, in which electrons move most freely
option_b: over which the conduction band itself extends from its lowest to its highest energy
option_c: required to remove an electron completely from the surface of the solid into free space
option_d: between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band, in which no electron state exists
correct_answer_text: between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band, in which no electron state exists
solution: The forbidden gap is the range of energies between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band. No allowed electron state lies in it, so an electron can only cross it in one jump if it is given at least Eg of energy.
formula_principle: Eg = E_conduction band minimum minus E_valence band maximum.
common_misconception: Students confuse the band gap with the work function of the material.

concept_tested: Room temperature band gaps of silicon and germanium
stem: The forbidden energy gaps of silicon and germanium at room temperature are respectively about
solution: Silicon has a forbidden gap of about 1.1 eV and germanium about 0.7 eV at room temperature. Both are well below the 3 eV mark that separates semiconductors from insulators, and germanium, with the smaller gap, generates more electron hole pairs at a given temperature.
formula_principle: Eg for Si is about 1.1 eV and for Ge about 0.7 eV at 300 K.
common_misconception: Learners interchange the two values, or quote the diamond gap of 5.4 eV as a semiconductor value.

concept_tested: Band structure of a good conductor
stem: In the band picture of a good conductor
option_a: the valence band and the conduction band overlap, and no forbidden gap exists between them
option_b: the forbidden gap is narrow, about 1 eV wide
option_c: the forbidden gap is wide, more than 3 eV across
option_d: the conduction band is completely empty and the valence band completely full at every temperature
correct_answer_text: the valence band and the conduction band overlap, and no forbidden gap exists between them
solution: In a metal the highest band containing electrons is only partly filled, or else the empty conduction band overlaps the filled valence band. In either case there are unoccupied states immediately above the occupied ones, so even a very weak field can accelerate electrons and a large current flows.
formula_principle: In a conductor the valence and conduction bands overlap, or the highest occupied band is only partly filled.
common_misconception: Students look for a small gap in a metal instead of recognising that no gap exists.

concept_tested: Classifying a solid from its band gap
stem: A solid whose forbidden energy gap is about 6 eV is best described as
solution: Thermal energy at room temperature is only about 0.026 eV, so a gap of 6 eV is enormous compared with it and virtually no electron can cross. Such a solid conducts negligibly and is classed as an insulator; diamond, with a gap of 5.4 eV, is the standard example.
formula_principle: Eg = 0 for conductors, Eg less than about 3 eV for semiconductors, Eg greater than about 3 eV for insulators.
common_misconception: Learners assume that any solid with a stated band gap must be a semiconductor.

concept_tested: Band occupation of a pure semiconductor at absolute zero
stem: At absolute zero, the occupation of the bands of a pure semiconductor is
option_a: the valence band partly full and the conduction band partly full
option_b: the valence band completely full and the conduction band completely empty
option_c: the valence band completely empty and the conduction band completely full
correct_answer_text: the valence band completely full and the conduction band completely empty
solution: At 0 K there is no thermal energy to lift an electron across the gap. Every valence electron sits in the valence band, filling it completely, and the conduction band above the gap is completely empty. A completely full band carries no current, so the crystal behaves as an insulator.
formula_principle: At 0 K electrons occupy the lowest available states, filling the valence band exactly.
common_misconception: Students imagine a few electrons remain in the conduction band even at 0 K.

concept_tested: Why germanium conducts better than silicon at the same temperature
stem: At the same temperature a pure germanium sample conducts better than a pure silicon sample chiefly because
option_a: germanium has the larger forbidden gap, so more electrons are released from its bonds
option_b: germanium has the smaller forbidden gap, so many more electron hole pairs are generated in it
option_c: germanium atoms are pentavalent while silicon atoms are tetravalent
option_d: germanium has a very much higher density of atoms than silicon
correct_answer_text: germanium has the smaller forbidden gap, so many more electron hole pairs are generated in it
solution: The number of electron hole pairs generated at a given temperature depends exponentially on the ratio of the band gap to the thermal energy. Germanium, with Eg about 0.7 eV, has a much smaller exponent than silicon with Eg about 1.1 eV, and its intrinsic carrier concentration is about a thousand times larger, giving it the higher conductivity.
formula_principle: The concentration of thermally generated pairs falls off exponentially as the forbidden gap increases.
common_misconception: Learners think a larger gap means more energy available and hence more carriers.

concept_tested: Converting a band gap from electron volt to joule
stem: Taking 1 eV = 1.6 x 10^-19 J, the forbidden gap of silicon, 1.1 eV, expressed in joule is
solution: E = 1.1 x 1.6 x 10^-19 = 1.76 x 10^-19 J. The energy needed to break one covalent bond of silicon is therefore a little under two parts in 10^19 of a joule.
formula_principle: E in joule = E in eV multiplied by 1.6 x 10^-19.
common_misconception: Students divide by the conversion factor instead of multiplying when going from eV to joule.

concept_tested: Longest wavelength that can excite an electron across a gap
stem: A semiconductor has a forbidden gap of 2.48 eV. Using hc = 1240 eV nm, the longest wavelength of light that can lift an electron from the valence band to the conduction band is
solution: lambda_max = 1240 / 2.48 = 500 nm. A photon of wavelength longer than 500 nm carries less than 2.48 eV and cannot lift an electron across the gap, however intense the beam.
formula_principle: lambda_max = hc / Eg, with hc = 1240 eV nm when Eg is in eV and lambda in nm.
common_misconception: Learners multiply hc by the gap instead of dividing, so the wavelength comes out thousands of times too large.

concept_tested: Minimum photon frequency for band to band excitation
stem: The minimum frequency of a photon that can excite an electron across a forbidden gap of 1.32 eV is (take h = 6.6 x 10^-34 J s and 1 eV = 1.6 x 10^-19 J)
formula_principle: Eg = h nu_min, so nu_min = Eg / h with Eg in joule.
common_misconception: Students forget to convert the gap from eV to joule before dividing by Planck constant.

concept_tested: Condition on band filling for an electron to conduct
stem: An electron contributes to electric conduction in a solid only when it is
option_a: in a band that is not completely filled, with empty states lying immediately above it
option_b: in a completely filled band, where every allowed state is occupied
option_c: in the forbidden gap, midway between the valence and conduction bands
option_d: bound in the innermost shell of an atom of the crystal
correct_answer_text: in a band that is not completely filled, with empty states lying immediately above it
solution: An electric field can change an electron energy only slightly. If the band is full there is no vacant state at a slightly higher energy, so the field cannot accelerate the electron and no current flows. Only a partly filled band, or a band with a few electrons in it, supports conduction.
formula_principle: Conduction requires empty allowed states immediately above the occupied ones so that carriers can gain energy from the field.
common_misconception: Learners believe that any electron in the solid can be pushed along by a field, whatever the band occupation.

concept_tested: Link between excitation across the gap and the creation of holes
stem: Consider two statements about a pure semiconductor at room temperature. The first says that a few electrons cross the forbidden gap. The second says that each such electron leaves a vacancy behind in the valence band. The correct verdict is
option_a: both statements are correct, but the second describes the origin of donor ions rather than of holes
option_b: the first is correct while the second is wrong, since the valence band stays completely full
option_c: the first is wrong while the second is correct, since bonds break only above 500 K
option_d: both statements are correct, and the second describes the origin of holes
correct_answer_text: both statements are correct, and the second describes the origin of holes
solution: At room temperature a small fraction of the valence electrons acquire enough thermal energy to reach the conduction band. Each such electron leaves an empty state in the valence band. That vacancy is a hole, so the process always creates carriers in pairs and keeps the electron and hole concentrations equal in a pure sample.
formula_principle: Thermal excitation across Eg creates one conduction electron and one valence band vacancy, that is one electron hole pair.
common_misconception: Students accept that electrons reach the conduction band but forget that the vacancy left behind is itself a carrier.

concept_tested: Comparison of bond breaking energies of germanium and silicon
stem: The energy required to break a covalent bond in germanium, compared with that in silicon, is
option_c: the same for both, roughly 1.1 eV in each case
solution: Breaking a covalent bond means lifting a valence electron across the forbidden gap into the conduction band, so the bond energy equals Eg. For germanium this is about 0.7 eV and for silicon about 1.1 eV, which is why germanium devices are more sensitive to temperature.
formula_principle: The forbidden gap of a semiconductor equals the energy needed to break one covalent bond.
common_misconception: Learners quote the small donor ionisation energy of a doped crystal in place of the band gap of the host.

concept_tested: Effect of illumination on the resistance of a semiconductor
stem: A slab of pure silicon of forbidden gap 1.1 eV is first kept in the dark and its resistance measured. It is then illuminated with light whose photons each carry 2 eV. The resistance of the slab
option_a: falls, because photons of 2 eV exceed the gap and create extra electron hole pairs
option_b: rises, because the absorbed photons heat the lattice and hinder the motion of the carriers
option_c: stays unchanged, because light cannot alter the number of charge carriers inside a solid
option_d: falls, because photons of 2 eV knock electrons right out of the surface of the slab
correct_answer_text: falls, because photons of 2 eV exceed the gap and create extra electron hole pairs
solution: Each photon carries 2 eV, which is more than the 1.1 eV gap, so it can be absorbed by a valence electron and lift it into the conduction band. Every such event adds one free electron and one hole. The carrier concentration therefore rises above the thermal value, the conductivity rises and the measured resistance falls.
formula_principle: Photons of energy greater than Eg are absorbed and generate electron hole pairs, raising the conductivity.
common_misconception: Students confuse internal band to band excitation with photoelectric emission from the surface.

concept_tested: Band gap criterion for a semiconductor
stem: A solid is usually classed as a semiconductor when its forbidden gap is
option_c: less than about 3 eV but not zero
correct_answer_text: less than about 3 eV but not zero
solution: The dividing line is set by whether thermal energy at ordinary temperatures can lift an appreciable number of electrons across the gap. Gaps up to about 3 eV allow this to a measurable extent, so silicon at 1.1 eV and germanium at 0.7 eV are semiconductors, while diamond at 5.4 eV is an insulator.
formula_principle: Semiconductors have 0 less than Eg less than about 3 eV; conductors have no gap; insulators have Eg above about 3 eV.
common_misconception: Learners forget the lower limit and call a metal with overlapping bands a semiconductor of zero gap.

concept_tested: Deciding whether a given photon can excite two different semiconductors
stem: Light of wavelength 620 nm falls on separate samples of silicon of gap 1.1 eV and germanium of gap 0.7 eV. Taking hc = 1240 eV nm, the light
option_a: carries 2 eV per photon and can create electron hole pairs in both samples
option_b: carries 2 eV per photon and can create pairs in germanium only
option_c: carries 0.5 eV per photon and can create pairs in neither sample
option_d: carries 2 eV per photon and can create pairs in silicon only
correct_answer_text: carries 2 eV per photon and can create electron hole pairs in both samples
solution: E = 1240 / 620 = 2 eV per photon. Since 2 eV is greater than 1.1 eV and also greater than 0.7 eV, the photon can lift an electron across the gap in either material, so pairs are created in both samples.
formula_principle: E = hc / lambda, and band to band excitation occurs when E is at least Eg.
common_misconception: Students test the photon energy against only one of the two gaps and forget that the smaller gap is easier to cross.

concept_tested: Threshold wavelengths for two different gaps
stem: Two semiconductor samples have forbidden gaps of 1.24 eV and 0.62 eV. With hc = 1240 eV nm, the longest wavelengths that can just create an electron hole pair in them are respectively
solution: For the first sample lambda_max = 1240 / 1.24 = 1000 nm. For the second lambda_max = 1240 / 0.62 = 2000 nm. Halving the gap doubles the threshold wavelength, so the narrower gap material responds to longer wavelength infrared light.
formula_principle: lambda_max = hc / Eg, so the threshold wavelength varies inversely as the band gap.
common_misconception: Learners suppose that a smaller gap corresponds to a smaller threshold wavelength.

concept_tested: Conduction in a divalent metal with a filled valence band
stem: In a divalent metal the valence band is completely filled, and yet the metal conducts extremely well. The reason is that
option_a: a completely filled band by itself can carry a current once a field is applied
option_b: the forbidden gap of such a metal is about 1 eV and is crossed easily at room temperature
option_c: the empty conduction band overlaps the filled valence band, so unoccupied states lie immediately above the filled ones
option_d: the metal contains pentavalent impurities that donate electrons to its conduction band
correct_answer_text: the empty conduction band overlaps the filled valence band, so unoccupied states lie immediately above the filled ones
solution: Counting electrons alone would suggest that a divalent metal has a full valence band and should be an insulator. In the real crystal the next band dips down and overlaps the valence band in energy, so electrons spill into it and both bands end up partly filled. Vacant states then lie immediately above occupied ones and conduction is easy.
formula_principle: Metallic conduction requires either a partly filled band or an overlap of a filled band with an empty one.
common_misconception: Students conclude from a filled valence band alone that the solid must be an insulator.

concept_tested: Comparing band occupation at 300 K with that at 0 K
stem: Which comparison of a pure semiconductor at 300 K with the same semiconductor at 0 K is correct?
option_a: at 300 K the conduction band is half filled and the valence band is half empty
option_b: at 300 K some electrons occupy states inside the forbidden gap of the pure crystal
option_c: at 300 K the conduction band holds electrons while the valence band still remains completely full
option_d: at 300 K a small number of electrons occupy the conduction band and an equal number of vacancies exist in the valence band
correct_answer_text: at 300 K a small number of electrons occupy the conduction band and an equal number of vacancies exist in the valence band
solution: At 0 K the valence band is full and the conduction band empty. At 300 K roughly one valence electron in 10^12 is excited across the gap. The conduction band therefore holds a small number n_i of electrons and the valence band holds the same number n_i of vacancies, so the two bands are still almost completely full and almost completely empty respectively.
formula_principle: Thermal excitation transfers a very small equal number of electrons and vacancies between the two bands.
common_misconception: Learners exaggerate the fraction of electrons excited and picture the bands as substantially redistributed.

concept_tested: Why a wide gap solid has far fewer conduction electrons
stem: Diamond of gap 5.4 eV and silicon of gap 1.1 eV have the same crystal structure. At room temperature the ratio of their conduction electron populations is enormous. The best physical reason is that
option_a: the number excited across a gap falls off in direct proportion to the gap, so the ratio is close to five
option_b: diamond has far fewer atoms per unit volume than silicon and therefore fewer electrons in total
option_c: diamond has no valence electrons available for excitation while silicon has four per atom
option_d: the number of electrons excited across a gap falls off exponentially as the gap grows, and 5.4 eV is far beyond the thermal energy available at 300 K
correct_answer_text: the number of electrons excited across a gap falls off exponentially as the gap grows, and 5.4 eV is far beyond the thermal energy available at 300 K
solution: The fraction of electrons able to cross a gap is governed by an exponential factor in which the gap is compared with the thermal energy k T, about 0.026 eV at 300 K. Increasing the gap from 1.1 eV to 5.4 eV increases the exponent by a factor of about five, and since the dependence is exponential the population drops by many tens of powers of ten. Diamond is therefore an excellent insulator.
formula_principle: The thermally excited carrier concentration varies as exp(-Eg / 2 k T), so it is exponentially sensitive to Eg.
common_misconception: Students treat the carrier population as linearly related to the band gap instead of exponentially.

concept_tested: Excess energy of an electron excited by an energetic photon
stem: A photon of wavelength 400 nm is absorbed by a semiconductor of forbidden gap 2.0 eV. Taking hc = 1240 eV nm, the energy handed to the excited electron over and above the bottom of the conduction band is about
solution: E_photon = 1240 / 400 = 3.1 eV. Of this, 2.0 eV is used up in lifting the electron across the forbidden gap, so the electron arrives in the conduction band with about 3.1 - 2.0 = 1.1 eV of extra energy, which it then loses to the lattice as it settles to the band edge.
formula_principle: E_photon = hc / lambda; excess energy = E_photon minus Eg.
common_misconception: Learners quote the full photon energy as the kinetic energy and forget that the gap must first be paid for.

concept_tested: Nature of the bonding in pure silicon and germanium
stem: The crystals of pure silicon and germanium are held together by
option_a: ionic bonds between positive and negative ions formed by transfer of electrons
option_b: covalent bonds, each atom sharing its four valence electrons with four neighbouring atoms
option_c: metallic bonds in which all the valence electrons form a common free pool
option_d: hydrogen bonds between neighbouring atoms of the lattice
correct_answer_text: covalent bonds, each atom sharing its four valence electrons with four neighbouring atoms
solution: Each silicon or germanium atom has four valence electrons. It shares one electron with each of four neighbours, so every atom finds itself with a stable set of eight shared electrons. All the valence electrons are locked in these bonds, which is why a pure crystal is an insulator at 0 K.
formula_principle: Silicon and germanium are tetravalent and form four covalent bonds per atom in a tetrahedral lattice.
common_misconception: Students describe silicon bonding as metallic because silicon conducts a little at room temperature.

concept_tested: Relation between electron and hole concentrations in a pure sample
stem: In a pure semiconductor at any temperature above absolute zero,
option_a: the electron concentration is very much larger than the hole concentration
option_b: the hole concentration is very much larger than the electron concentration
option_c: the electron concentration equals the hole concentration
option_d: holes are present but free electrons are entirely absent
correct_answer_text: the electron concentration equals the hole concentration
solution: In a pure crystal the only source of carriers is the breaking of covalent bonds, and every broken bond releases exactly one electron and leaves exactly one hole. The two concentrations must therefore be equal, and their common value is called the intrinsic carrier concentration n_i.
formula_principle: n_e = n_h = n_i in an intrinsic semiconductor.
common_misconception: Learners assume electrons always outnumber holes because electrons are the more familiar carriers.

concept_tested: Physical meaning of a hole
stem: A hole in a semiconductor is
option_a: a positively charged particle of the same mass as a proton sitting in the lattice
option_b: a vacancy left in a covalent bond when an electron leaves it, behaving as a carrier of positive charge
option_c: an atom of the crystal that has lost its nucleus
option_d: an empty lattice site from which a whole atom is missing
correct_answer_text: a vacancy left in a covalent bond when an electron leaves it, behaving as a carrier of positive charge
solution: When thermal energy breaks a covalent bond the freed electron wanders through the crystal, and the incomplete bond it leaves behind is short of one electron. Relative to the neutral crystal that site carries a net positive charge of magnitude e, and because a neighbouring bonding electron can jump into it the vacancy itself moves. It is therefore treated as a mobile positive carrier.
formula_principle: A hole is the vacancy in a broken covalent bond and carries an effective charge of +e.
common_misconception: Students imagine a hole as a real positive particle rather than as a missing electron in a bond.

concept_tested: Direction in which holes drift in an applied field
stem: In a semiconductor placed in an electric field, the holes move
option_a: in the same direction as the electrons
option_b: opposite to the conventional current, alongside the electrons
option_c: in the direction of the conventional current, that is opposite to the electrons
option_d: at right angles to the applied field
correct_answer_text: in the direction of the conventional current, that is opposite to the electrons
solution: The applied field pushes the positively charged hole along the field direction, which is the direction of conventional current, and pushes the negatively charged electron the opposite way. Because their charges are also opposite, the two motions give current contributions in the same sense, and they add.
formula_principle: Force on a hole is +eE along the field; force on an electron is -eE opposite to the field.
common_misconception: Learners assume both carriers move the same way because both contribute to the same current.

concept_tested: Free electron count in pure silicon at absolute zero
stem: In a pure silicon crystal at 0 K the number of free electrons is
option_a: equal to the number of atoms, since each atom releases one electron
option_b: zero, since every valence electron is locked in a covalent bond
option_c: four times the number of atoms, since each atom has four valence electrons
option_d: about 10^16 per cubic metre, the same as at room temperature
correct_answer_text: zero, since every valence electron is locked in a covalent bond
solution: At 0 K no thermal energy is available to break a bond. Each of the four valence electrons of every silicon atom is shared in a covalent bond and none is free. Hence there are no free electrons and no holes, and the crystal is a perfect insulator.
formula_principle: At 0 K all bonds are intact, so n_e = n_h = 0 in a pure semiconductor.
common_misconception: Students count the four valence electrons per atom as free electrons.

concept_tested: Why the carrier concentration is steady at a fixed temperature
stem: At a fixed temperature the carrier concentration of a pure semiconductor stays steady because
option_a: once an electron hole pair has been generated it can never recombine
option_b: generation stops as soon as a fixed number of pairs has been produced
option_c: electron hole pairs are generated and recombine at exactly equal rates
option_d: every electron that is freed immediately leaves the crystal through its surface
correct_answer_text: electron hole pairs are generated and recombine at exactly equal rates
solution: Thermal agitation continually breaks bonds and creates pairs, while free electrons continually meet broken bonds and recombine, destroying pairs. At a given temperature the two rates settle to the same value, so the concentrations stay constant even though individual carriers are constantly being created and destroyed.
formula_principle: Dynamic equilibrium: rate of thermal generation of pairs equals rate of recombination at a given temperature.
common_misconception: Learners think of the carriers as a fixed set of particles rather than as a population in dynamic equilibrium.

concept_tested: Total number of mobile carriers in a given volume
stem: The intrinsic carrier concentration of a pure semiconductor at 300 K is 2 x 10^19 m^-3. The total number of mobile charge carriers in a sample of volume 1 cm^3 is
solution: 1 cm^3 = 10^-6 m^3. Electrons in this volume = 2 x 10^19 x 10^-6 = 2 x 10^13, and there are equally many holes. Total mobile carriers = 2 x 2 x 10^13 = 4 x 10^13.
formula_principle: Total carriers = (n_e + n_h) V = 2 n_i V for an intrinsic sample.
common_misconception: Students forget that a pure sample contains an equal number of holes as well as electrons.

concept_tested: Conductivity of a pure semiconductor from n_i and the two mobilities
stem: A pure semiconductor has n_i = 2.5 x 10^19 m^-3, electron mobility 0.36 m^2 V^-1 s^-1 and hole mobility 0.14 m^2 V^-1 s^-1. Taking e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, its conductivity is
solution: mu_e + mu_h = 0.36 + 0.14 = 0.50 m^2 V^-1 s^-1. Then sigma = e n_i (mu_e + mu_h) = 1.6 x 10^-19 x 2.5 x 10^19 x 0.50 = 4.0 x 0.50 = 2.0 S m^-1, so the resistivity is 0.5 ohm m.
formula_principle: sigma = e n_i (mu_e + mu_h) for an intrinsic semiconductor.
common_misconception: Learners include only the electron term, forgetting that holes carry a comparable share of the current.

concept_tested: Fraction of atoms with a broken bond at room temperature
stem: A silicon crystal contains 5 x 10^28 atoms per cubic metre, and at 300 K its intrinsic carrier concentration is 1.5 x 10^16 m^-3. The fraction of the atoms that have a broken covalent bond is about
solution: Fraction = (1.5 x 10^16) / (5 x 10^28) = 0.3 x 10^-12 = 3 x 10^-13. So only about three atoms in every ten million million have lost a bonding electron, which is why pure silicon is such a poor conductor.
formula_principle: Fraction = n_i divided by the atomic number density.
common_misconception: Students invert the ratio and obtain an impossibly large fraction greater than one.

concept_tested: How hole current is actually carried
stem: Hole conduction in a pure semiconductor takes place because
option_a: the hole is a real particle that is pushed along by the field just like a free electron in vacuum
option_b: a valence electron of a neighbouring bond jumps into the vacancy, and the vacancy itself shifts the other way
option_c: the positively charged lattice ions drift slowly through the crystal towards the negative terminal
option_d: the nucleus of a silicon atom migrates towards the negative terminal
correct_answer_text: a valence electron of a neighbouring bond jumps into the vacancy, and the vacancy itself shifts the other way
solution: When a bond is broken the vacancy can be filled by an electron from an adjacent bond. That bond is then incomplete instead, so the vacancy has effectively moved one step in the direction opposite to the electron jump. Repeating this, the vacancy drifts along the field and behaves exactly like a mobile positive charge.
formula_principle: Hole motion is the successive transfer of bound valence electrons into neighbouring vacancies.
common_misconception: Learners take the hole to be a genuine positive particle instead of a description of bound electron motion.

concept_tested: Shape of the conductivity against temperature curve
stem: For a pure semiconductor, the graph of electrical conductivity against absolute temperature is best described as
option_a: a straight line that falls uniformly as the temperature increases
option_b: a curve that rises, with the rise becoming steeper as the temperature increases
option_c: a horizontal straight line, since conductivity is a fixed property of the material
option_d: a curve that falls steeply at first and then levels off
correct_answer_text: a curve that rises, with the rise becoming steeper as the temperature increases
solution: The carrier concentration of a pure semiconductor grows with temperature through an exponential factor, and the conductivity follows it. The curve therefore starts near zero at very low temperature and climbs, its slope increasing steadily, which is the opposite of the gently falling straight line characteristic of a metal.
formula_principle: n_i varies as exp(-Eg / 2 k T), so sigma rises rapidly and with increasing steepness as T increases.
common_misconception: Students draw the metallic behaviour, a straight line of negative slope, for a semiconductor as well.

concept_tested: Relative mobilities of electrons and holes
stem: In the same semiconductor at the same temperature,
option_a: the mobility of the holes is greater than the mobility of the electrons
option_b: the mobility of the electrons is greater than the mobility of the holes
option_c: the two mobilities are exactly equal because the two concentrations are equal in a pure sample
option_d: the holes have no mobility at all, since they are not real particles
correct_answer_text: the mobility of the electrons is greater than the mobility of the holes
solution: A free electron in the conduction band moves through the crystal almost unhindered except by scattering. A hole moves only by successive jumps of bound valence electrons into the vacancy, a more sluggish process. Hence for the same field the electron drift speed is larger, and mu_e exceeds mu_h in both silicon and germanium.
formula_principle: mu_e is greater than mu_h in silicon and germanium; for germanium mu_e is about 0.39 and mu_h about 0.19 m^2 V^-1 s^-1.
common_misconception: Learners assume equal concentrations of the two carriers must imply equal mobilities as well.

concept_tested: How the two carrier currents combine
stem: In a pure semiconductor carrying a steady current, the electron current and the hole current
option_a: flow in opposite directions and cancel each other, leaving zero net current
option_b: are exactly equal in magnitude, because the two mobilities are equal
option_c: flow in opposite directions as motions but add together as currents, because the carriers have opposite charges
option_d: consist entirely of hole current, since the electrons stay bound in the lattice
correct_answer_text: flow in opposite directions as motions but add together as currents, because the carriers have opposite charges
solution: The field drives electrons one way and holes the other. A negative charge moving one way is equivalent to a positive charge moving the opposite way, so both motions correspond to conventional current in the same sense. The two contributions therefore add, and because mu_e exceeds mu_h the electrons carry the larger share.
formula_principle: I = I_e + I_h, since reversing both the sign of the charge and the direction of motion leaves the current direction unchanged.
common_misconception: Students subtract the two contributions because the carriers physically move in opposite directions.

concept_tested: Current from intrinsic conductivity, field and area
stem: A bar of pure germanium of cross sectional area 2 x 10^-4 m^2 has n_i = 2.5 x 10^19 m^-3, mu_e = 0.36 m^2 V^-1 s^-1 and mu_h = 0.14 m^2 V^-1 s^-1. A uniform field of 500 V m^-1 is set up along its length. Taking e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, the current in the bar is
formula_principle: sigma = e n_i (mu_e + mu_h); J = sigma E; I = J A.
common_misconception: Learners stop after finding the current density and report it as the current.

concept_tested: Resistance of a rod given its conductivity and dimensions
stem: A rod of pure semiconductor has length 0.1 m, cross sectional area 1 x 10^-4 m^2 and conductivity 2 S m^-1. The resistance offered by the rod is
solution: rho = 1 / sigma = 0.5 ohm m. Then R = rho l / A = 0.5 x 0.1 / (1 x 10^-4) = 0.05 / 10^-4 = 500 ohm. Equivalently R = l / (sigma A) = 0.1 / (2 x 10^-4) = 500 ohm.
formula_principle: R = rho l / A with rho = 1 / sigma, so R = l / (sigma A).
common_misconception: Students substitute the conductivity directly into R = rho l / A without first taking its reciprocal.

concept_tested: Conclusion from unequal carrier concentrations
stem: A sample believed to be a pure semiconductor is found to have unequal electron and hole concentrations. The only acceptable conclusion is that
option_a: the mass action law has broken down at the temperature of the measurement
option_b: the sample has been cooled below the temperature at which holes can exist
option_c: charge is not conserved in semiconductors
option_d: the sample is not truly pure and contains some doping impurity
correct_answer_text: the sample is not truly pure and contains some doping impurity
solution: In a pure crystal every carrier generating event produces one electron and one hole together, so the two concentrations must stay equal. An excess of one type can only be balanced by fixed ionised impurity centres of the opposite sign, which means donors or acceptors are present. The sample is therefore extrinsic.
formula_principle: In an intrinsic sample carriers appear only in pairs, so n_e = n_h; any inequality requires ionised impurities.
common_misconception: Learners look for exotic explanations rather than the simple one that the crystal is not pure.

subtopic: Comparing n_i of Si and Ge
concept_tested: Reason for the very different intrinsic concentrations of Ge and Si
stem: At the same temperature the intrinsic carrier concentration of germanium is about a thousand times that of silicon. This is because
option_a: germanium has a thousand times as many atoms per unit volume as silicon
option_b: germanium has the smaller forbidden gap, and the pair concentration depends exponentially on the gap
option_c: germanium atoms have more valence electrons than silicon atoms
option_d: germanium has the larger forbidden gap, and a larger gap releases more electron hole pairs
correct_answer_text: germanium has the smaller forbidden gap, and the pair concentration depends exponentially on the gap
solution: The gap of germanium is 0.7 eV against 1.1 eV for silicon, a difference of 0.4 eV. With k T about 0.026 eV at 300 K, this difference appears in an exponential factor and multiplies the carrier concentration by roughly a thousand. Hence n_i for germanium is about 2.4 x 10^19 m^-3 while for silicon it is about 1.5 x 10^16 m^-3.
formula_principle: n_i varies as exp(-Eg / 2 k T), so a change of a few tenths of an eV in Eg alters n_i by orders of magnitude.
common_misconception: Students attribute the difference to the number of atoms or of valence electrons rather than to the band gap.

concept_tested: Fraction of the intrinsic current carried by electrons
stem: In a pure semiconductor the electron mobility is 0.38 m^2 V^-1 s^-1 and the hole mobility is 0.19 m^2 V^-1 s^-1. The fraction of the total current carried by the electrons is
solution: Electron current is proportional to n_i mu_e and hole current to n_i mu_h. The electron share is therefore mu_e / (mu_e + mu_h) = 0.38 / (0.38 + 0.19) = 0.38 / 0.57 = 2/3. The holes carry the remaining one third.
formula_principle: In an intrinsic sample the current share of each carrier is proportional to its mobility, since the concentrations are equal.
common_misconception: Learners report the ratio of the two currents when the question asks for a fraction of the total.

concept_tested: Behaviour of the current as a pure semiconductor is cooled
stem: A pure semiconductor sample is cooled steadily from 400 K towards 0 K while a fixed potential difference is maintained across it. The current through it
option_a: rises steadily, because the mobility of the carriers rises as lattice scattering weakens
option_b: falls steadily and approaches zero, because the number of thermally generated pairs falls towards zero
option_c: stays constant, because the sample is pure and its carrier number is therefore fixed
option_d: first falls and then rises again once the sample has become an insulator
correct_answer_text: falls steadily and approaches zero, because the number of thermally generated pairs falls towards zero
solution: Cooling has two competing effects. Mobility increases because lattice vibrations weaken, which alone would raise the current. But the pair concentration contains an exponential factor in the gap divided by the thermal energy, and as the temperature falls this factor collapses. The carrier number therefore wins decisively, the conductivity falls towards zero and the current vanishes as 0 K is approached.
formula_principle: sigma = e n_i (mu_e + mu_h); n_i falls exponentially on cooling while mu rises only slowly.
common_misconception: Students see only the rise in mobility on cooling and predict a larger current.

concept_tested: Combining carrier and mobility changes to find the new conductivity
stem: The conductivity of a pure semiconductor at 300 K is 4 S m^-1. At 350 K its carrier concentration becomes 5 times larger while both mobilities fall to 60 percent of their earlier values. Its conductivity at 350 K is
solution: Conductivity is proportional to n multiplied by mobility. The factor by which it changes is 5 x 0.60 = 3. Hence the new conductivity is 4 x 3 = 12 S m^-1, which is larger than before even though the mobility has fallen.
formula_principle: sigma = e n (mu_e + mu_h), so sigma is proportional to the product of carrier concentration and mobility.
common_misconception: Learners apply only one of the two changes, or divide by the mobility factor instead of multiplying.

concept_tested: Meaning of doping
stem: Doping a semiconductor means
option_a: heating a pure semiconductor until its carrier concentration has doubled
option_b: removing every last trace of impurity from a semiconductor crystal
option_c: adding a small controlled amount of a suitable impurity to an otherwise pure crystal
option_d: applying a strong electric field across a semiconductor crystal
correct_answer_text: adding a small controlled amount of a suitable impurity to an otherwise pure crystal
solution: Doping is the deliberate addition of a tiny, carefully controlled amount of a pentavalent or trivalent element to a very pure semiconductor. Even one impurity atom in a million raises the conductivity enormously and fixes which type of carrier is in the majority.
formula_principle: Doping introduces about one impurity atom per 10^6 to 10^8 host atoms to fix the majority carrier type.
common_misconception: Students think doping means any contamination, rather than a controlled addition of a chosen valency.

concept_tested: Result of doping silicon with a pentavalent element
stem: Silicon doped with arsenic becomes
option_a: p type material, with holes as the majority carriers
option_b: n type material, with electrons as the majority carriers
option_c: n type material, with holes as the majority carriers
option_d: p type material, with electrons as the majority carriers
correct_answer_text: n type material, with electrons as the majority carriers
solution: Arsenic is pentavalent. Four of its five valence electrons complete covalent bonds with the neighbouring silicon atoms, and the fifth is only very loosely held. It is released at room temperature into the conduction band, so free electrons greatly outnumber holes and the material is n type.
formula_principle: Pentavalent dopants such as P, As and Sb are donors and produce n type material.
common_misconception: Learners memorise the letters n and p without linking them to the sign of the majority carrier.

concept_tested: Identifying a set of trivalent dopants
stem: Which set contains only trivalent dopants?
solution: Boron, aluminium, gallium and indium each have three valence electrons, so when one replaces a silicon atom one of the four bonds is left short of an electron. That incomplete bond is an acceptor site, and the material becomes p type.
formula_principle: Trivalent acceptors: B, Al, Ga, In. Pentavalent donors: P, As, Sb, Bi.
common_misconception: Students confuse the list of trivalent acceptors with the list of pentavalent donors.

concept_tested: Why a pentavalent atom is called a donor
