stem: A pentavalent impurity atom in a silicon crystal is called a donor because
option_a: four of its valence electrons form covalent bonds and the fifth is very easily released to the crystal
option_b: it accepts an electron from a neighbouring silicon atom and so creates a hole
option_c: it donates a proton to the silicon lattice
option_d: it gives up all five of its valence electrons to the conduction band at room temperature
correct_answer_text: four of its valence electrons form covalent bonds and the fifth is very easily released to the crystal
solution: A pentavalent atom sits in a silicon site and uses four of its five valence electrons to complete the four covalent bonds. The fifth electron has no bond to join and is held only weakly by the parent atom, needing about 0.05 eV to break away. At room temperature it is released, so the atom donates a conduction electron.
formula_principle: A donor supplies one extra electron that needs only about 0.05 eV to reach the conduction band.
common_misconception: Learners believe all five valence electrons of a donor become free.

concept_tested: Majority and minority carriers in p type material
stem: In a p type semiconductor the majority carriers and the minority carriers are respectively
solution: A trivalent dopant leaves one covalent bond short of an electron, creating a hole for every acceptor atom. Holes therefore vastly outnumber electrons and are the majority carriers. The few electrons present come only from thermal breaking of host bonds and are the minority carriers.
formula_principle: In p type material n_h is much greater than n_e; the small electron population is thermally generated.
common_misconception: Students count the immobile ionised impurity centres among the charge carriers.

concept_tested: Net charge on an n type sample
stem: An n type semiconductor sample taken as a whole is
option_a: negatively charged, because it contains extra free electrons
option_b: positively charged, because it contains fixed positive donor ions
option_c: electrically neutral at every point and at all times
option_d: negatively charged only while a current is flowing through it
correct_answer_text: electrically neutral at every point and at all times
solution: The donor atoms are added as neutral atoms. When one releases its extra electron it becomes a fixed positive ion, but the electron released remains within the same crystal. Adding up all the charges therefore gives zero, and the sample is electrically neutral even though it is rich in mobile electrons.
formula_principle: Doping adds neutral atoms, so the crystal stays neutral: n_e = N_D positive ions plus n_h.
common_misconception: Learners assume the names n type and p type refer to a net charge on the material.

concept_tested: Position of the acceptor level in the band diagram
stem: In a p type semiconductor the acceptor energy level lies
option_a: just below the bottom of the conduction band
option_b: just above the top of the valence band
option_c: exactly at the middle of the forbidden gap
correct_answer_text: just above the top of the valence band
solution: The trivalent impurity provides an empty state a very small energy above the valence band edge. A valence electron needs only about 0.05 eV to jump into it, which thermal energy easily supplies at room temperature. The electron leaves a hole behind in the valence band and the impurity becomes a fixed negative ion.
formula_principle: Acceptor levels lie about 0.05 eV above the valence band edge; donor levels lie about 0.05 eV below the conduction band edge.
common_misconception: Students place the acceptor level near the conduction band, confusing it with a donor level.

concept_tested: Consequence of the donor level lying just below the conduction band
stem: In an n type semiconductor the donor level lies just below the conduction band. The practical consequence is that
option_a: about 1.1 eV is needed, so the extra electron stays bound until the crystal is heated strongly
option_b: the extra electron falls into the valence band and produces a hole there
option_c: the donor atom becomes negatively charged once the electron has been released
option_d: only about 0.05 eV is needed to move the extra electron into the conduction band, so it is already free at room temperature
correct_answer_text: only about 0.05 eV is needed to move the extra electron into the conduction band, so it is already free at room temperature
solution: Thermal energy at 300 K is about 0.026 eV, comparable with the 0.05 eV donor ionisation energy but tiny compared with the 1.1 eV band gap. Practically every donor is therefore ionised at room temperature, and the electron concentration is close to the donor concentration.
formula_principle: Donor ionisation energy is about 0.05 eV in Si and about 0.01 eV in Ge, far smaller than the band gap.
common_misconception: Learners assume the donor electron must cross the whole forbidden gap to become free.

concept_tested: State of a donor atom after it has released its electron
stem: When the extra electron of a donor atom enters the conduction band, the donor atom left behind is
option_a: a negative ion that is fixed in the lattice and cannot move
option_b: a positive ion that is fixed in the lattice and cannot move
option_c: a positive ion that is free to drift towards the negative terminal
option_d: a neutral atom, since the released electron is still inside the crystal
correct_answer_text: a positive ion that is fixed in the lattice and cannot move
solution: The donor atom is covalently bonded into the lattice. When its fifth electron leaves, the atom retains its full nuclear charge but one fewer electron, so it becomes a positive ion. Being locked into the crystal it cannot contribute to conduction, but it does keep the crystal electrically neutral overall.
formula_principle: Ionised donors are immobile positive charges; ionised acceptors are immobile negative charges.
common_misconception: Students count the ionised donors as mobile positive carriers alongside the holes.

concept_tested: Minority carrier concentration in a doped sample
stem: A silicon sample has n_i = 1.5 x 10^16 m^-3. It is doped so that its electron concentration becomes 4.5 x 10^22 m^-3. Its hole concentration is then
solution: n_i^2 = (1.5 x 10^16)^2 = 2.25 x 10^32 m^-6. Then n_h = n_i^2 / n_e = (2.25 x 10^32) / (4.5 x 10^22) = 0.5 x 10^10 = 5 x 10^9 m^-3. The holes are now more than ten million million times fewer than the electrons.
formula_principle: n_e n_h = n_i^2.
common_misconception: Learners assume that doping leaves the minority carrier concentration at its intrinsic value.

concept_tested: Donor concentration from a stated doping ratio
stem: A silicon crystal contains 5 x 10^28 atoms per cubic metre. It is doped with phosphorus in the ratio of one phosphorus atom for every 10^7 silicon atoms. The donor concentration is
solution: N_D = (5 x 10^28) / 10^7 = 5 x 10^21 m^-3. Even this very light doping puts about a hundred thousand times more electrons into the crystal than the intrinsic value of 1.5 x 10^16 m^-3.
formula_principle: N_D = (atomic number density) divided by (doping ratio).
common_misconception: Students multiply by the doping ratio instead of dividing by it.

concept_tested: Hole concentration in a lightly doped n type sample
stem: An n type silicon sample has an electron concentration of 5 x 10^21 m^-3, and for the same material n_i = 1.5 x 10^16 m^-3. Its hole concentration is
formula_principle: n_h = n_i^2 / n_e.
common_misconception: Learners forget to square n_i before dividing by the majority carrier concentration.

concept_tested: Neutrality condition for an n type sample
stem: For an n type semiconductor containing donors only, the condition of electrical neutrality is
option_a: n_e = N_D + n_h, where N_D is the concentration of ionised donors
option_b: n_e = N_D - n_h, where N_D is the concentration of ionised donors
option_c: n_e = n_h, whatever the donor concentration may be
option_d: n_e + N_D = n_h, where N_D is the concentration of ionised donors
correct_answer_text: n_e = N_D + n_h, where N_D is the concentration of ionised donors
solution: The mobile negative charges are the electrons, of concentration n_e. The positive charges are the mobile holes, of concentration n_h, together with the fixed ionised donors, of concentration N_D. Neutrality of the crystal requires n_e = N_D + n_h, which for heavy doping reduces to n_e approximately equal to N_D.
formula_principle: Total negative charge density equals total positive charge density: n_e = N_D(ionised) + n_h.
common_misconception: Students omit the fixed ionised impurity centres from the charge balance.

concept_tested: Effect of heavy doping on conductivity
stem: A silicon sample is doped so that its majority carrier concentration becomes a million times the intrinsic value. Its conductivity
option_a: falls, because the impurity atoms obstruct the motion of the carriers
option_b: rises enormously, because the majority carriers now far outnumber the intrinsic carriers
option_c: stays the same, because the minority carriers fall in exactly the same proportion
option_d: rises by exactly a factor of two, since only one of the two carrier types has changed
correct_answer_text: rises enormously, because the majority carriers now far outnumber the intrinsic carriers
solution: Before doping both concentrations equal n_i. After doping the majority concentration is 10^6 n_i and the minority concentration is n_i divided by 10^6. The majority term therefore dominates and the conductivity rises by roughly a factor of 10^6. This is why doping is the standard way of controlling semiconductor conductivity.
formula_principle: sigma = e (n_e mu_e + n_h mu_h); doping raises one term by many powers of ten.
common_misconception: Learners think that because the product n_e n_h is fixed the conductivity must also be fixed.

concept_tested: Carriers and fixed ions in indium doped germanium
stem: Germanium is doped with indium. The resulting material has
option_a: electrons as majority carriers and positive donor ions fixed in the lattice
option_b: holes as majority carriers and positive donor ions fixed in the lattice
option_c: holes as majority carriers and negative acceptor ions fixed in the lattice
option_d: electrons as majority carriers and negative acceptor ions fixed in the lattice
correct_answer_text: holes as majority carriers and negative acceptor ions fixed in the lattice
solution: Indium is trivalent, so when it replaces a germanium atom one bond is left short of an electron. A neighbouring valence electron fills that bond, which makes the indium atom a fixed negative ion and creates a mobile hole in the valence band. Holes are therefore the majority carriers and the sample is p type.
formula_principle: Trivalent acceptors capture a valence electron, becoming fixed negative ions and leaving mobile holes.
common_misconception: Students give the correct carrier type but the wrong sign for the ionised impurity.

concept_tested: Origin of the minority carriers in an n type sample
stem: The minority carriers in an n type semiconductor are produced
option_a: by the thermal breaking of covalent bonds of the host crystal
option_b: by the pentavalent impurity atoms only
option_c: by the applied electric field only
option_d: only when the material is illuminated by light of a suitable wavelength
correct_answer_text: by the thermal breaking of covalent bonds of the host crystal
solution: Doping fixes the majority carrier concentration but does not stop the thermal breaking of silicon or germanium bonds. Every such event still creates one electron and one hole, and those holes are the minority carriers. Their concentration is set by the mass action law, n_h = n_i^2 / n_e, and it rises rapidly with temperature.
formula_principle: In n type material n_h = n_i^2 / n_e, and these holes come from thermally broken host bonds.
common_misconception: Learners think the dopant supplies both kinds of carrier.

concept_tested: Correcting the loose description of p type material as positive
stem: A p type semiconductor is often described loosely as positive material. The correct statement is that
option_a: it carries a net positive charge equal to the total charge of all its holes
option_b: it carries a net negative charge because the acceptor ions are negative
option_c: it is electrically neutral, the holes being balanced by an equal number of fixed negative acceptor ions
option_d: it becomes positively charged as soon as a battery is connected across it
correct_answer_text: it is electrically neutral, the holes being balanced by an equal number of fixed negative acceptor ions
solution: Each trivalent acceptor is added as a neutral atom. When it captures a valence electron it becomes a negative ion and simultaneously creates one positive hole elsewhere in the crystal. The two charges are equal and opposite and both stay inside the sample, so the material as a whole carries no net charge.
formula_principle: Doping conserves charge, so both n type and p type materials are electrically neutral.
common_misconception: Students read the letter p as meaning that the material carries a positive charge.

concept_tested: Finding n_i from majority and minority concentrations
stem: A doped semiconductor has an electron concentration of 9 x 10^21 m^-3 and a hole concentration of 1 x 10^11 m^-3. The intrinsic concentration of this material is
solution: n_e n_h = (9 x 10^21)(1 x 10^11) = 9 x 10^32 m^-6. Taking the square root, n_i = 3 x 10^16 m^-3. Note that the square root of 10^32 is 10^16, so both the number and the exponent must be treated.
formula_principle: n_i = square root of (n_e n_h).
common_misconception: Learners halve the exponent of a power of ten incorrectly, or take an arithmetic mean instead of a geometric one.

concept_tested: Conductivity from majority carrier concentration and mobility
stem: An n type silicon sample has an electron concentration of 5 x 10^22 m^-3 and an electron mobility of 0.25 m^2 V^-1 s^-1. Its hole concentration is negligible. Taking e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, its conductivity is
solution: e n_e = 1.6 x 10^-19 x 5 x 10^22 = 8.0 x 10^3. Then sigma = 8.0 x 10^3 x 0.25 = 2.0 x 10^3 S m^-1, so the resistivity of the sample is 5 x 10^-4 ohm m, close to metallic values.
formula_principle: sigma = e n_e mu_e when the minority carrier contribution is negligible.
common_misconception: Students stop at the product of charge and carrier concentration and omit the mobility factor.

concept_tested: Ratio of majority to minority carriers for a given doping level
stem: In an n type sample the electron concentration is 10^4 times the intrinsic concentration of the same material. The ratio of the majority carrier concentration to the minority carrier concentration is
solution: Write n_e = 10^4 n_i. The mass action law gives n_h = n_i^2 / n_e = n_i / 10^4. Hence n_e / n_h = (10^4 n_i) divided by (n_i / 10^4) = 10^8. Doping thus improves the carrier ratio by the square of the doping factor.
formula_principle: n_e n_h = n_i^2, so if n_e = k n_i then n_h = n_i / k and n_e / n_h = k^2.
common_misconception: Learners quote the doping factor as the carrier ratio, forgetting that the minority population falls as well.

concept_tested: Effect of increased doping on the minority carrier population
stem: In an n type semiconductor, as the donor concentration is increased at a fixed temperature the hole concentration
option_a: increases in the same proportion, because both carrier types are supplied by the dopant
option_b: decreases, because the product of the two concentrations is fixed at n_i squared
option_c: stays exactly at the intrinsic value, since holes come only from broken host bonds
option_d: becomes exactly zero, since all the bonds are filled by the donated electrons
correct_answer_text: decreases, because the product of the two concentrations is fixed at n_i squared
solution: The extra electrons supplied by the donors increase the chance that a thermally generated hole meets an electron and recombines. Equilibrium is restored at a lower hole concentration, and the balance is expressed by the mass action law n_e n_h = n_i^2. Since n_i depends only on temperature, raising n_e must lower n_h in exact proportion.
formula_principle: n_e n_h = n_i^2 at a fixed temperature, so n_h is inversely proportional to n_e.
common_misconception: Students expect both carrier concentrations to rise together when a crystal is doped more heavily.

subtopic: Comparing n type and p type
concept_tested: Which of two equally doped samples conducts better
stem: Two silicon samples are doped to the same majority carrier concentration, one with phosphorus and the other with boron. At the same temperature
option_a: the boron doped sample has the higher conductivity, because hole mobility exceeds electron mobility
option_b: the phosphorus doped sample has the higher conductivity, because electron mobility exceeds hole mobility
option_c: both samples have exactly the same conductivity, because the carrier concentrations are equal
option_d: the boron doped sample has the higher conductivity, because it also keeps all its free electrons
correct_answer_text: the phosphorus doped sample has the higher conductivity, because electron mobility exceeds hole mobility
solution: Phosphorus is pentavalent and gives n type material in which the majority carriers are electrons, while boron is trivalent and gives p type material with holes as majority carriers. With the same majority concentration the conductivities are in the ratio of the mobilities, and since mu_e exceeds mu_h the n type sample conducts better.
formula_principle: sigma is approximately e n mu for the majority carrier, and mu_e is greater than mu_h.
common_misconception: Learners assume equal doping must mean equal conductivity, forgetting the difference in mobility.

concept_tested: Energy needed to free a donor electron, in joule
stem: The donor level in a doped silicon crystal lies 0.05 eV below the bottom of the conduction band. Taking 1 eV = 1.6 x 10^-19 J, the energy needed to free the extra electron is
solution: E = 0.05 x 1.6 x 10^-19 = 8 x 10^-21 J. For comparison, thermal energy k T at 300 K is about 4 x 10^-21 J, so a large fraction of the donors are ionised at room temperature.
formula_principle: E in joule = E in eV multiplied by 1.6 x 10^-19.
common_misconception: Students substitute the band gap of the host crystal instead of the donor ionisation energy.

concept_tested: Identifying carrier concentration and material type together
stem: A germanium sample with n_i = 2 x 10^19 m^-3 is doped until its hole concentration is 8 x 10^22 m^-3. Its electron concentration and the type of the material are
solution: n_i^2 = (2 x 10^19)^2 = 4 x 10^38 m^-6. Then n_e = n_i^2 / n_h = (4 x 10^38) / (8 x 10^22) = 0.5 x 10^16 = 5 x 10^15 m^-3. Since holes greatly outnumber electrons the material is p type.
formula_principle: n_e n_h = n_i^2; the material is named after whichever carrier is in the majority.
common_misconception: Learners name the material after the carrier that is fewer in number.

concept_tested: Type of a crystal doped with both donors and acceptors
stem: A silicon sample is first doped with phosphorus and then, in a second step, doped with boron so that the acceptor concentration is twice the donor concentration. The final material is
option_a: n type, because the donors were added first and their electrons are already free
option_b: intrinsic, because the two kinds of impurity cancel each other out completely
option_c: p type, because the acceptors in excess of the donors decide the majority carrier
option_d: p type, with a hole concentration equal to the sum of the donor and acceptor concentrations
correct_answer_text: p type, because the acceptors in excess of the donors decide the majority carrier
solution: Electrons released by the donors are captured by acceptor sites, so donor and acceptor doping cancel one for one. With twice as many acceptors as donors, half of the acceptors remain uncompensated and each of these provides a hole. Holes are therefore in the majority and the crystal is p type, with a hole concentration equal to N_A minus N_D.
formula_principle: In a compensated sample the majority carrier concentration is set by the difference between N_A and N_D.
common_misconception: Students believe the impurity added last, or the one added first, decides the type regardless of the numbers.

concept_tested: Minority carrier concentration in a compensated sample
stem: A semiconductor with n_i = 2 x 10^16 m^-3 is doped with donors of concentration 4 x 10^22 m^-3 and acceptors of concentration 3 x 10^22 m^-3. Assuming complete ionisation, and that the majority carrier concentration equals the net doping, the minority carrier concentration is
solution: Net donor concentration = 4 x 10^22 - 3 x 10^22 = 1 x 10^22 m^-3, so the sample is n type with n_e = 1 x 10^22 m^-3. n_i^2 = (2 x 10^16)^2 = 4 x 10^32 m^-6, so the minority carrier concentration is n_h = (4 x 10^32) / (1 x 10^22) = 4 x 10^10 m^-3.
formula_principle: n_e = N_D - N_A for a compensated n type sample, and n_h = n_i^2 / n_e.
common_misconception: Learners use the total donor concentration and forget that the acceptors compensate most of it.

concept_tested: Meaning of carrier mobility
stem: The mobility of a charge carrier in a semiconductor is defined as
option_a: the drift speed acquired by the carrier per unit applied electric field
option_b: the drift speed acquired by the carrier per unit applied potential difference
option_c: the charge carried by the carrier per unit applied electric field
option_d: the current density produced per unit charge of the carrier
correct_answer_text: the drift speed acquired by the carrier per unit applied electric field
solution: Mobility measures how readily a carrier responds to a field. It is the drift speed per unit field, mu = v_d / E, and it is a property of the carrier and the material at a given temperature, independent of the size and shape of the sample.
formula_principle: mu = v_d / E.
common_misconception: Students define mobility with the applied voltage rather than the field, which makes it depend on sample length.

concept_tested: SI unit of carrier mobility
stem: The SI unit of the mobility of a charge carrier is
solution: The drift speed is measured in m s^-1 and the electric field in V m^-1. Dividing gives (m s^-1) x (m V^-1) = m^2 V^-1 s^-1. Typical values are a few tenths of this unit for electrons and holes in silicon and germanium.
formula_principle: mu = v_d / E, so the unit is (m s^-1) divided by (V m^-1).
common_misconception: Learners drop one power of metre by forgetting that the field itself contains a reciprocal length.

concept_tested: Statement of the mass action law
stem: The mass action law for a semiconductor in thermal equilibrium states that
option_a: n_e + n_h = 2 n_i at a given temperature, for pure as well as for doped material
option_b: n_e n_h = n_i^2 at a given temperature, for pure as well as for doped material
option_c: n_e n_h = n_i for doped material only
option_d: n_e divided by n_h equals n_i^2 for doped material only
correct_answer_text: n_e n_h = n_i^2 at a given temperature, for pure as well as for doped material
solution: Doping raises one carrier concentration and lowers the other in such a way that their product remains fixed at the square of the intrinsic concentration for that material and temperature. The relation applies to intrinsic samples too, where n_e = n_h = n_i satisfies it trivially.
formula_principle: n_e n_h = n_i^2 in thermal equilibrium at a given temperature.
common_misconception: Students quote the law as a sum of the two concentrations rather than a product.

concept_tested: Computing mobility from drift speed and field
stem: In a semiconductor a carrier acquires a drift speed of 3 m s^-1 in a uniform field of 15 V m^-1. Its mobility is
solution: mu = v_d / E = 3 / 15 = 0.2 m^2 V^-1 s^-1. This is a typical value for holes in germanium at room temperature.
formula_principle: mu = v_d / E.
common_misconception: Learners invert the defining relation and compute field divided by drift speed.

concept_tested: Drift speed from an applied potential difference and sample length
stem: A potential difference of 2 V is applied across a semiconductor bar of length 1 cm. If the electron mobility is 0.35 m^2 V^-1 s^-1, the electron drift speed is
solution: E = V / l = 2 / (1 x 10^-2) = 200 V m^-1. Then v_d = mu E = 0.35 x 200 = 70 m s^-1. Note how much larger this is than the drift speed of order 10^-4 m s^-1 found in a metal wire, because the carrier concentration here is far smaller.
formula_principle: E = V / l and v_d = mu E.
common_misconception: Students forget to convert the length from centimetre to metre before computing the field.

concept_tested: General expression for the conductivity of a semiconductor
stem: For a semiconductor containing both types of carrier, the conductivity is given by
solution: Each carrier type contributes a current density e n mu E, with its own concentration and its own mobility. The two contributions are in the same sense, so they add, giving sigma = e (n_e mu_e + n_h mu_h). Setting n_e = n_h = n_i recovers the intrinsic result sigma = e n_i (mu_e + mu_h).
formula_principle: sigma = e (n_e mu_e + n_h mu_h); for an intrinsic sample this reduces to e n_i (mu_e + mu_h).
common_misconception: Learners pair the wrong mobility with each concentration, or subtract the two contributions.

concept_tested: Ratio of electron and hole drift speeds in the same field
stem: In a given semiconductor the electron mobility is 0.36 m^2 V^-1 s^-1 and the hole mobility is 0.18 m^2 V^-1 s^-1. In the same applied field the ratio of the electron drift speed to the hole drift speed is
solution: Both carriers experience the same field E, so v_e / v_h = mu_e / mu_h = 0.36 / 0.18 = 2. The electrons therefore drift twice as fast as the holes, which is why electrons carry the larger share of the current in an intrinsic sample.
formula_principle: v_d = mu E, so for a common field v_e / v_h = mu_e / mu_h.
common_misconception: Students think the same field must produce the same drift speed for both carriers.

concept_tested: Carrier motion in the absence of a field
stem: In the absence of an applied electric field, the charge carriers in a semiconductor
option_a: are completely at rest at every point of the crystal
option_b: all move together in one direction with a small drift speed
option_c: move rapidly in random directions, giving zero net current through any section
option_d: move only lengthwise along the sample from one end to the other
correct_answer_text: move rapidly in random directions, giving zero net current through any section
solution: Carriers in a semiconductor share the thermal energy of the lattice and move at high random speeds, colliding frequently. Because all directions are equally likely, the velocities average to zero and no current flows. A field superposes a small common drift velocity v_d = mu E on this random motion, and that drift is the current.
formula_principle: Random thermal motion gives zero average velocity; an applied field superposes a small drift velocity.
common_misconception: Learners believe carriers are motionless until a battery is connected.

concept_tested: Current density from conductivity and field
stem: A semiconductor of conductivity 5 S m^-1 is subjected to a uniform electric field of 40 V m^-1. The current density in it is
solution: J = sigma E = 5 x 40 = 200 A m^-2. To obtain an actual current one would still have to multiply by the area of cross section of the sample.
formula_principle: J = sigma E.
common_misconception: Students report a current density as a current, dropping the per unit area part of the unit.

concept_tested: Conductivity when both carrier concentrations matter
stem: A doped semiconductor has n_e = 3 x 10^21 m^-3, n_h = 1 x 10^21 m^-3, mu_e = 0.3 m^2 V^-1 s^-1 and mu_h = 0.1 m^2 V^-1 s^-1. Taking e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, its conductivity is
formula_principle: sigma = e (n_e mu_e + n_h mu_h).
common_misconception: Learners assume the minority term is always negligible and drop it even when it is not.

concept_tested: Extracting mobility from a measured conductivity
stem: An n type sample of conductivity 800 S m^-1 has an electron concentration of 5 x 10^22 m^-3 and a negligible hole concentration. Taking e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, its electron mobility is
formula_principle: sigma = e n_e mu_e, so mu_e = sigma / (e n_e).
common_misconception: Students invert the final division and obtain a mobility a hundred times too large.

concept_tested: Current from carrier concentration, area and drift speed
stem: In an n type bar of cross sectional area 1 x 10^-6 m^2 the electron concentration is 5 x 10^22 m^-3 and the electron drift speed is 0.25 m s^-1. Taking e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C and neglecting holes, the current in the bar is
formula_principle: I = n e A v_d.
common_misconception: Learners omit one factor, most often the area, and report a current density as a current.

concept_tested: Temperature dependence of carrier mobility
stem: As the temperature of a semiconductor is raised, the mobility of its charge carriers
option_a: rises, because the carriers acquire larger thermal speeds at higher temperature
option_b: rises, because more carriers become available to share the current between them
option_c: stays constant, because mobility depends only on the strength of the applied field
option_d: falls, because stronger lattice vibrations scatter the carriers more frequently
correct_answer_text: falls, because stronger lattice vibrations scatter the carriers more frequently
solution: Mobility is proportional to the average time a carrier travels between collisions. Heating increases the amplitude of the lattice vibrations, so collisions occur more often and this time falls. The mobility therefore decreases with temperature, even though the conductivity of the semiconductor rises because far more carriers become available.
formula_principle: mu = e tau / m, where the mean free time tau falls as lattice scattering increases with temperature.
common_misconception: Students confuse the increase in carrier number with an increase in mobility.

subtopic: Range of validity of the mass action law
concept_tested: When the mass action law applies
stem: The relation n_e n_h = n_i^2 holds
option_a: for a pure sample and for a doped sample alike, provided the material is in thermal equilibrium
option_b: only for a pure sample, since doping destroys the relation
option_c: only for an n type sample, in which the hole population is negligible
option_d: only while a current is being driven through the sample
correct_answer_text: for a pure sample and for a doped sample alike, provided the material is in thermal equilibrium
solution: The product of the two concentrations is fixed by the balance between thermal generation and recombination, both of which depend only on the material and its temperature. Doping shifts the two concentrations in opposite directions but leaves the product unchanged, so the relation is valid for pure, n type and p type samples alike whenever the sample is in equilibrium.
formula_principle: n_e n_h = n_i^2 is an equilibrium relation, valid for intrinsic and extrinsic material at a stated temperature.
common_misconception: Students think the relation applies only to pure crystals, since it is first derived for them.

concept_tested: Ratio of doped to intrinsic conductivity
stem: A pure semiconductor with n_i = 4 x 10^18 m^-3 has mu_e = 0.45 m^2 V^-1 s^-1 and mu_h = 0.15 m^2 V^-1 s^-1. It is then doped so that n_e = 8 x 10^22 m^-3, the minority carriers becoming negligible. Assuming the mobilities are unchanged, the ratio of the conductivity after doping to that before doping is
solution: sigma before doping = 1.6 x 10^-19 x 4 x 10^18 x (0.45 + 0.15) = 0.64 x 0.60 = 0.384 S m^-1. sigma after doping = 1.6 x 10^-19 x 8 x 10^22 x 0.45 = 1.28 x 10^4 x 0.45 = 5760 S m^-1. The ratio is 5760 / 0.384 = 1.5 x 10^4. Equivalently the ratio is (n_e / n_i) multiplied by mu_e / (mu_e + mu_h) = 2 x 10^4 x 0.75.
formula_principle: sigma_intrinsic = e n_i (mu_e + mu_h) and sigma_doped = e n_e mu_e.
common_misconception: Learners use the sum of the mobilities for the doped sample as well, although only one carrier is left there.

concept_tested: Why oppositely drifting carriers give currents that add
stem: In a semiconductor the electrons and the holes drift in opposite directions, and their mobilities are different. Which statement about the resulting current is correct?
option_a: the two contributions point in opposite directions, so the net current is the difference of the two
option_b: only the carrier with the larger mobility contributes, the other being effectively at rest
option_c: the two carriers have opposite charges as well as opposite drift directions, so both contributions point the same way and simply add
option_d: the two contributions add only in the special case where the two mobilities happen to be equal
correct_answer_text: the two carriers have opposite charges as well as opposite drift directions, so both contributions point the same way and simply add
solution: A hole of charge +e drifts along E, giving a conventional current along E. An electron of charge -e drifts opposite to E, and a negative charge moving backwards is again a conventional current along E. Both contributions therefore point along the field and add, giving J = e (n_e mu_e + n_h mu_h) E. The mobilities fix only how large each share is.
formula_principle: J = e n_e mu_e E + e n_h mu_h E; the sign reversal of charge and of velocity cancel.
common_misconception: Students subtract the two contributions because the two carriers physically move in opposite directions.

concept_tested: How a p n junction is made
stem: A p n junction is formed by
option_a: pressing a piece of p type material firmly against a piece of n type material
option_b: joining a semiconductor to a metal with a thin insulating layer between them
option_c: doping one region of a crystal first with donors and then with an equal number of acceptors
option_d: doping one region of a single semiconductor crystal with acceptors and the adjoining region with donors
correct_answer_text: doping one region of a single semiconductor crystal with acceptors and the adjoining region with donors
solution: The two regions must belong to one single crystal, with the lattice continuing unbroken from the p side to the n side. This is achieved by diffusing or growing the two dopings into adjacent parts of the same wafer. Only then can carriers diffuse freely across the boundary and set up the depletion region.
formula_principle: A p n junction must be formed within one continuous crystal so that the lattice is unbroken across the boundary.
common_misconception: Students imagine a junction can be made by simply touching two doped pieces together.

concept_tested: Contents of the depletion region
stem: The depletion region of an unbiased p n junction
option_a: has the largest concentration of mobile carriers to be found anywhere in the crystal
option_b: contains only mobile electrons and no ions at all
option_c: has almost no mobile charge carriers and contains immobile ions of both signs
option_d: lies entirely inside the p region and does not extend into the n region
correct_answer_text: has almost no mobile charge carriers and contains immobile ions of both signs
solution: Holes diffusing out of the p side and electrons diffusing out of the n side leave behind the fixed acceptor and donor ions near the boundary. This thin layer, typically of the order of 10^-6 m wide, holds almost no mobile carriers and is therefore called the depletion region.
formula_principle: Diffusion of majority carriers across the boundary leaves a thin layer of uncompensated immobile ions.
common_misconception: Learners picture the depletion region as crowded with carriers because it is where the action occurs.

concept_tested: Typical barrier potentials of silicon and germanium diodes
stem: The barrier potential of a junction diode at room temperature is about
option_a: 0.3 V for silicon and 0.7 V for germanium
option_b: 1.1 V for silicon and 0.7 V for germanium
option_c: 7 V for silicon and 3 V for germanium
option_d: 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium
correct_answer_text: 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium
solution: The built in potential difference across an unbiased junction is about 0.7 V for silicon and about 0.3 V for germanium. It is smaller than the band gap expressed in volt, and it is the voltage that a forward bias must largely cancel before appreciable current flows.
formula_principle: Barrier potential is about 0.7 V for Si and about 0.3 V for Ge at room temperature.
common_misconception: Students quote the band gap in eV as the barrier potential in volt.

concept_tested: Meaning of the arrowhead in the junction diode symbol
stem: In the circuit symbol of a junction diode, the arrowhead represents
option_a: the n region, and it points in the direction of the conventional current under forward bias
option_b: the p region, and it points opposite to the conventional current under forward bias
option_c: the p region, and it points in the direction of the conventional current under forward bias
option_d: the depletion region, which lies between the two terminals of the device
correct_answer_text: the p region, and it points in the direction of the conventional current under forward bias
solution: The solid triangle of the symbol stands for the p region and the bar it touches for the n region. Under forward bias conventional current enters the p region and leaves through the n region, so it flows in the direction in which the triangle points. Under reverse bias this path is blocked.
formula_principle: In the diode symbol the triangle is the p region (anode) and the bar is the n region (cathode).
common_misconception: Learners take the arrowhead to mark the n region and reverse the conducting direction of the device.

concept_tested: Direction of carrier diffusion when the junction is formed
stem: Immediately after a p n junction is formed,
option_a: holes diffuse from the p side to the n side and electrons diffuse from the n side to the p side
option_b: holes diffuse from the n side to the p side and electrons from the p side to the n side
option_c: both holes and electrons diffuse from the p side to the n side
option_d: no diffusion takes place at all until an external voltage is applied
correct_answer_text: holes diffuse from the p side to the n side and electrons diffuse from the n side to the p side
solution: Holes are the majority carriers on the p side and are scarce on the n side, so they diffuse from p to n. Electrons are the majority on the n side and scarce on the p side, so they diffuse from n to p. Both flows constitute a conventional current from the p side to the n side, the diffusion current.
formula_principle: Diffusion of a carrier proceeds from the region of higher concentration to the region of lower concentration.
common_misconception: Students reverse the diffusion directions by thinking of attraction to the opposite region rather than concentration differences.

concept_tested: Sign of the fixed charge on either side of the boundary
stem: In the depletion region of a p n junction, the layer on the p side and the layer on the n side carry respectively
option_a: negative acceptor ions and positive donor ions
option_b: positive donor ions and negative acceptor ions
option_c: negative acceptor ions and free electrons
correct_answer_text: negative acceptor ions and positive donor ions
solution: The p side was doped with acceptors, which become fixed negative ions once they have captured an electron. When the holes near the boundary diffuse away, these negative ions are left uncovered. On the n side the donors are fixed positive ions, uncovered when the electrons diffuse away. The result is a negative layer on the p side facing a positive layer on the n side.
formula_principle: Uncovered acceptor ions on the p side are negative; uncovered donor ions on the n side are positive.
common_misconception: Learners attach the sign of the majority carrier to the fixed ions of the same side.

concept_tested: Direction of the built in field across the depletion region
stem: The internal electric field in the depletion region of an unbiased p n junction is directed
option_a: from the p side towards the n side
option_b: from the n side towards the p side
option_c: along the junction plane, parallel to the boundary between the two regions
option_d: outward from the middle of the depletion region towards both sides
correct_answer_text: from the n side towards the p side
solution: The uncovered donor ions on the n side form a positive sheet and the uncovered acceptor ions on the p side form a negative sheet. The field between them runs from the positive sheet to the negative sheet, that is from the n side towards the p side, and it opposes further diffusion of majority carriers.
formula_principle: The field points from the positive donor ion layer on the n side to the negative acceptor ion layer on the p side.
common_misconception: Students take the field to point from p to n because conventional current in forward bias flows that way.

concept_tested: Effect of forward bias on the barrier and the depletion width
stem: When a junction diode is forward biased,
option_a: the barrier potential is reduced but the width of the depletion region increases
option_b: the barrier potential and the width of the depletion region both increase
option_c: the barrier potential increases but the width of the depletion region is reduced
option_d: the barrier potential and the width of the depletion region are both reduced
correct_answer_text: the barrier potential and the width of the depletion region are both reduced
solution: The external supply drives holes towards the junction from the p side and electrons towards it from the n side. These carriers neutralise part of the uncovered ion charge, so the depletion region shrinks and the potential difference across it falls. With a lower barrier many more majority carriers have enough energy to cross, and the current rises sharply.
formula_principle: Forward bias opposes the built in potential, lowering the barrier and narrowing the depletion region.
common_misconception: Learners change the barrier height but forget that the depletion width changes with it in the same sense.

concept_tested: Source of the small reverse current
stem: The very small current that flows through a reverse biased junction diode is due to
option_a: the minority carriers present on the two sides of the junction
option_b: majority carriers that manage to cross the widened barrier
option_c: the immobile ions of the depletion region drifting across the junction
option_d: electrons emitted from the metal contacts at the two ends of the diode
correct_answer_text: the minority carriers present on the two sides of the junction
solution: Reverse bias raises the barrier for the majority carriers, so their flow practically stops. But the field across the junction sweeps minority carriers the other way, and these are helped rather than hindered. Their number is fixed by thermal generation, so the reverse current is very small, of the order of microampere, and almost independent of the applied voltage.
formula_principle: Reverse current is a drift current of thermally generated minority carriers and is nearly independent of the applied voltage.
common_misconception: Students think the reverse current is a leakage of majority carriers over the barrier.

concept_tested: Correct connection for forward bias
stem: A junction diode is forward biased when
option_a: the p region is joined to the positive terminal and the n region to the negative terminal of the cell
option_b: the p region is joined to the negative terminal and the n region to the positive terminal of the cell
option_c: both regions are joined to the positive terminal of the cell
option_d: the cell is connected across the depletion region only, leaving both doped regions free
correct_answer_text: the p region is joined to the positive terminal and the n region to the negative terminal of the cell
solution: The barrier makes the n side positive with respect to the p side. Connecting the p region to the positive terminal of the cell applies a potential difference in the opposite sense, which reduces the net barrier. Once the applied voltage approaches the barrier value of about 0.7 V for silicon, majority carriers cross freely and a large current flows.
formula_principle: Forward bias: p side positive with respect to n side, so the applied voltage opposes the barrier potential.
common_misconception: Learners connect the positive terminal to the n side by analogy with attracting the electrons.

concept_tested: Comparison of forward and reverse resistance
stem: Compared with its forward resistance, the reverse resistance of a junction diode is
option_a: very much smaller, typically by a factor of the order of 10^5
option_b: very much larger, typically by a factor of the order of 10^5
option_c: almost the same, since the same barrier is present in both cases
option_d: exactly twice as large, since the barrier is doubled when the supply is reversed
correct_answer_text: very much larger, typically by a factor of the order of 10^5
solution: In forward bias the current for a fraction of a volt is measured in milliampere, giving a resistance of tens of ohm. In reverse bias the same or a larger voltage produces only microampere, giving a resistance of megaohm. The ratio is therefore of the order of 10^5, and this asymmetry is what makes the diode useful.
formula_principle: Forward resistance is of the order of a few tens of ohm; reverse resistance is of the order of megaohm.
common_misconception: Students judge the two resistances to be comparable because the same junction is involved in both.

concept_tested: Balance of diffusion and drift in an unbiased junction
stem: In an unbiased p n junction in equilibrium,
option_a: the diffusion current and the drift current are equal and opposite, so the net current is zero
option_b: both the diffusion current and the drift current have fallen to zero
option_c: only the diffusion current exists, and it is balanced by the external circuit
option_d: only the drift current exists, diffusion having stopped once the ions were formed
correct_answer_text: the diffusion current and the drift current are equal and opposite, so the net current is zero
solution: Majority carriers continue to diffuse across the boundary because the concentration difference remains. The built in field sweeps minority carriers the other way, producing a drift current. The barrier grows until these two opposing currents are exactly equal, after which the net current is zero although both processes continue.
formula_principle: At equilibrium the diffusion current of majority carriers exactly cancels the drift current of minority carriers.
common_misconception: Learners take zero net current to mean that nothing at all is happening at the junction.

concept_tested: Electric field from barrier potential and depletion width
stem: The barrier potential of a junction is 0.5 V and its depletion region is 5 x 10^-7 m wide. Assuming a uniform field, the electric field in the depletion region is
solution: E = V / d = 0.5 / (5 x 10^-7) = 0.1 x 10^7 = 1 x 10^6 V m^-1. Although the barrier is only half a volt, the depletion region is so thin that the field inside it is enormous.
formula_principle: E = V / d for a uniform field across a layer of thickness d.
common_misconception: Students are surprised by the very large field and adjust the arithmetic to get a smaller number.

concept_tested: Work done by an electron crossing the barrier
stem: An electron crosses a silicon junction against a barrier potential of 0.7 V. Taking e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, the work it must do is
solution: W = e V = 1.6 x 10^-19 x 0.7 = 1.12 x 10^-19 J, which is the same as 0.7 eV. Only carriers whose thermal energy reaches this value can cross an unbiased silicon junction, which is why the equilibrium current is so small.
formula_principle: W = q V, so for one electron W = e V_barrier.
common_misconception: Learners quote the potential difference in volt as though it were an energy in joule.

concept_tested: Net barrier height when a forward bias is applied
stem: A silicon junction diode of barrier potential 0.7 V is connected so that its p side is 0.3 V positive with respect to its n side. The effective height of the barrier becomes
solution: Making the p side positive applies a potential difference that opposes the built in barrier, so the two subtract. The effective barrier is 0.7 - 0.3 = 0.4 V. The remaining barrier is still large enough to keep the forward current small, which is why a silicon diode begins to conduct appreciably only near 0.7 V.
formula_principle: Under forward bias the net barrier is V_barrier minus V_applied; under reverse bias it is V_barrier plus V_applied.
common_misconception: Students add the applied voltage to the barrier without checking which way the bias is applied.

concept_tested: Why the barrier potential cannot be read with a voltmeter
stem: A p n junction has a barrier potential across it, and yet a voltmeter connected across an isolated junction diode reads zero. The reason is that
option_a: the barrier potential exists only after the diode has been connected into a circuit
option_b: the voltmeter has too large a resistance to record the barrier potential
option_c: the barrier potential is far too small for any voltmeter to record
option_d: equal and opposite contact potentials appear where the leads meet the semiconductor, so the potentials round the closed loop cancel
correct_answer_text: equal and opposite contact potentials appear where the leads meet the semiconductor, so the potentials round the closed loop cancel
solution: The barrier is a contact potential set up inside the crystal. Connecting metal leads introduces further contact potentials at the metal to semiconductor boundaries, and in the closed loop formed by the voltmeter these exactly cancel the junction barrier. If it were otherwise, an isolated diode could drive a steady current round a loop and act as a source of energy for ever.
formula_principle: The barrier is an internal contact potential; around any closed loop the sum of all contact potentials is zero.
common_misconception: Students expect a real internal potential difference always to appear on an external meter.

concept_tested: Effect of heavier doping on width and barrier
stem: As the doping concentration on both sides of a p n junction is increased, the width of the depletion region and the barrier potential respectively
solution: The depletion region must uncover enough fixed ion charge to support the built in potential. Heavier doping packs more ions into each cubic metre, so the necessary charge is uncovered within a thinner layer and the width falls. At the same time the concentration difference of carriers between the two sides is larger, which raises the built in potential. Hence the region becomes narrower and the barrier taller.
formula_principle: The uncovered ion charge per unit volume rises with doping, so a thinner layer suffices, while the built in potential rises with the carrier concentration difference.
common_misconception: Learners assume the width and the barrier must always change in the same direction.

concept_tested: Accounting for the very different currents in the two biases
stem: A junction diode is connected in series with a resistor and a cell. When the cell is reversed the current falls from a few milliampere to a few microampere. The correct account of the two situations is that
option_a: in the first case majority carriers cross, and in the second the same majority carriers cross a thinner barrier
option_b: in the first case the barrier is lowered and majority carriers cross in large numbers, while in the second the barrier is raised and only minority carriers cross
option_c: in the first case minority carriers cross, and in the second majority carriers cross
option_d: in both cases the current is carried by minority carriers, the only difference being the width of the barrier
correct_answer_text: in the first case the barrier is lowered and majority carriers cross in large numbers, while in the second the barrier is raised and only minority carriers cross
solution: With the p side positive the applied voltage opposes the built in barrier, the depletion region narrows and enormous numbers of majority carriers diffuse across, giving milliampere currents. With the cell reversed the applied voltage adds to the barrier, the region widens and majority carriers are blocked. Only the thermally generated minority carriers are swept across, and since their number is tiny the current is only a few microampere.
formula_principle: Forward bias lowers the barrier and gives a large majority carrier diffusion current; reverse bias raises it and leaves only the minority carrier drift current.
common_misconception: Students explain the reverse current by majority carriers leaking over the barrier rather than by minority carrier drift.

concept_tested: v = r omega
stem: A particle moves in a circle of radius 0.5 m with angular velocity 4 rad s^-1. Its linear speed is
solution: v = r omega = 0.5 x 4 = 2 m s^-1.
formula_principle: v = r omega
common_misconception: Dividing instead of multiplying r and omega.

concept_tested: a = v^2/r
stem: A body moves along a circle of radius 2 m with a constant speed of 4 m s^-1. Its centripetal acceleration is
formula_principle: a_c = v^2 / r
common_misconception: Forgetting to square the speed before dividing by the radius.

concept_tested: Nature of velocity
stem: In uniform circular motion, the quantity that remains constant is
solution: In uniform circular motion the magnitude of velocity (speed) is constant, but its direction, and hence velocity, acceleration and force, keep changing.
formula_principle: Uniform circular motion
common_misconception: Treating constant speed as constant velocity in circular motion.

concept_tested: Direction
stem: The centripetal force acting on a body in uniform circular motion is directed
option_a: towards the centre of the circle
option_b: away from the centre of the circle
option_c: along the tangent to the circle
option_d: perpendicular to the plane of the circle
correct_answer_text: towards the centre of the circle
solution: Centripetal force always points radially inward, towards the centre of the circular path.
formula_principle: Centripetal force
common_misconception: Confusing the real inward centripetal force with the pseudo outward centrifugal force.

concept_tested: Pseudo force
stem: Centrifugal force is regarded as a pseudo force because it
option_a: appears only in a rotating (non-inertial) frame of reference
option_b: is always smaller than the centripetal force
option_c: acts only on bodies at rest
correct_answer_text: appears only in a rotating (non-inertial) frame of reference
solution: Centrifugal force has no physical agent and is introduced only to apply Newton's laws within a rotating, non-inertial frame.
formula_principle: Pseudo forces in non-inertial frames
common_misconception: Believing centrifugal force is a real interaction force in the ground frame.

concept_tested: Force with mass and omega
stem: A body of mass 2 kg moves in a circle of radius 3 m with angular velocity 2 rad s^-1. The centripetal force is
solution: F = m r omega^2 = 2 x 3 x (2)^2 = 2 x 3 x 4 = 24 N.
formula_principle: F = m r omega^2
common_misconception: Failing to square the angular velocity in F = m r omega^2.

concept_tested: Relation with omega
stem: The angular velocity of a body completing one revolution in 4 s is
solution: omega = 2 pi / T = 2 pi / 4 = pi/2 rad s^-1.
formula_principle: omega = 2 pi / T
common_misconception: Forgetting to divide the full angle 2 pi by the period.

concept_tested: Doubling speed
stem: If the speed of a body in uniform circular motion is doubled while the radius is unchanged, its centripetal acceleration becomes
solution: Since a_c is proportional to v^2, doubling v multiplies the acceleration by 2^2 = 4.
formula_principle: a_c = v^2 / r
common_misconception: Assuming a linear rather than quadratic dependence on speed.

concept_tested: Definition
stem: Angular acceleration is defined as the rate of change of
solution: Angular acceleration alpha is the time rate of change of angular velocity omega.
formula_principle: alpha = d omega / dt
common_misconception: Confusing angular acceleration with angular velocity.

concept_tested: Relation a_t = r alpha
stem: A wheel of radius 0.2 m has angular acceleration 5 rad s^-2. The tangential acceleration of a point on its rim is
solution: a_t = r alpha = 0.2 x 5 = 1 m s^-2.
formula_principle: a_t = r alpha
common_misconception: Confusing tangential acceleration r alpha with centripetal acceleration r omega^2.

concept_tested: Two components
stem: In non-uniform circular motion, the net acceleration of the particle has
solution: Non-uniform circular motion has a centripetal (radial) component v^2/r and a tangential component r alpha due to changing speed.
formula_principle: Components of acceleration
common_misconception: Assuming circular motion always has purely centripetal acceleration.

concept_tested: Source of force
stem: For a car taking a turn on a level road, the centripetal force is provided by
option_a: the force of friction between the tyres and the road
option_c: the normal reaction of the road
correct_answer_text: the force of friction between the tyres and the road
solution: On a level road only friction acts horizontally, so friction supplies the required centripetal force.
formula_principle: Centripetal force on a level road
common_misconception: Assuming the normal reaction or weight can provide horizontal centripetal force on a level road.

concept_tested: Maximum safe speed
stem: The maximum speed with which a car can turn on a level road of radius r with coefficient of friction mu is
solution: Setting friction equal to the required centripetal force, mu m g = m v^2 / r gives v_max = sqrt(mu r g).
formula_principle: mu m g = m v^2 / r
common_misconception: Placing the radius in the denominator instead of the numerator.

concept_tested: Numerical maximum speed
stem: A car turns on a level road of radius 20 m with coefficient of friction 0.5. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the maximum safe speed is
solution: v_max = sqrt(0.5 x 20 x 10) = sqrt(100) = 10 m s^-1.
formula_principle: v_max = sqrt(mu r g)
common_misconception: Forgetting to take the square root of the product.

concept_tested: Angle of banking
stem: For a frictionless banked road of radius r, the angle of banking theta for a design speed v satisfies
solution: Resolving the normal reaction on a frictionless banked road gives tan theta = v^2 / (r g).
formula_principle: tan theta = v^2 / (r g)
common_misconception: Inverting the ratio or forgetting to square the speed.

concept_tested: Optimum speed
stem: On a road banked at angle theta with radius r, the speed for which no friction is needed is
solution: From tan theta = v^2/(r g), the optimum (no friction) speed is v = sqrt(r g tan theta).
formula_principle: v = sqrt(r g tan theta)
common_misconception: Using sin theta in place of tan theta.

concept_tested: Numerical banking angle
stem: A road of radius 100 m is designed for a speed of 30 m s^-1. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the value of tan theta for the banking angle is
formula_principle: tan theta = v^2 / (r g)
common_misconception: Failing to square the speed before dividing.

concept_tested: Independence of mass
stem: The angle of banking required for a curved road is independent of
solution: Mass cancels from both sides when the equations of motion are written, so the banking angle does not depend on it.
formula_principle: tan theta = v^2 / (r g)
common_misconception: Assuming heavier vehicles need a larger banking angle.

concept_tested: Maximum speed
stem: For a road banked at angle theta with coefficient of friction mu, the maximum safe speed is
option_a: sqrt(r g (mu - tan theta)/(1 + mu tan theta))
option_c: sqrt(r g (mu + tan theta)/(1 - mu tan theta))
option_d: sqrt(r g (1 - mu tan theta)/(mu + tan theta))
correct_answer_text: sqrt(r g (mu + tan theta)/(1 - mu tan theta))
solution: With friction acting down the slope at maximum speed, v_max = sqrt(r g (mu + tan theta)/(1 - mu tan theta)).
formula_principle: Banking with friction
common_misconception: Interchanging the expressions for maximum and minimum safe speed.

concept_tested: Purpose of banking
stem: Roads are banked at curves mainly to
option_a: increase the friction between tyres and road
option_b: reduce the weight of the vehicle
option_c: provide a component of the normal reaction as centripetal force
option_d: increase the speed limit without any centripetal force
correct_answer_text: provide a component of the normal reaction as centripetal force
solution: Tilting the road allows the horizontal component of the normal reaction to supply centripetal force, reducing reliance on friction.
formula_principle: Banking of roads
common_misconception: Believing banking works by increasing friction.

concept_tested: Period formula
stem: The period of a conical pendulum of string length L making angle theta with the vertical is
solution: The vertical height of the cone is h = L cos theta, and the period is T = 2 pi sqrt(h/g) = 2 pi sqrt(L cos theta / g).
formula_principle: T = 2 pi sqrt(L cos theta / g)
common_misconception: Using sin theta instead of cos theta for the vertical height of the cone.

concept_tested: Tension component
stem: In a conical pendulum, the vertical component of the string tension
option_a: balances the weight of the bob
correct_answer_text: balances the weight of the bob
solution: The vertical component T cos theta balances mg, while the horizontal component T sin theta supplies the centripetal force.
formula_principle: Force resolution in a conical pendulum
common_misconception: Interchanging the roles of the vertical and horizontal tension components.

concept_tested: Minimum speed at top
stem: The minimum speed of a body at the highest point of a vertical circle of radius r, so that the string remains taut, is
solution: At the top with zero tension, gravity alone supplies the centripetal force: m g = m v^2/r, giving v = sqrt(g r).
formula_principle: At the top: m g = m v^2 / r when tension is zero
common_misconception: Quoting the lowest-point condition sqrt(5gr) for the highest point.

concept_tested: Minimum speed at bottom
stem: For a body to just complete a vertical circle of radius r, its minimum speed at the lowest point must be
solution: Using energy conservation between the lowest and highest points with v_top^2 = g r gives v_bottom^2 = g r + 4 g r = 5 g r.
formula_principle: Energy conservation with v_top = sqrt(gr)
common_misconception: Forgetting the 4gr contribution from the rise through height 2r.

concept_tested: Tension difference
stem: For a body moving in a vertical circle, the difference between the tensions at the lowest and highest points is
solution: Using energy conservation, T_bottom - T_top = 6 m g for any speed sufficient to complete the circle.
formula_principle: Tension in a vertical circle
common_misconception: Considering only the weight difference 2mg and omitting the kinetic energy contribution.

concept_tested: Numerical minimum speed
stem: A stone tied to a string of length 0.4 m is whirled in a vertical circle. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the minimum speed at the top is
solution: v_top = sqrt(g r) = sqrt(10 x 0.4) = sqrt(4) = 2 m s^-1.
formula_principle: v_top = sqrt(g r)
common_misconception: Forgetting to take the square root of the product gr.

concept_tested: Critical condition
stem: At the highest point of a vertical circle, when a body just completes the circle, the tension in the string is
solution: At the critical speed the string just goes slack at the top, so the tension there is zero and gravity alone provides the centripetal force.
formula_principle: Critical condition in a vertical circle
common_misconception: Assuming the tension at the top equals the weight of the body.

concept_tested: Position of maximum tension
stem: In vertical circular motion, the tension in the string is maximum at
solution: At the lowest point the tension must both support the weight and supply the centripetal force, so it is greatest there.
formula_principle: Tension variation in a vertical circle
common_misconception: Assuming the tension is uniform around the circle.

concept_tested: Work done
stem: The work done by the centripetal force on a body in uniform circular motion over one complete revolution is
option_b: positive and equal to the kinetic energy
option_d: equal to the centripetal force times the circumference
solution: The centripetal force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so the angle is 90 degrees and the work done is zero.
formula_principle: W = F d cos theta
common_misconception: Multiplying force by path length without accounting for the perpendicular direction.

concept_tested: Radian measure
stem: A wheel turns through 5 revolutions. The angular displacement in radian is
solution: Angular displacement = 5 x 2 pi = 10 pi radian.
formula_principle: One revolution = 2 pi radian
common_misconception: Taking one revolution as pi radian instead of 2 pi radian.

concept_tested: Physical meaning
stem: Moment of inertia of a body about an axis is a measure of its
option_a: opposition to a change in its translational motion
option_c: opposition to a change in its rotational motion
correct_answer_text: opposition to a change in its rotational motion
solution: Moment of inertia plays the role in rotation that mass plays in translation, measuring resistance to angular acceleration.
formula_principle: Moment of inertia
common_misconception: Equating moment of inertia with mass or with angular momentum.

concept_tested: Factors affecting I
stem: The moment of inertia of a rigid body depends on
option_b: the angular velocity of the body
option_d: the mass, its distribution and the axis chosen
correct_answer_text: the mass, its distribution and the axis chosen
solution: Since I = sum m r^2, it depends on how much mass lies at what distance from the chosen axis.
formula_principle: I = sum m r^2
common_misconception: Assuming moment of inertia is a fixed property like mass, independent of the axis.

concept_tested: Ring about central axis
stem: The moment of inertia of a ring of mass M and radius R about an axis through its centre and perpendicular to its plane is
solution: All the mass of a ring lies at distance R from the central perpendicular axis, so I = M R^2.
formula_principle: I = M R^2 for a ring
common_misconception: Confusing the ring result with the disc result M R^2 / 2.

concept_tested: Disc about central axis
stem: The moment of inertia of a uniform disc of mass M and radius R about an axis through its centre and perpendicular to its plane is
solution: For a uniform disc about its central perpendicular axis, I = M R^2 / 2.
formula_principle: I = M R^2 / 2 for a disc
common_misconception: Using the ring formula M R^2 for a solid disc.

concept_tested: Solid sphere
stem: The moment of inertia of a solid sphere of mass M and radius R about a diameter is
solution: For a uniform solid sphere about any diameter, I = 2 M R^2 / 5.
common_misconception: Confusing the solid sphere (2/5) with the hollow sphere (2/3).

concept_tested: Hollow sphere
stem: The moment of inertia of a thin hollow sphere of mass M and radius R about a diameter is
solution: For a thin spherical shell about a diameter, I = 2 M R^2 / 3.
common_misconception: Interchanging the solid sphere and hollow sphere coefficients.

concept_tested: Rod about centre
stem: The moment of inertia of a thin uniform rod of mass M and length L about an axis through its centre and perpendicular to its length is
solution: For a thin rod about a perpendicular axis through its centre, I = M L^2 / 12.
common_misconception: Using the end-axis result M L^2 / 3 for the central axis.

concept_tested: Rod about end
stem: The moment of inertia of a thin uniform rod of mass M and length L about a perpendicular axis through one end is
solution: Applying the parallel axis theorem to M L^2/12 with d = L/2 gives M L^2/12 + M L^2/4 = M L^2/3.
common_misconception: Quoting the central-axis value when the axis is at one end.

concept_tested: Definition
stem: The radius of gyration k of a body of mass M and moment of inertia I is given by
solution: By definition I = M k^2, so the radius of gyration is k = sqrt(I/M).
formula_principle: I = M k^2
common_misconception: Inverting the ratio or omitting the square root.

concept_tested: Numerical
stem: A body of mass 8 kg has moment of inertia 200 kg m^2 about an axis. Its radius of gyration is
solution: k = sqrt(I/M) = sqrt(200/8) = sqrt(25) = 5 m.
formula_principle: k = sqrt(I / M)
common_misconception: Forgetting the square root after dividing I by M.

concept_tested: Parallel axis theorem
stem: According to the theorem of parallel axes, the moment of inertia about an axis parallel to one through the centre of mass at distance d is
solution: The theorem states I = I_cm + M d^2, where d is the perpendicular distance between the two parallel axes.
formula_principle: Parallel axis theorem
common_misconception: Subtracting rather than adding the M d^2 term.

concept_tested: Perpendicular axis theorem
stem: The theorem of perpendicular axes, applicable to a plane lamina, states that
solution: For a plane lamina, the moment of inertia about an axis perpendicular to its plane equals the sum of those about two perpendicular axes in the plane.
formula_principle: Perpendicular axis theorem
common_misconception: Applying the theorem to three-dimensional bodies, where it does not hold.

concept_tested: Applicability
stem: The theorem of perpendicular axes can be applied only to
option_c: bodies rotating about a fixed point
solution: The derivation assumes all mass lies in a single plane, so the theorem applies only to plane laminae.
formula_principle: Perpendicular axis theorem
common_misconception: Applying the perpendicular axis theorem to a sphere or a cylinder.

concept_tested: Ring about diameter
stem: Using the theorem of perpendicular axes, the moment of inertia of a ring of mass M and radius R about its diameter is
solution: For a ring I_z = M R^2 and by symmetry I_x = I_y, so 2 I_x = M R^2 giving I_diameter = M R^2/2.
formula_principle: I_z = I_x + I_y with I_x = I_y
common_misconception: Forgetting to halve the central perpendicular value when using symmetry.

concept_tested: Disc about diameter
stem: The moment of inertia of a uniform disc of mass M and radius R about its diameter is
solution: For a disc I_z = M R^2/2, and by symmetry 2 I_diameter = M R^2/2, giving I_diameter = M R^2/4.
formula_principle: I_z = I_x + I_y with I_x = I_y
common_misconception: Using the central perpendicular value directly for the diameter.

concept_tested: Ring about tangent
stem: The moment of inertia of a ring of mass M and radius R about a tangent lying in its own plane is
solution: I = I_diameter + M R^2 = M R^2/2 + M R^2 = 3 M R^2/2.
formula_principle: Parallel axis theorem applied to the diameter
common_misconception: Starting from the central perpendicular value instead of the diameter value.

concept_tested: Ring about perpendicular tangent
stem: The moment of inertia of a ring of mass M and radius R about a tangent perpendicular to its plane is
solution: I = I_centre + M R^2 = M R^2 + M R^2 = 2 M R^2.
formula_principle: Parallel axis theorem
common_misconception: Forgetting to add the M R^2 term from the parallel axis theorem.

concept_tested: Solid sphere about tangent
stem: The moment of inertia of a solid sphere of mass M and radius R about a tangent is
formula_principle: Parallel axis theorem
common_misconception: Omitting the M R^2 term when moving from the diameter to a tangent.

concept_tested: Largest moment of inertia
stem: Four bodies of equal mass and equal radius rotate about their central axes. The largest moment of inertia belongs to
solution: The coefficients are ring 1, hollow sphere 2/3, disc 1/2 and solid sphere 2/5, so the ring has the greatest moment of inertia.
formula_principle: Compare I = c M R^2
common_misconception: Assuming a solid body always has a larger moment of inertia than a hollow one.

stem: A disc of mass 4 kg and radius 0.5 m rotates about its central perpendicular axis. Its moment of inertia is
common_misconception: Using the ring formula and omitting the factor of one half.

concept_tested: Solid sphere value
stem: A solid sphere of mass 5 kg and radius 0.2 m rotates about a diameter. Its moment of inertia is
common_misconception: Applying the hollow sphere coefficient 2/3 to a solid sphere.

concept_tested: Ring value
stem: The radius of gyration of a ring of radius R about its central perpendicular axis is
solution: Since I = M R^2 = M k^2, the radius of gyration is k = R.
formula_principle: I = M k^2 with I = M R^2
common_misconception: Confusing the ring value with the disc value R/sqrt(2).

concept_tested: Disc value
stem: The radius of gyration of a disc of radius R about its central perpendicular axis is
solution: M k^2 = M R^2/2 gives k^2 = R^2/2, so k = R/sqrt(2).
formula_principle: I = M k^2 with I = M R^2 / 2
common_misconception: Taking k = R/2 by halving the radius instead of the squared radius.

concept_tested: Torque formula
stem: The torque acting on a body about an axis is given by
option_a: the product of force and its perpendicular distance from the axis
option_b: the product of force and the time for which it acts
option_c: the product of mass and angular acceleration
option_d: the product of force and the displacement along the force
correct_answer_text: the product of force and its perpendicular distance from the axis
solution: Torque is the moment of a force, equal to force times the perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation.
formula_principle: tau = F r sin theta
common_misconception: Confusing torque with work, both of which have the same dimensions.

concept_tested: tau = I alpha
stem: The rotational analogue of Newton's second law of motion is
solution: Torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration, mirroring F = m a in translation.
formula_principle: tau = I alpha
common_misconception: Writing tau = I omega, which is the expression for angular momentum.

concept_tested: Torque from I and alpha
stem: A body of moment of inertia 5 kg m^2 has angular acceleration 4 rad s^-2. The torque acting on it is
solution: tau = I alpha = 5 x 4 = 20 N m.
formula_principle: tau = I alpha
common_misconception: Adding I and alpha instead of multiplying them.

concept_tested: Angular acceleration from torque
stem: A torque of 12 N m acts on a wheel of moment of inertia 3 kg m^2. The angular acceleration produced is
solution: alpha = tau / I = 12/3 = 4 rad s^-2.
formula_principle: alpha = tau / I
common_misconception: Multiplying torque by moment of inertia instead of dividing.

concept_tested: Zero torque condition
stem: The torque acting on a body is zero when the applied force
option_a: is perpendicular to the axis of rotation
option_c: acts for a very short time
option_d: passes through the axis of rotation
correct_answer_text: passes through the axis of rotation
solution: If the line of action of the force passes through the axis, the perpendicular distance is zero and so is the torque.
formula_principle: tau = F r sin theta
common_misconception: Assuming any large force must produce a torque, regardless of its line of action.

concept_tested: L = I omega
stem: The angular momentum of a rotating rigid body is given by
solution: Angular momentum L equals moment of inertia times angular velocity.
formula_principle: L = I omega
common_misconception: Confusing L = I omega with tau = I alpha.

concept_tested: L from I and omega
stem: A flywheel of moment of inertia 6 kg m^2 rotates at 5 rad s^-1. Its angular momentum is
solution: L = I omega = 6 x 5 = 30 kg m^2 s^-1.
formula_principle: L = I omega
common_misconception: Adding rather than multiplying I and omega.

concept_tested: Condition
stem: The angular momentum of a system is conserved when
option_a: the net external torque on the system is zero
option_b: the net external force on the system is zero
option_c: the moment of inertia is constant
correct_answer_text: the net external torque on the system is zero
solution: From tau = dL/dt, zero net external torque implies that L remains constant.
formula_principle: Conservation of angular momentum
common_misconception: Requiring zero external force instead of zero external torque.

concept_tested: Ice skater
stem: When a spinning ice skater pulls her arms inward, her angular velocity
option_a: decreases because her moment of inertia decreases
option_b: increases because her moment of inertia decreases
option_c: remains unchanged because angular momentum is conserved
option_d: increases because her angular momentum increases
correct_answer_text: increases because her moment of inertia decreases
solution: With negligible external torque, L = I omega is constant; pulling the arms in reduces I, so omega increases.
formula_principle: L = I omega constant
common_misconception: Assuming angular momentum increases when the skater spins faster.

concept_tested: Numerical
stem: A body rotating at 10 rad s^-1 has its moment of inertia reduced to one half its original value with no external torque. Its new angular velocity is
solution: I x 10 = (I/2) x omega2, so omega2 = 20 rad s^-1.
formula_principle: I1 omega1 = I2 omega2
common_misconception: Applying the change in the wrong direction and halving the angular velocity.

concept_tested: tau = dL/dt
stem: The rate of change of angular momentum of a body equals
option_c: the net external force acting on it
option_d: the net external torque acting on it
correct_answer_text: the net external torque acting on it
solution: Just as force is the rate of change of linear momentum, torque is the rate of change of angular momentum.
formula_principle: tau = dL / dt
common_misconception: Associating the rate of change of angular momentum with force rather than torque.

concept_tested: Formula
stem: The kinetic energy of a body rotating with angular velocity omega about a fixed axis is
solution: Rotational kinetic energy is I omega^2/2, the analogue of m v^2/2.
formula_principle: KE = I omega^2 / 2
common_misconception: Omitting the factor of one half or the square on omega.

concept_tested: Rotational KE
stem: A wheel of moment of inertia 4 kg m^2 rotates at 3 rad s^-1. Its rotational kinetic energy is
formula_principle: KE = I omega^2 / 2
common_misconception: Failing to square the angular velocity before halving.

concept_tested: Work by torque
stem: The work done by a constant torque tau in rotating a body through angle theta is
solution: Work done in rotation is the product of torque and angular displacement, W = tau theta.
formula_principle: W = tau theta
common_misconception: Confusing work tau theta with power tau omega.

concept_tested: Rotational power
stem: The power delivered by a torque tau to a body rotating with angular velocity omega is
solution: Rotational power is P = tau omega, the analogue of P = F v in translation.
formula_principle: P = tau omega
common_misconception: Using the work expression tau theta in place of power.
