concept_tested: Same L different I
stem: Two bodies have the same angular momentum. The body with the larger moment of inertia has
solution: Since L = I omega is fixed, omega is inversely proportional to I, so a larger I gives a smaller omega.
formula_principle: L = I omega
common_misconception: Assuming a larger moment of inertia implies a larger angular velocity.

concept_tested: KE in terms of L
stem: The rotational kinetic energy of a body in terms of its angular momentum L and moment of inertia I is
solution: Substituting omega = L/I into KE = I omega^2/2 gives KE = I (L/I)^2/2 = L^2/(2I).
formula_principle: KE = I omega^2/2 with L = I omega
common_misconception: Mishandling the substitution and leaving an extra factor of I.

concept_tested: Rolling without slipping
stem: For a body rolling without slipping on a surface, the relation between its linear speed v and angular speed omega is
solution: Rolling without slipping requires the contact point to be instantaneously at rest, giving v = R omega.
formula_principle: v = R omega for rolling
common_misconception: Inverting the relation between linear and angular speed.

concept_tested: Total KE
stem: The total kinetic energy of a body of mass m rolling without slipping with speed v and radius of gyration k about radius R is
solution: Total KE = m v^2/2 + I omega^2/2 with I = m k^2 and omega = v/R, giving m v^2(1 + k^2/R^2)/2.
formula_principle: KE = translational + rotational
common_misconception: Counting only the translational kinetic energy of a rolling body.

concept_tested: Rolling ring
stem: For a ring rolling without slipping, the ratio of its rotational kinetic energy to its total kinetic energy is
solution: For a ring k^2/R^2 = 1, so rotational KE equals translational KE and each is half the total.
formula_principle: k^2/R^2 = 1 for a ring
common_misconception: Using the disc ratio for a ring.

concept_tested: Rolling disc total KE
stem: The total kinetic energy of a disc of mass m rolling without slipping with speed v is
common_misconception: Confusing the disc, ring and sphere coefficients.

concept_tested: Rolling sphere total KE
stem: The total kinetic energy of a solid sphere of mass m rolling without slipping with speed v is
formula_principle: k^2/R^2 = 2/5 for a solid sphere
common_misconception: Using the disc coefficient for a solid sphere.

concept_tested: Acceleration formula
stem: A body rolls without slipping down an incline of angle theta. Its linear acceleration is
solution: Rotational inertia reduces the acceleration by the factor (1 + k^2/R^2) in the denominator.
formula_principle: a = g sin theta / (1 + k^2/R^2)
common_misconception: Using the sliding result g sin theta for a rolling body.

concept_tested: Sphere acceleration
stem: A solid sphere rolls without slipping down an incline of angle theta. Its acceleration is
solution: With k^2/R^2 = 2/5, a = g sin theta/(1 + 2/5) = g sin theta/(7/5) = 5 g sin theta/7.
formula_principle: a = g sin theta / (1 + 2/5)
common_misconception: Using the disc or ring coefficient for a solid sphere.

concept_tested: Fastest body
stem: A ring, a disc and a solid sphere of equal mass and radius roll without slipping from rest down the same incline. The body reaching the bottom first is
solution: The smallest k^2/R^2 gives the largest acceleration; for the sphere it is 2/5, less than the disc 1/2 and ring 1, so the sphere arrives first.
formula_principle: a = g sin theta / (1 + k^2/R^2)
common_misconception: Assuming the heaviest or largest body rolls down fastest.

concept_tested: Independence of mass
stem: The acceleration of a body rolling without slipping down an incline is independent of
solution: Mass and radius cancel out, leaving the acceleration dependent only on g, theta and the shape factor k^2/R^2.
formula_principle: a = g sin theta / (1 + k^2/R^2)
common_misconception: Assuming a heavier or larger rolling body accelerates faster.

concept_tested: Speed at bottom
stem: A body of radius of gyration k and radius R rolls from rest down a height h. Its speed at the bottom is
solution: Equating m g h to m v^2(1 + k^2/R^2)/2 gives v = sqrt(2 g h/(1 + k^2/R^2)).
formula_principle: Energy conservation for rolling
common_misconception: Using the free-fall result sqrt(2gh) and ignoring rotational kinetic energy.

concept_tested: Role of friction
stem: In rolling without slipping on a horizontal surface at constant speed, the work done by friction is
option_a: positive, because friction drives the rolling
option_b: negative and equal to the kinetic energy
option_c: zero, because the contact point is instantaneously at rest
option_d: equal to the rotational kinetic energy
correct_answer_text: zero, because the contact point is instantaneously at rest
solution: In rolling without slipping the point of contact has zero instantaneous velocity, so static friction acts through zero displacement and does no work.
formula_principle: Rolling constraint and work
common_misconception: Assuming friction always dissipates energy, even in ideal rolling.

concept_tested: Breaking string
stem: A stone whirled in a horizontal circle flies off when the string breaks. It then moves
option_b: along the tangent to the circle at that point
correct_answer_text: along the tangent to the circle at that point
solution: Once the centripetal force vanishes, the stone continues in a straight line along its instantaneous velocity, which is tangential.
formula_principle: Newton's first law
common_misconception: Believing the stone flies radially outward because of centrifugal force.

concept_tested: Rod axis change
stem: The moment of inertia of a rod about a perpendicular axis through one end, compared with that through its centre, is
solution: The ratio is (M L^2/3)/(M L^2/12) = 12/3 = 4, so the end value is four times the central value.
formula_principle: Compare ML^2/3 with ML^2/12
common_misconception: Assuming the moment of inertia merely doubles when the axis moves to the end.

concept_tested: Minimum speed with friction
stem: On a banked road with friction, the minimum safe speed is given by
option_a: sqrt(r g (tan theta + mu)/(1 - mu tan theta))
option_c: sqrt(r g (tan theta - mu)/(1 + mu tan theta))
correct_answer_text: sqrt(r g (tan theta - mu)/(1 + mu tan theta))
solution: At minimum speed friction acts up the slope, giving v_min = sqrt(r g (tan theta - mu)/(1 + mu tan theta)).
formula_principle: Banking with friction acting up the slope
common_misconception: Interchanging the maximum and minimum safe speed expressions.

concept_tested: SI unit
stem: The SI unit of angular momentum is
solution: L = I omega has units kg m^2 x s^-1 = kg m^2 s^-1.
formula_principle: L = I omega
common_misconception: Confusing the unit of angular momentum with that of torque.

concept_tested: SI unit of torque
stem: The SI unit of torque is
solution: Torque is force times perpendicular distance, so its unit is the newton metre.
formula_principle: tau = F r
common_misconception: Writing the unit as newton alone and omitting the distance factor.

concept_tested: Dimensional formula
stem: The dimensional formula of torque is
solution: Torque = force x distance = [M L T^-2][L] = [M L^2 T^-2].
formula_principle: tau = F r
common_misconception: Confusing torque with angular momentum, which is [M L^2 T^-1].

concept_tested: Ring value
stem: A ring of mass 2 kg and radius 0.3 m rotates about its central perpendicular axis. Its moment of inertia is
formula_principle: I = M R^2
common_misconception: Applying the disc formula M R^2/2 to a ring.

concept_tested: Angular velocity from rpm
stem: A wheel rotates at 300 revolutions per minute. Its angular velocity is
solution: n = 300/60 = 5 rev s^-1, so omega = 2 pi x 5 = 10 pi rad s^-1.
formula_principle: omega = 2 pi n with n in rev per second
common_misconception: Forgetting to convert revolutions per minute into revolutions per second.

concept_tested: Same KE different I
stem: Two bodies have the same rotational kinetic energy. The body with the larger moment of inertia has
solution: Since I omega^2 is fixed, omega is inversely proportional to the square root of I, so a larger I gives a smaller omega.
formula_principle: KE = I omega^2 / 2
common_misconception: Assuming a larger moment of inertia means a faster rotation at the same energy.

concept_tested: Speed at lowest point numerical
stem: A body is whirled in a vertical circle of radius 0.8 m and just completes the circle. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, its speed at the lowest point is
solution: v_bottom = sqrt(5 g r) = sqrt(5 x 10 x 0.8) = sqrt(40) = 6.32, about 6.3 m s^-1.
formula_principle: v_bottom = sqrt(5 g r)
common_misconception: Using the highest-point condition sqrt(gr) for the lowest point.

concept_tested: Not a vector
stem: Moment of inertia of a body about a given axis is
solution: For a fixed axis, moment of inertia is a scalar, defined as the sum of m r^2 over all mass elements.
formula_principle: I = sum m r^2
common_misconception: Treating moment of inertia as a vector because rotation has a direction.

concept_tested: Planetary motion
stem: A planet moving around the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times. This is a direct consequence of
option_d: the constancy of the gravitational force
solution: Gravity is a central force, so it exerts no torque about the Sun, and the planet's angular momentum, and hence its areal velocity, stays constant.
formula_principle: Central force and angular momentum
common_misconception: Attributing Kepler's second law to energy conservation.

concept_tested: Equal KE ranking
stem: A ring and a solid sphere of equal mass roll without slipping with equal speed. The ratio of the total kinetic energy of the ring to that of the sphere is
solution: Ring KE = m v^2 and sphere KE = 7 m v^2/10, so the ratio is 1 : 7/10 = 10 : 7.
common_misconception: Inverting the ratio by placing the sphere value first.

concept_tested: Force with period
stem: The centripetal force on a body of mass m moving in a circle of radius r with period T is
solution: F = m r (2 pi/T)^2 = 4 pi^2 m r / T^2.
formula_principle: F = m r omega^2 with omega = 2 pi / T
common_misconception: Forgetting to square both the factor 2 pi and the period.

concept_tested: Rod value
stem: A rod of mass 3 kg and length 2 m rotates about a perpendicular axis through its centre. Its moment of inertia is
common_misconception: Using M L^2/3 when the axis passes through the centre.

concept_tested: Torque from force and distance
stem: A force of 20 N acts at a perpendicular distance of 0.4 m from the axis of rotation. The torque is
solution: tau = F r = 20 x 0.4 = 8 N m.
formula_principle: tau = F r
common_misconception: Dividing force by distance instead of multiplying.

concept_tested: Tension at lowest point
stem: For a body of mass m moving in a vertical circle of radius r with speed v at the lowest point, the tension in the string there is
solution: At the lowest point T - m g = m v^2/r, so T = m v^2/r + m g.
formula_principle: Newton's second law at the lowest point
common_misconception: Subtracting the weight instead of adding it at the lowest point.

concept_tested: Tension at highest point
stem: For a body of mass m moving in a vertical circle of radius r with speed v at the highest point, the tension there is
solution: At the top T + m g = m v^2/r, so T = m v^2/r - m g.
formula_principle: Newton's second law at the highest point
common_misconception: Adding the weight at the top instead of subtracting it.

concept_tested: Flywheel purpose
stem: A flywheel is fitted to an engine mainly because its large moment of inertia
option_a: stores rotational energy and smooths out speed fluctuations
option_b: increases the torque produced by the engine
option_c: reduces the mass of the engine
correct_answer_text: stores rotational energy and smooths out speed fluctuations
solution: The flywheel's large moment of inertia lets it store and release rotational energy, evening out variations in angular speed.
formula_principle: Rotational kinetic energy storage
common_misconception: Believing a flywheel increases the engine's torque output.

concept_tested: Parallel axis condition
stem: The theorem of parallel axes can be applied only when one of the axes
option_a: lies in the plane of the body
option_c: passes through a corner of the body
option_d: passes through the centre of mass
correct_answer_text: passes through the centre of mass
solution: The relation I = I_cm + M d^2 requires that I_cm be taken about an axis through the centre of mass.
formula_principle: Parallel axis theorem
common_misconception: Applying the theorem between two arbitrary parallel axes, neither through the centre of mass.

concept_tested: Sliding versus rolling
stem: A block slides down a frictionless incline and an identical sphere rolls down the same incline without slipping. Reaching the bottom first is
option_c: neither, as both remain at rest
solution: The block has acceleration g sin theta while the rolling sphere has only 5 g sin theta/7, so the block arrives first.
formula_principle: a_slide = g sin theta versus a_roll = 5 g sin theta/7
common_misconception: Assuming rolling is always faster because friction seems to help.

concept_tested: Angular momentum of a disc
stem: A disc of mass 2 kg and radius 0.5 m rotates about its central perpendicular axis at 8 rad s^-1. Its angular momentum is
formula_principle: L = I omega with I = M R^2/2
common_misconception: Using the ring formula M R^2 for the disc moment of inertia.

concept_tested: Angle dependence
stem: For a conical pendulum, as the angle of the string with the vertical increases, the period of revolution
solution: Since cos theta decreases as theta increases, the quantity L cos theta falls and the period decreases.
formula_principle: T = 2 pi sqrt(L cos theta / g)
common_misconception: Assuming a wider cone means a longer period.

concept_tested: Mass at greater distance
stem: Two bodies of equal mass have their mass distributed differently. The body with more mass concentrated far from the axis has
solution: Because each mass element contributes m r^2, mass placed farther from the axis raises the moment of inertia.
formula_principle: I = sum m r^2
common_misconception: Assuming equal masses must have equal moments of inertia.

concept_tested: Sphere speed at bottom
stem: A solid sphere rolls without slipping from rest down a height of 1.4 m. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, its speed at the bottom is
common_misconception: Using sqrt(2gh) and ignoring the rotational kinetic energy of the sphere.

concept_tested: Definition of a couple
stem: A couple consists of two forces that are
option_a: equal in magnitude, opposite in direction and not along the same line
option_b: equal in magnitude and acting along the same line
correct_answer_text: equal in magnitude, opposite in direction and not along the same line
solution: A couple is a pair of equal, opposite, non-collinear forces producing rotation without any net translational force.
formula_principle: Moment of a couple
common_misconception: Thinking a couple produces a net linear force as well as rotation.

concept_tested: Halving radius
stem: If the radius of the circular path is halved while the speed is unchanged, the centripetal force becomes
solution: At constant speed F is inversely proportional to r, so halving r doubles the force.
formula_principle: F = m v^2 / r
common_misconception: Applying the omega-based relation F = m r omega^2 when the speed, not omega, is fixed.

concept_tested: Rolling KE split for disc
stem: For a disc rolling without slipping, the fraction of its total kinetic energy that is rotational is
solution: For a disc rotational KE = m v^2/4 and total KE = 3 m v^2/4, so the fraction is 1/3.
formula_principle: Ratio of rotational to total KE
common_misconception: Using the ring fraction of one half for a disc.

concept_tested: Hollow sphere value
stem: A hollow sphere of mass 3 kg and radius 0.1 m rotates about a diameter. Its moment of inertia is
common_misconception: Applying the solid sphere coefficient to a hollow sphere.

concept_tested: Direction of L
stem: The direction of the angular momentum vector of a rotating rigid body is
option_a: along the tangent to the circular path
option_b: towards the centre of the circle
option_c: along the axis of rotation, given by the right hand rule
correct_answer_text: along the axis of rotation, given by the right hand rule
solution: For rotation about a fixed axis, L points along the axis in the same sense as omega, set by the right hand rule.
formula_principle: L = I omega as a vector
common_misconception: Assuming angular momentum points along the velocity of the rotating particle.

concept_tested: Washing machine dryer
stem: The drying action in a washing machine spinner works because
option_a: centrifugal force physically pushes water out of the clothes
option_b: water droplets lack sufficient centripetal force and move out through the holes
option_c: the spinning heats the water and evaporates it
option_d: the holes attract the water droplets
correct_answer_text: water droplets lack sufficient centripetal force and move out through the holes
solution: Clothes provide centripetal force to hold water, but at high speed the required force exceeds what the fabric supplies, so droplets move along tangents and escape through the holes.
formula_principle: Requirement of centripetal force
common_misconception: Explaining the effect as a real outward centrifugal push.

concept_tested: Using radius of gyration
stem: A body of mass 10 kg has radius of gyration 0.3 m about an axis. Its moment of inertia is
formula_principle: I = M k^2
common_misconception: Failing to square the radius of gyration.

concept_tested: Rotational equilibrium
stem: A rigid body is in rotational equilibrium when
option_a: the net torque acting on it is zero
option_b: the net force acting on it is zero
option_d: its moment of inertia is zero
correct_answer_text: the net torque acting on it is zero
solution: Rotational equilibrium requires that the vector sum of all torques about any axis be zero.
formula_principle: Conditions of equilibrium
common_misconception: Confusing the condition for translational equilibrium with that for rotational equilibrium.

concept_tested: Independence of incline result
stem: Two solid spheres of different masses and radii roll without slipping from rest down the same incline. They reach the bottom
option_a: at the same time, since the acceleration is independent of mass and radius
correct_answer_text: at the same time, since the acceleration is independent of mass and radius
solution: For a solid sphere a = 5 g sin theta/7 regardless of mass and radius, so both spheres arrive together.
formula_principle: a = 5 g sin theta / 7 for all solid spheres
common_misconception: Assuming heavier or larger rolling bodies descend faster.

concept_tested: Centripetal force from speed
stem: A car of mass 1000 kg turns a corner of radius 50 m at 10 m s^-1. The centripetal force required is
formula_principle: F = m v^2 / r
common_misconception: Failing to square the speed before dividing by the radius.

concept_tested: Effect of axis shift
stem: For a given rigid body, the moment of inertia is least about an axis that
option_a: passes through one of its edges
option_b: passes through its centre of mass
correct_answer_text: passes through its centre of mass
solution: Since M d^2 is never negative, shifting an axis away from the centre of mass can only increase the moment of inertia.
formula_principle: I = I_cm + M d^2
common_misconception: Assuming the moment of inertia can be reduced by moving the axis off centre.

concept_tested: Diver tucking
stem: A diver curls up during a somersault in order to
option_a: increase her angular momentum in mid air
option_c: reduce her moment of inertia and increase her rate of spin
correct_answer_text: reduce her moment of inertia and increase her rate of spin
solution: With angular momentum conserved, curling up reduces I and therefore raises the angular velocity.
formula_principle: L = I omega conserved
common_misconception: Believing the diver gains angular momentum by changing body shape.

concept_tested: KE of a rolling body
stem: A ring of mass 2 kg rolls without slipping at 3 m s^-1. Its total kinetic energy is
solution: For a ring total KE = m v^2 = 2 x (3)^2 = 18 J.
formula_principle: KE = m v^2 for a rolling ring
common_misconception: Counting only m v^2/2 and omitting the equal rotational contribution.

concept_tested: Angle turned under constant alpha
stem: A wheel starting from rest has constant angular acceleration 2 rad s^-2. The angle turned in 3 s is
formula_principle: theta = omega_0 t + alpha t^2 / 2
common_misconception: Forgetting the factor of one half in the rotational kinematic equation.

subtopic: Pressure due to a liquid column
concept_tested: Gauge pressure at a depth depends only on depth, density and g
stem: A tank is filled with a liquid up to a depth h. The gauge pressure at a point on the base of the tank is decided by
option_a: the depth of the point below the free surface and the area of the base of the tank
option_b: the depth of the point below the free surface, the density of the liquid and the acceleration due to gravity
option_c: the total weight of the liquid held in the tank and the area of the base of the tank
option_d: the shape of the tank and the total volume of liquid that it holds
correct_answer_text: the depth of the point below the free surface, the density of the liquid and the acceleration due to gravity
solution: The pressure at a depth h inside a static liquid is P = h rho g. Only the depth h, the density rho and g appear. Neither the area of the base nor the shape or the volume of the vessel enters the expression.
formula_principle: P = h rho g for a liquid column of uniform density
common_misconception: Students believe a wider vessel gives a larger pressure at the base because it holds more liquid.

subtopic: Pressure due to a liquid column
concept_tested: Numerical use of P = h rho g
stem: Water of density 1000 kg m^-3 fills a tank. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the gauge pressure at a point 5 m below the free surface is
solution: P = h rho g = 5 x 1000 x 10 = 50000 Pa = 5 x 10^4 Pa. This is the gauge pressure, that is the excess over atmospheric pressure.
formula_principle: P = h rho g
common_misconception: Students add atmospheric pressure even when the gauge pressure is asked for.

concept_tested: Statement of Pascal's law
stem: Pascal's law for an enclosed fluid at rest states that a change of pressure applied at any point of the fluid
option_a: is transmitted to every point of the fluid but falls off with distance from the point of application
option_b: is transmitted undiminished to every point of the fluid and to the walls of the container
option_c: is transmitted only along the direction in which the external force is applied
option_d: is transmitted only to the walls of the container and not to the interior of the fluid
correct_answer_text: is transmitted undiminished to every point of the fluid and to the walls of the container
solution: Pascal's law says that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid at rest is transmitted equally and undiminished in all directions, reaching every point of the fluid and every part of the containing walls. This is the basis of hydraulic machines.
formula_principle: Pascal's law for transmission of pressure in an enclosed incompressible fluid
common_misconception: Students think the transmitted pressure decreases with distance from the piston.

concept_tested: Relation between gauge, absolute and atmospheric pressure
stem: For a point inside a liquid that is open to the atmosphere, the gauge pressure is
option_a: the absolute pressure at the point plus the atmospheric pressure
option_b: the atmospheric pressure minus the absolute pressure at the point
option_c: the absolute pressure at the point minus the atmospheric pressure
option_d: the absolute pressure at the point divided by the atmospheric pressure
correct_answer_text: the absolute pressure at the point minus the atmospheric pressure
solution: A pressure gauge open to the atmosphere on one side reads the excess of the true pressure over atmospheric pressure. Hence P_gauge = P_absolute - P_atmospheric, and for a liquid column P_gauge = h rho g.
formula_principle: P_gauge = P_absolute - P_atmospheric
common_misconception: Students use gauge and absolute pressure interchangeably and add atmospheric pressure twice.

concept_tested: Absolute pressure at a depth in an open tank
stem: A lake holds water of density 1000 kg m^-3. Atmospheric pressure is 1.0 x 10^5 Pa and g = 10 m s^-2. The absolute pressure at a depth of 20 m below the surface is
solution: The water column contributes h rho g = 20 x 1000 x 10 = 2.0 x 10^5 Pa. Adding the atmospheric pressure, P = 1.0 x 10^5 + 2.0 x 10^5 = 3.0 x 10^5 Pa.
formula_principle: P_absolute = P_atmospheric + h rho g
common_misconception: Students report the gauge value when the absolute pressure is demanded.

concept_tested: Force multiplication in a hydraulic lift
stem: In a hydraulic lift the two pistons have areas in the ratio 1 : 50. A force of 100 N is applied on the smaller piston. The maximum load that can be raised on the larger piston is
solution: The same pressure acts on both pistons, so F2 = F1 x (A2 / A1) = 100 x 50 = 5000 N. The lift multiplies force by the area ratio, while the smaller piston must be pushed through a correspondingly larger distance.
formula_principle: Pascal's law: F1 / A1 = F2 / A2
common_misconception: Students think the force, and not the pressure, is transmitted unchanged.

concept_tested: Pressure at the base is independent of vessel shape
stem: Three vessels of very different shapes, one cylindrical, one flaring outwards and one tapering inwards, stand on a table. Each has the same base area and each is filled with water to the same height. The pressure exerted by the water on the base is
option_a: largest for the vessel that flares outwards
option_b: largest for the vessel that tapers inwards
option_d: the same for all three vessels
correct_answer_text: the same for all three vessels
solution: Pressure at the base is h rho g and depends only on the vertical depth of liquid. Since h and rho are the same in all three vessels the base pressure is identical, even though the vessels hold different amounts of water. The extra weight in the flaring vessel is supported by the vertical component of the reaction of the slanting walls.
formula_principle: P = h rho g, the hydrostatic paradox
common_misconception: Students equate pressure on the base with the weight of the liquid divided by the base area for every vessel shape.

concept_tested: Mercury barometer reading converted to pascal
stem: A mercury barometer stands at a height of 0.75 m. The density of mercury is 13600 kg m^-3 and g = 10 m s^-2. The atmospheric pressure indicated is
solution: P = h rho g = 0.75 x 13600 x 10 = 102000 Pa = 1.02 x 10^5 Pa. The barometric height measures atmospheric pressure directly because the space above the mercury is very nearly a vacuum.
formula_principle: P = h rho g for the mercury column of a barometer
common_misconception: Students forget to convert centimetres of mercury to metres before applying h rho g.

subtopic: Pressure due to a liquid column
concept_tested: Pressure at equal depths in liquids of different density
stem: Two wide vessels, one holding water of density 1000 kg m^-3 and the other holding an oil of density 800 kg m^-3, are open to the atmosphere. The ratio of the gauge pressure at a depth of 2 m in water to that at a depth of 2 m in oil is
solution: At equal depth h and equal g, P is proportional to rho. Hence the ratio is 1000 : 800 = 5 : 4. Numerically the values are 2 x 1000 x 10 = 2.0 x 10^4 Pa and 2 x 800 x 10 = 1.6 x 10^4 Pa.
formula_principle: P = h rho g at a given depth
common_misconception: Students assume the same depth always means the same pressure whatever the liquid.

concept_tested: Thrust on a horizontal base from the pressure at that depth
stem: A tank with a flat horizontal base of area 2 m^2 holds water of density 1000 kg m^-3 to a depth of 3 m. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the force exerted by the water on the base, over and above the force due to the atmosphere, is
solution: Every point of a horizontal base lies at the same depth, so the pressure is uniform: P = 3 x 1000 x 10 = 3 x 10^4 Pa. Therefore F = P A = 3 x 10^4 x 2 = 6 x 10^4 N.
formula_principle: F = P A with P = h rho g
common_misconception: Students apply the average pressure factor of one half, which belongs to a vertical wall, to a horizontal base.

concept_tested: Dimensional formula of pressure
stem: In fluid mechanics, pressure is defined as thrust per unit area. Its dimensional formula is
solution: Pressure = F / A. The dimensions of force are [M L T^-2] and of area are [L^2], so pressure has dimensions [M L T^-2] divided by [L^2], that is [M^1 L^-1 T^-2]. The same result follows from h rho g, namely [L][M L^-3][L T^-2].
formula_principle: Pressure = force per unit area
common_misconception: Students quote the dimensions of force in place of those of pressure.

subtopic: Pressure balance in a U tube
concept_tested: Equating pressures at the level of the interface of two immiscible liquids
stem: A U tube contains water of density 1000 kg m^-3. Oil of density 800 kg m^-3 is poured into the left arm and forms a column of height 20 cm standing above the oil to water interface. The difference between the levels of the two free surfaces is
solution: Take the horizontal level of the oil to water interface. The oil column of 20 cm gives a pressure 0.20 x 800 x g. The balancing water column of height x in the other arm gives x x 1000 x g. Hence x = 0.20 x 800 / 1000 = 0.16 m = 16 cm. The oil surface stands 20 cm above the interface while the water surface stands 16 cm above it, so the free surfaces differ by 20 - 16 = 4 cm.
formula_principle: Pressures are equal at points at the same horizontal level in a connected liquid at rest
common_misconception: Students report the equivalent water column height as the level difference instead of subtracting it from the oil column height.

concept_tested: Volume of incompressible liquid displaced is the same for both pistons
stem: In a hydraulic lift the cross sectional areas of the small and the large piston are in the ratio 1 : 25. The small piston is pushed down through 20 cm. The large piston rises through
solution: The liquid is incompressible, so the volume pushed out from under the small piston equals the volume that lifts the large piston: A1 d1 = A2 d2. Hence d2 = d1 x (A1 / A2) = 20 x (1 / 25) = 0.8 cm. The force is multiplied by 25 while the displacement is reduced by 25, so the work done is unchanged.
formula_principle: A1 d1 = A2 d2 for an incompressible liquid, together with Pascal's law
common_misconception: Students think a hydraulic lift multiplies force without any penalty in distance moved.

concept_tested: Adding the contributions of two immiscible layers
stem: A vessel holds a 0.5 m layer of oil of density 800 kg m^-3 floating on a 1.0 m layer of water of density 1000 kg m^-3. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the gauge pressure at the bottom of the vessel is
solution: The oil layer contributes 0.5 x 800 x 10 = 4000 Pa at the oil to water interface. Below that the water adds 1.0 x 1000 x 10 = 10000 Pa. The total gauge pressure at the bottom is 4000 + 10000 = 14000 Pa = 1.4 x 10^4 Pa.
formula_principle: P = sum of h rho g over each layer
common_misconception: Students apply h rho g once using the total depth together with a single density.

concept_tested: Depth at which the absolute pressure doubles
stem: Atmospheric pressure at the surface of a lake is 1.0 x 10^5 Pa. The density of water is 1000 kg m^-3 and g = 10 m s^-2. The depth at which the absolute pressure becomes twice the atmospheric pressure is
solution: We need P_atmospheric + h rho g = 2 P_atmospheric, that is h rho g = P_atmospheric. Hence h = 1.0 x 10^5 divided by (1000 x 10), which gives 10 m. Every further 10 m of water adds one more atmosphere.
formula_principle: P_absolute = P_atmospheric + h rho g
common_misconception: Students set the water column pressure equal to twice the atmospheric pressure instead of equal to it.

concept_tested: Average pressure on a vertical wall is half the pressure at the bottom
stem: A rectangular tank has a vertical side wall 3 m wide. Water of density 1000 kg m^-3 stands against this wall to a depth of 2 m. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the net force exerted by the water on this wall is
solution: Pressure on the wall grows linearly with depth from zero at the surface to h rho g = 2 x 1000 x 10 = 2 x 10^4 Pa at the bottom. The average pressure over the wetted area is therefore half of this, that is 1 x 10^4 Pa. The wetted area is 2 x 3 = 6 m^2, so F = 1 x 10^4 x 6 = 6 x 10^4 N.
formula_principle: Average pressure on a vertical wall = h rho g / 2, then F = P_average x A
common_misconception: Students multiply the maximum pressure at the bottom by the whole wall area, forgetting that pressure varies with depth on a vertical surface.

concept_tested: Surface tension as force per unit length
stem: The SI unit of surface tension is
solution: Surface tension is defined as the force acting per unit length of an imaginary line drawn on the liquid surface, so its unit is newton per metre. The same quantity read as surface energy per unit area gives J m^-2, which is identical to N m^-1.
formula_principle: T = F / l, force per unit length of the surface
common_misconception: Students treat surface tension as a pressure and quote N m^-2.

concept_tested: Dimensional formula of surface tension
stem: Surface tension is defined as the force acting per unit length of a surface. Its dimensional formula is
solution: Surface tension is force per unit length, so its dimensions are [M L T^-2] divided by [L], that is [M^1 L^0 T^-2]. Checking with surface energy per unit area gives [M L^2 T^-2] divided by [L^2], the same result.
formula_principle: T = F / l
common_misconception: Students confuse the dimensions of surface tension with those of pressure.

concept_tested: Surface energy per unit area equals surface tension
stem: The work done in increasing the free surface area of a liquid by one square metre at constant temperature is numerically equal to
option_a: twice the surface tension of the liquid
option_b: half the surface tension of the liquid
option_c: the surface tension of the liquid
option_d: the surface tension divided by the density of the liquid
correct_answer_text: the surface tension of the liquid
solution: Isothermal work done in creating extra surface is W = T dA. For dA = 1 m^2 the work equals T numerically, which is why surface tension can be quoted in J m^-2 as well as in N m^-1.
formula_principle: Surface energy per unit area = T
common_misconception: Students apply the two surface factor of a soap film to an ordinary liquid surface.

concept_tested: Excess pressure inside a liquid drop
stem: The excess of pressure inside a spherical liquid drop of radius R, for a liquid of surface tension T, over the pressure just outside is
solution: A liquid drop has one single curved surface separating liquid from air. Balancing the surface tension force against the pressure difference over a hemisphere gives P_inside minus P_outside = 2 T / R.
formula_principle: Excess pressure inside a drop = 2 T / R
common_misconception: Students quote 4 T / R for a drop by confusing it with a soap bubble.

concept_tested: Excess pressure inside a soap bubble
stem: A soap bubble of radius R is blown from a solution of surface tension T. The pressure inside the bubble exceeds the atmospheric pressure by
solution: The thin soap film has two surfaces in contact with air, an inner one and an outer one. Each contributes 2 T / R, so the total excess pressure is 4 T / R.
formula_principle: Excess pressure inside a soap bubble = 4 T / R
common_misconception: Students forget that a soap bubble has two free surfaces and use the drop result.

concept_tested: Net inward pull on a molecule at the surface
stem: According to the molecular theory of surface tension, a molecule lying exactly on the free surface of a liquid experiences
option_a: a net outward force directed away from the bulk of the liquid
option_b: a net inward force directed into the bulk of the liquid
option_c: no net force at all because its sphere of influence is complete
option_d: a net force directed along the surface towards the walls of the vessel
correct_answer_text: a net inward force directed into the bulk of the liquid
solution: A molecule deep inside the liquid is pulled equally in all directions and the resultant is zero. For a molecule on the surface the upper half of its sphere of influence is nearly empty, so the cohesive pull from below is unbalanced and the resultant force is directed inwards. This is why a surface molecule has extra potential energy and why the liquid tends to minimise its surface area.
formula_principle: Unbalanced cohesive forces within the sphere of influence of a surface molecule
common_misconception: Students think surface molecules are pulled outwards, which would make the surface expand rather than contract.

concept_tested: Numerical excess pressure inside a drop
stem: A spherical water drop has radius 1 mm. The surface tension of water is 0.05 N m^-1. The excess pressure inside the drop is
solution: R = 1 mm = 1 x 10^-3 m. Excess pressure = 2 T / R = 2 x 0.05 divided by 1 x 10^-3 = 0.1 divided by 0.001 = 100 Pa.
formula_principle: Excess pressure inside a drop = 2 T / R
common_misconception: Students forget to convert millimetres to metres before substituting.

concept_tested: Numerical excess pressure inside a soap bubble
stem: A soap bubble of radius 2 mm is blown from a solution of surface tension 0.03 N m^-1. The excess pressure inside the bubble is
solution: R = 2 mm = 2 x 10^-3 m. Excess pressure = 4 T / R = 4 x 0.03 divided by 2 x 10^-3 = 0.12 divided by 0.002 = 60 Pa.
formula_principle: Excess pressure inside a soap bubble = 4 T / R
common_misconception: Students apply the single surface result to a soap bubble.

concept_tested: Comparing a drop and a soap bubble of equal radius
stem: A liquid drop and a soap bubble of the same liquid have the same radius. The ratio of the excess pressure inside the drop to that inside the bubble is
solution: The drop has one liquid to air surface and gives 2 T / R. The soap bubble has an inner and an outer surface and gives 4 T / R. The ratio is therefore 2 T / R to 4 T / R, that is 1 : 2.
formula_principle: 2 T / R for a drop and 4 T / R for a soap bubble
common_misconception: Students believe the number of surfaces does not matter as long as the radius is the same.

concept_tested: A soap film stretched in a frame has two surfaces
stem: A soap film is formed in a rectangular frame whose movable wire is 10 cm long. The wire is pulled out slowly through 5 cm at constant temperature. The surface tension of the solution is 0.03 N m^-1. The work done is
solution: The extra area on each face is 0.10 x 0.05 = 5 x 10^-3 m^2. The film has two faces, so the total increase in surface area is 1 x 10^-2 m^2. Hence W = T x dA = 0.03 x 1 x 10^-2 = 3 x 10^-4 J.
formula_principle: W = T x (increase in total surface area), a soap film having two surfaces
common_misconception: Students forget that a soap film has two free surfaces and halve the correct work.

concept_tested: Force on a wire supporting a soap film
stem: A soap film is formed on a frame carrying a movable wire of length 20 cm. The surface tension of the solution is 0.04 N m^-1. The force that must be applied to the wire to keep the film from contracting is
solution: F = 2 T l = 2 x 0.04 x 0.20 = 0.016 N. The factor of two arises because the film has an upper and a lower surface, each pulling on the wire with force T l.
formula_principle: F = 2 T l for a soap film with two surfaces
common_misconception: Students apply F = T l, which is correct only for a single liquid surface.

concept_tested: Work needed to blow a soap bubble
stem: The work done in blowing a soap bubble of radius R from a solution of surface tension T is
solution: A soap bubble has an inner surface and an outer surface, each of area 4 pi R^2 to a good approximation. The total new area is 8 pi R^2, so the isothermal work done is W = 8 pi R^2 T.
formula_principle: W = T x total new surface area, with two surfaces of area 4 pi R^2 each
common_misconception: Students use 4 pi R^2 T, which is the surface energy of a drop and not of a bubble.

concept_tested: Surface energy scales as the square of the radius
stem: The radius of a spherical liquid drop is doubled at constant temperature. Its surface energy becomes
solution: Surface energy is T times the surface area, and the area of a sphere is 4 pi R^2. Doubling R multiplies the area, and hence the surface energy, by 2^2 = 4.
formula_principle: Surface energy of a drop = 4 pi R^2 T
common_misconception: Students scale surface energy with the volume of the drop instead of with its surface area.

concept_tested: Two connected soap bubbles of unequal radius
stem: Two soap bubbles of unequal radii are blown at the two ends of a tube and the connecting tap between them is opened. Then
option_a: the larger bubble shrinks and the smaller bubble grows
option_b: the smaller bubble shrinks and the larger bubble grows
option_c: both bubbles adjust until they reach the same radius
option_d: both bubbles stay exactly as they were because the surface tension is the same
correct_answer_text: the smaller bubble shrinks and the larger bubble grows
solution: The excess pressure inside a bubble is 4 T / R, which is greater for the bubble of smaller radius. When the tap is opened air flows from the region of higher pressure to that of lower pressure, that is from the smaller bubble into the larger one. The smaller bubble therefore collapses further while the larger one expands.
formula_principle: Excess pressure inside a soap bubble = 4 T / R, so smaller radius means larger pressure
common_misconception: Students assume the bigger bubble must contain the higher pressure because it holds more air.

concept_tested: Effect of temperature on surface tension
stem: As the temperature of a liquid is raised towards its critical temperature, the surface tension of the liquid
option_a: decreases and becomes zero at the critical temperature
option_b: increases and becomes maximum at the critical temperature
option_c: remains constant because surface tension is a property of the liquid alone
option_d: first decreases and then increases sharply near the critical temperature
correct_answer_text: decreases and becomes zero at the critical temperature
solution: Rising temperature increases the average separation and the thermal motion of the molecules, which weakens the cohesive forces responsible for surface tension. At the critical temperature the distinction between liquid and vapour disappears and the surface tension falls to zero. This is why hot water cleans better than cold water.
formula_principle: Temperature dependence of surface tension
common_misconception: Students assume surface tension is a fixed constant for a given liquid regardless of temperature.

concept_tested: Energy released when small drops merge into one
stem: Eight identical spherical drops of a liquid, each of radius 1 mm, coalesce isothermally into a single large drop. The surface tension of the liquid is 0.05 N m^-1. The energy released is
solution: Volume conservation gives R = 8^(1/3) x r = 2 x 1 mm = 2 mm. Initial total area = 8 x 4 pi r^2 = 32 pi x 10^-6 m^2. Final area = 4 pi R^2 = 4 pi x 4 x 10^-6 = 16 pi x 10^-6 m^2. The area decreases by 16 pi x 10^-6 m^2, so the energy released is T x 16 pi x 10^-6 = 0.05 x 16 pi x 10^-6 = 0.8 pi x 10^-6 J.
formula_principle: Volume is conserved, so R = n^(1/3) r; energy released = T x (decrease in surface area)
common_misconception: Students forget that the merged drop still has a surface and subtract nothing from the initial area.

concept_tested: General expression for the work done in splitting a drop
stem: A spherical drop of radius R and surface tension T is broken up isothermally into n identical smaller drops. The work that must be done is
solution: Conserving volume, n x (4/3) pi r^3 = (4/3) pi R^3, so r = R divided by n^(1/3). The total final area is n x 4 pi r^2 = 4 pi R^2 x n^(1/3). The initial area is 4 pi R^2. The increase is 4 pi R^2 (n^(1/3) - 1), and the work done is T times this, that is 4 pi T R^2 (n^(1/3) - 1).
formula_principle: Volume conservation r = R / n^(1/3), then W = T x (increase in surface area)
common_misconception: Students take the final area as n times the original area, forgetting that each small drop is smaller in radius.

concept_tested: Numerical work done in splitting a drop into a thousand droplets
stem: A drop of a liquid of surface tension 0.05 N m^-1 and radius 1 mm is sprayed into 1000 identical droplets. The work done in the process is
solution: Here n^(1/3) = 1000^(1/3) = 10, so the factor n^(1/3) minus 1 equals 9. With R = 1 x 10^-3 m, R^2 = 1 x 10^-6 m^2. Hence W = 4 pi x 0.05 x 1 x 10^-6 x 9 = 1.8 pi x 10^-6 J, which is about 5.7 x 10^-6 J. Each droplet has radius 1 mm divided by 10, that is 0.1 mm.
common_misconception: Students multiply the parent area by n instead of by n^(1/3) when finding the final total area.

concept_tested: An air bubble inside a liquid has only one surface
stem: An air bubble of radius R is formed well inside a large body of a liquid of surface tension T. The pressure inside the bubble exceeds the pressure of the liquid just outside it by
solution: An air bubble sitting inside a liquid has just one interface between air and liquid, exactly like a liquid drop in air. Therefore the excess pressure is 2 T / R. Only a soap bubble in air, whose thin film has an inner and an outer face, gives 4 T / R.
formula_principle: Number of liquid to air surfaces decides the numerical factor in the excess pressure
common_misconception: Students see the word bubble and automatically apply 4 T / R without counting the interfaces.

concept_tested: Two soap bubbles coalescing isothermally
stem: Two soap bubbles of radii 3 cm and 4 cm coalesce isothermally under vacuum to form a single bubble. The radius of the resulting bubble is
solution: For a soap bubble the pressure inside is 4 T / R above the outside pressure, which is zero here. Applying Boyle's law to the enclosed air, (4 T / R1)(4/3 pi R1^3) + (4 T / R2)(4/3 pi R2^3) = (4 T / R)(4/3 pi R^3), which simplifies to R1^2 + R2^2 = R^2. Hence R = square root of (9 + 16) = 5 cm.
formula_principle: Isothermal coalescence under vacuum conserves the enclosed air, giving R^2 = R1^2 + R2^2 for soap bubbles
common_misconception: Students add the radii or the volumes directly instead of applying Boyle's law to the enclosed air.

concept_tested: Radius of each droplet after splitting
stem: A single spherical drop of radius R is broken into 64 identical smaller drops. The radius of each smaller drop is
solution: The total volume is unchanged, so 64 x (4/3) pi r^3 = (4/3) pi R^3, giving r^3 = R^3 divided by 64 and hence r = R divided by 4. The total surface area rises by the factor 64^(1/3) = 4, which is why energy must be supplied.
formula_principle: Volume conservation: r = R / n^(1/3)
common_misconception: Students divide the radius by the number of drops instead of by the cube root of that number.

concept_tested: Work done in expanding a soap bubble
stem: The radius of a soap bubble made from a solution of surface tension T is increased isothermally from r to 2 r. The work done is
solution: The total area of a soap bubble of radius r is 2 x 4 pi r^2 = 8 pi r^2. For radius 2 r it is 8 pi (2r)^2 = 32 pi r^2. The increase is 32 pi r^2 minus 8 pi r^2 = 24 pi r^2, so the work done is 24 pi T r^2.
formula_principle: W = 2 T x (4 pi R2^2 - 4 pi R1^2) for a soap film with two surfaces
common_misconception: Students forget to subtract the initial surface area, or count only a single surface.

concept_tested: Radius of curvature of the common film between two bubbles
stem: Two soap bubbles of radii 3 cm and 6 cm are blown from the same solution and are made to stick to each other. The radius of curvature of the common film separating them is
solution: Let a = 3 cm be the smaller radius and b = 6 cm the larger. The pressure inside the small bubble exceeds atmospheric by 4 T / a and that inside the large bubble by 4 T / b. The common film separates these two, so it must support 4 T / a minus 4 T / b = 4 T / R. Hence 1 / R = 1 / a minus 1 / b, giving R = a b divided by (b minus a) = 18 divided by 3 = 6 cm. The film bulges into the larger bubble.
formula_principle: The common film must support the difference of the two excess pressures: 4T/R = 4T/a - 4T/b
common_misconception: Students add the excess pressures instead of taking their difference across the common film.

concept_tested: Ratio of surface energies before and after splitting
stem: A mercury drop is broken into 27 identical smaller drops at constant temperature. The ratio of the total surface energy of the parent drop to that of all the smaller drops taken together is
solution: Each small drop has radius r = R divided by 27^(1/3) = R divided by 3. The total area of the small drops is 27 x 4 pi (R/3)^2 = 27 x 4 pi R^2 divided by 9 = 3 x 4 pi R^2. Since surface energy is T times area, the ratio of the parent energy to the total final energy is 4 pi R^2 T to 12 pi R^2 T, that is 1 : 3. The extra energy comes from the work done in splitting.
formula_principle: r = R / n^(1/3), total final area = n^(1/3) x 4 pi R^2
common_misconception: Students take the total final surface area as 27 times that of the parent drop.

concept_tested: Definition of the angle of contact
stem: The angle of contact for a liquid in contact with a solid is the angle measured
option_a: outside the liquid, between the tangent to the liquid surface at the point of contact and the solid surface
option_b: between the free horizontal surface of the liquid and the wall of the containing vessel
option_c: between the vertical wall of the vessel and the horizontal base of the vessel
option_d: inside the liquid, between the tangent to the liquid surface at the point of contact and the solid surface
correct_answer_text: inside the liquid, between the tangent to the liquid surface at the point of contact and the solid surface
solution: At the line where the liquid surface meets the solid, a tangent is drawn to the liquid surface. The angle between this tangent and the solid surface, measured through the liquid, is the angle of contact. It is fixed by the relative strengths of the adhesive and cohesive forces.
formula_principle: Angle of contact theta measured within the liquid at the solid to liquid to air junction
common_misconception: Students measure the angle on the air side and report its supplement.

concept_tested: Meniscus shape for water and for mercury in glass
stem: In a clean glass tube, water forms a concave meniscus while mercury forms a convex meniscus. This is because
option_a: for water the cohesive force exceeds the adhesive force with glass, while for mercury the adhesive force is the greater
option_b: water is less dense than mercury, so its surface curves downwards at the walls
option_c: water has a larger surface tension than mercury, so it is pulled up along the walls
option_d: for water the adhesive force with glass exceeds the cohesive force, while for mercury the cohesive force is the greater
correct_answer_text: for water the adhesive force with glass exceeds the cohesive force, while for mercury the cohesive force is the greater
solution: When adhesion between liquid and solid is stronger than cohesion within the liquid, the liquid climbs the wall, the angle of contact is acute and the meniscus is concave, as for water on glass. When cohesion dominates, as for mercury on glass, the angle of contact is obtuse and the meniscus is convex.
formula_principle: Adhesion versus cohesion decides the angle of contact and hence the shape of the meniscus
common_misconception: Students think the liquid with the larger surface tension always rises higher and wets the solid.

concept_tested: Formula for capillary rise
stem: For a liquid of surface tension T, density rho and angle of contact theta in a capillary tube of radius r, the height of capillary rise is given by
option_a: 2 T cos theta x r / (rho g)
option_d: T cos theta / (2 r rho g)
solution: The upward pull of surface tension around the circle of contact is T x 2 pi r x cos theta. This supports the weight of the raised column, pi r^2 h rho g. Equating the two gives h = 2 T cos theta divided by (r rho g).
formula_principle: h = 2 T cos theta / (r rho g)
common_misconception: Students place the radius in the numerator and conclude that wider tubes give a greater rise.

concept_tested: Rise varies inversely with the radius
stem: For a given liquid and a given tube material, the height to which the liquid rises in a capillary tube is
option_a: directly proportional to the radius of the tube
option_b: inversely proportional to the radius of the tube
option_c: inversely proportional to the square of the radius of the tube
option_d: independent of the radius of the tube
correct_answer_text: inversely proportional to the radius of the tube
solution: In the expression for capillary rise the radius appears once, in the denominator. Hence h is inversely proportional to r, and the product h r is a constant for a given liquid and tube material. This is Jurin's law.
formula_principle: h = 2 T cos theta / (r rho g), so h r = constant
common_misconception: Students believe a wider tube holds more liquid and therefore lifts it higher.

concept_tested: Mercury is depressed in a glass capillary
stem: A clean glass capillary tube is dipped into mercury, whose angle of contact with glass is about 140 degrees. The mercury in the tube
option_a: is depressed below the level of mercury in the vessel
option_b: rises above the level of mercury in the vessel
option_c: stands exactly at the level of mercury in the vessel
option_d: rises and then falls back until it just reaches the vessel level
correct_answer_text: is depressed below the level of mercury in the vessel
solution: For mercury on glass the angle of contact is about 140 degrees, so cos theta is negative. The computed height h is therefore negative, which means the mercury is pushed down and stands below the level in the vessel. The meniscus is convex upwards.
formula_principle: h = 2 T cos theta / (r rho g) with theta greater than 90 degrees
common_misconception: Students expect every liquid to rise in a capillary tube because they have only seen water demonstrations.

concept_tested: Numerical capillary rise for a wetting liquid
stem: A capillary tube of radius 0.2 mm is dipped in a liquid of surface tension 0.06 N m^-1 and density 1000 kg m^-3. The angle of contact is zero and g = 10 m s^-2. The liquid rises through
solution: With cos theta = 1 and r = 2 x 10^-4 m, h = 2 x 0.06 divided by (2 x 10^-4 x 1000 x 10) = 0.12 divided by 2 = 0.06 m = 6 cm.
formula_principle: h = 2 T cos theta / (r rho g)
common_misconception: Students mix up radius and diameter, or forget to convert millimetres to metres.

concept_tested: Comparing rises in two tubes of different radius
stem: Two capillary tubes whose radii are in the ratio 1 : 2 are dipped in the same liquid. The heights to which the liquid rises in the two tubes are in the ratio
solution: Since h = 2 T cos theta divided by (r rho g), the product h r is constant. If the radii are in the ratio 1 : 2, the rises are in the inverse ratio 2 : 1, so the narrower tube lifts the liquid twice as high.
formula_principle: h is proportional to 1 / r for a given liquid and tube material
common_misconception: Students invert the proportionality and expect the wider tube to give the larger rise.

concept_tested: Wetting and non wetting liquids
stem: A liquid is said to wet the surface of a solid when its angle of contact with that solid is
option_a: acute, that is less than 90 degrees
option_b: obtuse, that is greater than 90 degrees
correct_answer_text: acute, that is less than 90 degrees
solution: When adhesion dominates, the liquid spreads over the solid, the meniscus is concave and the angle of contact measured inside the liquid is acute. Such a liquid wets the solid and rises in a capillary tube. Water on clean glass, with an angle of contact near zero, is the standard example.
formula_principle: Acute angle of contact corresponds to adhesion stronger than cohesion
common_misconception: Students associate wetting with large surface tension rather than with a small angle of contact.

concept_tested: Effect of reduced gravity on capillary rise
stem: A capillary tube dipped in water on the Earth shows a rise h. The same experiment is repeated on the surface of the Moon, where the acceleration due to gravity is one sixth of its value on the Earth. Assuming the tube is long enough, the rise becomes
solution: The surface tension force at the meniscus is unchanged, but the weight of a given column of liquid is six times smaller on the Moon. The same upward pull can therefore support a column six times as tall, so the rise becomes 6 h provided the tube is at least that long.
formula_principle: h = 2 T cos theta / (r rho g), so h is proportional to 1 / g
common_misconception: Students think weaker gravity should reduce the rise because everything feels lighter.

concept_tested: Finding surface tension from an observed rise
stem: Water rises through 4 cm in a capillary tube of radius 0.25 mm. The density of water is 1000 kg m^-3, the angle of contact is zero and g = 10 m s^-2. The surface tension of water is
solution: Rearranging the capillary rise formula with cos theta = 1 gives T = h r rho g divided by 2. Substituting h = 0.04 m and r = 2.5 x 10^-4 m, T = 0.04 x 2.5 x 10^-4 x 1000 x 10 divided by 2 = 0.10 divided by 2 = 0.05 N m^-1.
formula_principle: T = h r rho g / (2 cos theta)
common_misconception: Students forget the factor of two when inverting the capillary rise formula.

concept_tested: Mass of liquid raised varies directly with the radius
stem: The same liquid is drawn up by two capillary tubes of different radii. The mass of liquid held above the outside level in a tube is
option_a: inversely proportional to the radius of the tube
option_b: directly proportional to the square of the radius of the tube
option_c: directly proportional to the radius of the tube
option_d: independent of the radius of the tube
correct_answer_text: directly proportional to the radius of the tube
solution: The mass raised is m = pi r^2 h rho. Since h is proportional to 1 / r, the product r^2 x (1/r) leaves a single factor of r, so m is proportional to r. Equivalently, the weight supported equals the vertical surface tension force 2 pi r T cos theta, which is plainly proportional to r.
formula_principle: m = pi r^2 h rho with h proportional to 1 / r
common_misconception: Students assume that because a narrow tube gives a greater rise it must also hold more liquid.

concept_tested: Condition for a flat meniscus
stem: A liquid stands with a perfectly flat surface right up to the wall of the tube in which it is placed. For this liquid and this solid, the angle of contact is
option_a: exactly 90 degrees, so that the liquid neither rises nor falls in a capillary
option_b: exactly 0 degrees, so that the liquid climbs the wall as far as it can
option_c: exactly 180 degrees, so that the liquid pulls away from the wall completely
option_d: exactly 45 degrees, midway between the wetting and the non wetting extremes
correct_answer_text: exactly 90 degrees, so that the liquid neither rises nor falls in a capillary
solution: The rise is proportional to cos theta. At theta = 90 degrees the cosine is zero, so there is neither rise nor depression and the liquid surface meets the wall horizontally. This is the borderline between wetting behaviour and non wetting behaviour.
formula_principle: h = 2 T cos theta / (r rho g), which vanishes when cos theta = 0
common_misconception: Students think a flat meniscus means the liquid has no surface tension.

concept_tested: Effect of raising the temperature on capillary rise
stem: The temperature of the water in a capillary rise experiment is raised, the tube and its radius being unchanged. Neglecting the small change in the density of water, the height of the rise
option_a: increases because the surface tension of water rises with rising temperature
option_b: stays the same because surface tension is a fixed constant for a given liquid
option_c: increases because the water becomes less viscous when heated
option_d: decreases because the surface tension of water falls with rising temperature
correct_answer_text: decreases because the surface tension of water falls with rising temperature
solution: Heating reduces the cohesive forces between the molecules and hence reduces T. Since the rise is directly proportional to T, with the radius and the density essentially unchanged the equilibrium rise is smaller at the higher temperature.
formula_principle: h = 2 T cos theta / (r rho g) with T decreasing as temperature rises
common_misconception: Students confuse the effect of temperature on viscosity, which controls the rate of rise, with its effect on the final height.

subtopic: Capillary tube shorter than the rise
concept_tested: Behaviour of a liquid when the tube is too short
stem: A capillary tube whose length is less than the height to which the liquid would normally rise is dipped vertically in that liquid. The liquid
option_a: rises to the top of the tube and stays there, the radius of curvature of the meniscus increasing so that equilibrium is maintained
option_b: rises to the top of the tube and then overflows continuously as a fountain
option_c: rises only to the height it would reach in a long tube and leaves the top part of the tube empty
option_d: does not rise at all because the tube is too short to support a meniscus
correct_answer_text: rises to the top of the tube and stays there, the radius of curvature of the meniscus increasing so that equilibrium is maintained
solution: The equilibrium condition is h rho g = 2 T divided by R, where R is the radius of curvature of the meniscus. In a long tube with zero angle of contact R equals the tube radius r. If the tube is shorter than the computed rise, the liquid climbs to the top and then the meniscus flattens, that is R increases, until h rho g R = 2 T is satisfied with h equal to the tube length. The liquid never spills over.
formula_principle: h R = 2 T / (rho g) is fixed, so if h is limited the radius of curvature R adjusts
common_misconception: Students expect the liquid to overflow and keep running out of a short capillary tube.

subtopic: Capillary tube shorter than the rise
concept_tested: Numerical value of the adjusted radius of curvature
stem: A capillary tube of radius 0.2 mm would raise a liquid of surface tension 0.04 N m^-1 and density 1000 kg m^-3 through 4 cm if the tube were long enough, the angle of contact being zero and g being 10 m s^-2. The tube actually used projects only 2 cm above the liquid surface. The radius of curvature of the meniscus at the top of this tube is
solution: For the full rise, 0.04 m of liquid is supported with R equal to the tube radius 0.2 mm. In the short tube only 0.02 m is available, that is half the height, so R must be twice as large: R = 0.2 x (4 / 2) = 0.4 mm. Equivalently cos theta at the top is r divided by R = 0.5, so the meniscus meets the wall at 60 degrees and the liquid does not overflow.
formula_principle: h rho g = 2 T / R, so R is inversely proportional to the height actually available
common_misconception: Students assume the meniscus must always have the tube radius as its radius of curvature.

concept_tested: Vertical rise is unchanged when the tube is tilted
stem: A capillary tube in which a liquid rises to a vertical height h is now tilted so that its axis makes an angle of 60 degrees with the vertical, the lower end staying in the liquid. The length of the liquid column measured along the tube is
solution: The equilibrium condition balances the surface tension force against the weight of the raised column, which depends only on the vertical height. Tilting the tube therefore leaves the vertical rise h unchanged. If L is the length along the axis and the axis makes 60 degrees with the vertical, then h = L cos 60 = L / 2, so L = 2 h.
formula_principle: The vertical rise h is fixed by 2 T cos theta / (r rho g); the length along the tube is h / cos(tilt)
common_misconception: Students think tilting the tube lowers the liquid because the column looks longer.

concept_tested: Compensating changes in radius and density
stem: In a capillary rise experiment the tube radius is halved and at the same time the liquid is replaced by another of twice the density but the same surface tension and the same angle of contact. The height of the rise
option_a: becomes four times the original value
option_b: becomes one quarter of the original value
solution: The rise varies as 1 divided by the product r rho. Halving r would double the rise, while doubling rho would halve it. The two effects exactly cancel, so the final height is the same as before.
formula_principle: h = 2 T cos theta / (r rho g), so h is proportional to 1 / (r rho)
common_misconception: Students track only one of the two changes and forget that the other pulls in the opposite direction.

concept_tested: Difference of rise in two tubes
stem: Two capillary tubes of radii 0.5 mm and 1.5 mm are dipped in the same liquid, whose surface tension is 0.075 N m^-1 and density is 1000 kg m^-3. The angle of contact is zero and g = 10 m s^-2. The difference between the two rises is
solution: For the narrow tube, h1 = 2 x 0.075 divided by (5 x 10^-4 x 1000 x 10) = 0.15 divided by 5 = 0.03 m = 3 cm. For the wide tube, h2 = 2 x 0.075 divided by (1.5 x 10^-3 x 1000 x 10) = 0.15 divided by 15 = 0.01 m = 1 cm. The difference is 3 cm minus 1 cm = 2 cm.
formula_principle: h = 2 T / (r rho g) applied separately to each tube
common_misconception: Students substitute the difference of the radii into the formula instead of computing the two heights separately.

concept_tested: Capillary rise inside a freely falling lift
stem: A beaker of water with a capillary tube standing in it is placed inside a lift that is falling freely. In the usual capillary rise relation h = 2 T cos theta / (r rho g), the effect of the free fall is that
option_a: the surface tension term 2 T cos theta vanishes, so the liquid falls back to the beaker level
option_b: every term is unchanged, so the liquid stays at exactly its earlier height
option_c: the radius r effectively becomes zero, so the rise is unbounded and a jet is produced
option_d: the term rho g vanishes, so the relation defines no finite equilibrium rise
correct_answer_text: the term rho g vanishes, so the relation defines no finite equilibrium rise
solution: In the capillary rise relation h = 2 T cos theta / (r rho g), free fall makes the effective acceleration due to gravity zero, so the product rho g vanishes and the denominator goes to zero. The relation therefore defines no finite equilibrium height: there is no weight for the surface tension force to balance. What the liquid finally does depends on the tube length, the liquid volume, the contact angle and the conditions at the open end, none of which are fixed by this relation alone.
formula_principle: h = 2 T cos theta / (r rho g_effective), with g_effective = 0 in free fall
common_misconception: Students expect the water either to fall back or to spray out of the tube in free fall.

concept_tested: Pressure just below a concave meniscus is below atmospheric
stem: Water rises to a height h in a capillary tube of radius r, the angle of contact being zero. The pressure of the water at a point just below the concave meniscus at the top of the column, compared with the atmospheric pressure just above it, is
option_a: greater by 2 T / r, which is the same as h rho g
option_b: less by 2 T / r, which is the same as h rho g
option_c: less by 4 T / r, twice the value set by the single curved surface
option_d: equal to the atmospheric pressure, since the tube is open at both ends
correct_answer_text: less by 2 T / r, which is the same as h rho g
solution: The meniscus is concave upwards, so the pressure on the liquid side is lower than that on the air side by 2 T divided by R, and with a zero angle of contact R equals the tube radius r. Coming down the column from the meniscus to the level of the outside liquid surface adds h rho g, and at that level the pressure must again equal atmospheric. Hence 2 T divided by r equals h rho g, which is exactly the capillary rise condition.
formula_principle: Excess pressure across a curved surface 2 T / R, combined with h = 2 T / (r rho g)
common_misconception: Students think a liquid surface open to the air must always be at atmospheric pressure, even when it is curved.

concept_tested: SI unit of the coefficient of viscosity
stem: The SI unit of the coefficient of viscosity is
solution: From Newton's law of viscous flow, eta = F divided by the product of area and velocity gradient. The unit is therefore N divided by (m^2 x s^-1), that is N s m^-2, which is also written as Pa s or as deca poise.
formula_principle: eta = F / (A x velocity gradient)
common_misconception: Students quote N m^-2 by treating the coefficient of viscosity as a pressure.

concept_tested: Dimensional formula of the coefficient of viscosity
stem: From Stokes' law F = 6 pi eta r v, the dimensional formula of the coefficient of viscosity eta is
solution: Force has dimensions [M L T^-2], area has [L^2] and the velocity gradient has [T^-1]. Hence eta has dimensions [M L T^-2] divided by ([L^2][T^-1]), which gives [M^1 L^-1 T^-1].
formula_principle: eta = F / (A x dv/dx)
common_misconception: Students carry over the dimensions of pressure and forget the extra factor of time.

concept_tested: Statement of Newton's law of viscosity
stem: According to Newton's law of viscosity, the viscous force between two adjacent layers of a flowing liquid is directly proportional to
option_a: the area of contact of the layers and the relative velocity of the layers alone
option_b: the square of the velocity gradient and the area of contact of the layers
option_c: the area of contact of the layers and the velocity gradient perpendicular to them
option_d: the volume of the liquid between the layers and the velocity gradient
correct_answer_text: the area of contact of the layers and the velocity gradient perpendicular to them
solution: Newton's law of viscous flow states that the tangential force between adjacent layers is F = eta A dv/dx, where A is the area of contact and dv/dx is the velocity gradient normal to the layers. The constant eta is the coefficient of viscosity of the liquid.
formula_principle: F = eta A dv/dx, the negative sign indicating opposition to relative motion
common_misconception: Students write the force as proportional to the relative velocity and forget to divide by the separation of the layers.

concept_tested: Unit of velocity gradient
stem: The SI unit of velocity gradient is
solution: Velocity gradient is the change of velocity per unit distance measured perpendicular to the flow. Its unit is (m s^-1) divided by m, that is s^-1.
formula_principle: Velocity gradient = dv/dx
common_misconception: Students confuse velocity gradient with acceleration because both involve a rate of change of velocity.

concept_tested: Viscosity of a liquid falls when it is heated
stem: When the temperature of a liquid is raised, its coefficient of viscosity
option_a: increases, because the molecules move faster and collide more often
option_b: remains unchanged, because viscosity is a fixed property of the liquid
option_c: decreases, because the cohesive forces between the molecules become weaker
option_d: first increases and then decreases as the boiling point is approached
correct_answer_text: decreases, because the cohesive forces between the molecules become weaker
solution: In a liquid the viscous drag arises mainly from cohesive forces between neighbouring molecules. Heating increases the average molecular separation and weakens these forces, so the liquid flows more easily and its viscosity falls. Warm engine oil is thinner than cold engine oil for this reason.
formula_principle: Temperature dependence of the viscosity of a liquid
common_misconception: Students apply the gas behaviour, in which viscosity rises with temperature, to liquids as well.

concept_tested: Viscosity of a gas rises when it is heated
stem: When the temperature of a gas is raised at constant pressure, its coefficient of viscosity
option_a: decreases, because the cohesive forces between the molecules become weaker
option_b: increases, because faster molecules transfer momentum between layers more rapidly
option_c: remains unchanged, because the molecules of a gas are already far apart
option_d: decreases, because the gas expands and its density falls
correct_answer_text: increases, because faster molecules transfer momentum between layers more rapidly
solution: In a gas the layers are coupled not by cohesion but by molecules wandering from one layer to another and carrying momentum with them. Raising the temperature raises the mean molecular speed, so momentum is transported faster and the viscosity increases. This is the exact opposite of the behaviour of a liquid.
formula_principle: Viscosity of a gas arises from transport of momentum by molecular motion
common_misconception: Students assume that heating always makes a fluid flow more easily and so lowers its viscosity.

concept_tested: Viscous drag on a plate sliding over a thin film
stem: A flat plate of area 0.2 m^2 slides at 0.5 m s^-1 over a layer of liquid 1 mm thick that rests on a fixed horizontal surface. The coefficient of viscosity of the liquid is 0.1 N s m^-2 and the velocity gradient across the layer is uniform. The viscous force on the plate is
solution: The velocity falls uniformly from 0.5 m s^-1 at the plate to zero at the fixed surface across 1 x 10^-3 m, so the gradient is 500 s^-1. Hence F = eta A x gradient = 0.1 x 0.2 x 500 = 10 N.
formula_principle: F = eta A v / d for a uniform velocity gradient across a thin film
common_misconception: Students multiply by the film thickness instead of dividing, which reverses the dependence on d.

concept_tested: Computing a velocity gradient
stem: In a liquid flowing over a fixed surface, the velocity rises steadily from zero at the surface to 4 m s^-1 at a perpendicular distance of 2 mm from it. The velocity gradient in this region is
solution: The change in velocity is 4 m s^-1 and it occurs over a perpendicular distance of 2 x 10^-3 m. Hence the gradient is 4 divided by 2 x 10^-3 = 2000 s^-1.
formula_principle: Velocity gradient = dv / dx
common_misconception: Students forget to convert millimetres to metres and report a gradient a thousand times too small.

concept_tested: Relation between the poise and the SI unit
stem: One poise, the unit of viscosity in the centimetre gram second system, is equal to
solution: One poise is one dyne second per square centimetre. Since 1 dyne = 10^-5 N and 1 cm^2 = 10^-4 m^2, one poise equals 10^-5 divided by 10^-4 = 0.1 N s m^-2. Equivalently the SI unit N s m^-2 equals 10 poise and is called the deca poise.
formula_principle: 1 poise = 1 dyne s cm^-2
common_misconception: Students reverse the direction of the conversion and take one poise as ten SI units.

concept_tested: Direction in which the viscous force acts
stem: A layer of a liquid moves faster than the layer immediately below it. The viscous force exerted by the faster layer on the slower layer acts
option_a: along the direction of flow, tending to speed the slower layer up
option_b: opposite to the direction of flow, tending to slow the slower layer down further
option_c: perpendicular to the direction of flow, tending to push the layers apart
option_d: along the direction of flow, tending to speed the faster layer up further
correct_answer_text: along the direction of flow, tending to speed the slower layer up
solution: Viscosity acts like an internal friction between adjacent layers. The faster layer drags the slower one forwards while, by Newton's third law, the slower layer drags the faster one backwards. The overall effect is always to reduce the relative velocity between the layers.
formula_principle: Viscous forces act tangentially and always oppose relative motion between layers
common_misconception: Students think the viscous force is always backwards on every layer, forgetting Newton's third law.

concept_tested: Physical meaning of a large coefficient of viscosity
stem: Honey has a much larger coefficient of viscosity than water at the same temperature. This means that, for the same area of contact and the same velocity gradient,
option_a: a much smaller tangential force is needed to maintain the flow in honey than in water
option_b: honey has a much larger density than water and therefore resists motion more
option_c: honey has a much larger surface tension than water and therefore clings to the walls
option_d: a much larger tangential force is needed to maintain the flow in honey than in water
correct_answer_text: a much larger tangential force is needed to maintain the flow in honey than in water
solution: For a fixed area of contact and a fixed velocity gradient the viscous force is directly proportional to the coefficient of viscosity. Honey therefore demands a far larger tangential force than water for the same flow pattern, which is what we mean by calling it thick.
formula_principle: F = eta A dv/dx, so F is proportional to eta at fixed A and gradient
common_misconception: Students equate high viscosity with high density or with high surface tension.

concept_tested: Finding eta from force, area and velocity gradient
stem: A tangential force of 6 N maintains a uniform velocity gradient of 10 s^-1 across an area of 3 m^2 inside a flowing liquid. The coefficient of viscosity of the liquid is
solution: eta = F divided by (A x velocity gradient) = 6 divided by (3 x 10) = 6 divided by 30 = 0.2 N s m^-2.
formula_principle: eta = F / (A x dv/dx)
common_misconception: Students forget to divide by the velocity gradient and report a force per unit area instead.

concept_tested: What the coefficient of viscosity does and does not depend on
stem: Consider the following statements about the coefficient of viscosity of a given liquid. Statement X: it depends on the nature of the liquid and on its temperature. Statement Y: it depends on the area of contact between the layers of the liquid. The correct assessment is
option_a: Both X and Y are correct
option_b: X is incorrect and Y is correct
option_c: X is correct and Y is incorrect
option_d: Both X and Y are incorrect
correct_answer_text: X is correct and Y is incorrect
solution: The coefficient of viscosity is defined as the tangential force per unit area per unit velocity gradient. Because the area has already been divided out, eta is a property of the liquid and of its state, in particular its temperature, and does not depend on the size of the sample or on the area of contact chosen. Statement X is therefore correct and statement Y is not.
formula_principle: eta = F / (A x dv/dx) defines a property of the liquid alone
common_misconception: Students see the area in F = eta A dv/dx and conclude that eta itself must depend on area.

concept_tested: Finding the thickness of a lubricating film
