stem: A metal plate of area 0.5 m^2 is dragged at a steady 2 m s^-1 over a horizontal oil film by a force of 5 N. The coefficient of viscosity of the oil is 0.01 N s m^-2 and the velocity gradient across the film is uniform. The thickness of the oil film is
solution: Rearranging Newton's law of viscous flow, d = eta A v divided by F = 0.01 x 0.5 x 2 divided by 5 = 0.01 divided by 5 = 0.002 m = 2 mm. A thinner film would demand a larger force for the same speed.
formula_principle: F = eta A v / d, rearranged to give d = eta A v / F
common_misconception: Students solve for the wrong unknown and leave the thickness in the numerator of the force expression.

concept_tested: Where the velocity gradient is largest in a pipe
stem: A viscous liquid flows steadily along a horizontal pipe of circular cross section. The magnitude of the velocity gradient is
option_a: greatest on the axis of the pipe and zero at the wall
option_b: the same at every point of the cross section of the pipe
option_c: zero everywhere, because the flow is steady
option_d: greatest at the wall of the pipe and zero on the axis
correct_answer_text: greatest at the wall of the pipe and zero on the axis
solution: The layer touching the wall is held at rest by adhesion, while the layer along the axis moves fastest. The speed therefore changes most steeply just beside the wall, so the velocity gradient and the viscous drag are largest there. On the axis the speed passes through its maximum, so the gradient falls to zero.
formula_principle: Layer in contact with the wall is at rest, speed is maximum on the axis
common_misconception: Students confuse the point of maximum speed with the point of maximum velocity gradient.

concept_tested: Compensating changes of area and film thickness
stem: A plate slides at a fixed speed over a thin oil film. The area of the plate is doubled and at the same time the thickness of the film is doubled, the oil and the speed being unchanged. The force needed to keep the plate moving at that speed
solution: The force varies as the ratio A divided by d. Doubling the area doubles the force, while doubling the film thickness halves the velocity gradient and so halves the force. The two changes cancel exactly and the required force is unaltered.
formula_principle: F = eta A v / d, so F is proportional to A / d
common_misconception: Students track only the change in area and forget that a thicker film gives a gentler velocity gradient.

concept_tested: Steady sliding of a block down a lubricated incline
stem: A block of mass 2 kg and base area 0.02 m^2 slides down an incline on an oil film 0.1 mm thick. The incline is such that the component of the weight along the slope is one half of the weight. The coefficient of viscosity of the oil is 0.5 N s m^-2 and g = 10 m s^-2. The steady speed with which the block slides is
solution: The driving force along the slope is one half of m g = 0.5 x 2 x 10 = 10 N. At the steady speed this is balanced by the viscous drag eta A v divided by d. Hence v = F d divided by (eta A) = 10 x 1 x 10^-4 divided by (0.5 x 0.02) = 1 x 10^-3 divided by 1 x 10^-2 = 0.1 m s^-1.
formula_principle: At steady speed the driving force equals the viscous force: m g sin(slope) = eta A v / d
common_misconception: Students use the whole weight of the block rather than its component along the slope as the driving force.

concept_tested: Plate dragged between two liquid layers
stem: A thin plate of area 1 m^2 on each face is pulled at 1 m s^-1 midway between two fixed horizontal walls. The gap above the plate is filled with a liquid of viscosity 0.2 N s m^-2 and is 2 mm wide, and the gap below is filled with a liquid of viscosity 0.3 N s m^-2 and is 3 mm wide. The total force needed to maintain the motion is
solution: Upper face: F1 = eta1 A v divided by d1 = 0.2 x 1 x 1 divided by 2 x 10^-3 = 100 N. Lower face: F2 = eta2 A v divided by d2 = 0.3 x 1 x 1 divided by 3 x 10^-3 = 100 N. The two viscous forces both oppose the motion of the plate and therefore add, giving a total of 200 N.
formula_principle: Each face experiences its own drag eta A v / d and the two drags add
common_misconception: Students compute the drag on one face only, or try to average the two viscosities instead of adding the two forces.

concept_tested: Expression for the viscous drag on a small sphere
stem: A small sphere of radius r moves with speed v through a fluid of coefficient of viscosity eta. According to Stokes law the viscous drag on the sphere is
solution: For a small sphere moving slowly through a large body of fluid, so that the flow around it stays streamlined, the retarding force is F = 6 pi eta r v. It is directly proportional to the coefficient of viscosity, to the radius and to the speed.
formula_principle: F = 6 pi eta r v
common_misconception: Students square the radius or the speed in the expression for Stokes drag.

concept_tested: Condition that defines terminal velocity
stem: A small sphere released in a deep column of a viscous liquid finally attains a terminal velocity. At that stage
option_a: the weight of the sphere is balanced by the sum of the upthrust and the viscous drag
option_b: the weight of the sphere is balanced by the upthrust alone, the viscous drag having fallen to zero
option_c: the viscous drag alone balances the weight, the upthrust being negligible for a solid sphere
option_d: the weight, the upthrust and the viscous drag all act downwards and add up to zero
correct_answer_text: the weight of the sphere is balanced by the sum of the upthrust and the viscous drag
solution: As the sphere speeds up the viscous drag 6 pi eta r v grows, while the weight and the upthrust stay fixed. When the drag has grown enough that the upward forces balance the weight, the acceleration becomes zero and the sphere continues at a constant terminal velocity.
formula_principle: At terminal velocity the net force is zero: weight = upthrust + viscous drag
common_misconception: Students think the drag vanishes at terminal velocity because the acceleration has vanished.

concept_tested: Terminal velocity varies as the square of the radius
stem: For small spheres of the same material falling through the same liquid, the terminal velocity is
option_a: directly proportional to the radius of the sphere
option_b: inversely proportional to the radius of the sphere
option_c: independent of the radius of the sphere
option_d: directly proportional to the square of the radius of the sphere
correct_answer_text: directly proportional to the square of the radius of the sphere
solution: The effective weight of the sphere grows as r^3 while the Stokes drag grows only as r, so the balance is struck at a speed that grows as r^2. Hence doubling the radius makes the terminal velocity four times as large.
formula_principle: v = 2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g / (9 eta)
common_misconception: Students take the terminal velocity as simply proportional to the radius because the drag is.

concept_tested: Expression for the terminal velocity of a sphere
stem: A sphere of radius r and density rho falls through a liquid of density sigma and coefficient of viscosity eta. Its terminal velocity is
solution: Setting the weight equal to the sum of the upthrust and the Stokes drag gives (4/3) pi r^3 rho g = (4/3) pi r^3 sigma g + 6 pi eta r v. Solving for v gives v = 2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g divided by (9 eta).
formula_principle: v = 2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g / (9 eta)
common_misconception: Students add the two densities instead of subtracting, thereby leaving out the upthrust.

concept_tested: Numerical terminal velocity of a metal sphere
stem: A sphere of radius 1 mm and density 10000 kg m^-3 falls through a liquid of density 1000 kg m^-3 and coefficient of viscosity 0.2 N s m^-2. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, its terminal velocity is
solution: Here r^2 = 1 x 10^-6 m^2 and rho minus sigma = 9000 kg m^-3. The numerator is 2 x 1 x 10^-6 x 9000 x 10 = 0.18, and the denominator is 9 x 0.2 = 1.8. Hence v = 0.18 divided by 1.8 = 0.1 m s^-1.
formula_principle: v = 2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g / (9 eta)
common_misconception: Students forget the upthrust and use the density of the sphere alone in the numerator.

concept_tested: Comparing two spheres of different radius
stem: Two spheres of the same material and of radii in the ratio 1 : 2 are dropped into the same deep column of a viscous liquid. Their terminal velocities are in the ratio
solution: Since the densities and the viscosity are common to both, the terminal velocity varies as r^2. With radii in the ratio 1 : 2, the terminal velocities are in the ratio 1^2 : 2^2, that is 1 : 4.
formula_principle: v is proportional to r^2 for spheres of the same material in the same liquid
common_misconception: Students use the ratio of the radii or of the volumes instead of the ratio of their squares.

concept_tested: Shape of the velocity against time graph for a falling sphere
stem: A small steel ball is released gently at the surface of a tall jar of glycerine. A graph of its speed against time from the moment of release is best described as
option_a: a straight line through the origin that continues to rise at the same rate throughout
option_b: a curve that rises to a peak and then falls back before levelling off
option_c: a horizontal straight line right from the moment of release
option_d: a curve that rises steeply at first, then bends over and finally becomes a horizontal straight line
correct_answer_text: a curve that rises steeply at first, then bends over and finally becomes a horizontal straight line
solution: At release the speed and hence the drag are zero, so the ball accelerates under its weight less the upthrust. As the speed grows, the drag grows with it and the net force shrinks, so the graph bends over. Once the drag has grown enough to balance the effective weight, the acceleration is zero and the graph becomes a horizontal line at the terminal velocity.
formula_principle: Acceleration falls as the drag 6 pi eta r v grows, until the net force is zero
common_misconception: Students draw a straight line, forgetting that the drag depends on the speed already attained.

concept_tested: Numerical value of the Stokes drag
stem: A sphere of radius 1 cm moves at 0.2 m s^-1 through a fluid of coefficient of viscosity 0.5 N s m^-2, the flow around it remaining streamlined. The viscous drag on the sphere is
solution: With r = 1 x 10^-2 m, F = 6 pi x 0.5 x 1 x 10^-2 x 0.2 = 6 pi x 1 x 10^-3 N, which is about 1.9 x 10^-2 N.
formula_principle: F = 6 pi eta r v
common_misconception: Students substitute the radius in centimetres and obtain a value a hundred times too large.

concept_tested: Effect of using a more viscous liquid
stem: A sphere is dropped into a liquid of coefficient of viscosity eta and attains a terminal velocity v. The same sphere is dropped into a second liquid of the same density but of coefficient of viscosity 3 eta. Its terminal velocity in the second liquid is
solution: Since the densities and the radius are unchanged, the terminal velocity varies inversely as the coefficient of viscosity. Tripling eta therefore reduces the terminal velocity to one third of its former value.
formula_principle: v = 2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g / (9 eta), so v is proportional to 1 / eta
common_misconception: Students expect a thicker liquid to have no effect once the sphere has stopped accelerating.

concept_tested: A sphere less dense than the liquid
stem: A small sphere whose density is less than that of the surrounding liquid is released at the bottom of a deep tank of that liquid. After a short time the sphere
option_a: moves downward with a constant terminal speed
option_b: stays exactly where it was released, since the upthrust and the weight are equal
option_c: moves upward with a constant terminal speed
option_d: moves upward with a steadily increasing speed all the way to the surface
correct_answer_text: moves upward with a constant terminal speed
solution: When rho is less than sigma the quantity rho minus sigma is negative, so the terminal velocity comes out negative, meaning that the steady motion is upward. Physically the upthrust exceeds the weight, the sphere accelerates upward, and the drag now acts downward and grows until the three forces balance. An air bubble rising steadily through water is the familiar example.
formula_principle: v = 2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g / (9 eta), which is negative when rho is less than sigma
common_misconception: Students apply the terminal velocity formula only to sinking bodies and overlook the negative sign.

concept_tested: Dimensional check of the Stokes expression
stem: The combination 6 pi eta r v, where eta is a coefficient of viscosity, r a radius and v a speed, has the dimensions of
solution: Multiplying the dimensions gives [M L^-1 T^-1] x [L] x [L T^-1] = [M^1 L^1 T^-2], which is the dimensional formula of force. This confirms that Stokes expression represents a drag force.
formula_principle: eta has dimensions [M L^-1 T^-1]
common_misconception: Students misremember the dimensions of the coefficient of viscosity and obtain a pressure instead of a force.

concept_tested: Terminal velocity after small drops merge
stem: Twenty seven identical rain drops, each falling with the same terminal velocity v, coalesce to form a single large drop. Assuming the flow around the large drop is still streamlined, its terminal velocity is
solution: Conserving volume, R = 27^(1/3) x r = 3 r. Since terminal velocity varies as the square of the radius, the new terminal velocity is (3)^2 = 9 times the old one, that is 9 v. This is why merged raindrops fall so much faster than the fine droplets of a cloud.
formula_principle: Volume conservation gives R = n^(1/3) r, and terminal velocity is proportional to the square of the radius
common_misconception: Students multiply the terminal velocity directly by the number of drops that merged.

concept_tested: Scaling the terminal velocity with radius
stem: A small sphere of a certain radius falls through a liquid with a terminal velocity of 2 cm s^-1. Another sphere of the same material and of three times the radius is dropped into the same liquid. Its terminal velocity is
solution: The densities and the coefficient of viscosity are the same for both spheres, so v is proportional to r^2. Tripling the radius multiplies the terminal velocity by 3^2 = 9, giving 9 x 2 = 18 cm s^-1.
formula_principle: v is proportional to r^2 when the material and the liquid are unchanged
common_misconception: Students scale by the first or the third power of the radius instead of the second.

concept_tested: Finding the coefficient of viscosity from a terminal velocity measurement
stem: A sphere of radius 3 mm and density 3000 kg m^-3 falls with a terminal velocity of 0.2 m s^-1 through a liquid of density 1000 kg m^-3. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the coefficient of viscosity of the liquid is
solution: Rearranging, eta = 2 r^2 (rho minus sigma) g divided by (9 v). With r^2 = 9 x 10^-6 m^2 and rho minus sigma = 2000 kg m^-3, the numerator is 2 x 9 x 10^-6 x 2000 x 10 = 0.36. The denominator is 9 x 0.2 = 1.8. Hence eta = 0.36 divided by 1.8 = 0.2 N s m^-2.
formula_principle: eta = 2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g / (9 v)
common_misconception: Students forget to subtract the density of the liquid before substituting.

concept_tested: Why fog droplets appear to hang in the air
stem: The tiny water droplets of a fog appear to remain suspended in the air for a very long time. The main reason is that
option_a: the upthrust of the air on them exactly balances their weight
option_b: the surface tension of water holds the droplets up against gravity
option_c: the coefficient of viscosity of air increases sharply when fog forms
option_d: their terminal velocity is extremely small because it varies as the square of the radius
correct_answer_text: their terminal velocity is extremely small because it varies as the square of the radius
solution: Fog droplets have radii of the order of a few micrometres. Because the terminal velocity varies as the square of the radius, reducing the radius by a factor of a thousand compared with a raindrop reduces the terminal velocity by a factor of a million. The droplets therefore settle so slowly that the slightest air current keeps them aloft.
formula_principle: v = 2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g / (9 eta), with r of the order of 10^-5 m
common_misconception: Students invoke buoyancy or surface tension instead of the strong dependence of terminal velocity on radius.

concept_tested: Terminal velocity of each droplet after a drop breaks up
stem: A large drop falling with terminal velocity v breaks up into eight identical smaller drops. The terminal velocity of each smaller drop, in the same medium, is
solution: Volume conservation gives r = R divided by 8^(1/3) = R divided by 2. Since terminal velocity varies as the square of the radius, each small drop falls with (1/2)^2 = 1/4 of the original terminal velocity, that is v divided by 4.
formula_principle: r = R / n^(1/3) and v is proportional to the square of the radius
common_misconception: Students divide the terminal velocity by the number of drops produced.

concept_tested: Magnitude of the viscous drag at terminal velocity
stem: A metal sphere of volume 2 x 10^-4 m^3 and density 8000 kg m^-3 falls with its terminal velocity through a liquid of density 1000 kg m^-3. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the viscous drag acting on the sphere at that stage is
solution: Weight = V rho g = 2 x 10^-4 x 8000 x 10 = 16 N. Upthrust = V sigma g = 2 x 10^-4 x 1000 x 10 = 2 N. Since the sphere moves with constant velocity the net force is zero, so the drag makes up the difference: 16 minus 2 = 14 N. Notice that no value of the coefficient of viscosity is needed for this balance.
formula_principle: At terminal velocity, viscous drag = weight - upthrust = V (rho - sigma) g
common_misconception: Students equate the viscous drag to the full weight of the sphere and ignore the upthrust.

concept_tested: Changing radius and viscosity together
stem: A sphere falls through a liquid with terminal velocity v. A second sphere of the same material but of twice the radius is dropped into a different liquid of the same density but of twice the coefficient of viscosity. The terminal velocity of the second sphere is
solution: The densities of the sphere and of the liquid are unchanged, so the terminal velocity varies as r^2 divided by eta. Doubling the radius multiplies it by 4, while doubling the coefficient of viscosity divides it by 2. The net factor is 4 divided by 2 = 2, so the terminal velocity becomes 2 v.
formula_principle: v is proportional to r^2 / eta when the two densities are unchanged
common_misconception: Students apply only one of the two changes, or assume that any two changes must cancel.

major_topic: Streamline Flow and Equation of Continuity
concept_tested: Property of streamlines in steady flow
stem: In the steady streamline flow of a liquid, two streamlines can never cross each other because
option_a: the liquid is incompressible and its density cannot change at a crossing point
option_b: a crossing point would give the fluid particle there two different velocities at the same instant
option_c: the pressure would become infinitely large at the point where they crossed
option_d: the viscosity of the liquid prevents adjacent layers from ever meeting
correct_answer_text: a crossing point would give the fluid particle there two different velocities at the same instant
solution: The velocity of the fluid at any point of a streamline is directed along the tangent to that streamline. If two streamlines crossed, the particle at the crossing point would have to move along two different tangents at the same instant, which is impossible. Hence streamlines never intersect in steady flow.
formula_principle: A streamline is the path along which the velocity at each point is tangential to the line
common_misconception: Students think streamlines cannot cross because the liquid would pile up there.

major_topic: Streamline Flow and Equation of Continuity
concept_tested: Physical principle behind the equation of continuity
stem: The equation of continuity A1 v1 = A2 v2 for the steady flow of an incompressible liquid through a pipe expresses the conservation of
solution: In steady flow the mass entering one cross section per second must equal the mass leaving another, since none can accumulate in between. For an incompressible liquid of constant density this reduces to A1 v1 = A2 v2, that is the volume flow rate is the same everywhere.
formula_principle: A v = constant for an incompressible liquid in steady flow
common_misconception: Students associate the equation of continuity with conservation of energy instead of mass.

major_topic: Streamline Flow and Equation of Continuity
concept_tested: Reynolds number is a pure number
stem: The Reynolds number of a flowing fluid is
option_a: measured in metre per second, like the critical velocity
option_b: measured in N s m^-2, like the coefficient of viscosity
option_c: measured in kg m^-3, like the density of the fluid
option_d: a dimensionless quantity with no unit
correct_answer_text: a dimensionless quantity with no unit
solution: Substituting dimensions, [M L^-3][L T^-1][L] divided by [M L^-1 T^-1] gives [M^0 L^0 T^0]. The Reynolds number is therefore a pure number, which is why the same critical values apply to pipes of every size.
formula_principle: R_n = rho v d / eta
common_misconception: Students expect every physical quantity to carry a unit and assign one to the Reynolds number.

major_topic: Streamline Flow and Equation of Continuity
concept_tested: Effect of halving the radius of a pipe
stem: Water flows steadily along a horizontal pipe. At a certain section the radius of the pipe narrows to half its earlier value. Compared with the earlier section, the speed of the water at the narrow section is
solution: The area of a circular cross section varies as r^2, so halving the radius reduces the area to one quarter. Since A v must stay constant, the speed rises by a factor of four.
formula_principle: A1 v1 = A2 v2 with A proportional to r^2
common_misconception: Students scale the speed with the ratio of the radii rather than with the ratio of the areas.

major_topic: Streamline Flow and Equation of Continuity
concept_tested: Definition of the Reynolds number
stem: For a fluid of density rho and coefficient of viscosity eta flowing with speed v through a pipe of diameter d, the Reynolds number is given by
solution: The Reynolds number compares the inertial effects in the flow with the viscous effects. It is defined as rho v d divided by eta, where d is a characteristic length such as the diameter of the pipe. The combination is dimensionless.
formula_principle: R_n = rho v d / eta
common_misconception: Students misplace the coefficient of viscosity in the numerator instead of the denominator.

major_topic: Streamline Flow and Equation of Continuity
concept_tested: Numerical use of A1 v1 = A2 v2
stem: Water flows steadily through a pipe whose cross sectional area falls from 10 cm^2 to 5 cm^2. Where the area is 10 cm^2 the speed of the water is 2 m s^-1. Where the area is 5 cm^2 the speed is
solution: A1 v1 = 10 x 2 = 20 in units of cm^2 m s^-1. Hence v2 = 20 divided by 5 = 4 m s^-1. Converting both areas to square metres would give the same ratio, so the conversion is not needed here.
formula_principle: A1 v1 = A2 v2
common_misconception: Students think steady flow means the speed is the same at every cross section.

major_topic: Streamline Flow and Equation of Continuity
concept_tested: Reynolds number and the type of flow
stem: For a liquid flowing through a pipe, the flow is expected to be
option_a: streamline when the Reynolds number is below about 1000 and turbulent when it is above about 2000
option_b: turbulent when the Reynolds number is below about 1000 and streamline when it is above about 2000
option_c: streamline at every value of the Reynolds number provided the pipe is smooth
option_d: turbulent at every value of the Reynolds number provided the liquid has some viscosity
correct_answer_text: streamline when the Reynolds number is below about 1000 and turbulent when it is above about 2000
solution: A small Reynolds number means viscous forces dominate and the layers slide smoothly over one another, giving streamline flow. A large Reynolds number means inertial effects dominate and the flow becomes turbulent. For flow in a pipe the flow is streamline up to about 1000 and turbulent beyond about 2000, with an unstable region in between.
formula_principle: Critical values of the Reynolds number for pipe flow
common_misconception: Students reverse the criterion and expect turbulence at low Reynolds numbers.

major_topic: Streamline Flow and Equation of Continuity
concept_tested: Expression for the critical velocity
stem: The critical velocity of a liquid of density rho and coefficient of viscosity eta flowing through a pipe of diameter d, for a critical Reynolds number R_n, is
solution: The critical velocity is the speed at which the Reynolds number reaches its critical value. Rearranging R_n = rho v d divided by eta gives v = R_n eta divided by (rho d). A more viscous liquid can therefore flow faster before turbulence sets in, while a wider pipe goes turbulent at a lower speed.
formula_principle: Rearranging R_n = rho v d / eta gives v_critical = R_n eta / (rho d)
common_misconception: Students place the coefficient of viscosity in the denominator by carrying over the form of the Reynolds number itself.

major_topic: Streamline Flow and Equation of Continuity
concept_tested: Flow through a pipe that branches
stem: A main pipe of cross sectional area 12 cm^2 carries water at 2 m s^-1. It branches into four identical smaller pipes, each of cross sectional area 2 cm^2. The speed of the water in each smaller pipe is
solution: The volume flow rate in the main pipe is 12 x 2 = 24 in units of cm^2 m s^-1. The four branches together offer a cross sectional area of 4 x 2 = 8 cm^2. Hence the speed in each branch is 24 divided by 8 = 3 m s^-1. Note that the total branch area is smaller than the main pipe area, so the water speeds up.
formula_principle: The volume flow rate is conserved: A_main v_main = n A_branch v_branch
common_misconception: Students forget to add the areas of all the branches before applying the continuity equation.

major_topic: Streamline Flow and Equation of Continuity
concept_tested: Spacing of streamlines and speed of flow
stem: In a diagram of the steady flow of a liquid, the streamlines are seen to crowd closely together in one region and to be widely spaced in another. In the region where they crowd together, the liquid is
option_a: moving more slowly, because the crowded streamlines obstruct one another
option_b: moving at the same speed as elsewhere, since the flow is steady
option_c: moving faster, because the same volume must pass through a smaller cross section each second
option_d: at rest, because the streamlines have merged into a single line
correct_answer_text: moving faster, because the same volume must pass through a smaller cross section each second
solution: The region between neighbouring streamlines is a tube of flow, and no liquid crosses its walls. Where the streamlines crowd together the cross section of the tube of flow is small, so by the equation of continuity the speed there must be large. This is the basis of reading a flow diagram at a glance, and combined with Bernoulli's principle it also tells us that the pressure there is low.
formula_principle: A v = constant applied to a tube of flow bounded by streamlines
common_misconception: Students read crowded streamlines as congestion and conclude that the liquid must be moving slowly.

major_topic: Streamline Flow and Equation of Continuity
concept_tested: Narrowing of a falling stream of water
stem: Water leaves a tap of radius 4 mm with a speed of 1 m s^-1 and falls freely as a smooth stream. Taking g = 10 m s^-2 and neglecting any effect of surface tension, the radius of the stream at a point 0.75 m below the tap is
solution: The speed after falling 0.75 m is given by v2^2 = 1 + 2 x 10 x 0.75 = 16, so v2 = 4 m s^-1. Applying the equation of continuity to the circular stream, r1^2 v1 = r2^2 v2, so r2^2 = 16 x 1 divided by 4 = 4, giving r2 = 2 mm. The stream narrows because it speeds up as it falls.
formula_principle: Free fall v2^2 = v1^2 + 2 g h, then the equation of continuity r1^2 v1 = r2^2 v2
common_misconception: Students apply the equation of continuity to the radii directly instead of to the areas.

major_topic: Streamline Flow and Equation of Continuity
concept_tested: Numerical value of the critical velocity for water in a pipe
stem: Water of density 1000 kg m^-3 and coefficient of viscosity 1 x 10^-3 N s m^-2 flows through a pipe of diameter 2 cm. Taking the critical Reynolds number as 2000, the critical velocity of the water is
solution: Substituting, v = 2000 x 1 x 10^-3 divided by (1000 x 0.02) = 2 divided by 20 = 0.1 m s^-1. Above this speed the flow of water in such a pipe ceases to be streamline, which is why laminar flow of water is confined to slow speeds or narrow tubes.
formula_principle: v_critical = R_n eta / (rho d)
common_misconception: Students substitute the radius instead of the diameter, or forget to convert centimetres to metres.

concept_tested: Bernoulli's equation expresses conservation of energy
stem: Bernoulli's equation for the steady streamline flow of an ideal fluid is a statement of the conservation of
solution: Bernoulli's equation states that the sum of the pressure energy per unit volume, the kinetic energy per unit volume and the potential energy per unit volume is the same at all points of a streamline in the steady flow of an ideal fluid. It is the work energy theorem applied to a small element of the fluid.
formula_principle: P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant along a streamline
common_misconception: Students associate Bernoulli's equation with conservation of mass because it is derived alongside the equation of continuity.

concept_tested: Toricelli's law
stem: A small hole is made in the side wall of a large open tank at a depth h below the free surface of the liquid. The speed with which the liquid emerges from the hole is
solution: Applying Bernoulli's equation between the free surface, where the pressure is atmospheric and the speed is negligible, and the hole, where the pressure is again atmospheric, gives (1/2) rho v^2 = rho g h. Hence v = square root of (2 g h), the same as the speed of a body that has fallen freely through the height h.
formula_principle: Toricelli's law: v = square root of (2 g h)
common_misconception: Students forget the square root and quote 2 g h as a speed.

concept_tested: Where a fluid moves faster the pressure is lower
stem: Along a horizontal streamline in the steady flow of an ideal fluid, at a point where the speed of the fluid is greater the pressure is
option_a: greater than at a point where the speed is less
option_b: smaller than at a point where the speed is less
option_c: the same as at a point where the speed is less
option_d: smaller only if the fluid is also rising along the streamline
correct_answer_text: smaller than at a point where the speed is less
solution: For a horizontal streamline the potential term is unchanged, so P plus (1/2) rho v^2 is constant. An increase in speed must therefore be paid for by a decrease in pressure. This is why a narrow section of a pipe carries fast moving liquid at low pressure.
formula_principle: P + (1/2) rho v^2 = constant along a horizontal streamline
common_misconception: Students expect fast moving fluid to press harder on the walls.

concept_tested: Numerical speed of efflux
stem: A large tank of water has a small hole in its side wall 5 m below the free surface. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the speed with which water emerges from the hole is
solution: v = square root of (2 x 10 x 5) = square root of 100 = 10 m s^-1. The result is the same as the speed of a stone dropped from a height of 5 m.
formula_principle: v = square root of (2 g h)
common_misconception: Students omit the square root and report a value ten times too large.

concept_tested: Working principle of a venturi meter
stem: A venturi meter measures the rate of flow of a liquid through a pipe by
option_a: measuring the rise in pressure at a deliberately narrowed section, where the liquid must flow faster
option_b: measuring the change in the temperature of the liquid as it passes the narrowed section
option_c: measuring the fall in pressure at a deliberately narrowed section, where the liquid must flow faster
option_d: measuring the time taken by a floating marker to travel between two fixed sections of the pipe
correct_answer_text: measuring the fall in pressure at a deliberately narrowed section, where the liquid must flow faster
solution: The meter has a constriction in the pipe. By the equation of continuity the liquid speeds up there, and by Bernoulli's principle its pressure therefore drops. The pressure difference between the wide and the narrow sections, read from a manometer, gives the speed and hence the rate of flow.
formula_principle: Continuity plus Bernoulli: A1 v1 = A2 v2 and P1 + (1/2) rho v1^2 = P2 + (1/2) rho v2^2
common_misconception: Students expect the pressure to build up where the pipe is squeezed, as though the liquid were being compressed.

concept_tested: Lift on an aerofoil
stem: An aeroplane wing is shaped so that air travels faster over its upper surface than along its lower surface. The upward lift arises because
option_a: the pressure on the upper surface is larger than that on the lower surface
option_b: the air above the wing is warmer and therefore less dense than the air below it
option_c: the pressure on the upper surface is smaller than that on the lower surface
option_d: the wing is lighter than the volume of air it displaces, so it floats upward
correct_answer_text: the pressure on the upper surface is smaller than that on the lower surface
solution: The curved upper surface makes the air travel faster over the top of the wing than beneath it. By Bernoulli's principle the faster stream is at the lower pressure, so the pressure below the wing exceeds that above it. The resulting upward force per unit area, multiplied by the wing area, is the lift.
formula_principle: P + (1/2) rho v^2 = constant applied to the air just above and just below the wing
common_misconception: Students explain lift by imagining the wing is buoyant rather than by comparing the pressures on its two faces.

concept_tested: Every term of Bernoulli's equation has the dimensions of pressure
stem: In Bernoulli's equation P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant, the term (1/2) rho v^2 has the dimensions of
solution: Substituting, rho v^2 has dimensions [M L^-3][L^2 T^-2] = [M^1 L^-1 T^-2], which is the dimensional formula of pressure. The same is true of rho g h and of P itself, which is why the three terms may be added. Each is an energy per unit volume, and energy per unit volume is dimensionally a pressure.
formula_principle: Every term of Bernoulli's equation is an energy per unit volume, which is the same as a pressure
common_misconception: Students describe the kinetic term as an energy and then wonder how it can be added to a pressure.

concept_tested: Pressure drop in a pipe that rises
stem: Water of density 1000 kg m^-3 flows steadily through a pipe of uniform cross section. One section of the pipe is 2 m higher than another. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the pressure at the higher section is
option_a: 2 x 10^4 Pa greater than that at the lower section
option_b: 2 x 10^4 Pa less than that at the lower section
option_c: 1 x 10^4 Pa less than that at the lower section
option_d: the same as that at the lower section, since the pipe has a uniform cross section
correct_answer_text: 2 x 10^4 Pa less than that at the lower section
solution: The cross section is uniform, so by the equation of continuity the speed is the same at both sections and the kinetic terms cancel. Bernoulli's equation then reduces to P1 + rho g h1 = P2 + rho g h2, so the pressure difference is rho g times the height difference = 1000 x 10 x 2 = 2 x 10^4 Pa, the higher section being at the lower pressure.
formula_principle: P1 + (1/2) rho v1^2 + rho g h1 = P2 + (1/2) rho v2^2 + rho g h2
common_misconception: Students assume that if the speed is unchanged then the pressure must be unchanged as well.

concept_tested: Depth of the hole that gives the greatest horizontal range
stem: A tall tank standing on the ground is filled with water to a height H. A small hole is made in the side wall at a depth h below the free surface, and the emerging jet strikes the ground at a horizontal distance R from the tank. The range R is greatest when h equals
solution: The jet leaves horizontally with speed square root of (2 g h) and then falls freely through the remaining height H minus h, taking a time square root of (2 (H - h) divided by g). Multiplying gives R = 2 x square root of (h (H minus h)). The product h (H minus h) is greatest when the two factors are equal, that is when h = H divided by 2, and the maximum range is then H itself.
formula_principle: v = square root of (2 g h) and the time of fall from height (H - h) gives R = 2 square root of (h (H - h))
common_misconception: Students assume the deepest hole gives the longest range because it produces the fastest jet.

concept_tested: Efflux speed does not depend on the density of the liquid
stem: Two identical open tanks stand side by side, one filled with water and the other with a liquid of twice the density, both to the same depth. A small hole is made in the side wall of each tank at the same depth below the free surface. The speeds of efflux from the two holes are
option_a: in the ratio 1 : 2, the denser liquid emerging twice as fast
option_b: in the ratio 2 : 1, the lighter liquid emerging twice as fast
option_c: equal, because the speed of efflux depends only on the depth of the hole and on g
option_d: in the ratio 1 : square root of 2, the denser liquid emerging faster
correct_answer_text: equal, because the speed of efflux depends only on the depth of the hole and on g
solution: Applying Bernoulli's equation between the free surface and the hole, both of which are at atmospheric pressure, gives (1/2) rho v^2 = rho g h. The density cancels from both sides, leaving v = square root of (2 g h). The result is exactly the free fall speed through the depth h, and it is the same for every liquid.
formula_principle: (1/2) rho v^2 = rho g h, in which the density cancels
common_misconception: Students reason that a denser liquid presses harder and so must squirt out faster.

concept_tested: Numerical range of a jet from a hole in a tank
stem: An open tank standing on level ground is filled with water to a height of 2.0 m above the base. A small hole is made in the side wall at a height of 0.2 m above the base. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the horizontal distance from the tank at which the jet strikes the ground is
solution: The hole lies at a depth of 2.0 minus 0.2 = 1.8 m below the free surface, so the efflux speed is v = square root of (2 x 10 x 1.8) = square root of 36 = 6 m s^-1, directed horizontally. The jet then falls freely through 0.2 m, taking a time t = square root of (2 x 0.2 divided by 10) = square root of 0.04 = 0.2 s. The horizontal range is therefore 6 x 0.2 = 1.2 m.
formula_principle: v = square root of (2 g h) for the efflux, then projectile motion with horizontal launch
common_misconception: Students use the height of the water above the base, rather than the depth of the hole below the free surface, when finding the efflux speed.

concept_tested: Rate of flow from a venturi pressure difference
stem: Water of density 1000 kg m^-3 flows through a horizontal pipe whose cross sectional area falls from 10 cm^2 to 5 cm^2. The pressure at the wide section exceeds that at the narrow section by 6000 Pa. The volume of water flowing through the pipe each second is
solution: The narrow section has half the area, so by the equation of continuity v2 = 2 v1. Bernoulli's equation for a horizontal pipe gives P1 minus P2 = (1/2) rho (v2^2 minus v1^2) = (1/2) x 1000 x (4 v1^2 minus v1^2) = 1500 v1^2. Setting this equal to 6000 Pa gives v1^2 = 4, so v1 = 2 m s^-1. The volume flow rate is A1 v1 = 10 x 10^-4 x 2 = 2 x 10^-3 m^3 s^-1, that is 2 litre per second.
formula_principle: A1 v1 = A2 v2 together with P1 - P2 = (1/2) rho (v2^2 - v1^2)
common_misconception: Students take the pressure difference as (1/2) rho v2^2 alone, forgetting to subtract the kinetic term at the wide section.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Nature of molecular collisions in an ideal gas
stem: According to the kinetic theory of gases, the collisions of gas molecules with one another and with the walls of the container are
option_a: perfectly inelastic, so that the molecules move together after collision
option_b: partially elastic, a small fraction of the kinetic energy being lost as heat in every collision
option_c: perfectly elastic, so that the total kinetic energy of the colliding molecules is conserved
option_d: elastic with the walls but inelastic among the molecules themselves
correct_answer_text: perfectly elastic, so that the total kinetic energy of the colliding molecules is conserved
solution: Kinetic theory assumes that a gas molecule suffers no loss of kinetic energy in a collision. Momentum and kinetic energy are both conserved. This is why a gas kept at constant temperature in an insulated vessel maintains a steady pressure indefinitely; if any energy were lost per collision the pressure would keep decreasing.
formula_principle: Postulate of kinetic theory: intermolecular and molecule to wall collisions are perfectly elastic
common_misconception: Students often think real bouncing bodies lose energy so molecules must also lose energy in every collision.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Volume occupied by the molecules themselves
stem: In the kinetic theory of an ideal gas, the actual volume occupied by all the molecules put together is taken to be
option_a: negligible in comparison with the volume of the container
option_b: equal to the volume of the container
option_c: exactly one third of the volume of the container
option_d: larger than the volume of the container at high pressure
correct_answer_text: negligible in comparison with the volume of the container
solution: A gas at ordinary pressure has molecules separated by roughly ten molecular diameters, so the summed molecular volume is a very small fraction of the vessel volume. Therefore the free volume available for motion is taken as the whole volume V of the container. This assumption breaks down at high pressure, which is why the van der Waals correction subtracts a volume term.
formula_principle: Postulate: size of a molecule is negligible compared with the average separation between molecules
common_misconception: Learners confuse the free volume available to the molecules with the volume of the molecules themselves.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Motion of a molecule between successive collisions
stem: Between two successive collisions, a molecule of an ideal gas moves
option_a: along a curved path because of the mutual attraction of the other molecules
option_b: along a straight line but with continuously decreasing speed
option_c: in a random zig zag path even without collisions
option_d: along a straight line with constant velocity
correct_answer_text: along a straight line with constant velocity
solution: Kinetic theory neglects intermolecular forces except during the brief collision. With zero net force the acceleration is zero, so the molecule travels in a straight line at constant speed. The straight segment between two collisions is exactly what is called a free path, and its average value is the mean free path.
formula_principle: Postulate: no force acts on a molecule except during collision, so Newton's first law gives uniform velocity
common_misconception: Students imagine gravity or mutual attraction bending the path of every molecule all the time.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Conditions under which a real gas behaves like an ideal gas
stem: A real gas behaves most nearly like an ideal gas at
solution: At low pressure the molecules are far apart, so their own volume is a negligible fraction of the vessel and the attractive forces are weak. At high temperature the average kinetic energy is large compared with the potential energy of attraction, so the attractive forces hardly affect the motion. Both requirements of the ideal gas model are therefore best satisfied at low pressure and high temperature.
formula_principle: Ideal behaviour requires negligible molecular volume and negligible intermolecular force
common_misconception: Students remember only one of the two conditions and pick a combination that satisfies pressure or temperature alone.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Identifying a statement that is not an assumption
stem: Which of the following is NOT an assumption of the kinetic theory of an ideal gas?
option_a: The molecules are in ceaseless random motion in all directions
option_b: The molecules exert appreciable attractive forces on one another at all separations
option_c: The duration of a collision is negligible compared with the time between two collisions
option_d: The molecules of a given gas are identical, rigid and perfectly elastic spheres
correct_answer_text: The molecules exert appreciable attractive forces on one another at all separations
solution: Kinetic theory deliberately switches off intermolecular forces except for the instant of contact during a collision. Random ceaseless motion, negligible collision time and identical rigid elastic spheres are all standard postulates. A continuous attractive force at all separations belongs to the van der Waals description of a real gas, not to the ideal gas model.
formula_principle: The ideal gas model neglects intermolecular forces except during collisions
common_misconception: Learners import the van der Waals attraction term into the ideal gas postulates because both are studied together.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Physical reason for deviation from ideal behaviour
stem: The two corrections that must be applied to the ideal gas equation to describe a real gas arise because
option_a: the molecules occupy a finite volume and they attract one another
option_b: the molecules move with different speeds and collide with the walls
option_c: the collisions between molecules are inelastic and the gas loses energy
option_d: gravity acts on the molecules and makes the density non uniform
correct_answer_text: the molecules occupy a finite volume and they attract one another
solution: The ideal gas model assumes point molecules with no mutual force. A real molecule has a finite size, so the space available for motion is less than the vessel volume, which requires a volume correction. A real molecule also attracts its neighbours, so a molecule about to strike the wall is pulled back by the gas behind it and the measured pressure is smaller than the ideal value, which requires a pressure correction.
formula_principle: Real gas corrections: excluded volume term and intermolecular attraction term
common_misconception: Students blame deviation on inelastic collisions rather than on molecular size and attraction.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Effect of intermolecular attraction on measured pressure
stem: Because of the attractive forces between the molecules of a real gas, the pressure actually exerted on the walls is
option_a: greater than the pressure predicted for an ideal gas under the same conditions
option_b: equal to the ideal value because attraction acts equally in all directions
option_c: zero at the wall because attraction cancels the molecular momentum completely
option_d: less than the pressure predicted for an ideal gas under the same conditions
correct_answer_text: less than the pressure predicted for an ideal gas under the same conditions
solution: Deep inside the gas a molecule is pulled equally in all directions, so the net force is zero. A molecule approaching the wall has gas only on one side, so it experiences a net inward pull that slows it down slightly. It therefore delivers less momentum to the wall than an ideal molecule would, and the observed pressure falls below the ideal value. The van der Waals equation restores this by adding a positive correction term to the measured pressure.
formula_principle: Inward pull on a molecule near the wall reduces the momentum transferred per impact
common_misconception: Students think attraction should push molecules harder against the wall instead of holding them back.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Comparison of collision time with free flight time
stem: Kinetic theory assumes that the time taken for one collision is negligible compared with the time between two successive collisions. The direct consequence of this assumption is that
option_a: a molecule spends almost all of its time in free straight line motion
option_b: the number of collisions per second becomes extremely small
option_c: the pressure on the wall is produced only during the free flight
option_d: the molecules must all move with the same speed
correct_answer_text: a molecule spends almost all of its time in free straight line motion
solution: If each collision lasts for a vanishingly small time, then almost the entire lifetime of a molecule is spent travelling freely in a straight line. This is what makes it meaningful to define a free path and a mean free path, and it also justifies calculating pressure as a sequence of instantaneous momentum transfers. The frequency of collisions can still be very large; a short duration does not mean a small number.
formula_principle: Postulate on negligible collision duration and its link to free path motion
common_misconception: Learners confuse the duration of a single collision with the collision frequency.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Average velocity vector versus mean square speed
stem: For a large number of molecules of a gas in a closed container at rest, the average of the velocity vectors of all the molecules and the average of the squares of their speeds are respectively
option_b: zero and a non zero positive quantity
option_c: a non zero positive quantity and zero
option_d: non zero and non zero, both directed along the container axis
correct_answer_text: zero and a non zero positive quantity
solution: Molecular motion is completely random, so for every molecule moving with a certain velocity there is on average another moving with the opposite velocity. The vector sum, and hence the average velocity, is zero for a container at rest. The square of a speed is always positive, so no cancellation is possible and the mean square speed is a definite positive number. That is exactly why pressure is written using the mean square speed and not the average velocity.
formula_principle: Randomness makes the vector sum of velocities zero while the mean of squared speeds stays positive
common_misconception: Students conclude that the root mean square speed must also be zero because the average velocity is zero.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Which assumptions are essential for deriving the pressure expression
stem: In deriving the expression P = (1/3) rho v_rms^2 for an ideal gas, the assumptions that are essential are that the collisions with the wall are elastic, that the molecular motion is random and isotropic, and that
option_a: the molecules all travel with the same speed equal to v_rms
option_b: the collisions between molecules must be neglected altogether or the result changes
option_c: intermolecular forces are absent between collisions so that a molecule crosses the vessel at constant speed
option_d: the gas must be monatomic so that rotation cannot store energy
correct_answer_text: intermolecular forces are absent between collisions so that a molecule crosses the vessel at constant speed
solution: The standard derivation follows one molecule bouncing between two opposite faces. Force free flight lets the transit time be written as twice the side length divided by the velocity component. Elastic collision at the wall makes the momentum change equal to twice the momentum component. Isotropy allows the mean square components along the three axes to be set equal, which produces the factor one third. A single common speed is never assumed; averaging over the distribution is what converts the sum of squared speeds into the mean square speed.
formula_principle: P = (1/3) rho v_rms^2 follows from elastic wall collisions, isotropy and force free flight between collisions
common_misconception: Students believe that all molecules must have the same speed for the pressure formula to hold.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Direct use of P = (1/3) rho v_rms^2
stem: A gas of density 1.2 kg m^-3 has a root mean square speed of 500 m s^-1. The pressure exerted by the gas is
formula_principle: P = (1/3) rho v_rms^2
common_misconception: Students substitute the factor 1/2 from kinetic energy in place of the factor 1/3.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Pressure in terms of number of molecules
concept_tested: Form of the pressure expression using N, m and V
stem: For a gas containing N molecules each of mass m in a vessel of volume V, the kinetic theory expression for pressure is
solution: The density of the gas is the total mass N m divided by the volume V. Substituting rho = N m / V into P = (1/3) rho v_rms^2 gives P = (1/3) (N m / V) v_rms^2. The quantity N m / V has units kg m^-3 and multiplying by the square of a speed gives Pa.
formula_principle: P = (1/3) rho v_rms^2 with rho = N m / V
common_misconception: Learners mix up the factor 1/3 in the pressure formula with the factor 2/3 in the energy relation.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Root mean square speed from pressure
concept_tested: Rearranging the pressure expression to find v_rms
stem: The pressure of a gas of density 3 kg m^-3 is 1.6 x 10^5 Pa. The root mean square speed of its molecules is
solution: From P = (1/3) rho v_rms^2 we get v_rms^2 = 3P / rho = 3 x 1.6 x 10^5 / 3 = 1.6 x 10^5. Taking the square root, v_rms = 400 m s^-1.
formula_principle: v_rms = sqrt(3P / rho)
common_misconception: Students forget to carry the factor 3 across when inverting the pressure relation.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Pressure and kinetic energy per unit volume
concept_tested: Relation between pressure and translational kinetic energy density
stem: If E is the translational kinetic energy of the molecules of an ideal gas per unit volume, then the pressure of the gas is
solution: Kinetic energy per unit volume is E = (1/2) rho v_rms^2, so rho v_rms^2 = 2E. Substituting in P = (1/3) rho v_rms^2 gives P = (1/3) x 2E = (2/3) E. Equivalently the energy density is one and a half times the pressure.
formula_principle: P = (1/3) rho v_rms^2 and E = (1/2) rho v_rms^2 give P = (2/3) E
common_misconception: Students quote the reciprocal relation and write pressure as three halves of the energy density.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Pressure and kinetic energy per unit volume
concept_tested: Computing energy density from a given pressure
stem: The pressure of an ideal gas is 1.5 x 10^5 Pa. The translational kinetic energy of its molecules per unit volume is
solution: Since P = (2/3) E, the energy density is E = (3/2) P = 1.5 x 1.5 x 10^5 = 2.25 x 10^5 J m^-3. Note that a joule per cubic metre and a pascal are the same combination of base units, so the answer is dimensionally consistent.
common_misconception: Learners apply the factor 2/3 in the wrong direction when converting between pressure and energy density.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Pressure from mass and volume of gas
concept_tested: Two step calculation of density and then pressure
stem: A closed vessel of volume 0.02 m^3 contains 60 g of a gas whose molecules have a root mean square speed of 500 m s^-1. The pressure of the gas is
formula_principle: rho = mass / volume, then P = (1/3) rho v_rms^2
common_misconception: Students forget to convert gram to kilogram before computing the density.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Proportionality of pressure to the square of v_rms
stem: The root mean square speed of the molecules of a gas is doubled while the density is kept unchanged. The pressure of the gas becomes
solution: At constant density, P = (1/3) rho v_rms^2 shows P proportional to v_rms^2. Doubling v_rms multiplies the pressure by 2^2 = 4. Physically each molecule now delivers twice the momentum per impact and strikes the wall twice as often, giving four times the force.
formula_principle: P proportional to v_rms^2 at constant density
common_misconception: Students forget that the speed enters the pressure formula squared.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Isothermal compression seen through the kinetic theory expression
stem: A fixed mass of gas is compressed to half its volume while the temperature is held constant. Using P = (1/3) rho v_rms^2, the pressure
option_a: doubles, because the density doubles while v_rms stays the same
option_b: doubles, because v_rms doubles while the density stays the same
option_c: becomes four times, because both the density and v_rms double
option_d: remains unchanged, because the number of molecules does not change
correct_answer_text: doubles, because the density doubles while v_rms stays the same
solution: The root mean square speed depends only on temperature through v_rms = sqrt(3RT/M), so an isothermal change leaves it unaltered. Halving the volume for a fixed mass doubles the density. Since P = (1/3) rho v_rms^2 with v_rms fixed, the pressure doubles, which is exactly Boyle's law recovered from kinetic theory.
formula_principle: At constant temperature v_rms is fixed, so P is proportional to rho
common_misconception: Learners think squeezing a gas makes the molecules move faster even when the temperature is held constant.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Equal pressure and equal density imply equal v_rms
stem: Two different gases are found to have the same pressure and the same density. Then
option_a: their molecules have the same mass
option_b: their molecules have the same root mean square speed
option_c: they are necessarily at the same temperature
option_d: their molecules have the same average kinetic energy
correct_answer_text: their molecules have the same root mean square speed
solution: Rearranging the pressure expression gives v_rms = sqrt(3P / rho). If both P and rho are the same for the two gases, then v_rms must be the same. Nothing follows about the molecular mass, since a gas of heavy molecules can reach the same density with fewer molecules per unit volume, and nothing follows about temperature because v_rms = sqrt(3RT/M) involves the molar mass as well.
formula_principle: v_rms = sqrt(3P / rho) depends only on pressure and density
common_misconception: Students jump from equal root mean square speed to equal temperature without noticing the molar mass factor.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Dimensions of the quantity rho v_rms^2
stem: The dimensions of the quantity rho v_rms^2, where rho is density and v_rms is the root mean square speed, are
solution: Density has dimensions M^1 L^-3 and speed squared has dimensions L^2 T^-2. Their product is M^1 L^-3 x L^2 T^-2 = M^1 L^-1 T^-2, which is exactly the dimensional formula of pressure. This confirms that P = (1/3) rho v_rms^2 is dimensionally consistent, the numerical factor 1/3 being dimensionless.
formula_principle: Dimensions of pressure are M^1 L^-1 T^-2
common_misconception: Students combine the length powers with the wrong sign when multiplying density by speed squared.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Origin of the factor one third
concept_tested: Why the factor 1/3 appears in the pressure expression
stem: In the kinetic theory expression for pressure, the factor 1/3 arises because
option_a: only one third of the molecules strike a given wall at any instant
option_b: each molecule loses one third of its momentum at the wall
option_c: a cube has three pairs of opposite faces and pressure acts on one pair
option_d: the mean square speed is shared equally among the three mutually perpendicular directions
correct_answer_text: the mean square speed is shared equally among the three mutually perpendicular directions
solution: For any molecule the squared speed is the sum of the squares of its three velocity components. Because the motion is random and isotropic, the averages of the three squared components are equal, so each equals one third of the mean square speed. Only the component perpendicular to a wall contributes to the momentum transfer at that wall, and this introduces the factor 1/3 into the pressure expression.
formula_principle: Isotropy gives mean square component along each axis equal to one third of the mean square speed
common_misconception: Learners believe the factor 1/3 counts the fraction of molecules moving towards a chosen wall.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Total kinetic energy of a gas from pressure and volume
stem: A gas at a pressure of 2 x 10^5 Pa occupies a volume of 0.5 m^3. The total translational kinetic energy of all its molecules is
solution: Energy per unit volume is (3/2)P, so the total translational kinetic energy in a volume V is (3/2) P V = 1.5 x 2 x 10^5 x 0.5 = 1.5 x 10^5 J. The same result follows from (3/2) n R T combined with P V = n R T.
formula_principle: Total translational kinetic energy = (3/2) P V
common_misconception: Students use PV as the energy directly instead of three halves of PV.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Combined change of density and speed
concept_tested: Pressure when density and v_rms both change
stem: The density of a gas is reduced to half its initial value while the root mean square speed of its molecules is made three times the initial value. The new pressure is
solution: Write P_new / P_old = (rho_new / rho_old) x (v_new / v_old)^2 = (1/2) x (3)^2 = (1/2) x 9 = 4.5. The pressure therefore becomes 4.5 times the initial value.
formula_principle: P proportional to rho v_rms^2
common_misconception: Learners apply the square to the density factor as well as to the speed factor.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Link between pressure formula and v_rms
concept_tested: Deriving v_rms = sqrt(3RT/M) from the pressure expression
stem: Starting from P = (1/3) rho v_rms^2 and using the ideal gas equation for one mole, PV = RT, the root mean square speed is obtained as
option_a: v_rms = sqrt(3 R T / M), where M is the molar mass
correct_answer_text: v_rms = sqrt(3 R T / M), where M is the molar mass
solution: For one mole the density is rho = M / V. Substituting gives P = (1/3)(M / V) v_rms^2, that is P V = (1/3) M v_rms^2. Since P V = R T for one mole, R T = (1/3) M v_rms^2, so v_rms^2 = 3 R T / M and v_rms = sqrt(3 R T / M). The molar mass must be taken in kilogram per mole for SI units.
formula_principle: P = (1/3) rho v_rms^2 with rho = M / V and PV = RT for one mole
common_misconception: Students misplace the molar mass and end up with a speed that increases with molecular mass.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Effect of doubling temperature at constant volume on energy density
stem: A gas in a rigid container is at a pressure of 1.5 x 10^5 Pa. Its absolute temperature is then doubled. The translational kinetic energy per unit volume of the gas becomes
solution: At constant volume the pressure is proportional to the absolute temperature, so doubling T raises the pressure to 3.0 x 10^5 Pa. The translational kinetic energy per unit volume is E = (3/2) P = 1.5 x 3.0 x 10^5 = 4.5 x 10^5 J m^-3.
formula_principle: At constant volume P is proportional to T, and energy density E = (3/2) P
common_misconception: Students treat kinetic energy as proportional to the square of temperature because speed involves a square root.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Pressure with changed molecule number and speed
concept_tested: Combined effect of losing molecules and increasing v_rms
stem: A rigid vessel contains a gas at pressure P. Half the molecules are allowed to escape and the root mean square speed of the remaining molecules is then made twice its original value. The final pressure is
solution: With the volume and molecular mass unchanged, the pressure is proportional to the product of the number of molecules and the square of the root mean square speed. The number falls to one half and the square of the speed rises by a factor of 2^2 = 4. Hence P_final / P = (1/2) x 4 = 2, so the final pressure is 2P.
formula_principle: P = (1/3)(N m / V) v_rms^2 with V and m fixed
common_misconception: Learners cancel the halved molecule count against the doubled speed without squaring the speed factor.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Standard formula for the root mean square speed
stem: For a gas of molar mass M at absolute temperature T, the root mean square speed of the molecules is given by
solution: For one mole, P V = R T and P V = (1/3) M v_rms^2 from kinetic theory. Equating the two gives v_rms^2 = 3 R T / M, so v_rms = sqrt(3 R T / M) with M in kilogram per mole.
formula_principle: v_rms = sqrt(3 R T / M)
common_misconception: Students confuse the coefficient 3 of the root mean square speed with the coefficient 2 of the most probable speed.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Dependence of v_rms on the square root of absolute temperature
stem: The absolute temperature of a gas is made four times its initial value. The root mean square speed of its molecules becomes
solution: Since v_rms = sqrt(3 R T / M), the speed is proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature. Multiplying T by 4 multiplies v_rms by sqrt(4) = 2.
formula_principle: v_rms proportional to sqrt(T)
common_misconception: Learners forget the square root and scale the speed by the same factor as the temperature.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Ordering of root mean square, mean and most probable speeds
stem: For the molecules of a gas at a given temperature, the correct order of the root mean square speed v_rms, the mean speed v_mean and the most probable speed v_mp is
solution: Writing each speed as a coefficient times sqrt(R T / M), the coefficients are sqrt(3) = 1.73 for the root mean square speed, sqrt(8/pi) = 1.60 for the mean speed and sqrt(2) = 1.41 for the most probable speed. Hence v_rms is the largest and v_mp is the smallest.
formula_principle: v_rms : v_mean : v_mp = sqrt(3) : sqrt(8/pi) : sqrt(2) = 1.73 : 1.60 : 1.41
common_misconception: Students think the most probable speed must be the largest because most molecules have it.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Expression for v_rms using Boltzmann constant and molecular mass
stem: If k is the Boltzmann constant and m is the mass of one molecule, the root mean square speed at absolute temperature T is
solution: Divide both numerator and denominator of 3 R T / M by the Avogadro number. Since R / N_A = k and M / N_A = m, the expression becomes 3 k T / m, so v_rms = sqrt(3 k T / m). The molar form and the molecular form are the same statement written on two different scales.
formula_principle: v_rms = sqrt(3 k T / m), with k = R / N_A and m = M / N_A
common_misconception: Learners pair the Boltzmann constant with the molar mass or the gas constant with the molecular mass.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Comparison of v_rms for two gases at the same temperature
stem: Hydrogen and oxygen are kept at the same temperature. Compared with an oxygen molecule, a hydrogen molecule has
option_a: a larger root mean square speed because v_rms varies inversely as the square root of molar mass
option_b: a smaller root mean square speed because a lighter molecule carries less energy
option_c: the same root mean square speed because the temperature is the same
option_d: a larger root mean square speed because hydrogen molecules are diatomic
correct_answer_text: a larger root mean square speed because v_rms varies inversely as the square root of molar mass
solution: At the same temperature every molecule has the same average translational kinetic energy (3/2)kT. Since this equals (1/2) m v_rms^2, a smaller mass must be balanced by a larger speed. Numerically v_rms is proportional to 1 / sqrt(M), and hydrogen with molar mass 2 g mol^-1 is far lighter than oxygen with 32 g mol^-1.
formula_principle: At fixed T, v_rms proportional to 1 / sqrt(M)
common_misconception: Students think a lighter molecule must be slower because it seems less energetic.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Numerical scaling of v_rms with temperature
stem: The root mean square speed of the molecules of a gas at 300 K is 500 m s^-1. At 1200 K the root mean square speed of the same gas is
solution: The temperature ratio is 1200 / 300 = 4, so the speed ratio is sqrt(4) = 2. Hence the new speed is 2 x 500 = 1000 m s^-1.
formula_principle: v_rms proportional to sqrt(T), so v2 / v1 = sqrt(T2 / T1)
common_misconception: Learners scale the speed directly with the temperature ratio.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Ratio of v_rms for hydrogen and oxygen at the same temperature
stem: Hydrogen of molar mass 2 g mol^-1 and oxygen of molar mass 32 g mol^-1 are at the same temperature. The ratio of the root mean square speed of hydrogen to that of oxygen is
solution: The ratio is sqrt(M_oxygen / M_hydrogen) = sqrt(32 / 2) = sqrt(16) = 4. So hydrogen molecules have a root mean square speed four times that of oxygen molecules at the same temperature.
formula_principle: v_rms proportional to 1 / sqrt(M) at constant temperature
common_misconception: Students use the molar mass ratio itself rather than the square root of that ratio.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Ratio of root mean square speed to most probable speed
stem: The ratio of the root mean square speed to the most probable speed of the molecules of a gas at a given temperature is approximately
solution: Dividing the two expressions, v_rms / v_mp = sqrt(3RT/M) / sqrt(2RT/M) = sqrt(3/2) = 1.2247, which is about 1.22. Equivalently the coefficients 1.73 and 1.41 give 1.73 / 1.41 = 1.22.
formula_principle: v_rms = sqrt(3RT/M), v_mp = sqrt(2RT/M), so the ratio is sqrt(3/2)
common_misconception: Learners divide the coefficients 3 and 2 without remembering that both sit under a square root.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Using the fixed ratio between the three characteristic speeds
stem: The root mean square speed of the molecules of a gas is 1730 m s^-1. The mean speed of the molecules at the same temperature is nearly
solution: Since the root mean square speed corresponds to the coefficient 1.73, a value of 1730 m s^-1 means that sqrt(R T / M) equals 1000 m s^-1. The mean speed then equals 1.60 x 1000 = 1600 m s^-1.
common_misconception: Students pick the coefficient of the most probable speed when the mean speed is asked for.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Temperature at which a heavy gas matches a light gas
stem: At what temperature will the root mean square speed of oxygen molecules of molar mass 32 g mol^-1 equal the root mean square speed of hydrogen molecules of molar mass 2 g mol^-1 kept at 300 K?
solution: Setting 3 R T_oxygen / 32 = 3 R x 300 / 2 gives T_oxygen / 32 = 300 / 2 = 150, so T_oxygen = 150 x 32 = 4800 K. The heavier gas must be much hotter to match the speed of the lighter one.
formula_principle: Equal v_rms means T / M is the same for both gases
common_misconception: Learners apply the square root factor 4 to the temperature, but temperature scales with the molar mass ratio itself.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Finding the temperature increase needed to double v_rms
stem: The root mean square speed of the molecules of a gas at 300 K has to be doubled. The temperature must be raised by
solution: To double the speed the absolute temperature must become 2^2 = 4 times, that is 4 x 300 = 1200 K. The required rise is 1200 minus 300 = 900 K.
formula_principle: v_rms proportional to sqrt(T), so doubling v_rms needs T to become four times
common_misconception: Students report the final temperature instead of the increase in temperature.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Effect of changing pressure at constant temperature on v_rms
stem: The pressure of a fixed mass of gas is doubled while its temperature is kept constant. The root mean square speed of its molecules
option_a: becomes sqrt(2) times the initial value, since v_rms depends on pressure
option_b: remains unchanged, since v_rms depends only on temperature and molar mass
option_c: becomes two times the initial value
correct_answer_text: remains unchanged, since v_rms depends only on temperature and molar mass
solution: For a given gas the root mean square speed is fixed by the absolute temperature alone. The alternative form v_rms = sqrt(3P / rho) may look pressure dependent, but in an isothermal change the density rises in exactly the same proportion as the pressure, so the ratio P / rho and hence v_rms are unaltered.
formula_principle: v_rms = sqrt(3 R T / M) contains no pressure term
common_misconception: Learners use the pressure form of the formula and change P while leaving rho fixed.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Using v_rms = sqrt(3 k T / m) for a change of temperature
stem: The molecules of a gas at 200 K have a root mean square speed of 400 m s^-1. Take k = 1.38 x 10^-23 J K^-1. At 800 K the root mean square speed of the same molecules is
solution: The molecular mass is unchanged, so v_rms is proportional to sqrt(T). The temperature ratio is 800 / 200 = 4, giving a speed ratio of sqrt(4) = 2. The new speed is 2 x 400 = 800 m s^-1. The value of the Boltzmann constant is not needed for a ratio question.
formula_principle: v_rms = sqrt(3 k T / m), so v_rms proportional to sqrt(T) for a given molecule
common_misconception: Students multiply by the temperature ratio directly instead of taking its square root.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Distinguishing the average of velocities from the average of speeds
stem: For a gas enclosed in a stationary container, the average of the velocities of all the molecules and the mean speed of the molecules are respectively
option_b: zero and about 1.60 times sqrt(R T / M)
option_c: about 1.60 times sqrt(R T / M) and zero
option_d: both equal to about 1.73 times sqrt(R T / M)
correct_answer_text: zero and about 1.60 times sqrt(R T / M)
solution: Velocity is a vector, and in a stationary container every direction is equally likely, so the components cancel in pairs and the average velocity is zero. Speed is the magnitude of velocity and is always positive, so no cancellation is possible. The mean speed equals sqrt(8 R T / pi M), which is 1.60 times sqrt(R T / M).
formula_principle: Average velocity is a vector average and vanishes; mean speed uses magnitudes and equals sqrt(8 R T / pi M)
common_misconception: Learners treat mean velocity and mean speed as the same quantity.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Inverting v_rms = sqrt(3RT/M) to obtain the molar mass
stem: The root mean square speed of the molecules of a gas at 300 K is 500 m s^-1. Taking R = 8.3 J mol^-1 K^-1, the molar mass of the gas is nearly
solution: M = 3 x 8.3 x 300 / (500)^2 = 7470 / 250000 = 0.0299 kg mol^-1, which is about 0.03 kg mol^-1, that is nearly 30 g mol^-1.
formula_principle: M = 3 R T / v_rms^2
common_misconception: Students forget that the molar mass obtained from the SI formula is in kilogram per mole and must be converted to gram per mole.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Halving the root mean square speed
concept_tested: Temperature needed to reduce v_rms to one half
stem: At 1200 K the root mean square speed of the molecules of a gas has a certain value. The temperature at which the root mean square speed of the same gas becomes half of that value is
solution: If v_rms is to fall by a factor of 2, then T must fall by a factor of 2^2 = 4. Hence the required temperature is 1200 / 4 = 300 K.
formula_principle: v_rms proportional to sqrt(T), so halving v_rms needs T to become one quarter
common_misconception: Learners halve the temperature when they want to halve the speed.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Combined effect of molar mass and temperature on v_rms
stem: Gas A has a molar mass four times that of gas B, and gas A is kept at twice the absolute temperature of gas B. The ratio of the root mean square speed of A to that of B is
solution: The ratio is sqrt((T_A / M_A) / (T_B / M_B)) = sqrt((2 T_B / 4 M_B) x (M_B / T_B)) = sqrt(2 / 4) = sqrt(1/2) = 1 / sqrt(2), which is about 0.71. So gas A is the slower of the two despite being hotter.
formula_principle: v_rms proportional to sqrt(T / M)
common_misconception: Students let the higher temperature decide the answer and overlook the larger molar mass.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Converting the most probable speed into the root mean square speed
stem: At a certain temperature the most probable speed of the molecules of a gas is 400 m s^-1. The root mean square speed at the same temperature is nearly
solution: v_rms = v_mp x sqrt(3/2) = 400 x 1.2247 = 489.9 m s^-1, which is nearly 490 m s^-1. Using the coefficient form, 400 corresponds to 1.41 times sqrt(R T / M), so sqrt(R T / M) is about 283.7 and 1.73 times this is about 490 m s^-1.
formula_principle: v_rms / v_mp = sqrt(3/2) = 1.2247
common_misconception: Learners apply the factor 3/2 directly without the square root.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Fractional increase in v_rms when temperature is doubled
stem: The absolute temperature of a gas is doubled. The percentage increase in the root mean square speed of its molecules is nearly
solution: The new speed is sqrt(2) = 1.414 times the old speed. The increase is 1.414 minus 1 = 0.414 of the original, that is about 41 per cent.
formula_principle: v_rms proportional to sqrt(T), so the ratio becomes sqrt(2) = 1.414
common_misconception: Students report the factor as a percentage without subtracting the original value.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Speed and energy in a mixture
concept_tested: Comparing v_rms and kinetic energy for two gases in the same vessel
