stem: Hydrogen of molar mass 2 g mol^-1 and oxygen of molar mass 32 g mol^-1 are mixed in a vessel and allowed to reach thermal equilibrium. For a hydrogen molecule compared with an oxygen molecule,
option_a: both the root mean square speed and the average kinetic energy are 4 times larger
option_b: the root mean square speed is 4 times larger while the average kinetic energy is the same
option_c: the root mean square speed is 16 times larger while the average kinetic energy is the same
option_d: the root mean square speed is the same while the average kinetic energy is 16 times larger
correct_answer_text: the root mean square speed is 4 times larger while the average kinetic energy is the same
solution: Thermal equilibrium means a common temperature, so every molecule of either gas has the same average translational kinetic energy (3/2)kT. Since (1/2) m v_rms^2 is the same for both, the speed ratio is sqrt(32 / 2) = 4 in favour of hydrogen.
formula_principle: Average kinetic energy per molecule = (3/2)kT for all gases; v_rms proportional to 1 / sqrt(M)
common_misconception: Learners assume that the faster molecules must also carry more kinetic energy.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Matching v_mp of one gas to v_rms of another
concept_tested: Temperature at which the most probable speed equals a given root mean square speed
stem: At what temperature will the most probable speed of oxygen molecules of molar mass 32 g mol^-1 equal the root mean square speed of hydrogen molecules of molar mass 2 g mol^-1 kept at 300 K?
solution: Set sqrt(2 R T / 0.032) = sqrt(3 R x 300 / 0.002). Squaring and cancelling R gives 2T / 32 = 900 / 2 = 450, so 2T = 450 x 32 = 14400 and T = 7200 K.
formula_principle: v_mp = sqrt(2 R T / M) and v_rms = sqrt(3 R T / M)
common_misconception: Students forget that the most probable speed carries the coefficient 2 while the root mean square speed carries the coefficient 3.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Effect of leakage on speed and energy
concept_tested: What changes and what does not when gas escapes at constant temperature
stem: A vessel of fixed volume contains a gas at 300 K. Gas is allowed to leak out slowly until the pressure falls to half its initial value, the temperature being held at 300 K throughout. As a result,
option_a: both the root mean square speed and the total translational kinetic energy are halved
option_b: the root mean square speed is unchanged and the total translational kinetic energy is unchanged
option_c: the root mean square speed is unchanged and the total translational kinetic energy of the gas in the vessel is halved
option_d: the root mean square speed falls to 1 / sqrt(2) times its value and the total energy is halved
correct_answer_text: the root mean square speed is unchanged and the total translational kinetic energy of the gas in the vessel is halved
solution: The temperature is constant, so v_rms = sqrt(3 R T / M) is unchanged. At constant volume and temperature the pressure is proportional to the number of molecules, so halving the pressure means half the molecules remain. The total translational kinetic energy is (3/2) N k T, which therefore falls to half. The same conclusion follows from (3/2) P V with V fixed and P halved.
formula_principle: v_rms depends only on T; total translational kinetic energy = (3/2) N k T = (3/2) P V
common_misconception: Learners assume that a fall in pressure must slow the molecules down.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Standard result for average translational kinetic energy
stem: The average translational kinetic energy of a molecule of an ideal gas at absolute temperature T is
solution: Each of the three translational degrees of freedom carries an average energy (1/2) k T by the law of equipartition. The total translational energy of one molecule is therefore 3 x (1/2) k T = (3/2) k T, and this value is the same for every ideal gas at a given temperature.
formula_principle: Average translational kinetic energy per molecule = (3/2) k T
common_misconception: Students substitute the molar gas constant in place of the Boltzmann constant when speaking about one molecule.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Translational kinetic energy of one mole of a gas
stem: The total translational kinetic energy of one mole of an ideal gas at absolute temperature T is
solution: One mole contains N_A molecules and each has an average translational kinetic energy (3/2) k T. The total is N_A x (3/2) k T = (3/2) (N_A k) T = (3/2) R T, because the gas constant is the product of the Avogadro number and the Boltzmann constant.
formula_principle: Energy per mole = N_A x (3/2) k T = (3/2) R T since R = N_A k
common_misconception: Learners interchange the molar and the molecular constants.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Independence of the nature of gas
concept_tested: Comparing average kinetic energy of different gases at the same temperature
stem: Helium, nitrogen and carbon dioxide are all kept at the same temperature. The average translational kinetic energy of one molecule is
option_a: the same for all three gases
option_b: largest for carbon dioxide because its molecules are heaviest
option_c: largest for helium because its molecules move fastest
option_d: largest for carbon dioxide because it has the most atoms per molecule
correct_answer_text: the same for all three gases
solution: The expression (3/2) k T contains only the Boltzmann constant and the absolute temperature. Neither the mass of the molecule nor the number of atoms in it appears. A heavier molecule compensates its larger mass with a smaller root mean square speed so that (1/2) m v_rms^2 stays the same.
formula_principle: Average translational kinetic energy per molecule = (3/2) k T, independent of the nature of the gas
common_misconception: Students believe heavier molecules must carry more kinetic energy at the same temperature.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Temperature as a measure of energy
concept_tested: Physical meaning of absolute zero in kinetic theory
stem: On the kinetic theory picture, the absolute zero of temperature is the temperature at which
option_a: the molecules move with the most probable speed
option_b: the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules becomes zero
option_c: the pressure of the gas becomes maximum
option_d: the density of the gas becomes zero
correct_answer_text: the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules becomes zero
solution: Because the average translational kinetic energy per molecule is directly proportional to the absolute temperature, it vanishes only when T = 0. Absolute zero is therefore the temperature at which the translational motion assumed by kinetic theory ceases, and it is why no lower temperature is possible on the Kelvin scale.
formula_principle: Average translational kinetic energy per molecule = (3/2) k T, so it vanishes when T = 0
common_misconception: Learners connect absolute zero with vanishing volume or vanishing density instead of vanishing molecular energy.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Computing (3/2) k T for a given temperature
stem: The average translational kinetic energy of a gas molecule at 200 K, taking k = 1.38 x 10^-23 J K^-1, is
formula_principle: Average kinetic energy per molecule = (3/2) k T
common_misconception: Students drop the factor 1/2 and compute three times k T.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Numerical value of (3/2) R T
stem: The translational kinetic energy of one mole of an ideal gas at 400 K, taking R = 8.3 J mol^-1 K^-1, is
formula_principle: Energy per mole = (3/2) R T
common_misconception: Learners multiply by 3 rather than by 3/2.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Effect of doubling the absolute temperature on molecular energy
stem: The absolute temperature of an ideal gas is doubled. The average translational kinetic energy of a molecule becomes
solution: Since the energy equals (3/2) k T, it is directly proportional to T. Doubling T doubles the energy. It is the root mean square speed that grows only as sqrt(T), by a factor of 1.41 in this case.
formula_principle: Average kinetic energy per molecule is directly proportional to absolute temperature
common_misconception: Students transfer the square root rule of speed to the energy.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Comparison of moles of two gases
concept_tested: Translational kinetic energy of equal numbers of moles
stem: One mole of helium and one mole of oxygen are kept at the same temperature. The ratio of the total translational kinetic energy of the helium sample to that of the oxygen sample is
solution: The translational kinetic energy of n moles is (3/2) n R T and involves neither the molar mass nor the atomicity. With n = 1 and the same T for both samples, the two energies are equal, so the ratio is 1 : 1. The atomicity would matter only if the total internal energy including rotation were asked for.
formula_principle: Total translational kinetic energy of n moles = (3/2) n R T
common_misconception: Learners bring in the molar mass or the atomicity when only the translational part is asked.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Total translational kinetic energy of a given number of moles
stem: The total translational kinetic energy of 2 moles of an ideal gas at 300 K, taking R = 8.3 J mol^-1 K^-1, is
formula_principle: Total translational kinetic energy = (3/2) n R T
common_misconception: Students compute the energy per mole and forget the factor n.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Converting between Celsius and Kelvin in an energy problem
stem: A gas is at 27 degree celsius. The temperature to which it must be raised so that the average kinetic energy of its molecules is doubled is
solution: The initial absolute temperature is 27 + 273 = 300 K. To double the energy the absolute temperature must become 600 K. Converting back, 600 minus 273 = 327 degree celsius.
formula_principle: Energy proportional to absolute temperature; T(K) = t(degree celsius) + 273
common_misconception: Learners double the Celsius reading instead of the Kelvin temperature.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Identifying the quantities on which molecular kinetic energy depends
stem: The average translational kinetic energy of the molecules of an ideal gas depends on
option_b: the absolute temperature and the pressure
option_c: the absolute temperature and the molar mass
option_d: the volume of the container only
solution: The expression contains only the Boltzmann constant, a universal number, and the absolute temperature. Pressure, volume, molar mass and the chemical identity of the gas are all absent. This is precisely why temperature can be interpreted as a direct measure of average molecular kinetic energy.
formula_principle: Average kinetic energy per molecule = (3/2) k T
common_misconception: Students add pressure or molar mass to the list because both appear in other gas formulas.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Inverting the energy relation to find temperature
stem: The average translational kinetic energy of the molecules of a gas is 6.21 x 10^-21 J. Taking k = 1.38 x 10^-23 J K^-1, the temperature of the gas is
common_misconception: Learners invert the factor 3/2 incorrectly and multiply where they should divide.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Comparing kinetic energy per kilogram for two gases
stem: Hydrogen of molar mass 2 g mol^-1 and oxygen of molar mass 32 g mol^-1 are at the same temperature. The ratio of the translational kinetic energy per unit mass of hydrogen to that of oxygen is
solution: For one kilogram the number of moles is 1 / M, so the translational kinetic energy per kilogram is (3/2) R T / M, which varies inversely as the molar mass. The ratio is therefore M_oxygen / M_hydrogen = 32 / 2 = 16, so hydrogen has sixteen times the energy per kilogram.
formula_principle: Energy per unit mass = (3/2) R T / M at a given temperature
common_misconception: Students carry over the per molecule equality to a per kilogram comparison.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Number of molecules from total energy
concept_tested: Finding N from the total translational kinetic energy
stem: The total translational kinetic energy of a sample of gas at 200 K is 4.14 x 10^-18 J. Taking k = 1.38 x 10^-23 J K^-1, the number of molecules in the sample is
solution: Energy per molecule = 1.5 x 1.38 x 10^-23 x 200 = 4.14 x 10^-21 J. Hence N = 4.14 x 10^-18 / 4.14 x 10^-21 = 1000 molecules.
formula_principle: Total energy = N x (3/2) k T
common_misconception: Learners forget the factor 3/2 when converting total energy into a molecule count.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Temperature change required to double the root mean square speed
stem: The root mean square speed of the molecules of a gas at 250 K is doubled. The average translational kinetic energy per molecule and the final temperature are respectively
option_a: two times the initial energy and 500 K
option_b: four times the initial energy and 500 K
option_c: four times the initial energy and 1000 K
option_d: two times the initial energy and 1000 K
correct_answer_text: four times the initial energy and 1000 K
solution: Since the energy varies as the square of the speed, doubling v_rms makes the energy 2^2 = 4 times its original value. Because the energy is directly proportional to the absolute temperature, the temperature must also become 4 times, that is 4 x 250 = 1000 K.
formula_principle: Kinetic energy = (1/2) m v_rms^2 and also (3/2) k T
common_misconception: Students scale energy linearly with speed instead of with the square of the speed.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Kinetic energy of 1 gram samples of two different gases
stem: One gram of hydrogen of molar mass 2 g mol^-1 and one gram of oxygen of molar mass 32 g mol^-1 are kept at the same temperature. The ratio of the total translational kinetic energy of the hydrogen sample to that of the oxygen sample is
solution: One gram of hydrogen is 1/2 mole and one gram of oxygen is 1/32 mole. Since the energy is (3/2) n R T at a common temperature, the ratio equals the ratio of the numbers of moles, that is (1/2) divided by (1/32) = 16. So the hydrogen sample carries sixteen times the translational energy.
formula_principle: Total translational kinetic energy = (3/2) n R T with n = mass / molar mass
common_misconception: Learners equate equal masses with equal numbers of molecules.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Total translational kinetic energy of a mixture of two gases
stem: A vessel contains 2 moles of helium and 3 moles of oxygen at 300 K. Taking R = 8.3 J mol^-1 K^-1, the total translational kinetic energy of the mixture is
solution: Translational energy per mole depends only on temperature, so both gases contribute (3/2) R T per mole. The total number of moles is 2 + 3 = 5. Energy = 1.5 x 5 x 8.3 x 300 = 1.5 x 12450 = 18675 J.
formula_principle: Translational kinetic energy = (3/2) n R T summed over all the gases in the mixture
common_misconception: Students use different coefficients for the monatomic and diatomic parts although the translational share is three halves R T per mole for every gas.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Energy in terms of P and V
concept_tested: Effect on total translational energy when P and V change oppositely
stem: The pressure of a fixed mass of an ideal gas is doubled while its volume is simultaneously halved. The total translational kinetic energy of the gas
option_a: becomes four times, because both pressure and volume changes raise the energy
option_b: becomes two times, because the pressure has doubled
option_c: remains unchanged, because it equals (3/2) P V and the product P V is unaltered
option_d: becomes half, because the volume has halved
correct_answer_text: remains unchanged, because it equals (3/2) P V and the product P V is unaltered
solution: The energy density of an ideal gas is (3/2) P, so the total translational kinetic energy in a volume V is (3/2) P V. Doubling P and halving V leaves the product P V unchanged, so the energy is unchanged. Since P V = n R T for a fixed mass, this also tells us that the temperature has not changed.
formula_principle: Total translational kinetic energy = (3/2) P V = (3/2) n R T
common_misconception: Learners look at only one of the two changes and forget that the energy depends on the product P V.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Degrees of freedom of a monatomic gas molecule
stem: The number of degrees of freedom of a monatomic gas molecule at ordinary temperature is
solution: A monatomic molecule is treated as a point mass, so its position needs three coordinates and its motion is fully described by three independent translational velocity components. Rotation of a point mass stores no energy and there are no interatomic bonds to vibrate, so the total is 3.
formula_principle: A point like atom has only three translational degrees of freedom
common_misconception: Students add rotational modes to a single atom by analogy with diatomic molecules.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Degrees of freedom of a rigid diatomic molecule
stem: A rigid diatomic molecule at moderate temperature has degrees of freedom equal to
option_c: 7, consisting of 3 translational, 2 rotational and 2 vibrational
solution: A diatomic molecule is a dumb bell. Its centre of mass can move along three independent directions, giving 3 translational modes. It can rotate about two axes perpendicular to the line joining the atoms, giving 2 rotational modes. Rotation about the bond axis itself has a negligible moment of inertia and is not counted, and the rigid model excludes vibration.
formula_principle: Rigid diatomic: 3 translational plus 2 rotational degrees of freedom
common_misconception: Learners count three rotational modes for a linear molecule.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Energy associated with one degree of freedom
stem: According to the law of equipartition of energy, the average energy associated with each degree of freedom of a molecule at absolute temperature T is
solution: In thermal equilibrium the total energy of a molecule is shared equally among all its degrees of freedom, each receiving an average of (1/2) k T. Three translational modes therefore give 3 x (1/2) k T = (3/2) k T, which reproduces the standard translational result.
formula_principle: Law of equipartition: each quadratic degree of freedom carries an average energy (1/2) k T
common_misconception: Students confuse the share of one degree of freedom with the total translational energy.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Relation between the two molar specific heats
stem: For one mole of an ideal gas, the molar specific heat at constant pressure C_p and that at constant volume C_v are related by
solution: At constant volume all the heat supplied raises the internal energy. At constant pressure the gas also does work R T per mole for a unit rise in temperature, so extra heat equal to R is needed per mole per kelvin. Hence C_p exceeds C_v by exactly R.
formula_principle: C_p - C_v = R for one mole of an ideal gas
common_misconception: Learners write the difference in the wrong order and obtain a negative gas constant.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Value of gamma for a monatomic gas
stem: The ratio of specific heats gamma for a monatomic ideal gas such as helium is
solution: A monatomic molecule has f = 3, so C_v = (3/2) R and C_p = C_v + R = (5/2) R. Therefore gamma = C_p / C_v = (5/2) / (3/2) = 5/3 = 1.67. The same follows from gamma = 1 + 2/3 = 1.67.
formula_principle: gamma = 1 + 2/f with f = 3 for a monatomic gas
common_misconception: Students memorise the diatomic value and apply it to every gas.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Value of gamma for a rigid diatomic gas
stem: For a rigid diatomic gas such as nitrogen at ordinary temperature, the ratio C_p / C_v is
solution: With f = 5, C_v = (5/2) R and C_p = (7/2) R, so gamma = 7/5 = 1.40. Equivalently gamma = 1 + 2/5 = 1.40.
formula_principle: gamma = 1 + 2/f with f = 5 for a rigid diatomic gas
common_misconception: Learners include vibrational modes at room temperature, where they remain frozen out.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Numerical values of C_v and C_p for a monatomic gas
stem: Taking R = 8.3 J mol^-1 K^-1, the molar specific heats at constant volume and at constant pressure for a monatomic ideal gas are respectively
formula_principle: C_v = (f/2) R and C_p = C_v + R, with f = 3
common_misconception: Students report the larger value as the constant volume specific heat.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Finding f when gamma is given
stem: The ratio of specific heats of a gas is 1.5. The number of degrees of freedom of its molecules is
solution: From gamma = 1 + 2/f we get gamma - 1 = 2/f, so f = 2 / (gamma - 1) = 2 / 0.5 = 4.
formula_principle: gamma = 1 + 2/f, so f = 2 / (gamma - 1)
common_misconception: Learners guess the atomicity from a remembered table rather than inverting the relation.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Internal energy of a diatomic gas sample
stem: The internal energy of 2 moles of a rigid diatomic ideal gas at 300 K, taking R = 8.3 J mol^-1 K^-1, is
formula_principle: Internal energy U = (f/2) n R T with f = 5 for a rigid diatomic gas
common_misconception: Students use the translational coefficient 3/2 when the whole internal energy is asked for.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Degrees of freedom and gamma for a non linear triatomic gas
stem: A triatomic gas molecule that is not linear has 3 translational and 3 rotational degrees of freedom and no excited vibration. For this gas the ratio of specific heats is
solution: With f = 6, C_v = 3R and C_p = 4R, so gamma = 4R / 3R = 4/3 = 1.33. Equivalently gamma = 1 + 2/6 = 1.33.
formula_principle: gamma = 1 + 2/f with f = 6
common_misconception: Learners count degrees of freedom atom by atom rather than for the molecule as a rigid body.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Deducing atomicity and gamma from a measured C_v
stem: The molar specific heat at constant volume of a gas is 20.75 J mol^-1 K^-1. Taking R = 8.3 J mol^-1 K^-1, the gas is
option_c: non linear triatomic with gamma equal to 1.33
solution: f = 2 x 20.75 / 8.3 = 41.5 / 8.3 = 5, so the molecule has five degrees of freedom and is a rigid diatomic. Then gamma = 1 + 2/5 = 1.40. Note that 20.75 J mol^-1 K^-1 is also the value of C_p for a monatomic gas, which is why the identification must be made from the definition and not from the number alone.
formula_principle: C_v = (f/2) R, so f = 2 C_v / R; then gamma = 1 + 2/f
common_misconception: Students recognise the number 20.75 as a monatomic C_p and answer monatomic without reading which capacity was given.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Effect of exciting vibration in a diatomic molecule
stem: At a sufficiently high temperature a diatomic molecule also vibrates, adding two more degrees of freedom. The ratio of specific heats then becomes nearly
solution: A vibrating diatomic molecule has f = 3 + 2 + 2 = 7. Then C_v = (7/2) R, C_p = (9/2) R and gamma = 9/7 = 1.286, which is nearly 1.29.
formula_principle: gamma = 1 + 2/f with f = 7 for a vibrating diatomic molecule
common_misconception: Learners add only one degree of freedom for vibration, forgetting that a vibrational mode contributes both kinetic and potential energy terms.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Ratio of C_p values for monatomic and diatomic gases
stem: The ratio of the molar specific heat at constant pressure of a monatomic gas to that of a rigid diatomic gas is
solution: For the monatomic gas C_p = (3/2) R + R = (5/2) R. For the rigid diatomic gas C_p = (5/2) R + R = (7/2) R. The required ratio is (5/2) R divided by (7/2) R = 5/7.
formula_principle: C_p = (f/2 + 1) R, giving (5/2) R for f = 3 and (7/2) R for f = 5
common_misconception: Students compare the constant volume capacities when the constant pressure ones are asked for.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Energy per degree of freedom per mole
concept_tested: Numerical energy share of one degree of freedom for a mole
stem: For one mole of a gas at 300 K, the energy associated with each degree of freedom, taking R = 8.3 J mol^-1 K^-1, is
solution: Energy = 0.5 x 8.3 x 300 = 0.5 x 2490 = 1245 J. Multiplying by 3 gives 3735 J, the translational energy per mole, which confirms the arithmetic.
formula_principle: Energy per degree of freedom per mole = (1/2) R T
common_misconception: Learners quote the total translational energy in place of the share of one mode.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Effective gamma of a mixture of monatomic and diatomic gases
stem: One mole of a monatomic gas is mixed with one mole of a rigid diatomic gas. For the mixture the molar specific heat at constant volume and the ratio of specific heats are respectively
solution: C_v of the mixture = (1 x 1.5R + 1 x 2.5R) / 2 = 4R / 2 = 2R, which is 16.6 J mol^-1 K^-1 for R = 8.3. Then C_p = C_v + R = 3R and gamma = 3R / 2R = 1.5. The mixture behaves like a gas with four effective degrees of freedom.
formula_principle: C_v of a mixture = (n1 C_v1 + n2 C_v2) / (n1 + n2); gamma = 1 + R / C_v
common_misconception: Students simply average the two values of gamma instead of averaging the specific heats first.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Fraction of heat that goes into translational motion
stem: A rigid diatomic gas is heated at constant volume. The fraction of the supplied heat that appears as translational kinetic energy of the molecules is
solution: Heating one mole through one kelvin at constant volume requires C_v = (5/2) R of heat. Of the five degrees of freedom, three are translational, so the translational part of the energy rise is (3/2) R. The fraction is (3/2) R divided by (5/2) R = 3/5 = 0.6, the remaining 0.4 going into rotation.
formula_principle: At constant volume all heat becomes internal energy; translational share is (3/2) R out of (5/2) R per mole
common_misconception: Learners assume that all the heat supplied at constant volume speeds the molecules up.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Meaning of the mean free path of a gas molecule
stem: The mean free path of a molecule of a gas is
option_a: the average distance between the walls of the container
option_b: the average distance travelled by a molecule between two successive collisions
option_c: the total distance travelled by a molecule in one second
option_d: the shortest distance a molecule can travel before it stops
correct_answer_text: the average distance travelled by a molecule between two successive collisions
solution: Between two collisions a molecule travels a straight segment called a free path. These segments have different lengths, and their average value is the mean free path, usually written as lambda. For air at room temperature and atmospheric pressure it is of the order of 10^-7 m, far smaller than the size of any container.
formula_principle: Mean free path is the mean of the free paths travelled between successive collisions
common_misconception: Students confuse the mean free path with the mean speed because both describe the travel of a molecule.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Variation of mean free path with number of molecules per unit volume
stem: The mean free path of the molecules of a gas varies with the number of molecules per unit volume n as
option_b: inversely proportional to the square of n
solution: The more molecules there are in a given volume, the sooner a moving molecule meets one. In the standard expression lambda = 1 / (sqrt(2) pi d^2 n), the number density appears in the denominator to the first power, so the mean free path is inversely proportional to n.
formula_principle: lambda = 1 / (sqrt(2) pi d^2 n)
common_misconception: Learners assume more molecules means more room to travel.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Effect of doubling the molecular diameter
stem: Two gases have the same number density but the molecular diameter of the second is twice that of the first. The mean free path in the second gas compared with the first is
solution: The collision cross section is proportional to the square of the molecular diameter, and it appears in the denominator of lambda = 1 / (sqrt(2) pi d^2 n). Doubling d multiplies d^2 by 4, so the mean free path falls to one fourth of its earlier value.
formula_principle: lambda proportional to 1 / d^2 at constant number density
common_misconception: Students use the first power of the diameter rather than its square.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Effect of doubling pressure at constant temperature
stem: The pressure of a gas is doubled while the temperature is held constant. The mean free path of its molecules becomes
option_c: one fourth of its initial value
option_d: unchanged, because the temperature has not changed
solution: At constant temperature the number density is proportional to the pressure, so doubling P doubles n. Since lambda varies inversely as n, the mean free path falls to half. The same follows directly from lambda = k T / (sqrt(2) pi d^2 P) with T fixed.
formula_principle: lambda = k T / (sqrt(2) pi d^2 P)
common_misconception: Learners think pressure has no effect because the molecules are moving at the same speed.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Effect of doubling temperature at constant pressure
stem: The absolute temperature of a gas is doubled while its pressure is held constant. The mean free path of its molecules becomes
solution: At constant pressure a rise in temperature expands the gas and lowers the number density in proportion to 1/T. Since lambda varies inversely as n, it varies directly as T. Doubling the absolute temperature therefore doubles the mean free path.
formula_principle: lambda = k T / (sqrt(2) pi d^2 P), so lambda proportional to T at constant P
common_misconception: Students apply the square root of temperature because they are thinking of the root mean square speed.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Combined change of n and d
concept_tested: Effect of changing both number density and molecular diameter
stem: The number density of a gas is reduced to one fourth of its initial value and, in a different sample, the effective molecular diameter is also halved. Taken together, these two changes make the mean free path
solution: Reducing n to one fourth multiplies lambda by 4. Halving d divides d^2 by 4 and therefore multiplies lambda by another 4. The combined factor is 4 x 4 = 16.
formula_principle: lambda proportional to 1 / (d^2 n)
common_misconception: Learners forget to square the diameter factor when combining two changes.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Mean free path in terms of density
concept_tested: Expressing lambda using mass density instead of number density
stem: If m is the mass of a molecule, d its diameter and rho the mass density of the gas, the mean free path is
solution: The number of molecules per unit volume is the mass density divided by the mass of one molecule, that is n = rho / m. Substituting this in lambda = 1 / (sqrt(2) pi d^2 n) gives lambda = m / (sqrt(2) pi d^2 rho). A denser gas or a heavier packing of molecules therefore shortens the free path.
formula_principle: lambda = 1 / (sqrt(2) pi d^2 n) with n = rho / m
common_misconception: Students substitute the density directly in place of the number density without dividing by the molecular mass.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Combined change of T and P
concept_tested: Effect on lambda when temperature and pressure both change
stem: The absolute temperature of a gas is doubled and at the same time its pressure is made four times the initial value. The mean free path of its molecules becomes
solution: The mean free path is proportional to T and inversely proportional to P. The combined factor is (T_new / T_old) x (P_old / P_new) = 2 x (1/4) = 1/2. Hence the mean free path falls to half its initial value.
formula_principle: lambda = k T / (sqrt(2) pi d^2 P), so lambda proportional to T / P
common_misconception: Learners treat both changes as increasing the mean free path and multiply the factors together.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Coefficients of absorption, reflection and transmission
concept_tested: Relation among a, r and t for any body
stem: For a body on which thermal radiation is incident, the coefficient of absorption a, the coefficient of reflection r and the coefficient of transmission t satisfy
solution: The radiant energy falling on a body is either absorbed, reflected or transmitted. Dividing the energy conservation statement Q_a + Q_r + Q_t = Q by the incident energy Q gives a + r + t = 1, where each coefficient is a pure number between 0 and 1.
formula_principle: Conservation of energy: absorbed plus reflected plus transmitted equals incident
common_misconception: Students forget that the three coefficients are fractions of the same incident energy and must add to unity.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Values of a, r and t for a perfectly black body
stem: For a perfectly black body, the coefficients of absorption, reflection and transmission are respectively
solution: A perfectly black body absorbs the whole of the radiant energy incident on it at every wavelength, so a = 1. Since a + r + t = 1, both r and t must be zero. Such a body is also the best possible emitter at any given temperature.
formula_principle: Perfectly black body: a = 1, hence r = 0 and t = 0
common_misconception: Learners think a black body must also be black in appearance rather than defined by complete absorption.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Definition and SI unit of emissive power
stem: The emissive power of a body at a given temperature is the quantity of radiant energy emitted per unit time per unit area, and its SI unit is
solution: Emissive power is defined as energy divided by area and by time. Joule per second is watt, so the unit is watt per square metre, written W m^-2. The Stefan constant carries the extra factor K^-4 because it multiplies the fourth power of temperature.
formula_principle: Emissive power = energy emitted per unit area per unit time
common_misconception: Students omit the time factor and quote joule per square metre.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Meaning and value of emissivity
stem: The coefficient of emission of a body is defined as the ratio of its emissive power to that of a perfectly black body at the same temperature. For a perfectly black body its value is
option_a: 0, and it is a dimensionless quantity
option_b: 1, and it has the unit W m^-2
option_c: 5.67 x 10^-8, and it has the unit W m^-2 K^-4
option_d: 1, and it is a dimensionless quantity
correct_answer_text: 1, and it is a dimensionless quantity
solution: The coefficient of emission, or emissivity, compares a body with the best possible emitter at the same temperature. Being a ratio of two quantities with the same unit, it is dimensionless. A perfectly black body is the reference, so its coefficient of emission is exactly 1, and every real body has a value less than 1.
formula_principle: e = E_body / E_black body at the same temperature, so 0 is less than or equal to e which is at most 1
common_misconception: Learners give the emissivity a unit because emissive power has one.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Using a plus r plus t equals 1
concept_tested: Finding the transmission coefficient from the other two
stem: A body absorbs 30 per cent and reflects 50 per cent of the radiant energy incident on it. The coefficient of transmission of the body is
solution: Here a = 0.3 and r = 0.5, so t = 1 minus (0.3 + 0.5) = 1 minus 0.8 = 0.2. Twenty per cent of the incident energy passes through the body.
formula_principle: a + r + t = 1
common_misconception: Students report the sum of the two given coefficients rather than the leftover fraction.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Statement of Kirchhoff's law
stem: Kirchhoff's law of thermal radiation states that at a given temperature and for a given wavelength,
option_a: the emissive power of a body is inversely proportional to its coefficient of absorption
option_b: the product of the emissive power and the coefficient of absorption is the same for all bodies
option_c: the ratio of the emissive power of a body to its coefficient of absorption is the same for all bodies and equals the emissive power of a perfectly black body
option_d: the emissive power of every body is the same irrespective of its coefficient of absorption
correct_answer_text: the ratio of the emissive power of a body to its coefficient of absorption is the same for all bodies and equals the emissive power of a perfectly black body
solution: Kirchhoff's law follows from the requirement of thermal equilibrium inside an enclosure. A body that absorbs strongly at a wavelength must also emit strongly at that wavelength, otherwise it would heat up or cool down relative to its surroundings. In symbols E / a is a universal function of temperature and wavelength, equal to the emissive power of a perfectly black body, so emissivity and absorptivity are numerically equal.
formula_principle: E / a = E_black body at the same temperature and wavelength, so good absorbers are good emitters
common_misconception: Learners state the law as an inverse relation, believing shiny bodies emit better than dark ones.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Distinguishing substances by their transmission of heat radiation
stem: A substance that does not transmit heat radiation through it is called athermanous. On this basis,
option_a: rock salt is athermanous while water vapour is diathermanous
option_b: water vapour and ordinary glass are athermanous while rock salt is diathermanous
option_c: all transparent substances are necessarily diathermanous
option_d: a substance can be athermanous only if its coefficient of reflection is one
correct_answer_text: water vapour and ordinary glass are athermanous while rock salt is diathermanous
solution: Athermanous substances stop infrared radiation, and glass and water vapour are standard examples, which is why a glasshouse warms up and why the atmosphere traps outgoing heat radiation. Rock salt transmits infrared radiation freely and is therefore diathermanous, which is why it is used for prisms and windows in infrared work. Transparency to visible light is a separate property.
formula_principle: Athermanous means t = 0 for heat radiation; diathermanous means the radiation is transmitted
common_misconception: Students assume that anything clear to the eye must also let heat radiation through.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Design feature of Ferry's black body
stem: In Ferry's black body, a hollow double walled sphere is blackened on the inside and has a small aperture, with a conical projection placed opposite the aperture. The purpose of the conical projection is
option_a: to increase the temperature of the inner wall of the sphere
option_b: to prevent radiation entering the aperture from being reflected straight back out
option_c: to allow the radiation to be transmitted through the wall of the sphere
option_d: to focus the emitted radiation into a parallel beam
correct_answer_text: to prevent radiation entering the aperture from being reflected straight back out
solution: Radiation entering the small aperture strikes the blackened inner surface and is largely absorbed, the small remainder being reflected repeatedly until practically nothing is left. If the wall directly opposite the aperture were smooth, a single reflection could send radiation straight back out. The conical projection points at the aperture so that any radiation striking it is reflected sideways onto the walls, ensuring near total absorption.
formula_principle: A cavity with a small aperture behaves as a perfectly black body
common_misconception: Learners think the cone has a thermal role rather than a geometrical one.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Coefficients for a perfectly transparent body
stem: For a body that transmits the whole of the radiant energy incident on it,
option_a: the coefficient of absorption is 1 and the other two are zero
option_b: the coefficient of reflection is 1 and the other two are zero
option_c: the coefficient of transmission is 1 and the coefficients of absorption and reflection are both zero
option_d: all three coefficients equal one third
correct_answer_text: the coefficient of transmission is 1 and the coefficients of absorption and reflection are both zero
solution: Complete transmission means the whole of the incident energy passes through, so t = 1. Because the three coefficients must add to one, both the absorption and the reflection coefficients are zero. Such an ideal body is described as perfectly transparent or perfectly diathermanous.
formula_principle: a + r + t = 1 with t = 1 forces a = 0 and r = 0
common_misconception: Students set the absorption coefficient to one whenever an extreme case is described.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Emissive power of a real body
concept_tested: Relating emissive power of a body to that of a black body
stem: At a certain temperature a perfectly black body has emissive power E_b. A body whose coefficient of emission is 0.4 at the same temperature has emissive power
solution: The coefficient of emission is by definition the ratio E / E_b, so E = e E_b = 0.4 E_b. No body can emit more than a perfectly black body at the same temperature, which rules out any answer greater than E_b.
formula_principle: E = e x E_b, where e is the coefficient of emission
common_misconception: Learners divide by the emissivity and obtain a body that outshines a black body.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Combining the coefficients with Kirchhoff's law
concept_tested: Finding reflection coefficient and emissivity of an opaque body
stem: An opaque body absorbs 60 per cent of the radiation incident on it. Its coefficient of reflection and its coefficient of emission are respectively
solution: Opaque means t = 0, so a + r = 1 and r = 1 minus 0.6 = 0.4. By Kirchhoff's law the coefficient of emission of a body equals its coefficient of absorption at the same temperature, so e = 0.6. The body reflects two fifths of what falls on it and radiates three fifths of what a black body would radiate.
formula_principle: a + r + t = 1 with t = 0 for an opaque body; Kirchhoff's law gives e = a
common_misconception: Students equate emissivity with reflectivity rather than with absorptivity.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Explanation of dark absorption lines in the solar spectrum
stem: The dark Fraunhofer lines seen in the solar spectrum are explained by Kirchhoff's law because
option_a: the cooler gases in the sun's outer layers absorb exactly those wavelengths that they would themselves emit strongly
option_b: the cooler outer gases reflect those wavelengths back into the sun
option_c: those wavelengths are never produced in the interior of the sun
option_d: the earth's atmosphere transmits only certain wavelengths and blocks the rest
correct_answer_text: the cooler gases in the sun's outer layers absorb exactly those wavelengths that they would themselves emit strongly
solution: The dense hot interior of the sun emits a continuous spectrum. The cooler vapours in the outer layers are strong emitters at the characteristic wavelengths of their elements, and by Kirchhoff's law they must be equally strong absorbers at those same wavelengths. They therefore remove energy from the continuous spectrum at exactly those positions. Being cooler, they re emit less than they absorb along the line of sight, so those wavelengths appear as dark lines.
formula_principle: Kirchhoff's law: a good emitter at a wavelength is an equally good absorber at that wavelength
common_misconception: Learners explain the dark lines as wavelengths that were never emitted in the first place.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Deducing emissivity, absorptivity and reflectivity together
stem: At a given temperature a body radiates 200 W m^-2 while a perfectly black body at the same temperature radiates 800 W m^-2. If the body is opaque, its coefficient of emission and its coefficient of reflection are respectively
solution: The coefficient of emission is e = 200 / 800 = 0.25. By Kirchhoff's law the coefficient of absorption is also 0.25. For an opaque body the transmission coefficient is zero, so the coefficient of reflection is 1 minus 0.25 = 0.75.
formula_principle: e = E / E_b, Kirchhoff's law gives a = e, and a + r = 1 for an opaque body
common_misconception: Students invert the ratio of the two emissive powers and obtain an emissivity greater than one.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Why a poor emitter is also a poor absorber
stem: A polished silver ball and a soot coated ball of the same size are placed inside a large evacuated enclosure kept at a constant temperature and are left until each reaches a steady state. In that steady state,
option_a: each ball emits exactly as much energy per second as it absorbs, the soot coated ball doing both at a much greater rate
option_b: the soot coated ball becomes hotter than the silver ball because it absorbs more
option_c: the silver ball becomes hotter because it emits very little
option_d: the silver ball absorbs more than it emits and keeps gaining energy indefinitely
correct_answer_text: each ball emits exactly as much energy per second as it absorbs, the soot coated ball doing both at a much greater rate
solution: In a steady state neither ball changes temperature, so for each of them the energy emitted per second must equal the energy absorbed per second. Both therefore settle at the temperature of the enclosure. The soot coated ball has a high absorption coefficient, so it absorbs a large amount, and Kirchhoff's law requires its coefficient of emission to be equally large, so it also radiates a large amount. The silver ball absorbs and emits little. The balance is maintained in both cases, which is precisely the argument that establishes Kirchhoff's law.
formula_principle: Kirchhoff's law follows from the requirement of thermal equilibrium inside an isothermal enclosure
common_misconception: Learners conclude that a dark body must run hotter than a shiny one in the same enclosure.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Statement of the fourth power law
stem: According to the Stefan Boltzmann law, the energy radiated per unit time per unit area by a perfectly black body at absolute temperature T is proportional to
solution: Stefan's law states that the emissive power of a perfectly black body is E = sigma T^4, where sigma = 5.67 x 10^-8 W m^-2 K^-4 is the Stefan constant and T is the absolute temperature. For a body of coefficient of emission e the law reads E = e sigma T^4.
formula_principle: E = sigma T^4 for a perfectly black body
common_misconception: Students recall a linear dependence because Newton's law of cooling is linear in the temperature difference.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Relation between lambda_max and temperature
stem: According to Wien's displacement law, the wavelength at which a black body radiates most strongly and its absolute temperature are related so that
option_a: the wavelength increases as the temperature increases, their ratio being a constant
option_b: the wavelength is independent of the temperature
option_c: the wavelength decreases as the temperature increases, their product being a constant
option_d: the wavelength is proportional to the fourth power of the temperature
correct_answer_text: the wavelength decreases as the temperature increases, their product being a constant
solution: Wien's law states lambda_max T = b, a constant. The peak of the emission curve therefore shifts towards shorter wavelengths as the temperature rises, which is why a heated body glows first dull red, then orange and finally bluish white.
formula_principle: lambda_max x T = b, with b = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K
common_misconception: Learners think a hotter body must emit longer wavelengths because it emits more energy.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Effect of doubling the absolute temperature
stem: The absolute temperature of a black body is doubled. The energy radiated by it per unit time per unit area becomes
solution: Since E = sigma T^4, doubling T multiplies the emissive power by 2^4 = 16.
formula_principle: E proportional to T^4
common_misconception: Students apply a cube or a square instead of the fourth power.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Emissive power of a black body at a stated temperature
stem: The energy radiated per second per square metre by a perfectly black body at 1000 K, taking sigma = 5.67 x 10^-8 W m^-2 K^-4, is
formula_principle: E = sigma T^4
common_misconception: Learners mishandle the powers of ten when raising the temperature to the fourth power.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Finding temperature from the peak wavelength
stem: The radiation from a black body is most intense at a wavelength of 2.9 x 10^-6 m. Taking the Wien constant as 2.9 x 10^-3 m K, the temperature of the body is
formula_principle: T = b / lambda_max
common_misconception: Students multiply the two quantities instead of dividing the Wien constant by the wavelength.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Finding lambda_max for a given temperature
stem: A black body is at a temperature of 5000 K. Taking the Wien constant as 2.9 x 10^-3 m K, the wavelength at which it radiates maximum energy is
solution: lambda_max = 2.9 x 10^-3 / 5000 = 5.8 x 10^-7 m, that is 580 nm, which lies in the visible part of the spectrum near the yellow green region.
formula_principle: lambda_max = b / T
common_misconception: Learners drop powers of ten when dividing by a four figure temperature.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Expression for net loss of energy by a body in surroundings
stem: A black body at absolute temperature T is placed in surroundings at absolute temperature T0, where T is greater than T0. The net energy lost by the body per unit time per unit area is
solution: The body radiates sigma T^4 per unit area per unit time and simultaneously absorbs sigma T0^4 from its surroundings. The net loss is the difference, sigma (T^4 - T0^4). This vanishes when T equals T0, which is the condition of thermal equilibrium, and it is not the same as raising the temperature difference to the fourth power.
formula_principle: Net rate of loss per unit area = sigma (T^4 - T0^4)
common_misconception: Students write the fourth power of the difference instead of the difference of the fourth powers.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Statement and range of validity
stem: Newton's law of cooling states that the rate of loss of heat by a body is proportional to the excess of its temperature over that of the surroundings. This law is
option_a: valid for any temperature difference however large
option_b: valid only when the excess of temperature over the surroundings is small
option_c: valid only when the body is a perfectly black body
option_d: valid only when the surroundings are at absolute zero
correct_answer_text: valid only when the excess of temperature over the surroundings is small
solution: Newton's law of cooling is an approximation of Stefan's law. If T = T0 + dT with dT small compared with T0, then T^4 - T0^4 is nearly 4 T0^3 dT, which is proportional to the excess temperature. The approximation therefore holds only while the excess is small, and it also requires that the surroundings stay at a steady temperature and that the loss is not dominated by forced convection.
formula_principle: For small excess temperature, sigma (T^4 - T0^4) reduces to a term proportional to (T - T0)
common_misconception: Learners treat Newton's law of cooling as exact for all temperature differences.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Shift of the emission peak with rising temperature
stem: As a metal block is heated to higher and higher temperatures, the colour of the light it emits changes from dull red to bluish white. This happens because
option_a: the wavelength of maximum emission increases as the temperature rises
option_b: the total energy radiated increases as the fourth power of the temperature
option_c: the wavelength of maximum emission decreases as the temperature rises
option_d: the emissivity of the metal increases with temperature
correct_answer_text: the wavelength of maximum emission decreases as the temperature rises
solution: By Wien's displacement law the peak of the emission curve lies at lambda_max = b / T. At a modest temperature the peak is in the infrared and only the long wavelength red tail is visible, so the block looks dull red. As T rises the peak moves to shorter wavelengths and the emission spreads across the whole visible range, so the block appears orange, then yellow and finally bluish white.
formula_principle: lambda_max = b / T, so the peak shifts to shorter wavelength as T rises
common_misconception: Students explain the change of colour by the increase in total energy rather than by the shift of the peak.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Two stage cooling problem
stem: A body cools from 60 degree celsius to 50 degree celsius in 5 minutes in surroundings at 20 degree celsius. Assuming Newton's law of cooling, the time it takes to cool from 50 degree celsius to 40 degree celsius is
solution: In the first stage the mean temperature is (60 + 50) / 2 = 55, so the excess over the surroundings is 35. The rate is 10 / 5 = 2 degree per minute, giving 2 = 35 k, so k = 2/35. In the second stage the mean temperature is (50 + 40) / 2 = 45 and the excess is 25. The rate is 25 k = 25 x 2 / 35 = 10/7 degree per minute, so the time for a 10 degree fall is 10 divided by 10/7 = 7 minutes.
formula_principle: Rate of cooling = k x (mean temperature of the body minus temperature of surroundings)
common_misconception: Learners use the instantaneous temperatures instead of the mean temperature of each stage, or assume equal drops take equal times.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Computing net loss using the difference of fourth powers
stem: A black body at 400 K is kept in surroundings at 200 K. Taking sigma = 5.67 x 10^-8 W m^-2 K^-4, the net energy radiated by it per second per square metre is
formula_principle: Net rate per unit area = sigma (T^4 - T0^4)
common_misconception: Students raise the temperature difference to the fourth power instead of taking the difference of the fourth powers.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Simultaneous change of emissive power and peak wavelength
stem: The temperature of a black body is raised from 300 K to 600 K. Its emissive power and the wavelength of maximum emission respectively become
option_a: 16 times the earlier value and twice the earlier value
option_b: 4 times the earlier value and half the earlier value
option_c: 16 times the earlier value and half the earlier value
option_d: 2 times the earlier value and half the earlier value
correct_answer_text: 16 times the earlier value and half the earlier value
solution: The temperature ratio is 600 / 300 = 2. Stefan's law gives an emissive power ratio of 2^4 = 16. Wien's law gives lambda_max = b / T, so doubling the temperature halves the wavelength of maximum emission.
formula_principle: E proportional to T^4 and lambda_max proportional to 1 / T
common_misconception: Learners apply the same factor to both quantities, forgetting that one grows as the fourth power while the other falls as the reciprocal.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Deducing temperature ratio from peak wavelengths and then the power ratio
stem: Two stars behave as black bodies. The radiation from the first is most intense at 6.0 x 10^-7 m and that from the second at 3.0 x 10^-7 m. The ratio of the energy radiated per unit area per unit time by the first star to that by the second is
solution: Since lambda_max is inversely proportional to temperature, halving the peak wavelength doubles the temperature, so T1 : T2 = 1 : 2. Stefan's law then gives E1 : E2 = 1^4 : 2^4 = 1 : 16. The star with the shorter peak wavelength is hotter and radiates sixteen times as strongly per unit area.
formula_principle: lambda_max T = b gives T proportional to 1 / lambda_max; then E proportional to T^4
common_misconception: Students report the temperature ratio as the answer without applying the fourth power law.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Total power radiated when radius and temperature both change
stem: A solid sphere behaves as a black body. Its radius is doubled while its absolute temperature is reduced to half. The total power radiated by the sphere becomes
option_b: one sixteenth of the initial value
option_d: one fourth of the initial value
correct_answer_text: one fourth of the initial value
solution: Doubling the radius makes the surface area 2^2 = 4 times larger. Halving the absolute temperature multiplies T^4 by (1/2)^4 = 1/16. The net factor is 4 x 1/16 = 1/4, so the total power falls to one quarter of its initial value.
formula_principle: Total power P = sigma A T^4 with A = 4 pi r^2, so P proportional to r^2 T^4
common_misconception: Learners think a bigger but cooler sphere must radiate the same as before.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Stefan's law for a real body
concept_tested: Total power from emissivity, area and temperature
stem: A body of surface area 0.1 m^2 and coefficient of emission 0.5 is maintained at 1000 K. Taking sigma = 5.67 x 10^-8 W m^-2 K^-4 and neglecting the absorption from the surroundings, the power radiated by it is
formula_principle: P = e sigma A T^4
common_misconception: Students forget that the coefficient of emission multiplies the whole expression exactly once.

chapter_name: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
concept_tested: Showing that the fourth power law reduces to a linear law
stem: A body at absolute temperature T is placed in surroundings at absolute temperature T0, with the excess T minus T0 very small compared with T0. Under this condition the net rate of loss of energy per unit area, sigma (T^4 - T0^4), reduces to a form proportional to
option_a: (T - T0), the constant of proportionality involving sigma T0
option_b: (T - T0)^4, the constant of proportionality being sigma
option_c: (T^2 - T0^2), the constant of proportionality involving 2 sigma T0
option_d: (T - T0), the constant of proportionality involving 4 sigma T0^3
correct_answer_text: (T - T0), the constant of proportionality involving 4 sigma T0^3
solution: Write T = T0 + dT. Then T^4 - T0^4 = (T^2 - T0^2)(T^2 + T0^2) = (T - T0)(T + T0)(T^2 + T0^2). For a small excess, T is nearly T0, so (T + T0) is nearly 2 T0 and (T^2 + T0^2) is nearly 2 T0^2. The product becomes (T - T0) x 2 T0 x 2 T0^2 = 4 T0^3 (T - T0). Hence the net rate of loss is nearly 4 sigma T0^3 (T - T0), which is directly proportional to the excess of temperature. This is exactly Newton's law of cooling, and it shows why that law holds only for a small excess temperature.
formula_principle: sigma (T^4 - T0^4) is approximately 4 sigma T0^3 (T - T0) when T - T0 is small
common_misconception: Learners try to obtain the linear law by simply replacing the difference of fourth powers with the fourth power of the difference.

concept_tested: Zeroth law of thermodynamics
stem: Which statement is the zeroth law of thermodynamics?
option_a: If two systems are each separately in thermal equilibrium with a third system, then they are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
option_b: If two systems are each separately in thermal equilibrium with a third system, heat flows from the hotter of the two to the colder one.
option_c: The heat supplied to a system equals the rise in its internal energy plus the work done by the system.
option_d: Heat cannot flow on its own from a colder body to a hotter body.
correct_answer_text: If two systems are each separately in thermal equilibrium with a third system, then they are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
solution: The zeroth law states that if system X is in thermal equilibrium with system Z, and system Y is also in thermal equilibrium with Z, then X and Y are in thermal equilibrium with each other. This transitivity is what allows a single number, the temperature, to be attached to every system.
formula_principle: Zeroth law: thermal equilibrium is a transitive relation, which allows temperature to be defined.
common_misconception: Students confuse the zeroth law with the first or the second law because all three are stated in similar language.

concept_tested: Equality of temperature at equilibrium
stem: Two bodies in thermal contact are found to be in thermal equilibrium. Which quantity is necessarily the same for the two bodies?
option_c: The total heat stored in them
solution: Thermal equilibrium is signalled by the absence of any net heat exchange between the bodies. The single property whose equality guarantees this is temperature, so the temperatures of the two bodies must be equal.
formula_principle: Thermal equilibrium between two bodies means their temperatures are equal and there is no net heat exchange.
common_misconception: Students think that equal internal energy or equal heat content, rather than equal temperature, is the condition for equilibrium.

concept_tested: Temperature difference drives heat flow
stem: Bodies X and Y are placed in thermal contact and heat is observed to flow from X to Y. This observation shows that
option_a: the internal energy of X is greater than the internal energy of Y
option_b: the temperature of X is higher than the temperature of Y
option_c: the mass of X is greater than the mass of Y
option_d: the specific heat capacity of X is greater than that of Y
correct_answer_text: the temperature of X is higher than the temperature of Y
solution: Spontaneous heat flow is governed only by the temperature difference. Since heat flows from X to Y, X must be at the higher temperature. Nothing can be concluded about masses or internal energies from this single observation.
formula_principle: Heat flows spontaneously from the body at higher temperature to the body at lower temperature.
common_misconception: Students believe that the body containing more heat energy always loses heat to the other body.

concept_tested: Zeroth law defines temperature
stem: The zeroth law of thermodynamics makes it logically possible to define
option_a: internal energy, as a function of the state of a system alone
option_b: temperature, as a property whose equality decides thermal equilibrium
option_c: heat, as the energy transferred because of a temperature difference
option_d: efficiency, as the fraction of absorbed heat converted into work
correct_answer_text: temperature, as a property whose equality decides thermal equilibrium
solution: Because thermal equilibrium is transitive, all systems in equilibrium with one another can be given one common label. That label is temperature. Hence the zeroth law is the basis of the very concept of temperature.
formula_principle: Transitivity of thermal equilibrium allows a unique label, the temperature, to be assigned to every system.
common_misconception: Students treat the zeroth law as a trivial statement and do not connect it with the definition of temperature.

concept_tested: Thermometry rests on the zeroth law
stem: A clinical thermometer is kept in contact with a patient and read only after the mercury column stops moving. The reading is taken as the temperature of the patient. This procedure is justified by
solution: Waiting until the column stops means the thermometer has reached thermal equilibrium with the patient. By the zeroth law, since the thermometer is also in equilibrium with its own calibrated scale, the scale reading equals the patient temperature.
formula_principle: A thermometer in equilibrium with a body shares its temperature; equilibrium with the scale then gives the reading.
common_misconception: Students memorise the zeroth law but do not recognise it as the working principle of every thermometer.

concept_tested: Equal temperature means no net heat exchange
stem: A sample of 1 kg of water at 50 degree celsius is brought into contact with a sample of 100 g of water at 50 degree celsius. Which statement describes what happens?
option_a: Heat flows from the 1 kg sample to the 100 g sample, because it holds more heat energy.
option_b: There is no net exchange of heat, because both samples are at the same temperature.
option_c: Heat flows from the 100 g sample to the 1 kg sample until the energy per unit mass becomes equal.
option_d: Heat flows from the 1 kg sample until the two samples hold equal internal energies.
correct_answer_text: There is no net exchange of heat, because both samples are at the same temperature.
solution: Both samples are at 50 degree celsius, so the temperature difference driving heat flow is zero. Even though the 1 kg sample contains ten times the internal energy of the 100 g sample, there is no net transfer of energy between them.
formula_principle: No net heat flows between systems at the same temperature, whatever their sizes.
common_misconception: Students assume the body with more stored energy must give energy to the one with less.

concept_tested: Temperature, not stored energy, drives heat flow
stem: Block X of mass 2 kg and block Y of mass 1 kg are made of the same metal. X is at 300 K and Y is at 320 K. They are brought into thermal contact and isolated from the surroundings. Which statement is correct?
option_a: Heat flows from X to Y, because X holds the larger internal energy.
option_b: No heat flows, because the products of mass and temperature are nearly equal for the two blocks.
option_c: Heat flows from Y to X, even though X may hold the larger internal energy.
option_d: Heat flows from Y to X until the two blocks hold equal internal energies.
correct_answer_text: Heat flows from Y to X, even though X may hold the larger internal energy.
solution: Y is at the higher temperature of 320 K, so heat flows from Y to X. For the same metal, internal energy is proportional to mass times temperature, so X with 2 kg at 300 K holds more energy than Y with 1 kg at 320 K, yet it still receives heat. Flow stops when both reach a common temperature between 300 K and 320 K.
formula_principle: Heat flows from higher to lower temperature; equilibrium is equality of temperature, not of internal energy.
common_misconception: Students expect heat to flow out of the body with the greater total thermal energy.

concept_tested: Nature of the separating wall
stem: Two gas samples occupy two chambers separated by a fixed wall that lets the samples settle to a common temperature but does not let any gas cross. Such a wall is described as
solution: Since the two samples reach a common temperature, energy must be able to cross the wall, so the wall is diathermic. Since no matter crosses and the chambers keep fixed volumes, the wall is also rigid and non porous.
formula_principle: A diathermic wall permits heat exchange; an adiabatic wall prevents it. A rigid wall permits no volume change.
common_misconception: Students mix up adiabatic and diathermic, treating any solid partition as an insulator.

concept_tested: Applying the zeroth law to three systems
stem: System X is found to be in thermal equilibrium with system Z, and system Y is separately found to be in thermal equilibrium with the same system Z. Without bringing X and Y into contact, it can be stated that
option_a: X and Y are at the same temperature and no heat would flow if they were joined
option_b: X and Y are at the same temperature only if they are made of the same material
option_c: heat would flow from X to Y if they were joined, since X reached equilibrium with Z first
option_d: X and Y hold equal internal energies and therefore cannot exchange energy
correct_answer_text: X and Y are at the same temperature and no heat would flow if they were joined
solution: By the zeroth law, thermal equilibrium is transitive. X in equilibrium with Z and Y in equilibrium with Z together force X and Y to be in equilibrium, that is, to be at the same temperature, so joining them would produce no net heat flow.
formula_principle: Zeroth law: equilibrium with a common third system implies equilibrium with each other.
common_misconception: Students think a direct contact test is necessary before any conclusion can be drawn about X and Y.

concept_tested: Equilibrium does not require equal internal energy
stem: Two moles of a monatomic ideal gas labelled X and one mole of a diatomic ideal gas labelled Y occupy two chambers separated by a rigid diathermic wall. Both samples are at 300 K. Take R = 8.3 J mol^-1 K^-1. Which statement is correct?
option_a: Heat flows from X to Y, because the internal energy of X is larger than that of Y.
option_b: Heat flows from Y to X, because each molecule of Y carries more energy than each molecule of X.
option_c: There is no net heat flow, because the two samples hold equal internal energies at 300 K.
option_d: There is no net heat flow, although the internal energy of X, about 7470 J, exceeds that of Y, about 6225 J.
correct_answer_text: There is no net heat flow, although the internal energy of X, about 7470 J, exceeds that of Y, about 6225 J.
solution: For X, U = (3/2) x 2 x 8.3 x 300 = 7470 J. For Y, U = (5/2) x 1 x 8.3 x 300 = 6225 J. The internal energies differ, yet both samples sit at 300 K, so the temperature difference is zero and no net heat crosses the diathermic wall.
formula_principle: U = (f/2) n R T with f = 3 for a monatomic gas and f = 5 for a diatomic gas; equilibrium needs equal T only.
common_misconception: Students assume that two systems in contact must exchange energy until their internal energies match.

subtopic: Internal energy as a state function
concept_tested: State function property of internal energy
stem: The internal energy of a thermodynamic system is called a state function because
option_a: it always keeps the same value while the system passes through any process
option_b: its value is fixed by the present state of the system and not by the way that state was reached
option_c: it can be measured directly with a thermometer for any system
option_d: it is always equal to the heat supplied to the system in every process
correct_answer_text: its value is fixed by the present state of the system and not by the way that state was reached
solution: For a system taken from one state to another by different routes, the change in internal energy is the same for every route. That is precisely what is meant by calling internal energy a state function.
formula_principle: A state function has a value determined by the thermodynamic state alone, so its change is path independent.
common_misconception: Students read state function as constant and think internal energy never changes.

concept_tested: Definition of heat
stem: In thermodynamics, heat is best described as
option_a: the total energy stored in the random motion of the molecules of a system
option_b: the energy a system possesses because of its pressure and volume
option_c: the energy that must be supplied to raise the temperature of unit mass by one kelvin
option_d: energy in transit between a system and its surroundings because of a temperature difference
correct_answer_text: energy in transit between a system and its surroundings because of a temperature difference
solution: Heat exists only while it is crossing a boundary. Once it has entered the system it becomes part of the internal energy, so a body cannot be said to contain a certain amount of heat.
formula_principle: Heat is energy transferred across a boundary owing to a temperature difference; a body holds internal energy, not heat.
common_misconception: Students say a hot body contains more heat instead of more internal energy.

concept_tested: Work done by an expanding gas
stem: In the convention used with the first law of thermodynamics, the work associated with a gas that expands against an external pressure is
option_a: negative, because the gas loses energy while it expands
option_b: zero, because the pressure of the gas does not change during the expansion
option_c: positive, because the gas does work on the surroundings
option_d: positive only if heat is supplied to the gas at the same time
correct_answer_text: positive, because the gas does work on the surroundings
solution: Work done by a gas is the integral of P dV. When the volume increases, dV is positive, so dW is positive and the work is counted as done by the gas on the surroundings.
formula_principle: dW is taken positive when the system does work on the surroundings, that is when the volume increases.
common_misconception: Students carry over the chemistry convention in which work done by the system is written with a negative sign.

concept_tested: dW = P dV
stem: A gas at pressure P expands slowly by a small volume dV. The small amount of work done by the gas is
solution: If the piston of area A moves out through a small distance dx, the gas exerts force P A on it, so the work is P A dx. Since A dx is the small volume change dV, the work done is P dV.
formula_principle: For a quasi static change, dW = P dV, where P is the pressure of the gas.
common_misconception: Students write V dP by mistakenly differentiating the wrong factor of the product P V.

subtopic: Internal energy of an ideal gas
concept_tested: Internal energy depends only on temperature
stem: For a fixed mass of an ideal gas, the internal energy depends on
solution: There is no intermolecular potential energy in an ideal gas, so the whole internal energy is molecular kinetic energy, which is fixed by temperature. Hence U depends only on T for a given amount of gas.
formula_principle: For an ideal gas U = (f/2) n R T, so U is a function of temperature only.
common_misconception: Students think that compressing a gas must raise its internal energy even when the temperature is held fixed.

concept_tested: Signs of dQ and dW
stem: A gas is compressed while at the same time it gives out heat to its surroundings. In the convention used with dQ = dU + dW, the signs are
solution: Heat leaving the system makes dQ negative. Compression means dV is negative, so dW, which equals P dV, is also negative. Then dU = dQ minus dW can still be positive if the magnitude of the work done on the gas exceeds the heat lost.
formula_principle: dQ is positive when heat is absorbed by the system; dW is positive when the system expands.
common_misconception: Students apply the sign of work from the point of view of the surroundings instead of the system.

concept_tested: Numerical use of W = P dV
stem: A gas kept at a constant pressure of 1.5 x 10^5 Pa expands from a volume of 0.02 m^3 to a volume of 0.05 m^3. The work done by the gas is
solution: The change in volume is 0.05 minus 0.02, that is 0.03 m^3. Then W = 1.5 x 10^5 x 0.03 = 4.5 x 10^3 J, so the gas does 4500 J of work.
formula_principle: For an isobaric change, W = P (V2 minus V1).
common_misconception: Students substitute a single volume rather than the change in volume into W = P dV.

subtopic: Internal energy of a monatomic gas
concept_tested: U = (3/2) n R T for a monatomic gas
stem: Two moles of a monatomic ideal gas are heated from 300 K to 400 K. Taking R = 8.3 J mol^-1 K^-1, the increase in the internal energy of the gas is
solution: Here n = 2 and dT = 100 K, so dU = (3/2) x 2 x 8.3 x 100 = 3 x 830 = 2490 J. The result is the same whatever process is used, since internal energy depends only on temperature.
formula_principle: dU = (3/2) n R dT for a monatomic ideal gas.
common_misconception: Students use the wrong number of degrees of freedom or forget the number of moles.

concept_tested: Work in expansion into vacuum
stem: An insulated rigid container is divided by a partition. One half holds an ideal gas and the other half is evacuated. The partition is suddenly removed and the gas fills the whole container. For this process,
option_a: the work done by the gas is n R T ln 2 and its temperature falls
option_b: the work done by the gas is zero and its temperature stays the same
option_c: the work done by the gas is zero and its temperature falls
option_d: the work done by the gas is P dV and its temperature rises
correct_answer_text: the work done by the gas is zero and its temperature stays the same
solution: The gas expands into vacuum, so there is no opposing pressure and no work is done. The walls are insulating, so no heat enters. From the first law dU = dQ minus dW = 0, and since the internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature, the temperature is unchanged.
formula_principle: In free expansion dQ = 0 and dW = 0, so dU = 0 and the temperature of an ideal gas is unchanged.
common_misconception: Students assume every expansion cools a gas and apply the isothermal work formula where no external pressure exists.

concept_tested: Path dependence of work
stem: A gas is taken from one given state to another given state. Which of the following depends on the particular route followed?
option_a: The work done by the gas
option_b: The change in the internal energy of the gas
option_c: The change in the temperature of the gas
option_d: The change in the pressure of the gas
correct_answer_text: The work done by the gas
solution: Work equals the area under the path drawn on a pressure volume diagram, and different routes between the same end points enclose different areas. All of pressure, volume, temperature and internal energy are fixed once the state is fixed, so only the work is route dependent.
formula_principle: U, P, V and T are state functions; heat and work are path functions.
