common_misconception: Students classify work as a state function because they can compute it from P and V values.

subtopic: Two paths between the same states
concept_tested: Using path independence of dU
stem: A gas is carried from state X to state Y along two different paths. Along the first path it absorbs 600 J of heat and does 200 J of work. Along the second path it does 500 J of work. The heat absorbed along the second path is
solution: Along the first path, dU = 600 minus 200 = 400 J. The same 400 J change occurs along the second path, since the end states are identical. Hence the heat absorbed along the second path is 400 plus 500 = 900 J.
formula_principle: dU is the same for all paths between the same states, so dQ = dU + dW must be applied path by path.
common_misconception: Students assume the heat exchanged is the same along both paths because the end states agree.

concept_tested: Work done on a system
stem: A system gives out 300 J of heat while 500 J of work is done on it by the surroundings. The internal energy of the system
solution: Heat rejected gives dQ = minus 300 J. Work done on the system gives dW = minus 500 J. Then dU = dQ minus dW = minus 300 minus (minus 500) = plus 200 J, so the internal energy rises by 200 J.
formula_principle: dU = dQ minus dW, with dQ negative for heat rejected and dW negative for work done on the system.
common_misconception: Students drop one of the two negative signs and obtain a decrease of 800 J or 200 J.

concept_tested: Fraction of supplied heat that appears as work
stem: One mole of a monatomic ideal gas is heated at constant pressure. The fraction of the supplied heat that appears as work done by the gas is
solution: For a temperature rise dT of one mole, the work done is R dT and the heat supplied is (5/2) R dT. The ratio is R dT divided by (5/2) R dT, which is 2/5. This equals (gamma minus 1) divided by gamma with gamma = 5/3.
formula_principle: At constant pressure dQ = (5/2) n R dT, dW = n R dT and dU = (3/2) n R dT for a monatomic gas.
common_misconception: Students quote 3/5, the share that goes into internal energy, when asked for the share that goes into work.

subtopic: Work in a two step process
concept_tested: Net work from two isobaric stages
stem: A gas at a constant pressure of 2 x 10^5 Pa expands from 2 x 10^-3 m^3 to 5 x 10^-3 m^3. It is then compressed at a constant pressure of 1 x 10^5 Pa back to 2 x 10^-3 m^3. The net work done by the gas is
solution: First stage: W1 = 2 x 10^5 x (5 minus 2) x 10^-3 = 600 J. Second stage: W2 = 1 x 10^5 x (2 minus 5) x 10^-3 = minus 300 J. Net work = 600 minus 300 = 300 J done by the gas.
formula_principle: W = P dV applied stage by stage, with dV negative during compression.
common_misconception: Students add the magnitudes of the two stages and forget that compression contributes negative work.

subtopic: Internal energy change by two routes
concept_tested: Same temperature change gives same dU
stem: Two moles of an ideal gas are taken from 300 K to 500 K, once at constant volume and once at constant pressure. The change in internal energy
option_a: is larger in the constant pressure case, since more heat has to be supplied there
option_b: is larger in the constant volume case, since no work is done there
option_c: is zero in the constant pressure case, since the gas expands as it is heated
option_d: is the same in the two cases, since internal energy depends only on temperature
correct_answer_text: is the same in the two cases, since internal energy depends only on temperature
solution: In both cases the temperature rises by 200 K for the same two moles of gas, so dU = n Cv dT is the same. The processes differ in the heat supplied, since at constant pressure part of the heat leaves as work, but the change in internal energy is identical.
formula_principle: For an ideal gas dU = n Cv dT whatever the process, since U is a function of T alone.
common_misconception: Students think the change in internal energy depends on how much heat was supplied.

subtopic: Heat on a straight line path
concept_tested: Combining work and internal energy on a linear P against V path
stem: One mole of a monatomic ideal gas is taken along a straight line on a pressure volume diagram from the state with pressure 1 x 10^5 Pa and volume 1 x 10^-3 m^3 to the state with pressure 2 x 10^5 Pa and volume 2 x 10^-3 m^3. The heat absorbed by the gas is
solution: The area under the straight line is the mean pressure times the change in volume, that is (1 x 10^5 plus 2 x 10^5)/2 x 1 x 10^-3 = 150 J. The products of pressure and volume are 100 J initially and 400 J finally, so dU = (3/2)(400 minus 100) = 450 J. Hence dQ = 450 plus 150 = 600 J.
formula_principle: W is the area under the straight line; dU = (3/2)(P2 V2 minus P1 V1) for a monatomic gas; dQ = dU + dW.
common_misconception: Students forget that on a sloping path the work is the trapezium area, or they use only one of the two contributions to the heat.

concept_tested: dQ = dU + dW
stem: The first law of thermodynamics is expressed as
option_a: dQ = dU minus dW, where dQ is the heat supplied, dU the change in internal energy and dW the work done by the system
option_b: dW = dU + dQ, where dQ is the heat supplied, dU the change in internal energy and dW the work done by the system
option_c: dQ = dU + dW, where dQ is the heat supplied, dU the change in internal energy and dW the work done by the system
option_d: dU = dQ + dW, where dQ is the heat supplied, dU the change in internal energy and dW the work done by the system
correct_answer_text: dQ = dU + dW, where dQ is the heat supplied, dU the change in internal energy and dW the work done by the system
solution: Energy supplied as heat has only two destinations. Part of it raises the internal energy of the system and the rest leaves as work done by the system, giving dQ = dU + dW.
formula_principle: First law: heat supplied to a system is shared between raising its internal energy and doing external work.
common_misconception: Students mix the two sign conventions and write dU = dQ + dW while still calling dW the work done by the gas.

subtopic: Physical content of the first law
concept_tested: Energy conservation including heat
stem: The first law of thermodynamics is essentially a statement of
option_a: the conservation of energy applied to systems that exchange heat and work
option_b: the impossibility of converting all the absorbed heat into work in a cycle
option_c: the transitive property of thermal equilibrium between systems
option_d: the fact that entropy of an isolated system never decreases
correct_answer_text: the conservation of energy applied to systems that exchange heat and work
solution: By recognising heat as a form of energy transfer, the first law simply says that energy is conserved in any thermodynamic process. It puts no restriction on the direction of a process.
formula_principle: The first law extends the principle of conservation of energy to thermal processes.
common_misconception: Students attribute the limitation on efficiency to the first law rather than the second.

subtopic: First law for an isochoric process
concept_tested: dQ = dU when volume is constant
stem: When heat is supplied to a gas held in a rigid closed vessel, the first law reduces to
solution: A rigid vessel keeps the volume fixed, so dV is zero and no work is done. The first law dQ = dU + dW then becomes dQ = dU, and all the heat supplied raises the internal energy.
formula_principle: In an isochoric process dV = 0, so dW = 0 and dQ = dU.
common_misconception: Students still include a work term in a constant volume process because the pressure changes.

subtopic: First law for an isothermal process
concept_tested: dQ = dW when temperature is constant
stem: For an ideal gas taken through an isothermal process, the first law reduces to
solution: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature. In an isothermal process the temperature is fixed, so dU = 0 and the first law gives dQ = dW: all the heat absorbed leaves as work.
formula_principle: For an ideal gas at constant temperature dU = 0, so dQ = dW.
common_misconception: Students set dQ to zero for an isothermal process, confusing it with an adiabatic process.

subtopic: State and path quantities in the first law
concept_tested: dU exact, dQ and dW inexact
stem: In the relation dQ = dU + dW applied to a process between two fixed states,
option_a: dQ has the same value for every path, while dU and dW depend on the path
option_b: dW has the same value for every path, while dQ and dU depend on the path
option_c: dU has the same value for every path, while dQ and dW depend on the path
option_d: all three of dQ, dU and dW have the same value for every path
correct_answer_text: dU has the same value for every path, while dQ and dW depend on the path
solution: Whatever route is taken between two given states, the change in internal energy is the same. The heat absorbed and the work done individually vary with the route, though their difference dQ minus dW always equals the same dU.
formula_principle: Internal energy is a state function; heat and work are path functions.
common_misconception: Students assume that if dU is fixed then dQ and dW must each be fixed as well.

subtopic: Direct use of the first law
concept_tested: Finding dU from dQ and dW
stem: A gas absorbs 200 J of heat and does 120 J of work on its surroundings. The change in the internal energy of the gas is
solution: Here dQ = plus 200 J and dW = plus 120 J, so dU = 200 minus 120 = plus 80 J. The internal energy of the gas increases by 80 J.
formula_principle: dU = dQ minus dW.
common_misconception: Students add heat and work instead of subtracting the work done by the gas.

concept_tested: Heat rejected equals work done on the gas
stem: An ideal gas is compressed isothermally and 150 J of work is done on it by the piston. During this process the gas
option_a: absorbs 150 J of heat from the surroundings
option_b: rejects 150 J of heat to the surroundings
option_c: rejects 75 J of heat to the surroundings
option_d: neither absorbs nor rejects heat, since the temperature is constant
correct_answer_text: rejects 150 J of heat to the surroundings
solution: For an isothermal change of an ideal gas dU = 0, hence dQ = dW. Work done on the gas means dW = minus 150 J, so dQ = minus 150 J and the gas rejects 150 J of heat.
formula_principle: Isothermal ideal gas: dU = 0, so dQ = dW.
common_misconception: Students equate an isothermal process with a zero heat process.

concept_tested: What the first law does not decide
stem: Which of the following cannot be decided using the first law of thermodynamics alone?
option_a: The heat that must be supplied to produce a given change of state and work output
option_b: Whether a given process will actually take place in a particular direction
option_c: The change in internal energy of a gas between two given states
option_d: The work done by a gas when the heat absorbed and the internal energy change are known
correct_answer_text: Whether a given process will actually take place in a particular direction
solution: Energy conservation is satisfied both by heat flowing from hot to cold and by the reverse. The first law therefore cannot rule out the reverse process, and a separate principle, the second law, is needed to fix the direction.
formula_principle: The first law is silent about the direction of a process; that is settled by the second law.
common_misconception: Students believe the first law forbids heat flowing from a cold body to a hot body.

subtopic: First law for an adiabatic process
concept_tested: dU = minus dW when dQ is zero
stem: For a gas expanding adiabatically, the first law gives
option_a: a rise in internal energy equal in magnitude to the work done by the gas
option_b: no change in internal energy, since no heat is exchanged
option_c: a fall in internal energy equal in magnitude to the work done by the gas
option_d: a fall in internal energy equal in magnitude to the heat absorbed
correct_answer_text: a fall in internal energy equal in magnitude to the work done by the gas
solution: With dQ = 0 the first law becomes 0 = dU + dW, that is dU = minus dW. In an expansion dW is positive, so dU is negative and the gas cools; the work done comes entirely from the store of internal energy.
formula_principle: Adiabatic process: dQ = 0, so dU = minus dW.
common_misconception: Students think that no heat exchange implies no change in internal energy or temperature.

concept_tested: Rapid compression raises temperature
stem: The barrel of a bicycle pump becomes noticeably warm when air inside it is pumped rapidly. The best explanation is that
option_a: the air is compressed isothermally, so the heat produced is passed to the barrel
option_b: the air expands adiabatically, so its internal energy is converted into heat
option_c: the air is compressed almost adiabatically, so the work done on it raises its internal energy
option_d: friction at the piston is the only source of the heating, the gas playing no part
correct_answer_text: the air is compressed almost adiabatically, so the work done on it raises its internal energy
solution: Pumping quickly gives the gas no time to exchange heat with the surroundings, so the process is nearly adiabatic. Work is done on the gas, making dW negative, so dU = minus dW is positive and the temperature of the trapped air rises.
formula_principle: Fast compression leaves no time for heat exchange, so dQ = 0 and dU = minus dW is positive.
common_misconception: Students call every fast process isothermal because they associate slowness with adiabatic behaviour.

concept_tested: Temperature rise from heat at constant volume
stem: Two moles of a monatomic ideal gas in a rigid vessel are supplied 1245 J of heat. Taking R = 8.3 J mol^-1 K^-1, the rise in temperature of the gas is
solution: Since the vessel is rigid, all the heat raises the internal energy. So 1245 = (3/2) x 2 x 8.3 x dT = 24.9 dT, giving dT = 1245 divided by 24.9 = 50 K.
formula_principle: At constant volume dQ = dU = (3/2) n R dT for a monatomic gas.
common_misconception: Students use Cp instead of Cv when the container is rigid.

concept_tested: Which term vanishes in which process
stem: Match the process with the term that vanishes in dQ = dU + dW. In an isochoric process, an isothermal process of an ideal gas and an adiabatic process, the vanishing terms are respectively
solution: A rigid container makes the volume constant, so no work is done and dW = 0. A constant temperature process of an ideal gas leaves the internal energy unchanged, so dU = 0. An adiabatic process is defined by the absence of heat exchange, so dQ = 0.
formula_principle: Isochoric: dV = 0 so dW = 0. Isothermal ideal gas: dT = 0 so dU = 0. Adiabatic: dQ = 0 by definition.
common_misconception: Students swap the isothermal and adiabatic conditions, setting dQ = 0 for the isothermal case.

concept_tested: Using dQ = dU + dW
stem: During a process the internal energy of a gas rises by 500 J while the gas does 300 J of work on its surroundings. The heat supplied to the gas is
solution: The heat supplied must cover both destinations of energy, so dQ = 500 + 300 = 800 J.
formula_principle: dQ = dU + dW.
common_misconception: Students subtract instead of adding, because they recall the rearranged form dU = dQ minus dW without care.

subtopic: Comparing heat needed in two processes
concept_tested: Cp exceeds Cv
stem: The same mass of an ideal gas is given the same rise in temperature, once at constant volume and once at constant pressure. Compared with the constant volume case, the heat needed in the constant pressure case is
option_a: smaller, since the expanding gas returns some energy to the surroundings
option_b: the same, since the change in internal energy is the same in the two cases
option_c: greater, since the internal energy change is larger at constant pressure
option_d: greater, since the gas also does work while expanding
correct_answer_text: greater, since the gas also does work while expanding
solution: In both cases the internal energy rises by n Cv dT. At constant pressure the gas additionally does work n R dT, and this extra energy must come from the heat supplied. Hence more heat is needed at constant pressure, and Cp exceeds Cv by R.
formula_principle: dQ at constant volume is n Cv dT while dQ at constant pressure is n Cv dT plus n R dT.
common_misconception: Students think expansion reduces the heat requirement because the gas seems to release energy.

subtopic: Isobaric heating of a monatomic gas
concept_tested: Splitting dQ into dU and dW
stem: One mole of a monatomic ideal gas is heated at constant pressure from 300 K to 400 K. Taking R = 8.3 J mol^-1 K^-1, the heat supplied and the work done by the gas are respectively
solution: With n = 1 and dT = 100 K, n R dT = 8.3 x 100 = 830 J. Hence the work done is 830 J, the rise in internal energy is (3/2) x 830 = 1245 J and the heat supplied is 830 + 1245 = 2075 J.
formula_principle: Isobaric: dW = n R dT, dU = (3/2) n R dT, dQ = (5/2) n R dT for a monatomic gas.
common_misconception: Students interchange the roles of the work term and the internal energy term in an isobaric process.

concept_tested: Work share for a diatomic gas at constant pressure
stem: A diatomic ideal gas with gamma = 1.4 is heated at constant pressure. The fraction of the heat supplied that leaves the gas as work is
solution: The work done is n R dT and the heat supplied is n Cp dT. Since Cp = gamma R divided by (gamma minus 1), the ratio is (gamma minus 1) divided by gamma = 0.4 divided by 1.4 = 2/7.
formula_principle: At constant pressure the ratio of work to heat is n R dT divided by n Cp dT, which is (gamma minus 1)/gamma.
common_misconception: Students quote the monatomic result 2/5 for every gas, ignoring the value of gamma.

concept_tested: Compression with heat rejection
stem: A gas is compressed so that 400 J of work is done on it, and during the process it rejects 250 J of heat. The internal energy of the gas
solution: Heat rejected gives dQ = minus 250 J. Work done on the gas gives dW = minus 400 J. Then dU = minus 250 minus (minus 400) = plus 150 J, so the internal energy rises by 150 J and the gas gets hotter.
formula_principle: dU = dQ minus dW, with dQ = minus 250 J and dW = minus 400 J.
common_misconception: Students mishandle the double negative and report a decrease of 150 J.

concept_tested: dU = 0 over a closed cycle
stem: A gas is taken round a closed cycle. During the cycle it absorbs 900 J of heat from a hot source and rejects 600 J to a cold sink. Over one complete cycle,
option_a: the internal energy increases by 300 J and the net work done by the gas is zero
option_b: the internal energy is unchanged and the net work done by the gas is 1500 J
option_c: the internal energy is unchanged and the net work done by the gas is 300 J
option_d: the internal energy decreases by 600 J and the net work done by the gas is 900 J
correct_answer_text: the internal energy is unchanged and the net work done by the gas is 300 J
solution: Since the gas returns to its initial state, the change in internal energy over the cycle is zero. The first law then gives net work = net heat = 900 minus 600 = 300 J done by the gas.
formula_principle: Over a cycle dU = 0, so the net heat absorbed equals the net work done.
common_misconception: Students believe the gas stores the difference between the two heats as internal energy.

concept_tested: Applying the first law with a volume change on melting
stem: A block of ice is melted at constant pressure. During melting the substance contracts in volume. For the ice water system during this change,
option_a: the increase in internal energy is slightly less than the heat absorbed
option_b: the increase in internal energy is slightly greater than the heat absorbed
option_c: the internal energy does not change, since the temperature stays constant
option_d: the internal energy falls, since work is done on the system by the atmosphere
correct_answer_text: the increase in internal energy is slightly greater than the heat absorbed
solution: Melting ice contracts, so dV is negative and dW = P dV is negative: the atmosphere does work on the system. Then dU = dQ minus dW = dQ plus a small positive amount, so the internal energy rises by slightly more than the heat absorbed.
formula_principle: dU = dQ minus dW; contraction makes dW negative, so dU exceeds dQ.
common_misconception: Students think that internal energy cannot change during a phase change because the temperature stays fixed.

concept_tested: Heat over a sequence of two processes
stem: A gas at 2 x 10^5 Pa occupying 3 x 10^-3 m^3 is first expanded at constant pressure to 5 x 10^-3 m^3. Its pressure is then lowered at constant volume until the internal energy returns to its original value. For the two stages taken together, the heat absorbed by the gas is
solution: Work in the first stage is 2 x 10^5 x (5 minus 3) x 10^-3 = 400 J. No work is done in the second stage since the volume is fixed. The internal energy ends where it began, so dU total is zero and dQ total = 0 plus 400 = 400 J.
formula_principle: dQ total = dU total + dW total; dU total = 0 here and work arises only in the isobaric stage.
common_misconception: Students conclude that zero change in internal energy means zero heat exchange.

subtopic: Process with given P against V relation
concept_tested: Work and heat for a linear pressure volume path
stem: One mole of a monatomic ideal gas expands so that its pressure falls linearly with volume from 3 x 10^5 Pa at 1 x 10^-3 m^3 to 1 x 10^5 Pa at 3 x 10^-3 m^3. Taking R = 8.3 J mol^-1 K^-1, the heat absorbed by the gas is
solution: The mean pressure is (3 x 10^5 plus 1 x 10^5)/2 = 2 x 10^5 Pa and the volume increases by 2 x 10^-3 m^3, so W = 400 J. The products of pressure and volume are 300 J at both ends, so the temperature is unchanged and dU = 0. Hence dQ = 0 plus 400 = 400 J.
formula_principle: W is the trapezium area under the straight line; dU = (3/2)(P2 V2 minus P1 V1); dQ = dU + dW.
common_misconception: Students assume that a process with no change of internal energy must involve no heat exchange.

concept_tested: Heat exchange over three consecutive stages
stem: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat while doing 200 J of work, then rejects 150 J of heat while 250 J of work is done on it, and is finally brought back to its original state by a third stage carried out at constant volume. The heat exchanged during the third stage is
solution: Stage one gives dU1 = 500 minus 200 = 300 J. Stage two gives dU2 = minus 150 minus (minus 250) = plus 100 J. So the internal energy has risen by 400 J. For the cycle to close, the third stage must give dU3 = minus 400 J, and since the volume is fixed no work is done, so dQ3 = minus 400 J, that is 400 J of heat is rejected.
formula_principle: Over a complete cycle dU = 0; at constant volume dW = 0, so dQ for the last stage equals its dU.
common_misconception: Students forget that the change in internal energy over a full cycle must be zero.

concept_tested: Isothermal process
stem: For a gas to undergo a nearly isothermal change, it should be
option_a: kept in a thick walled insulating vessel and made to change very slowly
option_b: kept in a thin walled conducting vessel and made to change very rapidly
option_c: kept in a thin walled conducting vessel and made to change very slowly
option_d: kept in a thick walled insulating vessel and made to change very rapidly
correct_answer_text: kept in a thin walled conducting vessel and made to change very slowly
solution: To hold the temperature fixed, heat must flow freely between the gas and its surroundings. This calls for thin conducting walls, and the change must be slow enough for that exchange to keep pace.
formula_principle: An isothermal change needs free heat exchange with a reservoir, which requires conducting walls and a slow change.
common_misconception: Students associate slow changes with adiabatic behaviour and fast changes with isothermal behaviour.

concept_tested: Adiabatic process
stem: An adiabatic process is one in which
option_a: the temperature of the system stays constant throughout
option_b: the pressure of the system stays constant throughout
option_c: no heat is exchanged between the system and its surroundings
option_d: the internal energy of the system stays constant throughout
correct_answer_text: no heat is exchanged between the system and its surroundings
solution: The defining condition of an adiabatic process is that no heat crosses the boundary, so dQ = 0. The temperature, pressure, volume and internal energy may all change.
formula_principle: Adiabatic process: dQ = 0.
common_misconception: Students confuse zero heat exchange with constant temperature.

concept_tested: W = 0 at constant volume
stem: The work done by a gas during an isochoric change is
option_a: zero, whatever the change in pressure
option_b: equal to V times the change in pressure
option_c: equal to the change in the product of pressure and volume
option_d: equal to the heat supplied divided by the number of moles
correct_answer_text: zero, whatever the change in pressure
solution: With the volume held fixed, dV is zero at every stage, so the integral of P dV vanishes. The gas does no work however much its pressure and temperature change.
formula_principle: W = integral of P dV; if V is constant then dV = 0 and W = 0.
common_misconception: Students think a change of pressure must be accompanied by some work.

concept_tested: W = P (V2 minus V1)
stem: A gas expands at a constant pressure P from volume V1 to volume V2. The work done by the gas is
option_c: P V2 minus P V2 divided by 2
option_d: 2.303 P V1 log (V2 divided by V1)
solution: Since P is constant it comes out of the integral, giving W = P times the change in volume, that is P (V2 minus V1). On a pressure volume diagram this is the rectangular area under the horizontal path.
formula_principle: For a constant pressure change, W = P dV = P (V2 minus V1).
common_misconception: Students apply the isothermal logarithmic formula to a constant pressure change.

subtopic: Adiabatic relation between P and V
concept_tested: P V^gamma = constant
stem: For a quasi static adiabatic change of an ideal gas, the pressure and the volume are related by
solution: Combining dU = minus dW for an adiabatic change with the ideal gas equation gives P V^gamma = constant, where gamma is the ratio of the two principal molar heat capacities.
formula_principle: Adiabatic relations: P V^gamma = constant, T V^(gamma minus 1) = constant, P^(1 minus gamma) T^gamma = constant.
common_misconception: Students place the exponent gamma on the wrong variable or use the temperature volume relation for pressure and volume.

subtopic: Isothermal relation between P and V
concept_tested: P V = constant at constant temperature
stem: For a fixed mass of an ideal gas held at constant temperature, the pressure volume curve is
option_a: a straight line through the origin, since P is proportional to V
option_b: a rectangular hyperbola, since P V is constant
option_c: a horizontal straight line, since the pressure does not change
option_d: a vertical straight line, since the volume does not change
correct_answer_text: a rectangular hyperbola, since P V is constant
solution: At constant temperature the ideal gas equation gives P V = constant, so P varies as the reciprocal of V. A graph of P against V is therefore a rectangular hyperbola.
formula_principle: Isothermal ideal gas: P V = n R T = constant.
common_misconception: Students draw the isothermal curve as a straight line because P V = constant looks like a linear relation.

concept_tested: W = 2.303 n R T log (V2/V1)
stem: One mole of an ideal gas at 300 K expands isothermally until its volume is doubled. Taking R = 8.3 J mol^-1 K^-1 and log 2 = 0.301, the work done by the gas is about
solution: Here W = 2.303 x 1 x 8.3 x 300 x log 2 = 2.303 x 2490 x 0.301. Since 2.303 x 0.301 = 0.693, the work is 0.693 x 2490 = 1726 J approximately.
formula_principle: Isothermal work: W = 2.303 n R T log (V2 divided by V1).
common_misconception: Students omit the logarithm and quote n R T as the isothermal work.

subtopic: Adiabatic relation between T and V
concept_tested: T V^(gamma minus 1) = constant
stem: For an adiabatic change of an ideal gas, the temperature and the volume are related by
solution: Write P = n R T divided by V and put it into P V^gamma = constant. The volume powers combine to give T V^(gamma minus 1) = constant for a fixed amount of gas.
formula_principle: Substituting P = n R T divided by V into P V^gamma = constant gives T V^(gamma minus 1) = constant.
common_misconception: Students carry the exponent gamma over unchanged from the pressure volume form.

concept_tested: W = n R dT at constant pressure
stem: Two moles of an ideal gas are heated at constant pressure so that the temperature rises by 100 K. Taking R = 8.3 J mol^-1 K^-1, the work done by the gas is
solution: Using P V = n R T at constant pressure gives P dV = n R dT. Hence W = 2 x 8.3 x 100 = 1660 J. Note that the answer does not depend on whether the gas is monatomic or diatomic.
formula_principle: At constant pressure, W = P dV = n R dT.
common_misconception: Students think the work at constant pressure depends on the atomicity of the gas.

concept_tested: Adiabatic curve is steeper
stem: An isothermal curve and an adiabatic curve for the same gas are drawn through a common point on a pressure volume diagram. Near that point,
option_a: the isothermal curve is steeper than the adiabatic curve
option_b: the two curves have the same slope, since both pass through the same state
option_c: the isothermal curve is steeper only for a monatomic gas
option_d: the adiabatic curve is steeper than the isothermal curve
correct_answer_text: the adiabatic curve is steeper than the isothermal curve
solution: Differentiating P V = constant gives a slope of minus P divided by V. Differentiating P V^gamma = constant gives a slope of minus gamma P divided by V. Since gamma exceeds one, the adiabatic curve falls more steeply at the common point.
formula_principle: Isothermal slope is minus P divided by V; adiabatic slope is minus gamma P divided by V.
common_misconception: Students remember that the curves differ but cannot recall which one is steeper.

concept_tested: Speed of the process decides the type
stem: A gas in a cylinder is compressed so quickly that there is no time for heat exchange with the surroundings. This compression is best described as
option_a: isothermal, with the temperature of the gas staying constant
option_b: adiabatic, with the temperature of the gas staying constant
option_c: adiabatic, with the temperature of the gas rising
option_d: isobaric, with the pressure of the gas staying constant
correct_answer_text: adiabatic, with the temperature of the gas rising
solution: With no time for heat exchange, dQ = 0 and the process is adiabatic. Work is done on the gas, so dW is negative and dU = minus dW is positive, meaning the internal energy and hence the temperature rise.
formula_principle: Rapid change means dQ = 0, so dU = minus dW; compression makes dW negative and dU positive.
common_misconception: Students say adiabatic but then also claim the temperature is unchanged.

subtopic: Adiabatic compression of a monatomic gas
concept_tested: Using T V^(gamma minus 1) = constant
stem: A monatomic ideal gas at 300 K is compressed adiabatically until its volume becomes one eighth of the original value. Taking gamma = 5/3, the final temperature is
solution: Here V1 divided by V2 is 8 and gamma minus 1 is 2/3, so the temperature ratio is 8^(2/3) = 4. Hence T2 = 300 x 4 = 1200 K.
formula_principle: T2 = T1 (V1 divided by V2)^(gamma minus 1) with gamma minus 1 = 2/3 for a monatomic gas.
common_misconception: Students apply the exponent gamma rather than gamma minus 1 in the temperature volume relation.

subtopic: Adiabatic relation between P and T
concept_tested: P^(1 minus gamma) T^gamma = constant
stem: For an adiabatic change of an ideal gas, the correct relation between pressure and temperature is
solution: From the gas equation V is proportional to T divided by P. Substituting into P V^gamma = constant gives P (T divided by P)^gamma = constant, that is P^(1 minus gamma) T^gamma = constant.
formula_principle: Eliminating V between P V^gamma = constant and T V^(gamma minus 1) = constant gives P^(1 minus gamma) T^gamma = constant.
common_misconception: Students swap the exponents between pressure and temperature.

concept_tested: Cooling on sudden expansion
stem: When a tyre bursts, the air rushing out is found to be noticeably cooler than the air inside the tyre was. This happens because the escaping air
option_a: expands isothermally and gives out heat to the surrounding air
option_b: is compressed adiabatically by the atmosphere outside the tyre
option_c: expands adiabatically and does work at the cost of its own internal energy
option_d: loses molecules of high speed first, so the average speed of those left falls
correct_answer_text: expands adiabatically and does work at the cost of its own internal energy
solution: The escape is too fast for heat exchange, so dQ = 0. The air pushes back the atmosphere, making dW positive, so dU = minus dW is negative. The internal energy and hence the temperature of the escaping air fall.
formula_principle: Sudden expansion is adiabatic, so dQ = 0 and dU = minus dW is negative for expansion.
common_misconception: Students explain the cooling by heat being carried away rather than by work done at the cost of internal energy.

concept_tested: W = n R (T1 minus T2) divided by (gamma minus 1)
stem: One mole of a monatomic ideal gas expands adiabatically and its temperature falls from 400 K to 300 K. Taking R = 8.3 J mol^-1 K^-1 and gamma = 5/3, the work done by the gas is
solution: Here gamma minus 1 = 2/3, so the work is 1 x 8.3 x 100 divided by (2/3) = 830 x 1.5 = 1245 J. This equals the fall in internal energy, as it must when no heat is exchanged.
formula_principle: Adiabatic work: W = n R (T1 minus T2) divided by (gamma minus 1).
common_misconception: Students forget the division by gamma minus 1 in the adiabatic work formula.

subtopic: Molar heat capacity in special processes
concept_tested: Zero molar heat capacity
stem: The molar heat capacity of an ideal gas is zero for
solution: In an adiabatic change no heat is exchanged although the temperature does change, so dQ divided by n dT is zero. In an isothermal change heat is exchanged with no temperature change, so the same ratio becomes infinite.
formula_principle: Molar heat capacity is dQ divided by n dT; it is zero when dQ = 0 with dT not zero.
common_misconception: Students assign zero heat capacity to the isothermal process and infinite to the adiabatic one.

subtopic: Adiabatic compression of a diatomic gas
concept_tested: Using P V^gamma = constant
stem: A diatomic ideal gas with gamma = 1.4 is compressed adiabatically until its volume becomes one thirty second of the original value. The pressure of the gas becomes
solution: The volume ratio is 32, so P2 divided by P1 = 32^1.4. Writing 32 as 2^5 gives 2^(5 x 1.4) = 2^7 = 128. Hence the pressure becomes 128 times the original value.
formula_principle: P2 = P1 (V1 divided by V2)^gamma.
common_misconception: Students use P V = constant for an adiabatic compression and lose the factor from the temperature rise.

concept_tested: Comparing work between the same volume limits
stem: Starting from the same state, a fixed mass of ideal gas is expanded to the same final volume, once isothermally and once adiabatically. The work done by the gas is
option_a: greater in the adiabatic expansion, since no heat has to be supplied to the gas
option_b: the same in the two cases, since the volume limits are the same
option_c: greater in the isothermal expansion, since the pressure stays higher throughout
option_d: greater in the adiabatic expansion, since the temperature of the gas falls
correct_answer_text: greater in the isothermal expansion, since the pressure stays higher throughout
solution: From the common starting point, the adiabatic curve falls more steeply because its slope is gamma times as large in magnitude. Hence at every larger volume the adiabatic pressure is lower, the area under the adiabatic curve is smaller, and the isothermal expansion delivers more work.
formula_principle: The adiabatic curve is steeper, so it lies below the isothermal curve after the common starting point.
common_misconception: Students think that not having to supply heat means the gas can deliver more work.

subtopic: Adiabatic work from P and V values
concept_tested: W = (P1 V1 minus P2 V2) divided by (gamma minus 1)
stem: A monatomic ideal gas with gamma = 5/3 expands adiabatically from a pressure of 8 x 10^5 Pa and a volume of 1 x 10^-3 m^3 to a volume of 8 x 10^-3 m^3, at which its pressure is 2.5 x 10^4 Pa. The work done by the gas is
solution: P1 V1 = 8 x 10^5 x 1 x 10^-3 = 800 J and P2 V2 = 2.5 x 10^4 x 8 x 10^-3 = 200 J. Their difference is 600 J, and dividing by gamma minus 1 = 2/3 gives 600 x 1.5 = 900 J.
formula_principle: Adiabatic work: W = (P1 V1 minus P2 V2) divided by (gamma minus 1).
common_misconception: Students multiply by gamma minus 1 instead of dividing by it.

concept_tested: Reading an isothermal and an adiabatic curve
stem: Two curves for the same fixed mass of ideal gas cross at a point on a pressure volume diagram. Curve X falls more steeply through the crossing point than curve Y. It follows that
option_a: curve X is the isothermal and curve Y is the adiabatic
option_b: curve X is the adiabatic and curve Y is the isothermal
option_c: curve X is the isobaric and curve Y is the isothermal
option_d: curve X is the isochoric and curve Y is the adiabatic
correct_answer_text: curve X is the adiabatic and curve Y is the isothermal
solution: At the crossing point both curves share the same P and V. The magnitudes of the slopes are P divided by V for the isothermal and gamma P divided by V for the adiabatic. Since gamma exceeds one, the steeper curve X must be the adiabatic and Y the isothermal.
formula_principle: Magnitude of isothermal slope is P/V; magnitude of adiabatic slope is gamma P/V, with gamma greater than one.
common_misconception: Students identify the steeper curve as the isothermal by mistaking the direction of the inequality.

subtopic: Pressure change in an adiabatic expansion
concept_tested: Combining the adiabatic relation with the gas equation
stem: A monatomic ideal gas with gamma = 5/3 expands adiabatically and its temperature falls from 400 K to 100 K. The final pressure of the gas is
option_a: one thirty second of the initial pressure
option_b: one eighth of the initial pressure
option_c: one quarter of the initial pressure
option_d: one hundred and twenty eighth of the initial pressure
correct_answer_text: one thirty second of the initial pressure
solution: From T V^(gamma minus 1) = constant with gamma minus 1 = 2/3, the volume ratio is (T1 divided by T2) raised to the power 3/2, that is 4^(3/2) = 8. Then from P V = n R T, the pressure ratio is (T2 divided by T1) times (V1 divided by V2) = (1/4) x (1/8) = 1/32.
formula_principle: T V^(gamma minus 1) = constant gives the volume ratio; then P V = n R T gives the pressure ratio.
common_misconception: Students quote only the temperature ratio and forget that the volume has changed as well.

subtopic: Adiabatic work for a diatomic gas
concept_tested: Work from the temperature drop
stem: One mole of a diatomic ideal gas with gamma = 1.4 expands adiabatically and its temperature falls from 400 K to 100 K. Taking R = 8.3 J mol^-1 K^-1, the work done by the gas is
solution: The temperature drop is 300 K, so n R (T1 minus T2) = 1 x 8.3 x 300 = 2490 J. Dividing by gamma minus 1 = 0.4 gives 2490 divided by 0.4 = 6225 J.
formula_principle: W = n R (T1 minus T2) divided by (gamma minus 1).
common_misconception: Students use the monatomic value of gamma minus 1 for a diatomic gas.

subtopic: Heat capacity in an isothermal change
concept_tested: Infinite molar heat capacity
stem: For an isothermal change of an ideal gas, the molar heat capacity is
option_a: zero, since the internal energy of the gas does not change
option_b: equal to R, since the whole of the heat appears as work
option_c: infinite, since heat is exchanged with no change in temperature
option_d: equal to Cp minus Cv, since pressure and volume both change
correct_answer_text: infinite, since heat is exchanged with no change in temperature
solution: In an isothermal change of an ideal gas the whole of the heat absorbed leaves as work, so dQ is not zero, while dT is zero. The ratio dQ divided by n dT therefore has no finite value and the molar heat capacity is said to be infinite.
formula_principle: Molar heat capacity C = dQ divided by n dT; isothermal means dT = 0 with dQ not zero.
common_misconception: Students associate constant temperature with zero heat capacity instead of an unbounded one.

concept_tested: Chaining an adiabatic and an isochoric stage
stem: One mole of a monatomic ideal gas at 300 K is compressed adiabatically until its volume is one eighth of the original. It is then cooled at constant volume back to 300 K. Taking R = 8.3 J mol^-1 K^-1 and gamma = 5/3, the heat rejected during the cooling stage is
solution: The adiabatic compression raises the temperature to 300 x 8^(2/3) = 300 x 4 = 1200 K. Cooling at constant volume from 1200 K to 300 K gives a drop of 900 K, so the heat rejected is (3/2) x 1 x 8.3 x 900 = 12.45 x 900 = 11205 J.
formula_principle: T2 = T1 (V1/V2)^(gamma minus 1); then at constant volume dQ = (3/2) n R dT.
common_misconception: Students use the initial temperature of 300 K as the starting point of the cooling stage.

concept_tested: Adiabatic slope is gamma times the isothermal slope
stem: At the point where an isothermal curve and an adiabatic curve for the same ideal gas intersect on a pressure volume diagram, the ratio of the magnitude of the slope of the adiabatic curve to that of the isothermal curve is
solution: Differentiating P V = constant gives P dV + V dP = 0, so the isothermal slope is minus P divided by V. Differentiating P V^gamma = constant gives gamma P dV + V dP = 0, so the adiabatic slope is minus gamma P divided by V. At the common point P and V are shared, so the ratio of the magnitudes is gamma.
formula_principle: Differentiating P V = constant gives dP/dV = minus P/V; differentiating P V^gamma = constant gives dP/dV = minus gamma P/V.
common_misconception: Students recall that the adiabatic curve is steeper but quote gamma minus 1 as the factor.

subtopic: Adiabatic work with a general gamma
concept_tested: Consistent adiabatic states and the work formula
stem: A gas for which gamma = 1.5 expands adiabatically from a pressure of 8 x 10^5 Pa and a volume of 1 x 10^-3 m^3 to a volume of 4 x 10^-3 m^3. The work done by the gas is
solution: The volume ratio is 4, so the pressure falls by a factor 4^1.5 = 8, giving P2 = 1 x 10^5 Pa. Then P1 V1 = 800 J and P2 V2 = 1 x 10^5 x 4 x 10^-3 = 400 J. The work is (800 minus 400) divided by 0.5 = 800 J.
formula_principle: P2 = P1 (V1/V2)^gamma, then W = (P1 V1 minus P2 V2) divided by (gamma minus 1).
common_misconception: Students find the final pressure from P V = constant instead of from P V^gamma = constant.

concept_tested: Work as area on a pressure volume diagram
stem: For a gas taken from one state to another, the area under the path drawn on a pressure volume diagram represents
option_a: the work done by the gas
option_b: the heat absorbed by the gas
option_c: the change in internal energy of the gas
option_d: the change in temperature of the gas
correct_answer_text: the work done by the gas
solution: Since the work done in a small step is P dV, adding the strips of width dV and height P gives the whole area under the path, which is therefore the work done by the gas.
formula_principle: W = integral of P dV, which is the area between the path and the volume axis.
common_misconception: Students think the area under the curve gives the heat supplied.

concept_tested: dU = 0 for a closed cycle
stem: When a gas is taken round a complete cycle and returns to its starting state, the change in its internal energy over the cycle is
option_a: equal to the net work done by the gas
option_b: equal to the heat absorbed from the source
option_c: equal to the area enclosed by the cycle
option_d: zero, because internal energy is a state function
correct_answer_text: zero, because internal energy is a state function
solution: The gas ends in exactly the state it began in, with the same pressure, volume and temperature. Since internal energy depends only on the state, its change over the cycle is zero.
formula_principle: Internal energy is a state function, so it returns to its initial value after any closed cycle.
common_misconception: Students think that the difference between heat absorbed and heat rejected is stored in the gas.

concept_tested: Clockwise cycle gives positive net work
stem: A cycle traced in the clockwise sense on a pressure volume diagram corresponds to
option_a: net work done by the gas on the surroundings
option_b: net work done on the gas by the surroundings
option_c: no net work, since the gas returns to its starting state
option_d: net heat rejected exactly equal to the net heat absorbed
correct_answer_text: net work done by the gas on the surroundings
solution: In a clockwise loop the upper branch is the expansion and the lower branch is the compression. The gas therefore does more work while expanding than is done on it while being compressed, so the net work is positive and equal to the enclosed area.
formula_principle: Clockwise traversal means expansion at higher pressure than compression, so the enclosed area is positive work done by the gas.
common_misconception: Students believe that a closed cycle must give zero net work because the gas returns to its starting state.

concept_tested: Net work equals the enclosed area
stem: For a gas taken round a closed loop on a pressure volume diagram, the area enclosed by the loop is equal in magnitude to
option_a: the net change in internal energy during the cycle
option_b: the net work done during the cycle
option_c: the heat absorbed from the hot reservoir during the cycle
option_d: the sum of the heat absorbed and the heat rejected during the cycle
correct_answer_text: the net work done during the cycle
solution: The work along the outward branch is the area under it and the work along the return branch is the area under that branch taken with the opposite sign. The difference is the area enclosed by the loop, which is the net work.
formula_principle: Net work over a cycle equals the area enclosed by the loop, and by the first law it also equals the net heat.
common_misconception: Students equate the enclosed area with the heat taken from the source rather than with the net heat.

concept_tested: Net work from a rectangular loop
stem: A gas is taken clockwise round a rectangular cycle on a pressure volume diagram in which the pressure varies between 1 x 10^5 Pa and 3 x 10^5 Pa and the volume varies between 2 x 10^-3 m^3 and 5 x 10^-3 m^3. The net work done by the gas per cycle is
solution: The pressure range is 2 x 10^5 Pa and the volume range is 3 x 10^-3 m^3. The enclosed area is 2 x 10^5 x 3 x 10^-3 = 600 J, and since the traversal is clockwise this work is done by the gas.
formula_principle: Net work equals the enclosed area, which for a rectangle is the pressure range times the volume range.
common_misconception: Students compute only the expansion work and forget the negative work of the compression branch.

concept_tested: Meaning of an anticlockwise loop
stem: A fixed mass of gas is taken round a cycle in the anticlockwise sense on a pressure volume diagram. Over one complete cycle,
option_a: net work is done by the gas and the gas absorbs more heat than it rejects
option_b: net work is done on the gas and the gas rejects more heat than it absorbs
option_c: no net work is done and the heat absorbed equals the heat rejected
option_d: net work is done on the gas and the internal energy of the gas falls
correct_answer_text: net work is done on the gas and the gas rejects more heat than it absorbs
solution: In an anticlockwise loop the compression occurs at the higher pressure, so more work is done on the gas than by it. Since the internal energy returns to its initial value, the net heat must be negative as well, that is more heat is rejected than absorbed. This is the sense in which a refrigerator operates.
formula_principle: Anticlockwise traversal makes the enclosed area negative, so the net work is done on the gas and the net heat is rejected.
common_misconception: Students assume every closed cycle delivers useful work regardless of the sense of traversal.

concept_tested: Net heat equals net work
stem: In one complete cycle a gas absorbs 1000 J of heat and does 400 J of net work on its surroundings. The heat rejected by the gas during the cycle is
solution: Since the internal energy returns to its starting value, 1000 minus Q rejected = 400. Hence the heat rejected is 600 J.
formula_principle: Over a cycle dU = 0, so Q absorbed minus Q rejected equals the net work.
common_misconception: Students add the work to the absorbed heat instead of subtracting it.

concept_tested: Vertical segment means no work
stem: On a pressure volume diagram with pressure on the vertical axis, a stage of a cycle appears as a vertical straight line segment. During this stage,
option_a: no work is done, since the volume does not change
option_b: no work is done, since the pressure does not change
option_c: the work done equals the product of the volume and the change in pressure
option_d: the work done is the largest of all the stages, since the pressure changes most
correct_answer_text: no work is done, since the volume does not change
solution: A vertical segment has a fixed volume, so dV = 0 at every point and the area under it is zero. Hence the work done during that stage is zero, however large the pressure change may be.
formula_principle: A vertical line on a P against V plot is an isochoric stage, for which dV = 0 and W = 0.
common_misconception: Students associate a large pressure change with a large amount of work.

concept_tested: Trapezium area under a straight line
stem: A gas expands along a straight line on a pressure volume diagram from a pressure of 2 x 10^5 Pa at a volume of 1 x 10^-3 m^3 to a pressure of 1 x 10^5 Pa at a volume of 3 x 10^-3 m^3. The work done by the gas is
solution: The mean pressure is (2 x 10^5 plus 1 x 10^5) divided by 2 = 1.5 x 10^5 Pa and the volume increases by 2 x 10^-3 m^3. Hence W = 1.5 x 10^5 x 2 x 10^-3 = 300 J.
formula_principle: For a straight line path, W is the trapezium area, that is the mean pressure times the change in volume.
common_misconception: Students use one of the end pressures instead of the mean pressure for a sloping path.

concept_tested: Path lying higher gives more work
stem: A gas is expanded between the same two volumes along two different paths on a pressure volume diagram. Path X lies entirely above path Y. The work done by the gas is
option_a: greater along path X, since the area under it is larger
option_b: greater along path Y, since the pressure is lower and the gas expands more easily
option_c: the same along both paths, since the volume limits are the same
option_d: greater along path X only if the gas absorbs heat along it
correct_answer_text: greater along path X, since the area under it is larger
solution: Between the same volume limits, the area under the higher path is larger at every value of the volume. Hence the gas does more work along path X than along path Y, even though both start and end at the same volumes.
formula_principle: W is the area under the path, so a path at higher pressure between the same volumes gives more work.
common_misconception: Students assume that equal volume changes must give equal work.

subtopic: Heat in a constant volume stage
concept_tested: Isochoric heat for a monatomic gas from P and V
stem: During one stage of a cycle, a monatomic ideal gas kept at a fixed volume of 1 x 10^-3 m^3 has its pressure raised from 1 x 10^5 Pa to 3 x 10^5 Pa. The heat supplied to the gas during this stage is
solution: The change in the product of pressure and volume is (3 x 10^5 minus 1 x 10^5) x 1 x 10^-3 = 200 J, and this equals n R dT. For a monatomic gas dU = (3/2) n R dT = 300 J, and since no work is done the heat supplied is 300 J.
formula_principle: At constant volume dQ = dU = (3/2) V dP for a monatomic ideal gas, since n R dT = V dP.
common_misconception: Students forget the factor 3/2 and quote the change in the product of pressure and volume as the heat.

subtopic: What must vanish over a cycle
concept_tested: Only dU is necessarily zero
stem: For a gas taken round any complete cycle, which quantity is necessarily zero?
option_a: The net heat exchanged with the surroundings
option_c: The net work done by the gas
option_d: The heat rejected to the cold reservoir
solution: Internal energy is a state function, so after a complete cycle it returns to its original value and its change is zero. Heat and work are path functions, and for a loop of finite area both the net heat and the net work are non zero and equal to each other.
formula_principle: Over a cycle every state function returns to its initial value, so dU = 0, while path functions need not vanish.
common_misconception: Students assume that everything returns to zero over a cycle, including the net work.

subtopic: Two routes between the same states
concept_tested: Extra heat along the route with more work
stem: A gas is taken from the state with pressure 3 x 10^5 Pa and volume 1 x 10^-3 m^3 to the state with pressure 1 x 10^5 Pa and volume 3 x 10^-3 m^3 by two routes. Route X is an expansion at the constant pressure 3 x 10^5 Pa followed by a fall of pressure at constant volume. Route Y is a fall of pressure at constant volume followed by an expansion at the constant pressure 1 x 10^5 Pa. The heat absorbed along route X exceeds that along route Y by
solution: Along route X the work is 3 x 10^5 x 2 x 10^-3 = 600 J, the constant volume stage contributing nothing. Along route Y the work is 1 x 10^5 x 2 x 10^-3 = 200 J. Since the end states are the same, dU is common, so the heat difference equals 600 minus 200 = 400 J.
formula_principle: dU is the same for both routes, so the difference in heat equals the difference in work.
common_misconception: Students expect the heat absorbed to be the same along both routes because the end states agree.

subtopic: Direction of a cycle and the device
concept_tested: Anticlockwise cycles describe refrigerating devices
stem: A working substance is carried round a loop on a pressure volume diagram in the anticlockwise sense, and the loop encloses an area of 250 J. Over each cycle the device
option_a: delivers 250 J of net work and transfers heat from the hotter body to the colder body
option_b: takes in 250 J of net work and stores it as internal energy of the working substance
option_c: takes in 250 J of net work and transfers heat from the colder body to the hotter body
option_d: delivers 250 J of net work and stores an equal amount of heat in the colder body
correct_answer_text: takes in 250 J of net work and transfers heat from the colder body to the hotter body
solution: In an anticlockwise loop the compression branch lies above the expansion branch, so the surroundings do 250 J of net work on the substance each cycle. Since the internal energy is unchanged over a cycle, this work together with the heat drawn from the colder body is delivered to the hotter body. That is the operation of a refrigerator or heat pump.
formula_principle: Anticlockwise loop: net work is negative, so external work is supplied and heat is pumped from cold to hot.
common_misconception: Students read every closed loop as a heat engine without checking the sense of traversal.

subtopic: Total heat absorbed in a cycle
concept_tested: Stage by stage analysis of a rectangular cycle
stem: One sample of a monatomic ideal gas is taken clockwise round a rectangular cycle whose corners are at pressures 1 x 10^5 Pa and 3 x 10^5 Pa and volumes 1 x 10^-3 m^3 and 3 x 10^-3 m^3. The total heat absorbed by the gas during those stages in which it takes in heat is
solution: The four corner values of the product of pressure and volume are 100 J, 300 J, 900 J and 300 J. Heating at the fixed smaller volume gives dQ = (3/2)(300 minus 100) = 300 J. Expansion at 3 x 10^5 Pa gives dU = (3/2)(900 minus 300) = 900 J and W = 600 J, so dQ = 1500 J. The other two stages both reject heat. Hence the total heat taken in is 300 plus 1500 = 1800 J.
formula_principle: For each stage use dU = (3/2) d(P V) and dW = P dV, then dQ = dU + dW.
common_misconception: Students take the enclosed area as the heat absorbed rather than as the difference between heat absorbed and heat rejected.

concept_tested: Net work from a triangular loop
stem: A gas is carried round a triangular cycle whose corners are at the states with pressure 1 x 10^5 Pa and volume 1 x 10^-3 m^3, pressure 3 x 10^5 Pa and volume 1 x 10^-3 m^3, and pressure 1 x 10^5 Pa and volume 3 x 10^-3 m^3, taken in that order and back to the first. The net work per cycle is
solution: The triangle has a vertical side of height 2 x 10^5 Pa and a horizontal side of length 2 x 10^-3 m^3, so its area is one half of 2 x 10^5 x 2 x 10^-3 = 200 J. Along the sloping side the gas expands, doing (3 x 10^5 plus 1 x 10^5)/2 x 2 x 10^-3 = 400 J, and along the return at 1 x 10^5 Pa the surroundings do 200 J on the gas, leaving 200 J of net work done by the gas.
formula_principle: Net work equals the enclosed area; for a right triangle this is half the base times the height.
common_misconception: Students use the full rectangle area rather than half of it for a triangular loop.

concept_tested: Second law in engine language
stem: According to the Kelvin Planck statement of the second law of thermodynamics, it is impossible to construct a device that, working in a cycle,
option_a: takes heat from a single reservoir and converts all of it into work
option_b: takes heat from a hot reservoir and converts part of it into work
option_c: takes in work and delivers heat to a hot reservoir
option_d: takes heat from a hot reservoir and rejects part of it to a cold reservoir
correct_answer_text: takes heat from a single reservoir and converts all of it into work
solution: A heat engine must reject some heat to a colder body. A device that drew heat from one reservoir alone and delivered an equal amount of work would have an efficiency of one, which the second law forbids.
formula_principle: Kelvin Planck: no cyclic device can convert heat from a single reservoir completely into work.
common_misconception: Students think the second law forbids converting any heat into work rather than converting all of it.

concept_tested: eta = 1 minus Q2/Q1
stem: A heat engine absorbs heat Q1 from a source and rejects heat Q2 to a sink in each cycle. Its efficiency is
solution: Over a cycle the internal energy is unchanged, so the net work is W = Q1 minus Q2. The efficiency is the ratio of this useful work to the heat drawn from the source, giving eta = (Q1 minus Q2) divided by Q1 = 1 minus Q2 divided by Q1.
formula_principle: eta = W divided by Q1 with W = Q1 minus Q2, so eta = 1 minus Q2/Q1.
common_misconception: Students invert the ratio of the two heats in the efficiency expression.

concept_tested: Source, working substance and sink
stem: Every heat engine working in a cycle must have
option_a: a hot source and a working substance, with no need for a sink
option_b: a cold sink and a working substance, with no need for a source
option_c: a hot source, a working substance and a cold sink
option_d: a hot source and a cold sink, with no need for a working substance
correct_answer_text: a hot source, a working substance and a cold sink
solution: Heat is drawn from the source, part of it is converted into work by the working substance, and the remainder must be given to a sink at a lower temperature so that the working substance can return to its initial state.
formula_principle: A heat engine needs two reservoirs at different temperatures and a working substance taken round a cycle.
common_misconception: Students think that a sufficiently well designed engine can dispense with the sink.

concept_tested: Second law in refrigerator language
stem: The Clausius statement of the second law of thermodynamics says that it is impossible for a self acting device, working in a cycle and unaided by any external agency, to
option_a: transfer heat from a colder body to a hotter body
option_b: transfer heat from a hotter body to a colder body
option_d: keep two bodies at different temperatures in permanent contact
correct_answer_text: transfer heat from a colder body to a hotter body
solution: A refrigerator does move heat from a colder region to a warmer one, but only because external work is supplied by the compressor. Without that external agency the transfer is impossible.
formula_principle: Clausius: heat cannot flow on its own from a colder to a hotter body without external work.
common_misconception: Students think the Clausius statement forbids refrigerators altogether.

concept_tested: Computing eta and W
stem: In each cycle a heat engine absorbs 500 J from a source and rejects 300 J to a sink. Its efficiency and the work obtained per cycle are
solution: The work per cycle is 500 minus 300 = 200 J. The efficiency is 200 divided by 500 = 0.4, that is 40 per cent.
formula_principle: W = Q1 minus Q2 and eta = W divided by Q1.
common_misconception: Students divide the work by the rejected heat instead of by the heat absorbed.

subtopic: Why efficiency is less than one
concept_tested: Necessity of rejecting heat
stem: The efficiency of a practical heat engine is always less than one because
option_a: the first law of thermodynamics forbids the complete conversion of heat into work
option_b: some heat must always be rejected to the sink for the cycle to be completed
option_c: the work done by the engine is always stored partly as internal energy of the gas
option_d: the heat absorbed from the source is always smaller than the work obtained
correct_answer_text: some heat must always be rejected to the sink for the cycle to be completed
solution: For the working substance to return to its initial state, part of the absorbed heat must be given up to a colder body. Since Q2 is never zero, the efficiency 1 minus Q2 divided by Q1 is always less than one. This restriction comes from the second law, not from the first.
formula_principle: eta = 1 minus Q2/Q1 with Q2 greater than zero, a requirement of the second law.
common_misconception: Students attribute the limitation on efficiency to the first law or to friction alone.

subtopic: Work and rejected heat from efficiency
concept_tested: Using eta to find W and Q2
stem: An engine of efficiency 25 per cent absorbs 800 J of heat in each cycle. The work done and the heat rejected per cycle are
solution: The work per cycle is 0.25 x 800 = 200 J. The heat rejected is 800 minus 200 = 600 J.
formula_principle: W = eta Q1 and Q2 = Q1 minus W.
common_misconception: Students apply the efficiency to the rejected heat instead of to the absorbed heat.

concept_tested: Second law adds a restriction the first law does not
stem: A machine is proposed that in each cycle draws 500 J of heat from the sea and delivers 500 J of work, rejecting nothing. Such a machine
option_a: violates the first law but satisfies the second law
option_b: satisfies the first law but violates the second law
option_c: violates both the first law and the second law
option_d: satisfies both laws and can in principle be built
correct_answer_text: satisfies the first law but violates the second law
solution: The proposal balances energy exactly, so the first law is respected. However it uses only one reservoir and rejects no heat, so its efficiency would be one, which the Kelvin Planck statement of the second law forbids. Such a device is called a perpetual motion machine of the second kind.
formula_principle: Kelvin Planck rules out complete conversion of heat from a single reservoir into work, even though energy is conserved.
common_misconception: Students look only at the energy balance and conclude that the machine is possible.

concept_tested: Why heat is rejected in every cycle
stem: In a heat engine, the purpose served by rejecting heat to the sink is that it
option_a: increases the work obtained from the engine in each cycle
option_b: keeps the internal energy of the working substance rising steadily
option_c: brings the working substance back to its initial state so that the cycle can repeat
option_d: compensates for the energy lost as friction in the moving parts
correct_answer_text: brings the working substance back to its initial state so that the cycle can repeat
solution: After expanding and doing work the working substance must be brought back to its starting state before the next cycle. Compressing it along the same path would use up all the work gained, so it is compressed at a lower temperature, which requires heat to be given up to the sink.
formula_principle: A cyclic device must restore its working substance to the initial state, which requires rejecting heat.
common_misconception: Students see the rejected heat purely as an avoidable practical loss rather than a necessity of cyclic operation.

subtopic: Heat input from work and efficiency
concept_tested: Reversing the efficiency relation
stem: An engine of efficiency 25 per cent delivers 300 J of work in each cycle. The heat absorbed from the source and the heat rejected to the sink per cycle are
solution: The heat absorbed is 300 divided by 0.25 = 1200 J. The heat rejected is 1200 minus 300 = 900 J.
formula_principle: Q1 = W divided by eta and Q2 = Q1 minus W.
common_misconception: Students multiply the work by the efficiency instead of dividing by it.

subtopic: Efficiency from work and rejected heat
concept_tested: Finding eta when Q2 and W are given
stem: In each cycle an engine delivers 200 J of work and rejects 300 J of heat to the sink. Its efficiency is
solution: The heat absorbed must be 200 plus 300 = 500 J. Hence the efficiency is 200 divided by 500 = 0.4, that is 40 per cent.
formula_principle: Q1 = W plus Q2, then eta = W divided by Q1.
common_misconception: Students take the rejected heat as the heat input when computing the efficiency.

concept_tested: Kelvin Planck and Clausius are equivalent
stem: Suppose a device existed that could take heat from a single reservoir and convert all of it into work. Coupling this device to an ordinary refrigerator would then make it possible to
option_a: create energy out of nothing, contradicting the first law
option_b: build a refrigerator whose coefficient of performance is exactly one
option_c: raise the efficiency of the refrigerator above that of a Carnot engine working between the same temperatures
option_d: move heat from a colder body to a hotter body with no external work, contradicting the Clausius statement
correct_answer_text: move heat from a colder body to a hotter body with no external work, contradicting the Clausius statement
solution: The work produced by the hypothetical device could be fed straight into the refrigerator, which would then pump heat from the cold body to the hot body. The net result of the combination would be a transfer of heat from cold to hot with no external agency, which the Clausius statement forbids. Hence violating one statement violates the other.
formula_principle: The Kelvin Planck and Clausius statements of the second law imply each other.
common_misconception: Students treat the two statements as unrelated assertions rather than as equivalent forms of one law.

concept_tested: Rate of heat intake from work per cycle
stem: An engine of efficiency 20 per cent completes 10 cycles per second and delivers 400 J of work in each cycle. The rate at which it absorbs heat from the source is
solution: The mechanical power is 400 x 10 = 4000 W. Since the efficiency is 0.2, the rate of heat intake is 4000 divided by 0.2 = 20000 W, that is 20 kW. The rate of heat rejection is then 16 kW.
formula_principle: Power output = W times cycles per second; heat input rate = power output divided by eta.
common_misconception: Students report the mechanical power when asked for the rate of heat intake.

concept_tested: Irreversibility
stem: A drop of ink spreads through a glass of water but is never observed to gather back into a drop. This one way character of the process is accounted for by
option_d: the law of conservation of linear momentum
solution: Gathering the spread ink back into a drop would not create or destroy any energy, so the first law permits it. The second law, through the requirement that disorder in an isolated system does not decrease, is what makes the process one way.
formula_principle: The second law selects a preferred direction for natural processes; energy conservation alone does not.
common_misconception: Students think energy conservation alone explains why processes run one way.

concept_tested: Combining efficiency, cycles and heat rates
stem: An engine takes in 1000 J of heat in each cycle at an efficiency of 30 per cent and runs at 5 cycles per second. The mechanical power delivered and the rate at which heat is rejected are
solution: Per cycle the work is 0.3 x 1000 = 300 J and the heat rejected is 700 J. At 5 cycles per second the power delivered is 300 x 5 = 1500 W and the rate of heat rejection is 700 x 5 = 3500 W. The total heat intake rate is 5000 W, which balances the two.
formula_principle: Power = eta Q1 times cycles per second; heat rejection rate = (1 minus eta) Q1 times cycles per second.
common_misconception: Students give per cycle values when a rate is asked for.

concept_tested: Overall efficiency of a compound arrangement
stem: The heat rejected by an engine of efficiency 40 per cent is fed entirely to a second engine of efficiency 25 per cent. If the first engine takes in 1000 J, the total work delivered by the two engines together is
solution: The first engine delivers 0.4 x 1000 = 400 J and rejects 600 J. The second engine receives 600 J and delivers 0.25 x 600 = 150 J. The total work is 400 plus 150 = 550 J, so the overall efficiency of the pair is 55 per cent.
formula_principle: Work of each stage is its efficiency times the heat it receives; the second stage receives the heat rejected by the first.
common_misconception: Students add the two efficiencies directly instead of applying the second one to the heat actually passed on.

concept_tested: eta = 1 minus T2/T1
stem: A Carnot engine works between a source at absolute temperature T1 and a sink at absolute temperature T2. Its efficiency is
solution: In a Carnot cycle the ratio of the heats exchanged equals the ratio of the absolute temperatures of the two reservoirs. Substituting this into eta = 1 minus Q2 divided by Q1 gives eta = 1 minus T2 divided by T1.
formula_principle: For a Carnot cycle Q2 divided by Q1 equals T2 divided by T1, so eta = 1 minus T2/T1.
common_misconception: Students invert the temperature ratio or put the sink temperature in the denominator.

concept_tested: Efficiency from two absolute temperatures
stem: A Carnot engine operates between a source at 500 K and a sink at 300 K. Its efficiency is
solution: Here eta = 1 minus 300 divided by 500 = 1 minus 0.6 = 0.4, that is 40 per cent.
formula_principle: eta = 1 minus T2 divided by T1 with both temperatures in kelvin.
common_misconception: Students report the ratio T2 divided by T1 as the efficiency.

concept_tested: Converting celsius to kelvin
stem: A Carnot engine works between a source at 127 degree celsius and a sink at 27 degree celsius. Its efficiency is
solution: The source is at 127 plus 273 = 400 K and the sink at 27 plus 273 = 300 K. Then eta = 1 minus 300 divided by 400 = 0.25, that is 25 per cent.
formula_principle: eta = 1 minus T2/T1 with T in kelvin; T in kelvin equals the celsius reading plus 273.
common_misconception: Students substitute celsius readings straight into the Carnot efficiency expression.

concept_tested: Two isothermal and two adiabatic stages
stem: The Carnot cycle consists of
option_a: two isobaric stages and two isochoric stages taken alternately
option_b: two isothermal stages and two adiabatic stages taken alternately
option_c: two isothermal stages and two isochoric stages taken alternately
option_d: two adiabatic stages and two isobaric stages taken alternately
correct_answer_text: two isothermal stages and two adiabatic stages taken alternately
solution: Heat is taken in only during the isothermal expansion at the source temperature and given out only during the isothermal compression at the sink temperature. The two adiabatic stages carry the working substance between the two temperatures without any heat exchange, which keeps the cycle reversible.
formula_principle: Carnot cycle: isothermal expansion, adiabatic expansion, isothermal compression, adiabatic compression.
common_misconception: Students describe the Carnot cycle as a rectangle of isobars and isochors.

concept_tested: Reversing the efficiency relation
stem: A Carnot engine with its sink at 300 K has an efficiency of 50 per cent. To raise the efficiency to 60 per cent while keeping the same sink, the source temperature must be raised from
solution: For an efficiency of 0.5 the source must satisfy 300 divided by T1 = 0.5, so T1 = 600 K. For an efficiency of 0.6 we need 300 divided by T1 = 0.4, so T1 = 750 K. The source temperature must therefore be raised from 600 K to 750 K.
formula_principle: T1 = T2 divided by (1 minus eta).
common_misconception: Students scale the source temperature in proportion to the required efficiency.

concept_tested: Efficiency one needs a sink at absolute zero
stem: A Carnot engine could have an efficiency of 100 per cent only if
option_a: its sink were at the absolute zero of temperature, which cannot be attained
option_b: its source were at the absolute zero of temperature, which cannot be attained
option_c: its working substance had no friction and no heat leaked from the cylinder
option_d: the source and the sink were at the same temperature
correct_answer_text: its sink were at the absolute zero of temperature, which cannot be attained
solution: The Carnot efficiency reaches one only when the sink temperature T2 is zero on the absolute scale. Since absolute zero cannot be reached, no engine, however perfectly built, can convert the whole of the absorbed heat into work.
formula_principle: eta = 1 minus T2/T1 equals one only if T2 = 0 K, which is unattainable.
common_misconception: Students believe perfect engineering and zero friction would allow 100 per cent efficiency.

subtopic: Heat exchanges in a Carnot cycle
concept_tested: Ratio of heats equals ratio of temperatures
stem: A Carnot engine working between 500 K and 300 K absorbs 1000 J of heat from the source in each cycle. The work done and the heat rejected per cycle are
solution: The efficiency is 1 minus 300 divided by 500 = 0.4. So the work is 0.4 x 1000 = 400 J and the heat rejected is 1000 minus 400 = 600 J. As a check, Q2 divided by Q1 = 600 divided by 1000 = 0.6, which equals T2 divided by T1.
formula_principle: eta = 1 minus T2/T1, W = eta Q1, and Q2 = Q1 minus W.
common_misconception: Students compute the efficiency correctly but then assign the larger share to the work.

concept_tested: Which change helps more
stem: A Carnot engine works between a source at 500 K and a sink at 300 K. Consider raising the source temperature by 50 K and, as an alternative, lowering the sink temperature by 50 K. Compared with the original efficiency of 40 per cent, these two changes give
option_a: about 45.5 per cent and 50 per cent respectively, so lowering the sink helps more
option_b: about 50 per cent and 45.5 per cent respectively, so raising the source helps more
option_c: 50 per cent in both cases, since the temperature difference is the same either way
option_d: about 45.5 per cent in both cases, since only the ratio of the change to the source matters
correct_answer_text: about 45.5 per cent and 50 per cent respectively, so lowering the sink helps more
solution: Raising the source gives eta = 1 minus 300 divided by 550 = 1 minus 0.545 = 0.455, about 45.5 per cent. Lowering the sink gives eta = 1 minus 250 divided by 500 = 1 minus 0.5 = 0.5, that is 50 per cent. Hence lowering the sink temperature by a given amount is the more effective of the two changes.
formula_principle: eta = 1 minus T2/T1; changing T2 alters both the numerator and the denominator of the ratio while changing T1 alters only the denominator.
common_misconception: Students assume that equal changes in the two temperatures must produce equal gains in efficiency because the difference is the same.

concept_tested: Definition of the coefficient of performance
stem: The coefficient of performance of a refrigerator is defined as the ratio of
option_a: the work supplied to the heat removed from the cold body
option_b: the heat removed from the cold body to the work supplied
option_c: the heat delivered to the hot body to the heat removed from the cold body
option_d: the heat removed from the cold body to the heat delivered to the hot body
correct_answer_text: the heat removed from the cold body to the work supplied
solution: The useful effect of a refrigerator is the heat drawn out of the cold interior, and the cost is the work supplied by the compressor. The coefficient of performance is therefore the ratio of that heat to that work, and unlike an efficiency it can exceed one.
formula_principle: Coefficient of performance = Q2 divided by W, where Q2 is the heat drawn from the cold body.
common_misconception: Students define the coefficient of performance as an efficiency and expect it to be less than one.

concept_tested: COP = T2 divided by (T1 minus T2)
stem: An ideal refrigerator keeps its interior at 270 K while rejecting heat to a room at 300 K. Its coefficient of performance is
solution: Here T2 = 270 K and T1 minus T2 = 30 K, so the coefficient of performance is 270 divided by 30 = 9. For every joule of work supplied, 9 J of heat is drawn from the interior.
formula_principle: For an ideal refrigerator, coefficient of performance = T2 divided by (T1 minus T2).
common_misconception: Students place the hot reservoir temperature in the numerator, which belongs to a heat pump.

concept_tested: COP = (1 minus eta) divided by eta
stem: A Carnot engine working between two reservoirs has an efficiency of 20 per cent. If the same cycle is run in reverse as a refrigerator between the same two reservoirs, its coefficient of performance is
solution: With eta = 0.2, the ratio Q2 divided by Q1 is 0.8 and W divided by Q1 is 0.2. Hence the coefficient of performance is 0.8 divided by 0.2 = 4.
formula_principle: Coefficient of performance of a refrigerator = Q2 divided by W = (1 minus eta) divided by eta.
common_misconception: Students quote the reciprocal of the efficiency, which is the heat pump value and exceeds the refrigerator value by one.

concept_tested: Energy balance in a reversed cycle
stem: In each cycle a refrigerator removes 300 J of heat from its cold interior while 100 J of work is supplied to it. Its coefficient of performance and the heat delivered to the room per cycle are
