solution: The coefficient of performance is 300 divided by 100 = 3. Since the internal energy of the working substance is unchanged over a cycle, the heat delivered to the room is 300 plus 100 = 400 J.
formula_principle: Coefficient of performance = Q2 divided by W; energy balance gives Q1 = Q2 plus W.
common_misconception: Students forget that the work supplied also ends up as heat delivered to the room.

concept_tested: Two coefficients differ by one
stem: For a reversed Carnot cycle working between the same two reservoirs, the coefficient of performance of a heat pump compared with that of a refrigerator is
option_b: larger by exactly the efficiency of the corresponding engine
option_d: the same, since the same cycle is being described in two ways
solution: Since Q1 = Q2 plus W, dividing by W gives Q1 divided by W = Q2 divided by W plus 1. In terms of temperatures, T1 divided by (T1 minus T2) minus T2 divided by (T1 minus T2) = 1. Hence the heat pump value always exceeds the refrigerator value by one.
formula_principle: Heat pump coefficient = Q1/W = T1/(T1 minus T2); refrigerator coefficient = Q2/W = T2/(T1 minus T2).
common_misconception: Students treat the two coefficients as identical because the same machine is involved.

concept_tested: Power required by an ideal refrigerator
stem: An ideal refrigerator maintains a cold chamber at 250 K while rejecting heat to surroundings at 300 K, and it removes heat from the chamber at the rate of 1000 J per second. The power that must be supplied to it and the rate at which heat is delivered to the surroundings are
solution: The coefficient of performance is 250 divided by 50 = 5. The power required is 1000 divided by 5 = 200 W. The rate at which heat is delivered to the surroundings is 1000 plus 200 = 1200 W.
formula_principle: Coefficient of performance = T2 divided by (T1 minus T2); W rate = Q2 rate divided by the coefficient; Q1 rate = Q2 rate plus W rate.
common_misconception: Students multiply by the coefficient of performance instead of dividing, or omit the work from the heat delivered.

concept_tested: Direction of restoring force in linear SHM
stem: In linear simple harmonic motion, the restoring force acting on the particle is always directed
option_a: along the instantaneous displacement of the particle
option_c: along the direction of motion of the particle
solution: The defining property of linear SHM is F = -k x. The negative sign means that whatever the sign of x, the force has the opposite sign, so it always points back to the point where x = 0, that is, the mean position.
formula_principle: F = -k x, the restoring force is proportional to displacement and opposite in direction
common_misconception: Students often assume the force acts in the direction of motion, forgetting that from mean to extreme the particle slows down because force opposes motion.

concept_tested: Relation a = -omega^2 x
stem: For a particle performing linear SHM, the acceleration is
option_a: directly proportional to the displacement and in the same direction as it
option_b: directly proportional to the displacement and opposite in direction to it
option_c: inversely proportional to the displacement and opposite in direction to it
option_d: directly proportional to the square of the displacement
correct_answer_text: directly proportional to the displacement and opposite in direction to it
solution: Dividing F = -k x by the mass m gives a = -(k/m) x = -omega^2 x. So the magnitude of acceleration grows in direct proportion to x, and its sign is always opposite to that of x.
formula_principle: a = -omega^2 x for linear SHM
common_misconception: Learners recall a proportional to x but forget the sign, and then cannot explain why the particle turns back at the extreme positions.

concept_tested: Differential equation of linear SHM
stem: The differential equation of linear simple harmonic motion is
solution: Acceleration is the second derivative of displacement. Substituting a = -omega^2 x gives d^2x/dt^2 = -omega^2 x, which on rearranging becomes d^2x/dt^2 + omega^2 x = 0.
formula_principle: a = d^2x/dt^2 = -omega^2 x, hence d^2x/dt^2 + omega^2 x = 0
common_misconception: The minus sign is often shifted to the wrong side, giving an equation whose solutions are exponentials rather than sines and cosines.

concept_tested: SI unit of force constant
stem: The SI unit of the force constant k appearing in F = -k x is
solution: From F = -k x, the magnitude of k is force divided by displacement. Force is measured in N and displacement in m, so k is measured in N per m, written N m^-1.
formula_principle: k = magnitude of F divided by x
common_misconception: Students sometimes quote N m because they associate k with energy stored in a spring rather than with the defining ratio of force to displacement.

concept_tested: Numerical use of F = -k x
stem: A particle performing SHM has a force constant of 200 N m^-1. The magnitude of the restoring force when the displacement is 0.05 m is
solution: Magnitude of F = k x = 200 x 0.05 = 10 N. The direction is towards the mean position.
formula_principle: Magnitude of F = k x
common_misconception: The one half that belongs to the potential energy expression is often carried into the force expression by mistake.

concept_tested: Positions of maximum and zero acceleration
stem: Which of the following statements about a particle performing linear SHM is correct?
option_a: The magnitude of acceleration is maximum at the mean position and zero at the extreme positions
option_b: The acceleration and the speed are both maximum at the same position
option_c: The acceleration is constant in magnitude throughout the motion
option_d: The magnitude of acceleration is maximum at the extreme positions and zero at the mean position
correct_answer_text: The magnitude of acceleration is maximum at the extreme positions and zero at the mean position
solution: Since the magnitude of acceleration is omega^2 times the magnitude of x, it is largest where x is largest, that is at x equal to plus or minus A, and it is zero where x = 0, the mean position.
formula_principle: a = -omega^2 x, so magnitude of a is proportional to magnitude of x
common_misconception: Speed and acceleration are frequently assumed to peak together, whereas in SHM one is maximum exactly where the other is zero.

concept_tested: State of motion at the mean position
stem: As a particle performing SHM passes through the mean position, its
option_a: speed is zero and acceleration is maximum
option_b: speed is maximum and acceleration is zero
option_c: speed and acceleration are both maximum
option_d: speed and acceleration are both zero
correct_answer_text: speed is maximum and acceleration is zero
solution: Putting x = 0 gives v = omega sqrt(A^2) = A omega, the largest possible speed, and a = -omega^2 x = 0.
formula_principle: v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2) and a = -omega^2 x
common_misconception: The mean and extreme positions are often interchanged when recalling where speed and acceleration take extreme values.

concept_tested: Dimensions of angular frequency
stem: The dimensional formula of the angular frequency omega of a particle performing SHM is
solution: omega is an angle divided by time. Angle in radian is dimensionless, so omega has the dimensions of the reciprocal of time, that is M^0 L^0 T^-1, measured in rad s^-1.
formula_principle: omega = 2 pi / T, and angle is dimensionless
common_misconception: Because omega^2 appears in a = -omega^2 x, students sometimes assign the dimensions of omega^2 to omega itself.

concept_tested: Extracting omega from a = -omega^2 x
stem: The acceleration of a particle performing SHM is given by a = -16 x, where a is in m s^-2 and x is in m. The period of the motion is
solution: Comparing a = -16 x with a = -omega^2 x gives omega^2 = 16, so omega = 4 rad s^-1. Then T = 2 pi / omega = 2 pi / 4 = pi/2 s, which is about 1.57 s.
formula_principle: Compare a = -omega^2 x with the given relation, then T = 2 pi / omega
common_misconception: The coefficient of x is omega^2 and not omega; forgetting the square root doubles or quarters the answer.

concept_tested: Testing whether a motion is simple harmonic
stem: A particle moves along a straight line such that its acceleration is a = -k x^3, where k is a positive constant and x is the displacement from a fixed point. The motion is
option_a: oscillatory and periodic but not simple harmonic
option_b: simple harmonic with angular frequency equal to sqrt(k)
option_d: simple harmonic with a period that depends on k alone
correct_answer_text: oscillatory and periodic but not simple harmonic
solution: The acceleration is directed towards x = 0 because of the negative sign, so the particle oscillates about x = 0. However SHM demands a = -omega^2 x, a first power relation. Here a varies as the cube of x, so the motion is oscillatory and periodic but not simple harmonic.
formula_principle: SHM requires a proportional to x to the first power, with a negative sign
common_misconception: Any restoring type acceleration is often labelled SHM, but only the first power dependence gives sinusoidal motion with an amplitude independent period.

concept_tested: Linear SHM as a projection of uniform circular motion
stem: Linear simple harmonic motion can be described as the motion of
option_a: the projection of a particle in uniform circular motion on the tangent to the reference circle
option_b: the projection of a uniformly accelerated straight line motion on a diameter
option_c: the projection of a particle in uniform circular motion on any diameter of the reference circle
option_d: a particle moving on a circle with uniformly increasing speed
correct_answer_text: the projection of a particle in uniform circular motion on any diameter of the reference circle
solution: If a reference particle moves on a circle of radius A with constant angular speed omega, its position vector makes an angle omega t + phi with a chosen axis. The foot of the perpendicular from this particle to any diameter has displacement A cos(omega t + phi), which is exactly linear SHM of amplitude A.
formula_principle: x = A cos(omega t + phi) is the projection of uniform circular motion of radius A
common_misconception: The reference circle is often thought to be the actual path of the oscillating particle, whereas only the projection performs SHM.

concept_tested: Meaning of the ratio k over m
stem: For a particle of mass m performing SHM under a restoring force of force constant k, the ratio k/m is equal to
solution: Newton second law gives m a = -k x, so a = -(k/m) x. Comparing with a = -omega^2 x shows that omega^2 = k/m, so omega = sqrt(k/m) and T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k).
formula_principle: a = -(k/m) x compared with a = -omega^2 x
common_misconception: Students sometimes write omega = k/m directly, which is dimensionally impossible and gives wrong periods.

concept_tested: Period from a given force law
stem: A body of mass 2 kg experiences a restoring force F = -8 x N, where x is in m. The period of its oscillation is
solution: Here k = 8 N m^-1 and m = 2 kg, so omega^2 = k/m = 8/2 = 4 and omega = 2 rad s^-1. Then T = 2 pi / omega = 2 pi / 2 = pi s, which is about 3.14 s.
formula_principle: omega = sqrt(k/m) and T = 2 pi / omega
common_misconception: The mass is often ignored, so that the coefficient of x alone is taken as omega^2.

concept_tested: Necessary and sufficient condition for linear SHM
stem: The necessary and sufficient condition for a particle to perform linear SHM is that
option_a: the speed of the particle remains constant throughout the motion
option_b: the net force on it is constant in magnitude and always directed towards the mean position
option_c: the net force on it is proportional to its displacement from the mean position and is directed opposite to that displacement
option_d: the particle moves along a circular path with constant angular speed
correct_answer_text: the net force on it is proportional to its displacement from the mean position and is directed opposite to that displacement
solution: SHM is defined by F = -k x with k positive. This single condition guarantees a = -omega^2 x, sinusoidal displacement, and a period independent of amplitude.
formula_principle: F = -k x is the defining condition of linear SHM
common_misconception: Motion that merely repeats is often called SHM, but periodicity alone is not sufficient.

concept_tested: Comparing accelerations at two displacements
stem: A particle performs SHM of amplitude A. The ratio of the magnitude of its acceleration at x = A/2 to that at x = A is
solution: Magnitude of acceleration at A/2 is omega^2 A/2 and at A it is omega^2 A. Their ratio is (omega^2 A/2) divided by (omega^2 A), which equals 1/2, that is 1 : 2.
formula_principle: Magnitude of a = omega^2 x
common_misconception: The square in omega^2 is sometimes wrongly attached to x as well, producing a ratio of 1 : 4.

concept_tested: Maximum restoring force in SHM
stem: A particle of mass 0.1 kg performs SHM of amplitude 0.05 m with angular frequency 20 rad s^-1. The maximum restoring force acting on it is
solution: a_max = omega^2 A = 20^2 x 0.05 = 400 x 0.05 = 20 m s^-2. Maximum force = m a_max = 0.1 x 20 = 2 N.
formula_principle: Maximum force = m x a_max = m omega^2 A
common_misconception: Maximum acceleration is often quoted as the answer for maximum force because the mass factor is dropped.

concept_tested: Interpreting the acceleration versus displacement graph
stem: For a particle performing SHM, the graph of acceleration against displacement is a straight line passing through the origin with slope -100 s^-2. The frequency of the motion is
solution: The slope of the a versus x line equals -omega^2, so omega^2 = 100 and omega = 10 rad s^-1. Then f = omega / (2 pi) = 10 / (2 pi) = 5/pi Hz, which is about 1.59 Hz.
formula_principle: a = -omega^2 x, so slope = -omega^2; f = omega / (2 pi)
common_misconception: Angular frequency in rad s^-1 and frequency in Hz are treated as the same quantity, dropping the factor 2 pi.

concept_tested: Time from mean position to extreme position
stem: A particle performs SHM with acceleration a = -(4 pi^2) x m s^-2. Starting from the mean position, the time it takes to reach an extreme position for the first time is
solution: Comparing with a = -omega^2 x gives omega^2 = 4 pi^2, so omega = 2 pi rad s^-1 and T = 2 pi / (2 pi) = 1 s. The journey from the mean position to an extreme position is a quarter of a full oscillation, so the time is T/4 = 0.25 s.
formula_principle: omega^2 from the acceleration relation, T = 2 pi / omega, mean to extreme takes T/4
common_misconception: The path from mean to extreme is sometimes counted as half an oscillation, giving twice the correct time.

concept_tested: Acceleration at a given displacement
stem: A particle performs SHM of period 2 s and amplitude 5 cm. Taking pi^2 = 10, the magnitude of its acceleration when the displacement is 2.5 cm is
solution: omega = 2 pi / 2 = pi rad s^-1, so omega^2 = pi^2 = 10 s^-2. With x = 2.5 cm = 0.025 m, magnitude of a = 10 x 0.025 = 0.25 m s^-2.
formula_principle: omega = 2 pi / T and magnitude of a = omega^2 x
common_misconception: Centimetres are carried into the final SI answer, inflating the result by a factor of one hundred.

concept_tested: Time to cover half the amplitude from the mean position
stem: A particle starts from the mean position and performs SHM with acceleration a = -9 x m s^-2. The time it takes to reach a displacement equal to half the amplitude for the first time is
solution: Comparing a = -9 x with a = -omega^2 x gives omega = 3 rad s^-1. Starting from the mean position, x = A sin(3 t). Setting x = A/2 gives sin(3 t) = 0.5, so 3 t = pi/6 and t = pi/18 s, which is about 0.175 s.
formula_principle: x = A sin(omega t) for a start from the mean position, with omega from a = -omega^2 x
common_misconception: The sine form for a start at the mean position and the cosine form for a start at the extreme are interchanged, doubling the phase angle.

concept_tested: Meaning of the constant phi in the displacement equation
stem: In the equation x = A sin(omega t + phi) for linear SHM, the constant phi is called
option_a: the angular frequency of the motion
option_b: the phase of the motion at time t
option_c: the initial phase or epoch of the motion
correct_answer_text: the initial phase or epoch of the motion
solution: Putting t = 0 in the phase omega t + phi leaves phi. Hence phi is the phase at the instant from which time is measured, and it is called the initial phase or epoch.
formula_principle: x = A sin(omega t + phi), where omega t + phi is the phase and phi is the phase at t = 0
common_misconception: The whole angle omega t + phi and its constant part phi are often both loosely called the phase.

concept_tested: Maximum speed in SHM
stem: A particle performs SHM of amplitude A and angular frequency omega. Its maximum speed is
solution: The velocity is v = A omega cos(omega t + phi). The cosine has a largest magnitude of one, so the largest speed is A omega, and it occurs where the cosine equals plus or minus one, that is at the mean position.
formula_principle: v = A omega cos(omega t + phi), so v_max = A omega
common_misconception: Maximum speed and maximum acceleration expressions are frequently interchanged because both contain A and omega.

concept_tested: Maximum acceleration in SHM
stem: For a particle performing SHM of amplitude A with angular frequency omega, the magnitude of the maximum acceleration is
solution: Differentiating the velocity gives a = -A omega^2 sin(omega t + phi). The largest magnitude of the sine is one, so the maximum magnitude of acceleration is A omega^2, occurring at the extreme positions.
formula_principle: a = -A omega^2 sin(omega t + phi), so magnitude of a_max = A omega^2
common_misconception: The number of powers of omega in the velocity and acceleration expressions is easily mixed up.

concept_tested: Phase difference between displacement and velocity
stem: In SHM, the phase difference between the displacement and the velocity of the particle is
solution: Writing the velocity as A omega sin(omega t + pi/2) shows that its phase exceeds that of the displacement by pi/2 rad, which is a quarter of a cycle.
formula_principle: x = A sin(omega t) and v = A omega cos(omega t) = A omega sin(omega t + pi/2)
common_misconception: The pi rad separation of displacement and acceleration is often quoted for velocity as well.

concept_tested: Using v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2)
stem: For SHM of amplitude A and angular frequency omega, the speed of the particle at the mean position obtained from v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2) is
solution: At the mean position x = 0, so v = omega sqrt(A^2 - 0) = omega A. This is the largest speed reached during the oscillation.
formula_principle: v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2)
common_misconception: The mean position is sometimes taken as x = A, giving zero speed where in fact the speed is greatest.

concept_tested: Maximum speed from a given displacement equation
stem: The displacement of a particle is x = 5 sin(4 t) cm, with t in second. Its maximum speed is
solution: Comparing with x = A sin(omega t) gives A = 5 cm and omega = 4 rad s^-1. Hence v_max = A omega = 5 x 4 = 20 cm s^-1.
formula_principle: v_max = A omega
common_misconception: The number multiplying t inside the sine is sometimes read as the frequency in Hz rather than as omega in rad s^-1.

concept_tested: Maximum acceleration from a given displacement equation
stem: A particle moves according to x = 0.2 sin(10 t + pi/3) m, with t in second. The magnitude of its maximum acceleration is
solution: Here A = 0.2 m and omega = 10 rad s^-1, so omega^2 = 100 s^-2. Magnitude of a_max = A omega^2 = 0.2 x 100 = 20 m s^-2. The epoch pi/3 does not affect the maximum value.
formula_principle: Magnitude of a_max = A omega^2
common_misconception: The epoch is sometimes thought to change the maximum values, whereas it only shifts the instants at which they occur.

concept_tested: Speed at a given displacement
stem: A particle performing SHM has amplitude 10 cm and angular frequency 2 rad s^-1. Its speed when the displacement is 6 cm is
formula_principle: v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2)
common_misconception: The difference A^2 minus x^2 is sometimes written as (A - x)^2, which gives a different and wrong value.

concept_tested: Phase difference between velocity and acceleration
stem: In SHM, the acceleration leads the velocity in phase by
solution: If x = A sin(omega t), then v = A omega sin(omega t + pi/2) and a = A omega^2 sin(omega t + pi). Subtracting the phase of v from the phase of a gives pi minus pi/2, which is pi/2 rad.
formula_principle: Each differentiation of a sinusoid advances the phase by pi/2
common_misconception: The phase separations of the three quantities are memorised as one number instead of a quarter cycle step at each differentiation.

concept_tested: Choosing the correct form for a given starting point
stem: A particle performing SHM of amplitude A starts from an extreme position at t = 0. Its displacement at any later time t is best written as
solution: At an extreme position the displacement equals the amplitude. Substituting t = 0 in x = A cos(omega t) gives x = A, which matches the stated start. The other forms give x = 0 at t = 0.
formula_principle: The epoch is fixed by the displacement at t = 0
common_misconception: The sine form is used automatically for every problem, regardless of where the timing actually begins.

concept_tested: Amplitude of a sum of a sine and a cosine of the same frequency
stem: The displacement of a particle is x = 3 sin(pi t) + 4 cos(pi t) cm. The amplitude of the resulting SHM is
solution: The two terms have the same angular frequency pi rad s^-1 but differ in phase by pi/2, so they combine like perpendicular vectors. The resultant amplitude is sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5 cm.
formula_principle: For a sin(omega t) + b cos(omega t), the resultant amplitude is sqrt(a^2 + b^2)
common_misconception: Amplitudes of terms with a phase difference are added arithmetically instead of being combined using the square root of the sum of squares.

concept_tested: Displacement at which the speed is half its maximum
stem: A particle performs SHM of amplitude A. Its speed becomes half of its maximum value at a displacement of
solution: Setting omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2) = (1/2) A omega gives sqrt(A^2 - x^2) = A/2. Squaring, A^2 - x^2 = A^2/4, so x^2 = (3/4) A^2 and x = (sqrt(3)/2) A, about 0.87 A.
formula_principle: v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2) with v = (1/2) A omega
common_misconception: The velocity is assumed to vary linearly with displacement, whereas the relation involves a square root.

concept_tested: Ordering of displacement, velocity and acceleration in phase
stem: Which statement correctly describes the phase relations in linear SHM?
option_a: Velocity leads displacement by pi/2 rad and acceleration leads velocity by pi/2 rad
option_b: Displacement leads velocity by pi/2 rad and velocity leads acceleration by pi/2 rad
option_c: Velocity and acceleration are in phase with each other
option_d: Acceleration leads displacement by pi/2 rad
correct_answer_text: Velocity leads displacement by pi/2 rad and acceleration leads velocity by pi/2 rad
solution: Each differentiation with respect to time advances the phase of a sinusoid by pi/2. Hence velocity is ahead of displacement by pi/2 and acceleration is ahead of velocity by a further pi/2, making it pi ahead of displacement.
formula_principle: x = A sin(omega t), v = A omega sin(omega t + pi/2), a = A omega^2 sin(omega t + pi)
common_misconception: Leading and lagging are swapped, so students place displacement ahead of velocity.

concept_tested: Ratio of speed at half amplitude to maximum speed
stem: For a particle in SHM of amplitude A, the ratio of its speed at x = A/2 to its maximum speed is
solution: At x = A/2, v = omega sqrt(A^2 - A^2/4) = omega sqrt(3 A^2/4) = (sqrt(3)/2) A omega. Dividing by v_max = A omega gives sqrt(3)/2, that is sqrt(3) : 2, about 0.87 : 1.
formula_principle: v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2) and v_max = A omega
common_misconception: Energy fractions and speed fractions are confused, since kinetic energy varies as the square of the speed.

concept_tested: Time to reach a given displacement from the mean position
stem: A particle performs SHM of period 12 s and amplitude 6 cm, starting from the mean position. The time it takes to acquire a displacement of 3 cm is
solution: Here A = 6 cm and T = 12 s, so x = 6 sin(2 pi t / 12) = 6 sin(pi t / 6). Setting x = 3 cm gives sin(pi t / 6) = 0.5, so pi t / 6 = pi/6 and t = 1 s.
formula_principle: x = A sin(2 pi t / T) for a start from the mean position
common_misconception: A displacement of half the amplitude is wrongly assumed to take half the quarter period, ignoring the sine relation.

concept_tested: Shortest time between two displacements
stem: A particle performs SHM of period T and amplitude A. The shortest time it takes to move from x = A/2 to x = A is
solution: Taking the start from the mean position, x = A/2 corresponds to a phase of pi/6, reached at t1 = T/12, and x = A corresponds to a phase of pi/2, reached at t2 = T/4. The interval is T/4 minus T/12 = 3T/12 minus T/12 = 2T/12 = T/6.
formula_principle: x = A sin(2 pi t / T); compare the times at the two displacements
common_misconception: Because the last half of the amplitude is covered more slowly, students wrongly assume equal times for equal distances.

concept_tested: Reading amplitude and period from a velocity relation
stem: The motion of a particle obeys v^2 = 144 - 16 x^2, where v is in m s^-1 and x is in m. The amplitude and the period of the motion are
solution: Comparing coefficients, omega^2 = 16 so omega = 4 rad s^-1, and omega^2 A^2 = 144 so A^2 = 144/16 = 9 and A = 3 m. The period is T = 2 pi / omega = 2 pi / 4 = pi/2 s, about 1.57 s.
formula_principle: v^2 = omega^2 (A^2 - x^2) = omega^2 A^2 - omega^2 x^2
common_misconception: The constant term is read directly as the square of the amplitude, without dividing by omega^2.

concept_tested: Speed at a given displacement with the period given
stem: A particle performs SHM of amplitude 5 cm and period 4 s. Its speed when the displacement is 3 cm is
option_d: 2 pi cm s^-1, about 6.28 cm s^-1
correct_answer_text: 2 pi cm s^-1, about 6.28 cm s^-1
solution: omega = 2 pi / 4 = pi/2 rad s^-1. Then v = (pi/2) x sqrt(5^2 - 3^2) = (pi/2) x sqrt(16) = (pi/2) x 4 = 2 pi cm s^-1, about 6.28 cm s^-1.
formula_principle: omega = 2 pi / T and v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2)
common_misconception: The quantity sqrt(A^2 - x^2) is replaced by A minus x, which underestimates the speed.

concept_tested: Maximum acceleration for a high frequency oscillation
stem: A particle oscillates according to x = 2 sin(50 pi t) cm, with t in second. Taking pi^2 = 10, the magnitude of its maximum acceleration is
option_a: pi m s^-2, about 3.14 m s^-2
solution: Here A = 2 cm = 0.02 m and omega = 50 pi rad s^-1, so omega^2 = 2500 pi^2 = 2500 x 10 = 25000 s^-2. Hence a_max = 0.02 x 25000 = 500 m s^-2.
formula_principle: Magnitude of a_max = A omega^2
common_misconception: Units are not converted before substitution, so an answer in centimetre based units is reported as if it were in SI.

concept_tested: Displacement after one sixth of a period from the extreme
stem: A particle performing SHM of amplitude A starts from an extreme position. Its displacement after a time equal to T/6 is
solution: With t = T/6, the phase is 2 pi (T/6)/T = pi/3 rad. Hence x = A cos(pi/3) = A x 0.5 = A/2.
formula_principle: x = A cos(2 pi t / T) for a start from the extreme position
common_misconception: The cosine appropriate to a start at the extreme position is replaced by a sine, which swaps the answers A/2 and 0.87 A.

concept_tested: Time interval between two specified displacements
stem: A particle performs SHM of amplitude A and period T, starting from the mean position. The time it takes to move from x = A/2 to x = (sqrt(3)/2) A while continuing to move away from the mean position is
solution: For x = A/2, sin gives a phase of pi/6. For x = (sqrt(3)/2) A, sin gives a phase of pi/3. The phase interval is pi/3 minus pi/6 = pi/6. Dividing by omega = 2 pi / T gives t = (pi/6) x T/(2 pi) = T/12.
formula_principle: x = A sin(2 pi t / T); the time interval is the phase interval divided by omega
common_misconception: The two phase angles are subtracted incorrectly, or one of them is read from a cosine instead of a sine.

concept_tested: Finding the period from two speed and displacement pairs
stem: A particle performing SHM has a speed of 4 cm s^-1 when its displacement is 3 cm, and a speed of 3 cm s^-1 when its displacement is 4 cm. The period of the motion is
solution: From the two conditions, 16 = omega^2 (A^2 - 9) and 9 = omega^2 (A^2 - 16). Subtracting gives 7 = omega^2 x 7, so omega = 1 rad s^-1. Substituting back gives A^2 = 25, that is A = 5 cm. Hence T = 2 pi / 1 = 2 pi s, about 6.28 s.
formula_principle: v^2 = omega^2 (A^2 - x^2) applied at two points, then T = 2 pi / omega
common_misconception: Students try to solve for the amplitude first, which leads to messy algebra; subtracting the two equations eliminates A^2 at once.

subtopic: Period of a spring mass system
concept_tested: Standard expression for the period
stem: The period of oscillation of a body of mass m attached to a spring of force constant k is
solution: Since omega = sqrt(k/m), the period T = 2 pi / omega = 2 pi sqrt(m/k). A heavier mass gives a longer period and a stiffer spring gives a shorter one.
formula_principle: omega = sqrt(k/m) and T = 2 pi / omega
common_misconception: The ratio m/k and k/m are frequently interchanged, which reverses the effect of stiffness on the period.

concept_tested: Relation between period and frequency
stem: A particle performing SHM completes one oscillation in 0.2 s. Its frequency is
solution: f = 1/T = 1/0.2 = 5 Hz, meaning the particle completes five oscillations every second.
formula_principle: f = 1/T
common_misconception: Frequency and angular frequency are confused, so an extra factor of 2 pi is included.

concept_tested: Relation omega = 2 pi f
stem: A tuning fork prong performs SHM at a frequency of 50 Hz. Its angular frequency is
solution: omega = 2 pi f = 2 pi x 50 = 100 pi rad s^-1, which is about 314 rad s^-1.
formula_principle: omega = 2 pi f
common_misconception: The factor 2 pi is either omitted or placed in the denominator when converting frequency to angular frequency.

concept_tested: SI unit of frequency
stem: The SI unit of frequency of an oscillation is the hertz, which is equivalent to
solution: Frequency counts oscillations per unit time. Since the oscillation count is a pure number, the unit is simply the reciprocal second, s^-1, given the special name hertz.
formula_principle: f = 1/T, so the unit of f is the reciprocal of the unit of time
common_misconception: Hertz and radian per second are treated as identical, ignoring the factor 2 pi between them.

subtopic: Period of a spring mass system
concept_tested: Numerical evaluation of the period
stem: A block of mass 0.5 kg is attached to a spring of force constant 200 N m^-1. Its period of oscillation is
solution: m/k = 0.5/200 = 0.0025 s^2, and sqrt(0.0025) = 0.05 s. Hence T = 2 pi x 0.05 = 0.1 pi s, which is about 0.314 s.
formula_principle: T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k)
common_misconception: The factor 2 pi is dropped after the square root is evaluated, giving a period about six times too small.

concept_tested: Effect of changing the mass
stem: The mass attached to a spring is made four times as large while the spring is unchanged. The period of oscillation becomes
solution: Since T is proportional to the square root of m, multiplying m by four multiplies T by sqrt(4) = 2. The period therefore doubles.
formula_principle: T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k), so T is proportional to sqrt(m)
common_misconception: The mass independence of the simple pendulum period is wrongly carried over to the spring mass system.

concept_tested: Effect of changing the spring constant
stem: The same mass is attached to a spring whose force constant is four times that of the original spring. The new period is
option_a: one quarter of the original period
option_d: the same as the original period
solution: Multiplying k by four divides T by sqrt(4) = 2. The new period is therefore half the original period.
formula_principle: T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k), so T is inversely proportional to sqrt(k)
common_misconception: The square root is dropped, so a fourfold change in stiffness is thought to change the period fourfold.

concept_tested: Simultaneous change of mass and spring constant
stem: In a spring mass oscillator both the mass and the force constant of the spring are doubled. The period of oscillation
solution: The new ratio is (2 m)/(2 k) = m/k, exactly the original ratio. Since the period depends only on this ratio, T is unchanged.
formula_principle: T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k) depends only on the ratio m/k
common_misconception: Each change is considered in isolation, so one of the two compensating effects is overlooked.

concept_tested: Independence of period from amplitude
stem: For an ideal linear oscillator, which statement about the period is correct?
option_a: The period increases in direct proportion to the amplitude
option_b: The period is independent of the amplitude of oscillation
option_c: The period decreases as the amplitude increases
option_d: The period is proportional to the square root of the amplitude
correct_answer_text: The period is independent of the amplitude of oscillation
solution: The period expression involves only the inertia and the stiffness of the system. Increasing the amplitude increases both the distance to be covered and the restoring force in the same proportion, so the time taken per oscillation does not change. This property is called isochronism.
formula_principle: T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k) contains no amplitude term
common_misconception: It seems intuitive that a longer path must take longer, but the higher speeds exactly compensate.

concept_tested: Maximum acceleration from frequency and amplitude
stem: A particle performs SHM of frequency 5 Hz and amplitude 2 cm. Taking pi^2 = 10, the magnitude of its maximum acceleration is
solution: omega = 2 pi x 5 = 10 pi rad s^-1, so omega^2 = 100 pi^2 = 100 x 10 = 1000 s^-2. With A = 2 cm = 0.02 m, a_max = 0.02 x 1000 = 20 m s^-2.
formula_principle: omega = 2 pi f and magnitude of a_max = A omega^2
common_misconception: The instruction pi^2 = 10 is applied to pi rather than to pi^2, which changes the answer by a factor of ten.

concept_tested: Angular frequency from a count of oscillations
stem: A particle completes 40 oscillations in 20 s. Its angular frequency is
option_b: 4 pi rad s^-1, about 12.6 rad s^-1
correct_answer_text: 4 pi rad s^-1, about 12.6 rad s^-1
solution: f = 40/20 = 2 Hz, so the period is 0.5 s. Then omega = 2 pi f = 2 pi x 2 = 4 pi rad s^-1, about 12.6 rad s^-1.
formula_principle: f = number of oscillations divided by time, then omega = 2 pi f
common_misconception: Frequency in hertz is reported directly as angular frequency, dropping the factor 2 pi.

subtopic: Period of a spring mass system
concept_tested: Frequency of a spring mass oscillator
stem: A body of mass 2 kg is attached to a spring of force constant 800 N m^-1. The frequency of its oscillation is
solution: omega = sqrt(800/2) = sqrt(400) = 20 rad s^-1. Then f = omega / (2 pi) = 20 / (2 pi) = 10/pi Hz, which is about 3.18 Hz.
formula_principle: omega = sqrt(k/m) and f = omega / (2 pi)
common_misconception: The step from angular frequency to frequency is skipped, leaving an answer that is 2 pi times too large.

concept_tested: Change of mass needed to halve the period
stem: A block on a spring oscillates with period T. Keeping the same spring, the mass must be changed to
option_a: one half of its original value to make the period T/2
option_b: twice its original value to make the period T/2
option_c: four times its original value to make the period T/2
option_d: one quarter of its original value to make the period T/2
correct_answer_text: one quarter of its original value to make the period T/2
solution: Since T is proportional to sqrt(m), halving T requires sqrt(m) to be halved, that is m must become one quarter of its original value. Checking, sqrt(m/4) = (1/2) sqrt(m).
formula_principle: T is proportional to sqrt(m) for a fixed spring constant
common_misconception: The square root relation is inverted, so students change the mass by a factor of two instead of four.

subtopic: Period of a spring mass system
concept_tested: Finding the force constant from the period
stem: A body of mass 200 g attached to a spring oscillates with a period of 0.4 pi s. The force constant of the spring is
solution: omega = 2 pi / (0.4 pi) = 5 rad s^-1, so omega^2 = 25 s^-2. With m = 200 g = 0.2 kg, k = m omega^2 = 0.2 x 25 = 5 N m^-1.
formula_principle: omega = 2 pi / T and k = m omega^2
common_misconception: The mass is left in gram, which makes the force constant one thousand times too large.

concept_tested: Number of oscillations per minute
stem: A particle performs SHM with acceleration a = -100 x m s^-2. The number of oscillations it completes in one minute is
solution: From a = -100 x, omega^2 = 100 so omega = 10 rad s^-1. Then f = 10/(2 pi) = 5/pi Hz. In 60 s the number of oscillations is 60 x 5/pi = 300/pi, which is about 95.
formula_principle: omega from a = -omega^2 x, then f = omega/(2 pi) and count = 60 f
common_misconception: Angular frequency is used directly as the number of oscillations per second, overcounting by a factor of 2 pi.

concept_tested: Deducing the mass from two periods
stem: A spring mass system has a period of 2 s. When an extra mass of 2 kg is attached to the same spring, the period becomes 3 s. The original mass is
solution: Squaring the ratio of periods gives (3/2)^2 = (m + 2)/m, that is 9/4 = (m + 2)/m. Cross multiplying, 9 m = 4 m + 8, so 5 m = 8 and m = 1.6 kg.
formula_principle: T is proportional to sqrt(m), so (T2/T1)^2 = (m + 2)/m
common_misconception: Periods are compared directly instead of their squares, which loses the square root in T proportional to sqrt(m).

concept_tested: Expression for the total energy in SHM
stem: The total energy of a particle of mass m performing SHM of amplitude A and angular frequency omega is
solution: At an extreme position the particle is momentarily at rest, so all the energy is potential and equals (1/2) k A^2. Writing k = m omega^2 gives E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2. This value is the same at every point of the path.
formula_principle: Total energy E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2 = (1/2) k A^2
common_misconception: The displacement x is left in place of the amplitude A, giving the potential energy rather than the constant total energy.

concept_tested: Position of maximum kinetic energy
stem: The kinetic energy of a particle performing SHM is maximum at
option_b: the position where the displacement is half the amplitude
option_d: the position where displacement is A divided by sqrt(2)
solution: The kinetic energy expression is largest when the subtracted term x^2 is smallest, that is at x = 0, the mean position, where KE equals the total energy (1/2) m omega^2 A^2.
formula_principle: KE = (1/2) m omega^2 (A^2 - x^2)
common_misconception: The extreme position is associated with maximum energy of all kinds, whereas only the potential energy peaks there.

concept_tested: Position of maximum potential energy
stem: The potential energy of a particle performing SHM is maximum at
option_b: the position midway between the mean and an extreme position
option_d: every point of the path, since it is constant
solution: The potential energy grows as the square of the displacement, so it is largest where the displacement is largest, that is at x equal to plus or minus A, where it equals the total energy.
formula_principle: PE = (1/2) m omega^2 x^2
common_misconception: Constancy of the total energy is wrongly attributed to the potential energy as well.

concept_tested: Interchange of kinetic and potential energy
stem: Which statement about the energy of a particle performing ideal SHM is correct?
option_a: The kinetic and potential energies are both constant throughout the motion
option_b: The total energy is largest at the mean position and smallest at the extremes
option_c: The kinetic and potential energies are equal at every point of the path
option_d: The kinetic and potential energies keep changing but their sum stays constant
correct_answer_text: The kinetic and potential energies keep changing but their sum stays constant
solution: Adding (1/2) m omega^2 (A^2 - x^2) and (1/2) m omega^2 x^2 gives (1/2) m omega^2 A^2, in which x does not appear. So energy is continually exchanged between the two forms while the total remains fixed.
formula_principle: KE + PE = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2, a constant
common_misconception: The constancy of the total energy is confused with constancy of each separate part.

concept_tested: Kinetic energy at half the amplitude
stem: A particle performs SHM of amplitude A and total energy E. Its kinetic energy when the displacement is A/2 is
solution: KE/E = (A^2 - x^2)/A^2. With x = A/2, this is (A^2 - A^2/4)/A^2 = (3/4). Hence KE = 3E/4, that is 75 percent of the total energy.
formula_principle: KE = (1/2) m omega^2 (A^2 - x^2) and E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2
common_misconception: Kinetic and potential fractions are swapped, since at half the amplitude the potential share is only one quarter.

concept_tested: Potential energy at half the amplitude
stem: For a particle performing SHM of amplitude A and total energy E, the potential energy at a displacement of A/2 is
solution: PE/E = (A/2)^2 divided by A^2 = (A^2/4)/A^2 = 1/4. Hence the potential energy is E/4, that is 25 percent of the total.
formula_principle: PE = (1/2) m omega^2 x^2, so PE/E = x^2/A^2
common_misconception: The square in PE proportional to x^2 is forgotten, so half the amplitude is thought to hold half the energy.

concept_tested: Displacement at which kinetic and potential energies are equal
stem: The kinetic energy of a particle performing SHM of amplitude A equals its potential energy at a displacement of
option_d: A divided by sqrt(2), about 0.71 A
correct_answer_text: A divided by sqrt(2), about 0.71 A
solution: Cancelling the common factor gives A^2 - x^2 = x^2, so 2 x^2 = A^2 and x^2 = A^2/2. Therefore x = A divided by sqrt(2), which is about 0.707 A. At that point each energy is half the total.
formula_principle: Set (1/2) m omega^2 (A^2 - x^2) equal to (1/2) m omega^2 x^2
common_misconception: Students guess x = A/2 because the energies are split in half, forgetting that the energies depend on the square of x.

concept_tested: Numerical value of the total energy
stem: A particle of mass 0.2 kg performs SHM of amplitude 0.1 m with angular frequency 10 rad s^-1. Its total energy is
formula_principle: E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2
common_misconception: One of the two squares, on omega or on A, is dropped during substitution.

concept_tested: Effect of doubling the amplitude
stem: The amplitude of a particle performing SHM is doubled while its frequency and mass remain unchanged. Its total energy becomes
solution: Doubling A multiplies A^2 by four, so the total energy becomes four times as large.
formula_principle: E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2, so E is proportional to A^2
common_misconception: Energy is assumed to scale linearly with amplitude, as displacement and force do.

concept_tested: Effect of doubling both amplitude and frequency
stem: For a particle performing SHM, both the amplitude and the frequency are doubled while the mass is unchanged. The total energy becomes
solution: The energy is proportional to f^2 and to A^2. Doubling f multiplies the energy by four, and doubling A multiplies it by another four. The overall factor is 4 x 4 = 16.
formula_principle: E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2 = 2 pi^2 m f^2 A^2
common_misconception: Only one of the two squared factors is applied, since students stop after handling the amplitude.

concept_tested: Shape of the potential energy versus displacement graph
stem: For a particle performing linear SHM, the graph of potential energy against displacement is
option_a: an upward opening parabola with its minimum at the mean position
option_b: a straight line through the origin
option_c: a downward opening parabola with its maximum at the mean position
correct_answer_text: an upward opening parabola with its minimum at the mean position
solution: The potential energy is proportional to x^2 with a positive constant of proportionality, which is the equation of a parabola opening upwards. Its lowest point, zero, occurs at x = 0.
formula_principle: PE = (1/2) m omega^2 x^2
common_misconception: The kinetic energy curve and the potential energy curve are interchanged, since they are mirror images about the horizontal line of total energy.

concept_tested: Frequency of variation of kinetic energy
stem: A particle performs SHM of frequency f. The frequency with which its kinetic energy varies with time is
solution: The kinetic energy depends on the square of the cosine. Using cos^2(theta) = (1 + cos 2 theta)/2 shows that the time varying part has angular frequency 2 omega, so the frequency of the energy variation is 2 f. Physically, the particle passes the mean position twice per oscillation, so kinetic energy peaks twice per period.
formula_principle: KE = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2 cos^2(omega t), and cos^2 has twice the frequency of cos
common_misconception: The kinetic energy is assumed to repeat with the same frequency as the displacement, ignoring the squaring.

concept_tested: Kinetic energy at a given displacement
stem: A block of mass 0.5 kg on a spring of force constant 50 N m^-1 oscillates with amplitude 0.2 m. Its kinetic energy at a displacement of 0.1 m is
solution: E = 0.5 x 50 x 0.2^2 = 0.5 x 50 x 0.04 = 1 J. PE at x = 0.1 m is 0.5 x 50 x 0.01 = 0.25 J. Hence KE = 1 minus 0.25 = 0.75 J. The mass is not needed because the force constant is given.
common_misconception: The mass is substituted into (1/2) k x^2 by habit, although the force constant already contains the mass dependence.

concept_tested: Displacement at which kinetic energy is one quarter of the total
stem: The kinetic energy of a particle performing SHM of amplitude A is one fourth of its total energy at a displacement of
solution: Setting (A^2 - x^2)/A^2 = 1/4 gives A^2 - x^2 = A^2/4, so x^2 = (3/4) A^2 and x = (sqrt(3)/2) A, about 0.87 A.
common_misconception: Displacement fractions and energy fractions are equated directly, forgetting that energy depends on x^2.

concept_tested: Ratio of kinetic to potential energy at a given displacement
stem: A particle performs SHM of amplitude A. At a displacement of A/3, the ratio of its kinetic energy to its potential energy is
solution: With x = A/3, x^2 = A^2/9 and A^2 minus x^2 = A^2 minus A^2/9 = 8 A^2/9. The ratio is (8 A^2/9) : (A^2/9), that is 8 : 1.
common_misconception: The subtraction A^2 minus x^2 is skipped, so the total energy is compared with the potential energy instead.

concept_tested: Maximum kinetic energy from the displacement equation
stem: A particle of mass 1 kg moves according to x = 0.1 sin(20 t) m, with t in second. Its maximum kinetic energy is
solution: Here A = 0.1 m and omega = 20 rad s^-1, so v_max = 0.1 x 20 = 2 m s^-1. Then KE_max = 0.5 x 1 x 2^2 = 0.5 x 4 = 2 J. This also equals the total energy of the oscillation.
formula_principle: v_max = A omega and KE_max = (1/2) m v_max^2
common_misconception: The factor one half is dropped, or the maximum acceleration is used where the maximum speed is required.

concept_tested: Comparing total energies of two oscillators
stem: Two particles of equal mass perform SHM with the same amplitude, but their periods are in the ratio 1 : 2. The ratio of their total energies is
solution: For equal masses and amplitudes, the energy varies as 1/T^2. With periods in the ratio 1 : 2, the energies are in the ratio (1/1^2) : (1/2^2) = 1 : 1/4, that is 4 : 1. The particle with the shorter period carries four times the energy.
formula_principle: E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2 with omega = 2 pi / T, so E is proportional to 1/T^2
common_misconception: The period ratio is used directly instead of the ratio of the squares of the reciprocal periods.

concept_tested: Total energy from mass, amplitude and period
stem: A body of mass 2 kg performs SHM of amplitude 0.5 m with a period of pi s. Its total energy is
solution: omega = 2 pi / pi = 2 rad s^-1, so omega^2 = 4 s^-2. Then E = 0.5 x 2 x 4 x 0.5^2 = 0.5 x 2 x 4 x 0.25 = 1 J.
formula_principle: omega = 2 pi / T and E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2
common_misconception: The pi in the period is cancelled incorrectly, leaving an angular frequency that is off by a factor of two.

concept_tested: Displacement at which potential energy is a given fraction of the total
stem: The potential energy of a particle performing SHM of amplitude A is 36 percent of its total energy at a displacement of
solution: Setting x^2/A^2 = 0.36 gives x/A = sqrt(0.36) = 0.6, so x = 0.6 A. As a check, the kinetic energy fraction there is 1 minus 0.36 = 0.64, corresponding to a speed of 0.8 times the maximum speed.
formula_principle: PE/E = x^2/A^2
common_misconception: The square root is not taken, so the energy fraction is quoted straight away as the displacement fraction.

concept_tested: Period deduced from the total energy
stem: A particle of mass 0.1 kg performs SHM of amplitude 0.1 m. If its total energy is 0.2 J, the period of the motion is
solution: Substituting, 0.2 = 0.5 x 0.1 x omega^2 x 0.1^2 = 0.0005 omega^2. Hence omega^2 = 400 and omega = 20 rad s^-1. Then T = 2 pi / 20 = pi/10 s, which is about 0.314 s.
formula_principle: E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2, then T = 2 pi / omega
common_misconception: Errors creep in while rearranging the energy relation, most often by forgetting to square the amplitude before dividing.

concept_tested: Standard expression for the period
stem: The period of a simple pendulum of length L at a place where the acceleration due to gravity is g is
solution: For small oscillations the restoring force on the bob is proportional to displacement with an effective force constant m g / L. Substituting in T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k) gives T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).
formula_principle: For small angular amplitude, T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g)
common_misconception: The ratio L/g is inverted, which reverses how length affects the period.

concept_tested: Independence of period from the mass of the bob
stem: Two simple pendulums of equal length carry bobs of mass 50 g and 200 g. At the same place, their periods are
option_a: in the ratio 1 : 2, because the period varies as the square root of the mass
option_b: equal, because the period does not depend on the mass of the bob
option_c: in the ratio 1 : 4, because the period varies directly with the mass
option_d: in the ratio 2 : 1, because a heavier bob swings faster
correct_answer_text: equal, because the period does not depend on the mass of the bob
solution: The restoring force is m g sin(theta) and the inertia is m, so the acceleration g sin(theta) is independent of m. The period expression therefore contains only L and g, and the two pendulums have equal periods.
formula_principle: T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g) contains no mass term
common_misconception: Because a heavier bob feels a larger force, students expect it to swing faster, forgetting its larger inertia.

concept_tested: Definition of a second pendulum
stem: The period of a second pendulum is
solution: A second pendulum is defined so that each one way swing takes exactly 1 s. Since one complete oscillation contains two such swings, the period is 2 s and the frequency is 0.5 Hz.
formula_principle: A second pendulum takes 1 s for each swing, so its period is 2 s
common_misconception: The one second per swing is mistaken for the full period, halving the answer.

concept_tested: Length of a second pendulum
stem: Taking g = 10 m s^-2 and pi^2 = 10, the length of a second pendulum is
solution: L = g T^2 / (4 pi^2) = 10 x 2^2 / (4 x 10) = 40/40 = 1 m. With the more accurate values g = 9.8 m s^-2 the length is about 0.993 m, close to 1 m.
formula_principle: From T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g), L = g T^2 / (4 pi^2)
common_misconception: A period of 1 s is used because the pendulum is called a second pendulum, which gives a quarter of the correct length.

concept_tested: Effect of increasing the length
stem: The length of a simple pendulum is made four times as long. Its period becomes
solution: Since T is proportional to sqrt(L), multiplying L by four multiplies T by sqrt(4) = 2. The period therefore doubles.
formula_principle: T is proportional to sqrt(L)
common_misconception: The square root in T proportional to sqrt(L) is dropped, so the period is thought to scale directly with length.

concept_tested: Numerical evaluation of the period
stem: A simple pendulum of length 0.4 m oscillates at a place where g = 10 m s^-2. Its period is
solution: L/g = 0.4/10 = 0.04 s^2 and sqrt(0.04) = 0.2 s. Hence T = 2 pi x 0.2 = 0.4 pi s, which is about 1.26 s.
formula_principle: T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g)
common_misconception: The square root step is skipped, leaving an answer smaller than the correct one by a factor of five.

concept_tested: Frequency of a second pendulum
stem: The frequency of oscillation of a second pendulum is
solution: A second pendulum has a period of 2 s, so f = 1/T = 1/2 = 0.5 Hz. It completes half an oscillation every second.
formula_principle: f = 1/T with T = 2 s for a second pendulum
common_misconception: The numerical value of the period is repeated as the frequency without taking its reciprocal.

concept_tested: Effect of a change in the acceleration due to gravity
stem: A simple pendulum is taken from the Earth to the Moon, where the acceleration due to gravity is one sixth of its value on the Earth. Its period becomes
option_a: sqrt(6) times the value on the Earth, about 2.45 times
option_b: six times the value on the Earth
option_c: one sixth of the value on the Earth
option_d: unchanged, since the mass of the bob is unchanged
correct_answer_text: sqrt(6) times the value on the Earth, about 2.45 times
solution: Dividing g by six multiplies 1/sqrt(g) by sqrt(6). Hence the new period is sqrt(6) times the original, about 2.45 times longer, so the pendulum swings noticeably more slowly on the Moon.
formula_principle: T is inversely proportional to sqrt(g) for a fixed length
common_misconception: The square root is omitted, so students expect the period to become six times longer.

concept_tested: Pendulum in an accelerating lift
stem: A simple pendulum is suspended from the ceiling of a lift that moves upward with a constant acceleration a. Compared with its period when the lift is at rest, the period of the pendulum
option_a: increases, because the effective acceleration due to gravity becomes g - a
option_b: decreases, because the effective acceleration due to gravity becomes g + a
option_c: remains the same, because the mass of the bob is unchanged
option_d: becomes zero, because the bob is pressed against the ceiling
correct_answer_text: decreases, because the effective acceleration due to gravity becomes g + a
solution: In the frame of the accelerating lift a pseudo force acts downward on the bob, so the effective acceleration due to gravity is g + a. Since T is inversely proportional to sqrt(g_eff), a larger g_eff gives a shorter period.
formula_principle: T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g_eff) with g_eff = g + a for upward acceleration
common_misconception: The sign of the pseudo force is taken wrongly, so upward acceleration is thought to reduce the effective gravity.

concept_tested: Pendulum in a freely falling lift
stem: A simple pendulum is set oscillating inside a lift whose cable then snaps, so that the lift falls freely. The pendulum
option_a: stops oscillating, since the effective acceleration due to gravity becomes zero
option_b: oscillates with the same period as before
option_c: oscillates with half its earlier period
option_d: oscillates with twice its earlier period
correct_answer_text: stops oscillating, since the effective acceleration due to gravity becomes zero
solution: In a freely falling lift the bob and the lift have the same downward acceleration g, so relative to the lift the bob experiences no net gravitational effect. With g_eff = 0 the restoring force vanishes, the period becomes infinitely large, and the bob simply stays where it is relative to the lift.
formula_principle: T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g_eff); in free fall g_eff = 0 and T tends to infinity
common_misconception: Free fall is thought to leave the pendulum unaffected because the bob still has weight in the ground frame.

concept_tested: Why the small amplitude condition is needed
stem: The relation T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g) is valid only for oscillations of small angular amplitude because
option_a: for large angles the mass of the bob starts to affect the period
option_b: for large angles the string tension becomes zero
option_c: for large angles the acceleration due to gravity changes with height
option_d: only for small angles can sin(theta) be replaced by theta, which makes the restoring force proportional to the displacement
correct_answer_text: only for small angles can sin(theta) be replaced by theta, which makes the restoring force proportional to the displacement
solution: The tangential restoring force on the bob is m g sin(theta). SHM requires a force proportional to the displacement, which is satisfied only when sin(theta) can be replaced by theta, that is for small theta expressed in radian. For larger amplitudes the true period is slightly greater than 2 pi sqrt(L/g).
formula_principle: Restoring force = m g sin(theta), approximated as m g theta for small theta
common_misconception: Students take the small amplitude condition as an arbitrary rule instead of recognising it as the step that makes the motion harmonic.

concept_tested: Percentage change in length and period
stem: The length of a simple pendulum whose period is 2 s is increased by 21 percent. The new period is
solution: L2/L1 = 1.21, so T2/T1 = sqrt(1.21) = 1.1. Hence T2 = 1.1 x 2 = 2.2 s, an increase of 10 percent in the period for a 21 percent increase in length.
formula_principle: T is proportional to sqrt(L), so T2/T1 = sqrt(L2/L1)
common_misconception: The percentage increase in length is applied straight to the period, ignoring the square root.

concept_tested: Period of a second pendulum on another planet
stem: A second pendulum is taken from the Earth, where g = 10 m s^-2, to a planet where g = 2.5 m s^-2. Its length is unchanged. Its new period is
solution: T2/T1 = sqrt(10/2.5) = sqrt(4) = 2. Since T1 = 2 s for a second pendulum, T2 = 2 x 2 = 4 s. On that planet the pendulum is no longer a second pendulum.
formula_principle: For fixed length, T2/T1 = sqrt(g1/g2)
common_misconception: The ratio of the g values, four, is used directly as the ratio of the periods.

concept_tested: Length change required to treble the period
stem: The length of a simple pendulum of period T must be changed to make its period 3 T. The new length must be
option_d: one ninth of the original length
solution: Since L varies as T^2, trebling the period multiplies the length by 3^2 = 9. Checking, 2 pi sqrt(9 L/g) = 3 x 2 pi sqrt(L/g) = 3 T.
formula_principle: T is proportional to sqrt(L), so L is proportional to T^2
common_misconception: The proportionality is inverted, so the length factor of three is used in place of nine.

concept_tested: Period inside an accelerating lift
stem: A simple pendulum has a period of 2 s at rest. It is now placed in a lift moving upward with an acceleration of 10 m s^-2 at a place where g = 10 m s^-2. Its new period is
solution: g_eff = 10 + 10 = 20 m s^-2. Hence T2 = T1 sqrt(g/g_eff) = 2 x sqrt(10/20) = 2 divided by sqrt(2) = sqrt(2) s, which is about 1.41 s.
formula_principle: g_eff = g + a for upward acceleration, and T is inversely proportional to sqrt(g_eff)
common_misconception: The effective gravity is doubled correctly but then used without the square root, halving the period instead.

concept_tested: Length of a second pendulum on the Moon
stem: Taking pi^2 = 10, the length of a second pendulum on the surface of the Moon, where g = 1.6 m s^-2, is
solution: L = 1.6 x 2^2 / (4 x 10) = 1.6 x 4 / 40 = 6.4/40 = 0.16 m, that is 16 cm. The weaker lunar gravity requires a much shorter pendulum to keep a period of 2 s.
formula_principle: L = g T^2 / (4 pi^2) with T = 2 s
common_misconception: The Earth value of g is used out of habit even though the problem specifies a different planet or satellite.

concept_tested: Small percentage change in g
stem: A second pendulum is carried to a place where the acceleration due to gravity is smaller by 2 percent. Its new period is nearly
solution: A decrease of 2 percent in g gives dg/g = -0.02. Then dT/T = -(1/2)(-0.02) = +0.01, an increase of 1 percent. Hence T = 2 x 1.01 = 2.02 s, and the pendulum clock would run slow.
formula_principle: T is proportional to g raised to the power minus one half, so a small fractional change gives dT/T = -(1/2)(dg/g)
common_misconception: The factor one half from the square root is dropped, doubling the estimated change in the period.

concept_tested: Two pendulums returning to the same phase
stem: Two simple pendulums of lengths 1 m and 1.21 m are set swinging together in the same phase at the same place. They will again be exactly in phase after the longer pendulum has completed
solution: The ratio of periods is sqrt(1.21/1) = 1.1, so the longer pendulum has the longer period. If the longer one completes n oscillations while the shorter completes n + 1 in the same time, then n x 1.1 T1 = (n + 1) T1, giving 1.1 n = n + 1, so 0.1 n = 1 and n = 10. The longer pendulum completes 10 oscillations while the shorter completes 11.
formula_principle: T proportional to sqrt(L); they are in phase again when the shorter pendulum has gained exactly one full oscillation
common_misconception: The counts for the two pendulums are interchanged, since the shorter one always completes one extra oscillation.

concept_tested: Equivalent force constant of springs in parallel
stem: Two springs of force constants k1 and k2 are connected in parallel to support the same mass. The equivalent force constant is
solution: Springs in parallel undergo the same extension x. The total restoring force is k1 x + k2 x = (k1 + k2) x, so the equivalent force constant is k1 + k2. A parallel combination is always stiffer than either spring alone.
formula_principle: In parallel the extensions are equal and the forces add, so k_eq = k1 + k2
common_misconception: Series and parallel formulae are interchanged, which is easy because the resistance analogy runs the opposite way.

concept_tested: Two identical springs in series
stem: Two identical springs, each of force constant k, are joined end to end in series. The force constant of the combination is
solution: For two identical springs in series, 1/k_eq = 1/k + 1/k = 2/k, so k_eq = k/2. The same force stretches each spring by the same amount, so the total extension doubles and the combination is softer.
formula_principle: In series 1/k_eq = 1/k1 + 1/k2
common_misconception: The reciprocal addition rule is applied directly to the force constants instead of to their reciprocals.

concept_tested: Numerical series combination
stem: Springs of force constants 3 N m^-1 and 6 N m^-1 are joined in series. The equivalent force constant is
solution: 1/k_eq = 1/3 + 1/6 = 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6 = 1/2, so k_eq = 2 N m^-1. Note that the series value is smaller than either individual constant, as it must be.
common_misconception: Students stop after computing 1/k_eq and report that value as the answer instead of taking its reciprocal.

subtopic: Period of a spring mass system
concept_tested: Period of a single spring and mass
stem: A mass of 1 kg attached to a spring of force constant 100 N m^-1 oscillates with a period of
solution: m/k = 1/100 = 0.01 s^2, and sqrt(0.01) = 0.1 s. Hence T = 2 pi x 0.1 = 0.2 pi s, which is about 0.628 s.
formula_principle: T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k)
common_misconception: The square root is omitted, so the answer comes out ten times too small.

concept_tested: Effect of cutting a spring
stem: A spring of force constant k is cut into two equal halves. The force constant of each half is
solution: For a given force, a full spring of length L extends by x, and each half of it contributes x/2. So a half spring extends only x/2 under the same force, meaning its force constant is 2 k. Shorter springs are stiffer.
formula_principle: Force constant is inversely proportional to the natural length of the spring
common_misconception: Force constant is treated as if it scaled directly with length, so a shorter spring is thought to be softer.

concept_tested: Frequency when the mass is increased
stem: A spring mass system oscillates with frequency f. The same spring is now used with a mass four times as large. The new frequency is
solution: Since f varies as 1/sqrt(m), multiplying m by four divides f by sqrt(4) = 2. The new frequency is therefore f/2.
formula_principle: f = (1/2 pi) sqrt(k/m), so f is inversely proportional to sqrt(m)
common_misconception: The square root is skipped, so a fourfold mass change is expected to reduce the frequency fourfold.

concept_tested: Period with two identical springs in parallel
stem: A block of mass m is supported by two identical springs, each of force constant k, connected in parallel. The period of vertical oscillation is
solution: The two springs in parallel give k_eq = k + k = 2 k. Substituting in T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k_eq) gives T = 2 pi sqrt(m/(2 k)), which is shorter than the period with a single spring by a factor of sqrt(2).
formula_principle: For parallel springs k_eq = k1 + k2, then T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k_eq)
common_misconception: The series rule is used because the springs look like they are acting together, whereas equal extensions mean they are in parallel.

concept_tested: Force constant from a static extension
stem: A spring stretches by 5 cm when a force of 10 N is applied to it. Its force constant is
formula_principle: k = F/x for a spring obeying Hooke law
common_misconception: Centimetres are used directly in an SI calculation, making the force constant one hundred times too small.

concept_tested: Period of a mass on two parallel springs
stem: A block of mass 2 kg is attached to two springs, each of force constant 100 N m^-1, connected in parallel. The period of oscillation is
solution: k_eq = 100 + 100 = 200 N m^-1. Then m/k_eq = 2/200 = 0.01 s^2 and sqrt(0.01) = 0.1 s. Hence T = 2 pi x 0.1 = 0.2 pi s, about 0.628 s.
formula_principle: k_eq = k1 + k2 for parallel springs, then T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k_eq)
common_misconception: Parallel and series combinations are confused, which changes the equivalent constant by a factor of four here.

concept_tested: Comparing series and parallel arrangements
stem: The same mass m is attached first to two identical springs of constant k in series and then to the same two springs in parallel. The ratio of the period in the series arrangement to that in the parallel arrangement is
solution: T_series = 2 pi sqrt(m/(k/2)) = 2 pi sqrt(2 m/k) and T_parallel = 2 pi sqrt(m/(2 k)). Their ratio is sqrt(2 m/k) divided by sqrt(m/(2 k)) = sqrt(4) = 2, that is 2 : 1.
formula_principle: k_series = k/2, k_parallel = 2 k, and T is inversely proportional to sqrt(k_eq)
common_misconception: Only one arrangement is changed from the single spring case, so a factor of sqrt(2) is obtained instead of 2.

subtopic: Period of a spring mass system
concept_tested: Period from the static extension of a vertical spring
stem: A mass hung from a vertical spring stretches it by 0.1 m at equilibrium. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the period of small vertical oscillations of the mass is
solution: The static extension gives m/k = x0/g = 0.1/10 = 0.01 s^2. Hence T = 2 pi sqrt(0.01) = 2 pi x 0.1 = 0.2 pi s, about 0.628 s. Neither the mass nor the force constant needs to be known separately.
formula_principle: At equilibrium m g = k x0, so m/k = x0/g and T = 2 pi sqrt(x0/g)
common_misconception: Students look for the mass and the force constant separately, missing that the static extension already fixes their ratio.

concept_tested: Cutting a spring and recombining the pieces
stem: A spring of force constant k is cut into three equal parts, and the three parts are then joined in parallel. The force constant of the combination is
solution: Each of the three pieces has a force constant of 3 k because a shorter spring is stiffer in inverse proportion to its length. Placing three such pieces in parallel gives 3 k + 3 k + 3 k = 9 k.
formula_principle: Cutting into n equal parts gives each part a constant n k; parallel constants add
common_misconception: Only one of the two steps is carried out, so students report either 3 k or k/3 instead of combining both effects.

concept_tested: Mass between two springs on opposite sides
stem: A block of mass 1 kg rests on a smooth horizontal surface and is connected to two fixed walls on opposite sides by springs of force constants 3 N m^-1 and 1 N m^-1. The period of horizontal oscillation of the block is
option_c: 2 pi divided by sqrt(3) s, about 3.63 s
solution: When the block moves a distance x to one side, one spring is stretched and the other is compressed, and both push it back. The restoring forces add, so k_eq = 3 + 1 = 4 N m^-1. Then omega = sqrt(k_eq/m) = sqrt(4/1) = 2 rad s^-1 and T = 2 pi / 2 = pi s, about 3.14 s.
formula_principle: Springs on opposite sides both oppose the same displacement, so they act in parallel and k_eq = k1 + k2
common_misconception: Springs on opposite sides look like a series chain through the block, but since both oppose the same displacement they combine as a parallel pair.

concept_tested: Period after a spring is cut in half
stem: A spring mass system has a period of 2 s. The spring is cut into two equal halves and the same mass is attached to one half. The new period is
solution: Cutting the spring in half doubles its force constant to 2 k. Since T is inversely proportional to sqrt(k), the new period is T divided by sqrt(2) = 2 divided by 1.414 = sqrt(2) s, about 1.41 s.
formula_principle: Half a spring has force constant 2 k, and T is inversely proportional to sqrt(k)
common_misconception: The stiffening effect of cutting a spring is reversed, so students expect the shorter spring to give a longer period.

concept_tested: Variation of amplitude with time in damped oscillation
stem: In a damped oscillation with a damping force proportional to velocity, the amplitude of the oscillation
solution: Solving the equation of damped motion gives an amplitude A0 exp(-b t / 2 m). The amplitude therefore falls off exponentially, quickly at first and then more slowly, and never becomes exactly zero in a finite time.
formula_principle: A = A0 exp(-b t / 2 m) for a damping force F = -b v
common_misconception: Amplitude is assumed to fall by equal amounts in equal times, which corresponds to linear rather than exponential decay.

concept_tested: Condition for resonance
stem: Resonance in a forced oscillation occurs when the frequency of the applied periodic force is
option_a: twice the natural frequency of the system
option_b: half the natural frequency of the system
option_c: equal to the natural frequency of the oscillating system
option_d: zero, so that the force is steady
correct_answer_text: equal to the natural frequency of the oscillating system
solution: When the driving frequency matches the natural frequency, the driving force stays in step with the motion and feeds energy into the system in every cycle. The amplitude then grows to a large value that is limited only by the damping present.
formula_principle: Resonance occurs when the driving frequency matches the natural frequency of the system
common_misconception: Resonance is thought to occur at any whole number multiple of the natural frequency, as with harmonics in sound.

concept_tested: Nature of the damping force
stem: In the usual treatment of damped oscillations, the damping force acting on the body is taken to be proportional to
option_a: the displacement of the body and opposite to it in direction
option_b: the acceleration of the body and opposite to it in direction
option_c: the square of the displacement of the body
option_d: the velocity of the body and opposite to it in direction
correct_answer_text: the velocity of the body and opposite to it in direction
solution: For a body moving slowly through a fluid the resistive force is proportional to speed and acts against the motion, so F = -b v. This term removes energy from the oscillator because the force is always opposite to the velocity.
formula_principle: Damping force F = -b v, where b is the damping constant
common_misconception: The damping force is confused with the restoring force, since both are written with a negative sign.

concept_tested: Frequency of forced vibrations in the steady state
stem: A body is driven by an external periodic force. After the steady state is reached, the body vibrates with
option_a: its own natural frequency, whatever the driving frequency may be
option_b: the frequency of the applied periodic force
option_c: the mean of the driving frequency and the natural frequency
option_d: a frequency equal to the difference between the driving and natural frequencies
correct_answer_text: the frequency of the applied periodic force
solution: The transient part of the motion, at the natural frequency, dies away because of damping. What remains is the steady state, in which the body follows the driver and oscillates at exactly the driving frequency, with an amplitude that depends on how close that frequency is to the natural frequency.
formula_principle: In the steady state a forced oscillator responds at the driving frequency
common_misconception: Students expect the body always to vibrate at its own natural frequency, which is true only for free vibrations.

concept_tested: Unit of the damping constant
stem: The SI unit of the damping constant b defined through the damping force F = -b v is
option_c: kg s^-1, equivalently N s m^-1
correct_answer_text: kg s^-1, equivalently N s m^-1
solution: From F = -b v, the magnitude of b is force divided by speed, that is N divided by m s^-1, which equals N s m^-1. Writing N as kg m s^-2 shows that this is the same as kg s^-1.
formula_principle: b = magnitude of F divided by v
common_misconception: The damping constant is given the unit of the force constant because both appear with a negative sign in the equation of motion.

concept_tested: Time for the amplitude to fall to one over e of its initial value
stem: A damped oscillator of mass 0.5 kg has a damping constant of 0.1 kg s^-1. The time in which its amplitude falls to 1/e of its initial value is
solution: The amplitude falls to A0/e when b t / (2 m) = 1, that is t = 2 m / b. Substituting, t = 2 x 0.5 / 0.1 = 1/0.1 = 10 s.
formula_principle: A = A0 exp(-b t / 2 m); set the exponent equal to minus one
common_misconception: The factor two in the denominator of the exponent is dropped, halving the estimated decay time.

concept_tested: Energy loss when the amplitude halves
stem: In a damped oscillation the amplitude falls to half its initial value. The total energy of the oscillator at that instant, as a fraction of its initial energy, is
solution: Since the energy of an oscillator varies as the square of its amplitude, halving the amplitude reduces the energy by a factor of 2^2 = 4. The remaining energy is therefore one quarter of the initial value, so three quarters of the energy has been dissipated.
formula_principle: E is proportional to A^2
common_misconception: Energy is assumed to fall in the same proportion as the amplitude, ignoring the square relation.

concept_tested: Effect of damping on the resonance curve
stem: As the damping in a driven oscillator is increased, the graph of steady state amplitude against driving frequency
option_a: develops a lower and broader peak, with the maximum shifted slightly below the natural frequency
option_b: develops a taller and sharper peak at exactly the natural frequency
option_c: keeps the same peak height but shifts to a much higher frequency
option_d: becomes a horizontal straight line at all driving frequencies
correct_answer_text: develops a lower and broader peak, with the maximum shifted slightly below the natural frequency
solution: The amplitude at resonance is set by how much energy the damping removes each cycle. Light damping gives a tall narrow peak, so the response is sharp. Heavier damping lowers and widens the peak and moves the maximum a little below the undamped natural frequency, because the damped angular frequency is itself smaller than the natural one.
formula_principle: Steady state amplitude is largest near the natural frequency, and its peak height falls as damping rises
common_misconception: Damping is thought to shift the peak sideways without changing its height, whereas the height is exactly what damping controls.

concept_tested: Period of a damped oscillation
stem: A damped oscillator has mass 0.5 kg, force constant 50 N m^-1 and damping constant 6 kg s^-1. The period of its damped oscillation is
solution: omega0 = sqrt(50/0.5) = sqrt(100) = 10 rad s^-1 and b/(2 m) = 6/(2 x 0.5) = 6 s^-1. Hence omega_damped = sqrt(10^2 - 6^2) = sqrt(100 - 36) = sqrt(64) = 8 rad s^-1. The period is T = 2 pi / 8 = pi/4 s, about 0.785 s, which is longer than the undamped period of pi/5 s.
formula_principle: omega_damped = sqrt(omega0^2 - (b/2m)^2) with omega0 = sqrt(k/m), then T = 2 pi / omega_damped
common_misconception: The two angular frequencies are subtracted directly instead of combining their squares under a square root.

concept_tested: Distinguishing free, forced and resonant oscillations
stem: Which of the following statements about oscillations is correct?
option_a: A freely vibrating body oscillates at the driving frequency, while a forced oscillator settles at its own natural frequency
option_b: At resonance the amplitude of a real oscillator becomes infinitely large whatever the damping
option_c: The natural frequency of a system depends on the strength of the applied periodic force
option_d: A freely vibrating body oscillates at its natural frequency, while a body under a periodic external force settles into oscillation at the driving frequency with an amplitude that grows as the two frequencies approach each other
correct_answer_text: A freely vibrating body oscillates at its natural frequency, while a body under a periodic external force settles into oscillation at the driving frequency with an amplitude that grows as the two frequencies approach each other
solution: A body displaced and released oscillates at its natural frequency set by its inertia and stiffness. When a periodic force is applied, the transient at the natural frequency dies away and the steady state follows the driver. The steady state amplitude rises as the driving frequency nears the natural frequency and reaches its largest, finite, value at resonance, where damping alone fixes the peak.
formula_principle: Free vibration is at the natural frequency; forced vibration in the steady state is at the driving frequency; resonance is the amplitude peak where the two coincide
common_misconception: Resonance is described as giving an infinite amplitude, which would be true only if there were no damping at all.

concept_tested: What a progressive wave carries forward
stem: A progressive wave travels through a material medium. What is actually carried forward from one point of the medium to another?
