option_a: Energy and momentum, while each particle only oscillates about its own mean position
option_b: The particles of the medium themselves, which move bodily along with the wave
option_c: Only the shape of the disturbance, with no energy being transported
option_d: Mass of the medium, which piles up at the crests of the wave
correct_answer_text: Energy and momentum, while each particle only oscillates about its own mean position
solution: In a progressive wave each particle performs oscillation about its own fixed mean position and passes the disturbance on to the next particle. The pattern and the energy move forward, but the average position of every particle stays where it was.
formula_principle: A progressive wave transports energy and momentum without net transport of matter
common_misconception: Learners often picture the medium flowing along with the wave, which would make a sound wave a wind.

concept_tested: Use of v = f lambda
stem: A progressive sound wave of frequency 500 Hz travels in air. The speed of sound in air is 330 m s^-1. The wavelength of the wave is
solution: Rearranging v = f lambda gives lambda = v/f = 330/500 = 0.66 m.
formula_principle: v = f lambda, so lambda = v/f
common_misconception: Students frequently invert the ratio and write lambda = f/v, which gives a number with the wrong units.

concept_tested: SI unit of the propagation constant k
stem: In the equation of a progressive wave y = A sin(omega t - k x), the SI unit of the propagation constant k is
solution: The argument of the sine must be an angle, so k x must be in radian. Since x is in metre, k must be in radian per metre, written rad m^-1.
formula_principle: k = 2 pi/lambda, so k has the dimension of reciprocal length
common_misconception: The propagation constant is often mixed up with omega because both appear inside the same bracket.

concept_tested: Reading the direction of travel from the wave equation
stem: The wave described by y = A sin(omega t - k x) travels
option_d: nowhere, since the equation represents a stationary wave
solution: Keeping the phase constant, omega t - k x = constant, so x = (omega/k) t + constant. As time increases, x increases, so the wave advances along the positive x direction.
formula_principle: For constant phase, omega t - k x = constant gives x increasing with t
common_misconception: Many students memorise the sign without linking it to the condition of constant phase, and then reverse the direction.

concept_tested: Extracting omega and k from a given equation
stem: The equation of a progressive wave is y = 0.05 sin(200 pi t - pi x), where all quantities are in SI units. The speed of the wave is
solution: Comparing with y = A sin(omega t - k x) gives omega = 200 pi rad s^-1 and k = pi rad m^-1. Hence v = omega/k = 200 pi/pi = 200 m s^-1. As a check, f = omega/2 pi = 100 Hz and lambda = 2 pi/k = 2 m, so v = 100 x 2 = 200 m s^-1.
formula_principle: v = omega/k for a progressive wave
common_misconception: Students often compute f and lambda separately and then slip by a factor of 2 pi in one of them.

concept_tested: Converting path difference into phase difference
stem: The wavelength of a progressive wave is 40 cm. Two points on the wave are separated by a path difference of 10 cm along the direction of propagation. The phase difference between them is
solution: Path difference is 10 cm out of a wavelength of 40 cm, that is one quarter of a wavelength. Phase difference = (2 pi/40) x 10 = pi/2 rad.
formula_principle: phase difference = (2 pi/lambda) x path difference
common_misconception: The factor 2 pi/lambda is often written as pi/lambda, which halves every answer.

concept_tested: Finding wave speed from a given phase relation
stem: Two points on a progressive wave of frequency 500 Hz are 25 cm apart along the direction of propagation and differ in phase by pi/2 rad. The speed of the wave is
solution: A phase difference of pi/2 rad corresponds to a path difference of lambda/4. So lambda/4 = 0.25 m, giving lambda = 1 m. Then v = f lambda = 500 x 1 = 500 m s^-1.
formula_principle: path difference = (lambda/2 pi) x phase difference, then v = f lambda
common_misconception: The quarter wavelength step is often skipped and the given separation is used directly as the wavelength.

concept_tested: Distinguishing particle velocity from wave velocity
stem: For a progressive wave travelling through a medium, which statement is correct?
option_a: Both the wave velocity and the particle velocity are constant in magnitude and direction
option_b: The particle velocity is always equal to the wave velocity
option_c: The wave velocity is maximum at the crest and zero at the mean position
option_d: The wave velocity is constant for a given medium, while the particle velocity changes continuously during each oscillation
correct_answer_text: The wave velocity is constant for a given medium, while the particle velocity changes continuously during each oscillation
solution: The wave velocity omega/k is fixed by the elastic and inertial properties of the medium and does not change with time. The particle velocity is the time derivative of the displacement and varies from zero at the extreme positions to A omega at the mean position.
formula_principle: Particle velocity = A omega cos(omega t - k x); wave velocity = omega/k
common_misconception: Learners assume that a fast wave means fast moving particles, whereas the two speeds are independent of each other.

subtopic: Wave equation in the t and x form
concept_tested: Reading period and wavelength from the 2 pi form
stem: A progressive wave is given by y = 2 sin 2 pi (t/0.02 - x/40), where y and x are in centimetre and t is in second. The speed of the wave is
solution: Comparison gives T = 0.02 s and lambda = 40 cm = 0.4 m. Hence v = lambda/T = 0.4/0.02 = 20 m s^-1.
formula_principle: Comparing with y = A sin 2 pi (t/T - x/lambda) gives T and lambda, and v = lambda/T
common_misconception: Failing to convert centimetre to metre inflates the answer by a factor of one hundred.

concept_tested: Condition for maximum particle speed to equal wave speed
stem: In a progressive wave of amplitude A and wavelength lambda, the maximum particle velocity equals the wave velocity when
solution: Setting A omega = omega/k gives A = 1/k. Since k = 2 pi/lambda, this becomes A = lambda/(2 pi), that is lambda = 2 pi A.
formula_principle: Maximum particle velocity = A omega; wave velocity = omega/k
common_misconception: The relation A omega = v is often solved without substituting k = 2 pi/lambda, so the factor 2 pi is lost.

subtopic: Minimum separation for a given phase
concept_tested: Path difference for a phase difference of 60 degrees
stem: A sound wave of frequency 250 Hz travels in air with speed 330 m s^-1. The minimum distance between two points of the wave that differ in phase by 60 degrees is
solution: First lambda = v/f = 330/250 = 1.32 m. A phase difference of 60 degrees is 60/360 = 1/6 of a cycle, so the path difference is 1.32/6 = 0.22 m.
formula_principle: lambda = v/f and path difference = (phase difference/360 degrees) x lambda
common_misconception: Students convert 60 degrees to pi/3 radian and then divide the wavelength by 3 instead of by 6.

concept_tested: Relating amplitude to wavelength through particle speed
stem: In a progressive wave the maximum particle velocity is twice the wave velocity. The amplitude of the wave in terms of its wavelength lambda is
solution: The condition A omega = 2 omega/k gives A = 2/k. Substituting k = 2 pi/lambda gives A = 2 lambda/(2 pi) = lambda/pi.
formula_principle: A omega = 2 (omega/k) with k = 2 pi/lambda
common_misconception: The factor of two is often applied to the wavelength instead of to the reciprocal of k.

concept_tested: Ratio of maximum particle speed to wave speed
stem: A progressive wave is given by y = 0.02 sin(300 t - 1.5 x) in SI units. The ratio of the maximum particle speed to the wave speed is
solution: Here A = 0.02 m, omega = 300 rad s^-1 and k = 1.5 rad m^-1. Maximum particle speed = 0.02 x 300 = 6 m s^-1 and wave speed = 300/1.5 = 200 m s^-1. The ratio is 6/200 = 0.03, which is also A k = 0.02 x 1.5.
formula_principle: Maximum particle speed = A omega, wave speed = omega/k, so the ratio is A k
common_misconception: Learners stop after finding A omega and forget that a ratio is asked for.

concept_tested: Solving for the time at which a chosen particle reaches its positive extreme
stem: A progressive wave is described by y = 0.1 sin(100 pi t - 0.5 pi x) in SI units. The particle at x = 2 m attains its maximum positive displacement for the first time at
solution: At x = 2 m the phase is 100 pi t - 0.5 pi x = 100 pi t - pi. Setting this equal to pi/2 gives 100 pi t = 3 pi/2, so t = 1.5/100 = 0.015 s. This is the first such instant because smaller values of the phase are negative.
formula_principle: Displacement is maximum and positive when the total phase equals pi/2
common_misconception: The spatial phase term is frequently dropped, which shifts every predicted instant by a fixed amount.

concept_tested: Resultant displacement when two waves meet
stem: When two or more waves arrive simultaneously at a point of a medium, the principle of superposition states that
option_a: the resultant displacement at that point is the vector sum of the displacements produced by the individual waves
option_b: the resultant displacement is the product of the individual displacements
option_c: only the wave with the larger amplitude decides the displacement
option_d: the resultant displacement is the arithmetic mean of the individual displacements
correct_answer_text: the resultant displacement at that point is the vector sum of the displacements produced by the individual waves
solution: Because the wave equation is linear, if y1 and y2 are separately solutions then their sum is also a solution. Hence the net displacement of a particle is obtained by adding the individual displacements with their proper signs.
formula_principle: y = y1 + y2 + y3 and so on, taken as a vector sum
common_misconception: Learners sometimes add amplitudes rather than instantaneous displacements, which is correct only when the waves are in phase.

concept_tested: Adding amplitudes of two waves in phase
stem: Two waves of the same frequency, of amplitudes 3 units and 4 units, arrive at a point in the same phase. The amplitude of the resultant wave is
solution: With phi = 0, cos phi = 1, so R = sqrt(9 + 16 + 24) = sqrt(49) = 7 units. Equivalently R = 3 + 4 = 7 units.
formula_principle: R = sqrt(a1^2 + a2^2 + 2 a1 a2 cos phi), with phi = 0 giving R = a1 + a2
common_misconception: The Pythagorean combination is applied out of habit even when the phase difference is zero.

concept_tested: Path difference condition for reinforcement
stem: Two waves of the same frequency reinforce each other completely at a point when
option_a: the path difference is an odd integral multiple of half the wavelength
option_b: the path difference between them is an integral multiple of the wavelength
option_c: the path difference is an odd integral multiple of a quarter of the wavelength
option_d: the two waves happen to have equal amplitudes
correct_answer_text: the path difference between them is an integral multiple of the wavelength
solution: Phase difference and path difference are related by phase = (2 pi/lambda) x path. For the phase difference to be 0, 2 pi, 4 pi and so on, the path difference must be 0, lambda, 2 lambda and so on.
formula_principle: Constructive superposition requires phase difference 2 n pi, that is path difference n lambda
common_misconception: The two conditions are memorised as a pair and are frequently exchanged under examination pressure.

concept_tested: Amplitude when the phase difference is pi
stem: Two waves of the same frequency, of amplitudes 5 units and 3 units, superpose with a phase difference of pi. The amplitude of the resultant wave is
solution: With phi = pi, cos phi = -1, so R = sqrt(25 + 9 - 30) = sqrt(4) = 2 units, which is the difference of the two amplitudes.
formula_principle: R = sqrt(a1^2 + a2^2 + 2 a1 a2 cos phi), with phi = pi giving R = |a1 - a2|
common_misconception: The magnitude sign is forgotten, and students sometimes report a negative amplitude.

concept_tested: Resultant of two equal amplitudes with phase difference pi/3
stem: Two waves, each of amplitude A, superpose with a phase difference of pi/3. The amplitude of the resultant wave is
solution: With a1 = a2 = A and cos(pi/3) = 0.5, R = sqrt(A^2 + A^2 + 2 A^2 x 0.5) = sqrt(3 A^2) = A sqrt(3), which is about 1.73 A.
formula_principle: R = sqrt(a1^2 + a2^2 + 2 a1 a2 cos phi)
common_misconception: The shortcut R = 2 A cos(phi/2) is often written as 2 A cos(phi), which gives the wrong angle.

concept_tested: Resultant when the phase difference is pi/2
stem: Two waves of amplitudes 3 units and 4 units superpose with a phase difference of pi/2. The amplitude of the resultant wave is
solution: Since cos(pi/2) = 0, the cross term vanishes and R = sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5 units.
formula_principle: R = sqrt(a1^2 + a2^2 + 2 a1 a2 cos phi), with cos(pi/2) = 0
common_misconception: The cross term is sometimes retained with cos taken as 1, which turns the answer into 7 units.

concept_tested: Where the principle of superposition applies
stem: Which statement about the principle of superposition of waves is correct?
option_a: It applies only to transverse waves and fails for longitudinal waves
option_b: It applies only when the two waves have exactly the same frequency
option_c: It applies only when the two waves travel in the same direction
option_d: It follows from the linearity of the wave equation and applies to waves of every kind, including sound and light
correct_answer_text: It follows from the linearity of the wave equation and applies to waves of every kind, including sound and light
solution: If y1 and y2 each satisfy the linear wave equation, then any sum of them also satisfies it. Nothing in the argument refers to the type of wave, the direction of travel or the equality of frequencies.
formula_principle: Linearity of the wave equation implies superposition
common_misconception: Students restrict the principle to the special cases they first meet, such as interference of identical waves.

concept_tested: Recovering individual amplitudes from the extremes
stem: Two waves of the same frequency travelling in the same direction give a maximum resultant amplitude of 8 units and a minimum resultant amplitude of 2 units. The amplitudes of the individual waves are
solution: From a1 + a2 = 8 and a1 - a2 = 2, adding gives 2 a1 = 10 so a1 = 5 units, and then a2 = 3 units.
formula_principle: a1 + a2 = R maximum and a1 - a2 = R minimum
common_misconception: The minimum resultant is mistaken for one of the amplitudes rather than for their difference.

concept_tested: Amplitude and phase of the resultant wave
stem: Two waves y1 = 4 sin(omega t) and y2 = 3 sin(omega t + pi/2) superpose. The resultant wave has
option_a: amplitude 7 units and is in phase with y1
option_b: amplitude 1 unit and is in phase with y2
option_c: amplitude 5 units and leads y1 by tan inverse (4/3)
option_d: amplitude 5 units and leads y1 by tan inverse (3/4)
correct_answer_text: amplitude 5 units and leads y1 by tan inverse (3/4)
solution: With phi = pi/2, R = sqrt(16 + 9) = 5 units. The phase angle satisfies tan(alpha) = 3 sin(pi/2)/(4 + 3 cos(pi/2)) = 3/4, so the resultant leads y1 by tan inverse (3/4), about 37 degrees.
formula_principle: R = sqrt(a1^2 + a2^2 + 2 a1 a2 cos phi) and tan(alpha) = a2 sin phi/(a1 + a2 cos phi)
common_misconception: The phase angle is often quoted as tan inverse of the ratio of the two amplitudes without regard to which one is perpendicular.

concept_tested: Superposition of three equally spaced phases
stem: Three waves, each of amplitude A and of the same frequency, superpose at a point with phases 0, 2 pi/3 and 4 pi/3. The resultant amplitude is
solution: The three phasors of equal length A are separated by 120 degrees, so they form a closed equilateral triangle. Adding components, A cos 0 + A cos 120 + A cos 240 = A - 0.5 A - 0.5 A = 0, and A sin 0 + A sin 120 + A sin 240 = 0 as well. Hence the resultant amplitude is zero.
formula_principle: Phasors of equal length spaced equally over 2 pi close into a polygon and give zero resultant
common_misconception: Students assume that three waves must give something larger than one wave, forgetting that phases can cancel completely.

concept_tested: Fate of energy at points of destructive superposition
stem: At the points where two identical waves cancel each other completely, what happens to the energy that the waves were carrying?
option_a: It is not destroyed; it is redistributed so that points of constructive superposition receive correspondingly more energy
option_b: It is destroyed at those points, since the displacement there is zero
option_c: It is entirely converted into heat within the medium
option_d: It is stored in the medium and released only after the two waves have separated
correct_answer_text: It is not destroyed; it is redistributed so that points of constructive superposition receive correspondingly more energy
solution: Energy in a wave depends on the square of the amplitude. Where the amplitude falls to zero the energy density is zero, but where the amplitude doubles the energy density becomes four times as large. Averaged over the whole pattern the total energy equals the sum of the energies of the two waves.
formula_principle: Conservation of energy in an interference pattern
common_misconception: The zero displacement at a point of cancellation is wrongly read as the disappearance of energy.

concept_tested: Resultant amplitude for a path difference of one third of a wavelength
stem: Two waves, each of amplitude A and of the same frequency, arrive at a point with a path difference of lambda/3. The resultant amplitude at that point is
solution: The phase difference is (2 pi/lambda) x (lambda/3) = 2 pi/3. For two equal amplitudes, R = 2 A cos(phi/2) = 2 A cos(pi/3) = 2 A x 0.5 = A.
formula_principle: phase difference = (2 pi/lambda) x path difference, then R = 2 A cos(phase difference/2)
common_misconception: The path difference is inserted directly into the cosine as if it were already a phase angle.

concept_tested: Phase change of pi at a fixed end
stem: A transverse pulse travelling along a string is reflected at a rigidly clamped end. The reflected pulse
option_a: returns without any phase change, so that a crest comes back as a crest
option_b: returns with a phase change of pi/2
option_c: is completely absorbed, so that nothing comes back along the string
option_d: returns with a phase change of pi, so that a crest comes back as a trough
correct_answer_text: returns with a phase change of pi, so that a crest comes back as a trough
solution: The clamped point cannot move at any instant. The only way the incident and reflected displacements can cancel there at all times is for the reflected pulse to be inverted, which is a phase change of pi.
formula_principle: Reflection from a denser or rigid medium introduces a phase change of pi
common_misconception: The inversion is memorised without the reason, so it is easily attached to the wrong boundary.

concept_tested: No phase change at a free end
stem: When a wave is reflected from a free boundary, that is from a rarer medium, the reflected wave suffers
solution: At a free boundary the end is able to move and in fact reaches maximum displacement. Incident and reflected displacements must add there rather than cancel, which requires zero phase change.
formula_principle: Reflection from a rarer or free boundary occurs without any phase change
common_misconception: Students expect every reflection to invert the wave, by analogy with a fixed end.

subtopic: Longitudinal wave at a rigid wall
concept_tested: Compression reflected from a rigid wall
stem: A compression pulse of a sound wave travelling in air strikes a rigid wall. On reflection
option_a: a compression is returned as a rarefaction
option_b: a compression is returned as a wave of double the frequency
option_c: a compression is returned as a compression
option_d: a compression is returned as a transverse wave
correct_answer_text: a compression is returned as a compression
solution: The rigid wall holds the air displacement at zero, so the wall is a displacement node and a pressure antinode. The pressure variation therefore adds up at the wall, which means a compression comes back as a compression.
formula_principle: At a rigid boundary the pressure variation is reinforced while the displacement reverses
common_misconception: The displacement inversion is wrongly transferred to the pressure, leading to the answer that a compression returns as a rarefaction.

subtopic: Boundary condition at a rigid support
concept_tested: Node formed at a fixed boundary
stem: When a wave is reflected at a rigid boundary and superposes on the incident wave, the boundary point itself is
option_a: an antinode, because the incident and reflected waves reinforce each other there
option_b: a node, because the displacement there must remain zero at every instant
option_c: a node for a transverse wave but an antinode for a longitudinal wave
option_d: neither a node nor an antinode, because the boundary lies outside the wave pattern
correct_answer_text: a node, because the displacement there must remain zero at every instant
solution: The clamp forces the displacement at that point to be zero for all time. Since the resultant displacement there is permanently zero, the point is a node by definition.
formula_principle: A rigid boundary is always a displacement node
common_misconception: Learners look for a node only inside the medium and forget that the boundary itself is one.

concept_tested: Different phase behaviour of displacement and pressure
stem: When a longitudinal sound wave is reflected from a rigid wall, the reflected wave shows
option_a: a phase change of pi in both the displacement and the pressure variation
option_b: no phase change in either the displacement or the pressure variation
option_c: a phase change of pi in the displacement but no phase change in the pressure variation
option_d: a phase change of pi in the pressure variation but none in the displacement
correct_answer_text: a phase change of pi in the displacement but no phase change in the pressure variation
solution: Zero net displacement at the wall requires the reflected displacement to be the negative of the incident displacement, a phase change of pi. Pressure is related to the spatial gradient of displacement, so where displacement reverses the pressure does not, and the pressure variations add at the wall.
formula_principle: Rigid boundary: displacement node and pressure antinode
common_misconception: The single phrase phase change of pi is applied to every quantity without asking which quantity is meant.

subtopic: Reflection at the open end of a pipe
concept_tested: Compression reflected as a rarefaction
stem: At the open end of an organ pipe, an incident compression is reflected as
option_a: a compression, and the open end behaves as a displacement node
option_b: a rarefaction, and the open end behaves as a displacement node
option_c: a rarefaction, and the open end behaves as a displacement antinode
option_d: a compression, and the open end behaves as a displacement antinode
correct_answer_text: a rarefaction, and the open end behaves as a displacement antinode
solution: At the open end the air is free to expand into the atmosphere, so the excess pressure there must stay close to zero. The reflected pressure wave is therefore inverted, and a compression returns as a rarefaction, while the displacement is unreversed and maximum, making the end an antinode.
formula_principle: Open end: pressure node and displacement antinode
common_misconception: Because a compression returns as a compression at a wall, students expect the same at an open end.

concept_tested: Path difference corresponding to the phase change on reflection
stem: A wave of wavelength 0.6 m is reflected from a rigid boundary. The extra path difference that is equivalent to the phase change introduced by this reflection is
solution: Path difference and phase difference are related by path = (lambda/2 pi) x phase. For a phase change of pi this gives (0.6/2 pi) x pi = 0.3 m, that is half a wavelength.
formula_principle: A phase change of pi is equivalent to an extra path of lambda/2
common_misconception: The equivalence between a phase change of pi and a path of lambda/2 is often quoted as lambda/4.

concept_tested: What reflection can and cannot alter
stem: A wave is reflected back into the same medium from which it came. Which quantities are altered by this reflection?
option_a: the frequency, the wavelength and the speed all change
option_b: only the direction of propagation and, at a rigid boundary, the phase
option_c: the wavelength changes while the frequency stays the same
option_d: the speed changes while the frequency and the wavelength stay the same
correct_answer_text: only the direction of propagation and, at a rigid boundary, the phase
solution: The source continues to vibrate at the same rate, so the frequency of the reflected wave equals that of the incident wave. The medium is the same, so the speed is the same, and therefore lambda = v/f is also the same. Only the direction reverses, together with a phase change of pi if the boundary is rigid.
formula_principle: Frequency is set by the source; speed by the medium; hence wavelength is also unchanged
common_misconception: Reflection is confused with refraction, in which the speed and wavelength genuinely do change.

concept_tested: Judging two statements on reflection at a free end
stem: Consider the following two statements. Statement 1: at a free boundary the reflected transverse pulse is not inverted. Statement 2: at a free boundary the particle at the boundary has zero displacement. Which of the following is true?
option_a: Statement 1 is correct and statement 2 is incorrect
option_b: Statement 1 is incorrect and statement 2 is correct
option_c: Statement 1 and statement 2 are both correct
option_d: Statement 1 and statement 2 are both incorrect
correct_answer_text: Statement 1 is correct and statement 2 is incorrect
solution: At a free end the boundary particle is unconstrained and is driven to twice the incident displacement, so it is an antinode and its displacement is certainly not zero. The uninverted reflection is exactly what makes this large displacement possible.
formula_principle: Free boundary: no phase change, displacement antinode
common_misconception: The two features are learnt separately and are often paired with the wrong type of boundary.

subtopic: Pulse at a junction of two strings
concept_tested: Reflection when a light string is joined to a heavy string
stem: A pulse travelling along a light string reaches a junction where the light string is joined to a much heavier string. Which statement describes what happens?
option_a: The reflected pulse is erect, because the junction is free to move
option_b: There is no reflected pulse at all, since the whole pulse is transmitted into the heavy string
option_c: The transmitted pulse is inverted while the reflected pulse remains erect
option_d: The reflected pulse is inverted, because the heavier string behaves as the denser and more rigid medium
correct_answer_text: The reflected pulse is inverted, because the heavier string behaves as the denser and more rigid medium
solution: The wave speed on a string is sqrt(T/m), so a heavier string carries the wave more slowly and acts as the denser medium. Reflection from a denser medium introduces a phase change of pi, which appears as an inverted reflected pulse, while the pulse transmitted into the heavy string stays erect.
formula_principle: Reflection from a denser medium is accompanied by a phase change of pi
common_misconception: Students judge denseness by thickness alone and forget that it is the linear density that decides the wave speed.

concept_tested: Distance between two consecutive nodes
stem: In a stationary wave of wavelength lambda, the distance between two consecutive nodes is
solution: The space factor of a stationary wave is sin(k x), which vanishes whenever k x is a multiple of pi. Successive zeros are separated by pi/k = lambda/2.
formula_principle: Consecutive nodes are separated by lambda/2
common_misconception: The node separation is frequently quoted as a full wavelength, which halves every calculated frequency.

concept_tested: Distance from a node to the neighbouring antinode
stem: In a stationary wave of wavelength lambda, the distance between a node and the antinode nearest to it is
solution: Each loop extends from one node to the next and is lambda/2 long. The antinode lies at the centre of the loop, so it is lambda/4 from either node.
formula_principle: A node and the adjacent antinode are separated by lambda/4
common_misconception: Students halve the wavelength once and stop, forgetting that a further halving is needed.

subtopic: Behaviour of a particle at a node
concept_tested: Amplitude at a node
stem: A particle situated exactly at a node of a stationary wave
option_a: has the largest amplitude and moves with the greatest speed
option_b: has half the amplitude of a particle at an antinode
option_c: has zero amplitude and stays permanently at rest
option_d: vibrates with the same amplitude as every other particle of the medium
correct_answer_text: has zero amplitude and stays permanently at rest
solution: The amplitude factor 2 A sin(k x) vanishes at the nodes for every value of time, so a particle located there never moves.
formula_principle: Amplitude of a stationary wave is 2 A sin(k x), which is zero at a node
common_misconception: Learners think a node is merely a point of small motion rather than a point of no motion at all.

concept_tested: Absence of energy transport
stem: Which statement about the flow of energy in a stationary wave is correct?
option_a: Energy is carried forward at twice the speed of the component progressive waves
option_b: No net energy crosses a node, so energy stays confined within each loop
option_c: Energy flows in the direction of whichever component wave has the larger amplitude
option_d: Energy is carried through the nodes but not through the antinodes
correct_answer_text: No net energy crosses a node, so energy stays confined within each loop
solution: Power transmitted across a point is force multiplied by particle velocity. At a node the particle velocity is permanently zero, so no energy can cross it. Energy merely changes back and forth between kinetic and potential form inside each loop.
formula_principle: A stationary wave stores energy but does not transport it
common_misconception: The word wave suggests transport, so students assume energy must be flowing somewhere.

concept_tested: Phase relation of particles between two nodes
stem: All the particles lying between two consecutive nodes of a stationary wave
option_a: vibrate in phase with one another and with equal amplitudes
option_b: vibrate in phase with one another but with different amplitudes
option_c: vibrate in opposite phase to one another
option_d: vibrate with a phase difference of pi/2 between neighbouring particles
correct_answer_text: vibrate in phase with one another but with different amplitudes
solution: Within one loop sin(k x) keeps the same sign, so every particle reaches its extreme at the same instant. Only the magnitude 2 A sin(k x) changes from point to point.
formula_principle: y = 2 A sin(k x) cos(omega t): the time factor is the same for all particles
common_misconception: The steady phase lag familiar from progressive waves is wrongly carried over to stationary waves.

concept_tested: Recognising the stationary wave form
stem: Which of the following equations represents a stationary wave?
option_a: y = A sin(omega t - k x)
option_b: y = 2 A sin(k x) cos(omega t)
option_c: y = A sin(omega t + k x)
option_d: y = A sin(omega t) + A sin(k x)
correct_answer_text: y = 2 A sin(k x) cos(omega t)
solution: Adding y1 = A sin(omega t - k x) and y2 = A sin(omega t + k x) gives y = 2 A sin(k x) cos(omega t) after using the sum to product identity. The position fixes the amplitude and the time factor is shared by all particles.
formula_principle: A stationary wave has the space and time dependence in separate factors
common_misconception: Any equation containing both x and t is assumed to be a stationary wave, without checking whether they are separated.

concept_tested: Finding wave speed from the node separation
stem: In a stationary wave pattern the distance between two consecutive nodes is 20 cm and the frequency of vibration is 250 Hz. The speed of the component progressive waves is
solution: Since lambda/2 = 20 cm, lambda = 40 cm = 0.4 m. Then v = f lambda = 250 x 0.4 = 100 m s^-1.
formula_principle: Consecutive nodes are lambda/2 apart, then v = f lambda
common_misconception: The factor of two between node spacing and wavelength is the single most common slip in this calculation.

concept_tested: Node separation from a given stationary wave equation
stem: A stationary wave is given by y = 0.06 sin(pi x/3) cos(100 pi t), where x and y are in metre and t is in second. The distance between two consecutive nodes is
solution: Here k = pi/3 rad m^-1, so lambda = 2 pi/k = 6 m. Consecutive nodes are separated by lambda/2 = 3 m. Directly, sin(pi x/3) vanishes at x = 0, 3, 6 metre and so on.
formula_principle: k = 2 pi/lambda, and consecutive nodes are lambda/2 apart
common_misconception: Students substitute k = pi/3 into lambda = 2 pi/k incorrectly and obtain a wavelength containing pi.

concept_tested: Locating the first antinode
stem: For the stationary wave y = 2 sin(pi x/4) cos(50 pi t), in SI units, the first antinode lies at a distance from x = 0 of
solution: Here k = pi/4 rad m^-1, so lambda = 8 m. The amplitude 2 sin(pi x/4) is maximum when pi x/4 = pi/2, that is x = 2 m, which is lambda/4 as expected.
formula_principle: Antinodes occur where sin(k x) equals plus or minus one
common_misconception: The condition for an antinode is sometimes taken as sin(k x) = 0, which actually locates the nodes.

concept_tested: Amplitude behaviour in the two kinds of wave
stem: Which statement correctly compares a progressive wave with a stationary wave?
option_a: In both waves every particle vibrates with the same amplitude
option_b: In a progressive wave the amplitude varies with position while in a stationary wave it is the same everywhere
option_c: In a progressive wave every particle has the same amplitude, while in a stationary wave the amplitude varies with position from zero to a maximum
option_d: In both waves the amplitude varies with position in exactly the same way
correct_answer_text: In a progressive wave every particle has the same amplitude, while in a stationary wave the amplitude varies with position from zero to a maximum
solution: In the progressive form the coefficient of the oscillating factor is the constant A. In the stationary form the coefficient is 2 A sin(k x), which depends on where the particle is, giving zero at nodes and 2 A at antinodes.
formula_principle: Progressive wave: y = A sin(omega t - k x); stationary wave: y = 2 A sin(k x) cos(omega t)
common_misconception: The variation of displacement with position is confused with a variation of amplitude with position.

concept_tested: Amplitude one eighth of a wavelength from a node
stem: In the stationary wave y = 2 A sin(k x) cos(omega t), the amplitude of a particle located at a distance lambda/8 from a node is
solution: With x = lambda/8, k x = (2 pi/lambda)(lambda/8) = pi/4. Hence the amplitude is 2 A sin(pi/4) = 2 A/sqrt(2) = A sqrt(2), about 1.41 A.
formula_principle: Amplitude = 2 A sin(k x) with k = 2 pi/lambda
common_misconception: The distance is inserted directly into the sine without first multiplying by 2 pi/lambda.

concept_tested: How often all particles cross the mean position
stem: In a stationary wave of period T, all the particles of the medium pass simultaneously through their mean positions
option_d: never, because the particles at the nodes are always at rest
solution: The whole pattern becomes flat when cos(omega t) = 0, which happens at t = T/4 and t = 3T/4 in each period, that is twice in every period.
formula_principle: y = 2 A sin(k x) cos(omega t) vanishes whenever cos(omega t) = 0
common_misconception: The four turning points of a cycle are confused with the crossings of the mean position.

concept_tested: Frequency of a stationary sound wave
stem: In a stationary sound wave set up in air, two consecutive antinodes are 15 cm apart. If the speed of sound in air is 330 m s^-1, the frequency of the wave is
solution: Since lambda/2 = 15 cm, lambda = 30 cm = 0.3 m. Hence f = v/lambda = 330/0.3 = 1100 Hz.
formula_principle: Consecutive antinodes are lambda/2 apart, then f = v/lambda
common_misconception: Antinode spacing is sometimes taken as lambda/4 by confusing it with the node to antinode distance.

concept_tested: Conditions needed to form a stationary wave
stem: A stationary wave is produced when
option_a: two progressive waves of the same frequency and amplitude travel in opposite directions along the same line
option_b: two progressive waves of the same frequency travel in the same direction
option_c: two progressive waves of slightly different frequencies travel in the same direction
option_d: two progressive waves of different frequencies travel in opposite directions
correct_answer_text: two progressive waves of the same frequency and amplitude travel in opposite directions along the same line
solution: Adding A sin(omega t - k x) and A sin(omega t + k x) gives 2 A sin(k x) cos(omega t). Equal frequency keeps the nodes fixed and equal amplitude makes the nodes points of complete rest.
formula_principle: Superposition of two identical waves travelling in opposite directions
common_misconception: Stationary waves and beats are both amplitude effects and are easily interchanged.

concept_tested: Phase relation between adjacent loops
stem: Particles in two adjacent loops of a stationary wave
option_a: are in phase with one another
solution: Since sin(k x) is positive in one loop and negative in the next, the displacements of particles in adjacent loops always have opposite signs, which corresponds to a phase difference of pi.
formula_principle: The amplitude factor 2 A sin(k x) changes sign at every node
common_misconception: The sign change of the amplitude factor is overlooked, so all particles are thought to move together.

concept_tested: Speed of the progressive waves forming a stationary wave
stem: A stationary wave is represented by y = 0.1 cos(pi x/6) sin(20 pi t), where all quantities are in SI units. The speed of the component progressive waves is
solution: Here k = pi/6 rad m^-1, so lambda = 2 pi/k = 12 m, and omega = 20 pi rad s^-1, so f = 10 Hz. Hence v = f lambda = 10 x 12 = 120 m s^-1, which is also omega/k = 20 pi/(pi/6).
formula_principle: v = omega/k for the component waves of a stationary wave
common_misconception: Students take the coefficient of t as the frequency in hertz and inflate the speed by a factor of 2 pi.

concept_tested: Node spacing when the two component waves are given
stem: Two waves y1 = 5 sin(4 t - 2 x) and y2 = 5 sin(4 t + 2 x), in SI units, superpose to form a stationary wave. The distance between two consecutive nodes is
option_a: pi m, that is about 3.14 m
option_b: pi/4 m, that is about 0.79 m
option_c: pi/2 m, that is about 1.57 m
correct_answer_text: pi/2 m, that is about 1.57 m
solution: Adding the two waves gives y = 10 sin(2 x) cos(4 t) apart from sign conventions. The nodes are where sin(2 x) = 0, that is 2 x = 0, pi, 2 pi and so on, so consecutive nodes are pi/2 m apart. Equivalently lambda = 2 pi/2 = pi m and lambda/2 = pi/2 m.
formula_principle: Superposition gives 2 A sin(k x) cos(omega t) with node spacing pi/k
common_misconception: The propagation constant of 2 rad m^-1 is read as a wavelength of 2 m, which changes the answer completely.

concept_tested: Which quantity is maximum at a node of a stationary sound wave
stem: At the displacement nodes of a stationary sound wave in an air column, which quantity has its maximum value?
option_a: the displacement of the air particles
option_c: nothing is maximum there, since every physical quantity vanishes at a node
option_d: the pressure variation, because a displacement node is a pressure antinode
correct_answer_text: the pressure variation, because a displacement node is a pressure antinode
solution: If the displacement varies as sin(k x), the strain varies as cos(k x). Where sin(k x) is zero the cosine is largest, so points of zero displacement are points of greatest compression and rarefaction.
formula_principle: Pressure variation is proportional to the spatial gradient of displacement
common_misconception: Students assume that everything about the wave is zero at a node, when only the displacement is.

concept_tested: Wave speed from the number of loops
stem: A stationary wave pattern on a string 1 m long shows five complete loops. If the frequency of vibration is 300 Hz, the speed of the wave along the string is
solution: Each loop is 1/5 = 0.2 m long and equals lambda/2, so lambda = 0.4 m. Then v = f lambda = 300 x 0.4 = 120 m s^-1.
formula_principle: Each loop is lambda/2 long, so L = p lambda/2 for p loops
common_misconception: The number of loops is treated as the number of wavelengths rather than the number of half wavelengths.

concept_tested: Interval between successive instants when the medium is at rest
stem: In a stationary wave of period T, the time interval between two successive instants at which all the particles are momentarily at rest is
solution: The velocity of every particle is proportional to sin(omega t), which vanishes at omega t = 0, pi, 2 pi and so on. These instants are separated by pi/omega = T/2, at which the pattern is alternately at one extreme and then at the other.
formula_principle: All particles are at rest when the time factor cos(omega t) equals plus or minus one
common_misconception: The pattern at the two extremes looks like a mirror image, so students count only one of them per period.

subtopic: Frequency from node to antinode distance
concept_tested: Frequency of a stationary sound wave from a quarter wavelength
stem: In a stationary sound wave in air, the distance between a node and the antinode next to it is 5 cm. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m s^-1, the frequency of the wave is
solution: Since lambda/4 = 5 cm, lambda = 20 cm = 0.2 m. Hence f = v/lambda = 330/0.2 = 1650 Hz.
formula_principle: Node to antinode distance is lambda/4, then f = v/lambda
common_misconception: The quarter wavelength relation is confused with the half wavelength relation, doubling the answer.

concept_tested: Amplitude at lambda/12 from a node compared with the antinode
stem: In a stationary wave, the ratio of the amplitude of a particle situated at a distance lambda/12 from a node to the amplitude of a particle at an antinode is
solution: With x = lambda/12, k x = (2 pi/lambda)(lambda/12) = pi/6. The amplitude is 2 A sin(pi/6) = 2 A x 0.5 = A, while the antinode amplitude is 2 A. The ratio is A : 2 A, that is 1 : 2.
formula_principle: Amplitude = 2 A sin(k x), maximum value 2 A at an antinode
common_misconception: The sinusoidal variation of amplitude along a loop is replaced by a linear one.

concept_tested: Frequency of the fundamental mode of a stretched string
stem: A string of length L is stretched with tension T and has mass per unit length m. Its fundamental frequency is
option_d: n = (1/2L) sqrt(T/M), where M is the total mass of the wire
solution: In the fundamental mode the string carries one loop, so L = lambda/2 and lambda = 2L. Since v = sqrt(T/m), the frequency is n = v/lambda = (1/2L) sqrt(T/m).
formula_principle: n = v/(2L) with v = sqrt(T/m)
common_misconception: The total mass of the wire is used in place of the mass per unit length, which changes the units of the answer.

concept_tested: Dependence of frequency on vibrating length
stem: For a stretched string kept at constant tension and made of the same material, the fundamental frequency is
option_a: directly proportional to the vibrating length
option_b: inversely proportional to the square of the vibrating length
option_c: inversely proportional to the vibrating length
correct_answer_text: inversely proportional to the vibrating length
solution: Since n = (1/2L) sqrt(T/m), keeping T and m fixed makes n proportional to 1/L, so the product n L stays constant.
formula_principle: Law of length: n L = constant at constant T and m
common_misconception: The everyday observation that longer strings sound deeper is not linked to the formula, so the proportionality is reversed.

concept_tested: First overtone of a string fixed at both ends
stem: A string fixed at both ends has fundamental frequency n. Its first overtone is
option_a: the third harmonic, of frequency 3 n
option_b: the second harmonic, of frequency 2 n
option_c: the second harmonic, of frequency n/2
option_d: the third harmonic, of frequency 2 n
correct_answer_text: the second harmonic, of frequency 2 n
solution: The allowed modes have L = p lambda/2, giving frequencies p v/(2L) = p n for p = 1, 2, 3 and so on. The first tone above the fundamental is p = 2, of frequency 2 n.
formula_principle: A string fixed at both ends supports all harmonics n, 2n, 3n and so on
common_misconception: The rule for a pipe closed at one end, which skips even harmonics, is wrongly applied to a string.

concept_tested: SI unit of mass per unit length
stem: The SI unit of the quantity m that appears in the expression n = (1/2L) sqrt(T/m) for a stretched string is
solution: For the expression sqrt(T/m) to have the unit of speed, T in N divided by m must give m^2 s^-2. Since N is kg m s^-2, m must be in kg m^-1, which is indeed mass per unit length.
formula_principle: m = mass of the wire divided by its length
common_misconception: The symbol m is read as ordinary mass because the same letter is used for both quantities.

concept_tested: Nodes and antinodes in the fundamental mode
stem: A sonometer wire of vibrating length L sounds its fundamental note. The pattern on the wire consists of
option_a: two antinodes at the ends and one node at the middle, with L = lambda/2
option_b: two nodes at the ends and two antinodes, with L = lambda
option_c: two nodes at the ends and one antinode at the middle, with L = lambda/2
option_d: one node and one antinode, with L = lambda/4
correct_answer_text: two nodes at the ends and one antinode at the middle, with L = lambda/2
solution: Both ends are held fixed and must be nodes. The simplest pattern satisfying this has a single loop with one antinode in the middle, and one loop spans half a wavelength, so L = lambda/2.
formula_principle: In the fundamental mode of a string, L = lambda/2
common_misconception: The closed pipe quarter wavelength condition is transferred to the string, halving the calculated frequency.

concept_tested: Fundamental frequency from length and wave speed
stem: Transverse waves travel along a stretched string at 200 m s^-1. If the vibrating length of the string is 0.5 m, its fundamental frequency is
solution: The fundamental wavelength is lambda = 2L = 1 m, so n = v/lambda = 200/1 = 200 Hz.
formula_principle: n = v/(2L) for the fundamental mode of a string
common_misconception: The factor of two in the fundamental wavelength is dropped, doubling the answer.

concept_tested: Effect of quadrupling the tension
stem: The tension in a sonometer wire is made four times as large while the vibrating length and the linear density are kept unchanged. The fundamental frequency
option_a: becomes four times the original value
option_d: remains unchanged because the length has not been altered
solution: Since n = (1/2L) sqrt(T/m), multiplying T by four multiplies sqrt(T) by two, so the frequency doubles.
formula_principle: Law of tension: n is proportional to sqrt(T) at constant L and m
common_misconception: The square root is ignored, so the frequency is scaled by the same factor as the tension.

subtopic: Combined change of length and tension
concept_tested: Effect of doubling length and quadrupling tension together
stem: The vibrating length of a stretched wire is doubled and at the same time its tension is made four times as large. The linear density is unchanged. The fundamental frequency
option_d: becomes four times the original value
solution: Frequency scales as sqrt(T)/L. Quadrupling T multiplies the numerator by two and doubling L multiplies the denominator by two, so the two effects cancel and the frequency is unchanged.
formula_principle: n is proportional to sqrt(T)/L
common_misconception: Only one of the two changes is applied because the other is forgotten midway through the calculation.

concept_tested: Fundamental frequency from T, m and L
stem: A wire of linear density 0.01 kg m^-1 is stretched with a tension of 100 N. If its vibrating length is 0.5 m, its fundamental frequency is
solution: The wave speed is v = sqrt(100/0.01) = sqrt(10000) = 100 m s^-1. The fundamental frequency is n = v/(2L) = 100/(2 x 0.5) = 100 Hz.
formula_principle: v = sqrt(T/m) and n = v/(2L)
common_misconception: The tension and the linear density are multiplied instead of divided inside the square root.

concept_tested: Second overtone of a string
stem: The fundamental frequency of a stretched string is 150 Hz. The frequency of its second overtone is
option_a: 450 Hz, which is the third harmonic
option_b: 300 Hz, which is the second harmonic
option_c: 600 Hz, which is the fourth harmonic
option_d: 450 Hz, which is the fifth harmonic
correct_answer_text: 450 Hz, which is the third harmonic
solution: The second overtone corresponds to p = 2, so it is the third harmonic with frequency 3 x 150 = 450 Hz.
formula_principle: For a string, the pth overtone is the (p + 1)th harmonic of frequency (p + 1) n
common_misconception: The words overtone and harmonic are treated as synonyms, so every mode number is out by one.

concept_tested: Frequencies of two wires of different radii
stem: Two wires of the same material and the same length are stretched with the same tension. Their radii are in the ratio 1 : 2. The ratio of their fundamental frequencies is
solution: The linear density is m = pi r^2 rho, so sqrt(m) is proportional to r. Since n is proportional to 1/sqrt(m), it is proportional to 1/r. With radii in the ratio 1 : 2, the frequencies are in the ratio 2 : 1.
formula_principle: m = pi r^2 rho, so n is proportional to 1/r at constant L, T and rho
common_misconception: The square of the radius from the area is carried through without the compensating square root.

concept_tested: Statement of the third law of vibrating strings
stem: The law of linear density for a vibrating string states that, at constant length and tension, the fundamental frequency is
option_a: inversely proportional to the linear density itself
option_b: directly proportional to the square root of the linear density
option_c: inversely proportional to the square root of the linear density
option_d: independent of the linear density as long as the tension is unchanged
correct_answer_text: inversely proportional to the square root of the linear density
solution: From n = (1/2L) sqrt(T/m), holding L and T fixed makes n proportional to 1/sqrt(m), so the product n sqrt(m) is constant.
formula_principle: Law of linear density: n sqrt(m) = constant at constant L and T
common_misconception: The square root is dropped, which exaggerates the effect of using a thicker or heavier wire.

concept_tested: New length for a required frequency
stem: A sonometer wire of vibrating length 0.4 m sounds a note of 256 Hz. Keeping the tension unchanged, the vibrating length required to obtain a note of 320 Hz is
formula_principle: n L = constant at constant tension and linear density
common_misconception: The proportionality is set up the wrong way round, giving a longer wire for a higher note.

concept_tested: Speed from the fundamental frequency and length
stem: A string of vibrating length 0.6 m sounds its fundamental note of frequency 250 Hz. The speed of the transverse wave along the string is
solution: The fundamental wavelength is lambda = 2 x 0.6 = 1.2 m, so v = f lambda = 250 x 1.2 = 300 m s^-1.
formula_principle: In the fundamental mode lambda = 2L, then v = f lambda
common_misconception: The relation v = 2 L n is remembered as v = L n, halving every answer.

concept_tested: Tension needed to sound the same note in the fundamental mode
stem: A wire vibrating in three loops gives a note of frequency 300 Hz. Keeping the length and the linear density unchanged, the tension must be made how many times as large so that the wire gives the same 300 Hz note while vibrating in its fundamental mode?
option_b: one ninth of the original value
solution: With three loops the frequency is 3 times the fundamental, so the present fundamental is 300/3 = 100 Hz. To make the fundamental itself 300 Hz the frequency must be tripled, and since n is proportional to sqrt(T), the tension must be multiplied by 3^2 = 9.
formula_principle: n is proportional to p sqrt(T), so a change of mode must be compensated by a change of tension
common_misconception: The tripling of frequency is applied directly to the tension without squaring.

concept_tested: Finding the tension in a wire
stem: A wire of length 1 m and linear density 0.01 kg m^-1 is to sound a fundamental note of 100 Hz. The tension required in the wire is
solution: The fundamental wavelength is 2L = 2 m, so v = f lambda = 100 x 2 = 200 m s^-1. Since v = sqrt(T/m), T = m v^2 = 0.01 x 200^2 = 0.01 x 40000 = 400 N.
formula_principle: v = 2 L n and T = m v^2
common_misconception: The square on the speed is forgotten when the relation v = sqrt(T/m) is inverted.

concept_tested: New frequency when the tension is increased
stem: A sonometer wire under a tension of 100 N sounds a fundamental note of 200 Hz. Keeping the length unchanged, the tension is increased to 225 N. The new fundamental frequency is
solution: The ratio of tensions is 225/100 = 2.25, whose square root is 1.5. Hence n2 = 200 x 1.5 = 300 Hz.
formula_principle: n2/n1 = sqrt(T2/T1) at constant length and linear density
common_misconception: The square root step is skipped, which greatly exaggerates the rise in pitch.

concept_tested: Wave speed when the string vibrates in four loops
stem: A string of length 1.2 m vibrates in four loops at a frequency of 200 Hz. The speed of the transverse wave along the string is
solution: Each loop is 1.2/4 = 0.3 m long and equals lambda/2, so lambda = 0.6 m. Hence v = f lambda = 200 x 0.6 = 120 m s^-1.
formula_principle: L = p lambda/2 for p loops, then v = f lambda
common_misconception: The number of loops is confused with the number of wavelengths on the string.

subtopic: Two wires of different length and diameter
concept_tested: Comparing fundamental frequencies of two wires
stem: Two wires of the same material are stretched with the same tension. Their lengths are in the ratio 1 : 2 and their diameters are in the ratio 1 : 2. The ratio of their fundamental frequencies is
solution: The linear density is proportional to d^2, so sqrt(m) is proportional to d and n is proportional to 1/(L d). Hence n1/n2 = (L2 d2)/(L1 d1) = (2 x 2)/(1 x 1) = 4, giving 4 : 1.
formula_principle: n is proportional to 1/(L d) for wires of the same material under the same tension
common_misconception: Only one of the two differences is used because the other is assumed not to matter.

concept_tested: Fundamental from two successive resonances
stem: A string fixed at both ends resonates at 420 Hz and the next higher resonance occurs at 490 Hz. The fundamental frequency of the string is
solution: The allowed frequencies are n, 2n, 3n and so on, so any two consecutive resonances differ by n. Here 490 - 420 = 70 Hz, so the fundamental is 70 Hz. As a check, 420 = 6 x 70 and 490 = 7 x 70.
formula_principle: For a string, consecutive harmonics differ by the fundamental frequency
common_misconception: The rule for a closed pipe, where consecutive resonances differ by twice the fundamental, is used instead.

concept_tested: General relation between overtone number and frequency
stem: A string fixed at both ends has fundamental frequency n. The frequency of its pth overtone is
solution: The modes are n, 2n, 3n and so on. Calling the fundamental the first harmonic, the first overtone is 2n, the second overtone is 3n, and in general the pth overtone is (p + 1) n.
formula_principle: For a string every harmonic is present, so the pth overtone is the (p + 1)th harmonic
common_misconception: Students memorise (2p + 1) n from the closed pipe case and apply it to strings as well.

subtopic: Tension from a three loop resonance
concept_tested: Tension when a wire resonates in three loops
stem: A wire of length 1.5 m and linear density 0.02 kg m^-1 vibrates in three loops when excited by a tuning fork of frequency 100 Hz. The tension in the wire is
solution: Three loops in 1.5 m means each loop is 0.5 m, so lambda = 1 m. The wave speed is v = f lambda = 100 x 1 = 100 m s^-1. Hence T = m v^2 = 0.02 x 100^2 = 0.02 x 10000 = 200 N.
formula_principle: L = 3 lambda/2 for three loops, v = f lambda and T = m v^2
common_misconception: The number of loops is left out of the wavelength calculation, which multiplies the tension by nine.

concept_tested: Tension needed to change the number of loops
stem: A string of fixed length vibrates in two loops under a tension T. To make the same string vibrate in three loops at the same frequency, the tension must be changed to
solution: For constant frequency and length, p sqrt(T) must remain constant. Hence 2 sqrt(T) = 3 sqrt(T dash), giving sqrt(T dash) = (2/3) sqrt(T) and T dash = 4 T/9.
formula_principle: n = (p/2L) sqrt(T/m), so at constant n and L the product p sqrt(T) is constant
common_misconception: Students expect more loops to need more tension, forgetting that the frequency is being held fixed.

concept_tested: Frequencies of three segments of a sonometer wire
stem: A sonometer wire under constant tension is divided into three segments by two movable bridges, so that the lengths of the segments are in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3. The fundamental frequencies of the three segments are in the ratio
solution: The tension and linear density are common to all three segments, so n is proportional to 1/L. The reciprocals of 1, 2 and 3 are 1, 1/2 and 1/3, which on multiplying throughout by 6 become 6 : 3 : 2.
formula_principle: n is proportional to 1/L when T and m are the same for all segments
common_misconception: The reciprocals are taken but not cleared of fractions, so the answer is left in an unrecognisable form or reversed.

concept_tested: Fundamental frequency of a pipe closed at one end
stem: A pipe of length L is closed at one end. If the speed of sound in air is v, the fundamental frequency of the air column is
solution: The closed end is a displacement node and the open end is a displacement antinode, so the shortest possible pattern occupies a quarter of a wavelength. Hence lambda = 4 L and n = v/lambda = v/(4 L).
formula_principle: Closed pipe fundamental: L = lambda/4, so n = v/(4 L)
common_misconception: The open pipe relation is used for both kinds of pipe, doubling the calculated fundamental of a closed pipe.

concept_tested: Which harmonics a closed pipe supports
stem: A pipe closed at one end can sound
option_a: all the harmonics, in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3
option_b: only the even harmonics, in the ratio 2 : 4 : 6
option_c: only the first two harmonics and nothing beyond them
option_d: only the odd harmonics, in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5
correct_answer_text: only the odd harmonics, in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5
solution: The node at the closed end and the antinode at the open end allow only patterns containing an odd number of quarter wavelengths. The frequencies are therefore v/(4L), 3v/(4L), 5v/(4L) and so on, in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5.
formula_principle: Closed pipe modes: L = (2p + 1) lambda/4, giving frequencies (2p + 1) v/(4 L)
common_misconception: The complete harmonic series of a string is assumed to hold for every vibrating system.

subtopic: First overtone of a closed pipe
concept_tested: Identifying the first overtone of a closed pipe
stem: The fundamental frequency of a pipe closed at one end is n. Its first overtone is
option_a: the second harmonic, of frequency 2 n
option_b: the third harmonic, of frequency 3 n
option_c: the third harmonic, of frequency n/3
option_d: the fifth harmonic, of frequency 5 n
correct_answer_text: the third harmonic, of frequency 3 n
solution: The available frequencies are n, 3n, 5n and so on. The first frequency above the fundamental is 3n, so the first overtone is the third harmonic.
formula_principle: For a closed pipe the pth overtone is the (2p + 1)th harmonic
common_misconception: The string rule that the first overtone is the second harmonic is applied to a closed pipe as well.

subtopic: Boundary conditions in a closed pipe
concept_tested: Nodes and antinodes at the two ends
stem: In the air column of a pipe closed at one end there is
option_a: a displacement antinode at the closed end and a displacement node at the open end
option_b: a displacement node at each of the two ends
option_c: a displacement node at the closed end and a displacement antinode at the open end
option_d: a displacement antinode at each of the two ends
correct_answer_text: a displacement node at the closed end and a displacement antinode at the open end
solution: The closed end blocks the motion of the air, forcing zero displacement there, while at the open end the air is free to move and the displacement is largest.
formula_principle: Rigid end is a displacement node; open end is a displacement antinode
common_misconception: The two ends are treated as equivalent because both are boundaries of the pipe.

concept_tested: Fundamental frequency of a pipe open at both ends
stem: A pipe of length L is open at both ends. If the speed of sound in air is v, the fundamental frequency of the air column is
solution: Both ends are displacement antinodes with a single node in between, so the pipe holds half a wavelength. Hence lambda = 2 L and n = v/(2 L).
formula_principle: Open pipe fundamental: L = lambda/2, so n = v/(2 L)
common_misconception: The quarter wavelength condition is applied to an open pipe, halving the calculated fundamental.

concept_tested: Fundamental of a closed pipe of given length
stem: A pipe closed at one end has length 0.25 m. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m s^-1, its fundamental frequency is
solution: The fundamental wavelength is 4 L = 1 m, so n = 330/1 = 330 Hz.
formula_principle: n = v/(4 L) for a pipe closed at one end
common_misconception: The factor four in the closed pipe relation is often replaced by two.

concept_tested: Fundamental of an open pipe of given length
stem: A pipe open at both ends has length 0.5 m. Taking the speed of sound in air as 340 m s^-1, its fundamental frequency is
solution: The fundamental wavelength is 2 L = 1 m, so n = 340/1 = 340 Hz.
formula_principle: n = v/(2 L) for a pipe open at both ends
common_misconception: The relations for open and closed pipes are interchanged because both contain v and L.

concept_tested: First overtone frequency of an open pipe
stem: A pipe open at both ends has length 0.33 m. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m s^-1, the frequency of its first overtone is
solution: The fundamental is n = 330/(2 x 0.33) = 330/0.66 = 500 Hz. The first overtone of an open pipe is the second harmonic, so its frequency is 2 x 500 = 1000 Hz.
formula_principle: Open pipe: n = v/(2 L) and the first overtone is the second harmonic 2 n
common_misconception: The first overtone is sometimes quoted as three times the fundamental by borrowing the closed pipe rule.

concept_tested: First overtone frequency of a closed pipe
stem: A pipe closed at one end has length 0.5 m. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m s^-1, the frequency of its first overtone is
solution: The fundamental is n = 330/(4 x 0.5) = 330/2 = 165 Hz. The first overtone of a closed pipe is the third harmonic, so its frequency is 3 x 165 = 495 Hz.
formula_principle: Closed pipe: n = v/(4 L) and the first overtone is the third harmonic 3 n
common_misconception: The missing even harmonics of a closed pipe are forgotten, so 2 n is quoted as the first overtone.

concept_tested: Ratio of fundamentals for equal lengths
stem: An open pipe and a closed pipe have exactly the same length. The ratio of the fundamental frequency of the open pipe to that of the closed pipe is
solution: For the same length the ratio is [v/(2L)] divided by [v/(4L)] = 4L/2L = 2, that is 2 : 1.
formula_principle: Open pipe n = v/(2 L); closed pipe n = v/(4 L)
common_misconception: The ratio of the wavelengths 2L : 4L is quoted directly as the ratio of the frequencies.

subtopic: Overtone series of an open pipe
concept_tested: Ratio of the first three modes of an open pipe
stem: The frequencies of the fundamental, the first overtone and the second overtone of a pipe open at both ends are in the ratio
solution: The allowed frequencies are v/(2L), 2v/(2L), 3v/(2L) and so on. The first three are therefore in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3.
formula_principle: Open pipe modes: L = p lambda/2, giving frequencies p v/(2 L)
common_misconception: Because closed pipes are studied alongside open pipes, the odd only series is applied to both.

concept_tested: Size of the end correction at an open end
stem: For a cylindrical pipe of inner diameter d, the end correction to be added at one open end is taken as
option_b: 0.3 L, where L is the length of the pipe
solution: The displacement antinode does not sit exactly at the geometric opening but a little beyond it, at a distance of about 0.3 times the inner diameter. A closed pipe has one open end and so needs one such correction, while an open pipe needs two.
formula_principle: End correction e = 0.3 d per open end, so effective length = L + e for a closed pipe
common_misconception: The correction is wrongly linked to the length of the pipe rather than to its bore.

concept_tested: Fundamental of a closed pipe including end correction
stem: A pipe closed at one end has length 0.49 m and the end correction for its open end is 0.01 m. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m s^-1, the fundamental frequency of the air column is
solution: The effective length is L + e = 0.49 + 0.01 = 0.50 m. Hence n = 330/(4 x 0.50) = 330/2 = 165 Hz.
formula_principle: n = v/[4 (L + e)] for a pipe closed at one end
common_misconception: The end correction is applied with the wrong sign, which raises rather than lowers the calculated frequency.

concept_tested: Frequency from two resonance positions
stem: In a resonance tube experiment the first resonance occurs when the air column is 0.24 m long and the second when it is 0.74 m long. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m s^-1, the frequency of the tuning fork used is
solution: The difference of the two resonance lengths is 0.74 - 0.24 = 0.50 m, which equals lambda/2, so lambda = 1 m. Hence f = v/lambda = 330/1 = 330 Hz. This method automatically eliminates the end correction.
formula_principle: l2 - l1 = lambda/2, then f = v/lambda
common_misconception: The first resonance length alone is used as a quarter wavelength, which builds the end correction into the answer.

concept_tested: Relative lengths for equal fundamental frequencies
stem: An open pipe and a closed pipe sound the same fundamental note in the same air. Comparing their lengths,
option_a: the open pipe is half as long as the closed pipe
option_b: the open pipe is twice as long as the closed pipe
option_c: the two pipes have equal lengths
option_d: the open pipe is four times as long as the closed pipe
correct_answer_text: the open pipe is twice as long as the closed pipe
solution: Setting the two fundamentals equal, v/(2 Lo) = v/(4 Lc), so 4 Lc = 2 Lo and Lo = 2 Lc. The open pipe must be twice as long.
formula_principle: v/(2 Lo) = v/(4 Lc) gives Lo = 2 Lc
common_misconception: Because a closed pipe sounds deeper for a given length, students expect it to be the longer pipe here.

subtopic: Nodes and antinodes in a mode
concept_tested: Counting nodes and antinodes in the second overtone of an open pipe
stem: In the second overtone of a pipe open at both ends, the air column contains
solution: The second overtone of an open pipe is the third harmonic, so the pipe holds three half wavelengths. Counting along the pipe there are antinodes at both ends and at two interior points, giving 4 antinodes, with 3 nodes in between.
formula_principle: For the pth harmonic of an open pipe there are p nodes and p + 1 antinodes
common_misconception: The antinodes at the open ends are omitted because attention is fixed on the interior of the pipe.

subtopic: Consecutive resonances of a closed pipe
concept_tested: Fundamental from two successive closed pipe resonances
stem: A pipe closed at one end resonates strongly at 500 Hz and at 700 Hz, with no resonance in between. The fundamental frequency of the pipe is
solution: Consecutive odd harmonics differ by twice the fundamental, so 2 n = 700 - 500 = 200 Hz and n = 100 Hz. As a check, 500 = 5 x 100 and 700 = 7 x 100, which are indeed consecutive odd multiples.
formula_principle: Closed pipe frequencies are odd multiples of the fundamental, so consecutive resonances differ by 2 n
common_misconception: The difference of consecutive resonances is quoted as the fundamental, which is the rule for open pipes and strings.

subtopic: End correction from a resonance tube
concept_tested: Computing the end correction from two resonance lengths
stem: In a resonance tube the first resonance is obtained at an air column length of 0.23 m and the second at 0.71 m. The end correction of the tube is
formula_principle: l1 + e = lambda/4 and l2 + e = 3 lambda/4, giving e = (l2 - 3 l1)/2
common_misconception: The formula is remembered as l2 - 3 l1 without the division by two, doubling the end correction.

concept_tested: How many closed pipe harmonics lie below a given frequency
stem: A pipe closed at one end has length 0.5 m. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m s^-1, the number of harmonics of this pipe that lie below 1000 Hz is
solution: The fundamental is 330/(4 x 0.5) = 165 Hz. The permitted frequencies are the odd multiples 165, 495, 825, 1155 Hz and so on. Of these, 165 Hz, 495 Hz and 825 Hz are below 1000 Hz, so there are 3 such harmonics.
formula_principle: Closed pipe frequencies are (2p + 1) v/(4 L)
common_misconception: All integral multiples of the fundamental are counted, which doubles the number obtained.

concept_tested: Effect of half filling an open pipe with water
stem: An organ pipe open at both ends has fundamental frequency n. It is now half filled with water, so that it behaves as a pipe closed at one end. The new fundamental frequency is
solution: Originally n = v/(2 L). After half filling, the air column is L/2 long and closed at the water surface, so its fundamental is v/[4 (L/2)] = v/(2 L), which is exactly n again.
formula_principle: Open pipe n = v/(2 L); closed pipe of length L/2 gives v/[4 (L/2)]
common_misconception: Only one of the two changes is applied, so the frequency is reported as halved or doubled.

concept_tested: Length ratio when two chosen modes coincide
stem: The third overtone of a pipe closed at one end has the same frequency as the fifth harmonic of a pipe open at both ends. The ratio of the length of the closed pipe to that of the open pipe is
solution: The third overtone of the closed pipe is its seventh harmonic, of frequency 7 v/(4 Lc). The fifth harmonic of the open pipe has frequency 5 v/(2 Lo). Equating, 7/(4 Lc) = 5/(2 Lo), so 7 x 2 Lo = 5 x 4 Lc, giving 14 Lo = 20 Lc and Lc/Lo = 14/20 = 7/10.
formula_principle: Closed pipe pth overtone is the (2p + 1)th harmonic; open pipe pth harmonic is p v/(2 L)
common_misconception: The overtone number is used in place of the harmonic number for the closed pipe.

concept_tested: Ratio of first overtones of pipes of equal length
stem: A closed pipe and an open pipe have the same length. The ratio of the frequency of the first overtone of the closed pipe to that of the first overtone of the open pipe is
solution: The closed pipe first overtone is its third harmonic, 3 v/(4 L). The open pipe first overtone is its second harmonic, 2 x v/(2 L) = v/L. The ratio is [3 v/(4 L)] divided by [v/L] = 3/4, that is 3 : 4.
formula_principle: Closed pipe first overtone = 3 v/(4 L); open pipe first overtone = 2 x v/(2 L) = v/L
common_misconception: Overtones and harmonics are mixed between the two pipes, so the wrong pair of modes is compared.

concept_tested: Length of air column at the second resonance
stem: A resonance tube is sounded with a tuning fork of frequency 425 Hz. The speed of sound in air is 340 m s^-1 and the end correction may be neglected. The length of the air column at the second resonance is
solution: The wavelength is lambda = v/f = 340/425 = 0.8 m. The first resonance is at lambda/4 = 0.2 m and the second at 3 lambda/4 = 0.6 m.
formula_principle: Resonances of a closed tube occur at lambda/4, 3 lambda/4, 5 lambda/4 and so on
common_misconception: The successive resonance lengths are assumed to be in the ratio 1 : 2 rather than 1 : 3 : 5.

concept_tested: Length of a closed pipe sounding with an open pipe
stem: An open pipe of length 0.4 m sounds its third harmonic and is found to be in unison with a closed pipe sounding its first overtone. The length of the closed pipe is
solution: The open pipe third harmonic has frequency 3 v/(2 x 0.4) = 3 v/0.8. The closed pipe first overtone is its third harmonic, of frequency 3 v/(4 Lc). Equating gives 4 Lc = 0.8, so Lc = 0.2 m.
formula_principle: Open pipe third harmonic = 3 v/(2 Lo); closed pipe first overtone = 3 v/(4 Lc)
common_misconception: The first overtone of the closed pipe is taken as its second harmonic, which does not exist for that pipe.

concept_tested: Beat frequency as the difference of two frequencies
stem: Two tuning forks of frequencies 256 Hz and 260 Hz are sounded together. The number of beats heard per second is
solution: The beat frequency is the magnitude of the difference of the two frequencies, that is 260 - 256 = 4 beats per second.
formula_principle: Beat frequency = |n1 - n2|
common_misconception: The mean frequency, which decides the pitch of the sound heard, is quoted as the beat frequency.

concept_tested: Meaning of waxing and waning in beats
stem: In the phenomenon of beats, the terms waxing and waning refer to
option_a: the rise and the fall of the pitch of the resultant note
option_b: the instants of maximum loudness and of minimum loudness in the resultant sound
option_c: an increase in the frequency of one fork and a decrease in that of the other
option_d: the two halves of a single cycle of the resultant sound wave
correct_answer_text: the instants of maximum loudness and of minimum loudness in the resultant sound
solution: When two nearly equal frequencies superpose, the two waves drift slowly in and out of phase. When they are in phase the sound is loudest, which is waxing, and when they are in opposite phase it is faintest, which is waning.
formula_principle: Beats: periodic waxing and waning of intensity due to slowly varying resultant amplitude
common_misconception: The slow variation of loudness is mistaken for a wobble in the pitch of the note.

concept_tested: When beats are produced
stem: Beats are produced when
option_a: two notes of exactly the same frequency superpose
option_b: two notes of the same frequency travel in opposite directions
option_c: two notes of very different frequencies, such as 200 Hz and 800 Hz, superpose
option_d: two notes of slightly different frequencies travelling in the same direction superpose
correct_answer_text: two notes of slightly different frequencies travelling in the same direction superpose
solution: The resultant amplitude of two superposing waves varies as cos[pi (n1 - n2) t]. This gives a slow rise and fall of loudness only when n1 and n2 differ by a small amount.
formula_principle: Beats require two waves of slightly different frequencies superposing at the same place
common_misconception: Beats and stationary waves are both described as amplitude effects and are easily confused.

concept_tested: Practical uses of the phenomenon of beats
stem: Which of the following is a genuine application of beats?
option_a: Tuning a musical instrument and determining an unknown frequency by comparison with a standard fork
option_b: Measuring the speed of sound in a solid rod directly
option_c: Producing a stationary wave in an air column
option_d: Increasing the loudness of a note permanently
correct_answer_text: Tuning a musical instrument and determining an unknown frequency by comparison with a standard fork
solution: If a fork of unknown frequency gives a known number of beats with a standard fork, the unknown frequency differs from the standard by that number. Adjusting the instrument until the beats vanish brings it into tune, which is exactly how strings are tuned.
formula_principle: Beat frequency equals the difference of the two frequencies, which allows an unknown frequency to be found
common_misconception: Any effect involving two sound sources is loosely labelled an application of beats.

concept_tested: Effect of wax on the frequency of a fork
stem: A tuning fork A of frequency 288 Hz produces 4 beats per second with a fork B. When B is loaded with a little wax, the number of beats rises to 6 per second. The original frequency of B was
solution: Before loading, B is either 292 Hz or 284 Hz. Wax lowers the frequency of B. Starting from 292 Hz the frequency would fall towards 288 Hz and the beats would decrease, which contradicts the observation. Starting from 284 Hz the frequency falls to 282 Hz, making the difference 6 Hz, which agrees. Hence B was 284 Hz.
formula_principle: Loading a fork with wax increases its mass and lowers its frequency; beat frequency = |n1 - n2|
common_misconception: Students forget that wax lowers the frequency and choose the value above the standard fork.

concept_tested: Effect of filing the prongs of a fork
stem: A tuning fork A of frequency 512 Hz gives 5 beats per second with a fork B. When the prongs of B are filed slightly, the beat rate falls to 2 per second. The original frequency of B was
solution: Before filing, B is either 517 Hz or 507 Hz. Filing raises the frequency of B. From 517 Hz the frequency would move away from 512 Hz and the beats would increase, which contradicts the observation. From 507 Hz it rises towards 512 Hz, for example to 510 Hz, giving 2 beats, which agrees. Hence B was 507 Hz.
formula_principle: Filing a fork reduces its mass and raises its frequency; beat frequency = |n1 - n2|
common_misconception: The effects of waxing and of filing are interchanged, which reverses the choice between the two candidates.

concept_tested: Time between successive maxima of loudness
stem: Two tuning forks sounded together produce 5 beats per second. The time interval between two successive instants of maximum loudness is
solution: The interval between successive waxings is the beat period, T = 1/5 = 0.2 s.
formula_principle: Beat period = 1/beat frequency
common_misconception: The reciprocal is not taken, so the numerical value of the beat frequency is reported as a time.

subtopic: Number of beats in a time interval
