concept_tested: Counting beats over several seconds
stem: Two sources of sound of frequencies 300 Hz and 306 Hz are sounded together for 4 s. The total number of beats heard is
solution: The beat frequency is 306 - 300 = 6 beats per second. Over 4 s the total number of beats is 6 x 4 = 24.
formula_principle: Number of beats = beat frequency x time
common_misconception: The per second beat count is given as the final answer because the duration is overlooked.

subtopic: Beats from two given wave equations
concept_tested: Reading frequencies from equations and finding the beat rate
stem: Two sound waves are described by y1 = A sin(2 pi x 300 t) and y2 = A sin(2 pi x 304 t), with t in second. The number of times per second that the resultant amplitude becomes maximum is
solution: Comparison gives n1 = 300 Hz and n2 = 304 Hz. The resultant amplitude is maximum at the beat frequency, that is 304 - 300 = 4 times per second.
formula_principle: Comparing with y = A sin(2 pi n t) gives the two frequencies; beat frequency = |n1 - n2|
common_misconception: The coefficient of t is read as the frequency itself, leaving an unwanted factor of 2 pi in the answer.

concept_tested: Using a tension change to decide the wire frequency
stem: A tuning fork of frequency 300 Hz gives 4 beats per second with a sonometer wire. When the tension in the wire is slightly increased, the beat rate falls. The original frequency of the wire was
solution: The wire is either 304 Hz or 296 Hz. Increasing the tension increases the frequency of the wire. From 304 Hz the frequency would move further above 300 Hz and the beats would increase, which contradicts the observation. From 296 Hz it moves towards 300 Hz and the beats fall, which agrees. So the wire was at 296 Hz.
formula_principle: n is proportional to sqrt(T), and beat frequency = |n fork - n wire|
common_misconception: The direction in which tension shifts the frequency is guessed rather than taken from n proportional to sqrt(T).

concept_tested: Beat frequency from two open pipes of different lengths
stem: Two pipes open at both ends have lengths 1.0 m and 1.1 m. They are sounded together in their fundamental modes. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m s^-1, the number of beats produced per second is
solution: The first pipe gives n1 = 330/(2 x 1.0) = 165 Hz and the second gives n2 = 330/(2 x 1.1) = 330/2.2 = 150 Hz. The beat frequency is 165 - 150 = 15 beats per second.
formula_principle: Open pipe fundamental n = v/(2 L), then beat frequency = |n1 - n2|
common_misconception: The two fundamental frequencies are computed correctly but then added rather than subtracted.

concept_tested: Why rapid beats are not heard separately
stem: Two notes of frequencies 400 Hz and 412 Hz are sounded together. The individual beats cannot be distinguished by the ear mainly because
option_a: the two frequencies are too high for the human ear to detect
option_b: the beat frequency of 12 Hz lies below the audible range, so nothing at all is produced
option_c: the ear cannot resolve loudness variations occurring more than about ten times per second, owing to the persistence of hearing
option_d: the two waves cancel each other completely so that no sound is produced
correct_answer_text: the ear cannot resolve loudness variations occurring more than about ten times per second, owing to the persistence of hearing
solution: The beat frequency here is 412 - 400 = 12 beats per second. Since a sound impression lasts about one tenth of a second in the ear, successive waxings separated by less than that time overlap and the listener hears a continuous rough sound instead of separate beats.
formula_principle: Persistence of hearing is about one tenth of a second, so beats faster than about 10 per second merge
common_misconception: The beat frequency is treated as if it were an audible tone whose pitch must lie in the audible range.

concept_tested: Finding a frequency using two standard forks
stem: A tuning fork X gives 5 beats per second with a standard fork of 384 Hz and 3 beats per second with a standard fork of 376 Hz. The frequency of X is
solution: From the first observation X is 389 Hz or 379 Hz. From the second observation X is 379 Hz or 373 Hz. The only value common to both lists is 379 Hz.
formula_principle: Beat frequency = |n unknown - n standard|, applied to two standards
common_misconception: Only one of the two conditions is used, so both candidates from that condition seem acceptable.

concept_tested: Tracking the beat rate through repeated loading
stem: Two tuning forks A and B produce 4 beats per second. Fork A is loaded with a little wax and the beat rate falls to 2 per second. On adding more wax the beats vanish, and on adding still more wax the beat rate becomes 3 per second. If the frequency of B is 512 Hz, the original frequency of A was
solution: Initially A is either 516 Hz or 508 Hz. Wax lowers the frequency of A. Starting from 516 Hz, the frequency falls to about 514 Hz giving 2 beats, then to 512 Hz giving no beats, then to about 509 Hz giving 3 beats, which matches the whole sequence. Starting from 508 Hz the beat rate would only increase, so that possibility is ruled out. Hence A was 516 Hz.
formula_principle: Loading with wax lowers the frequency; beat frequency = |n A - n B|
common_misconception: Students settle for the first candidate that fits the initial beat count without testing it against the later observations.

concept_tested: Definition of a wavefront
stem: A wavefront of light is best described as
option_a: the path along which the light energy travels
option_b: the surface on which the amplitude of the wave is always zero
option_c: the locus of all points of the medium that vibrate in the same phase
option_d: the boundary between two media at which light bends
correct_answer_text: the locus of all points of the medium that vibrate in the same phase
solution: Every point on a wavefront is reached by the disturbance at the same instant, so all such points oscillate in the same phase. Hence a wavefront is the locus of points having the same phase of vibration.
formula_principle: A wavefront is a surface of constant phase.
common_misconception: Students often say a wavefront is the path of light; the path is the ray, which is perpendicular to the wavefront.

concept_tested: Wavefront from a point source
stem: A point source of light is placed in a homogeneous isotropic medium. At a short distance from the source the wavefront is
solution: In time t the disturbance from the point source covers the same distance v x t in every direction, so all points in the same phase lie on a sphere of radius v x t centred on the source. The wavefront is therefore spherical.
formula_principle: In an isotropic medium light travels with the same speed in all directions.
common_misconception: Learners forget that isotropy is what makes the wavefront spherical; in an anisotropic crystal it need not be.

concept_tested: Plane wavefront from a distant source
stem: Light coming from a distant star is treated as a plane wavefront near the Earth because
option_a: only a very small portion of the enormous spherical wavefront reaches the Earth and its curvature is negligible
option_b: a star emits plane wavefronts right from its surface
option_c: the wavefront becomes plane because light loses energy on the way
option_d: the atmosphere of the Earth converts spherical wavefronts into plane wavefronts
correct_answer_text: only a very small portion of the enormous spherical wavefront reaches the Earth and its curvature is negligible
solution: The radius of the wavefront at the Earth is of the order of the star distance, which is enormous. A tiny patch of a sphere whose radius is huge has almost zero curvature, so it is treated as a plane wavefront.
formula_principle: A small part of a sphere of very large radius is practically a plane.
common_misconception: Students think distant sources emit plane waves; in fact the wavefront is spherical but with a radius so large that the patch we receive is flat.

concept_tested: Wavefront from a linear source
stem: A long narrow illuminated slit acts as a source of light. The wavefront produced by it is
solution: Each point of the slit sends out light; the set of points reached in the same time lies at a constant perpendicular distance from the line of the slit. That surface is a cylinder with the slit as its axis.
formula_principle: Points equidistant from a straight line source lie on a cylinder.
common_misconception: Learners apply the point source result blindly and answer spherical for a slit source.

concept_tested: Relation between ray and wavefront
stem: Which statement about a ray of light and the corresponding wavefront is correct?
option_a: The ray always lies along the wavefront
option_b: The ray is always perpendicular to the wavefront at the point where it meets it
option_c: The ray is the locus of points having the same phase
option_d: The ray and the wavefront always make an angle of 45 degree with each other
correct_answer_text: The ray is always perpendicular to the wavefront at the point where it meets it
solution: Energy travels outward along the shortest path from one wavefront to the next, which is along the normal to the wavefront. Hence the ray is drawn perpendicular to the wavefront everywhere.
formula_principle: Rays are normals to the wavefront and give the direction of energy propagation.
common_misconception: Students sometimes draw rays tangential to the wavefront instead of normal to it.

concept_tested: Statement of Huygens principle
stem: According to Huygens principle, every point on a given wavefront
option_a: acts as a sink that absorbs the incoming wave energy
option_b: sends out secondary wavelets only in the backward direction
option_c: acts as a secondary source and sends out secondary wavelets in the forward direction
option_d: remains at rest while the neighbouring points vibrate
correct_answer_text: acts as a secondary source and sends out secondary wavelets in the forward direction
solution: The disturbance reaching a point sets it vibrating, and that vibrating point radiates fresh spherical wavelets into the medium ahead. Drawing the common tangent to these forward wavelets after time t gives the wavefront at that later instant.
formula_principle: Huygens principle: each point of a wavefront is a secondary source; the envelope of secondary wavelets gives the new wavefront.
common_misconception: Learners quote the principle but forget that the new wavefront is the envelope of the wavelets, not one single wavelet.

concept_tested: Predictions of wave theory
stem: Which of the following statements is NOT true according to the wave theory of light?
option_a: Light travels faster in water than in air
option_b: Light is propagated as a wave motion
option_c: Every point on a wavefront behaves as a secondary source of light
option_d: The frequency of light does not change when it passes from one medium to another
correct_answer_text: Light travels faster in water than in air
solution: For water mu is about 1.33, so the wave theory speed is c divided by 1.33, which is less than c. Wave theory therefore predicts light to be slower in water than in air, and the experiment of Foucault confirmed this.
formula_principle: Wave theory gives v = c / mu, so a denser medium means a smaller speed.
common_misconception: The corpuscular picture predicted a greater speed in the denser medium and students often carry that wrong idea into wave theory.

concept_tested: Evidence for transverse nature
stem: The phenomenon that establishes the transverse nature of light waves is
solution: In a longitudinal wave the vibration is along the direction of propagation, so no direction across the ray is special and polarisation is impossible. Light can be polarised by a polaroid, hence its vibrations must be perpendicular to the direction of propagation.
formula_principle: Only transverse waves can be polarised.
common_misconception: Students quote interference or diffraction as proof of transverse nature; those only prove the wave nature.

concept_tested: Corpuscular theory versus wave theory
stem: Newton's corpuscular theory and Huygens wave theory differ in their prediction of the speed of light in a denser medium. The experiment on the speed of light in water showed that
option_a: the speed in water is greater than that in air, supporting the corpuscular theory
option_b: the speed in water equals that in air, so both theories fail
option_c: the speed in water is less than that in air, supporting the wave theory
option_d: the speed in water depends only on the intensity of the light used
correct_answer_text: the speed in water is less than that in air, supporting the wave theory
solution: Wave theory requires the speed in water to be c divided by 1.33, that is about 2.25 x 10^8 m per second, which is smaller than 3 x 10^8 m per second. Measurement gave the smaller value, so the wave theory prediction was confirmed.
formula_principle: Wave theory gives mu = c / v, corpuscular theory gave mu = v / c.
common_misconception: Learners mix up which theory predicted the higher speed in the denser medium.

concept_tested: Direction of energy flow
stem: In a light wave travelling through a homogeneous medium, the energy is transported
option_a: along the normals to the wavefront
option_b: along the surface of the wavefront
option_c: in a direction making an angle of 45 degree with the wavefront
option_d: equally in all directions from every point of the wavefront
correct_answer_text: along the normals to the wavefront
solution: Successive wavefronts are separated by the shortest distance along their common normal, and the disturbance moves from one to the next along that normal. Hence the flow of energy is along the rays, which are the normals to the wavefront.
formula_principle: Rays are normals to the wavefront and show the direction of energy transport.
common_misconception: Students confuse the spreading of the wavefront surface with the direction in which energy actually moves.

concept_tested: Inverse square law for a point source
stem: A point source radiates light uniformly in all directions in a non absorbing medium. At a distance of 3 m from the source the intensity is 8 W per square metre. The distance at which the intensity becomes 2 W per square metre and the ratio of the amplitudes at 3 m and at that distance are
solution: Intensity falls from 8 to 2 W per square metre, a factor of 4, so r^2 must increase 4 times and r must double: the new distance is 2 x 3 m = 6 m. Since amplitude varies as 1 / r, the amplitude at 3 m is twice that at 6 m, giving a ratio 2 : 1.
formula_principle: For a spherical wave, intensity I is proportional to 1 / r^2 and amplitude A is proportional to 1 / r.
common_misconception: Learners apply the inverse square law to amplitude as well; amplitude follows an inverse first power law.

concept_tested: Amplitude of a spherical wave
stem: For a spherical wavefront spreading out from a point source in a non absorbing medium, the amplitude at a distance r from the source varies as
solution: The same power spreads over the area 4 x pi x r^2, so I varies as 1 / r^2. Since I is proportional to A^2, A^2 varies as 1 / r^2 and therefore A varies as 1 / r.
formula_principle: Intensity I is proportional to A^2 and also to 1 / r^2 for a spherical wave.
common_misconception: Students quote the inverse square law for amplitude by mistake.

concept_tested: Amplitude of a cylindrical wave
stem: For a cylindrical wavefront produced by a long linear source, the amplitude of the wave at perpendicular distance r from the source varies as
solution: The energy crossing a cylindrical surface of radius r per second is fixed, and that area is proportional to r. Hence I varies as 1 / r. Using I proportional to A^2 gives A^2 proportional to 1 / r, so A varies as 1 divided by the square root of r.
formula_principle: For a cylinder of length L the area is 2 x pi x r x L, so I varies as 1 / r and A varies as 1 / square root of r.
common_misconception: Learners use the spherical result 1 / r for every kind of source without checking the geometry.

concept_tested: Combined amplitude and intensity variation
stem: A point source emits light uniformly in all directions in a non absorbing medium. At a distance of 10 m the amplitude of the wave is A and the intensity is 1 W per square metre. At the point where the amplitude has fallen to A / 5, the distance from the source and the intensity are
option_a: 50 m and 0.2 W per square metre
option_b: 50 m and 0.04 W per square metre
option_c: 250 m and 0.04 W per square metre
option_d: 2 m and 25 W per square metre
correct_answer_text: 50 m and 0.04 W per square metre
solution: Amplitude falls by a factor 5, and since A varies as 1 / r the distance must become 5 x 10 m = 50 m. Intensity varies as A^2, so it falls by 5^2 = 25 times, giving 1 divided by 25 = 0.04 W per square metre.
formula_principle: A is proportional to 1 / r and I is proportional to 1 / r^2 for a spherical wave.
common_misconception: Students scale intensity by the same factor as amplitude instead of by its square.

concept_tested: Constructing the new wavefront
stem: In Huygens geometrical construction, the position of the wavefront after a time t is obtained by drawing
option_a: the largest single secondary wavelet only
option_b: a line joining the centres of all the secondary wavelets
option_c: the common tangent, that is the envelope, to all the secondary wavelets
option_d: a circle passing through the centre of the original wavefront
correct_answer_text: the common tangent, that is the envelope, to all the secondary wavelets
solution: Each point of the old wavefront emits a wavelet of radius v x t. The surface that touches all of these wavelets in the forward direction is the new wavefront at that instant.
formula_principle: New wavefront is the forward envelope of secondary wavelets of radius v x t.
common_misconception: Learners draw only one wavelet and mistake it for the new wavefront.

concept_tested: Laws of reflection from wavefronts
stem: Huygens construction applied to a plane wavefront striking a plane mirror shows that
option_a: the angle of incidence is twice the angle of reflection
option_b: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal
option_c: the reflected wavefront travels with half the speed of the incident wavefront
option_d: the wavelength of light doubles on reflection
correct_answer_text: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal
solution: In the construction the distance travelled by the wavelet from the first point and the distance travelled by the incident wavefront to reach the mirror are both v x t. The two right triangles formed share the same hypotenuse and have equal perpendiculars, so they are congruent and the two angles are equal.
formula_principle: The two triangles in the reflection construction have a common hypotenuse and equal sides v x t.
common_misconception: Students memorise the law but cannot connect it to the equality of the two distances v x t.

concept_tested: Changes on entering a denser medium
stem: When light travels from air into glass, which set of changes is correct?
option_a: speed decreases, wavelength remains the same, frequency decreases
option_b: speed increases, wavelength increases, frequency remains the same
option_c: speed decreases, wavelength decreases, frequency remains the same
option_d: speed remains the same, wavelength decreases, frequency increases
correct_answer_text: speed decreases, wavelength decreases, frequency remains the same
solution: The frequency is set by the source and is the same in every medium. Since v = c / mu is smaller in glass and v = f x lambda, the wavelength in glass must be lambda divided by mu, that is smaller than in air.
formula_principle: v = f x lambda with f fixed by the source and v = c / mu.
common_misconception: A very common error is to think the frequency of light changes inside glass.

concept_tested: Snell law from wavefront construction
stem: Light passes from medium 1 of refractive index mu1 and speed v1 into medium 2 of refractive index mu2 and speed v2. Huygens construction gives sin i divided by sin r as
option_a: v2 / v1, which equals mu1 / mu2
option_d: v1 / v2, which equals mu2 / mu1
correct_answer_text: v1 / v2, which equals mu2 / mu1
solution: In the construction the incident wavefront covers v1 x t along the surface while the refracted wavelet covers v2 x t inside medium 2. Dividing the two sine expressions built on the common hypotenuse gives sin i / sin r = v1 / v2, and since mu = c / v this equals mu2 / mu1.
formula_principle: sin i / sin r = v1 / v2 = mu2 / mu1.
common_misconception: Students invert the speed ratio and end up predicting bending away from the normal in a denser medium.

concept_tested: Speed from refractive index
stem: The refractive index of a certain glass is 1.5. Taking the speed of light in vacuum as 3 x 10^8 m per second, the speed of light in this glass is
solution: v = c / mu = (3 x 10^8) / 1.5 = 2 x 10^8 m per second.
formula_principle: v = c / mu.
common_misconception: Learners multiply c by mu and obtain a speed larger than the speed of light in vacuum.

concept_tested: Wavelength change on refraction
stem: Light of wavelength 6000 angstrom in air enters glass of refractive index 1.5. The wavelength of this light inside the glass is
solution: lambda inside glass = 6000 / 1.5 = 4000 angstrom.
formula_principle: lambda in medium = lambda in air divided by mu.
common_misconception: Students sometimes change the frequency instead of the wavelength.

concept_tested: Invariant quantity at a boundary
stem: A beam of monochromatic light passes from air into water. The quantity that remains unchanged is its
solution: The number of wave crests generated per second by the source is the number arriving per second at any point, so the frequency is the same in air and in water. Since v = f x lambda and v falls, lambda must fall in the same proportion.
formula_principle: Frequency is decided by the source and is the same in all media.
common_misconception: Learners think a change of colour inside a medium implies a change of frequency; the colour is set by frequency and does not change.

concept_tested: Refractive index from angles
stem: A plane wavefront in air strikes the flat surface of a transparent medium at an angle of incidence 45 degree and the angle of refraction is 30 degree. The refractive index of the medium is
solution: mu = sin 45 degree divided by sin 30 degree = (1 divided by square root of 2) divided by (1 divided by 2) = 2 divided by square root of 2 = square root of 2, about 1.41.
formula_principle: mu = sin i / sin r.
common_misconception: Students invert the ratio and obtain a refractive index smaller than one.

concept_tested: Absence of the back wave
stem: In Huygens construction the secondary wavelets are taken only in the forward direction because
option_a: the backward wavelets are absorbed by the source
option_b: the amplitude of a secondary wavelet is maximum in the forward direction and falls to zero in the backward direction
option_c: the backward wavelets travel with a much smaller speed
option_d: the medium behind the wavefront becomes optically denser
correct_answer_text: the amplitude of a secondary wavelet is maximum in the forward direction and falls to zero in the backward direction
solution: The strength of a secondary wavelet depends on the angle theta measured from the forward normal. It is greatest at theta = 0 degree and becomes zero at theta = 180 degree, so no backward travelling wavefront is produced.
formula_principle: The obliquity factor of a secondary wavelet varies as (1 + cos theta) / 2 and vanishes at theta = 180 degree.
common_misconception: Students think Huygens simply ignored the back wave; it actually has zero effective amplitude.

concept_tested: Time to cross a slab
stem: A glass slab of thickness 3 cm has refractive index 1.5. Taking the speed of light in vacuum as 3 x 10^8 m per second, the time taken by light to cross the slab normally is
solution: Speed in glass v = (3 x 10^8) / 1.5 = 2 x 10^8 m per second. Thickness = 3 cm = 3 x 10^-2 m. Time t = (3 x 10^-2) / (2 x 10^8) = 1.5 x 10^-10 s.
formula_principle: v = c / mu and t = thickness divided by v.
common_misconception: Learners forget to reduce the speed inside the medium and use c throughout.

concept_tested: Refractive index and wavelength from speed
stem: Light of wavelength 6000 angstrom in air travels with a speed of 1.5 x 10^8 m per second inside a certain liquid. Taking c as 3 x 10^8 m per second, the refractive index of the liquid and the wavelength of the light inside it are
solution: mu = (3 x 10^8) / (1.5 x 10^8) = 2. Wavelength inside the liquid = 6000 / 2 = 3000 angstrom. The frequency stays 5 x 10^14 Hz in both media.
formula_principle: mu = c / v and lambda in medium = lambda in air divided by mu.
common_misconception: Students change the frequency instead of the wavelength when the speed changes.

concept_tested: Extra optical path through a slab
stem: A plane wavefront of light of wavelength 6000 angstrom in air falls normally on an aperture. A glass slab of refractive index 1.5 and thickness 6 cm covers one half of the aperture. The extra optical path introduced by the slab and the number of wavelengths corresponding to it are
solution: Extra optical path = (1.5 minus 1) x 6 cm = 0.5 x 6 = 3 cm = 3 x 10^-2 m. With lambda = 6000 angstrom = 6 x 10^-7 m, the number of wavelengths = (3 x 10^-2) / (6 x 10^-7) = 5 x 10^4.
formula_principle: Extra optical path = (mu minus 1) x t; number of wavelengths = extra path divided by lambda.
common_misconception: Learners use mu x t for the extra path; the air path of thickness t that the slab replaces must be subtracted.

concept_tested: Condition for coherence
stem: Two sources of light are said to be coherent if the waves emitted by them have
option_a: the same frequency and a constant phase difference between them
option_b: the same amplitude but a continuously changing phase difference
option_c: different frequencies but a constant phase difference
option_d: the same frequency but a rapidly and randomly changing phase difference
correct_answer_text: the same frequency and a constant phase difference between them
solution: The positions of the maxima depend on the phase difference between the arriving waves. Only if that phase difference is fixed do the maxima stay at the same places long enough for the eye to see a steady pattern.
formula_principle: Coherence requires equal frequency and a phase difference that is constant in time.
common_misconception: Students think equal intensity or equal amplitude is what makes sources coherent.

concept_tested: Constructive interference condition
stem: Two coherent waves meet at a point. The interference at that point is constructive if the path difference between them is
solution: A path difference of a whole number of wavelengths corresponds to a phase difference of 2 x pi x n, so the two displacements are in step and the amplitudes add.
formula_principle: Constructive interference: path difference = n x lambda; destructive: path difference = (2n minus 1) x lambda / 2.
common_misconception: Learners interchange the bright and dark fringe conditions.

concept_tested: Destructive interference condition
stem: For two coherent waves of equal amplitude, complete destructive interference occurs at a point where the path difference is
solution: An odd number of half wavelengths corresponds to a phase difference of an odd multiple of pi, so one displacement is exactly opposite to the other and for equal amplitudes the resultant is zero.
formula_principle: Destructive interference: path difference = (2n minus 1) x lambda / 2.
common_misconception: Students write lambda / 2 only for the first minimum and forget the general odd multiples.

concept_tested: Relation between phase and path difference
stem: The phase difference between two waves at a point is related to the path difference between them by the relation
option_a: phase difference = (lambda / 2 x pi) x path difference
option_b: phase difference = (pi / lambda) x path difference
option_c: phase difference = (2 x pi / lambda) x path difference
option_d: phase difference = lambda x path difference
correct_answer_text: phase difference = (2 x pi / lambda) x path difference
solution: One full wavelength of path difference corresponds to one complete cycle, that is 2 x pi radian. Scaling in proportion gives phase difference = (2 x pi / lambda) x path difference.
formula_principle: Phase difference = (2 x pi / lambda) x path difference.
common_misconception: Learners drop the factor 2 and use pi divided by lambda.

concept_tested: Conservation of energy
stem: In an interference pattern, bright and dark bands are formed. This shows that
option_a: light energy is destroyed at the dark bands
option_b: light energy is only redistributed, the total energy remaining the same
option_c: light energy is created at the bright bands
option_d: the law of conservation of energy does not apply to light waves
correct_answer_text: light energy is only redistributed, the total energy remaining the same
solution: At a bright band the intensity of two equal sources rises to 4 x I0 and at a dark band it falls to zero. The average over the pattern is 2 x I0, exactly the sum of the two separate intensities, so the total energy is unchanged and only its distribution alters.
formula_principle: The average intensity over the whole pattern equals the sum of the individual intensities.
common_misconception: Students believe interference destroys light energy at the dark fringes.

concept_tested: Nature of a point from path difference
stem: Two coherent waves of equal amplitude arrive at a point with a path difference of 1.5 lambda. At this point the waves interfere
option_a: destructively, the phase difference being 3 pi radian
option_b: constructively, the phase difference being 3 pi radian
option_c: destructively, the phase difference being 1.5 pi radian
option_d: constructively, the phase difference being 6 pi radian
correct_answer_text: destructively, the phase difference being 3 pi radian
solution: Phase difference = (2 x pi / lambda) x 1.5 lambda = 3 pi radian. Since 3 pi is an odd multiple of pi, the two equal displacements are exactly opposite and the resultant amplitude is zero, so the point is dark.
formula_principle: Phase difference = (2 x pi / lambda) x path difference.
common_misconception: Learners see 1.5 as a fraction and jump to constructive interference without converting to phase.

concept_tested: Phase difference from a quarter wave path
stem: The phase difference between two coherent waves that reach a point with a path difference of lambda / 4 is
solution: Phase difference = (2 x pi / lambda) x (lambda / 4) = 2 x pi / 4 = pi / 2 radian, which is 90 degree.
formula_principle: Phase difference = (2 x pi / lambda) x path difference.
common_misconception: Students convert by multiplying the fraction of a wavelength by pi instead of 2 pi.

concept_tested: Maximum and minimum intensity from amplitudes
stem: Two coherent light waves of amplitudes 5a and 3a superpose. The ratio of the maximum to the minimum intensity in the resulting pattern is
solution: Maximum amplitude = 5a plus 3a = 8a and minimum amplitude = 5a minus 3a = 2a. Hence Imax / Imin = (8a)^2 / (2a)^2 = 64 / 4 = 16 : 1.
formula_principle: Imax / Imin = (a1 plus a2)^2 / (a1 minus a2)^2.
common_misconception: Learners report the amplitude ratio 4 : 1 as the intensity ratio.

concept_tested: Maximum and minimum intensity from intensities
stem: Two coherent sources have intensities in the ratio 9 : 1. The ratio of the maximum to the minimum intensity in the interference pattern produced by them is
solution: Since amplitude is the square root of intensity, a1 : a2 = 3 : 1. Then Imax / Imin = (3 plus 1)^2 / (3 minus 1)^2 = 16 / 4 = 4 : 1.
formula_principle: a is proportional to square root of I; Imax / Imin = (a1 plus a2)^2 / (a1 minus a2)^2.
common_misconception: Students forget the square root step and use the intensities directly in the sum and difference.

concept_tested: Why two lamps do not interfere
stem: Light from two identical electric lamps placed side by side does not produce an interference pattern because
option_a: the two lamps emit light of different frequencies only
option_b: the intensity of the lamps is too large for fringes to form
option_c: light from a lamp is longitudinal and cannot interfere
option_d: the two lamps emit light in independent bursts, so the phase difference between them changes randomly and very rapidly
correct_answer_text: the two lamps emit light in independent bursts, so the phase difference between them changes randomly and very rapidly
solution: Atoms in each lamp radiate independently in wave trains lasting about 10^-8 s. The phase relation between the two lamps therefore changes millions of times per second, so the maxima shift about far too quickly to be seen and the screen looks uniformly lit.
formula_principle: A steady pattern needs a phase difference that stays constant for a time long enough to be observed.
common_misconception: Learners think two identical lamps must be coherent because they are the same in every visible way.

concept_tested: Conditions for a sustained pattern
stem: For a steady and clearly visible interference pattern, which condition is essential?
option_a: The two sources must be coherent and must emit light of the same wavelength
option_b: The two sources must be at least one metre apart
option_c: The two sources must have exactly equal intensities
option_d: The two sources must emit light continuously in all possible wavelengths
correct_answer_text: The two sources must be coherent and must emit light of the same wavelength
solution: If the sources are not coherent the positions of the maxima shift randomly, and if the wavelengths differ the two patterns of different fringe width overlap. Both conditions must hold for a steady visible pattern.
formula_principle: Coherence and equal wavelength are necessary; equal amplitude and small separation improve contrast.
common_misconception: Students list equal intensity as an essential condition; it only improves the contrast.

concept_tested: Resultant intensity at a given phase difference
stem: Two coherent waves, each of intensity I0, meet at a point where the phase difference between them is pi / 2 radian. The resultant intensity at that point is
solution: I = I0 plus I0 plus 2 x square root of (I0 x I0) x cos 90 degree = 2 I0 plus 2 I0 x 0 = 2 I0.
formula_principle: I = I1 plus I2 plus 2 x square root of (I1 x I2) x cos of the phase difference.
common_misconception: Learners assume a phase difference of pi / 2 gives complete cancellation.

concept_tested: Minimum intensity for unequal sources
stem: Two coherent sources of unequal intensities I1 and I2 interfere. The intensity at a point of destructive interference is
option_c: (square root of I1 minus square root of I2)^2, which is greater than zero
correct_answer_text: (square root of I1 minus square root of I2)^2, which is greater than zero
solution: Amplitudes are proportional to the square roots of the intensities, so at destructive interference the resultant amplitude is the square root of I1 minus the square root of I2. Squaring gives the minimum intensity, which is zero only if I1 = I2.
formula_principle: Imin = (a1 minus a2)^2 with a proportional to square root of I.
common_misconception: Students state that dark fringes are always perfectly black even for unequal sources.

concept_tested: Intensity from the cosine squared law
stem: Two coherent sources each of intensity I0 interfere. At a point where the phase difference is 120 degree, the resultant intensity is
solution: I = 4 x I0 x cos^2 (120 / 2) degree = 4 x I0 x (cos 60 degree)^2 = 4 x I0 x (0.5)^2 = I0.
formula_principle: I = 4 x I0 x cos^2 (phase difference / 2).
common_misconception: Learners forget to halve the phase difference before taking the cosine.

concept_tested: Source intensities from the fringe contrast
stem: In an interference pattern the ratio of the maximum to the minimum intensity is 25 : 9. The ratio of the intensities of the two interfering waves is
solution: Taking square roots, (a1 plus a2) / (a1 minus a2) = 5 / 3. Cross multiplying gives 3 a1 plus 3 a2 = 5 a1 minus 5 a2, so 8 a2 = 2 a1 and a1 / a2 = 4. Hence I1 / I2 = 4^2 = 16 : 1.
formula_principle: Imax / Imin = (a1 plus a2)^2 / (a1 minus a2)^2 and I is proportional to a^2.
common_misconception: Students stop at the amplitude ratio and forget to square it for intensities.

concept_tested: Slit widths and intensity ratio
stem: In an interference experiment the widths of the two slits are in the ratio 16 : 1. Taking the intensity from a slit to be proportional to its width, the ratio of the maximum to the minimum intensity in the pattern is
solution: Intensities are in the ratio 16 : 1, so amplitudes are in the ratio 4 : 1. Then Imax / Imin = (4 plus 1)^2 / (4 minus 1)^2 = 25 / 9, that is 25 : 9.
formula_principle: I is proportional to slit width; a is proportional to square root of I; Imax / Imin = (a1 plus a2)^2 / (a1 minus a2)^2.
common_misconception: Learners treat the width ratio as an amplitude ratio and skip the square root step.

concept_tested: Intensity at a fractional path difference
stem: In an interference pattern produced by two identical coherent sources, the intensity at the centre of a bright fringe is Imax. The intensity at a point where the path difference is lambda / 3 is
solution: Phase difference = (2 x pi / lambda) x (lambda / 3) = 2 pi / 3, that is 120 degree. Then I = Imax x cos^2 60 degree = Imax x 0.25 = Imax / 4.
formula_principle: Phase difference = (2 x pi / lambda) x path difference and I = Imax x cos^2 (phase difference / 2).
common_misconception: Students take the intensity to fall in direct proportion to the path difference.

concept_tested: Average intensity of the pattern
stem: Two coherent sources, each of intensity I0, produce an interference pattern on a screen. The average intensity over a large number of fringes is
solution: I = 4 x I0 x cos^2 (phase difference / 2). The average value of cos^2 over many fringes is 1 / 2, so the average intensity is 4 x I0 x 0.5 = 2 I0, which is exactly the sum of the two source intensities and confirms that energy is conserved.
formula_principle: Average of cos^2 over a whole number of cycles is 1 / 2, so average I = I1 plus I2.
common_misconception: Learners quote the maximum value 4 I0 as the average intensity of the pattern.

concept_tested: Resultant amplitude from a phase difference
stem: Two coherent waves each of amplitude a arrive at a point with a phase difference of 60 degree. The resultant amplitude at that point is
solution: Resultant amplitude = 2 x a x cos (60 / 2) degree = 2 x a x cos 30 degree = 2 x a x (square root of 3) / 2 = a x square root of 3, about 1.73a.
formula_principle: Resultant amplitude for equal amplitudes = 2 x a x cos (phase difference / 2).
common_misconception: Students use the full phase difference in the cosine instead of half of it.

concept_tested: Effect of unequal frequencies
stem: Two sources emit light waves of equal amplitude but of slightly different frequencies. On a screen placed in the region of overlap one observes
option_a: a permanent pattern with fringes of double the usual width
option_b: no steady fringe pattern, because the positions of the maxima keep shifting with time
option_c: a permanent pattern in which the bright and dark fringes are interchanged
option_d: complete darkness everywhere on the screen
correct_answer_text: no steady fringe pattern, because the positions of the maxima keep shifting with time
solution: If the frequencies differ by delta f, the phase difference between the waves at any point increases steadily at the rate 2 x pi x delta f. The maxima therefore sweep across the screen, and over the time of observation the eye records only a uniform illumination.
formula_principle: A steady pattern needs a phase difference that does not change with time, which requires equal frequencies.
common_misconception: Learners assume that equal amplitude alone is enough to give visible fringes.

concept_tested: Resultant of unequal intensities at a phase difference
stem: Two coherent sources of intensities I and 4I interfere. At a point where the phase difference between the waves is 120 degree, the resultant intensity is
solution: Here I1 = I, I2 = 4I, so square root of (I1 x I2) = square root of 4 I^2 = 2 I. Then I resultant = I plus 4I plus 2 x 2I x cos 120 degree = 5I plus 4I x (minus 0.5) = 5I minus 2I = 3I.
formula_principle: I = I1 plus I2 plus 2 x square root of (I1 x I2) x cos of the phase difference.
common_misconception: Students use the cosine of the half phase difference here; that shortcut applies only to equal intensities.

concept_tested: Fringe visibility from source intensities
stem: Two coherent sources have intensities in the ratio 1 : 4. For the interference pattern produced, the value of (Imax minus Imin) divided by (Imax plus Imin) is
solution: Amplitudes are in the ratio 1 : 2, so Imax is proportional to (1 plus 2)^2 = 9 and Imin is proportional to (2 minus 1)^2 = 1. Then (9 minus 1) divided by (9 plus 1) = 8 / 10 = 4 / 5.
formula_principle: Imax = (a1 plus a2)^2, Imin = (a1 minus a2)^2 with a proportional to square root of I.
common_misconception: Learners forget that the amplitude ratio is the square root of the intensity ratio.

concept_tested: Fringe width formula
stem: In Young's double slit experiment, the distance between two consecutive bright fringes on the screen is given by
option_a: lambda x D / d, where d is the slit separation and D is the slit to screen distance
correct_answer_text: lambda x D / d, where d is the slit separation and D is the slit to screen distance
solution: The nth bright fringe lies at y = n x lambda x D / d, so the gap between consecutive bright fringes is lambda x D / d, which is the fringe width beta.
formula_principle: Fringe width beta = lambda x D / d.
common_misconception: Students interchange d and D and then predict that fringes get narrower as the screen is moved back.

concept_tested: Numerical value of fringe width
stem: In a double slit experiment light of wavelength 6000 angstrom is used, the slit separation is 1 mm and the screen is 1 m from the slits. The fringe width is
formula_principle: beta = lambda x D / d.
common_misconception: Learners slip by one power of ten while converting angstrom to metre.

concept_tested: Uniform spacing of fringes
stem: In Young's double slit experiment with monochromatic light, the fringes near the centre of the screen are
option_a: equally spaced, the spacing being the same for all orders
option_b: closer together as the order increases
option_c: farther apart as the order increases
option_d: spaced at random with no fixed pattern
correct_answer_text: equally spaced, the spacing being the same for all orders
solution: Since the position of a bright fringe increases in direct proportion to the order n, the difference between consecutive positions is the constant lambda x D / d. Hence the fringes are of equal width near the centre.
formula_principle: y(n) = n x lambda x D / d, so y(n plus 1) minus y(n) = lambda x D / d for every n.
common_misconception: Students carry over the unequal spacing of diffraction maxima into the interference pattern.

concept_tested: Position of the nth bright fringe
stem: In Young's double slit experiment the distance of the nth bright fringe from the centre of the pattern is
option_a: n x lambda x D / d
option_b: (2n minus 1) x lambda x D / (2 x d)
option_c: n x lambda x d / D
option_d: (n plus 1) x lambda x D / d
correct_answer_text: n x lambda x D / d
solution: A bright fringe requires the path difference y x d / D to equal n x lambda. Solving for y gives y = n x lambda x D / d.
formula_principle: Bright fringe: y = n x lambda x D / d; dark fringe: y = (2n minus 1) x lambda x D / (2 x d).
common_misconception: Learners use the dark fringe expression for bright fringes and get positions shifted by half a fringe.

concept_tested: Effect of screen distance
stem: In a double slit experiment, if the screen is moved so that its distance from the slits becomes twice the original value while everything else stays the same, the fringe width becomes
solution: Doubling D in beta = lambda x D / d doubles the value of beta while lambda and d stay fixed.
formula_principle: beta = lambda x D / d, so beta is directly proportional to D.
common_misconception: Students think the pattern only becomes fainter and not wider when the screen is moved back.

concept_tested: Effect of slit separation
stem: In Young's experiment the separation between the two slits is doubled without changing anything else. The fringe width then becomes
option_b: one fourth of the original value
solution: Replacing d by 2d in beta = lambda x D / d gives a new fringe width lambda x D / (2 x d), which is half the original value.
formula_principle: beta = lambda x D / d, so beta is inversely proportional to d.
common_misconception: Learners expect wider slits separation to give wider fringes, which is the opposite of the truth.

concept_tested: Nature of the central fringe
stem: Young's double slit experiment is performed with white light. The fringe formed at the centre of the screen is
option_a: violet, because violet has the shortest wavelength
option_b: red, because red has the longest wavelength
option_c: dark, because the different colours cancel one another
option_d: white, because the path difference is zero for every wavelength there
correct_answer_text: white, because the path difference is zero for every wavelength there
solution: The point equidistant from both slits has zero path difference. The condition for a maximum, path difference = n x lambda with n = 0, is met by all the colours in white light at once, so their sum appears white.
formula_principle: At the centre the path difference is zero for all wavelengths, so every colour has a maximum.
common_misconception: Students assume white light can never produce a definite central fringe.

concept_tested: Finding the slit separation
stem: In a double slit experiment with light of wavelength 5000 angstrom and a screen 1 m from the slits, the fringe width measured is 0.5 mm. The separation between the slits is
formula_principle: beta = lambda x D / d, so d = lambda x D / beta.
common_misconception: Learners rearrange the formula wrongly and place beta in the numerator.

concept_tested: Distance of a given bright fringe
stem: In Young's experiment light of wavelength 5000 angstrom falls on two slits 0.5 mm apart and the screen is 1 m away. The distance of the fourth bright fringe from the centre of the pattern is
solution: beta = lambda x D / d = (5 x 10^-7 x 1) / (5 x 10^-4) = 10^-3 m = 1 mm. The fourth bright fringe is at y = 4 x 1 mm = 4 mm.
formula_principle: y(n) = n x lambda x D / d.
common_misconception: Students confuse the order of the fringe with the number of fringe widths for dark fringes.

concept_tested: Position of a dark fringe
stem: In a double slit experiment the fringe width is 0.4 mm. The distance of the third dark fringe from the centre of the pattern is
solution: For the third dark fringe n = 3, so y = (2 x 3 minus 1) x beta / 2 = 5 x 0.4 / 2 = 1.0 mm.
formula_principle: Dark fringe position y = (2n minus 1) x beta / 2.
common_misconception: Learners count the central bright fringe as a dark one and shift all the dark fringe orders by one.

concept_tested: Separation of a bright and a dark fringe
stem: In Young's experiment the fringe width is 0.6 mm. The distance between the second bright fringe and the second dark fringe, both on the same side of the centre, is
solution: The second bright fringe is at 2 x 0.6 = 1.2 mm and the second dark fringe is at (2 x 2 minus 1) x 0.6 / 2 = 1.5 x 0.6 = 0.9 mm. The separation is 1.2 minus 0.9 = 0.3 mm, that is half a fringe width.
formula_principle: Bright fringe at n x beta; dark fringe at (2n minus 1) x beta / 2.
common_misconception: Students take the gap between any bright and any dark fringe as one full fringe width.

concept_tested: Fringe width inside water
stem: A double slit apparatus gives a fringe width of 0.8 mm in air. The whole apparatus is now immersed in water of refractive index 4 / 3. The new fringe width is
solution: New fringe width = 0.8 divided by (4 / 3) = 0.8 x 3 / 4 = 0.6 mm.
formula_principle: In a medium of refractive index mu, lambda becomes lambda / mu, so beta becomes beta / mu.
common_misconception: Learners think immersion widens the pattern; the shorter wavelength in water actually brings the fringes closer.

concept_tested: Effect of changing the wavelength
stem: A double slit experiment is first done with light of wavelength 6000 angstrom and then repeated with light of wavelength 4000 angstrom, everything else unchanged. The fringe width in the second case, compared with the first, is
option_d: unchanged, because only the colour of the fringes alters
solution: The ratio of the new fringe width to the old one equals 4000 / 6000 = 2 / 3. The fringes therefore become closer together in the ratio 2 : 3.
formula_principle: beta = lambda x D / d, so beta is directly proportional to lambda.
common_misconception: Students remember that blue light gives a different pattern but not that it gives narrower fringes.

concept_tested: Effect of covering one slit
stem: In a working double slit experiment, one of the two slits is completely covered with an opaque sheet. On the screen one now observes
option_a: the same interference fringes but with half the intensity
option_b: interference fringes of double the fringe width
option_c: the single slit diffraction pattern of the open slit, with no interference fringes
correct_answer_text: the single slit diffraction pattern of the open slit, with no interference fringes
solution: With only one slit open there is a single beam, so there is no path difference and no interference. What remains is the broad diffraction pattern produced by that one slit.
formula_principle: Interference requires superposition of two coherent beams.
common_misconception: Learners think covering a slit only halves the brightness of the fringes.

concept_tested: Order of colours in white light fringes
stem: In a double slit experiment with white light, the coloured fringes on either side of the central white fringe appear such that
option_a: red lies nearest to the central fringe and violet lies farthest from it
option_b: violet lies nearest to the central fringe and red lies farthest from it
option_c: all the colours lie at exactly the same distance from the central fringe
option_d: the colours appear only on one side of the central fringe
correct_answer_text: violet lies nearest to the central fringe and red lies farthest from it
solution: For the first order, y = lambda x D / d. Violet has the smallest wavelength of the visible range, so its first maximum is the nearest to the centre, while red with the largest wavelength has its first maximum farthest out.
formula_principle: beta is proportional to lambda, so the fringe of the smallest wavelength is closest to the centre.
common_misconception: Students recall the order of colours in a prism spectrum, where the deviation is largest for violet, and apply it here in reverse.

concept_tested: Angular separation of fringes
stem: In Young's double slit experiment the slits are 1 mm apart and light of wavelength 6000 angstrom is used. The angular fringe width is
option_a: 6 x 10^-4 radian per metre of screen distance
solution: Angular fringe width = lambda / d = (6 x 10^-7) / (10^-3) = 6 x 10^-4 radian. Note that D cancels out, so moving the screen does not change this angle.
formula_principle: Angular fringe width = beta / D = lambda / d.
common_misconception: Learners think the angular width changes when the screen is moved farther away.

concept_tested: Counting fringes in a given width
stem: In a double slit experiment lambda = 5000 angstrom, d = 1 mm and D = 1 m. The number of bright fringes contained in a 1 cm wide region of the screen near the centre is
solution: beta = (5 x 10^-7 x 1) / 10^-3 = 5 x 10^-4 m = 0.5 mm. In a region of 1 cm = 10 mm, the number of bright fringes = 10 divided by 0.5 = 20.
formula_principle: beta = lambda x D / d; number of fringes = width of region divided by beta.
common_misconception: Students divide by the distance between a bright and the next dark fringe and so double the count.

concept_tested: Qualitative effect of immersion
stem: The entire Young's double slit set up is taken from air into a transparent liquid of refractive index greater than one. The fringes on the screen
option_a: move farther apart, because the light slows down in the liquid
option_b: stay exactly as they were, because the frequency of light does not change
option_c: disappear completely, because the two beams stop being coherent
option_d: come closer together, because the wavelength inside the liquid is smaller
correct_answer_text: come closer together, because the wavelength inside the liquid is smaller
solution: Inside the liquid the wavelength becomes lambda divided by mu, so the fringe width becomes beta divided by mu. Since mu is greater than one, the new fringe width is smaller and the fringes crowd together.
formula_principle: beta = lambda x D / (mu x d) when the whole set up is in a medium of refractive index mu.
common_misconception: Learners connect a slower speed with a bigger pattern instead of a smaller wavelength.

concept_tested: Combined change of D and d
stem: In a double slit experiment the fringe width is 0.6 mm when D = 1 m and d = 1 mm. The screen is now moved to D = 1.5 m and the slit separation is reduced to 0.5 mm, with the same light. The new fringe width is
solution: The screen distance rises by the factor 1.5 / 1 = 1.5 and the slit separation falls by the factor 0.5 / 1 = 0.5, which multiplies the fringe width by 1 / 0.5 = 2. New beta = 0.6 x 1.5 x 2 = 1.8 mm.
formula_principle: beta = lambda x D / d, so beta scales as D and inversely as d.
common_misconception: Students apply one of the two changes and forget the other.

concept_tested: Coincidence of fringe orders
stem: A double slit is illuminated at the same time with light of wavelengths 4000 angstrom and 6000 angstrom. The first position away from the centre at which a bright fringe of one wavelength falls exactly on a bright fringe of the other is where
option_a: the second bright fringe of 4000 angstrom meets the third bright fringe of 6000 angstrom
option_b: the third bright fringe of 4000 angstrom meets the second bright fringe of 6000 angstrom
option_c: the fourth bright fringe of 4000 angstrom meets the third bright fringe of 6000 angstrom
option_d: the sixth bright fringe of 4000 angstrom meets the fourth bright fringe of 6000 angstrom
correct_answer_text: the third bright fringe of 4000 angstrom meets the second bright fringe of 6000 angstrom
solution: The condition is n1 x 4000 = n2 x 6000, that is n1 / n2 = 6000 / 4000 = 3 / 2. The smallest whole numbers satisfying this are n1 = 3 and n2 = 2, so the third fringe of 4000 angstrom coincides with the second fringe of 6000 angstrom.
formula_principle: Coincidence needs n1 x lambda1 = n2 x lambda2.
common_misconception: Learners give the higher order to the longer wavelength, which is the wrong way round.

concept_tested: Shift due to a thin transparent sheet
stem: In a double slit experiment with light of wavelength 6000 angstrom, a thin sheet of refractive index 1.5 and thickness 6 x 10^-6 m is placed in front of one slit. The number of fringes by which the pattern shifts is
solution: Extra optical path = (1.5 minus 1) x 6 x 10^-6 = 3 x 10^-6 m. Dividing by lambda = 6 x 10^-7 m gives 5, so the whole pattern shifts by 5 fringes towards the slit that carries the sheet.
formula_principle: Number of fringes shifted = (mu minus 1) x t / lambda.
common_misconception: Students use mu x t rather than (mu minus 1) x t and get three times the correct shift.

concept_tested: Nature of a point from its position
stem: In Young's experiment lambda = 6000 angstrom, d = 1 mm and D = 1 m. The point on the screen at a distance of 0.9 mm from the centre is
option_a: bright, being the first bright fringe
option_b: dark, being the second dark fringe
option_c: dark, being the first dark fringe
option_d: bright, being the second bright fringe
correct_answer_text: dark, being the second dark fringe
solution: Path difference = (0.9 x 10^-3 x 10^-3) / 1 = 9 x 10^-7 m. Dividing by lambda = 6 x 10^-7 m gives 1.5, so the path difference is 1.5 lambda. This is an odd multiple of half a wavelength with n = 2, so the point is the second dark fringe.
formula_principle: Path difference = y x d / D; dark when it equals (2n minus 1) x lambda / 2.
common_misconception: Learners compare 0.9 mm with the fringe width and guess an order without computing the path difference.

concept_tested: Wavelength from a measured fringe position
stem: In a double slit experiment with d = 1 mm and D = 1 m, the tenth bright fringe is found 6 mm from the centre of the pattern. The wavelength of the light used is
solution: beta = 6 mm divided by 10 = 0.6 mm = 6 x 10^-4 m. Then lambda = beta x d / D = (6 x 10^-4 x 10^-3) / 1 = 6 x 10^-7 m = 6000 angstrom.
formula_principle: y(n) = n x lambda x D / d, so lambda = y x d / (n x D).
common_misconception: Students forget to divide the measured distance by the order before using the fringe width formula.

concept_tested: Intensity at a point between fringes
stem: In Young's experiment the intensity at the centre of a bright fringe is I0 and the fringe width is beta. The intensity at a point that is a distance beta / 4 from the centre of the pattern is
solution: At y = beta / 4 the path difference is (beta / 4) x d / D = lambda / 4, since beta x d / D = lambda. The phase difference is therefore (2 x pi / lambda) x lambda / 4 = pi / 2. Then I = I0 x cos^2 (pi / 4) = I0 x 0.5 = I0 / 2.
formula_principle: Path difference = y x d / D and I = I0 x cos^2 (phase difference / 2).
common_misconception: Learners assume the intensity falls in direct proportion to the distance from the fringe centre.

concept_tested: Separation of fringes on opposite sides
stem: In a double slit experiment the fringe width is 0.4 mm. The distance between the third bright fringe on one side and the fifth dark fringe on the other side of the centre is
solution: Third bright fringe is at 3 x 0.4 = 1.2 mm on one side. Fifth dark fringe is at (2 x 5 minus 1) x 0.4 / 2 = 4.5 x 0.4 = 1.8 mm on the other side. Since they lie on opposite sides, the separation is 1.2 plus 1.8 = 3.0 mm.
formula_principle: Bright fringe at n x beta; dark fringe at (2n minus 1) x beta / 2; add the distances for opposite sides.
common_misconception: Students subtract the two distances without noticing that the fringes are on opposite sides of the centre.

concept_tested: Least distance of coincidence
stem: A double slit with d = 1 mm and a screen at D = 1 m is illuminated with light containing wavelengths 4800 angstrom and 6000 angstrom. The least distance from the centre at which bright fringes of the two wavelengths coincide is
solution: The condition n1 x 6000 = n2 x 4800 gives n1 / n2 = 4800 / 6000 = 4 / 5, so the smallest whole numbers are n1 = 4 for 6000 angstrom and n2 = 5 for 4800 angstrom. Then y = 4 x (6 x 10^-7) x 1 / 10^-3 = 2.4 x 10^-3 m = 2.4 mm. The same value follows from 5 x (4.8 x 10^-7) x 1 / 10^-3.
formula_principle: Coincidence: n1 x lambda1 = n2 x lambda2; then y = n2 x lambda2 x D / d.
common_misconception: Learners pick any pair of orders instead of the smallest whole number pair.

concept_tested: Orders missing from the pattern
stem: In a double slit arrangement each slit has width a and the separation between the slit centres is d = 2a. Because of the single slit diffraction envelope, the interference maxima that are missing from the pattern are of order
option_c: every order, so that no fringes are seen at all
solution: Setting the two directions equal gives n / m = d / a = 2, so n = 2m. Taking m = 1, 2, 3 gives the missing orders n = 2, 4, 6 and so on.
formula_principle: Interference maxima: d x sin theta = n x lambda; diffraction minima: a x sin theta = m x lambda; a maximum is missing when n / m = d / a.
common_misconception: Students expect the interference pattern to be unaffected by the width of each slit.

concept_tested: Refractive index from the change in fringe width
stem: A double slit apparatus gives a fringe width of 0.6 mm in air. When the whole apparatus is immersed in a transparent liquid, the fringe width becomes 0.4 mm. The refractive index of the liquid is
solution: mu = 0.6 divided by 0.4 = 1.5. As a check, the wavelength inside the liquid is 1 / 1.5 of its value in air, which shrinks the fringe width in the same proportion.
formula_principle: beta in medium = beta in air divided by mu, so mu = beta in air divided by beta in medium.
common_misconception: Learners invert the ratio and obtain a refractive index below one, which is impossible for a transparent liquid.

concept_tested: Definition of diffraction
stem: Diffraction of light is the phenomenon of
option_a: splitting of white light into its constituent colours by a prism
option_b: bending of light around the edges of an obstacle or an aperture into the region of the geometrical shadow
option_c: restriction of the vibrations of light to a single plane
option_d: change in the direction of light when it passes from one medium to another
correct_answer_text: bending of light around the edges of an obstacle or an aperture into the region of the geometrical shadow
solution: When a wavefront is partly blocked, the secondary wavelets from the exposed part spread sideways, so light appears inside the region that geometrical optics would call a shadow.
formula_principle: Diffraction is the spreading of a wave after it passes an obstacle or aperture.
common_misconception: Students confuse diffraction with dispersion because both spread the light out.

concept_tested: Condition for minima
stem: For Fraunhofer diffraction at a single slit of width a, the directions of the dark bands are given by
option_a: a x sin theta = n x lambda, with n = 1, 2, 3 and so on
option_b: a x sin theta = n x lambda, with n = 0, 1, 2 and so on
option_c: a x sin theta = (2n plus 1) x lambda / 2
option_d: d x sin theta = n x lambda, where d is the distance to the screen
correct_answer_text: a x sin theta = n x lambda, with n = 1, 2, 3 and so on
solution: The slit is imagined as split into pairs of strips whose contributions cancel in pairs when the extreme path difference a x sin theta equals a whole number of wavelengths. The value n = 0 must be excluded because there all the strips arrive in step, giving the central maximum.
formula_principle: Single slit minima: a x sin theta = n x lambda with n a non zero integer.
common_misconception: Learners include n = 0 in the minima condition and wrongly make the centre dark.

concept_tested: Nature of the central maximum
stem: In the single slit diffraction pattern, the central maximum is
option_a: as bright and as wide as each of the secondary maxima
option_b: the brightest band and twice as wide as any of the secondary maxima
option_c: twice as wide as the secondary maxima but fainter than them
option_d: half as wide as the secondary maxima
correct_answer_text: the brightest band and twice as wide as any of the secondary maxima
solution: The first minima on the two sides are each at lambda x D / a from the centre, so the central band spans 2 x lambda x D / a. Successive minima are separated by lambda x D / a, so each secondary maximum is only half as wide, and its peak intensity is a small fraction of the central one.
formula_principle: Central maximum lies between the first minima on either side, so its width is 2 x lambda x D / a while a secondary maximum spans lambda x D / a.
common_misconception: Students draw the single slit pattern with all bands equal, as in the interference pattern.

concept_tested: When diffraction is noticeable
stem: Diffraction effects of light become easily noticeable when
option_a: the obstacle is very much larger than the wavelength of the light
option_b: the light used is of very high intensity
option_c: the light is made to pass through a very thick glass slab
option_d: the size of the obstacle or aperture is comparable with the wavelength of the light
correct_answer_text: the size of the obstacle or aperture is comparable with the wavelength of the light
solution: The half angular width of the central maximum is lambda / a. For visible light of about 5 x 10^-7 m passing an aperture of a few millimetres this angle is only about 10^-4 radian, which is too small to notice, but for an aperture of the order of a micrometre it becomes large.
formula_principle: The angular spread of the central maximum is about lambda / a, which is appreciable only when a is of the order of lambda.
common_misconception: Learners expect brighter light or bigger obstacles to show more diffraction.

concept_tested: Angle of the first minimum
stem: Light of wavelength 6000 angstrom falls normally on a slit of width 1 mm. The angle at which the first diffraction minimum is formed is nearly
solution: theta = lambda / a = (6 x 10^-7) / (10^-3) = 6 x 10^-4 radian.
formula_principle: First minimum: a x sin theta = lambda, so for small angles theta = lambda / a.
common_misconception: Students give the full angular width instead of the angle of the first minimum.

concept_tested: Formula for the width of the central maximum
stem: For a single slit of width a with a screen at distance D, the linear width of the central maximum is
solution: The first minimum on each side lies at y = lambda x D / a from the centre. The central maximum extends from one to the other, so its total width is 2 x lambda x D / a.
formula_principle: Width of central maximum = 2 x lambda x D / a.
common_misconception: Learners quote the half width as the width of the central maximum.

concept_tested: Numerical width of the central maximum
stem: Light of wavelength 4000 angstrom falls on a single slit of width 0.4 mm and the pattern is observed on a screen 1 m away. The width of the central maximum is
formula_principle: Width of central maximum = 2 x lambda x D / a.
common_misconception: Students forget the factor 2 and report half of the correct width.

concept_tested: Comparison of the two patterns
stem: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a two slit interference pattern from a single slit diffraction pattern?
option_a: In interference the bright bands are of equal width and nearly equal brightness, while in diffraction the central band is much wider and much brighter than the rest
option_b: In interference the bands become narrower with order, while in diffraction all bands are of equal width
option_c: Interference occurs only with white light while diffraction occurs only with monochromatic light
option_d: Interference needs a single wavefront while diffraction needs two separate coherent sources
correct_answer_text: In interference the bright bands are of equal width and nearly equal brightness, while in diffraction the central band is much wider and much brighter than the rest
solution: In two slit interference the maxima satisfy y = n x lambda x D / d, so consecutive bands are equally spaced and of comparable intensity. In single slit diffraction the minima satisfy y = n x lambda x D / a, so the central band spans twice the spacing of the others and carries most of the energy.
formula_principle: Interference arises from two coherent beams; diffraction arises from secondary wavelets of the same wavefront.
common_misconception: Learners think diffraction bands are also equally bright, as in the interference pattern.

concept_tested: Condition for secondary maxima
stem: In single slit diffraction the secondary maxima occur approximately in the directions given by
option_a: a x sin theta = n x lambda, with n = 1, 2, 3 and so on
option_b: a x sin theta = n x lambda / 4
option_c: a x sin theta = (2n plus 1) x lambda / 2, with n = 1, 2, 3 and so on
option_d: a x sin theta = 2 x n x lambda
correct_answer_text: a x sin theta = (2n plus 1) x lambda / 2, with n = 1, 2, 3 and so on
solution: The minima occur at a x sin theta = n x lambda. Between two consecutive minima there is a weak maximum, which lies close to the odd half wavelength values of the path difference across the slit.
formula_principle: Secondary maxima lie approximately midway between consecutive minima, at a x sin theta = (2n plus 1) x lambda / 2.
common_misconception: Students interchange the maxima and minima conditions of the single slit with those of two slit interference.

concept_tested: Half angular width
stem: For a single slit of width a illuminated normally with light of wavelength lambda, the half angular width of the central maximum is
solution: The central maximum extends up to the first minimum, whose direction satisfies a x sin theta = lambda. For small angles this gives theta = lambda / a, which is the half angular width.
formula_principle: Half angular width of the central maximum = lambda / a.
common_misconception: Learners mix up the half width with the full width of the central band.

concept_tested: Effect of widening the slit
stem: In a single slit diffraction experiment the width of the slit is doubled while the wavelength and the screen distance are unchanged. The central maximum then becomes
solution: Doubling a halves the value of 2 x lambda x D / a, so the central band narrows to half. At the same time twice as much light passes through the slit and is concentrated into a narrower band, so it looks brighter.
formula_principle: Width of central maximum = 2 x lambda x D / a, and the transmitted energy rises with a.
common_misconception: Students expect a wider slit to give a wider bright patch, thinking in terms of ray optics.

concept_tested: Effect of changing the colour
stem: In a single slit diffraction experiment the red light used is replaced by blue light, everything else being unchanged. The central maximum
option_a: becomes narrower, because blue light has a shorter wavelength
option_b: becomes wider, because blue light has a higher frequency
option_c: remains of the same width, because the slit width is unchanged
option_d: disappears, because blue light is not diffracted
correct_answer_text: becomes narrower, because blue light has a shorter wavelength
solution: Blue light of about 4500 angstrom has a smaller wavelength than red light of about 6500 angstrom, so 2 x lambda x D / a is smaller and the central band contracts.
formula_principle: Width of central maximum is directly proportional to lambda.
common_misconception: Learners link the higher frequency of blue light with more spreading.

concept_tested: Separation of two minima on the same side
stem: Light of wavelength 6000 angstrom falls on a single slit of width 0.5 mm and the screen is 1 m away. The distance between the first and the third minima on the same side of the centre is
solution: Spacing of one order = lambda x D / a = (6 x 10^-7 x 1) / (5 x 10^-4) = 1.2 x 10^-3 m = 1.2 mm. The first minimum is at 1.2 mm and the third at 3.6 mm, so the required distance is 3.6 minus 1.2 = 2.4 mm.
formula_principle: y(n) = n x lambda x D / a for the minima of a single slit.
common_misconception: Students give the position of the third minimum instead of the separation asked for.

concept_tested: Slit width from the observed pattern
stem: In a single slit experiment with light of wavelength 5000 angstrom and a screen 1 m from the slit, the central maximum is 5 mm wide. The width of the slit is
formula_principle: Width of central maximum W = 2 x lambda x D / a, so a = 2 x lambda x D / W.
common_misconception: Learners rearrange the formula without the factor 2 and get a slit width half as large.

concept_tested: Slit width equal to the wavelength
stem: In a single slit diffraction experiment the width of the slit is made exactly equal to the wavelength of the light used. The first minimum then occurs at
option_b: 90 degree, so no minimum is seen and the light spreads over the whole forward region
option_c: 0 degree, so the whole screen is dark
option_d: 45 degree, because the slit and the wavelength are equal
correct_answer_text: 90 degree, so no minimum is seen and the light spreads over the whole forward region
solution: With a = lambda, sin theta = lambda / lambda = 1, so theta = 90 degree. The first minimum is pushed to the edge of the forward hemisphere, which means the central maximum fills the entire region beyond the slit and no dark band is observed.
formula_principle: First minimum: sin theta = lambda / a.
common_misconception: Students try to compute a small angle and do not notice that sin theta reaches its maximum value of one.

concept_tested: Distance up to which ray optics holds
stem: A parallel beam of light of wavelength 6000 angstrom passes through an aperture of width 3 mm. The Fresnel distance, up to which the beam may be treated as travelling in a straight line, is
formula_principle: Fresnel distance Z = a^2 / lambda.
common_misconception: Learners forget to square the aperture width in the Fresnel distance formula.

concept_tested: Angular position of a higher order minimum
stem: Light of wavelength 6000 angstrom falls normally on a slit of width 0.1 mm. The angular position of the third minimum from the centre is nearly
formula_principle: Minima: a x sin theta = n x lambda, so for small angles theta = n x lambda / a.
common_misconception: Students leave out the order number and quote the first minimum angle.

concept_tested: Diffraction inside a medium
stem: A single slit diffraction apparatus is taken from air into a liquid of refractive index mu. The angular width of the central maximum
option_a: becomes 1 / mu times its value in air
option_b: becomes mu times its value in air
option_c: remains the same, because the slit width is unchanged
option_d: becomes mu^2 times its value in air
correct_answer_text: becomes 1 / mu times its value in air
solution: Inside the liquid the wavelength becomes lambda divided by mu, so the half angular width becomes lambda divided by (mu x a). Every angle of the pattern therefore shrinks by the factor mu.
formula_principle: Half angular width = lambda / a with lambda inside a medium equal to lambda in air divided by mu.
common_misconception: Learners assume the pattern is unaffected because the slit width and the frequency do not change.

concept_tested: Central width and a higher order minimum together
stem: Light of wavelength 5000 angstrom falls normally on a slit of width 1 mm and the pattern is seen on a screen 2 m away. The width of the central maximum and the distance of the third minimum from the centre are respectively
solution: lambda x D / a = (5 x 10^-7 x 2) / (10^-3) = 10^-3 m = 1 mm. Hence the central maximum is 2 x 1 mm = 2 mm wide and the third minimum lies at 3 x 1 mm = 3 mm from the centre.
formula_principle: Half width = lambda x D / a; central width = 2 x lambda x D / a; nth minimum at n x lambda x D / a.
common_misconception: Students apply the factor 2 to every minimum instead of only to the total width of the central band.

concept_tested: Matching minima of two wavelengths
stem: In a single slit diffraction experiment the first minimum for light of wavelength 6000 angstrom is formed in the same direction as the second minimum for light of another wavelength. That wavelength, and the ratio of the widths of the central maximum for 6000 angstrom to that for the other wavelength, are
solution: Equating the two directions gives 1 x 6000 = 2 x lambda dash, so lambda dash = 3000 angstrom. Since the central maximum width 2 x lambda x D / a is proportional to lambda, the ratio of the widths is 6000 : 3000 = 2 : 1.
formula_principle: a x sin theta = n x lambda; width of central maximum is proportional to lambda.
common_misconception: Learners take the higher order to belong to the longer wavelength.

concept_tested: Meaning of plane polarised light
stem: Plane polarised light is light in which
option_a: the vibrations take place along the direction of propagation
option_b: the vibrations occur equally in all directions perpendicular to the direction of propagation
option_c: the amplitude of vibration is the same at every point of the beam
option_d: the vibrations of the electric field are confined to a single plane containing the direction of propagation
correct_answer_text: the vibrations of the electric field are confined to a single plane containing the direction of propagation
solution: Unpolarised light contains vibrations in every direction perpendicular to the ray. A polariser removes all of these except those parallel to one direction, so the surviving vibrations lie in a single plane that contains the ray.
formula_principle: In plane polarised light the electric field vibrates in one fixed plane.
common_misconception: Students describe polarised light as vibrating along the ray, which would make it longitudinal.

concept_tested: Intensity after a single polaroid
stem: Unpolarised light of intensity I0 is passed through a single ideal polaroid. The intensity of the emergent light is
solution: The incident vibrations are spread uniformly over all directions perpendicular to the ray, so the average value of cos^2 of the angle is 1 / 2. The transmitted intensity is therefore I0 / 2, whatever the orientation of the polaroid.
formula_principle: For unpolarised light the average of cos^2 over all directions is 1 / 2.
common_misconception: Learners apply the law of Malus with a specific angle to unpolarised light instead of averaging.

concept_tested: Statement of the law of Malus
stem: According to the law of Malus, when plane polarised light of intensity I0 is passed through an analyser whose axis makes an angle theta with the plane of polarisation, the transmitted intensity is
solution: The analyser passes only the component of the electric field along its axis, which is E0 x cos theta. Since intensity is proportional to the square of the field, the transmitted intensity is I0 x cos^2 theta.
formula_principle: Law of Malus: I = I0 x cos^2 theta.
common_misconception: Students use cos theta rather than cos^2 theta for the intensity.

concept_tested: Transmitted intensity at a given angle
stem: Plane polarised light of intensity I0 falls on an analyser whose axis makes an angle of 60 degree with the plane of vibration of the light. The transmitted intensity is
solution: I = I0 x cos^2 60 degree = I0 x (0.5)^2 = I0 / 4.
formula_principle: I = I0 x cos^2 theta.
common_misconception: Learners forget to square the cosine.

concept_tested: Crossed polaroids
stem: Two ideal polaroids are placed one behind the other with their transmission axes perpendicular to each other. Unpolarised light of intensity I0 falls on the first one. The intensity coming out of the second polaroid is
solution: After the first polaroid the intensity is I0 / 2 and the light is plane polarised. The second polaroid then gives (I0 / 2) x cos^2 90 degree = (I0 / 2) x 0 = 0.
formula_principle: I = (I0 / 2) x cos^2 theta with theta = 90 degree.
common_misconception: Students think some light always leaks through a pair of polaroids.

concept_tested: Statement of Brewster law
stem: According to Brewster law, the refractive index mu of a medium and the polarising angle theta B for light incident from air on it are related by
