solution: At the polarising angle the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular, so the angle of refraction is 90 degree minus theta B. Putting this in Snell law, mu = sin theta B divided by sin (90 degree minus theta B) = sin theta B divided by cos theta B = tan theta B.
formula_principle: Brewster law: mu = tan of theta B.
common_misconception: Learners quote Snell law in place of Brewster law and use the sine instead of the tangent.

concept_tested: Polarising angle from the refractive index
stem: The refractive index of a certain glass is the square root of 3. The polarising angle for light going from air into this glass is
solution: tan of theta B = square root of 3, and since tan 60 degree = square root of 3, the polarising angle is 60 degree.
formula_principle: tan of theta B = mu.
common_misconception: Students take the inverse tangent of the reciprocal of mu.

concept_tested: Angle of refraction at the polarising angle
stem: Unpolarised light falls on a glass surface at the polarising angle of 60 degree. The angle of refraction inside the glass is
solution: r = 90 degree minus 60 degree = 30 degree. As a check, mu = sin 60 degree divided by sin 30 degree = square root of 3, which is also tan 60 degree.
formula_principle: At the polarising angle the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular, so r = 90 degree minus theta B.
common_misconception: Learners set the angle of refraction itself equal to 90 degree instead of the angle between the two rays.

concept_tested: Polarisation of sound waves
stem: Sound waves travelling in air cannot be polarised because
option_a: their wavelength is much larger than that of light
option_b: they travel much more slowly than light
option_c: they are longitudinal, so the vibrations are along the direction of propagation and no plane can be selected
option_d: they cannot pass through a polaroid sheet
correct_answer_text: they are longitudinal, so the vibrations are along the direction of propagation and no plane can be selected
solution: In a sound wave in air the particles move back and forth along the ray, so all directions perpendicular to the ray are equivalent and there is nothing for a polariser to select. Polarisation is therefore impossible for a longitudinal wave.
formula_principle: Only transverse waves can be polarised.
common_misconception: Students think polarisation fails for sound because of the size of its wavelength.

concept_tested: Two polaroids at a given angle
stem: Unpolarised light of intensity I0 passes through two polaroids whose transmission axes make an angle of 60 degree with each other. The intensity emerging from the second polaroid is
solution: After the first polaroid the intensity is I0 / 2. The second polaroid gives (I0 / 2) x cos^2 60 degree = (I0 / 2) x 0.25 = I0 / 8.
formula_principle: I = (I0 / 2) x cos^2 theta for unpolarised light entering a pair of polaroids.
common_misconception: Learners apply the law of Malus straight to the unpolarised beam and omit the factor one half.

concept_tested: Three polaroids with a middle one inserted
stem: Two polaroids are crossed so that no light passes through them. A third polaroid is now introduced between them with its axis at 45 degree to the axis of the first. If unpolarised light of intensity I0 falls on the first polaroid, the intensity emerging from the last one is
solution: After the first polaroid the intensity is I0 / 2. After the middle polaroid at 45 degree it is (I0 / 2) x cos^2 45 degree = I0 / 4. The last polaroid is at 45 degree to the middle one, so the final intensity is (I0 / 4) x cos^2 45 degree = I0 / 8.
formula_principle: Apply I = I x cos^2 theta at each polaroid in turn, with a factor one half at the first for unpolarised light.
common_misconception: Students expect crossed polaroids to stay dark no matter what is placed between them.

concept_tested: Refractive index and speed from the angle of refraction
stem: Unpolarised light falls from air on the flat surface of a transparent medium at the polarising angle, and the angle of refraction is found to be 30 degree. Taking c as 3 x 10^8 m per second, the refractive index of the medium and the speed of light inside it are
option_a: 0.58 and about 5.2 x 10^8 m per second
option_c: square root of 3 and about 5.2 x 10^8 m per second
option_d: square root of 3, that is about 1.73, and about 1.73 x 10^8 m per second
correct_answer_text: square root of 3, that is about 1.73, and about 1.73 x 10^8 m per second
solution: Since the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular at the polarising angle, theta B = 90 degree minus 30 degree = 60 degree. Then mu = tan 60 degree = square root of 3, about 1.73, and v = (3 x 10^8) divided by 1.73 = about 1.73 x 10^8 m per second.
formula_principle: theta B = 90 degree minus r; mu = tan of theta B; v = c / mu.
common_misconception: Learners take the given 30 degree as the polarising angle itself.

concept_tested: State of the reflected and refracted beams
stem: Unpolarised light falls on a glass plate at the polarising angle. The reflected and the refracted beams are respectively
option_a: partially polarised and completely plane polarised
option_b: completely plane polarised and partially polarised
correct_answer_text: completely plane polarised and partially polarised
solution: At this angle the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular. The vibrations lying in the plane of incidence cannot be radiated along the reflected direction, so the reflected beam contains only vibrations perpendicular to the plane of incidence and is fully polarised, while the refracted beam keeps both components in unequal amounts and is partially polarised.
formula_principle: At the polarising angle the reflected light is completely plane polarised with vibrations perpendicular to the plane of incidence.
common_misconception: Students believe the refracted beam is the completely polarised one because it carries most of the energy.

concept_tested: Effect of rotating the analyser
stem: An analyser is first set parallel to the plane of vibration of a beam of plane polarised light and then rotated through 30 degree. The transmitted intensity
option_a: falls to 50 per cent of its earlier value
option_b: falls to 25 per cent of its earlier value
option_c: falls to 75 per cent of its earlier value
option_d: rises to 125 per cent of its earlier value
correct_answer_text: falls to 75 per cent of its earlier value
solution: I = I0 x cos^2 30 degree = I0 x (square root of 3 divided by 2)^2 = I0 x 3 / 4 = 0.75 I0, that is 75 per cent of the earlier value.
formula_principle: I = I0 x cos^2 theta with I0 the intensity at the parallel setting.
common_misconception: Learners assume the intensity falls in direct proportion to the angle of rotation.

concept_tested: Three polaroids in series
stem: Unpolarised light of intensity I0 passes through three polaroids placed one behind the other. The axis of the second makes 30 degree with that of the first, and the axis of the third makes 30 degree with that of the second, in the same sense. The final emergent intensity is
solution: After the first polaroid the intensity is I0 / 2. After the second it is (I0 / 2) x cos^2 30 degree = (I0 / 2) x 3 / 4 = 3 I0 / 8. After the third it is (3 I0 / 8) x cos^2 30 degree = (3 I0 / 8) x 3 / 4 = 9 I0 / 32.
formula_principle: I = (I0 / 2) x cos^2 theta1 x cos^2 theta2 for three polaroids in series.
common_misconception: Students use the angle between the first and the third polaroid, which is 60 degree, in a single application of the law of Malus.

concept_tested: Polarising angle and critical angle together
stem: The polarising angle for a certain transparent medium in contact with air is 60 degree. The critical angle for total internal reflection at the same surface is
option_a: 30 degree, since it is the complement of the polarising angle
option_b: 60 degree, the same as the polarising angle
option_c: the angle whose sine equals the refractive index of the medium
option_d: the angle whose sine is 1 divided by the square root of 3, that is about 35 degree
correct_answer_text: the angle whose sine is 1 divided by the square root of 3, that is about 35 degree
solution: From Brewster law, mu = tan 60 degree = square root of 3, about 1.73. Then sin of the critical angle = 1 divided by 1.73 = 0.577, so the critical angle is about 35 degree.
formula_principle: mu = tan of theta B and sin of the critical angle = 1 / mu.
common_misconception: Learners take the critical angle to be the complement of the polarising angle.

concept_tested: Statement of the Rayleigh criterion
stem: According to the Rayleigh criterion, two point objects are just resolved when
option_a: the central maxima of the two diffraction patterns fall exactly on each other
option_b: the first minima of the two patterns fall exactly on each other
option_c: the central maximum of the diffraction pattern of one falls on the first minimum of the pattern of the other
option_d: the two objects are of exactly equal brightness
correct_answer_text: the central maximum of the diffraction pattern of one falls on the first minimum of the pattern of the other
solution: In this position the combined intensity shows a clear dip between the two peaks, so the eye can just distinguish two separate images instead of one.
formula_principle: Rayleigh criterion: the central maximum of one image coincides with the first minimum of the other.
common_misconception: Students state that the two images must not overlap at all, which is a far stricter condition.

concept_tested: Resolving power of a telescope
stem: For a telescope of objective aperture D used with light of wavelength lambda, the limit of resolution and the resolving power are respectively
option_a: 1.22 x D / lambda and lambda / (1.22 x D)
option_b: lambda / (2 x D) and 2 x D / lambda
option_c: 1.22 x lambda x D and 1 / (1.22 x lambda x D)
option_d: 1.22 x lambda / D and D / (1.22 x lambda)
correct_answer_text: 1.22 x lambda / D and D / (1.22 x lambda)
solution: The diffraction pattern of a circular aperture has its first dark ring at an angle 1.22 x lambda / D, and by the Rayleigh criterion this angle is the smallest angular separation that can be resolved. The resolving power, being the ability to resolve, is the reciprocal of this angle.
formula_principle: Limit of resolution of a telescope = 1.22 x lambda / D; resolving power is its reciprocal.
common_misconception: Learners write the limit of resolution and the resolving power as the same expression.

concept_tested: Resolving power of a microscope
stem: For a compound microscope, the smallest distance between two points that can just be resolved is given by
option_a: 1.22 x lambda / D, where D is the diameter of the objective
option_b: 2 x mu x sin theta / (1.22 x lambda)
option_c: 1.22 x lambda / (2 x mu x sin theta), where mu x sin theta is the numerical aperture
option_d: 1.22 x lambda x mu x sin theta
correct_answer_text: 1.22 x lambda / (2 x mu x sin theta), where mu x sin theta is the numerical aperture
solution: The numerical aperture mu x sin theta measures the cone of light collected by the objective. A larger numerical aperture or a shorter wavelength reduces the smallest resolvable distance and so improves the microscope.
formula_principle: Smallest resolvable distance = 1.22 x lambda / (2 x mu x sin theta) = 0.61 x lambda / (mu x sin theta).
common_misconception: Students quote the reciprocal expression and call it the limit of resolution.

concept_tested: Improving the resolving power
stem: The resolving power of an astronomical telescope can be increased by
option_a: increasing the diameter of the objective or using light of a shorter wavelength
option_b: increasing the focal length of the eyepiece
option_c: using light of a longer wavelength
option_d: reducing the diameter of the objective
correct_answer_text: increasing the diameter of the objective or using light of a shorter wavelength
solution: The resolving power is directly proportional to the aperture D and inversely proportional to the wavelength. Hence a wider objective or a shorter wavelength gives a larger resolving power, while the eyepiece plays no part in it.
formula_principle: Resolving power of a telescope = D / (1.22 x lambda).
common_misconception: Learners confuse magnifying power, which depends on the eyepiece, with resolving power, which depends on the objective aperture.

concept_tested: Limit of resolution of a telescope
stem: A telescope has an objective of diameter 1.22 m and is used with light of wavelength 5000 angstrom. Its limit of resolution is
solution: Limit of resolution = (1.22 x 5 x 10^-7) divided by 1.22 = 5 x 10^-7 radian, since the factor 1.22 cancels with the aperture of 1.22 m.
formula_principle: Limit of resolution = 1.22 x lambda / D.
common_misconception: Students report the reciprocal, which is the resolving power, when the limit of resolution is asked for.

concept_tested: Combined change of aperture and wavelength
stem: The aperture of a telescope objective is doubled and at the same time the wavelength of the light used is halved. The resolving power of the telescope becomes
option_c: unchanged, because the two effects cancel
solution: Doubling D multiplies the resolving power by 2, and halving lambda multiplies it by another 2. The total factor is 2 x 2 = 4.
formula_principle: Resolving power = D / (1.22 x lambda).
common_misconception: Learners take the halving of the wavelength as a factor of one half and cancel the two changes.

concept_tested: Smallest resolvable distance of a microscope
stem: A microscope objective has a numerical aperture of 0.61 and is used with light of wavelength 6000 angstrom. The smallest distance between two points that it can just resolve is
solution: Smallest distance = (0.61 x 6 x 10^-7) divided by 0.61 = 6 x 10^-7 m, since the factor 0.61 cancels with the numerical aperture.
formula_principle: Smallest resolvable distance = 1.22 x lambda / (2 x mu x sin theta) = 0.61 x lambda / (mu x sin theta).
common_misconception: Students forget the factor 2 in the denominator and double the answer.

concept_tested: Least separation resolved at a large distance
stem: A telescope of objective diameter 2 m is used with light of wavelength 5 x 10^-7 m to look at two points on the surface of the moon, which is 4 x 10^8 m away. The least separation between the two points that can just be resolved is about
solution: Angular limit = (1.22 x 5 x 10^-7) divided by 2 = 3.05 x 10^-7 radian. Multiplying by the distance, the separation = 3.05 x 10^-7 x 4 x 10^8 = 122 m.
formula_principle: Angular limit = 1.22 x lambda / D; linear separation = angular limit x distance.
common_misconception: Learners stop at the angular limit and forget to convert it into a linear separation.

concept_tested: Direct substitution in F = k q1 q2 / r^2
stem: Two point charges of 2 microC and 3 microC are held 3 m apart in vacuum. Taking k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, the magnitude of the electrostatic force between them is
formula_principle: F = k q1 q2 / r^2 with k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2
common_misconception: Students often forget to square the separation, or mishandle the microcoulomb to coulomb conversion.

subtopic: Effect of medium and dielectric constant
concept_tested: Force in a medium is the vacuum force divided by K
stem: Two point charges separated by a fixed distance experience a force F in vacuum. Keeping the separation unchanged, the charges are immersed in a liquid of dielectric constant 5. The force between them now becomes
solution: In a medium the permittivity becomes epsilon = K epsilon_0, so F = q1 q2 / (4 pi K epsilon_0 r^2) = F_vacuum / K. With K = 5 the force falls to F / 5.
formula_principle: F_medium = F_vacuum / K, where K is the dielectric constant of the medium
common_misconception: Believing that a dielectric strengthens the interaction, or applying the sqrt K factor that belongs to the equivalent separation problem.

concept_tested: Scaling of Coulomb force with charge and separation
stem: Each of two point charges is doubled and at the same time the distance between them is doubled. Compared with its original value, the electrostatic force between them is
option_d: one fourth of the original value
solution: F' = k (2 q1)(2 q2) / (2 r)^2 = 4 k q1 q2 / (4 r^2) = k q1 q2 / r^2 = F. The two effects cancel exactly.
formula_principle: F is proportional to q1 q2 / r^2
common_misconception: Applying only one of the two changes, most often the charge change, and ignoring the other.

concept_tested: Dimensional formula of permittivity of free space
stem: Coulomb's law is written F = q1 q2 / (4 pi epsilon_0 r^2). From this relation the dimensional formula of epsilon_0 is
solution: epsilon_0 has dimensions of (A T)^2 divided by (M L T^-2)(L^2), that is A^2 T^2 / (M L^3 T^-2) = M^-1 L^-3 T^4 A^2.
formula_principle: epsilon_0 = q1 q2 / (4 pi F r^2)
common_misconception: Forgetting that charge carries dimensions A T, so that its square contributes T^2 in addition to the T^2 from force.

concept_tested: Charge redistribution between identical conducting spheres
stem: Two identical conducting spheres carrying charges of 6 microC and -2 microC attract each other with a force F when their centres are 10 cm apart. They are brought into contact and then replaced at the same separation. The force between them is now
option_a: one third of F and repulsive
option_b: four thirds of F and repulsive
option_d: one third of F and attractive
correct_answer_text: one third of F and repulsive
solution: Total charge = 6 + (-2) = 4 microC, so each sphere carries 2 microC after contact. The product of magnitudes changes from 6 x 2 = 12 to 2 x 2 = 4, a factor of 1/3. Both charges are now positive, so the force is repulsive and equals F / 3.
formula_principle: On contact identical spheres share the total charge equally; F is proportional to the product of the charges
common_misconception: Averaging the magnitudes of the charges rather than the algebraic total, which ignores the partial neutralisation.

concept_tested: Null point for unlike charges lies outside the pair, nearer the smaller charge
stem: Point charges of 4q and -q are fixed 30 cm apart. A third point charge is to be placed on the line joining them so that the net electrostatic force on it is zero. It must be placed
option_a: 10 cm from the -q charge, between the two charges
option_b: 30 cm from the -q charge, on the side away from the 4q charge
option_c: 15 cm from the 4q charge, midway between the two charges
option_d: 30 cm from the 4q charge, on the side away from the -q charge
correct_answer_text: 30 cm from the -q charge, on the side away from the 4q charge
solution: For unlike charges the null point lies outside the pair and nearer the smaller charge. Let it be at distance d beyond the -q charge. Then 4 / (0.30 + d)^2 = 1 / d^2, so 2 d = 0.30 + d and d = 0.30 m, that is 30 cm beyond the -q charge.
formula_principle: At the null point k (4q) Q / r1^2 = k q Q / r2^2
common_misconception: Assuming the zero force point always lies between the two charges, which is only true for like charges.

subtopic: Effect of medium and dielectric constant
concept_tested: Equivalent separation in a medium
stem: Two point charges placed 20 cm apart in air experience a force F. They are now placed in a medium of dielectric constant 4. The separation at which the force is again exactly F is
solution: Equating the two forces gives 1 / r^2 = 1 / (K r'^2), so r'^2 = r^2 / K and r' = r / sqrt K = 20 / 2 = 10 cm.
formula_principle: k q1 q2 / r^2 = k q1 q2 / (K r'^2), giving r' = r / sqrt K
common_misconception: Dividing by K rather than by sqrt K, because the K appears with r^2 in the denominator.

concept_tested: Validity conditions for the point charge form of Coulomb's law
stem: The expression F = k q1 q2 / r^2 may be applied directly to two uniformly charged conducting spheres, with r taken as the distance between their centres, provided that
option_a: the two spheres carry charges of the same sign
option_b: the two spheres have exactly equal radii
option_c: the two spheres are made of the same metal
option_d: their separation is very large compared with their radii
correct_answer_text: their separation is very large compared with their radii
solution: When the spheres are close together each sphere induces a redistribution of charge on the other, so the charge is no longer uniformly distributed and the centres are no longer the effective locations of the charge. Only when the separation is much larger than the radii can each sphere be treated as a point charge at its centre.
formula_principle: Coulomb's law in point charge form requires the charge distributions to be effectively concentrated at the centres
common_misconception: Believing that the inverse square law fails for conductors altogether, or that the sign or size of the spheres decides its validity.

concept_tested: Null point for like charges lies between them, nearer the smaller charge
stem: Two point charges of 9 microC and 1 microC are fixed 20 cm apart. A small test charge placed on the line joining them experiences zero net force at a point which is
solution: Taking x as the distance from the 1 microC charge, 9 / (0.20 - x)^2 = 1 / x^2 gives 3 x = 0.20 - x, so x = 0.05 m = 5 cm from the 1 microC charge and 15 cm from the 9 microC charge.
formula_principle: 9 / (0.20 - x)^2 = 1 / x^2 for a point at distance x from the smaller charge
common_misconception: Dividing the separation in the ratio of the charges instead of in the ratio of the square roots of the charges.

concept_tested: Principle of superposition of electrostatic forces
stem: According to the principle of superposition, the electrostatic force on a point charge due to a group of other point charges is
option_a: the vector sum of the forces due to each of the other charges taken one at a time, each force being unaffected by the presence of the remaining charges
option_b: the algebraic sum of the magnitudes of the forces due to each of the other charges taken one at a time
option_c: the vector sum of the forces due to each of the other charges, each force being reduced by the screening action of the remaining charges
option_d: the force due to the nearest charge alone, since the inverse square dependence makes the others negligible
correct_answer_text: the vector sum of the forces due to each of the other charges taken one at a time, each force being unaffected by the presence of the remaining charges
solution: Coulomb's law describes a two body interaction. The force between any pair of charges is exactly the same whether or not other charges are present, and the resultant is obtained by vector addition of these pairwise forces.
formula_principle: F_net = F_1 + F_2 + F_3 + ... as a vector sum
common_misconception: Adding forces as scalars, or supposing that intervening charges shield one charge from another.

concept_tested: Resultant force on one charge of an equilateral triangle of like charges
stem: Three point charges of 1 microC each are placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side 10 cm in vacuum. Taking k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, the magnitude of the net force on any one charge is about
solution: F = 9 x 10^9 x (10^-6)^2 / (0.10)^2 = 9 x 10^-3 / 0.01 = 0.90 N. The two forces on a corner charge are equal in magnitude and inclined at 60 degrees, so the resultant is 2 F cos 30 = sqrt 3 x 0.90 = 1.56 N, directed away from the centre of the triangle.
formula_principle: Each pair force F = k q^2 / a^2; the resultant of two equal forces at 60 degrees is sqrt 3 times either
common_misconception: Adding the two equal forces arithmetically instead of using the 60 degree angle between them.

concept_tested: Maximising the force by dividing a fixed total charge
stem: A total charge Q is to be split into two parts q and Q - q, which are then held a fixed distance apart. The force between the two parts is greatest when q equals
solution: F = k q (Q - q) / r^2. Writing the product as q Q - q^2 and setting the derivative with respect to q to zero gives Q - 2 q = 0, so q = Q / 2. Equivalently, the product of two numbers with a fixed sum is largest when they are equal.
formula_principle: F is proportional to q (Q - q); the product is maximum when the two factors are equal
common_misconception: Assuming that a lopsided division gives the larger product, or that the answer depends on the separation.

concept_tested: Net force on one corner charge of a square of like charges
stem: Four equal point charges q are fixed at the corners of a square of side a. The magnitude of the net electrostatic force on any one of them is
solution: The two adjacent charges each exert k q^2 / a^2 along perpendicular directions, giving a resultant sqrt 2 k q^2 / a^2 along the diagonal. The diagonal charge is at distance a sqrt 2 and exerts k q^2 / (2 a^2) along the same diagonal. The total is (sqrt 2 + 1/2) k q^2 / a^2.
formula_principle: Edge charges are at distance a, the diagonal charge at a sqrt 2; forces are combined vectorially
common_misconception: Forgetting that the diagonal separation is a sqrt 2, so that its square contributes a factor of 2 in the denominator.

concept_tested: Third charge required to keep a pair of like charges in equilibrium
stem: Two equal point charges q are fixed at the ends of a line of length r. A third charge is placed at the midpoint of this line so that the whole system is in equilibrium. That third charge must be
solution: Consider one of the end charges. The other end charge repels it with k q^2 / r^2 outward. The midpoint charge Q is at distance r / 2 and must attract it inward with k q |Q| / (r/2)^2 = 4 k q |Q| / r^2. Equating gives |Q| = q / 4, and the charge must be negative, so it is -q / 4. The midpoint charge is itself in equilibrium by symmetry.
formula_principle: For an end charge, k q^2 / r^2 must be balanced by k q |Q| / (r/2)^2
common_misconception: Forgetting that halving the distance multiplies the force by four, and so obtaining -q / 2.

concept_tested: Separation of two charged pith balls suspended from a common point
stem: Two small identical balls, each of mass m and charge q, hang from a common point by insulating threads of equal length L. In equilibrium the threads make a small angle with the vertical and the balls are a distance x apart. For small angles, x varies with q as
solution: For each ball the horizontal Coulomb force is balanced through the thread tension: k q^2 / x^2 = m g tan theta. For small angles tan theta is approximately (x/2) / L, so k q^2 / x^2 = m g x / (2 L), giving x^3 = 2 k q^2 L / (m g). Hence x is proportional to q^(2/3).
formula_principle: k q^2 / x^2 = m g tan theta and tan theta is approximately (x/2) / L for small angles
common_misconception: Forgetting that the separation itself appears in the small angle expression, which converts the q^2 dependence into a q^(2/3) dependence.

concept_tested: Successive contacts with an identical uncharged sphere
stem: Two identical metal spheres X and Y carry charges of 5 microC and -3 microC and are held 40 cm apart, attracting each other with a force F. A third identical uncharged sphere is touched first to X, then to Y, and is then removed far away. With X and Y still 40 cm apart, the force between them is now
solution: After the third sphere touches X, both carry (5 + 0) / 2 = 2.5 microC. The third sphere, now at 2.5 microC, touches Y, and the two share (2.5 - 3) / 2 = -0.25 microC each. So X finally carries 2.5 microC and Y carries -0.25 microC. The product of magnitudes changes from 5 x 3 = 15 to 2.5 x 0.25 = 0.625, a factor of 1/24. The charges are still of opposite sign, so the force is attractive and equals F / 24.
formula_principle: Identical spheres in contact share their total charge equally; F is proportional to the product of the final charges
common_misconception: Not tracking the charge carried away by the third sphere into the second contact, or losing the sign of the final charge on Y.

subtopic: Field due to a point charge
concept_tested: Direct substitution in E = k q / r^2
stem: A point charge of 4 microC is placed in vacuum. Taking k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, the magnitude of the electric field at a point 3 m from the charge is
solution: E = 9 x 10^9 x 4 x 10^-6 / (3)^2 = 3.6 x 10^4 / 9 = 4 x 10^3 N C^-1, directed radially away from the positive charge.
formula_principle: E = k q / r^2
common_misconception: Using the potential expression k q / r in place of the field expression k q / r^2.

concept_tested: Properties of electrostatic field lines
stem: Which of the following is a correct property of electrostatic field lines?
option_a: Field lines always form closed loops
option_b: Two field lines can never cross each other
option_c: Field lines pass continuously through the body of a conductor
option_d: Field lines start on negative charges and end on positive charges
correct_answer_text: Two field lines can never cross each other
solution: If two field lines crossed, the field at the point of crossing would have two different directions at once, which is impossible. Electrostatic lines begin on positive charges and end on negative charges, are never closed, and do not pass through conductors.
formula_principle: The electrostatic field has a unique direction at every point
common_misconception: Carrying over the closed loop property of magnetic field lines to electrostatic field lines.

subtopic: Field due to a dipole on axial and equatorial lines
concept_tested: Axial field of a short dipole
stem: For a short electric dipole of moment p, the magnitude of the electric field at a point on its axis at a distance r from the centre, with r much larger than the dipole length, is
solution: The two charges of the dipole are at slightly different distances from an axial point, and their fields subtract but do not cancel. The net field works out to 2 k p / r^3 directed along the dipole moment.
formula_principle: E_axial = 2 k p / r^3 for a short dipole
common_misconception: Interchanging the axial and equatorial expressions, or using the potential formula for the field.

subtopic: Field due to a dipole on axial and equatorial lines
concept_tested: Ratio of axial to equatorial dipole field at equal distances
stem: For a short electric dipole, the ratio of the magnitude of the electric field at a point on the axis to that at a point on the equatorial line, both at the same distance r from the centre, is
solution: Dividing 2 k p / r^3 by k p / r^3 gives 2. The axial field is twice the equatorial field at the same distance, and the two point in opposite senses relative to the dipole moment.
formula_principle: E_axial = 2 k p / r^3 and E_equatorial = k p / r^3
common_misconception: Remembering that the two differ but not which one is larger.

concept_tested: Field line picture of a uniform electric field
stem: A uniform electric field is represented by
option_a: straight lines directed radially outward from a point
option_b: parallel straight lines drawn at equal spacing
option_c: concentric circles drawn around a central point
option_d: straight lines that crowd closer together along the direction of the field
correct_answer_text: parallel straight lines drawn at equal spacing
solution: A uniform field has the same magnitude and direction at every point. Constant direction requires parallel lines and constant magnitude requires uniform spacing, since the number of lines per unit area represents the field strength.
formula_principle: Field line density represents field magnitude and line direction represents field direction
common_misconception: Assuming that any set of straight lines represents a uniform field, without checking that the spacing is constant.

concept_tested: Balancing weight with an electrostatic force
stem: A small ball of mass 2 g carrying a charge of 5 microC is held stationary in mid air by a uniform vertical electric field. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the magnitude of the field is
formula_principle: q E = m g for equilibrium in a vertical field
common_misconception: Failing to convert grams to kilograms before equating the weight to the electric force.

subtopic: Field due to a point charge
concept_tested: Superposition of fields of two unlike charges at the midpoint
stem: Point charges of 5 microC and -5 microC are fixed 20 cm apart in vacuum. Taking k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, the magnitude of the electric field at the midpoint of the line joining them is
solution: Each charge is 0.10 m from the midpoint, so each produces 9 x 10^9 x 5 x 10^-6 / (0.10)^2 = 4.5 x 10^6 N C^-1. The field of the positive charge points away from it and the field of the negative charge points towards it, so both point in the same direction and add: 9 x 10^6 N C^-1.
formula_principle: E = k q / r^2 for each charge, added as vectors
common_misconception: Confusing the vector addition of fields with the scalar addition of potentials, and so concluding that the field vanishes.

subtopic: Field due to a point charge
concept_tested: Graphical test of the inverse square law
stem: For the electric field E of an isolated point charge at a distance r from it, a straight line passing through the origin is obtained when
solution: Writing E = (k q) x (1 / r^2) shows that E is directly proportional to 1 / r^2. A plot of E against 1 / r^2 is therefore a straight line through the origin with slope k q.
formula_principle: E = k q / r^2, so E is a linear function of the variable 1 / r^2
common_misconception: Choosing 1 / r because the potential varies that way, or plotting against r and expecting linearity.

subtopic: Field due to a dipole on axial and equatorial lines
concept_tested: Numerical use of the axial dipole field
stem: A short electric dipole has a moment of 4 x 10^-9 C m. Taking k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, the electric field at a point on its axis at a distance of 0.1 m from the centre is
solution: E = 2 x 9 x 10^9 x 4 x 10^-9 / (0.1)^3 = 72 / 10^-3 = 7.2 x 10^4 N C^-1, directed along the dipole moment.
formula_principle: E_axial = 2 k p / r^3
common_misconception: Forgetting the factor of 2 in the axial field, or cubing the distance incorrectly.

concept_tested: Field lines meet a conductor surface normally
stem: In electrostatic equilibrium the electric field just outside the surface of a charged conductor is always normal to the surface because
option_a: the conductor offers a very high resistance to charge flow along its surface
option_b: electric field lines are unable to enter any material medium
option_c: any tangential component would drive the free surface charges along the surface, so equilibrium would not have been reached
option_d: the surface charge density on a conductor is always the same at every point
correct_answer_text: any tangential component would drive the free surface charges along the surface, so equilibrium would not have been reached
solution: Free charges on a conductor respond to any tangential field by moving. In the final static state there can be no such motion, so the tangential component must be zero and the field is purely normal to the surface.
formula_principle: Electrostatic equilibrium requires zero tangential field at a conductor surface
common_misconception: Attributing the normal direction to a property of the material rather than to the condition for static equilibrium.

subtopic: Field due to a dipole on axial and equatorial lines
concept_tested: Equatorial field from the charges and separation of a dipole
stem: An electric dipole consists of charges of 2 microC and -2 microC held 2 cm apart. Taking k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, the electric field at a point on the equatorial line 10 cm from the centre of the dipole is
solution: p = 2 x 10^-6 x 0.02 = 4 x 10^-8 C m. Then E = 9 x 10^9 x 4 x 10^-8 / (0.10)^3 = 360 / 10^-3 = 3.6 x 10^5 N C^-1, directed antiparallel to the dipole moment.
formula_principle: p = q x 2l and E_equatorial = k p / r^3
common_misconception: Using half the separation in the dipole moment, since 2l rather than l is the full charge separation.

subtopic: Field due to a point charge
concept_tested: Field is a property of the source, independent of the test charge
stem: At a certain point a test charge of 2 microC experiences a force of 0.1 N. The test charge is then removed and replaced by a charge of -4 microC. The electric field at that point is
option_a: 5 x 10^4 N C^-1 before and 2.5 x 10^4 N C^-1 after the replacement
option_b: 5 x 10^4 N C^-1 both before and after the replacement
option_c: 5 x 10^4 N C^-1 before and 1 x 10^5 N C^-1 after the replacement
option_d: 2 x 10^4 N C^-1 both before and after the replacement
correct_answer_text: 5 x 10^4 N C^-1 both before and after the replacement
solution: E = 0.1 / (2 x 10^-6) = 5 x 10^4 N C^-1. The field at a point is created by the source charges and does not depend on the size or sign of the charge used to probe it, so it is unchanged when the test charge is replaced. Only the force on the new charge changes.
formula_principle: E = F / q, and E is determined by the source charges alone
common_misconception: Believing that a larger test charge changes the field, when in fact it only changes the force it experiences.

subtopic: Field due to a point charge
concept_tested: Field at the centre of a square with two positive and two negative charges
stem: Charges of q, q, -q and -q are placed at the corners of a square of side a, the two positive charges occupying one pair of adjacent corners and the two negative charges the other pair. The magnitude of the electric field at the centre of the square is
solution: Each charge is at a distance a / sqrt 2 from the centre, so each produces a field of magnitude k q / (a^2 / 2) = 2 k q / a^2. The components perpendicular to the line separating the positive pair from the negative pair cancel, while the components parallel to it add. Each charge contributes 2 k q / a^2 times cos 45, that is sqrt 2 k q / a^2, and all four contributions point the same way, giving 4 sqrt 2 k q / a^2 directed from the positive pair towards the negative pair.
formula_principle: Each corner is at a distance a / sqrt 2 from the centre; contributions are added as vectors
common_misconception: Assuming that any symmetric arrangement of four charges gives zero field at the centre, without checking the signs.

concept_tested: Deflection of a charged particle projected across a uniform field
stem: A particle of mass 1 g and charge 1 microC enters a uniform electric field of 1000 N C^-1 with a speed of 10 m s^-1 directed at right angles to the field. Neglecting gravity, its sideways deflection after it has travelled 1 m along its original direction is
solution: a = 1 x 10^-6 x 1000 / (1 x 10^-3) = 1 m s^-2. The time to cover 1 m along the initial direction is t = 1 / 10 = 0.1 s. The sideways displacement is y = 0.5 x 1 x (0.1)^2 = 5 x 10^-3 m = 5 mm.
formula_principle: a = q E / m, t = x / v and y = (1/2) a t^2
common_misconception: Treating the motion along the field as uniform velocity motion and dropping the factor of one half.

concept_tested: A field line is not in general the trajectory of a charge
stem: A positive point charge is released from rest at a point in a non uniform electrostatic field. Which statement about its subsequent motion is correct?
option_a: Its initial acceleration is along the field line through that point, but its later path need not coincide with that field line
option_b: It moves along the field line through its starting point for the whole of its motion
option_c: It moves at right angles to the field lines, along an equipotential surface
option_d: It stays at rest because the field is not uniform
correct_answer_text: Its initial acceleration is along the field line through that point, but its later path need not coincide with that field line
solution: The force, and hence the acceleration, is always tangent to the field line at the particle position. Starting from rest the first motion is along that tangent. Once the particle has velocity, a curved field line would require a component of force perpendicular to the velocity of exactly the right size, which is not generally available, so the path departs from the line.
formula_principle: F = q E gives the acceleration, not the velocity, so field lines are not trajectories
common_misconception: Reading field lines as paths of motion, which is only valid when the lines are straight.

subtopic: Field due to a dipole on axial and equatorial lines
concept_tested: Comparing axial and equatorial fields at different distances
stem: For a short electric dipole, the ratio of the axial field at a distance r from the centre to the equatorial field at a distance r / 2 from the centre is
solution: The axial field at r is 2 k p / r^3. The equatorial field at r / 2 is k p / (r / 2)^3 = 8 k p / r^3. The ratio is 2 : 8, that is 1 : 4.
formula_principle: E_axial = 2 k p / r^3 and E_equatorial = k p / r^3
common_misconception: Handling only one of the two changes, either the axial factor or the cube of the halved distance.

subtopic: Field due to a dipole on axial and equatorial lines
concept_tested: Equatorial field without the short dipole approximation
stem: Charges of 10 microC and -10 microC are held 6 cm apart. Taking k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, the magnitude of the electric field at a point on the perpendicular bisector of the line joining them, 4 cm from its midpoint, is
solution: Each charge is at a distance d = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = 5 cm = 0.05 m from the point. Each contributes 9 x 10^9 x 10 x 10^-6 / (0.05)^2 = 9 x 10^4 / 2.5 x 10^-3 = 3.6 x 10^7 N C^-1. The components perpendicular to the dipole axis cancel and the parallel components add, each carrying a factor 3 / 5. The net field is 2 x 3.6 x 10^7 x 0.6 = 4.32 x 10^7 N C^-1, directed from the positive towards the negative charge.
formula_principle: Each charge contributes k q / d^2, and only the components parallel to the dipole axis survive
common_misconception: Applying the short dipole formula k p / r^3 even though the separation is comparable with the distance to the point.

concept_tested: Charged pendulum bob in a horizontal uniform field
stem: A small bob of mass 1 g carrying a charge of 10 microC hangs from a light insulating thread in a horizontal uniform electric field of 1000 N C^-1. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, in equilibrium the thread makes an angle with the vertical, and the tension in it is
option_a: 45 degrees, with a tension of 1.0 x 10^-2 N
option_b: 30 degrees, with a tension of 1.2 x 10^-2 N
option_c: 45 degrees, with a tension of 1.4 x 10^-2 N
option_d: 60 degrees, with a tension of 2.0 x 10^-2 N
correct_answer_text: 45 degrees, with a tension of 1.4 x 10^-2 N
solution: q E = 10 x 10^-6 x 1000 = 1 x 10^-2 N and m g = 1 x 10^-3 x 10 = 1 x 10^-2 N. Since the two are equal, tan theta = 1 and theta = 45 degrees. The tension balances their resultant: T = sqrt((10^-2)^2 + (10^-2)^2) = 1.41 x 10^-2 N, about 1.4 x 10^-2 N.
formula_principle: tan theta = q E / (m g) and T = sqrt((q E)^2 + (m g)^2)
common_misconception: Taking the tension as equal to the weight, forgetting that the thread must also balance the horizontal electric force.

concept_tested: Direction of the electric dipole moment vector
stem: The electric dipole moment of a pair of equal and opposite point charges is directed
option_a: from the negative charge towards the positive charge
option_b: from the positive charge towards the negative charge
option_c: perpendicular to the line joining the two charges
option_d: always along the external electric field in which the dipole is placed
correct_answer_text: from the negative charge towards the positive charge
solution: By convention the dipole moment vector points from the negative charge to the positive charge, along the line joining them. Its magnitude is the product of either charge and the separation between them.
formula_principle: p = q x 2l, directed from -q to +q
common_misconception: Aligning the dipole moment with the field lines that run from the positive to the negative charge.

concept_tested: Computation of dipole moment from charge and separation
stem: Charges of 2 microC and -2 microC are held 5 cm apart. The magnitude of the electric dipole moment of this pair is
solution: p = 2 x 10^-6 x 0.05 = 1 x 10^-7 C m, directed from the negative charge to the positive charge.
formula_principle: p = q x 2l
common_misconception: Halving the separation, since the symbol 2l for the separation is often misread as l.

concept_tested: Orientation giving maximum torque
stem: An electric dipole is placed in a uniform electric field. The torque acting on it is maximum when the angle between the dipole moment and the field is
solution: The torque magnitude p E sin theta is largest when sin theta = 1, that is at theta = 90 degrees, where the dipole axis is perpendicular to the field.
formula_principle: tau = p E sin theta
common_misconception: Confusing the position of maximum torque with the position of minimum potential energy, which is at zero degrees.

concept_tested: Stable equilibrium of a dipole in a uniform field
stem: A dipole of moment p is free to rotate in a uniform electric field E. Its potential energy is least, and its equilibrium is stable, when the angle between p and E is
option_a: 180 degrees, and this position is one of stable equilibrium
option_b: 90 degrees, and this position is one of minimum potential energy
option_c: 0 degrees, and this position is one of unstable equilibrium
option_d: 0 degrees, and this position is one of stable equilibrium
correct_answer_text: 0 degrees, and this position is one of stable equilibrium
solution: U = -p E cos theta is smallest, equal to -p E, when cos theta = 1, that is theta = 0. A small displacement from this position produces a restoring torque, so the alignment with the field is stable.
formula_principle: U = -p E cos theta
common_misconception: Believing that the antiparallel orientation is stable because the potential energy there is positive and largest.

concept_tested: Numerical evaluation of torque on a dipole
stem: A dipole of moment 2 x 10^-6 C m is placed in a uniform electric field of 5 x 10^5 N C^-1 with its axis at 30 degrees to the field. The torque acting on the dipole is
solution: tau = 2 x 10^-6 x 5 x 10^5 x sin 30 = 1 x 0.5 = 0.5 N m, directed so as to turn the dipole into alignment with the field.
formula_principle: tau = p E sin theta
common_misconception: Using cosine instead of sine, by confusing the torque expression with the potential energy expression.

concept_tested: Work done in rotating a dipole through a finite angle
stem: A dipole of moment 1 x 10^-6 C m lies along a uniform field of 1 x 10^5 N C^-1. The work that must be done to turn it until its axis makes 60 degrees with the field is
solution: p E = 1 x 10^-6 x 1 x 10^5 = 0.1 J. Starting at theta = 0 and ending at theta = 60 degrees, W = p E (cos 0 - cos 60) = 0.1 x (1 - 0.5) = 0.05 J.
formula_principle: W = U_final - U_initial = p E (cos theta_1 - cos theta_2)
common_misconception: Using the sine of the final angle, which belongs to the torque, instead of the change in cosine, which gives the work.

concept_tested: Net force and torque on a dipole in a uniform field
stem: An electric dipole is placed in a uniform electric field with its axis inclined to the field. It experiences
option_a: a non zero net force and zero torque
option_b: zero net force and zero torque in every orientation
option_c: a non zero net force and a non zero torque
option_d: zero net force and a non zero torque
correct_answer_text: zero net force and a non zero torque
solution: In a uniform field the forces q E and -q E on the two charges are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so they cancel and the net force is zero. Their lines of action are different, so they constitute a couple of moment p E sin theta, which is non zero unless the dipole is aligned or antialigned with the field.
formula_principle: Equal and opposite forces at different points form a couple
common_misconception: Expecting a net translational force in a uniform field, which only arises when the field varies from point to point.

concept_tested: Dependence of the oscillation period on the field strength
stem: A dipole performs small angular oscillations about its equilibrium position in a uniform electric field. If the field strength is made four times as large, the period of oscillation becomes
solution: The restoring torque for small angular displacements is p E theta, giving T = 2 pi sqrt(I / (p E)). The period varies as 1 / sqrt E, so multiplying E by 4 divides T by 2.
formula_principle: T = 2 pi sqrt(I / (p E))
common_misconception: Forgetting that the field appears under a square root, and so scaling the period by 4 or by 1 / 4.

concept_tested: Potential energy of an aligned dipole
stem: A dipole of moment 5 x 10^-6 C m is aligned along a uniform electric field of 2 x 10^4 N C^-1. Its potential energy in this position is
solution: With theta = 0, U = -p E = -(5 x 10^-6)(2 x 10^4) = -0.1 J. The negative value shows that work must be done against the field to disturb the dipole from alignment.
formula_principle: U = -p E cos theta
common_misconception: Taking the zero of dipole potential energy at theta = 0 rather than at theta = 90 degrees, which changes the sign and the reference.

subtopic: Dipole in a non uniform field
concept_tested: Force and torque on a dipole aligned with a non uniform field
stem: A short dipole is placed in a non uniform electric field with its axis pointing along the local field direction. The dipole experiences
option_a: zero net force and a non zero torque
option_b: zero net force and zero torque
option_c: a net force and a non zero torque
option_d: a net force and zero torque
correct_answer_text: a net force and zero torque
solution: Because the field is stronger at one charge than at the other, the two forces no longer cancel and a net force of magnitude p times the rate of change of E along the axis appears. Since the dipole moment is parallel to the field, sin theta = 0 and the torque is zero.
formula_principle: Net force is p dE/dx along the axis; torque is p E sin theta
common_misconception: Assuming that a dipole always feels a torque and never a net force, which is only correct in a uniform field.

concept_tested: Work to invert a dipole, deduced from the maximum torque
stem: The maximum torque that a certain uniform electric field can exert on a given dipole is 4 N m. The work that must be done to turn that dipole from its stable equilibrium position to its unstable equilibrium position in the same field is
solution: The maximum torque equals p E, so p E = 4 N m. Turning the dipole from theta = 0 to theta = 180 degrees requires W = p E (cos 0 - cos 180) = p E (1 + 1) = 2 p E = 8 J.
formula_principle: tau_max = p E and W = p E (cos theta_1 - cos theta_2)
common_misconception: Not recognising that the maximum torque itself supplies the value of p E, or forgetting the factor of 2 for a complete inversion.

concept_tested: Period of small oscillations of a dipole
stem: A dipole of moment 2 x 10^-6 C m and moment of inertia 1 x 10^-6 kg m^2 oscillates with small amplitude about its equilibrium position in a uniform field of 5 x 10^3 N C^-1. Its period of oscillation is about
solution: p E = 2 x 10^-6 x 5 x 10^3 = 1 x 10^-2 N m. Then I / (p E) = 1 x 10^-6 / 1 x 10^-2 = 1 x 10^-4 s^2, so the angular frequency is 100 rad s^-1 and T = 2 pi / 100 = 0.063 s.
formula_principle: T = 2 pi sqrt(I / (p E))
common_misconception: Placing p E in the numerator of the square root, which reverses the dependence on the field.

concept_tested: Distance at which the equatorial field matches a given axial field
stem: For a short dipole, the axial field at a distance r from the centre is equal in magnitude to the equatorial field at a distance
solution: Setting 2 k p / r^3 equal to k p / r'^3 gives r'^3 = r^3 / 2, so r' = r divided by 2^(1/3), which is about 0.79 r. The equatorial point must be nearer the dipole to give the same field strength.
formula_principle: 2 k p / r^3 = k p / r'^3
common_misconception: Applying the factor of 2 linearly to the distance rather than taking its cube root.

concept_tested: Maximum angular speed of a dipole released perpendicular to the field
stem: A dipole of moment p and moment of inertia I is held with its axis perpendicular to a uniform field E and then released from rest. Its maximum angular speed during the subsequent motion is
solution: At 90 degrees the potential energy is -p E cos 90 = 0 and at 0 degrees it is -p E. The energy released is therefore p E, all of which appears as rotational kinetic energy at the aligned position: (1/2) I omega^2 = p E, so omega = sqrt(2 p E / I).
formula_principle: Energy conservation: (1/2) I omega^2 = U_initial - U_final
common_misconception: Equating (1/2) I omega^2 with p E and then forgetting to clear the factor of one half.

concept_tested: Force on a point charge placed on the axis of a dipole
stem: A short dipole of moment 2 x 10^-9 C m lies along a straight line. A point charge of 5 microC is placed on that line, 0.1 m from the centre of the dipole. Taking k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, the force on the point charge is
solution: E = 2 x 9 x 10^9 x 2 x 10^-9 / (0.1)^3 = 36 / 10^-3 = 3.6 x 10^4 N C^-1. The force on the charge is F = 5 x 10^-6 x 3.6 x 10^4 = 0.18 N, directed along the dipole axis.
formula_principle: E_axial = 2 k p / r^3 and F = q E
common_misconception: Using the equatorial expression for an axial point, which halves the answer.

subtopic: Dipole in a non uniform field
concept_tested: Net force on a dipole from the gradient of the field
stem: A short dipole of moment 1 x 10^-6 C m is placed with its axis along the x axis in a region where the electric field is directed along the x axis and its magnitude increases as E = 1000 x newton per coulomb, with x in metres. The magnitude of the net force on the dipole is
solution: The two charges sit at slightly different values of x, where the field magnitudes differ. The net force is p times the rate of change of E with x. Here that rate is 1000 N C^-1 per metre, so F = 1 x 10^-6 x 1000 = 1 x 10^-3 N, directed towards the region of stronger field.
formula_principle: Net force on an aligned dipole in a non uniform field is p times the rate of change of E along the axis
common_misconception: Assuming a dipole always experiences zero net force, which holds only when the field is uniform.

concept_tested: Total flux through a closed surface equals enclosed charge divided by epsilon_0
stem: Gauss's law states that the total electric flux through any closed surface is equal to
option_a: the net charge enclosed by the surface divided by epsilon_0
option_b: the net charge enclosed by the surface multiplied by epsilon_0
option_c: the total of all charges in the region, whether inside or outside the surface, divided by epsilon_0
option_d: the net charge enclosed by the surface divided by 4 pi epsilon_0
correct_answer_text: the net charge enclosed by the surface divided by epsilon_0
solution: Charges outside the closed surface send as many field lines in as they send out, so they contribute zero net flux. Only the algebraic sum of the charges inside determines the flux, and the constant of proportionality is 1 / epsilon_0.
formula_principle: Total flux = q_enclosed / epsilon_0
common_misconception: Including charges lying outside the Gaussian surface in the enclosed charge.

concept_tested: Direct evaluation of flux from enclosed charge
stem: A charge of 8.85 x 10^-6 C is enclosed by a closed surface. Taking epsilon_0 = 8.85 x 10^-12 C^2 N^-1 m^-2, the total electric flux through that surface is
formula_principle: Total flux = q / epsilon_0
common_misconception: Multiplying by epsilon_0 rather than dividing, which also produces an absurdly small answer.

concept_tested: Flux is independent of the shape and size of the surface
stem: A point charge is placed somewhere inside a closed surface. The total electric flux through the surface
option_a: increases as the surface is made larger, because a larger surface intercepts more field lines
option_b: is largest when the charge is at the centre and falls as the charge moves towards the surface
option_c: depends only on the charge and is the same whatever the shape, size or position of the surface, as long as the charge stays inside
option_d: depends on the shape of the surface, being greatest for a sphere of the same volume
correct_answer_text: depends only on the charge and is the same whatever the shape, size or position of the surface, as long as the charge stays inside
solution: Gauss's law gives the flux as q / epsilon_0, which contains no reference at all to the shape, size or orientation of the surface, or to where inside it the charge sits. Enlarging the surface increases the area but reduces the field at the surface in exactly the same proportion.
formula_principle: Total flux = q_enclosed / epsilon_0, independent of the geometry of the surface
common_misconception: Believing that a bigger Gaussian surface must collect more flux.

subtopic: Field due to an infinite plane sheet
concept_tested: Field of an infinite charged plane sheet
stem: The electric field due to an infinite plane sheet carrying a uniform surface charge density sigma has magnitude
option_a: sigma / epsilon_0, the same at all distances from the sheet
option_b: sigma / (2 epsilon_0), the same at all distances from the sheet
option_c: sigma / (2 epsilon_0) at the surface, falling off as the distance from the sheet increases
option_d: sigma / (2 epsilon_0 r) at a distance r from the sheet
correct_answer_text: sigma / (2 epsilon_0), the same at all distances from the sheet
solution: A cylindrical Gaussian surface with its flat faces of area A parallel to the sheet gives 2 E A = sigma A / epsilon_0, so E = sigma / (2 epsilon_0). The result contains no distance, so the field is uniform on either side of the sheet.
formula_principle: E = sigma / (2 epsilon_0) for an infinite plane sheet
common_misconception: Expecting every electrostatic field to weaken with distance, which is not so for an infinite sheet.

subtopic: Field due to an infinite line charge
concept_tested: Field of a long straight line charge
stem: A very long straight wire carries a uniform linear charge density of 2 x 10^-6 C m^-1. Taking k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, the electric field at a point 0.1 m from the wire is
solution: E = 2 x 9 x 10^9 x 2 x 10^-6 / 0.1 = 3.6 x 10^4 / 0.1 = 3.6 x 10^5 N C^-1, directed radially away from the wire.
formula_principle: E = lambda / (2 pi epsilon_0 r) = 2 k lambda / r
common_misconception: Using an inverse square dependence for a line charge, whose field actually falls as 1 / r.

concept_tested: Flux through one face of a cube with a charge at its centre
stem: A point charge q is placed at the centre of a cube. The electric flux through one face of the cube is
solution: The charge at the centre sits symmetrically with respect to all six faces, so the total flux q / epsilon_0 is shared equally among them. Each face therefore carries q / (6 epsilon_0).
formula_principle: Total flux q / epsilon_0 shared equally among six identical faces
common_misconception: Reporting the total flux through the cube when only one face is asked about.

concept_tested: Charge just outside a closed surface
stem: A point charge is placed just outside a closed surface. For that surface,
option_a: both the net flux and the field at every point of the surface are zero
option_b: the net flux is not zero because the charge is very close to the surface
option_c: the net flux is not zero, although the field at every point of the surface is zero
option_d: the net flux is zero, although the electric field at points on the surface is not zero
correct_answer_text: the net flux is zero, although the electric field at points on the surface is not zero
solution: The enclosed charge is zero, so the net flux is zero: every field line that enters the surface also leaves it. The field itself is certainly not zero on the surface, since the external charge produces a strong field nearby. Zero net flux means the inward and outward contributions cancel.
formula_principle: Total flux = q_enclosed / epsilon_0
common_misconception: Concluding from zero flux that the field must vanish everywhere on the Gaussian surface.

subtopic: Field due to a charged spherical shell
concept_tested: Field inside and outside a uniformly charged shell
stem: A thin spherical shell of radius 10 cm carries a uniformly distributed charge of 4 microC. Taking k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, the electric fields at a point 5 cm from the centre and at a point 30 cm from the centre are respectively
solution: A Gaussian sphere of radius 5 cm encloses no charge, so the field there is zero. At 30 cm the whole charge is enclosed and behaves as if concentrated at the centre: E = 9 x 10^9 x 4 x 10^-6 / (0.30)^2 = 3.6 x 10^4 / 0.09 = 4 x 10^5 N C^-1.
formula_principle: E = 0 inside a uniformly charged shell and E = k Q / r^2 outside
common_misconception: Assuming the shell produces a field inside itself, or forgetting to square the external distance.

concept_tested: Range of validity and practical usefulness of Gauss's law
stem: Which statement about Gauss's law is correct?
option_a: It holds only for spherical surfaces, since it is derived from the inverse square law
option_b: It holds for every closed surface and can be used to find the field in every charge distribution
option_c: It holds for every closed surface, but it can be used to find the field only when the charge distribution has enough symmetry
option_d: It holds only when the enclosed charge is a single point charge at the centre of the surface
correct_answer_text: It holds for every closed surface, but it can be used to find the field only when the charge distribution has enough symmetry
solution: Gauss's law is a general result valid for any closed surface and any charge distribution. To extract the field from it, however, one must choose a surface on which the field magnitude is constant and its direction is known, and that is only possible for spherical, cylindrical or planar symmetry.
formula_principle: Total flux = q_enclosed / epsilon_0 for any closed surface
common_misconception: Confusing the general validity of the law with the special circumstances in which it is a practical tool.

concept_tested: Flux through a cube with a charge at one corner
stem: A point charge q is placed at one corner of a cube. The total electric flux through the cube is
solution: Imagine eight identical cubes packed around the corner charge so that the charge sits at their common vertex. Together they form a closed region enclosing the charge, so they share the total flux q / epsilon_0 equally. Each cube, including the given one, receives q / (8 epsilon_0).
formula_principle: Eight identical cubes stacked around the charge share the total flux q / epsilon_0 equally
common_misconception: Assuming that a charge sitting on the boundary is fully enclosed, and quoting q / epsilon_0.

concept_tested: Net enclosed charge from several charges inside and outside
stem: A closed surface encloses charges of 5 microC, -3 microC and 2 microC, while a further charge of -8 microC lies outside it. Taking epsilon_0 = 8.85 x 10^-12 C^2 N^-1 m^-2, the total flux through the surface is about
solution: The enclosed charge is 5 - 3 + 2 = 4 microC. The charge outside contributes nothing. Flux = 4 x 10^-6 / (8.85 x 10^-12) = 4.5 x 10^5 N m^2 C^-1.
formula_principle: Total flux = q_enclosed / epsilon_0, with q_enclosed the algebraic sum of the charges inside
common_misconception: Adding the charges as magnitudes, or letting the external charge into the calculation.

subtopic: Field due to an infinite plane sheet
concept_tested: Field of a pair of oppositely charged parallel sheets
stem: Two very large parallel plane sheets carry uniform surface charge densities of sigma and -sigma. The magnitude of the electric field between them and outside them is respectively
option_a: zero between the sheets and sigma / epsilon_0 outside them
option_b: sigma / (2 epsilon_0) between the sheets and sigma / (2 epsilon_0) outside them
option_c: 2 sigma / epsilon_0 between the sheets and zero outside them
option_d: sigma / epsilon_0 between the sheets and zero outside them
correct_answer_text: sigma / epsilon_0 between the sheets and zero outside them
solution: Each sheet alone produces sigma / (2 epsilon_0) pointing away from the positive sheet and towards the negative sheet. Between the sheets both contributions point from the positive to the negative sheet and add to sigma / epsilon_0. Outside, they point in opposite directions and cancel exactly, leaving zero field.
formula_principle: Each sheet contributes sigma / (2 epsilon_0), and the contributions are superposed
common_misconception: Applying the single sheet formula without superposing the second sheet, which gives the same value everywhere.

subtopic: Field due to a charged spherical shell
concept_tested: Point charge at the centre of a charged conducting shell
stem: A thin conducting spherical shell of radius 10 cm carries a charge of 6 microC. A point charge of 2 microC is placed at its centre. Taking k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, the electric field at a point 5 cm from the centre is
solution: A Gaussian sphere of radius 5 cm lies inside the shell, so it encloses only the central 2 microC. The shell charge lies outside it and contributes nothing. E = 9 x 10^9 x 2 x 10^-6 / (0.05)^2 = 1.8 x 10^4 / 2.5 x 10^-3 = 7.2 x 10^6 N C^-1.
formula_principle: E = k q_enclosed / r^2, with q_enclosed the charge inside the Gaussian sphere
common_misconception: Quoting the standard result that the field inside a shell is zero without checking whether any charge lies within the Gaussian surface.

subtopic: Field due to an infinite line charge
concept_tested: Finding the linear charge density from a measured field
stem: The electric field at a point 2 m from a very long straight charged wire is 9 x 10^3 N C^-1. Taking k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, the linear charge density on the wire is
formula_principle: E = 2 k lambda / r, so lambda = E r / (2 k)
common_misconception: Rearranging the line charge result with an inverse square dependence, which changes the answer by a factor equal to the distance.

concept_tested: Flux of a uniform field through a hemispherical surface
stem: A uniform electric field of magnitude E_0 is directed along the axis of a hemispherical surface of radius R. The flux of this field through the curved hemispherical surface is
solution: Close the hemisphere with its flat circular face of radius R. The closed surface contains no charge, so the total flux is zero, which means the flux through the curved part equals in magnitude the flux through the flat circular face. That face has area pi R^2 perpendicular to the field, so the flux is E_0 pi R^2.
formula_principle: Flux through an open surface in a uniform field equals E times the area projected perpendicular to the field
common_misconception: Multiplying the field by the actual curved area instead of the projected area.

concept_tested: Flux through a cube with a charge at the centre of one face
stem: A point charge q is placed at the centre of one face of a cube. The total electric flux through the cube is
solution: Place a second identical cube against the face carrying the charge. The charge is then at the centre of the combined region, and the pair of cubes encloses it completely, so together they carry a flux q / epsilon_0. By symmetry each cube carries half of it, that is q / (2 epsilon_0).
formula_principle: A second identical cube placed against that face makes the charge fully enclosed by the pair
common_misconception: Assuming the charge is entirely inside the given cube, so that the whole flux q / epsilon_0 passes through it.

subtopic: Potential due to a point charge
concept_tested: Direct substitution in V = k q / r
stem: A point charge of 2 microC is placed in vacuum. Taking k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, the electric potential at a point 3 m from it is
formula_principle: V = k q / r
common_misconception: Using the inverse square dependence of the field for the potential, which falls only as 1 / r.

concept_tested: Work done in moving a charge over an equipotential surface
stem: A charge is carried from one point to another along a path that lies entirely on a single equipotential surface. The work done by the electric force is
option_a: zero, because the electric field vanishes on an equipotential surface
option_b: positive and equal to the charge times the potential of the surface
option_c: zero, because the two points are at the same potential
option_d: dependent on the particular path followed over the surface
correct_answer_text: zero, because the two points are at the same potential
solution: Work done by the electric force depends only on the potential difference between the end points. Both points lie on the same equipotential surface, so that difference is zero and no work is done, no matter which path over the surface is taken.
formula_principle: W = q (V_initial - V_final)
common_misconception: Believing that zero work implies zero field, when in fact the field is merely perpendicular to the displacement.

concept_tested: Relative orientation of equipotential surfaces and field lines
stem: Equipotential surfaces are always
option_a: parallel to the electric field lines at every point
option_b: inclined at 45 degrees to the electric field lines
option_c: perpendicular to the electric field lines at every point
option_d: spherical in shape whatever the charge distribution
correct_answer_text: perpendicular to the electric field lines at every point
solution: Moving a charge along an equipotential surface involves no change of potential and hence no work. Since the work equals q E times the displacement along E, the field must have no component along the surface, so it is perpendicular to the surface everywhere.
formula_principle: No work is done in moving a charge along an equipotential surface, so E is perpendicular to it
common_misconception: Picturing equipotential surfaces as running along the field lines rather than across them.

concept_tested: Direction of the field relative to changing potential
stem: In a region where the electric potential varies from point to point, the electric field at any point is directed
option_a: along the direction in which the potential increases most rapidly
option_b: along any direction in which the potential does not change
option_c: always from a point of lower potential to a point of higher potential
option_d: along the direction in which the potential decreases most rapidly
correct_answer_text: along the direction in which the potential decreases most rapidly
solution: The negative sign in E = -dV/dr means the field points from higher to lower potential, and its magnitude equals the maximum rate at which the potential falls with distance.
formula_principle: E = -dV/dr
common_misconception: Dropping the negative sign, which reverses the direction of the field.

concept_tested: Work done in moving a charge between two potentials
stem: A charge of 2 microC is carried slowly from a point at a potential of 10 V to a point at a potential of 60 V. The work done by the external agent is
solution: W = 2 x 10^-6 x (60 - 10) = 2 x 10^-6 x 50 = 1 x 10^-4 J. The work is positive because a positive charge is being pushed towards a region of higher potential.
formula_principle: W_external = q (V_final - V_initial)
common_misconception: Using a single potential value rather than the difference, or reversing the order of subtraction.

concept_tested: Potential and field on the equatorial line of a dipole
stem: At a point on the equatorial line of a short electric dipole,
option_a: the electric field is zero while the potential is not zero
option_b: the potential is zero while the electric field is not zero
option_c: both the potential and the electric field are zero
option_d: both the potential and the electric field have their largest values
correct_answer_text: the potential is zero while the electric field is not zero
solution: An equatorial point is equidistant from the two charges, so the positive and negative contributions to the potential, which are scalars, cancel exactly. The field contributions are vectors: their components along the equatorial line cancel while the components parallel to the dipole axis add, giving k p / r^3 antiparallel to the dipole moment.
formula_principle: V_equatorial = 0 while E_equatorial = k p / r^3
common_misconception: Assuming that zero potential at a point forces the field there to vanish as well.

concept_tested: Axial potential of a short dipole
stem: A short dipole has a moment of 4 x 10^-9 C m. Taking k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, the electric potential at a point on its axis 0.3 m from the centre is
formula_principle: V_axial = k p / r^2 for a short dipole
common_misconception: Carrying the factor of 2 from the axial field expression into the axial potential, where it does not belong.

subtopic: Potential due to a point charge
concept_tested: Potential at the midpoint between two like charges
stem: Point charges of 2 microC and 3 microC are held 1 m apart. Taking k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, the potential at the midpoint of the line joining them is
formula_principle: Potential is a scalar, so contributions add algebraically: V = k q1 / r1 + k q2 / r2
common_misconception: Forgetting that the distance from each charge to the midpoint is half the separation.

subtopic: Potential due to a point charge
concept_tested: Potential and field inside a charged conducting shell
stem: A thin conducting spherical shell of radius 20 cm carries a charge of 4 microC. Taking k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, the potential and the field at the centre of the shell are
solution: The field inside the shell is zero, so the potential does not vary inside and equals the surface value: V = 9 x 10^9 x 4 x 10^-6 / 0.20 = 3.6 x 10^4 / 0.20 = 1.8 x 10^5 V. The field at the centre is zero.
formula_principle: Inside a charged conducting shell E = 0 and V is constant, equal to its surface value k Q / R
common_misconception: Confusing zero field with zero potential, whereas zero field only means the potential is constant.

concept_tested: Constant potential implies zero field
stem: Throughout a certain region of space the electric potential has the same value at every point. In that region
option_a: the electric field is uniform but not zero
option_b: the electric field is zero only at the centre of the region
option_c: the electric field is zero everywhere
option_d: the electric field is directed along the boundary of the region
correct_answer_text: the electric field is zero everywhere
solution: The field is the negative rate of change of potential with position. If the potential does not change from point to point, that rate of change is zero in every direction, and so the field is zero throughout the region.
formula_principle: E = -dV/dr
common_misconception: Confusing a constant potential with a constant, non zero field, which corresponds to a potential varying linearly with position.

concept_tested: Field from a given potential function
stem: In a certain region the electric potential varies as V = 5 x^2 volt, with x measured in metres. The electric field at x = 2 m is
option_a: 20 N C^-1 directed along the negative x direction
option_b: 20 N C^-1 directed along the positive x direction
option_c: 10 N C^-1 directed along the negative x direction
option_d: 40 N C^-1 directed along the negative x direction
correct_answer_text: 20 N C^-1 directed along the negative x direction
solution: dV/dx = 10 x, so E = -10 x. At x = 2 m, E = -20 N C^-1, that is a field of magnitude 20 N C^-1 pointing in the negative x direction, towards lower potential.
formula_principle: E = -dV/dx
common_misconception: Reporting the value of V rather than of its derivative, or losing the negative sign and hence the direction.

concept_tested: Potential difference across a displacement in a uniform field
stem: Two points X and Y in a uniform electric field of 200 N C^-1 are 0.5 m apart along the field direction. The potential difference between them is
option_a: 100 V, the point farther along the field direction being at the lower potential
option_b: 100 V, the point farther along the field direction being at the higher potential
option_c: 400 V, the point farther along the field direction being at the lower potential
option_d: zero, since the field is the same at both points
correct_answer_text: 100 V, the point farther along the field direction being at the lower potential
solution: The magnitude of the potential difference is E d = 200 x 0.5 = 100 V. Since the field points from higher to lower potential, the point reached by moving along the field lies 100 V lower.
formula_principle: V_X - V_Y = E d for a displacement d along a uniform field E
common_misconception: Thinking that a uniform field means a uniform potential, so that no potential difference exists.

concept_tested: Direction of spontaneous motion of positive and negative charges
stem: A proton and an electron are each released from rest in an electrostatic field. Left to themselves,
option_a: both the proton and the electron move towards regions of lower potential
option_b: the proton moves towards regions of higher potential and the electron towards regions of lower potential
option_c: the proton moves towards regions of lower potential and the electron towards regions of higher potential
option_d: both the proton and the electron move along the equipotential surfaces through their starting points
correct_answer_text: the proton moves towards regions of lower potential and the electron towards regions of higher potential
solution: Every free particle moves so as to lower its own potential energy U = q V. For the positively charged proton this requires V to decrease, so it moves towards lower potential, along the field. For the electron q is negative, so U falls when V rises, and it moves towards higher potential, against the field.
formula_principle: F = q E and E points from higher to lower potential
common_misconception: Applying the same rule to both signs of charge, forgetting that potential energy depends on the sign of q.

subtopic: Potential due to a point charge
concept_tested: Points of zero potential on the line joining unlike charges
stem: Point charges of 9 microC and -1 microC are fixed 20 cm apart. On the line through them the potential is zero at
option_a: one point only, 18 cm from the 9 microC charge
option_b: two points, 18 cm and 22.5 cm from the 9 microC charge
option_c: two points, 10 cm and 20 cm from the 9 microC charge
option_d: one point only, 2 cm from the -1 microC charge
correct_answer_text: two points, 18 cm and 22.5 cm from the 9 microC charge
solution: Between the charges, at distance x from the 9 microC charge, 9 / x = 1 / (0.20 - x), so 1.8 = 10 x and x = 0.18 m, that is 18 cm. Beyond the -1 microC charge, at distance d from it, 9 / (0.20 + d) = 1 / d, so 9 d = 0.20 + d and d = 0.025 m, which is 22.5 cm from the 9 microC charge. There are therefore two such points.
formula_principle: V = k q1 / r1 + k q2 / r2 = 0 gives 9 / r1 = 1 / r2
common_misconception: Using the ratio of square roots of the charges, which is the condition for zero field and not for zero potential.

concept_tested: Speed gained by a charge accelerated through a potential difference
stem: A particle of mass 4 x 10^-6 kg and charge 2 microC starts from rest and is accelerated through a potential difference of 100 V. Its final speed is
common_misconception: Dropping the factor of one half in the kinetic energy, which changes the speed by a factor of sqrt 2.

subtopic: Potential due to a point charge
