stem: Two batteries of emf 6 V and 4 V, each of internal resistance 1 ohm, are connected in parallel with their like terminals joined, and the combination feeds an external resistance of 2 ohm. The current through the external resistance is
solution: Let V be the potential difference across the external resistance. The junction rule gives (6 - V) / 1 + (4 - V) / 1 = V / 2, that is 10 - 2 V = 0.5 V, so 2.5 V = 10 and V = 4 V. The current through the external resistance is 4 / 2 = 2 A. The 6 V battery supplies (6 - 4) / 1 = 2 A while the 4 V battery happens to supply no current.
formula_principle: Junction rule at the common node together with Ohm's law in each branch.
common_misconception: Adding the emfs of cells that are connected in parallel.

concept_tested: Reading of a real voltmeter in a divider
stem: A 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance is connected across a series combination of a 4 ohm and an 8 ohm resistor. A voltmeter of resistance 8 ohm is then connected across the 8 ohm resistor. The reading of the voltmeter is
solution: The voltmeter of 8 ohm in parallel with the 8 ohm resistor gives 4 ohm. Total resistance = 4 + 4 = 8 ohm, so the current from the battery is 12 / 8 = 1.5 A. The potential difference across the parallel section, which is what the voltmeter reads, is 1.5 x 4 = 6 V.
formula_principle: A real voltmeter draws current, so it appears in parallel with the element across which it is joined.
common_misconception: Assuming a voltmeter never changes the circuit it is connected to.

concept_tested: Finding a branch resistance from the total current
stem: A 6 V cell of negligible internal resistance is connected across a 2 ohm resistor in series with a parallel combination of an unknown resistance R and a 6 ohm resistor. The current drawn from the cell is 1.5 A. The value of R is
solution: R_total = 6 / 1.5 = 4 ohm, so the parallel section has 4 - 2 = 2 ohm. Then 1 / R + 1 / 6 = 1 / 2, giving 1 / R = 1 / 2 - 1 / 6 = 1 / 3, so R = 3 ohm.
formula_principle: R_total = V / I, then subtract the series resistance and solve the parallel relation.
common_misconception: Stopping at the value of the parallel section and reporting it as the unknown resistance.

concept_tested: Terminal potential difference in a two source network
stem: Batteries of emf 12 V and 6 V, with internal resistances 2 ohm and 3 ohm respectively, are connected in parallel with their like terminals joined, and the combination is connected to an external resistance of 6 ohm. The potential difference across the external resistance is
solution: Let V be the potential difference across the load. Then (12 - V) / 2 + (6 - V) / 3 = V / 6. Multiplying throughout by 6 gives 3 (12 - V) + 2 (6 - V) = V, that is 36 - 3 V + 12 - 2 V = V, so 48 = 6 V and V = 8 V. Checking, the 12 V battery delivers (12 - 8) / 2 = 2 A while the 6 V battery receives (8 - 6) / 3 = 0.67 A, leaving 1.33 A for the load, which matches 8 / 6.
formula_principle: Junction rule at the common node: sum of currents delivered by the sources equals the current in the load.
common_misconception: Assuming that every source in a parallel group must deliver current to the load.

concept_tested: Steady state charge on a capacitor in a resistive circuit
stem: A 10 V cell of negligible internal resistance is connected in series with a 2 ohm and a 3 ohm resistor. A capacitor of 4 microfarad is connected across the 3 ohm resistor. In the steady state the charge on the capacitor is
solution: In the steady state the capacitor branch carries no current, so the current in the series loop is 10 / (2 + 3) = 2 A. The potential difference across the 3 ohm resistor is 2 x 3 = 6 V, and this is also the potential difference across the capacitor. Hence Q = C V = 4 x 10^-6 x 6 = 24 x 10^-6 C, that is 24 microcoulomb.
formula_principle: In the steady state no current flows into a capacitor branch, so the capacitor holds the potential difference of the element across which it is joined.
common_misconception: Concluding that a capacitor carries no charge merely because it carries no steady current.

concept_tested: Statement of the balance condition
stem: In a Wheatstone network the resistances P, Q, R and S occupy the arms AB, BC, AD and DC, a galvanometer is joined between B and D and a cell between A and C. The bridge is balanced when
solution: At balance no current passes through the galvanometer, so B and D are at the same potential. The same current flows through P and Q and likewise through R and S, and equal potential drops across P and R require P / Q = R / S.
formula_principle: At balance the two branches divide the potential in the same ratio, giving P / Q = R / S.
common_misconception: Writing the second ratio upside down and obtaining P S = Q R in the wrong arrangement.

concept_tested: Galvanometer current at balance
stem: When a Wheatstone bridge is balanced, the current through the galvanometer is
option_a: maximum, because the network then offers the least resistance
option_b: zero, because its two terminals are at the same potential
option_c: equal to the current drawn from the cell
option_d: independent of the arm resistances but not zero
correct_answer_text: zero, because its two terminals are at the same potential
solution: The balance condition makes the potentials at B and D equal. With zero potential difference across it, the galvanometer carries zero current whatever its own resistance may be.
formula_principle: Balance means the galvanometer terminals are at equal potential.
common_misconception: Thinking that a balanced bridge means the largest possible deflection.

concept_tested: Finding an unknown arm at balance
stem: In a balanced Wheatstone bridge, P = 10 ohm, Q = 20 ohm and R = 15 ohm. The value of S is
formula_principle: At balance P / Q = R / S, so S = R Q / P.
common_misconception: Setting up the proportion with the arms in the wrong order.

concept_tested: Working relation of the metre bridge
stem: In a metre bridge an unknown resistance X and a known resistance R occupy the two gaps, and the balance point is found at a distance l centimetre from the end of the wire on the side of X. Then
solution: The two segments of the uniform wire act as the remaining two arms of the bridge, with resistances proportional to l and to (100 - l). The balance condition X / R = l / (100 - l) then gives X = R l / (100 - l).
formula_principle: The bridge wire is uniform, so the resistances of its two segments are proportional to their lengths.
common_misconception: Measuring the balancing length from the wrong end of the bridge wire.

concept_tested: Unknown resistance from a balancing length
stem: In a metre bridge the balance point is at 40 cm from the end at which the unknown resistance X is connected, the known resistance in the other gap being 6 ohm. The value of X is
common_misconception: Using the total length of the wire in the ratio instead of the second segment.

concept_tested: Effect of interchanging the resistances in the gaps
stem: In a metre bridge the balance point is at 30 cm from the left end. If the resistances in the two gaps are interchanged, the new balance point will be at
solution: Originally X / R = 30 / 70. After interchanging, the same pair of resistances must satisfy R / X = l' / (100 - l'), so l' / (100 - l') = 70 / 30, giving l' = 70 cm from the left end.
formula_principle: Interchanging the gaps replaces the balancing length l by 100 - l.
common_misconception: Believing that the balance point cannot move when the two gap resistances are swapped.

concept_tested: Interchanging the cell and the galvanometer
stem: In a balanced Wheatstone bridge the positions of the cell and the galvanometer are interchanged. The bridge then
option_a: becomes unbalanced and the galvanometer shows a deflection
option_b: remains balanced only if the galvanometer resistance equals the internal resistance of the cell
option_c: remains balanced, since the balance condition contains neither the galvanometer resistance nor the cell
option_d: becomes balanced at a different ratio of the arm resistances
correct_answer_text: remains balanced, since the balance condition contains neither the galvanometer resistance nor the cell
solution: The balance condition is derived by requiring the two galvanometer terminals to be at equal potential, and it contains only P, Q, R and S. Interchanging the cell and the galvanometer branches does not alter this condition, so the bridge stays balanced.
formula_principle: The balance condition P / Q = R / S involves only the four arms.
common_misconception: Assuming the balance point depends on the sensitivity of the galvanometer or the strength of the cell.

concept_tested: Shifting the balance point towards the middle of the wire
stem: In a metre bridge experiment the balance point is found at 20 cm from one end. To bring the balance point nearer the middle of the wire, one should
option_a: increase the emf of the cell used to drive the bridge
option_b: use a galvanometer of smaller resistance
option_c: change the known resistance so that the two gap resistances become closer in value
option_d: use a longer bridge wire of the same material
correct_answer_text: change the known resistance so that the two gap resistances become closer in value
solution: A balance point at 20 cm means X / R = 20 / 80 = 1 / 4. Choosing a known resistance closer in value to X brings the ratio closer to unity, which brings l closer to 50 cm, where the fractional error in the reading is least.
formula_principle: X / R = l / (100 - l), so l is near 50 cm when X is near R.
common_misconception: Trying to shift the null point by changing the cell or the galvanometer.

concept_tested: New balance point after shunting one gap
stem: In a metre bridge the null point is at 25 cm from the left end when the left gap contains 2 ohm. A resistance of 3 ohm is now connected in parallel with the resistance in the right gap. The new balance length measured from the left end is
solution: First balance: 2 / X = 25 / 75 = 1 / 3, so X = 6 ohm. After shunting, the right gap has (6 x 3) / (6 + 3) = 2 ohm. The new condition is 2 / 2 = l / (100 - l), which gives l = 50 cm.
formula_principle: Left / right = l / (100 - l), applied before and after shunting.
common_misconception: Halving the shunted resistance instead of using the parallel combination formula.

concept_tested: Condition for maximum sensitivity of the bridge
stem: A Wheatstone bridge gives the sharpest null point, that is it is most sensitive, when
option_a: the four arm resistances differ from one another as widely as possible
option_b: all four arm resistances are of the same order of magnitude
option_c: the galvanometer resistance is very much larger than every arm resistance
option_d: the cell used has a very large internal resistance
correct_answer_text: all four arm resistances are of the same order of magnitude
solution: The deflection produced by a small change in one arm is greatest when the four arms are comparable, which is also why the metre bridge is used near the middle of the wire. Very unequal arms, a very high resistance galvanometer or a cell of high internal resistance all reduce the response.
formula_principle: Sensitivity is greatest when the four arms are comparable in magnitude.
common_misconception: Assuming that a more sensitive galvanometer alone can compensate for badly chosen arm resistances.

concept_tested: Equivalent resistance of a balanced bridge
stem: In a Wheatstone network P = 2 ohm, Q = 4 ohm, R = 3 ohm and S = 6 ohm, with a galvanometer of 10 ohm between the junctions B and D. The equivalent resistance of the network between A and C is
solution: P / Q = 2 / 4 = 0.5 and R / S = 3 / 6 = 0.5, so the bridge is balanced and the galvanometer carries no current. The network reduces to (2 + 4) = 6 ohm in parallel with (3 + 6) = 9 ohm, giving (6 x 9) / 15 = 54 / 15 = 3.6 ohm.
formula_principle: If P / Q = R / S the galvanometer branch may be removed, leaving two series branches in parallel.
common_misconception: Including the galvanometer resistance in the reduction without first testing the balance condition.

concept_tested: Effect of doubling both gap resistances
stem: In a metre bridge the null point is at 40 cm from the left end. Both resistances in the gaps are now replaced by resistances of twice their earlier values. The new null point is at
option_b: 40 cm from the left end, that is unchanged
correct_answer_text: 40 cm from the left end, that is unchanged
solution: The balance condition is X / R = l / (100 - l). Replacing X by 2 X and R by 2 R leaves the ratio X / R unchanged, so the ratio l / (100 - l) and therefore the balancing length of 40 cm are unchanged.
formula_principle: The balance condition depends only on the ratio of the two gap resistances.
common_misconception: Assuming that any change in the gap resistances must move the null point.

concept_tested: Resistance to be added in parallel to balance a bridge
stem: In a Wheatstone bridge P = 10 ohm, Q = 20 ohm, R = 30 ohm and S = 100 ohm. To balance the bridge, a resistance must be connected in parallel with S. Its value is
solution: Balance requires R / S' = P / Q = 10 / 20 = 0.5, so S' = 2 R = 60 ohm. With x in parallel with 100 ohm we need 1 / 60 = 1 / 100 + 1 / x, so 1 / x = 1 / 60 - 1 / 100 = (5 - 3) / 300 = 2 / 300, giving x = 150 ohm.
formula_principle: Balance needs R / S' = P / Q; then find x from 1 / S' = 1 / S + 1 / x.
common_misconception: Subtracting the resistances directly instead of subtracting their reciprocals.

concept_tested: Galvanometer current and cell current together
stem: In a Wheatstone bridge P = 2 ohm, Q = 4 ohm, R = 3 ohm and S = 6 ohm, with a galvanometer of 15 ohm between B and D. A cell of emf 7.2 V of negligible internal resistance is connected between A and C. The galvanometer current and the current drawn from the cell are respectively
solution: Since 2 / 4 = 3 / 6, the bridge is balanced and the galvanometer current is zero. Removing that branch leaves 2 + 4 = 6 ohm in parallel with 3 + 6 = 9 ohm, that is (6 x 9) / 15 = 3.6 ohm. The current from the cell is 7.2 / 3.6 = 2 A.
formula_principle: Test the balance condition, remove the galvanometer branch and reduce the remaining network.
common_misconception: Trying to compute a galvanometer current in a balanced bridge, or adding all the arms in series.

concept_tested: Potential difference proportional to length
stem: The principle of the potentiometer is that, for a wire of uniform cross section carrying a steady current, the potential difference across any portion of the wire is
option_a: inversely proportional to the length of that portion
option_b: directly proportional to the length of that portion
option_c: independent of the length of that portion
option_d: proportional to the square of the length of that portion
correct_answer_text: directly proportional to the length of that portion
solution: For a uniform wire carrying a steady current, the resistance of a portion is proportional to its length, so the potential drop I R across that portion is proportional to its length. The constant of proportionality is the potential gradient.
formula_principle: V = I R and R = rho L / A, so with I, rho and A fixed, V is proportional to L.
common_misconception: Confusing the potential gradient with the potential difference itself.

concept_tested: Why a potentiometer measures emf accurately
stem: A potentiometer measures the emf of a cell more accurately than a voltmeter does, because
option_a: the potentiometer wire has a very low resistance
option_b: at the balance point the potentiometer draws no current from the cell being tested
option_c: the potentiometer uses a very sensitive galvanometer
option_d: the potentiometer wire is very long
correct_answer_text: at the balance point the potentiometer draws no current from the cell being tested
solution: At balance the galvanometer shows no deflection, which means the test cell supplies no current. With I equal to zero the internal drop I r vanishes, so the balancing potential difference equals the emf itself. A voltmeter always draws some current and hence reads a value smaller than the emf.
formula_principle: V = E - I r, so the measured value equals E only when I is zero.
common_misconception: Thinking that a high resistance voltmeter and a potentiometer are equally exact.

concept_tested: Potential gradient along a potentiometer wire
stem: A potentiometer wire of length 10 m has a potential difference of 5 V across its full length. The potential gradient along the wire is
formula_principle: Potential gradient k = V / L.
common_misconception: Inverting the ratio while computing the potential gradient.

concept_tested: Ratio of emfs from balancing lengths
stem: Two cells give balancing lengths of 250 cm and 400 cm on the same potentiometer with the same potential gradient. The ratio of their emfs is
formula_principle: E = k l with the same k, so E1 / E2 = l1 / l2.
common_misconception: Inverting the ratio, or comparing differences of lengths instead of the lengths themselves.

concept_tested: emf from potential gradient and balancing length
stem: A potentiometer wire of length 4 m has a potential gradient of 0.25 V m^-1. A cell balances at 240 cm along the wire. The emf of the cell is
solution: Balancing length l = 240 cm = 2.4 m. Hence E = k l = 0.25 x 2.4 = 0.6 V.
formula_principle: E = k l.
common_misconception: Forgetting to convert the balancing length into metre before multiplying by the gradient.

concept_tested: Working relation for internal resistance
stem: In the measurement of the internal resistance of a cell by a potentiometer, the balancing length is l1 with the cell on open circuit and l2 when a resistance R is joined across the cell. The internal resistance of the cell is
solution: The open circuit balance gives E proportional to l1 and the balance with the shunt gives V proportional to l2. Substituting into r = R (E - V) / V gives r = R (l1 - l2) / l2.
formula_principle: l1 corresponds to E and l2 to the terminal potential difference V, with r = R (E - V) / V.
common_misconception: Dividing by the open circuit length rather than by the loaded length.

concept_tested: Numerical value of internal resistance
stem: In a potentiometer experiment a cell balances at 120 cm on open circuit and at 100 cm when a resistance of 5 ohm is joined across it. The internal resistance of the cell is
common_misconception: Using the wrong length in the denominator of the working relation.

concept_tested: How to increase the sensitivity of a potentiometer
stem: The sensitivity of a potentiometer can be increased by
option_a: increasing the current through the potentiometer wire
option_b: using a driving cell of larger emf with no other change
option_c: decreasing the potential gradient along the potentiometer wire
option_d: using a shorter wire with the same potential difference across it
correct_answer_text: decreasing the potential gradient along the potentiometer wire
solution: A smaller potential gradient means that a given emf balances over a greater length, so the null point can be located with a smaller fractional error. The gradient is lowered by using a longer wire, a smaller current or a larger series resistance in the primary circuit.
formula_principle: Sensitivity improves as the potential gradient k = V / L becomes smaller.
common_misconception: Believing that a stronger driving cell always improves a potentiometer measurement.

concept_tested: Potential gradient with a series resistance
stem: A potentiometer wire of length 10 m has a total resistance of 10 ohm and is connected to a driving cell of emf 4 V of negligible internal resistance through a series resistance of 30 ohm. The potential gradient along the wire is
solution: Current in the primary circuit = 4 / (30 + 10) = 0.1 A. Potential difference across the wire = 0.1 x 10 = 1 V. Potential gradient = 1 / 10 = 0.1 V m^-1.
formula_principle: I = E / (R_series + R_wire), V_wire = I R_wire and k = V_wire / L.
common_misconception: Assuming that the whole emf of the driving cell appears across the potentiometer wire.

concept_tested: Largest emf that can be balanced
stem: A potentiometer wire of length 6 m has a potential gradient of 0.5 V m^-1. A cell of emf 4 V is connected in the secondary circuit with the correct polarity. The result is that
option_a: the balance point lies at 8 m along the wire
option_b: no balance point is obtained, since the largest emf that can be balanced is 3 V
option_c: the balance point lies at 6 m, that is at the far end of the wire
option_d: the balance point lies at 3 m along the wire
correct_answer_text: no balance point is obtained, since the largest emf that can be balanced is 3 V
solution: The total potential difference available along the wire is k L = 0.5 x 6 = 3 V. Since the cell has an emf of 4 V, which exceeds 3 V, the galvanometer deflects in the same sense at every point and no null point can be found.
formula_principle: The largest measurable emf equals k times the total length of the wire.
common_misconception: Extrapolating the balancing length beyond the physical end of the wire.

concept_tested: Readings of a potentiometer and a real voltmeter
stem: A cell of emf 6 V and internal resistance 1 ohm is connected to an external resistance of 4 ohm. The potential difference across the external resistance is measured first with a potentiometer and then with a voltmeter of resistance 12 ohm. The two readings are respectively
solution: Without the voltmeter, the current is 6 / (4 + 1) = 1.2 A and the potential difference across the 4 ohm resistor is 1.2 x 4 = 4.8 V, which is what the potentiometer reads. With the voltmeter connected, the load becomes (4 x 12) / 16 = 3 ohm, the current is 6 / (3 + 1) = 1.5 A and the reading is 1.5 x 3 = 4.5 V.
formula_principle: A potentiometer at balance draws no current; a real voltmeter loads the circuit as a parallel resistance.
common_misconception: Assuming a voltmeter of finite resistance gives the same value as a potentiometer.

concept_tested: Ratio of emfs from aiding and opposing connections
stem: Two cells connected in series so as to support each other balance at 600 cm on a potentiometer, and when connected in opposition they balance at 200 cm. The ratio of their emfs is
solution: E1 + E2 corresponds to 600 and E1 - E2 corresponds to 200. Hence E1 / E2 = (600 + 200) / (600 - 200) = 800 / 400 = 2, that is 2 : 1.
formula_principle: E1 + E2 is proportional to l1 and E1 - E2 is proportional to l2, so E1 / E2 = (l1 + l2) / (l1 - l2).
common_misconception: Reading the ratio of the balancing lengths directly as the ratio of the emfs.

concept_tested: Series rheostat resistance from a standard cell reading
stem: A potentiometer wire of length 10 m has a resistance of 20 ohm and is connected in series with a driving cell of emf 5 V of negligible internal resistance and a rheostat. A standard cell of emf 1.02 V balances at 510 cm. The resistance of the rheostat is
solution: Potential gradient k = 1.02 / 5.10 = 0.2 V m^-1, so the potential difference across the whole 10 m wire is 0.2 x 10 = 2 V. The primary current is 2 / 20 = 0.1 A. The total resistance of the primary circuit is 5 / 0.1 = 50 ohm, so the rheostat contributes 50 - 20 = 30 ohm.
formula_principle: k = E_standard / l, V_wire = k L, I = V_wire / R_wire, and the rheostat carries the remaining potential drop.
common_misconception: Quoting the total primary resistance instead of subtracting the resistance of the wire.

concept_tested: One sided deflection of the galvanometer
stem: In a potentiometer experiment the galvanometer deflects in the same sense for every position of the jockey along the wire, although the polarities have been checked and are correct. The most likely reason is that
option_a: the driving cell has a very small internal resistance
option_b: the potentiometer wire is too thick
option_c: the two cells being compared have nearly equal emfs
option_d: the emf in the secondary circuit exceeds the total potential difference across the potentiometer wire
correct_answer_text: the emf in the secondary circuit exceeds the total potential difference across the potentiometer wire
solution: The potential difference tapped from the wire rises from zero at one end to k L at the other. If the emf in the secondary circuit is larger than k L, it cannot be balanced anywhere and the galvanometer deflects in the same sense at every position. The remedy is to raise the potential gradient by reducing the series resistance in the primary circuit or by using a driving cell of larger emf.
formula_principle: A null point exists only if the emf to be balanced is smaller than k L, the total potential difference along the wire.
common_misconception: Attributing one sided deflection to a faulty galvanometer rather than to an out of range emf.

concept_tested: Power from potential difference and current
stem: An electric heater draws a current of 5 A from a 220 V supply. The power consumed by the heater is
formula_principle: P = V I.
common_misconception: Confusing power with energy and quoting the answer in joule.

concept_tested: Energy consumed in kilowatt hour
stem: A geyser rated 2 kW is used for 3 hours every day. The electrical energy it consumes in 10 days is
solution: Energy = 2 x 3 x 10 = 60 kWh.
formula_principle: Energy in kWh = power in kW x time in hours.
common_misconception: Forgetting either the daily hours of use or the number of days.

concept_tested: Which bulb glows brighter in series
stem: Two bulbs rated 100 W, 220 V and 60 W, 220 V are connected in series across a 220 V supply. Assuming their resistances stay constant,
option_a: the 100 W bulb glows more brightly, because it has the higher power rating
option_b: both bulbs glow equally brightly, because the current through them is the same
option_c: the 100 W bulb glows more brightly, because it carries the larger current
option_d: the 60 W bulb glows more brightly, because it has the greater resistance
correct_answer_text: the 60 W bulb glows more brightly, because it has the greater resistance
solution: Resistance of the 100 W bulb = 220^2 / 100 = 484 ohm and that of the 60 W bulb = 220^2 / 60 = 807 ohm. In series the current is common, so the power I^2 R is larger in the 807 ohm bulb, that is in the bulb marked 60 W.
formula_principle: R = V^2 / P at the rated values; in series P = I^2 R, so the larger resistance dissipates more power.
common_misconception: Assuming the bulb with the higher rating always glows brighter, whatever the connection.

concept_tested: Working resistance of a lamp
stem: The resistance of a lamp marked 60 W, 120 V at its working temperature is
formula_principle: P = V^2 / R, so R = V^2 / P.
common_misconception: Using V / P in place of V^2 / P.

concept_tested: Monthly cost of running an appliance
stem: An electric iron of 1000 W is used for 2 hours a day for 30 days. If electrical energy costs 5 rupees per kWh, the cost for the month is
solution: Power = 1000 W = 1 kW. Energy = 1 x 2 x 30 = 60 kWh. Cost = 60 x 5 = 300 rupees.
formula_principle: Energy in kWh = power in kW x hours; cost = energy x rate.
common_misconception: Forgetting to convert watt into kilowatt before using the tariff.

concept_tested: Heat produced by a coil in a given time
stem: A heating coil of resistance 20 ohm is connected to a 200 V supply. The heat produced in 5 minutes is
formula_principle: P = V^2 / R and heat H = P t.
common_misconception: Forgetting to convert minutes into seconds, or quoting the power in place of the heat.

concept_tested: Time to boil water with coils in parallel
stem: Two identical heating coils, each of resistance R, take 10 minutes to boil a given quantity of water when used one at a time on a fixed supply. The time taken when the two coils are connected in parallel across the same supply is
solution: Two identical coils in parallel present R / 2 to the supply, so the power V^2 / (R / 2) is twice that of a single coil. The same quantity of heat is therefore delivered in half the time, that is in 10 / 2 = 5 minutes.
formula_principle: At fixed supply voltage, P = V^2 / R and the time to supply a fixed amount of heat is proportional to R.
common_misconception: Assuming that using two coils always doubles the time or leaves it unchanged.

concept_tested: Power dissipated in one resistor of a parallel pair
stem: A battery of emf 12 V and internal resistance 2 ohm is connected across a parallel combination of a 3 ohm and a 6 ohm resistor. The power dissipated in the 3 ohm resistor is
solution: Parallel combination = (3 x 6) / 9 = 2 ohm, so the total resistance is 2 + 2 = 4 ohm and the current from the battery is 12 / 4 = 3 A. The terminal potential difference is 3 x 2 = 6 V, which appears across both resistors. Hence the power in the 3 ohm resistor is 6^2 / 3 = 36 / 3 = 12 W.
formula_principle: Reduce the parallel pair, find the terminal potential difference, then use P = V^2 / R for the chosen branch.
common_misconception: Using the emf instead of the terminal potential difference across the parallel branches.

concept_tested: Power consumed at a voltage below the rating
stem: A bulb marked 100 W, 250 V is operated on a 200 V supply. Assuming its resistance does not change, the power it consumes is
formula_principle: R = V_rated^2 / P_rated is fixed, and P = V^2 / R at any applied voltage.
common_misconception: Scaling the power directly with the voltage instead of with its square.

concept_tested: Total power of a mixed grouping of identical bulbs
stem: Three bulbs, each marked 60 W, 120 V, are connected with two of them in parallel and this pair in series with the third, and the whole arrangement is joined to a 120 V supply. Assuming the resistances stay constant, the total power consumed is
solution: Each bulb has R = 120^2 / 60 = 14400 / 60 = 240 ohm. The two in parallel give 240 / 2 = 120 ohm, and adding the third in series gives 120 + 240 = 360 ohm. The total power is P = 120^2 / 360 = 14400 / 360 = 40 W.
formula_principle: R = V_rated^2 / P_rated for each bulb; reduce the network and use P = V^2 / R_eq.
common_misconception: Adding the marked wattages of bulbs that are not each working at their rated voltage.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Dependence of dB on distance from the current element
stem: According to the Biot Savart law, the magnitude of the magnetic field dB produced at a point by a small current element I dl depends on the distance r of the point from the element as
option_a: dB is inversely proportional to r
option_b: dB is directly proportional to r^2
option_c: dB is inversely proportional to r^2
option_d: dB does not depend on r
correct_answer_text: dB is inversely proportional to r^2
solution: The Biot Savart law states dB = (mu_0 / 4 pi) x I dl sin theta / r^2. The distance appears as r^2 in the denominator, so dB falls off as the inverse square of the distance from the current element.
formula_principle: dB = (mu_0 / 4 pi) x I dl sin theta / r^2
common_misconception: Students often carry over the 1/r dependence of the infinite straight wire, which is the result of integrating the law, and apply it to a single element.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Numerical value of mu_0 / 4 pi
stem: In SI units the constant mu_0 / 4 pi appearing in the Biot Savart law has the value
solution: Dividing mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1 by 4 pi gives exactly 10^-7 T m A^-1.
common_misconception: Learners mix up mu_0, mu_0 / 2 pi and mu_0 / 4 pi, and often substitute the wrong one into the Biot Savart law.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Vector character of dB and the cross product dl x r
stem: The direction of the magnetic field dB produced at a point P by a current element I dl is
option_a: along the direction of dl itself
option_b: along the line joining the element to P
option_c: perpendicular to the plane containing dl and the line joining the element to P
option_d: opposite to the direction of dl
correct_answer_text: perpendicular to the plane containing dl and the line joining the element to P
solution: Because dB involves the cross product dl x r_hat, dB must be perpendicular to both dl and to the position vector r drawn from the element to the point. That is, dB is normal to the plane containing these two vectors.
formula_principle: dB = (mu_0 / 4 pi) x I (dl x r_hat) / r^2
common_misconception: Students often assume the magnetic field points radially outward, copying the pattern of the electrostatic field of a point charge.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Points at which the field of a current element vanishes
stem: A short current element I dl lies along a straight line. The magnetic field due to this element is zero at points lying
option_a: on the perpendicular drawn to the element through its midpoint
option_b: on a circle drawn around the element
option_c: on the line along which the element itself is directed
option_d: at every point equally distant from the element
correct_answer_text: on the line along which the element itself is directed
solution: The magnitude is dB = (mu_0 / 4 pi) x I dl sin theta / r^2. For points lying along the axis of the element, theta is 0 degrees or 180 degrees, so sin theta = 0 and dB = 0. The field is largest at theta = 90 degrees.
formula_principle: dB proportional to sin theta, where theta is the angle between dl and r
common_misconception: The sine factor is frequently dropped, so students wrongly conclude that the element produces a field of the same strength in every direction.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: SI unit of mu_0
stem: The SI unit of the permeability of free space mu_0 is
solution: Rearranging B = mu_0 I / (2 pi r) gives mu_0 = 2 pi r B / I, so the unit is (m x T) / A, that is T m A^-1. This is the same as N A^-2.
formula_principle: From B = mu_0 I / (2 pi r), mu_0 = B x r / I in unit terms
common_misconception: Confusing the unit of magnetic flux, Wb = T m^2, with the unit of magnetic field leads to an extra power of length.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Direct substitution in the Biot Savart law
stem: A current element of length 2 cm carries a current of 5 A. Calculate the magnitude of the magnetic field produced by this element at a point 20 cm away, the point lying on the perpendicular drawn to the element. Take mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1.
formula_principle: dB = (mu_0 / 4 pi) x I dl sin theta / r^2
common_misconception: Mixing centimetres and metres in the same substitution is the commonest source of error in this calculation.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Using sin theta correctly for an inclined position vector
stem: A current element of length 1 cm carries a current of 10 A. Find the magnitude of the magnetic field at a point 10 cm from the element, the line joining the element to the point making an angle of 30 degrees with the element. Take mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1.
formula_principle: dB = (mu_0 / 4 pi) x I dl sin theta / r^2
common_misconception: The angle theta is measured between the current element and the line drawn to the point, not between the element and the field, so cos theta must never be used.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Writing the Biot Savart law in vector notation
stem: The vector form of the Biot Savart law for the field of a current element I dl at position vector r from the element is
option_a: dB = (mu_0 / 4 pi) x I (dl . r_hat) / r^2
option_b: dB = (mu_0 / 4 pi) x I (r_hat x dl) / r^2
option_c: dB = (mu_0 / 4 pi) x I (dl x r_hat) / r
option_d: dB = (mu_0 / 4 pi) x I (dl x r_hat) / r^2
correct_answer_text: dB = (mu_0 / 4 pi) x I (dl x r_hat) / r^2
solution: The field of an element is a vector perpendicular to both dl and r_hat, so a vector product of dl with r_hat is required, taken in that order, and the magnitude carries an inverse square factor 1 / r^2.
formula_principle: dB = (mu_0 / 4 pi) x I (dl x r_hat) / r^2
common_misconception: Reversing the order of a vector product is not harmless; it flips the sign, and therefore the direction of the magnetic field.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Similarities and differences between the two inverse square laws
stem: Which statement correctly compares the Biot Savart law with Coulomb's law in electrostatics?
option_a: Both are inverse square laws and in both cases the field lies along the line joining the source and the point
option_b: The Biot Savart law is an inverse law while Coulomb's law is an inverse square law
option_c: Coulomb's law depends on the angular position of the point while the Biot Savart law does not
option_d: Both are inverse square laws, but the Coulomb field is directed along the line joining the source and the point whereas the Biot Savart field is perpendicular to that line
correct_answer_text: Both are inverse square laws, but the Coulomb field is directed along the line joining the source and the point whereas the Biot Savart field is perpendicular to that line
solution: Both laws vary as 1 / r^2 and both are linear in their sources. The Coulomb field of a point charge is central, directed along the joining line, and has no angular dependence. The Biot Savart field carries a factor sin theta and is perpendicular to the plane of dl and r, so it is not a central field.
formula_principle: dB proportional to I dl sin theta / r^2; F proportional to q1 q2 / r^2
common_misconception: The presence of an inverse square factor tempts students to assume the magnetic field of an element is also radial.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Recognising when sin theta vanishes
stem: A very short conductor carrying a steady current lies along the x axis. At a point on the x axis, some distance away from the conductor, the magnetic field due to this conductor is
option_a: maximum, because the point lies closest to the direction of current flow
option_b: zero, because the angle between the current element and the line joining it to the point is 0 degrees
option_c: equal to mu_0 I / (2 pi r)
correct_answer_text: zero, because the angle between the current element and the line joining it to the point is 0 degrees
solution: For a point on the line of the element, the vectors dl and r are parallel, so theta = 0 degrees and sin theta = 0. Hence dB = 0 at every point on the axis of the element.
formula_principle: dB = (mu_0 / 4 pi) x I dl sin theta / r^2
common_misconception: Students assume that a point close to the current always experiences a strong field and forget that the direction of the point relative to the element matters.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
subtopic: Direction from the right hand rule
concept_tested: Applying the cross product to fix the direction of dB
stem: A current element at the origin points along the positive x direction. The magnetic field due to this element at a point on the positive y axis is directed along
solution: Here dl is along x_hat and r_hat is along y_hat. The vector product x_hat x y_hat gives z_hat, so the field at that point is along the positive z direction, that is out of the xy plane.
formula_principle: dB is along dl x r_hat
common_misconception: Reversing the order of the vector product, or using the left hand instead of the right hand, gives exactly the opposite direction.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Combined effect of changing distance and angle
stem: The magnetic field due to a small current element at a point 10 cm away, on the perpendicular to the element, is 2 x 10^-7 T. The field due to the same element at a point 20 cm away, along a line making 30 degrees with the element, is
solution: Doubling the distance from 10 cm to 20 cm reduces the field by a factor of 2^2 = 4. Changing the angle from 90 degrees to 30 degrees multiplies the field by sin 30 / sin 90 = 0.5. Hence the new field is 2 x 10^-7 x (1 / 4) x 0.5 = 2.5 x 10^-8 T.
formula_principle: dB proportional to sin theta / r^2
common_misconception: Both changes must be applied together; applying only one of the two factors is the usual mistake.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Why the current element is not an independently measurable quantity
stem: Which statement about the Biot Savart law is correct?
option_a: An isolated current element can be produced in the laboratory and its field measured directly
option_b: The law applies only to circular circuits and fails for straight conductors
option_c: An isolated current element cannot exist by itself, so the law is verified only through the fields of complete current circuits obtained by integration
option_d: The law gives the force between two current elements directly
correct_answer_text: An isolated current element cannot exist by itself, so the law is verified only through the fields of complete current circuits obtained by integration
solution: A steady current must flow in a closed loop, so a current element cannot be isolated. The Biot Savart law is therefore a statement about the contribution of an element, and it is tested by integrating over a full circuit and comparing the resulting field of a straight wire, a loop or a solenoid with measurement.
formula_principle: dB = (mu_0 / 4 pi) x I dl sin theta / r^2, applied by integration over a closed circuit
common_misconception: The law is often treated as if the element were an experimentally accessible object, like a point charge in electrostatics.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Dimensional formula of the permeability of free space
stem: The dimensional formula of the permeability of free space mu_0 is
solution: Magnetic field has dimensions [M^1 L^0 T^-2 A^-1]. From mu_0 = 2 pi r B / I, the dimensions are [L] x [M^1 L^0 T^-2 A^-1] / [A] = [M^1 L^1 T^-2 A^-2]. This is consistent with the unit N A^-2.
common_misconception: Students confuse the dimensions of B, of flux, and of mu_0, because all three involve the ampere in a negative power.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
subtopic: Field at an off axis point
concept_tested: Finding sin theta from the geometry before substituting
stem: A current element of length 2 mm carrying 10 A lies at the origin along the x axis. Find the magnitude of the magnetic field it produces at the point whose coordinates are x = 3 cm, y = 4 cm. Take mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1.
solution: The distance is r = square root of (3^2 + 4^2) cm = 5 cm = 0.05 m. The angle theta is measured from the x axis, so sin theta = 4 / 5 = 0.8. Then dB = 10^-7 x (10 x 0.002 x 0.8) / (0.05)^2 = 10^-7 x 0.016 / 0.0025 = 10^-7 x 6.4 = 6.4 x 10^-7 T.
formula_principle: dB = (mu_0 / 4 pi) x I dl sin theta / r^2 with sin theta = y / r
common_misconception: Learners often take the perpendicular coordinate divided by r as cos theta, or use the coordinate along the element in the sine.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Vector addition of the fields of two perpendicular current elements
stem: Two identical current elements, each of length 1 cm and carrying 10 A, are placed at the origin, one directed along the positive x axis and the other along the positive y axis. Find the magnitude of the resultant magnetic field at a point on the positive z axis, 10 cm from the origin. Take mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1.
solution: Each element makes an angle of 90 degrees with the line to the point on the z axis, so each contributes dB = 10^-7 x (10 x 0.01) / (0.10)^2 = 10^-7 x 0.1 / 0.01 = 1 x 10^-6 T. The element along x gives a field along the negative y direction and the element along y gives a field along the positive x direction, so the two contributions are mutually perpendicular. The resultant is square root of (1 + 1) x 10^-6 = 1.414 x 10^-6 T, that is about 1.4 x 10^-6 T.
formula_principle: dB = (mu_0 / 4 pi) x I dl / r^2 for each element, then vector addition of perpendicular components
common_misconception: Equal magnitudes tempt students either to add them directly or to assume cancellation, without checking the actual directions given by the vector products.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Standard expression for the field of a long straight wire
stem: The magnetic field at a perpendicular distance r from a very long straight conductor carrying a steady current I is
solution: Integrating the Biot Savart law along an infinite straight wire gives B = mu_0 I / (2 pi r). The field falls off as the first power of the distance, not as its square, because contributions come from the whole length of the wire.
formula_principle: B = mu_0 I / (2 pi r)
common_misconception: The inverse square dependence of a single element is often retained after integration, which is wrong.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Computing B for a given current and distance
stem: A long straight wire carries a current of 5 A. Find the magnetic field at a point 10 cm from the wire. Take mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1.
solution: B = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 5) / (2 pi x 0.10). The factor pi cancels, leaving B = (2 x 10^-7 x 5) / 0.10 = 1 x 10^-6 / 0.10 = 1 x 10^-5 T.
formula_principle: B = mu_0 I / (2 pi r)
common_misconception: Writing mu_0 / (2 pi) as 10^-7 instead of 2 x 10^-7 halves every answer of this type.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Shape and sense of the magnetic lines around a straight wire
stem: The magnetic lines of force around a long straight current carrying wire are
option_a: straight lines parallel to the wire
option_b: concentric circles lying in planes perpendicular to the wire, with the sense given by the right hand thumb rule
option_c: straight lines radiating outward from the wire
option_d: concentric circles lying in planes containing the wire
correct_answer_text: concentric circles lying in planes perpendicular to the wire, with the sense given by the right hand thumb rule
solution: Point the right thumb along the direction of conventional current; the curled fingers then give the sense in which the circular field lines are traced. These circles lie in planes at right angles to the wire, centred on the wire.
formula_principle: Right hand thumb rule for a straight conductor
common_misconception: Radial field lines belong to electrostatics; magnetic field lines around a straight wire are closed circles.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Inverse first power dependence
stem: The magnetic field at a point 4 cm from a long straight current carrying wire is B. At a point 8 cm from the same wire the field will be
solution: Since B = mu_0 I / (2 pi r), the field varies inversely as the first power of r. Doubling the distance from 4 cm to 8 cm therefore halves the field, giving B / 2.
formula_principle: B proportional to 1 / r for a long straight wire
common_misconception: The inverse square habit built up in electrostatics and gravitation is wrongly transferred to the long straight wire.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Applying the right hand rule to a vertical wire
stem: A long vertical wire carries a current directed vertically upward. At a point due east of the wire, the magnetic field points towards
solution: Take the current along the upward vertical and the point to the east. The field direction is given by the vector product of the upward direction with the eastward radial direction, which points to the north. Equivalently, curling the right hand fingers around the upward thumb sends the field anticlockwise seen from above, which is northward on the eastern side.
formula_principle: B is along the direction of (current direction) x (radial unit vector)
common_misconception: Using the left hand, which belongs to the force rule, reverses the field direction.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Field at a point on the perpendicular through one end
stem: A very long straight wire carries a current of 10 A. Find the magnetic field at a point 5 cm from the wire, on the perpendicular drawn to the wire at one of its ends, the wire extending only on one side of this perpendicular. Take mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1.
solution: Only half the wire contributes, so the field is half the infinite wire value: B = mu_0 I / (4 pi a) = 10^-7 x 10 / 0.05 = 10^-6 / 0.05 = 2 x 10^-5 T.
formula_principle: B = mu_0 I / (4 pi a) for a semi infinite straight conductor
common_misconception: Students forget that a semi infinite wire gives exactly half the field of a wire extending on both sides.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Inverting the straight wire formula
stem: The magnetic field at a distance of 5 cm from a long straight wire is 2 x 10^-5 T. The current flowing in the wire is (take mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1)
formula_principle: I = 2 pi r B / mu_0
common_misconception: The factor mu_0 / (2 pi) = 2 x 10^-7 T m A^-1 is often replaced by 10^-7 T m A^-1, doubling the computed current.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Simultaneous change of current and distance
stem: Wire P carries a current I and the field is measured at a distance r from it. Wire Q carries a current 2 I and the field is measured at a distance 2 r from it. Both wires are long and straight. The fields at these two points are related as
option_a: the field near Q is twice that near P
option_b: the field near Q is half that near P
option_c: the field near Q is four times that near P
solution: For wire P, B_P = mu_0 I / (2 pi r). For wire Q, B_Q = mu_0 (2 I) / (2 pi x 2 r) = mu_0 I / (2 pi r). The doubling of the current is exactly cancelled by the doubling of the distance, so the two fields are the same.
formula_principle: B = mu_0 I / (2 pi r)
common_misconception: Applying one change and forgetting the other is the usual slip in ratio problems of this kind.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Locating the null point between parallel currents in the same sense
stem: Two long parallel wires 10 cm apart carry currents of 2 A and 3 A in the same direction. The point on the line joining them at which the resultant magnetic field is zero lies
option_c: 20 cm from the 2 A wire on the outer side
solution: For currents in the same sense the fields oppose each other only between the wires, so the null point lies between them. Let it be at x from the 2 A wire. Then 2 / x = 3 / (10 - x), giving 20 - 2 x = 3 x, so 5 x = 20 and x = 4 cm. The null point is 4 cm from the 2 A wire and 6 cm from the 3 A wire, that is nearer the smaller current.
formula_principle: mu_0 I1 / (2 pi x) = mu_0 I2 / (2 pi (d - x))
common_misconception: Students often place the null point nearer the larger current; it always lies nearer the smaller current.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Field at a point on the line of the conductor
stem: A straight conductor of finite length carries a steady current. At a point lying on the line along which the conductor lies, beyond one of its ends, the magnetic field due to this conductor is
option_c: zero, since every current element of the conductor makes an angle of 0 degrees or 180 degrees with the line to that point
correct_answer_text: zero, since every current element of the conductor makes an angle of 0 degrees or 180 degrees with the line to that point
solution: Each element I dl of the conductor and the line joining it to the given point are collinear, so theta is 0 degrees or 180 degrees and sin theta = 0. Every element contributes zero, so the resultant field at such a point is zero.
formula_principle: dB proportional to sin theta, integrated along the conductor
common_misconception: The expression mu_0 I / (2 pi r) is valid only for points on a perpendicular drawn to the wire, never for points on its own line.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Uniformity of B on a circle around the wire
stem: Which statement about the magnetic field of a long straight current carrying conductor is correct?
option_a: Both the magnitude and the direction of B are the same at every point of such a circle
option_b: The magnitude of B is greatest on the side of the wire towards which the current flows
option_c: B is zero at all points in the plane perpendicular to the wire
option_d: The magnitude of B is the same at every point of a circle drawn around the wire in a perpendicular plane, but its direction changes from point to point
correct_answer_text: The magnitude of B is the same at every point of a circle drawn around the wire in a perpendicular plane, but its direction changes from point to point
solution: The magnitude depends only on r, so all points of a given circle have equal field strength. The direction is tangential to that circle, so it rotates continuously as one moves around the circle. This constancy of magnitude with a tangential direction is precisely what makes such a circle a convenient Amperian loop.
formula_principle: B = mu_0 I / (2 pi r), directed tangentially
common_misconception: Constant magnitude is often read as constant vector, which is false for a circulating field.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Resultant field at the midpoint
stem: Two long parallel wires 20 cm apart carry currents of 5 A each in opposite directions. Find the magnitude of the resultant magnetic field at the midpoint of the line joining them. Take mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1.
solution: Each wire is 0.10 m from the midpoint, so each produces B = 2 x 10^-7 x 5 / 0.10 = 1 x 10^-5 T. For currents in opposite directions the two fields at a point between the wires point the same way, so they add: B = 1 x 10^-5 + 1 x 10^-5 = 2 x 10^-5 T.
formula_principle: B = mu_0 I / (2 pi r) for each wire, then vector addition
common_misconception: Students assume opposite currents mean opposite fields everywhere; between the wires the fields actually reinforce each other.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Using the sin theta_1 plus sin theta_2 result
stem: A straight wire of length 20 cm carries a current of 10 A. Find the magnetic field at a point 10 cm from the wire on the perpendicular drawn through its midpoint. Take mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1.
solution: Here the half length is 0.10 m and the perpendicular distance is a = 0.10 m, so each angle satisfies sin theta = 0.10 / square root of (0.10^2 + 0.10^2) = 1 / square root of 2. The sum of the two sines is 2 / square root of 2 = square root of 2 = 1.414. Then B = 10^-7 x 10 / 0.10 x 1.414 = 1 x 10^-5 x 1.414 = 1.41 x 10^-5 T.
formula_principle: B = (mu_0 I / (4 pi a)) x (sin theta_1 + sin theta_2)
common_misconception: Applying the infinite wire formula to a wire whose length is comparable with the distance overestimates the field.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Null point for antiparallel currents
stem: Two long parallel wires 10 cm apart carry currents of 1 A and 3 A in opposite directions. The resultant magnetic field is zero at a point
option_a: 2.5 cm from the 1 A wire, between the two wires
option_b: 5 cm from the 3 A wire, on the side away from the 1 A wire
option_d: 5 cm from the 1 A wire, on the side away from the 3 A wire
correct_answer_text: 5 cm from the 1 A wire, on the side away from the 3 A wire
solution: For antiparallel currents the two fields point the same way at every point between the wires, so no null point can lie between them. Outside, on the side of the smaller current, let the point be x from the 1 A wire. Then 1 / x = 3 / (x + 10), giving 3 x = x + 10, so x = 5 cm. The null point lies 5 cm from the 1 A wire, on the far side from the 3 A wire.
formula_principle: mu_0 I1 / (2 pi x) = mu_0 I2 / (2 pi (x + d))
common_misconception: Students apply the between the wires condition without first checking whether the currents are parallel or antiparallel.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Superposition of the fields of two perpendicular conductors
stem: Two long insulated straight wires cross each other at right angles at the origin without touching. One lies along the x axis with a current of 10 A in the positive x direction and the other lies along the y axis with a current of 10 A in the positive y direction. Find the resultant magnetic field at the point x = 10 cm, y = 10 cm. Take mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1.
solution: Each wire is at a perpendicular distance 0.10 m from the point, so each gives 2 x 10^-7 x 10 / 0.10 = 2 x 10^-5 T. The wire along x, with current towards positive x, produces a field out of the xy plane at that point. The wire along y, with current towards positive y, produces a field into the xy plane there. The two are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so the resultant is zero.
formula_principle: B = mu_0 I / (2 pi r) for each wire, with directions from the right hand rule
common_misconception: Both contributions are along the z axis, not perpendicular to each other, so combining them as perpendicular vectors is wrong.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Distance at which the wire field equals a given value
stem: A long straight wire carries a current of 100 A. At what distance from the wire is the magnetic field equal to 4 x 10^-5 T? Take mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1.
formula_principle: r = mu_0 I / (2 pi B)
common_misconception: Substituting mu_0 itself, or mu_0 / 4 pi, in place of mu_0 / 2 pi shifts the answer by a factor of two either way.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Locating the point of zero resultant horizontal field
stem: A long vertical wire carries a current of 20 A vertically upward. The horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field at the place is 4 x 10^-5 T directed towards the north. The resultant horizontal magnetic field is zero at a point that lies (take mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1)
option_a: 10 cm to the east of the wire
option_b: 10 cm to the west of the wire
option_c: 5 cm to the west of the wire
option_d: 10 cm to the north of the wire
correct_answer_text: 10 cm to the west of the wire
solution: For cancellation the wire must produce a field of 4 x 10^-5 T pointing south. Equating magnitudes, 2 x 10^-7 x 20 / r = 4 x 10^-5, so r = 4 x 10^-6 / 4 x 10^-5 = 0.10 m = 10 cm. For an upward current, the circular field lines run anticlockwise when seen from above, so the field points south only on the western side of the wire. Hence the point is 10 cm to the west.
formula_principle: mu_0 I / (2 pi r) = B_H, with the wire field directed opposite to B_H
common_misconception: Getting the magnitude right but the side wrong is very common; the direction must be fixed by the right hand thumb rule.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
subtopic: Field at the apex of a triangle
concept_tested: Vector addition of fields at 120 degrees
stem: Two long parallel wires are perpendicular to the plane of the paper and 10 cm apart. Each carries 10 A, one directed out of the paper and the other into the paper. Find the magnitude of the resultant magnetic field at a point P which is 10 cm from each wire. Take mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1.
solution: Each wire is 0.10 m from P, so each contributes 2 x 10^-7 x 10 / 0.10 = 2 x 10^-5 T. Each field is perpendicular to the line joining that wire to P. Since the wires and P form an equilateral triangle and the currents are oppositely directed, the two field vectors turn out to be inclined at 120 degrees to each other. For two equal vectors of magnitude B at 120 degrees, the resultant magnitude is B square root of (1 + 1 + 2 cos 120) = B. Hence the resultant is 2 x 10^-5 T, directed perpendicular to the line joining the two wires.
formula_principle: B = mu_0 I / (2 pi r) for each wire, resultant of two equal vectors at 120 degrees is equal to either one
common_misconception: Students rarely check the actual angle between the two tangential field vectors and simply add or subtract the magnitudes.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Standard expression for a coil of N turns
stem: The magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil of N turns, radius R, carrying a current I is
solution: Every element of the loop is at the same distance R from the centre and every element makes an angle of 90 degrees with the line to the centre, so the contributions add directly to give B = mu_0 I / (2 R) for one turn, and N times this for N turns.
formula_principle: B = mu_0 N I / (2 R)
common_misconception: The factor 2 pi from the straight wire result is frequently carried over to the loop, where it does not belong.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Direct substitution for a single turn
stem: A circular loop of radius 5 cm carries a current of 5 A. Find the magnetic field at its centre. Take mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1.
formula_principle: B = mu_0 I / (2 R)
common_misconception: Unlike the straight wire case, pi does not cancel here, so an answer free of pi signals that the wrong formula has been used.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Right hand rule for a current loop
stem: A circular loop lies in the plane of the paper and carries a current in the anticlockwise sense as seen by the reader. At the centre of the loop the magnetic field is directed
option_a: out of the plane of the paper, towards the reader
option_b: into the plane of the paper
option_c: along the circumference in the anticlockwise sense
correct_answer_text: out of the plane of the paper, towards the reader
solution: Curl the fingers of the right hand along the anticlockwise current; the extended thumb then points out of the paper. Hence the field at the centre, and everywhere on the axis, is directed out of the plane of the loop towards the reader. That face of the loop behaves as a north pole.
formula_principle: Right hand rule: fingers along the current, thumb gives the direction of B on the axis
common_misconception: Learners often use the left hand, which belongs to the force rule, and obtain the opposite direction.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Proportionality of B to N
stem: A circular coil of 1 turn and radius R carrying a current I produces a field B at its centre. If the coil is replaced by one of 50 turns of the same radius carrying the same current, the field at the centre becomes
solution: With the radius and current unchanged, B is directly proportional to N. Increasing N from 1 to 50 therefore increases the field fifty fold, giving 50 B.
formula_principle: B = mu_0 N I / (2 R)
common_misconception: The N squared dependence, which arises only when a wire of fixed length is rewound into more turns of smaller radius, is wrongly used here where the radius stays the same.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Inverse dependence of B on R at the centre
stem: Two circular loops carry the same current. The radius of the second loop is twice that of the first. The magnetic field at the centre of the second loop, compared with that at the centre of the first, is
solution: For a single turn the field at the centre varies inversely as the first power of the radius. Doubling R therefore halves the field at the centre.
formula_principle: B = mu_0 I / (2 R), so B proportional to 1 / R
common_misconception: The inverse square habit from electrostatics is often applied here, giving one quarter instead of one half.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Field at the centre of a half turn
stem: A wire bent in the form of a semicircle of radius 10 cm carries a current of 4 A. Find the magnetic field at the centre of the semicircle, ignoring the straight lead wires. Take mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1.
solution: A semicircle is half of a full turn, so the field at the centre is half of mu_0 I / (2 R), that is mu_0 I / (4 R). Substituting, B = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 4) / (4 x 0.10) = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 4) / 0.40 = 4 pi x 10^-6 T, about 1.26 x 10^-5 T.
formula_principle: B = mu_0 I / (4 R) for a semicircular arc
common_misconception: The straight lead wires, if they lie along the diameter produced, contribute nothing at the centre, which students often forget to justify.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Fraction of the full loop field
stem: A wire in the shape of a circular arc of radius R subtending an angle of 60 degrees at its centre carries a current I. The magnetic field at the centre due to this arc is
solution: An arc of 60 degrees is one sixth of a full circle, so it contributes one sixth of the full loop field: B = (1 / 6) x mu_0 I / (2 R) = mu_0 I / (12 R).
formula_principle: B = (theta / 2 pi) x mu_0 I / (2 R), with theta in radian
common_misconception: The fraction must be applied to the complete loop result mu_0 I / (2 R), not to mu_0 I / R.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Ratio of axial field to centre field at x equal to R
stem: For a circular current loop of radius R, the ratio of the magnetic field at an axial point distant R from the centre to the field at the centre itself is
solution: Dividing, B_axis / B_centre = R^3 / (R^2 + x^2)^(3/2). With x = R this becomes R^3 / (2 R^2)^(3/2) = R^3 / (2^(3/2) R^3) = 1 / (2 square root of 2), which is about 0.354.
formula_principle: B_axis = mu_0 I R^2 / (2 (R^2 + x^2)^(3/2)); B_centre = mu_0 I / (2 R)
common_misconception: The three halves power is often reduced to a first power or to a cube during simplification.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Dipole behaviour of a current loop at large distances
stem: At an axial point very far from a circular current loop, so that the distance x is much greater than the radius R, the magnetic field varies as
solution: When x is much greater than R, the term R^2 in the bracket may be neglected, giving B = mu_0 I R^2 / (2 x^3). Writing the magnetic moment as m = I pi R^2, this becomes B = mu_0 x 2 m / (4 pi x^3), the standard axial field of a magnetic dipole, which falls off as the cube of the distance.
formula_principle: B_axis = mu_0 I R^2 / (2 (R^2 + x^2)^(3/2)) tends to mu_0 I R^2 / (2 x^3) when x is much greater than R
common_misconception: Students expect an inverse square law because the loop looks like a point source from far away, but a dipole field always falls as the inverse cube.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Superposition at a common centre
stem: Two concentric circular loops of radii R and 2 R lie in the same plane and carry equal currents I in opposite senses. The magnitude of the resultant magnetic field at their common centre is
solution: The inner loop gives mu_0 I / (2 R) and the outer loop gives mu_0 I / (2 x 2 R) = mu_0 I / (4 R). Because the currents circulate in opposite senses, the two axial fields are oppositely directed, so the resultant is mu_0 I / (2 R) minus mu_0 I / (4 R) = mu_0 I / (4 R), in the sense of the inner loop.
formula_principle: B = mu_0 I / (2 R) for each loop, combined with due regard to sense
common_misconception: Equal currents do not mean equal fields; the smaller loop always produces the stronger field at the common centre.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Numerical for a coil of many turns
stem: A circular coil of 100 turns has a radius of 10 cm and carries a current of 1 A. Find the magnetic field at its centre. Take mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1.
formula_principle: B = mu_0 N I / (2 R)
common_misconception: The number of turns is often dropped because the formula for a single loop is memorised without N.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
subtopic: Rewinding a fixed length of wire
concept_tested: Dependence of the centre field on N squared
stem: A wire of a certain length carrying a current I is first bent into a single circular turn and then rewound into two turns of half the original radius, the current remaining the same. The magnetic field at the centre in the second case, compared with the first, is
solution: For one turn of radius R the field is mu_0 I / (2 R). For two turns each of radius R / 2 the field is mu_0 x 2 x I / (2 x R / 2) = 2 mu_0 I / R. Dividing, the second field is 4 times the first. In general, rewinding a fixed length into N turns multiplies the centre field by N^2.
formula_principle: B = mu_0 N I / (2 R) with R = L / (2 pi N) for a wire of fixed length L
common_misconception: Only the increase in the number of turns is usually counted; the accompanying reduction in radius contributes an equal factor.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Pole character of the two faces of a loop
stem: Which statement about a plane circular current loop is correct?
option_a: The face of the loop from which the current appears anticlockwise behaves as a north pole
option_b: The face of the loop from which the current appears anticlockwise behaves as a south pole
option_c: Both faces of the loop behave as north poles
option_d: A current loop has no magnetic dipole character because it carries no permanent magnet
correct_answer_text: The face of the loop from which the current appears anticlockwise behaves as a north pole
solution: Curling the right hand fingers along the current, the thumb points out of the face from which the current looks anticlockwise. The field emerges from that face, so it acts as the north pole, while the other face, where the current looks clockwise, acts as the south pole.
formula_principle: Magnetic moment m = I A, directed along the outward normal given by the right hand rule
common_misconception: The two faces are often thought to be identical because the loop is symmetric, but the sense of the current breaks the symmetry.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Adding the contributions of concentric semicircles
stem: A conductor consists of two concentric semicircular arcs of radii 10 cm and 20 cm lying in the same plane and joined by short radial pieces, and it carries a current of 10 A. Both arcs are traversed in the same sense. Find the magnetic field at the common centre. Ignore the radial pieces. Take mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1.
solution: The inner arc gives (4 pi x 10^-7 x 10) / (4 x 0.10) = 10 pi x 10^-6 T. The outer arc gives (4 pi x 10^-7 x 10) / (4 x 0.20) = 5 pi x 10^-6 T. Both arcs are traversed in the same sense, so their axial fields point the same way and add to 15 pi x 10^-6 T, that is about 4.7 x 10^-5 T. The radial pieces pass through the centre line and contribute nothing.
formula_principle: B = mu_0 I / (4 R) for each semicircular arc
common_misconception: The radial connecting pieces are sometimes credited with a field, but every element of a radial piece is collinear with the line to the centre, so its contribution vanishes.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
subtopic: Axial field from the centre field
concept_tested: Using the three halves power relation
stem: The magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil of radius 3 cm is 125 x 10^-6 T. The magnetic field at a point on its axis, 4 cm from the centre, is
solution: Here square root of (3^2 + 4^2) = 5 cm, so the ratio is 3^3 / 5^3 = 27 / 125. Hence B_axis = 125 x 10^-6 x 27 / 125 = 27 x 10^-6 T.
formula_principle: B_axis / B_centre = R^3 / (R^2 + x^2)^(3/2)
common_misconception: Reducing the three halves power to a first power or to a simple square root is the standard error in axial field problems.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
subtopic: Coil made from a given length of wire
concept_tested: Expressing the centre field in terms of wire length
stem: A wire of total length L is wound into a flat circular coil of N turns and carries a current I. The magnetic field at the centre of the coil is
solution: The total wire length gives N x 2 pi R = L, so R = L / (2 pi N). Substituting, B = mu_0 N I / (2 R) = mu_0 N I x 2 pi N / (2 L) = pi mu_0 N^2 I / L. The field at the centre therefore grows as the square of the number of turns for a fixed length of wire.
formula_principle: B = mu_0 N I / (2 R) with 2 pi R N = L
common_misconception: Forgetting that the radius itself shrinks as N grows leads to a result proportional to N instead of N^2.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
subtopic: Square loop compared with circular loop
concept_tested: Comparing centre fields for equal wire lengths
stem: The same length of wire carrying the same current is bent once into a circle and once into a square. The ratio of the magnetic field at the centre of the square to that at the centre of the circle is
option_c: 8 square root of 2 : pi^2, that is about 1.15 : 1
correct_answer_text: 8 square root of 2 : pi^2, that is about 1.15 : 1
solution: For the circle, 2 pi R = L gives R = L / (2 pi), so B_circle = mu_0 I / (2 R) = pi mu_0 I / L. For the square, 4 a = L gives a = L / 4. Each side is a finite wire whose perpendicular distance from the centre is a / 2, and each side subtends 45 degrees on either side of that perpendicular. One side therefore gives (mu_0 I / (4 pi x a / 2)) x (sin 45 + sin 45) = (mu_0 I / (2 pi a)) x square root of 2. Four sides give B_square = 2 square root of 2 mu_0 I / (pi a) = 8 square root of 2 mu_0 I / (pi L). Dividing, B_square / B_circle = 8 square root of 2 / pi^2 = 11.31 / 9.87 = 1.15. The square gives the slightly stronger central field because parts of it lie closer to the centre.
formula_principle: Circle: B = mu_0 I / (2 R) with 2 pi R = L. Square: B = 4 x (mu_0 I / (4 pi (a / 2))) x 2 sin 45 with 4 a = L
common_misconception: Students assume the shape does not matter once the length and current are fixed, but the field at the centre depends strongly on how close the wire comes to that point.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Vector addition of two perpendicular axial fields
stem: Two circular loops, of radii 10 cm and 5 cm, have a common centre but lie in mutually perpendicular planes. Each carries a current of 10 A. Find the magnitude of the resultant magnetic field at the common centre. Take mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1.
solution: The 10 cm loop gives (4 pi x 10^-7 x 10) / (2 x 0.10) = 2 pi x 10^-5 T, about 6.28 x 10^-5 T. The 5 cm loop gives (4 pi x 10^-7 x 10) / (2 x 0.05) = 4 pi x 10^-5 T, about 1.26 x 10^-4 T. Since the planes are perpendicular, the two axial fields are perpendicular, so the resultant is 2 pi x 10^-5 x square root of (1 + 4) = 2 pi square root of 5 x 10^-5 T, which is about 1.4 x 10^-4 T.
formula_principle: B = mu_0 I / (2 R) for each loop; resultant of perpendicular vectors is the square root of the sum of squares
common_misconception: Perpendicular fields must be combined by the square root of the sum of squares, not by simple addition or subtraction.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Line integral of B around a closed path
stem: Ampere's circuital law states that the line integral of the magnetic field taken around any closed path is equal to
option_a: mu_0 times the sum of all currents in the neighbourhood
option_b: mu_0 times the net current passing through the area bounded by that path
option_c: mu_0 times the net current divided by 2 pi r
option_d: mu_0 times the total charge enclosed by the path
correct_answer_text: mu_0 times the net current passing through the area bounded by that path
solution: Ampere's law relates the circulation of B around a closed path to the net current threading that path. Currents lying outside the path contribute nothing to the integral, although they do contribute to the field at individual points on the path.
formula_principle: The line integral of B dot dl around a closed path equals mu_0 x I_enclosed
common_misconception: Students include every nearby current in the enclosed current, forgetting that only the currents linking the loop matter.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Why a circle is chosen for a straight wire
stem: In applying Ampere's circuital law to a long straight current carrying wire, a circle centred on the wire and lying in a plane perpendicular to it is chosen as the closed path because
option_a: on such a circle B is zero everywhere
option_b: on such a circle B is everywhere perpendicular to the path
option_c: such a circle is the only closed path for which Ampere's law is valid
option_d: on such a circle the magnitude of B is constant and B is everywhere tangential to the path
correct_answer_text: on such a circle the magnitude of B is constant and B is everywhere tangential to the path
solution: Symmetry ensures that B has the same magnitude at every point of the circle and is directed along the tangent, so B dot dl reduces to B dl and the integral becomes B x 2 pi r. This makes it possible to solve for B.
formula_principle: The line integral of B dot dl = B x (2 pi r) when B is constant and tangential
common_misconception: The law itself is valid for any closed path, but it becomes useful only for paths chosen to exploit the symmetry of the problem.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Deriving the straight wire field
stem: Applying Ampere's circuital law to a circular path of radius r around a long straight wire carrying current I gives
option_a: B x 2 pi r^2 = mu_0 I
option_b: B x 2 pi r = mu_0 I, so that B = mu_0 I / (2 pi r)
option_c: B x pi r^2 = mu_0 I
option_d: B x 2 pi r = mu_0 I / 2
correct_answer_text: B x 2 pi r = mu_0 I, so that B = mu_0 I / (2 pi r)
solution: Since B is constant and tangential on the circle, the line integral equals B multiplied by the circumference 2 pi r. Equating this to mu_0 I gives B = mu_0 I / (2 pi r).
formula_principle: The line integral of B dot dl = B x 2 pi r = mu_0 I
common_misconception: The circumference, not the area, appears in a line integral; substituting pi r^2 is a frequent slip.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Effect of an external current on the line integral
stem: A closed Amperian loop is drawn in a region where a current carrying wire passes entirely outside the loop. For this loop,
option_a: both the line integral and the field B are zero at every point of the loop
option_b: the line integral equals mu_0 times that external current
option_c: the line integral is undefined because Ampere's law cannot be applied when a current lies outside
option_d: the line integral of B dot dl is zero, although B is not zero at points on the loop
correct_answer_text: the line integral of B dot dl is zero, although B is not zero at points on the loop
solution: The external current produces a magnetic field at every point of the loop, so B is not zero there. However, its circulation around a loop that it does not thread is zero, so the contribution of this current to the line integral vanishes.
formula_principle: The line integral of B dot dl = mu_0 x I_enclosed
common_misconception: A zero line integral is wrongly read as a zero field; the law constrains only the circulation, not the pointwise value.

chapter_name: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
concept_tested: Net enclosed current from several currents
