stem: According to Faraday's second law of electromagnetic induction, the magnitude of the induced emf in a circuit is equal to
option_a: the magnetic flux linked with the circuit
option_b: the rate of change of the current in the circuit
option_c: the product of the magnetic flux and the time for which it acts
option_d: the rate of change of magnetic flux linked with the circuit
correct_answer_text: the rate of change of magnetic flux linked with the circuit
solution: Faraday's second law states that the magnitude of the induced emf equals the time rate of change of the flux linkage, e = N d(phi)/dt in magnitude.
formula_principle: e = -N d(phi)/dt
common_misconception: Thinking that a large steady flux produces a large emf, when only a changing flux does.

subtopic: Induced emf in a multi turn coil
concept_tested: e = N d(phi)/dt applied directly
stem: The flux through each turn of a 100 turn coil changes at a steady rate of 0.02 Wb s^-1. The magnitude of the induced emf is
solution: e = N x d(phi)/dt = 100 x 0.02 = 2 V.
formula_principle: e = N d(phi)/dt
common_misconception: Omitting the number of turns when the flux is quoted per turn.

concept_tested: Physical significance of the minus sign in Faraday's law
stem: The negative sign in the relation e = -N d(phi)/dt indicates that
option_a: the induced emf is always negative in value
option_b: the induced emf opposes the change in flux that produces it, which follows from conservation of energy
option_c: the magnetic flux always decreases with time
option_d: energy is lost during the process of induction
correct_answer_text: the induced emf opposes the change in flux that produces it, which follows from conservation of energy
solution: The minus sign is the mathematical statement of Lenz's law. The induced emf drives a current whose effect opposes the change in flux, so that work must be done to maintain the change and energy is conserved.
formula_principle: e = -N d(phi)/dt expresses Lenz's law
common_misconception: Reading the minus sign as meaning the emf has a negative numerical value.

concept_tested: Average emf from a finite flux change
stem: The magnetic flux through a single turn coil changes from 0.06 Wb to 0.02 Wb in 0.2 s. The average induced emf is
formula_principle: e_average = delta(phi)/delta(t)
common_misconception: Multiplying by the time interval instead of dividing by it.

concept_tested: Weber per second is the volt
stem: One weber per second is equivalent to
solution: Faraday's law equates emf to the rate of change of flux, so the unit weber per second must be identical with the unit volt.
formula_principle: e = d(phi)/dt so 1 Wb s^-1 = 1 V
common_misconception: Dividing flux by area or by current out of habit instead of by time.

subtopic: Induced emf from a flux change
concept_tested: Average emf in a coil of many turns
stem: The flux through each turn of a coil of 200 turns falls from 4 x 10^-3 Wb to 1 x 10^-3 Wb in 0.1 s. The average induced emf is
solution: delta(phi) per turn = 4 x 10^-3 minus 1 x 10^-3 = 3 x 10^-3 Wb. Then e = 200 x 3 x 10^-3/0.1 = 200 x 0.03 = 6 V.
formula_principle: e = N delta(phi)/delta(t)
common_misconception: Adding the initial and final flux values instead of subtracting them.

concept_tested: q = N delta(phi)/R
stem: A coil of 50 turns and total circuit resistance 10 ohm experiences a flux change of 2 x 10^-3 Wb per turn. The charge that circulates in the circuit is
formula_principle: q = N delta(phi)/R
common_misconception: Multiplying by the resistance instead of dividing, which would make a better conductor carry less charge.

concept_tested: Induced charge is independent of the time taken
stem: A magnet is brought up to a closed coil, first quickly and then slowly, producing the same total flux change each time. Compared with the slow motion, the fast motion produces
option_a: a larger induced emf but the same total induced charge
option_b: a larger induced emf and a larger total induced charge
option_c: the same induced emf and the same total induced charge
option_d: a smaller induced emf but a larger total induced charge
correct_answer_text: a larger induced emf but the same total induced charge
solution: The emf is inversely proportional to the time taken, so faster motion gives a larger emf. The charge is q = integral of i dt = N delta(phi)/R, in which the time interval cancels, so the same flux change always circulates the same charge.
formula_principle: e = N delta(phi)/delta(t) but q = N delta(phi)/R
common_misconception: Believing that a bigger deflection of the galvanometer means more charge has flowed.

subtopic: Flux given as a function of time
concept_tested: Instantaneous emf by differentiation
stem: The magnetic flux linked with a single turn coil varies as phi = (3 t^2 + 4 t + 9) Wb, where t is in second. The magnitude of the induced emf at t = 2 s is
solution: d(phi)/dt = 6 t + 4. At t = 2 s this is 6 x 2 + 4 = 16, so the induced emf has magnitude 16 V.
formula_principle: e = d(phi)/dt
common_misconception: Reporting the value of the flux at the given instant instead of its rate of change.

concept_tested: Induced current from a changing field
stem: A coil of 500 turns and area 1 x 10^-2 m^2 has its plane perpendicular to a magnetic field that rises steadily from 0.2 T to 0.6 T in 0.4 s. The resistance of the circuit is 10 ohm. The induced current is
formula_principle: e = N A dB/dt and i = e/R
common_misconception: Stopping at the emf and quoting it as the current.

concept_tested: Duration of the induced emf
stem: Faraday's first law of electromagnetic induction tells us that an induced emf
option_a: exists so long as the circuit is placed in a magnetic field
option_b: exists only if the circuit is closed
option_c: continues for some time after the flux stops changing
option_d: exists only so long as the flux linked with the circuit is changing
correct_answer_text: exists only so long as the flux linked with the circuit is changing
solution: The first law states that whenever the magnetic flux linked with a circuit changes, an emf is induced in it, and this emf lasts only as long as the change in flux continues.
formula_principle: An emf is induced whenever the flux linked with a circuit changes, and it lasts only while the change lasts
common_misconception: Assuming a closed circuit is necessary for an emf; it is necessary only for a current.

concept_tested: Relative motion between magnet and coil
stem: A bar magnet is held stationary inside a closed coil connected to a galvanometer. The galvanometer shows
option_a: a steady deflection, because the flux linked with the coil is large
option_b: no deflection, because the flux linked with the coil is not changing
option_c: a deflection that slowly dies away
option_d: an oscillating deflection at the natural frequency of the coil
correct_answer_text: no deflection, because the flux linked with the coil is not changing
solution: With the magnet at rest the flux linked with the coil is constant in time, so d(phi)/dt = 0 and no emf and no current are produced.
formula_principle: e = -N d(phi)/dt is zero when phi is constant
common_misconception: Believing that the mere presence of a magnet inside a coil drives a current.

concept_tested: Average emf when a coil is turned through 180 degrees
stem: A coil of 40 turns and area 0.05 m^2 is held with its plane perpendicular to a uniform field of 0.2 T. It is turned through 180 degrees about a diameter in 0.1 s. The average induced emf is
solution: Flux per turn changes from +B A = 0.2 x 0.05 = 0.01 Wb to -0.01 Wb, so delta(phi) = 0.02 Wb. Then e = 40 x 0.02/0.1 = 8 V.
formula_principle: delta(phi) = 2 B A for a 180 degree turn; e = N delta(phi)/delta(t)
common_misconception: Forgetting the factor of two that arises because the flux reverses direction, not merely vanishes.

concept_tested: Joule heating from an induced current
stem: A coil of 100 turns, area 0.05 m^2 and total resistance 20 ohm has its plane perpendicular to a field which falls steadily from 0.5 T to 0.1 T in 0.5 s. The heat produced in the coil during this interval is
formula_principle: e = N A dB/dt, i = e/R, H = i^2 R t
common_misconception: Quoting the dissipated power instead of the heat produced over the stated interval.

concept_tested: Charge circulated when a coil is turned through 90 degrees
stem: A coil of 100 turns and area 0.01 m^2 lies with its plane perpendicular to a field of 0.5 T. The total resistance of the circuit is 5 ohm. The coil is turned through 90 degrees. The charge that circulates is
solution: delta(phi) per turn = B A cos 0 minus B A cos 90 = 0.5 x 0.01 = 5 x 10^-3 Wb. Then q = 100 x 5 x 10^-3/5 = 0.5/5 = 0.1 C.
formula_principle: q = N delta(phi)/R with delta(phi) = B A for a 90 degree turn
common_misconception: Applying the 180 degree factor of two to a 90 degree rotation.

concept_tested: Setting the derivative of the flux to zero
stem: The flux linked with a single turn coil varies as phi = (t^2 - 8 t + 12) Wb, with t in second. The induced emf is zero at
solution: d(phi)/dt = 2 t - 8. Setting 2 t - 8 = 0 gives t = 4 s, the instant at which the flux passes through its minimum value and the induced emf vanishes.
formula_principle: e = d(phi)/dt; e = 0 when d(phi)/dt = 0
common_misconception: Setting the flux itself to zero instead of setting its time derivative to zero.

concept_tested: Finding B from the induced charge
stem: A search coil of 100 turns and area 2 x 10^-3 m^2 is connected to a circuit of total resistance 10 ohm. When the coil is quickly pulled out of a uniform field with its plane initially perpendicular to the field, a charge of 4 x 10^-4 C flows. The magnetic field is
formula_principle: q = N B A/R, so B = q R/(N A)
common_misconception: Dividing by the resistance instead of multiplying, because the charge formula has R in the denominator.

subtopic: Effect of the material of the coil
concept_tested: emf depends on flux change, current depends on resistance
stem: Two identical coils, one of copper and one of nichrome of much higher resistivity, are subjected to exactly the same rate of change of magnetic flux. Then
option_a: both the induced emf and the induced current are larger in the copper coil
option_b: the induced emf is larger in the nichrome coil and the current is larger in the copper coil
option_c: the induced emf is the same in both, while the induced current is larger in the copper coil
option_d: the induced emf and the induced current are the same in both
correct_answer_text: the induced emf is the same in both, while the induced current is larger in the copper coil
solution: The induced emf depends only on the number of turns and the rate of change of flux, so it is identical for the two coils. The current is e/R, and since copper has the smaller resistance it carries the larger current.
formula_principle: e = N d(phi)/dt is material independent; i = e/R
common_misconception: Believing that a good conductor develops a larger induced emf.

concept_tested: Heat from a uniformly changing field
stem: A coil of 1000 turns and area 5 x 10^-3 m^2 is placed with its plane perpendicular to a field that falls uniformly from 0.8 T to 0.2 T in 0.3 s. The total resistance of the circuit is 100 ohm. The heat generated during this interval is
solution: dB/dt = 0.6/0.3 = 2 T s^-1, so e = 1000 x 5 x 10^-3 x 2 = 10 V. The power is e^2/R = 100/100 = 1 W, and over 0.3 s the heat is 1 x 0.3 = 0.3 J.
formula_principle: e = N A dB/dt and H = e^2 t/R
common_misconception: Confusing the rate of dissipation of energy with the total energy dissipated.

concept_tested: Peak emf from a sinusoidal flux
stem: The flux linked with each turn of a 200 turn coil varies as phi = 0.02 sin(100 t) Wb, with t in second. The peak value of the induced emf is
solution: d(phi)/dt = 0.02 x 100 x cos(100 t), whose peak value is 2 Wb s^-1. Multiplying by the 200 turns gives a peak emf of 200 x 2 = 400 V.
formula_principle: e = -N d(phi)/dt; for phi = phi_0 sin(omega t) the peak emf is N phi_0 omega
common_misconception: Forgetting that differentiating sin(omega t) brings down a factor of omega.

concept_tested: Direction of the induced current
stem: Lenz's law states that the direction of the induced current is such that it
option_a: always flows in the clockwise sense when seen from the magnet
option_b: opposes the change in magnetic flux that produces it
option_c: assists the change in magnetic flux that produces it
option_d: is always in the same direction as the applied magnetic field
correct_answer_text: opposes the change in magnetic flux that produces it
solution: The induced current always flows so that its own magnetic effect opposes the change in flux that caused it. This is expressed by the minus sign in e = -N d(phi)/dt.
formula_principle: Lenz's law: the induced effect opposes its cause
common_misconception: Treating the sense of the induced current as fixed rather than determined by the cause.

concept_tested: Lenz's law and conservation of energy
stem: Lenz's law is a direct consequence of the law of conservation of
solution: If the induced current aided the change, the change would grow on its own and energy would appear from nowhere. Opposition ensures that work must be done by an external agent, and that work appears as electrical and then thermal energy.
formula_principle: Work done against the opposing force appears as electrical energy
common_misconception: Associating the minus sign with conservation of charge instead of energy.

concept_tested: Sense of the induced current for an approaching north pole
stem: The north pole of a bar magnet is moved towards one face of a closed circular coil. As seen from the magnet, the induced current in that face flows
option_a: anticlockwise, so that the near face behaves as a north pole
option_b: clockwise, so that the near face behaves as a south pole
option_c: anticlockwise, so that the near face behaves as a south pole
option_d: in no direction, since the magnet does not touch the coil
correct_answer_text: anticlockwise, so that the near face behaves as a north pole
solution: The flux towards the coil increases, so the coil opposes the approach by presenting a north pole to the magnet. A face behaves as a north pole when the current in it runs anticlockwise as seen from the side facing the magnet.
formula_principle: Lenz's law with the right hand rule for the face of a current loop
common_misconception: Choosing the sense that attracts the magnet, which would violate conservation of energy.

concept_tested: Sense of the induced current for a receding north pole
stem: The north pole of a bar magnet is pulled away from a closed coil. The coil then
option_a: repels the magnet, its near face behaving as a north pole
option_b: neither attracts nor repels the magnet
option_c: attracts the magnet, its near face behaving as a north pole
option_d: attracts the magnet, its near face behaving as a south pole
correct_answer_text: attracts the magnet, its near face behaving as a south pole
solution: As the magnet recedes the flux linked with the coil decreases, so the induced current acts to maintain it by attracting the magnet. The near face therefore behaves as a south pole for the receding north pole.
formula_principle: Lenz's law: the induced effect opposes the relative motion
common_misconception: Applying the repulsion rule to both approach and recession.

concept_tested: Source of the electrical energy in induction
stem: When a magnet is pushed towards a closed coil against the opposing magnetic force, the electrical energy that appears in the coil comes from
option_a: the magnetic energy stored permanently in the bar magnet
option_b: the mechanical work done by the agent pushing the magnet
option_c: the thermal energy of the surrounding air
option_d: the electric charges already resident in the coil
correct_answer_text: the mechanical work done by the agent pushing the magnet
solution: The coil opposes the approach, so the agent must do work against that opposition. This mechanical work is converted into electrical energy in the coil and finally into heat, keeping the total energy constant.
formula_principle: Work done against the induced opposition equals the electrical energy developed
common_misconception: Believing that induction extracts energy from the magnet itself.

concept_tested: Retardation of a falling magnet
stem: A small bar magnet is dropped from rest along the axis of a fixed horizontal copper ring, passing through it. During the fall the acceleration of the magnet near the ring is
option_a: greater than g, because the induced current pulls the magnet towards the ring
option_b: exactly g, because the ring carries no battery
option_c: less than g, because the induced current in the ring opposes the relative motion
option_d: exactly g, because copper is a non magnetic material
correct_answer_text: less than g, because the induced current in the ring opposes the relative motion
solution: The moving magnet changes the flux through the ring, so an induced current appears. By Lenz's law this current opposes the relative motion, exerting an upward force on the descending magnet. The net downward force is less than the weight, so the acceleration is less than g.
formula_principle: Lenz's law with e = -N d(phi)/dt and the retarding magnetic force
common_misconception: Assuming a non ferromagnetic ring cannot influence a magnet.

concept_tested: Why the induced effect must oppose its cause
stem: Suppose the induced current in a coil flowed in the sense opposite to that required by Lenz's law. The immediate consequence would be that
option_a: the motion causing the flux change would be assisted and energy would be produced from nothing
option_b: the induced emf would become infinite in a finite time
option_c: no current would flow at all in the coil
option_d: the coil would gain charge continuously
correct_answer_text: the motion causing the flux change would be assisted and energy would be produced from nothing
solution: If the induced current aided the change, the magnet would be pulled in faster, increasing the flux change and the current further. Both kinetic energy and electrical energy would grow with no external supply, which is impossible.
formula_principle: Lenz's law is required by conservation of energy
common_misconception: Thinking the direction rule is an arbitrary convention rather than a requirement of energy conservation.

concept_tested: Force between a coil and a nearby ring at switch on
stem: A closed metal ring is placed coaxially near a coil. At the instant the current in the coil is switched on and is rising, the ring
option_a: is attracted to the coil, its induced current being in the same sense as the coil current
option_b: is repelled from the coil, its induced current being in the same sense as the coil current
option_c: is repelled from the coil, its induced current being opposite in sense to the coil current
option_d: stays at rest, because the ring carries no source of emf
correct_answer_text: is repelled from the coil, its induced current being opposite in sense to the coil current
solution: While the coil current rises, the flux through the ring rises. The ring opposes this by driving a current in the opposite sense. Antiparallel currents repel, so the ring is pushed away from the coil.
formula_principle: Lenz's law; antiparallel currents repel
common_misconception: Assuming that the induced current always mirrors the source current.

concept_tested: Current sense and force on a loop pulled out of a field
stem: A rectangular conducting loop is pulled to the right, out of a region in which a uniform magnetic field points into the plane of the page. The induced current and the magnetic force on the loop are
option_a: anticlockwise, with the force on the loop directed to the left
option_b: clockwise, with the force on the loop directed to the left
option_c: clockwise, with the force on the loop directed to the right
option_d: anticlockwise, with the force on the loop directed to the right
correct_answer_text: clockwise, with the force on the loop directed to the left
solution: The into the page flux through the loop is falling, so the induced current flows clockwise to maintain that flux. The side still inside the field carries this current, and the force B i l on it points to the left, opposing the pulling motion.
formula_principle: Lenz's law and F = B i l on the current carrying side inside the field
common_misconception: Choosing the sense of current that produces a forward force, which would make the loop accelerate on its own.

concept_tested: emf without current
stem: The same changing magnetic flux threads two identical loops, one closed and one having a small gap cut in it. Then
option_a: an emf is induced only in the closed loop
option_b: a current flows in both loops but the emf appears only in the closed loop
option_c: an emf is induced in both loops but a current flows only in the closed loop
option_d: neither an emf nor a current appears in the loop with the gap
correct_answer_text: an emf is induced in both loops but a current flows only in the closed loop
solution: Faraday's law gives the same induced emf in both loops, since it depends only on the rate of change of flux. A steady current needs a complete conducting path, so only the closed loop carries a current, while a potential difference appears across the gap of the other.
formula_principle: e = -N d(phi)/dt holds for any loop; i = e/R needs a closed path
common_misconception: Assuming no emf exists unless a current can flow.

concept_tested: Sense of the induced current when the source current is cut
stem: A steady current flows in coil P placed close to a closed coil Q. When the switch in the circuit of P is opened, the current induced in Q, during the brief interval while the current in P falls to zero,
option_a: flows in the sense opposite to that of the current that was flowing in P
option_b: flows in the same sense as the current that was flowing in P
option_c: is zero, because coil P no longer carries any current
option_d: reverses its direction twice before dying away
correct_answer_text: flows in the same sense as the current that was flowing in P
solution: As the current in P collapses, the flux through Q falls. Coil Q opposes this fall by trying to maintain the flux, which requires a current in the same sense as the original current in P.
formula_principle: Lenz's law applied to a decreasing flux
common_misconception: Applying the switch on rule, in which the induced current opposes the source current, to the switch off case as well.

concept_tested: Division of labour between Faraday and Lenz
stem: For a coil in a changing magnetic field, the magnitude of the induced emf is given by Faraday's law while its direction is given by
solution: Faraday's laws fix how large the induced emf is, namely N times the rate of change of flux. Lenz's law fixes its sense, requiring the induced effect to oppose its cause; together they are written as e = -N d(phi)/dt.
formula_principle: e = -N d(phi)/dt; the magnitude comes from Faraday, the minus sign from Lenz
common_misconception: Attributing the direction rule to Ampere's law because both concern currents and magnetic fields.

concept_tested: Energy balance for a loop pulled at constant velocity
stem: A conducting loop of resistance R is pulled at constant velocity out of a region of uniform magnetic field. The work done by the external agent is
option_a: equal to the heat dissipated in the loop, since the kinetic energy does not change
option_b: equal to the gain in kinetic energy of the loop
option_c: zero, because the magnetic force does no net work on the charges
option_d: stored as magnetic energy and recovered when the loop re enters the field
correct_answer_text: equal to the heat dissipated in the loop, since the kinetic energy does not change
solution: At constant velocity the applied force exactly balances the retarding magnetic force B i l. The power delivered by the agent is F v, and this equals e^2/R, the rate at which heat is produced in the loop. With no change in kinetic energy, all the work done appears as heat.
formula_principle: W_external = heat dissipated when the kinetic energy is constant
common_misconception: Assuming that because magnetic forces do no work, no work is needed to pull the loop out.

concept_tested: Repulsion of a ring at switch on
stem: A closed aluminium ring rests loosely around the top of a vertical solenoid with an iron core. When the solenoid is connected to a source, the ring flies upward because
option_a: the ring is heated by the current and rises with the hot air
option_b: the induced current in the ring is opposite in sense to the solenoid current, so the two repel each other
option_c: the induced current in the ring is in the same sense as the solenoid current, so the two repel each other
option_d: the iron core magnetises the aluminium ring and repels it
correct_answer_text: the induced current in the ring is opposite in sense to the solenoid current, so the two repel each other
solution: At switch on, the flux through the ring rises sharply. The ring opposes the rise by carrying a current in the opposite sense to that in the solenoid. Two antiparallel currents repel, and the repulsive force exceeds the weight of the light ring, so it jumps.
formula_principle: Lenz's law; antiparallel currents repel
common_misconception: Attributing the jump to heating or to magnetisation of the aluminium.

subtopic: Loop moving inside a uniform field
concept_tested: No emf when the flux is unchanged
stem: A square conducting loop moves with constant velocity entirely within a large region of uniform magnetic field perpendicular to its plane. The induced current in the loop is
option_a: constant and non zero, because the loop is moving in a magnetic field
option_b: zero, because the magnetic field is perpendicular to the plane of the loop
option_c: zero, because the flux linked with the loop does not change
option_d: non zero only while the loop is accelerating
correct_answer_text: zero, because the flux linked with the loop does not change
solution: Inside the uniform region the field and the enclosed area are the same at every instant, so the flux is constant and d(phi)/dt = 0. The motional emfs of the leading and trailing sides are equal and opposite around the loop, so no net current flows.
formula_principle: e = -N d(phi)/dt; uniform B and constant area give constant flux
common_misconception: Believing that a loop moving in any magnetic field must carry an induced current.

concept_tested: Induced current and force on a small coaxial loop
stem: A small closed loop is held coaxially above a large loop in which the current is being increased steadily. Just after the increase begins, the small loop
option_a: carries a current opposite in sense to that in the large loop and is pushed away from it
option_b: carries a current in the same sense as that in the large loop and is pulled towards it
option_c: carries a current opposite in sense to that in the large loop and is pulled towards it
option_d: carries no current, because the two loops are not connected to each other
correct_answer_text: carries a current opposite in sense to that in the large loop and is pushed away from it
solution: The rising current in the large loop increases the flux through the small loop, so by Lenz's law the small loop drives a current in the opposite sense to oppose the increase. Coaxial loops carrying antiparallel currents repel, so the small loop is pushed away, and the work done in holding it in place accounts for the extra energy drawn from the source.
formula_principle: Lenz's law; force between coaxial current loops
common_misconception: Assuming induced currents always flow in the same sense as the current that causes them.

concept_tested: e = B l v for a rod moving perpendicular to the field
stem: A straight conducting rod of length 0.5 m moves with a speed of 4 m s^-1 perpendicular to both its own length and a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T. The emf induced between its ends is
formula_principle: e = B l v
common_misconception: Adding contributions from the two halves of the rod, which are already included in the full length l.

concept_tested: Magnetic force on free charges in a moving conductor
stem: The emf induced across the ends of a conductor moving in a magnetic field arises because
option_a: the moving conductor becomes electrically charged by friction with the air
option_b: the resistance of the conductor changes as it moves
option_c: the magnetic field exerts a force on the fixed positive ions of the lattice
option_d: the magnetic force q v x B pushes the free charges towards one end of the conductor
correct_answer_text: the magnetic force q v x B pushes the free charges towards one end of the conductor
solution: Free charges inside the moving rod share its velocity, so each experiences a magnetic force q v x B along the rod. Charges pile up at the ends until the electric field they set up balances this force, and the resulting potential difference is the motional emf B l v.
formula_principle: F = q(v x B) acting on free carriers gives e = B l v
common_misconception: Looking for a chemical or frictional source of emf instead of the magnetic force on the carriers.

concept_tested: Condition for zero motional emf
stem: A conducting rod is moved with a uniform velocity that is parallel to a uniform magnetic field. The emf induced across its ends is
option_a: B l v, the same as for perpendicular motion
option_b: B l v divided by two
option_c: infinite, because the rod cuts no field lines
option_d: zero, because the velocity has no component perpendicular to the field
correct_answer_text: zero, because the velocity has no component perpendicular to the field
solution: The motional emf comes from v x B. If v is parallel to B their cross product vanishes, no force acts along the rod, and no emf is induced. In field line language the rod slides along the lines without cutting any of them.
formula_principle: e = B l v sin(angle between v and B), with l perpendicular to both
common_misconception: Applying e = B l v without checking that v is perpendicular to B.

concept_tested: Motional emf due to the vertical component of the earth's field
stem: An aeroplane with a wingspan of 20 m flies horizontally at 300 m s^-1 in a region where the vertical component of the earth's magnetic field is 5 x 10^-5 T. The emf induced between the wing tips is
formula_principle: e = B_vertical x l x v
common_misconception: Using the total earth's field instead of the vertical component for horizontal flight.

concept_tested: Induced current in a rod and rail circuit
stem: A rod of length 0.4 m slides at 5 m s^-1 on frictionless horizontal rails in a vertical magnetic field of 0.5 T. The rails are joined by a 2 ohm resistor and all other resistances are negligible. The current in the circuit is
formula_principle: e = B l v and i = e/R
common_misconception: Stopping at the emf and quoting its numerical value as the current.

concept_tested: Mechanical power equals the electrical power dissipated
stem: A rod of length 0.2 m slides at 10 m s^-1 on frictionless rails in a field of 0.5 T, the circuit having a total resistance of 1 ohm. The mechanical power that must be supplied to keep the rod moving uniformly is
solution: e = 0.5 x 0.2 x 10 = 1 V and i = 1/1 = 1 A. The retarding force is F = B i l = 0.5 x 1 x 0.2 = 0.1 N, so P = F v = 0.1 x 10 = 1 W, which agrees with e^2/R = 1/1 = 1 W.
formula_principle: e = B l v, i = e/R, F = B i l, P = F v = e^2/R
common_misconception: Double counting the energy by adding the mechanical work to the heat, when they are the same energy.

concept_tested: e = B omega l^2/2 for a rod rotating about one end
stem: A rod of length 0.4 m rotates about an axis through one end, perpendicular to a uniform field of 0.5 T, with an angular speed of 10 rad s^-1. The emf between its ends is
formula_principle: e = B omega l^2/2
common_misconception: Using B l v with the tip speed, which ignores that points nearer the axis move more slowly.

concept_tested: Dependence of the power on speed
stem: A rod slides on fixed rails in a constant magnetic field with a constant total circuit resistance. If the speed of the rod is doubled, the power that must be supplied becomes
solution: The emf B l v doubles and the current e/R doubles with it, so the power, being the product of the two, increases by a factor of four.
common_misconception: Scaling the power linearly with the speed by tracking only the emf.

subtopic: Rod rotating at a stated rate
concept_tested: Converting revolutions per minute to angular speed
stem: A conducting rod of length 1 m rotates about one end at 60 revolutions per minute in a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T directed perpendicular to the plane of rotation. Take pi = 3.14. The emf between the ends of the rod is
solution: 60 revolutions per minute is 1 revolution per second, so omega = 2 pi = 6.28 rad s^-1. Then e = 0.5 x 6.28 x (1)^2/2 = 1.57 V.
formula_principle: omega = 2 pi n; e = B omega l^2/2
common_misconception: Forgetting to convert revolutions per minute into radians per second.

concept_tested: Using F = q v x B to find the positive end
stem: A vertical conducting rod PQ, with P at the top, moves to the right with velocity v in a uniform magnetic field directed into the plane of the page. The end at higher potential is
option_a: Q, because the magnetic force on the free positive charges is directed downward
option_b: P, because electrons are heavier than protons and settle at the bottom
option_c: neither, because the rod is not part of a closed circuit
option_d: P, because the magnetic force on the free positive charges is directed upward
correct_answer_text: P, because the magnetic force on the free positive charges is directed upward
solution: With v to the right and B into the page, the cross product v x B points upward along the rod. Positive carriers are therefore pushed to the top end P, which becomes positive, while the lower end Q is left negative.
formula_principle: F = q(v x B); the end towards which positive charge is pushed is at higher potential
common_misconception: Mixing up the sign of the cross product when the field points into the page.

concept_tested: emf without a circuit
stem: An isolated straight rod moves perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field, with no rails or external circuit connected. Then
option_a: a steady potential difference exists between its ends but no current flows
option_b: neither a potential difference nor a current appears
option_c: a current flows inside the rod continuously from one end to the other
option_d: the potential difference grows without limit as the rod keeps moving
correct_answer_text: a steady potential difference exists between its ends but no current flows
solution: Charges are pushed to the ends until the electric field between them exerts a force equal and opposite to the magnetic force. At that point the redistribution stops, leaving a constant potential difference B l v across the ends with no continuing current.
formula_principle: Equilibrium of q E and q v B gives a steady emf B l v with no current
common_misconception: Believing that no emf exists unless there is a closed circuit.

concept_tested: Balance of weight and magnetic retarding force
stem: A rod of mass 0.02 kg and length 0.5 m slides down frictionless vertical rails in a horizontal magnetic field of 0.4 T perpendicular to the plane of the rails. The circuit resistance is 2 ohm. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the terminal velocity of the rod is
solution: The retarding force is B i l = B^2 l^2 v/R. Setting this equal to m g gives v = m g R/(B^2 l^2) = (0.02 x 10 x 2)/((0.4)^2 x (0.5)^2) = 0.4/(0.16 x 0.25) = 0.4/0.04 = 10 m s^-1.
formula_principle: At terminal velocity m g = B^2 l^2 v/R, so v = m g R/(B^2 l^2)
common_misconception: Forgetting that both the emf and the force contain a factor of B l, so the denominator carries the square.

concept_tested: Force and power for a rod on rails
stem: A rod of length 0.5 m moves at a constant 4 m s^-1 on frictionless rails in a field of 0.4 T, the circuit resistance being 0.2 ohm. The power supplied by the external agent is
solution: e = 0.4 x 0.5 x 4 = 0.8 V and i = 0.8/0.2 = 4 A. The retarding force is F = B i l = 0.4 x 4 x 0.5 = 0.8 N, so P = F v = 0.8 x 4 = 3.2 W, equal to e^2/R = 0.64/0.2 = 3.2 W.
formula_principle: e = B l v, i = e/R, F = B i l, P = F v
common_misconception: Adding the mechanical power and the dissipated power, although they are the same energy flow.

concept_tested: Symmetry of the emf about the midpoint
stem: A rod of length 1 m rotates in a horizontal plane about a vertical axis through its midpoint at 20 rad s^-1, in a vertical magnetic field of 0.1 T. The emf between the two ends of the rod is
solution: Each half of length 0.5 m develops an emf of B omega l^2/2 = 0.1 x 20 x 0.25/2 = 0.25 V, with the centre at the same polarity relative to both ends. Going from one end to the other, the two equal emfs oppose each other, so the potential difference between the ends is zero although each end differs from the centre by 0.25 V.
formula_principle: e = B omega l^2/2 for each half, measured from the axis
common_misconception: Treating the two halves as though their emfs add along the rod.

concept_tested: emf between axle and rim is independent of the number of spokes
stem: A wheel with 10 conducting spokes, each of length 0.5 m, rotates at 60 revolutions per minute about its axle in a uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T parallel to the axle. Take pi = 3.14. The emf between the axle and the rim is
solution: omega = 2 pi x 1 = 6.28 rad s^-1. For one spoke, e = 0.4 x 6.28 x (0.5)^2/2 = 0.4 x 6.28 x 0.125 = 0.314 V. All spokes join the axle to the rim, so they are identical sources in parallel and the emf between axle and rim stays 0.314 V whatever the number of spokes.
formula_principle: e = B omega l^2/2; identical spokes are sources in parallel
common_misconception: Multiplying by the number of spokes as if they added like cells in series.

concept_tested: Dependence of the dissipated power on B and v
stem: For a rod sliding on fixed rails with a fixed circuit resistance, both the magnetic field and the speed of the rod are doubled. The rate at which heat is produced becomes
solution: The emf B l v becomes four times as large when both B and v are doubled. The power varies as the square of the emf, so it becomes 4^2 = 16 times its earlier value.
common_misconception: Forgetting that the power depends on the square of the emf, not on the emf itself.

subtopic: Charge circulated as a rod stops
concept_tested: Total charge from the impulse of the magnetic force
stem: A rod of mass 0.1 kg and length 0.4 m is given an initial speed of 10 m s^-1 along frictionless rails in a field of 0.5 T and is then left alone. The total charge that circulates in the circuit before the rod finally comes to rest is
solution: The retarding force is B i l, and its impulse over the whole motion is B l times the integral of i dt, that is B l q. This impulse must remove all the momentum, so B l q = m v and q = (0.1 x 10)/(0.5 x 0.4) = 1/0.2 = 5 C. Note that the resistance does not enter.
formula_principle: The impulse of the retarding force gives m v = B l q, so q = m v/(B l)
common_misconception: Assuming the charge must depend on the resistance, as the distance travelled does.

concept_tested: Only the velocity component perpendicular to the rod matters
stem: A rod of length 0.4 m moves with a speed of 5 m s^-1 in a plane perpendicular to a uniform field of 0.2 T. The velocity makes an angle of 30 degrees with the length of the rod. The emf induced between its ends is
solution: Only the velocity component perpendicular to the rod sweeps out area, and that component is v sin 30 = 5 x 0.5 = 2.5 m s^-1. Hence e = 0.2 x 0.4 x 2.5 = 0.2 V. The component along the rod merely slides the rod along its own length and links no extra flux.
formula_principle: e = B l v_perpendicular, where v_perpendicular is the component of v at right angles to the rod
common_misconception: Resolving the velocity along the rod instead of perpendicular to it.

concept_tested: The henry
stem: The self inductance of a coil is one henry if
option_a: a steady current of one ampere flows through it under one volt
option_b: a flux of one weber passes through it in one second
option_c: a current changing at one ampere per second induces an emf of one volt in it
option_d: it stores one joule of energy when carrying one ampere
correct_answer_text: a current changing at one ampere per second induces an emf of one volt in it
solution: The defining relation is e = L dI/dt in magnitude. If a rate of change of one ampere per second produces one volt, then L = 1 H. Equivalently one henry is one weber of flux linkage per ampere.
formula_principle: e = -L dI/dt, so 1 H = 1 V/(1 A s^-1) = 1 Wb A^-1
common_misconception: Confusing the henry with the ohm by thinking of a steady current instead of a changing one.

concept_tested: e = L dI/dt
stem: The current in a coil of self inductance 0.5 H changes at the steady rate of 4 A s^-1. The magnitude of the self induced emf is
solution: e = L dI/dt = 0.5 x 4 = 2 V.
formula_principle: e = L dI/dt in magnitude
common_misconception: Dividing instead of multiplying when the numbers happen to look convenient.

stem: A coil of self inductance 2 H carries a steady current of 3 A. The energy stored in its magnetic field is
common_misconception: Dropping the factor of one half from the energy expression.

concept_tested: Analogy between inductance and mass
stem: Self inductance is often called the inertia of electricity because
option_a: it stores charge in the coil in the way a capacitor does
option_b: it converts electrical energy into heat at a steady rate
option_c: it keeps the current constant at all times in every circuit
option_d: it opposes any change in the current through the coil, just as mass opposes a change in velocity
correct_answer_text: it opposes any change in the current through the coil, just as mass opposes a change in velocity
solution: The self induced emf always opposes the change in current, so a larger inductance makes the current harder to change. This is exactly the role mass plays in mechanics, where a larger mass makes the velocity harder to change.
formula_principle: e = -L dI/dt is analogous to F = m dv/dt
common_misconception: Equating inductance with capacitance because both store energy.

concept_tested: N phi = L I

formula_principle: L = N phi/I
common_misconception: Inverting the ratio of flux linkage to current.

concept_tested: L = mu_0 N^2 A/l

formula_principle: L = mu_0 N^2 A/l
common_misconception: Forgetting that 1 cm^2 equals 10^-4 m^2.

subtopic: Effect of the number of turns
concept_tested: Dependence of L on N squared
stem: The number of turns of a solenoid is doubled while its length, cross sectional area and core are kept unchanged. Its self inductance becomes
option_d: unchanged, since the length and area are the same
solution: The field inside the solenoid is proportional to N for fixed length, and the flux linkage brings in another factor of N. Hence L varies as N^2 and doubling N makes the inductance four times as large.
formula_principle: L = mu_0 N^2 A/l
common_misconception: Scaling the inductance linearly with the number of turns.

concept_tested: emf from a finite change of current

formula_principle: e = L delta(I)/delta(t)
common_misconception: Using one of the current values instead of the change in current.

concept_tested: Geometry and core, not current
stem: The self inductance of a given coil depends on
option_a: its number of turns, its dimensions and the permeability of its core
option_d: the rate at which the current through it changes
correct_answer_text: its number of turns, its dimensions and the permeability of its core
solution: The expression for a solenoid contains only the number of turns, the area, the length and the permeability of the core. The current cancels in the ratio N phi/I because the flux is directly proportional to the current.
formula_principle: L = mu_0 mu_r N^2 A/l for a solenoid
common_misconception: Concluding from L = N phi/I that L must change if the current changes.

subtopic: Energy built up in an inductor
concept_tested: Energy stored when the current is raised from zero
stem: The current in a coil of self inductance 0.1 H is raised from zero to 4 A. The energy now stored in its magnetic field is
common_misconception: Forgetting that the energy grows with the square of the final current.

concept_tested: Role of relative permeability
stem: A soft iron core of relative permeability 800 is inserted into an air cored solenoid without changing its winding or dimensions. The self inductance
option_b: remains unchanged, since the number of turns is unchanged
solution: With a core of relative permeability mu_r the field and hence the flux for the same current become mu_r times larger, so the inductance becomes mu_r times larger, that is 800 times the air cored value.
formula_principle: L = mu_0 mu_r N^2 A/l
common_misconception: Treating the relative permeability as an additive rather than a multiplicative factor.

concept_tested: No emf without a change of current
stem: An ideal inductor of 2 H carries a steady current of 5 A. The emf induced across it is
solution: The current is steady, so dI/dt = 0 and the self induced emf is zero, however large the inductance or the current may be. An ideal inductor behaves like a plain wire for a direct current that does not change.
formula_principle: e = -L dI/dt
common_misconception: Multiplying inductance by current and calling the product an emf.

concept_tested: Large dI/dt at switch off
stem: A bright spark is seen at the switch when a circuit containing a large inductance is suddenly broken because
option_a: the inductor stores charge which is released at the switch
option_b: the current falls to zero in a very short time, so L dI/dt becomes very large
option_c: the resistance of the switch contacts falls to zero as they separate
option_d: the supply voltage rises automatically when the switch is opened
correct_answer_text: the current falls to zero in a very short time, so L dI/dt becomes very large
solution: Opening the switch forces the current to vanish almost instantly, making dI/dt enormous. The self induced emf L dI/dt then greatly exceeds the supply voltage and is large enough to break down the air gap, producing a spark that dissipates the stored energy (1/2) L I^2.
formula_principle: e = -L dI/dt with a very small dt
common_misconception: Thinking of the inductor as a store of charge like a capacitor.

concept_tested: Combining L of a solenoid with the energy expression
stem: A solenoid of length 0.5 m has 500 turns wound on a circular cross section of radius 2 cm and carries a current of 2 A. Take mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1 and pi = 3.14. The energy stored in it is about
formula_principle: L = mu_0 N^2 A/l and U = (1/2) L I^2
common_misconception: Stopping at the inductance and reporting it as the stored energy.

concept_tested: Dependence of L on the length
stem: A solenoid of self inductance L is stretched to twice its original length, the number of turns and the cross sectional area remaining the same. Its new self inductance is
solution: With N and A fixed, L is inversely proportional to l. Doubling the length halves the number of turns per unit length, so the field and the flux for a given current are halved and the inductance falls to L/2.
formula_principle: L = mu_0 N^2 A/l
common_misconception: Confusing the strong N^2 dependence with the dependence on length.

concept_tested: Combination of inductances with no mutual coupling
stem: Two inductors of 4 H and 6 H, with no mutual coupling between them, are connected in parallel. The equivalent inductance is
formula_principle: 1/L = 1/L1 + 1/L2 for uncoupled inductors in parallel
common_misconception: Forgetting the final inversion after adding the reciprocals.

concept_tested: Difference of the squares of the currents
stem: The current in a coil of self inductance 5 H is increased from 2 A to 4 A. The energy supplied to the magnetic field of the coil is
common_misconception: Writing (I_2 - I_1)^2 in place of I_2^2 - I_1^2.

concept_tested: Interpreting L = N phi/I correctly
stem: For a coil with a non magnetic core, which statement is correct?
option_a: The self inductance falls as the current is increased, because I appears in the denominator
option_b: The self inductance is zero when no current flows, because the flux is then zero
option_c: The self inductance changes sign when the current is reversed
option_d: The self inductance is a constant of the coil even though it is written as the ratio N phi/I
correct_answer_text: The self inductance is a constant of the coil even though it is written as the ratio N phi/I
solution: For a non magnetic core the flux produced by the coil is directly proportional to the current, so the ratio N phi/I is fixed by the geometry and the core alone. It stays the same whether the current is large, small, zero in the limit, or reversed.
formula_principle: L = N phi/I with phi proportional to I for a non magnetic core
common_misconception: Treating L = N phi/I as though L must vary inversely with the current.

concept_tested: L = mu_r mu_0 N^2 A/l
stem: A solenoid of length 1 m has 1000 turns wound on an iron core of relative permeability 500 and cross sectional area 5 cm^2. Take mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1 and pi = 3.14. Its self inductance is
formula_principle: L = mu_r mu_0 N^2 A/l
common_misconception: Omitting the relative permeability, which for iron changes the answer by two or three orders of magnitude.

concept_tested: Inverting U = (1/2) L I^2
stem: An inductor stores 2 J of energy when it carries 4 A. The current needed for it to store 4.5 J is
solution: From 2 = (1/2) L (4)^2 we get L = 4/16 = 0.25 H. Then 4.5 = (1/2) x 0.25 x I^2 gives I^2 = 36 and I = 6 A. Equivalently the current scales as the square root of the energy, and 4 x sqrt(4.5/2) = 4 x 1.5 = 6 A.
formula_principle: U = (1/2) L I^2, so I is proportional to the square root of U
common_misconception: Assuming the current is directly proportional to the stored energy.

concept_tested: Mutual inductance of a pair of coils
stem: The mutual inductance of a pair of coils is numerically equal to the
option_a: flux linked with one coil when unit current flows in the same coil
option_b: current in one coil when unit flux is linked with the other
option_c: emf in one coil when a steady current flows in the other
option_d: flux linked with one coil when unit current flows in the other
correct_answer_text: flux linked with one coil when unit current flows in the other
solution: Mutual inductance is defined as the flux linkage produced in the secondary coil per unit current in the primary coil, and is measured in henry.
formula_principle: N_2 phi_2 = M I_1, so M = N_2 phi_2/I_1
common_misconception: Describing self inductance when the question asks about mutual inductance.

concept_tested: e_2 = M dI_1/dt
stem: Two coils have a mutual inductance of 0.2 H. The current in the first coil changes at 5 A s^-1. The emf induced in the second coil is
formula_principle: e_2 = M dI_1/dt in magnitude
common_misconception: Mixing up which quantity divides which in the product M dI/dt.

concept_tested: M = k sqrt(L1 L2) with k = 1
stem: Two coils of self inductance 2 H and 8 H are wound on the same core so that all the flux of one links the other. Their mutual inductance is
solution: All the flux is shared, so k = 1 and M = sqrt(2 x 8) = sqrt(16) = 4 H.
formula_principle: M = k sqrt(L1 L2), with k = 1 for perfect coupling
common_misconception: Using an arithmetic mean or a sum in place of the geometric mean.

concept_tested: M for partially coupled coils
stem: Two coils of self inductance 8 mH and 2 mH have a coefficient of coupling of 0.75. Their mutual inductance is
solution: sqrt(L1 L2) = sqrt(8 x 2) = sqrt(16) = 4 mH, so M = 0.75 x 4 = 3 mH.
formula_principle: M = k sqrt(L1 L2)
common_misconception: Applying the coupling factor before taking the square root.

concept_tested: N_2 phi_2 = M I_1
stem: Two coils have a mutual inductance of 0.5 H. When a current of 4 A flows in the first coil, the total flux linked with the second coil is
formula_principle: N_2 phi_2 = M I_1
common_misconception: Confusing the units of henry and weber and quoting M itself.

concept_tested: Meaning and limits of k
stem: The coefficient of coupling k between two coils
option_a: can take any value greater than 1 for coils on an iron core
option_b: lies between 0 and 1, being 1 when all the flux of one coil links the other
option_c: is always exactly 1 for any two coils placed near each other
option_d: is measured in henry like the mutual inductance
correct_answer_text: lies between 0 and 1, being 1 when all the flux of one coil links the other
solution: The coupling coefficient is the fraction of the flux of one coil that links the other, so it cannot be negative or exceed one. It is a dimensionless number, equal to one only for ideal coupling with no leakage.
formula_principle: k = M/sqrt(L1 L2), 0 <= k <= 1
common_misconception: Believing an iron core can push the coupling coefficient above unity.

concept_tested: M_12 equals M_21
stem: For any two coils placed in a fixed relative position, the mutual inductance of coil 1 with respect to coil 2 and that of coil 2 with respect to coil 1 are
option_b: equal only if the two coils have the same number of turns
option_c: in the ratio of the numbers of turns of the two coils
option_d: equal only if the two coils have the same self inductance
solution: The reciprocity theorem shows that the flux linkage in coil 2 per unit current in coil 1 is exactly equal to the flux linkage in coil 1 per unit current in coil 2, whatever the shapes, sizes or turn numbers of the coils.
common_misconception: Assuming the coil with more turns must have the larger mutual inductance.

concept_tested: Geometry, separation, orientation and core
stem: The mutual inductance of two given coils will not change if
option_a: the current in the primary coil is doubled while everything else is fixed
option_b: the distance between the coils is increased
option_c: one coil is turned so that its plane becomes perpendicular to the other
option_d: a soft iron rod is inserted through both coils
correct_answer_text: the current in the primary coil is doubled while everything else is fixed
solution: Mutual inductance is the ratio of flux linkage to current. Since the shared flux is itself proportional to the current, the ratio is unchanged when the current is doubled. Separation, orientation and the core material all change the ratio.
formula_principle: M depends on geometry, relative orientation, separation and the medium, not on the current
common_misconception: Assuming the mutual inductance rises when the primary current is increased.

concept_tested: M = mu_0 N_1 N_2 A/l
stem: A long solenoid of length 0.4 m and cross sectional area 4 x 10^-3 m^2 has 500 turns. A second coil of 200 turns is wound closely over its middle. Take mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1 and pi = 3.14. The mutual inductance of the pair is
formula_principle: M = mu_0 N_1 N_2 A/l
common_misconception: Adding the turn numbers of the two windings instead of multiplying them.

concept_tested: No induced emf without a change of current
stem: A steady direct current flows in the primary of a pair of closely coupled coils. The emf induced in the secondary is
option_a: large, because the coupling between the coils is strong
option_b: zero, because the current in the primary is not changing
option_c: equal to M times the primary current
option_d: equal to the primary emf multiplied by the turns ratio
correct_answer_text: zero, because the current in the primary is not changing
solution: The induced emf in the secondary depends on the rate of change of the primary current. For a steady direct current dI_1/dt = 0, so no emf is induced however strong the coupling.
formula_principle: e_2 = -M dI_1/dt
common_misconception: Assuming strong coupling by itself guarantees an induced emf.

concept_tested: q = M delta(I_1)/R
stem: Two coils have a mutual inductance of 0.05 H. The current in the primary falls from 10 A to 2 A in 0.4 s. The secondary circuit has a resistance of 2 ohm. The charge circulated in the secondary is
solution: delta(I_1) = 10 - 2 = 8 A. The charge is q = M delta(I_1)/R = 0.05 x 8/2 = 0.4/2 = 0.2 C. The time interval cancels, so the answer does not depend on the 0.4 s.
formula_principle: e_2 = M delta(I_1)/delta(t) and q = e_2 delta(t)/R = M delta(I_1)/R
common_misconception: Dividing by the time interval as well, having assumed the charge must depend on how fast the change occurs.

concept_tested: k = M/sqrt(L1 L2)
stem: Two coils have self inductances of 20 mH and 80 mH and a mutual inductance of 30 mH. Their coefficient of coupling is
solution: sqrt(L1 L2) = sqrt(20 x 80) = sqrt(1600) = 40 mH. Hence k = 30/40 = 0.75, which is properly less than one.
formula_principle: k = M/sqrt(L1 L2)
common_misconception: Dividing by one self inductance instead of by the geometric mean of both.

concept_tested: Coaxial solenoids of different radii
stem: A short coil of small radius is wound at the middle of a long solenoid of larger radius. In the expression for their mutual inductance, the area that appears is
option_a: the cross sectional area of the outer solenoid
option_b: the cross sectional area of the inner coil, since only that area carries the shared field
option_c: the sum of the two cross sectional areas
option_d: the difference of the two cross sectional areas
correct_answer_text: the cross sectional area of the inner coil, since only that area carries the shared field
solution: The uniform field of the long solenoid exists inside it, and the flux linked with the smaller coil is that field multiplied by the smaller of the two areas. By reciprocity the same value of M is obtained whichever coil is treated as primary, so the inner area is the one that enters.
formula_principle: M = mu_0 n_1 N_2 A_inner for coaxial windings of unequal radii
common_misconception: Automatically using the area of the coil that is treated as the primary.

concept_tested: Working back from the secondary flux to M
stem: A secondary coil of 500 turns is placed near a primary. When the primary current changes uniformly by 4 A in 0.2 s, the flux through each turn of the secondary changes by 8 x 10^-5 Wb. The mutual inductance is
solution: e_2 = 500 x 8 x 10^-5/0.2 = 0.04/0.2 = 0.2 V. The rate of change of the primary current is 4/0.2 = 20 A s^-1, so M = 0.2/20 = 0.01 H.
formula_principle: e_2 = N_2 delta(phi_2)/delta(t) and M = e_2/(dI_1/dt)
common_misconception: Dividing the emf by the change in current rather than by the rate of change of current.

concept_tested: Series aiding combination
stem: Two coils of self inductance 2 H and 8 H have a coefficient of coupling of 0.5. They are connected in series so that their fluxes aid each other. The equivalent inductance is
solution: M = 0.5 x sqrt(2 x 8) = 0.5 x 4 = 2 H. For fluxes that aid each other, L = L1 + L2 + 2M = 2 + 8 + 4 = 14 H.
formula_principle: M = k sqrt(L1 L2); L_series aiding = L1 + L2 + 2M
common_misconception: Including the mutual inductance once rather than twice in the series combination.

subtopic: emf induced in a secondary winding
concept_tested: Combining M of coaxial solenoids with e = M dI/dt
stem: A long solenoid of length 0.5 m and cross sectional area 1 x 10^-3 m^2 has 1000 turns. A secondary coil of 50 turns is wound over its middle. The current in the solenoid changes at 100 A s^-1. Take mu_0 = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1 and pi = 3.14. The emf induced in the secondary is
formula_principle: M = mu_0 N_1 N_2 A/l and e_2 = M dI_1/dt
common_misconception: Stopping at the mutual inductance and reporting it as the induced emf.

concept_tested: Circulating currents in a bulk conductor
stem: Eddy currents are
option_a: currents that flow along the surface of a conductor because of static charges
option_b: currents that flow only in wires wound into closed loops
option_c: circulating currents induced in the body of a conductor placed in a changing magnetic flux
option_d: currents produced by the chemical action inside a conductor
correct_answer_text: circulating currents induced in the body of a conductor placed in a changing magnetic flux
solution: A changing magnetic flux induces emfs along every closed path inside a solid conductor. Because the conductor offers many such paths, whirling currents are set up in its body; these are called eddy or Foucault currents.
formula_principle: Faraday's law applied to closed paths within a solid conductor
common_misconception: Believing that induced currents need a wire loop and cannot arise in a solid block.

concept_tested: Why cores are laminated
stem: The core of a transformer is built from thin sheets insulated from one another in order to
option_a: break up the paths available to eddy currents and so raise their resistance
option_b: increase the magnetic flux through the core
option_c: make the core lighter and cheaper to manufacture
option_d: prevent the core from becoming permanently magnetised
correct_answer_text: break up the paths available to eddy currents and so raise their resistance
solution: Laminations lie parallel to the flux, so they do not obstruct it, but the insulation between them confines each eddy current to a thin sheet. The narrow paths have a much higher resistance, so the induced currents and the heat they produce are greatly reduced.
formula_principle: Eddy current loss falls when the resistance of the induced current paths rises
common_misconception: Thinking lamination reduces the magnetic flux rather than the induced currents.

concept_tested: Heating by eddy currents
stem: In an induction furnace, a metal placed inside a coil carrying a high frequency alternating current melts because
option_a: the coil conducts heat to the metal by direct contact
option_b: the alternating magnetic field breaks the chemical bonds of the metal
option_c: the metal loses its resistance and therefore becomes hot
option_d: strong eddy currents induced in the metal dissipate heat within its own body
correct_answer_text: strong eddy currents induced in the metal dissipate heat within its own body
solution: The rapidly changing flux induces very large eddy currents throughout the metal. The i^2 R heating produced by these currents is generated inside the metal itself and is intense enough to raise the metal to its melting point.
formula_principle: H = i^2 R t applied to eddy currents induced by a rapidly changing flux
common_misconception: Looking for a conduction path from the coil instead of recognising internal induction heating.

concept_tested: Damping in a moving coil galvanometer
stem: The coil of a dead beat galvanometer is wound on a metallic frame so that
option_a: the frame increases the magnetic field acting on the coil
option_b: the frame carries part of the measured current and protects the coil
option_c: the frame stores the electrical energy of the coil for later use
option_d: eddy currents induced in the frame oppose the motion and bring the coil quickly to rest
correct_answer_text: eddy currents induced in the frame oppose the motion and bring the coil quickly to rest
solution: As the coil turns, the flux through the metal frame changes and eddy currents appear in it. By Lenz's law these currents oppose the rotation, dissipating the energy of the oscillation as heat so the pointer settles at its reading without swinging.
formula_principle: Lenz's law applied to eddy currents in a moving conductor
common_misconception: Assuming the metal frame is there for mechanical rigidity or magnetic reasons only.

concept_tested: How laminations must be placed
stem: In a laminated core the individual sheets are placed so that their planes are
option_a: parallel to the magnetic flux and perpendicular to the plane of the eddy currents
option_b: perpendicular to the magnetic flux, so that the flux is cut into small parts
option_c: parallel to the eddy currents, so that the currents can flow freely
option_d: at 45 degrees to the flux, so that the loss is shared equally
correct_answer_text: parallel to the magnetic flux and perpendicular to the plane of the eddy currents
solution: The flux has to pass freely along the core, so the sheets lie parallel to it. The eddy currents circulate in planes perpendicular to the flux, and the insulation between the sheets cuts those circulating paths into thin, high resistance loops.
formula_principle: Laminations must not interrupt the flux but must interrupt the eddy current paths
common_misconception: Placing the laminations across the flux, which would block the very flux the core is meant to carry.

concept_tested: Eddy current loss varies as the square of the frequency
stem: The eddy current power loss in a given core is proportional to the square of the frequency of the alternating flux. If the frequency is doubled with the peak flux density unchanged, the loss becomes
option_c: unchanged, since the peak flux density is the same
solution: Doubling the frequency doubles the rate of change of flux and so doubles the induced emf and the eddy currents. The power dissipated varies as the square of the current, so it rises by a factor of four.
formula_principle: Induced emf is proportional to frequency and the loss is proportional to the square of the emf
common_misconception: Following the emf only and forgetting the squaring in i^2 R.

concept_tested: Effect of cutting slots in a swinging plate
stem: A solid copper plate swinging between the poles of a strong magnet comes to rest very quickly. If deep slots are cut in the same plate, it will
option_a: come to rest even faster, because the slots make the plate lighter
option_b: swing for exactly the same time, because copper is not magnetic
option_c: swing for a much longer time, because the slots interrupt the eddy current paths
option_d: swing for a longer time, because the slots reduce the magnetic field between the poles
correct_answer_text: swing for a much longer time, because the slots interrupt the eddy current paths
solution: In the solid plate large eddy currents circulate and, by Lenz's law, oppose the swing, damping it rapidly. The slots break these wide circulating paths into narrow ones of much higher resistance, so the currents and the retarding force become small and the plate swings for far longer.
formula_principle: Slots raise the resistance of the eddy current paths, reducing the retarding force
common_misconception: Explaining the change by the mass of the plate instead of by the induced currents.

concept_tested: Speed dependence of the braking force
stem: In the electromagnetic brakes of a train, the retarding force produced by eddy currents
option_a: stays constant at all speeds, so the train stops with uniform deceleration
option_b: decreases as the train slows down, so this braking alone cannot bring the train fully to rest
option_c: increases as the train slows down, giving a sharp final stop
option_d: acts only after the train has already stopped
correct_answer_text: decreases as the train slows down, so this braking alone cannot bring the train fully to rest
solution: The eddy currents are driven by an emf proportional to the speed, so the retarding force is also proportional to the speed. As the train slows, the braking force falls in proportion, giving a smooth jerk free retardation that becomes weaker and weaker, so mechanical brakes are needed for the final stop. The kinetic energy removed appears as heat in the rails and discs.
formula_principle: Induced emf is proportional to speed, so the eddy current retarding force is proportional to speed
common_misconception: Assuming eddy current braking behaves like ordinary friction with a constant force.

concept_tested: Working principle of an AC generator
stem: An AC generator works on the principle of
option_a: the heating effect of an electric current
option_b: electromagnetic induction, converting mechanical energy into electrical energy
option_c: the magnetic effect of an electric current
correct_answer_text: electromagnetic induction, converting mechanical energy into electrical energy
solution: A coil rotated in a magnetic field experiences a continuously changing flux linkage, so an emf is induced in it according to Faraday's law. The mechanical work done in turning the coil appears as electrical energy in the circuit.
formula_principle: e = -N d(phi)/dt for a coil rotating in a magnetic field
common_misconception: Confusing the generator with a motor, which uses the magnetic effect of a current.

concept_tested: e_0 = N B A omega
stem: A coil of 100 turns and area 0.02 m^2 rotates at 100 rad s^-1 in a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T about an axis perpendicular to the field. The peak emf generated is
formula_principle: e_0 = N B A omega
common_misconception: Reporting the rms value when the peak value has been asked for.

concept_tested: Function of slip rings
stem: The slip rings in an AC generator
option_a: reverse the connections of the coil twice in every rotation
option_b: increase the emf generated by the rotating coil
option_c: keep the rotating coil permanently connected to the same external terminals, so the output alternates
option_d: convert the alternating emf of the coil into a steady direct emf
correct_answer_text: keep the rotating coil permanently connected to the same external terminals, so the output alternates
solution: Each end of the coil is joined to its own slip ring, and each ring presses against a fixed brush. The connection to the external circuit never changes, so the reversal of the emf inside the rotating coil appears as an alternating emf across the load.
formula_principle: Slip rings preserve the alternating output; split rings rectify it
common_misconception: Interchanging the roles of slip rings and split ring commutators.

concept_tested: Relation between rotation rate and frequency
stem: The armature of an AC generator makes 3000 revolutions per minute. The frequency of the emf generated is
solution: f = 3000/60 = 50 revolutions per second, that is 50 Hz. The corresponding angular speed is omega = 2 pi x 50 = 314 rad s^-1.
formula_principle: f = n/60 when n is in revolutions per minute; omega = 2 pi f
common_misconception: Confusing the angular speed in radian per second with the frequency in hertz.

subtopic: Peak emf from the rotation rate
concept_tested: Converting revolutions per minute before using e_0 = N B A omega
stem: A generator coil of 200 turns and area 100 cm^2 rotates at 600 revolutions per minute in a field of 0.5 T. Take pi = 3.14. The peak emf is
solution: 600 revolutions per minute is 10 revolutions per second, so omega = 2 x 3.14 x 10 = 62.8 rad s^-1. The area is 100 cm^2 = 1 x 10^-2 m^2. Then e_0 = 200 x 0.5 x 1 x 10^-2 x 62.8 = 1 x 62.8 = 62.8 V.
formula_principle: omega = 2 pi n with n in revolutions per second; e_0 = N B A omega
common_misconception: Forgetting to convert revolutions per minute into radians per second.

concept_tested: Orientation of the coil at maximum emf
stem: In an AC generator the induced emf has its maximum value at the instant when
option_a: the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field, so that the flux linked with it is maximum
option_c: the plane of the coil is parallel to the magnetic field, so that the flux linked with it is zero
option_d: the flux linked with the coil is maximum and is still increasing
correct_answer_text: the plane of the coil is parallel to the magnetic field, so that the flux linked with it is zero
solution: The emf depends on the rate of change of flux, not on the flux. When the plane of the coil lies along the field the flux linkage is momentarily zero, but it is changing at its fastest rate, and the sine term reaches unity so the emf takes its peak value N B A omega.
formula_principle: phi = N B A cos(omega t) and e = N B A omega sin(omega t)
common_misconception: Assuming the emf is largest when the flux is largest.

concept_tested: Scaling of peak emf and frequency
stem: The speed of rotation of the armature of an AC generator is doubled, everything else remaining the same. Then
option_a: the peak emf is doubled but the frequency is unchanged
option_b: the frequency is doubled but the peak emf is unchanged
option_c: the peak emf becomes four times as large and the frequency is doubled
option_d: both the peak emf and the frequency of the output are doubled
correct_answer_text: both the peak emf and the frequency of the output are doubled
solution: The peak emf is directly proportional to omega, so it doubles. The frequency is omega divided by 2 pi, so it doubles as well. Both change in the same proportion as the speed of rotation.
formula_principle: e_0 = N B A omega and f = omega/(2 pi)
common_misconception: Assuming the frequency is fixed by the design of the generator alone.

concept_tested: Peak emf converted to rms
stem: A generator coil of 50 turns and area 0.02 m^2 rotates 50 times per second in a magnetic field of 0.4 T. Take pi = 3.14 and root two as 1.414. The rms value of the generated emf is
formula_principle: omega = 2 pi n, e_0 = N B A omega, e_rms = e_0/sqrt(2)
common_misconception: Reporting the peak value when the rms value has been asked for.

concept_tested: Relation between peak value and rms value of a sinusoidal emf
stem: An alternating voltage is given by e = 311 sin(314 t) volt. The rms value of this voltage is nearly (take sqrt(2) = 1.414)
solution: Comparing e = e0 sin(omega t) with the given equation, e0 = 311 V. Then e_rms = 311 / 1.414 = 220 V.
formula_principle: e_rms = e0 / sqrt(2) for a sinusoidal alternating voltage
common_misconception: Students often quote the coefficient of the sine function as the rms value; it is actually the peak value.

concept_tested: Extracting frequency from the angular frequency in an AC equation
stem: For an alternating current i = 10 sin(314 t) ampere, the frequency of the supply is nearly (take pi = 3.14)
solution: Here omega = 314 rad/s. Therefore f = 314 / (2 x 3.14) = 314 / 6.28 = 50 Hz.
formula_principle: omega = 2 pi f, so f = omega / (2 pi)
common_misconception: Confusing angular frequency omega measured in rad/s with frequency f measured in Hz.

concept_tested: Average value of a sinusoidal current over one half cycle
stem: The peak value of an alternating current is 10 A. Its average value over one half cycle is nearly (take pi = 3.14)
formula_principle: i_mean over half cycle = 2 I0 / pi = 0.637 I0
common_misconception: Mixing up the half cycle mean value 0.637 I0 with the rms value 0.707 I0.

subtopic: Average value over a full cycle
concept_tested: Average of a symmetric sinusoid over one complete period
stem: Over one complete cycle, the average value of a sinusoidal alternating current is
option_a: equal to the peak value of the current
option_b: equal to 0.707 times the peak value
option_c: zero, because the positive and negative halves are equal and opposite
option_d: equal to 0.637 times the peak value
correct_answer_text: zero, because the positive and negative halves are equal and opposite
solution: During the first half cycle the current is positive and during the second half cycle it is equally negative, so the areas under the current time graph cancel and the full cycle mean is zero.
formula_principle: Average of sin(omega t) over a full period is zero
common_misconception: Assuming the full cycle average equals the half cycle average of 0.637 I0.

concept_tested: Form factor as the ratio of rms value to half cycle mean value
stem: For a sinusoidal alternating voltage, the form factor, defined as the ratio of the rms value to the mean value over half a cycle, is nearly
formula_principle: Form factor = e_rms / e_mean = (e0 / sqrt(2)) / (2 e0 / pi) = pi / (2 sqrt(2))
common_misconception: Interchanging the form factor 1.11 with the peak factor 1.414.

concept_tested: Simultaneous extraction of rms value and frequency from an AC equation
stem: An AC source has emf e = 100 sin(200 pi t) volt. The rms voltage and the frequency of the source are respectively
solution: Peak value e0 = 100 V, so e_rms = 100 / 1.414 = 70.7 V. Also omega = 200 pi rad/s, so 2 pi f = 200 pi giving f = 100 Hz.
formula_principle: e_rms = e0 / sqrt(2) and omega = 2 pi f
common_misconception: Multiplying rather than dividing by sqrt(2) when converting peak value to rms value.

concept_tested: Evaluating the instantaneous current of an AC waveform at a given instant
stem: An alternating current is i = 5 sin(100 pi t + pi/3) ampere. The instantaneous current at t = 0 is nearly
formula_principle: i = I0 sin(omega t + phi); substitute the given instant
common_misconception: Forgetting that a nonzero initial phase means the current is not zero at t = 0.

concept_tested: Physical definition of the root mean square value of an alternating current
stem: The rms value of an alternating current is defined as
option_a: the average of the instantaneous values of the current over one complete cycle
option_b: the maximum value attained by the current during one cycle
option_c: the average of the instantaneous values over one half cycle
option_d: the value of the steady current that produces the same heat in a given resistance in the same time
correct_answer_text: the value of the steady current that produces the same heat in a given resistance in the same time
solution: Heat produced in a resistance depends on the square of the current. Averaging i^2 over a cycle and taking the square root gives I_rms, which by construction produces the same heating as an equal steady current.
formula_principle: I_rms is defined through the equal heating effect, since heat depends on i^2
common_misconception: Believing the rms value is just a mathematical average of the current rather than of its square.

concept_tested: Using the rms current to compute heat developed in a resistor
stem: An alternating current of peak value 2 A flows through a 100 ohm resistor for 1 minute. The heat produced is
formula_principle: H = I_rms^2 R t with I_rms = I0 / sqrt(2)
common_misconception: Substituting the peak current into the heating formula, which doubles the answer.

concept_tested: Number of times an alternating current becomes zero in one second
stem: A 50 Hz alternating current becomes zero how many times in one second
solution: In one cycle the current is zero at the start of the cycle and again at the midpoint, that is twice per cycle. With 50 cycles per second the count is 2 x 50 = 100 times per second.
formula_principle: A sinusoid passes through zero twice in every complete cycle
common_misconception: Counting only one zero per cycle and answering 50.

concept_tested: Ratio of peak value to rms value for a sinusoidal waveform
stem: For a sinusoidal alternating voltage, the ratio of the peak value to the rms value is
solution: Since e_rms = e0 / sqrt(2), the ratio e0 / e_rms = sqrt(2) = 1.414.
formula_principle: Peak factor = e0 / e_rms = sqrt(2)
common_misconception: Assuming a simple factor of 2 relates peak and rms values.

concept_tested: Relating quarter period to the first instant of maximum voltage
stem: An alternating voltage e = 200 sin(100 pi t) volt starts from zero at t = 0. The time taken by it to reach its peak value for the first time is
solution: omega = 100 pi rad/s gives f = 50 Hz and T = 1 / 50 = 0.02 s. Starting from zero, the sine first reaches its maximum after a quarter period, that is 0.02 / 4 = 0.005 s = 5 milliseconds.
