formula_principle: omega = 2 pi f, T = 1 / f, and the peak of a sine starting at zero occurs at T / 4
common_misconception: Using half the period instead of a quarter of the period for the first maximum.

subtopic: Time to reach half the peak
concept_tested: Solving the sine equation for a specified fraction of the peak value
stem: An alternating current i = I0 sin(100 pi t) ampere starts from zero at t = 0. The time in which it first attains half of its peak value is
solution: I0 / 2 = I0 sin(100 pi t) gives sin(100 pi t) = 0.5, so 100 pi t = pi/6. Hence t = 1 / 600 s, which is about 1.67 milliseconds.
formula_principle: Set i = I0 / 2 in i = I0 sin(omega t) and solve for t
common_misconception: Taking half the peak value to occur at half the quarter period, which is not true for a sinusoid.

concept_tested: Peak emf of an AC generator from N, B, A and omega
stem: A coil of 100 turns and area 0.02 m^2 rotates at 50 revolutions per second in a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T about an axis perpendicular to the field. The peak emf induced is nearly (take pi = 3.14)
formula_principle: e0 = N B A omega with omega = 2 pi f
common_misconception: Forgetting to convert revolutions per second into angular frequency by multiplying by 2 pi.

subtopic: RMS value of a mixed waveform
concept_tested: RMS value of a current having a steady part and a sinusoidal part
stem: A current i = 3 + 4 sin(omega t) ampere flows through a circuit. The rms value of this current is nearly
solution: i^2 = 9 + 24 sin(omega t) + 16 sin^2(omega t). Over a full cycle the mean of sin(omega t) is 0 and the mean of sin^2(omega t) is 0.5. Hence mean of i^2 = 9 + 0 + 8 = 17, so I_rms = sqrt(17) = 4.12 A.
formula_principle: I_rms = sqrt(mean of i^2); the cross term averages to zero over a cycle
common_misconception: Treating the constant 3 A as though it too must be divided by sqrt(2).

concept_tested: Dimensions of the combination sqrt(LC) in an AC circuit
stem: In an AC circuit containing an inductance L and a capacitance C, the quantity sqrt(LC) has the same dimensions as
option_a: frequency, with dimensional formula [M^0 L^0 T^-1]
option_b: velocity, with dimensional formula [M^0 L^1 T^-1]
option_c: time, with dimensional formula [M^0 L^0 T^1]
option_d: angular acceleration, with dimensional formula [M^0 L^0 T^-2]
correct_answer_text: time, with dimensional formula [M^0 L^0 T^1]
solution: Since omega = 1 / sqrt(LC) and omega has the dimensions of inverse time, sqrt(LC) must have the dimensions of time, that is [M^0 L^0 T^1].
formula_principle: The resonant angular frequency is omega = 1 / sqrt(LC), and omega has dimensions of [T^-1]
common_misconception: Quoting the dimensions of 1 / sqrt(LC) instead of sqrt(LC) itself.

concept_tested: Voltage and current are in phase in a purely resistive AC circuit
stem: When an alternating voltage is applied across a pure resistor, the phase difference between the applied voltage and the current is
option_a: pi/2 with the current lagging the voltage
option_b: pi/2 with the current leading the voltage
solution: Ohm law holds instant by instant in a resistor, so i = (e0 / R) sin(omega t) when e = e0 sin(omega t). Both reach zero and reach their maxima at the same instants, giving zero phase difference.
formula_principle: For a resistor, i = e / R at every instant, so i and e vary together
common_misconception: Assuming every AC element introduces some phase difference.

concept_tested: Applying Ohm law with rms quantities
stem: A 44 ohm resistor is connected across a 220 V, 50 Hz AC supply. The rms current through it is
formula_principle: I_rms = V_rms / R for a pure resistor
common_misconception: Mixing rms voltage with peak current in the same Ohm law step.

concept_tested: Power factor equals unity for a purely resistive circuit
stem: The power factor of a purely resistive AC circuit is
solution: In a pure resistor the phase angle between voltage and current is zero, so power factor = cos(0) = 1.
formula_principle: Power factor = cos(phi) and phi = 0 for a resistor
common_misconception: Believing the power factor is always less than one in AC circuits.

concept_tested: Simultaneous maxima of current and voltage in a resistor
stem: In a purely resistive AC circuit, which statement is correct
option_a: The current attains its peak value a quarter cycle after the voltage does
option_b: The current and voltage attain their peak values at the same instant and become zero at the same instant
option_c: The current attains its peak value a quarter cycle before the voltage does
option_d: The current is maximum exactly when the voltage is zero
correct_answer_text: The current and voltage attain their peak values at the same instant and become zero at the same instant
solution: Because the current is proportional to the instantaneous voltage with no phase shift, both waveforms rise, peak, fall and cross zero together.
formula_principle: i = (e0 / R) sin(omega t) when e = e0 sin(omega t)
common_misconception: Assuming that current always lags voltage in any AC circuit.

concept_tested: Computing average power from rms voltage and resistance
stem: An AC source of rms voltage 100 V is connected across a 50 ohm resistor. The average power dissipated is
formula_principle: P_avg = V_rms^2 / R for a pure resistor
common_misconception: Applying the factor of one half twice, once through rms values and again explicitly.

concept_tested: Writing the current equation for a resistor across a given AC source
stem: An AC source e = 141.4 sin(314 t) volt is connected across a 20 ohm resistor. The instantaneous current is
solution: Peak voltage e0 = 141.4 V, so peak current I0 = 141.4 / 20 = 7.07 A. Since a resistor introduces no phase shift, i = 7.07 sin(314 t) A.
formula_principle: For a resistor i = (e0 / R) sin(omega t), with no phase difference
common_misconception: Adding a phase angle to a purely resistive circuit.

subtopic: Effect of frequency on a resistor
concept_tested: Independence of resistance from the frequency of the supply
stem: A resistor is connected to an AC source of fixed rms voltage. If the frequency of the source is doubled, the rms current through the resistor
option_a: remains unchanged, because resistance does not depend on frequency
option_b: becomes half, because the opposition doubles with frequency
option_c: becomes double, because the opposition halves with frequency
option_d: becomes four times, because power varies as the square of the frequency
correct_answer_text: remains unchanged, because resistance does not depend on frequency
solution: Since I_rms = V_rms / R and R does not contain omega, changing the frequency leaves the current unaltered.
formula_principle: R is a constant of the material and geometry, independent of omega
common_misconception: Extending the frequency dependence of reactance to ordinary resistance.

concept_tested: Comparing power for equal peak AC voltage and DC voltage
stem: A resistor connected to a 200 V DC source dissipates power P. The same resistor is now connected to an AC source whose peak voltage is 200 V. The power dissipated now is
solution: For DC, P = (200)^2 / R. For AC, V_rms = 200 / sqrt(2), so the power becomes (200)^2 / (2 R), which is exactly half of P.
formula_principle: P = V_rms^2 / R and V_rms = V0 / sqrt(2)
common_misconception: Comparing peak AC voltage directly with steady DC voltage.

concept_tested: Combining power calculation with the periodicity of instantaneous power
stem: A 100 ohm resistor is connected to a 220 V, 50 Hz AC supply. The average power consumed and the number of times per second at which the instantaneous power becomes zero are respectively
solution: P_avg = (220)^2 / 100 = 48400 / 100 = 484 W. The current is zero twice in each cycle, and with 50 cycles per second the instantaneous power becomes zero 2 x 50 = 100 times per second.
formula_principle: P_avg = V_rms^2 / R; instantaneous power p = i^2 R vanishes whenever i = 0
common_misconception: Forgetting that a sinusoid crosses zero twice per cycle when counting power zeros.

concept_tested: Relating average power to the product of peak voltage and peak current
stem: The peak voltage across a resistor is 100 V and the peak current through it is 2 A. The average power dissipated in the resistor is
solution: V_rms = 100 / sqrt(2) and I_rms = 2 / sqrt(2). Their product is (100 x 2) / 2 = 100 W, which is half the peak power of 200 W.
formula_principle: P_avg = V_rms x I_rms = (V0 / sqrt(2)) x (I0 / sqrt(2)) = V0 I0 / 2 for a resistor
common_misconception: Treating the product of peak voltage and peak current as the average power.

concept_tested: Computing X_L from omega and L
stem: An inductor of 0.1 H is connected to an AC source of angular frequency 100 rad/s. Its inductive reactance is
formula_principle: X_L = omega L
common_misconception: Confusing the inductive reactance omega L with the capacitive form 1 / (omega C).

concept_tested: Current lags the applied voltage by a quarter cycle in a pure inductor
stem: In a purely inductive AC circuit, the current
option_a: leads the applied voltage by pi/2 radian
option_b: is in phase with the applied voltage
option_c: lags behind the applied voltage by pi radian
option_d: lags behind the applied voltage by pi/2 radian
correct_answer_text: lags behind the applied voltage by pi/2 radian
solution: The self induced emf opposes the change of current, so the current builds up a quarter cycle behind the applied voltage. Hence the current lags the voltage by pi/2 radian.
formula_principle: For e = e0 sin(omega t) across L, i = (e0 / X_L) sin(omega t - pi/2)
common_misconception: Swapping the lead and lag behaviours of inductors and capacitors.

concept_tested: Inductive reactance vanishes at zero frequency
stem: An ideal inductor is connected to a steady DC source. Its inductive reactance is
option_a: infinite, because the inductor blocks steady current
option_b: zero, because X_L = omega L and omega is zero for DC
option_c: equal to L, because reactance equals inductance at zero frequency
option_d: equal to 1 / L, because reactance is inversely proportional to inductance
correct_answer_text: zero, because X_L = omega L and omega is zero for DC
solution: For steady DC the frequency is zero, so omega = 0 and X_L = 0 x L = 0. The inductor then offers only its ohmic resistance.
formula_principle: X_L = omega L = 2 pi f L, and f = 0 for steady DC
common_misconception: Interchanging the DC behaviour of inductors and capacitors.

concept_tested: Using X_L = 2 pi f L with numerical data
stem: A 0.5 H inductor is connected to a 50 Hz AC supply. Its inductive reactance is nearly (take pi = 3.14)
formula_principle: X_L = 2 pi f L
common_misconception: Dropping the factor 2 while converting frequency to angular frequency.

concept_tested: Ohm law analogue for a pure inductor
stem: A pure inductor of reactance 44 ohm is connected across a 220 V, 50 Hz supply. The rms current is
formula_principle: I_rms = V_rms / X_L
common_misconception: Using peak voltage with rms current in the same relation.

concept_tested: Current through an inductor when the supply frequency is doubled
stem: A pure inductor is connected to an AC source of constant rms voltage. If the frequency of the source is doubled, the current through the inductor
option_a: becomes double, because the reactance halves
option_b: becomes half, because the inductive reactance doubles
option_c: remains unchanged, because reactance is independent of frequency
option_d: becomes one fourth, because reactance varies as the square of frequency
correct_answer_text: becomes half, because the inductive reactance doubles
solution: Doubling f doubles X_L. Since I = V / X_L with V fixed, the current falls to half its earlier value.
formula_principle: X_L = 2 pi f L, so I = V / X_L is inversely proportional to f
common_misconception: Applying the capacitive frequency dependence to an inductor.

concept_tested: Comparing the opposition offered by a coil to DC and to AC
stem: A coil of negligible resistance carries a large current when connected to a DC source but a much smaller current when connected to an AC source of the same rms voltage. The reason is that
option_a: the resistance of the coil increases when AC is passed through it
option_b: the coil stores all the AC energy permanently and none of it flows
option_c: the coil offers inductive reactance omega L to AC but no reactance to steady DC
option_d: AC cannot pass through a coil of wire at all
correct_answer_text: the coil offers inductive reactance omega L to AC but no reactance to steady DC
solution: With steady DC the current is limited only by the small ohmic resistance. With AC the current is limited by omega L, which can be large, so the current is much smaller.
formula_principle: X_L = omega L is zero for DC and nonzero for AC
common_misconception: Thinking that the resistance of a wire itself changes when the source is changed.

concept_tested: Average power over a complete cycle in a pure inductor
stem: The average power consumed by a pure inductor over one complete cycle of AC is
option_a: V_rms x I_rms, the same as in a resistor
option_b: zero, since energy is stored and returned to the source in equal amounts
option_d: V_rms^2 divided by the inductive reactance
correct_answer_text: zero, since energy is stored and returned to the source in equal amounts
solution: Since cos(pi/2) = 0, the average power is zero. During one quarter cycle the inductor draws energy to build its magnetic field and during the next quarter cycle it returns exactly that energy to the source.
formula_principle: P_avg = V_rms I_rms cos(phi) with phi = pi/2 for a pure inductor
common_misconception: Assuming that a large current through an inductor must mean large power consumption.

concept_tested: Finding the peak voltage from the peak current and reactance
stem: A current i = 5 sin(100 t) ampere flows through a pure inductor of 0.2 H. The peak voltage across the inductor is
formula_principle: V0 = I0 X_L with X_L = omega L
common_misconception: Forgetting to multiply the inductance by the angular frequency before using it as a reactance.

concept_tested: Writing the instantaneous current including the lagging phase
stem: An AC source e = 100 sin(100 t) volt is connected across a pure inductor of 1 H. The instantaneous current is
solution: X_L = 100 x 1 = 100 ohm, so the peak current is 100 / 100 = 1 A. The current lags the voltage by pi/2, giving i = 1 sin(100 t - pi/2) A.
formula_principle: i = (e0 / X_L) sin(omega t - pi/2) with X_L = omega L
common_misconception: Writing the correct magnitude but the wrong sign for the phase angle.

concept_tested: Working back from measured current and voltage to the inductance
stem: A pure inductor draws 2 A when connected to a 200 V, 50 Hz supply. Its inductance is nearly (take pi = 3.14)
formula_principle: X_L = V_rms / I_rms and L = X_L / (2 pi f)
common_misconception: Reporting the reactance in ohm as though it were the inductance in henry.

subtopic: RMS current from a source equation
concept_tested: Extracting rms voltage and reactance from a given source equation
stem: An inductor of 0.1 H is connected across a source e = 220 sqrt(2) sin(100 pi t) volt. The rms current through it is nearly (take pi = 3.14)
solution: Here omega = 100 pi = 314 rad/s, so X_L = 314 x 0.1 = 31.4 ohm. The peak voltage is 220 sqrt(2), so V_rms = 220 V. Hence I_rms = 220 / 31.4 = 7.0 A.
formula_principle: X_L = omega L and I_rms = V_rms / X_L
common_misconception: Reading 100 pi as 100 and so underestimating the reactance by a factor of about 3.

concept_tested: Quarter cycle relationship between current and voltage maxima in an inductor
stem: In a pure inductor carrying alternating current, at the instant when the current is maximum, the voltage across the inductor is
option_a: zero, because the rate of change of current is zero at that instant
option_b: also maximum, because voltage and current peak together
option_c: half of its peak value, because the phase difference is 60 degrees
option_d: equal to the peak current multiplied by the inductance
correct_answer_text: zero, because the rate of change of current is zero at that instant
solution: At the peak of the current waveform the slope di/dt is zero, and since v = L di/dt, the voltage across the inductor is zero at that instant. This is exactly the quarter cycle phase difference expressed instant by instant.
formula_principle: v = L di/dt, so v is proportional to the slope of the current waveform
common_misconception: Assuming that the largest current must accompany the largest voltage.

subtopic: Instantaneous current at a given time
concept_tested: Combining reactance, phase lag and evaluation at a specified instant
stem: An AC source e = 20 sin(100 t) volt is connected across a pure inductor of 0.1 H. The instantaneous current at t = pi/600 second is
formula_principle: X_L = omega L, I0 = e0 / X_L, and i = I0 sin(omega t - pi/2)
common_misconception: Forgetting the phase lag term, which changes both the magnitude and the sign of the answer.

concept_tested: Computing X_C from omega and C
stem: A capacitor of 100 microF is connected to an AC source of angular frequency 100 rad/s. Its capacitive reactance is
formula_principle: X_C = 1 / (omega C)
common_misconception: Slipping by a power of ten while converting microfarad to farad.

concept_tested: Current leads the applied voltage by a quarter cycle in a pure capacitor
stem: In a purely capacitive AC circuit, the current
option_a: lags behind the applied voltage by pi/2 radian
option_b: leads the applied voltage by pi/2 radian
option_c: is in phase with the applied voltage
option_d: leads the applied voltage by pi/4 radian
correct_answer_text: leads the applied voltage by pi/2 radian
solution: The current into a capacitor is i = C dv/dt, so it is largest when the voltage is changing fastest, that is when the voltage is zero. The current therefore reaches its peak a quarter cycle before the voltage does.
formula_principle: For e = e0 sin(omega t) across C, i = (e0 / X_C) sin(omega t + pi/2)
common_misconception: Interchanging the lead of a capacitor with the lag of an inductor.

concept_tested: Capacitive reactance becomes infinite at zero frequency
stem: A capacitor is said to block direct current because
option_a: its reactance becomes zero at zero frequency
option_b: the dielectric between the plates conducts only alternating current
option_c: the charge on its plates keeps increasing without limit
option_d: its reactance 1 / (2 pi f C) becomes infinitely large as the frequency tends to zero
correct_answer_text: its reactance 1 / (2 pi f C) becomes infinitely large as the frequency tends to zero
solution: With f = 0 the denominator 2 pi f C vanishes and X_C becomes infinitely large, so no steady current can be maintained through the capacitor.
formula_principle: X_C = 1 / (2 pi f C), which tends to infinity as f tends to zero
common_misconception: Attributing the DC blocking property to conduction through the dielectric.

concept_tested: Variation of capacitive reactance with frequency
stem: As the frequency of the AC supply across a capacitor is increased, the capacitive reactance
option_a: increases, being directly proportional to the frequency
option_b: remains constant, being independent of frequency
option_c: decreases, being inversely proportional to the frequency
option_d: decreases, being inversely proportional to the square of the frequency
correct_answer_text: decreases, being inversely proportional to the frequency
solution: Since f appears in the denominator to the first power, doubling the frequency halves the capacitive reactance.
formula_principle: X_C = 1 / (2 pi f C)
common_misconception: Assuming both reactances change with frequency in the same direction.

concept_tested: Numerical evaluation of X_C for a small capacitance
stem: A 1 microF capacitor is connected to a 50 Hz AC supply. Its capacitive reactance is nearly (take pi = 3.14)
formula_principle: X_C = 1 / (2 pi f C)
common_misconception: Mishandling the 10^-6 factor for microfarad, which shifts the answer by powers of ten.

concept_tested: Ohm law analogue for a pure capacitor
stem: A pure capacitor of reactance 55 ohm is connected across a 220 V, 50 Hz supply. The rms current through it is
formula_principle: I_rms = V_rms / X_C
common_misconception: Using peak and rms values inconsistently in the same relation.

concept_tested: Average power over a complete cycle in a pure capacitor
stem: The average power consumed by an ideal capacitor connected to an AC source over one full cycle is
option_a: zero, because the energy stored while charging is returned while discharging
option_b: V_rms x I_rms, as in a resistor
option_d: V_rms^2 multiplied by the capacitive reactance
correct_answer_text: zero, because the energy stored while charging is returned while discharging
solution: Since cos(pi/2) = 0, the average power is zero. The capacitor takes energy from the source while charging and gives exactly that energy back while discharging in each half cycle.
formula_principle: P_avg = V_rms I_rms cos(phi) with phi = pi/2 for a pure capacitor
common_misconception: Believing that a capacitor dissipates energy the way a resistor does.

concept_tested: Writing the instantaneous current including the leading phase
stem: An AC source e = e0 sin(omega t) is applied across a pure capacitor C. The instantaneous current is
option_a: i = e0 omega C sin(omega t - pi/2)
option_b: i = e0 omega C sin(omega t + pi/2)
option_d: i = e0 omega C sin(omega t)
correct_answer_text: i = e0 omega C sin(omega t + pi/2)
solution: The peak current is e0 / X_C = e0 omega C, and the current leads the voltage by pi/2. Hence i = e0 omega C sin(omega t + pi/2).
formula_principle: i = (e0 / X_C) sin(omega t + pi/2) and 1 / X_C = omega C
common_misconception: Writing e0 / (omega C) for the peak current instead of e0 omega C.

subtopic: Combined change of frequency and capacitance
concept_tested: Effect on current when both frequency and capacitance are doubled
stem: A capacitor is connected to an AC source of fixed rms voltage. If both the frequency of the source and the capacitance are doubled, the rms current becomes
solution: Since I = V omega C, doubling omega doubles the current and doubling C doubles it again, giving four times the original current.
formula_principle: X_C = 1 / (omega C), so I = V omega C
common_misconception: Assuming that increasing capacitance opposes the effect of increasing frequency.

concept_tested: Identifying the SI unit of capacitive reactance
stem: The SI unit of the quantity 1 / (omega C) is
solution: Reactance is the ratio of an rms voltage to an rms current, so it carries the unit volt per ampere, that is ohm.
formula_principle: X_C = 1 / (omega C) is the opposition offered by a capacitor and is measured like resistance
common_misconception: Assuming that any expression containing C must carry the unit farad.

concept_tested: Working back from measured current and voltage to the capacitance
stem: A pure capacitor draws 5 A when connected to a 200 V, 50 Hz supply. Its capacitance is nearly (take pi = 3.14)
formula_principle: X_C = V_rms / I_rms and C = 1 / (2 pi f X_C)
common_misconception: Making a power of ten error when expressing the answer in microfarad.

subtopic: Capacitor in series with a lamp
concept_tested: Brightness of a lamp in series with a capacitor as frequency changes
stem: A lamp is connected in series with a capacitor across an AC source of fixed rms voltage. If the frequency of the source is increased, the lamp
option_a: glows dimmer, because the capacitive reactance rises with frequency
option_b: shows no change, because reactance does not affect the current
option_c: goes out completely, because the capacitor blocks high frequency current
option_d: glows brighter, because the capacitive reactance falls and the current rises
correct_answer_text: glows brighter, because the capacitive reactance falls and the current rises
solution: Raising the frequency lowers X_C, so the total opposition sqrt(R^2 + X_C^2) falls and the series current rises. Greater current through the lamp filament means greater brightness.
formula_principle: X_C = 1 / (2 pi f C) and the series current is I = V / sqrt(R^2 + X_C^2)
common_misconception: Applying the frequency behaviour of an inductor to a capacitor.

concept_tested: Relating peak charge to peak voltage across a capacitor
stem: An AC source e = 100 sin(100 t) volt is connected across a capacitor of 100 microF. The peak charge stored on the capacitor is
solution: C = 100 microF = 1 x 10^-4 F and V0 = 100 V. Hence q0 = 1 x 10^-4 x 100 = 0.01 C.
formula_principle: q0 = C V0 for a capacitor
common_misconception: Substituting the capacitance in microfarad without converting it to farad.

subtopic: Instantaneous current at a given time
concept_tested: Combining reactance, phase lead and evaluation at a specified instant
stem: A capacitor of 50 microF is connected across an AC source e = 200 sin(200 t) volt. The instantaneous current at t = pi/400 second is
solution: X_C = 1 / (200 x 50 x 10^-6) = 1 / 0.01 = 100 ohm, so I0 = 200 / 100 = 2 A and i = 2 sin(200 t + pi/2). At t = pi/400 s, 200 t = pi/2, so i = 2 sin(pi/2 + pi/2) = 2 sin(pi) = 0 A. At this instant the voltage is at its peak, so the current is momentarily zero.
formula_principle: X_C = 1 / (omega C), I0 = e0 / X_C, and i = I0 sin(omega t + pi/2)
common_misconception: Omitting the phase lead and so obtaining the peak current instead of zero.

concept_tested: Combining resistance and inductive reactance through the impedance triangle
stem: A series LR circuit has R = 3 ohm and X_L = 4 ohm. The impedance of the circuit is
formula_principle: Z = sqrt(R^2 + X_L^2)
common_misconception: Adding resistance and reactance like ordinary resistances in series.

concept_tested: Combining resistance and capacitive reactance through the impedance triangle
stem: A series CR circuit has R = 6 ohm and X_C = 8 ohm. The impedance of the circuit is
formula_principle: Z = sqrt(R^2 + X_C^2)
common_misconception: Treating reactance as an ordinary series resistance.

concept_tested: Sign and range of the phase angle in a series LR circuit
stem: In a series LR circuit connected to an AC source, the current
option_a: lags behind the applied voltage by an angle between 0 and pi/2
option_b: leads the applied voltage by an angle between 0 and pi/2
option_c: lags behind the applied voltage by exactly pi/2
option_d: is exactly in phase with the applied voltage
correct_answer_text: lags behind the applied voltage by an angle between 0 and pi/2
solution: Because both R and X_L are present, tan(phi) = X_L / R is a finite positive number, so phi lies strictly between 0 and pi/2 and the current lags the voltage.
formula_principle: tan(phi) = X_L / R, which is positive and finite for nonzero R and X_L
common_misconception: Assuming the presence of an inductor always gives a full quarter cycle lag.

concept_tested: Finding the rms current after computing impedance
stem: A series LR circuit with R = 3 ohm and X_L = 4 ohm is connected to a 100 V AC source. The rms current is
solution: Z = sqrt(9 + 16) = 5 ohm. Hence I = 100 / 5 = 20 A.
formula_principle: Z = sqrt(R^2 + X_L^2) and I = V / Z
common_misconception: Dividing by the arithmetic sum of R and X_L rather than by the impedance.

subtopic: Phase angle of an LR circuit
concept_tested: Computing the phase angle from the ratio of reactance to resistance
stem: In a series LR circuit R = 3 ohm and X_L = 4 ohm. The angle by which the current lags the applied voltage is nearly
solution: tan(phi) = 4 / 3 = 1.333, so phi = 53 degrees, with the current lagging the applied voltage.
formula_principle: tan(phi) = X_L / R
common_misconception: Inverting the ratio and quoting the complementary angle of 37 degrees.

subtopic: Phase angle of a CR circuit
concept_tested: Phase angle and its direction in a series CR circuit
stem: A series CR circuit has R = 6 ohm and X_C = 8 ohm. The phase relation between the current and the applied voltage is
option_a: the current lags the voltage by nearly 53 degrees
option_b: the current leads the voltage by nearly 37 degrees
option_c: the current leads the voltage by exactly 90 degrees
option_d: the current leads the voltage by nearly 53 degrees
correct_answer_text: the current leads the voltage by nearly 53 degrees
solution: tan(phi) = 8 / 6 = 1.333, so phi = 53 degrees. Since the circuit is capacitive, the current leads the applied voltage by this angle.
formula_principle: tan(phi) = X_C / R and the current leads in a capacitive circuit
common_misconception: Getting the magnitude of the phase angle right but the direction wrong.

concept_tested: Converting inductance to reactance before finding the current
stem: A coil of resistance 30 ohm and inductance 0.4/pi H is connected to a 200 V, 50 Hz AC supply. The current in the circuit is
formula_principle: X_L = 2 pi f L, Z = sqrt(R^2 + X_L^2), I = V / Z
common_misconception: Forgetting to convert the inductance into a reactance before combining it with the resistance.

concept_tested: Adding component voltages as perpendicular phasors
stem: In a series LR circuit the rms voltage across the resistor is 60 V and that across the inductor is 80 V. The rms voltage of the source is
formula_principle: V = sqrt(V_R^2 + V_L^2) because V_R and V_L are pi/2 apart in phase
common_misconception: Adding rms voltages of different circuit elements arithmetically as in a DC circuit.

concept_tested: How extra series resistance changes the phase angle of an LR circuit
stem: An additional resistance is connected in series with an inductor already carrying alternating current. The phase angle between the source voltage and the current
option_a: increases, because more elements always increase the phase difference
option_b: remains unchanged, because the phase angle depends only on the inductance
option_c: decreases, because tan(phi) = X_L / R falls when R increases
option_d: becomes exactly 90 degrees, because the circuit becomes purely inductive
correct_answer_text: decreases, because tan(phi) = X_L / R falls when R increases
solution: Increasing R with X_L fixed reduces the ratio X_L / R, hence phi becomes smaller and the circuit behaves more like a pure resistor.
formula_principle: tan(phi) = X_L / R
common_misconception: Assuming the phase angle depends on the inductance alone.

subtopic: Current and power factor in CR
concept_tested: Finding both current and power factor for a CR circuit
stem: A series CR circuit with R = 40 ohm and X_C = 30 ohm is connected to a 100 V AC source. The current and the power factor are respectively
solution: Z = sqrt(40^2 + 30^2) = sqrt(1600 + 900) = 50 ohm. Then I = 100 / 50 = 2 A and power factor = 40 / 50 = 0.8.
formula_principle: Z = sqrt(R^2 + X_C^2), I = V / Z, power factor = R / Z
common_misconception: Taking the ratio of reactance to impedance as the power factor.

concept_tested: Working back from measured current to the reactance of a coil
stem: A coil of resistance 6 ohm draws 10 A when connected to a 100 V AC source. The inductive reactance of the coil is
formula_principle: Z = V / I and X_L = sqrt(Z^2 - R^2)
common_misconception: Subtracting the resistance directly from the impedance instead of subtracting the squares.

concept_tested: Why measured component voltages can exceed the source voltage
stem: In a series LR circuit connected to a 100 V source, a voltmeter reads 80 V across the resistor and 60 V across the inductor, a total of 140 V. This is because
option_a: the two voltages are pi/2 out of phase and must be combined as perpendicular phasors, giving 100 V
option_b: one of the voltmeter readings must be faulty since voltages cannot exceed the source
option_c: the inductor generates extra emf that adds energy to the circuit
option_d: the voltmeter reads peak values across the inductor and rms values across the resistor
correct_answer_text: the two voltages are pi/2 out of phase and must be combined as perpendicular phasors, giving 100 V
solution: Since sqrt(80^2 + 60^2) = sqrt(6400 + 3600) = sqrt(10000) = 100 V, the readings are entirely consistent with a 100 V source. The arithmetic sum has no physical meaning because the two voltages peak at different instants.
formula_principle: V = sqrt(V_R^2 + V_L^2), not V_R + V_L
common_misconception: Expecting Kirchhoff voltage law to apply to rms values in the same way as to DC values.

subtopic: Coil tested with DC and AC
concept_tested: Separating resistance and reactance using DC and AC measurements
stem: A coil draws 4 A when connected to a 12 V DC source and 2.4 A when connected to a 12 V, 50 Hz AC source. The inductance of the coil is nearly (take pi = 3.14)
solution: With DC the reactance is zero, so R = 12 / 4 = 3 ohm. With AC, Z = 12 / 2.4 = 5 ohm, so X_L = sqrt(25 - 9) = 4 ohm. Hence L = 4 / (2 x 3.14 x 50) = 4 / 314 = 0.0127 H = 12.7 mH.
formula_principle: R = V_dc / I_dc, Z = V_ac / I_ac, X_L = sqrt(Z^2 - R^2), L = X_L / (2 pi f)
common_misconception: Using the AC impedance directly as the inductive reactance without removing the resistance.

subtopic: Full analysis of a CR circuit
concept_tested: Using component voltages to obtain current and then capacitance
stem: In a series CR circuit connected to a 50 V, 50 Hz source, the voltage across the 15 ohm resistor is 30 V and that across the capacitor is 40 V. The capacitance is nearly (take pi = 3.14)
solution: Check the phasor sum first: sqrt(30^2 + 40^2) = 50 V, matching the source. The current is I = 30 / 15 = 2 A. Then X_C = 40 / 2 = 20 ohm and C = 1 / (2 x 3.14 x 50 x 20) = 1 / 6280 = 1.59 x 10^-4 F = 159 microF.
formula_principle: I = V_R / R, X_C = V_C / I, C = 1 / (2 pi f X_C)
common_misconception: Finding the current from the capacitor voltage and the resistance, mixing quantities that belong to different elements.

concept_tested: Using the net reactance in the impedance formula
stem: A series LCR circuit has R = 3 ohm, X_L = 8 ohm and X_C = 4 ohm. The impedance of the circuit is
solution: Net reactance = 8 - 4 = 4 ohm. Then Z = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(9 + 16) = 5 ohm.
formula_principle: Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2)
common_misconception: Adding the two reactances instead of subtracting them, since they act in opposite senses.

concept_tested: Deciding whether a series LCR circuit is inductive or capacitive
stem: In a series LCR circuit the inductive reactance is greater than the capacitive reactance. The circuit is
option_a: inductive, with the current lagging behind the applied voltage
option_b: capacitive, with the current leading the applied voltage
option_c: purely resistive, with the current in phase with the applied voltage
option_d: inductive, with the current leading the applied voltage
correct_answer_text: inductive, with the current lagging behind the applied voltage
solution: With X_L greater than X_C the net reactance is inductive and tan(phi) is positive, so the current lags the applied voltage and the circuit is called inductive.
formula_principle: tan(phi) = (X_L - X_C) / R; a positive value means a lagging current
common_misconception: Naming the circuit after the element with the larger value rather than the larger reactance.

concept_tested: Correct expression for the phase angle of a series LCR circuit
stem: For a series LCR circuit, the phase angle phi between the applied voltage and the current is given by
solution: In the impedance triangle the base is R and the perpendicular is the net reactance X_L - X_C, so the tangent of the angle at the base is (X_L - X_C) / R.
formula_principle: tan(phi) = (X_L - X_C) / R from the impedance triangle
common_misconception: Placing the impedance rather than the resistance in the denominator of the tangent.

concept_tested: Combining V_R, V_L and V_C as phasors
stem: In a series LCR circuit the rms voltages are V_R = 40 V, V_L = 60 V and V_C = 30 V. The rms voltage of the source is
solution: Net reactive voltage = 60 - 30 = 30 V. Then V = sqrt(40^2 + 30^2) = sqrt(1600 + 900) = sqrt(2500) = 50 V.
formula_principle: V = sqrt(V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2)
common_misconception: Forgetting that V_L and V_C are exactly opposite in phase and so partly cancel.

subtopic: Current in a capacitive LCR circuit
concept_tested: Finding the current when the capacitive reactance dominates
stem: A series LCR circuit has R = 6 ohm, X_L = 10 ohm and X_C = 18 ohm and is connected to a 100 V source. The rms current is
solution: Net reactance = 10 - 18 = -8 ohm, whose magnitude is 8 ohm. Then Z = sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = 10 ohm and I = 100 / 10 = 10 A.
formula_principle: Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2) and I = V / Z
common_misconception: Worrying about the negative sign of the net reactance; only its magnitude enters the impedance.

concept_tested: Numerical phase angle when net reactance equals resistance
stem: A series LCR circuit has R = 10 ohm, X_L = 30 ohm and X_C = 20 ohm. The phase angle between the applied voltage and the current is
solution: Net reactance = 30 - 20 = 10 ohm, equal to R. Hence tan(phi) = 10 / 10 = 1 and phi = 45 degrees, with the current lagging since the net reactance is inductive.
formula_principle: tan(phi) = (X_L - X_C) / R
common_misconception: Getting the correct magnitude but misidentifying whether the current leads or lags.

concept_tested: Obtaining current and power factor from given reactances
stem: A series LCR circuit with R = 8 ohm, X_L = 16 ohm and X_C = 10 ohm is connected to a 200 V source. The current and power factor are respectively
solution: Net reactance = 16 - 10 = 6 ohm. Then Z = sqrt(8^2 + 6^2) = 10 ohm, so I = 200 / 10 = 20 A and power factor = 8 / 10 = 0.8.
formula_principle: Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2), I = V / Z, power factor = R / Z
common_misconception: Using the reactance rather than the resistance in the numerator of the power factor.

concept_tested: Relative phase of the voltages across the inductor and the capacitor
stem: In a series LCR circuit, the voltage across the inductor and the voltage across the capacitor are
option_d: opposite in phase, that is pi radian apart
correct_answer_text: opposite in phase, that is pi radian apart
solution: The same current flows through both elements. The inductor voltage leads that current by pi/2 and the capacitor voltage lags it by pi/2, so the two voltages are separated by pi radian and act in opposite directions in the phasor diagram.
formula_principle: V_L leads the common current by pi/2 while V_C lags it by pi/2
common_misconception: Assuming that because each is pi/2 from the current, they must be pi/2 from each other.

concept_tested: Identifying the phase behaviour when X_C exceeds X_L
stem: In a series LCR circuit the capacitive reactance is larger than the inductive reactance. Then
option_a: the current lags the applied voltage and the circuit behaves inductively
option_b: the current is in phase with the applied voltage
option_c: no current flows because the reactances cancel the source voltage
option_d: the current leads the applied voltage and the circuit behaves capacitively
correct_answer_text: the current leads the applied voltage and the circuit behaves capacitively
solution: With X_C greater than X_L the quantity X_L - X_C is negative, so phi is negative and the current leads the applied voltage. The circuit is then said to be capacitive.
formula_principle: tan(phi) = (X_L - X_C) / R; a negative value means a leading current
common_misconception: Judging the character of the circuit by the size of L and C rather than by their reactances.

concept_tested: Meaning of the net reactance of a series LCR circuit
stem: The net reactance of a series LCR circuit is
option_a: the difference X_L - X_C, since the two reactive voltages act in opposite senses
option_b: the sum X_L + X_C, since both oppose the current
option_c: the geometric mean sqrt(X_L X_C), since both are reactances
option_d: the larger of X_L and X_C, since the smaller one has no effect
correct_answer_text: the difference X_L - X_C, since the two reactive voltages act in opposite senses
solution: The inductor voltage leads the current by pi/2 and the capacitor voltage lags it by pi/2, so in the phasor diagram they point in opposite directions and their magnitudes subtract.
formula_principle: Net reactance X = X_L - X_C
common_misconception: Adding the two reactances because both are forms of opposition to current.

concept_tested: Recovering the source voltage from the three measured voltages
stem: In a series LCR circuit, voltmeters read 30 V across R, 80 V across L and 40 V across C. The rms voltage of the source is
solution: Net reactive voltage = 80 - 40 = 40 V. Then V = sqrt(30^2 + 40^2) = sqrt(900 + 1600) = sqrt(2500) = 50 V.
formula_principle: V = sqrt(V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2)
common_misconception: Applying the DC form of Kirchhoff voltage law to rms readings.

concept_tested: Behaviour of a capacitive LCR circuit as frequency is increased
stem: A series LCR circuit is operating at a frequency at which the capacitive reactance exceeds the inductive reactance. If the supply frequency is now slowly increased, the impedance of the circuit
option_a: first decreases, reaches a minimum equal to R, and then increases
option_b: increases continuously, since inductive reactance always grows with frequency
option_c: decreases continuously, since capacitive reactance always falls with frequency
option_d: remains unchanged, since the two reactances change by equal amounts
correct_answer_text: first decreases, reaches a minimum equal to R, and then increases
solution: Raising the frequency increases X_L and decreases X_C, so the magnitude of X_L - X_C first shrinks to zero at resonance, where Z = R, and then grows again as X_L overtakes X_C.
formula_principle: Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2), minimum when X_L = X_C
common_misconception: Tracking only one of the two reactances while ignoring the other.

concept_tested: Converting L and C to reactances before computing the current
stem: A series circuit of R = 30 ohm, L = 0.8 H and C = 250 microF is connected to a source e = 100 sqrt(2) sin(100 t) volt. The rms current is
solution: Here omega = 100 rad/s, so X_L = 100 x 0.8 = 80 ohm and X_C = 1 / (100 x 250 x 10^-6) = 1 / 0.025 = 40 ohm. Net reactance = 40 ohm, so Z = sqrt(30^2 + 40^2) = 50 ohm. The rms voltage is 100 V, hence I = 100 / 50 = 2 A.
formula_principle: X_L = omega L, X_C = 1 / (omega C), Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2), I = V_rms / Z
common_misconception: Using the peak source voltage with the impedance and calling the result an rms current.

concept_tested: Component voltage exceeding the source voltage
stem: A series LCR circuit with R = 40 ohm, X_L = 90 ohm and X_C = 60 ohm is connected to a 100 V source. The rms voltage across the inductor is
solution: Net reactance = 90 - 60 = 30 ohm, so Z = sqrt(40^2 + 30^2) = 50 ohm and I = 100 / 50 = 2 A. Then V_L = 2 x 90 = 180 V, which exceeds the source voltage because it is largely cancelled by V_C = 2 x 60 = 120 V. A check gives sqrt(80^2 + 60^2) = 100 V.
formula_principle: I = V / Z with Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2), then V_L = I X_L
common_misconception: Assuming that the voltage across any single element must be smaller than the supply voltage.

concept_tested: Working back from the power factor to the net reactance
stem: A series LCR circuit has R = 12 ohm and a power factor of 0.6. The magnitude of its net reactance is
solution: From cos(phi) = R / Z we get Z = 12 / 0.6 = 20 ohm. Then the net reactance is sqrt(20^2 - 12^2) = sqrt(400 - 144) = sqrt(256) = 16 ohm.
formula_principle: cos(phi) = R / Z, then X = sqrt(Z^2 - R^2)
common_misconception: Reporting the impedance in place of the reactance.

concept_tested: Finding current and source voltage from three voltmeter readings
stem: In a series LCR circuit the resistance is 5 ohm, and voltmeters read 15 V across R, 30 V across L and 10 V across C. The current in the circuit and the source voltage are respectively
solution: The current follows from the resistor alone: I = 15 / 5 = 3 A. Net reactive voltage = 30 - 10 = 20 V, so the source voltage is sqrt(15^2 + 20^2) = sqrt(225 + 400) = sqrt(625) = 25 V.
formula_principle: I = V_R / R and V = sqrt(V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2)
common_misconception: Using the inductor or capacitor reading with the resistance to find the current.

concept_tested: When Kirchhoff voltage law can be applied directly in AC circuits
stem: For a series LCR circuit driven by an alternating source, which statement is correct
option_a: The instantaneous voltages across R, L and C always add to the instantaneous source voltage, but their rms values do not add arithmetically
option_b: Both the instantaneous and the rms voltages add arithmetically to the source voltage
option_c: Neither the instantaneous nor the rms voltages satisfy any addition rule
option_d: The rms voltages add arithmetically but the instantaneous voltages do not
correct_answer_text: The instantaneous voltages across R, L and C always add to the instantaneous source voltage, but their rms values do not add arithmetically
solution: At any instant the sum v_R + v_L + v_C equals the source voltage, because Kirchhoff voltage law is an instantaneous statement. The rms values, however, describe waveforms that peak at different instants, so they combine as V = sqrt(V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2).
formula_principle: Kirchhoff voltage law holds instant by instant; rms values require phasor addition
common_misconception: Applying Kirchhoff voltage law directly to meter readings in an AC circuit.

concept_tested: Multi-step analysis leading to a large capacitor voltage
stem: A series LCR circuit has R = 60 ohm, X_L = 80 ohm and X_C = 160 ohm and is connected to a 200 V AC source. The rms voltage across the capacitor is
solution: Net reactance = 80 - 160 = -80 ohm, magnitude 80 ohm. Then Z = sqrt(60^2 + 80^2) = 100 ohm and I = 200 / 100 = 2 A. Hence V_C = 2 x 160 = 320 V. As a check, V_R = 120 V, V_L = 160 V and sqrt(120^2 + (320 - 160)^2) = sqrt(14400 + 25600) = 200 V.
formula_principle: Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2), I = V / Z, V_C = I X_C
common_misconception: Capping the capacitor voltage at the source voltage instead of computing it from I X_C.

concept_tested: Interpreting a circuit in which V_L and V_C are equal
stem: In a series LCR circuit connected to a 100 V AC source, the rms voltage across the inductor is 200 V and that across the capacitor is also 200 V. The rms voltage across the resistor is
option_a: zero, because the inductor and capacitor voltages have used up the whole source voltage
option_b: 500 V, because all three voltages must add up arithmetically
option_c: 283 V, because the three voltages must combine in quadrature
option_d: 100 V, and the circuit behaves as a purely resistive circuit
correct_answer_text: 100 V, and the circuit behaves as a purely resistive circuit
solution: Since V_L = V_C = 200 V, the term V_L - V_C is zero. Therefore V = V_R, giving V_R = 100 V. With the reactances equal the circuit is at resonance and the current is in phase with the applied voltage.
formula_principle: V = sqrt(V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2)
common_misconception: Believing that large reactive voltages must reduce the voltage available to the resistor.

concept_tested: Finding the combined voltage across the series L and C section
stem: A series LCR circuit with R = 9 ohm, X_L = 24 ohm and X_C = 12 ohm is connected to a 150 V AC source. The rms voltage across the series combination of L and C taken together is
solution: Net reactance = 24 - 12 = 12 ohm, so Z = sqrt(9^2 + 12^2) = sqrt(81 + 144) = 15 ohm and I = 150 / 15 = 10 A. The combined LC voltage is 10 x 12 = 120 V. As a check, V_R = 90 V and sqrt(90^2 + 120^2) = 150 V, matching the source.
formula_principle: Net reactance X = X_L - X_C, I = V / Z, V_LC = I x |X_L - X_C|
common_misconception: Adding V_L and V_C arithmetically instead of recognising that they are in opposition.

concept_tested: Equality of inductive and capacitive reactance at resonance
stem: A series LCR circuit is in resonance when
option_b: the inductive reactance equals the capacitive reactance
option_c: the resistance equals the inductive reactance
option_d: the capacitive reactance equals the resistance
correct_answer_text: the inductive reactance equals the capacitive reactance
solution: When omega L = 1 / (omega C) the two reactive voltages cancel exactly, the net reactance becomes zero and the impedance reduces to the resistance R.
formula_principle: At resonance X_L = X_C, so the net reactance vanishes
common_misconception: Equating the values of L and C instead of their reactances.

concept_tested: Expression for the resonant frequency of a series LCR circuit
stem: The resonant frequency of a series LCR circuit is given by
solution: Setting omega L equal to 1 / (omega C) gives omega^2 = 1 / (LC), so omega = 1 / sqrt(LC) and therefore f = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(LC)).
formula_principle: omega L = 1 / (omega C) gives omega = 1 / sqrt(LC) and f = omega / (2 pi)
common_misconception: Dropping the square root, which destroys the dimensional correctness of the formula.

concept_tested: Minimum impedance and maximum current at resonance
stem: At resonance in a series LCR circuit
option_a: the impedance is maximum and the current is minimum
option_b: the impedance is minimum and equal to R, and the current is maximum
option_c: the impedance is zero and the current is infinite
option_d: the impedance equals the inductive reactance and the current is maximum
correct_answer_text: the impedance is minimum and equal to R, and the current is maximum
solution: Since the net reactance vanishes at resonance, the impedance takes its smallest possible value R, and by I = V / Z the current takes its largest value V / R.
formula_principle: Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2); at resonance the bracket is zero so Z = R
common_misconception: Applying the parallel resonance behaviour of maximum impedance to a series circuit.

concept_tested: Why a series resonant circuit is called an acceptor circuit
stem: A series LCR circuit at resonance is called an acceptor circuit because
option_a: it rejects the signal at the resonant frequency and passes all others
option_b: it accepts energy continuously without returning any to the source
option_c: it offers least opposition and so accepts most strongly the signal at the resonant frequency
option_d: it accepts direct current and blocks alternating current
correct_answer_text: it offers least opposition and so accepts most strongly the signal at the resonant frequency
solution: Of all the frequencies present in a signal, the series circuit passes the resonant one with the largest current because its impedance is least there. It therefore selects or accepts that frequency.
formula_principle: At resonance Z = R is minimum, so current is maximum at that one frequency
common_misconception: Confusing the acceptor behaviour of series resonance with the rejector behaviour of parallel resonance.

concept_tested: Numerical evaluation of omega at resonance
stem: A series LCR circuit contains L = 2 H and C = 8 microF. Its resonant angular frequency is
solution: LC = 2 x 8 x 10^-6 = 1.6 x 10^-5. Then sqrt(LC) = 4 x 10^-3 and omega_r = 1 / (4 x 10^-3) = 250 rad/s.
formula_principle: omega_r = 1 / sqrt(LC)
common_misconception: Reporting the answer in hertz when the question asks for angular frequency.

subtopic: Capacitance for a given resonant frequency
concept_tested: Designing a circuit to resonate at a stated frequency
stem: A series circuit containing an inductance of 1 H is to resonate at 50 Hz. The required capacitance is nearly (take pi^2 = 9.87)
formula_principle: f = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(LC)) rearranged as C = 1 / (4 pi^2 f^2 L)
common_misconception: Forgetting to square the frequency when rearranging the resonance condition.

concept_tested: Computing the Q factor from L, C and R
stem: A series LCR circuit has L = 2 H, C = 8 microF and R = 10 ohm. Its quality factor is
formula_principle: Q = (1 / R) sqrt(L / C)
common_misconception: Forgetting to divide by the resistance, which is what makes Q depend on the circuit losses.

concept_tested: Value of the power factor at series resonance
stem: The power factor of a series LCR circuit at resonance is
option_a: 1, because the current is in phase with the applied voltage
option_b: 0, because the reactances cancel and no power is drawn
option_c: 0.707, because the phase angle is 45 degrees at resonance
option_d: 0.5, because the average power is half the apparent power
correct_answer_text: 1, because the current is in phase with the applied voltage
solution: At resonance the net reactance is zero so Z = R, giving power factor = R / R = 1. The phase angle is zero and the circuit behaves like a pure resistor.
formula_principle: Power factor = R / Z, and Z = R at resonance
common_misconception: Assuming that the cancellation of reactances also cancels the power drawn.

concept_tested: Dependence of the sharpness of resonance on resistance
stem: The sharpness of resonance of a series LCR circuit
option_a: increases as the resistance of the circuit is increased
option_b: depends only on the resonant frequency and not on the resistance
option_c: increases as the resistance of the circuit is reduced
option_d: is independent of the inductance of the circuit
correct_answer_text: increases as the resistance of the circuit is reduced
solution: A smaller R gives a larger quality factor and a narrower bandwidth R / L, so the current peak becomes taller and narrower, which is what is meant by a sharper resonance.
formula_principle: Q = omega_r L / R and bandwidth = R / L
common_misconception: Believing that adding resistance improves the frequency selectivity of the circuit.

concept_tested: Maximum current in a series LCR circuit at resonance
stem: A series LCR circuit with R = 20 ohm is connected to a 200 V AC source of adjustable frequency. The maximum current that can be obtained is
solution: The current is largest at resonance, where Z = R = 20 ohm. Hence I_max = 200 / 20 = 10 A.
formula_principle: At resonance Z = R, so I_max = V_rms / R
common_misconception: Trying to include reactance terms that have already cancelled at resonance.

concept_tested: Behaviour of V_L and V_C at resonance
stem: At resonance in a series LCR circuit, the voltages across the inductor and the capacitor
option_a: are both zero, since the reactances have cancelled
option_b: are equal in magnitude and in the same phase, so they add up
option_c: are equal in magnitude and opposite in phase, so their combined effect is zero
option_d: are unequal, with the inductor voltage always the larger
correct_answer_text: are equal in magnitude and opposite in phase, so their combined effect is zero
solution: The same current flows through both elements and the two reactances are equal, so V_L = V_C in magnitude. Since the two phasors point in opposite directions, their resultant is zero and the source voltage appears entirely across R.
formula_principle: V_L = I X_L and V_C = I X_C with X_L = X_C at resonance
common_misconception: Concluding that each reactive voltage is separately zero at resonance.

concept_tested: Computing the bandwidth of a series resonant circuit
stem: A series LCR circuit has R = 10 ohm and L = 2 H. Its bandwidth in angular frequency is
solution: Bandwidth = R / L = 10 / 2 = 5 rad/s. This is the width of the resonance curve between the two half power points.
formula_principle: Bandwidth in angular frequency = R / L
common_misconception: Inverting the ratio and quoting L / R, which is the time constant and not the bandwidth.

concept_tested: Large reactive voltage produced by a high Q circuit
stem: A series LCR circuit with R = 10 ohm, L = 1 H and C = 1 microF is driven at its resonant frequency by a 100 V source. The rms voltage across the inductor is
solution: omega_r = 1 / sqrt(1 x 10^-6) = 1000 rad/s, so X_L = 1000 x 1 = 1000 ohm. At resonance Z = R = 10 ohm, so I = 100 / 10 = 10 A. Hence V_L = 10 x 1000 = 10000 V. This is Q = 100 times the source voltage, and V_C is equally large and opposite.
formula_principle: omega_r = 1 / sqrt(LC), I = V / R at resonance, V_L = I omega_r L
common_misconception: Refusing to accept a component voltage far larger than the source voltage.

concept_tested: Application of series resonance in radio tuning
stem: The tuning circuit of a radio receiver uses a series LCR circuit with a variable capacitor. Tuning to a desired station works because
option_a: the capacitance is adjusted until the resonant frequency is far from the station frequency, so that only the station is amplified
option_b: increasing the capacitance always increases the resonant frequency and hence the selectivity
option_c: the capacitance is adjusted until the resonant frequency matches the station frequency, giving maximum current for that signal
option_d: the resistance of the circuit is adjusted to match the station frequency
correct_answer_text: the capacitance is adjusted until the resonant frequency matches the station frequency, giving maximum current for that signal
solution: All broadcast signals reach the aerial. Varying C changes f_r, and when f_r equals the frequency of the chosen station the impedance for that frequency drops to R, so that signal alone drives a large current while others are strongly attenuated.
formula_principle: f_r = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(LC)) and the current peaks at f_r
common_misconception: Thinking that tuning means moving the resonant frequency away from the signal frequency.

concept_tested: What changes and what does not when R is increased
stem: In a series LCR circuit the resistance is increased while L and C are kept unchanged. Then
option_a: both the resonant frequency and the peak current decrease
option_b: the resonant frequency is unchanged but the peak current and the sharpness both decrease
option_c: the resonant frequency increases while the peak current decreases
option_d: the resonant frequency is unchanged and the peak current also stays the same
correct_answer_text: the resonant frequency is unchanged but the peak current and the sharpness both decrease
solution: Resonance occurs when X_L = X_C, a condition involving only L and C, so f_r is unaffected. However the peak current V / R falls and the quality factor omega_r L / R falls, so the resonance curve becomes lower and broader.
formula_principle: f_r = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(LC)) is independent of R, while I_max = V / R and Q = omega_r L / R both depend on R
common_misconception: Assuming that any change in a circuit element must shift the resonant frequency.

concept_tested: Using the known reactances at one frequency to find resonance
stem: At a frequency of 50 Hz, a series LCR circuit has X_L = 10 ohm and X_C = 40 ohm. The circuit will resonate at a frequency of
solution: Let the resonant frequency be f_r and the given frequency f. At f_r, X_L (f_r / f) = X_C (f / f_r), so (f_r / f)^2 = X_C / X_L = 40 / 10 = 4. Hence f_r / f = 2 and f_r = 2 x 50 = 100 Hz. Check: at 100 Hz, X_L = 20 ohm and X_C = 20 ohm.
formula_principle: X_L is proportional to f and X_C is inversely proportional to f; at resonance they are equal
common_misconception: Taking the ratio of the reactances as the frequency ratio without extracting the square root.

concept_tested: Locating the two half power points around resonance
stem: A series LCR circuit has R = 10 ohm, L = 0.2 H and C = 20 microF. The two half power angular frequencies are nearly
solution: LC = 0.2 x 20 x 10^-6 = 4 x 10^-6, so sqrt(LC) = 2 x 10^-3 and the resonant angular frequency is omega_r = 500 rad/s. The bandwidth is R / L = 10 / 0.2 = 50 rad/s. In the narrow-band approximation the two half power points sit symmetrically at omega_r +/- R/(2L), that is 475 rad/s and 525 rad/s. The exact roots of the half power condition are [-R + sqrt(R^2 + 4L/C)]/(2L) and [R + sqrt(R^2 + 4L/C)]/(2L), which give 475.6 rad/s and 525.6 rad/s; the stem therefore asks for the values to the nearest whole number.
formula_principle: omega_r = 1 / sqrt(LC), bandwidth = R / L, half power points at omega_r +/- (bandwidth / 2)
common_misconception: Placing the half power points a full bandwidth away from resonance on each side.

subtopic: Designing for a given Q factor
concept_tested: Finding the resistance that gives a specified quality factor
stem: A series LCR circuit has L = 1 H and C = 25 microF. The resistance needed to give the circuit a quality factor of 10 is
solution: LC = 1 x 25 x 10^-6 = 2.5 x 10^-5, so sqrt(LC) = 5 x 10^-3 and omega_r = 200 rad/s. Then R = omega_r L / Q = (200 x 1) / 10 = 20 ohm. The same result follows from Q = (1 / R) sqrt(L / C) with sqrt(L / C) = 200.
formula_principle: omega_r = 1 / sqrt(LC) and Q = omega_r L / R, so R = omega_r L / Q
common_misconception: Multiplying by the quality factor instead of dividing by it when solving for R.

concept_tested: Definition of power factor in terms of R and Z
stem: The power factor of a series AC circuit is given by
solution: In the impedance triangle the resistance forms the base and the impedance the hypotenuse, so cos(phi) = R / Z. This factor multiplies V_rms I_rms to give the true average power.
formula_principle: Power factor = cos(phi) = R / Z
common_misconception: Using the sine of the phase angle in place of the cosine.

concept_tested: Meaning of the wattless component of current
stem: The wattless current in an AC circuit is
option_a: the component I cos(phi) of the current that is along the voltage phasor
option_b: the total current flowing when the circuit contains no resistance at all
option_c: the current that flows only during the first quarter of every cycle
option_d: the component I sin(phi) of the current that is perpendicular to the voltage phasor and consumes no average power
correct_answer_text: the component I sin(phi) of the current that is perpendicular to the voltage phasor and consumes no average power
solution: The perpendicular component I sin(phi) is a quarter cycle out of step with the voltage, so the power it carries is positive for half the time and negative for the other half, averaging to zero. It is therefore called the wattless current.
formula_principle: The current is resolved into I cos(phi) along V and I sin(phi) perpendicular to V
common_misconception: Identifying the wattless current with the in phase component.

concept_tested: Using P = V I cos(phi) with a given phase angle
stem: An AC circuit draws 5 A from a 200 V supply with the current lagging the voltage by 60 degrees. The average power consumed is
solution: cos(60 degrees) = 0.5, so P_avg = 200 x 5 x 0.5 = 500 W.
formula_principle: P_avg = V_rms I_rms cos(phi)
common_misconception: Reporting the product V I as the power, which is the apparent power in volt ampere.

subtopic: Power factor from R and Z
concept_tested: Numerical value of the power factor
stem: A series AC circuit has R = 3 ohm and impedance Z = 5 ohm. Its power factor is
solution: Power factor = 3 / 5 = 0.6.
formula_principle: Power factor = R / Z
common_misconception: Using the reactance instead of the resistance in the numerator.

concept_tested: Purpose and working of a choke coil
stem: A choke coil is used in a fluorescent tube circuit because
option_a: it reduces the current by converting the excess electrical energy into heat
option_b: it reduces the current using inductive reactance while consuming almost no power
option_c: it increases the current through the tube at the moment of starting
option_d: it converts the alternating supply into direct current for the tube
correct_answer_text: it reduces the current using inductive reactance while consuming almost no power
solution: The large inductive reactance limits the current, while the very small resistance makes the power factor nearly zero, so the average power V I cos(phi) dissipated in the choke is almost nil. A resistor doing the same job would waste large amounts of energy as heat.
formula_principle: A choke has large L and very small R, so its power factor R / Z is nearly zero
common_misconception: Assuming that any device limiting current must dissipate the corresponding energy.

concept_tested: Distinguishing apparent power from average power
stem: In an AC circuit, the product of the rms voltage and the rms current is called the apparent power. The true average power is
option_a: smaller than or equal to the apparent power, being the apparent power multiplied by cos(phi)
option_b: always exactly equal to the apparent power
option_c: always larger than the apparent power
option_d: equal to the apparent power multiplied by sin(phi)
correct_answer_text: smaller than or equal to the apparent power, being the apparent power multiplied by cos(phi)
solution: The power factor cos(phi) lies between 0 and 1, so the true power V I cos(phi) is at most equal to the apparent power V I, and equals it only when the phase angle is zero.
formula_principle: P_avg = V_rms I_rms cos(phi) while apparent power = V_rms I_rms
common_misconception: Treating the volt ampere rating of a device as its actual power consumption in watt.

concept_tested: Power factor for purely inductive and purely capacitive circuits
stem: The power factor of a circuit containing only a pure inductor, and that of a circuit containing only a pure capacitor, are respectively
solution: In a pure inductor the current lags the voltage by pi/2 and in a pure capacitor it leads by pi/2. In both cases cos(phi) = cos(pi/2) = 0, so neither element consumes average power.
formula_principle: Power factor = cos(phi), with phi = pi/2 for both pure L and pure C
common_misconception: Assuming that a lead and a lag must give power factors of opposite sign.

concept_tested: Computing average power from impedance and current
stem: A series LR circuit with R = 6 ohm and X_L = 8 ohm is connected to a 100 V AC source. The average power consumed is
solution: Z = sqrt(36 + 64) = 10 ohm, so I = 100 / 10 = 10 A. Then P = I^2 R = 100 x 6 = 600 W. The same follows from V I cos(phi) = 100 x 10 x 0.6 = 600 W.
formula_principle: Z = sqrt(R^2 + X_L^2), I = V / Z, P = I^2 R = V I cos(phi)
common_misconception: Including the reactance in the power calculation, although only resistance dissipates energy.

concept_tested: Computing the wattless component from the phase angle
stem: An AC circuit carries a current of 10 A with the current lagging the applied voltage by 60 degrees. The wattless component of the current is nearly
solution: sin(60 degrees) = 0.866, so the wattless component is 10 x 0.866 = 8.66 A. The power carrying component is 10 x cos(60 degrees) = 5 A.
formula_principle: Wattless current = I sin(phi)
common_misconception: Swapping the sine and cosine components of the current.

concept_tested: Deducing the power factor from wattmeter, voltmeter and ammeter readings
stem: A device connected to a 200 V AC supply draws 4 A and consumes 400 W. Its power factor is
solution: Apparent power = 200 x 4 = 800 VA. Hence cos(phi) = 400 / 800 = 0.5, corresponding to a phase angle of 60 degrees.
formula_principle: cos(phi) = P_avg / (V_rms I_rms)
common_misconception: Dividing apparent power by true power instead of the other way round.

concept_tested: Why a choke is preferred to a resistor for limiting AC current
stem: To reduce the current in an AC circuit, a choke coil is preferred to a resistor because
option_a: the choke limits the current only for direct current, which is safer
option_b: the choke limits the current with almost no dissipation, whereas a resistor wastes energy as heat
option_c: a resistor cannot reduce alternating current
option_d: the choke increases the power factor of the circuit towards unity
correct_answer_text: the choke limits the current with almost no dissipation, whereas a resistor wastes energy as heat
solution: A resistor limiting the same current dissipates I^2 R as heat. A choke of large reactance and negligible resistance limits the current equally well, but since its power factor is almost zero the average power it consumes is nearly zero, so the energy is returned to the source rather than lost.
formula_principle: P = I^2 R for a resistor, while for an ideal choke cos(phi) is nearly zero
common_misconception: Believing that a choke saves energy because it stores it permanently.

subtopic: Power in a series LCR circuit
concept_tested: Full power calculation for an LCR circuit
stem: A series LCR circuit with R = 30 ohm, X_L = 70 ohm and X_C = 30 ohm is connected to a 250 V AC source. The average power consumed is
solution: Net reactance = 70 - 30 = 40 ohm, so Z = sqrt(30^2 + 40^2) = 50 ohm and I = 250 / 50 = 5 A. The power factor is 30 / 50 = 0.6, so P = 250 x 5 x 0.6 = 750 W, which agrees with I^2 R = 25 x 30 = 750 W.
formula_principle: Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2), I = V / Z, P = I^2 R
common_misconception: Assuming that reactive elements share in the dissipation of power.

subtopic: Power consumed by a choke coil
concept_tested: Small but nonzero power in a real choke
stem: A choke coil of resistance 2 ohm draws 5 A when connected to a 200 V, 50 Hz supply. The power consumed by the coil is
solution: Z = 200 / 5 = 40 ohm, so the power factor is 2 / 40 = 0.05. The power is P = I^2 R = 25 x 2 = 50 W, which also equals V I cos(phi) = 200 x 5 x 0.05 = 50 W. The apparent power is 1000 VA, twenty times the true power.
formula_principle: Z = V / I, power factor = R / Z, P = I^2 R
common_misconception: Treating the volt ampere product of a choke as the power it actually consumes.

subtopic: Resistance and reactance from power data
concept_tested: Separating R and X of a coil from voltage, current and power readings
stem: A coil connected to a 100 V AC supply draws 5 A and consumes 300 W. The reactance of the coil is
solution: Z = 100 / 5 = 20 ohm. Since only the resistance dissipates power, R = P / I^2 = 300 / 25 = 12 ohm. Then X = sqrt(20^2 - 12^2) = sqrt(400 - 144) = sqrt(256) = 16 ohm. The power factor is 12 / 20 = 0.6.
formula_principle: Z = V / I, R = P / I^2, X = sqrt(Z^2 - R^2)
common_misconception: Subtracting resistance directly from impedance instead of using the impedance triangle.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Historical discovery of photoelectric emission
stem: The photoelectric effect was first observed as an accidental increase in spark discharge when the electrodes were illuminated. The scientist who first noticed this in 1887 was
option_b: Albert Einstein, who first observed the spark enhancement in his own discharge tube
option_c: J J Thomson, during his measurement of the charge to mass ratio
option_d: Max Planck, while studying black body radiation
solution: Hertz observed in 1887 that a spark jumped more readily across a gap when the negative electrode was illuminated by ultraviolet light. Hallwachs and Lenard studied it in detail; Einstein explained it in 1905.
formula_principle: Photoelectric emission: light incident on a metal ejects electrons.
common_misconception: Students credit Einstein with the discovery because he supplied the explanation.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Particles ejected in photoelectric emission
stem: In photoelectric emission from a metal surface, the particles ejected from the metal are
option_a: protons, since the metal nucleus is loosened by the incident light
option_b: photons of lower frequency re-emitted by the metal
option_d: neutral atoms of the metal evaporated by the light
solution: Light supplies energy to the loosely bound conduction electrons of the metal. If the energy exceeds the work function the electron escapes. The emitted particles carry negative charge and have the charge to mass ratio of the electron.
formula_principle: Photoelectrons are the free conduction electrons of the metal given energy by photons.
common_misconception: Students think 'photoelectrons' are a special particle different from ordinary electrons.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Role of the evacuated tube and collector plate
stem: In the standard photoelectric experiment the photosensitive plate and the collector are enclosed in an evacuated glass tube mainly because
option_a: air molecules would scatter and absorb the emitted electrons before they reach the collector
option_b: air would absorb all the incident light before it reaches the emitter plate
option_c: the vacuum increases the work function of the emitter so that emission becomes measurable
option_d: electrons cannot be accelerated by an electric field in the presence of a gas
correct_answer_text: air molecules would scatter and absorb the emitted electrons before they reach the collector
solution: Photoelectrons emitted with a few eV of kinetic energy would collide with gas molecules, lose energy and be deflected, so the measured current and stopping potential would not correspond to the emitted energies. Evacuation gives the electrons a free path.
formula_principle: Photoelectrons must travel from emitter to collector without collisions.
common_misconception: Students think the vacuum is needed to stop the light from being absorbed.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Dependence of photocurrent on intensity
stem: For monochromatic light of a fixed frequency above the threshold, the saturation photocurrent from a metal plate is doubled when
option_a: the frequency of the incident light is doubled at the same intensity
option_b: the accelerating potential of the collector is doubled beyond saturation
option_c: the intensity of the incident light is doubled, the frequency being unchanged
option_d: the wavelength of the incident light is doubled at the same intensity
correct_answer_text: the intensity of the incident light is doubled, the frequency being unchanged
solution: Each absorbed photon can release at most one electron. Doubling the intensity at fixed frequency doubles the number of photons arriving per second, so the number of photoelectrons per second and the saturation current both double.
formula_principle: Saturation current is proportional to the number of photons per second, hence to intensity.
common_misconception: Students link photocurrent to frequency instead of to intensity.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Time lag predicted by wave theory
stem: The classical wave theory of light fails to explain the photoelectric effect chiefly because it predicts that
option_a: no electrons should be emitted at all from a metal surface by light of any frequency
option_b: the photocurrent should be independent of the intensity of the incident light
option_c: a measurable time lag should occur before emission when the light is very feeble, whereas emission is observed to be practically instantaneous
option_d: the emission should stop when the accelerating potential is made zero
correct_answer_text: a measurable time lag should occur before emission when the light is very feeble, whereas emission is observed to be practically instantaneous
solution: On the wave picture a very dim source would take hours to deliver the work function to a single electron spread over an atomic area. Experiment shows emission within about 10^-9 s even for feeble light, because a single photon delivers its whole energy to one electron at once.
formula_principle: Wave theory spreads energy continuously over the wavefront, so a weak beam needs time to supply the work function.
common_misconception: Students say wave theory fails because it cannot explain the current, when in fact it fails on threshold frequency, instantaneous emission and the intensity independence of KE_max.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Existence of a threshold frequency
stem: Which observed feature of photoelectric emission is completely inexplicable on the wave theory of light?
option_a: The photocurrent increases when the intensity of the light is increased
option_b: The photocurrent saturates at a large positive collector potential
option_c: Emission does not occur below a certain frequency however intense the light is
option_d: The emitted electrons are negatively charged
correct_answer_text: Emission does not occur below a certain frequency however intense the light is
solution: On the wave picture, intensity controls the energy delivered, so a sufficiently intense low frequency beam should always eject electrons. Experimentally red light of any intensity gives no emission from a metal whose threshold lies in the ultraviolet, which requires the photon idea E = h nu.
formula_principle: Existence of threshold frequency nu_0 with W = h nu_0.
common_misconception: Students accept increasing intensity as the anomaly, but it is the frequency threshold that breaks the wave picture.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Effect of intensity on maximum kinetic energy
stem: Light of fixed frequency above the threshold falls on a metal. When the intensity of this light is increased four times, the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons
option_d: is reduced to one fourth of its original value
solution: KE_max is fixed by the energy of a single photon minus the work function. Increasing intensity increases the number of photons per second, hence the current, but not the energy h nu carried by each photon. So KE_max stays the same.
formula_principle: KE_max = h nu - W, independent of intensity.
common_misconception: Students confuse brightness with photon energy.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Effect of reversing the collector potential
stem: In a photoelectric experiment the collector plate is made increasingly negative with respect to the emitter. The photocurrent
option_a: increases steadily because the negative plate repels electrons towards the collector
option_b: stays at its saturation value until the potential is reversed completely
option_c: decreases and becomes zero at a definite negative potential
option_d: becomes negative, that is it reverses direction
correct_answer_text: decreases and becomes zero at a definite negative potential
solution: As the collector is made negative, electrons must climb a potential barrier of energy e V. Electrons with lower kinetic energy are turned back, so the current falls. At V = V_0 even the fastest electrons are stopped and the current is zero.
formula_principle: Retarding potential filters out electrons with kinetic energy less than e V.
common_misconception: Students expect a reverse current to appear beyond the stopping potential.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Photon absorption is a one to one process
stem: In photoelectric emission a single electron inside the metal
option_a: absorbs a fraction of the energy of each of many photons until it collects enough to escape
option_b: absorbs one whole photon and either escapes or gives the energy back to the lattice
option_c: absorbs several photons simultaneously in ordinary light so that low frequencies also work
option_d: is emitted only if it is a nuclear electron of the metal atom
correct_answer_text: absorbs one whole photon and either escapes or gives the energy back to the lattice
solution: The elementary photoelectric process is the absorption of one photon by one electron. The electron gains h nu at once. If h nu exceeds the work function W the electron can escape with kinetic energy up to h nu - W, otherwise the energy is shared with the lattice as heat.
formula_principle: Photon energy is delivered in a single indivisible quantum h nu.
common_misconception: Students believe several photons can pool their energy in an ordinary light beam.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Instantaneous nature of emission
