stem: Experiments show that photoelectric emission begins within about 10^-9 s of the light striking the surface, even for very feeble light. This shows that
option_a: the electrons in the metal move at speeds close to the speed of light before emission
option_b: the energy of the light is concentrated in localised quanta rather than spread over the wavefront
option_c: light travels with a very large speed so the wave reaches the plate quickly
option_d: the work function of every metal is extremely small, of the order of 10^-9 eV
correct_answer_text: the energy of the light is concentrated in localised quanta rather than spread over the wavefront
solution: If light energy were spread uniformly over the wavefront, a dim beam would need minutes or hours to supply a few eV to one electron. Because energy arrives as photons of energy h nu, a single absorption event immediately supplies the whole energy, so emission is essentially instantaneous.
formula_principle: Photon picture: energy arrives in packets, so absorption is a single instantaneous event.
common_misconception: Students attribute the promptness to the speed of light rather than to energy quantisation.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Purpose of the quartz window
stem: The photoelectric cell used to demonstrate emission with ultraviolet light is fitted with a quartz window instead of an ordinary glass window because
option_a: quartz has a much smaller work function than glass and so emits electrons itself
option_b: quartz can withstand the vacuum inside the tube whereas glass cannot
option_c: quartz slows the light down and so increases the energy of each photon
option_d: ordinary glass absorbs ultraviolet light strongly while quartz transmits it
correct_answer_text: ordinary glass absorbs ultraviolet light strongly while quartz transmits it
solution: Metals such as zinc have a threshold in the ultraviolet. Ordinary soda glass cuts off wavelengths shorter than about 350 nm, so the light that could cause emission would never reach the plate. Quartz is transparent well into the ultraviolet.
formula_principle: Photoelectric emission from most metals needs ultraviolet light, which must reach the emitter.
common_misconception: Students think the window material affects the work function of the emitter.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Which quantity does not change with intensity
stem: For a given emitter illuminated by monochromatic light, which of the following changes when only the intensity is increased?
option_a: The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons
option_b: The stopping potential of the emitted electrons
option_c: The threshold frequency of the emitter
option_d: The number of photoelectrons emitted per second
correct_answer_text: The number of photoelectrons emitted per second
solution: Intensity is the energy delivered per unit area per second, which at fixed frequency is proportional to the photon rate. More photons per second means more electrons per second. Energies per electron, and hence the stopping potential and the threshold, are untouched.
formula_principle: Intensity controls photon rate; frequency controls photon energy.
common_misconception: Students think a brighter beam gives faster electrons.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Wave theory prediction for maximum kinetic energy
stem: According to the classical wave theory of light, the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons should
option_a: depend only on the frequency of the incident light and not on its intensity
option_b: be zero for all frequencies below a threshold frequency
option_c: increase when the intensity of the incident light is increased
option_d: be exactly equal to h nu for every incident frequency
correct_answer_text: increase when the intensity of the incident light is increased
solution: In the wave picture the electric field of the wave drives the electron; a larger amplitude, that is a larger intensity, would give the electron more energy. Experiment shows KE_max is completely independent of intensity and grows linearly with frequency, which is what Einstein's equation gives.
formula_principle: Wave theory: energy absorbed grows with the amplitude squared, that is with intensity.
common_misconception: Students mix up the wave theory prediction with the observed result.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Effect of changing the emitter material
stem: Two different metals are illuminated in turn by the same monochromatic ultraviolet source of fixed intensity, and both emit photoelectrons. Compared with the metal of larger work function, the metal of smaller work function gives photoelectrons of
option_c: the same maximum kinetic energy since the light is the same
solution: With h nu fixed, KE_max = h nu - W is larger when W is smaller. The metal with the lower work function therefore releases faster electrons and shows a larger stopping potential.
formula_principle: KE_max = h nu - W.
common_misconception: Students assume the same light must give the same electron energy from any metal.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Saturation current
stem: In a photoelectric experiment the photocurrent becomes constant at large positive collector potential. This saturation occurs because
option_a: the emitter runs out of free electrons at that potential
option_b: every electron emitted from the plate is then collected, so no further increase is possible
option_c: the incident photons are all used up at that potential
option_d: the electric field becomes so strong that electrons are pushed back into the plate
correct_answer_text: every electron emitted from the plate is then collected, so no further increase is possible
solution: At small positive potential some slow electrons emitted sideways or backwards fail to reach the collector. As the potential rises, more of them are drawn in until all emitted electrons are collected. Then the current equals e times the number emitted per second and cannot rise further.
formula_principle: Saturation current equals the electronic charge times the emission rate.
common_misconception: Students think saturation means the source has been exhausted.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Photoelectric current with different frequencies at equal intensity
stem: Two monochromatic beams, one blue and one violet, both above the threshold, fall in turn on the same emitter with equal intensity. The saturation current is
option_a: larger for the violet beam because each violet photon carries more energy
option_b: larger for the blue beam because it delivers more photons per second at the same intensity
option_c: the same for both beams because the intensities are equal
option_d: zero for the blue beam because only violet light can cause emission
correct_answer_text: larger for the blue beam because it delivers more photons per second at the same intensity
solution: At equal power P, the photon rate is n = P / (h nu). Blue light has the smaller frequency, so h nu is smaller and n is larger. More photons per second give more photoelectrons per second and a larger saturation current, while the violet beam gives faster electrons and a larger stopping potential.
formula_principle: Number of photons per second n = P / (h nu); saturation current is proportional to n.
common_misconception: Students assume equal intensity means equal photon flux.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Distribution of photoelectron energies
stem: Photoelectrons emitted from a metal by monochromatic light have kinetic energies ranging from nearly zero up to a maximum value. The electrons with less than the maximum energy are those which
option_a: absorbed photons of smaller frequency present in the same monochromatic beam
option_b: came from deeper inside the metal and lost energy in collisions before escaping
option_c: absorbed only a part of the energy of the photon they met
option_d: were emitted after the light had been switched off
correct_answer_text: came from deeper inside the metal and lost energy in collisions before escaping
solution: All electrons absorb the same energy h nu. The most weakly bound electrons at the surface need only the work function W to escape, so they emerge with KE_max = h nu - W. Electrons from deeper layers must do extra work and suffer collisions, so they emerge with less, giving a continuous spread from zero up to KE_max.
formula_principle: KE_max corresponds to the most weakly bound surface electrons; deeper electrons lose energy.
common_misconception: Students think monochromatic light contains a spread of photon energies.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Combined statement evaluation
stem: Consider the statements: (i) the photoelectric current depends on the intensity of the light; (ii) the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons depends on the intensity of the light. Which is correct?
option_a: Statement (i) is true and statement (ii) is false
option_c: Statement (i) is false and statement (ii) is true
correct_answer_text: Statement (i) is true and statement (ii) is false
solution: Doubling the intensity at fixed frequency doubles the photon rate and hence the saturation current, so the first statement is correct. The energy given to each electron is h nu - W, which does not contain intensity, so the second statement is wrong.
formula_principle: Intensity controls current; frequency controls KE_max.
common_misconception: Students accept both statements because they associate 'more light' with 'more of everything'.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Work function as minimum energy for escape
stem: The work function of a metal is defined as the
option_a: average kinetic energy of the free electrons inside the metal at room temperature
option_b: minimum energy required to just free an electron from the metal surface
option_c: energy of the photon that produces the maximum photoelectric current
option_d: total energy of all the electrons emitted from unit area of the metal per second
correct_answer_text: minimum energy required to just free an electron from the metal surface
solution: The work function W is the least energy that must be supplied to a conduction electron at the Fermi level for it to escape from the surface with zero kinetic energy. It is characteristic of the metal and its surface condition and is usually a few eV.
formula_principle: W = h nu_0.
common_misconception: Students confuse the work function with the kinetic energy of the emitted electron.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Computing work function from threshold frequency
stem: The threshold frequency of a metal is 5 x 10^14 Hz. Taking h = 6.6 x 10^-34 J s and e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, the work function of the metal in eV is about
formula_principle: W = h nu_0.
common_misconception: Students forget to divide by the electronic charge when converting joule to eV.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Threshold wavelength from work function
stem: A metal has a work function of 2.48 eV. Using h c = 12400 eV angstrom, the threshold wavelength of the metal is about
solution: lambda_0 = h c / W = 12400 / 2.48 = 5000 angstrom. Light of wavelength shorter than 5000 angstrom, that is of higher frequency, will eject photoelectrons from this metal.
formula_principle: lambda_0 = h c / W.
common_misconception: Students invert the relation and multiply instead of divide.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Ordering metals by work function
stem: Caesium, sodium and platinum have work functions 2.14 eV, 2.75 eV and 5.65 eV respectively. Illuminated by the same light of photon energy 3.0 eV, photoemission occurs from
option_b: platinum only, because it has the largest work function
option_c: caesium only, because it alone has a work function below 2.5 eV
option_d: all three metals, since 3.0 eV is a fairly large photon energy
solution: Emission needs h nu greater than W. Here h nu = 3.0 eV, which exceeds 2.14 eV for caesium and 2.75 eV for sodium but falls well short of 5.65 eV for platinum. So caesium and sodium emit; platinum does not.
formula_principle: Emission occurs when photon energy h nu is greater than or equal to W.
common_misconception: Students think the metal with the largest work function emits most readily.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Threshold frequency from work function in eV
stem: The work function of a metal is 3.3 eV. Taking h = 6.6 x 10^-34 J s and e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, its threshold frequency is
formula_principle: nu_0 = W / h.
common_misconception: Students use the work function in eV without converting it to joule.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Effect of longer wavelength than threshold
stem: The threshold wavelength of a metal is 6200 angstrom. Light of wavelength 7000 angstrom of very high intensity is made to fall on it. Then
option_a: photoelectrons are emitted with very small kinetic energy because the intensity is high
option_b: photoelectrons are emitted after a long time lag when enough energy has accumulated
option_c: no photoelectrons are emitted at all
option_d: photoelectrons are emitted with kinetic energy equal to h c divided by 7000 angstrom
correct_answer_text: no photoelectrons are emitted at all
solution: Photon energy at 7000 angstrom is 12400 / 7000 = 1.77 eV, while the work function is 12400 / 6200 = 2.0 eV. Since 1.77 eV is less than 2.0 eV no electron can escape, no matter how many such photons arrive per second.
formula_principle: Emission requires lambda less than or equal to lambda_0.
common_misconception: Students believe a very intense beam can always cause emission.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Relation between work function and threshold wavelength
stem: Metal P has a larger threshold wavelength than metal Q. It follows that
option_a: the work function of P is smaller than that of Q
option_b: the work function of P is larger than that of Q
option_c: the threshold frequency of P is larger than that of Q
option_d: P and Q must have the same work function since both are metals
correct_answer_text: the work function of P is smaller than that of Q
solution: Since W = h c / lambda_0, a larger lambda_0 for P means a smaller W for P. Equivalently nu_0 = c / lambda_0 is smaller for P, so P responds to light of lower frequency and is the more sensitive photoemitter.
formula_principle: W = h c / lambda_0, so W is inversely proportional to lambda_0.
common_misconception: Students treat threshold wavelength as directly proportional to work function.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Units of work function
stem: The work function of a metal has the same dimensions as
option_a: power, because it involves the rate of emission of electrons
option_b: force, since it is the force binding the electron to the metal
option_c: electric potential, because it is often quoted in volts
solution: Planck constant has dimensions of energy times time, and frequency has dimensions of inverse time, so h nu_0 has the dimensions of energy, M L^2 T^-2. It is measured in joule or in electron volt.
formula_principle: W = h nu_0, which has the dimensions of Planck constant times frequency, that is energy.
common_misconception: Students see 'electron volt' and think the quantity is a potential difference.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Work function of a metal from threshold wavelength in nm
stem: The threshold wavelength for a certain metal is 620 nm. Using h c = 1240 eV nm, its work function is
solution: W = 1240 / 620 = 2 eV. So photons of energy greater than 2 eV, that is of wavelength shorter than 620 nm, can eject electrons from this metal.
formula_principle: W = h c / lambda_0.
common_misconception: Students forget the division and quote the constant itself.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Choosing a photocathode for visible light
stem: A photocell is to respond to ordinary visible light of wavelength about 550 nm. Using h c = 1240 eV nm, the photocathode material should have a work function of at most
solution: Photon energy at 550 nm is 1240 / 550 = 2.25 eV. For emission the work function must not exceed this, so a low work function material such as caesium coated antimony is used. Platinum with 5.65 eV would be useless in the visible region.
formula_principle: Emission requires W less than or equal to h c / lambda.
common_misconception: Students select a high work function metal thinking it is more sensitive.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Threshold and emission condition in terms of frequency
stem: Photoelectric emission from a metal of threshold frequency nu_0 occurs when the incident light has frequency nu such that
option_c: nu is less than nu_0 but the intensity is large
option_d: nu equals zero, that is for a steady electric field
solution: Each photon carries h nu. Escape needs at least W = h nu_0, that is nu greater than or equal to nu_0, with KE_max = h (nu - nu_0). Exactly at nu_0 an electron can just escape but with zero kinetic energy, so no measurable photocurrent is produced; observable emission therefore requires nu greater than nu_0, which is the condition asked for here.
formula_principle: Condition for emission: h nu greater than or equal to h nu_0 = W.
common_misconception: Students think a strong enough beam of low frequency light will eventually work.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Work function in joule from threshold wavelength
stem: The threshold wavelength of a metal is 4000 angstrom. Taking h = 6.6 x 10^-34 J s and c = 3 x 10^8 m s^-1, the work function of the metal in joule is
formula_principle: W = h c / lambda_0.
common_misconception: Students mis-convert angstrom to metre; 1 angstrom = 10^-10 m.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Same light on two metals with different work functions
stem: Light of wavelength 3100 angstrom falls in turn on metal X of work function 1 eV and metal Y of work function 2 eV. Using h c = 12400 eV angstrom, the ratio of the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons from X to that from Y is
solution: Photon energy = 12400 / 3100 = 4 eV. For X, KE_max = 4 - 1 = 3 eV. For Y, KE_max = 4 - 2 = 2 eV. The required ratio is therefore 3 : 2, which is quite different from the 1 : 2 ratio of the work functions.
formula_principle: KE_max = h c / lambda - W.
common_misconception: Students take the ratio of the work functions instead of the ratio of the kinetic energies.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Surface dependence of the work function
stem: The work function of a metal surface
option_a: depends on the nature of the metal and on the condition of its surface
option_b: depends only on the frequency of the light used to illuminate it
option_c: is the same for all metals since all metals contain free electrons
option_d: increases in proportion to the intensity of the incident light
correct_answer_text: depends on the nature of the metal and on the condition of its surface
solution: The work function measures how tightly the least bound electrons are held at the surface. It differs from metal to metal and is also sensitive to adsorbed layers, oxidation and surface roughness, which is why photocathodes are prepared and kept in vacuum.
formula_principle: W is a property of the emitting surface.
common_misconception: Students treat work function as a property of the light rather than of the metal.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Metal that will not respond to a given source
stem: A source emits photons of energy 1.8 eV. Which of the following metals will definitely not show photoelectric emission with this source? Work functions: caesium 2.14 eV, sodium 2.75 eV, potassium 2.30 eV, and a hypothetical metal Z of 1.5 eV
option_a: caesium, sodium and potassium all fail while Z emits
option_b: only sodium fails while the rest emit
option_c: all four metals emit because 1.8 eV is a visible photon
option_d: only Z fails while the other three emit
correct_answer_text: caesium, sodium and potassium all fail while Z emits
solution: Compare 1.8 eV with each work function. It is smaller than 2.14 eV, 2.75 eV and 2.30 eV, so caesium, sodium and potassium give no emission. It exceeds 1.5 eV, so metal Z emits with KE_max = 0.3 eV.
formula_principle: Emission requires photon energy greater than W.
common_misconception: Students compare in the wrong direction and pick the metals with the largest work function.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Work function from a stated threshold in nm and eV together
stem: For a metal the threshold wavelength is 300 nm. Using h c = 1240 eV nm, the least frequency of light that can cause emission is (c = 3 x 10^8 m s^-1)
solution: lambda_0 = 300 nm = 3 x 10^-7 m. nu_0 = c / lambda_0 = 3 x 10^8 / 3 x 10^-7 = 1 x 10^15 Hz. The corresponding work function is 1240 / 300 = 4.13 eV.
formula_principle: nu_0 = c / lambda_0.
common_misconception: Students mishandle the nm to m conversion; 1 nm = 10^-9 m.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Ratio of threshold wavelengths
stem: Two metals have work functions in the ratio 2 : 3. The ratio of their threshold wavelengths is
solution: Since lambda_0 W = h c is the same constant for both metals, lambda_1 / lambda_2 = W_2 / W_1 = 3 / 2. The metal with the smaller work function has the longer threshold wavelength.
formula_principle: lambda_0 = h c / W, so lambda_0 is inversely proportional to W.
common_misconception: Students carry the ratio straight through without inverting.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Threshold wavelengths deduced from two stopping potentials
stem: Light of wavelength 4000 angstrom gives a stopping potential of 1.1 V with metal P and 0.6 V with metal Q. Using h c = 12400 eV angstrom, the ratio of the threshold wavelength of P to that of Q is
solution: Photon energy = 12400 / 4000 = 3.1 eV. For P, W = 3.1 - 1.1 = 2.0 eV, so lambda_0 = 12400 / 2.0 = 6200 angstrom. For Q, W = 3.1 - 0.6 = 2.5 eV, so lambda_0 = 12400 / 2.5 = 4960 angstrom. The ratio is 6200 : 4960 = 5 : 4.
formula_principle: W = h c / lambda - e V_0 and lambda_0 = h c / W.
common_misconception: Students assume the ratio of threshold wavelengths equals the ratio of the stopping potentials.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Determining work function from two frequencies
stem: When light of frequency 6 x 10^14 Hz falls on a metal the photoelectrons have maximum kinetic energy 0.66 eV. Taking h = 6.6 x 10^-34 J s and e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, the threshold frequency of the metal is
formula_principle: h nu = W + KE_max, so nu_0 = nu - KE_max / h.
common_misconception: Students subtract an energy in eV from a frequency in Hz without dividing by h.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Metal with smaller work function under identical illumination
stem: Two metals M and N of work functions 2 eV and 4 eV are illuminated by the same light of photon energy 6 eV. The ratio of the maximum speeds of photoelectrons from M and from N is
solution: For M, KE_max = 6 - 2 = 4 eV. For N, KE_max = 6 - 4 = 2 eV. Since v_max is proportional to sqrt(KE_max), the ratio of speeds is sqrt(4) : sqrt(2) = 2 : sqrt(2) = sqrt(2) : 1, that is about 1.41 : 1.
formula_principle: KE_max = h nu - W and KE_max = (1/2) m v_max^2, so v_max is proportional to sqrt(KE_max).
common_misconception: Students forget that speed varies as the square root of kinetic energy.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Form of Einstein's photoelectric equation
stem: Einstein's photoelectric equation for a metal of work function W illuminated by light of frequency nu is
solution: A photon of energy h nu is absorbed by one electron. Part of this energy, W, is used in escaping from the surface, and the rest appears as kinetic energy. The most weakly bound electrons keep the largest share, so KE_max = h nu - W.
formula_principle: Conservation of energy for one photon and one electron.
common_misconception: Students write the work function with the wrong sign.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Maximum kinetic energy from wavelength and work function
stem: Light of wavelength 4000 angstrom falls on a metal of work function 2.1 eV. Using h c = 12400 eV angstrom, the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is
solution: Photon energy = 12400 / 4000 = 3.1 eV. Then KE_max = 3.1 - 2.1 = 1.0 eV. The corresponding stopping potential is 1.0 V.
formula_principle: KE_max = h c / lambda - W.
common_misconception: Students report the photon energy as the kinetic energy.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Doubling the frequency does not double KE_max
stem: Light of frequency nu, greater than the threshold frequency nu_0, gives photoelectrons of maximum kinetic energy K. If the frequency is doubled to 2 nu, the new maximum kinetic energy is
option_d: K, since the work function also doubles
solution: Originally K = h nu - W. At doubled frequency K' = h (2 nu) - W = 2 h nu - W = (h nu - W) + h nu = K + h nu. So the increase is exactly h nu, and K' is more than 2K because 2K = 2 h nu - 2W is smaller by W.
formula_principle: KE_max = h nu - W.
common_misconception: Students assume KE_max is directly proportional to frequency, forgetting the constant offset W.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Slope of the KE_max versus frequency graph
stem: For a photosensitive metal, the graph of maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons against the frequency of incident light is a straight line whose slope equals
option_a: the work function of the metal
option_d: the threshold frequency of the metal
solution: Comparing KE_max = h nu - W with y = m x + c, the slope m is h and the intercept c is -W. Since h is a universal constant, the graph is a straight line of the same slope for every metal; only the intercept shifts.
formula_principle: KE_max = h nu - W is of the form y = m x + c with m = h.
common_misconception: Students identify the slope with the work function.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Parallel lines for different metals
stem: The graphs of maximum kinetic energy against frequency of incident light are plotted for three different metals on the same axes. The three lines are
option_a: straight lines of different slopes meeting at a common point on the energy axis
option_b: three curves that bend upwards at high frequency
option_c: parallel straight lines cutting the frequency axis at different points
option_d: straight lines all passing through the origin
correct_answer_text: parallel straight lines cutting the frequency axis at different points
solution: Every metal obeys KE_max = h nu - W with the same h, so all lines have slope h and are parallel. The metal with the larger work function has its line shifted to the right, cutting the frequency axis at a larger nu_0 and the energy axis at a more negative -W.
formula_principle: KE_max = h nu - W with universal slope h and metal dependent intercept.
common_misconception: Students expect metals with larger work functions to give steeper lines.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Kinetic energy in joule
stem: Light of frequency 10^15 Hz falls on a metal of work function 3.3 eV. Taking h = 6.6 x 10^-34 J s and e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is
formula_principle: KE_max = h nu - W.
common_misconception: Students subtract 3.3 x 10^-19 J, forgetting to multiply the eV value by e.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Independence of KE_max from intensity
stem: In Einstein's photoelectric equation KE_max = h nu - W, the intensity of the incident light
option_a: appears hidden inside the symbol h, so KE_max grows with intensity
option_b: appears hidden inside W, so a brighter beam lowers the work function
option_c: appears as a multiplying factor on nu, so KE_max is proportional to intensity
option_d: does not appear at all, so KE_max is independent of intensity
correct_answer_text: does not appear at all, so KE_max is independent of intensity
solution: The equation involves only the photon energy h nu and the metal's work function W. Intensity determines how many such photons arrive per second, and so fixes the current, but the energy transaction for each individual electron is unchanged.
formula_principle: KE_max = h nu - W contains only frequency and work function.
common_misconception: Students look for an intensity term somewhere in the equation.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Maximum speed from wavelength and threshold wavelength
stem: Light of wavelength 2000 angstrom falls on a metal whose threshold wavelength is 4000 angstrom. Taking h c = 12400 eV angstrom, electron mass 9.1 x 10^-31 kg and e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, the maximum speed of the photoelectrons is about
formula_principle: W = h c / lambda_0, KE_max = h c / lambda - W and v_max = sqrt(2 KE_max / m).
common_misconception: Students use the full photon energy instead of the excess over the work function when finding the speed.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Intercept on the energy axis
stem: For a metal, the straight line graph of maximum kinetic energy against the frequency of incident light, extended backwards, cuts the kinetic energy axis at a value
option_b: h nu_0, a positive value equal to the work function
option_c: -W, the negative of the work function
option_d: zero, so the line passes through the origin
correct_answer_text: -W, the negative of the work function
solution: Setting nu = 0 in KE_max = h nu - W gives KE_max = -W. The extrapolated line therefore meets the vertical axis at -W. Physically no emission occurs for nu below nu_0, so this part of the line is only an extrapolation.
formula_principle: KE_max = h nu - W compared with y = m x + c.
common_misconception: Students expect the intercept to be positive.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Kinetic energy with hc shortcut in nm
stem: Ultraviolet light of wavelength 200 nm falls on a metal of work function 4.2 eV. Using h c = 1240 eV nm, the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is
solution: Photon energy = 1240 / 200 = 6.2 eV. KE_max = 6.2 - 4.2 = 2.0 eV, so the stopping potential for this arrangement would be 2.0 V.
formula_principle: KE_max = h c / lambda - W.
common_misconception: Students quote the photon energy instead of the excess over the work function.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Finding the work function from two data sets
stem: Photons of energy 5 eV eject electrons of maximum kinetic energy 3 eV from a metal. Photons of energy 7 eV incident on the same metal will eject electrons of maximum kinetic energy
solution: From the first case W = 5 - 3 = 2 eV. For the second case KE_max = 7 - 2 = 5 eV. Note that the kinetic energy rose by 2 eV, exactly the rise in photon energy, since W is unchanged.
formula_principle: KE_max = h nu - W with W fixed for the metal.
common_misconception: Students scale kinetic energy proportionally to photon energy, ignoring the fixed work function.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Change of KE_max with a given change of frequency
stem: When the frequency of the light incident on a photosensitive metal is increased by 2 x 10^14 Hz, the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons increases by (h = 6.6 x 10^-34 J s, e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C)
solution: Delta KE = h Delta nu = 6.6 x 10^-34 x 2 x 10^14 = 1.32 x 10^-19 J. In eV this is 1.32 x 10^-19 / 1.6 x 10^-19 = 0.825 eV. The work function cancels because it is unchanged.
formula_principle: Change in KE_max equals h times the change in frequency.
common_misconception: Students try to compute absolute kinetic energies although the work function is not given.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Same power at a wavelength that falls to the threshold
stem: Light of wavelength 3100 angstrom falls on a metal of work function 2.0 eV and a steady photocurrent flows. The source is replaced by one of wavelength 6200 angstrom delivering exactly the same power. Assume every incident photon of sufficient energy releases an electron and that a collecting field gathers all released electrons. Using h c = 12400 eV angstrom, the result is that
option_a: the saturation photocurrent doubles while the stopping potential falls to zero
option_b: the photocurrent falls practically to zero because the released electrons have no kinetic energy
option_c: the photocurrent is unchanged because the power delivered to the metal is unchanged
option_d: the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons doubles because the wavelength has doubled
correct_answer_text: the saturation photocurrent doubles while the stopping potential falls to zero
solution: At 3100 angstrom the photon energy is 12400 / 3100 = 4.0 eV, so KE_max = 4.0 - 2.0 = 2.0 eV. At 6200 angstrom the photon energy is 12400 / 6200 = 2.0 eV, exactly the work function, so KE_max = 0 and the stopping potential falls to zero. Photon energy has halved at the same power, so the photon rate doubles. Under the stated assumption that each sufficiently energetic photon releases an electron and all released electrons are collected, the saturation current follows the photon rate and therefore doubles. Note that maximum kinetic energy and emission rate are separate quantities: frequency fixes the former, intensity fixes the latter.
formula_principle: E = h c / lambda; emission needs E greater than or equal to W; photon rate n = P / E.
common_misconception: Confusing zero maximum kinetic energy at threshold with zero emission rate; under the stated model threshold photons still release electrons, which are then collected.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Work function from wavelength and kinetic energy
stem: Light of wavelength 2480 angstrom ejects photoelectrons of maximum kinetic energy 1.0 eV from a metal. Using h c = 12400 eV angstrom, the work function of the metal is
solution: Photon energy = 12400 / 2480 = 5.0 eV. W = 5.0 - 1.0 = 4.0 eV. The threshold wavelength is then 12400 / 4.0 = 3100 angstrom.
formula_principle: W = h c / lambda - KE_max.
common_misconception: Students add the kinetic energy rather than subtract it.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Reading the work function off a graph
stem: In a plot of maximum kinetic energy against frequency for a metal, the line meets the frequency axis at 6 x 10^14 Hz. Taking h = 6.6 x 10^-34 J s and e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, the work function of the metal is
solution: At the point where the line meets the frequency axis KE_max is zero, so nu = nu_0 = 6 x 10^14 Hz. Then W = h nu_0 = 6.6 x 10^-34 x 6 x 10^14 = 3.96 x 10^-19 J = 3.96 x 10^-19 / 1.6 x 10^-19 = 2.475 eV.
formula_principle: The intercept on the frequency axis is nu_0, and W = h nu_0.
common_misconception: Students read the frequency intercept but forget to convert the resulting energy to eV.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Ratio of kinetic energies for two wavelengths
stem: A metal of work function 2 eV is illuminated first by light of 4 eV photons and then by light of 6 eV photons. The maximum kinetic energies are in the ratio
solution: First case KE_max = 4 - 2 = 2 eV. Second case KE_max = 6 - 2 = 4 eV. The ratio is 2 : 4 = 1 : 2. The ratio of kinetic energies is not the ratio of photon energies because of the constant work function.
formula_principle: KE_max = h nu - W.
common_misconception: Students take the ratio of photon energies directly.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Emission with photon energy exactly equal to work function
stem: Light whose photon energy is exactly equal to the work function of a metal falls on it. Then
option_a: electrons are emitted with kinetic energy equal to the work function
option_b: electrons are just barely liberated with essentially zero kinetic energy
option_c: no electrons are emitted under any circumstances
option_d: electrons are emitted with kinetic energy equal to twice the work function
correct_answer_text: electrons are just barely liberated with essentially zero kinetic energy
solution: Setting h nu = W in KE_max = h nu - W gives KE_max = 0. The most weakly bound electrons reach the surface with just enough energy to escape and emerge with vanishing speed, so the stopping potential is zero and the current is extremely small.
formula_principle: KE_max = h nu - W, which is zero at nu = nu_0.
common_misconception: Students think the whole photon energy always appears as kinetic energy.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Multi step: wavelength, work function and speed
stem: Light of wavelength 3100 angstrom falls on a metal of work function 3.0 eV. Using h c = 12400 eV angstrom, electron mass 9.1 x 10^-31 kg and e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, the maximum speed of the photoelectrons is about
formula_principle: KE_max = h c / lambda - W and v_max = sqrt(2 KE_max / m).
common_misconception: Students use the photon energy rather than the excess energy when finding the speed.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Determining Planck constant from a graph
stem: The graph of maximum kinetic energy in joule against frequency in Hz for a metal is a straight line. Two points on it are (5 x 10^14 Hz, 0) and (10 x 10^14 Hz, 3.3 x 10^-19 J). The value of Planck constant obtained from this graph is
solution: Slope = (3.3 x 10^-19 - 0) / (10 x 10^14 - 5 x 10^14) = 3.3 x 10^-19 / 5 x 10^14 = 6.6 x 10^-34 J s. This is Planck constant. The intercept at 5 x 10^14 Hz is the threshold frequency, giving W = 3.3 x 10^-19 J.
formula_principle: Slope of the KE_max against nu graph equals h.
common_misconception: Students divide by the final frequency instead of by the frequency difference.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Why some electrons have less than KE_max
stem: Einstein's equation gives the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons rather than the kinetic energy of every electron because
option_a: the incident light always contains a range of frequencies
option_b: Planck constant has a small uncertainty in its measured value
option_c: some electrons absorb two photons and others only one
option_d: electrons from below the surface lose part of their energy before escaping
correct_answer_text: electrons from below the surface lose part of their energy before escaping
solution: The work function is the minimum energy for escape and applies to the least tightly bound electrons at the surface. Electrons originating deeper must expend extra energy in collisions with the lattice, so they emerge with less than h nu - W. The observed spectrum therefore extends from zero up to KE_max.
formula_principle: KE_max corresponds to electrons needing only the work function to escape.
common_misconception: Students believe every photoelectron emerges with exactly h nu - W.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Half the threshold wavelength
stem: The threshold wavelength of a metal is lambda_0. Light of wavelength lambda_0 / 2 falls on it. The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is
solution: Work function W = h c / lambda_0. Photon energy at lambda_0 / 2 is 2 h c / lambda_0. So KE_max = 2 h c / lambda_0 - h c / lambda_0 = h c / lambda_0, which equals the work function itself.
formula_principle: KE_max = h c / lambda - h c / lambda_0.
common_misconception: Students halve or double the wrong term in the difference.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Kinetic energy for one third of the threshold wavelength
stem: The work function of a metal corresponds to a threshold wavelength lambda_0. If light of wavelength lambda_0 / 3 falls on it, the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons expressed as a multiple of the work function is
solution: Photon energy at lambda_0 / 3 is 3 h c / lambda_0 = 3W. Hence KE_max = 3W - W = 2W. In general for wavelength lambda_0 / n the maximum kinetic energy is (n - 1) W.
formula_principle: KE_max = h c / lambda - W with W = h c / lambda_0.
common_misconception: Students report the photon energy as the kinetic energy, forgetting to subtract W.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Meaning of stopping potential
stem: The stopping potential in a photoelectric experiment is the
option_a: positive potential of the collector at which the photocurrent becomes saturated
option_b: least negative potential of the collector at which the photocurrent becomes zero
option_c: potential difference at which the emitter stops emitting electrons
option_d: potential energy of an electron at the surface of the emitter
correct_answer_text: least negative potential of the collector at which the photocurrent becomes zero
solution: As the collector is made more negative, electrons must overcome a retarding barrier. At V_0 even the fastest electron, of energy KE_max, is just turned back, so the current falls to zero. Hence e V_0 = KE_max.
formula_principle: e V_0 = KE_max.
common_misconception: Students confuse stopping potential with the potential at which the current saturates.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Stopping potential from kinetic energy in eV
stem: Photoelectrons ejected from a metal have maximum kinetic energy 1.6 x 10^-19 J. Taking e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, the stopping potential is
solution: V_0 = KE_max / e = 1.6 x 10^-19 / 1.6 x 10^-19 = 1 V. Whenever the maximum kinetic energy is expressed in eV, its numerical value equals the stopping potential in volt.
formula_principle: V_0 = KE_max / e.
common_misconception: Students forget that dividing an energy in joule by e gives a potential in volt.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Stopping potential unchanged by intensity
stem: In a photoelectric experiment the intensity of the incident monochromatic light is trebled while the frequency is kept fixed. The stopping potential
option_c: becomes one third of its earlier value
solution: Trebling the intensity trebles the number of photons per second, so the saturation current is trebled. Each photon still has energy h nu, so KE_max and hence V_0 = (h nu - W) / e are unchanged.
formula_principle: e V_0 = h nu - W, independent of intensity.
common_misconception: Students expect a brighter beam to need a larger retarding voltage.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Slope of the stopping potential versus frequency graph
stem: For a photosensitive metal, the graph of stopping potential against the frequency of incident light is a straight line of slope
solution: Dividing Einstein's equation by e gives V_0 = (h / e) nu - W / e. Comparing with y = m x + c, the slope is h / e, about 4.14 x 10^-15 V s, the same for every metal. Millikan used exactly this slope to measure h.
formula_principle: e V_0 = h nu - W, so V_0 = (h / e) nu - W / e.
common_misconception: Students quote h as the slope, forgetting the conversion from energy to potential.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Intercept of the V_0 versus nu graph on the potential axis
stem: The straight line graph of stopping potential against frequency for a metal, extrapolated to zero frequency, meets the potential axis at
solution: Putting nu = 0 in V_0 = (h / e) nu - W / e gives V_0 = -W / e. So the magnitude of the intercept on the potential axis multiplied by e gives the work function directly.
formula_principle: V_0 = (h / e) nu - W / e.
common_misconception: Students quote the work function itself rather than the work function divided by e.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Stopping potential from wavelength and work function
stem: Light of wavelength 2000 angstrom is incident on a metal of work function 4.2 eV. Using h c = 12400 eV angstrom, the stopping potential is
solution: Photon energy = 12400 / 2000 = 6.2 eV. KE_max = 6.2 - 4.2 = 2.0 eV, so V_0 = 2.0 V since a kinetic energy of n eV corresponds to a stopping potential of n volt.
formula_principle: e V_0 = h c / lambda - W.
common_misconception: Students confuse the photon energy in eV with the stopping potential in volt.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Increase of stopping potential with frequency
stem: In a photoelectric cell, the frequency of the incident light is increased while the intensity is kept constant. The stopping potential
option_b: remains constant because the intensity is unchanged
option_c: increases in proportion to the square of the frequency
solution: The equation is linear in nu with positive slope h / e, so V_0 rises steadily as the frequency rises. At constant intensity the photon rate actually falls slightly, so the saturation current falls even as V_0 rises.
formula_principle: V_0 = (h / e) nu - W / e.
common_misconception: Students believe stopping potential follows intensity.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Change in stopping potential with change in frequency
stem: The frequency of the light incident on a photocell is raised from 6 x 10^14 Hz to 8 x 10^14 Hz. Taking h = 6.6 x 10^-34 J s and e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, the stopping potential increases by
solution: Delta nu = 2 x 10^14 Hz. Delta V_0 = h Delta nu / e = (6.6 x 10^-34 x 2 x 10^14) / 1.6 x 10^-19 = 1.32 x 10^-19 / 1.6 x 10^-19 = 0.825 V. The work function cancels since it is unchanged.
formula_principle: Delta V_0 = h Delta nu / e.
common_misconception: Students use the absolute frequency instead of the frequency change.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Effect of intensity on the I against V curve
stem: Two current against collector voltage curves are drawn for the same emitter with the same monochromatic light at two different intensities. The two curves
option_a: saturate at the same current but cut the voltage axis at different negative potentials
option_b: are exactly the same curve since the frequency is the same
option_c: both pass through the origin with the same slope
option_d: saturate at different currents but meet the voltage axis at the same negative potential
correct_answer_text: saturate at different currents but meet the voltage axis at the same negative potential
solution: Higher intensity means more photoelectrons per second, so the curve saturates at a larger current. Since the frequency is the same for both, KE_max and hence the stopping potential are identical, so both curves reach zero current at the same negative voltage.
formula_principle: Saturation current is proportional to intensity; stopping potential depends only on frequency.
common_misconception: Students shift the stopping potential when they change the intensity.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Effect of frequency on the I against V curve
stem: Curves of photocurrent against collector voltage are drawn for the same emitter with two frequencies of light adjusted to give equal saturation currents. The curve for the higher frequency
option_b: cuts the voltage axis at a more negative potential
option_c: cuts the voltage axis at a less negative potential
option_d: does not reach zero current at any retarding potential
correct_answer_text: cuts the voltage axis at a more negative potential
solution: With saturation currents matched, the two curves rise to the same plateau. The higher frequency gives KE_max = h nu - W larger, so V_0 = KE_max / e is larger in magnitude and that curve reaches zero current at a more negative collector voltage.
formula_principle: e V_0 = h nu - W; saturation current depends on photon rate.
common_misconception: Students associate a more negative stopping potential with a larger current.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Predicting the stopping potential at a second wavelength
stem: For a certain metal, light of wavelength 4000 angstrom gives a stopping potential of 1.0 V. Using h c = 12400 eV angstrom, the stopping potential obtained from the same metal with light of wavelength 3100 angstrom is
solution: At 4000 angstrom the photon energy is 12400 / 4000 = 3.1 eV, so W = 3.1 - 1.0 = 2.1 eV. At 3100 angstrom the photon energy is 12400 / 3100 = 4.0 eV, so the new maximum kinetic energy is 4.0 - 2.1 = 1.9 eV and the stopping potential is 1.9 V.
formula_principle: e V_0 = h c / lambda - W, with W the same for both wavelengths.
common_misconception: Students scale the stopping potential in proportion to the photon energy, forgetting the fixed work function.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Work function from stopping potential and wavelength
stem: Light of wavelength 4960 angstrom produces a stopping potential of 0.5 V for a certain metal. Using h c = 12400 eV angstrom, the work function of the metal is
solution: Photon energy = 12400 / 4960 = 2.5 eV. The maximum kinetic energy is e V_0 = 0.5 eV. Hence W = 2.5 - 0.5 = 2.0 eV, giving a threshold wavelength of 12400 / 2.0 = 6200 angstrom.
formula_principle: W = h c / lambda - e V_0.
common_misconception: Students add the stopping potential energy instead of subtracting it.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Combined statement about stopping potential
stem: Consider two statements about the stopping potential V_0 in a photoelectric experiment: (i) V_0 depends on the frequency of the incident light; (ii) V_0 depends on the material of the emitter. Which is correct?
solution: The relation contains both nu and W. Raising the frequency raises V_0 at fixed metal; changing to a metal of larger work function lowers V_0 at fixed frequency. Only the intensity is absent from the relation.
formula_principle: V_0 = (h nu - W) / e.
common_misconception: Students remember that intensity is irrelevant and wrongly conclude the material is irrelevant too.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Determining h from the V_0 against nu graph
stem: In a Millikan type experiment the stopping potential is plotted against frequency and the slope of the straight line is found to be 4.125 x 10^-15 V s. Taking e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, the value of Planck constant is
solution: h = e x slope = 1.6 x 10^-19 x 4.125 x 10^-15 = 6.6 x 10^-34 J s. Millikan measured this slope for several metals and found the same value each time, confirming Einstein's equation and giving an independent determination of h.
formula_principle: Slope of V_0 against nu equals h / e, so h = e x slope.
common_misconception: Students divide by e instead of multiplying.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: What happens below the threshold
stem: Monochromatic light of frequency below the threshold frequency of a metal falls on it. The stopping potential measured for this metal is
option_a: negative and large, because the electrons come out very slowly
option_b: meaningless, because no photoelectrons are emitted at all
option_c: equal to W / e for that metal
option_d: equal to h nu / e for the incident light
correct_answer_text: meaningless, because no photoelectrons are emitted at all
solution: For nu less than nu_0 no photon carries enough energy to free an electron, so the photocurrent is zero at every collector voltage. There is no current to reduce to zero, so the stopping potential is not defined. The graph of V_0 against nu exists only for nu greater than nu_0.
formula_principle: Emission requires nu greater than or equal to nu_0; a measurable stopping potential exists only for nu greater than nu_0.
common_misconception: Students extrapolate the V_0 against nu line into the region below nu_0 and treat it as physical.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Work function deduced from two stopping potentials at nu and 2 nu
stem: The stopping potential for a metal is 1 V when light of frequency nu is used and 3 V when the frequency is doubled to 2 nu. The work function of the metal is
solution: Let the photon energy at frequency nu be E, in eV. Then 1 = E - W and 3 = 2E - W. Subtracting the first from the second gives 2 = E, so E = 2 eV. Substituting back, W = E - 1 = 2 - 1 = 1 eV. The threshold frequency is therefore half of nu.
formula_principle: e V_0 = h nu - W applied at two frequencies and solved simultaneously.
common_misconception: Students assume the stopping potential doubles when the frequency doubles, which would require a zero work function.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Stopping potential when wavelength is halved
stem: Light of wavelength lambda gives a stopping potential of 1 V for a metal of work function 2 eV. Using h c = 12400 eV angstrom, the stopping potential when light of wavelength lambda / 2 is used is
solution: Initially e V_0 = 1 eV, so h c / lambda = 1 + 2 = 3 eV. At wavelength lambda / 2 the photon energy is 6 eV. Then the new maximum kinetic energy is 6 - 2 = 4 eV, so the new stopping potential is 4 V.
formula_principle: e V_0 = h c / lambda - W.
common_misconception: Students simply double the stopping potential when the wavelength is halved.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Choosing the retarding supply
stem: A photocell using a cathode of work function 1.9 eV is illuminated by light of wavelength 3100 angstrom (h c = 12400 eV angstrom). To ensure that no photocurrent flows, the collector must be held at a potential of at least
option_a: 2.1 V negative with respect to the cathode
option_b: 4.0 V negative with respect to the cathode
option_c: 1.9 V negative with respect to the cathode
option_d: 2.1 V positive with respect to the cathode
correct_answer_text: 2.1 V negative with respect to the cathode
solution: Photon energy = 12400 / 3100 = 4.0 eV. KE_max = 4.0 - 1.9 = 2.1 eV. The retarding voltage must therefore be at least 2.1 V with the collector negative; any smaller magnitude leaves the fastest electrons still able to cross.
formula_principle: e V_0 = h c / lambda - W and the collector must be negative.
common_misconception: Students give the correct magnitude but the wrong sign of the applied potential.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Photon has zero rest mass
stem: The rest mass of a photon is
option_a: equal to the rest mass of an electron
option_b: equal to h nu / c, which is its momentum divided by c
option_c: infinite, since it moves at the speed of light
option_d: zero, which is why it can travel with the speed of light
correct_answer_text: zero, which is why it can travel with the speed of light
solution: A photon always travels at c in vacuum. Relativistic mechanics allows this only for particles of zero rest mass. Its energy is E = h nu and its momentum p = E / c = h / lambda, consistent with the relation E^2 = p^2 c^2 + m_0^2 c^4 with m_0 = 0.
formula_principle: Relativity requires zero rest mass for a particle moving at c.
common_misconception: Students quote the effective mass h nu / c^2 as the rest mass.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Photon energy from wavelength
stem: Using h c = 12400 eV angstrom, the energy of a photon of wavelength 6200 angstrom is
solution: E = 12400 / 6200 = 2 eV. Red light near 6200 angstrom therefore carries about 2 eV per photon, which is why only low work function metals such as caesium respond to it.
formula_principle: E = h c / lambda.
common_misconception: Students invert the relation between energy and wavelength.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Photon momentum from wavelength
stem: The momentum of a photon of wavelength 6.6 x 10^-7 m, taking h = 6.6 x 10^-34 J s, is
solution: p = h / lambda = 6.6 x 10^-34 / 6.6 x 10^-7 = 1 x 10^-27 kg m s^-1. Equivalently p = E / c, since a photon of this wavelength has energy 3 x 10^-19 J and 3 x 10^-19 / 3 x 10^8 gives the same result.
formula_principle: p = h / lambda.
common_misconception: Students multiply instead of dividing, or attach an energy unit to a momentum.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Photon emission rate of a lamp
stem: A monochromatic source emits 20 W of light of photon energy 4 x 10^-19 J. The number of photons emitted per second is
solution: n = P / E = 20 / (4 x 10^-19) = 5 x 10^19 photons per second. The very large number explains why the granular nature of light is not apparent in everyday experience.
formula_principle: n = P / E, where E is the energy per photon.
common_misconception: Students multiply power by photon energy instead of dividing.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Photon energy in joule from frequency
stem: The energy of a photon of frequency 5 x 10^14 Hz, taking h = 6.6 x 10^-34 J s, is
solution: E = h nu = 6.6 x 10^-34 x 5 x 10^14 = 3.3 x 10^-19 J. Dividing by 1.6 x 10^-19 gives 2.06 eV, which lies in the visible region.
formula_principle: E = h nu.
common_misconception: Students confuse the values in joule and in eV.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Relation between photon energy and momentum
stem: For a photon, the relation between energy E and momentum p is
solution: E = h nu = h c / lambda and p = h / lambda. Dividing, E / p = c, so E = p c. This is the massless limit of the relativistic relation E^2 = p^2 c^2 + m_0^2 c^4.
formula_principle: E = h nu and p = h / lambda with c = nu lambda.
common_misconception: Students apply the classical E = p^2 / (2 m) to the photon.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Photon rate for a laser of given wavelength
stem: A laser of power 3.3 mW emits light of wavelength 6000 angstrom. Using h = 6.6 x 10^-34 J s and c = 3 x 10^8 m s^-1, the number of photons emitted per second is about
solution: Energy per photon = h c / lambda = (6.6 x 10^-34 x 3 x 10^8) / (6 x 10^-7) = 3.3 x 10^-19 J. Then n = P / E = 3.3 x 10^-3 / 3.3 x 10^-19 = 1 x 10^16 photons per second.
formula_principle: n = P lambda / (h c).
common_misconception: Students mishandle the milliwatt to watt conversion.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Effect of entering a denser medium
stem: A beam of light passes from vacuum into glass. The energy of each photon in the glass, compared with its value in vacuum,
option_a: decreases because the speed of light in glass is smaller
option_b: increases because the wavelength in glass is smaller
option_c: stays the same because the frequency does not change
option_d: becomes zero because the photon is absorbed by the glass
correct_answer_text: stays the same because the frequency does not change
solution: On entering a medium the frequency is fixed by the source and does not change; the speed falls to c / n and the wavelength shortens to lambda / n. Since E = h nu, the photon energy is unaltered. The momentum in the medium is h / (lambda / n), which does change.
formula_principle: E = h nu, and nu is unchanged on refraction while lambda and v change.
common_misconception: Students use E = h c / lambda with the shortened wavelength and the vacuum value of c.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Ratio of energies and momenta of two photons
stem: Two photons have wavelengths in the ratio 1 : 2. The ratio of their momenta is
solution: Since p is inversely proportional to lambda, p_1 / p_2 = lambda_2 / lambda_1 = 2 / 1. The shorter wavelength photon carries the larger momentum, and by E = p c also the larger energy.
formula_principle: p = h / lambda.
common_misconception: Students carry the wavelength ratio through unchanged.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Behaviour of a photon in an electric field
stem: A narrow beam of light is passed through a region of strong uniform electric field. The beam is
option_a: deflected towards the positive plate, because photons behave as negative particles
option_b: deflected towards the negative plate, because photons carry positive charge
option_c: stopped completely, because the field does work against the photon momentum
option_d: undeviated, because the photon carries no electric charge
correct_answer_text: undeviated, because the photon carries no electric charge
solution: The photon is a chargeless quantum of the electromagnetic field. Since the electric force is q E and q = 0, no deflection occurs. This is one way to distinguish a beam of photons from a beam of electrons, which would be strongly deflected.
formula_principle: Photons are electrically neutral, so electric and magnetic fields exert no force on them.
common_misconception: Students assign a charge to the photon because it is associated with electromagnetic waves.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Comparing photon energies across the spectrum
stem: Among X ray photons, visible light photons and radio wave photons, the ordering by energy from largest to smallest is
option_d: all three are equal since all are electromagnetic waves
solution: X rays have the highest frequency and shortest wavelength, so their photons carry the largest energy, typically thousands of eV. Visible photons carry a few eV. Radio photons, with wavelengths of metres, carry only about 10^-6 eV.
formula_principle: E = h nu = h c / lambda.
common_misconception: Students order the spectrum by wavelength and forget the inverse relation to energy.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Photons falling on a surface per second
stem: Light of wavelength 5000 angstrom and intensity 2 W m^-2 falls normally on a surface of area 1 cm^2. Using h c = 12400 eV angstrom and e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, the number of photons striking the surface per second is about
solution: Power on the surface = 2 x 10^-4 W. Energy per photon = 12400 / 5000 = 2.48 eV = 2.48 x 1.6 x 10^-19 = 3.97 x 10^-19 J. So n = 2 x 10^-4 / 3.97 x 10^-19 = 5.0 x 10^14 photons per second.
formula_principle: n = P / E with P = intensity x area and E = h c / lambda.
common_misconception: Students forget that 1 cm^2 equals 10^-4 m^2.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Radiation pressure idea from photon momentum
stem: A photon of wavelength lambda strikes a perfectly reflecting surface normally and bounces straight back. The magnitude of the momentum transferred to the surface is
option_b: zero, because the photon has no rest mass
solution: Incoming momentum is +h / lambda and outgoing is -h / lambda, so the photon's momentum changes by 2h / lambda. By conservation of momentum the surface receives 2h / lambda. For an absorbing surface the transfer would be only h / lambda, which is why a mirror feels twice the radiation pressure of a black surface.
formula_principle: p = h / lambda; on reflection the momentum reverses, so the change is 2p.
common_misconception: Students forget the reversal of direction and use h / lambda.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Force exerted by a beam on an absorbing surface
stem: A parallel laser beam of power 3.3 W and wavelength 6600 angstrom falls normally on a perfectly absorbing black surface. Taking h = 6.6 x 10^-34 J s and c = 3 x 10^8 m s^-1, the force exerted on the surface is
solution: Energy per photon = h c / lambda = (6.6 x 10^-34 x 3 x 10^8) / (6.6 x 10^-7) = 3.0 x 10^-19 J, so n = 3.3 / 3.0 x 10^-19 = 1.1 x 10^19 photons per second. Momentum per photon = h / lambda = 6.6 x 10^-34 / 6.6 x 10^-7 = 1.0 x 10^-27 kg m s^-1. Force = n x p = 1.1 x 10^19 x 1.0 x 10^-27 = 1.1 x 10^-8 N, which is just P / c = 3.3 / 3 x 10^8.
formula_principle: n = P lambda / (h c), p = h / lambda, force F = n p = P / c for full absorption.
common_misconception: Students apply the reflecting surface factor of two to an absorbing surface.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Two beams of equal power but different colour
stem: Two beams of equal power, one of red light and one of blue light, fall on identical detectors. Compared with the red beam, the blue beam delivers
option_a: more photons per second, each of larger energy
option_b: fewer photons per second, each of larger energy
option_c: fewer photons per second, each of smaller energy
option_d: the same number of photons per second with the same energy each
correct_answer_text: fewer photons per second, each of larger energy
solution: Blue light has the higher frequency, so each blue photon carries more energy. Since the power P = n h nu is the same for both beams, n = P / (h nu) is smaller for the blue beam. Equal power means equal energy per second shared among fewer, more energetic packets.
formula_principle: P = n h nu, so at fixed P, n is inversely proportional to nu.
common_misconception: Students think the more energetic beam must also deliver more photons.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Effective mass of a photon
stem: The effective mass associated with a photon of frequency nu, obtained from its energy through E = m c^2, is
solution: Setting h nu = m c^2 gives m = h nu / c^2. This is a dynamic or effective mass reflecting the photon's energy content; the rest mass of the photon remains exactly zero. Note also p = m c = h nu / c = h / lambda, which is consistent.
formula_principle: E = h nu equated with E = m c^2 gives m = h nu / c^2.
common_misconception: Students confuse the effective mass with the momentum, which differs by one factor of c.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: de Broglie wavelength formula
stem: According to de Broglie, a particle of mass m moving with speed v is associated with a wave of wavelength
solution: de Broglie extended the photon relation p = h / lambda to material particles, proposing lambda = h / p. For a particle of mass m and speed v this is lambda = h / (m v). Larger momentum means shorter wavelength.
formula_principle: lambda = h / p = h / (m v).
common_misconception: Students invert the relation and write m v / h.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Heavier particle at the same speed
stem: A proton and an electron move with the same speed. Compared with the electron, the de Broglie wavelength of the proton is
option_a: much longer, because the proton is heavier
option_b: exactly the same, because both move with the same speed
option_c: zero, because a proton is a composite particle
option_d: much shorter, because the proton has much larger momentum
correct_answer_text: much shorter, because the proton has much larger momentum
solution: At the same speed, lambda_proton / lambda_electron = m_electron / m_proton, about 1 / 1836. The proton wave is therefore about 1836 times shorter. A heavier particle at the same speed always has the shorter de Broglie wavelength.
formula_principle: lambda = h / (m v); at fixed v, lambda is inversely proportional to m.
common_misconception: Students associate a heavier particle with a longer wave.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Standard formula for an accelerated electron
stem: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of V volt. Its de Broglie wavelength in angstrom is given by
solution: The electron gains kinetic energy e V, so p = sqrt(2 m e V) and lambda = h / sqrt(2 m e V). Substituting h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s, m = 9.1 x 10^-31 kg and e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C gives lambda = 12.27 / sqrt(V) angstrom.
formula_principle: lambda = h / sqrt(2 m e V), which reduces to 12.27 / sqrt(V) angstrom for an electron.
common_misconception: Students omit the square root on V.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Wavelength for 100 V accelerating potential
stem: An electron accelerated from rest through 100 V has a de Broglie wavelength of about
solution: lambda = 12.27 / sqrt(100) = 12.27 / 10 = 1.227 angstrom. This is comparable to atomic spacings in crystals, which is exactly why electrons of about 100 eV are diffracted by crystal lattices.
formula_principle: lambda = 12.27 / sqrt(V) angstrom.
common_misconception: Students divide by V rather than by the square root of V.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Wavelength for 150 V, and comparison of voltages
stem: The de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through 25 V is
solution: lambda = 12.27 / sqrt(25) = 12.27 / 5 = 2.454 angstrom. Note that to quarter the wavelength the accelerating voltage must be increased sixteen fold.
formula_principle: lambda = 12.27 / sqrt(V) angstrom.
common_misconception: Students use V rather than sqrt(V) in the denominator.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Wavelength in terms of kinetic energy
stem: For a non relativistic particle of mass m and kinetic energy K, the de Broglie wavelength is
solution: From K = (1/2) m v^2 = p^2 / (2 m) we get p = sqrt(2 m K). Substituting into lambda = h / p gives lambda = h / sqrt(2 m K). Both larger mass and larger kinetic energy shorten the wavelength.
formula_principle: K = p^2 / (2 m), so p = sqrt(2 m K) and lambda = h / p.
common_misconception: Students forget the square root in the momentum.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Same kinetic energy, different masses
stem: An alpha particle and a proton have the same kinetic energy. The ratio of the de Broglie wavelength of the alpha particle to that of the proton is (mass of alpha particle is four times that of the proton)
solution: With K the same for both, lambda_alpha / lambda_proton = sqrt(m_proton / m_alpha) = sqrt(1 / 4) = 1 / 2. So the alpha particle wave is half as long as the proton wave. At the same kinetic energy a heavier particle always has the shorter wavelength.
formula_principle: lambda = h / sqrt(2 m K); at fixed K, lambda is inversely proportional to sqrt(m).
common_misconception: Students use the mass ratio without taking the square root.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Why matter waves are not seen for everyday objects
stem: The wave nature of a cricket ball of mass 0.15 kg moving at 20 m s^-1 is never observed because
option_a: large objects have exactly zero de Broglie wavelength
option_b: its de Broglie wavelength, about 2 x 10^-34 m, is far too small to be detected by any means
option_c: de Broglie's relation applies only to charged particles
option_d: the ball moves too slowly for a wave to form
correct_answer_text: its de Broglie wavelength, about 2 x 10^-34 m, is far too small to be detected by any means
solution: lambda = 6.6 x 10^-34 / (0.15 x 20) = 6.6 x 10^-34 / 3 = 2.2 x 10^-34 m. No aperture or grating of that spacing exists, so diffraction effects can never be exhibited. The wave nature becomes apparent only for very light particles such as electrons.
formula_principle: lambda = h / (m v).
common_misconception: Students think macroscopic objects have no matter wave at all.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Nature of matter waves
stem: Matter waves associated with moving particles
option_a: are electromagnetic waves emitted by the moving particle
option_b: are ordinary mechanical waves needing a material medium
option_c: are neither mechanical nor electromagnetic in nature
option_d: travel always with the speed of light in vacuum
correct_answer_text: are neither mechanical nor electromagnetic in nature
solution: A matter wave requires no medium, so it is not mechanical, and it is associated with neutral particles such as neutrons as well as charged ones, so it is not electromagnetic. Its amplitude relates to the probability of finding the particle, and the wavelength is h / p.
formula_principle: Matter waves are probability waves associated with particles.
common_misconception: Students classify matter waves as electromagnetic because both travel in vacuum.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Effect of doubling the speed
stem: The speed of an electron is doubled. Its de Broglie wavelength becomes
option_d: one fourth of its earlier value
solution: Since lambda is inversely proportional to v at fixed mass, doubling v halves lambda. Note that the kinetic energy in this case becomes four times as large, consistent with lambda being inversely proportional to sqrt(K).
formula_principle: lambda = h / (m v).
common_misconception: Students confuse the speed dependence with the kinetic energy dependence.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Wavelength of an electron of given momentum
stem: An electron has momentum 3.3 x 10^-24 kg m s^-1. Taking h = 6.6 x 10^-34 J s, its de Broglie wavelength is
solution: lambda = 6.6 x 10^-34 / 3.3 x 10^-24 = 2 x 10^-10 m, that is 2 angstrom. This is of the order of interatomic spacings, so such electrons can be diffracted by crystals.
formula_principle: lambda = h / p.
common_misconception: Students invert the division.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Matching an electron wavelength to a photon wavelength
stem: An X ray photon has energy 12400 eV. Using h c = 12400 eV angstrom and lambda = 12.27 / sqrt(V) angstrom, the potential difference through which an electron must be accelerated from rest so that it has the same wavelength as this photon is about
solution: The photon wavelength is 12400 / 12400 = 1 angstrom. For the electron to have the same wavelength, 12.27 / sqrt(V) = 1, so sqrt(V) = 12.27 and V = 150.6, that is about 150 V. Note that the electron then carries only about 150 eV while the photon carries 12400 eV, although their wavelengths are equal.
formula_principle: lambda = h c / E for a photon and lambda = 12.27 / sqrt(V) angstrom for an accelerated electron.
common_misconception: Students assume that equal wavelength implies equal energy for a photon and an electron.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Electron and photon of the same wavelength
stem: An electron and a photon have the same de Broglie wavelength. Then they have
option_a: the same momentum but different energies
option_b: the same energy but different momenta
option_c: the same energy and the same momentum
correct_answer_text: the same momentum but different energies
solution: Both satisfy p = h / lambda, so equal wavelengths mean equal momenta. The photon energy is p c while the electron kinetic energy is p^2 / (2 m) = p c x (p / (2 m c)). Since p is far smaller than m c for slow electrons, the electron energy is far less than the photon energy.
formula_principle: p = h / lambda for both; E = p c for a photon, E = p^2 / (2 m) for an electron.
common_misconception: Students assume equal wavelength implies equal energy.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Alpha particle and proton through the same potential difference
stem: An alpha particle of mass 4m and charge 2e and a proton of mass m and charge e are each accelerated from rest through the same potential difference. The ratio of the de Broglie wavelength of the alpha particle to that of the proton is
solution: For the alpha particle the product m q is 4m x 2e = 8 m e, while for the proton it is m e. Since lambda is inversely proportional to sqrt(m q), the ratio is sqrt(m e / 8 m e) = 1 / sqrt(8) = 1 / (2 sqrt(2)), which is about 1 : 2.83. The alpha particle wave is the shorter of the two.
formula_principle: For charge q accelerated through V, KE = q V, p = sqrt(2 m q V) and lambda = h / sqrt(2 m q V).
common_misconception: Students account for the mass but overlook the doubled charge, or omit the square root altogether.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: de Broglie wavelength of an electron of given speed
stem: An electron moves with speed 2.2 x 10^6 m s^-1. Taking h = 6.6 x 10^-34 J s and electron mass 9.1 x 10^-31 kg, its de Broglie wavelength is about
solution: Momentum p = 9.1 x 10^-31 x 2.2 x 10^6 = 2.0 x 10^-24 kg m s^-1. Then lambda = 6.6 x 10^-34 / 2.0 x 10^-24 = 3.3 x 10^-10 m, which is 3.3 angstrom.
formula_principle: lambda = h / (m v).
common_misconception: Students stop at the momentum and report it as the wavelength.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Proton and electron accelerated through the same potential
stem: A proton and an electron, both starting from rest, are accelerated through the same potential difference. The ratio of the de Broglie wavelength of the electron to that of the proton is
option_d: 1, because both carry the same magnitude of charge
solution: Both gain kinetic energy e V, so lambda = h / sqrt(2 m e V). Hence lambda_e / lambda_p = sqrt(m_p / m_e) = sqrt(1836) = 42.8. The electron, being far lighter, ends with a much smaller momentum despite the equal energy, and so has the far longer wavelength.
formula_principle: lambda = h / sqrt(2 m q V), with q the same magnitude for both.
common_misconception: Students use the mass ratio directly instead of its square root.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Ratio of wavelengths for two accelerating voltages
stem: An electron is accelerated first through 100 V and then through 400 V. The ratio of the two de Broglie wavelengths, for 100 V to that for 400 V, is
solution: lambda at 100 V is 12.27 / 10 = 1.227 angstrom and at 400 V is 12.27 / 20 = 0.6135 angstrom. The ratio is 1.227 : 0.6135 = 2 : 1, which is simply sqrt(400 / 100).
formula_principle: lambda = 12.27 / sqrt(V) angstrom.
common_misconception: Students take the ratio of voltages rather than of their square roots.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Condition for a wave to be associated with a particle
stem: A de Broglie wave is associated with
option_a: only charged particles such as electrons and protons
option_b: only particles moving at speeds comparable to the speed of light
option_c: particles at rest as well, with wavelength equal to h / m
option_d: every particle that is in motion, whether charged or neutral
correct_answer_text: every particle that is in motion, whether charged or neutral
solution: The de Broglie relation involves only Planck constant and the momentum. Charge does not appear, so neutrons, atoms and even molecules show wave behaviour. Since p must be non zero for a finite wavelength, the particle must be in motion.
formula_principle: lambda = h / p applies to any particle with non zero momentum.
common_misconception: Students restrict matter waves to charged particles because most demonstrations use electrons.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: What the Davisson and Germer experiment demonstrated
stem: The Davisson and Germer experiment provided direct experimental confirmation of
option_a: the particle nature of light proposed by Einstein
option_b: the wave nature of electrons predicted by de Broglie
option_c: the existence of the neutron inside the nucleus
correct_answer_text: the wave nature of electrons predicted by de Broglie
