solution: Davisson and Germer scattered a beam of low energy electrons from a nickel single crystal and found a pronounced peak in the scattered intensity at a particular angle. This peak can only arise from constructive interference of waves, confirming that electrons possess a wavelength given by h / p.
formula_principle: Electron diffraction from a crystal confirms lambda = h / p.
common_misconception: Students link the experiment to the photoelectric effect instead of to matter waves.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Target used in the Davisson and Germer experiment
stem: In the Davisson and Germer experiment the electron beam was scattered from
option_a: a thin film of gold foil as in the Rutherford scattering experiment
option_b: a narrow slit cut in a metal plate of width about one millimetre
option_c: a single crystal of nickel acting as a three dimensional grating
option_d: a drop of mercury in a vacuum chamber
correct_answer_text: a single crystal of nickel acting as a three dimensional grating
solution: Electron wavelengths at about 54 eV are near 1.67 angstrom. Only a regular array with spacing of that order can diffract them, and the atomic planes of a nickel single crystal, spaced about 0.91 angstrom apart in the relevant direction, serve exactly this purpose.
formula_principle: A crystal lattice provides spacings comparable with the electron de Broglie wavelength.
common_misconception: Students confuse this experiment with Rutherford's gold foil scattering.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Observation of a scattering peak
stem: In the Davisson and Germer experiment, a sharp peak in the intensity of scattered electrons at a definite angle indicates that
option_a: all the electrons happened to be emitted in that one direction by the electron gun
option_b: the electron waves scattered from successive atomic planes interfere constructively at that angle
option_c: the crystal surface is a perfect mirror at that particular angle
option_d: the electrons lose energy in that direction and pile up there
correct_answer_text: the electron waves scattered from successive atomic planes interfere constructively at that angle
solution: The regularly spaced atomic planes scatter the incident electron waves. In directions where the path difference between waves from successive planes is a whole number of wavelengths the amplitudes add, producing a strong maximum. The angular position depends on the electron energy exactly as the de Broglie wavelength predicts.
formula_principle: Bragg type condition: constructive interference when the path difference equals a whole number of wavelengths.
common_misconception: Students explain the peak as ordinary reflection rather than as interference.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Effect of accelerating voltage on the diffraction peak
stem: In an electron diffraction experiment the accelerating voltage of the electron gun is increased. The diffraction maximum then occurs at
option_a: a larger scattering angle, because faster electrons are deflected more
option_b: the same angle, because the crystal spacing has not changed
option_c: no angle at all, because high energy electrons are not diffracted
option_d: a smaller scattering angle, because the electron wavelength has become shorter
correct_answer_text: a smaller scattering angle, because the electron wavelength has become shorter
solution: Increasing V shortens lambda as 1 / sqrt(V). For a fixed lattice spacing d, the constructive interference condition of the form d sin theta = n lambda then gives a smaller sin theta, so the maximum moves to a smaller angle. This voltage dependence is itself strong evidence for the de Broglie relation.
formula_principle: lambda = 12.27 / sqrt(V) angstrom, and the diffraction angle satisfies a sin theta proportional to lambda.
common_misconception: Students think faster particles are always scattered through larger angles.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Numerical value of the electron wavelength at 54 V
stem: In the Davisson and Germer experiment electrons were accelerated through about 54 V. Using lambda = 12.27 / sqrt(V) angstrom, the de Broglie wavelength of these electrons was about
solution: sqrt(54) = 7.35, so lambda = 12.27 / 7.35 = 1.67 angstrom. The observed diffraction maximum at 50 degrees corresponded to a wavelength of about 1.65 angstrom from the crystal spacing, in excellent agreement with the de Broglie prediction.
formula_principle: lambda = 12.27 / sqrt(V) angstrom.
common_misconception: Students divide by V rather than by sqrt(V).

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Meaning of wave particle duality
stem: The principle of wave particle duality states that
option_a: radiation is always a wave while matter is always a stream of particles
option_b: a single experiment can display both the wave and the particle behaviour simultaneously
option_c: light behaves as a particle only when it travels through a vacuum
option_d: radiation and matter both show wave behaviour in some experiments and particle behaviour in others
correct_answer_text: radiation and matter both show wave behaviour in some experiments and particle behaviour in others
solution: Interference and diffraction of light require a wave description, while the photoelectric and Compton effects require photons. Similarly electrons show diffraction from crystals yet leave sharp tracks in a cloud chamber. Each experiment reveals one aspect; the two are complementary and never contradictory.
formula_principle: Complementarity of wave and particle descriptions.
common_misconception: Students expect a single experiment to display both aspects at once.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Why electron microscopes resolve fine detail
stem: An electron microscope can resolve much finer detail than an optical microscope chiefly because
option_a: electrons travel much faster than light in the instrument
option_b: electrons carry charge and so are focused perfectly with no aberration at all
option_c: the de Broglie wavelength of the accelerated electrons is far shorter than the wavelength of visible light
option_d: electrons have zero rest mass like photons and so form sharper images
correct_answer_text: the de Broglie wavelength of the accelerated electrons is far shorter than the wavelength of visible light
solution: Visible light has a wavelength around 5000 angstrom, so an optical microscope cannot resolve detail much finer than that. Electrons accelerated through say 10000 V have lambda = 12.27 / 100 = 0.1227 angstrom, thousands of times shorter, so the attainable resolution is enormously better.
formula_principle: Resolving power improves as the wavelength decreases; lambda = 12.27 / sqrt(V) angstrom for electrons.
common_misconception: Students attribute the resolving power to the speed or the charge of the electron rather than to its wavelength.

chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
concept_tested: Voltage change needed to halve the diffraction angle scale
stem: In an electron diffraction experiment with a fixed crystal, the accelerating voltage is changed so that the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons is reduced to one third of its earlier value. The accelerating voltage must be made
solution: Since lambda is inversely proportional to sqrt(V), we have V proportional to 1 / lambda^2. Reducing lambda by a factor of 3 multiplies 1 / lambda^2 by 9, so V must be increased nine fold. For example 100 V giving 1.227 angstrom becomes 900 V giving 0.409 angstrom.
formula_principle: lambda = 12.27 / sqrt(V) angstrom, so V is proportional to 1 / lambda^2.
common_misconception: Students change the voltage by the same factor as the wavelength.

concept_tested: Interpretation of undeviated alpha particles
stem: In Rutherford's alpha particle scattering experiment almost all the alpha particles passed through the thin gold foil without any appreciable deviation. This observation leads directly to the conclusion that
option_a: most of the space inside an atom is empty
option_b: the alpha particles are much heavier than the gold atoms
option_c: the positive charge of the atom is spread uniformly over its whole volume
option_d: the electrons in the atom are at rest at fixed points
correct_answer_text: most of the space inside an atom is empty
solution: An alpha particle is deflected only when it comes close to a concentrated centre of positive charge. Since the overwhelming majority of alpha particles emerge along their original direction, they must have travelled through regions containing no such centre. Hence the volume of an atom is mostly empty space, with the positive charge and nearly all the mass packed into a very small nucleus.
formula_principle: Rutherford scattering: the fraction of alpha particles deviated measures how much of the atomic volume is occupied by the scattering centre.
common_misconception: Students often quote the large mass of the alpha particle as the reason for zero deflection, instead of the emptiness of the atom.

concept_tested: Statistics of large angle scattering
stem: In the alpha particle scattering experiment the number of alpha particles that were turned back through angles greater than 90 degrees was found to be roughly
solution: Geiger and Marsden found that only about one alpha particle in every eight thousand was scattered through an angle exceeding 90 degrees. Rutherford described this as being as surprising as a shell bouncing back from tissue paper. The rarity of the event shows that the target responsible for it occupies only a minute fraction of the atomic cross section, of the order of 10^-5 of the atomic radius in linear size.
formula_principle: Rutherford's counting result: the rare large angle events fix the size of the scattering centre.
common_misconception: Learners frequently misremember the order of magnitude of the backscattered fraction and quote it as one in eight or one in eighty.

concept_tested: Choice of gold and of a thin foil
stem: In the alpha particle scattering experiment gold was rolled into an extremely thin foil mainly because
option_a: gold is the only metal that does not absorb alpha particles at all
option_b: a thin foil makes multiple successive scatterings of the same alpha particle very unlikely
option_c: a thin foil increases the total number of nuclei that each alpha particle meets
option_d: gold nuclei are lighter than the alpha particles and so recoil strongly
correct_answer_text: a thin foil makes multiple successive scatterings of the same alpha particle very unlikely
solution: Rutherford's analysis assumes that a given deflection is produced by one encounter with one nucleus. If the foil were thick, an alpha particle would suffer many small deflections whose combined effect could not be traced to a single Coulomb encounter, and the angular distribution would be meaningless. Gold was chosen because it can be beaten into foils only a few hundred atoms thick and because its large atomic number gives strong Coulomb deflection.
formula_principle: Single scattering condition: the foil thickness must be small enough that each alpha particle interacts with at most one nucleus.
common_misconception: Students attribute the choice of gold to a supposed transparency to alpha particles rather than to the single scattering requirement.

concept_tested: Dependence of closest approach on kinetic energy
stem: An alpha particle fired head on at a heavy nucleus comes to rest momentarily at a distance r from the centre of the nucleus. If an identical alpha particle is fired head on at the same nucleus with twice the kinetic energy, the corresponding distance becomes
solution: Equating the initial kinetic energy to the electrostatic potential energy at the turning point gives K = (1/(4 pi epsilon_0)) x (2e)(Ze)/r_0. Rearranging, r_0 = (1/(4 pi epsilon_0)) x 2 Z e^2 / K, so r_0 varies inversely with the kinetic energy. Doubling K therefore halves the distance of closest approach, giving r/2.
formula_principle: At the distance of closest approach the whole kinetic energy has become Coulomb potential energy: K = (1/(4 pi epsilon_0)) x 2 Z e^2 / r_0, so r_0 is proportional to 1/K.
common_misconception: The inverse relation between closest approach and kinetic energy is often inverted, so that a faster projectile is wrongly said to stop further away.

concept_tested: Numerical evaluation of the turning point
stem: An alpha particle of kinetic energy 7.2 MeV is fired head on towards a stationary nucleus of atomic number 50. Taking (1/(4 pi epsilon_0)) e^2 = 1.44 MeV fm, the distance of closest approach is
solution: Substituting the data, r_0 = 2 x 50 x 1.44 MeV fm / 7.2 MeV. The numerator is 100 x 1.44 = 144 MeV fm. Dividing by 7.2 MeV gives r_0 = 20 fm, that is 2.0 x 10^-14 m. Note that this is much larger than an actual nuclear radius, which is why the alpha particle never touches the nucleus and pure Coulomb scattering applies.
formula_principle: r_0 = (1/(4 pi epsilon_0)) x 2 Z e^2 / K with (1/(4 pi epsilon_0)) e^2 = 1.44 MeV fm.
common_misconception: The factor 2 for the alpha particle charge is dropped, halving the calculated distance of closest approach.

concept_tested: Comparing two projectiles of equal energy
stem: An alpha particle and a proton, each of kinetic energy 5 MeV, are fired head on at the same heavy nucleus. The ratio of the distance of closest approach of the alpha particle to that of the proton is
solution: For a projectile of charge z e the turning point satisfies K = (1/(4 pi epsilon_0)) z Z e^2 / r_0, so at fixed kinetic energy and fixed target r_0 is proportional to z. The alpha particle has z = 2 and the proton has z = 1, hence the ratio of closest approaches is 2 : 1. The alpha particle, being more strongly repelled, is turned back sooner.
formula_principle: r_0 = (1/(4 pi epsilon_0)) z Z e^2 / K, where z e is the charge of the projectile.
common_misconception: The proportionality of the closest approach to the projectile charge is confused with a dependence on projectile mass.

concept_tested: What large angle scattering establishes
stem: The occurrence of a small number of alpha particles scattered through very large angles was taken by Rutherford as evidence that
option_a: the electrons inside the atom are arranged in fixed circular shells
option_b: the atom contains an equal number of positive and negative charges
option_c: the positive charge and almost the whole mass of the atom are concentrated in a very small volume
option_d: the nuclear force between the alpha particle and the target is attractive
correct_answer_text: the positive charge and almost the whole mass of the atom are concentrated in a very small volume
solution: To turn an energetic alpha particle through more than 90 degrees the repulsive Coulomb force must be enormous, which is possible only if the alpha particle can approach very close to a large positive charge. In a uniformly spread positive charge the field inside falls towards zero at the centre and no such force arises. The rare violent deflections therefore require the positive charge to be compressed into a tiny volume, and since the alpha particle is scarcely able to move that centre, essentially all the atomic mass must sit there too.
formula_principle: A large deflection requires a large repulsive force, which requires a large charge acting over a very small distance.
common_misconception: Students credit the scattering experiment with results such as electron shells or neutrality that it does not actually establish.

concept_tested: Relation between impact parameter and scattering angle
stem: In Rutherford scattering, the alpha particles that are scattered through the largest angles are those for which the impact parameter is
option_a: largest, so that the alpha particle spends the longest time near the nucleus
option_b: smallest, tending to zero for a head on collision
option_c: equal to the nuclear radius, so that the alpha particle grazes the nuclear surface
option_d: equal to the atomic radius, so that the alpha particle enters the electron cloud
correct_answer_text: smallest, tending to zero for a head on collision
solution: The impact parameter is the perpendicular distance between the initial line of motion and the parallel line through the nucleus. A small impact parameter brings the alpha particle deep into the strong Coulomb field near the nucleus, so the repulsive impulse is large and the deflection is large. In the limit b tending to zero the alpha particle travels straight at the nucleus, is brought to rest at the distance of closest approach and is thrown straight back, giving a scattering angle of 180 degrees. Large impact parameters correspond to weak, distant encounters and small angles.
formula_principle: The scattering angle theta increases as the impact parameter b decreases; b = 0 corresponds to a head on collision and theta = 180 degrees.
common_misconception: The impact parameter is thought of as increasing with scattering angle because a bigger number is loosely associated with a bigger effect.

concept_tested: Combined change of charge and energy
stem: A proton of kinetic energy K is fired head on at a fixed nucleus and stops at a distance d from its centre. An alpha particle of kinetic energy 4K is then fired head on at the same nucleus. Its distance of closest approach is
solution: For the proton, d = (1/(4 pi epsilon_0)) (1)(Z) e^2 / K. For the alpha particle the projectile charge is doubled and the kinetic energy is four times larger, so its closest approach is (1/(4 pi epsilon_0)) (2)(Z) e^2 / (4K), which equals one half of the proton value. Hence the alpha particle stops at d/2.
formula_principle: r_0 = (1/(4 pi epsilon_0)) z Z e^2 / K, so r_0 is proportional to z/K.
common_misconception: Only one of the two changes is applied, most often the energy change, leaving the doubled projectile charge out of the account.

concept_tested: Instability of the classical orbiting electron
stem: The principal failure of Rutherford's nuclear model of the atom is that, according to classical electromagnetism, the orbiting electron should
option_a: be pulled out of the atom by the repulsion of the nuclear charge
option_b: radiate continuously, lose energy and spiral into the nucleus in a very short time
option_c: move with a speed greater than the speed of light in the innermost orbit
option_d: have an angular momentum that decreases in fixed steps of h/(2 pi)
correct_answer_text: radiate continuously, lose energy and spiral into the nucleus in a very short time
solution: In the Rutherford picture the electron moves in a circle, so it has a centripetal acceleration. Classical electrodynamics requires an accelerated charge to emit electromagnetic radiation, so the electron would steadily lose energy, its orbital radius would shrink and it would fall into the nucleus in a time of the order of 10^-8 s. The model therefore predicts that no atom can be stable. It also predicts a continuously changing frequency of emitted radiation, that is a continuous spectrum, whereas atoms in fact emit sharp lines.
formula_principle: A charge in circular motion is accelerated, and an accelerated charge radiates electromagnetic energy.
common_misconception: The instability is attributed to a supposed repulsion or to a collision with the nucleus rather than to radiation by an accelerated charge.

concept_tested: Inverse fourth power sine law
stem: The number of alpha particles scattered per unit time into a given small angular range about a scattering angle theta is proportional to 1/(sin(theta/2))^4. The ratio of the number scattered at 60 degrees to the number scattered at 120 degrees is
solution: At theta = 60 degrees, sin(theta/2) = sin 30 degrees = 1/2, so (sin(theta/2))^4 = 1/16 and N is proportional to 16. At theta = 120 degrees, sin(theta/2) = sin 60 degrees = 0.866, so (sin(theta/2))^4 = (0.75)^2 = 0.5625 and N is proportional to 1/0.5625 = 1.78. The required ratio is 16 divided by 1.78, which is 9. So nine times as many alpha particles appear at 60 degrees as at 120 degrees.
formula_principle: Rutherford scattering law: N(theta) is proportional to 1/(sin(theta/2))^4.
common_misconception: The fourth power is applied to sin theta rather than to sin(theta/2), or the half angle is forgotten altogether.

concept_tested: Relative sizes of nucleus and atom
stem: According to the nuclear model of the atom, the ratio of the radius of the nucleus to the radius of the atom is of the order of
solution: A typical nuclear radius is a few times 10^-15 m while a typical atomic radius is about 10^-10 m. Dividing gives a ratio of order 10^-5, so the nucleus is about one hundred thousand times smaller in linear size than the atom. In terms of volume the nucleus occupies only about 10^-15 of the atomic volume, which is why the atom is described as almost entirely empty.
formula_principle: Nuclear radius about 10^-15 m, atomic radius about 10^-10 m, so the ratio is about 10^-5.
common_misconception: The dimensionless ratio is replaced by one of the two absolute sizes, usually the nuclear radius in metres.

concept_tested: Quantisation of angular momentum
stem: According to Bohr's second postulate, the angular momentum of an electron revolving in a stationary orbit of a hydrogen atom can only take the values
option_a: n h, where n is a positive integer
option_b: n h/(4 pi), where n is a positive integer
option_c: h/(2 pi n), where n is a positive integer
option_d: n h/(2 pi), where n is a positive integer
correct_answer_text: n h/(2 pi), where n is a positive integer
solution: Bohr postulated that an electron can occupy only those circular orbits in which its angular momentum is an integral multiple of h/(2 pi). Writing L = m v r, the condition is m v r = n h/(2 pi) with n = 1, 2, 3 and so on. The integer n is the principal quantum number and it labels the stationary orbit.
formula_principle: Bohr quantisation condition: L = m v r = n h/(2 pi).
common_misconception: The factor 2 pi is dropped or replaced by 4 pi, which belongs to the uncertainty principle rather than to Bohr quantisation.

concept_tested: Radius of the second orbit of hydrogen
stem: The radius of the first Bohr orbit of the hydrogen atom is 0.53 angstrom. The radius of the second orbit is
solution: The Bohr radius grows as the square of the principal quantum number, r_n = 0.53 n^2 angstrom. For n = 2 this gives r = 0.53 x 4 = 2.12 angstrom. The second orbit is therefore four times as far from the nucleus as the first.
formula_principle: r_n = 0.53 n^2 angstrom for hydrogen.
common_misconception: The n squared dependence of the Bohr radius is replaced by a simple proportionality to n.

concept_tested: Ground state energy of hydrogen
stem: For the hydrogen atom the energy of the electron in the nth stationary orbit is E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV. The energy of the atom in its ground state is
solution: The ground state is the lowest energy state, for which n = 1. Substituting gives E_1 = -13.6/1 = -13.6 eV. The energy is negative because the electron is bound to the proton; energy must be supplied to free it.
formula_principle: E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV; the ground state is n = 1.
common_misconception: The negative sign is discarded, or the ground state is confused with the first excited state.

concept_tested: Variation of orbital speed with quantum number
stem: In the Bohr model of the hydrogen atom, the speed of the electron in the nth orbit varies with n as
solution: Combining the quantisation condition m v r = n h/(2 pi) with the radius result r proportional to n squared gives v proportional to n/r, that is v proportional to n/n^2 = 1/n. The electron therefore moves more slowly in the outer orbits. For hydrogen the speed in the first orbit is about 2.18 x 10^6 m s^-1.
formula_principle: v_n = 2 pi k Z e^2/(n h), so v is proportional to 1/n.
common_misconception: The orbital speed is assumed to increase with the quantum number, by analogy with kinetic energy rising in higher orbits.

concept_tested: Absence of radiation from a stationary orbit
stem: Bohr's first postulate resolves the instability of the Rutherford atom by asserting that an electron moving in a permitted circular orbit
option_a: moves with uniform velocity and hence has no acceleration
option_b: radiates energy only when the orbit is very close to the nucleus
option_c: is held in place by the nuclear force acting between it and the protons
option_d: does not radiate energy even though it is accelerated
correct_answer_text: does not radiate energy even though it is accelerated
solution: Bohr simply asserted, in contradiction to classical electromagnetism, that an electron in one of the allowed orbits is in a stationary state and does not radiate. Radiation occurs only when the electron makes a transition from one stationary state to another. This postulate removes the collapse predicted by classical theory and permits stable atoms.
formula_principle: Bohr's first postulate: certain circular orbits are stationary states in which the electron does not emit radiation.
common_misconception: Students try to save the atom by denying the acceleration of the electron rather than by denying the radiation.

concept_tested: Energy of the first excited state
stem: For the hydrogen atom E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV. The energy of the atom when the electron is in the first excited state is
solution: The ground state is n = 1, so the first excited state is n = 2. Then E_2 = -13.6/4 = -3.4 eV. The atom is less tightly bound in this state, which is why the energy is closer to zero.
formula_principle: E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV; the first excited state is n = 2.
common_misconception: The numbering of excited states is shifted, so that the first excited state is taken to be n = 1.

concept_tested: Ratio of radii of two orbits
stem: In a hydrogen atom the ratio of the radius of the third Bohr orbit to that of the first Bohr orbit is
solution: Since r_n = 0.53 n^2 angstrom, the ratio r_3/r_1 equals 9/1. In absolute terms r_3 = 0.53 x 9 = 4.77 angstrom while r_1 = 0.53 angstrom.
formula_principle: r_n is proportional to n^2, so r_3/r_1 = 3^2/1^2.
common_misconception: The square in the radius formula is dropped when a ratio is being formed.

concept_tested: Angular momentum in a specified orbit
stem: The angular momentum of the electron of a hydrogen atom in the third Bohr orbit is
solution: The Bohr condition gives L = n h/(2 pi). For the third orbit n = 3, so L = 3h/(2 pi), which may also be written as 1.5 h/pi. Angular momentum increases in equal steps of h/(2 pi) from one orbit to the next.
formula_principle: L = n h/(2 pi).
common_misconception: The angular momentum is taken to depend on the square of the quantum number, as the radius does.

concept_tested: Energy of the third orbit
stem: Given E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV for hydrogen, the energy of the electron in the orbit with n = 3 is nearest to
solution: For n = 3, E_3 = -13.6/9 eV. Carrying out the division, 13.6/9 = 1.511, so E_3 = -1.51 eV. The levels crowd together as n increases, approaching zero for a free electron.
common_misconception: The quantum number is not squared before the division, giving -4.53 eV instead of -1.51 eV.

concept_tested: Kinetic and potential energy in a Bohr orbit
stem: For a hydrogen atom in the state n = 2 the total energy of the electron is -3.4 eV. Its kinetic energy and potential energy in this state are respectively
solution: For a circular orbit under the inverse square Coulomb attraction the electrostatic force supplies the centripetal force, which leads to KE = k e^2/(2r) and PE = -k e^2/r. Hence PE = -2 KE and the total energy E = KE + PE = -KE. With E = -3.4 eV the kinetic energy is +3.4 eV and the potential energy is 2 x (-3.4) = -6.8 eV. Adding them returns -3.4 eV, as required.
formula_principle: In a Coulomb orbit, KE = -E and PE = 2E, so PE = -2 KE.
common_misconception: The magnitudes of kinetic and potential energy are swapped, or the sign of the potential energy is taken positive.

concept_tested: Ratio of kinetic to potential energy
stem: For an electron in any Bohr orbit of a hydrogen atom the ratio of its kinetic energy to its potential energy is
solution: Balancing the Coulomb attraction against the centripetal requirement, m v^2/r = k e^2/r^2, gives m v^2 = k e^2/r and hence KE = k e^2/(2r). The electrostatic potential energy of the electron and proton is PE = -k e^2/r. Dividing, KE/PE = -1/2, independent of the orbit. This is the virial result for an inverse square attraction.
formula_principle: KE = k e^2/(2r) and PE = -k e^2/r for a Coulomb orbit, so KE/PE = -1/2.
common_misconception: The negative sign of the potential energy is omitted, so the ratio is quoted as a positive one half.

concept_tested: Ratio of speeds in two orbits
stem: The speed of the electron in the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen is v. Its speed in the third Bohr orbit is
solution: Since the orbital speed varies as 1/n, moving from n = 1 to n = 3 divides the speed by 3, giving v/3. Numerically, if v = 2.18 x 10^6 m s^-1 in the first orbit, the speed in the third orbit is about 7.3 x 10^5 m s^-1.
formula_principle: v_n is proportional to 1/n.
common_misconception: The inverse first power dependence of speed on n is confused with the inverse square or with the radius dependence.

concept_tested: Dependence of the orbital period on n
stem: In the Bohr model of hydrogen the period of revolution of the electron in the nth orbit is proportional to
solution: The period of a circular orbit is T = 2 pi r/v. Substituting r proportional to n^2 and v proportional to 1/n gives T proportional to n^2 divided by 1/n, that is T proportional to n^3. The electron therefore takes twenty seven times as long to complete an orbit at n = 3 as at n = 1.
formula_principle: T = 2 pi r/v with r proportional to n^2 and v proportional to 1/n.
common_misconception: Only the change of radius is taken into account, so the period is wrongly said to vary as the square of the quantum number.

concept_tested: Comparing revolution frequencies
stem: The frequency of revolution of the electron in the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen is f. Its frequency of revolution in the second Bohr orbit is
solution: Since the period varies as n cubed, the frequency of revolution varies as 1/n cubed. Going from n = 1 to n = 2 divides the frequency by 2 cubed, that is by 8, giving f/8.
formula_principle: f = 1/T and T is proportional to n^3, so f is proportional to 1/n^3.
common_misconception: The cube in the period dependence is reduced to a first or second power when the frequency is computed.

concept_tested: Identifying the orbit from its radius
stem: In a hydrogen atom the radius of an orbit is measured to be 4.77 angstrom. Given that the first Bohr radius is 0.53 angstrom, the principal quantum number of this orbit is
solution: Dividing the given radius by the first Bohr radius, 4.77/0.53 = 9. Since this ratio equals n squared, n = 3. A quick check confirms that 0.53 x 9 = 4.77 angstrom.
formula_principle: r_n = 0.53 n^2 angstrom, so n = square root of (r_n/0.53).
common_misconception: The ratio of radii is reported as the quantum number without taking the square root.

concept_tested: de Broglie interpretation of quantisation
stem: The Bohr condition that angular momentum is an integral multiple of h/(2 pi) follows from de Broglie's hypothesis if one requires that the circumference of the orbit
option_a: equals one de Broglie wavelength of the electron in every orbit
option_b: contains a whole number of half de Broglie wavelengths of the electron
option_c: is inversely proportional to the de Broglie wavelength of the electron
option_d: contains a whole number of de Broglie wavelengths of the electron
correct_answer_text: contains a whole number of de Broglie wavelengths of the electron
solution: De Broglie proposed that the electron in an orbit behaves as a wave that must close on itself, so the circumference must be an integral number of wavelengths, 2 pi r = n lambda. Substituting lambda = h/(m v) gives 2 pi r = n h/(m v), which rearranges to m v r = n h/(2 pi). This is exactly Bohr's quantisation postulate, now given a physical basis.
formula_principle: Standing wave condition 2 pi r = n lambda with lambda = h/(m v) gives m v r = n h/(2 pi).
common_misconception: The half wavelength condition appropriate to a string clamped at its ends is transferred to a closed circular orbit.

concept_tested: Current due to the orbiting electron
stem: The electron revolving in the nth Bohr orbit of hydrogen constitutes an equivalent electric current. This current varies with the principal quantum number as
solution: The electron passes a given point once per revolution, so the equivalent current is I = e/T = e v/(2 pi r). Substituting v proportional to 1/n and r proportional to n squared gives I proportional to (1/n)/(n^2) = 1/n^3. The current therefore falls off very rapidly for the outer orbits.
formula_principle: I = e/T = e v/(2 pi r) with v proportional to 1/n and r proportional to n^2.
common_misconception: Only one of the two factors, speed or radius, is allowed to change with the quantum number.

concept_tested: Orbital magnetic moment of the electron
stem: The magnetic dipole moment associated with the electron revolving in the nth Bohr orbit of hydrogen is proportional to
solution: The magnetic moment of a current loop is the current times the enclosed area, so mu = (e v/(2 pi r)) x pi r^2, which simplifies to e v r/2. Since v is proportional to 1/n and r is proportional to n squared, the product v r is proportional to n. Hence mu is proportional to n. Equivalently mu = (e/2m) L, and L itself is proportional to n.
formula_principle: mu = I x area = (e v/(2 pi r)) x pi r^2 = e v r/2.
common_misconception: The current dependence 1/n^3 is quoted as the answer without multiplying by the orbital area.

concept_tested: Radius and energy for a singly ionised helium ion
stem: For a hydrogen like ion of atomic number Z the Bohr results become r_n = 0.53 n^2/Z angstrom and E_n = -13.6 Z^2/n^2 eV. For a singly ionised helium ion in the state n = 2 the radius and the energy are
solution: A singly ionised helium ion has one electron and Z = 2. For n = 2 the radius is r = 0.53 x 4/2 = 1.06 angstrom, which is twice the hydrogen ground state radius. The energy is E = -13.6 x 4/4 = -13.6 eV, which happens to equal the hydrogen ground state energy. The stronger nuclear charge pulls the orbit in and deepens the binding.
formula_principle: r_n = 0.53 n^2/Z angstrom and E_n = -13.6 Z^2/n^2 eV.
common_misconception: The factor Z is applied to the radius but the factor Z squared is forgotten in the energy expression.

concept_tested: Ground state energy of a doubly ionised lithium ion
stem: The ground state energy of the hydrogen atom is -13.6 eV. For a doubly ionised lithium ion, which has a single electron and a nuclear charge of 3e, the ground state energy is
solution: For a one electron ion the energy scales as the square of the nuclear charge. With Z = 3 and n = 1, E_1 = -13.6 x 9 = -122.4 eV. The electron is bound nine times more tightly than in hydrogen, so the ionisation energy of this ion is 122.4 eV.
formula_principle: E_n = -13.6 Z^2/n^2 eV for a one electron ion.
common_misconception: The nuclear charge enters as the first power instead of the square, giving -40.8 eV.

concept_tested: Angular momentum from a stated radius
stem: In a hydrogen atom the electron is found in an orbit of radius 2.12 angstrom. Taking the first Bohr radius as 0.53 angstrom, the angular momentum of the electron in this orbit is
solution: Dividing, 2.12/0.53 = 4, and since this equals n squared, n = 2. The angular momentum is then L = 2h/(2 pi) = h/pi. Note that the radius grows as the square of n while the angular momentum grows only as the first power of n.
formula_principle: r_n = 0.53 n^2 angstrom to find n, then L = n h/(2 pi).
common_misconception: The ratio of radii is taken directly as the quantum number, so the angular momentum comes out four times too large.

concept_tested: Matching a radius across different ions
stem: For a one electron ion the Bohr radius is r_n = 0.53 n^2/Z angstrom. Among one electron ions in the state n = 2, the nuclear charge for which the orbital radius equals the ground state radius of hydrogen is
solution: The requirement is 0.53 x 2^2/Z = 0.53, that is 4/Z = 1, so Z = 4. A triply ionised beryllium ion in its state n = 2 therefore has the same orbital radius as hydrogen in its ground state, although its energy, -13.6 x 16/4 = -54.4 eV, is four times deeper.
formula_principle: r_n = 0.53 n^2/Z angstrom; set this equal to 0.53 angstrom with n = 2.
common_misconception: The nuclear charge is squared in the radius formula by analogy with the quantum number, giving Z = 16.

concept_tested: Effect of changing the quantisation rule
stem: Suppose the angular momentum of the electron in a hydrogen atom were quantised as n h/(4 pi) instead of n h/(2 pi), all other physics being unchanged. The ground state energy of hydrogen would then become
solution: Writing the Coulomb force as the centripetal force, m v^2/r = k e^2/r^2, and eliminating v using L = m v r, one obtains r = L^2/(m k e^2). The total energy is E = -k e^2/(2r) = -m k^2 e^4/(2 L^2), so the magnitude of the binding energy varies as 1/L^2. Halving the quantised angular momentum therefore multiplies the binding energy by four, giving E_1 = 4 x (-13.6) = -54.4 eV. The corresponding radius would shrink to one quarter, that is 0.1325 angstrom.
formula_principle: Balancing forces with m v r = L gives r = L^2/(m k e^2) and E = -m k^2 e^4/(2 L^2), so E is proportional to 1/L^2.
common_misconception: The energy is assumed to scale linearly with angular momentum, so the answer is doubled rather than quadrupled.

concept_tested: Muonic hydrogen radius
stem: In a muonic hydrogen atom the electron is replaced by a muon of the same charge but 207 times the mass, the proton being unchanged. Given that the first Bohr radius of ordinary hydrogen is 0.53 angstrom, the radius of the first orbit of muonic hydrogen is about
solution: Eliminating the speed between the force balance and the quantisation condition gives r_1 proportional to 1/m for a fixed charge and fixed quantisation rule. Replacing the electron by a particle 207 times heavier therefore shrinks the first orbit by the same factor. Numerically r = 0.53 x 10^-10 m divided by 207, which is 2.56 x 10^-13 m, so about 2.6 x 10^-13 m. This is why the muon spends much of its time close to the nucleus and is sensitive to the nuclear size.
formula_principle: r_1 = h^2 epsilon_0/(pi m e^2), so the first Bohr radius is inversely proportional to the mass of the orbiting particle.
common_misconception: The dependence of the Bohr radius on the mass of the orbiting particle is overlooked, or the mass ratio is applied the wrong way round.

concept_tested: Region of the Lyman series
stem: All the lines of the Lyman series of atomic hydrogen lie in the
solution: Every Lyman line corresponds to an electron falling to n = 1, so the smallest photon energy in the series is 13.6 - 3.4 = 10.2 eV and the largest is 13.6 eV. Using h c = 12400 eV angstrom, these correspond to wavelengths of 1216 angstrom and 912 angstrom, both well short of the violet limit of about 4000 angstrom. The whole series therefore lies in the ultraviolet.
formula_principle: Lyman series: transitions ending at n = 1, photon energies from 10.2 eV to 13.6 eV.
common_misconception: The Lyman series is placed in the visible region because it is the first series that students meet.

concept_tested: Final level of the Balmer series
stem: The lines of the Balmer series of atomic hydrogen arise from transitions in which the electron finally arrives at the level
solution: In the Balmer series the electron drops from any level with n greater than 2 down to n = 2. The first line, from n = 3 to n = 2, has a photon energy of 1.89 eV and a wavelength of about 6563 angstrom, which is red light. Four Balmer lines fall in the visible region, which is why this series was discovered first.
formula_principle: Balmer series: n_final = 2, n_initial = 3, 4, 5 and so on.
common_misconception: The final levels of the different series are interchanged, most often Lyman and Balmer.

concept_tested: The Paschen series
stem: The Paschen series of atomic hydrogen consists of transitions ending at n = 3 and its lines lie in the
solution: The most energetic Paschen photon is the series limit, of energy 13.6/9 = 1.51 eV, and its wavelength is 12400/1.51 = 8200 angstrom. Since visible light stops at about 7500 angstrom, every Paschen line is longer in wavelength than visible red light and so lies in the infrared.
formula_principle: Paschen series: n_final = 3, largest photon energy 1.51 eV.
common_misconception: The Paschen series is placed in the visible region because its final level is only one step above that of the Balmer series.

concept_tested: Correct form of the Rydberg relation
stem: For a transition in atomic hydrogen from an upper level n_2 to a lower level n_1, the wave number of the emitted radiation is given by
solution: The photon energy is E_2 - E_1 in magnitude, that is 13.6 (1/n_1^2 - 1/n_2^2) eV with n_1 the lower level. Dividing by h c converts this into a wave number, giving 1/lambda = R (1/n_1^2 - 1/n_2^2) where R is the Rydberg constant, about 1.097 x 10^7 m^-1. Because n_2 is larger than n_1 the bracket is positive, as it must be for emission.
formula_principle: Rydberg formula 1/lambda = R (1/n_1^2 - 1/n_2^2) with n_2 greater than n_1.
common_misconception: The lower and upper levels are interchanged inside the bracket, producing a negative wave number.

concept_tested: Meaning of a series limit
stem: The series limit of the Lyman series of atomic hydrogen corresponds to a transition from
solution: As the upper level rises, the term 1/n_2^2 tends to zero and the photon energy approaches its greatest value. For the Lyman series this limiting energy is 13.6 eV, produced when a free electron with negligible kinetic energy is captured into the ground state. The corresponding wavelength, 912 angstrom, is the shortest in the series.
formula_principle: The series limit is the shortest wavelength line of a series, obtained by setting n_2 = infinity.
common_misconception: The series limit is confused with the first line of the series, which is the longest wavelength member.

concept_tested: Wavelength of the Lyman series limit
stem: Taking the ground state energy of hydrogen as -13.6 eV and h c = 12400 eV angstrom, the shortest wavelength present in the Lyman series is nearest to
solution: The series limit photon carries the full ionisation energy of the ground state, 13.6 eV. Using lambda = 12400/13.6 angstrom gives 911.8 angstrom, so about 912 angstrom. Every other Lyman line has a smaller photon energy and hence a longer wavelength.
formula_principle: lambda = h c/E with E = 13.6 eV for the Lyman series limit.
common_misconception: The energy of the first line, 10.2 eV, is used instead of the full 13.6 eV of the series limit.

concept_tested: Wavelength of the Balmer series limit
stem: For hydrogen E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV and h c = 12400 eV angstrom. The shortest wavelength of the Balmer series is nearest to
solution: For the Balmer series n_1 = 2, so the limiting photon energy is 13.6/4 = 3.4 eV. Then lambda = 12400/3.4 = 3647 angstrom. This lies just beyond the violet end of the visible spectrum, which is why the Balmer series is only partly visible.
formula_principle: Series limit energy for a series ending at n_1 is 13.6/n_1^2 eV; lambda = h c/E.
common_misconception: The ionisation energy from the ground state is used for every series limit, regardless of the final level.

concept_tested: Wavelength of the first Balmer line
stem: In atomic hydrogen the electron falls from n = 3 to n = 2. Given E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV and h c = 12400 eV angstrom, the wavelength of the emitted photon is nearest to
solution: The photon energy is 13.6 (1/4 - 1/9) = 13.6 x (9 - 4)/36 = 13.6 x 5/36 = 1.889 eV. The wavelength follows as 12400/1.889 = 6564 angstrom, so about 6563 angstrom. This is the familiar red line of hydrogen.
formula_principle: E = 13.6 (1/n_1^2 - 1/n_2^2) eV, then lambda = 12400/E angstrom.
common_misconception: The two reciprocal squares are subtracted the wrong way round, or the quantum numbers are not squared.

concept_tested: Longest wavelength of the Lyman series
stem: For hydrogen E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV and h c = 12400 eV angstrom. The longest wavelength line of the Lyman series has a wavelength nearest to
solution: The smallest photon energy in the Lyman series comes from the closest pair of levels, n = 2 down to n = 1. That energy is 13.6 (1/1 - 1/4) = 13.6 x 0.75 = 10.2 eV. The wavelength is 12400/10.2 = 1215.7 angstrom, so about 1216 angstrom.
formula_principle: The longest wavelength of a series comes from the smallest energy jump, here n = 2 to n = 1.
common_misconception: Longest wavelength is confused with largest photon energy, so the series limit is quoted instead.

concept_tested: Which transition gives the shortest wavelength
stem: Among the following transitions in atomic hydrogen, the one that produces radiation of the shortest wavelength is
option_a: from a very high level to n = 2
option_c: from a very high level to n = 1
correct_answer_text: from a very high level to n = 1
solution: The photon energy is the difference between the two level energies. The greatest possible difference is obtained by falling from the top of the ladder, where the energy is essentially zero, to the deepest level, n = 1, at -13.6 eV. That gives 13.6 eV and a wavelength of 912 angstrom. Every other listed transition releases less energy and so gives a longer wavelength.
formula_principle: Shortest wavelength means largest photon energy, which means the largest drop in level energy.
common_misconception: Students associate a large quantum number jump with a large energy release, forgetting that upper levels crowd together near zero energy.

concept_tested: Ratio of extreme wavelengths in a series
stem: The ratio of the longest wavelength to the shortest wavelength in the Lyman series of atomic hydrogen is
solution: The longest wavelength member of the Lyman series has photon energy 13.6 x (1 - 1/4) = 10.2 eV and the shortest has 13.6 eV. Since wavelength varies inversely with energy, the ratio of wavelengths is 13.6 : 10.2, which simplifies to 4 : 3. The same result follows from the Rydberg formula as (1/(3/4)) divided by (1/1).
formula_principle: lambda is proportional to 1/E; longest wavelength comes from 10.2 eV and shortest from 13.6 eV.
common_misconception: The energy ratio is quoted directly as the wavelength ratio, without inverting it.

concept_tested: Counting lines from an excited level
stem: A sample of hydrogen atoms is excited so that the electrons occupy the level n = 4. The maximum number of different spectral lines that can be emitted as the atoms return to the ground state is
solution: Each distinct pair of levels among n = 1, 2, 3 and 4 gives one spectral line. The number of such pairs is 4 x 3/2 = 6. Listing them, the transitions are from 4 to 3, 4 to 2, 4 to 1, 3 to 2, 3 to 1 and 2 to 1. Three of these belong to the Lyman series, two to the Balmer series and one to the Paschen series.
formula_principle: Number of possible lines from level n is n(n - 1)/2.
common_misconception: Only the transitions that terminate at the ground state are counted, giving three instead of six.

concept_tested: Wavelength in terms of the Rydberg constant
stem: In terms of the Rydberg constant R, the wavelength of the first line of the Lyman series of atomic hydrogen is
solution: Substituting the quantum numbers, 1/lambda = R (1/1 - 1/4) = 3R/4. Taking the reciprocal gives lambda = 4/(3R). With R = 1.097 x 10^7 m^-1 this evaluates to 1.216 x 10^-7 m, in agreement with the value 1216 angstrom.
formula_principle: 1/lambda = R (1/n_1^2 - 1/n_2^2) with n_1 = 1 and n_2 = 2.
common_misconception: The reciprocal is not taken at the end, so the wave number is reported as if it were the wavelength.

concept_tested: Numerical series limit using the Rydberg constant
stem: Taking the Rydberg constant as 1.1 x 10^7 m^-1, the shortest wavelength of the Balmer series of atomic hydrogen is nearest to
solution: For the Balmer series n_1 = 2, so lambda = 4/R = 4/(1.1 x 10^7) m. Carrying out the division gives 3.64 x 10^-7 m, that is 364 nm. This agrees with the value 3647 angstrom obtained from the energy of 3.4 eV.
formula_principle: For the series limit 1/lambda = R/n_1^2, so lambda = n_1^2/R.
common_misconception: The square of the final quantum number is omitted, so the answer comes out four times too small.

concept_tested: Lines emitted after absorbing a given photon
stem: A hydrogen atom in its ground state absorbs a photon of energy 12.75 eV. Taking E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV, the number of different spectral lines the atom can subsequently emit is
solution: After absorption the energy of the atom is -13.6 + 12.75 = -0.85 eV. Setting -13.6/n^2 = -0.85 gives n^2 = 16, so n = 4. From the level n = 4 the number of distinct downward transitions is 4 x 3/2 = 6.
formula_principle: Absorbed energy = E_n - E_1; number of emission lines = n(n - 1)/2.
common_misconception: The excited level is misidentified because the absorbed energy is equated to the level energy instead of to the difference of level energies.

concept_tested: Transition producing a given photon energy
stem: A hydrogen atom emits a photon of energy 2.55 eV. Taking E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV, the transition responsible is
solution: The levels are E_1 = -13.6 eV, E_2 = -3.40 eV, E_3 = -1.51 eV and E_4 = -0.85 eV. The difference between the level at -0.85 eV and the level at -3.40 eV is 2.55 eV, which matches the emitted photon exactly. So the electron has fallen from n = 4 to n = 2, giving the second line of the Balmer series at 4863 angstrom.
formula_principle: Photon energy = 13.6 (1/n_1^2 - 1/n_2^2) eV.
common_misconception: Students test only neighbouring levels and overlook transitions that skip a level.

concept_tested: Which hydrogen line is visible
stem: Of the hydrogen lines listed below, the one that can be seen by the unaided eye is produced by the transition
solution: Working out the photon energies, the transition from n = 3 to n = 2 gives 1.89 eV, from n = 2 to n = 1 gives 10.2 eV, from n = 4 to n = 3 gives 1.51 - 0.85 = 0.66 eV and from n = 5 to n = 4 gives 0.85 - 0.54 = 0.31 eV. Only 1.89 eV falls inside the visible band, and the corresponding wavelength of 6563 angstrom is the red hydrogen line.
formula_principle: The visible band runs from about 4000 angstrom to about 7000 angstrom, corresponding to photon energies from about 1.8 eV to about 3.1 eV.
common_misconception: Any transition between low lying levels is assumed to be visible, without checking the photon energy against the visible band.

concept_tested: Wavelength of the second Balmer line
stem: For hydrogen E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV and h c = 12400 eV angstrom. The wavelength of the second line of the Balmer series is nearest to
solution: The first Balmer line comes from n = 3 to n = 2, so the second comes from n = 4 to n = 2. Its photon energy is 13.6 (1/4 - 1/16) = 13.6 x 3/16 = 2.55 eV. The wavelength is 12400/2.55 = 4863 angstrom, which is blue green light.
formula_principle: The second line of a series comes from the second lowest upper level; here n = 4 down to n = 2.
common_misconception: The counting of lines within a series is shifted by one, so the first line is reported as the second.

concept_tested: Ratio of two series limits
stem: The ratio of the shortest wavelength of the Lyman series to the shortest wavelength of the Balmer series of atomic hydrogen is
solution: Setting the upper level to infinity, the shortest wavelength of a series is lambda = n_1^2/R. For the Lyman series n_1 = 1, giving 1/R, and for the Balmer series n_1 = 2, giving 4/R. The ratio is therefore 1 : 4. Numerically this is 912 angstrom against 3647 angstrom, which indeed differ by a factor of four.
formula_principle: For a series limit, 1/lambda = R/n_1^2, so lambda_min is proportional to n_1^2.
common_misconception: The square of the final quantum number is omitted, so the ratio is quoted as one to two.

concept_tested: Matching a helium ion line to a hydrogen line
stem: For a one electron ion of atomic number Z the level energies are E_n = -13.6 Z^2/n^2 eV. In a singly ionised helium ion the transition that emits a photon of exactly the same energy as the transition from n = 2 to n = 1 in hydrogen is
solution: In hydrogen the transition from n = 2 to n = 1 releases 13.6 (1 - 1/4) = 10.2 eV. For the helium ion Z = 2, so the level energies are E_n = -54.4/n^2 eV, giving E_1 = -54.4, E_2 = -13.6, E_3 = -6.04 and E_4 = -3.4 eV. The difference between the level at -3.4 eV and the level at -13.6 eV is 10.2 eV, matching the hydrogen line exactly. In general, multiplying every quantum number by Z reproduces the hydrogen spectrum.
formula_principle: For a one electron ion, E_n = -13.6 Z^2/n^2 eV, so doubling both Z and n leaves the energy unchanged.
common_misconception: The Z squared scaling of the level energies is ignored, so the same pair of quantum numbers is assumed to give the same photon energy in every one electron ion.

concept_tested: Ionisation energy of hydrogen from the ground state
stem: The energy needed to remove the electron completely from a hydrogen atom that is in its ground state is
solution: Ionisation means raising the electron from its bound level to the free state of zero energy. From the ground state at -13.6 eV, the energy required is 0 - (-13.6) = 13.6 eV. Any photon of higher energy will also ionise the atom, the surplus appearing as kinetic energy of the freed electron.
formula_principle: Ionisation energy = 0 - E_n, so from the ground state it equals 13.6 eV.
common_misconception: The first excitation energy is quoted as the ionisation energy because both refer to energy supplied to a ground state atom.

concept_tested: Ionisation potential of hydrogen
stem: The ionisation potential of the hydrogen atom in its ground state is
solution: The ionisation potential is the accelerating potential difference through which an electron must fall to acquire just enough energy to ionise the atom. Since an electron accelerated through V volt gains V electron volt of energy, an ionisation energy of 13.6 eV corresponds to an ionisation potential of 13.6 V. The number is the same but the unit is the volt, not the electron volt.
formula_principle: Ionisation potential in volt = ionisation energy in eV divided by the electronic charge in units of e.
common_misconception: Energy and potential are used interchangeably, so the answer is given in electron volt instead of volt.

concept_tested: First excitation energy of hydrogen
stem: For hydrogen E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV. The first excitation energy of the hydrogen atom is
solution: The first excited state is n = 2, whose energy is -3.4 eV. Starting from the ground state at -13.6 eV, the energy that must be supplied is -3.4 - (-13.6) = 10.2 eV. This is the first excitation energy.
formula_principle: Excitation energy = E_final - E_initial with the initial state the ground state.
common_misconception: The magnitude of the upper level energy is quoted directly instead of the difference between the two levels.

concept_tested: First excitation potential of hydrogen
stem: The first excitation potential of the hydrogen atom is
solution: An electron accelerated through 10.2 V arrives with 10.2 eV of kinetic energy, exactly the amount needed to lift a ground state hydrogen atom to n = 2. Hence the first excitation potential is 10.2 V. In the Franck and Hertz type experiment this shows up as the first dip in the transmitted electron current.
formula_principle: Excitation potential in volt equals the excitation energy in eV.
common_misconception: The excitation potential is computed from the energy of the upper level alone rather than from the difference of two levels.

concept_tested: Ionisation energy from n = 2
stem: A hydrogen atom is in the state n = 2, for which the energy is -3.4 eV. The minimum energy that must be supplied to ionise this atom is
solution: Ionising from n = 2 means raising the atom from -3.4 eV to zero energy, so 3.4 eV suffices. An excited atom is easier to ionise than a ground state atom, which is why ionisation energy always refers to the ground state unless another state is named.
formula_principle: Ionisation energy from level n = 0 - E_n = 13.6/n^2 eV.
common_misconception: The ground state ionisation energy is applied to every state, ignoring that the electron is already partly raised.

concept_tested: Second excitation energy of hydrogen
stem: For hydrogen E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV. The second excitation energy of the hydrogen atom is nearest to
solution: The second excited state is n = 3, whose energy is -13.6/9 = -1.51 eV. Starting from the ground state at -13.6 eV, the energy needed is -1.51 - (-13.6) = 12.09 eV. So the second excitation potential of hydrogen is 12.09 V.
formula_principle: Second excitation energy = E_3 - E_1.
common_misconception: The excitation is measured from the first excited state instead of from the ground state, giving 1.89 eV.

concept_tested: Ionisation energy of a helium ion
stem: The ionisation energy of the hydrogen atom is 13.6 eV. The energy required to remove the remaining electron from a singly ionised helium ion in its ground state is
solution: A singly ionised helium ion has a single electron moving around a nucleus of charge 2e, so Z = 2. Its ground state energy is -13.6 x 4 = -54.4 eV and the energy needed to free the electron is 54.4 eV. This is why the second ionisation energy of helium is much larger than the first.
formula_principle: For a one electron ion, ionisation energy from the ground state = 13.6 Z^2 eV.
common_misconception: The nuclear charge is taken to the first power in the energy expression instead of being squared.

concept_tested: Ionisation energy from n = 3
stem: For hydrogen E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV. The energy needed to remove the electron from a hydrogen atom that is in the state n = 3 is nearest to
solution: The energy of the level n = 3 is -13.6/9 = -1.51 eV, so 1.51 eV lifts the electron to the free state of zero energy. The higher the initial level, the smaller this binding energy becomes, tending to zero for very large n.
formula_principle: Ionisation energy from level n = 13.6/n^2 eV.
common_misconception: Excitation energy to a level and ionisation energy from that level are treated as the same quantity.

concept_tested: A collision below the excitation threshold
stem: An electron with a kinetic energy of 10 eV collides with a hydrogen atom in its ground state. Taking the first excitation energy of hydrogen as 10.2 eV, the outcome is that
option_a: the collision is elastic and the electron retains practically all of its kinetic energy
option_b: the atom is raised to the level n = 2 and the electron loses 10 eV
option_c: the atom is ionised and a free electron of 10 eV is released
option_d: the atom absorbs 10 eV and re-emits a photon of 10 eV
correct_answer_text: the collision is elastic and the electron retains practically all of its kinetic energy
solution: The lowest amount of energy a ground state hydrogen atom can accept is 10.2 eV, the gap to the level n = 2. A projectile electron carrying only 10 eV has less than this, so no internal transition is possible. The collision is therefore elastic, and because the atom is about eighteen hundred times heavier than the electron, the electron rebounds with essentially unchanged kinetic energy.
formula_principle: An atom can accept energy in a collision only in amounts equal to a difference between two of its energy levels.
common_misconception: Students assume that any energetic electron can excite an atom partially, treating atomic energy as continuously variable.

concept_tested: Identifying the level reached by an absorbed photon
stem: A hydrogen atom in its ground state absorbs a photon of energy 12.09 eV. Taking E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV, the electron is raised to the level
solution: After absorbing the photon the energy of the atom is -13.6 + 12.09 = -1.51 eV. Setting -13.6/n^2 = -1.51 gives n^2 = 9, so n = 3. Note that the photon energy matches this gap exactly, which is precisely why absorption is possible.
formula_principle: Absorption occurs only when the photon energy equals E_n - E_1 exactly.
common_misconception: The photon energy is equated to the final level energy rather than to the difference between the final and initial levels.

concept_tested: A photon that cannot be absorbed
stem: A beam of photons each of energy 11.0 eV passes through a gas of hydrogen atoms that are all in the ground state. Taking E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV, the beam
option_a: passes through essentially unabsorbed because 11.0 eV matches no energy gap from the ground state
option_b: is strongly absorbed and raises the atoms to the level n = 2
option_c: is strongly absorbed and ionises the atoms, freeing electrons of 11.0 eV
option_d: is partly absorbed, each atom taking 10.2 eV and passing on the remaining 0.8 eV
correct_answer_text: passes through essentially unabsorbed because 11.0 eV matches no energy gap from the ground state
solution: From the ground state the permitted absorption energies are 10.2 eV to reach n = 2, 12.09 eV to reach n = 3, 12.75 eV to reach n = 4 and so on up to 13.6 eV for ionisation. The value 11.0 eV lies between two of these and matches none of them, and it is below the ionisation threshold, so no free electron state is available either. The photon is therefore not absorbed and the gas is transparent at this energy. This is unlike a collision with an electron, where the surplus energy can be carried away as kinetic energy.
formula_principle: Photon absorption by a bound atom is all or nothing and requires an exact match with a level difference.
common_misconception: Students allow an atom to absorb part of a photon, treating photon energy as divisible in the way collision energy is.

concept_tested: Excitation energy of a helium ion
stem: For a singly ionised helium ion the level energies are E_n = -54.4/n^2 eV. The first excitation energy of this ion is
solution: For this ion E_1 = -54.4 eV and E_2 = -54.4/4 = -13.6 eV. The first excitation energy is therefore -13.6 - (-54.4) = 40.8 eV. This is four times the corresponding hydrogen value, as expected from the Z squared scaling of the level energies.
formula_principle: Excitation energy = E_2 - E_1 for the given set of levels.
common_misconception: The magnitude of the second level energy is quoted as the excitation energy instead of the difference between the two levels.

concept_tested: Threshold wavelength for ionising an excited atom
stem: A hydrogen atom is in the state n = 2, whose energy is -3.4 eV. Taking h c = 12400 eV angstrom, the longest wavelength of a photon that can ionise this atom is nearest to
solution: The atom needs at least 3.4 eV to reach the free state of zero energy. The longest wavelength corresponds to exactly this threshold energy, so lambda = 12400/3.4 = 3647 angstrom. Photons of shorter wavelength carry more energy and also ionise, the excess appearing as kinetic energy of the released electron.
formula_principle: Threshold energy for ionisation from level n is 13.6/n^2 eV; lambda_max = h c/E.
common_misconception: The ground state ionisation energy is used, or longest wavelength is confused with largest photon energy.

concept_tested: Highest level reached and lines produced
stem: Electrons of kinetic energy 12.5 eV are fired into a gas of hydrogen atoms all in the ground state, for which E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV. The number of distinct spectral lines that this gas can then emit is
solution: The energies needed from the ground state are 10.2 eV for n = 2, 12.09 eV for n = 3 and 12.75 eV for n = 4. A 12.5 eV electron can supply the 12.09 eV needed for n = 3, keeping the remaining 0.41 eV as kinetic energy, but it cannot supply the 12.75 eV needed for n = 4. So the highest populated level is n = 3, and the number of distinct downward transitions is 3 x 2/2 = 3, namely from 3 to 2, from 3 to 1 and from 2 to 1.
formula_principle: A colliding electron can transfer any amount up to its kinetic energy; the highest level reached satisfies E_n - E_1 less than or equal to the electron energy. Lines = n(n - 1)/2.
common_misconception: The electron energy is treated like a photon energy that must match a gap exactly, or the highest reachable level is overestimated.

concept_tested: Definition of isotopes
stem: Two nuclides are said to be isotopes of each other when they have
option_a: the same atomic number but different mass numbers
option_b: the same mass number but different atomic numbers
option_c: the same number of neutrons but different atomic numbers
option_d: the same number of neutrons and the same number of protons
correct_answer_text: the same atomic number but different mass numbers
solution: The atomic number Z fixes the chemical element, so isotopes are different forms of the same element. They contain the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so their mass numbers differ. Hydrogen with mass numbers 1, 2 and 3 is the standard example. Isotopes have almost identical chemical behaviour because chemistry depends on the electron count, which equals Z.
formula_principle: Isotopes: equal Z, unequal A, and therefore unequal neutron number.
common_misconception: Isotopes and isobars are interchanged because both words describe nuclides that share one of the two numbers.

concept_tested: Definition of isobars
stem: Nuclides that have the same mass number but different atomic numbers are called
solution: Isobars contain the same total number of nucleons but distribute them differently between protons and neutrons, so they are different chemical elements. The nuclide with Z = 18 and A = 40 and the nuclide with Z = 20 and A = 40 form a familiar pair. Since the mass number is the same, isobars have very nearly equal masses and, by the relation R = R_0 A^(1/3), equal nuclear radii.
formula_principle: Isobars: equal A, unequal Z.
common_misconception: The term isobar is applied to nuclides of the same element, confusing it with isotope.

concept_tested: Definition of isotones
stem: Two nuclides are isotones when they contain
option_c: the same total number of nucleons
option_d: the same ratio of neutrons to protons
solution: The neutron number is N = A - Z. Isotones have equal N but different Z and different A. The nuclide with Z = 6 and A = 14 has eight neutrons, and so does the nuclide with Z = 8 and A = 16, so these two are isotones.
formula_principle: Isotones: equal neutron number N = A - Z.
common_misconception: Isotones are defined by the neutron number, but students often define them by the proton number or by the mass number.

concept_tested: The empirical radius relation
stem: The radius R of a nucleus of mass number A is well described by the relation
solution: Experiments show that the volume of a nucleus is proportional to the number of nucleons it contains. Since volume is proportional to the cube of the radius, R^3 is proportional to A and hence R is proportional to A^(1/3). Writing the constant of proportionality as R_0 gives R = R_0 A^(1/3) with R_0 about 1.2 fm.
formula_principle: R = R_0 A^(1/3) with R_0 about 1.2 x 10^-15 m.
common_misconception: The exponent one third is replaced by one, which would contradict the observed constancy of nuclear density.

concept_tested: Counting neutrons in a heavy nuclide
stem: A nuclide has atomic number 92 and mass number 238. The number of neutrons in its nucleus is
solution: The mass number counts protons and neutrons together, so the neutron number is N = A - Z = 238 - 92 = 146. Heavy nuclei carry many more neutrons than protons because the extra neutrons help to offset the mutual electrostatic repulsion of the protons.
formula_principle: N = A - Z.
common_misconception: The mass number and atomic number are added rather than subtracted, or the two are assumed equal.

concept_tested: Ratio of radii of two nuclei
stem: Two nuclei have mass numbers 27 and 125. The ratio of their nuclear radii is
solution: Taking cube roots, the cube root of 27 is 3 and the cube root of 125 is 5. Hence the radii are in the ratio 3 : 5. The mass numbers differ by a factor of about 4.6 while the radii differ by less than a factor of 2, which shows how slowly nuclear size grows with mass.
formula_principle: R is proportional to A^(1/3), so R_1/R_2 = (A_1/A_2)^(1/3).
common_misconception: The cube root is not taken, so the ratio of mass numbers is reported as the ratio of radii.

concept_tested: Dependence of nuclear density on mass number
stem: As the mass number of a nucleus increases, the density of nuclear matter
option_a: increases in direct proportion to the mass number
option_b: decreases in inverse proportion to the mass number
option_c: increases in proportion to the cube root of the mass number
option_d: stays practically the same for all nuclei
correct_answer_text: stays practically the same for all nuclei
solution: The mass of a nucleus is about A times the nucleon mass m, while its volume is (4/3) pi R^3 = (4/3) pi R_0^3 A. Dividing, the mass number cancels and the density becomes 3m/(4 pi R_0^3), a constant of about 2.3 x 10^17 kg m^-3. Nuclear matter therefore has the same density in a light nucleus as in a heavy one, which is why nuclear matter is often described as incompressible.
formula_principle: Density = A m/((4/3) pi R_0^3 A) = 3m/(4 pi R_0^3), independent of A.
common_misconception: Heavier nuclei are assumed to be denser because they are more massive, ignoring the matching growth in volume.

concept_tested: Radius of a specified nucleus
stem: Taking R_0 = 1.2 x 10^-15 m, the radius of a nucleus of mass number 27 is
solution: The cube root of 27 is 3, so R = 1.2 x 10^-15 x 3 = 3.6 x 10^-15 m, that is 3.6 fm. This is roughly one hundred thousand times smaller than the radius of the corresponding atom.
common_misconception: The mass number is used without taking the cube root, giving a radius almost ten times too large.

concept_tested: Mass number from a doubled radius
stem: The nucleus of a nuclide X has twice the radius of the nucleus of a nuclide Y. The mass number of X is greater than that of Y by a factor of
solution: Inverting the radius relation gives A = (R/R_0)^3, so the mass number varies as the cube of the radius. Doubling the radius therefore multiplies the mass number by 2 cubed, that is by 8. Equivalently the nuclear volume, and hence the number of nucleons, has increased eightfold.
formula_principle: R is proportional to A^(1/3), so A is proportional to R^3.
common_misconception: The cube relation between mass number and radius is reduced to a first or second power.

concept_tested: Recognising a pair of isotones
stem: Consider the nuclide P with Z = 6 and A = 14 and the nuclide Q with Z = 8 and A = 16. These two nuclides are
solution: For the nuclide P the neutron number is 14 - 6 = 8. For the nuclide Q it is 16 - 8 = 8. The neutron numbers agree while both the atomic numbers and the mass numbers differ, so the pair are isotones.
formula_principle: Compute N = A - Z for each nuclide and compare.
common_misconception: Students compare the mass numbers or the atomic numbers and never compute the neutron number that the classification actually requires.

concept_tested: Numerical value of nuclear density
stem: Taking R_0 = 1.2 x 10^-15 m and the mass of a nucleon as 1.67 x 10^-27 kg, the density of nuclear matter is nearest to
solution: The mass number cancels, leaving rho = m divided by (4/3) pi R_0^3. First R_0^3 = (1.2 x 10^-15)^3 = 1.728 x 10^-45 m^3. Multiplying by 4 pi/3 = 4.19 gives a volume per nucleon of 7.24 x 10^-45 m^3. Dividing the nucleon mass by this, rho = 1.67 x 10^-27/7.24 x 10^-45 = 2.3 x 10^17 kg m^-3.
common_misconception: The factor 4 pi/3 is omitted, or the cube of R_0 is taken as R_0 multiplied by 3.

concept_tested: Ratio of nuclear volumes
stem: Two nuclei have mass numbers 16 and 128. The ratio of their nuclear volumes is
solution: Since R = R_0 A^(1/3), the volume (4/3) pi R^3 equals (4/3) pi R_0^3 A, which is directly proportional to the mass number. Hence the volumes are in the ratio 16 : 128, that is 1 : 8. The radii themselves are in the ratio 1 : 2, being the cube roots of 16 and 128.
formula_principle: Volume is proportional to R^3, and R^3 is proportional to A, so volume is proportional to A.
common_misconception: The cube root taken for the radius is applied again to the volume, so the direct proportionality between volume and mass number is missed.

concept_tested: Mass number from a measured radius
stem: The radius of a certain nucleus is measured to be 4.8 x 10^-15 m. Taking R_0 = 1.2 x 10^-15 m, the mass number of this nuclide is
solution: Dividing, R/R_0 = 4.8/1.2 = 4. Cubing this gives A = 4^3 = 64. As a check, the cube root of 64 is 4 and 1.2 x 4 = 4.8 fm, which is the given radius.
common_misconception: The ratio of radii is reported directly as the mass number, without cubing it.

concept_tested: Fractional change of radius with mass number
stem: A nucleus of mass number 64 has radius R. Among the nuclides listed, the one whose nuclear radius is 1.25 R has mass number
solution: The mass number varies as the cube of the radius, so A_2 = 64 x (1.25)^3. Now (1.25)^3 = 1.953125, and 64 x 1.953125 = 125. So a nuclide of mass number 125 has a radius 1.25 times that of a nuclide of mass number 64, since the cube roots are 5 and 4 respectively.
formula_principle: A is proportional to R^3, so A_2 = A_1 (R_2/R_1)^3.
common_misconception: The ratio of radii is applied to the mass number as a first power, so a 25 per cent increase in radius is taken to mean a 25 per cent increase in mass number.

concept_tested: Radius and density compared together
stem: Two nuclei X and Y have mass numbers 8 and 216 respectively. The ratio of the radius of X to that of Y and the ratio of the density of X to that of Y are respectively
solution: The cube root of 8 is 2 and the cube root of 216 is 6, so the radii are in the ratio 2 : 6, that is 1 : 3. For the density, the mass is proportional to A and the volume is also proportional to A, so the two dependences cancel exactly and every nucleus has the same density. The density ratio is therefore 1 : 1. This constancy is the physical content behind the empirical radius relation.
formula_principle: R = R_0 A^(1/3) gives the radius ratio; rho = 3m/(4 pi R_0^3) is independent of A.
common_misconception: Students correctly obtain the radius ratio but then assume the heavier nucleus must also be the denser one.

concept_tested: Nuclear density compared with ordinary matter
stem: The density of nuclear matter is about 2.3 x 10^17 kg m^-3 and the density of water is 1.0 x 10^3 kg m^-3. Nuclear matter is denser than water by a factor of about
solution: Dividing, 2.3 x 10^17 divided by 1.0 x 10^3 gives 2.3 x 10^14. So a spoonful of nuclear matter would weigh as much as a mountain of ordinary matter. The huge factor reflects the fact that atoms are almost entirely empty, with the mass confined to a volume about 10^-15 of the atomic volume.
formula_principle: Ratio of densities = rho_nuclear/rho_water.
common_misconception: The exponents are added instead of subtracted, or the ratio is confused with the nuclear density itself.

concept_tested: Definition of mass defect
stem: The mass defect of a nucleus is defined as
option_a: the amount by which the mass of the nucleus exceeds the sum of the masses of its free nucleons
option_b: the difference between the mass of the nucleus and the mass of an equal number of protons
option_c: the amount by which the sum of the masses of its free nucleons exceeds the mass of the nucleus
option_d: the difference between the mass number and the atomic number of the nuclide
correct_answer_text: the amount by which the sum of the masses of its free nucleons exceeds the mass of the nucleus
solution: When free nucleons combine to form a nucleus, energy is released, and by the mass energy relation the assembled nucleus is lighter than its separated constituents. The missing mass is the mass defect. For a stable nucleus it is always positive, and multiplying it by c squared gives the binding energy.
formula_principle: Mass defect delta m = [Z m_p + (A - Z) m_n] - M_nucleus.
common_misconception: The order of subtraction is reversed, giving a negative mass defect and an apparently unstable nucleus.

concept_tested: Energy equivalent of one atomic mass unit
stem: One unified atomic mass unit is equivalent to an energy of
solution: Multiplying 1.66 x 10^-27 kg by the square of 3 x 10^8 m s^-1 gives 1.49 x 10^-10 J. Dividing by 1.6 x 10^-19 J per eV gives 9.315 x 10^8 eV, that is 931.5 MeV. This conversion turns any mass defect expressed in atomic mass units straight into a binding energy in MeV.
formula_principle: 1 u = 1.66 x 10^-27 kg, and E = m c^2 gives 931.5 MeV.
common_misconception: The order of magnitude of the conversion is misremembered, most often as keV instead of MeV.

concept_tested: Position of the peak of the curve
stem: The curve of binding energy per nucleon against mass number reaches its maximum near
solution: The binding energy per nucleon rises steeply for light nuclei, reaches a broad maximum near mass number 56, in the iron region, and then falls slowly as the mass number increases. Iron group nuclei are therefore the most tightly bound and neither fusion nor fission of them releases energy.
formula_principle: The binding energy per nucleon curve peaks around A = 56, in the region of iron.
common_misconception: The peak is placed at helium because helium is often described as a particularly stable light nucleus.

concept_tested: Maximum value of binding energy per nucleon
stem: The greatest value reached by the binding energy per nucleon on the binding energy curve is about
solution: Across most of the periodic table the binding energy per nucleon lies between 7 and 9 MeV, and the maximum, reached near mass number 56, is about 8.8 MeV. That the value is nearly constant over a wide range of A is evidence that the nuclear force saturates, each nucleon interacting only with its immediate neighbours.
formula_principle: Peak binding energy per nucleon is about 8.8 MeV near A = 56.
common_misconception: The total binding energy of a small nucleus is quoted where the binding energy per nucleon is asked for.

concept_tested: Binding energy per nucleon as a measure of stability
stem: Among several nuclides, the most stable is the one with the largest
solution: The total binding energy of a heavy nucleus is large simply because it contains many nucleons. To compare nuclei of different sizes one must ask how tightly each individual nucleon is held, which is the binding energy divided by the mass number. Iron group nuclei, with about 8.8 MeV per nucleon, are the most stable on this measure even though uranium has a far larger total binding energy.
formula_principle: Stability is measured by binding energy per nucleon, that is by binding energy divided by A.
common_misconception: Total binding energy is used as the criterion of stability, which wrongly ranks heavy nuclei as the most stable.

concept_tested: Converting mass defect to energy
stem: The mass defect of a certain nucleus is 0.5 u. Taking 1 u as equivalent to 931.5 MeV, the binding energy of this nucleus is
