solution: Multiplying, 0.5 x 931.5 = 465.75 MeV. This is the energy that would have to be supplied to pull the nucleus apart into its separate free nucleons, and equally the energy that was released when they came together.
formula_principle: Binding energy in MeV = mass defect in u multiplied by 931.5.
common_misconception: The mass defect is divided into 931.5 instead of multiplied by it.

concept_tested: Computing binding energy from nucleon masses
stem: The mass of a proton is 1.00728 u, the mass of a neutron is 1.00867 u and the mass of a deuteron nucleus is 1.00728 u plus 1.00867 u less 0.00240 u. Taking 1 u as 931.5 MeV, the binding energy of the deuteron is nearest to
solution: The mass defect is stated to be 0.00240 u. Multiplying, 0.00240 x 931.5 = 2.2356 MeV, so about 2.24 MeV. Dividing by the two nucleons gives a binding energy per nucleon of only about 1.1 MeV, which is why the deuteron is a very loosely bound nucleus.
formula_principle: Binding energy = delta m x 931.5 MeV with delta m = 0.00240 u.
common_misconception: The mass defect is left in atomic mass units, or the conversion factor is applied per nucleon rather than to the whole nucleus.

concept_tested: Computing binding energy per nucleon
stem: A nucleus of mass number 16 has a total binding energy of 128 MeV. Its binding energy per nucleon is
solution: Dividing, 128/16 = 8 MeV per nucleon. This value sits close to the flat top of the binding energy curve, so a nuclide of this kind is comparatively tightly bound.
formula_principle: Binding energy per nucleon = total binding energy divided by A.
common_misconception: Total binding energy and binding energy per nucleon are treated as the same quantity.

concept_tested: Ranking nuclides by stability
stem: Four nuclides P, Q, R and S have binding energies per nucleon of 7.6 MeV, 8.8 MeV, 7.1 MeV and 1.1 MeV respectively. The most stable of them is
solution: Comparing the four values, 8.8 MeV per nucleon is the largest, so the nuclide Q is held together most tightly per nucleon and is the most stable. The value 8.8 MeV corresponds to the peak of the binding energy curve near mass number 56, while 1.1 MeV per nucleon is characteristic of the very loosely bound deuteron.
formula_principle: The nuclide with the greatest binding energy per nucleon is the most stable.
common_misconception: Students look for the largest total binding energy or the largest mass number instead of the largest value per nucleon.

concept_tested: Reversing the conversion
stem: The binding energy of a certain nucleus is 931.5 MeV. Its mass defect is
solution: Dividing, 931.5/931.5 = 1, so the mass defect is exactly 1 u, which is 1.66 x 10^-27 kg. A nucleus whose constituents lose a whole atomic mass unit on assembly is a moderately heavy one; for comparison, the helium nucleus loses only about 0.03 u.
formula_principle: delta m in u = binding energy in MeV divided by 931.5.
common_misconception: The conversion is applied in the wrong direction, so an energy in MeV is reported as a mass in atomic mass units.

concept_tested: Condition for a nuclear reaction to release energy
stem: A nuclear reaction releases energy whenever the products, compared with the reactants, have
option_c: a greater total number of nucleons
solution: Binding energy is the energy that was given up when nucleons assembled. If the products are more tightly bound than the reactants, the extra binding energy appears as kinetic energy of the products and as radiation. Equivalently, the total rest mass falls and the lost mass appears as energy. Both fission of very heavy nuclei and fusion of very light ones move the system towards the peak of the binding energy curve, so both release energy.
formula_principle: Energy released = total binding energy of products minus total binding energy of reactants.
common_misconception: Students reason from total mass or nucleon number rather than from the change in total binding energy.

concept_tested: Properties of the nuclear force
stem: The property of the nuclear force that is directly responsible for the binding energy per nucleon being nearly the same over a wide range of mass numbers is that the force is
option_a: short ranged, so that each nucleon interacts only with its nearest neighbours
option_b: much stronger than the electrostatic force at all separations
option_c: charge independent between any pair of nucleons
option_d: attractive at every separation, however small
correct_answer_text: short ranged, so that each nucleon interacts only with its nearest neighbours
solution: If every nucleon attracted every other nucleon, the total binding energy would grow roughly as the square of the mass number and the binding energy per nucleon would rise steadily with A. In fact the nuclear force acts only over about one femtometre, so a nucleon deep inside a nucleus is bound to a fixed small number of neighbours no matter how large the nucleus is. The total binding energy therefore grows in proportion to A and the binding energy per nucleon stays nearly constant, which is the property called saturation.
formula_principle: Saturation of the nuclear force: its range is about 10^-15 m, so the number of interacting pairs grows as A rather than as A squared.
common_misconception: The strength of the nuclear force is offered as the reason for saturation, when it is the short range that matters.

concept_tested: Helium binding energy per nucleon
stem: The total binding energy of a helium nucleus, which contains two protons and two neutrons, is 28 MeV. Its binding energy per nucleon is
solution: The helium nucleus contains four nucleons, so the binding energy per nucleon is 28/4 = 7 MeV. This is unusually high for such a light nucleus, which is why the helium nucleus is emitted as a unit in alpha decay.
formula_principle: Binding energy per nucleon = total binding energy divided by A.
common_misconception: The division is carried out using the atomic number rather than the mass number.

concept_tested: Full calculation from nucleon masses
stem: The mass of a proton is 1.00728 u, the mass of a neutron is 1.00867 u and the mass of a helium nucleus is 4.00151 u. Taking 1 u as 931.5 MeV, the binding energy of the helium nucleus is nearest to
solution: The constituent mass is 2 x 1.00728 + 2 x 1.00867 = 2.01456 + 2.01734 = 4.03190 u. Subtracting the actual nuclear mass, delta m = 4.03190 - 4.00151 = 0.03039 u. Multiplying by 931.5 gives 28.31 MeV. Dividing by four nucleons gives about 7.08 MeV per nucleon.
formula_principle: delta m = 2 m_p + 2 m_n - M_nucleus; binding energy = delta m x 931.5 MeV.
common_misconception: Only one proton and one neutron are included in the constituent mass, or the result is divided by four when the total is required.

concept_tested: Energy released in a fusion reaction
stem: Two deuterons, each of mass number 2 and binding energy per nucleon 1.1 MeV, fuse to form a helium nucleus of mass number 4 and binding energy per nucleon 7.0 MeV. The energy released is
solution: The helium nucleus has a total binding energy of 4 x 7.0 = 28.0 MeV. Each deuteron has 2 x 1.1 = 2.2 MeV, so the two together have 4.4 MeV. The energy released is 28.0 - 4.4 = 23.6 MeV. The reaction releases energy because the product lies much higher on the binding energy curve than the reactants.
formula_principle: Energy released = total binding energy of products minus total binding energy of reactants.
common_misconception: The binding energies per nucleon are subtracted directly, without first converting them into total binding energies.

concept_tested: Energy released in a fission reaction
stem: A nucleus of mass number 240 and binding energy per nucleon 7.6 MeV splits into two fragments each of mass number 120 and binding energy per nucleon 8.5 MeV. The energy released is
solution: The parent has a total binding energy of 240 x 7.6 = 1824 MeV. The two fragments together have 240 x 8.5 = 2040 MeV. The difference, 2040 - 1824 = 216 MeV, is released. Equivalently the gain of 0.9 MeV per nucleon is multiplied by the 240 nucleons involved.
formula_principle: Energy released = A x (binding energy per nucleon of products minus that of the reactant).
common_misconception: The gain in binding energy per nucleon is reported as the energy released, without multiplying by the number of nucleons.

concept_tested: Why the curve falls for heavy nuclei
stem: The binding energy per nucleon decreases for nuclides heavier than about mass number 60 mainly because
option_a: the nuclear force becomes repulsive in very large nuclei
option_b: heavy nuclei contain fewer neutrons than protons
option_c: the density of nuclear matter falls as the mass number increases
option_d: the electrostatic repulsion between the protons acts over the whole nucleus while the nuclear attraction acts only between neighbours
correct_answer_text: the electrostatic repulsion between the protons acts over the whole nucleus while the nuclear attraction acts only between neighbours
solution: Every proton repels every other proton, and this repulsion is not screened by distance within the nucleus, so the disruptive Coulomb energy grows roughly as the square of the proton number. The binding nuclear attraction, being short ranged, grows only in proportion to the number of nucleons. In heavy nuclei the rapidly growing repulsion eats into the binding, so the binding energy per nucleon falls from about 8.8 MeV near mass number 56 to about 7.6 MeV at mass number 238. This decline is what makes fission of heavy nuclei energetically favourable.
formula_principle: Coulomb repulsion is long ranged and grows as Z squared, while the nuclear attraction saturates and grows only as A.
common_misconception: The fall of the curve is blamed on a change in the nuclear force itself rather than on the accumulating Coulomb repulsion.

concept_tested: Why the curve is low for very light nuclei
stem: For very light nuclides the binding energy per nucleon is small mainly because
option_a: the electrostatic repulsion between the few protons present is very large
option_b: light nuclei contain more neutrons than protons
option_c: almost every nucleon is on the surface and so has few neighbours to bind it
option_d: the nuclear force does not act at all in nuclei of very small mass number
correct_answer_text: almost every nucleon is on the surface and so has few neighbours to bind it
solution: A nucleon in the interior of a nucleus is surrounded on all sides and is bound by several neighbours, whereas a nucleon on the surface has neighbours on one side only and is bound less strongly. In a very light nucleus almost every nucleon is a surface nucleon, so the average binding per nucleon is low. As the mass number grows the interior fraction increases and the binding energy per nucleon climbs steeply, reaching the flat top of the curve by about mass number 20 to 30.
formula_principle: Surface effect: the fraction of nucleons lying on the nuclear surface falls as A increases, so binding energy per nucleon rises steeply for small A.
common_misconception: The weak binding of light nuclei is attributed to Coulomb repulsion, which is in fact negligible there.

concept_tested: Energy to remove one neutron
stem: The total binding energy of a nuclide of mass number 16 is 128 MeV, and the total binding energy of the nuclide of the same element with mass number 15 is 112 MeV. The energy needed to remove one neutron from the heavier nuclide is
solution: Removing a neutron leaves a nuclide of the same element with one fewer nucleon. Since a free neutron has zero binding energy, the energy that must be supplied equals the loss of binding energy, that is 128 - 112 = 16 MeV. Note that this is twice the average binding energy per nucleon of 8 MeV, which shows that the separation energy of a particular nucleon can differ considerably from the average value.
formula_principle: Neutron separation energy = binding energy of the parent nucleus minus binding energy of the residual nucleus.
common_misconception: The average binding energy per nucleon is quoted as the energy needed to remove a specific nucleon.

concept_tested: Energy release expressed in joule
stem: In a nuclear reaction the total rest mass decreases by 0.02 u. Taking 1 u as 931.5 MeV and 1 eV as 1.6 x 10^-19 J, the energy released is nearest to
solution: First the energy in MeV is 0.02 x 931.5 = 18.63 MeV. Expressed in electron volt this is 1.863 x 10^7 eV. Multiplying by 1.6 x 10^-19 J per eV gives 2.98 x 10^-12 J, so about 3.0 x 10^-12 J. For comparison, a chemical reaction between two atoms releases only a few times 10^-19 J, which is why nuclear processes are millions of times more energetic.
formula_principle: E = delta m x 931.5 MeV, then convert using 1 MeV = 1.6 x 10^-13 J.
common_misconception: The factor of 10^6 in converting MeV to eV is dropped, so the final answer is a million times too small.

concept_tested: Changes in mass number and atomic number
stem: When a nucleus emits an alpha particle, its mass number and atomic number change by
option_a: a decrease of 2 in mass number and a decrease of 4 in atomic number
option_b: a decrease of 4 in mass number and a decrease of 2 in atomic number
option_c: a decrease of 4 in mass number with no change in atomic number
option_d: no change in mass number and a decrease of 2 in atomic number
correct_answer_text: a decrease of 4 in mass number and a decrease of 2 in atomic number
solution: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus containing two protons and two neutrons. When it is emitted the parent loses four nucleons in all, so the mass number falls by 4, and it loses two protons, so the atomic number falls by 2. The daughter is therefore two places to the left in the periodic table.
formula_principle: Alpha decay: A goes to A - 4 and Z goes to Z - 2.
common_misconception: The changes in mass number and atomic number are swapped, giving a decrease of 2 in A and 4 in Z.

concept_tested: Changes in mass number and atomic number
stem: When a nucleus undergoes beta minus decay, its mass number and atomic number change by
option_a: no change in mass number and an increase of 1 in atomic number
option_b: no change in mass number and a decrease of 1 in atomic number
option_c: a decrease of 1 in mass number and an increase of 1 in atomic number
option_d: an increase of 1 in mass number and no change in atomic number
correct_answer_text: no change in mass number and an increase of 1 in atomic number
solution: Inside the nucleus a neutron changes into a proton with the emission of an electron and an antineutrino. The total number of nucleons is unchanged, so the mass number stays the same, but the number of protons rises by one, so the atomic number increases by 1. The daughter lies one place to the right in the periodic table.
formula_principle: Beta minus decay: a neutron becomes a proton, an electron and an antineutrino, so A is unchanged and Z rises by 1.
common_misconception: The atomic number is taken to fall in beta minus decay, by analogy with the fall that occurs in alpha decay.

concept_tested: Effect of gamma emission on the nuclide
stem: When an excited nucleus emits a gamma ray photon,
option_a: the mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number by 2
option_b: the atomic number rises by 1 while the mass number is unchanged
option_c: the mass number falls by 1 while the atomic number is unchanged
option_d: neither the mass number nor the atomic number changes
correct_answer_text: neither the mass number nor the atomic number changes
solution: A gamma ray is a high energy photon, with zero charge and zero rest mass. Its emission takes energy away from an excited nucleus and leaves it in a lower energy state of the same nuclide. Both the mass number and the atomic number are unchanged, so gamma emission simply de-excites the nucleus, usually just after an alpha or beta decay has left it excited.
formula_principle: Gamma emission carries away energy only; it removes no nucleons and no charge.
common_misconception: Gamma emission is assumed to change the nuclide because alpha and beta emission do.

concept_tested: Order of penetrating power
stem: The three radiations emitted by radioactive nuclei, arranged in order of decreasing penetrating power, are
solution: Alpha particles are heavy and doubly charged, so they interact strongly with matter, lose energy rapidly and are stopped by a sheet of paper or a few centimetres of air. Beta particles are much lighter and singly charged, so they penetrate a few millimetres of aluminium. Gamma rays are uncharged photons that interact only weakly and need several centimetres of lead to be substantially attenuated.
formula_principle: Penetrating power: gamma greater than beta greater than alpha.
common_misconception: The order for penetrating power is confused with the order for ionising power, which is exactly reversed.

concept_tested: Order of ionising power
stem: The three radiations emitted by radioactive nuclei, arranged in order of decreasing ionising power, are
solution: An alpha particle carries a charge of 2e and moves comparatively slowly, so it spends a long time near each atom it passes and strips electrons very efficiently, producing about ten thousand ion pairs per millimetre of air. A beta particle has half the charge and a much higher speed, so it ionises about a hundred times less. A gamma photon is uncharged and ionises only indirectly, through the occasional electron it ejects. Because strong ionisation drains energy rapidly, the most strongly ionising radiation is also the least penetrating.
formula_principle: Ionising power: alpha greater than beta greater than gamma, the reverse of penetrating power.
common_misconception: The two orderings are memorised as the same list, so ionising and penetrating power are given in the same sequence.

concept_tested: Daughter of an alpha decay
stem: A nuclide with atomic number 92 and mass number 238 emits an alpha particle. The daughter nuclide has
solution: Subtracting, the atomic number becomes 92 - 2 = 90 and the mass number becomes 238 - 4 = 234. Both charge and nucleon number balance, since the emitted alpha particle carries away 2 units of charge and 4 nucleons.
formula_principle: Alpha decay: Z goes to Z - 2 and A goes to A - 4.
common_misconception: The reductions of 4 in mass number and 2 in atomic number are applied to the wrong quantities.

concept_tested: Net effect of one alpha and two beta emissions
stem: A radioactive nucleus emits one alpha particle followed by two beta minus particles. The final nuclide, compared with the original one, is
option_a: an isobar of the original nuclide, with atomic number lower by 2
option_b: an isotone of the original nuclide, with the same number of neutrons
option_c: the same nuclide as the original, since the changes cancel exactly
option_d: an isotope of the original element, with mass number lower by 4
correct_answer_text: an isotope of the original element, with mass number lower by 4
solution: Starting from atomic number Z and mass number A, the alpha emission gives Z - 2 and A - 4. The two beta emissions then raise the atomic number by 1 each, restoring it to Z, while leaving the mass number at A - 4. The final nuclide therefore has the same atomic number as the original but a mass number smaller by 4, so it is an isotope of the original element.
formula_principle: Alpha decay lowers Z by 2 and A by 4; each beta minus decay raises Z by 1 and leaves A unchanged.
common_misconception: The changes in atomic number are added without noticing that alpha and beta decay move it in opposite directions.

concept_tested: Composition of an alpha particle
stem: An alpha particle emitted in radioactive decay is
option_a: a helium atom containing two protons, two neutrons and two electrons
option_b: a helium nucleus containing two protons and two neutrons
option_c: a hydrogen nucleus, that is a single proton
option_d: a fast electron created in the nucleus at the moment of decay
correct_answer_text: a helium nucleus containing two protons and two neutrons
solution: An alpha particle consists of two protons and two neutrons bound together, that is a bare helium nucleus of charge plus 2e and mass number 4. Its high binding energy per nucleon of about 7 MeV is why this particular grouping, rather than separate nucleons, is ejected from heavy nuclei.
formula_principle: Alpha particle: charge plus 2e, mass number 4.
common_misconception: The alpha particle is described as a neutral helium atom, ignoring the charge it must carry away.

concept_tested: Origin of the beta particle
stem: The electron emitted in beta minus decay comes from
option_a: one of the orbital electrons of the atom being thrown out by the nucleus
option_b: the splitting of a proton in the nucleus into a neutron and an electron
option_c: the conversion of a neutron in the nucleus into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino
option_d: the direct conversion of a gamma ray photon inside the nucleus into a single electron
correct_answer_text: the conversion of a neutron in the nucleus into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino
solution: Nuclei contain no electrons. In beta minus decay a neutron within the nucleus is transformed into a proton, and the electron and antineutrino created in the process are ejected immediately. This explains why the mass number is unchanged while the atomic number rises by one, and the sharing of energy with the antineutrino explains why beta particles emerge with a continuous range of energies rather than a single value.
formula_principle: Beta minus decay: neutron gives proton plus electron plus antineutrino.
common_misconception: The beta particle is thought to be an orbital electron expelled by the nucleus, which would not change the element at all.

concept_tested: Counting alpha and beta emissions in a chain
stem: A nuclide with atomic number 92 and mass number 238 decays through a series of steps into a nuclide with atomic number 82 and mass number 206. The numbers of alpha and beta minus particles emitted in the whole chain are respectively
solution: The mass number falls by 238 - 206 = 32, and since each alpha emission removes 4 nucleons while beta emission removes none, the number of alpha particles is 32/4 = 8. These eight alpha emissions alone would lower the atomic number by 16, from 92 to 76. The observed final atomic number is 82, which is 6 higher, and since each beta minus emission raises the atomic number by 1, there must have been 6 beta emissions.
formula_principle: Only alpha decay changes A, so the number of alphas is (A_initial - A_final)/4; then Z_final = Z_initial - 2 x (number of alphas) + (number of betas).
common_misconception: The change in atomic number is attributed entirely to beta decay, so the beta count is taken as 10.

concept_tested: A second decay chain
stem: A nuclide with atomic number 90 and mass number 232 decays into a nuclide with atomic number 82 and mass number 208. The numbers of alpha and beta minus particles emitted are respectively
solution: The mass number falls by 232 - 208 = 24, so the number of alpha emissions is 24/4 = 6. Six alpha emissions lower the atomic number by 12, from 90 to 78. Since the final atomic number is 82, the beta emissions must have raised it by 4, so there were 4 beta minus particles.
formula_principle: Number of alphas = (A_initial - A_final)/4; number of betas = Z_final - Z_initial + 2 x (number of alphas).
common_misconception: The number of alpha particles is obtained from the change in atomic number instead of from the change in mass number.

concept_tested: Deflection of the three radiations
stem: A narrow beam containing alpha, beta and gamma radiation enters a uniform magnetic field at right angles to the field. It is found that
option_a: all three are deflected in the same sense, gamma being deflected the most
option_b: alpha and beta are deflected in opposite senses and gamma is not deflected
option_c: alpha and beta are deflected in the same sense and gamma is not deflected
option_d: only gamma is deflected, since it travels at the speed of light
correct_answer_text: alpha and beta are deflected in opposite senses and gamma is not deflected
solution: The alpha particle carries a positive charge and the beta particle a negative one, so for the same direction of motion the magnetic forces on them point in opposite directions and the two beams separate to opposite sides. The gamma ray is an uncharged photon and experiences no magnetic force, so it continues straight through. Moreover the alpha particle, having a much larger mass to charge ratio, moves on a path of much larger radius and so is bent far less than the beta particle.
formula_principle: Magnetic force F = q v B sin theta; the sense of deflection follows the sign of the charge and the radius of the path is m v/(q B).
common_misconception: Students expect gamma rays to be deflected because they are the most energetic of the three radiations.

concept_tested: Tracking a four step decay sequence
stem: A nuclide with atomic number 88 and mass number 226 emits, in order, one alpha particle, then two beta minus particles, then one more alpha particle. The final nuclide has
solution: Start with atomic number 88 and mass number 226. The first alpha emission gives 86 and 222. The two beta emissions leave the mass number at 222 and raise the atomic number to 87 and then to 88. The second alpha emission gives 86 and 218. So the final nuclide has atomic number 86 and mass number 218. Note that in total the mass number fell by 8, from the two alpha emissions, while the atomic number fell by only 2, because the two beta emissions cancelled the effect of one alpha emission.
formula_principle: Alpha: A falls by 4 and Z falls by 2. Beta minus: A unchanged and Z rises by 1.
common_misconception: The beta emissions are ignored or are taken to lower the atomic number, so the final atomic number comes out too small.

concept_tested: Relationship between members of a decay chain
stem: A radioactive nuclide P decays by alpha emission to Q, which decays by beta minus emission to R, which in turn decays by beta minus emission to S. Comparing the four nuclides,
option_a: P and S are isotopes, while Q, R and S are isobars
option_b: P and S are isobars, while Q, R and S are isotopes
option_c: P and Q are isotopes, while R and S are isobars
option_d: all four nuclides are isotopes of one another
correct_answer_text: P and S are isotopes, while Q, R and S are isobars
solution: Let P have atomic number Z and mass number A. Then Q has Z - 2 and A - 4. The first beta emission gives R with Z - 1 and A - 4, and the second gives S with Z and A - 4. Comparing P and S, the atomic numbers are equal at Z while the mass numbers differ by 4, so they are isotopes of the same element. Comparing Q, R and S, all three have the same mass number A - 4 while their atomic numbers are Z - 2, Z - 1 and Z, so those three are isobars.
formula_principle: Alpha: A falls by 4, Z falls by 2. Beta minus: A unchanged, Z rises by 1. Isotopes share Z; isobars share A.
common_misconception: Students track only the atomic number or only the mass number and so cannot distinguish isotopes from isobars in a decay chain.

concept_tested: Identification of the band formed by valence electrons
stem: The continuous range of energies formed by the levels of the valence electrons of the atoms of a solid is called
solution: When atoms come close in a crystal, the sharp energy levels of their valence electrons spread out into a continuous band. This band, which is completely filled at 0 K in a semiconductor, is the valence band. The next higher allowed band, empty at 0 K, is the conduction band, and the energy range between the two contains no allowed states and is the forbidden band.
formula_principle: In a solid the discrete levels of the valence electrons broaden into a continuous allowed band called the valence band.
common_misconception: Students often think the valence band is the empty one; it is the filled band, while the conduction band is empty at 0 K.

concept_tested: Standard band gap value of silicon
stem: The forbidden energy gap of pure silicon at room temperature is nearly
solution: Silicon is the most widely used semiconductor and its forbidden energy gap at room temperature is about 1.1 eV. Germanium, the other common elemental semiconductor, has a smaller gap of about 0.7 eV, while insulators such as diamond have gaps of several electron volt.
formula_principle: Standard band gap values: silicon about 1.1 eV, germanium about 0.7 eV.
common_misconception: The silicon and germanium gap values are frequently interchanged; silicon always has the larger gap of the two.

concept_tested: Band gap criterion for an insulator
stem: For a solid to behave as an insulator at room temperature, its forbidden energy gap must be
solution: Thermal energy at room temperature is only about 0.026 eV. A gap larger than about 3 eV cannot be crossed by such energy, so practically no electron reaches the conduction band and the solid does not conduct. Gaps near 1 eV allow measurable excitation, giving semiconducting behaviour, and a zero gap gives metallic conduction.
formula_principle: Conductor: bands overlap, gap zero. Semiconductor: gap about 0.7 eV to 1.1 eV. Insulator: gap larger than about 3 eV.
common_misconception: Learners assume any material with a gap is an insulator; semiconductors also have a gap, only a much smaller one.

concept_tested: Band picture of a metallic conductor
stem: In a good conductor such as copper, the valence band and the conduction band
option_a: are separated by a gap of about 1 eV
option_b: are separated by a gap of more than 5 eV
option_c: overlap each other, so that there is no forbidden gap between them
option_d: are both completely empty at room temperature
correct_answer_text: overlap each other, so that there is no forbidden gap between them
solution: A metal has either a partly filled valence band or overlapping valence and conduction bands. Because empty allowed levels lie immediately above the occupied ones, even a small applied field accelerates electrons into those levels and a large current flows. There is no forbidden gap to be crossed.
formula_principle: In metals the valence band and the conduction band overlap, so electrons find empty levels immediately above the filled ones.
common_misconception: Students look for a small gap in metals; the correct picture is that there is no gap at all.

concept_tested: Behaviour of a pure semiconductor at absolute zero
stem: A pure semiconductor crystal held at absolute zero temperature behaves as
option_a: a perfect insulator, because its conduction band is completely empty
option_b: a good conductor, because the carriers are no longer scattered
option_c: a superconductor of exactly zero resistance
option_d: an n-type semiconductor, because electrons collect in the conduction band
correct_answer_text: a perfect insulator, because its conduction band is completely empty
solution: Conduction requires carriers in a partly filled band. At 0 K there is no thermal energy to lift electrons across the forbidden gap, so the valence band stays completely full and the conduction band completely empty. With no free carrier the crystal cannot conduct and behaves as an insulator.
formula_principle: At 0 K the valence band of a pure semiconductor is full and the conduction band is empty, so no free carriers exist.
common_misconception: Cooling a semiconductor is often thought to improve conduction as in a metal; in fact it reduces the carrier number and raises the resistance.

concept_tested: Effect of band gap on intrinsic conduction
stem: At room temperature a germanium sample carries a larger intrinsic current than an identical silicon sample mainly because
option_a: germanium has a larger forbidden energy gap, which pushes electrons across more easily
option_b: germanium is pentavalent while silicon is tetravalent
option_c: germanium has a smaller forbidden energy gap, so many more electron hole pairs are generated thermally
option_d: germanium has no forbidden energy gap at room temperature
correct_answer_text: germanium has a smaller forbidden energy gap, so many more electron hole pairs are generated thermally
solution: The gap of germanium is about 0.7 eV and that of silicon about 1.1 eV. At the same temperature the smaller gap of germanium lets a far greater number of electrons be lifted into the conduction band, and each such electron leaves a hole behind. With more carriers of both kinds, germanium shows the larger intrinsic conductivity.
formula_principle: The number of thermally generated electron hole pairs increases sharply as the forbidden gap decreases at a fixed temperature.
common_misconception: The valency of the two elements is sometimes blamed; both are tetravalent and the real difference lies in the width of the forbidden gap.

concept_tested: Conversion of band gap energy from eV to joule
stem: The forbidden energy gap of germanium is 0.7 eV. Expressed in joule this is (take 1 eV = 1.6 x 10^-19 J)
solution: Multiplying, 0.7 x 1.6 x 10^-19 = 1.12 x 10^-19 J. The electron volt is simply the energy gained by one electronic charge falling through one volt, so the conversion is a plain multiplication by 1.6 x 10^-19.
formula_principle: Energy in joule = energy in eV x 1.6 x 10^-19.
common_misconception: The conversion factor is sometimes divided rather than multiplied, which gives a number that is far too large.

concept_tested: Longest wavelength that can excite an electron across the gap
stem: The longest wavelength of a photon that can just lift an electron across a forbidden gap of 2.48 eV is (take hc = 1240 eV nm)
solution: Using lambda = hc / Eg with hc = 1240 eV nm gives lambda = 1240 / 2.48 = 500 nm. A photon of longer wavelength carries less than 2.48 eV and cannot lift an electron across the gap, so 500 nm is the longest usable wavelength.
formula_principle: Threshold condition: hc / lambda = Eg, so lambda(max) = hc / Eg.
common_misconception: The relation is often inverted, giving a wavelength that grows with the band gap, whereas the two are inversely related.

concept_tested: Meaning of a forbidden band of energies
stem: Which statement about the forbidden energy gap of a crystalline solid is correct?
option_a: No electron of the solid can possess an energy that lies inside the gap
option_b: Electrons drift freely inside the gap while carrying current
option_c: The forbidden gap is widest in conductors
option_d: The holes of the crystal are stored inside the forbidden gap
correct_answer_text: No electron of the solid can possess an energy that lies inside the gap
solution: The gap is defined as the energy interval between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band in which the crystal provides no allowed state. An electron may be in the valence band or in the conduction band but never at an energy inside the gap. Holes are vacancies in the valence band and conductors show no gap at all.
formula_principle: The forbidden gap is a range of energies for which the crystal offers no allowed electron states.
common_misconception: The gap is imagined as physical space inside the crystal; it is a range of energy and not a region of the sample.

concept_tested: Formation of a hole when an electron is excited
stem: An electron in a pure semiconductor absorbs thermal energy and moves from the valence band to the conduction band. The vacancy it leaves behind
option_a: behaves as a mobile positively charged hole in the valence band
option_b: behaves as a negatively charged hole in the conduction band
option_c: disappears at once and plays no part in conduction
option_d: becomes a donor impurity level inside the gap
correct_answer_text: behaves as a mobile positively charged hole in the valence band
solution: The missing electron leaves the bond short of one negative charge, so the site appears positively charged. A valence electron from an adjacent bond can move into it, which shifts the vacancy in the opposite direction. This shifting vacancy is the hole, and it is a valence band entity carrying an effective positive charge.
formula_principle: Thermal breaking of a covalent bond creates one free electron in the conduction band and one hole in the valence band.
common_misconception: A hole is often thought of as a free positive particle in the conduction band; it is a vacancy inside the valence band.

concept_tested: Change of forbidden gap and carrier number with temperature
stem: When the temperature of a semiconductor crystal is raised, its forbidden energy gap
option_a: increases, so that conduction becomes progressively harder
option_b: stays exactly constant and the carrier number is also unaffected
option_c: decreases slightly, while the number of electron hole pairs increases sharply
option_d: falls to zero at room temperature, turning the crystal into a metal
correct_answer_text: decreases slightly, while the number of electron hole pairs increases sharply
solution: Lattice expansion and stronger lattice vibrations narrow the forbidden gap by a small amount as the temperature rises. Much more important is that the number of electron hole pairs generated grows very rapidly with temperature. The combined effect is a sharp rise in conductivity, that is, a fall in resistance.
formula_principle: Heating a semiconductor slightly narrows the gap and greatly increases the number of thermally generated carriers.
common_misconception: The dominant effect is often thought to be the change in the gap itself; the change in carrier number is far larger.

concept_tested: Ordering three materials by conductivity from their band gaps
stem: Three samples have forbidden energy gaps of 0 eV, 0.7 eV and 6 eV. Arranged in increasing order of electrical conductivity at room temperature they are
option_a: the 0 eV sample, the 0.7 eV sample, the 6 eV sample
option_b: the 6 eV sample, the 0.7 eV sample, the 0 eV sample
option_c: the 0.7 eV sample, the 6 eV sample, the 0 eV sample
option_d: the 6 eV sample, the 0 eV sample, the 0.7 eV sample
correct_answer_text: the 6 eV sample, the 0.7 eV sample, the 0 eV sample
solution: A 6 eV gap cannot be crossed by thermal energy, so that sample is an insulator and conducts least. A 0.7 eV gap allows plenty of electron hole pairs, so that sample is a semiconductor and conducts more. A zero gap means overlapping bands and metallic conduction, which is the largest of the three. Increasing conductivity therefore runs from 6 eV to 0.7 eV to 0 eV.
formula_principle: Conductivity falls as the forbidden gap widens; zero gap gives a conductor, about 1 eV a semiconductor and more than 3 eV an insulator.
common_misconception: Increasing order is frequently written as increasing band gap; here the ordering asked for is by conductivity, which runs the other way.

concept_tested: Photon energy smaller than the band gap
stem: Photons of energy 2 eV fall on a crystal whose forbidden energy gap is 3 eV. The crystal will
option_a: transmit the photons, since their energy is less than the energy needed to cross the gap
option_b: absorb the photons strongly and become conducting
option_c: absorb the photons in pairs so that 4 eV is delivered across the gap
option_d: emit electrons from its surface by the photoelectric effect
correct_answer_text: transmit the photons, since their energy is less than the energy needed to cross the gap
solution: An electron can be raised from the valence band to the conduction band only if a single photon supplies at least 3 eV. A 2 eV photon has no allowed final state to take the electron to, so it is not absorbed by that process and passes through. This is exactly why materials with wide gaps look transparent to visible light.
formula_principle: Interband absorption occurs only when the photon energy is at least equal to the forbidden gap energy.
common_misconception: Photons are assumed to add their energies; ordinary absorption is a one photon process and the single photon energy must exceed the gap.

concept_tested: Threshold frequency corresponding to a given band gap
stem: A semiconductor has a forbidden energy gap of 1.24 eV. The minimum frequency of radiation that can create an electron hole pair in it is nearly (h = 6.6 x 10^-34 J s, 1 eV = 1.6 x 10^-19 J)
solution: First convert the gap: Eg = 1.24 x 1.6 x 10^-19 = 1.984 x 10^-19 J. Then nu = Eg / h = 1.984 x 10^-19 / 6.6 x 10^-34 = 3.0 x 10^14 Hz. Radiation of lower frequency carries less energy per photon than the gap and cannot create a pair.
formula_principle: Threshold condition h x nu = Eg, so nu(min) = Eg / h with Eg expressed in joule.
common_misconception: The conversion from eV to joule is skipped, which makes the answer larger by a factor of about 10^19.

concept_tested: Equality of electron and hole concentrations in a pure crystal
stem: In a pure semiconductor at room temperature the free electron concentration n_e and the hole concentration n_h are related by
option_a: n_e is very much greater than n_h
option_c: n_h is very much greater than n_e
solution: Carriers in a pure crystal arise only from thermal breaking of covalent bonds. Each broken bond releases exactly one free electron and leaves exactly one hole, so the two populations are always equal and each is written as the intrinsic concentration n_i.
formula_principle: In an intrinsic semiconductor every broken bond gives one electron and one hole, so n_e = n_h = n_i.
common_misconception: The equality is thought to hold in doped crystals as well; after doping the two concentrations differ greatly although their product stays fixed.

concept_tested: Recognising a pentavalent dopant
stem: Which impurity, when added to pure silicon, produces an n-type semiconductor?
solution: An n-type crystal needs an impurity with five valence electrons. Four of them form covalent bonds with the neighbouring silicon atoms and the fifth is left loosely bound and becomes free. Antimony is pentavalent and behaves in exactly this way, while boron, aluminium and indium all have three valence electrons and act as acceptors.
formula_principle: Pentavalent dopants such as phosphorus, arsenic and antimony are donors and give n-type material.
common_misconception: The dopant lists are often mixed up; phosphorus, arsenic and antimony are donors while boron, aluminium and indium are acceptors.

concept_tested: Majority and minority carriers in n-type material
stem: In an n-type semiconductor the majority carriers and the minority carriers are respectively
option_b: electrons and the positive donor ions
option_d: holes and the negative acceptor ions
solution: Each donor atom releases one free electron, so electrons far outnumber every other carrier and are the majority carriers. Holes are still produced by thermal breaking of bonds, but in far smaller numbers, so they are the minority carriers. Ionised donors are locked in the lattice and never move.
formula_principle: Donor doping makes electrons the majority carriers, while the few thermally generated holes remain as minority carriers.
common_misconception: Ionised dopant atoms are counted as carriers; they are fixed in the lattice and cannot drift.

concept_tested: Role of a trivalent impurity
stem: A trivalent atom such as boron is added to pure germanium. The impurity atom and the resulting crystal are called
option_a: a donor and an n-type crystal
option_b: an acceptor and an n-type crystal
option_c: an acceptor and a p-type crystal
option_d: a donor and a p-type crystal
correct_answer_text: an acceptor and a p-type crystal
solution: Boron has three valence electrons, so when it substitutes for a germanium atom one of the four covalent bonds is left incomplete. That incomplete bond readily accepts an electron from a neighbouring bond, so boron is an acceptor. The vacancy created is a hole and holes become the majority carriers, which is p-type material.
formula_principle: A trivalent dopant leaves one bond incomplete and accepts an electron, creating a hole and giving p-type material.
common_misconception: The words donor and acceptor are interchanged; the atom that accepts an electron creates the hole and gives p-type material.

concept_tested: Negative temperature coefficient of resistance
stem: When the temperature of a semiconductor is raised, its electrical resistance
option_a: increases, because the increased vibrations scatter the carriers as in a metal
option_b: remains unchanged, since the number of atoms in the sample is fixed
option_c: first increases and then becomes infinite
option_d: decreases, because far more electron hole pairs are generated
correct_answer_text: decreases, because far more electron hole pairs are generated
solution: Heating a semiconductor breaks many more covalent bonds, so the numbers of free electrons and holes both grow rapidly. Although the mobility falls a little because of increased lattice vibrations, the rise in carrier number is much larger, so the conductivity rises and the resistance falls.
formula_principle: A semiconductor has a negative temperature coefficient of resistance because thermal generation of carriers dominates.
common_misconception: The metallic rule that resistance rises with temperature is carried over to semiconductors, where the opposite happens.

concept_tested: Minority carriers in a p-type crystal
stem: In a p-type semiconductor kept at room temperature the minority charge carriers are
option_a: electrons produced by the thermal breaking of covalent bonds
option_b: holes produced by the acceptor atoms
option_d: protons released from the nuclei of the atoms
correct_answer_text: electrons produced by the thermal breaking of covalent bonds
solution: Acceptor doping creates a large number of holes, so holes dominate. Thermal breaking of bonds still produces electron hole pairs, and the electrons from these pairs form the small minority population. Ionised acceptors carry a fixed negative charge but cannot move.
formula_principle: In p-type material holes are the majority carriers and thermally generated electrons are the minority carriers.
common_misconception: Any negatively charged entity is taken as the minority carrier; only the free electrons move, not the acceptor ions.

concept_tested: Position of the donor level in the energy band diagram
stem: The energy level created inside the forbidden gap of silicon by a pentavalent donor impurity lies
option_a: just above the top of the valence band
option_b: just below the bottom of the conduction band
option_c: exactly at the centre of the forbidden gap
correct_answer_text: just below the bottom of the conduction band
solution: The fifth electron of a donor atom is very loosely bound, so only about 0.01 eV to 0.05 eV is needed to set it free. On the band diagram this corresponds to a level lying just below the bottom of the conduction band, so that thermal energy at room temperature ionises practically every donor.
formula_principle: Donor levels lie a few hundredths of an electron volt below the conduction band edge.
common_misconception: Donor and acceptor levels are placed on the wrong sides of the gap; donors sit near the conduction band and acceptors near the valence band.

concept_tested: Ionisation energy of an acceptor level
stem: The energy required to lift a valence electron into the acceptor level of a p-type crystal is
option_a: equal to the full forbidden gap of the crystal
option_c: zero, because holes are present even at 0 K
option_d: very small, of the order of 0.01 eV to 0.05 eV
correct_answer_text: very small, of the order of 0.01 eV to 0.05 eV
solution: Because the acceptor level lies only a few hundredths of an electron volt above the top of the valence band, thermal energy at room temperature is enough to move valence electrons into it. Each such transfer leaves a hole in the valence band, which is why p-type material has plenty of holes at ordinary temperatures.
formula_principle: The acceptor level lies just above the valence band edge, so its ionisation energy is a small fraction of the band gap.
common_misconception: The full band gap is used as the ionisation energy, which would make doping useless at room temperature.

concept_tested: Use of n_e x n_h = n_i squared
stem: A semiconductor has an intrinsic carrier concentration of 2 x 10^16 per m^3. After doping, its free electron concentration becomes 4 x 10^22 per m^3. The hole concentration in the doped sample is
solution: Here n_i^2 = (2 x 10^16)^2 = 4 x 10^32. Dividing by the electron concentration, n_h = 4 x 10^32 / 4 x 10^22 = 1 x 10^10 per m^3. Doping has raised the electron population enormously and pushed the hole population far below the intrinsic value.
formula_principle: Law of mass action: n_e x n_h = n_i^2 at a given temperature.
common_misconception: The product relation is applied as a sum, or the intrinsic value is assumed to survive doping.

concept_tested: Overall electrical charge of a doped crystal
stem: An n-type semiconductor crystal taken as a whole is
option_a: negatively charged, because of the extra free electrons it contains
option_b: positively charged, because of the ionised donor atoms
option_c: electrically neutral, since the fixed positive donor ions balance the free electrons
option_d: neutral only while a battery is connected across it
correct_answer_text: electrically neutral, since the fixed positive donor ions balance the free electrons
solution: Each donor atom joins the lattice as a neutral atom. When it gives up its fifth electron it becomes a fixed positive ion, and the electron released is an equal negative charge somewhere in the same crystal. Adding up all such pairs leaves the total charge exactly zero.
formula_principle: Doping adds neutral atoms, so the crystal as a whole remains electrically neutral.
common_misconception: The words n-type and p-type are read as negatively and positively charged; they refer only to the sign of the majority carrier.

concept_tested: Expression for conductivity with two carrier types
stem: The electrical conductivity of a semiconductor carrying both electrons and holes is given by
solution: Each carrier type contributes a current density equal to its charge times its concentration times its mobility times the field. Electrons and holes carry opposite charges but drift in opposite directions, so the two current densities are in the same sense and their contributions add. This gives sigma = e (n_e mu_e + n_h mu_h).
formula_principle: sigma = e (n_e mu_e + n_h mu_h), where mu is the drift mobility of the carrier.
common_misconception: The opposite signs of the two charges lead students to subtract; the opposite drift directions make the contributions add.

concept_tested: Number of free electrons contributed by one donor atom
stem: Each pentavalent impurity atom substituted into a silicon lattice contributes
option_a: five free electrons, one for each of its valence electrons
option_c: one free electron, because four of its valence electrons are used in covalent bonds
correct_answer_text: one free electron, because four of its valence electrons are used in covalent bonds
solution: Silicon is tetravalent, so a substituting impurity can form only four covalent bonds. A pentavalent atom uses four of its valence electrons for these bonds and its fifth electron is left very loosely bound. A tiny amount of thermal energy sets that one electron free, so each donor gives exactly one free electron.
formula_principle: A donor atom forms four covalent bonds and releases its fifth valence electron as a free carrier.
common_misconception: All five valence electrons are assumed to become free; four of them are locked into covalent bonds.

concept_tested: Relative mobilities of electrons and holes
stem: In silicon at room temperature the drift mobility of electrons compared with that of holes is
option_a: smaller, so holes are the better carriers in every semiconductor
option_b: larger, so electrons contribute more to the current for the same concentration
option_c: exactly equal, because a hole is only a missing electron
option_d: zero, because electrons remain bound in covalent bonds
correct_answer_text: larger, so electrons contribute more to the current for the same concentration
solution: A conduction band electron moves through the crystal almost freely. A hole moves only because a valence electron from a neighbouring bond hops into the vacancy, and this step by step process is slower. Hence for the same applied field the electron drift velocity is larger, so electron mobility exceeds hole mobility and electrons carry more current for equal concentrations.
formula_principle: Electron mobility in a semiconductor is roughly two to three times the hole mobility.
common_misconception: Holes are pictured as free positive particles identical in behaviour to electrons, which would make the two mobilities equal.

concept_tested: Physical reason for the rise of n_i with temperature
stem: The intrinsic carrier concentration of a semiconductor rises rapidly with temperature because
option_a: the number of atoms in the crystal increases on heating
option_b: impurity atoms diffuse into the crystal from outside as it is heated
option_c: thermal energy breaks covalent bonds and creates fresh electron hole pairs
option_d: the drift velocity of the carriers rises while their number stays fixed
correct_answer_text: thermal energy breaks covalent bonds and creates fresh electron hole pairs
solution: Raising the temperature increases the vibrational energy of the lattice, and a bond breaks whenever an electron gains at least the gap energy. Every such event yields one free electron and one hole, so both concentrations climb sharply and stay equal to each other in a pure crystal.
formula_principle: n_i increases with temperature because thermal energy generates electron hole pairs across the forbidden gap.
common_misconception: The rise in n_i is attributed to faster carriers; speed is a mobility effect and does not change how many carriers exist.

concept_tested: Effect of a very small amount of dopant on conductivity
stem: Adding a very small controlled amount of a suitable impurity to a pure semiconductor
option_a: raises its conductivity enormously while the crystal stays electrically neutral
option_b: lowers its conductivity, because the impurity atoms obstruct the carriers
option_c: turns it into a metal whose bands overlap
option_d: has no effect at all until the sample is heated strongly
correct_answer_text: raises its conductivity enormously while the crystal stays electrically neutral
solution: Even one impurity atom in a very large number of host atoms supplies carriers in numbers far above the intrinsic concentration, so the conductivity may rise by several orders of magnitude. Since each dopant atom enters the lattice neutral, the crystal as a whole remains neutral throughout.
formula_principle: Controlled doping supplies majority carriers in numbers far greater than the intrinsic concentration, so conductivity rises steeply.
common_misconception: The small proportion of dopant is taken to mean a small effect; the effect on conductivity is very large.

concept_tested: Numerical use of the conductivity formula
stem: For an intrinsic semiconductor n_i = 2.5 x 10^19 per m^3, the electron mobility is 0.4 m^2/V s and the hole mobility is 0.2 m^2/V s. Its conductivity is (e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C)
solution: Here n_i e = 2.5 x 10^19 x 1.6 x 10^-19 = 4.0. Adding the mobilities, mu_e + mu_h = 0.4 + 0.2 = 0.6 m^2/V s. Hence sigma = 4.0 x 0.6 = 2.4 S/m. Both carrier types must be counted because in a pure sample their concentrations are equal.
formula_principle: For an intrinsic sample sigma = n_i e (mu_e + mu_h).
common_misconception: One of the two mobility terms is dropped, which halves or nearly doubles the answer depending on which is kept.

concept_tested: Extrinsic material at very high temperature
stem: An n-type germanium sample is heated to a very high temperature. Its behaviour then approaches that of
option_a: a p-type semiconductor, because heating creates holes
option_b: an intrinsic semiconductor, because thermally generated pairs greatly outnumber the donor electrons
option_c: a perfect insulator, because the donors are exhausted
option_d: a metallic conductor whose resistance is independent of temperature
correct_answer_text: an intrinsic semiconductor, because thermally generated pairs greatly outnumber the donor electrons
solution: The number of donor atoms is fixed, so the electrons they supply do not increase with temperature. Thermal generation, on the other hand, grows very rapidly. Once the generated pairs greatly outnumber the donor electrons, the electron and hole concentrations become nearly equal and the sample behaves like a pure crystal.
formula_principle: At high temperature the thermally generated pair concentration far exceeds the fixed dopant concentration, so extrinsic material behaves intrinsically.
common_misconception: The donors are thought to be used up or destroyed; they remain, but their fixed contribution simply becomes negligible.

concept_tested: Effect of donor doping on the hole population
stem: When a pure semiconductor is doped with donors so that the electron concentration rises, the equilibrium hole concentration
option_a: falls, because the product of the two concentrations must stay equal to n_i squared
option_b: rises in the same proportion as the electron concentration
option_d: becomes exactly zero, since all holes are filled by donor electrons
correct_answer_text: falls, because the product of the two concentrations must stay equal to n_i squared
solution: The extra electrons supplied by donors increase the rate at which holes are removed by recombination, while thermal generation continues at the same rate. Equilibrium is restored at a smaller hole concentration, such that the product of the two concentrations is still n_i squared. The hole population is reduced but never becomes zero.
formula_principle: n_e x n_h = n_i^2 at a fixed temperature, so raising one concentration lowers the other.
common_misconception: Doping is assumed to add carriers of both kinds; it increases one kind and suppresses the other.

concept_tested: Resistance from conductivity and geometry
stem: A silicon bar of length 0.1 m and area of cross section 1 x 10^-4 m^2 has a conductivity of 2 S/m. The resistance offered between its ends is
solution: The resistivity is rho = 1 / 2 = 0.5 ohm m. Then R = rho L / A = 0.5 x 0.1 / (1 x 10^-4) = 0.05 / 10^-4 = 500 ohm. Equivalently R = L / (sigma A) = 0.1 / (2 x 10^-4) = 500 ohm.
formula_principle: R = rho L / A and rho = 1 / sigma, so R = L / (sigma A).
common_misconception: Conductivity is used directly in place of resistivity, which inverts the answer.

concept_tested: Carrier populations and dominant carrier after doping
stem: A germanium crystal with n_i = 2 x 10^19 per m^3 is doped with 1 x 10^22 per m^3 donor atoms, all of which are ionised. The hole concentration and the dominant carrier are
option_a: 4 x 10^16 per m^3, with holes dominant
option_b: 4 x 10^16 per m^3, with electrons dominant
option_c: 2 x 10^19 per m^3, with electrons dominant
option_d: 4 x 10^38 per m^3, with electrons dominant
correct_answer_text: 4 x 10^16 per m^3, with electrons dominant
solution: Since the donor concentration of 1 x 10^22 per m^3 far exceeds n_i, the electron concentration equals 1 x 10^22 per m^3. Now n_i^2 = (2 x 10^19)^2 = 4 x 10^38, so n_h = 4 x 10^38 / 1 x 10^22 = 4 x 10^16 per m^3. Electrons outnumber holes by about a million times, so electrons are dominant.
formula_principle: n_e is set by the donor concentration and n_h = n_i^2 / n_e.
common_misconception: The dominant carrier is judged from the material name only; here the numbers themselves show electrons in huge excess.

concept_tested: Definition of the depletion region
stem: The narrow region on either side of a p-n junction which is practically free of mobile charge carriers is called
solution: When the junction is formed, electrons diffuse into the p-side and holes into the n-side, and they recombine near the boundary. This leaves a thin layer on both sides that has lost its mobile carriers and contains only fixed ionised impurity atoms. That layer is the depletion region.
formula_principle: Diffusion and recombination near the junction leave a carrier free layer called the depletion region.
common_misconception: The depletion region is imagined to be empty of everything; it still contains the fixed donor and acceptor ions.

concept_tested: Standard barrier potential values
stem: The barrier potentials of an unbiased silicon junction and an unbiased germanium junction are respectively about
solution: The barrier potential is the built-in potential difference established across the depletion layer at equilibrium. Its value depends on the material, being about 0.7 V for silicon and about 0.3 V for germanium. These are also the approximate forward voltages at which the two kinds of diode begin to conduct freely.
formula_principle: Barrier potential: about 0.7 V for a silicon junction and about 0.3 V for a germanium junction.
common_misconception: The band gaps of 1.1 eV and 0.7 eV are quoted as barrier potentials; the barrier potentials are the smaller numbers 0.7 V and 0.3 V.

concept_tested: Carriers responsible for the diffusion current
stem: The diffusion current across an unbiased p-n junction is carried by
option_a: minority carriers swept across by the junction field
option_b: the immobile donor and acceptor ions
option_d: majority carriers moving from the side where they are plentiful to the side where they are scarce
correct_answer_text: majority carriers moving from the side where they are plentiful to the side where they are scarce
solution: There are many holes on the p-side and very few on the n-side, and many electrons on the n-side and very few on the p-side. These concentration differences drive holes to the right and electrons to the left, and both flows constitute the diffusion current, which is therefore a majority carrier current.
formula_principle: Diffusion current arises from the concentration gradient of majority carriers across the junction.
common_misconception: Diffusion and drift currents are interchanged; diffusion belongs to majority carriers and drift to minority carriers.

concept_tested: Sign of the space charge on each side of the junction
stem: Immediately after a p-n junction is formed, the part of the depletion region lying on the n-side acquires
option_a: a positive charge, due to the uncovered donor ions left behind
option_b: a negative charge, due to uncovered acceptor ions
option_c: no charge at all, since the crystal as a whole is neutral
option_d: a positive charge, due to holes that are trapped there
correct_answer_text: a positive charge, due to the uncovered donor ions left behind
solution: Electrons diffuse out of the n-side and recombine on the p-side. The donor atoms they leave behind are locked in the lattice and are now positively charged, so the n-side of the depletion layer carries a positive space charge. By the same argument the p-side of the layer carries a negative space charge from the ionised acceptors.
formula_principle: Electrons leaving the n-side uncover positive donor ions there, while holes leaving the p-side uncover negative acceptor ions.
common_misconception: The sign is chosen from the majority carrier rather than from the ion left behind, which reverses the answer.

concept_tested: Balance of diffusion and drift at an unbiased junction
stem: In an unbiased p-n junction in equilibrium, the diffusion current and the drift current are
option_a: both exactly zero, since no carrier moves at all
option_b: equal in magnitude and in the same direction, giving a large steady current
option_c: unequal, giving a steady current of a few milliampere
option_d: equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so that the net current is zero
correct_answer_text: equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so that the net current is zero
solution: Diffusion drives majority carriers across the junction, which builds up the space charge and the barrier field. That field drives minority carriers the other way as a drift current. The barrier grows until the two currents are exactly equal and opposite, so the net current through an isolated junction is zero.
formula_principle: At equilibrium the majority carrier diffusion current is exactly cancelled by the minority carrier drift current.
common_misconception: Zero net current is read as no motion at all; two large opposing flows are actually present and cancel.

concept_tested: Direction of the built-in electric field
stem: The built-in electric field in the depletion layer of a p-n junction is directed
option_a: from the p-side towards the n-side
option_b: from the n-side towards the p-side
option_c: along the plane of the junction, parallel to it
option_d: radially outwards from the centre of the junction
correct_answer_text: from the n-side towards the p-side
solution: The n-side of the depletion layer holds fixed positive donor ions and the p-side holds fixed negative acceptor ions. An electric field always points from positive charge towards negative charge, so the built-in field runs from the n-side to the p-side. This field opposes further diffusion of majority carriers.
formula_principle: The field points from the positive space charge to the negative space charge, that is, from the n-side to the p-side.
common_misconception: The direction is guessed from the motion of electrons; electrons move against the field, so the field points the other way.

concept_tested: Effect of forward bias on barrier and depletion width
stem: When a p-n junction is forward biased, the width of the depletion layer and the height of the potential barrier
option_d: remain unchanged while only the current through the diode changes
solution: The external supply pushes holes towards the junction from the p-side and electrons towards it from the n-side. These carriers neutralise part of the space charge, so the layer becomes thinner and the potential step across it becomes smaller. A lower barrier lets many more majority carriers cross, which is why the forward current grows rapidly.
formula_principle: Forward bias opposes the built-in potential, lowering the barrier and narrowing the depletion layer.
common_misconception: Only the barrier height is thought to change; the depletion width changes in exactly the same sense.

concept_tested: Electric field from barrier potential and depletion width
stem: The barrier potential of a germanium junction is 0.3 V and its depletion layer is 1 x 10^-6 m wide. The average electric field inside the layer is
solution: Treating the field as uniform, E = 0.3 / (1 x 10^-6) = 3 x 10^5 V/m. Such a large field inside a very thin layer is what sweeps every minority carrier that wanders into the depletion region straight across the junction.
formula_principle: For a uniform field, E = V / d.
common_misconception: The very small width makes students multiply instead of divide, giving an absurdly small field.

concept_tested: Work needed to carry an electron across the barrier
stem: The work that must be done to carry one electron across a silicon junction whose barrier potential is 0.7 V is
solution: The work is W = 1.6 x 10^-19 x 0.7 = 1.12 x 10^-19 J, which is the same as 0.7 eV. This is the energy an electron must gain to climb the barrier of an unbiased silicon junction.
formula_principle: W = q V, with q = 1.6 x 10^-19 C.
common_misconception: Volt and joule are treated as the same unit; the potential must be multiplied by the charge to give energy.

concept_tested: Effective barrier height under reverse bias
stem: A junction whose barrier potential is 0.7 V is reverse biased by an external supply of 5 V. The effective height of the barrier becomes
solution: Reverse bias makes the n-side more positive and the p-side more negative, which is the same sense as the built-in space charge. The two potentials therefore add, giving 0.7 + 5 = 5.7 V. The depletion layer widens and the diffusion of majority carriers is almost completely stopped.
formula_principle: In reverse bias the applied voltage adds to the built-in barrier, giving an effective barrier of V0 + V.
common_misconception: The applied voltage is subtracted out of habit from forward bias problems; in reverse bias the voltages add.

concept_tested: Why a junction cannot be made mechanically
stem: A p-type crystal and an n-type crystal are simply pressed firmly against each other. The combination
option_a: does not act as a p-n junction, because a single continuous crystal lattice is needed at the boundary
option_b: acts as a perfect p-n junction with a barrier of 0.7 V
option_c: acts as a p-n junction only after it is heated strongly
option_d: acts as two junctions connected back to back
correct_answer_text: does not act as a p-n junction, because a single continuous crystal lattice is needed at the boundary
solution: Diffusion of carriers and the formation of a proper depletion layer require an unbroken crystal lattice across the boundary. Two pressed surfaces have a discontinuity, surface oxide and trapped impurities in between, so the ordered exchange of carriers that builds the barrier cannot occur. Real junctions are made by growing or diffusing one region into the other.
formula_principle: A p-n junction must be grown or diffused so that the crystal lattice runs continuously from the p-region into the n-region.
common_misconception: The junction is thought of as a mere meeting of two materials; it is a single crystal with two doped regions.

concept_tested: Why the drift current is nearly independent of reverse voltage
stem: The drift current across a p-n junction is almost independent of the applied reverse voltage because it depends on
option_a: the number of majority carriers, which the applied voltage controls
option_b: the width of the depletion layer alone
option_c: the doping concentration of the p-side alone
option_d: the number of thermally generated minority carriers, which is fixed at a given temperature
correct_answer_text: the number of thermally generated minority carriers, which is fixed at a given temperature
solution: Every minority carrier that wanders into the depletion layer is swept across by the strong barrier field, whatever the reverse voltage may be. So the current is limited not by the field but by how many such carriers are produced, and that number depends on temperature and not on voltage. Hence the reverse current saturates.
formula_principle: Reverse current is a saturation current set by the rate of thermal generation of minority carriers.
common_misconception: Saturation is read as meaning independent of temperature; it means independent of voltage, and it does grow with temperature.

concept_tested: Dependence of depletion width on doping level
stem: Two silicon junctions have identical geometry but one is far more heavily doped than the other. The heavily doped junction has
option_d: a depletion layer of exactly the same width
solution: The barrier potential is supported by the charge of the uncovered ions. In heavily doped material the ions are packed far more densely, so the required charge is uncovered within a much shorter distance on each side. The layer is therefore narrow, and the field inside it is correspondingly large. This is exactly why a Zener diode, which is heavily doped, breaks down at a low reverse voltage.
formula_principle: The space charge needed to support the barrier is provided by fewer ions over a shorter distance when the doping is heavy.
common_misconception: Heavier doping is assumed to make everything larger; it actually shrinks the depletion width and raises the junction field.

concept_tested: Resistance of the depletion layer
stem: Which of the following is true of the depletion region of an unbiased p-n junction?
option_a: It has the lowest resistance in the crystal, because of the strong field inside it
option_b: It has a very high resistance, since it is nearly free of mobile carriers
option_c: It contains mobile electrons only and no fixed ions
option_d: Its width is the same as the width of the whole crystal
correct_answer_text: It has a very high resistance, since it is nearly free of mobile carriers
solution: The depletion layer has lost its mobile electrons and holes through diffusion and recombination, leaving only fixed ionised impurity atoms. With practically no carriers available to move, that thin layer offers a very high resistance, which is why almost the whole applied voltage appears across it in reverse bias.
formula_principle: Resistance depends on the availability of mobile carriers, and the depletion layer has almost none.
common_misconception: The strong internal field suggests easy conduction; conduction needs carriers, and this region is nearly empty of them.

concept_tested: What the potential barrier opposes
stem: The potential barrier of an unbiased p-n junction opposes
option_a: the drift of minority carriers across the junction
option_b: the diffusion of majority carriers across the junction
option_c: both diffusion and drift equally, so nothing can cross
option_d: the recombination of electrons and holes anywhere in the crystal
correct_answer_text: the diffusion of majority carriers across the junction
solution: The field points from the n-side to the p-side. An electron trying to diffuse from the n-side to the p-side must move against this field, so majority carrier diffusion is opposed. A minority electron on the p-side, on the other hand, is pushed by the same field towards the n-side, so the barrier assists minority carrier drift. Equilibrium is the balance of these two effects.
formula_principle: The built-in field opposes majority carrier diffusion and assists minority carrier drift.
common_misconception: The barrier is assumed to block everything; it blocks majority carriers while sweeping minority carriers across.

concept_tested: Force on an electron inside the depletion layer
stem: A silicon junction has a barrier potential of 0.7 V across a depletion layer 0.5 micrometre wide. The force on an electron inside this layer is (e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C)
solution: First the field: E = 0.7 / (0.5 x 10^-6) = 1.4 x 10^6 V/m. Then the force: F = 1.6 x 10^-19 x 1.4 x 10^6 = 2.24 x 10^-13 N. Although the number looks tiny, it is enormous compared with the force on an electron in an ordinary conductor, which is why carriers are swept across the layer almost instantly.
formula_principle: E = V / d and F = e E.
common_misconception: The second step is skipped and the field itself is offered as the force, or charge times voltage is quoted, which is an energy.

concept_tested: Combined barrier of a silicon and a germanium junction
stem: A silicon diode and a germanium diode are joined in series in the forward direction across a supply whose voltage is raised slowly from zero. Appreciable current begins to flow when the supply just exceeds
solution: The same current must pass through both junctions, so the supply has to overcome both barriers at once. The silicon junction needs about 0.7 V and the germanium junction about 0.3 V, giving a total of 1.0 V before the pair conducts appreciably. Below this the germanium diode may pass a small current but the silicon diode still blocks the path.
formula_principle: Barrier potentials of junctions in series add: V(total) = 0.7 V + 0.3 V for silicon and germanium.
common_misconception: Only the larger barrier is taken as decisive; in series both barriers must be overcome and the voltages add.

concept_tested: Temperature dependence of the reverse saturation current
stem: The temperature of a reverse biased p-n junction is raised from 300 K to 350 K while the reverse voltage is kept constant. The reverse current
option_a: stays exactly the same, because it is called a saturation current
option_b: decreases, because the mobility of the carriers falls as the temperature rises
option_c: falls to zero once the barrier has been crossed
option_d: increases markedly, because many more minority carriers are generated thermally
correct_answer_text: increases markedly, because many more minority carriers are generated thermally
solution: The reverse current is limited by how fast minority carriers are produced, not by the voltage. Heating breaks many more covalent bonds, so minority carriers appear at a much greater rate on both sides of the junction. Every one that reaches the depletion layer is swept across, so the reverse current rises sharply. In silicon it roughly doubles for each 10 degree Celsius rise.
formula_principle: Reverse saturation current is proportional to the thermally generated minority carrier concentration, which rises steeply with temperature.
common_misconception: The word saturation is misread; the current is voltage independent but strongly temperature dependent.

concept_tested: Correct connection for forward bias
stem: A junction diode is said to be forward biased when
option_a: the p-region is joined to the negative terminal and the n-region to the positive terminal
option_b: both regions are joined to the positive terminal of the source
option_c: the p-region is joined to the positive terminal and the n-region to the negative terminal of the source
option_d: the diode is joined across an open switch with no source in the circuit
correct_answer_text: the p-region is joined to the positive terminal and the n-region to the negative terminal of the source
solution: Connecting the p-side to the positive terminal drives holes towards the junction and connecting the n-side to the negative terminal drives electrons towards it. This opposes the built-in field, lowers the barrier, narrows the depletion layer and allows a large majority carrier current.
formula_principle: Forward bias means the p-side is at the higher potential, which reduces the barrier.
common_misconception: The bias is judged from the diode symbol drawn on paper instead of from which region sits at the higher potential.

concept_tested: Cut in voltage of a silicon diode
stem: The knee voltage, also called the cut in voltage, of a silicon junction diode is nearly
solution: Below the knee voltage the applied forward voltage is not enough to overcome the barrier, so the current stays very small. Once the applied voltage reaches about 0.7 V in silicon the barrier is largely cancelled and the current rises very steeply with any further increase in voltage.
formula_principle: Knee voltage: about 0.7 V for silicon, about 0.3 V for germanium.
common_misconception: The knee voltage is confused with the band gap; the two are different quantities with different units.

concept_tested: Order of magnitude of the reverse saturation current
stem: In a good silicon diode the reverse saturation current is typically of the order of
solution: In reverse bias the majority carrier flow is stopped, and only the few minority carriers that reach the depletion layer are swept across. Since their number is very small, the resulting current is of the order of microampere in silicon, small enough for the diode to be treated as an open circuit in most calculations.
formula_principle: Reverse saturation current is set by thermally generated minority carriers and is very small.
common_misconception: The reverse current is taken as exactly zero; it is small but real, and it grows rapidly with temperature.

concept_tested: Resistance of an ideal diode in the two directions
stem: An ideal diode is one which has
option_a: infinite resistance in forward bias and zero resistance in reverse bias
option_b: the same finite resistance in both directions
option_c: zero resistance in forward bias and infinite resistance in reverse bias
