correct_answer_text: zero resistance in forward bias and infinite resistance in reverse bias
solution: The ideal diode is a convenient approximation in circuit problems. It drops no voltage at all when it conducts and passes no current at all when it is reverse biased. A real silicon diode differs by having a forward drop of about 0.7 V and a small reverse leakage.
formula_principle: An ideal diode is a perfect conductor when forward biased and a perfect insulator when reverse biased.
common_misconception: The ideal model is applied even where the 0.7 V forward drop matters; the model should be used only when that drop is negligible.

concept_tested: Static resistance from a point on the characteristic
stem: A silicon diode carries a forward current of 7 mA when the voltage across it is 0.7 V. Its static resistance at this point is
solution: Converting the current, I = 7 mA = 7 x 10^-3 A. Then R = 0.7 / (7 x 10^-3) = 100 ohm. This is the ratio of the coordinates of one point on the characteristic and it changes from point to point because the curve is not a straight line through the origin.
formula_principle: Static or dc resistance R = V / I at the chosen operating point.
common_misconception: The current is left in milliampere, which makes the resistance smaller by a factor of one thousand.

concept_tested: Dynamic resistance from small changes in voltage and current
stem: The forward voltage of a diode changes from 0.70 V to 0.75 V while its current changes from 10 mA to 15 mA. The dynamic resistance of the diode is
solution: The change in voltage is 0.75 - 0.70 = 0.05 V and the change in current is 15 - 10 = 5 mA = 5 x 10^-3 A. Hence r = 0.05 / (5 x 10^-3) = 10 ohm. Note how much smaller this is than the static resistance at the same point, which shows how steeply the forward curve rises.
formula_principle: Dynamic or ac resistance r = change in V divided by change in I.
common_misconception: Total values are used in place of changes, which gives the static resistance rather than the dynamic resistance.

concept_tested: Current in a series diode and resistor circuit
stem: A silicon diode is joined in series with a 1 kohm resistor across a 10 V battery, with the diode forward biased. The current in the circuit is
solution: The diode holds about 0.7 V, so the resistor takes 10 - 0.7 = 9.3 V. Hence I = 9.3 / 1000 = 9.3 x 10^-3 A = 9.3 mA. The same current flows through the diode and the resistor because they are in series.
formula_principle: For a conducting silicon diode in series with R, I = (V - 0.7) / R.
common_misconception: The diode drop is forgotten, which is acceptable only when the supply is very large compared with 0.7 V.

concept_tested: Current in a germanium diode circuit
stem: A germanium diode in series with a 470 ohm resistor is forward biased by a 5 V supply. The current through the resistor is
solution: The germanium diode drops about 0.3 V, leaving 5 - 0.3 = 4.7 V across the resistor. Hence I = 4.7 / 470 = 0.01 A = 10 mA. Using the silicon figure by mistake would change the answer by nearly one milliampere.
formula_principle: For a conducting germanium diode in series with R, I = (V - 0.3) / R.
common_misconception: The 0.7 V figure is applied to every diode; germanium diodes drop only about 0.3 V.

concept_tested: Total drop across two dissimilar diodes in series
stem: A silicon diode and a germanium diode are joined in series in the forward direction. Once both are conducting, the total voltage drop across the pair is about
solution: Both diodes carry the same current and their drops appear one after the other along the loop, so the drops add to give 0.7 + 0.3 = 1.0 V. This is the reason a series chain of diodes is sometimes used to obtain a roughly fixed voltage reference.
formula_principle: Voltage drops of series elements add: 0.7 V + 0.3 V.
common_misconception: The two drops are treated as alternatives, so only the larger one is counted.

concept_tested: Voltage distribution when a diode is reverse biased
stem: A diode is joined in reverse bias in series with a 2 kohm resistor across a 6 V supply. The potential difference across the resistor is very nearly
option_a: 6 V, since a diode offers no resistance
option_b: 5.3 V, after allowing a 0.7 V drop for the diode
option_c: 3 V, since the supply divides equally between the two elements
option_d: 0 V, since only a tiny leakage current flows
correct_answer_text: 0 V, since only a tiny leakage current flows
solution: In reverse bias only a leakage current of a few microampere flows. Across 2 kohm this gives a drop of only a few millivolt, which is negligible. Practically the whole of the 6 V therefore appears across the diode and the resistor drop is taken as zero.
formula_principle: A reverse biased diode behaves almost as an open circuit, so nearly the whole supply appears across it.
common_misconception: The 0.7 V rule is applied automatically; it belongs to forward conduction only.

concept_tested: Behaviour of a diode beyond reverse breakdown
stem: When the reverse voltage across a junction diode is raised past its breakdown value, the reverse current
option_b: rises very sharply while the voltage across the diode stays nearly constant
option_c: rises in direct proportion to the voltage, as in a resistor
option_d: reverses its direction and becomes a forward current
correct_answer_text: rises very sharply while the voltage across the diode stays nearly constant
solution: Beyond the breakdown voltage, either the intense junction field frees bound electrons directly or accelerated carriers create fresh pairs by collision. Either way carriers are produced in large numbers and the reverse current climbs steeply, while the voltage across the diode remains close to the breakdown value. This constant voltage property is what a Zener diode exploits.
formula_principle: At breakdown the reverse characteristic becomes almost vertical, so current changes greatly while voltage hardly changes.
common_misconception: Breakdown is thought to destroy the diode; it is reversible provided the current is limited by an external resistance.

concept_tested: Shape of the forward characteristic curve
stem: In the forward characteristic of a junction diode the current
option_a: increases linearly with voltage right from zero
option_b: decreases as the forward voltage is increased
option_c: remains constant at all forward voltages
option_d: stays very small up to the knee voltage and then rises steeply
correct_answer_text: stays very small up to the knee voltage and then rises steeply
solution: Below the knee the applied voltage cancels only part of the barrier, so very few majority carriers get across and the current is negligible. Once the knee is passed the barrier is nearly cancelled and the current rises almost vertically, so a small extra voltage produces a large extra current.
formula_principle: The forward characteristic is nonlinear, with a knee near 0.7 V for silicon.
common_misconception: The curve is remembered as a straight line, which would make the static and dynamic resistances equal.

concept_tested: Dynamic resistance in the reverse region
stem: In the reverse characteristic of a diode the current changes from 5 microampere to 6 microampere when the reverse voltage changes from 10 V to 20 V. The dynamic reverse resistance is
solution: The change in voltage is 20 - 10 = 10 V and the change in current is 6 - 5 = 1 microampere = 1 x 10^-6 A. Hence r = 10 / (1 x 10^-6) = 1 x 10^7 ohm. Such a huge value shows how nearly the reverse current saturates.
formula_principle: r = change in V divided by change in I, using consistent units.
common_misconception: The microampere prefix is dropped, which changes the answer by a factor of a million.

concept_tested: Doubling rule for reverse saturation current
stem: The reverse saturation current of a silicon diode nearly doubles for every rise of 10 degree Celsius. If it is 2 microampere at 300 K, its value at 320 K is about
solution: A rise from 300 K to 320 K is 20 degrees, which is two steps of 10 degrees. The current doubles at each step: 2 becomes 4 and 4 becomes 8. Hence the reverse current is about 8 microampere. The growth is geometric and not proportional to the temperature rise.
formula_principle: I(reverse) doubles for each 10 degree Celsius rise, so a rise of 20 degrees multiplies it by 2 x 2.
common_misconception: The doubling is treated as a proportionality, so the rise of 20 degrees is used as a multiplying factor.

concept_tested: Which of two dissimilar parallel diodes conducts
stem: A silicon diode and a germanium diode are joined in parallel in the same sense, and the pair is forward biased through a series resistor. In the steady state
option_a: almost the whole current passes through the germanium diode, which holds the voltage near 0.3 V
option_b: almost the whole current passes through the silicon diode
option_c: the current divides equally between the two diodes
option_d: no current flows, because the two diodes oppose each other
correct_answer_text: almost the whole current passes through the germanium diode, which holds the voltage near 0.3 V
solution: As the voltage across the pair rises, the germanium diode reaches its knee of about 0.3 V first and starts conducting heavily. Because both diodes have the same voltage across them, that voltage is now held near 0.3 V, which is well below the 0.7 V the silicon diode needs. The silicon diode therefore stays almost off.
formula_principle: Parallel elements share the same voltage; the diode with the lower knee voltage conducts first and clamps that voltage.
common_misconception: Students assume the two diodes share the current; the one that conducts first clamps the common voltage and keeps the other off.

concept_tested: Whether a diode obeys Ohm's law
stem: A student argues that a diode obeys Ohm's law because a graph of current against voltage can be drawn for it. The correct comment is that
option_a: the diode obeys Ohm's law in reverse bias where the graph is flat
option_b: the diode obeys Ohm's law because a resistance can be worked out at every point
option_c: the diode obeys Ohm's law above the knee where the curve rises steeply
option_d: the graph is not a straight line through the origin, so the diode is nonlinear and does not obey Ohm's law
correct_answer_text: the graph is not a straight line through the origin, so the diode is nonlinear and does not obey Ohm's law
solution: A ratio of voltage to current can always be worked out, but Ohm's law demands that this ratio be the same at every operating point. For a diode the ratio changes enormously along the curve, being of the order of megaohm below the knee and only tens of ohm above it. Hence the diode is a nonlinear device.
formula_principle: Ohm's law requires the ratio V / I to be constant, that is, a straight line characteristic through the origin.
common_misconception: Any current voltage graph is taken as evidence for Ohm's law; only a straight line through the origin qualifies.

concept_tested: Series resistance needed to limit the diode current
stem: A 12 V supply is to drive a silicon diode in series with a resistance R, with the current limited to 10 mA. The value of R should be
solution: The diode holds about 0.7 V, so the resistor must drop 12 - 0.7 = 11.3 V while carrying 10 mA. Hence R = 11.3 / (10 x 10^-3) = 1130 ohm. In practice the nearest standard value above this would be chosen so that the current never exceeds the limit.
formula_principle: R = (V(supply) - V(diode)) / I(required).
common_misconception: The diode drop is left out, which makes the calculated resistance too large and the actual current too small.

concept_tested: Static resistance compared with dynamic resistance
stem: For a junction diode operating well above its knee voltage, the static resistance is generally
option_a: larger than the dynamic resistance at the same operating point
option_b: smaller than the dynamic resistance at the same point
option_c: exactly equal to the dynamic resistance
correct_answer_text: larger than the dynamic resistance at the same operating point
solution: Take a typical point such as 0.7 V and 10 mA, which gives a static resistance of 70 ohm. Around the same point a change of 0.05 V may produce a change of 5 mA, giving a dynamic resistance of only 10 ohm. Because the curve rises far more steeply than the line joining the point to the origin, the static value always exceeds the dynamic value in this region.
formula_principle: Static resistance is V / I while dynamic resistance is the slope reciprocal; for a steeply rising forward curve the slope reciprocal is much smaller.
common_misconception: The two resistances are assumed to be the same quantity; they are equal only for a device obeying Ohm's law.

concept_tested: Current with two identical diodes in series
stem: Two identical silicon diodes are joined in series with a 100 ohm resistor across a 3.4 V supply, both diodes being forward biased. The current in the circuit is
solution: Each silicon diode drops about 0.7 V, so the two together drop 1.4 V. The resistor therefore receives 3.4 - 1.4 = 2.0 V, giving I = 2.0 / 100 = 0.02 A = 20 mA. Both diodes and the resistor carry this same current since they form a single loop.
formula_principle: I = (V(supply) - sum of diode drops) / R.
common_misconception: Only one diode drop is subtracted, which overestimates the current by about a third here.

concept_tested: Current through two oppositely connected diodes
stem: Two silicon diodes are joined back to back, that is anode to anode, and the pair is placed in series with a 1 kohm resistor across a 6 V battery. The current in the circuit is
option_a: 6 mA, because the two diodes conduct in turn
option_b: 4.6 mA, after subtracting the drops of both diodes
option_c: 5.3 mA, after subtracting the drop of one diode
option_d: almost zero, because one of the two diodes is always reverse biased
correct_answer_text: almost zero, because one of the two diodes is always reverse biased
solution: With the anodes joined, current entering from the battery must pass through one diode from anode to cathode and then through the other from cathode to anode. The second passage is against the arrow, so that diode blocks. Reversing the battery merely swaps the roles of the two diodes. Only the microampere level leakage flows, so the current is taken as zero.
formula_principle: Two diodes in opposition always leave one of them reverse biased, so the path is blocked for direct current of either polarity.
common_misconception: Each diode is checked separately and one is found to conduct; the series path requires both to conduct at the same time.

concept_tested: Number of diodes in half wave and bridge rectifiers
stem: The numbers of diodes used in a half wave rectifier and in a bridge type full wave rectifier are respectively
solution: A half wave circuit uses a single diode which conducts during one half cycle only. A bridge circuit uses four diodes arranged so that two opposite arms conduct during each half cycle, which routes current through the load in the same direction both times. The centre tap version of the full wave circuit uses two diodes and a centre tapped transformer.
formula_principle: Half wave rectifier: 1 diode. Centre tap full wave: 2 diodes. Bridge full wave: 4 diodes.
common_misconception: The three diode counts get mixed up; the two full wave versions differ, one using two diodes and the other four.

concept_tested: Output frequency of a half wave rectifier
stem: A half wave rectifier is fed by an alternating voltage of frequency 50 Hz. The fundamental frequency of its pulsating output is
solution: In a half wave circuit one pulse appears in each complete input cycle, because the diode conducts during one half cycle and blocks during the other. Hence the pulses repeat exactly as often as the input cycles, and the output frequency is 50 Hz, the same as the input.
formula_principle: Half wave output frequency equals the input frequency; full wave output frequency is twice the input.
common_misconception: The doubling rule is applied to every rectifier; only the full wave circuit doubles the frequency.

concept_tested: Ripple frequency of a full wave rectifier
stem: A full wave rectifier is fed from a 50 Hz supply. The ripple frequency at its output is
solution: Both halves of the input cycle are used and each produces a pulse of the same polarity through the load. Two pulses per input cycle means the output repeats twice as often, giving 2 x 50 = 100 Hz. This is one reason a full wave output is easier to smooth than a half wave output.
formula_principle: A full wave rectifier delivers two pulses per input cycle, so its ripple frequency is twice the input frequency.
common_misconception: The frequency is thought to be a property of the supply alone; the rectifier circuit changes the repetition rate of the output.

concept_tested: Maximum rectification efficiencies
stem: The maximum theoretical rectification efficiencies of a half wave rectifier and of a full wave rectifier are respectively
solution: Rectification efficiency is the ratio of dc output power to ac input power. Because the full wave circuit uses both halves of every cycle, its maximum efficiency of 81.2 percent is exactly twice the 40.6 percent of the half wave circuit. These maxima are reached only when the diode forward resistance is negligible compared with the load.
formula_principle: Maximum rectification efficiency: 40.6 percent for half wave and 81.2 percent for full wave.
common_misconception: The efficiencies are guessed as 50 percent and 100 percent from the fraction of the cycle used; the correct figures are lower because the output is pulsating.

concept_tested: Standard ripple factor values
stem: The ripple factors of a half wave rectifier and of a full wave rectifier are respectively
solution: The ripple factor measures how much alternating component remains in the output relative to the dc component. A half wave output has long gaps and so a very large ripple factor of 1.21, meaning the ac component actually exceeds the dc component. A full wave output has no gaps and its ripple factor is only 0.48.
formula_principle: Ripple factor: 1.21 for a half wave rectifier and 0.48 for a full wave rectifier.
common_misconception: A smaller ripple factor is sometimes thought to mean poorer output; a smaller ripple factor means a smoother and better output.

concept_tested: Function of a capacitor filter
stem: A capacitor is joined across the load of a rectifier. Its purpose is
option_a: to raise the output frequency of the rectifier
option_b: to convert alternating voltage into alternating voltage of higher value
option_c: to block the dc component and pass only the ripple to the load
option_d: to reduce the ripple by charging at the peaks and discharging slowly through the load
correct_answer_text: to reduce the ripple by charging at the peaks and discharging slowly through the load
solution: During each pulse the capacitor charges to nearly the peak value. When the pulse falls away the diode stops conducting and the capacitor supplies the load, so the output voltage sags only a little before the next pulse arrives. The result is a much smaller ripple riding on a higher average voltage.
formula_principle: A shunt capacitor filter stores charge at the peaks and supplies the load between the peaks, smoothing the output.
common_misconception: The filter is thought to remove the ripple completely; it reduces the ripple but never abolishes it.

concept_tested: When the diode of a half wave rectifier conducts
stem: In a half wave rectifier using a single diode, the diode conducts
option_a: during both half cycles of the input
option_b: during the half cycle in which its cathode is positive with respect to its anode
option_c: during the half cycle in which its anode is positive with respect to its cathode
option_d: only at the instants when the input voltage passes through zero
correct_answer_text: during the half cycle in which its anode is positive with respect to its cathode
solution: During one half cycle the transformer secondary makes the anode positive, the diode is forward biased and current flows through the load. During the next half cycle the polarity reverses, the diode is reverse biased and the current is essentially zero. Hence only alternate half cycles reach the load.
formula_principle: A diode conducts only when it is forward biased, that is, when its anode is at the higher potential.
common_misconception: Conduction is imagined to occur throughout the cycle with only the size varying; the diode is completely off for one half of every cycle.

concept_tested: Average load current of a half wave rectifier
stem: The peak value of the current through the load of a half wave rectifier is 31.4 mA. The average value of the load current is (take pi = 3.14)
solution: Substituting, I(dc) = 31.4 / 3.14 = 10 mA. The averaging is taken over the whole cycle, including the half in which the diode does not conduct, which is why the average is so much smaller than the peak.
formula_principle: For a half wave rectifier I(dc) = Im / pi.
common_misconception: The peak is halved because half the cycle is used; the correct division is by pi, not by two.

concept_tested: Average load current of a full wave rectifier
stem: In a full wave rectifier the peak load current is 15.7 mA. The average value of the load current is (take pi = 3.14)
solution: Substituting, I(dc) = 2 x 15.7 / 3.14 = 31.4 / 3.14 = 10 mA. Because both halves of each cycle contribute, the average is exactly twice what the same peak would give in a half wave circuit.
formula_principle: For a full wave rectifier I(dc) = 2 Im / pi.
common_misconception: The half wave formula is applied to a full wave circuit, which halves the answer.

concept_tested: Operation of a centre tap full wave rectifier
stem: In a centre tap full wave rectifier
option_a: two diodes are used and both conduct together during every half cycle
option_b: two diodes are used and each conducts during alternate half cycles
option_c: four diodes are used, two of them conducting at a time
option_d: one diode is used and it conducts throughout the cycle
correct_answer_text: two diodes are used and each conducts during alternate half cycles
solution: The centre tap divides the secondary into two halves whose ends are always of opposite polarity with respect to the tap. During one half cycle the upper half drives its diode into conduction, and during the next half cycle the lower half drives the other diode. Both currents pass through the load in the same direction, so a full wave output is obtained.
formula_principle: The centre tap circuit uses two diodes, one for each half of the secondary winding, conducting alternately.
common_misconception: Simultaneous conduction is assumed; the opposite polarities of the two secondary halves make that impossible.

concept_tested: Diodes conducting in a bridge rectifier
stem: In a bridge rectifier, during any one half cycle of the input
option_a: two diodes in opposite arms conduct while the other two are reverse biased
option_b: all four diodes conduct at the same time
option_d: three diodes conduct and one is reverse biased
correct_answer_text: two diodes in opposite arms conduct while the other two are reverse biased
solution: The four diodes form a ring. In one half cycle the two diodes whose arrows point away from the positive terminal and towards the load are forward biased, while the other two are reverse biased. When the input reverses, the roles swap. In both cases the current traverses the load in the same direction, giving full wave rectification without a centre tap.
formula_principle: In a bridge, one diagonal pair conducts in one half cycle and the other pair in the next, sending current through the load in the same direction each time.
common_misconception: Students count all four diodes as conducting; only the diagonal pair matching the input polarity conducts at any moment.

concept_tested: Advantage of a bridge over a centre tap circuit
stem: A bridge rectifier is often preferred to a centre tap full wave rectifier because
option_a: it needs no centre tapped transformer and gives a higher output voltage from the same secondary
option_c: its output frequency is twice that of a centre tap circuit
option_d: it converts direct current into alternating current
correct_answer_text: it needs no centre tapped transformer and gives a higher output voltage from the same secondary
solution: In a centre tap circuit only one half of the secondary is in the circuit at any moment, so the peak voltage available is half of the full secondary voltage. A bridge places the whole secondary across the conducting path, so it delivers roughly twice the output from the same winding and needs no centre tap. The price paid is two extra diodes and two diode drops.
formula_principle: In a bridge the whole secondary voltage is applied to the load, whereas in a centre tap circuit only half of it is used at a time.
common_misconception: The bridge is assumed to be simpler in every way; it actually needs more diodes and has a larger total forward drop.

concept_tested: Definition of the ripple factor
stem: The ripple factor of the output of a rectifier is defined as
option_a: the ratio of the dc value to the rms value of the alternating component
option_b: the ratio of the output frequency to the input frequency
option_c: the ratio of the rms value of the alternating component to the dc value of the output
option_d: the ratio of the dc output power to the ac input power
correct_answer_text: the ratio of the rms value of the alternating component to the dc value of the output
solution: The rectifier output is a steady dc component with an unwanted alternating component riding on it. The ripple factor compares the size of the unwanted part with the useful part, so a smaller value means a smoother output. Adding a filter reduces the ac component and therefore reduces the ripple factor.
formula_principle: Ripple factor = rms value of the ac component divided by the dc value of the output.
common_misconception: Ripple factor and efficiency are confused; one compares two currents and the other compares two powers.

concept_tested: Description of an unfiltered rectifier output
stem: The output of a rectifier without any filter is best described as
option_a: a unidirectional pulsating voltage containing both a dc component and an ac component
option_c: an alternating voltage of twice the input amplitude
option_d: a square wave of the same frequency as the input
correct_answer_text: a unidirectional pulsating voltage containing both a dc component and an ac component
solution: The diode allows current in one direction only, so the output never reverses sign. However its magnitude still rises and falls with each pulse, so the output can be analysed as a steady average value with an alternating component superposed. The filter is added to reduce that alternating component.
formula_principle: Rectification makes the current unidirectional but leaves it pulsating, so filtering is needed for a steady output.
common_misconception: Rectified output is assumed to be pure dc; it is unidirectional but far from steady until it is filtered.

concept_tested: Peak inverse voltage of a half wave rectifier
stem: In a half wave rectifier the transformer secondary has a peak voltage Vm. The peak inverse voltage that the diode must withstand is
solution: During the non conducting half cycle no current flows, so there is no drop across the load and the whole secondary voltage appears across the diode in the reverse sense. Its largest value in that half cycle is Vm. A diode with a peak inverse voltage rating below Vm would break down.
formula_principle: Peak inverse voltage is the largest reverse voltage across a non conducting diode; it is Vm for a half wave circuit.
common_misconception: The value 2 Vm is quoted for every rectifier; that figure belongs to the centre tap full wave circuit.

concept_tested: Efficiency with a finite diode forward resistance
stem: In a half wave rectifier the load resistance is 900 ohm and the forward resistance of the diode is 100 ohm. The rectification efficiency is about
solution: Here rf / RL = 100 / 900 = 0.111, so the denominator is 1.111. Then the efficiency is 40.6 / 1.111 = 36.5 percent. The diode resistance wastes part of the power, so the practical efficiency always falls short of the ideal 40.6 percent.
formula_principle: Efficiency of a half wave rectifier = 40.6 / (1 + rf / RL) percent.
common_misconception: The ideal figure is quoted directly; the forward resistance of the diode must be allowed for whenever it is given.

concept_tested: Ripple factor computed from rms and dc currents
stem: For a rectifier output the rms value of the load current is 10 mA and its dc value is 8 mA. The ripple factor is
solution: First the ratio: 10 / 8 = 1.25. Squaring gives 1.5625, and subtracting one gives 0.5625. The square root of 0.5625 is 0.75, so the ripple factor is 0.75. This value lies between the standard half wave and full wave figures, which suggests a full wave output with some additional ripple.
formula_principle: Ripple factor r = square root of ((Irms / Idc)^2 - 1).
common_misconception: The square root at the end is omitted, or the simple ratio is quoted as the ripple factor.

concept_tested: Action of a series inductor filter
stem: An inductor is placed in series with the load of a rectifier to act as a filter. It smooths the output because
option_a: it opposes changes in current, offering a high impedance to the ripple while passing the dc easily
option_b: it stores charge at the peaks and gives it back during the gaps
option_c: it offers a high resistance to the dc component
option_d: it doubles the frequency of the output
correct_answer_text: it opposes changes in current, offering a high impedance to the ripple while passing the dc easily
solution: For the steady component the frequency is zero, so the reactance is zero and the inductor passes it with only its small winding resistance in the way. For the ripple component the reactance is large, so most of the ripple voltage is dropped across the inductor rather than across the load. The current through the load is therefore much smoother.
formula_principle: An inductor has reactance 2 pi f L, which is large for the ripple frequency and zero for direct current.
common_misconception: Capacitor and inductor filters are described interchangeably; the capacitor is connected across the load and the inductor in series with it.

concept_tested: Identifying a rectifier from its measured performance
stem: A rectifier fed from a 50 Hz supply gives an output whose ripple frequency is measured as 50 Hz and whose efficiency is about 40 percent. The circuit is
option_b: a centre tap full wave rectifier
option_d: a full wave rectifier whose filter has failed
solution: Two independent measurements point the same way. A ripple frequency equal to the input frequency means one pulse per cycle, which only a half wave circuit gives. An efficiency near 40 percent matches the half wave maximum of 40.6 percent. Both full wave versions would give 100 Hz and about 81 percent.
formula_principle: Half wave: ripple frequency equal to input, efficiency 40.6 percent. Full wave: ripple frequency twice the input, efficiency 81.2 percent.
common_misconception: A poor efficiency is blamed on a faulty filter; the ripple frequency identifies the circuit type independently of any filter.

concept_tested: Dc output voltage of a full wave rectifier
stem: The transformer secondary supplies a peak voltage of 20 V to a full wave rectifier. Neglecting the diode drops, the dc output voltage across the load is (take pi = 3.14)
solution: Substituting, V(dc) = 2 x 20 / 3.14 = 40 / 3.14 = 12.7 V. This is the true average of the rectified waveform without a filter. Adding a large capacitor filter would raise the output towards the peak value of 20 V.
formula_principle: For a full wave rectifier V(dc) = 2 Vm / pi.
common_misconception: The peak or the rms value is reported as the dc output; the average of a rectified sine wave is smaller than both.

concept_tested: Dc power delivered by a half wave rectifier
stem: A half wave rectifier feeds a 1 kohm load from a supply of peak voltage 31.4 V. Neglecting the diode resistance, the dc power delivered to the load is (take pi = 3.14)
solution: The peak current is Im = 31.4 / 1000 = 31.4 mA. Then I(dc) = 31.4 / 3.14 = 10 mA = 0.01 A. Hence P(dc) = (0.01)^2 x 1000 = 0.1 W. Only the dc component of the current contributes to the dc power delivered.
formula_principle: Im = Vm / R, I(dc) = Im / pi and P(dc) = I(dc)^2 x R.
common_misconception: The peak or rms current is squared in the power formula; the dc power must be computed from the dc current.

concept_tested: Effect of load resistance on the ripple of a filtered supply
stem: A full wave rectifier working from a 50 Hz mains has a capacitor filter across its load. If the load resistance is increased, the ripple in the output
option_a: increases, because a smaller current is drawn from the capacitor
option_b: stays exactly the same, since the ripple depends only on the mains frequency
option_c: decreases, because the capacitor discharges more slowly through the larger resistance
option_d: becomes exactly zero, since no current flows at all
correct_answer_text: decreases, because the capacitor discharges more slowly through the larger resistance
solution: The output sags between successive pulses by an amount governed by how fast the capacitor discharges. That rate is set by the time constant R x C, so a larger load resistance means a slower discharge and a smaller sag. The ripple therefore falls, which is why regulation problems appear at heavy loads and not at light ones.
formula_principle: Between pulses the capacitor discharges through the load with time constant R x C; a larger time constant means less droop and less ripple.
common_misconception: A larger resistance is assumed to make everything worse; here it lengthens the time constant and improves the smoothing.

concept_tested: Operating region of a Zener diode
stem: A Zener diode used as a voltage regulator is always operated
option_a: in forward bias, above its knee voltage
option_b: in reverse bias, well below its breakdown voltage
option_c: in reverse bias, beyond its breakdown voltage
correct_answer_text: in reverse bias, beyond its breakdown voltage
solution: In the breakdown region the reverse characteristic is almost vertical, so the voltage across the diode stays close to the Zener voltage even when the current through it changes a great deal. That is exactly the property needed to hold a load voltage steady. Below breakdown the diode simply blocks and above the knee in forward bias it behaves as an ordinary diode.
formula_principle: A Zener diode regulates only in the reverse breakdown region, where its voltage is nearly independent of current.
common_misconception: The Zener diode is connected like a rectifier diode; it must be reverse biased to regulate.

concept_tested: Bias condition for an LED
stem: A light emitting diode gives out light when it is
option_b: forward biased, so that electrons and holes recombine near the junction
option_d: unbiased and simply exposed to sunlight
correct_answer_text: forward biased, so that electrons and holes recombine near the junction
solution: Forward bias injects electrons into the p-region and holes into the n-region. When an injected electron recombines with a hole, the energy released is close to the band gap energy and in suitable materials it appears as a photon. Since injection happens only in forward bias, an LED must be forward biased to glow.
formula_principle: An LED emits light by recombination of injected carriers, which requires forward bias.
common_misconception: The LED is confused with the photodiode; one is forward biased to emit and the other reverse biased to detect.

concept_tested: Bias condition for a photodiode
stem: A photodiode is normally operated in
option_a: reverse bias, so that the small light generated current is easily measured
option_b: forward bias, so that a large current flows through it
option_d: zero bias with its terminals short circuited
correct_answer_text: reverse bias, so that the small light generated current is easily measured
solution: Without light a reverse biased junction carries only a few microampere. Light falling on the depletion region creates extra electron hole pairs, which the strong junction field sweeps across, adding a current proportional to the intensity. Because the dark background is so small, this addition is easily measured, which makes reverse bias the natural choice.
formula_principle: In reverse bias the dark current is very small, so the change caused by illumination is easy to detect.
common_misconception: Forward bias is assumed to give a bigger and therefore better signal; the huge forward current would hide the light generated part.

concept_tested: How a solar cell differs from a photodiode
stem: A solar cell differs from a photodiode mainly in that a solar cell
option_a: works without any external bias and delivers electrical power to the load
option_b: works only under a heavy reverse bias
option_c: gives out light when it is illuminated
option_d: needs a large forward bias before it can generate a voltage
correct_answer_text: works without any external bias and delivers electrical power to the load
solution: Both devices generate carriers when light falls on the junction, but their purposes differ. A photodiode is reverse biased and is used to measure light, so it draws power from the supply. A solar cell has no external supply, has a large junction area to collect as much light as possible, and its photo generated carriers drive a current through the external load, so it supplies power.
formula_principle: A solar cell is an unbiased junction with a large area that converts light energy directly into electrical energy.
common_misconception: The two devices are treated as the same because both respond to light; only the solar cell acts as a source of energy.

concept_tested: Reason for the sharp breakdown of a Zener diode
stem: A Zener diode has a sharp and well defined breakdown voltage because
option_a: both its regions are very lightly doped, giving a wide depletion layer
option_b: it is made from an insulator with a very wide band gap
option_c: its junction area is made unusually large
option_d: both its regions are heavily doped, giving a very narrow depletion layer and a very intense junction field
correct_answer_text: both its regions are heavily doped, giving a very narrow depletion layer and a very intense junction field
solution: With heavy doping on both sides the space charge required to support the barrier is uncovered within a very short distance, so the depletion layer is extremely thin. A reverse voltage of a few volt across such a thin layer gives a field of the order of 10^8 V/m, which pulls electrons out of covalent bonds directly. Since this happens at a definite field, the breakdown voltage is sharp and reproducible.
formula_principle: Heavy doping narrows the depletion layer, so even a modest reverse voltage produces a field strong enough to break bonds directly.
common_misconception: Heavy doping is thought to widen the junction; it makes the depletion layer thinner and the field inside it much stronger.

concept_tested: Circuit arrangement of a Zener regulator
stem: In a simple Zener voltage regulator the Zener diode is connected
option_a: in series with the load and in parallel with a resistor
option_b: in series with the load and directly across the supply with no resistor
option_c: in parallel with the supply with no series resistor at all
option_d: in parallel with the load and in series with a current limiting resistor
correct_answer_text: in parallel with the load and in series with a current limiting resistor
solution: The Zener must be across the load so that the load sees the constant Zener voltage. The series resistor takes up the difference between the unregulated input and the Zener voltage, and it also limits the current so that the diode is not damaged. If the load current changes, the Zener current adjusts by the opposite amount and the total current through the resistor stays nearly the same.
formula_principle: The Zener is shunted across the load and a series resistor drops the surplus voltage and limits the current.
common_misconception: The Zener is placed in series with the load, which would put the load current entirely under its control and defeat the purpose.

concept_tested: Zener current with a given load current
stem: An unregulated 20 V supply feeds a 10 V Zener diode through a 1 kohm series resistor. If the load draws 5 mA, the current through the Zener is
solution: The resistor drops 20 - 10 = 10 V, so the series current is 10 / 1000 = 10 mA. Of this the load takes 5 mA, so the Zener carries the remaining 10 - 5 = 5 mA. If the load were removed the whole 10 mA would pass through the Zener.
formula_principle: I(series) = (V(in) - V(Z)) / R and I(Z) = I(series) - I(load).
common_misconception: The series current is reported as the Zener current; the load current must be subtracted from it.

concept_tested: Band gap corresponding to the emitted wavelength
stem: An LED emits red light of wavelength 620 nm. The band gap of the material used is about (take hc = 1240 eV nm)
solution: Substituting, Eg = 1240 / 620 = 2.0 eV. Materials with a gap near 2 eV therefore emit red light. A larger gap gives shorter wavelengths, which is why blue LEDs need materials with gaps near 3 eV.
formula_principle: The photon energy released on recombination is about equal to the band gap: Eg = hc / lambda.
common_misconception: The formula is inverted, which gives an energy far below anything that could produce visible light.

concept_tested: Dependence of photodiode current on light intensity
stem: In a reverse biased photodiode the current
option_a: decreases as the intensity of the incident light increases
option_b: is independent of the intensity and depends only on the reverse voltage
option_c: flows only when the frequency of the light is below the threshold
option_d: increases as the intensity of the incident light increases
correct_answer_text: increases as the intensity of the incident light increases
solution: A greater intensity means more photons arriving each second, and provided each photon has energy above the band gap, each one can create an electron hole pair in or near the depletion layer. The junction field sweeps these carriers across, so the current grows in proportion to the intensity. This linear response is what makes the photodiode useful for light measurement.
formula_principle: Each absorbed photon of sufficient energy creates one electron hole pair, so the photocurrent is proportional to the intensity.
common_misconception: The reverse voltage is thought to control the current; in the saturation region the voltage matters little and the intensity decides the current.

concept_tested: Property that makes a Zener useful for regulation
stem: The essential property that makes a Zener diode useful as a voltage regulator is that in the breakdown region
option_a: the current through it stays constant while the voltage across it varies widely
option_b: it behaves as a pure resistance of fixed value
option_c: the voltage across it stays nearly constant while the current through it varies widely
correct_answer_text: the voltage across it stays nearly constant while the current through it varies widely
solution: A nearly vertical characteristic means that a large change of current produces almost no change of voltage. So when the load current or the supply voltage changes, the Zener simply takes up or gives up current while the voltage across it, and hence across the load, hardly moves. That is precisely voltage regulation.
formula_principle: In the breakdown region the reverse characteristic is nearly vertical, which means a nearly constant voltage.
common_misconception: A vertical line on the graph is read as constant current; on a current against voltage plot a vertical line means constant voltage.

concept_tested: Selecting an LED material that emits visible light
stem: Three possible LED materials have forbidden gaps of 0.5 eV, 1.0 eV and 2.5 eV. Taking the visible range as 400 nm to 700 nm and hc = 1240 eV nm, the material that will emit visible light is
option_a: the 2.5 eV material, whose emission lies near 496 nm
option_b: the 1.0 eV material, whose emission lies near 1240 nm
option_c: the 0.5 eV material, whose emission lies near 2480 nm
option_d: the 2.5 eV material, whose emission lies near 3100 nm
correct_answer_text: the 2.5 eV material, whose emission lies near 496 nm
solution: Dividing hc by each gap gives 1240 / 0.5 = 2480 nm, 1240 / 1.0 = 1240 nm and 1240 / 2.5 = 496 nm. Only 496 nm falls inside the visible band from 400 nm to 700 nm, so the 2.5 eV material is the one that glows visibly. The other two emit infrared radiation, which is why such materials are used in remote controls rather than in indicator lamps.
formula_principle: Photon wavelength emitted on recombination is lambda = hc / Eg; visible light needs lambda between 400 nm and 700 nm.
common_misconception: A small band gap is thought to give visible light because it is easier to cross; a small gap gives a small photon energy and therefore a long, invisible wavelength.

concept_tested: Power dissipated in a Zener diode
stem: A 6 V Zener diode carries a current of 20 mA. The power dissipated in it is
solution: Converting the current, I = 20 mA = 0.02 A. Then P = 6 x 0.02 = 0.12 W. The chosen diode must have a power rating comfortably above this figure, otherwise it will overheat in the breakdown region.
formula_principle: P = V(Z) x I(Z), with the current expressed in ampere.
common_misconception: The milliampere is not converted, which inflates the answer by a factor of one thousand.

concept_tested: Open circuit voltage of solar cells in series
stem: Four identical solar cells, each giving an open circuit voltage of 0.5 V in bright sunlight, are joined in series. The open circuit voltage of the combination is
solution: Each cell contributes 0.5 V and the four are in series in the same sense, so the voltages add to give 4 x 0.5 = 2.0 V. Had the cells been placed in parallel instead, the voltage would have stayed at 0.5 V while the available current would have become four times as large.
formula_principle: Sources in series add their voltages, provided they are joined in the same sense.
common_misconception: Series and parallel behaviour of sources is interchanged; series adds voltage while parallel adds current.

concept_tested: Distinction between Zener and avalanche breakdown
stem: Zener breakdown differs from avalanche breakdown in that Zener breakdown
option_a: occurs in lightly doped junctions at high reverse voltages through collisions that multiply carriers
option_b: occurs only when the junction is forward biased
option_c: occurs in heavily doped junctions at low reverse voltages by direct field ionisation of covalent bonds
option_d: permanently destroys the junction every time it happens
correct_answer_text: occurs in heavily doped junctions at low reverse voltages by direct field ionisation of covalent bonds
solution: In a heavily doped junction the depletion layer is very thin, so a reverse voltage of only a few volt produces an enormous field that tears electrons directly out of covalent bonds. That is Zener breakdown. In a lightly doped junction the layer is wide, the field is smaller, and breakdown occurs only at a higher voltage when carriers gain enough kinetic energy between collisions to create new pairs. That is avalanche breakdown.
formula_principle: Zener breakdown is field ionisation in a very thin heavily doped junction; avalanche breakdown is carrier multiplication by collision in a wider junction.
common_misconception: The two mechanisms are treated as one; they differ in doping, in breakdown voltage and in physical cause.

concept_tested: Zener current when the load is removed
stem: In a Zener regulator the series resistance is 500 ohm and the Zener voltage is 5 V. When the input is 10 V and the load is disconnected, the current through the Zener is
solution: The resistor drops 10 - 5 = 5 V, so the series current is 5 / 500 = 0.01 A = 10 mA. With the load disconnected there is nowhere else for this current to go, so the Zener carries all of it. This no load condition is the worst case for the power rating of the diode.
formula_principle: With no load, the whole series current passes through the Zener: I(Z) = (V(in) - V(Z)) / R.
common_misconception: Removing the load is assumed to stop the current; in fact it forces the entire series current through the Zener.

concept_tested: Maximum load current for a Zener regulator
stem: A 12 V unregulated supply feeds a 9 V Zener through a 300 ohm resistor. The Zener current must never fall below 5 mA. The largest load current that may be drawn is
solution: The resistor drops 12 - 9 = 3 V, so the series current is 3 / 300 = 0.01 A = 10 mA, and this stays nearly fixed while the Zener holds 9 V. The Zener must keep at least 5 mA to remain in breakdown, so the load can take at most 10 - 5 = 5 mA. Drawing more would pull the Zener out of breakdown and regulation would be lost.
formula_principle: I(series) = (V(in) - V(Z)) / R, and I(load,max) = I(series) - I(Z,min).
common_misconception: The whole series current is offered to the load; a minimum current must always be left for the Zener itself.

concept_tested: Output of a combination of AND and OR gates
stem: Two inputs P and Q are applied both to an AND gate and to an OR gate. The outputs of these two gates are then applied to the two inputs of a second AND gate. The final output is 1
option_a: only when both P and Q are 0
option_b: whenever at least one of P and Q is 1
option_c: for every combination of P and Q
option_d: only when both P and Q are 1
correct_answer_text: only when both P and Q are 1
solution: Take the combinations in order. With A = 0 and B = 0 the AND branch gives 0 and the OR branch gives 0, so the final AND gives 0. With A = 0 and B = 1 the AND branch gives 0 and the OR branch gives 1, so the final AND gives 0. With A = 1 and B = 0 the result is the same, namely 0. Only with A = 1 and B = 1 do both branches give 1, so the final output is 1. The whole network therefore behaves as a single AND gate.
formula_principle: Work through all four input combinations, evaluating each gate in turn.
common_misconception: The OR branch is allowed to decide the answer; the final AND stage cannot give 1 unless the AND branch is also 1.

concept_tested: Design of the base region
stem: In a junction transistor the base region is made
solution: Transistor action needs almost every carrier injected from the emitter to travel across the base and be collected. A thin base gives them a short distance to cross and light doping means few carriers of the opposite kind waiting to recombine with them. Together these ensure that the collector current is very nearly equal to the emitter current.
formula_principle: The base is thin and lightly doped so that nearly all carriers injected by the emitter reach the collector.
common_misconception: The base is imagined as a substantial middle layer; it is by far the thinnest and most lightly doped of the three regions.

concept_tested: Relation between the three transistor currents
stem: For a junction transistor the emitter, base and collector currents are related by
solution: The emitter injects carriers into the base. A small fraction recombines there and leaves through the base lead, while the rest is collected. Since all the current that enters must leave, the emitter current equals the sum of the base and collector currents, with the base contribution being only a percent or two of the total.
formula_principle: Charge conservation at the transistor gives I_E = I_B + I_C.
common_misconception: The relation is written with the collector current largest; the emitter current is always the largest of the three.

concept_tested: Collector current from emitter and base currents
stem: The emitter current of a transistor is 10 mA and its base current is 0.1 mA. The collector current is
solution: Substituting, I_C = 10 - 0.1 = 9.9 mA. The base takes only one percent of the emitter current here, which is typical, and this is why a small change in the base current can control a much larger collector current.
formula_principle: I_C = I_E - I_B.
common_misconception: The three currents are added in the wrong combination; the emitter current is the sum of the other two.

concept_tested: Conversion of alpha into beta
stem: For a transistor the current amplification factor alpha in the common base mode is 0.98. The corresponding beta in the common emitter mode is
solution: Here 1 - alpha = 1 - 0.98 = 0.02, so beta = 0.98 / 0.02 = 49. A value of alpha very close to one gives a large beta, which is why manufacturers try to make alpha as near unity as possible.
formula_principle: beta = alpha / (1 - alpha).
common_misconception: The subtraction 1 - alpha is done correctly but the numerator is taken as 1 instead of alpha.

concept_tested: Truth table of an OR gate
stem: The output of a two input OR gate is 0 only when
option_d: the two inputs are equal to each other
solution: Running through the four combinations, inputs 0 and 0 give output 0, inputs 0 and 1 give 1, inputs 1 and 0 give 1, and inputs 1 and 1 give 1. So the single case producing a zero output is the one with both inputs at 0.
formula_principle: OR gate: output is 1 if any input is 1, and 0 only when every input is 0.
common_misconception: The OR gate is confused with the exclusive OR, which gives 0 when both inputs are 1.

concept_tested: NAND gate with its inputs joined
stem: The two inputs of a NAND gate are joined together and a single input A is applied to the joined pair. The circuit then behaves as
option_d: a NOR gate whose output is always 1
solution: If A is 0 then both inputs are 0, their AND is 0 and the inverted output is 1. If A is 1 then both inputs are 1, their AND is 1 and the inverted output is 0. The output is thus always the complement of the input, which is exactly a NOT gate. This is one reason the NAND gate is called a universal gate.
formula_principle: NAND output = NOT (A AND B); with A = B this becomes NOT (A AND A) = NOT A.
common_misconception: The inversion in the NAND gate is forgotten, which turns the answer into an AND gate that would merely repeat the input.

concept_tested: Truth table of a NOR gate
stem: For a two input NOR gate the output is 1
option_c: whenever at least one input is 1
option_d: whenever the two inputs are different from each other
solution: An OR gate gives 1 unless both inputs are 0. Inverting that result, the NOR gate gives 0 unless both inputs are 0, and gives 1 in that single case. Checking all four rows: inputs 0 and 0 give 1, and the other three combinations all give 0.
formula_principle: NOR output = NOT (A OR B).
common_misconception: The NOR gate is treated as the opposite of the AND gate; it is the inverted OR gate.

concept_tested: Carriers responsible for the emitter current of an npn transistor
stem: In an npn transistor working in the active region, the current in the emitter lead is carried mainly by
option_a: holes injected from the emitter into the base
option_b: electrons injected from the emitter into the base
option_c: the immobile ionised impurity atoms of the base
option_d: minority carriers generated thermally in the collector region
correct_answer_text: electrons injected from the emitter into the base
solution: The emitter base junction is forward biased, so the heavily doped n-type emitter injects electrons into the p-type base. Because the base is thin and lightly doped, only a small fraction recombine there and the rest are swept into the reverse biased collector junction. The main current is therefore an electron current, and in a pnp transistor the corresponding current is a hole current.
formula_principle: In an npn transistor the n-type emitter injects electrons into the thin p-type base, most of which reach the collector.
common_misconception: The npn and pnp cases are interchanged; the type of the emitter region decides which carrier is injected.

concept_tested: Collector and emitter currents from beta and base current
stem: A transistor has beta equal to 100 and its base current is 20 microampere. Its collector current and emitter current are
solution: First the collector current: I_C = 100 x 20 microampere = 2000 microampere = 2 mA. Then the emitter current: I_E = 0.02 + 2 = 2.02 mA. The base current is only about one percent of the total, but it is the quantity that controls the other two.
formula_principle: I_C = beta x I_B and I_E = I_B + I_C.
common_misconception: The base current is dropped in the second step; although small, it must be added to obtain the emitter current.
